column5: Impossible to control or restrain.
column7: Her irrepressible laughter filled the entire room. / Her irrepressible enthusiasm lifted the whole team. / He has an irrepressible sense of humor.
column8: ir- (not) + repress (hold back) + -bile (able to) = not able to be held back. Common with positive energy and emotion: irrepressible enthusiasm, spirit, energy, laughter, smile. It suggests something keeps bursting out despite attempts to restrain it.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative topic::everyday_life discovery::emotional_intensity discovery::containment discovery::release

column5: 1. To formally repeal, abolish, or cancel a law, agreement, right, or rule. 2. To fail to fulfill or deliberately cast aside a duty, responsibility, or obligation.
column6: repeal, abolish, annul, revoke, rescind, invalidate; shirk, evade, renounce (a responsibility/duty, context-dependent)
column7: The government moved to abrogate the treaty. / Congress cannot simply abrogate constitutional protections. / Critics accused the board of abrogating its responsibilities to shareholders. / The old rule was formally abrogated.
column8: The legal/official sense is the core one: abrogate a law, treaty, agreement, right, or provision. With duties or responsibilities, it means to cast them aside or fail to discharge them. 'Abrogated' is commonly passive or adjectival in formal writing: 'the provision was abrogated.' Do not confuse with arrogate = claim or seize for oneself.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal topic::law topic::grammar discovery::evasive_language discovery::agreement

column5: In a way that prevents success or causes harm.
column7: The medication can adversely affect your blood pressure. / The delay adversely affected our travel plans. / Higher rates could adversely impact small businesses.
column8: Very common collocations: adversely affect, adversely impact. Contrast adverse = harmful/unfavorable with averse = opposed/unwilling ('averse to risk').

column5: Secret, mysterious, or known only to a few people who have special knowledge or understanding. It's often used to describe things that are complex, obscure, or esoteric.
column7: The professor specialized in arcane legal theory. This argument may seem arcane to those not closely involved in the world of finance. / The manual is full of arcane rules that only longtime users seem to understand.
column8:
Examples:
Arcane rituals, arcane knowledge, or arcane rules can all be described as things that require a degree of specialized understanding to comprehend. Already a strong early card. Useful combinations: arcane knowledge/rules/procedures/details. Arcane often implies specialized and obscure rather than literally secret.
column12: entry::word usage::specialist usage::instructional usage::rhetorical discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::debate_language

column5: Striking or eye-catching; demanding attention.
column7: Her arresting beauty left everyone speechless. / The film opens with an arresting image. / She has an arresting voice that immediately commands attention.
column8: Arresting = striking enough to stop and hold your attention. Common with image, appearance, design, voice, opening, contrast. Not related to being arrested by police in this use.

column5: 1. Severe, strict, or uncompromising in manner or discipline. 2. Plain, sparse, and without comfort or decoration. 3. Economically severe or restrictive, especially in 'austere measures/policies.'
column6: stern, strict, severe, ascetic, spare, stark, unadorned; stringent, restrictive (economic context)
column7: The headmaster had an austere manner. / The room was austere, with bare walls and almost no furniture. / The government introduced austere spending measures after the crisis.
column8: Austere can describe a person, lifestyle, design, or policy. The common thread is severity and lack of indulgence. 'Austere beauty' can be positive: simple, restrained, and striking rather than luxurious.

column5: 1. To give a false or misleading impression of something. 2. To show that a statement, appearance, or belief is false or inconsistent with the facts.
column6: misrepresent, disguise, mask, conceal; contradict, disprove, give the lie to
column7: His calm voice belied how angry he really was. / Her youthful appearance belied her age. / The latest figures belie the claim that demand is falling.
column8: Two closely related patterns matter: 'X belies Y' can mean X hides Y ('his smile belied his anxiety') or X proves Y false ('the evidence belies that claim'). The subject is the thing creating the misleading appearance or contradiction.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::form_family entry::word topic::grammar discovery::disagreement discovery::impression

column5: To talk at length in a pompous or boastful way.
column7: The politician bloviated for over an hour without saying much. / He spent ten minutes bloviating about a topic he barely understood.
column8: Usually humorous or critical, often about politicians, pundits, or self-important speakers. Bloviate emphasizes pompous, inflated talk more than ordinary rambling.

column5: The edge or threshold of something, often a dramatic change.
column7: The company was on the brink of bankruptcy. / The country stood on the brink of war. / One mistake pushed the project to the brink of collapse.
column8: Teach the fixed frame 'on the brink of X'. Literal brink = edge; figurative brink = threshold of an extreme state. Related: brinkmanship.

column5: Brown-nosing is trying to gain favor from someone in authority through excessive, insincere flattery or servile behavior. To brown-nose means to behave this way.
column6: sucking up, kissing up, bootlicking, fawning, toadying, currying favor; flatter excessively
column7: Everyone could see that his constant compliments were just brown-nosing. / He keeps brown-nosing the manager because he wants a promotion. / I don't want to suck up to anyone just to get ahead.
column8: Usually hyphenated as brown-nosing; the verb is brown-nose. Strongly informal and insulting. 'Suck up to' is the most natural everyday equivalent. 'Curry favor with' is more formal and does not necessarily sound as crude.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::disparaging usage::formal usage::critical usage::vulgar usage::persuasive topic::work topic::workplace topic::business topic::communication discovery::social_approval discovery::persuasion

column5: 1. A finishing stone placed at the top of a structure. 2. Figuratively, the culminating or crowning part of a project, course of study, career, or achievement.
column6: culmination, crowning achievement, finishing touch, pinnacle, climax
column7: The capstone completed the stone arch. / Her thesis was the capstone of her graduate program. / The final project serves as a capstone experience for the entire course.
column8: Very common in education: capstone course/project/experience. Figuratively it suggests the final piece that completes and summarizes what came before.

column5: 1. To create or establish a role, niche, career, reputation, or position through sustained effort. 2. To set aside or obtain a portion of time, space, territory, or resources.
column6: establish, create, build, forge; set aside, make room for, secure
column7: She's carved out a successful career in animation. / The channel carved out a niche for itself among older viewers. / I need to carve out an hour tonight to study. / They carved out a small workspace in the corner.
column8: The image is of cutting a distinct piece out of something larger. Common patterns: carve out a niche/career/role/reputation; carve out time/space. 'Carve out a niche' is especially frequent.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::phrasal_verb usage::debate-friendly topic::work topic::debate discovery::resource_allocation discovery::social_approval discovery::debate_language

column5: To pause and reflect on your thoughts, emotions, or needs.
column7: Take a moment to check in with yourself before making a decision. / Before replying, I checked in with myself and realized I was more frustrated than angry.
column8: Modern self-reflection phrase rather than a rigid idiom. Compare check in with someone = contact them / see how they are doing.

column5: A sudden and complete failure.
column7: The product launch was a total debacle. / The rollout became a public-relations debacle after the site crashed on launch day.
column8: Debacle usually suggests a conspicuous, often embarrassing collapse or failure. Close to fiasco; debacle can sound slightly more formal.

column5: Making someone weak or unable to function.
column7: She suffered from a debilitating illness for years. / Chronic pain can be physically and mentally debilitating. / The uncertainty had a debilitating effect on morale.
column8: Common with illness, pain, anxiety, injury, debt, fear, effects. Stronger than tiring: it seriously reduces someone's ability to function.

column5: Showing resistance or bold disobedience.
column7: His defiant tone made it clear he wouldn't back down. / She remained defiant even after repeated warnings. / He gave the interviewer a defiant stare.
column8: Common collocations: defiant tone/look/gesture/stance. Better synonyms than 'bold': rebellious, resistant, insubordinate, unyielding.

column5: A natural ability to do something.
column7: She showed great aptitude for mathematics at an early age. / He has a natural aptitude for languages. / The test measures spatial and numerical aptitude.
column8: Aptitude is natural potential/capacity to learn or perform well, not simply an acquired skill. Common: aptitude for, aptitude test. Skill can be trained; aptitude is underlying ability.

column5: Things that cause persistent annoyance or irritation.
column7: One of his biggest bugbears is people who chew loudly. / Late trains are one of my biggest bugbears. / Bureaucratic delays remain a major bugbear for small businesses.
column8: Especially common in British English. A bugbear can be a pet peeve or a persistent troublesome problem, not only a personal annoyance.

column5: 1. Relating to the brain or cerebrum. 2. Intellectual, analytical, or abstract rather than emotional, instinctive, or physical.
column6: intellectual, analytical, cerebral, brainy, thought-provoking; neurological/brain-related (literal context)
column7: The scan showed reduced cerebral blood flow. / It's a very cerebral film—fascinating, but emotionally distant. / Their conversation was more cerebral than personal.
column8: In reviews, 'cerebral' often means intellectually demanding or idea-driven. It can be praise ('thought-provoking') or mild criticism ('too detached or cold'). Literal medical uses relate to the brain.

column5: Funds or financial reserves of an organization or government.
column7: The city's coffers were depleted after years of overspending. / Tax increases helped refill the government's coffers. / The settlement put millions into the company's coffers.
column8: Literal coffer = strongbox/chest. Plural coffers is very common figuratively for the treasury or financial reserves of a government/organization.

column5: The act of conforming to rules or standards.
column7: The company was fined for non-compliance with safety regulations. / The system was redesigned to ensure compliance with privacy rules. / All staff must act in compliance with the policy.
column8: High-frequency frames: compliance with; in compliance with; regulatory/legal compliance. Compliance is conformity with a requirement, not necessarily enthusiastic agreement.

column4: noun / adjective; informal/slang; meanings vary by context
column5: 1. Drugs or an illegal drug, especially in older/informal use. 2. Information or inside knowledge ('the dope on...'), somewhat dated. 3. A foolish person, informal and dated. 4. Slang adjective: excellent, cool, impressive.
column6: drugs, narcotics; information, inside scoop; fool, idiot; awesome, cool, sick, fire (slang, sense-dependent)
column7: Police found dope in the car. / Give me the inside dope on what happened. / Don't be a dope—read the instructions first. / That new track is dope; I've had it on repeat all day.
column8: 'Dope' is highly polysemous, so context is essential. The positive adjective 'That's dope' is common slang. The drug sense is older and still widely understood. Never merge the different senses into one synonym list without labels.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::informal usage::slang usage::dated

column5: Small faults or malfunctions, especially in software or systems.
column7: The software update caused several unexpected glitches. / A temporary network glitch knocked the app offline for a few minutes.
column8: A glitch is usually a small, temporary, unexpected malfunction. A bug is often a reproducible flaw in code/design; everyday speakers may use them loosely.

column5: Not able to be forgotten or removed.
column7: That trip left an indelible mark on her memory. / The experience left an indelible impression on me. / The image is indelibly associated with the event.
column8: Common: indelible mark/impression/memory. Literal sense: ink/mark that cannot be erased; figuratively, an effect that cannot be forgotten.

column5: A positive or negative whole number, including zero; a number with no fractional part: ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
column6: whole-valued number (descriptive); no exact everyday synonym
column7: -7, 0, and 42 are integers, but 3.5 and 2/3 are not. / The program accepts only integer values for this field.
column8: Do NOT use digit or numeral as synonyms. A digit is one symbol from 0–9; a numeral is a written representation of a number; an integer is a mathematical type of number. 'Whole number' is sometimes used for nonnegative integers only, so it is not always an exact synonym.

column5: 1. A small cut, indentation, or mark, often used for counting or fitting. 2. A level or degree on a scale. 3. Figuratively, a small step in quality, intensity, status, or achievement.
column6: indentation, cut, mark; level, degree, step
column7: He cut a notch in the wood to mark the height. / This restaurant is a notch above the others nearby. / She took her performance up a notch in the finals. / The company notched up another record year.
column8: Useful patterns: a notch above/below; take/turn/kick something up a notch; notch up a win/success (verb). The figurative sense is extremely common.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::figurative discovery::process_details discovery::figurative_extension discovery::evaluation

column5: To spread or pass through every part of something, often by penetrating into its material, space, or members.
column6: penetrate, saturate, diffuse through, seep through, spread throughout, infuse
column7: The smell of garlic permeated the entire kitchen. / Water had permeated the walls. / A sense of optimism gradually permeated the organization.
column8: Compared with pervade, permeate more readily suggests entering or penetrating through a substance or structure, though both can be figurative. Common subjects: smell, moisture, light, ideas, attitudes.

column5: To be present, felt, or noticeable throughout a place, situation, group, or period.
column6: permeate, suffuse, fill, spread throughout, run through
column7: A sense of unease pervaded the room. / Optimism pervaded the campaign. / The smell of smoke pervaded the building.
column8: Pervade is especially natural with atmospheres, feelings, attitudes, smells, and qualities. Compared with permeate, it focuses more on widespread presence than on physical penetration.

column5: 1. Noun: the back part of something. 2. Adjective: at or toward the back. 3. Verb: to raise and care for children or animals. 4. Verb: to rise up, especially on the hind legs.
column6: back, hind part; raise, bring up; rise up
column7: The engine is mounted at the rear of the vehicle. / Please use the rear entrance. / She reared three children on her own. / The horse reared when it heard the explosion.
column8: Rear is highly polysemous. 'Rear a child/animal' = raise. 'A horse rears' = rises on its hind legs. In some varieties, 'rear' as a noun can also mean buttocks, usually informal.

column5: Having sharp judgment or practical intelligence.
column7: She made a shrewd investment that doubled in value. / It was a shrewd move to negotiate before prices rose. / She's a shrewd judge of character.
column8: Shrewd is practical, sharp, often unsentimental judgment. It can sound admiring but may imply calculating cleverness.

column5: 1. A small, scattered amount or number of something. 2. A slight or superficial knowledge of a subject or language.
column6: sprinkling, handful, scattering, trace; rudimentary knowledge, a little knowledge
column7: There were only a smattering of people in the audience. / The article contains a smattering of technical jargon. / I know a smattering of Italian, but nowhere near enough to hold a real conversation.
column8: Usually appears as 'a smattering of ...'. The knowledge sense is especially useful: 'a smattering of French/history/coding.' The plural 'smatterings' exists but the singular headword is much more useful.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::technical usage::specialist discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: In a disconnected or aimless manner.
column7: He wandered desultorily through the exhibit without focus. / He worked desultorily, jumping from one unfinished task to another.
column8: Desultory/desultorily suggests movement from one thing to another without clear plan, continuity, enthusiasm, or purpose. Formal/literary.

column5: To depart from an established course or norm.
column7: Try not to deviate from the original plan. / The results deviated significantly from the forecast. / We had to deviate from the original route.
column8: Core grammar: deviate from a path, plan, norm, standard, expected result. Deviation is the noun.

column5: To soak something thoroughly.
column7: The rain completely drenched his clothes. / We got drenched in the sudden storm. / The fries were drenched in sauce.
column8: Common patterns: be drenched in/with rain, sweat, blood, sauce; drench something with liquid. Stronger than simply wet.

column5: Deriving ideas or style from a broad and diverse range of sources.
column7: Her music taste is eclectic, ranging from jazz to metal. / The café has an eclectic playlist—jazz, metal, K-pop, and old soul.
column8: Eclectic means selecting or combining elements from many different sources/styles, often deliberately. More specific than merely 'diverse'.

column5: The practice of combining elements from different styles or ideas.
column7: His art reflects an eclecticism rarely seen in contemporary work. / The interior reflects deliberate eclecticism, mixing industrial furniture with antique art.
column8: Eclecticism is the approach or practice behind eclectic choices. Common in art, design, philosophy, architecture, and intellectual method.

column5: A person or thing that is mysterious or difficult to understand.
column7: Her sudden departure remains an enigma. / Even after years of interviews, the actor remains something of an enigma.
column8: Pattern: an enigma to someone / remain an enigma. An enigmatic person is difficult to read or understand.

column5: A weary feeling of boredom, listlessness, and dissatisfaction caused by having nothing interesting or meaningful to do, often prolonged rather than momentary.
column7: After months of doing the same routine, a deep sense of ennui set in. / The novel captures the ennui of wealthy characters who have everything except a sense of purpose.
column8: Ennui is more literary/formal than boredom and often implies weary dissatisfaction or emptiness, not simply 'I'm bored for ten minutes.' 'Melancholy' can overlap emotionally but is not a close synonym.

column5: To be a perfect example of something.
column7: She epitomizes grace and professionalism. / Her calm response epitomized the professionalism of the whole team.
column8: Epitomize = embody the defining qualities of something, not merely 'be an example'. Noun: epitome.

column5: To destroy or remove completely.
column7: The program aims to eradicate poverty in rural areas. / The campaign aims to eradicate polio worldwide. / It's almost impossible to eradicate every trace of mold.
column8: Very strong verb: remove completely. Common with disease, pests, poverty, corruption, weeds, errors. Stronger than reduce or control.

column2: every alternate day / every other day
column5: On one day, then not the next, repeating every two days.
column6: every other day, on alternate days, every second day
column7: He takes the medication every other day. / The clinic is open on alternate days. / In some varieties of English, 'every alternate day' is also used for the same schedule.
column8: 'Every other day' is the most natural everyday AmE form. 'On alternate days' is broadly standard. 'Every alternate day' is used in some varieties, especially South Asian English, but may sound less idiomatic to many AmE speakers.

column5: To clear someone from blame, fault, responsibility, or an accusation, especially when evidence shows they were not responsible.
column6: clear, absolve, vindicate, acquit (legal context only), clear of blame, clear of wrongdoing
column7: New DNA evidence could exonerate the suspect. / The investigation exonerated the company of wrongdoing. / Nothing in the report exonerates management from responsibility for the failure.
column8: Typical active patterns: evidence/investigation/report exonerates someone; exonerate someone of wrongdoing/blame; exonerate someone from responsibility/liability. 'Acquit' is specifically a legal judgment in a criminal case; 'vindicate' can also mean prove a decision or belief was right.

column4: past tense / past participle; often passive or adjectival
column5: Cleared from blame, accusation, wrongdoing, or responsibility; the past/past-participle form of exonerate, very often used in passive constructions.
column6: cleared, absolved, vindicated; acquitted (only when a court verdict is meant), cleared of wrongdoing
column7: She was exonerated after DNA evidence identified another suspect. / He was fully exonerated of any wrongdoing. / The exonerated defendant later sued the city. / Years later, the evidence finally exonerated him.
column8: KEEP separately because the usage profile is useful for learners: 'was exonerated', 'exonerated of wrongdoing', and 'the exonerated defendant' are common passive/adjectival patterns that differ from the active dictionary form 'exonerate someone'. This is more than simply memorizing a past-tense spelling.

column5: 1. The stated or printed monetary value of a coin, banknote, ticket, bond, etc. 2. In 'take/accept something at face value': accept its apparent meaning or truth without questioning or looking for hidden factors.
column6: nominal value, stated value; apparent meaning, surface meaning (figurative)
column7: The ticket has a face value of $80, but resale prices are much higher. / Don't take his promises at face value—he often exaggerates. / At face value, the proposal sounds reasonable.
column8: The literal financial meaning is important. The idiom is usually 'take X at face value'. 'Face value' does not itself mean 'superficial meaning' in every context.

column5: To waste time doing unnecessary or unproductive tasks.
column7: Stop faffing and get to work already! / Booking this trip has been such a faff. / Stop faffing about and pick one.
column8: Strongly British informal. Verb: faff / faff about/around = waste time fussing. Noun: a faff = an annoying hassle requiring unnecessary effort.

column5: A complete and embarrassing failure.
column7: The dinner party turned into a total fiasco. / What was meant to be a simple launch turned into a complete fiasco.
column8: Fiasco = conspicuous, embarrassing failure. Very close to debacle WID 15; keep both but cross-reference rather than duplicate identical notes.

column5: Recklessly bold or rash.
column7: It was foolhardy to go hiking alone in that storm. / Trying to cross the river during the flood would be foolhardy.
column8: Foolhardy is always negative: recklessly daring despite obvious danger. Brave/bold can be positive; foolhardy means the risk is foolish.

column5: Clothing or distinctive style of dress.
column7: The priest wore traditional ceremonial garb. / The performers appeared in elaborate ceremonial garb.
column8: Formal/literary word for distinctive clothing, especially ceremonial, traditional, religious, military, or occupational dress.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::literary usage::ceremonial usage::religious usage::military topic::fashion topic::culture

column5: Excessively talkative, especially on trivial matters.
column7: The garrulous host dominated the conversation all evening. / The otherwise quiet meeting became exhausting once the garrulous guest took over.
column8: Garrulous usually implies excessive, sometimes tiresome talkativeness. Loquacious is formal and can be more neutral.

column2: go/come to the brink of; bring/take to the brink
column5: To approach, or cause someone/something to approach, an extreme and usually dangerous point such as war, collapse, bankruptcy, or disaster.
column6: come close to, verge on, approach the edge of, nearly reach; push to the edge
column7: The crisis brought the two countries to the brink of war. / The company came to the brink of bankruptcy. / Negotiators went to the brink before finally reaching an agreement.
column8: The most useful pattern is 'the brink of + noun': the brink of war/collapse/disaster/bankruptcy. 'Go to the brink' can occur, but teach it as part of the wider brink phrase family rather than as an isolated fixed idiom.

column5: In open resistance or bold disobedience to something.
column7: She continued working in defiance of her doctor's advice. / They marched in defiance of the ban. / The structure seems to stand in defiance of gravity.
column8: 'In defiance of' implies deliberate/open resistance, stronger than simple despite. Common with orders, law, warnings, expectations, gravity.

column5: 1. Physics: the tendency of an object to remain at rest or keep moving at a constant velocity unless acted on by an external force. 2. Figuratively, a tendency to remain inactive or resist change once a situation is established.
column6: resistance to change, inactivity, stagnation, sluggishness (figurative); no exact synonym in physics
column7: A moving object continues because of inertia unless another force acts on it. / Organizational inertia made even small reforms difficult. / After a week off, pure inertia kept me from getting back into my routine.
column8: Do not equate inertia directly with apathy. Apathy is lack of interest or feeling; inertia is resistance to changing the current state, which may happen even when people care.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::figurative usage::scientific topic::physics topic::science discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Childish or immature.
column7: His infantile behavior annoyed everyone at the meeting. / The argument was embarrassingly infantile. / The study focuses on infantile developmental reflexes.
column8: Literal/formal sense relates to infants; figurative sense = childish/immature and is disparaging.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::figurative usage::disparaging usage::rhetorical usage::evaluative discovery::debate_language

column5: Innocent, candid, and free from deceit or calculation; sometimes naively trusting or straightforward.
column6: guileless, candid, innocent, sincere, artless, naive, trusting
column7: Her ingenuous questions made it clear she genuinely wanted to understand. / He gave an ingenuous account of what had happened, without trying to make himself look better.
column8: High-value contrast: ingenuous = innocent/candid; ingenious = clever/inventive. They look similar but are unrelated in meaning. 'Ingenuous' can be positive (refreshingly candid) or suggest naivety.

column5: Curious or eager for knowledge.
column7: Her inquisitive nature made her a great journalist. / She was inquisitive about how the machine worked. / The neighbor became uncomfortably inquisitive about my private life.
column8: Can be positive (curious, eager to learn) or negative (prying, nosy), depending on context.

column5: Buried a dead body in a grave or tomb.
column7: He was interred in the family cemetery. / The remains were interred in a private ceremony.
column8: Formal word for burial. High-value contrast: interred = buried; interned = detained/confined, often during wartime.

column5: 1. Dull, uninteresting, or lacking substance. 2. Naive, simplistic, superficial, or immature in thought.
column6: dull, insipid, tedious; naive, simplistic, shallow, immature
column7: The lecture was so jejune that even specialists struggled to stay interested. / The critic dismissed the argument as jejune and overly simplistic.
column8: Formal/literary word with two established senses. Context decides whether the criticism is 'boring/insubstantial' or 'naive/superficial'. Avoid reducing it to only 'childish'.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::formal usage::literary usage::rhetorical discovery::debate_language

column5: In a fair or morally correct way.
column7: She was justly praised for her honesty and dedication. / The book was justly praised as one of the year's best. / He wanted everyone involved to be treated justly.
column8: Two common ideas: fairly/according to justice; deservedly/rightly ('justly famous', 'justly criticized').

column5: Used to emphasize that something is even less likely or possible than another thing.
column6: much less, not to mention, still less
column7: He can't afford a bike, let alone a car. / She can barely walk to the store, let alone run a marathon. / I don't have time to read the article, let alone the whole book.
column8: 'Let alone B' presents B as even less possible/likely than A. It can also work in positive contexts when B is an even stronger claim.

column5: To incorrectly identify or interpret A as B.
column6: misidentify, confuse A with B, take A for B
column7: I mistook him for his brother—they look so alike. / Don't mistake kindness for weakness. / From a distance, I mistook the coat on the chair for a person.
column8: Core pattern: mistake A for B. Past tense is mistook; past participle mistaken. Compare 'confuse A with B'. 'Be mistaken for' is common passive: 'I was mistaken for an employee.'

column5: The essential customs and values of a community.
column7: Social mores vary widely from one culture to another. / Changing social mores have reshaped attitudes toward marriage and work.
column8: Usually plural. Mores are established social/moral customs regarded as important to a community. More value-laden than mere habits.

column5: A statement that does not logically follow from the previous one.
column7: His response was a complete non sequitur. / His answer was a complete non sequitur. / 'It's raining, so the movie must be bad' is a non sequitur.
column8: In logic, a non sequitur is a conclusion that does not follow from the premises; in conversation it can also mean an irrelevant or random remark. Latin non sequitur literally means 'it does not follow.' Related term: sequitur literally means 'it follows' and can mean a logical consequence that follows from what came before. Standalone English use of sequitur is uncommon and is often technical, playful, or used specifically as a contrast to 'non sequitur'.

column5: Noun: 1. a short written message or reminder; 2. an annotation or brief written record; 3. a particular quality or tone ('a note of sadness'); 4. a musical sound/symbol. Verb: to notice, observe, mention, or write something down.
column6: message, memo, annotation, remark; observe, notice, record, mention (sense-dependent)
column7: She left a note on the fridge. / I made a note of the address. / There was a note of irritation in his voice. / Please note that the schedule has changed. / The report notes several serious risks.
column8: This card was too narrow. High-frequency patterns: make/take a note of; note that...; please note...; a note of concern/sarcasm; musical note. Because 'note' is very polysemous, examples should signal the sense clearly.

column5: In an overly eager or submissive way, especially to gain favor.
column7: He bowed obsequiously to his boss. / He laughed obsequiously at every joke the executive made.
column8: Obsequious means excessively submissive/fawning toward someone powerful, usually to gain favor. Stronger and more negative than merely polite or deferential.

column5: An expression of surprise, realization, or awkwardness.
column7: Oh dip! I left my wallet at home. / Oh dip—I forgot the tickets. / Oh dip, that actually worked!
column8: Casual/playful exclamation of surprise, realization, alarm, or excitement. Often functions as a milder euphemistic alternative to stronger exclamations; not universal in all dialects/age groups.
column12: entry::interjection entry::slang_expression usage::casual usage::slang usage::playful usage::informal discovery::perception

column5: Adverb: completely, openly, immediately, or without qualification. Adjective: complete, total, direct, or unambiguous.
column6: completely, absolutely, flatly, categorically; total, complete, direct, unqualified
column7: She rejected the proposal outright. / He denied the accusation outright. / That claim is an outright lie. / We bought the car outright rather than financing it.
column8: Common combinations: reject/refuse/deny outright; outright ban/refusal/lie/victory. 'Buy/own outright' = without debt, installments, or shared ownership.

column5: Having keen understanding or insight.
column7: Her perspicacious observations impressed the whole panel. / Her perspicacious analysis caught a flaw everyone else had missed.
column8: Perspicacious = keenly perceptive and insightful. Noun: perspicacity. Do not confuse with perspicuous = clearly expressed/easy to understand.

column5: Something that especially annoys or irritates a person.
column7: Loud chewing is one of his biggest pet peeves. / One of my pet peeves is people who block the whole sidewalk.
column8: A pet peeve is a particular, often idiosyncratic annoyance. Very common frame: 'One of my pet peeves is...'. Cross-reference bugbear WID 19.

column5: Used humorously to refer to planning a life together or making domestic choices.
column6: settle down, plan a future, nest-build
column7: We're not picking out curtains just yet it's only our third date. / Relax—we've only had two dates. I'm not picking out curtains yet.
column8: Humorous romantic shorthand for acting as if a relationship is already serious/domestic. Often appears as 'We're not picking out curtains yet.' Not a rigid dictionary idiom.

column5: Verb: to arouse or stimulate interest, curiosity, or attention. Noun: a feeling of irritation or wounded pride, especially in 'in a fit of pique.'
column6: arouse, spark, stimulate, whet, provoke (interest); irritation, resentment, wounded pride (noun)
column7: The trailer piqued my curiosity. / That detail immediately piqued his interest. / She left in a fit of pique after her suggestion was ignored.
column8: Common confusion: pique interest/curiosity, not 'peak' or 'peek'. Peak = highest point; peek = quick look; pique = stimulate or irritate.

column5: Favoring or supporting commercial and economic interests.
column7: The candidate promoted a pro-business agenda. / The mayor ran on a pro-business platform focused on lowering regulation.
column8: A relative political/economic label meaning favorable to business interests, investment, enterprise, or reduced burdens. Not a precise synonym for capitalist.
column12: entry::word usage::persuasive usage::businesslike topic::business topic::economics discovery::promotion discovery::persuasion

column5: To try to convert someone to a belief, faith, or cause.
column7: He was known to proselytize at every social gathering. / He kept trying to proselytize for his diet at dinner. / The group proselytized among new arrivals.
column8: Originally strongly associated with religious conversion; now extended to ideologies, causes, products, lifestyles. Often disapproving when someone aggressively recruits or preaches.
column12: entry::word usage::critical usage::persuasive usage::religious topic::religion discovery::advocacy discovery::persuasion

column5: Extremely cool or awesome.
column7: That skateboard trick was totally rad! / That old arcade is rad. / The jacket looks totally rad.
column8: Strongly associated with 1980s–90s youth/surfer/skater slang, especially California; still used playfully or retro. Shortened from radical.

column5: 1. To restore friendly relations between people. 2. To make two facts, accounts, statements, or positions consistent with each other. 3. To reconcile oneself to something: to accept an unpleasant reality.
column6: make peace, reunite; harmonize, resolve, square, align; accept, come to terms with
column7: They reconciled after years of tension. / We need to reconcile the two sets of figures before publishing the report. / She eventually reconciled herself to the fact that the plan had failed.
column8: Three distinct grammar patterns: reconcile with someone; reconcile A with B; reconcile oneself to something. These are worth learning separately.

column5: To respond to an accusation with one of your own.
column7: Their argument turned bitter as they began to recriminate. / Instead of solving the problem, both sides spent hours recriminating. / The breakup was followed by months of mutual recriminations.
column8: Formal/rare verb; the plural noun recriminations is much more common. Recriminate = answer an accusation with a counteraccusation.

column5: To reject or refuse to accept; to deny the truth or validity of something.
column7: The scientist publicly repudiated the flawed research findings. / The party repudiated the extremist statement. / He repudiated the debt and denied that he had agreed to it.
column8: Formal, forceful rejection/disowning. Common objects: claim, belief, policy, debt, contract, statement, ideology. Stronger than ordinary reject.

column5: To move smoothly from one topic or situation to another.
column7: She expertly segued from small talk to serious discussion. / She segued smoothly from the budget update into the hiring discussion.
column8: Pronounced /ˈsɛɡweɪ/. Common pattern: segue into/from. Noun also exists ('a smooth segue'). Do not confuse spelling with the Segway brand.

column5: Deliberately avoided or rejected someone or something.
column7: He was shunned by his former colleagues after the scandal. / After the scandal, former allies shunned him. / She shuns social media entirely.
column8: Shun = deliberately avoid/reject, often because of disapproval, fear, or principle. More deliberate than simply avoid.

column2: off the cuff / speak off the cuff
column5: Without preparation, rehearsal, or advance planning; improvised spontaneously.
column7: She spoke off the cuff for twenty minutes and still sounded polished. / His off-the-cuff remark ended up becoming the headline. / I can explain the idea off the cuff, but I'd want notes for a formal presentation.
column8: 'Off the cuff' can function adverbially ('speak off the cuff') or adjectivally before a noun ('an off-the-cuff comment'). The original headword 'speaking off and cuff' was nonstandard.
column12: entry::idiom entry::adverbial_phrase usage::formal usage::journalistic usage::presentation-friendly topic::communication topic::planning discovery::improvement discovery::presentation_language

column5: Extremely surprising, shocking, or impressive, especially because of very large size, amount, or degree.
column6: astonishing, astounding, breathtaking, overwhelming, enormous, eye-watering (informal, amount/cost)
column7: The project cost a staggering $2 billion. / The number of people affected is staggering. / She made a staggering recovery after the accident.
column8: The adjective comes from stagger = move unsteadily or be shocked/overwhelmed. Common collocations: staggering amount/cost/number/figure/scale. The verb has separate senses: 'He staggered home' and 'The news staggered me.'

column5: With strong loyalty or firmness.
column7: She staunchly defended her beliefs despite criticism. / She staunchly opposed the proposal. / He remained a staunch supporter.
column8: Adverb staunchly commonly modifies support/oppose/defend. Adjective staunch = loyal, committed, firm. 'Stanch' traditionally means stop a flow, though staunch is also used as a variant.

column5: 1. stoicism: calm endurance of pain, hardship, or emotion without complaint or outward display. 2. Stoicism: the ancient philosophical tradition associated with virtue, reason, and focusing on what is within one's control.
column6: fortitude, endurance, composure, emotional restraint (lowercase sense); Stoic philosophy (proper-name sense)
column7: He faced the surgery with remarkable stoicism. / Her stoicism made it hard to tell how worried she really was. / Stoicism teaches that virtue matters more than external fortune.
column8: Do not reduce philosophical Stoicism to 'suppressing emotion'. Lowercase stoicism is the everyday trait; capitalized Stoicism is the philosophy.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::form_family entry::word topic::culture topic::philosophy discovery::complaint

column5: To bring under control or domination.
column7: The empire aimed to subjugate neighboring lands. / The regime tried to subjugate neighboring peoples. / They refused to be politically subjugated.
column8: Strong, often oppressive verb: bring under domination/control, frequently through force. Noun: subjugation.

column5: The legal or political right to vote in public elections.
column6: voting rights, the franchise; enfranchisement (related process/state)
column7: The movement campaigned for women's suffrage. / Universal suffrage means that adult citizens broadly have the right to vote. / Many activists fought for decades to secure suffrage.
column8: 'Ballot' is not a synonym: a ballot is the voting paper/process. 'Enfranchisement' is related but can mean the granting of voting rights, while suffrage is the right itself. Avoid the redundant phrase 'the right to suffrage'; say 'suffrage' or 'the right to vote'.

column5: A person who flatters someone important to gain advantage.
column7: The boss surrounded himself with sycophants instead of honest advisors. / The leader surrounded himself with sycophants who never challenged him.
column8: A sycophant flatters or agrees with a powerful person for personal advantage. Related: sycophantic, sycophancy.

column5: Limited or restricted by a specific period or deadline.
column7: The goals must be time-bound to ensure accountability. / A useful goal should be specific, measurable, and time-bound.
column8: Common in SMART goals. Time-bound = constrained by a time limit/deadline; 'deadline-driven' is related but not an exact synonym.

column5: 1. To happen or occur. 2. To become known or be revealed, especially after being secret or unclear.
column6: happen, occur, take place, unfold; emerge, come to light, become known
column7: No one could believe what had transpired at the meeting. / It later transpired that the figures had been altered. / As more details transpired, the original story began to fall apart.
column8: The 'happen' sense is standard in modern English, though older usage commentators sometimes objected to it. The 'become known' pattern is especially common in 'it transpired that...'.

column5: A formal criminal accusation that someone committed treason—an offense involving betrayal of one's state or sovereign as specifically defined by the law of that jurisdiction.
column6: charge of treason, accusation of treason, treason indictment (where applicable)
column7: He was arrested and later faced treason charges. / Prosecutors must satisfy the jurisdiction's specific legal definition before bringing a treason charge.
column8: Do not treat sedition as a synonym. Treason and sedition are distinct offenses with different legal elements, and definitions vary by jurisdiction. 'State crime' is also too broad to be a synonym.

column5: Lacking good manners or refinement.
column7: His uncouth remarks made everyone uncomfortable. / The host apologized for his guest's uncouth behavior.
column8: Can describe a person, manners, language, jokes, behavior, or taste. Implies lack of social refinement, often stronger than merely informal.

column5: In a way, at a rate, or on a scale that cannot be maintained over the long term without exhausting resources, causing harm, or eventually failing.
column6: at an unsustainable rate, nonviably, in a way that cannot be maintained (context-dependent)
column7: The company was growing unsustainably fast and burning through cash. / Groundwater is being extracted unsustainably. / He had been working at an unsustainably intense pace for months.
column8: 'Excessively' and 'recklessly' may describe some cases but are not synonyms. The core idea is inability to continue over time. Common domains: environment, finance, growth, workload, debt, resource use.

column5: For a very long time, often with the implication that continuing the activity will not change the outcome.
column6: for ages, endlessly, indefinitely, forever (informal exaggeration)
column7: You can argue until the cows come home, but I'm not changing my mind. / We could discuss tiny details until the cows come home and still never finish the project.
column8: The standard idiom is plural: 'until the cows come home'. Singular 'until the cow comes home' may occur as a variation or mistake, but it should not be the canonical headword.

column5: Using more words than necessary.
column7: His writing style is far too verbose for technical documentation. / The draft is accurate but far too verbose for a one-page memo.
column8: Verbose is usually negative: more wordy than necessary. Noun: verbosity. Detailed can be useful; verbose means unnecessarily wordy.

column5: 1. To clear someone from blame, criticism, or suspicion by showing that they were right or not responsible. 2. To show that a decision, belief, claim, or course of action was justified or correct.
column6: clear, exonerate, absolve; justify, validate, confirm, prove right
column7: The new evidence vindicated her. / The final results vindicated his decision to change strategy. / She felt vindicated when the investigation confirmed her account.
column8: 'Vindicate her innocence' is awkward because vindicate already carries the idea of clearing/justifying. Compared with exonerate, vindicate more readily applies to decisions, beliefs, reputations, or claims—not only accusations of wrongdoing.

column5: To impair, spoil, weaken, or destroy the effectiveness, quality, or validity of something; in legal/formal contexts, to make something defective or invalid.
column6: impair, undermine, weaken, spoil, corrupt, invalidate, nullify (legal/context-dependent)
column7: A serious methodological flaw can vitiate the study's conclusions. / The scandal had a vitiating effect on public trust. / Fraud may vitiate consent in some legal contexts.
column8: Formal word. Common objects include consent, agreement, reasoning, evidence, atmosphere, effect, and validity. 'Vitiating factor' is especially common in legal/technical writing.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal usage::technical topic::law topic::grammar discovery::evaluation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A mocking term used to ridicule someone who is being overly dramatic or whiny.
column7: Oh no, someone call the wahmbulance—he didn't get his way. / Stop complaining or I'm calling the wahmbulance.
column8: Mocking portmanteau of childish 'wah-wah' + ambulance. Used to ridicule whining/overdramatic complaining; intentionally dismissive and can sound mean. Often appears in 'call the wahmbulance'.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::humorous usage::disparaging usage::informal topic::communication topic::everyday_life discovery::complaint discovery::criticism discovery::excessive_emotion

column5: to decrease gradually in size, strength, or intensity
column7: Interest in the project began to wane after the initial excitement wore off.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add moon/phase sense ('waning moon'), wane in popularity/influence/confidence, and contrast wax and wane.

column5: removing unnecessary items to make a space cleaner or more organized
column7: She's been decluttering her apartment to create a more peaceful environment.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Prefer declutter / decluttering; include physical and digital decluttering and distinguish declutter from ordinary tidy/organize.

column5: left a place angrily and abruptly
column6: walked out, left angrily, stomped off
column7: He stormed out of the meeting after being interrupted for the third time.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add storm out of + place and storm off; stress anger/drama and distinguish walk out, which can also mean protest/abandon.

column5: to remain valid or applicable
column7: The old saying still holds true in today's fast-paced world.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add 'the same holds true for...', 'if this holds true...', and contrast hold true with be true: it often means remain valid/applicable across cases/time.

column5: used to express sorrow, regret, or disappointment
column7: Alas, their efforts were not enough to win the competition.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Mark literary/old-fashioned/playfully dramatic; add 'Alas, ...' sentence-position pattern and contrast unfortunately/sadly.

column5: a noisy or heated argument or disagreement
column7: The two drivers got into a loud altercation after the near collision.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Usually a brief heated confrontation, often verbal but potentially physical; add get into/have an altercation and contrast argument/fight.

column5: 1. arrest (verb): to take someone into legal custody. 2. arrest (verb, formal): to stop, check, or slow the progress or development of something. 3. arresting (adjective): striking, captivating, or capable of immediately catching and holding attention. 4. arrested (past participle/adjective): stopped or halted at a particular stage, as in arrested development.
column6: arresting: striking, stunning, captivating, eye-catching, attention-grabbing; arrest (stop sense): halt, stop, check, impede; arrested: halted, stopped, checked
column7: The police arrested the suspect outside the station. / Researchers hope the treatment can arrest the progression of the disease. / The film opens with an arresting image of the empty city. / The condition can lead to arrested physical development.
column8: KEEP as a distinct usage-cluster card rather than treating it as a trivial inflection. The adjective arresting has a lexicalized meaning ('striking/captivating') that is not predictable from the police sense of arrest. The formal verb sense 'stop/check the progress of' explains combinations such as arrest decay, arrest disease progression, and arrested development. 'Arrested development' broadly means development that has stopped or been impeded; in clinical contexts, use the specific field's terminology rather than assuming one universal psychological diagnosis.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal usage::specialist topic::law topic::grammar discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: a confident or forceful statement of fact or belief
column7: Her assertion that the results were flawed sparked debate among the researchers.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add unsupported/confident claim nuance, assertion of rights/authority, and programming assertion if useful; distinguish assertion from evidence/proof.

column5: A rough numerical estimate that is reasonably close to the likely or actual amount, without claiming precision.
column6: rough estimate, approximate figure, educated estimate, approximate amount
column7: Can you give me a ballpark figure for the repairs? / We don't have the final numbers yet, but $20,000 is probably in the ballpark.
column8: 'Ballpark figure' is the standard spelling. Related expression: 'in the ballpark' = approximately correct, reasonable, or within an acceptable range. Informal but very common in business and everyday conversation.

column5: to surround a place with armed forces or to overwhelm with requests or questions
column7: The reporters besieged the actor with questions as he left the courthouse.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Separate military siege from figurative 'besieged by reporters/requests/problems'; add besiege a city and be besieged with/by.

column5: a person's spouse or romantic partner, often used humorously or affectionately
column7: He always brings his better half to company events.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Mark informal/affectionate and sometimes dated/cutesy; traditionally spouse, now partner; note not literally 'better' person.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::dated usage::affectionate topic::relationships topic::romance

column5: high-sounding language with little meaning, used to impress people
column7: The politician's speech was full of bombast but lacked substance.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add bombastic adjective; emphasize inflated/pompous rhetoric intended to impress, often lacking substance.

column5: To invent or introduce a new word, term, phrase, or expression.
column7: The writer coined the term to describe a new kind of online behavior. / Who coined the phrase 'the American Dream'?
column8: Normalize from 'coin in English'. A person can coin an expression without being the person who later makes it popular. Common pattern: 'X coined the term/phrase ...'.

column5: hanging or swinging loosely
column7: The keys were dangling from the edge of the table.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add dangle something in front of someone = tempt/offer, dangling modifier/participle (grammar), and 'leave someone dangling' if useful.

column5: having or showing an ability to accurately assess situations or people and turn this to one's advantage
column7: She's an astute negotiator who always finds the best deal.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add astute observation/judgment/business move; nuance = quick, practical, perceptive judgment, often advantageous; contrast shrewd/canny.

column5: gives or grants something formally or officially
column7: The foundation bestows scholarships on deserving students every year.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Prefer bestow / bestows; teach bestow something on/upon someone, often honors/awards/powers/gifts; formal register.

column5: An internally generated biological rhythm of roughly 24 hours that helps regulate sleep and wakefulness, body temperature, hormone release, and other physiological processes.
column7: Jet lag occurs partly because your circadian rhythm is out of sync with the local day-night cycle.
column8: Do not equate circadian rhythm with a sleep cycle. A sleep cycle is the roughly 90-minute progression through sleep stages during sleep; circadian rhythm is the approximately 24-hour timing system. 'Biological clock' is a broader, less precise expression.
column12: entry::noun_phrase topic::wellness topic::biology topic::weather topic::science discovery::release discovery::iteration

column5: Verb /ˈkɒnsəmeɪt/: 1. to complete or bring a transaction, agreement, or process to completion; 2. traditionally/legal-historically, to complete a marriage by having sexual intercourse. Adjective consummate /ˈkɒnsəmət/: supremely skilled, accomplished, or complete.
column6: verb: complete, finalize, conclude; marriage sense: complete/consummate the marriage; adjective: accomplished, superb, masterful
column7: The companies consummated the merger after months of negotiations. / In traditional legal language, a marriage may be described as consummated after the spouses have sexual intercourse. / She is a consummate professional.
column8: High-value pronunciation/part-of-speech contrast: the verb ends in /-meɪt/, while the adjective ends in /-mət/. 'Consummated' is common in formal business/legal writing. The marriage sense is established but can sound formal or legalistic.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal usage::professional usage::legalistic topic::law topic::language_learning discovery::process_details discovery::expertise discovery::agreement discovery::professional_context

column5: not openly acknowledged or displayed; secretive
column7: The agent was on a covert mission overseas.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add covert operation/surveillance/action and contrast covert vs clandestine/undercover/overt; pronunciation contrast with 'cover' can help.

column5: expresses the essential features of something succinctly
column7: The introduction perfectly encapsulates the main argument of the book.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Prefer encapsulate / encapsulates; cover summarize/embody in compact form and literal enclose in capsule if useful.

column5: having or displaying passionate intensity
column7: She is a fervent supporter of environmental causes.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add fervent belief/support/hope/prayer; strong sincere intensity, often positive or ideological; contrast fervid/fervor if useful.

column5: fails to meet the required standard in a test or class
column7: If he flunks one more class, he won't graduate on time.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Prefer flunk / flunk out; cover fail a test/class, cause someone to fail (AmE), flunk out of school; informal.
column12: entry::word entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::american_english topic::testing discovery::evaluation

column5: encouraging the development or growth of something
column7: The school is committed to fostering creativity and independence.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Prefer foster / fostering; foster growth/creativity/relations; also foster child/parent as adjective/noun-related family.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::persuasive topic::grammar discovery::promotion discovery::encouragement discovery::persuasion

column5: the realization or fulfillment of a plan or project
column7: Her hard work finally came to fruition when she published her novel.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Teach come to fruition / bring to fruition; realization of plans/efforts, historically fruit-bearing; not simply 'completion'.

column5: the establishment or starting point of an institution or activity
column7: The company has grown significantly since its inception in 2010.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Common frame since/from its inception; formal; inception = beginning/establishment, not the process of developing.

column5: to instill an idea or habit by persistent instruction
column7: The teacher worked to inculcate respect and discipline in the students.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Inculcate values/habits/ideas in someone / inculcate someone with (less preferred); repeated instruction; formal, sometimes authoritarian nuance.

column5: lack of strictness or care
column7: Laxity in enforcing the rules led to a chaotic environment.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add laxity in security/enforcement/standards; distinguish laxity (insufficient strictness) from laziness.

column5: 1. Ordinary, routine, or lacking excitement or interest. 2. Formal/literary: relating to the earthly or worldly realm rather than the spiritual or heavenly.
column6: ordinary, routine, everyday, humdrum, prosaic; worldly, earthly (second sense)
column7: Most of the job consists of mundane administrative tasks. / The novel contrasts spiritual aspirations with mundane concerns.
column8: The everyday sense is by far the most common. 'Mundane' does not necessarily mean bad; it often simply means ordinary or routine.

column5: to last or endure permanently; to continue to exist
column7: Some traditions perdure despite the passage of centuries.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Mark literary/rare; perdure = endure/continue for a long time. Contrast persist/endure; perhaps lower retention priority.

column5: Verb: to propose or assume something as a basis for reasoning, theory, or discussion, often without first proving it. Noun: an assumption or proposition accepted as a starting point for reasoning.
column6: verb: posit, assume, hypothesize, propose; noun: assumption, premise, axiom (context-dependent)
column7: The theory postulates that language ability has an innate component. / Euclidean geometry begins from a small set of postulates.
column8: More formal and technical than ordinary 'suggest'. 'Postulate' emphasizes putting forward or accepting a proposition as a basis for further reasoning. An axiom/postulate distinction varies by field.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::technical discovery::speculation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: deserving of condemnation or criticism
column7: His actions were morally reprehensible and widely condemned.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Stronger than merely criticizable: deserving strong moral condemnation. Add reprehensible conduct/behavior and noun reprehensibility if useful.

column5: a sudden or aggressive series of acts or remarks; a simultaneous discharge of weapons
column7: The debate began with a salvo of pointed accusations.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Separate literal simultaneous gun/artillery discharge from figurative opening salvo/salvo of criticism/questions; add 'opening salvo'.

column5: Relating to meaning in language, symbols, logic, or other representational systems.
column7: The two sentences are grammatically similar but have an important semantic difference. / The word underwent a semantic shift over time.
column8: 'Linguistic' is much broader and is not a synonym. Common terms: semantic meaning, semantic difference, semantic shift, semantic field, semantic memory. Contrast semantic (meaning) with syntactic (structure/grammar).

column5: in a brief and clearly expressed manner
column7: She succinctly summarized the entire project in two sentences.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add succinct = brief without sacrificing clarity; succinctly put; contrast terse (can sound abrupt) and concise.

column5: not embarrassed, disconcerted, or ashamed
column7: He was unabashed about his love for cheesy rom-coms.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add unabashed enthusiasm/fan/supporter and 'unabashedly'; unlike shameless, often positive/playful because no embarrassment.

column5: pure and complete; not mixed or diluted with anything else
column7: The documentary captured the unadulterated joy of childhood.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Literal not diluted/mixed/contaminated; figurative complete/pure ('unadulterated joy/nonsense'). Contrast adulterated.

column5: steady or resolute; not changing or becoming weaker
column7: She remained unwavering in her support of the team through tough times.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add unwavering support/commitment/gaze/voice; steady despite pressure; contrast unwavering vs unchanging.

column5: the number below the line in a fraction; also used metaphorically to refer to a shared trait, characteristic, or factor that connects multiple things or situations. It can also be used to describe something of low quality or appeal designed to reach a broad but undemanding audience.
column6: divisor, common factor, base number, attribute, feature, manner
column7: In the fraction 3/4, the number 4 is the denominator. The common denominator for their success was hard work. The reality show was designed to appeal to the lowest common denominator, sacrificing depth for cheap laughs."
column8:
Common Denominator (figurative):
Something shared by all elements in a group.
e.g., A shared sense of responsibility was the common denominator among the team’s top performers.
Despite their different backgrounds, kindness was the common denominator that brought them together.
In every successful project we've led, clear communication was the common denominator.

Lowest Common Denominator (figurative):
A shared trait at the most basic or superficial level — often used to criticize something for being dumbed down.
e.g., The show caters to the lowest common denominator of public taste. They lowered the content to the lowest common denominator just to get more clicks. Depth-pass addition: Preserve current literal + common denominator + lowest common denominator coverage; only clean formatting/quote artifact if needed.

column5: having or showing good judgment and insight
column7: She's a discerning reader who prefers complex character development.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Discerning = able to notice fine distinctions and judge quality; common discerning reader/customer/palate; can imply selectiveness.

column5: unsettled or confused, typically due to an unexpected event
column7: He was disconcerted by the sudden change in her tone.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Use disconcert / disconcerted; disconcerted = unsettled, confused, thrown off; add be disconcerted by/at and contrast embarrassed.

column5: intended to explain or describe something
column7: The textbook is filled with expository passages that clarify key concepts.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Expository writing/text/essay explains or informs rather than narrates/persuades; distinguish exposition/expository from explanatory.

column5: medications used to stimulate ovulation or increase fertility
column7: The doctor prescribed fertility drugs to improve her chances of conception.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Use neutral medical wording; note umbrella term for medications used to induce/regulate ovulation or support fertility treatment; avoid treating all as identical.

column5: problems or challenges related to becoming pregnant or reproducing
column7: They sought medical help after struggling with fertility issues for years.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Note broad/nontechnical wording; fertility issues can affect any partner and do not automatically equal a diagnosis of infertility.

column5: used to indicate the immediate continuation of an activity, often after a delay
column6: delay, ceremony, fuss (in negative form: 'without further ado')
column7: Without further ado, let's begin the presentation.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Normalize headword; ado = fuss/delay/activity; 'without further ado' = without more delay or ceremony. Ado alone is uncommon outside set phrases.

column5: pointlessness or uselessness
column7: He gave up, realizing the futility of arguing with her.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add futility of doing something / sense of futility; contrast futile adjective and hopelessness (emotion) vs futility (ineffectiveness/pointlessness).

column5: to measure, estimate, or judge something
column7: It's hard to gauge the team's performance from just one game.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Gauge = measure/estimate/judge; noun instrument/measure/standard; gauge reaction/interest/distance; note common misspelling 'guage'.

column5: a retail store in a small town or rural area that sells a wide variety of goods
column6: country store, corner shop, local shop
column7: We stopped by the general store to grab some snacks and supplies.
column8: Depth-pass addition: General store traditionally rural/small-community shop selling varied everyday goods; distinguish convenience store and department store.

column2: greatest glory in living lies not in never falling but in rising every time we fall
column3: /ˈɡreɪ.təst ˈɡlɔr.i ɪn ˈlɪ.vɪŋ laɪz nɑt ɪn ˈnɛ.vɚ ˈfɑ.lɪŋ bət ɪn ˈraɪ.zɪŋ ˈɛv.ri taɪm wi fɔl/
column5: A motivational saying expressing the idea that real achievement or dignity lies not in never failing, but in recovering and continuing after failure.
column6: resilience, perseverance, getting back up, bouncing back (idea-level equivalents)
column7: After the project failed, she reminded the team that the real test was whether they could learn from it and rise again.
column8: Keep as a quotation card only if its source context is useful to the collection. Online versions are frequently attributed to different historical figures, so do not attach an author without reliable source verification. The learning value is the resilience idea and the wording, not an uncertain attribution.

column5: a series of words said as a magic spell or charm
column7: The wizard recited an incantation to unlock the ancient gate.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add figurative repetitive formula/ritual words if useful; distinguish incantation, invocation, chant, spell.

column5: 1. The process of keeping eggs, embryos, or organisms under conditions that allow development. 2. Medicine: the period between infection with a pathogen and the appearance of symptoms. 3. Figuratively, a period in which an idea, project, or plan develops before becoming visible or active.
column7: The virus has an incubation period of several days. / The eggs require careful incubation. / The idea spent years in incubation before becoming a real company.
column8: Do not reduce incubation to 'development' in every context. In infectious disease, incubation period specifically runs from infection to symptom onset; it is not automatically the same as a latent or infectious period.

column5: To gradually but firmly introduce an idea, value, feeling, habit, or quality into someone's mind or character.
column6: implant, inculcate, imbue, inspire, foster, impress upon
column7: Her parents instilled a strong work ethic in her. / The coach tries to instill confidence in every player. / Constant warnings can instill fear in children.
column8: Canonical card for WID 128 'instills'. Core pattern: instill something in/into someone. Common objects: confidence, fear, discipline, values, habits, respect. Compare inculcate: more formal and often emphasizes repeated teaching or instruction.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::instructional topic::self-help discovery::encouragement discovery::evaluation

column5: A species whose effect on the structure and functioning of an ecosystem is disproportionately large relative to its abundance; removing it can cause major ecological changes.
column6: no exact synonym; ecologically pivotal species (descriptive)
column7: Sea otters are often described as a keystone species because their predation on sea urchins can help maintain kelp forests.
column8: 'Central species' or 'ecosystem anchor' can help explain the idea but are not technical synonyms. Keystone species can be predators, ecosystem engineers, mutualists, or other organisms; the defining idea is disproportionate ecological impact.

column5: a boy or young man, often used informally or affectionately
column7: The lad ran off to join his friends at the park.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Especially BrE/Irish informal; 'the lads' can mean male friends/team; sometimes jocular. Contrast lad vs boy/guy.

column5: 1. Mechanical advantage gained by using a lever. 2. Influence or bargaining power that helps someone obtain a desired result. 3. Finance: use of borrowed money or debt to increase potential returns, also increasing risk. 4. Verb: to use a resource, advantage, information, or position effectively to achieve a result.
column6: mechanical advantage; influence, bargaining power, clout; financial gearing (BrE, finance); use, exploit, capitalize on (verb, context-dependent)
column7: A longer handle gives you more leverage. / The union used the deadline as leverage in negotiations. / Highly leveraged companies can be vulnerable when interest rates rise. / We can leverage the existing data instead of starting from scratch.
column8: Keep the senses separate. Business-verb 'leverage X to do Y' is extremely common but can sound corporate or jargon-heavy. Financial leverage magnifies both gains and losses.

column5: 1. Arranged in or resembling a straight line. 2. Proceeding in a direct, sequential order. 3. Mathematics: involving a relationship represented by a straight line or satisfying linearity properties. 4. Figuratively, progressing in a simple step-by-step way.
column6: straight-line, sequential, direct; proportional (only in some mathematical contexts)
column7: The story is told in a mostly linear sequence. / Recovery isn't always linear—you can improve for a while and then have a bad week. / The graph shows a roughly linear relationship between the variables.
column8: Contrast WID 164 nonlinear. 'Linear' does not automatically mean continuous, constant, or easy; its exact technical meaning depends on the field.
