column5: A form of protest in which participants lie down in a public place, often symbolically representing dead or affected people or physically occupying a space to draw attention to a cause.
column7: Activists staged a die-in outside the building to protest preventable deaths. / Students organized a lie-in in the lobby as a peaceful demonstration.
column8: Normalize from the vague/nonstandard headword 'lying down movement'. A die-in usually has symbolic associations with death or casualties; a lie-in can more broadly mean a protest involving people lying down. Do NOT confuse this with China's 'lying flat' (tang ping) movement in WID 161.

column2: lying flat / lying flat movement (tang ping, 躺平)
column5: A Chinese social attitude and trend, widely discussed from 2021 onward, in which people reject or disengage from intense work pressure, hypercompetition, and the relentless pursuit of conventional material success.
column6: tang ping; opting out (partial idea-level equivalent); low-desire lifestyle/passive resistance (descriptive, not exact synonyms)
column7: For some young people, lying flat means refusing the expectation that they must work extreme hours simply to keep competing. / The phrase tang ping became shorthand for stepping back from the conventional race for status and material success.
column8: Chinese: 躺平 (tǎng píng), literally 'lie flat'. The idea became especially associated with frustration over high-pressure work culture, competition, housing and living costs, and limited perceived rewards from relentless striving. It can range from a minimalist/low-desire lifestyle to symbolic passive resistance; it does not necessarily mean literally refusing all work. It is distinct from a die-in or lie-in protest (WID 160). Related Chinese slang such as 摆烂 (bǎi làn, roughly 'let it rot') can express a more resigned 'give up trying to fix it' attitude, but the terms are not identical.
column12: entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::informal topic::work topic::workplace topic::culture discovery::nonconformity discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: working a second job in addition to one's main employment, typically at night
column6: side hustling, freelancing, holding a second job, working extra
column7: She's been moonlighting as a graphic designer while working full-time in finance. She's moonlighting as a bartender to pay off student loans.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Prefer moonlight / moonlighting; second paid job in addition to primary job, often secretly/without employer knowledge in some contexts; moonlight as + role.

column5: 1. Illegally or informally distilled liquor, especially homemade high-proof spirits. 2. Literally, moonlight (older/literary). 3. Dated figurative use: nonsense or foolish talk.
column6: illicit liquor, homemade spirits; moonlight (older sense); nonsense (dated figurative)
column7: The family had once made moonshine in the mountains. / In older writing, moonshine can simply mean the light of the moon. / He dismissed the whole scheme as moonshine.
column8: The illicit-liquor sense is dominant in modern American English. A person who makes illicit spirits may be called a moonshiner. Do not assume the dated 'nonsense' sense from modern context without cues.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::literary usage::dated usage::figurative usage::american_english discovery::evidence

column5: 1. Not forming or following a straight line. 2. Not proceeding in a simple sequential order. 3. Mathematics/science: not satisfying a linear relationship or linearity conditions. 4. Figuratively, involving irregular changes, feedback, jumps, or multiple paths.
column7: The film uses a nonlinear narrative that jumps between different periods. / Language learning is nonlinear: progress can come in bursts. / The system exhibits nonlinear behavior.
column8: Standard closed spelling 'nonlinear' is common, though 'non-linear' is also accepted in many styles. Contrast WID 159 linear.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::form_family entry::word usage::scientific topic::relationships topic::science topic::mathematics discovery::figurative_extension

column5: new or unusual in an interesting way
column7: She proposed a novel solution to the recurring issue.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add novel approach/idea/solution/technology; distinguish adjective novel = new/original from noun novel = book-length fiction.

column5: exceptionally high or impressive in degree, extent, or intensity
column7: Her energy levels were off the charts during the performance.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Can mean extremely high/low/outside normal measurable range, not only impressive; off-the-charts popularity/pain/chemistry. Informal.

column5: unconventional or unusual in style or behavior
column7: He has an offbeat sense of humor that not everyone understands.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Offbeat = unconventional/quirky, often appealing; also musical offbeat noun/adjective sense if useful; distinguish odd/eccentric.

column5: to surpass someone in intelligence, strategy, or problem-solving
column7: The chess champion managed to outthink every opponent in the tournament.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Outthink = defeat by thinking/planning better; often strategy/problem-solving. Contrast outsmart/outwit/outmaneuver.

column5: 1. A raised platform on which a speaker, conductor, athlete, or other person stands. 2. Especially in American usage, also commonly used for the lectern—the stand that holds a speaker's notes or microphone.
column6: platform, dais; lectern (common AmE usage, though traditionally distinct)
column7: The conductor stepped onto the podium. / She walked to the podium and placed her notes on it.
column8: Traditional distinction: podium = raised platform you stand on; lectern = stand you stand behind and place notes on. In modern AmE, 'podium' is very commonly used for the lectern too, so treating that use as simply 'wrong' would be misleading.

column5: Charging prices viewed as excessively or unfairly high, especially by sharply raising prices for essential goods or services during shortages, emergencies, or sudden spikes in demand.
column6: excessive pricing, exploitative pricing, profiteering (overlapping, not always legally identical)
column7: The store was accused of price gouging after tripling the price of bottled water during the emergency.
column8: Correct the error 'price gauging' → 'price gouging'. Ordinary price increases or dynamic/surge pricing are not automatically price gouging. Legal definitions and restrictions vary by jurisdiction.

column5: Information, messaging, or material deliberately shaped and spread to influence attitudes or behavior in favor of a political cause, ideology, organization, or authority, often through selective or emotionally persuasive presentation.
column6: persuasive messaging, ideological messaging; agitprop (specific context)
column7: The regime used posters, films, and radio broadcasts as propaganda. / Both sides accused the other of spreading wartime propaganda.
column8: Misinformation is false or inaccurate information, whether intentional or not; disinformation is deliberately false or deceptive information. Propaganda is defined primarily by persuasive purpose and framing, so it can contain true, false, misleading, or selectively presented material. 'Spin' overlaps but is usually narrower and less systematic.
column12: entry::word usage::presentation-friendly topic::politics topic::presentations discovery::presentation_language discovery::public_discourse

column5: a key point or main message taken from a discussion, experience, or event
column7: Her biggest takeaway from the workshop was the importance of active listening.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add takeaway = key lesson/message; food bought to eat elsewhere (especially BrE; AmE takeout); takeaway point. Keep senses separated.

column5: to get or bring something back from a place
column7: He ran back to retrieve his forgotten backpack.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Retrieve object/data/information; retrieve a ball; regain/recover; computing information retrieval. Contrast fetch (go and bring) vs recover.

column5: 1. The art or practice of using language effectively and persuasively. 2. A particular style of persuasive language. 3. Often disapproving: impressive-sounding language that is seen as lacking substance, sincerity, or action.
column6: oratory, persuasive language, discourse; bombast, empty words (only in negative sense)
column7: She studied classical rhetoric and public speaking. / The campaign's rhetoric became increasingly aggressive. / Voters were tired of rhetoric and wanted concrete action.
column8: Do not define rhetoric only as empty talk. The neutral academic sense is central. Related: rhetorical device, rhetorical question, rhetorical strategy.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::academic usage::critical usage::rhetorical topic::art topic::rhetoric discovery::academic_discussion discovery::debate_language

column2: rocky intertidal zone / rocky shore intertidal zone
column5: The rocky coastal area between the usual high- and low-tide marks, alternately exposed to air and submerged by seawater as tides rise and fall.
column7: Tide pools in the rocky intertidal zone support organisms that must tolerate both exposure and submersion.
column8: 'Coastal reef' is not a synonym. Intertidal specifically refers to the zone affected by the regular rise and fall of tides.

column5: A figure of speech that explicitly compares one thing with another, typically using words such as 'like' or 'as'.
column7: 'Her smile was like sunshine' is a simile. / 'He fought like a lion' uses a simile to make the description more vivid.
column8: A metaphor is related but not a synonym: metaphor directly identifies one thing as another ('Time is a thief'), while a simile makes an explicit comparison ('Time is like a thief'). An analogy is usually a more extended comparison used to explain or reason about something.

column5: to find or encounter something by chance
column7: I stumbled upon an old photo album while cleaning the attic.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Add stumble across/on/upon and figurative chance discovery; distinguish literally stumble over something.

column5: A social insect that lives in colonies and feeds primarily on cellulose; some species can cause serious damage to wooden structures and other plant-based material.
column7: The inspector found termite damage in several wooden beams. / Not every termite species is a household pest.
column8: 'Destroyers' is not a synonym. Termites are ecologically important decomposers in many environments even though some species are major structural pests.

column5: 1. A person who secretly watches others engaged in private or intimate activity, especially for sexual pleasure. 2. Figuratively, a person or audience deriving fascination from observing other people's private lives, distress, or intimate experiences.
column6: Peeping Tom (informal, sexual/privacy sense); prying observer (figurative/descriptive)
column7: The man was accused of acting as a voyeur by secretly filming people in a private space. / Some critics said the documentary turned viewers into voyeurs of the family's grief.
column8: Ordinary observer/onlooker is too neutral to be a synonym. The core idea involves intrusive observation, privacy, and often sexual gratification in the primary sense.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::informal usage::figurative topic::public_speaking discovery::audience_engagement discovery::figurative_extension

column5: A person who reports or exposes suspected wrongdoing, illegality, danger, fraud, or misconduct within an organization or system, often using information gained through their position or access.
column6: internal reporter, wrongdoing reporter (descriptive); informant, leaker (overlapping but not equivalent)
column7: The whistleblower reported the accounting irregularities to regulators. / She blew the whistle on unsafe practices at the company.
column8: An informant provides information to authorities but need not be exposing wrongdoing from within an organization; a leaker discloses information, which may or may not concern wrongdoing. Legal definitions and whistleblower protections vary by jurisdiction.
column12: entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::news topic::debate topic::crime discovery::risk discovery::debate_language

column5: To become addicted to something or strongly absorbed in, enthusiastic about, or attached to it.
column6: become addicted to, get addicted to; get really into, become engrossed in (non-drug sense)
column7: I got hooked on the show after two episodes. / He got hooked on nicotine as a teenager. / Once I started the game, I was completely hooked.
column8: The severity depends on the object: 'hooked on a show' is casual enthusiasm, while 'hooked on a drug' can mean genuine addiction. Common adjective pattern: be hooked on.

column5: 1. To seek help, advice, comfort, or support from someone or something. 2. To begin using something as a solution, resource, occupation, or coping method. 3. To direct attention to a new topic or task. 4. To move to a specified page or section.
column6: seek help from, rely on, resort to; switch to, move on to; consult (context-dependent)
column7: When I'm stuck, I turn to a friend for advice. / Some people turn to alcohol when they're under stress. / Let's turn to the next issue on the agenda. / Turn to page 42.
column8: Do not reduce 'turn to' to 'rely on'. High-frequency patterns include turn to someone for help/advice, turn to something as a solution, turn to a new topic, and turn to page X. 'Resort to' often carries a stronger sense of using a last or undesirable option.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::phrasal_verb topic::problem-solving discovery::solution_framing discovery::resource_allocation discovery::transition discovery::support discovery::recommendation discovery::resolution

column5: a soothing ointment for wounds or pain; also used metaphorically for emotional relief
column7: Laughter can be a salve for the soul in tough times.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Literal medicinal ointment/balm; figurative comfort/remedy for emotional pain. Add salve a conscience/wound? Note verb salve exists but is less common.

column5: a magical or medicinal potion believed to cure or enhance
column7: Some claim this herbal drink is a modern-day elixir.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Elixir = medicinal/magical liquid historically; elixir of life/youth; figurative supposed cure/secret to success. Distinguish panacea = solution for all problems.

column5: A chemical messenger released by a neuron that carries a signal across a synapse to another neuron, muscle cell, gland cell, or other target cell.
column6: chemical messenger (descriptive); no exact simple synonym
column7: Dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, and GABA are neurotransmitters with different roles in neural signaling.
column8: 'Synaptic agent' is not a standard synonym. Neurotransmitters are one part of neural communication; they should not be reduced to simplistic labels such as one chemical = one emotion or behavior.

column5: to cause something to happen suddenly or unexpectedly
column7: The speech helped precipitate a wave of protests.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Precipitate a crisis/change = cause suddenly/prematurely; adjective precipitate = rash/sudden; noun chemistry precipitate if useful. Contrast precipitate vs precipitate out.

column5: relating to brain function and cognitive processes like memory or attention
column7: The study focuses on the neurocognitive effects of sleep deprivation.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Neurocognitive = involving relationship between brain/neurological function and cognition; common neurocognitive disorder/testing/deficit. Not simply synonym of mental.

column5: to lose strength, confidence, or momentum
column7: Her voice faltered as she tried to explain what happened.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Cover falter in speech/steps/confidence/economy/progress; hesitate or lose strength/momentum. Add 'without faltering'.

column5: Relating to older adults, especially their medical care, health, and diseases; as a noun, an older patient/person, though noun use can sound clinical or insensitive.
column6: geriatric-medicine-related, relating to older adults; elderly/older (not exact synonyms)
column7: She specializes in geriatric medicine. / The hospital expanded its geriatric care services.
column8: In medical contexts, geriatric is neutral and technical. Informal use to mean extremely old, decrepit, or outdated can be insulting when applied to people. Prefer 'older adult' in ordinary respectful reference to a person.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::technical topic::health topic::medicine discovery::impression discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: a medical professional trained to draw blood for tests, transfusions, or donations
column7: The phlebotomist was quick and gentle during the blood draw.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Phlebotomist specifically trained to collect blood, usually venipuncture; not generic medical technician. Add phlebotomy.

column5: A medication used primarily to treat psychotic symptoms and disorders, and also used in some other psychiatric conditions depending on the drug and clinical situation.
column6: neuroleptic (older/related term, not always perfectly interchangeable); antipsychotic medication
column7: The psychiatrist discussed the potential benefits and side effects of the antipsychotic medication.
column8: 'Tranquilizer' and generic 'psychiatric medication' are not synonyms. Antipsychotics are commonly grouped into first-generation and second-generation classes, but individual drugs differ substantially in effects and side-effect profiles.

column5: A prominent warning in U.S. prescription-drug labeling used to call attention to serious or life-threatening risks associated with a medication or its use.
column6: boxed warning; black box warning (common informal name)
column7: The prescribing information carries a boxed warning about a serious risk associated with the drug.
column8: 'Boxed warning' is the official FDA terminology; 'black box warning' is a very common informal name. A boxed warning does not mean a drug is banned or never appropriate—it signals that prescribers and patients need to consider a particularly serious risk.

column5: 1. Dental plaque: a sticky biofilm of microorganisms that forms on teeth. 2. Arterial/atherosclerotic plaque: deposits in artery walls associated with atherosclerosis. 3. A flat tablet or plate bearing an inscription, often commemorative. 4. Medicine: a raised or otherwise distinct patch/lesion, especially in dermatology and some disease terminology.
column6: biofilm (dental, technical); atherosclerotic deposit (arterial, descriptive); commemorative tablet/plate (inscription sense); lesion/patch (medical, context-dependent)
column7: Regular brushing helps remove dental plaque. / Plaque buildup can narrow an artery. / A plaque on the wall commemorates the building's founder. / The dermatologist examined a raised plaque on the skin.
column8: Highly polysemous: do not mix the dental, arterial, commemorative, and dermatological senses in one unlabeled synonym list.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::technical usage::specialist topic::health topic::medicine discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: to search thoroughly; also, to clean or scrub hard
column7: They scoured the beach for shells and sea glass.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Scour a surface = scrub vigorously; scour an area/web/records for = search thoroughly. Also geographical scouring/erosion if useful.

column5: a force or influence that makes something happen or develop more quickly
column7: The speech gave new impetus to the environmental movement.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Common 'give/provide impetus to', 'gain impetus'; force/stimulus that initiates or accelerates action. Contrast motivation (internal reason) vs impetus (triggering force).

column5: a male leader of a family or group; often the oldest or most respected male
column6: elder, father figure, head of family
column7: The patriarch of the clan was known for his wisdom and fairness.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Male head/founder/elder of family, tribe, organization, tradition; patriarchal relation. Can be neutral descriptive or carry power-hierarchy implications.

column5: a person who sells cannabis products and offers customer guidance in a dispensary
column6: dispensary staff, cannabis advisor, weed consultant
column7: The budtender explained the differences between the various strains available.
column8: Depth-pass addition: Cannabis dispensary retail worker advising customers; bud + bartender blend. Informal/industry-specific; responsibilities/legal status vary by jurisdiction.

column5: An acute, usually fluctuating disturbance in attention, awareness, and cognition that develops over a relatively short period and is often triggered by illness, medication, intoxication/withdrawal, surgery, or other medical causes.
column6: acute confusional state (clinical descriptive term); confusion (too broad for exact synonym)
column7: The infection caused sudden delirium, and his attention and awareness fluctuated throughout the day.
column8: Delirium is typically acute and fluctuating, unlike many dementias, which are usually more chronic and progressive. It is also not the same as psychosis, although hallucinations or delusions can occur during delirium. Medical evaluation is important because delirium often reflects an underlying physical cause.

column5: 1. Medicine: a sudden episode of abnormal electrical activity in the brain that can cause changes in movement, sensation, awareness, behavior, or consciousness. 2. The act of taking possession of property or goods by legal or official authority. 3. The sudden taking of power, control, territory, or an opportunity.
column6: medical: epileptic seizure (when epilepsy-related), fit (informal/variety-dependent); legal: confiscation, taking; power sense: takeover, capture
column7: Not every seizure involves convulsions or loss of consciousness. / Customs officials announced the seizure of illegal goods. / The coup resulted in the seizure of power by the military.
column8: Keep senses separate. A convulsion is a type of involuntary movement and can occur during some seizures, but seizure and convulsion are not synonyms. A single seizure does not by itself establish a diagnosis of epilepsy.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::technical usage::informal usage::military topic::health topic::law topic::engineering topic::television topic::medicine topic::entertainment discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: to stay at the same speed or level as someone or something
column6: match, stay abreast of, keep up with
column7: It's hard to keep pace with rapidly evolving technology.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Preserve the core sense; add the most natural collocations/patterns, register and close contrasts where useful, plus at least one natural real-world example if the current example is too narrow.

column5: In essential meaning, character, or content; when details of wording or form are set aside.
column6: essentially, fundamentally, in essence, at bottom
column7: The two proposals differ in wording but are the same in substance. / In substance, her argument has not changed.
column8: Normalize from 'in the substance'. The idiomatic expression for this meaning is usually 'in substance'. 'Substance' can separately mean the material/content of something, as in 'the substance of the report'.

column7: The crowd grew restive as the wait dragged on.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Preserve the core sense; add the most natural collocations/patterns, register and close contrasts where useful, plus at least one natural real-world example if the current example is too narrow.

column5: difficult to control or manage; disorderly
column7: The teacher struggled to calm the unruly students.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Preserve the core sense; add the most natural collocations/patterns, register and close contrasts where useful, plus at least one natural real-world example if the current example is too narrow.

column7: She came up with an ingenious solution to the problem.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Preserve the core sense; add the most natural collocations/patterns, register and close contrasts where useful, plus at least one natural real-world example if the current example is too narrow.

column5: arranged or organized to work well together
column7: The team executed a highly coordinated attack.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Preserve the core sense; add the most natural collocations/patterns, register and close contrasts where useful, plus at least one natural real-world example if the current example is too narrow.

column2: fly a plane / fly an airplane
column5: To pilot or control an airplane in flight. The past participle is flown: 'I've flown a plane before.'
column6: pilot, fly; operate an aircraft (broader/more technical, not an exact everyday synonym)
column7: Have you ever flown a plane? / I've never flown a plane before. / She learned to fly a small airplane before moving on to larger aircraft.
column8: Use 'fly a plane', not *drive a plane*, for ordinary piloting. 'Operate an aircraft' is valid but broader and more technical: it can refer to managing/using the aircraft and its systems and procedures, not merely physically maneuvering it through the air. A pilot can also 'operate' controls or systems. Useful forms: fly–flew–flown.

column5: silly or pointless, often in a self-satisfied way
column7: His fatuous remarks annoyed everyone in the room.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Preserve the core sense; add the most natural collocations/patterns, register and close contrasts where useful, plus at least one natural real-world example if the current example is too narrow.

column2: demographic / demographics / demography / age group / age bracket
column5: demographic (n.): a segment of a population, often defined by age or another characteristic; demographic (adj.): relating to population characteristics. demographics: statistical characteristics of a population or audience. demography: the study of populations and how their size/structure change. age group: people grouped by age; age bracket: a defined age range.
column6: population segment, target group, age group, age bracket; population characteristics
column7: Marketers often tailor ads to the 18–35 demographic. / People in the 18–35 age group were most likely to buy the product. / The survey divides respondents into several age brackets. / The demographics of the neighborhood have changed considerably. / Demography examines population structure and change, including age, births, deaths, and migration.
column8: Replace unnatural 'demographic age'. Demographics may include age, sex/gender, income, education, race/ethnicity, location, household characteristics, etc., depending on context. 'Age demographic' is possible for a segment defined by age, but 'the 18–35 demographic', 'age group', or 'age bracket' is often more natural. 'Demographic data/trends/change' use demographic adjectivally.

column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize singular paean / plural paeans; praise/tribute sense, often 'a paean to X'. Remove implication it must literally be sung.

column5: A high-school class or course in the U.S. Advanced Placement (AP) program, designed to offer college-level study and often prepare students for an AP exam.
column7: I'm taking three AP classes this year. / She took AP Biology and AP U.S. History in high school.
column8: Capitalize AP. An AP class is the course itself, not 'a class of students'. AP exams are separate standardized exams associated with AP subjects.

column5: The action or process of dividing into separate and often opposing groups.
column7: The polarization of opinions in politics has grown in recent years.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add political/social polarization, polarized/polarizing; 'polarization between groups/on an issue'; distinguish disagreement from entrenched division.

column5: A direct, blunt, or unembellished statement.
column7: His blunt statement offended many people in the room.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Consider headword blunt / bluntly rather than compositional 'blunt statement'; show blunt answer/comment/assessment and nuance direct vs tactless.

column5: An indirect or subtle reference, often negative or suggestive.
column7: His comments were full of innuendo about her personal life.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add sexual innuendo, innuendo about, by innuendo; distinguish insinuation and euphemism.

column5: To criticize or belittle someone or something.
column7: He was quick to put down anyone who disagreed with him.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Deepen put someone down (belittle), put something down (place/write/pay deposit/euthanize animal); if card is only insult sense, label clearly and cross-reference noun put-down.

column5: Language used to obscure or mislead, especially in politics or business.
column7: The politician's doublespeak made it hard to understand his true intentions.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add Orwellian/business euphemistic language nuance; distinguish doublespeak from double-talk and doublethink.

column5: A noticeable, important, and often unfair difference or inequality between people, groups, outcomes, or conditions.
column7: The report highlights racial disparities in health outcomes. / There is a large disparity between urban and rural incomes.
column8: Merge plural WID414 and singular WID415 into one productive card. Common patterns: disparity between A and B; disparity in income/outcomes/access; economic/health/racial disparities.

column5: Consequences or outcomes, especially negative ones.
column7: The repercussions of his actions were felt by everyone in the company.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add 'repercussions for/from', usually negative and often delayed/ripple effects; distinguish consequences (neutral).

column5: To the extent or degree that something is true or applicable.
column6: to the extent, as far as
column7: This argument is valid insofar as it applies to the current situation.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize 'insofar as' as full conjunction; 'insofar' alone is incomplete in most learner contexts. Also 'in so far as' variant.

column5: To set people, groups, ideas, or competitors against one another so that they compete, fight, or are compared as opponents.
column6: set against, turn against, make compete, play off against
column7: The format pits two teams against each other. / The policy risks pitting younger workers against older ones. / The article pits tradition against innovation.
column8: Normalize away from unnatural 'pit each other'. Core construction: pit A against B. Reciprocal: be pitted against each other.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::business topic::workplace topic::sports topic::communication discovery::disagreement discovery::escalation

column5: A real bag designed with bold outlines, flat colors, and visual perspective so that it appears like a two-dimensional cartoon drawing. In other contexts, 'toon bag' can simply mean a bag featuring cartoon characters, so the intended meaning depends on context.
column6: cartoon bag, 2D bag, cartoon-illusion bag, pop-art bag (context-dependent)
column7: Her toon bag looked like a flat cartoon drawing until she opened it and put her laptop inside. / The shop sells brightly outlined cartoon bags that create a 2D illusion.
column8: KEEP, but replace the fabricated animation-studio definition. The useful fashion sense is a descriptive/informal label rather than one tightly standardized dictionary term; brands such as JumpFromPaper popularized the 2D/cartoon-illusion style. In other contexts 'toon bag' may refer generically to cartoon-character merchandise, and an isolated occurrence could also be a typo/mishearing of another bag term. Preserve context sensitivity.

column5: To give in to a force or overwhelming influence.
column7: He succumbed to the pressure and agreed to their terms.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize succumb/succumbed; patterns succumb to pressure/temptation/injuries/disease. Often implies inability to resist; with illness/injuries can mean die.

column5: Focused on utility or practicality, often at the expense of aesthetics.
column7: The utilitarian design of the building prioritized function over form.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Separate everyday utilitarian = practical/function-first from philosophical Utilitarian/utilitarianism; capitalization/context.

column5: A contradiction in terms, combining two seemingly opposite ideas.
column7: The phrase 'jumbo shrimp' is an example of an oxymoronic expression.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Teach oxymoron/oxymoronic; distinguish paradox and contradiction; 'deafening silence' etc. are conventional examples.

column5: Too great to be overcome or dealt with.
column7: The mountain was insurmountable, and they turned back.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add insurmountable obstacle/problem/difficulty/odds; not literally 'unbeatable' in all contexts.

column5: The quality of being self-important or arrogantly assertive.
column7: His bumptiousness made him unpopular among his colleagues.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Rare/formal word; teach bumptious/bumptiousness with register note. Synonyms pushy, self-important, officious depending context.

column5: To officially declare someone or something as sacred or worthy of honor.
column7: The church decided to canonize the bishop for his devotion to the faith.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Cover Catholic/Orthodox formal saint declaration plus figurative canonize a cultural figure/work; distinguish canon/canonical.

column5: temper (v.): to moderate, soften, or balance something by adding a counteracting influence. tempered (adj.): moderated or restrained. In 'tempered glass', tempered means specially heat- or chemically-treated to increase strength and safety.
column6: moderate, soften, mitigate, restrain, balance; toughened (glass)
column7: Her optimism was tempered by caution. / The criticism was tempered with praise. / The door is made of tempered glass.
column8: Fix definition/example mismatch. 'Tempered glass' is a technical material sense, not simply 'moderated glass'. Common pattern: temper A with B / be tempered by B.
column12: entry::collocation entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical usage::softening discovery::containment discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To form or shape in a flawed or improper way.
column7: The artist misshapes the clay into abstract figures.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize misshape/misshapen. 'misshapes' is uncommon retrieval form; useful adjective misshapen likely higher value.

column5: Departing from what is normal, typical, expected, or accepted.
column7: The researchers treated the result as an aberrant data point. / His behavior that night was highly aberrant.
column8: Replace rare/nonstandard-looking 'aberrated' adjective with productive modern 'aberrant'. Related noun: aberration. Avoid 'deviant' as a blanket synonym when it adds moral/social judgment.

column5: Mentally unstable or insane.
column7: The demented man wandered the streets, confused and lost.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Update usage: demented can mean wildly irrational/crazy informally but referring to a person with dementia as 'demented' is dated/insensitive. Add figurative 'demented plan/laugh' with register caution.

column5: Extreme greed or selfishness.
column7: His avarice led him to make unethical decisions in business.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add avaricious; literary/formal stronger greed, especially wealth/money.

column5: To avoid or deliberately abstain from.
column7: She was eschewing the traditional path to follow her own dreams.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize eschew; transitive without 'from': eschew tradition/alcohol/violence. Formal/literary.

column5: A deep feeling of anxiety or dread.
column7: The film's themes of existential angst resonated with many viewers.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add existential/teenage angst; borrowed German but ordinary English; distinguish anxiety (clinical/general) from angst (brooding unease).

column5: Relating to or emphasizing individual elements over the whole.
column7: The atomistic approach broke the issue into smaller, manageable parts.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Explain technical/philosophical/social-science use: treating entities as independent units rather than relations/whole; contrast holistic/systemic.

column5: The geological epoch marking the last ice age, around 2.6 million years ago.
column7: The Pleistocene epoch was marked by the last ice age.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Correct geological precision: Pleistocene ~2.58 million to 11,700 years ago; not simply 'the last ice age'. Mention epoch capitalization.

column5: To become agitated or upset.
column7: She was so worked up about the situation that she could hardly think straight.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize get/be worked up about/over; emotionally agitated/excited, often negative. Also 'work someone up'.

column5: To lose control of one's temper and behave violently or irrationally.
column7: He went berserk when he found out what had happened.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add go berserk over/when; strong informal expression for losing control, not necessarily literal violence.

column5: A market selling fresh food, particularly meat, fish, and produce.
column7: The wet market was bustling with vendors selling fresh fish and produce.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Clarify wet market = market selling fresh meat/fish/produce and other perishables, historically contrasted with dry goods; not inherently exotic or unsanitary.

column5: Subject to decay or spoilage, especially in a short period of time.
column7: Milk is a perishable item that needs to be refrigerated.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add perishable goods/food; noun plural perishables; contrast nonperishable/shelf-stable.

column5: About to happen; forthcoming.
column7: The storm's imminent arrival caused panic in the coastal towns.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add imminent danger/arrival/collapse; distinguish eminent/immanent. Forthcoming is not always imminent.

column5: To assume or assert the existence or truth of something. to put forward as a fact or as a basis for argument
column6: assert, propose, suggest, hypothesize, postulate, presuppose
column7: He posited that the data would support his hypothesis. The theory posits that all matter is composed of tiny particles.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Already relatively strong; add formal/academic register and posit X / posit that; distinguish hypothesize/postulate/assume.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::academic usage::rhetorical discovery::assertion discovery::suggestion discovery::speculation discovery::academic_discussion discovery::debate_language

column5: Relating to or owned by a specific individual or company, often legally protected.
column7: The proprietary technology gave the company a competitive edge.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add proprietary software/data/formula/technology and ownership sense; distinguish confidential/trade secret/open-source.

column5: The state or quality of being proper, correct, or acceptable.
column7: She acted with propriety during the formal event.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add propriety of doing something, sense of propriety; distinguish proprietary (common confusable).

column5: Behavior that is appropriate or conforming to established conventions.
column7: He maintained a sense of decorum even in stressful situations.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add maintain/observe decorum, breach/lack of decorum; formal social behavior, not exactly etiquette.

column5: To be relevant or related to something.
column7: The details pertain to the original agreement.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add pertain to only; formal. Distinguish appertain if useful, and 'pertinent' adjective.

column5: The end or death of something, especially life or a system.
column7: The demise of the company was due to poor management.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add demise of person/company/system; formal/euphemistic for death; verb demise is specialized and not needed.

column5: Having a cheerful, energetic, or optimistic attitude.
column7: She was bright eyed and bushy tailed, ready to start the day.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize hyphens 'bright-eyed and bushy-tailed'; cheerful, alert, eager, often humorous/ironic especially early morning.

column5: Hidden or small, often in places that are hard to find or reach.
column7: The old house was full of nooks and crannies, hiding all sorts of treasures.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add every nook and cranny / search the nooks and crannies; small recesses/corners, often figurative exhaustive search.

column5: A long, formal written work, usually for an academic degree.
column7: She wrote a dissertation on modern architecture for her PhD.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Distinguish dissertation vs thesis across US/UK academic usage; PhD dissertation (US) vs thesis terminology varies.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::academic usage::specialist topic::work discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::academic_discussion

column5: In a childish or sulky manner, often in response to something unfair.
column7: He petulantly stomped out of the room after hearing the news.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize petulant/petulantly; childishly sulky/irritable especially when thwarted; add petulant tone/response.

column5: To congratulate or wish success to someone.
column7: I want to felicitate you on your recent success.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Rare/formal and much more common in Indian English/formal registers than everyday AmE/BrE; ordinary choice congratulate.

column5: verb: to support, strengthen, or reinforce an argument, structure, position, or system. noun: a projecting support built against a wall; figuratively, a source of support.
column6: support, reinforce, strengthen, bolster, shore up
column7: The new evidence buttressed her argument. / Additional beams were added to buttress the wall. / Flying buttresses support the cathedral walls.
column8: Current POS says noun while definition/example use the verb. Teach both. Figurative verb 'buttress an argument/claim' is especially useful.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::figurative_extension discovery::support discovery::debate_language

column5: To prove something to be false or incorrect.
column7: She refuted all the claims made against her.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Refute means show/prove claim false, not merely deny/contradict. Add refute claim/argument/allegation; distinguish rebut and deny.

column5: To perceive or recognize something clearly.
column7: He could discern the truth in her eyes.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add discern difference/pattern/meaning; discern A from B; formal, often difficult-to-perceive nuance; discerning adjective separate sense.

column5: Beginning to develop or exist; at an early stage, often before becoming fully formed or obvious.
column7: Doctors detected signs of incipient disease. / The government moved quickly to contain the incipient rebellion.
column8: Correct typo 'incipitent' → incipient. Common collocations: incipient disease, crisis, movement, rebellion, change.

column5: A refusal to accept, acknowledge, believe, or admit something; also a statement that something is not true. In psychology, denial can refer to avoiding an uncomfortable reality.
column7: He issued a firm denial of the allegations. / She was still in denial about how serious the problem had become.
column8: Remove obsolete note '(duplicate of #456)' because WID456 is absent. Useful patterns: denial of allegations/facts; be in denial; deny wrongdoing.

column5: Not justified or authorized by the circumstances.
column7: The unwarranted criticism was hurtful and unnecessary.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add unwarranted assumption/attack/intrusion/confidence; unjustified, not necessarily unauthorized.

column5: The deliberate refusal or restriction of one's own desires, pleasures, or comforts, often for moral, religious, practical, or disciplinary reasons.
column7: Saving that much money required years of self-denial. / The tradition emphasizes fasting and self-denial.
column8: Standard spelling is usually self-denial. Distinguish from denial of one's identity/feelings and from healthy self-control; context determines whether self-denial is praised or criticized.

column2: hold someone accountable for something / hold someone to something
column5: hold someone accountable for something: require them to accept responsibility for an action, decision, or outcome. hold someone to something: insist that they keep a promise, agreement, standard, or stated position.
column6: hold responsible, answer for; enforce, insist on, bind to
column7: We need to hold officials accountable for their decisions. / You said you'd finish by Friday, and I'm going to hold you to it. / The company should be held to the same standards as its competitors.
column8: Split the two constructions because 'accountable to' and 'hold someone to' are not interchangeable. A person can also be accountable to a boss/body (= answerable to them).
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::debate-friendly topic::decision-making topic::debate discovery::agreement discovery::evaluation discovery::debate_language

column5: To formally give up a position of power or responsibility.
column7: The king decided to abdicate the throne after much pressure.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add abdicate throne + abdicate responsibility; formal; distinguish resign, renounce, relinquish.

column5: Designed to work without depending on one particular model, algorithm, architecture, or implementation. In machine learning, a model-agnostic method can be applied across different models rather than being tied to one specific model type.
column7: Permutation feature importance is often described as model-agnostic because it can be applied to many different fitted models. / We wanted an algorithm-agnostic evaluation framework.
column8: Redesign vague 'agnostic approach in machine learning'. In technical compounds, -agnostic means 'not tied to / independent of a particular X', not 'open-minded'. The exact compound should match what is being abstracted away: model-agnostic, framework-agnostic, platform-agnostic, etc.
column12: entry::adjective_phrase usage::technical topic::work topic::technology topic::architecture discovery::implementation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The ability to move quickly and easily.
column7: Her agility on the dance floor impressed everyone at the competition.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Expand physical agility + mental/business/organizational agility; agile/agility; distinguish dexterity.

column5: Describes a process or method that is done repeatedly or in cycles.
column7: The iterative approach ensured that improvements were made after each cycle.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add iterate/iteration/iteratively; iterative design/process/development; distinguish repetitive (can imply mere repetition without learning).

column5: Belonging naturally; essential or inherent.
column7: The intrinsic value of the art lies in its cultural significance.
column8: KEEP as a distinct usage-profile card. Deepen intrinsic around intrinsic value/motivation/property and the sense of belonging to the essential nature of something or arising from within. Cross-reference WID480 inherent, but do not merge merely because meanings overlap.

column5: A person who opposes, distrusts, or is reluctant to adopt new technology or technological change; historically, a member of the early-19th-century English Luddite movement.
column7: I'm not a Luddite, but I don't need every appliance in my house connected to the internet. / He jokingly calls himself a Luddite because he still uses a flip phone.
column8: Correct typo 'lludite' → Luddite. Capitalized from the historical Luddites. Modern use is often humorous or critical and can oversimplify the historical movement; it does not simply mean 'old/outdated'.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::humorous usage::critical topic::technology topic::history

column5: Describes the phase of the moon when more than half of it is illuminated.
column7: The moon appeared gibbous, almost full but not quite.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Correct moon terminology: waxing gibbous vs waning gibbous; more than half illuminated but less than full. 'luminous/crescent' are not synonyms.

column5: To make a facial expression indicating displeasure or disapproval.
column7: He scowled at the proposal, clearly displeased with the idea.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add scowl at someone / scowl in disapproval; noun a scowl; stronger/darker than frown.

column5: To come together or assemble, typically for a formal meeting.
column7: The committee will convene tomorrow to discuss the new policies.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Transitive and intransitive: convene a meeting/committee; committee convenes. Formal/institutional.

column5: Fairness or justice in the way people are treated or resources/opportunities are distributed, often taking differing needs or circumstances into account. Also has important legal/financial senses.
column7: The program aims to improve equity in access to healthcare. / The company has $2 million in shareholders' equity. / She built substantial equity in her home.
column8: Keep separate because equity has major finance/legal senses beyond the social-policy contrast with equality. Cross-reference WID475 for equity vs. equality.

column5: The state of being equal in status, rights, opportunities, treatment, quantity, or value.
column6: equal status, parity, equal treatment, equivalence (context-dependent)
column7: The law guarantees equality before the law. / The organization campaigns for gender equality. / Equality of opportunity does not necessarily produce equality of outcome.
column8: Keep as a productive standalone concept. Cross-reference WID475; do not define equality merely as 'uniformity'.

column5: Equality generally focuses on people having equal status, rights, opportunities, treatment, or shares; equity focuses on fairness and may take different needs or starting conditions into account. The contrast is context-dependent, and the words are not simple opposites.
column6: equal treatment vs. fairness; parity vs. needs-sensitive fairness
column7: Giving every student the same device is an equality-based approach; providing additional accessibility tools to students who need them is an equity-based measure. / The debate involves both equality of opportunity and equity in access.
column8: Keep as comparison card because it teaches selection between two highly confusable words. Avoid oversimplified meme-style formulas such as 'equality = same, equity = fair' as universal definitions. Equity also has finance/legal senses not covered by this contrast.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::academic usage::debate-friendly topic::education topic::workplace topic::law topic::medicine topic::language_learning topic::health discovery::evaluation discovery::comparison discovery::contrast discovery::academic_discussion discovery::debate_language

column5: To have doubts, concerns, or misgivings about a plan, idea, person, or course of action.
column6: have doubts, have concerns, have misgivings, be hesitant about
column7: I have some reservations about signing a five-year contract. / She had serious reservations about the proposal but agreed to hear them out.
column8: Usually plural reservations in this sense: have reservations about something. Singular 'a reservation' more often means a booking or a specific reserved condition/right, though 'I have one reservation' can mean one specific concern.

column5: To tremble or shake, often due to fear or anxiety.
column7: The ground was quaking as the earthquake hit the city.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize quake/quaking; physical shaking, ground quake, quake with fear; distinguish quiver/tremble.

column5: A god or goddess, especially in a polytheistic religion.
column7: The deity of the sun was worshipped by the ancient civilization.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add deity vs god/goddess/divinity; deity can be gender-neutral and formal; 'a deity associated with the sun'.

column5: directive (n.): an official instruction or order. directive (adj.): intended to direct, guide, or control. In linguistics/pragmatics, a directive is an utterance intended to get someone to do something.
column6: instruction, order, command, mandate, guideline (depending force)
column7: The agency issued a directive requiring new safety checks. / 'Please close the door' can function as a directive even though it is phrased politely.
column8: Replace broken headword 'directive mean'. If original intent was 'What does directive mean?', the vocabulary item should simply be directive. Distinguish binding directives/orders from softer guidance.

column5: Belonging naturally; essential or inherent.
column7: Trust and compassion are inherent qualities of a good leader.
column8: KEEP as a distinct usage-profile card. Deepen inherent around 'inherent in', inherent risk/problem/limitation/quality: a feature inseparable from or characteristic of something. Cross-reference WID468 intrinsic and teach the selection contrast rather than merging on semantic similarity alone.

column5: A difficult or confusing problem or question.
column7: The conundrum of the puzzle baffled the team for hours.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Fix circular example 'conundrum of the puzzle'; difficult problem/dilemma, sometimes riddle historically. Add pose/face/solve a conundrum.

column5: A piece of land used for grazing or farming animals.
column7: The cows were grazing peacefully in the lush pasture.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add pasture vs meadow/field; grazing land; put/turn animals out to pasture; figurative 'put out to pasture' if useful.

column5: To feed on grass or other vegetation, typically by animals.
column6: feed, pasture; scrape, brush, skim (contact sense)
column7: Sheep grazed on the hillside all afternoon. / The bullet grazed his shoulder without causing a serious wound. / My bag grazed the wall as I squeezed past.
column8: Two major verb senses: animals feed on growing vegetation; something lightly touches/scrapes a surface or skin. The feeding sense is especially common with cattle/sheep; the contact sense often implies only slight damage. | Depth-pass guidance: Already enriched in earlier merge; KEEP unless later duplicate reconciliation finds another graze card.

column5: Covered in rich, green vegetation, or growing abundantly.
column7: The lush green landscape was breathtaking after the rain.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add lush vegetation/landscape + rich/luxurious 'lush production' and informal lush hair; avoid overexpanding noun 'lush' unless useful.

column4: contextual noun phrase; related idiom / pronoun usage
column5: A context-dependent phrase whose interpretation comes from 'one' plus its modifiers. It can mean a big, fast instance of a previously mentioned countable thing ('a big, fast one' = e.g. a big, fast car); in context it can refer to a notably fast case, process, approval, application, or other event under discussion ('this/that one was fast'); and it should also be learned alongside the separate idiom 'a fast one / pull a fast one', meaning a trick or deception.
column6: a big/fast case or instance (context-dependent); a fast one / pull a fast one = trick, deception, con
column7: Let's buy a new car. — Yeah, a big, fast one! / Wow, this one was fast. / That was a really big, fast one, huh? / That I-485 approval was incredibly fast—this one moved unusually quickly. / Don't let them pull a fast one on you.
column8: KEEP the original headword 'big fast one'; do not collapse it into a single interpretation. Usage cluster 1: one/ones substitution—'a big, fast one' can replace a previously mentioned countable noun such as car. Usage cluster 2: contextual one = the case/process/application/event currently under discussion; fast describes unusually quick completion or processing. Preserve the immigration/I-485-type context supplied by Jin as an example of this contextual reading: an unusually fast approval/application case can be described conversationally with 'this/that one was fast' or a modified 'fast one'. Do not claim 'big fast one' is an official USCIS term or a fixed immigration idiom. Usage cluster 3: separately, 'a fast one / pull a fast one on someone' is an established informal idiom meaning a trick/deception; 'big' can contextually intensify the scale. Punctuation depends on structure: 'a big, fast one' naturally coordinates adjectives modifying one.
column12: entry::idiom entry::noun_phrase usage::informal topic::automotive discovery::process_details discovery::social_approval

column5: Peasants or laborers who are bound to the land and work for a feudal lord.
column7: The serfs worked the land for the lord, never owning anything themselves.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize serf/serfs/serfdom; tied to land under feudal system, not simply any peasant/laborer.

column5: Burdening or causing difficulty, especially in terms of obligations or tasks.
column7: The onerous task of cleaning the entire building took all day.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add onerous burden/task/requirement/obligation; formal, burdensome because demanding, costly, or restrictive.

column5: A chemical compound used as a herbicide to kill weeds.
column7: Glyphosate is widely used in agriculture to control weeds.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Capitalize generically as glyphosate unless sentence-initial; define herbicide, not pesticide synonym exactly. Avoid safety claims beyond vocabulary scope.

column5: A chemical substance used to kill unwanted plants (weeds).
column7: Herbicide is sprayed on fields to prevent the growth of weeds.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Herbicide is a type of pesticide targeting plants; weedkiller informal. Add herbicidal.

column5: To give a name or label to someone or something.
column7: She was dubbed 'The Queen of the Day' for her excellent performance.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Expand dub someone/something X = give nickname/title; dub a film = replace dialogue with translated/other-language audio; distinguish subtitle.

column5: Greatly desired or in high demand.
column7: She's one of the most sought-after designers in the industry. / Apartments in that neighborhood are highly sought after.
column8: Use hyphen before a noun: a sought-after expert/product. Usually no hyphen after a linking verb: the tickets are highly sought after.

column5: To be drooling or showing excessive interest in something, usually in anticipation.
column7: The dog was salivating at the sight of the food.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize salivate/salivating; literal produce saliva + figurative salivate over/at prospect = eager/desirous, often humorous.

column5: Ordinary, not special or unique.
column7: The restaurant was run of the mill; nothing special, just basic food.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Hyphenate attributive/adjectival idiom 'run-of-the-mill'; ordinary/unexceptional; examples before noun and predicate.

column5: To gather people, animals, or things together; to find and collect what is needed. Also, in mathematics, to increase a number to the next specified place/value.
column7: Can you round up everyone for a quick meeting? / I need to round up the receipts before I file the claim. / Round 3.76 up to the nearest tenth.
column8: Fix POS from noun to phrasal verb. Noun is 'roundup/round-up' depending sense/style, e.g. a news roundup. Be cautious with law-enforcement 'round up people', which can sound coercive.

column5: Diseases or health conditions, often used in a general sense.
column7: The doctor treated several maladies, including a persistent cough and fever.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Normalize malady/maladies; somewhat formal/old-fashioned for illness/problem; figurative social/economic maladies.

column5: To attribute an event, result, or situation to a particular cause or explanation, often casually or provisionally.
column6: attribute to, put down to, ascribe to, blame on (negative contexts)
column7: I chalked the mistake up to inexperience. / Let's chalk it up to bad luck and move on.
column8: Normalize to the productive construction 'chalk it up to X'. Existing related cards should be checked during later global duplicate reconciliation; this WID is currently useful as the early canonical card in this range.

column5: Describing a position or movement that opposes abortion and generally supports legal protections for fetuses/unborn life; terminology is politically contested and may be self-identifying.
column6: anti-abortion (more descriptive in some contexts), abortion-opposing
column7: She describes herself as pro-life. / The bill drew support from several pro-life organizations.
column8: Use neutral descriptive framing. 'Pro-birth' is usually a critical label, not a neutral synonym, so remove it from synonyms. Cross-reference pro-choice WID311. Exact policy positions vary among people/groups using either label.
column12: entry::word usage::critical usage::specialist usage::debate-friendly topic::law topic::politics topic::debate discovery::terminology discovery::debate_language discovery::public_discourse discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Having a negative effect, harmful, or unfavorable.
column7: The adverse effects of the drug became evident after a few weeks.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add adverse effect/reaction/conditions/weather; distinguish averse (to) and adversity.

column5: To plot or scheme, usually with others, to achieve something secretly or illegally.
column7: They conspired to create a plan that would help them achieve their goal.
column8: Depth-pass guidance: Add conspire with someone to do / conspire against; also events/circumstances conspire to produce outcome (figurative, no secret plot).

column5: A situation in which two separate problems, disadvantages, or blows occur together or in close succession, making the overall effect worse.
column6: double blow, two setbacks at once, one-two punch (context-dependent)
column7: Losing my job and then having my rent raised was a double whammy. / The business was hit by the double whammy of rising costs and falling demand.
column8: Usually negative. Common pattern: the double whammy of A and B / be hit by a double whammy. It can also be used more loosely for two simultaneous strong effects.

column5: Having two parts, aspects, or purposes; or by a factor of two / to twice the degree.
column6: dual, two-part, two-pronged; twice, two times (adverbial sense)
column7: The benefit is twofold: it saves time and reduces costs. / Sales increased twofold over the decade.
column8: Very common pattern: 'The reason/benefit/problem is twofold: ...'. Distinguish 'twofold' = two aspects or twice as much from 'double' in constructions where only one is idiomatic.

column5: Very common, widespread, or abundant, especially something undesirable.
column7: The industry was rife with rumors. / The report found a system rife with corruption.
column8: Usually predicative and followed by with: be rife with rumors/corruption/speculation. Often negative. 'Rampant' is close but not interchangeable everywhere.

column5: 1) A conclusion reached by reasoning from evidence or premises. 2) The process of deductive reasoning. 3) An amount subtracted, especially from pay, tax, or a total.
column6: inference, conclusion; subtraction, reduction, allowance (financial contexts)
column7: From those clues, she made a reasonable deduction. / Taxes and other deductions are taken from my paycheck.
column8: Important polysemy: reasoning vs subtraction/financial deduction. Cross-reference deduct/deductive. 'Inference' is broader than deduction.

column5: Seeming reasonable, believable, or possible, especially on the basis of available facts, even if not proven true.
column7: That's a plausible explanation, but we still need evidence. / The ending felt plausible given what the character had been through.
column8: Plausible ≠ proven or necessarily likely. A story/explanation can be plausible yet false. Common: plausible explanation/scenario/argument.

column5: The act or amount of spending money, time, energy, or other resources; in finance, an amount spent.
column7: The company cut capital expenditure this year. / The trip required a considerable expenditure of time and money.
column8: Formal. Countable for specific amounts/items; uncountable for the act of spending. Common: government/public/capital expenditure; expenditure on X; expenditure of time/energy.

column5: In a clear, direct, and unambiguous way; stated rather than merely implied.
column7: The rules explicitly prohibit outside food. / She never explicitly said no, but her meaning was obvious.
column8: Contrast explicitly with implicitly. 'Expressly' often means specifically and deliberately stated.

column5: Not showing good judgment about risks or consequences; unwise or inadvisable.
column7: It would be imprudent to spend all our savings at once. / The company made an imprudent investment.
column8: Formal. Stronger and more judgment-oriented than merely careless. Direct contrast with prudent.

column5: Showing careful, sensible judgment, especially by considering future risks and consequences.
column7: It would be prudent to keep an emergency fund. / She took the prudent step of getting a second opinion.
column8: Often used for risk/finance/decisions: prudent decision, prudent investment, prudent to do. Contrast imprudent; prudent does not simply mean timid/cautious.

column5: slash (v.): to cut violently or deeply; to reduce something sharply; to strike with a sweeping cutting motion. slashing (adj.): cutting or sharply forceful; also used in compounds such as slashing attack.
column7: The company slashed prices by 30%. / He slashed the rope with a knife. / The budget faces another round of slashing cuts.
column8: Redesign because current 'slashing winds' example is unnatural for the intended lexical core. High-value figurative use: slash prices/costs/jobs/budgets. Related noun: slash.

column5: To perceive, detect, recognize, or distinguish something, especially when it is subtle, unclear, or difficult to notice.
column6: perceive, detect, recognize, distinguish, make out, identify
column7: I could barely discern a figure in the fog. / She quickly discerned a pattern in the data. / It's difficult to discern what he really wants from that answer.
column8: KEEP as the productive verb entry. Core patterns: discern something; discern A from B; discern that...; discern a pattern/difference/meaning. Do not merge merely because WID454 also contains discern-related material. Master-wide principle approved by Jin: discern and discerning should both exist as distinct, depth-rich learning entries. 'Discerning' should focus on good judgment/taste and the ability to notice subtle quality differences, while 'discern' focuses on the act of perceiving/distinguishing.

column5: To gradually accept and learn to deal with a difficult, painful, or unwanted reality.
column6: accept, reconcile oneself to, make peace with, adjust to
column7: It took him years to come to terms with the loss. / I'm still coming to terms with the fact that the project is over.
column8: Current card confuses this with 'come to terms' = reach an agreement. Keep the 'accept a difficult reality' idiom as headword. Separately, 'come to terms (with someone)' can mean reach agreement, but the constructions differ.

column5: To force or pressure someone into doing something by threats, intimidation, manipulation, or other strong pressure.
column7: They coerced him into signing the document. / She said the confession had been coerced.
column8: Normalize to coerce / coerced. Core pattern: coerce someone into doing something. Stronger than persuade or pressure; often implies lack of genuine consent.

column5: Excessively eager to obey, flatter, or please someone more powerful, usually in a way that seems servile or insincere.
column6: servile, fawning, sycophantic, ingratiating, deferential (too weak in some contexts)
column7: The waiter was almost comically obsequious toward the celebrity. / His obsequious praise made everyone uncomfortable.
column8: Build contrast cluster with servile, sycophantic, fawning: obsequious emphasizes excessive submissive attentiveness toward a superior.

column5: Excessively submissive or willing to obey and serve others, especially in a degrading or self-abasing way.
column7: He adopted a servile tone whenever the director entered the room. / The novel rejects blind, servile obedience.
column8: Not a synonym of itself. Compared with obsequious, servile emphasizes low/subordinate submissiveness; compared with sycophantic, it need not imply strategic flattery for gain.

column5: Excessively flattering or praising someone powerful in order to gain advantage or favor.
column7: The interview was so sycophantic that no difficult questions were asked. / He surrounded himself with sycophantic advisers.
column8: Emphasizes self-interested flattery toward power. Related noun: sycophant. Contrast servile = submissive; fawning = excessive display of admiration/affection.

column5: To give someone excessive, often insincere attention, praise, or affection in order to please or impress them.
column6: flatter, gush over, ingratiate oneself with, suck up to (informal)
column7: Everyone was fawning over the famous actor. / He fawned on the boss all evening.
column8: Normalize from adjective 'fawning' to productive verb pattern. Fawning can be adjective: fawning praise. Contrast sycophantic (motive of gaining favor) and obsequious (submissive manner).

column5: Literally, to cut and gather a crop; figuratively, to receive a result, reward, or consequence produced by earlier actions.
column7: Farmers reap the wheat in late summer. / Years of training finally allowed her to reap the benefits. / He reaped the consequences of his own decisions.
column8: Common figurative collocations: reap the benefits/rewards/profits; reap what you sow. Not all outcomes are positive.

column5: noun: a winner in a competition, or a strong advocate/supporter of a cause. verb: to actively support, defend, or promote a person, idea, or cause.
column6: winner, titleholder; advocate, defender, supporter; promote, support, defend
column7: She became world champion at 19. / He has long been a champion of free speech. / The organization champions accessible design.
column8: Major missing verb/advocate sense. 'Champion of X' and 'champion a cause/idea' are highly productive.
column12: entry::word usage::persuasive discovery::advocacy discovery::promotion discovery::support discovery::persuasion

column5: Containing a fault, weakness, defect, or error; imperfect in a way that may undermine quality or validity.
column7: The study was based on flawed assumptions. / He's a flawed but sympathetic character.
column8: Common with argument, logic, methodology, design, character. 'Faulty' often suits mechanisms/reasoning; 'flawed' can describe people/characters without meaning worthless.

column5: Expressing beliefs or principles as unquestionably true and refusing to seriously consider alternatives or evidence.
column7: He became dogmatic about his preferred teaching method. / The book is opinionated without being dogmatic.
column8: Usually negative. Related dogma/dogmatism. Stronger than merely confident or principled.

column5: A belief or idea accepted or considered as possibly true without firm proof; an assumption used as a basis for reasoning.
column7: The argument rests on the supposition that demand will remain stable. / That's only supposition; we don't know what happened.
column8: Formal. Compare conjecture: a conjecture is often a tentative conclusion/speculation formed from incomplete evidence; supposition emphasizes something supposed/assumed.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::rhetorical topic::research discovery::evidence discovery::possibility discovery::debate_language

column5: noun: an opinion or conclusion formed from incomplete evidence. verb: to form or express such a tentative conclusion.
column6: speculation, guess, hypothesis, supposition; speculate, surmise
column7: At this point, the cause is pure conjecture. / Historians have conjectured that the building was used for ceremonies.
column8: Often formal/academic. In mathematics, a conjecture is a proposition believed true but not yet proved. Distinguish from hypothesis depending field.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::academic usage::ceremonial usage::scientific topic::research discovery::evidence discovery::speculation discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::academic_discussion

column5: Directly relevant or applicable to the matter being considered.
column6: relevant, applicable, material, to the point
column7: Please include only information pertinent to the investigation. / She asked several pertinent questions.
column8: Common: pertinent to. Slightly formal. Cross-reference germane WID527; pertinent often means directly useful/relevant to the immediate matter.

column5: Closely and appropriately relevant to the subject being discussed or considered.
column7: That question isn't germane to the issue we're discussing. / The judge ruled that the evidence was germane to the case.
column8: Formal; normally germane to. Very close to pertinent, but often emphasizes relevance to the subject/topic. Keep both as a confusable pair rather than merge automatically.

column5: noun: an examination, trial, procedure, or challenge used to measure knowledge, ability, quality, condition, or truth. verb: to examine, measure, try, or challenge.
column6: exam, assessment, trial, check; examine, evaluate, try
column7: I have a math test tomorrow. / The lab tested the water for contaminants. / The crisis will test their leadership.
column8: Current card is too narrow. Add medical/lab/product/figurative senses and verb. Common patterns: test for, test whether, put to the test.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative topic::testing topic::assessment topic::courtroom topic::law discovery::process_details discovery::procedural_language discovery::evaluation

column5: A deep fissure or gorge; figuratively, a very large difference or division between people, groups, views, or conditions.
column6: gorge, abyss, ravine; gulf, divide, gap
column7: A narrow bridge crossed the chasm. / A political chasm has opened between the two groups.
column8: Figurative 'chasm between A and B' is common and high-value. Stronger/more dramatic than gap.

column5: Although; even though. Used to introduce a concessive phrase, adjective, adverb, or subordinate idea, often in formal writing.
column7: The room was small, albeit comfortable. / He agreed, albeit reluctantly.
column8: Fix example: 'Albeit challenging, the project...' is possible but less learner-friendly. Albeit often introduces a reduced phrase rather than a full finite clause: albeit slowly/expensive/with difficulty.

column5: The physical size, shape, layout, and configuration of a device or component, especially as constrained by a design standard.
column6: physical format, size and shape, hardware format
column7: The smaller form factor makes the laptop easier to carry. / ATX and Mini-ITX are different motherboard form factors.
column8: Technical term. Not just generic 'shape': often refers to standardized dimensions/layout or overall physical configuration.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::technical usage::specialist discovery::evaluation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: adjective: expressing contempt, disapproval, or a negative judgment. noun: a pejorative word or expression.
column7: The term can be pejorative in that context. / He rejected the label as a pejorative.
column8: Current definition says 'a word' while POS is adjective. Teach both adjective and noun. Contrast pejorative with slur: not every pejorative is a slur.
column12: entry::word usage::critical usage::derogatory usage::disparaging usage::evaluative discovery::evaluation

column5: A dated, insulting expression for a woman regarded as shamelessly bold, sexually improper, or socially brazen.
column7: In the old comedy, the scandalized aunt calls her a 'brazen hussy.'
column8: KEEP as a historical/literary insult, not a neutral description. 'Hussy' is dated and derogatory; using it seriously today can sound sexist or theatrical. Useful mainly for recognizing older dialogue.

column5: Bold and shameless, especially in openly doing something wrong, offensive, or audacious without embarrassment.
column7: It was a brazen attempt to cheat the system. / The thieves carried out the robbery in broad daylight with brazen confidence.
column8: Common: brazen lie/attack/theft/attempt. 'Bold' alone can be positive; brazen is usually disapproving.

column5: A comfortable, trusting, mutually understanding relationship that makes communication easy.
column6: connection, mutual understanding, affinity, good relationship
column7: She quickly established rapport with the students. / The interviewer built a good rapport with him.
column8: Usually uncountable: build/establish/develop rapport with someone; have a good rapport. Pronunciation is important: final t is silent.

column5: To believe or assume that someone or something is a particular person, thing, or type, sometimes mistakenly; also in 'take A for B' = mistake A for B.
column6: regard as, assume to be, mistake for
column7: I took him for a doctor because of the white coat. / Don't take my silence for agreement. / What do you take me for?
column8: Current example 'I take you for someone who...' is possible but not the most central pattern. Teach take A for B, take something for granted separately, and rhetorical 'What do you take me for?'

column5: adjective: suitable or proper for a particular situation. verb (formal): to take something for one's own use, often without permission; or to allocate money/resources for a purpose.
column6: suitable, fitting, proper; seize, commandeer; allocate
column7: Wear something appropriate for the interview. / The regime appropriated private property. / Congress appropriated funds for disaster relief.
column8: Major polysemy. Verb pronunciation/stress may differ in careful speech. Distinguish appropriate (suitable) from inappropriate and from cultural appropriation/appropriate funds.

column5: Relating to touch or the sense of touch; perceptible or designed to be experienced through physical contact.
column7: The controls provide tactile feedback when pressed. / I like the tactile feel of printed books. / The exhibit is highly tactile and encourages visitors to touch it.
