column8: 'Touchable/perceivable' are weak synonyms. Common: tactile sensation/feedback/experience/surface. Haptic is especially technical.

column5: A person who publicly supports, advocates, or argues in favor of an idea, policy, theory, or course of action.
column7: She's a leading proponent of nuclear energy. / Proponents argue that the reform will lower costs.
column8: Common: proponent of. Contrast opponent. Often used in balanced debate/reporting.
column12: entry::word usage::persuasive usage::debate-friendly discovery::advocacy discovery::policy_discussion discovery::persuasion discovery::debate_language

column5: Provided with openings, holes, windows, or perforations; used in architecture, anatomy, medicine, and technical design.
column7: The façade is heavily fenestrated. / The surgeon used a fenestrated drape with an opening over the operative site.
column8: Technical/formal. Related fenestration. In medicine/anatomy, a fenestration is an opening; 'fenestrated' does not necessarily mean literal glass windows.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::technical topic::medicine topic::anatomy topic::architecture topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To move repeatedly back and forth around a position; figuratively, to alternate between states, opinions, or values. Oscillating describes such repeated movement.
column7: The fan oscillates from side to side. / His mood oscillated between optimism and despair. / We bought an oscillating fan.
column8: Normalize to verb family. Distinguish oscillate (regular/repeated alternation) from fluctuate (irregular changes) and vacillate (indecision).
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::figurative_extension discovery::debate_language

column5: noun: an official request or demand for supplies, equipment, services, or action. verb: to formally request, obtain, or take something for official use.
column6: request, order, demand; commandeer (some verb contexts)
column7: Submit a purchase requisition before ordering the equipment. / The army requisitioned vehicles for emergency use.
column8: Formal/administrative. A requisition is not merely any request. Verb can imply official authority, especially requisition property/supplies.

column5: In a way that lacks order, planning, method, or care; randomly or irregularly.
column7: Boxes were piled haphazardly in the hallway. / The policy had been implemented haphazardly.
column8: Related adjective haphazard. 'Randomly' can be neutral/statistical; haphazardly usually suggests poor organization.

column5: Unpredictable, irregular, or inconsistent in movement, behavior, performance, or pattern.
column7: The car was moving erratically. / His attendance became increasingly erratic. / The stock has shown erratic price movements.
column8: Useful across behavior/motion/performance/data. Does not necessarily mean mentally unstable.

column5: To focus one's attention intensely or excessively on something; be fixated on = be unable or unwilling to stop focusing on it.
column6: obsess over, dwell on, become preoccupied with
column7: Don't fixate on one small mistake. / He became fixated on proving that he was right.
column8: Normalize grammar: current 'fixated' definition says 'to become'. Common construction be/get/become fixated on. Often negative, but intensity varies.

column5: The ability to judge, perceive, or distinguish things clearly and intelligently, especially subtle differences or what is good/appropriate.
column7: Choosing reliable sources requires discernment. / She showed excellent discernment in hiring the new manager.
column8: Related discern/discerning. Often implies good judgment, not merely perception. 'Discrimination' is a technical synonym only in the sense of distinguishing, and can mislead learners.
column12: entry::word usage::technical topic::courtroom topic::law discovery::perception discovery::evaluation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Difficult to find, catch, achieve, remember, define, or understand.
column6: hard to find, evasive, unattainable, hard to pin down
column7: The suspect remained elusive for months. / A simple solution has proved elusive. / The exact meaning of the phrase is elusive.
column8: Broad productive pattern: elusive goal/answer/quality/suspect. 'Evasive' usually describes deliberate avoidance, so not a general synonym.

column5: Very difficult or impossible to understand, interpret, or read, especially a person's expression, motives, or a complex mystery.
column7: She gave me an inscrutable look. / His motives remained inscrutable.
column8: Formal/literary. Stronger than merely unclear. Avoid stereotyped uses about ethnic groups/cultures.

column5: Shameful, dishonorable, or lacking glory, distinction, or success.
column7: The campaign came to an inglorious end. / After an inglorious defeat, the team returned home quietly.
column8: Common phrase: inglorious end/defeat. Can mean merely uncelebrated/undistinguished as well as disgraceful.

column5: Using indirect, secretive, or dishonest methods to achieve a goal; also following a winding or indirect route (less common literal sense).
column7: They used a devious scheme to hide the payments. / The path took a devious route through the hills.
column8: Usually negative for people/plans. 'Cunning' can be admiring or neutral; devious strongly suggests dishonesty or indirectness.

column5: A division or contrast between two categories or alternatives, especially when they are treated as sharply opposed.
column7: The debate creates a false dichotomy between security and privacy. / The book explores the dichotomy between public image and private life.
column8: High-value collocation: false dichotomy. A dichotomy need not mean the two things truly exhaust all possibilities; speakers often criticize an imposed binary.

column5: Unable to coexist, be combined, or work together successfully; mutually inconsistent or unsuitable.
column7: The software is incompatible with older devices. / Their goals turned out to be incompatible. / The two medications may be incompatible.
column8: Remove self-synonym. Common: incompatible with. Covers technology, goals, beliefs, people, substances.

column5: Past participle of work in certain formal/literary expressions, meaning made, created, shaped, or brought about; also used in fixed compounds such as wrought iron.
column7: The destruction wrought by the storm was enormous. / Years of neglect had wrought lasting damage. / The gate is made of wrought iron.
column8: Teach as irregular/historical form mainly surviving in formal 'damage/change wrought by X' and compounds. Not the ordinary past tense of work today (worked).

column5: Extremely bad, shocking, or morally disturbing.
column7: The conditions in the shelter were appalling. / He showed appalling judgment.
column8: Strong negative evaluation. Common: appalling conditions/behavior/lack of judgment. Related appall/appalled.

column5: Extremely bad, poor, or inadequate.
column7: The service was abysmal. / The team had an abysmal record last season.
column8: Often about quality/performance/conditions, not 'severe' generally. Stronger than poor; informal-to-neutral evaluative register.

column5: To irritate or make skin sore through rubbing; to rub against something; figuratively, to feel irritated or resentful under a restriction or situation.
column6: rub, irritate, abrade; resent, bridle at
column7: The backpack straps chafed my shoulders. / He chafed under the new restrictions.
column8: Important figurative pattern: chafe at/under restrictions, rules, authority. Related chafing.

column5: So abundant or enduring that it seems impossible to use up, exhaust, or deplete.
column7: She has an inexhaustible supply of energy. / His curiosity seems inexhaustible.
column8: Can be literal or figurative. Avoid asserting that a real-world resource is literally inexhaustible when 'renewable' or 'vast' is more accurate.

column5: A lively, exuberant enjoyment of life; a cheerful delight in living.
column6: zest for life, exuberance, love of life
column7: Her curiosity and joie de vivre were infectious. / Even in his eighties, he retained a remarkable joie de vivre.
column8: Correct form is joie de vivre, not 'joie vivre'. French borrowing used in English; pronunciation varies by speaker.

column5: Cheerful, lively enjoyment or festivity; brightness or merriment, often with a somewhat literary or old-fashioned tone.
column7: Music and laughter added to the gaiety of the evening. / The room was decorated with festive gaiety.
column8: Somewhat literary/old-fashioned in everyday AmE. Historical 'gay' senses are separate; do not assume modern sexual-orientation meaning from gaiety.

column5: Able to float or rise in a fluid; cheerful and optimistic; or strong/rising in economic or market contexts.
column7: The material is naturally buoyant. / She remained buoyant despite the setback. / Consumer demand has stayed buoyant.
column8: Three useful senses: physical buoyancy, mood/personality, economics/markets. Related buoyancy.

column5: Sensible, emotionally steady, and realistic; connected to practical reality. Also, depending context, prevented from flying/going out, or electrically connected to ground.
column7: Despite her success, she has stayed grounded. / Talking to old friends helps keep me grounded.
column8: Current emotional sense is good but broaden carefully. 'Grounded' has major unrelated senses: a grounded teenager, grounded aircraft, grounded electrical equipment.

column5: To obtain or acquire something, often with effort, planning, or special arrangements.
column7: She procured tickets at the last minute. / The hospital had difficulty procuring enough supplies.
column8: Formal. Common in procurement/business. In some legal contexts 'procure' can mean arrange or induce, so context matters.

column5: Impossible or very difficult to break; inviolable or not to be violated.
column7: The author describes the bond as infrangible. / They treated the principle as an infrangible rule.
column8: Rare word. Current example is possible but stiff. More useful for recognition than active everyday use. Distinguish intangible and infringe/infringement.

column5: A person's, animal's, or plant's offspring or descendants; figuratively, things produced by something.
column7: The stallion's progeny won several races. / Many of her artistic progeny adopted the same style.
column8: Formal. Often collective and can take singular or plural agreement depending style/context. Not limited to royal families.

column5: To officially cancel, withdraw, or make no longer valid a right, license, permission, law, offer, or decision.
column7: His driver's license was revoked. / The company revoked her access privileges.
column8: Usually formal/official. Common objects: license, permission, visa, access, offer. Distinguish rescind (contracts/decisions) and repeal (laws).

column5: A period, often about a year, taken between stages of education or before work to travel, work, volunteer, or pursue other experiences.
column7: She took a gap year before university and worked in Japan. / He's considering a gap year after graduation.
column8: Not necessarily exactly one calendar year. 'Sabbatical' is not a close synonym; sabbatical usually refers to an established leave from a job/academic post.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::academic usage::british_english topic::work topic::travel topic::education discovery::academic_discussion

column5: Experience gained directly through personal participation or observation rather than from another person's account.
column7: She has firsthand experience of the immigration process. / I know firsthand how difficult that exam can be.
column8: Standard modern spelling is usually firsthand in AmE; first-hand is common in BrE. Common: firsthand experience/knowledge/account; know/see firsthand.

column5: Connected spoken or written communication; discussion or debate about a subject; in linguistics/social theory, language and communication considered in a broader context.
column6: discussion, debate, communication, conversation; language use
column7: Public discourse around the issue has changed. / The course examines political discourse and media language.
column8: Broader and more formal than conversation. Can mean extended connected language in linguistics, or a body/mode of discussion in academic fields.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::conversational usage::academic usage::debate-friendly topic::communication topic::debate topic::linguistics discovery::debate_language discovery::academic_discussion

column5: A word or phrase that helps organize, connect, manage, or signal relationships in spoken or written discourse, often without contributing much propositional content.
column6: connector, pragmatic marker, linking expression (overlapping terms)
column7: Well, I think we should leave. / However, the results were different. / You know can function as a discourse marker in conversation.
column8: Examples include well, so, anyway, you know, I mean, however, therefore, depending framework. 'Connector' is only partial synonym; discourse markers also manage interaction, stance, topic shifts.

column2: get itchy feet / have itchy feet
column5: To become restless and strongly want to travel, move somewhere new, or change one's situation.
column6: feel restless, get wanderlust, want a change of scene
column7: After two years in the same city, I started getting itchy feet. / She always gets itchy feet after a few months at home.
column8: Especially common BrE but widely understood. Usually about travel/moving, sometimes broader restlessness. Do not confuse with literal itchy feet.

column5: A strong desire for exciting, unfamiliar, or challenging experiences.
column6: sense of adventure, wanderlust, craving for adventure
column7: His thirst for adventure took him across South America. / I still have a thirst for adventure, but I'm more careful now.
column8: Productive metaphor: thirst for knowledge/power/revenge/adventure. Useful to teach 'thirst for X' rather than only this fixed combination.

column5: The center of a target; figuratively, an exact or highly successful hit, answer, or assessment.
column6: center of the target, dead center; exact hit
column7: Her arrow landed in the bull's-eye. / Your diagnosis was right on the bullseye.
column8: Correct spelling from 'bulls eye'. Both bull's-eye and bullseye occur; style varies. Common: hit the bull's-eye; right on the bullseye.

column2: get a lemon / buy a lemon
column5: To end up with a defective or unsatisfactory product, especially a car; a lemon is something that proves faulty or disappointing.
column6: get a dud, buy a defective product, end up with a dud
column7: The used car looked great, but I realized I'd bought a lemon. / If the laptop keeps failing, you may have gotten a lemon.
column8: Current 'get the lemon = fail' is inaccurate. In AmE, a lemon is especially a defective vehicle/product. Also lemon law. 'When life gives you lemons...' is a separate expression.

column5: So small, slight, or unimportant that it can reasonably be ignored for a particular purpose.
column7: The difference in cost is negligible. / The risk is small enough to be negligible.
column8: Often technical/analytical: negligible effect/difference/risk/amount. Means negligible relative to context, not literally zero.

column5: To speak or write in an indirect, roundabout way; to use circumlocution.
column6: speak indirectly, talk around, beat around the bush (informal), circumlocute
column7: Instead of answering directly, he circumlocuted for several minutes.
column8: Rare back-formation. Much more useful forms are circumlocution (noun) and circumlocutory (adj.). Do not equate with babble/ramble: circumlocution specifically means indirect/roundabout wording.

column5: To communicate an idea, argument, or message successfully so that other people understand it.
column6: communicate, convey, make oneself understood, get through to
column7: I knew what I wanted to say, but I couldn't get my point across. / A simple example helped her get the point across.
column8: Can be get one's point across / get the point across. 'Clearly' is optional; the phrase already implies successful communication.
column12: entry::idiom entry::collocation entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::rhetorical topic::communication discovery::debate_language

column5: verb: to speak or complain at length in an angry, highly emotional, or forceful way. noun: a long angry or impassioned complaint or speech.
column6: rail, rave, complain angrily; tirade, diatribe
column7: He ranted about the new policy for twenty minutes. / Sorry for the rant—I needed to get that off my chest.
column8: Fix current verb example ('went on a ranting spree') to natural patterns: rant about/against, go on a rant. A rant can be humorous/self-aware online, not always shouting.

column5: To be convinced that an idea, plan, product, or person is good, worthwhile, or desirable.
column6: be convinced by, be persuaded about, be won over by
column7: I wasn't sold on the idea at first, but now I like it. / I'm still not completely sold on that candidate.
column8: Common negative: not sold on. Related sell someone on something = persuade them of its value.
column12: entry::idiom entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::persuasive discovery::persuasion

column5: A special, hard-to-define quality that makes a person or thing unusually attractive, effective, distinctive, or likely to succeed.
column6: special quality, edge, charisma, intangible quality
column7: She has the X factor that makes audiences pay attention. / The team is talented, but it still seems to lack an X factor.
column8: Capitalize X. Often deliberately vague/intangible. Also a TV-show title in some contexts, but generic expression predates/extends beyond it.

column5: Clever, useful, attractive, stylish, or pleasing in a neat/impressive way.
column7: That's a nifty little tool for opening jars. / The app has a nifty search feature.
column8: Informal, mildly enthusiastic, sometimes slightly old-fashioned/playful. More often clever/handy than simply fashionable.

column5: The practical, essential, or detailed realities of a matter, especially the less glamorous details.
column6: practical details, essentials, nuts and bolts, specifics
column7: Let's get down to the nitty-gritty. / Once we got into the nitty-gritty details, the plan became more complicated.
column8: Usually hyphenated nitty-gritty. Common: get down to the nitty-gritty. Historical origin is uncertain/contested; avoid confidently repeating folk etymologies.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::conversational usage::professional usage::presentation-friendly topic::communication topic::business topic::work topic::presentations topic::planning topic::problem-solving discovery::practical_details discovery::nuts_and_bolts discovery::presentation_language discovery::professional_context discovery::process_details discovery::implementation

column5: To remove material from inside something with a scooping motion, leaving a hollow or empty space.
column6: hollow out, remove, dig out, spoon out
column7: Scoop out the seeds before roasting the squash. / The inside had been scooped out to make room for the filling.
column8: Normalize to base phrasal verb. 'Scooped-out' can be adjective: a scooped-out pumpkin.

column5: 1) A natural mental or physical ability or power. 2) The teaching staff of a university/college or a division within one. Faculties can mean one's mental powers collectively.
column7: He retained all his mental faculties after the accident. / She joined the faculty at NYU. / The university has a Faculty of Arts.
column8: Current definition is circular. Major academic sense is essential. 'Faculty' is collective in AmE; institutional usage differs internationally.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::form_family entry::word usage::academic usage::american_english topic::work topic::education discovery::academic_discussion

column5: Cheerful readiness, eagerness, and prompt willingness to act.
column7: She accepted the invitation with alacrity. / He responded to the request with surprising alacrity.
column8: Formal/literary. Strong collocation: with alacrity. Implies willing promptness, not merely speed.

column5: A request, prompt, or response consisting of only one word.
column7: The form asks for a one-word response. / His entire request was a single word: 'Help.'
column8: Normalize hyphenation before noun: single-word request, one-word response. This is compositional rather than a fixed lexical item; KEEP only if source/context makes it useful.

column5: To spin on one foot or on the toes in ballet/dance; more loosely, to turn or spin gracefully. A pirouette is the turn itself.
column7: The dancer pirouetted across the stage. / She performed three clean pirouettes. / Leaves were pirouetting in the wind.
column8: Normalize to lemma. Figurative extension can describe graceful spinning motion outside dance.

column5: Great natural, physical, mechanical, or computational power in an unrefined or direct form, especially contrasted with skill, finesse, efficiency, or control.
column6: sheer power, brute force, strength, horsepower (specific contexts)
column7: He won through raw power rather than technique. / The new chip offers impressive raw computing power.
column8: Productive phrase across sports, machines, computing, politics. 'Raw' emphasizes magnitude before refinement/control, not necessarily 'ability to control'.

column5: Dangerously unstable, hazardous, or difficult; or likely to betray trust and act disloyally.
column7: The icy road was treacherous. / They crossed treacherous mountain terrain. / He discovered that his supposed ally was treacherous.
column8: Two major senses: hazardous conditions/terrain and betrayal/disloyalty. 'Harmful' is too broad.

column5: bristle: for hair/fur to stand stiffly upright; to react with anger or defensiveness; to be densely filled with projecting things. bristling: full of such projections, tension, anger, or abundance.
column6: stand on end; stiffen, take offense; teem with, be full of
column7: The dog bristled when the stranger approached. / She bristled at the suggestion that she had cheated. / The fortress was bristling with weapons.
column8: Current 'bristling attitude' is unnatural. High-value patterns: bristle at a remark/accusation; bristle with weapons/energy.

column5: The degree of detail, fineness, or subdivision at which information, data, analysis, permissions, or a system is represented or controlled.
column7: We need more granularity in the sales data, down to individual stores. / The permissions can be configured at a very fine level of granularity.
column8: Technical/business/data term. Higher/finer granularity usually means more detailed units; usage can vary, so 'fine/coarse granularity' is clearer than 'high/low' alone.

column5: noun: a count, score, or running total. verb: to count or total something; or to agree/correspond with something.
column6: count, total, score; count up; match, correspond
column7: The final tally was 52 votes to 48. / We tallied the receipts at the end of the day. / His account doesn't tally with the evidence.
column8: Current POS misses verb. Important intransitive sense tally with = agree/match.

column5: One of two equal or roughly equal parts of something; halves is the irregular plural of half.
column7: Cut the sandwich into two halves. / The two halves of the season felt completely different. / I'll take half.
column8: Teach irregular plural half → halves and common structures: half of, in half, by half, first/second half. Two halves are ideally equal, but figurative uses may be approximate.

column5: To formally or publicly give up, reject, or disown a claim, right, title, belief, allegiance, or way of life.
column6: relinquish, reject, disavow, abandon, give up
column7: He renounced his claim to the throne. / She publicly renounced violence. / He renounced his citizenship.
column8: Already fairly strong; deepen collocations and distinguish abdicate (office/throne), relinquish (give up possession/control), denounce (publicly condemn).

column5: A difficult, distressing, or dangerous situation, especially one that arouses concern or sympathy.
column7: The documentary drew attention to the plight of migrant workers. / Their plight worsened as winter approached.
column8: Common: the plight of X; draw attention to/highlight someone's plight. Usually serious and sympathy-evoking, unlike neutral predicament.

column5: A difficult, awkward, or unpleasant situation from which it is hard to find a good solution or escape.
column7: I found myself in a predicament when both meetings were scheduled for the same time. / How did you get into this predicament?
column8: Often less severe than plight and more focused on being stuck in a difficult problem. Common: be/find oneself in a predicament.

column5: A difficult state of uncertainty about what to do, especially when the available choices are problematic or competing.
column7: I'm in a quandary about whether to accept the offer or stay where I am. / The discovery left researchers in a quandary.
column8: Common: be in a quandary; a quandary over/about whether... Compared with dilemma, quandary emphasizes uncertainty/perplexity; predicament emphasizes being stuck in a difficult situation.

column5: A critical period when a deadline or decisive moment is close and intense effort or pressure is required.
column6: critical period, deadline pressure, make-or-break period
column7: It's crunch time—we have three days to finish the project. / The team usually performs well when crunch time arrives.
column8: KEEP despite earlier WID318 'crunch time' because current workflow does not mechanically delete repeated forms if a later global reconciliation may choose the stronger card. Core: at crunch time / when it comes to crunch time.

column5: To force yourself to face or do something difficult, unpleasant, or painful that can no longer reasonably be avoided.
column6: face it, tough it out, endure, take the plunge (some contexts)
column7: I hate going to the dentist, but I'll have to bite the bullet and make an appointment. / We finally bit the bullet and replaced the old furnace.
column8: Often means accepting an unavoidable unpleasant action/cost, not simply showing courage. Historical origin claims are disputed; avoid relying on folk etymology.

column5: A person who responds to a survey, questionnaire, research study, petition, appeal, or other formal inquiry; in law, the party responding to a proceeding or appeal.
column6: survey participant, interviewee (some studies), answering party
column7: Most respondents said they preferred the new design. / The respondent filed a brief opposing the appeal.
column8: Do not equate generally with defendant: legal meaning depends on proceeding. Survey respondent is especially common. Contrast participant: not every participant is necessarily a respondent.

column5: A prominent, influential, or highly respected person in a particular field.
column6: leading figure, notable, star, eminent person
column7: The conference attracted luminaries from science and technology. / Several literary luminaries attended the ceremony.
column8: Normalize singular + plural. Usually complimentary and somewhat elevated. Original literal sense relates to a source of light; modern common sense is figurative.

column5: A person living outside their country of origin, often for work, lifestyle, or long-term residence; expatriate can also be an adjective.
column6: expatriate, person living abroad, overseas resident
column7: She's a British expat living in Tokyo. / The company provides housing for expatriate employees.
column8: Expat is informal shortening of expatriate. Not a precise legal immigration category. It overlaps with immigrant/emigrant/migrant, but social usage differs and can carry class/cultural connotations; choose terms according to context rather than treating them as exact synonyms.

column5: Warm and enthusiastic; substantial and satisfying, especially food; strong, vigorous, or robust.
column6: warm, enthusiastic; substantial, filling; robust, vigorous
column7: They gave us a hearty welcome. / We ate a hearty breakfast before the hike. / He let out a hearty laugh.
column8: Productive collocations: hearty welcome/laugh/congratulations; hearty meal/breakfast; hale and hearty. Do not reduce to 'warm' only.

column5: To save time, money, or effort by omitting steps or doing something less thoroughly, often at the cost of quality, safety, or standards.
column7: They cut corners on construction, and the defects appeared within a year. / I don't mind saving money, but I won't cut corners on safety.
column8: Usually disapproving when quality/standards suffer. A shortcut is not necessarily bad; cutting corners often implies improper compromise.

column5: To use, spend, or consume a finite resource such as energy, effort, time, money, or ammunition.
column7: She expended a lot of energy worrying about something she couldn't control. / Considerable effort was expended on the redesign.
column8: Formal. Common: expend energy/effort/resources; expend something on/in doing something. Related expenditure, expendable.

column5: To spend, provide, or use less than is needed or advisable, especially to save money, time, or effort.
column7: Don't skimp on sleep before the exam. / They skimped on materials and the product felt cheap.
column8: Very common pattern skimp on something. Scrimp often appears in scrimp and save and emphasizes extreme economy; skimp emphasizes insufficient quantity/quality.
column12: entry::word entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern topic::finance topic::work topic::decision-making discovery::cost-cutting discovery::insufficient_quality discovery::resource_allocation discovery::trade-off

column5: Too small, meager, or insufficient in amount; of clothing, very small or revealing.
column7: The report gave only a skimpy explanation. / We were served a pretty skimpy portion. / The costume was deliberately skimpy.
column8: Two clusters: insufficient amount/details/portion and revealing clothing. Register informal. Do not make clothing the only salient sense.
column12: entry::word usage::informal topic::fashion topic::finance topic::work topic::decision-making discovery::insufficient_quality discovery::cost-cutting discovery::resource_allocation discovery::trade-off

column2: on the spur of the moment
column5: Suddenly and without advance planning; as an impulsive decision.
column7: We booked the trip on the spur of the moment. / On the spur of the moment, I decided to call her.
column8: Correct malformed headword 'spur the moment'. Fixed expression is on the spur of the moment. Related: spur-of-the-moment decision/purchase, with hyphens before a noun.

column5: noun: something that encourages or prompts action; also a pointed riding device and a projecting branch/route. verb: to stimulate, encourage, or prompt action or development.
column6: stimulus, incentive, impetus; encourage, prompt, drive
column7: The criticism gave her an extra spur to improve. / The announcement spurred investors to act. / Rising prices spurred demand for cheaper alternatives.
column8: High-value pattern: spur someone to do something; spur growth/action/change; spur someone on. Distinguish spur = stimulus from spurn = reject.

column5: Advance planning or deliberate thought before an action, especially before a crime; in criminal law, a concept whose exact requirements depend on jurisdiction.
column7: Prosecutors argued that the messages showed premeditation. / The attack appeared to have been carried out with premeditation.
column8: Especially legal. Avoid oversimplifying murder categories across jurisdictions. Related premeditate/premeditated; common phrase with premeditation.

column5: To speak, perform, compose, or devise something without advance preparation, using what is available at the moment.
column6: improvise, ad-lib, speak off the cuff
column7: When the slides failed, she extemporized for ten minutes. / The musicians extemporized a short ending.
column8: Normalize lemma. More formal than improvise. Can mean improvise a speech/performance or devise a temporary solution. Related extemporaneous.

column5: Secret, confidential, or deliberately kept from public knowledge.
column7: The negotiations were very hush-hush. / They're working on a hush-hush project.
column8: Hyphenated. Informal and often mildly playful/suspicious. Usually predicative or attributive: keep it hush-hush; a hush-hush meeting.

column5: To increase the standard, level of performance, or expectations that others are measured against.
column6: set a higher standard, increase expectations, set a new benchmark
column7: Her performance raised the bar for everyone else. / The new safety rules raise the bar for the entire industry.
column8: Correct malformed headword 'higher the bar'. Opposite: lower the bar. 'Set the bar high/low' is related but structurally different.

column5: An unwelcome, unpredictable, or difficult change in circumstances; vicissitudes = the changing fortunes and ups and downs of life or a situation.
column6: ups and downs, changes of fortune, fluctuations, reversals
column7: They survived the vicissitudes of war and economic crisis. / The business has weathered many vicissitudes over the decades.
column8: Formal/literary and most common in plural. Often: the vicissitudes of life/history/fortune. Not merely any neutral variation.

column5: Cheerful, playful, and not serious or burdensome in tone.
column7: The movie is a lighthearted comedy. / I was only making a lighthearted comment.
column8: Usually positive; can contrast with serious/heavy. Spelling lighthearted is common AmE; light-hearted also occurs.

column5: To sell or dispose of assets or investments; to remove or rid oneself/someone of something; in finance, to divest from a company or sector.
column6: sell off, dispose of, shed, relinquish
column7: The company plans to divest several non-core businesses. / The fund divested from fossil-fuel companies. / He divested himself of most of his possessions.
column8: Normalize from divesting. Finance/business use is common. Patterns: divest assets; divest a business of X; divest oneself of X; divest from X.

column5: A state or experience of feeling detached from oneself, one's thoughts, emotions, body, or actions, sometimes as though observing oneself from outside.
column7: The article describes depersonalization as a feeling of being detached from oneself. / The character says the experience made everything about himself feel strangely unreal.
column8: Keep definition descriptive rather than diagnosing the learner. Distinguish depersonalization (detachment from self) from derealization (surroundings feel unreal). Clinical interpretation belongs to qualified medical contexts.

column5: The work, maintenance, or expense required to keep a building, vehicle, property, system, or standard in good condition.
column7: The house is beautiful, but the upkeep is expensive. / Regular upkeep prevents small problems from becoming major repairs.
column8: Usually uncountable. Common: cost of upkeep; maintenance and upkeep. Can occasionally refer to maintaining a standard/appearance.

column5: Caregiver usually means a person who provides ongoing personal care or assistance to someone who needs it. Caretaker can mean a person responsible for a property/place and, in some varieties and contexts, can also mean caregiver.
column6: caregiver: carer, care provider; caretaker: custodian, property keeper; caregiver (some contexts)
column7: Her father became her primary caregiver after the surgery. / The caretaker lives on the grounds and maintains the property.
column8: Preserve regional nuance. In AmE, caregiver strongly suggests personal care; caretaker often property/temporary responsibility, but caretaker can also mean a person caring for another person. BrE often uses carer. Avoid presenting the distinction as absolute.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::noun_phrase usage::american_english usage::british_english topic::language_learning discovery::comparison discovery::contrast discovery::continuity

column5: Careful, tactful, and unobtrusive, especially in order to avoid embarrassment, attention, or disclosure of private information.
column7: She made a discreet inquiry about the problem. / The hotel has a discreet side entrance.
column8: Key confusable: discreet = tactful/private; discrete = separate/distinct. Common: discreet inquiry, discreet service, be discreet about something.

column5: A less experienced person whose career, skills, or development are guided and supported by an influential mentor.
column7: She was once the protégé of a famous director. / He helped his young protégé build a research career.
column8: Standard spelling protégé preserves accents, though protege is common in plain English text. A protégé is not necessarily an apprentice/student in a formal program; emphasis is sponsorship/mentorship.

column5: So firmly established in a position, habit, system, belief, or power structure that change is difficult.
column7: Long working hours are deeply entrenched in the company culture. / Both sides became more entrenched in their positions.
column8: From military trench imagery. Common: deeply entrenched; entrenched interests/attitudes/inequality/position. Can describe people becoming less willing to compromise.
column12: entry::word usage::military usage::debate-friendly topic::self-help topic::debate discovery::debate_language

column5: The process or state of becoming firmly established and resistant to change; also, literally, defensive fortification by trenches.
column7: The policy contributed to the entrenchment of existing inequalities. / Political polarization can lead to further entrenchment on both sides.
column8: Related entrench/entrenched. Abstract use often concerns power, inequality, attitudes, positions. Do not use generic 'establishment' as if fully synonymous.

column5: Lack of discipline, self-control, or adherence to rules, especially in a group, institution, or organization.
column6: lack of discipline, disorder, unruliness, misconduct
column7: The coach blamed the defeat partly on tactical indiscipline. / Repeated indiscipline disrupted the classroom.
column8: More common in BrE/institutional contexts than everyday AmE, where 'lack of discipline' is often more natural. Can describe behavior, finances, tactics, organizations.

column5: Showing strong self-control, orderly habits, or adherence to a method, training, or rules.
column7: She's very disciplined about studying every day. / The team played a disciplined defensive game.
column8: Not merely 'well-behaved'. Can describe a disciplined approach, investor, athlete, team. Related self-disciplined.

column2: hit the bull's-eye / hit the bullseye
column5: To hit the exact center of a target; figuratively, to be exactly right or achieve precisely the intended result.
column6: hit the mark, nail it, be spot-on
column7: The arrow hit the bull's-eye. / Your explanation hit the bullseye—you identified the real problem.
column8: Related to WID576 bull's-eye/bullseye. KEEP if retrieval value of the full expression is useful; later global duplicate reconciliation can decide whether noun + idiom should remain separate.

column5: A no-win situation in which contradictory or mutually dependent rules or conditions prevent a solution or escape.
column6: no-win situation, impossible bind, paradoxical trap
column7: It's a Catch-22: I need experience to get the job, but I need a job to get experience. / Small businesses can face a funding catch-22.
column8: Correct punctuation and broken example. Originates from Joseph Heller's novel Catch-22; generic use often lowercase. More specific than any dilemma: the conditions themselves trap you circularly.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word topic::problem-solving discovery::solution_framing discovery::prevention discovery::resolution

column5: Something that brings both benefits and disadvantages, so its overall value is ambiguous.
column6: double-edged sword, trade-off, blessing and curse
column7: Working from home has been a mixed blessing: I save commuting time, but I miss seeing colleagues. / Fame can be a mixed blessing.
column8: Compare double-edged sword: mixed blessing often emphasizes something beneficial that also has drawbacks; double-edged sword emphasizes a factor that can help and harm.
column12: entry::noun_phrase topic::decision-making discovery::compromise discovery::ambiguity discovery::trade-off discovery::summary

column5: Something that has both beneficial and harmful effects, or an advantage that also creates a corresponding risk or disadvantage.
column7: Social media can be a double-edged sword: it connects people but can also amplify misinformation. / Her perfectionism was a double-edged sword.
column8: Correct hyphenation. Often 'a double-edged sword'. Not identical to mixed blessing, though they overlap strongly.
column12: entry::idiom entry::noun_phrase topic::decision-making discovery::compromise discovery::risk discovery::trade-off

column5: A dangerous, malicious, or untrustworthy person or thing disguised as harmless, friendly, or beneficial.
column7: The investment looked safe, but it turned out to be a wolf in sheep's clothing. / He warned that the charming newcomer was a wolf in sheep's clothing.
column8: Can describe people, policies, products, ideas—not only a person. Biblical/fable-like imagery; common enough for active recognition/use.

column5: A situation or contest in which either of two or more outcomes seems about equally likely; a choice that is difficult because options are closely matched.
column6: coin toss, close call, fifty-fifty proposition
column7: It's a toss-up between the two restaurants. / The election is still a toss-up.
column8: Common patterns: it's a toss-up whether...; a toss-up between A and B. Hyphenated noun. 'Coin flip' is informal close synonym.

column5: A whistle, shout, sexual remark, jeer, or mocking call directed at someone in public; as a verb, to direct such calls at someone.
column6: wolf whistle, jeer, heckle; harass verbally
column7: She ignored the catcalls from across the street. / Several audience members catcalled the speaker.
column8: Broaden carefully: historically/general catcall can be a jeer or disapproving whistle, while contemporary use often means unsolicited sexual comments/whistles, especially toward women. Do not reduce it solely to one gender.

column5: A collection, situation, or result containing a varied mixture, often including both good and bad elements.
column6: mixture, assortment, uneven mix, mixed results
column7: The reviews were a mixed bag: some were glowing and others were brutal. / My first week at the new job was a mixed bag.
column8: Not always exactly 50/50 good and bad; can simply mean varied/uneven. Common: a mixed bag of X.

column2: vent / vent to someone / vent about
column5: verb: to express pent-up anger, frustration, or other strong feelings; noun: an opening that lets air/gas escape, and in some contexts an act/outlet of emotional expression.
column6: let off steam, unload, express frustration; outlet/opening
column7: Can I vent to you for a minute? / She vented about work all evening. / The dryer vent was blocked.
column8: Important patterns: vent to someone; vent about something; vent one's frustration/anger. Do not assume emotional sense is the only meaning; physical vent is common.

column5: The process or event of cutting wool from sheep.
column7: We visited a farm to watch a sheep-shearing demonstration. / Sheep shearing usually requires skill and proper handling.
column8: Correct typo 'sheep sharing'. Shear (v.) → shearing (n./gerund). A person who shears sheep is a shearer.

column5: A Hindi form meaning roughly 'will meet'; in leave-taking expressions such as phir milenge, it conveys 'we'll meet again / see you again.'
column6: see you again, we'll meet again (contextual translations)
column7: Phir milenge! — See you again! / She ended the conversation with 'milenge,' using it as a casual leave-taking expression.
column8: KEEP as source-language recognition card. More idiomatic leave-taking is often 'phir milenge' ('we'll meet again'). Romanization varies. Do not present isolated milenge as a universal one-word equivalent of goodbye.

column5: A genus of fungi that includes species containing psilocybin as well as taxonomically related species; the term refers to the genus, not to psychedelic mushrooms as a generic common noun.
column6: fungal genus; psilocybin-containing mushrooms (only for relevant species)
column7: The paper examined several species in the genus Psilocybe. / Psilocybe cubensis is one well-known species in the genus.
column8: Capitalize genus name and ideally italicize in scientific writing. Do not use 'Psilocybe' as an exact synonym for all 'magic mushrooms'; common labels cover multiple species/genera and taxonomic details matter.

column2: give someone a holler / give me a holler
column5: To call, contact, or get someone's attention, especially casually; literally, holler can mean shout.
column6: give someone a call, let someone know, hit someone up (slang)
column7: Give me a holler when you get home. / If you need a hand, just give us a holler.
column8: Informal, conversational, especially AmE. Depending context it can mean phone/message/contact rather than literally shout.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::conversational usage::slang usage::american_english

column5: To interpret or understand someone's words, actions, intentions, or a situation incorrectly.
column6: misinterpret, misunderstand, misread, take the wrong way
column7: Her friendliness was misconstrued as romantic interest. / Don't misconstrue my criticism as hostility.
column8: Normalize lemma. Common pattern misconstrue A as B. Usually concerns mistaken interpretation, not deliberate distortion.

column5: verb: to decorate or finish food/drink with an added item; noun: the decorative/flavoring item. In law/finance, garnish can also mean legally withhold money, especially wages, to satisfy a debt.
column7: Garnish the soup with chopped parsley. / Add a lemon twist as a garnish. / The court ordered his wages to be garnished.
column8: Major missing legal/financial sense: garnish wages. Do not confuse with garnishee, a related legal term.

column5: In a way that makes someone feel unsettled, uneasy, confused, or thrown off balance.
column7: She remained disconcertingly calm during the argument. / The two designs look disconcertingly similar.
column8: Related disconcert/disconcerted/disconcerting. Often means unexpectedly unsettling, not simply 'confusingly'.

column5: Impossible or extremely difficult to understand, explain, measure, or imagine.
column7: Why he did it remains unfathomable to me. / The ocean once seemed unfathomable in both depth and mystery.
column8: From fathom = measure depth / understand. Can intensify depth/scale metaphorically. Compare inscrutable: often motives/expressions that resist interpretation.

column5: Having many different aspects, features, dimensions, skills, or sides.
column7: It's a multifaceted problem with no simple solution. / She's a multifaceted performer who acts, sings, and writes.
column8: One-word multifaceted is now very common; multi-faceted also occurs. 'Versatile' works mainly for people/things with varied abilities, not every complex issue.

column5: verb: to enjoy or look forward to something greatly. noun: enjoyment/appetite for something; also a chopped or pickled condiment.
column6: savor, delight in, enjoy greatly; condiment
column7: She relished the chance to prove them wrong. / I'm not relishing the thought of another six-hour meeting. / He added pickle relish to the hot dog.
column8: Normalize lemma and include common negative progressive 'not relishing the prospect/thought'. Food noun is a separate major sense.

column2: poster boy / poster girl / poster child
column5: A person who is seen as a highly visible, representative, or emblematic example of a quality, movement, problem, or trend.
column6: symbol, emblem, representative example, public face
column7: He became the poster boy for reckless spending. / She was once described as the poster child for the reform movement.
column8: Normalize singular and broaden productive family. Can be positive, negative, or ironic. 'Poster child' is gender-neutral in many contexts and extremely common figuratively.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::figurative usage::ironic topic::family discovery::evaluation

column5: To think carefully about something for a period of time before deciding or forming an opinion.
column6: ponder, consider, think over, reflect on
column7: I need a day to mull it over. / She's mulling over whether to accept the offer.
column8: Mull over is very common; pronoun placement: mull it over. Plain mull can also be transitive in some usage. Separate unrelated mulled wine sense of mull if encountered.

column5: To cause something to happen; to persuade or lead someone to do something; in medicine, to initiate a physiological process such as labor or anesthesia.
column6: cause, bring about, trigger; persuade, prompt
column7: The medication may induce drowsiness. / Nothing could induce him to change his mind. / Doctors decided to induce labor.
column8: Normalize lemma. Patterns: induce X; induce someone to do; induce labor/sleep/anesthesia. Related induction. Not interchangeable with 'introduce'.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::persuasive topic::medicine topic::health discovery::persuasion discovery::process_details

column5: Causing unease, anxiety, or concern; troubling in a subtle or persistent way.
column7: There was something disquieting about his sudden silence. / The report contains several disquieting findings.
column8: Often more restrained/literary than alarming. Related disquiet (noun/verb) and disquieted.

column5: Out of place or not in harmony with its surroundings, context, style, or other elements.
column6: out of place, mismatched, inconsistent, discordant
column7: The modern glass tower looked incongruous beside the medieval church. / His cheerful tone seemed incongruous with the bad news.
column8: Common pattern incongruous with. Related incongruity. Focus is mismatch, not simply 'inappropriate'.

column5: An exclamation expressing relief, exhaustion, being impressed/overwhelmed, or reaction to something intense.
column6: whew, wow (some contexts), thank goodness (relief paraphrase)
column7: Phew, that was close! / Phew—I'm exhausted after that climb. / Whew, that's a lot of money.
column8: Phew and whew overlap; spelling/pronunciation vary. 'Whoa' is not a general synonym. Tone determines relief vs exhaustion vs amazement.

column5: Representing the highest, final, or most impressive achievement or feature of something.
column7: Winning the championship was the crowning achievement of her career. / The tower is the crowning feature of the building.
column8: High-value collocation: crowning achievement/glory. 'Crowning moment' also possible. Related crown (v.) = complete gloriously / put a crown on.

column5: verb: to increase an engine's speed; figuratively, rev up = increase activity, excitement, energy, or preparation. noun: an engine revolution, especially in plural revs.
column6: race an engine, accelerate; ramp up, energize
column7: He revved the engine at the light. / The campaign is revving up ahead of the election. / Keep the revs low until the engine warms up.
column8: Add productive phrasal verb rev up. Rev ≠ simply accelerate a vehicle; it specifically concerns engine speed in literal use.

column5: To untangle something physically or to resolve a complicated blockage, traffic jam, administrative problem, or tangled situation.
column7: She patiently unsnarled the knotted cord. / Police worked to unsnarl traffic after the crash. / Negotiators tried to unsnarl the dispute.
column8: Less common than untangle/disentangle but vivid and useful. Particularly natural with traffic/logistics/bureaucratic complications.

column5: To free something from a physical tangle; figuratively, to separate interconnected issues, relationships, causes, or oneself from a complicated involvement.
column7: I spent ten minutes disentangling my headphones. / It's difficult to disentangle cause from correlation. / The company is trying to disentangle itself from the partnership.
column8: Productive figurative patterns: disentangle A from B; disentangle oneself from. Compare unsnarl: often resolve a jam/mess; disentangle emphasizes separating intertwined elements.

column5: A systematic plan or routine, especially one involving diet, exercise, medication, treatment, training, or self-care.
column7: She follows a strict training regimen. / The doctor prescribed a new treatment regimen.
column8: Key confusable: regimen = planned routine; regime = system of rule/government (and sometimes regimen-like system); regiment = military unit / impose strict order.
column12: entry::word usage::military topic::wellness topic::planning topic::medicine topic::health

column5: verb: to smell very strongly and unpleasantly; figuratively, to strongly suggest an undesirable quality. noun: a strong unpleasant smell (less common than verb).
column6: stink; smack of, be redolent of (register differs); stench
column7: The room reeked of cigarette smoke. / The deal reeks of corruption. / A reek of chemicals hung in the air.
column8: Very common pattern reek of X, literal and figurative: reek of desperation/corruption/hypocrisy. Noun is less common in everyday AmE.
column12: entry::collocation entry::word usage::figurative usage::american_english discovery::figurative_extension discovery::suggestion discovery::evaluation

column5: A label used in some Western esoteric and occult traditions for approaches emphasizing individual autonomy, antinomian or taboo-breaking practices, self-deification, or other departures from conventional religious norms; meanings vary by tradition.
column7: The author contrasts Left-Hand Path traditions with what he calls the Right-Hand Path. / Different occult groups define the left-hand path differently.
column8: Hyphenate left-hand. Avoid defining it simply as 'dark' or immoral: the label is tradition-dependent and contested. In Western occultism it has specialized meanings; historical South Asian left/right-hand classifications have different contexts.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist usage::religious topic::culture topic::religion discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::emphasis discovery::specialist_register

column5: A person motivated by concern for others' welfare, especially someone willing to benefit others without expecting equivalent personal gain.
column6: selfless person, humanitarian (some contexts), benefactor (not exact)
column7: Even committed altruists have to decide where their help can do the most good. / The group attracted idealists and altruists.
column8: Normalize singular. Philanthropist/benefactor specifically imply giving resources and are not exact synonyms. Related altruism/altruistic.

column5: noun: a geometric angle; a particular perspective, approach, or way of presenting a subject; a strategic motive or 'angle.' verb: to position or present something at an angle or from a particular perspective.
column7: Let's look at the problem from another angle. / What's his angle—why is he offering this for free? / The article angles the story toward younger readers.
column8: Current figurative sense is useful but too narrow. High-value: from a different angle; what's your/his angle?; camera angle; angle for something (informal, seek).
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::debate_language

column5: A label used in some Western esoteric frameworks for traditions emphasizing alignment with a transcendent/divine order, conventional ethical constraints, or union with a higher principle; definitions vary widely by tradition.
column7: The book uses 'right-hand path' for traditions oriented toward union with a higher spiritual order. / Not all occultists accept the left-hand/right-hand path distinction.
column8: Hyphenate right-hand. Avoid simplistic equation with 'good/moral' versus left-hand = 'bad'. These are contested specialist categories, and historical South Asian uses differ from modern Western occult classifications.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist usage::religious topic::culture topic::religion discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::emphasis discovery::specialist_register

column5: A person, organization, state, account, or system participant that acts dishonestly, maliciously, irresponsibly, or in bad faith.
column6: wrongdoer, malicious actor, bad-faith participant, threat actor (cybersecurity-specific)
column7: The platform is trying to prevent bad actors from abusing the system. / A few bad actors can undermine trust in the whole market.
column8: Normalize singular. Common in policy, business, cybersecurity, geopolitics. 'Threat actor' is narrower cybersecurity/security jargon.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::specialist topic::religion discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: noun: an organized action that prevents people, goods, traffic, or supplies from entering or leaving a place. verb: to impose or create such an obstruction.
column6: siege (not exact), barrier, obstruction; seal off, obstruct
column7: The navy imposed a blockade on the port. / Protesters blockaded the entrance. / Aid deliveries were delayed by the blockade.
column8: A blockade is not identical to a siege: siege involves surrounding/attacking to force surrender; blockade focuses on preventing movement/supplies. Can be military, political, or protest-related.

column5: verb: to start, build, or improve something using one's own limited resources rather than substantial outside support; in computing/statistics, bootstrap has specialized meanings. noun: a loop/strap on a boot and several derived technical concepts.
column6: self-fund, build from scratch, start with limited resources
column7: She bootstrapped the company without outside investors. / The system uses a bootstrap process to load its core components.
column8: Business sense comes from 'pull oneself up by one's bootstraps,' originally an impossible feat later reinterpreted as self-reliance. Computing/statistics senses deserve context-specific treatment; do not collapse them into business self-funding.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::technical usage::specialist discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::resource_allocation discovery::support discovery::improvement discovery::specialist_register

column5: To move or balance unsteadily as if about to fall; figuratively, to be in an unstable situation close to a major change or failure.
column6: wobble, totter, sway; hover on the brink
column7: The glass teetered on the edge of the table. / The company was teetering on the brink of bankruptcy.
column8: High-value figurative construction teeter on the brink/edge of X. Compare totter = unsteady walking/movement; teeter emphasizes precarious balance.

column5: To tell someone unpleasant, disappointing, or surprising news, often carefully or reluctantly.
column6: tell, reveal, inform gently, let someone know
column7: I don't know how to break it to him that the trip was canceled. / Who's going to break the news to her?
column8: Pattern: break it to someone that... / break the news to someone. The phrase does not inherently mean the delivery itself is gentle, though speakers often try to be tactful.

column5: The act or process of breaking; damage caused by breaking; the quantity or cost of items that are broken.
column6: damage, broken items, loss through breakage
column7: Fragile items should be packed carefully to prevent breakage. / The store allows for a small amount of breakage.
column8: Usually uncountable. Common in shipping/retail/materials. Also technical senses such as hair breakage.

column5: Very friendly or familiar, often suddenly, conspicuously, or more intimately than the speaker thinks is natural or sincere.
column7: Why are you two suddenly so buddy-buddy? / He got buddy-buddy with the manager after the promotion was announced.
column8: Often mildly suspicious, teasing, or disapproving—not simply 'close friends'. Common get/be buddy-buddy with.

column5: A sudden painful muscle cramp or spasm, especially in the leg or calf.
column6: muscle cramp, leg cramp, muscle spasm
column7: I woke up with a charley horse in my calf. / Stretching helped the charley horse ease up.
column8: Informal North American expression. Usually a cramp, though sports usage historically can include muscle stiffness/injury. Spelling charley horse is standard; Charlie horse also appears.

column5: Abstaining from sexual activity according to a moral/religious ideal; sexually pure in traditional usage; also restrained, simple, or unadorned in style.
column6: celibate (not exact), sexually abstinent; pure, restrained, austere
column7: He had taken a vow to remain chaste. / The building's design is elegant and chaste, with almost no ornament.
column8: Do not equate chaste automatically with celibate: celibacy often means unmarried/abstinent by commitment/status; chastity depends on ethical/religious framework. Important nonsexual aesthetic sense = restrained/unornamented.

column5: Instead of; in place of something else as a substitute or alternative.
column6: instead of, in place of, as a substitute for
column7: Employees may take extra vacation days in lieu of overtime pay. / They sent a donation in lieu of flowers.
column8: Normalize from 'comes in lieu of'. Core fixed phrase is in lieu of. Formal but common in HR/legal/notices. Pronunciation of lieu in AmE often sounds like 'loo'.

column2: drive something home / drive the point home
column5: To make an idea, fact, warning, or lesson especially clear, forceful, or memorable through emphasis or evidence.
column7: The photos drove home the scale of the disaster. / She repeated the figure to drive the point home.
column8: Productive pattern drive home the point/fact/message/importance; pronoun/object variants possible. 'Bring something home to someone' is related but distinct.

column5: A playground seesaw; as a verb, to move or alternate back and forth between two positions, states, or choices.
column7: The kids played on the teeter-totter. / Public opinion teeter-tottered between the two positions.
column8: Noun is chiefly North American; seesaw is broader. Figurative verb exists but is less common than seesaw/oscillate.

column5: Expressing praise, gratitude, affection, enthusiasm, or emotion very freely and abundantly.
column7: She was effusive in her praise of the staff. / He received an effusive welcome.
column8: Can be sincere or imply excessive/gushing emotion depending tone. Common: effusive praise/thanks/welcome; be effusive about/in.

column5: noun: a plant that retains green foliage year-round. adjective: remaining useful, relevant, popular, or marketable over a long period; in media, 'evergreen content' stays timely.
column7: Pines are evergreens. / The site publishes evergreen articles that remain useful for years. / It's an evergreen favorite with audiences.
column8: Strong media/business sense: evergreen content/topic. 'Evergreen classic' can be redundant depending context but is used. Perennial overlaps figuratively.

column5: To look at someone or something carefully, often with attraction, interest, suspicion, or evaluation.
column6: look over, check out, size up, ogle (sexual/staring sense)
column7: She noticed a guy eyeing her up across the room. / He eyed up the competition before the race.
column8: Broader than romantic/physical interest. Especially BrE; AmE often eye someone/something, check out, size up. 'Ogle' is stronger and more explicitly prolonged/sexual.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::evaluation

column5: Based on faulty reasoning, a false assumption, or a logical error; misleading because the reasoning is unsound.
column7: The conclusion rests on fallacious reasoning. / It's fallacious to assume that correlation proves causation.
column8: Related fallacy. Fallacious specifically concerns false/invalid reasoning or belief, not simply any factually incorrect statement.

column5: Having effects, consequences, influence, or implications that extend widely across areas, people, or time.
column7: The ruling could have far-reaching consequences. / The invention had far-reaching effects on society.
column8: Hyphenated before/after noun in standard use. Common: far-reaching consequences/implications/reforms/changes.

column5: Artificial or imitation, made to resemble something genuine; figuratively, not genuine or affected.
column7: She bought a faux-fur coat. / The wall has a faux-marble finish. / His faux concern fooled nobody.
column8: From French; often used in compounds such as faux fur/leather/finish. Can sound more neutral/stylish than 'fake' for materials, but figurative faux outrage/concern is negative.

column5: From poverty or very humble circumstances to wealth, prominence, or major success.
column6: rise from poverty, rise to success, upward-mobility story
column7: The film tells a classic rags-to-riches story. / His rise from rags to riches became part of the company's mythology.
column8: Also attributive rags-to-riches story. 'Self-made' and 'against all odds' are related ideas, not exact synonyms.

column5: To become so excited, enthusiastic, emotional, or absorbed that you go further than intended or lose restraint.
column6: overdo it, get swept up, lose perspective, go overboard
column7: I got carried away and bought way more books than I needed. / Don't get carried away—we haven't won yet.
column8: Usually implies excess rather than total loss of control. Common: get carried away with something; get carried away by excitement/emotion.

column5: To learn or begin to understand how to do or use something through practice or experience.
column6: get used to, learn how to, master the basics of, pick up
column7: It took me a while to get the hang of driving stick. / Once you get the hang of the controls, the game is easy.
column8: Common: get the hang of it/doing something. Usually means reaching functional familiarity, not full mastery.

column2: give a rat's ass / not give a rat's ass
column5: To care at all; overwhelmingly common in the negative 'not give a rat's ass' = not care whatsoever.
column6: give a damn, give a shit (vulgar), care
column7: He doesn't give a rat's ass what they think. / Do you really think I give a rat's ass about that?
column8: Correct grammar/apostrophe from 'gives a rats ass'. Vulgar, emphatic AmE slang. Usually negative/interrogative. Avoid in polite/professional contexts.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::idiom usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::american_english usage::professional usage::informal discovery::professional_context

column5: To proceed through people, items, steps, or options one by one in sequence; in some contexts, to continue further along a route, hierarchy, or chain.
column6: go through one by one, proceed in order, work down the list
column7: Let's go down the line and hear from everyone. / We went down the line checking each requirement.
column8: Meaning depends on what 'the line' is. Compare 'down the line' = later in the future / further along, a related but separate expression.

column5: Inclined to touch, grab, or fondle other people excessively, especially in an unwanted, sexually suggestive, or boundary-crossing way.
column7: He got handsy at the party and made people uncomfortable. / She told him to stop being so handsy.
column8: Informal and usually negative. 'Touchy' is not a good synonym because touchy commonly means easily offended/sensitive. Can imply nonconsensual or inappropriate touching.

column5: Strong and able to withstand difficult conditions such as cold, disease, hardship, or rough treatment.
column7: These hardy plants can survive a harsh winter. / Only the hardiest hikers attempted the route.
column8: Common for plants/animals/people. Key confusable hearty: hearty = warm/enthusiastic/substantial; hardy = tough/resilient.

column5: With one's identity or true nature concealed by changed appearance or presentation; figuratively, something appearing to be one thing while actually being another.
column7: The detective entered the club in disguise. / The setback turned out to be a blessing in disguise.
column8: Broaden beyond literal clothing. Related 'a blessing in disguise' is a fixed idiom. Incognito usually concerns concealing identity, not every disguised object/quality.
column12: entry::idiom entry::prepositional_phrase usage::presentation-friendly topic::presentations topic::nature discovery::presentation_language discovery::figurative_extension

column5: The quality, practice, or policy of making people feel welcomed, respected, represented, and able to participate rather than excluded.
column7: The organization is trying to improve inclusiveness in its hiring and events. / The design was praised for its inclusiveness.
column8: Inclusion is generally the more common institutional term; inclusiveness emphasizes the quality of being inclusive. Diversity is not a synonym: a group can be diverse without being inclusive.

column5: To terminate someone's employment, typically because a position is eliminated or an employer reduces staff rather than because of individual misconduct; also informally, to stop bothering/criticizing/using something.
column6: make redundant (BrE), dismiss due to downsizing, let go; leave alone (other sense)
column7: The company laid off 200 employees after sales fell. / Lay off him—he's had a rough day. / I'm trying to lay off the caffeine.
column8: Important multiple senses. Employment layoff differs from being fired for misconduct, though everyday usage can blur. Noun: layoff. Separable: lay someone off.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::phrasal_verb usage::british_english usage::debate-friendly topic::work topic::debate discovery::release discovery::debate_language

column5: To learn the basic procedures, practical details, and unwritten conventions needed to function in a job, activity, or organization.
column6: get the hang of it, learn how things work, get up to speed
column7: It took me a few weeks to learn the ropes at my new job. / A senior editor showed her the ropes.
column8: Related show someone the ropes = teach them how things work. Usually practical familiarization rather than formal mastery.

column5: A small tablet or medicated sweet designed to dissolve slowly in the mouth, especially to soothe the throat; also a diamond/rhombus-shaped figure or object.
column6: throat lozenge, cough drop, pastille; diamond shape (other sense)
column7: I sucked on a throat lozenge to ease my sore throat. / The window was decorated with colored lozenge-shaped panes.
column8: Normalize singular + plural. In everyday AmE, cough drop is often more natural for throat medication. Important second sense: a lozenge is a diamond/rhombus shape, especially in heraldry/design.

column5: So unreasonable, absurd, or inappropriate that it seems laughable.
column7: The idea that we could finish all of this in ten minutes is ludicrous. / They were charging a ludicrous amount of money for a tiny room.
column8: Stronger than merely 'silly'. Common: ludicrous idea/claim/price/amount/situation. Often expresses disbelief plus ridicule.

column5: A sudden involuntary tightening or contraction of a muscle; it may be brief or sustained and can range from painless twitching to painful cramping.
column6: muscle contraction, cramp (some spasms), twitch (some cases)
column7: I had a painful muscle spasm in my calf after the run. / Stress can sometimes trigger muscle spasms.
column8: Do not equate every muscle spasm with a cramp: cramp is typically painful sustained contraction, while spasm is broader. Medical causes vary; card should remain vocabulary-focused, not diagnostic.

column5: To have a notary public formally witness, certify, or authenticate a signature/document according to applicable procedure.
column7: I need to get this form notarized before I submit it. / The document was notarised in the UK.
column8: Normalize lemma and variants. AmE notarize/notarized; BrE notarise/notarised. A notary does not necessarily certify that every factual statement in a document is true; the precise notarial act varies by jurisdiction.
column12: entry::word entry::form_family entry::variant_set usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::process_details discovery::procedural_language

column5: Long-established habits are difficult to change or stop, even when someone wants to change them.
column6: habits are hard to break, fall back into old ways
column7: I still reach for my old phone every morning—old habits die hard. / He retired years ago but still wakes up at six; old habits die hard.
column8: Usually a standalone comment after someone repeats an ingrained behavior. Can be affectionate, resigned, or critical.

column5: A game, match, or series used to determine advancement, qualification, or a championship after the regular competition; often plural playoffs for the postseason tournament.
column7: They clinched a spot in the playoffs. / The final playoff will determine who advances.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Sports structures differ: playoff can be one deciding contest or part of a postseason system. Common: make/reach/miss the playoffs; playoff berth/game.

column5: To outdo someone, especially by responding to their achievement, story, possession, or claim with something supposedly better or more impressive.
column7: Every time I tell a story, he tries to one-up me. / She one-upped his travel story with an even crazier one.
column8: Often carries annoyance about competitive conversational behavior. Related noun one-upmanship. Past tense one-upped.

column5: To succeed in accomplishing something difficult, surprising, or unlikely; also literally to remove something by pulling, and in driving to leave the main road and stop/turn aside.
column6: manage, accomplish, bring off, succeed in; remove (literal)
column7: I can't believe they pulled off that comeback. / She pulled off the disguise perfectly. / Pull off the highway at the next exit.
column8: Major active sense = successfully achieve something difficult: pull it off. Preserve polysemy rather than treating it as success-only.

column5: Claimed, alleged, or presented as being something, without the speaker necessarily accepting that the claim is true.
column7: The purported evidence turned out to be unreliable. / He denied meeting the purported leader of the group.
column8: Often signals skepticism or distance. Related verb purport: the document purports to show... Do not treat as simply 'reported'.

column2: jot down / put down an idea
column5: To write an idea, note, thought, or piece of information so it is not forgotten; jot down emphasizes writing something quickly and briefly.
column6: write down, jot down, note, record
column7: Let me jot that idea down before I forget it. / I put down a few ideas for the review while I was watching the episode.
column8: Current 'put down ideas' is grammatical in context but not the most useful standalone headword. For quick notes, jot down/write down is more idiomatic. Put something down also has many unrelated senses, so keep object/context explicit.

column5: Showing mild confusion, curiosity, or questioning, especially through a facial expression or tone.
column7: She gave me a quizzical look when I mentioned the name. / He raised an eyebrow quizzically.
column8: Very common collocation: quizzical look/expression. Usually suggests curious puzzlement rather than serious confusion.

column5: To betray or inform on someone by revealing their wrongdoing, secret, or rule-breaking to an authority or other person.
column6: snitch on, inform on, tell on, betray
column7: Who ratted us out to the teacher? / He refused to rat out his friends.
column8: Informal, strongly negative from the perspective of the person exposed. Compare tell on = common/childlike; snitch on = slang; inform on = more neutral/formal.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::formal usage::informal usage::slang discovery::betrayal

column5: Generally regarded as trustworthy, reliable, competent, or respectable because of a good reputation.
column7: Make sure you buy it from a reputable seller. / The study was published by a reputable journal.
column8: Common with source/company/dealer/seller/journal/institution. Reputable means having a good reputation; reputed means generally said/believed to be something and is not equivalent.

column2: be resigned to / be resigned to the fact that ...
column5: To have reluctantly accepted an unpleasant situation as unavoidable or unlikely to change.
column6: accept reluctantly, reconcile oneself to, come to terms with (overlap)
column7: I'm resigned to the fact that we'll probably have to start over. / She seemed resigned to waiting another hour.
column8: Productive pattern: be resigned to + noun/gerund; be resigned to the fact that... The feeling is reluctant/passive acceptance, stronger than neutral acceptance. Contrast resign from a job.

column5: The American family associated with Purdue Pharma, the maker of OxyContin; members of the family and the company became central subjects of litigation and public controversy over opioid marketing and the U.S. opioid crisis.
column7: The documentary examines the Sackler family's connection to Purdue Pharma and OxyContin. / Several museums reconsidered relationships with Sackler philanthropy.
column8: KEEP as a proper-name/context card, but avoid reducing a large family to a single undifferentiated legal claim. Use careful attribution: Purdue Pharma and members of the Sackler family have faced extensive litigation and criticism concerning opioid marketing.

column5: The quality or practice of including and welcoming different people, perspectives, or needs and enabling participation rather than exclusion.
column7: The city often presents inclusiveness as one of its core values. / The organization is trying to improve inclusiveness in its events.
column8: Normalize away from sentence headword 'Seattle is a city of inclusiveness'; preserve Seattle-style source context in examples if useful. Inclusion is usually the more common institutional noun. Diversity and inclusiveness are related but not synonyms.

column5: Conduct, speech, organization, or advocacy aimed at inciting resistance or revolt against lawful authority, especially government; its precise legal definition and criminal scope vary by jurisdiction.
column7: The government accused the organizers of sedition. / Historians debate how sedition laws have been used against political dissent.
column8: Legal/political term requiring jurisdictional caution. Do not define ordinary criticism of government as sedition. Related seditious.
