column12: entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::law topic::public_speaking topic::crime topic::government topic::politics discovery::nonconformity discovery::public_discourse discovery::debate_language

column5: To request a clearer explanation or additional information because something is ambiguous, incomplete, or uncertain.
column6: ask for clarification, request clarification, ask someone to clarify
column7: I emailed them to seek clarification on the new policy. / Could I ask for clarification about what you mean by 'final'?
column8: More idiomatic than 'seek a clarification' in most general contexts. A clarification is countable when referring to a specific clarifying statement, but seek clarification is the common collocation.
column12: entry::collocation entry::verb_pattern discovery::ambiguity discovery::clarification discovery::explanation discovery::expressing_need discovery::uncertainty

column5: Capable of experiencing sensations or feelings; in broader popular discussion, capable of subjective experience or awareness.
column6: feeling, conscious (overlap, not exact), capable of sensation
column7: The debate asks whether these animals should be regarded as sentient beings. / Science fiction often imagines sentient machines.
column8: Sentience and consciousness are related but not identical concepts, and definitions vary across philosophy/science. Avoid equating sentient simply with intelligent or self-aware.

column5: A distinctive routine, gimmick, style, persona, recurring bit, or habitual way of performing or presenting oneself.
column7: The fake outrage is part of his shtick. / Her whole shtick is pretending not to understand the obvious.
column8: From Yiddish. Shtick is common spelling; schtick also appears. Can be comedic but is broader than a formal comedy routine; often mildly dismissive.

column5: noun: an insulting or degrading term or remark, especially one targeting a group or identity; also a damaging accusation/insinuation. verb: to speak unclearly by running sounds together, or to insult/defame.
column6: insult, epithet, smear; mumble/slur speech (other sense)
column7: The comment contained an ethnic slur. / He considered the accusation a slur on his reputation. / Her speech became slurred as she grew exhausted.
column8: Important polysemy: identity-based slur; slur on someone's reputation; slurred speech/music notation. Avoid treating every insult as a slur in the narrower identity-based sense.

column5: A clever or plausible-looking but false, misleading, or logically unsound argument, especially one used to deceive or evade the real issue.
column6: specious argument, fallacy, sophistry, deceptive reasoning
column7: The claim sounds persuasive at first, but it's really a sophism. / He dismissed the argument as political sophistry.
column8: Formal/philosophical. Sophism can mean a particular deceptive argument; sophistry is the practice/use of such reasoning. Not every logical fallacy is intentionally deceptive.

column5: To spend more money than usual, often on something enjoyable or nonessential; as a noun, an instance of extravagant spending or indulgence.
column6: indulge, treat oneself, spend freely, splash out (BrE)
column7: I splurged on a nicer hotel for the last night of the trip. / The new headphones were a bit of a splurge.
column8: Common: splurge on something; splurge and buy... It can be playful/positive, not necessarily irresponsible. Contrast squander = waste money.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::word entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::playful usage::british_english

column5: Easily made uncomfortable, nauseated, shocked, or embarrassed by blood, injury, bodily matters, violence, or certain morally/socially unpleasant subjects.
column7: I'm squeamish about blood, so I looked away. / The film isn't for squeamish viewers.
column8: Common: squeamish about/at; not for the squeamish. Can extend beyond physical disgust to excessive delicacy about discussing/doing unpleasant things.

column2: take a leaf out of someone's book
column3: /teɪk ə liːf aʊt əv ˈsʌmwʌnz bʊk/
column5: To copy or learn from someone's good example, method, or behavior.
column6: follow someone's example, take a page from someone's book (AmE)
column7: You should take a leaf out of her book and start planning earlier. / Maybe I should take a page from your book and stop checking email at night.
column8: BrE commonly leaf; AmE equivalent is take a page out of someone's book. Usually implies the model is worth imitating.

column5: A long, forceful, angry speech or piece of criticism, often attacking a person, group, or issue.
column7: He launched into a tirade about the new rules. / We sat through a twenty-minute tirade against the media.
column8: Common: launch into/go on a tirade; tirade against/about. Rant is more everyday; diatribe more formal/written; harangue often forceful lecturing.

column5: The path an object follows through space; figuratively, the direction and pattern in which a career, trend, relationship, economy, or situation develops over time.
column7: The missile's trajectory changed after launch. / Her career trajectory shifted dramatically after that role. / The company is on a very different trajectory now.
column8: Preserve literal physics + highly common figurative use. Collocations: career/growth/upward/downward trajectory; change/alter a trajectory.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::scientific topic::work topic::relationships discovery::figurative_extension

column5: adjective: vertical or straight rather than leaning; behaving honestly and morally. noun: a vertical supporting part or an upright piano.
column7: Keep the bottle upright. / He was widely regarded as an upright public servant. / They bought a small upright piano.
column8: Current card only moral sense is too narrow. Important everyday physical sense. Contrast uptight = tense/overly strict, a common confusable.

column5: A tip or service payment that is genuinely optional rather than automatically required; wording often appears in hospitality, cruise, or service contexts.
column7: A voluntary gratuity may be added by the guest at the end of the meal. / Check whether the 'gratuity' is actually optional or automatically included.
column8: Useful distinction: gratuity commonly means tip, but an automatically imposed service charge is not voluntary merely because it is labeled gratuity. Exact legal treatment varies by jurisdiction.

column5: Displayed, expressed, or exemplified on a larger, clearer, or more conspicuous scale; sometimes used to mean an enlarged version of something.
column6: on a grand scale, magnified, clearly exemplified
column7: The scandal was the company's culture writ large. / The neighborhood is, in some ways, the city's inequality writ large.
column8: Formal/literary. Pattern X writ large = X manifested on a larger scale. 'Writ' here is an archaic past participle of write, not the legal noun writ.

column5: noun: an intuitive feeling or suspicion not based on firm evidence; also a bent posture. verb: to bend the body forward/upward, especially the shoulders.
column7: I have a hunch that he's going to cancel. / My hunch turned out to be right. / She hunched over the laptop for hours.
column8: Add physical verb/noun cluster. Common intuition patterns: have a hunch; on a hunch; my hunch is that... A hunch is weaker than evidence.

column5: Excessively sentimental, emotional, or self-pitying, especially in a tearful or drunken way.
column7: After a few drinks, he became maudlin and started talking about his childhood. / The ending is emotional without becoming maudlin.
column8: Usually negative. Stronger/more literary than sentimental. Often describes drunken sentimentality or art that feels cloyingly emotional.

column5: To place someone in an uncomfortable position where they must answer, decide, perform, or respond immediately under pressure.
column6: pressure, corner, force an immediate response
column7: I don't want to put you on the spot, but can you give us an answer today? / The interviewer put him on the spot with a very personal question.
column8: Very useful conversational softener: 'I don't mean to put you on the spot, but...' Not necessarily hostile; can happen unintentionally.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::conversational usage::debate-friendly topic::communication topic::debate discovery::debate_language

column5: To use every available resource, effort, technique, or advantage to achieve something or make an occasion impressive.
column6: go all out, spare no effort, do everything possible
column7: They pulled out all the stops to finish before the deadline. / The hotel pulled out all the stops for the wedding.
column8: Origin relates to organ stops, but active use does not require knowing etymology. Common with efforts/events/campaigns.

column5: To speak to someone suddenly and sharply, usually because of irritation, stress, or anger.
column6: snarl at, bark at, speak sharply to, bite someone's head off (stronger)
column7: Sorry I snapped at you earlier—I was stressed. / She snapped at him to leave her alone.
column8: Snap at is a brief sharp verbal reaction. Compare lash out = broader/stronger attack; bite someone's head off = exaggerated informal expression.

column5: To travel, move, extend, or pass across or through an area; in technical contexts, to move across a structure, surface, network, or data structure.
column6: cross, travel across, pass through, span
column7: We traversed the valley before sunset. / The cable traverses the entire building. / The algorithm traverses the tree recursively.
column8: Normalize lemma. More formal/technical than cross. Computing, climbing, surveying, and geography all use specialized senses.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal usage::technical usage::specialist topic::travel discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: verb: to pull, drag, carry, or transport something heavy or with effort; noun: an amount transported/caught/stolen/bought, or a long journey, especially a difficult one.
column6: drag, pull, transport, lug; load, catch, take
column7: We hauled the boxes up three flights of stairs. / The truck was hauling lumber. / The police recovered a large haul of stolen goods. / It was a long haul home.
column8: Major polysemy. Productive: haul something away/out/up; long haul; shopping haul; fishing haul. Do not keep only verb.

column5: The quantity or collection of fish or other catch taken during a fishing trip, netting, or period; haul more broadly means an amount obtained, carried, bought, or seized.
column7: The crew brought in a large fishing haul that morning. / Today's haul included tuna and mackerel.
column8: Could later merge with WID740 if global duplicate consolidation favors one deep haul card. For now KEEP because source phrase may aid retrieval; explicitly link to general noun haul.

column5: To preserve, protect, or establish an idea, right, principle, or rule as especially important or authoritative; literally, to place or preserve something in a shrine.
column6: embed, establish, protect, preserve, codify (some contexts)
column7: Freedom of expression is enshrined in the constitution. / The agreement enshrined the principle in law. / The relic was enshrined in the temple.
column8: Normalize lemma. Very common passive: be enshrined in law/the constitution. 'Codify' overlaps only when formally written into a code.

column5: Having a very strong, sharp smell or taste; figuratively, sharply expressive, biting, or penetrating in language or criticism.
column7: The kitchen was filled with the pungent smell of garlic. / The cheese has a pungent flavor. / She offered a pungent critique of the policy.
column8: Strong smell/taste can be pleasant or unpleasant. Figurative pungent wit/commentary is less common but useful. Compare acrid = usually harsh/unpleasant.

column2: have a bump on one's eyelid / eyelid bump
column5: To have a small lump or swelling on the eyelid; everyday description only, not the name of a specific condition.
column6: eyelid lump, eyelid swelling, bump on the eyelid
column7: I've got a small bump on my eyelid. / She noticed a tender lump near the edge of her eyelid.
column8: Keep as productive everyday symptom-description language, but remove diagnostic speculation from the definition. Specific causes require medical evaluation; vocabulary card should not imply every bump is an infection or stye.

column5: A localized, usually painful red lump near the edge of an eyelid caused by inflammation/infection of an eyelid gland or follicle.
column7: I woke up with a painful stye on my upper eyelid. / She gets styes occasionally when her eyelids are irritated.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Stye and sty are accepted spellings; stye avoids confusion with pigsty. Distinguish from chalazion, which is typically a blocked gland and often less acutely painful.

column5: A middle-school-aged person who deliberately adopts provocative, dark, shocking, cynical, or rebellious attitudes to seem bold, mature, or unconventional.
column7: That joke has the energy of an edgy middle schooler trying to shock everyone. / The character sounds less dangerous than like an edgy middle schooler.
column8: KEEP as source-driven descriptive/slang phrase, not a standardized lexical item. 'Edgy' itself has several meanings: tense/on edge; bold/innovative; deliberately provocative. Here the third cluster is intended.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::slang topic::education discovery::impression discovery::nonconformity

column5: A view or attitude that distrusts, challenges, or opposes established political, social, cultural, or economic institutions and power structures.
column6: anti-system stance, anti-institutional attitude, oppositional view
column7: The movement attracted voters with a strongly anti-establishment message. / His anti-establishment attitude shaped his criticism of both major parties.
column8: Hyphenate anti-establishment. It does not specify left/right ideology; movements across the political spectrum can be anti-establishment.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::debate-friendly topic::culture topic::politics topic::debate topic::economics discovery::debate_language discovery::public_discourse

column5: Carefully attentive to advice, warnings, risks, needs, or circumstances.
column7: Be heedful of the warning signs. / A good editor is heedful of both tone and context.
column8: Somewhat formal/literary and much less common than mindful/aware. Pattern heedful of. Related heed (v./n.) and heedless.

column5: Used to indicate that a claim can reasonably be argued or supported, while acknowledging that others may disagree.
column6: it can be argued that, plausibly, perhaps (weaker)
column7: This is arguably the best episode of the season. / She is arguably one of the most influential writers of her generation.
column8: Useful hedging device in analytical writing and conversation. It does not mean 'definitely'; nor does it necessarily mean the speaker personally doubts the claim.

column5: 1. To discuss or consult together. 2. To formally grant or bestow a degree, title, honor, right, status, or benefit.
column7: The lawyers conferred before answering. / The university conferred an honorary degree on her. / Citizenship confers certain rights.
column8: Two distinct constructions: confer with someone = consult; confer something on/upon someone = formally grant. Very useful contrast with bestow and award.

column5: To voluntarily or reluctantly give up, release, surrender, or stop holding a possession, right, claim, position, control, or responsibility.
column6: give up, surrender, yield, renounce, release
column7: He refused to relinquish control of the company. / She relinquished her claim to the property. / The champion was forced to relinquish the title.
column8: Formal. Relinquish emphasizes ceasing to hold/control something. Contrast waive = intentionally forgo a right/requirement; renounce = formally reject/abandon; surrender can imply yielding under pressure.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::assertion discovery::release discovery::debate_language

column5: To intentionally give up, forgo, or choose not to enforce a right, claim, requirement, fee, rule, or privilege.
column6: forgo, relinquish, give up, dispense with (some contexts)
column7: You may be asked to waive your right to a hearing. / The airline waived the change fee. / The requirement was waived for returning students.
column8: Normalize lemma. Key confusable wave. Common legal/admin patterns: waive a right/fee/requirement; waive enforcement. Unlike relinquish, waive often concerns a right or rule that could otherwise be invoked.

column5: An academic degree awarded by an institution as an honor, usually recognizing achievement or contribution, without the recipient completing the normal degree requirements.
column7: The university awarded her an honorary degree for her contributions to public health. / He received an honorary doctorate.
column8: An honorary degree is not the same as an earned academic qualification. Institutions differ in naming and conventions. Common verbs: award/confer/bestow an honorary degree.

column5: To formally give, present, or confer an honor, title, gift, right, quality, or benefit, often ceremonially or in elevated language.
column7: The foundation bestowed its highest honor on her. / The title was bestowed upon him after the ceremony.
column8: Formal/elevated. Pattern bestow something on/upon someone. Compare confer: confer also means consult; bestow only has the giving/granting cluster.

column5: Boldly rude, disrespectful, or contemptuous, especially toward someone in authority or someone considered deserving of respect.
column7: The officer considered his reply insolent. / She gave the teacher an insolent stare.
column8: Stronger/more formal than rude. Often implies defiant disrespect. Compare impudent/impertinent: close, with register and nuance differences.

column5: To make a usually small or accidental mistake, especially after trying to be careful; noun: slip-up.
column6: make a mistake, mess up, make an error
column7: I slipped up and sent the email to the wrong person. / One small slip-up cost them the game.
column8: Often implies an accidental lapse rather than incompetence. Noun is hyphenated: a slip-up. Compare screw up = stronger/more informal.

column5: A container, holder, or place designed to receive, contain, or collect something; also a technical term in botany/electrical contexts.
column7: Please put used batteries in the designated receptacle. / The wall receptacle needs to be replaced.
column8: Formal/generic. In North American electrical usage, receptacle can mean an electrical outlet/socket component. Context determines sense.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::technical usage::north_american_english usage::specialist topic::engineering discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::terminology discovery::containment discovery::specialist_register

column5: 1. Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably, especially in price, mood, politics, or conditions. 2. Easily evaporated at ordinary temperatures. 3. Potentially explosive or suddenly violent in behavior/situation.
column6: unstable, unpredictable, turbulent; evaporative; explosive, hot-tempered
column7: Markets have been extremely volatile this week. / Gasoline contains volatile compounds. / He has a volatile temper.
column8: Major polysemy: finance/politics, chemistry, temperament. Volatile does not inherently mean 'bad', though rapid unpredictability often creates risk.

column5: To leave or flee suddenly; to make/print copies quickly; to flow or drain away; to cause someone/something to leave. Related noun runoff = water or an additional election round.
column6: flee, dash away; print; drain; chase off
column7: He ran off before I could ask his name. / I'll run off a few copies. / Rainwater runs off the roof into the gutter. / The dog ran the deer off.
column8: Current card mixes verb with noun-like drainage. Keep phrasal verb senses distinct and note runoff is one word as a noun. Also 'run off with' = steal/elope with, a separate productive extension.

column5: To cancel a planned event, activity, search, attack, or arrangement; also to order a person/animal to stop attacking or pursuing.
column6: cancel, cancel plans, abort; recall, restrain
column7: They called off the game because of the storm. / The police called off the search at midnight. / Call off your dog!
column8: Separable: call it/the meeting off. 'Call off your dog' preserves literal order-to-stop sense. Compare put off = postpone, not cancel.

column5: To stop a process, mission, plan, or operation before completion, often because continuing is unsafe or impossible; in medicine, abort has specialized pregnancy-related meanings requiring context.
column7: The crew aborted the landing because of strong crosswinds. / The launch was aborted at the last second. / The program aborted after encountering a fatal error.
column8: Normalize lemma. Common technical/aviation/computing sense is important. Medical meanings are context-sensitive; avoid collapsing spontaneous pregnancy loss, induced abortion, and general 'stop early' into one vague definition.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical usage::specialist topic::grammar topic::medicine topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::process_details discovery::specialist_register

column5: To remove a ruler, government, or established system from power, especially by force or political upheaval; as a noun, the act of doing so.
column7: The rebels attempted to overthrow the government. / The coup led to the overthrow of the regime.
column8: Can be verb or noun. Strong political term; not every election defeat is an overthrow. Past tense overthrew; past participle overthrown.

column5: Not producing the intended or needed effect; lacking the ability, force, or competence to achieve results.
column7: The response was slow and ineffectual. / He was portrayed as an ineffectual leader who couldn't control his own cabinet.
column8: Often more personal/evaluative than ineffective: an ineffectual person/leader can imply weakness or inability to act effectively. Do not confuse with ineffective, which is more neutral/general.

column5: Literally, for a wound or sore to become infected or produce pus; figuratively, for resentment, conflict, problems, or grievances to worsen because they are ignored or unresolved.
column7: Don't let the resentment fester—talk to her about it. / The dispute had been festering for years. / The untreated wound began to fester.
column8: Normalize lemma and preserve literal + figurative. Figurative collocations: festering resentment/grievance/conflict/problem.

column5: A prolonged, bitter conflict or quarrel between people, families, groups, organizations, or public figures; as a verb, to remain in such conflict.
column7: The two families had been locked in a feud for decades. / The musicians feuded publicly for years.
column8: Often long-running and personal. Common: feud with; feud over; ongoing/bitter/longstanding feud. Rivalry can be competitive without hostility, so not exact.

column5: noun: a thorough investigation or inquiry; an instrument/device used to examine or explore. verb: to investigate closely or physically explore/examine.
column7: The agency launched a probe into the allegations. / Reporters probed the company's finances. / The spacecraft sent a probe into the outer solar system.
column8: Major polysemy. News collocation launch/open a probe into. Verb can sound intrusive: probe into someone's private life. Also medical/scientific instrument.

column5: To demand that someone be fired, removed from office, punished, or held personally responsible, especially after a failure or scandal.
column6: demand someone's resignation, demand someone be fired, call for removal
column7: After the loss, angry fans were calling for the coach's head. / Critics called for the minister's head over the scandal.
column8: Figurative; usually not a literal demand for execution in modern everyday use. Strong, dramatic expression common in politics/sports/media.

column5: To force a rule, tax, penalty, restriction, burden, or condition to be accepted; to place an unwelcome demand on someone; reflexively, impose on someone = take unfair advantage of their hospitality/time.
column7: The government imposed new restrictions. / The court imposed a fine. / I don't want to impose on you, but could I stay one more night?
column8: Normalize lemma and add interpersonal sense. Patterns: impose something on someone; impose a tax/ban/sentence; impose on someone's kindness/time.

column5: A serious break, disagreement, or estrangement in a relationship or group; literally, a crack, split, or fissure.
column7: The dispute caused a rift between the two friends. / A deep rift developed within the party. / Geologists studied the rift in the Earth's crust.
column8: Preserve literal geology + figurative relationship/political sense. Common: rift between; rift within; heal/widen/deepen a rift.

column5: A portion of a company's profits distributed to shareholders; figuratively, a benefit or return produced by an earlier investment, effort, or policy.
column7: The company increased its quarterly dividend. / Years of investment in education are beginning to pay dividends.
column8: Important figurative plural: pay dividends = produce benefits/results. Finance: dividend yield, declare/pay/cut a dividend. Not every company pays dividends.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative topic::business topic::finance discovery::policy_discussion discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Characteristically grumpy, irritable, cantankerous, or complaining, often in a way associated with an older or habitually grouchy person.
column7: The curmudgeonly neighbor complained about every little noise. / Beneath his curmudgeonly exterior, he was surprisingly generous.
column8: Often mildly humorous/literary rather than purely hostile. Related noun curmudgeon.

column5: To be represented at a higher rate than a comparison baseline; more loosely, especially in business/online discussion, to place disproportionate emphasis on or give too much weight to something.
column6: be overrepresented, skew high; overemphasize, overweight
column7: Young viewers over-index in this audience segment. / I think we're over-indexing on one bad review and ignoring the broader pattern.
column8: Correct headword from 'over indexing'. Two related jargon clusters: statistical/marketing overrepresentation and looser 'focus too much on'. Hyphenation over-index/over-indexing is common.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::word entry::verb_pattern usage::specialist topic::business topic::internet discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::comparison discovery::emphasis discovery::specialist_register

column5: To visibly or strongly display a quality, feeling, or impression; literally, for a substance to slowly release or ooze from something.
column7: She exudes confidence without seeming arrogant. / The room exuded warmth and calm. / The plant exudes a sticky sap when cut.
column8: Preserve literal + figurative. Common figurative: exude confidence/charm/warmth/authority. Often positive but not inherently.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::warm discovery::impression discovery::evaluation discovery::release

column5: Relating to exurbs: relatively low-density communities beyond the suburbs of a metropolitan area, often economically connected to the metro through commuting or employment.
column7: Housing expanded rapidly in exurban counties around the city. / The report compares urban, suburban, and exurban voting patterns.
column8: Do not define simply as 'inhabited by commuters'; exurbs vary. Related noun exurb. Boundaries are not universally standardized.

column5: A licensed eye-care professional trained to examine vision and eye health, prescribe corrective lenses, and provide certain forms of eye care; scope of practice varies by jurisdiction.
column6: eye doctor (broad everyday term), vision-care professional
column7: I made an appointment with an optometrist for an eye exam. / The optometrist updated my glasses prescription.
column8: Distinguish optometrist from ophthalmologist (medical doctor specializing in eye disease/surgery) and optician (fits/dispenses eyewear). Exact legal scope varies by location.

column2: tiptoe / on tiptoe / on one's tiptoes
column5: To walk quietly or carefully on the balls/front of the feet with the heels raised; to stand or rise with the heels raised.
column6: walk softly, creep; stand on one's toes
column7: I tiptoed out of the room so I wouldn't wake her. / She stood on tiptoe to reach the shelf. / He rose onto his tiptoes.
column8: Normalize nonstandard 'tippy toes'. Childlike tippy-toes/tiptoes exists informally, but productive standard vocabulary is tiptoe / on tiptoe / on one's tiptoes.

column5: Easy to tip or overturn; unstable because of a high center of gravity or poor balance. In some informal contexts, it can also mean slightly unsteady, but that use is less standardized.
column6: unstable, top-heavy, wobbly, easy to tip
column7: That little table is too tippy for a heavy lamp. / The canoe felt tippy when I first got in.
column8: Remove unsupported claim that it 'often' means mildly intoxicated. The robust sense is prone to tipping/unstable. For intoxication, tipsy is the standard word and a key confusable.

column5: Latin for 'queen'; also used historically in royal titles and in proper names/place names derived from Latin.
column7: In Latin, regina means 'queen.' / The phrase 'Regina Caeli' literally includes the word for queen.
column8: KEEP as Latin/source-language card. Do not imply every modern occurrence of Regina is a royal title; it is also a personal name and place name. Pronunciation varies by language/context.

column5: To experience consequences that correspond to one's earlier actions or choices, whether good or bad.
column6: face the consequences, get what you deserve (often negative), actions have consequences
column7: If you treat people badly for years, eventually you may reap what you sow. / The proverb can also be positive: invest patiently now and reap what you sow later.
column8: Agricultural metaphor: sow seeds → later reap the crop. Often used negatively, but the logic itself can apply to positive outcomes too.

column5: Able to chemically eat away or damage materials; figuratively, gradually destructive to relationships, institutions, trust, morale, or character.
column7: The chemical is highly corrosive to metal. / Constant suspicion can have a corrosive effect on a relationship.
column8: Literal chemistry + figurative social/emotional use. Corrosive ≠ poisonous; a substance can be corrosive because it damages tissue/material.

column5: Relating to infection or sepsis; contaminated by harmful microorganisms. Also used in septic tank/system, where it refers to an on-site sewage-treatment system rather than 'infected.'
column7: Doctors were concerned that the wound had become septic. / The house uses a septic system instead of a municipal sewer.
column8: Current definition is too narrow and risks conflating septic with sepsis. Add extremely common septic tank/system sense. Medical use should remain descriptive, not diagnostic.

column5: To suddenly surprise or frighten someone, causing a brief involuntary reaction.
column6: startle, give someone a fright, make someone jump
column7: You gave me a start—I didn't hear you come in. / The sudden knock gave her quite a start.
column8: Normalize from 'give me a start'. Especially BrE; AmE speakers more often say 'you startled me' / 'you scared me' / 'made me jump'. Not the same as give someone a head start.

column5: To interfere in a situation, activity, or other people's affairs without being invited or wanted; meddle with can also mean tamper with something.
column6: interfere, intrude, butt in; tamper with
column7: I wish he'd stop meddling in my personal life. / Don't meddle with the settings unless you know what you're doing.
column8: Patterns matter: meddle in someone's affairs/business; meddle with equipment. Usually disapproving. Compare intervene: can be legitimate/helpful.

column5: To know very little or nothing; most commonly used negatively as 'not know jack about something.'
column6: know nothing, not know a thing, not know squat (slang)
column7: He doesn't know jack about cars. / I knew jack about coding when I started.
column8: Normalize usage profile: affirmative 'know jack' is uncommon outside special constructions; negative not know jack is the productive slang idiom. Informal and mildly coarse; 'jack shit' is much more vulgar.

column5: To become detached; to happen or succeed as planned; to appear or make an impression in a particular way; in some constructions, to stop using a drug/medication or leave a stage/field.
column6: detach, fall off; succeed; seem, come across
column7: The handle came off in my hand. / The event came off better than expected. / I hope I didn't come off as rude. / He came off the medication gradually under medical guidance.
column8: Major polysemy. High-value conversational pattern come off as + adjective/noun. 'Come off it!' is a separate informal exclamation meaning stop talking nonsense/pretending.

column5: Extreme moral corruption, wickedness, or degradation; the state or quality of being depraved.
column7: The novel depicts both cruelty and human depravity. / Prosecutors described the crime in highly charged language about depravity.
column8: Strong moralizing word, often used for severe wrongdoing. Related depraved. Avoid using casually for mere bad manners or ordinary flaws.

column5: For a quality, habit, attitude, skill, or behavior to be gradually acquired from another person through contact or influence; literally, rub off = be removed by rubbing.
column6: influence, transfer, be picked up, wear off (literal removal differs)
column7: Her optimism is starting to rub off on me. / Spend enough time with him and some of his habits may rub off on you. / The ink rubbed off on my fingers.
column8: Normalize from 'rub off on you'. Figurative pattern: X rubs off on someone. Literal rub off is separate and common.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative topic::self-help discovery::evaluation

column5: A gland in the male reproductive system located below the bladder and surrounding part of the urethra; it contributes fluid to semen.
column7: The doctor explained where the prostate is located. / Prostate health becomes a common topic in men's health discussions with age.
column8: Anatomy vocabulary only; avoid implying symptoms/diagnoses. Key confusable spelling: prostate (gland) vs prostrate (lying flat/exhausted).

column5: Cancer that begins in the colon; colorectal cancer is the broader term covering cancers of the colon and rectum.
column7: The article discusses screening for colon cancer. / Colorectal cancer includes cancers of both the colon and rectum.
column8: Keep vocabulary precise: colon cancer is not exactly synonymous with all colorectal cancer. Avoid treatment/screening recommendations unless separately requested.

column5: Anxious, uneasy, or fearful about something that may happen in the future.
column7: I was apprehensive about speaking in front of the whole group. / She felt apprehensive as the deadline approached.
column8: Common: apprehensive about; apprehensive that... Usually anticipatory anxiety. Do not confuse with apprehend = understand/arrest.

column5: To establish or improve a favorable relationship with someone, often because their approval, influence, or help may be useful.
column6: get on someone's good side, curry favor with, ingratiate oneself with
column7: He's trying to get in good with the new manager. / She got in good with the organizers and started getting invited to every event.
column8: Often implies strategic/self-interested friendliness, though not always sinister. 'Curry favor' and 'ingratiate oneself' are more explicitly calculated/formal.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::formal usage::informal usage::american_english topic::relationships discovery::social_approval discovery::improvement

column5: Short, stiff hair that has grown back after shaving or cutting, especially facial hair; also short stalks left in a field after crops are harvested.
column6: short beard growth, five-o'clock shadow (specific); crop stubble
column7: He had two days of stubble on his face. / The fields were covered in wheat stubble after harvest.
column8: Add agricultural sense. Usually uncountable. Five-o'clock shadow is a specific light facial-stubble appearance, not exact synonym for all stubble.

column2: become second nature / be second nature
column5: To become so familiar through repetition or practice that an action feels automatic, effortless, or instinctive.
column6: become automatic, become instinctive, become habitual
column7: After a few months, using the shortcuts became second nature. / Checking mirrors before changing lanes is second nature to her.
column8: Normalize from full sentence 'it becomes second nature'. Common: become second nature; be second nature to someone; doing X is second nature.

column2: come back to bite someone / come back to bite someone in the ass
column3: /ɪt wɪl kʌm bæk tu baɪt ju/
column5: For an earlier action, decision, shortcut, lie, or neglected problem to cause trouble or negative consequences later.
column6: backfire, haunt someone, catch up with someone
column7: If you cut corners now, it may come back to bite you later. / That old lie eventually came back to bite him.
column8: Normalize productive pattern. 'In the ass' is a vulgar/emphatic extension. Often warns about delayed consequences. Compare reap what you sow: broader moral/consequence proverb.

column5: Offensive, obscene, irreverent, or taboo language, especially swear words; historically/religiously, language showing disrespect toward sacred things.
column6: swearing, curse words, obscenity (overlap), foul language
column7: The broadcast muted the profanity. / His speech was full of profanity.
column8: Usually uncountable as a category, though profanities can mean individual expressions. Profanity, obscenity, vulgarity, and slur overlap but are not identical.
column12: entry::word usage::offensive usage::profane usage::religious usage::evaluative topic::religion

column5: noun: a student who is absent from school without permission. adjective: absent without permission or neglecting a duty.
column7: The school contacted the parents of repeated truants. / He was reported truant after missing several days without permission.
column8: Related truancy. 'Truant' can be adjective: truant students. Absentee is broader and does not imply unauthorized absence.

column5: Unauthorized absence, especially from school; play hooky = deliberately skip school or sometimes work.
column6: skip school, ditch class, truant, skive (BrE)
column7: We played hooky and went to the movies. / He got caught playing hooky from school.
column8: Normalize to productive idiom play hooky. Hooky rarely functions as an ordinary standalone count noun. Compare truant/truancy = more formal; skive/skive off = BrE.
column12: entry::idiom entry::noun_phrase usage::formal usage::informal usage::american_english usage::british_english topic::work topic::education

column5: Full of anxiety, dissatisfaction, emotional tension, brooding, or existential frustration, often in a way associated with adolescence, art, or subculture.
column7: I listened to a lot of angsty music as a teenager. / The character is intense and angsty without being completely humorless.
column8: Informal derivative of angst. Can be teasing/dismissive, not a clinical description. Often collocates with teen/teenager/music/lyrics/character.

column5: A teenager characterized—often stereotypically or humorously—as brooding, anxious, emotionally intense, dissatisfied, or rebellious.
column6: brooding teenager, moody teen, troubled teen (not exact)
column7: The protagonist starts out as a classic angsty teen but becomes more self-aware. / I was an angsty teenager who wrote dramatic journal entries.
column8: KEEP as a source-driven phrase if retrieval value matters, but link explicitly to WID799 angsty. Do not define ordinary adolescent emotion as pathology. Possible later merge candidate if global reconciliation decides adjective + phrase are redundant.

column5: A Japanese slang term, literally 'second-year middle-school syndrome,' for adolescent-style grandiosity, affected edginess, fantasies of hidden powers or special destiny, or behavior seen as trying too hard to appear unique, mature, dark, or mysterious.
column6: eighth-grader syndrome (translation), adolescent grandiosity, edgy fantasy persona (contextual)
column7: The character acts like a classic chūnibyō, inventing secret powers and dramatic titles. / I went through a mild chuunibyou phase where everything had to sound mysterious.
column8: KEEP as Japanese cultural/slang vocabulary. The term is often humorous or teasing, not a clinical diagnosis. Anime/manga usage strongly features delusions of supernatural power, but real-world usage can be broader: pretentious, self-dramatizing adolescent behavior.
column12: entry::term entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::humorous usage::playful usage::evaluative usage::informal topic::anime topic::manga topic::fandom topic::culture topic::education discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::evaluation discovery::social_approval discovery::impression

column5: Using, involving, or combining multiple modes, channels, types of data, or forms of communication.
column7: The course uses a multimodal approach combining text, video, discussion, and hands-on work. / The model can perform multimodal reasoning across text and images.
column8: Broader than AI. Used in communication, education, transportation, medicine, interfaces, and machine learning. The exact 'modes' depend on domain.

column5: Artificial intelligence that can work with more than one data modality—such as text, images, audio, video, or sensor data—whether by understanding, generating, or connecting information across those modalities.
column6: multimodal model, multimodal system, vision-language model (narrower)
column7: A multimodal AI system might analyze an image while answering a spoken question about it. / Some multimodal models can accept text, images, and audio as input.
column8: Do not define multimodal AI as necessarily supporting every modality or every input/output combination. 'Vision-language model' is a narrower subtype involving vision and language.

column5: Existing beyond what is openly stated or immediately apparent; usually used of a hidden additional purpose or motive.
column7: I wondered whether there was some ulterior purpose behind the offer. / The question seemed innocent, but it may have had an ulterior aim.
column8: In modern everyday English, ulterior is strongly associated with motive/motives, purpose, agenda, reason. It does not simply mean 'secret' in every context.

column5: A hidden or undisclosed reason for doing something, especially one that is self-interested, manipulative, or different from the reason presented openly.
column6: hidden agenda, secret motive, underlying motive
column7: She offered to help with no ulterior motive. / He suspected that their sudden generosity came with an ulterior motive.
column8: Very common phrase. Often negative, but 'no ulterior motive' is also frequent. Distinguish motive (reason for action) from intention (what one plans to do).

column5: To use authority, pressure, or strict supervision to make people work harder, faster, or more obediently.
column6: push hard, pressure, drive, lay down the law (some contexts)
column7: The manager started cracking the whip as the deadline approached. / We need someone to crack the whip and keep the project moving.
column8: Usually figurative today and can sound joking or critical. Implies forceful management, not merely encouragement.
column12: entry::idiom usage::humorous usage::figurative usage::critical topic::work topic::law

column5: So close in a race, contest, poll, or competition that neither side has a clear lead.
column6: even, tied, too close to call, running level
column7: The two runners were neck and neck entering the final stretch. / The candidates are still neck and neck in the polls.
column8: Common: be/run neck and neck; a neck-and-neck race (hyphenated before noun). Origin is horse-racing imagery.

column5: noun: a shell-less terrestrial mollusk; a heavy punch; a small amount/shot of liquor; a projectile or various technical objects. verb: to hit hard; to move laboriously; in baseball, to hit for power.
column7: There was a slug on the garden path. / He took a slug to the shoulder. / She slugged the ball over the fence. / He took a slug of whiskey.
column8: Highly polysemous. For active vocabulary, prioritize animal + hard punch/slug someone + baseball slug. 'Slug of liquor' is informal. Avoid treating all technical senses as one concept.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::technical topic::sports discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The small cartilaginous projection of the outer ear immediately in front of the ear canal.
column7: The earbud rests near the tragus. / She got a tragus piercing.
column8: Anatomical term. Plural can be tragi or traguses depending register. Common everyday context: tragus piercing.

column5: For amusement, adventure, or curiosity, especially as a spontaneous or unserious impulse rather than a carefully planned decision.
column6: on a whim, for fun, impulsively, just for kicks
column7: We entered the contest on a lark and somehow won. / On a lark, they drove to the coast after dinner.
column8: Often implies playful spontaneity. Compare on a whim: spontaneous but not necessarily fun/playful.

column5: verb: to sit, rest, or be positioned on a high, narrow, or precarious place; noun: a place/position for sitting or a type of fish.
column6: sit, balance, roost; vantage point (some contexts)
column7: A bird perched on the fence. / She was perched on the edge of the sofa. / The village is perched high above the valley.
column8: Normalize lemma. Very productive passive/adjectival pattern be perched on/above/atop. Also noun perch and fish sense, though contextual priority is positional verb.

column5: Strikingly strange, bizarre, extravagant, or implausible, often beyond what seems normal or reasonable.
column7: He showed up in an outlandish costume. / At first the theory sounded outlandish, but part of it proved correct.
column8: Can describe appearance, behavior, claims, prices, plans. Not simply 'unfamiliar'; usually noticeably extreme or bizarre.

column5: An opening or aperture, especially a natural or artificial opening in the body, a machine, vessel, pipe, or other structure.
column7: The valve controls flow through a small orifice. / In anatomy, the term can refer to a bodily orifice.
column8: Formal/technical. Common in anatomy and engineering. In casual speech, bodily-orifice usage can sound clinical or deliberately comic.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::casual usage::technical usage::informal discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To drive back or repel an attack or advancing force; to cause intense disgust, aversion, or revulsion in someone.
column6: repel, drive back; disgust, revolt, sicken
column7: The defenders repulsed the attack. / His cruelty repulsed her. / I was repulsed by the smell.
column8: Two strong clusters: military/physical repel and emotional disgust. Related repulsive = disgusting; repulsion = aversion or physical force in science.

column5: To continue enduring a difficult, unpleasant, or discouraging situation until it ends or improves instead of quitting.
column6: persevere, tough it out, hang in there, see it through
column7: The first month was rough, but I decided to stick it out. / If you can stick it out until Friday, things should calm down.
column8: Often intransitive 'stick it out' or 'stick something out'. Emphasizes endurance despite wanting to quit.

column5: A smudge is a blurred, smeared, or dirty mark; to smudge is to make such a mark or blur something. Smudging can also refer to smoke-based ceremonial practices in some Indigenous and other spiritual contexts.
column7: I smudged the ink before it dried. / There was a dark smudge on the screen. / The article discusses ceremonial smudging in a specific cultural context.
column8: Normalize lemma and separate ordinary physical sense from ceremonial use. Avoid presenting diverse smoke-cleansing traditions as one generic practice; terminology and cultural significance vary.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::specialist usage::ceremonial discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: verb: to spread a substance messily over a surface; to make something dirty/blurred; figuratively, to damage someone's reputation with accusations. noun: a streak/mark or a damaging allegation/campaign.
column7: She smeared sunscreen across her face. / The wet ink smeared. / He called the allegation a political smear.
column8: Normalize lemma. Contrast smudge: smudge often emphasizes a blurred/dirty mark; smear emphasizes spreading a substance and has a strong figurative reputation-attack sense.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative topic::politics discovery::figurative_extension discovery::social_approval discovery::public_discourse

column5: Something that discourages or prevents an action by making it less attractive, more difficult, or more costly; also attributively, having a discouraging effect.
column7: The high fine is intended to act as a deterrent. / Visible security can have a deterrent effect.
column8: Common: deterrent to/against; act as a deterrent; deterrent effect. Deterrence is the strategy/process. A deterrent does not guarantee prevention.

column5: To worry a great deal about something, especially enough that it occupies one's thoughts; often used negatively to say something is not worth worrying about.
column6: worry about, fret over, agonize over
column7: I wouldn't lose sleep over one bad review. / She was losing sleep over the upcoming exam.
column8: Often figurative; actual insomnia is not required. Very common negative: 'I'm not going to lose any sleep over it.'

column5: To choose to do without, give up, or abstain from something that one could otherwise have or enjoy.
column6: go without, give up, abstain from, waive (some rights/benefits)
column7: We decided to forgo dessert and head home. / She forgone? No—she forwent the bonus to keep more staff employed.
column8: Irregular forms are rare but useful: forgo–forwent–forgone. Often writers avoid the awkward past by rephrasing. Distinguish forego, which historically can mean 'go before'; modern usage often confuses the spellings.

column5: To twist, squirm, or move the body repeatedly, especially because of pain, discomfort, strong emotion, or physical restraint.
column7: He was writhing in pain after the cramp. / The snake writhed in the grass. / She writhed with embarrassment at the memory.
column8: Normalize lemma. Common: writhe in pain/agony; writhe with embarrassment. Stronger/more dramatic than simply squirm.

column5: A twisted, strained, or unnatural position or movement of the body; figuratively, an elaborate or awkward distortion of reasoning, language, rules, or behavior.
column7: The performer twisted into astonishing contortions. / The argument requires some logical contortions to make it work.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Figurative 'mental/logical contortions' is highly useful. Related contort (verb).
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::figurative_extension discovery::debate_language

column5: To break apart into smaller pieces or components; figuratively, for an organization, relationship, plan, order, or situation to collapse or lose coherence.
column6: break apart, crumble, fall apart, decompose; collapse
column7: The old paper disintegrated when I touched it. / Their alliance began to disintegrate under pressure.
column8: Both physical and figurative. In science, disintegration can have specialized meanings. Compare dissolve: may become incorporated into liquid or disappear gradually, not necessarily fragment.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::specialist topic::relationships discovery::figurative_extension discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The process by which a gas or vapor becomes liquid; the resulting moisture droplets; also, in writing/science, the act of making something more compact or concentrated.
column6: moisture, water droplets; compression, abridgment (other sense)
column7: Condensation formed on the cold window. / Water vapor undergoes condensation as it cools. / The summary is a condensation of a much longer argument.
column8: Add less-common abstract sense. Common everyday pattern: condensation on windows/glass.

column5: A star near a celestial pole, especially Polaris in the Northern Hemisphere; figuratively, a guiding principle, ideal, or central point of reference.
column6: North Star, guiding star; guiding principle, lodestar
column7: Accuracy should be our polestar when we evaluate the data. / Polaris has long served as a pole star for navigation.
column8: Spelling pole star is common for astronomical literal sense; polestar is common figuratively. Lodestar is a close figurative synonym.

column5: To inform an authority or other person about someone's wrongdoing, rule-breaking, or secret behavior, usually with a negative implication of betrayal.
column6: rat someone out, tell on, inform on
column7: Who snitched on us to the teacher? / He said he wouldn't snitch on his friends.
column8: Compare WID714 rat someone out. Both are informal and negative; snitch can also be noun 'a snitch'. Later global reconciliation may retain both because they are independently common slang.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::slang discovery::betrayal

column2: hightail it / hightail it out of there
column5: To leave, flee, or move away very quickly, especially to escape trouble or because time is short.
column6: get out fast, flee, bolt, make a run for it
column7: As soon as we saw the storm coming, we hightailed it back to the car. / We should hightail it out of here before traffic gets worse.
column8: Very conversational AmE. Common extensions: hightail it home/back/out of there. Past: hightailed.

column5: A person, animal, phenomenon, or thing regarded as extraordinarily unusual or exceptional, sometimes admiringly and sometimes offensively.
column7: That athlete is a freak of nature—his speed at that size is unbelievable. / The storm was described as a freak of nature.
column8: Register warning: when applied to a person it can be admiring slang in sports, but 'freak' can also be insulting/dehumanizing. Context and tone matter.

column2: hang by a thread / hanging by a thread
column5: To be in an extremely precarious state, close to failure, loss, collapse, death, or termination.
column6: be on the brink, be in jeopardy, be precarious
column7: The deal is hanging by a thread. / His job hung by a thread after the investigation. / Their lead was hanging by a thread.
column8: Normalize productive verb. The 'thread' metaphor emphasizes a tiny remaining connection/support.

column5: To cause a sharp physical pain; figuratively, for words, criticism, rejection, or memories to cause sudden emotional pain.
column7: Her comment stung more than I expected. / Those words still sting years later. / My eyes stung from the smoke.
column8: Current phrase becomes a productive sting card while preserving 'words sting'. Past stung. Useful patterns: criticism stings; it stung to hear...; still stings.

column5: To behave in an excessively submissive, self-abasing, or pleading way, especially to gain forgiveness, favor, or mercy.
column7: I'm not going to grovel for forgiveness over a minor mistake. / The villain expected his enemies to grovel for mercy.
column8: Normalize lemma. Grovel can be literal 'lie/crawl low' historically but modern use is mainly figurative humiliation/subservience. Common: grovel to/before someone; grovel for forgiveness/mercy.

column5: To weaken, defeat, overwhelm, or cripple a person, organization, economy, system, or country so severely that it can barely function or resist.
column7: The cyberattack brought the company to its knees. / Years of war brought the economy to its knees.
column8: Broaden beyond 'humble someone'. Often used for systems/economies/businesses, not just people. Strong dramatic metaphor.

column5: A group, cluster, or network of related people, factors, ideas, symptoms, institutions, or other elements viewed together.
column7: The decision resulted from a constellation of political and economic pressures. / The region has a constellation of small research institutes.
column8: Figurative extension of constellation = group of stars. Often formal/analytical and suggests multiple interconnected factors rather than a random collection.

column5: Not religious, sacred, or controlled by a religious institution; relating to worldly/civil life. In some technical fields, secular can also mean occurring over a long time rather than cyclically.
column7: The country has a secular legal system. / She enjoys both sacred and secular music. / Economists sometimes distinguish secular trends from cyclical ones.
column8: Important polysemy: religion/social institutions + technical 'long-term/non-cyclical' sense in economics/science. 'Atheist' is not a synonym.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::religious topic::religion discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The main force, shock, burden, or worst impact of something unpleasant.
column7: Coastal towns bore the brunt of the storm. / Junior employees took the brunt of the criticism.
column8: Almost always in fixed pattern bear/take/feel the brunt of. Usually negative force/impact.

column5: One's deepest tender emotions, especially feelings of sympathy, affection, sadness, or sentimentality.
column7: The reunion scene really tugged at my heartstrings. / The ad was clearly designed to pull at viewers' heartstrings.
column8: Usually plural and especially in tug/pull at someone's heartstrings. Often sentimental and can imply deliberate emotional manipulation.

column5: To suddenly become hostile toward, attack, criticize, or betray someone who was previously tolerated, supported, or trusted.
column6: attack, betray, turn against, lash out at
column7: The crowd that had cheered him began to turn on him. / Even his closest allies eventually turned on him.
column8: Do not confuse with turn someone on = excite/interest/sexually arouse, which has different object placement. Here: turn on someone = become hostile.

column5: Freedom, flexibility, or available options to adjust one's actions, plans, position, or strategy as circumstances change.
column7: The tight budget leaves us very little room to maneuver. / She wants more room to manoeuvre in the negotiations.
column8: AmE maneuver; BrE manoeuvre. Can be literal physical room, but common figurative sense is strategic flexibility. Compare latitude and elbow room.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative usage::american_english usage::british_english usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::flexibility discovery::debate_language

column5: 1. Geographic distance north or south of the equator, measured in degrees. 2. Freedom or discretion to act, decide, interpret, or vary within limits.
column7: Managers have considerable latitude in how they schedule staff. / New York City lies at roughly 40.7 degrees north latitude.
column8: Major polysemy. Figurative pattern give/allow someone latitude; have considerable latitude. Not identical to room to maneuver: latitude often emphasizes permission/discretion.

column5: Enough physical space to move comfortably; figuratively, enough freedom or scope to act without excessive restriction or interference.
column7: The seats are cramped—I need more elbow room. / Give the team some elbow room to solve the problem their own way.
column8: Physical + figurative. More informal than latitude. Often implies freedom from crowding/micromanagement.

column5: noun: looseness or unused capacity; adjective: loose/not taut or insufficiently active/strict; verb: to reduce effort or loosen. Common idioms include cut someone some slack and pick/take up the slack.
column6: leeway, looseness, spare capacity; lax, loose
column7: There's too much slack in the rope. / Sales are slack this month. / Cut her some slack—she's new. / When he left, the rest of us had to pick up the slack.
column8: Highly polysemous. Do not reduce to 'freedom'. Productive idioms are important. Slack can also be a proper brand name, but that is separate.

column5: Habitual or repeated absence from work, school, or other expected attendance, especially when it creates an organizational problem.
column7: The company is trying to reduce employee absenteeism. / Chronic absenteeism has become a major concern for the school district.
column8: Does not always mean absence 'without good reason'; organizational statistics may include multiple kinds of absence. Truancy specifically implies unauthorized school absence.

column5: Floating without being anchored or controlled; figuratively, lacking direction, purpose, support, or stable connection.
column7: The boat was found adrift offshore. / After leaving college, he felt completely adrift. / The policy left local offices adrift without clear guidance.
column8: Literal maritime + figurative emotional/organizational. Common: set/cut adrift; feel adrift.

column2: rainbows and unicorns / all rainbows and unicorns
column5: An unrealistically cheerful, easy, idealized, or problem-free picture of reality; commonly used in negatives such as 'it's not all rainbows and unicorns.'
column6: sunshine and rainbows, rosy picture, utopia (contextual)
column7: Working for yourself isn't all rainbows and unicorns. / Her version of the story makes everything sound like rainbows and unicorns.
column8: Normalize productive family. Usually ironic/sarcastic, especially 'not all...'. Related 'sunshine and rainbows'.

column5: To reduce the strength, intensity, amplitude, effect, or concentration of something; in technical contexts, to weaken a signal, wave, pathogen, or force.
column7: The walls attenuate the wireless signal. / The intervention may attenuate the effect. / Some vaccines use attenuated organisms.
column8: Formal/technical. Common in engineering, physics, medicine, statistics. Related attenuation. 'Dampen' is good for signal/effect but not every technical context.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::technical usage::scientific discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Friendly, kindly, protective, or advisory in a way stereotypically associated with a good-natured uncle.
column7: He adopted an avuncular tone with the younger employees. / The host's avuncular manner put the nervous guest at ease.
column8: Formal/literary. Usually describes manner/tone/relationship, not literal kinship. Paternal can imply fatherly authority and is not exact.

column5: Relating to, forming, or situated around an axis; arranged along a central line or axis.
column7: The machine uses an axial fan. / The scan shows an axial view of the body. / Axial rotation occurs around a central axis.
column8: Technical term across anatomy, engineering, geometry, geology. Meaning depends on domain. Contrast radial = extending outward from a center/axis.

column5: To return to a worse condition, former bad habit, lower standard, or abandoned belief after a period of improvement or reform; backsliding is the process/state.
column7: I was exercising regularly, but I've started to backslide. / The report warns of democratic backsliding. / He worried about backsliding into old habits.
column8: Normalize lemma. Strong modern collocations: democratic backsliding; backslide into old habits. Relapse is closer for illness/addiction and not exact everywhere.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word topic::self-help discovery::process_details discovery::evaluation discovery::improvement

column5: To hesitate, refuse, or stop short because something seems unacceptable, difficult, expensive, or risky; also specialized sports/animal senses.
column7: They balked at the price. / She balked at signing the agreement without legal advice. / Investors balked when the terms changed.
column8: Normalize lemma. Very common pattern balk at + noun/gerund. In baseball, balk is a specific pitching violation; separate technical sense.
column12: entry::collocation entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical usage::specialist topic::animals discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::risk discovery::specialist_register

column5: verb: to uncover, reveal, or expose something; adjective: uncovered, minimal, empty, or lacking usual covering. Baring is the -ing form of bare.
column7: The dog bared its teeth. / She was baring her soul in the interview. / The room had bare walls and a bare wooden floor.
column8: Normalize lemma and distinguish bare from bear. Productive figurative: bare one's soul, bare one's teeth. Baring ≠ bearing.

column2: beat the dickens out of someone / the dickens
column5: The dickens is an old euphemistic exclamation meaning roughly 'the devil' or used for emphasis. In 'beat the dickens out of someone/something,' it intensifies the idea of beating, exhausting, or forcefully affecting.
column6: the devil, the heck; beat badly (phrase)
column7: That noise scared the dickens out of me. / The rough road beat the dickens out of the old car.
column8: Current definition is too narrow. 'The dickens' appears in scare the dickens out of, hurt like the dickens, what the dickens, etc. Old-fashioned/mildly humorous euphemism.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::dated usage::humorous discovery::emphasis discovery::escalation

column2: beat the fuck out of someone/something
column5: To beat, hit, damage, or overpower someone/something extremely severely; figuratively, it can also mean to outperform something by a huge margin in constructions like 'X beats the fuck out of Y.'
column6: beat badly, thrash, pummel; vastly outperform (figurative)
column7: He threatened to beat the fuck out of the guy. / This cheap setup beats the fuck out of my old one for convenience.
column8: Very vulgar and aggressive. Preserve recognition value but flag register strongly. Object can be a person or thing; figurative comparative use exists. Not appropriate in polite/professional contexts.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::figurative usage::vulgar usage::professional discovery::figurative_extension discovery::professional_context

column5: To impress, enchant, or overwhelm someone with brilliance, glamour, or spectacle; also to decorate something with sparkling rhinestones, gems, or similar ornaments.
column6: dazzle, impress, enchant; embellish with rhinestones
column7: The audience was bedazzled by the elaborate production. / She bedazzled the jacket with rhinestones.
column8: Normalize lemma. Modern decorative sense was popularized by the BeDazzler craft tool/brand but is now used generically as a verb. Figurative sense is older.

column5: To make something stronger, more substantial, more effective, larger, or better equipped.
column7: The company is beefing up security. / We need to beef up the examples in this section. / They beefed up the staff before the holiday rush.
column8: Normalize base form. Very productive with security, staff, defenses, résumé, argument, content. Informal but common.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::form_family entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::rhetorical discovery::debate_language

column5: To be appropriate, advisable, necessary, or in someone's interest; most commonly in 'it behooves someone to do something.'
column6: be advisable for, be wise for, be incumbent on (stronger/formal)
column7: It behooves us to check the numbers before making a claim. / It would behoove you to keep a copy of the receipt.
column8: Normalize from behooves. AmE behoove; BrE behove also occurs. Fixed impersonal construction is far more common than ordinary conjugated use.

column5: The quality or disposition of wishing to do good and act kindly toward others; also charitable generosity or a benevolent act/policy in formal contexts.
column7: He liked to present his philanthropy as an act of pure benevolence. / The ruler's supposed benevolence did not eliminate the power imbalance.
column8: Formal. Benevolence can describe kind intention, but in discussions of paternalism/power it may be critically framed. Related benevolent.

column5: A right, privilege, status, possession, or expectation regarded as belonging to someone by virtue of birth, ancestry, citizenship, or inherited tradition.
column6: inherited right, hereditary privilege, entitlement by birth
column7: He regarded access to the land as his birthright. / Citizenship by birth can confer rights that vary by country.
column8: Can be literal/legal, cultural, rhetorical, or biblical. Avoid implying a claimed birthright is necessarily legally valid.

column5: noun: a large covering for warmth. adjective: applying broadly to all cases without distinction. verb: to cover something completely or extensively.
column7: I grabbed an extra blanket. / The company imposed a blanket ban on personal devices. / Snow blanketed the city overnight.
column8: Major polysemy. Productive adjective: blanket ban/rule/statement/coverage. Verb: blanket an area in snow/smoke/advertising.

column5: In an obvious, conspicuous, and often shameless or offensive way, especially when violating a rule, truth, or expectation.
column7: The claim is blatantly false. / He was blatantly ignoring the rules.
column8: Usually negative. Common: blatantly obvious/false/unfair/illegal. 'Openly' is more neutral and not always equivalent.

column5: blue blood: aristocratic or noble ancestry, or a person of such ancestry; blue-blooded: aristocratic by birth.
column7: She came from an old blue-blood family. / The novel mocks a circle of wealthy blue bloods.
column8: Normalize morphology. Often historical, humorous, or critical. Plural noun 'blue bloods'. Hyphen usually in adjective blue-blooded.

column5: A serious or embarrassing mistake caused by carelessness, poor judgment, or ignorance; as a verb, to make such a mistake or move clumsily.
column7: The announcement was a major political blunder. / I blundered by sending the draft before checking it. / He blundered into the room in the dark.
column8: Noun often stronger than ordinary mistake. Verb also has physical 'move clumsily' and 'blunder into' figurative accidental-entry senses.

column5: Standardized text, language, code, or a formulaic method reused with little change; a boilerplate approach applies a generic template rather than tailoring to the situation.
column6: template, standard wording, stock language; cookie-cutter approach
column7: The contract contains several pages of boilerplate. / A boilerplate approach won't work for every client. / The generated code included a lot of framework boilerplate.
column8: Broaden beyond approach. Common in law, writing, software, business. Boilerplate is not necessarily bad; it becomes a criticism when generic reuse replaces needed customization.

column5: noun: an enthusiast or knowledgeable fan of a subject. adjective: muscular and physically fit; pale yellow-brown in color. verb: to polish; in games, to strengthen a character/item/ability.
column6: enthusiast, aficionado; muscular, ripped; polish; strengthen (gaming)
column7: He's a history buff. / The actor got buff for the role. / Buff the surface with a soft cloth. / The patch buffed several weaker characters.
column8: Major polysemy and modern gaming sense. As noun, film/history/train buff is common. Contrast nerf in gaming = weaken.

column5: To interrupt or interfere in a conversation, activity, or situation without being invited or welcomed.
column7: Sorry to butt in, but I think there's a mistake in that number. / He kept butting into conversations that didn't involve him.
column8: Base expression butt in is more general; butt into + conversation/business also occurs. Often softened with 'Sorry to butt in, but...'

column5: To perform, conduct, execute, or complete a task, plan, order, experiment, investigation, threat, or procedure.
column7: Researchers carried out three experiments. / The order was carried out immediately. / He never carried out the threat.
column8: Highly productive formal-neutral phrasal verb. Carry out a plan/task/order/survey/investigation/repair. Distinguish carryout/takeout food in some regional noun usage.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb usage::formal topic::research topic::finance discovery::implementation discovery::process_details discovery::procedural_language discovery::trial_and_error

column5: Two different forms of value or compensation: cash is money available in liquid form; equity is an ownership interest in a company or asset whose value and liquidity can vary.
column6: cash compensation and ownership stake, cash plus shares/stock (context-dependent)
column7: The startup offered a compensation package of cash and equity. / The acquisition was financed with a mix of cash and equity.
column8: Current definition overgeneralizes equity as merely a less-liquid financial asset. Equity can mean ownership/net value in multiple contexts. In compensation, it may involve shares, options, or other equity awards; details matter.

column5: A warning, qualification, limitation, or condition that should be kept in mind before accepting a statement, plan, or conclusion.
column7: The results look promising, with one important caveat: the sample was very small. / I'd recommend it, but there are a few caveats.
column8: Very common analytical phrase: with the caveat that...; one caveat is... Not necessarily a deal-breaker—often simply a limitation/qualification.

column5: Relating to or forming the climax—the most intense, important, or decisive point of a story, event, process, or sequence.
column7: The final battle is the movie's climactic scene. / The negotiations reached a climactic moment late that night.
column8: Key confusable: climactic = relating to climax; climatic = relating to climate. Not every 'important' event is climactic; it usually marks a culmination/peak.

column5: Characterized by a close-knit, socially comfortable, insider-oriented atmosphere; often implying exclusivity, informality among members, or difficulty for outsiders to enter.
column7: The industry still has a clubby culture dominated by personal connections. / The small restaurant has a warm, clubby atmosphere.
column8: Can be positive (cozy, sociable) or critical (exclusive/insular). Context determines tone.

column5: A group of people sharing a characteristic or experience, especially a group studied or tracked together; more broadly, a group/companion set. Historically, a Roman military unit.
column7: The study followed a cohort of 2,000 adults for ten years. / This year's graduate cohort is unusually large.
column8: Common in research, education, demographics, business. Avoid using 'cohort' as a fancy synonym for any random group when shared timing/characteristic is absent.

column2: come rain or shine / rain or shine
column5: Regardless of weather or other difficulties; no matter what happens.
column6: whatever happens, no matter what, without fail
column7: I'll be there at six, rain or shine. / She goes for a walk every morning, come rain or shine.
column8: Both forms common. Often emphasizes reliability/commitment. Literal weather origin but mostly figurative.

column5: noun: an agreement in which sides make concessions; verb: to reach such an agreement. Also, to weaken, damage, endanger, or expose something such as security, integrity, health, or a position.
column6: middle ground, settlement, concession; weaken, jeopardize, expose
column7: We reached a compromise after hours of negotiation. / Both sides had to compromise. / Reusing passwords can compromise your security. / The leak compromised the investigation.
column8: Critical polysemy: negotiated concession vs impair/endanger. 'Compromise one's principles' can mean abandon/weaken them. Do not teach only agreement sense.
column12: entry::word entry::discourse_expression usage::critical usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::security topic::health topic::debate topic::rhetoric discovery::compromise discovery::debate_language discovery::trade-off discovery::concession discovery::agreement

column5: In a way that is very noticeable, obvious, or attention-drawing, sometimes because something is unusually present or absent.
column7: He was conspicuously absent from the meeting. / The logo was conspicuously displayed at the entrance.
column8: High-value collocation conspicuously absent. Can be neutral or evaluative. Related conspicuous.

column5: Relating to, depending on, or interpreted through the surrounding circumstances, information, language, culture, or situation.
column7: The meaning is highly contextual, so the isolated sentence is misleading. / The model uses contextual information from the surrounding text.
column8: Common in language, analysis, AI, history. 'Contextual' does not merely mean 'related to background'; it often means meaning/behavior changes with context.

column5: To violate, conflict with, or act contrary to a law, rule, agreement, principle, or requirement.
column7: The policy may contravene federal law. / They were accused of contravening the terms of the agreement.
column8: Normalize lemma. Formal/legal. Usually takes direct object: contravene a law/rule/agreement; not normally 'contravene against'.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal topic::law discovery::agreement discovery::expressing_need

column5: verb: to avoid a responsibility, difficult choice, or commitment, often by making an excuse. noun: an avoidance/easy escape, or a person/answer regarded as evasive.
column6: duck out, evade, shirk; excuse, easy way out
column7: Don't cop out just because the conversation is uncomfortable. / Saying 'both sides are the same' felt like a cop-out.
column8: Hyphen noun/adjective cop-out; verb cop out. Often implies cowardly/evasive avoidance, not merely changing one's mind.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::variant_set entry::verb_pattern usage::informal topic::decision-making discovery::evasive_language discovery::prevention discovery::commitment

column5: Strongly desired, sought after, or prized, especially because something is scarce, prestigious, valuable, or difficult to obtain.
column7: She won a coveted spot in the program. / The award is one of the industry's most coveted honors.
column8: Usually before noun. Related covet (verb) can carry stronger/envying or biblical moral overtones; coveted itself is often neutral-positive.
