column5: Unnecessary, outdated, redundant, awkward, or accumulated code, files, configuration, features, or system debris that makes software harder to maintain.
column6: technical debt (overlap), legacy clutter, dead code, junk
column7: The refactor removed years of cruft from the codebase. / Old configuration files had accumulated as deployment cruft.
column8: Computing slang with flexible scope. Cruft overlaps with technical debt but is not identical: debt emphasizes future maintenance cost; cruft emphasizes accumulated unnecessary/messy residue.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::technical usage::informal topic::technology topic::finance discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: In modern usage, to destroy, kill, remove, or severely reduce a large proportion of something; historically, Roman decimation referred to killing one in ten as punishment.
column7: The disease decimated the local population. / Injuries decimated the team's defensive lineup.
column8: Modern standard usage is not restricted to exactly 10%. Historical 'one in ten' sense explains the word but should not be used to police ordinary modern usage.

column5: A feeling that someone or something is unworthy of respect or consideration; as a verb, to regard with contempt or to refuse something because one considers it beneath oneself.
column7: She spoke with open disdain for the proposal. / He disdained publicity and rarely gave interviews.
column8: Noun: disdain for. Verb can take object or infinitive in literary/formal use: disdain to answer. Stronger than simple dislike.

column5: A foolish, stupid, or incompetent person; a mild-to-moderate British insult whose force varies by region, age, and tone.
column6: idiot, fool, prat, muppet (UK slang; nuance differs)
column7: You absolute div—you left the keys inside. / He called himself a div for missing the obvious clue.
column8: British slang. Can be playful among friends or genuinely insulting. Etymology claims are uncertain/varied, so avoid presenting a single folk origin as fact.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::playful usage::informal topic::communication discovery::incompetence

column5: To move slowly without firm control or a fixed course; to gradually change position, state, topic, relationship, or opinion; noun: such movement/change, or the general meaning/tendency of what someone says ('get the drift').
column6: float, wander, stray; gradual shift, trend
column7: The boat drifted away from shore. / We gradually drifted apart after college. / The conversation drifted toward politics. / I think I get your drift.
column8: Major literal + figurative family. Productive: drift off (sleep/move away), drift apart, drift into, get the drift. Avoid overloading card with every phrasal extension but note them.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::relationships topic::debate discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::debate_language

column5: To draw out, evoke, or obtain a response, reaction, answer, information, or feeling from someone or something.
column6: evoke, draw out, prompt, bring forth
column7: The question elicited a laugh. / Investigators tried to elicit more information from the witness.
column8: Key confusable: elicit = draw out; illicit = illegal. Common objects: response/reaction/information/sympathy/laughter.

column5: The point on Earth's surface directly above an earthquake's underground focus; figuratively, the central or most intensely affected point of an activity, event, crisis, or trend.
column7: The city was close to the earthquake's epicenter. / The neighborhood became an epicenter of the music scene.
column8: Literal seismology sense is precise; figurative sense is now common. AmE epicenter, BrE epicentre. Figuratively it does not need to mean geometric center.
column12: entry::variant_set entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To deliberately avoid, reject, or abstain from something, especially as a matter of choice, principle, or style.
column7: The director eschews flashy effects in favor of practical sets. / She eschewed social media for years.
column8: Formal. Direct transitive verb: eschew something, not normally 'eschew from'. Often implies deliberate choice rather than accidental avoidance.

column5: Highly honored, elevated in rank/status, noble or lofty in character, or grand/elevated in tone; sometimes used ironically for an overly elevated status or opinion.
column7: He rose to an exalted position in the organization. / The essay uses an exalted style that can feel overly grand. / Even people in exalted positions make ordinary mistakes.
column8: Related exalt (verb) = praise highly/elevate. Can be sincerely reverential or ironic. Do not reduce to merely 'powerful'.
column12: entry::word usage::ironic usage::debate-friendly topic::communication discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::debate_language

column5: In a glaringly obvious and seriously wrong, offensive, or unlawful way.
column7: The company was flagrantly violating the rules. / The referee ignored a flagrantly obvious foul.
column8: Stronger and more condemnatory than merely openly/obviously. Common with violate, disregard, breach, unfair, illegal. Compare blatantly: both imply obviousness, but flagrantly strongly foregrounds offensiveness or serious wrongdoing.

column5: Likely or especially susceptible to flooding.
column6: susceptible to flooding, at risk of flooding, flood-vulnerable
column7: They avoid buying homes in flood-prone areas. / Heavy development has increased risk in this flood-prone region.
column8: Hyphenate before a noun. Productive pattern: X-prone = likely/susceptible to X, e.g. accident-prone, error-prone.

column5: The legal process by which a lender takes or sells property securing a loan after the borrower defaults, subject to the law of the jurisdiction.
column7: The family faced foreclosure after falling behind on the mortgage. / The bank began foreclosure proceedings.
column8: Usually associated with mortgages/real estate in AmE. Exact procedure varies by jurisdiction, so avoid defining it as one universal sequence. Related foreclose.

column5: Abandoned, deserted, or given up; often carrying a literary or emotional sense of isolation, neglect, or rejection.
column7: They found a forsaken cabin deep in the woods. / He felt utterly forsaken by the people he trusted.
column8: Forsake–forsook–forsaken. More literary/dramatic than abandoned in many contexts. Also in compounds/phrases such as God-forsaken, which is strongly negative.

column5: The person, team, candidate, product, or option currently considered most likely to win or succeed.
column6: leader, favorite, leading candidate, top contender
column7: She quickly emerged as the front-runner for the job. / The film is an early front-runner for best picture.
column8: Hyphenated. A front-runner is the current leader/favorite, not necessarily the eventual winner. Common: emerge as/become/remain the front-runner.

column5: 1. To travel or move from place to place. 2. To find a way around a rule, obstacle, or problem. 3. For news/information to become widely known. 4. To persuade or manage someone, in some contexts.
column6: get about, travel; circumvent, bypass; spread
column7: It's easy to get around the city by subway. / They found a way to get around the restriction. / Word soon got around that the store was closing.
column8: Major polysemy. Also 'get around to doing something' = finally find time to do it, which is a separate productive extension worth recognizing.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::phrasal_verb usage::persuasive topic::travel topic::news topic::problem-solving discovery::persuasion

column5: With obvious delight or excitement, often especially at a victory, another person's embarrassment, or something mischievous.
column7: He gleefully pointed out my mistake. / The kids gleefully tore open the packages.
column8: Glee can be innocent joy, but gleefully often acquires a mischievous, triumphant, or slightly malicious flavor from context.

column5: Fluent, smooth, and confident in speech or explanation, but often too easy, superficial, insincere, or insufficiently thoughtful.
column7: He gave a glib answer to a complicated ethical question. / Her glib charm worked at first, but people soon wanted specifics.
column8: Usually disapproving. Glib does not merely mean fluent. Common: glib answer/explanation/remark; glib assurances.

column5: To malfunction, become chaotic, behave unpredictably, or go badly out of control.
column6: go wrong, malfunction, go berserk, go off the rails
column7: My phone went haywire after the update. / The plan went haywire when three people canceled at once.
column8: Used for machines, systems, plans, schedules, emotions, data, etc. Informal and vivid.

column5: To tease, fool, or joke with someone by trying to make them believe something untrue, usually playfully.
column6: kid, tease, joke with, wind up (BrE)
column7: Relax—I'm just pulling your leg. / Are you serious, or are you pulling my leg?
column8: FIX current 'go pull one's leg'. Standard expression is pull someone's leg. Usually playful rather than malicious deception.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::playful usage::british_english topic::weather

column5: 1. Courage, perseverance, and determination in the face of difficulty. 2. Small rough particles such as sand or stone.
column6: determination, perseverance, resolve, toughness; sand, particles
column7: It took real grit to finish the race after that injury. / There was grit in my shoe.
column8: Important literal + figurative senses. In psychology/education, grit is often used for sustained perseverance toward long-term goals, though definitions and claims about it vary.

column5: To an extreme, excessive, or glaring degree, usually in a negative judgment.
column7: The figures were grossly inaccurate. / He was grossly underpaid for the work he was doing.
column8: Common: grossly unfair/inaccurate/negligent/inadequate/exaggerated. Not simply 'noticeably'; it intensifies a negative evaluation.

column5: verb: to severely restrict, cripple, or prevent someone/something from functioning effectively; noun: one of the tendons/muscle group at the back of the thigh/knee region in everyday usage.
column7: Budget cuts hamstrung the department. / The team was hamstrung by injuries. / He strained a hamstring during practice.
column8: Major literal/anatomical + figurative family. Figurative passive 'be hamstrung by' is especially common.

column5: noun: an amount caught, collected, stolen, bought, or transported at one time; verb: to pull, drag, transport, or move something with effort.
column6: load, catch, take, yield; pull, drag, transport
column7: The police displayed a large haul of stolen goods. / She posted a huge shopping haul online. / We hauled the boxes upstairs.
column8: Normalize from plural hauls and connect to WID740/741 family without deleting automatically. Modern noun clusters include fishing haul, drug haul, shopping haul, medal haul.

column5: Dominance, leadership, or controlling influence exercised by one state, group, class, culture, or system over others.
column7: The book examines regional hegemony and shifting alliances. / Critics challenged the cultural hegemony of the old elite.
column8: Formal academic/political term. Often implies dominance maintained through institutions, norms, influence, or consent as well as direct force; exact theoretical meaning varies by field.

column2: hell or high water / come hell or high water
column5: No matter what difficulties or obstacles arise; despite severe trouble.
column6: no matter what, whatever happens, at all costs, rain or shine
column7: I'll finish this by Friday, come hell or high water. / She was determined to get there through hell or high water.
column8: FIX headword: the established form is 'come hell or high water' (also 'through hell or high water'), not simply 'hell and high water'. Strong determination, often dramatic.

column5: Considering a whole system, person, problem, or situation and the relationships among its parts rather than treating each part in isolation.
column7: We need a holistic view of the problem, including cost, staffing, and user behavior. / The clinic describes its approach as holistic.
column8: Common in health, education, business, design, analysis. Does not automatically mean alternative medicine, spiritual, or scientifically superior; context determines what 'whole' includes.

column5: In a state of ongoing change, uncertainty, transition, or instability, with the final form or outcome not yet settled.
column7: The schedule is still in flux, so don't book anything yet. / The industry has been in flux for years.
column8: Very common with plans, rules, organizations, identity, markets, technology. Usually implies unsettled change rather than smooth predictable movement.

column5: In kind: in the same form or manner, or with goods/services rather than money depending on context. In-kind before a noun commonly means non-cash goods, services, or contributions.
column6: non-cash, goods-and-services; in the same manner (other sense)
column7: The charity received $20,000 in in-kind donations. / Instead of paying cash, the company contributed equipment in kind. / She returned the favor in kind.
column8: Important form distinction: adjective 'in-kind donation/contribution'; adverbial 'paid/contributed in kind'. Also 'respond/repay in kind' = in the same manner, sometimes retaliation.

column5: Lower in quality, rank, status, position, or performance; anatomically, situated below another structure. As a noun, a person of lower rank/status, now often formal or hierarchical.
column7: The cheaper material is clearly inferior to the original. / He hated being treated as an inferior. / In anatomy, inferior means lower or below.
column8: Pattern: inferior to, not 'inferior than'. Technical anatomical opposite is superior. Social noun use can sound hierarchical or insulting.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::technical usage::debate-friendly topic::performance topic::debate topic::anatomy topic::health discovery::evaluation discovery::debate_language discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Growing inward, especially into surrounding tissue; also figuratively, excessively inward-looking or isolated within a small group.
column7: I had an ingrown toenail. / The organization developed an ingrown culture that rarely listened to outsiders.
column8: Common medical collocations: ingrown hair, ingrown toenail. Figurative sense is less common but useful.

column5: To resolve, remove, or smooth out difficulties, disagreements, inconsistencies, or practical details.
column6: resolve, sort out, smooth out, work out
column7: We still need to iron out a few details before signing. / They ironed out their differences over lunch.
column8: Normalize base form. Very common: iron out problems/details/kinks/differences. Metaphor from smoothing wrinkles with an iron.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::form_family entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative topic::work discovery::practical_details discovery::removal discovery::resolution

column5: Showing sound, careful judgment, especially in choosing, using, or deciding something in a measured way.
column7: A judicious use of humor can make the presentation easier to follow. / She made a judicious choice to wait for more evidence.
column8: Often means not merely 'wise' but appropriately selective/measured: judicious use/choice/mix. Compare judicial = relating to courts/judges.

column5: On, toward, or being the side sheltered from or away from the direction the wind is coming from.
column7: We anchored on the leeward side of the island. / The smoke drifted leeward.
column8: Contrast windward = facing/toward the wind. Technical/navigation/geography vocabulary. Pronunciation and exact directional interpretation depend on wind reference, not compass direction.

column2: spoil someone rotten / let me spoil you rotten
column5: To indulge or pamper someone excessively, giving them many treats, comforts, gifts, or special attention.
column7: Come stay with us and let me spoil you rotten for a weekend. / Those grandparents spoil the kids rotten.
column8: Normalize productive idiom while preserving source phrase. Usually affectionate/playful, though 'spoil a child rotten' can criticize overindulgence.

column5: 1. Finance: using substantial borrowed money/debt relative to equity or assets. 2. More generally, used or exploited strategically to gain an advantage or result.
column6: debt-financed, highly geared (BrE finance); utilized, exploited (general)
column7: The buyout left the company highly leveraged. / The campaign leveraged social media to reach younger voters.
column8: Current card is too finance-only. Related leverage as verb is extremely common in business/tech, sometimes criticized as jargon. In finance, leverage magnifies both gains and losses.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::british_english usage::specialist topic::finance topic::grammar discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Relating to political philosophies that place strong emphasis on individual liberty and skepticism toward coercive state power; specific views on government, markets, property, and social issues vary among libertarian traditions.
column6: classical liberal (overlap, not identical), minarchist (narrower), libertarian thinker
column7: She describes herself as libertarian on many civil-liberty issues. / Libertarian theories differ sharply over the proper scope of government.
column8: NUANCE: do not define all libertarians simply as 'minimal government, especially personal and economic'. The label covers multiple traditions and differs across countries; capitalize when referring to a specific party only as appropriate.
column12: entry::word topic::politics topic::philosophy topic::government discovery::emphasis discovery::public_discourse

column5: The process or activity of resolving disputes through courts, including bringing, defending, and conducting lawsuits.
column6: legal action, court proceedings, lawsuit process
column7: The dispute led to years of litigation. / The company wants to avoid costly litigation.
column8: Usually uncountable as the general process. Litigate = pursue/contest through litigation; litigant = party in a case. Not every legal dispute becomes litigation.

column5: Used to introduce something surprising, unexpected, or ironically predictable that happened or appeared.
column6: wouldn't you know it, sure enough, surprisingly
column7: I checked the mailbox again and, lo and behold, the missing package was there. / He said the fix would fail and, lo and behold, it did.
column8: Often storytelling, humorous, ironic, or slightly old-fashioned. 'Lo' is not the ordinary verb look in modern usage.

column5: Generosity, nobility, and lack of pettiness, especially toward a defeated rival, opponent, or someone in a weaker position.
column7: She showed remarkable magnanimity toward the colleague who had attacked her. / In victory, he responded with magnanimity rather than gloating.
column8: Noun counterpart of magnanimous. Often specifically generosity when one has the power or opportunity to be vindictive.

column5: Generous, noble, and forgiving, especially toward a rival, defeated opponent, or someone less powerful.
column7: It was magnanimous of her to praise her opponent after such a bitter campaign. / He was surprisingly magnanimous in victory.
column8: Useful pattern: magnanimous in victory/defeat; magnanimous gesture. More elevated than simply kind/generous.

column5: A disease or illness; figuratively, a serious persistent problem or unhealthy condition in a society, organization, or system.
column7: The treatment was once used for a variety of maladies. / The essay treats corruption as a political malady.
column8: Somewhat formal/old-fashioned for ordinary illness. Figurative use remains common in elevated writing.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::dated usage::figurative topic::health discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Causing intense embarrassment, humiliation, or shame.
column7: I waved back and then realized she was waving at someone behind me—it was mortifying. / The mistake was absolutely mortifying at the time.
column8: Related mortified = extremely embarrassed. Modern everyday sense is embarrassment, not 'causing death'; historical senses differ.

column5: Dark or cloudy so that it is difficult to see through; figuratively, unclear, confusing, morally dubious, or poorly understood.
column7: The water was too murky to see the bottom. / The legal situation is still murky. / The deal has a murky history.
column8: Strong literal + figurative clusters. 'Murky ethics/past/deal' can imply suspicious or morally questionable, not merely unclear.

column5: noun: a small cut, notch, chip, or slight damage; verb: to make such a cut/notch. In BrE slang, nick has several additional meanings, including steal or arrest.
column7: There's a small nick in the blade. / I nicked my finger while shaving. / The table has a few nicks along the edge.
column8: Normalize singular + verb. BrE slang senses are common but context-sensitive: 'nick' = steal; 'the nick' = police station/prison in some usage; 'get nicked' = be arrested.

column5: Small cuts, nicks, scratches, or minor surface injuries/damage.
column7: My hands were covered in little nicks and cuts after moving the boxes. / The case protects the device from everyday nicks and cuts.
column8: KEEP as useful source phrase, but distinguish from WID940 lexical card. Can describe skin injuries or minor damage to objects.

column5: A null can be a zero, absence, empty/missing value, or point of zero response depending on the field; adjective null = having no legal force/value or no result; verb null is technical/rare outside computing.
column6: zero, absence, missing value; void, invalid
column7: The antenna pattern has several nulls where the signal drops sharply. / The database contains null values. / The contract was declared null and void.
column8: Current definition is too narrow. Statistics, computing, engineering, law all use null differently. Do not equate database NULL with numeric zero.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical topic::communication topic::law discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The act or result of making something difficult to understand, perceive, trace, or interpret, sometimes deliberately; in computing, deliberate transformation that makes code/data harder to inspect.
column7: The jargon felt like deliberate obfuscation. / The app uses code obfuscation to make reverse engineering harder.
column8: Related obfuscate. Deliberate intent is common but not required in every use. In cybersecurity/software, obfuscation can have legitimate or malicious purposes.
column12: entry::word usage::specialist topic::technology discovery::perception discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Slanting or not parallel/perpendicular; figuratively, indirect, not explicit, or approaching a subject at an angle.
column7: The sunlight entered at an oblique angle. / She made an oblique reference to the earlier dispute.
column8: Literal geometry/anatomy + figurative communication. Common: oblique angle/reference/approach. 'Oblique' is more formal than indirect.

column5: In a casual, unceremonious, or seemingly unconsidered way, often without giving something much attention.
column7: He offhandedly mentioned that he might move overseas. / She dismissed the concern rather offhandedly.
column8: Does not inherently mean rude; rudeness/dismissiveness comes from context. Related offhand adjective/adverb = without preparation or casual.

column2: on one's high horse / get off one's high horse
column5: In an arrogant, self-righteous, morally superior, or condescending attitude; 'get off your high horse' tells someone to stop acting that way.
column7: He gets on his high horse whenever anyone questions his taste. / Get off your high horse—we all make mistakes.
column8: Normalize productive possessive pattern rather than only 'their'. Often criticism of moral superiority, not just generic confidence.

column5: verb: to actively choose to participate, receive, or be included. noun/adjective: an opt-in is that choice or a system requiring affirmative consent.
column6: choose to participate, enroll, subscribe; affirmative consent
column7: Users must opt in to receive marketing emails. / The study uses an opt-in consent model. / Only a small percentage completed the opt-in.
column8: FIX POS: verb is 'opt in', not 'opt-in'. Hyphenate noun/adjective: opt-in system/option. Contrast opt out.

column5: 1. The movement of solvent through a semipermeable membrane toward a region of higher solute concentration, under the usual simplified description. 2. Figuratively, gradual or seemingly effortless absorption of knowledge, habits, or culture through exposure.
column7: Water moves across the membrane by osmosis. / I picked up a surprising amount of vocabulary by osmosis just from watching the show.
column8: Scientific osmosis is not identical to diffusion. Figurative 'learn by osmosis' is common and often slightly humorous because learning is not literally effortless.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::humorous usage::figurative usage::scientific topic::culture discovery::figurative_extension discovery::hedging

column5: Relating to osteopathy or osteopathic medicine. In the United States, osteopathic physicians (DOs) are fully licensed physicians; in other countries, 'osteopathy' may refer to a distinct manual-therapy profession.
column7: She graduated from an osteopathic medical school in the U.S. / The clinic offers osteopathic manual treatment.
column8: IMPORTANT geographic nuance. Do not define osteopathic practice universally as medicine emphasizing manipulation of muscles/bones; U.S. DO medicine is full-scope physician practice, while professional models differ internationally.
column12: entry::word usage::professional usage::instructional topic::mental_health topic::medicine topic::health discovery::professional_context

column5: verb: to criticize a work or performance severely, especially in a review; also to move a camera horizontally or wash material in a pan to separate gold. noun: a cooking vessel and various technical senses.
column6: slam, savage, trash (informal); sweep camera; cooking pan
column7: Critics panned the sequel. / The camera panned across the crowd. / Prospectors panned for gold in the river.
column8: Major polysemy. Review sense is informal journalism/criticism. Past panned, -ing panning.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::technical usage::journalistic topic::work topic::food topic::performance discovery::criticism discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Wild, noisy, confused disorder; a scene of chaotic commotion.
column7: Pandemonium broke out when the doors finally opened. / The kitchen was absolute pandemonium during the dinner rush.
column8: Strong vivid noun, usually uncountable. 'All hell broke loose' is more informal; mayhem overlaps but can imply violent disorder.

column5: A digital access restriction requiring payment, subscription, registration, or another qualifying entitlement before some or all content can be viewed.
column7: The article is behind a paywall. / The newspaper introduced a metered paywall that allows a few free articles each month.
column8: Common types include hard, soft/metered, and freemium paywalls. Productive: behind a paywall; put content behind a paywall.

column5: adjective: lasting for many years, recurring repeatedly, or persistently relevant/problematic; noun: a plant that lives for more than two years.
column6: recurring, enduring, persistent, long-standing; perennial plant
column7: Funding is a perennial problem for the organization. / She's a perennial favorite for the award. / Lavender is a perennial in many climates.
column8: FIX current 'lasting for an infinite time'. Perennial means recurring/enduring, not infinite. Contrast annual/biennial in botany.

column5: Likely to provoke strong political disagreement, emotion, symbolism, or partisan/ideological interpretation.
column7: Immigration is a politically charged issue in many countries. / Even the wording of the exhibit became politically charged.
column8: Does not simply mean 'influenced by politics'. Often describes topics, language, symbols, events, or environments carrying strong political stakes/emotions.

column5: The strength, power, or capacity of something to produce an effect, especially a drug, chemical, toxin, argument, symbol, or influence; historically also sexual potency.
column7: Heat and light can reduce the potency of some medications. / The image retained its political potency decades later.
column8: Potency is effect-producing power, not always concentration. Related potent. Medical/pharmacological meaning depends on substance and measurement.

column5: To spring or swoop suddenly to attack or seize; figuratively, to act immediately on an opportunity, mistake, weakness, or remark.
column6: spring, leap, swoop; seize on, jump on
column7: The cat pounced on the toy. / Reporters pounced on the contradiction. / She pounced on the chance to buy the tickets.
column8: Productive figurative pattern pounce on an opportunity/error/comment. Often implies speed and eagerness.

column5: A special right, power, privilege, or choice belonging to a particular person, office, group, or role.
column7: It's your prerogative to say no. / Hiring decisions are ultimately the manager's prerogative.
column8: Common conversational pattern 'That's your prerogative.' Historically/legal senses can involve sovereign or official powers. Not always 'exclusive' in an absolute sense.

column5: 1. Mentioned in or characteristic of a proverb. 2. So well known, stereotypical, or repeatedly referred to that it functions like a familiar saying or emblem; often used before a figurative noun.
column7: The project became the proverbial straw that broke the camel's back. / We finally found the proverbial needle in the haystack.
column8: Often signals that the following image/phrase is figurative and familiar: proverbial elephant in the room, can of worms, last straw. Not merely 'widely referred to'.

column5: verb: to cut back unwanted branches or parts to improve growth/shape; figuratively, to remove unnecessary items, options, data, or content. noun: a dried plum.
column6: trim, cut back, thin out; remove, pare down
column7: I pruned the rose bushes in early spring. / We pruned several redundant examples from the document. / Prunes are dried plums.
column8: Normalize lemma and add noun sense. Productive figurative use in data, writing, neural networks, budgets, lists.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative discovery::figurative_extension discovery::removal discovery::improvement

column5: To evoke strong feelings of sympathy, tenderness, sadness, or sentimentality in someone.
column6: move, touch, tug at the emotions
column7: That final scene really tugged at my heartstrings. / The charity ad is designed to pull at viewers' heartstrings.
column8: Normalize productive variants. Compare WID845 heartstrings. This card can remain as verb-pattern retrieval while WID845 teaches the noun/collocation family.

column5: noun: a question, request for information, or expression of doubt; computing: a request to retrieve/manipulate data. verb: to ask about, question, or challenge something.
column7: We received several customer queries. / Run a query against the database. / She queried the figure in the report.
column8: Merge lexical coverage of singular/plural conceptually but KEEP both WID963/964 pending duplicate-family reconciliation if retrieval history matters. Strong computing sense should be included.

column5: A question or request for information; an expression of doubt; in computing, a structured request for data. As a verb, to ask, question, or challenge.
column6: question, inquiry, request; ask, question, challenge
column7: I have a quick query about the invoice. / The database query returned 200 rows. / He queried whether the deadline was realistic.
column8: Near-duplicate family with WID963. Recommend eventual consolidation only if duplicate QA shows no independent source/retrieval value; do not delete automatically in this pass.

column5: 1. A loud, unpleasant noise. 2. An illegal, dishonest, or exploitative scheme/business. 3. A bat-like piece of sports equipment used in tennis, badminton, etc.
column6: din, noise, clamor; scam, scheme, criminal enterprise; racquet
column7: What's all that racket upstairs? / Prosecutors described it as an extortion racket. / He bought a new tennis racket.
column8: Major polysemy. Spelling racquet also exists for sports equipment, especially in some styles; racket is standard too. 'Protection racket' is a common criminal collocation.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::collocation entry::word topic::business topic::sports topic::crime

column5: To complain, protest, or criticize vehemently and at length against someone or something.
column6: denounce, rant against, inveigh against, attack verbally
column7: He railed against the new regulations for an hour. / The columnist regularly rails at corporate hypocrisy.
column8: Not necessarily literally loud, though forceful/angry language is typical. Formal-literary compared with rant. Patterns rail against/at.
column12: entry::phrase usage::formal usage::literary usage::professional usage::businesslike discovery::criticism discovery::complaint discovery::professional_context

column5: A supporter of, or something associated with, the political ideas, policies, style, or coalition of U.S. President Ronald Reagan.
column7: The essay contrasts Reaganite economic ideas with later conservative approaches. / Several Reaganites opposed the proposal.
column8: Capitalize. Historical/political label; exact policy bundle depends on context and speaker. Do not treat all conservatives of the era as identical.

column5: verb /rɪˈkaʊnt/: to tell or describe events in detail. noun /ˈriːkaʊnt/: a second count, especially of votes. 'Recounting' is the -ing form of the verb.
column6: relate, narrate, retell; count again (noun/other verb sense)
column7: She recounted what happened after the meeting. / His recounting of the trip was hilarious. / Officials ordered a recount of the ballots.
column8: Normalize lemma and flag pronunciation/sense split. Verb 'recount events'; noun 'a recount' = count again.

column5: To restore a person, rule, policy, benefit, system, or condition to a former position, status, or operation.
column7: The court ordered the company to reinstate the employee. / The city is reinstating the old parking rules.
column8: Normalize lemma. Patterns reinstate someone in/as; reinstate a policy/ban/benefit. Related reinstatement.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::policy_discussion discovery::debate_language

column5: 1. In relation to or with reference to. 2. Compared with or in proportion to something else.
column6: in relation to, compared with, with respect to
column7: The cost is small relative to the overall budget. / The position of the object is measured relative to the camera.
column8: Useful analytical phrase. 'Relative to' can express comparison, reference frame, or relationship; not always simple comparison.

column5: To assign or move someone/something to a lower, less important, less visible, or less desirable position/status; in sports, to demote a team to a lower division.
column7: The issue was relegated to a footnote. / She felt relegated to a supporting role. / The club was relegated after finishing last.
column8: Normalize lemma. Common passive be relegated to. Sports sense especially BrE/global football.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::british_english usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::debate_language

column5: A person who rejects, deserts, or breaks with a group, cause, authority, or established rules; adjective: rebellious, unauthorized, or operating independently.
column7: The story follows a renegade officer who ignores direct orders. / A group of renegade lawmakers opposed their own leadership.
column8: Can be approving ('independent rebel') or condemning ('traitor/rogue') depending viewpoint. Defector is narrower and more neutral.

column5: To fill, restore, or supply something again after it has been used, reduced, or depleted.
column7: I need to replenish my water bottle before we leave. / The body needs time to replenish its energy stores. / Staff replenished the shelves overnight.
column8: Common objects: supplies, stock, fluids, nutrients, energy, savings. Related replenishment.

column5: A person who owns or manages a restaurant, especially as a business professional.
column7: The chef later became a successful restaurateur. / Several local restaurateurs opposed the fee increase.
column8: Spelling trap: restaurateur, not *restauranteur in standard edited English, though the latter occurs. From French; no n after restaura-.

column5: To keep emphasizing or reminding someone of an embarrassing mistake, defeat, disadvantage, or misfortune, making them feel worse.
column6: gloat, taunt, twist the knife (stronger), keep reminding
column7: Okay, you won—you don't have to rub it in. / She kept rubbing it in that she'd predicted the result.
column8: Often used after someone is already aware of the bad outcome. 'Rub salt in the wound' is related but emphasizes worsening emotional pain.

column5: With regret, embarrassment, or self-aware sadness, often mixed with wry humor or resignation.
column7: He smiled ruefully and admitted that she'd been right. / She looked ruefully at the broken screen.
column8: Nuance is often regret + wry self-awareness, not pure sorrow. Related rueful.

column2: run low on refreshments / be running low on refreshments
column5: To have only a small amount of drinks/snacks or other refreshments left.
column6: be nearly out of, be short on, be running out of
column7: We're running low on refreshments, so I'll pick up more drinks. / By the end of the party, they were almost out of snacks.
column8: FIX number/naturalness: refreshments is normally plural/uncountable-like collective in this sense; 'running low on refreshments' is more natural than singular 'refreshment'. General productive pattern run low on X.

column5: Extremely harsh, cutting, and damaging in criticism or condemnation.
column7: The report delivered a scathing critique of the agency. / She wrote a scathing review of the sequel.
column8: Strong negative evaluation. Common: scathing attack/review/criticism/report. Related scathe is rare in modern everyday use.

column5: Mischievous, silly, tricky, dishonest, or questionable activity; the tone can range from playful antics to serious impropriety.
column6: antics, monkey business, funny business, mischief, trickery
column7: What kind of shenanigans are you two up to? / Investigators uncovered accounting shenanigans at the firm.
column8: Usually plural. Tone is highly context-dependent: playful with friends, euphemistically critical in business/politics.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::playful usage::critical topic::business topic::communication

column5: 1. To pass a dry substance through a sieve to separate particles. 2. To examine, sort, or separate information/evidence carefully to find what matters.
column6: sieve, screen; sort through, examine, filter
column7: Sift the flour before adding it. / We spent hours sifting through the evidence. / The software helps sift useful signals from noise.
column8: Productive figurative patterns: sift through data/evidence; sift out; sift A from B.

column5: To avoid work, school, or a duty, especially by being absent or doing something else instead.
column6: skip, shirk, play truant, bunk off (BrE), slack off (overlap)
column7: He skived off work to watch the match. / We used to skive off school on Friday afternoons.
column8: Chiefly British. Can be transitive-ish with activity: skive off work/school. Compare WID798 play hooky (chiefly AmE school/work absence).
column12: entry::phrasal_verb usage::informal usage::american_english usage::british_english topic::work topic::education discovery::prevention

column5: A film, song, book, game, or other release that attracts relatively little initial attention or expectation but later becomes unexpectedly successful, often through word of mouth.
column6: surprise hit, breakout success, slow-burn hit
column7: The film became a sleeper hit months after its quiet release. / The indie game turned into a sleeper hit through word of mouth.
column8: Not merely any unexpected success: usually low initial profile/expectations followed by later growth.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal topic::media topic::music topic::film topic::entertainment discovery::release

column5: To leave, disappear, escape, die, or gradually become lost/unreachable quietly or without being noticed; 'slip away from someone' can mean escape their control or grasp.
column7: We slipped away from the party without saying goodbye. / The lead began to slip away from them. / The memory is slowly slipping away.
column8: Broaden beyond movement. Can be literal departure, opportunity/time/control being lost, or euphemistic death depending context.

column5: A soft, aerated frozen dessert dispensed from a machine; 'soft-serve' is commonly hyphenated attributively before another noun.
column6: soft ice cream, soft-serve ice cream
column7: Let's get some soft serve after dinner. / They sell vanilla soft-serve ice cream.
column8: As a noun, both soft serve and soft-serve occur by style; hyphen is especially natural attributively. Definition should not overstate one exact production temperature/formula.

column5: 1. To plant or scatter seed. 2. Figuratively, to introduce, spread, or create the beginnings of an idea, emotion, conflict, doubt, confusion, etc.
column7: Farmers sow wheat in the fall. / The rumor sowed doubt among investors. / His comments only sowed confusion.
column8: Past sowed; past participle sown or sowed. High-value collocations: sow seeds, sow doubt/confusion/fear/discord. Pronounced /soʊ/, unlike sow 'female pig' /saʊ/.

column5: A general medical term for disease or disorder of the vertebrae/spinal column; the specific condition and cause must be identified from context.
column7: The report used spondylopathy as a broad diagnostic category and then specified the underlying spinal condition.
column8: Technical umbrella term, not one single disease. Do not infer diagnosis, severity, or treatment from the word alone. Related forms vary across specific spinal disorders.
column12: entry::word usage::technical topic::health discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Secretly or stealthily, especially because one wants to avoid being noticed, observed, or discovered.
column7: He surreptitiously checked his phone under the table. / Someone had surreptitiously recorded the conversation.
column8: Often implies concealment of the action itself. Compare discreetly: unobtrusively/tactfully, not necessarily secretly.

column5: noun: a large moving group, especially of insects; figuratively, a crowd/mass. verb: to move or gather in large numbers around/over a place or person.
column7: A swarm of bees settled on the branch. / Tourists swarmed the square. / Reporters swarmed around the actor.
column8: Normalize singular + verb. Common patterns swarm of bees/drones; swarm with people; swarm around/over.

column5: Made artificially by chemical or industrial processes rather than obtained directly in natural form; also figuratively, artificial or not genuine. As a noun, a synthetic material/substance.
column7: The jacket is made from synthetic fibers. / Researchers produced a synthetic version of the compound. / His enthusiasm sounded synthetic.
column8: Do not define as necessarily imitation: many synthetic substances are designed for their own properties. Contrast natural; artificial can be broader.

column5: Only indirectly or slightly related to the main subject; moving away from the central point. In geometry, relating to a tangent.
column7: That's interesting, but it's tangential to the question we're trying to answer. / The discussion drifted into tangential issues.
column8: Common analytical pattern tangential to. More precise than irrelevant: a tangential point is connected, but only indirectly.

column5: To cut, engrave, or chemically mark a design into a surface; figuratively, to fix an image, memory, expression, or experience vividly and enduringly in the mind.
column7: The design was etched into the glass. / That scene is etched in my memory. / Exhaustion was etched on his face.
column8: Normalize lemma. High-value figurative patterns etched in/into one's memory; etched on someone's face.

column5: To make something seem less important, serious, difficult, painful, or complex than it really is.
column7: Calling it 'just drama' trivializes what happened. / The joke risks trivializing a serious issue.
column8: Normalize lemma. Trivialize focuses on treating something as trivial; minimize/downplay may be strategic or quantitative and are not always identical.

column5: 1. Ungenerous or lacking kindness. 2. Unfairly harsh, unsympathetic, or inclined to interpret someone in the least favorable way.
column7: It would be uncharitable to assume he did it deliberately. / Her review was witty but unnecessarily uncharitable.
column8: Very useful figurative pattern 'an uncharitable interpretation/reading'. Often about judgment rather than literal charity.

column5: Clear, definite, and leaving no room for doubt, ambiguity, or multiple interpretations.
column7: She gave an unequivocal no. / The evidence is not unequivocal enough to support that conclusion.
column8: Common: unequivocal support/rejection/statement/evidence. Opposite equivocal = ambiguous/uncertain, not 'equal'.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::professional usage::academic usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::communication topic::debate topic::rhetoric topic::law topic::politics discovery::debate_language discovery::public_discourse discovery::professional_context discovery::academic_discussion discovery::certainty discovery::clarity discovery::definiteness discovery::assertion discovery::emphasis

column5: noun: short for veterinarian or veteran, depending on context. verb: to examine, investigate, or evaluate someone/something carefully before approval or acceptance.
column6: veterinarian, veteran; screen, check, investigate, evaluate
column7: Ask the vet whether the dog needs a booster. / Several military vets attended the ceremony. / We need to vet the source before citing it.
column8: Current card misses very common verb. Context disambiguates veterinarian vs veteran. Vetting is common in hiring, security, sourcing, politics.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::ceremonial usage::military topic::finance discovery::evaluation discovery::social_approval

column5: The power or act of making a conscious choice or decision; one's own will or deliberate choice.
column7: She left of her own volition. / He joined the project voluntarily, entirely of his own volition.
column8: Formal. Extremely common fixed phrase 'of one's own volition'. Volition is the capacity/act of willing, not merely any decision outcome.

column5: Bay Area Rapid Transit, the rapid-transit rail system serving the San Francisco Bay Area. 'Bart' separately can be a personal name, but that is not the same lexical item.
column7: We took BART from the airport into San Francisco. / BART service was delayed during the evening commute.
column8: FIX scope: uppercase BART is primarily the transit-system acronym in this card. Do not combine it with the unrelated given name Bart as though they were senses of one word.

column5: By which, through which, or in accordance with which; used to introduce the method, arrangement, or mechanism by which something happens.
column6: by which, through which, under which
column7: They created a system whereby users can recover deleted files. / The parties reached an agreement whereby payment would be made in stages.
column8: Formal. Very useful pattern 'a system/process/arrangement whereby...'. Often more natural in formal writing than conversation.

column5: A small amount of flexibility, discretion, extra time, space, or freedom to adjust a decision, rule, schedule, price, or interpretation.
column6: leeway, flexibility, latitude, breathing room, room to maneuver
column7: Is there any wiggle room on the price? / The deadline gives us almost no wiggle room. / The wording leaves some wiggle room for interpretation.
column8: Informal and highly productive. Compare WID847 room to maneuver (strategic flexibility), WID848 latitude (discretion), WID849 elbow room (space/freedom), WID850 slack (looseness/spare capacity).
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::conversational topic::business topic::work topic::planning topic::decision-making topic::finance topic::shopping discovery::minor_adjustment discovery::possibility discovery::flexibility discovery::constraints discovery::negotiation

column5: Severely scornful, contemptuous, or humiliating; also, literally causing something to wither or lose vitality.
column7: She gave him a withering look. / The proposal received withering criticism from reviewers.
column8: High-value collocations: withering look/glance/criticism/attack. Figurative sense is much more common than literal in everyday prose. Compare scathing: harshly critical; withering often suggests making the target shrink or feel small.

column5: Serious trouble, sorrow, distress, or misfortune; plural woes often means a person's or group's continuing problems.
column7: The company blamed its financial woes on falling demand. / Woe is me! is a deliberately dramatic or old-fashioned expression.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Modern everyday use strongly favors plural in compounds such as financial woes, legal woes, injury woes. Singular woe is literary or fixed-expression-heavy.

column5: To strike, destroy, remove, heat, transmit, or affect suddenly with energy or speed; zapped can also mean exhausted or depleted.
column6: blast, hit, destroy, nuke (contextual); exhausted, drained
column7: I zapped the leftovers in the microwave. / The bug zapper zapped another mosquito. / After that flight, I was completely zapped.
column8: Broaden beyond destroy/kill. Informal and highly context-dependent: microwave something, erase/kill, transmit electronically, suddenly affect; 'I'm zapped' = exhausted.

column5: To come into conflict or disagreement; to be incompatible in color/style; or to collide with a sharp metallic sound. As a noun, a conflict, confrontation, or mismatch.
column6: conflict, collide, disagree, conflict with, confrontation
column7: The two groups clashed over funding. / That tie clashes with the shirt. / We heard the clash of metal from the hallway.
column8: Major clusters: people/ideas clash over/on; colors/styles clash; objects clash together. Noun: clash between/with, personality clash.

column5: To collide violently; to fall or fail suddenly; for a computer/system to stop working; informally, to sleep somewhere or enter an event without invitation. A crash is such a collision, failure, or sudden decline.
column6: collide, smash, fail, collapse; sleep over (informal)
column7: The car crashed into a barrier. / My browser crashed again. / Stock prices crashed after the announcement. / Can I crash at your place tonight?
column8: Very polysemous. Productive: crash into, system crashes, market crash, crash a party, crash at someone's place, crash course (separate compound).

column5: To press or break by force; to defeat overwhelmingly; to suppress or overwhelm; noun: a strong romantic attraction, especially an early or informal one.
column6: squash, compress, pulverize; defeat, overwhelm; infatuation
column7: Crush the garlic before adding it. / Their team crushed us 8–0. / She had a crush on him in high school. / The workload was crushing me.
column8: Major physical, competitive, emotional, and romantic clusters. 'Crushing' can mean devastating/overwhelming. A crush is not necessarily temporary, though it often implies informal or unreciprocated attraction.

column5: To act before someone or something else in order to prevent, forestall, replace, or gain priority over it.
column7: The company preempted criticism by publishing the data first. / The emergency broadcast preempted the scheduled program.
column8: Normalize from pre-empting. AmE commonly preempt; BrE also pre-empt. Meanings include preventive action and replacing scheduled content. Related preemptive.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::prioritization discovery::prevention

column5: To gain an advantage over a competitor by acting earlier, faster, or unexpectedly.
column6: get a head start on, outmaneuver, get ahead of, beat to the punch
column7: The startup stole a march on its rivals by launching six months early.
column8: Often BrE/formal-ish. The advantage need not be literally secret, though surprise or early action is typical.

column5: An event or appointment at which someone is scheduled to give a speech, talk, presentation, or public remarks.
column7: She has three speaking engagements in Chicago next month. / He charges a fee for corporate speaking engagements.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Common with book, accept, schedule, cancel a speaking engagement; speaking fee.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::professional usage::businesslike usage::presentation-friendly topic::public_speaking topic::presentations topic::lectures discovery::lecture_language discovery::presentation_language discovery::professional_context

column5: To draw out, evoke, or obtain a response, reaction, answer, information, or feeling.
column6: evoke, draw out, prompt, bring forth
column7: The joke elicited a laugh. / The interviewer tried to elicit more detail from her.
column8: Normalize lemma. Related to WID896; likely duplicate-family. Key confusable: elicit = draw out; illicit = illegal.

column5: Not capable of being annulled, defeated, or made void under the relevant legal conditions; often used of rights, titles, or interests.
column7: The statute grants an indefeasible title once the registration requirements are met.
column8: Technical legal term. Do not gloss as universally 'permanent': legal rights can still be subject to specific statutory exceptions or conditions. Opposite defeasible.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::technical usage::legalistic topic::law discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: An heir whose right to inherit a title or position cannot normally be displaced by the birth of another person with a superior claim; figuratively, a person widely expected to succeed a leader.
column7: The prince is the heir apparent to the throne. / She is widely viewed as the CEO's heir apparent.
column8: Important contrast: heir apparent vs heir presumptive, whose claim can be displaced by a later-born heir with a stronger right. Figurative use is common in politics/business.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::title_language discovery::assertion discovery::figurative_extension discovery::debate_language

column5: To assume financial risk or guarantee financing, insurance, or securities issuance; more broadly, to fund, support, or make an undertaking financially possible.
column7: The insurer underwrites commercial property risks. / Several banks underwrote the bond issue. / A foundation underwrote the exhibition.
column8: Major finance/insurance + broader funding sense. Underwriter varies by industry. Do not reduce to simply 'pay for'.
column12: entry::word usage::businesslike topic::finance discovery::risk discovery::support discovery::speculation discovery::possibility

column5: Fire, attack, or weapons effects that unintentionally strike one's own or allied forces rather than the intended enemy; figuratively, criticism or harm coming from one's own side.
column6: fratricide (military technical, not exact in all cases), own-side fire
column7: The soldiers were injured by friendly fire. / The candidate took friendly fire from members of his own party.
column8: Military term with figurative political/business extension. 'Friendly' does not mean harmless; it identifies the source as one's own/allied side.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::technical usage::figurative usage::military topic::military discovery::figurative_extension discovery::criticism discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: In physics, mass multiplied by velocity; figuratively, the force or progress gained by a process, movement, campaign, or activity as it continues.
column7: The campaign gained momentum after the debate. / We need to keep the momentum going. / In physics, momentum is mass times velocity.
column8: Add literal physics sense. Common figurative patterns gain/build/lose/maintain momentum; momentum behind/for something.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::scientific usage::debate-friendly topic::politics topic::physics topic::science discovery::process_details discovery::figurative_extension discovery::building_on_success discovery::public_discourse discovery::debate_language

column5: Therefore; as a result; in this way or manner.
column6: therefore, consequently, hence; in this way
column7: The road was closed, thus delaying our arrival. / The device reduces friction and thus improves efficiency.
column8: Formal-neutral connector. Can mean result ('therefore') or manner ('in this way'). In modern prose, avoid using it as a vague ornament when the logical connection is weak.

column5: Up to this point in time, progress, discussion, or process.
column6: so far, up to now, to date
column7: Thus far, the experiment has produced consistent results. / We've had no major problems thus far.
column8: More formal than so far. Can refer to discourse/progress as well as clock time.

column2: keep up a front / put up a front
column5: To maintain or present an outward appearance that hides one's true feelings, problems, intentions, or circumstances.
column6: keep up appearances, put on an act, maintain a façade
column7: She kept up a cheerful front even though she was worried. / He put up a confident front during the interview.
column8: Add highly common 'put up a front'. 'Keep up' emphasizes maintaining it over time; 'put up' emphasizes presenting/creating it.

column5: Relating to discipline, punishment, or enforcement of rules; also, in academic contexts, relating to a field or discipline.
column7: The employee faced disciplinary action. / The project crosses traditional disciplinary boundaries.
column8: Major second sense: academic discipline. Common: disciplinary action/hearing/proceedings; disciplinary boundaries/norms.

column5: Not contaminated, corrupted, damaged, or negatively influenced; remaining pure, clean, or free from a particular stain or association.
column7: Investigators wanted evidence untainted by outside influence. / The spring water remained untainted by the spill.
column8: Literal contamination + figurative reputation/evidence/memory. Pattern untainted by.

column5: A practical rule, shortcut, or strategy used to make judgments, solve problems, or search efficiently without guaranteeing an optimal or correct result; adjective: heuristic method/approach.
column6: rule of thumb, shortcut, practical strategy
column7: A simple heuristic can reduce the search space dramatically. / People often rely on heuristics when making quick judgments.
column8: Normalize singular/plural and add adjective. Broader than 'mental shortcut': used in computer science, mathematics, design, decision-making. Heuristics trade certainty/optimality for speed or practicality.

column5: Having limits, boundaries, or a finite range; in mathematics and technical fields, constrained within specified bounds. Also past participle of bound in some senses.
column7: Human attention is bounded. / The function is bounded above by 1. / The field was bounded by a stone wall.
column8: Broaden technical and ordinary senses. Important phrase bounded rationality. Do not confuse with 'bound' = certain/obliged/destined.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::scientific topic::mathematics topic::grammar discovery::boundary-setting discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column2: in this vein / in the same vein
column5: In this same style, line of thought, approach, or manner.
column6: similarly, along these lines, in the same spirit
column7: In the same vein, we should examine how the policy affects small firms. / She made several comments in this vein.
column8: 'In the same vein' is especially common. Vein here means a distinctive style/line of thought, not merely 'context'.

column5: Similar enough in relevant respects to be meaningfully compared; sometimes approximately equivalent in quality, size, value, or function.
column7: The two studies used comparable methods. / Salaries are comparable to those at larger firms.
column8: Pattern comparable to/with. Comparable does not necessarily mean equal; it can simply mean suitable for comparison or broadly similar.

column5: Connected spoken or written communication; a way of discussing or framing a subject within a community or field; formal discussion/debate. As a verb, to speak or write at length, now uncommon.
column6: discussion, communication, debate, body of language
column7: The article examines political discourse around immigration. / Different academic discourses frame the problem differently.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Related to WID572; likely duplicate-family. In linguistics/social theory, discourse can mean language-in-use or structured ways of producing meaning, not just a single debate.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word entry::discourse_expression usage::formal usage::conversational usage::academic usage::debate-friendly topic::communication topic::debate discovery::debate_language discovery::academic_discussion

column5: Instead of; in place of; as a substitute for.
column6: instead of, in place of, as a substitute for
column7: Employees may take extra leave in lieu of overtime pay. / The family requested donations in lieu of flowers.
column8: Already normalized at WID677; this is a duplicate-family candidate. Very common in HR/legal/notices. Do not delete automatically until source/retrieval value is checked.

column5: An animal with a vertebral column/backbone; adjective: relating to such animals.
column7: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals are vertebrates. / The study focuses on vertebrate development.
column8: Add adjective. Biological classification term. Contrast invertebrate.

column5: A tough band or cord of dense connective tissue that typically connects muscle to bone and transmits muscular force.
column7: The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone. / She injured a tendon in her wrist.
column8: Contrast ligament: tendon typically connects muscle to bone; ligament typically connects bone to bone or stabilizes joints, though anatomy has exceptions and specialized structures.
column12: entry::word usage::specialist topic::anatomy topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A strong band of connective tissue that connects and stabilizes bones at joints or supports organs and other structures.
column7: He tore a ligament in his knee. / Ligaments help stabilize the joint.
column8: Contrast tendon, but avoid absolute oversimplification: ligaments can connect/support structures beyond bone-to-bone. Common: torn/sprained ligament, ligament damage.

column5: To draw or manipulate electoral district boundaries to advantage a political party, group, or incumbent; gerrymandering is the practice/result.
column6: redistrict for advantage, partisan gerrymandering, electoral boundary manipulation
column7: The lawsuit challenged the map as an unconstitutional racial gerrymander. / Critics accused lawmakers of gerrymandering the districts.
column8: Normalize productive family. Distinguish partisan and racial gerrymandering; legal standards differ by jurisdiction. A strangely shaped district alone does not prove gerrymandering.

column5: A mass of rock, earth, or debris moving down a slope; figuratively, an overwhelming victory, especially in an election or vote.
column6: landslip, slope failure; overwhelming victory, rout
column7: Heavy rain triggered a landslide. / The candidate won in a landslide.
column8: Literal + figurative. Common: landslide victory, win by/in a landslide. Figurative does not have a fixed numerical threshold.

column5: To become or make unfrozen; figuratively, for tension, hostility, restrictions, or a relationship to become warmer, less rigid, or more relaxed. A thaw is that process or period.
column6: defrost, melt; warm, ease, détente (political context)
column7: Let the chicken thaw in the refrigerator. / Relations between the countries began to thaw. / A diplomatic thaw followed the talks.
column8: Transitive/intransitive. Contrast melt: thaw focuses on becoming unfrozen; melt is broader phase change. Figurative political/relationship use is common.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::warm topic::relationships topic::politics discovery::process_details discovery::figurative_extension discovery::public_discourse

column5: To annoy, bother, or pressure someone repeatedly, especially with repeated questions, requests, or interruptions.
column7: The kids kept pestering me for snacks. / Reporters pestered him with questions.
column8: Normalize lemma. Common: pester someone for/about something; pester someone to do something. Usually less severe than harass.

column5: A recurring image, idea, theme, sound, design element, or pattern that contributes to the structure or meaning of a work; also a repeated decorative/design unit.
column7: The film repeatedly uses mirrors as a visual motif. / The fabric has a floral motif.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Motif is not identical to theme: a motif is a recurring element that may help develop a theme.

column5: Scatterbrained, silly, inattentive, or lacking practical seriousness; often used of a person or behavior.
column7: I was so ditzy this morning that I put the milk in the cupboard. / The character is written as charming but ditzy.
column8: Can be playful or insulting and has sometimes been applied in gendered/stereotyped ways. Not necessarily unintelligent; often suggests absent-mindedness or frivolity.

column5: Forgetful, disorganized, easily distracted, or unable to keep one's thoughts/tasks in order.
column7: I've been so scatterbrained today that I forgot my keys twice.
column8: Usually describes attention/organization rather than intelligence. Compare ditzy: can add silliness/frivolity and may sound more judgmental.

column5: Rude, insensitive, coarse, or socially ill-mannered.
column7: His boorish behavior embarrassed everyone at the table.
column8: More formal/literary than rude. Related boor = an ill-mannered person. Often implies lack of social refinement.

column5: Not courteous, honorable, or considerate according to traditional expectations associated with a 'gentleman.'
column7: The remark was criticized as ungentlemanly. / He apologized for what he called ungentlemanly conduct.
column8: Dated/traditional and gender-coded. Useful mainly for historical, literary, ironic, or quoted contexts; modern neutral alternatives are rude, discourteous, inappropriate, dishonorable.

column5: To stop dwelling on past disagreements, offenses, or problems and move forward without continuing the conflict.
column6: forgive and forget, move on, put the past behind you
column7: We've both made mistakes, so let's let bygones be bygones.
column8: Bygones = things from the past. Often conciliatory, but it can also be criticized if used to dismiss unresolved harm.

column5: Intended or likely to reduce hostility, repair relations, or encourage agreement; showing willingness to compromise or reconcile.
column7: She struck a conciliatory tone after the heated debate. / The government made a conciliatory gesture toward the opposition.
column8: Common: conciliatory tone/gesture/approach. Usually positive/neutral, though critics may see it as too accommodating.
column12: entry::word usage::debate-friendly discovery::compromise discovery::trade-off discovery::agreement discovery::encouragement discovery::possibility discovery::debate_language

column5: Intended to calm, appease, or satisfy someone who is angry, upset, or threatening.
column7: He made a placatory gesture and lowered his voice. / The company offered a placatory refund after the complaint.
column8: Less common than conciliatory/appeasing. Contrast conciliatory: aims to reconcile sides or reduce conflict; placatory focuses on calming the displeased party.

column5: Very carefully, cautiously, or delicately, especially because something may be painful, fragile, dangerous, or awkward.
column7: She gingerly touched the bruised area. / He stepped gingerly across the ice.
column8: Adverb is much more common. Often physical movement/touch, but can be figurative: approach a sensitive topic gingerly.

column5: To confront, deal seriously with, or take account of a difficult fact, force, person, consequence, or problem.
column6: confront, contend with, face, take into account
column7: The industry must reckon with declining demand. / She's a force to be reckoned with.
column8: Two important patterns: reckon with X = confront/take account of; a force/person to be reckoned with = powerful and not to be ignored.

column5: Used to represent or describe a sudden explosion, collapse, destruction, or dramatic failure: 'then—kablooey!'
column7: The old engine coughed twice and then went kablooey. / One wrong wire and—kablooey!
column8: Comic/cartoonish sound-symbolic slang. Spelling varies (kablooey, kablooie, etc.). Often used with go: go kablooey = explode/fail dramatically.

column2: take someone for all they're worth
column3: /teɪk ˈsʌmwʌn fər ɔl ˈsʌmwʌn ɪz wɝθ/
column5: To exploit, cheat, charge, sue, or extract as much money/value as possible from someone.
column6: clean someone out, fleece, exploit, take to the cleaners
column7: The scammers tried to take him for all he was worth. / She threatened to sue the company for all it was worth.
column8: FIX pronoun pattern. Usually 'take someone for all they're/he's/she's worth' or 'for everything they've got.' Can be financial exploitation or hyperbolic extraction.

column2: a fat lot of good / a fat lot of use / a fat lot of nothing
column5: A sarcastic way to say that something is of little or no use, benefit, value, or quantity.
column6: no use at all, no help, nothing worthwhile
column7: A fat lot of good that umbrella did us in the storm. / We waited two hours and got a fat lot of nothing.
column8: Broaden to the productive pattern. 'A fat lot of good/use' is especially established; 'fat lot of nothing' is possible and sarcastic. 'Fat lot' means very little, despite literal wording.

column5: A blurred, smeared, or dirty mark; to make such a mark, blur writing/ink, or become smeared.
column7: There's a smudge on the lens. / I smudged the ink before it dried.
column8: Duplicate-family with WID818. Current card is already lexical and useful, but WID818 has deeper ordinary + ceremonial coverage. Recommend later consolidation only after source/retrieval check; no deletion in this pass.

column2: a grape that thinks it's wine
column3: /ˈsʌmθɪŋ ɪz ˈnʌθɪŋ bət ə ɡreɪp ðət θɪŋks hi ɪz waɪn/
column5: A humorous insult or metaphor for someone or something seen as pretentious—ordinary or immature but acting refined, sophisticated, or superior.
column7: He talks like a connoisseur after one tasting—he's a grape that thinks it's wine.
column8: NORMALIZE grammar from 'something is nothing but a grape that thinks he is wine'. Treat as a creative/compositional joke, not a standard proverb. Pronoun 'it' fits grape; wording can vary.

column5: To have lively enthusiasm, enjoyment, or energetic interest in something.
column6: have enthusiasm for, be passionate about, relish, have an appetite for
column7: She has a real zest for travel and learning languages. / His zest for life is infectious.
column8: Productive noun zest: zest for life/travel/learning. Literal zest = outer colored peel of citrus fruit; this card can note the metaphorical sense while keeping phrase retrieval.

column5: A foolish, gullible, or unintelligent person; an old-fashioned or literary insult.
column7: The villain assumes everyone around him is a simpleton.
column8: Often old-fashioned and contemptuous. Can imply lack of sophistication/common sense as much as raw intelligence.

column5: A foolish, stupid, or muddle-headed person.
column7: You chowderhead—you left the map in the hotel room.
column8: Old-fashioned/comic insult, especially AmE. Usually more humorous than genuinely vicious.

column2: you bet your butt / you bet your ass / you bet your bottom dollar
column5: Used to say 'absolutely,' 'definitely,' or to express strong confidence that something is true or will happen.
column6: absolutely, definitely, you bet, damn right (stronger)
column7: You bet your butt I'm going. / You can bet your bottom dollar they'll raise the price again.
column8: Register ladder: bottom dollar is old-fashioned/mild; butt informal/mildly cheeky; ass is vulgarer/stronger. 'You bet' alone is very common and safe.

column5: To prepare or create something quickly; to stir, beat, or mix ingredients; or to arouse/intensify emotions, support, fear, excitement, or controversy.
column6: rustle up, throw together; stir up, arouse, foment
column7: I can whip up some pasta in ten minutes. / Whip the cream until thick. / The speech whipped up enthusiasm in the crowd.
column8: Distinguish whip up (quickly create/arouse) from plain whip (beat/mix). Common: whip up a meal, whip up support/fear/excitement.

column5: A foolish or stupid person in rare/old slang; also used in common names of certain fish, such as the jolthead porgy.
column7: The old story calls him a jolthead for ignoring the warning. / Jolthead porgy is a fish common name.
column8: Recognition card. Human-insult sense is rare/dated; do not present as current everyday slang. Fish-name sense may be more likely in modern factual contexts.

column5: Slow to understand, obtuse, or stubbornly unwilling to understand or change one's view.
column7: Don't be so thick-headed—the instructions are right there. / He was too thick-headed to admit the plan had failed.
column8: Hyphenate. Can target intelligence/comprehension or stubbornness. Insulting; 'dense' and 'obtuse' overlap but differ in tone.

column5: To reduce the intensity, volume, aggression, excitement, confidence, or extremity of something or someone's behavior.
column6: tone it down, dial it back, ease up, calm down
column7: You're coming in a little strong—take it down a notch. / We should bring the music down a notch.
column8: Both take it down a notch and bring it down a notch occur; 'take' is especially common as instruction to a person. Productive X down a notch.

column5: An unintended error in speech, memory, or action traditionally interpreted in psychoanalytic theory as revealing an unconscious thought or motive; in everyday use, often any suggestive verbal slip.
column7: Calling your new boss by your old boss's name might jokingly be called a Freudian slip.
column8: Capitalize Freudian. Modern casual use is often humorous and does not establish that the slip truly reveals an unconscious wish. Broader technical term parapraxis.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::casual usage::technical usage::humorous usage::specialist usage::informal topic::public_speaking discovery::suggestion discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Deserving contempt because of being morally bad, shameful, mean, or dishonorable.
column7: Exploiting vulnerable people for profit is contemptible.
column8: Strong moral condemnation. Compare contemptuous = showing contempt; contemptible = deserving contempt.

column5: Literally, a person who masturbates; commonly, a contemptible, foolish, arrogant, or obnoxious person used as a strong insult.
column7: Ignore him—he's being a complete wanker. / The crowd shouted abuse at the opposing player.
column8: British/Commonwealth vulgar insult; strength varies by context. Literal sexual origin remains transparent. Not appropriate in polite/professional speech.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::british_english usage::professional usage::informal discovery::professional_context

column5: Marks, wounds, sores, or sensations corresponding to the crucifixion wounds of Jesus, reported in some Christian religious traditions; singular stigma is possible but uncommon in this sense.
column7: Accounts of the saint describe the appearance of stigmata on her hands and feet.
column8: Religious/historical term. Do not present reported stigmata as medically verified fact. Distinguish from modern general stigma = mark of disgrace; plural of that sense can also be stigmas/stigmata in technical history.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::religious topic::religion discovery::possibility discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A state of extreme excitement, agitation, activity, or intensity.
column7: Excitement reached fever pitch before the final. / Speculation rose to fever pitch overnight.
column8: Common pattern reach/rise to fever pitch. Usually about collective excitement, media attention, tension, activity.

column4: acronym / name used by multiple programs
column5: An acronym for 'You Are Not Alone.' It is used by multiple unrelated organizations and programs, including safety check-in, community-support, and awareness initiatives.
column7: The local YANA program checks in on residents who live alone.
column8: FIX over-specificity: YANA is not one universal program. Meaning depends on source/context; 'You Are Not Alone' is the expansion, but many organizations use it.

column5: To suppress, restrain, smother, or prevent something from being expressed, developing, or continuing; literally, to make breathing difficult or suffocate.
column7: She stifled a laugh during the meeting. / Excessive rules can stifle innovation. / The room was hot and stifling.
column8: High-value patterns stifle a laugh/yawn/cry; stifle dissent/creativity/growth. Related stifling adjective = oppressively hot or restrictive.

column5: To make a word, name, pronunciation, custom, or form more English in spelling, sound, style, or character.
column6: Englishify (informal), adapt to English, render in English form
column7: The family Anglicized the spelling of its surname. / The Anglicized pronunciation became common locally.
