column8: Normalize lemma and capitalization by style: Anglicize/anglicize both occur; many dictionaries capitalize less consistently today. Distinguish translate: Anglicization may alter form without translating meaning.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal topic::culture topic::language_learning topic::grammar discovery::impression

column2: throw someone off / get thrown off
column5: To confuse, distract, mislead, disrupt someone's concentration/rhythm, or cause them to lose orientation; get thrown off = become affected that way.
column7: That unexpected question threw me off. / I got thrown off when the speaker changed topics suddenly.
column8: Normalize active + passive. Also literal senses exist (thrown off a horse, thrown off balance). Figurative is very common.

column5: Not attracting unnecessary attention; discreetly present, quiet, or visually inconspicuous.
column7: The microphone is small and unobtrusive. / Staff provided unobtrusive assistance throughout the event.
column8: Usually positive/neutral: present without getting in the way. Contrast inconspicuous = hard to notice; unobtrusive emphasizes not intruding on attention/experience.

column5: noun: a flat piece that hangs, folds, or covers an opening; informal: a commotion or controversy. verb: to move loosely back and forth, especially like wings or fabric.
column6: fold, panel; commotion, fuss; flutter, wave
column7: Close the envelope flap. / The bird flapped its wings. / The comment caused a brief media flap.
column8: Major polysemy. Also medical/anatomical 'flap' for tissue; aviation control-surface flaps. Keep common physical + controversy senses.

column5: Informal 'apron belly' refers to lower abdominal skin and/or fatty tissue that hangs downward; medical terms such as abdominal pannus/panniculus may be used depending on context.
column6: abdominal pannus, panniculus; overhanging abdominal tissue
column7: After major weight loss, some people have an apron belly with loose lower-abdominal skin.
column8: NORMALIZE away from 'flap belly,' which is not a standard general term. Avoid assuming cause (pregnancy, weight loss, obesity) from appearance alone. Medical terminology varies.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::specialist topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A flavorful, relatively thin and loose-grained cut of beef from the bottom sirloin area, often sold as flap meat or flap steak.
column7: Flap meat takes marinades well and cooks quickly over high heat.
column8: Culinary naming/butchery varies by country and retailer. Do not equate automatically with skirt steak or flank steak; they are distinct cuts despite similar uses.

column5: A long, flat, strongly flavored beef cut from the diaphragm area, commonly cooked quickly at high heat and sliced across the grain.
column6: inside skirt, outside skirt; fajita meat (contextual)
column7: Marinate the skirt steak, grill it quickly, and slice it across the grain.
column8: Distinct from flank steak and flap meat. Inside/outside skirt differ. Common in fajitas, tacos, stir-fries.

column5: To unsettle, disturb, embarrass, or throw someone off balance mentally or emotionally.
column7: The sudden silence disconcerted him. / I was slightly disconcerted by how confidently she said it.
column8: Usually stronger/more specific than confuse: it disrupts composure or confidence. Related disconcerted/disconcerting/disconcertingly (WID646).

column5: Something considered, added, or done later rather than as part of the original plan; a person or issue treated as secondary or insufficiently important.
column7: The accessibility features felt like an afterthought. / I added the last sentence as an afterthought.
column8: Common critical pattern 'X feels like an afterthought'. Also 'as an afterthought'.

column5: Sexual restraint or abstinence according to a moral, religious, personal, or cultural standard; historically, the concept can include sexual conduct considered 'pure' within marriage, not only total abstinence.
column7: The order required vows of chastity. / Medieval texts discuss chastity within different social and religious ideals.
column8: NUANCE: do not define universally as refraining from sexual intercourse. Contrast celibacy = state/commitment of remaining unmarried or abstaining from sex depending context; chastity is norm/value of sexual conduct.
column12: entry::word usage::religious topic::culture topic::religion topic::history discovery::evaluation

column5: To make, assemble, prepare, or organize something quickly, often with little advance planning but not necessarily poor quality.
column6: whip up, cobble together, put together quickly, improvise
column7: I threw together a quick dinner from what was in the fridge. / She threw the slides together the night before.
column8: Can imply roughness/improvisation, but result may still be good. Common for meals, outfits, presentations, documents.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal topic::planning discovery::evaluation discovery::improvement

column2: swing as hard as you can / take a full swing
column5: To swing with maximum force, literally in sports or hitting; figuratively, to make a wholehearted or high-effort attempt.
column6: swing with full force; give it everything, go all out
column7: Keep your eye on the ball and swing as hard as you can. / Figuratively, the team decided to take a full swing at the problem.
column8: Compositional phrase rather than a fixed idiom. Preserve source wording, but teach the productive concepts 'swing hard', 'take a swing at', and 'give it your best shot' separately.

column5: A word, phrase, or statement that can be understood in two ways, especially when one interpretation is sexual, risqué, or suggestive.
column7: The joke relies on a double entendre that children probably won't notice.
column8: French-derived term used in English. Not every ambiguous phrase is a double entendre; it usually involves deliberate or humorous dual interpretation, often suggestive.

column5: A substance, food, drug, image, or other stimulus believed or claimed to increase sexual desire; adjective: having such an effect.
column7: Oysters have long had a reputation as an aphrodisiac. / The evidence for many supposed aphrodisiac foods is weak.
column8: Avoid implying efficacy merely because something is called an aphrodisiac. Related to Aphrodite. Can be figurative: power as an aphrodisiac.

column5: In successive or rotating scheduled groups or periods, so different people perform the same activity at different times.
column6: on a shift system, in rotations, in relays (some contexts)
column7: The nurses work in shifts around the clock. / We slept in shifts so someone was always awake.
column8: Not limited to paid work: can sleep, guard, drive, eat in shifts. Compare take turns: alternation need not follow formal shifts.

column5: To eat a large amount of food, often quickly, greedily, or enthusiastically.
column6: pig out, gorge oneself, wolf down food
column7: I stuffed my face with pizza after the hike. / We spent the evening stuffing our faces with snacks.
column8: Normalize possessive pattern. Informal and self-deprecating/comic; can sound judgmental when applied to others.

column5: A pet-themed pun on positive, replacing 'pos-' with paws-, used in slogans, captions, brand names, or jokes about animals.
column7: The shelter posted a 'Stay pawsitive!' message with a photo of a dog.
column8: Not a standard lexical adjective for serious prose; recognition/wordplay card. Spelling pawsitive/paw-sitive varies.

column5: For two or more people to misunderstand each other, especially because messages, assumptions, or arrangements become confused.
column6: miscommunicate, misunderstand each other, get mixed up
column7: I think we got our wires crossed—I thought you were meeting me tomorrow. / Somewhere our wires got crossed.
column8: Normalize productive possessive/past pattern. Often about scheduling or instructions, not just verbal misunderstanding.

column5: To exhaust oneself by working, worrying, traveling, caring for others, or doing too many things without enough rest.
column6: wear oneself out, exhaust oneself, burn oneself out
column7: You've been running yourself ragged all week. / She ran herself ragged trying to please everyone.
column8: Normalize reflexive pattern. Ragged evokes worn/frayed condition. Burnout is a broader state, not exact synonym.

column5: In excellent physical condition, working order, or overall state.
column6: in excellent condition, in great shape, shipshape (some contexts)
column7: The mechanic got the old bike back into tip-top shape. / I want to be in tip-top shape before the hike.
column8: Not only health: machines, houses, organizations can be in tip-top shape. Informal, upbeat.

column5: An emphatically complete, blatant, or shameless lie.
column6: blatant lie, outright lie, bald-faced lie
column7: He told me he had never seen the message, which was a big fat lie.
column8: 'Big fat' is an informal intensifier here, not literal size/body description. Strong accusation; use carefully.

column5: A man who habitually pursues women for romantic or sexual attention, often aggressively or indiscriminately.
column6: womanizer, ladies' man (different tone), philanderer (if unfaithful)
column7: The old movie portrays him as a shameless skirt chaser.
column8: Dated expression that objectifies women through 'skirt'; mostly recognition/historical dialogue. Womanizer is more current but also negative; philanderer specifically suggests repeated casual affairs/infidelity.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::casual usage::slang usage::dated topic::romance topic::communication

column5: A U.S. National Weather Service marine alert for conditions hazardous to small craft, based on locally defined wind and/or sea thresholds.
column7: The National Weather Service issued a Small Craft Advisory for the coastal waters.
column8: FIX headword: standard U.S. term is Small Craft Advisory, not 'craft advisory'. Thresholds vary by forecast office/region; it is not a universal international alert name.

column5: Able to operate, live, or function both on land and in water; relating to military operations launched from sea to land.
column6: land-and-water, amphibian (not interchangeable in all senses)
column7: The vehicle is fully amphibious. / Marines trained for an amphibious landing.
column8: Animals can be amphibious without being amphibians, and amphibian is a biological class/noun. Military: amphibious assault/landing/operation.

column5: noun: a severe infectious disease or epidemic, especially historically the plague caused by Yersinia pestis; figuratively, a widespread persistent problem. verb: to trouble, afflict, or repeatedly cause problems for.
column7: The Black Death was a plague pandemic. / Software bugs plagued the release. / The city is plagued by chronic congestion.
column8: Major medical/historical + figurative. Avoid using 'plague' as a technical synonym for every epidemic. Productive passive: be plagued by/with.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::figurative topic::health discovery::figurative_extension discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To trouble, surround, attack, or burden persistently, especially with difficulties or problems.
column7: The project was beset by delays from the start. / She was beset with doubts.
column8: Usually literary/formal and often passive: be beset by/with problems, doubts, difficulties. Past/past participle beset.

column5: A word, phrase, pattern, image, device, or technique that helps memory; adjective: relating to memory or memory aids.
column7: 'ROYGBIV' is a mnemonic for the colors of the rainbow. / She uses mnemonic techniques to remember vocabulary.
column8: Pronunciation begins /nɪ-/; initial m is silent. Not limited to acronyms—rhymes, imagery, loci, stories, etc. can be mnemonics.

column2: have one's work cut out for one
column5: To face a difficult, demanding, or substantial amount of work that is already clearly defined or unavoidable.
column6: have a tough job ahead, face a difficult task, have a lot to do
column7: We have our work cut out for us if we want to finish by Friday. / You've got your work cut out for you with that repair.
column8: FIX: current 'cut out the work' is not the intended standard idiom. Do not confuse with 'cut out work' = remove tasks/work or 'cut out for' = suited to.

column5: A law-enforcement or public officer whose role and powers vary widely by country and jurisdiction; historically and in some places, a local peace officer.
column6: police officer, peace officer, law officer (context-dependent)
column7: In England and Wales, constable is a police rank/status term. / In parts of the U.S., elected constables perform duties defined by state or local law.
column8: CORRECT overgeneralization: not inherently rural, small-town, or limited-authority. Meaning differs substantially across the UK, U.S., Canada, and other jurisdictions.

column5: A tendency or readiness to believe claims too easily or without sufficient evidence.
column7: The story strains credulity. / His credulity made him an easy target for scams.
column8: High-value idiom 'strain/stretch credulity' = be very difficult to believe. Contrast credibility = believability/trustworthiness; credulous = too ready to believe.

column5: Sacred writings or texts regarded as authoritative within a religious tradition; capitalized Scripture often refers collectively to the Bible or another body of sacred text in a specific tradition.
column6: sacred text, holy writings, religious scripture
column7: She studies passages of Scripture every morning. / Different traditions interpret their scriptures in different ways.
column8: Usage and capitalization depend on context and tradition. 'Scripture' is often collective/uncountable when referring to the Bible; 'scriptures' can refer to multiple sacred texts or passages.

column5: A final remark, criticism, insult, or action delivered just before leaving or ending an exchange.
column6: final jab, last word, farewell dig
column7: As he walked out, he fired one last parting shot at the committee. / Her email ended with a sharp parting shot.
column8: Usually metaphorical and often hostile or sarcastic. Related expression 'Parthian shot' is historical and more literary.

column5: A performer or athlete who unexpectedly emerges as one of the standout successes of a work, season, or event despite limited initial attention or expectations.
column6: breakout star, surprise standout, unexpected star
column7: The supporting actor became the sleeper star of the series.
column8: Not a strongly fixed idiom like 'sleeper hit'. 'Breakout star' is more established. Keep as a compositional/source phrase rather than treating it as standard terminology.
column12: entry::idiom entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::specialist topic::work topic::performance topic::sports discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A recreation or staged performance of a past event, especially for historical education, commemoration, training, or entertainment.
column7: The museum hosts a Civil War reenactment every summer. / Police conducted a reenactment of the incident.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Both reenactment and re-enactment occur by style. Related reenact.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word topic::education topic::performance topic::entertainment topic::history

column5: A showy, decorative, or amusing object of little practical value and often little worth.
column7: The shelves were crowded with souvenir gewgaws. / She disliked ornate furniture covered in useless gewgaws.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Usually dismissive or humorous; somewhat literary/old-fashioned.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::literary usage::dated usage::humorous discovery::evaluation

column5: verb: to arouse interest, curiosity, or appetite; or to irritate/wound someone's pride. noun: a feeling of irritation or wounded pride.
column7: The headline piqued my curiosity. / He left in a fit of pique after being ignored.
column8: High-value phrase 'pique someone's interest/curiosity'. Do not confuse pique with peak or peek. Past/participle piqued.

column5: Deliberately expressionless or emotionally neutral, especially while saying something humorous; as a noun, a deadpan expression/style; as a verb, to say something in that manner.
column7: She deadpanned, 'Great, another meeting.' / His deadpan delivery made the joke even funnier.
column8: Core idea is delivery without visible emotion. Common in comedy. 'Dry' overlaps but is broader.

column5: To change or transform in form, character, function, or appearance, often gradually or smoothly.
column7: The discussion slowly morphed into an argument. / The animation shows one face morphing into another.
column8: Common pattern morph into. Originally associated with image/animation transformation but now broadly figurative.

column5: To push gently; figuratively, to encourage, prompt, or steer someone toward an action without forcing them. A nudge is a slight push or subtle prompt.
column7: She nudged me with her elbow. / The reminder nudged me to finally submit the form.
column8: Broader behavioral-policy sense is important: a nudge changes choice architecture or gives a subtle prompt without removing options.

column5: Puzzlement, confusion, or mild bewilderment; sometimes mixed with amusement in actual usage, but the core traditional meaning is being puzzled.
column7: He stared at the bizarre instructions in bemusement. / To my bemusement, everyone else seemed to understand the joke.
column8: Important nuance: bemusement is not simply amusement. Modern usage sometimes blends the two because of the sound similarity.

column5: A god, goddess, or divine being regarded as having supernatural or sacred status in a religion or belief system.
column7: The temple was dedicated to a local deity. / The mythology includes dozens of deities.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Not limited to polytheistic religions in a purely dictionary sense, though 'deities' is especially common when discussing multiple gods.

column5: Very unusual, eccentric, unconventional, bizarre, or unpredictable.
column7: That theory is a little off the wall, but it's interesting. / He has an off-the-wall sense of humor.
column8: NORMALIZE away from 'go off the wall' as the main headword. 'Off the wall' is the established phrase; 'go off the wall' is much less standard and context-dependent.

column2: to each their own / each to their own
column5: Used to acknowledge that different people have different tastes, preferences, choices, or opinions.
column6: different strokes for different folks, everyone has their own preference
column7: I wouldn't choose that color, but to each their own. / Each to their own—I actually like the ending.
column8: Both forms occur. Usually tolerant/neutral, though tone can sound dismissive depending on delivery.

column5: To wear, display, or show something conspicuously, often as a noticeable feature or with some pride.
column7: He sported a bright red jacket. / The car sports a new grille and redesigned headlights.
column8: Normalize lemma. Common with clothes, hairstyle, beard, logo, feature. Does not always imply pride.

column5: Based on conjecture rather than firm evidence; involving uncertain prediction; in finance, involving high risk in hope of high returns.
column7: The explanation is still speculative. / Speculative investments can produce large gains or losses.
column8: Major everyday + finance sense. Contrast conjectural, which is more purely 'based on conjecture' and less associated with markets.
column12: entry::word usage::speculative topic::finance discovery::risk discovery::evidence discovery::uncertainty discovery::speculation

column5: Based on conjecture, incomplete evidence, or an informed guess rather than established fact.
column7: The date is conjectural because the original records were lost.
column8: More formal than speculative. Usually about claims, reconstructions, interpretations, or dates rather than financial risk.

column5: Broad, comprehensive, or governing many smaller parts, aims, issues, or principles.
column7: The overarching goal is to reduce costs without reducing quality. / Trust is an overarching theme of the novel.
column8: Often used with goal, theme, principle, framework, concern. It means overarching in scope, not literally 'all-encompassing' in every case.

column5: To become deeply and energetically involved in something interesting, substantial, or challenging.
column6: dig into, dive into, tackle enthusiastically
column7: I finally have a project I can really sink my teeth into. / She sank her teeth into the research immediately.
column8: Normalize possessive pattern. Often implies the task has enough substance to be satisfying.

column2: a task with substance / something with substance
column5: A task, project, argument, or piece of content that has meaningful depth, importance, complexity, or value rather than being superficial or trivial.
column6: substantial task, meaningful work, something substantial
column7: He wanted a task with real substance instead of busywork.
column8: Compositional phrase, not a fixed idiom. 'Something with substance' and 'substantial work' are more general/productive alternatives.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::rhetorical topic::work discovery::triviality discovery::debate_language

column5: To meet the expectations, reputation, standard, promise, or ideal associated with someone or something.
column6: meet, fulfill, match, measure up to
column7: The sequel didn't live up to the hype. / It's difficult to live up to such a strong reputation.
column8: Common pattern live up to expectations/hype/reputation/name/promise. Usually evaluative.

column5: To make overly fine, subtle, or unnecessary distinctions, especially in an argument.
column7: We agree on the main point, so let's not split hairs over the wording.
column8: FIX: standard idiom is plural 'split hairs', not 'split a hair'. Singular wording can occur literally but is not the idiom.

column2: off the wall / being off the wall
column5: Unconventional, bizarre, eccentric, or wildly unexpected.
column7: His ideas are often off the wall, but some of them are brilliant.
column8: Duplicate-family with WID1113. Retain for now because this card may preserve a source phrase, but likely consolidate later unless retrieval value differs.

column5: Excessive, exaggerated, flamboyant, dramatic, or beyond what is reasonable or necessary.
column7: The decorations were completely over the top. / His reaction was a bit over the top.
column8: Normalize away from 'being over the top'. Can be negative or admiring/playful depending context.

column5: In a grimly mocking, scornful, cynical, or bitterly humorous way.
column7: 'Well, that went beautifully,' she said sardonically after everything failed.
column8: Sardonic humor is typically darker, more bitter, or contemptuous than ordinary sarcasm.

column5: To continue, transfer, or extend something from one period, place, context, account, or situation to another.
column7: Unused vacation days can carry over to next year. / The tension from the meeting carried over into dinner.
column8: Normalize active/passive family. Common in accounting, scheduling, sports, emotions, and effects.

column5: Used to introduce a related or secondary point: 'by the way'; also, in a manner that is incidental rather than central.
column6: by the way, in passing, parenthetically
column7: Incidentally, I saw your brother yesterday. / The policy also incidentally reduced paperwork.
column8: Usually not a synonym for accidentally. Related incidental = secondary or occurring as a minor consequence.

column5: To enter forcibly or illegally; to enter a career/market/field; to suddenly begin an activity such as laughing, singing, or running.
column6: force entry, enter; establish oneself; burst into
column7: Someone broke into the office overnight. / She's trying to break into publishing. / He broke into a grin.
column8: Major polysemy. Productive patterns break into a house, industry, song, laughter, sweat, run.

column5: To discourage or prevent someone from doing something by making it seem difficult, costly, risky, or undesirable.
column7: The fine is intended to deter people from parking there. / Bad weather didn't deter us from going out.
column8: Pattern deter someone from doing something. Fear can be involved but is not required.

column5: To choose one option, course, or alternative rather than another.
column7: We opted for the cheaper plan. / She opted for staying home instead of traveling.
column8: Normalize from opted for. Related opt to do something; opt in/out are separate productive patterns.

column5: To stop criticizing, bothering, pressuring, or attacking someone; separately, to dismiss employees because work is unavailable or costs are being reduced.
column6: back off, ease up, stop bothering; dismiss, make redundant
column7: Lay off him—he's trying his best. / The company laid off 200 workers.
column8: Related-family with WID699. Keep both senses explicit; this card's source meaning is the 'stop bothering' sense.

column5: Mealtime; time to eat, especially in military, camp, or joking contexts.
column6: mealtime, time to eat, grub time
column7: All right, everyone—chow time! / The kids came running when I called chow time.
column8: Casual/slangy and somewhat military/camp-flavored. Recognition/use card rather than a formal phrase.
column12: entry::phrase usage::formal usage::informal usage::casual usage::humorous usage::military topic::military

column5: Food, especially casual or hearty food; as a verb in 'chow down', to eat enthusiastically.
column7: We grabbed some chow after the game. / Let's chow down before the movie starts.
column8: Informal. 'Chow down' is the common verb phrase; plain transitive chow is less common.

column5: To drink quickly in large gulps; to move or operate with a repeated heavy sound; a chug is such a gulping action or rhythmic sound.
column7: He chugged the entire bottle of water. / The old train chugged up the hill.
column8: Broaden beyond drinking. Also productive in gaming/party contexts: chug a drink.

column5: To cause something to happen or exist; 'bring about misery' means cause suffering or unhappiness.
column6: cause, produce, lead to, result in
column7: The reforms brought about major changes. / The war brought about widespread misery.
column8: Teach productive phrasal verb 'bring about' rather than treating the whole source phrase as a fixed expression.

column5: To be finished with, no longer willing to deal with, or no longer wanting involvement with someone or something.
column6: be done with, have had enough of, finish with
column7: I'm through with this argument. / After the betrayal, she told him, 'I'm through with you.'
column8: Normalize away from 'being through with you'. Can refer to relationships, tasks, habits, or situations.

column5: To discover, uncover, or find something hidden or difficult to locate through persistent searching or investigation.
column6: dig out, uncover, track down, root out
column7: The reporter ferreted out several important details from old records.
column8: CORRECT likely error: current 'fret out' with the meaning 'work out/solve through persistent effort' is not standard. 'Ferret out' matches the intended meaning. 'Fret over/about' is a separate expression meaning worry.

column5: verb: to stagger, lose balance, or feel mentally shocked; to wind or draw in with a reel. noun: a spool/cylinder for winding line, film, cable, etc.
column7: He reeled backward from the blow. / I was still reeling from the news. / She reeled in the fish.
column8: Major literal + figurative family. Common: reel from shock/news; reel in a fish; film reel.

column5: The hottest, sultriest period of summer; figuratively, a sluggish, stagnant, or difficult period.
column6: hottest part of summer, summer doldrums; slump
column7: The dog days of August made everyone lethargic. / The team is trying to escape the dog days of its season.
column8: The original expression is tied to Sirius, the Dog Star. Figurative use can mean a languid or declining period, but context matters.

column5: noun: a legal tribunal, royal household, or marked playing area. verb: to seek someone's romantic attention or favor; to seek support/business; or to risk/provoke something.
column6: tribunal, court of law; woo, pursue, solicit
column7: The case went to court. / He courted her for months. / The company is courting new investors. / That decision courts disaster.
column8: Highly polysemous. Productive verb: court favor/support/controversy/danger/disaster.
column12: entry::word topic::business topic::romance topic::law discovery::risk discovery::support

column5: Stylish, attractive, smart, or flashy in a lively, eye-catching way.
column7: That's a snazzy new jacket. / The site has a snazzy redesign.
column8: Informal and upbeat, sometimes slightly playful or dated.

column5: Used to concede that someone may do or decide something as they wish, often with resignation or irritation.
column6: suit yourself, fine, do what you want
column7: I still think it's a bad idea, but have it your way.
column8: Tone is important: it often sounds exasperated or reluctant rather than generous.

column5: To avoid work, school, or a duty, especially by staying away, pretending to be ill, or doing something else instead.
column6: shirk, bunk off, skip, play hooky
column7: He skived off work to watch the match. / We used to skive school on Friday afternoons.
column8: Normalize family. Chiefly British. Related to WID981 skive off; likely duplicate-family.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::word entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::british_english topic::work topic::education discovery::prevention

column5: To surround a fortified place with armed forces; figuratively, to overwhelm someone with requests, messages, questions, or problems.
column7: The army besieged the city for months. / The office was besieged with calls after the announcement.
column8: Normalize lemma. Common figurative passive: be besieged by/with requests, reporters, complaints.

column5: In many legal systems, intentional unlawful or offensive physical contact with another person; precise elements and the relationship to assault differ by jurisdiction.
column6: unlawful touching, offensive contact; assault (not equivalent everywhere)
column7: He was charged with battery after allegedly striking another man.
column8: LEGAL PRECISION: definitions vary significantly by jurisdiction and between criminal law and tort law. Do not state that any unconsented contact automatically constitutes battery.

column5: A relationship entered into voluntarily by the people involved, with mutual agreement to the relationship itself.
column7: They described their relationship as consensual.
column8: Important consent nuance: calling a relationship consensual does not imply blanket consent to every act within it. Consent remains specific, ongoing, and revocable.

column5: Agreed to voluntarily by the people involved; based on mutual consent.
column7: The interaction was consensual. / The policy applies to consensual relationships between employees.
column8: Consent is specific and can be withdrawn. 'Consensual' does not automatically mean appropriate, ethical, or free of all power imbalances.

column5: Fellow members of a religious, fraternal, professional, or other close-knit group; historically also an old plural of brother.
column7: The preacher addressed his brethren. / He called on his legal brethren to support the reform.
column8: Formal, religious, fraternal, or old-fashioned. Not simply an archaic synonym for biological brothers.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::dated usage::archaic usage::professional usage::religious topic::religion discovery::professional_context

column5: Extremely high, strong, successful, intense, or exceptional—beyond the scale normally measured or expected.
column6: extreme, extraordinary, exceptional, through the roof
column7: Demand is off the charts. / Her energy level was off the charts that day.
column8: NORMALIZE: plural 'off the charts' is the standard idiom. Singular 'off the chart' can occur literally or in less fixed usage.

column5: The characteristic spirit, mood, ideas, attitudes, and cultural climate of a particular period.
column6: spirit of the age, cultural mood, ethos
column7: The film captured the zeitgeist of the early 2000s. / The product fit the political zeitgeist perfectly.
column8: German loanword literally 'spirit of the time'. Often used for broad cultural/intellectual atmosphere, not just a trend.

column5: To laugh or chuckle with gleeful, pleased, or sometimes smug amusement; a chortle is such a laugh.
column7: He chortled at his own joke. / She gave a satisfied chortle.
column8: Coined by Lewis Carroll from chuckle + snort. Often playful/literary.

column5: Basic, fundamental, or introductory; relating to elementary school; in technical contexts, relating to basic indivisible components such as elementary particles.
column7: The mistake was elementary. / She teaches elementary school. / The course introduces elementary statistics.
column8: Broaden beyond 'early learning'. Famous phrase 'Elementary, my dear Watson' is culturally associated with Sherlock Holmes, though not used in exactly that form in Conan Doyle's original stories.

column5: Used to acknowledge that a point is true before introducing a qualification, contrast, or counterargument; 'granted that...' means assuming/admitting that something is true.
column6: admittedly, to be sure, even accepting that
column7: Granted, the plan is risky, but it may still be our best option. / Granted that he's talented, he still lacks discipline.
column8: Already a strong card. Core rhetorical function is concession. Do not treat 'nevertheless' as a direct synonym; nevertheless typically introduces the counterpoint rather than the conceded point.
column12: entry::word entry::response_formula entry::discourse_expression entry::fixed_expression usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::debate topic::rhetoric topic::grammar discovery::debate_language discovery::contrast discovery::concession discovery::qualification

column2: spread the gospel / spreading the gospel
column5: Literally, to preach or share the Christian gospel; figuratively, to enthusiastically promote or advocate an idea, method, product, or cause.
column7: He spent years spreading the gospel abroad. / She travels widely spreading the gospel of open-source software.
column8: Add figurative extension. In literal religious use, gospel is often capitalized by style when referring to the Christian message or specific Gospel books.
column12: entry::phrase entry::collocation usage::figurative usage::persuasive usage::religious topic::religion topic::communication topic::business discovery::advocacy discovery::promotion discovery::religious_origin discovery::figurative_extension discovery::persuasion

column5: An irregular or repeated rise and fall or variation in level, amount, value, condition, or intensity.
column7: Currency fluctuations affected the company's profits. / Daily temperature fluctuations are normal.
column8: Common in finance, science, data, health metrics. Related fluctuate.

column5: Dangerously unstable, insecure, uncertain, or dependent on chance; at risk of falling, failing, or deteriorating.
column7: The ladder was in a precarious position. / Many workers remain in precarious employment.
column8: Literal physical + figurative social/economic senses. Common: precarious position/situation/balance/existence.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly discovery::risk discovery::uncertainty discovery::possibility discovery::debate_language

column5: Deeply moving or emotionally affecting, often because of sadness, tenderness, nostalgia, or bittersweet meaning.
column7: The final scene was especially poignant. / The photograph is a poignant reminder of what was lost.
column8: Broader than simply sadness/regret. It often combines emotional sharpness with tenderness or significance.

column5: Impossible or very difficult to explain, understand, or account for.
column7: His sudden change of mind seemed inexplicable. / The data contained an inexplicable spike.
column8: Stronger than surprising: there appears to be no satisfactory explanation.

column5: To remain hidden or unobtrusive, often while waiting or watching; figuratively, for a danger/problem to remain unseen; online, to read without actively posting.
column6: hide, skulk, lie in wait; browse silently
column7: Someone was lurking near the entrance. / A larger problem may be lurking beneath the surface. / I mostly lurk on that forum.
column8: Important modern internet sense: lurker = someone who reads but rarely participates.

column5: Causing intoxication; figuratively, producing intense excitement, pleasure, exhilaration, or fascination.
column7: The fumes can be intoxicating in high concentrations. / The sudden success was intoxicating.
column8: Literal substance effect + figurative emotional effect. 'Intoxicating scent' can mean powerfully pleasant rather than literally intoxicating.

column5: To take great pleasure or delight in something, especially in the pattern 'revel in'; older/literary use can mean celebrate noisily.
column6: delight in, glory in, enjoy immensely, celebrate
column7: She reveled in the freedom of working for herself. / Fans were reveling in the victory.
column8: Normalize lemma. The modern productive sense is revel in something; noisy partying is secondary/older.

column5: Ready and easy to take, exploit, acquire, recruit, or benefit from because conditions are favorable or the target is vulnerable.
column6: ready for the taking, vulnerable, easy pickings, opportune
column7: The weakened company looked ripe for the picking. / The market seemed ripe for the picking after competitors withdrew.
column8: NORMALIZE standard idiom with 'the'. Often carries exploitative or competitive undertone.

column5: Careful and economical in spending or using resources, avoiding unnecessary waste.
column7: She's frugal with money but still spends on things she values.
column8: Usually neutral or positive. Contrast cheap/stingy, which criticize unwillingness to spend appropriately.

column5: A sudden short burst of liquid, speed, activity, growth, effort, or output; to gush or increase suddenly for a short time.
column7: Water spurted from the pipe. / The runner put on a final spurt. / The company had a brief growth spurt.
column8: Literal liquid + figurative short burst. Related growth spurt.

column5: To experience a relatively sudden period of rapid physical growth, especially in childhood or adolescence; figuratively, rapid expansion can be called a growth spurt.
column6: grow rapidly, shoot up, expand quickly
column7: He hit a growth spurt at fourteen and grew several inches. / The startup went through a growth spurt last year.
column8: Both 'have a growth spurt' and 'hit a growth spurt' occur; 'have/go through' are broadly natural.

column5: A state of severely reduced alertness, responsiveness, or awareness; in everyday use, a dazed or near-unconscious state, often from alcohol, drugs, illness, or shock.
column7: He was found in a drunken stupor. / She sat in a stunned stupor for several minutes.
column8: Medical use can be more specific than casual use. Common phrase drunken stupor.

column5: verb: to outrank, surpass, or take precedence over. noun: in card games, a suit/card with special power; figuratively, a decisive advantage or resource.
column6: outweigh, override, surpass; winning card, advantage
column7: Safety concerns trump convenience. / Hearts were trumps in that round. / She kept one final trump card in reserve.
column8: Do not confuse the common noun/verb with the proper name Trump. Productive phrase trump card.

column5: Relating to catatonia, a serious psychomotor syndrome that can involve reduced movement/responsiveness, rigidity, agitation, mutism, or other symptoms; figuratively, extremely unresponsive or inert.
column7: The patient showed catatonic symptoms and required medical assessment. / Figuratively: I was practically catatonic after the overnight flight.
column8: CORRECT medical oversimplification. Catatonia is not simply 'lack of movement due to mental illness or shock'; it can occur with psychiatric, neurologic, medical, or drug-related conditions and has multiple possible presentations.

column5: To indicate, suggest, or foreshadow a future outcome, especially in the phrases bode well or bode ill.
column7: The early results bode well for the project. / Those dark clouds bode ill for the picnic.
column8: Most common patterns bode well/ill for. Not restricted to bad outcomes.

column5: noun: an uneasy feeling that something bad is going to happen. adjective: creating such a sense of threat or impending trouble.
column7: I had a strange sense of foreboding. / The soundtrack creates a foreboding atmosphere.
column8: Noun is especially common in 'a sense/feeling of foreboding'. Compare ominous = suggesting bad things are likely.

column5: Sad, gloomy, dejected, or visibly low in spirits.
column7: Why so glum? / He looked glum after hearing the news.
column8: NORMALIZE from 'be glum'. Common conversational 'Don't look so glum' / 'Why so glum?'

column5: Short for executive: a person in a senior managerial or decision-making role in an organization.
column7: Several company execs attended the meeting.
column8: Informal abbreviation common in business/media. Exact seniority depends on context.

column5: To be less strict, critical, or demanding with someone; to allow extra tolerance because of circumstances.
column6: go easy on, give someone a break, be lenient
column7: Cut her some slack—she just started the job.
column8: Related-family with WID850 slack. This card teaches the fixed idiom, so KEEP independently if retrieval value is useful.

column5: Away from keyboard; temporarily not available or not actively present online, even when literally using a phone rather than a keyboard.
column7: I'm AFK for ten minutes—back soon. / Sorry, I was AFK when you messaged me.
column8: Originally desktop/gaming slang; now used more broadly in online communication. Usually written uppercase, though lowercase afk is common informally.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::abbreviation usage::slang usage::informal topic::internet topic::games

column5: To accumulate, increase, or be earned gradually over time; also, for a right, benefit, cost, or obligation to arise or become due.
column7: Interest accrues daily. / Employees accrue vacation time each month. / Additional costs may accrue if payment is late.
column8: Common in finance, accounting, employment, and law. Can be intransitive ('interest accrues') or transitive ('accrue benefits').

column5: Secretly scheming, plotting, or manipulating in order to gain advantage, often dishonestly.
column7: The story's conniving adviser manipulates everyone around him.
column8: Strongly negative. Related connive = secretly cooperate in wrongdoing or scheme; exact verb sense varies by context.

column5: Extremely loving, attentive, and affectionate, especially toward a child, partner, or family member.
column7: He's a doting grandfather who never misses a birthday.
column8: Usually warm/positive; it can imply overindulgence, but excessive affection is not required.

column5: noun: a sloped surface connecting different levels. verb: to increase or decrease something, especially in 'ramp up/down'; also to move via a ramp.
column6: incline, slope; increase, scale up, intensify
column7: They installed an access ramp. / The company is ramping up production. / We'll ramp spending down next quarter.
column8: Major noun + phrasal-verb family. 'Ramp up' is far more common than plain transitive ramp in figurative business use.

column5: noun: an adult male sheep; a heavy device for striking; verb: to hit, force, or drive something violently into/through something.
column6: batter, crash into, force; male sheep
column7: The truck rammed the gate. / He rammed the box into the trunk. / A ram stood beside the flock.
column8: FIX POS and priorities. Vulgar sexual use exists but is not a core everyday sense and should be treated as explicit slang if retained. Also distinguish RAM (computer memory acronym), a separate lexical item.

column5: In GTA Online slang, EWO refers to using 'Easy Way Out'—historically an in-game self-kill option—or otherwise deliberately killing one's own character to reset or deny an opponent a kill/advantage.
column7: Players accused him of EWO-ing to avoid giving the opponent the kill.
column8: CORRECT corrupted current definition. 'Exit Without Option' is not the intended expansion. This is game-specific slang whose exact mechanics/availability can vary by game version and community usage.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::abbreviation usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::informal topic::internet topic::games topic::decision-making

column5: To betray, sacrifice, or abandon someone, especially for one's own advantage.
column7: He sold his partner down the river to protect himself.
column8: Normalize base form from sold. Strong negative betrayal idiom.

column5: 1. A conventional closing in correspondence. 2. Informally or humorously, a way to refer to oneself: 'me.'
column7: Yours truly, Alex Morgan. / And who had to clean up the mess? Yours truly.
column8: Current synonyms mix two different senses. The self-reference use is often playful, ironic, or mildly self-important.

column5: Deprecating = expressing disapproval or belittling something; self-deprecating = modestly or humorously criticizing oneself.
column7: He made a self-deprecating joke about his cooking. / The reviewer used a deprecating tone toward the proposal.
column8: Important distinction: 'deprecating' alone does not mean humble/self-critical. In everyday English, 'self-deprecating' is the common phrase for humor directed at oneself.

column5: Treating a serious subject with deliberately flippant, joking, or inappropriate humor; not meant literally or seriously.
column7: I was being facetious—I don't actually think we should cancel the whole project.
column8: Often misunderstood as simply funny. Facetiousness can be inappropriate because the subject is serious.

column5: 1. A venue filled to capacity. 2. In poker, a hand containing three cards of one rank and two of another. 3. Informally, a home/room with all expected people present.
column7: The theater played to a full house. / She won the pot with a full house.
column8: Add major poker sense. 'A full house' is countable; 'the concert was a full house' is natural, though 'played to a full house' is especially idiomatic.

column5: To argue or object over a minor detail; a quibble is a small objection or criticism.
column7: We can quibble over the exact wording later. / I have one small quibble with the proposal.
column8: Common pattern quibble over/about. Less hostile than bicker; often intellectual/detail-focused.

column5: To bring someone into a group or system, often to neutralize opposition or gain support; to appropriate an idea, movement, symbol, or practice for a different purpose; formally, to appoint someone into a group.
column7: The movement's language was co-opted by advertisers. / The committee co-opted two additional members.
column8: Current 'take over' definition is too narrow. Often the original group still exists; the issue is absorption, appropriation, or neutralization.

column5: Defensive end: a defensive-line position in American football, typically responsible for pass rushing, setting the edge, and defending the run depending on scheme.
column7: The DE beat the tackle and pressured the quarterback.
column8: FIX current POS/definition contamination: this card is about the football abbreviation DE, not French/Spanish 'de'. Role varies by defensive scheme.

column5: Done without careful selection, distinction, or discrimination; affecting targets broadly rather than selectively.
column7: The indiscriminate use of antibiotics can create problems. / The attack was condemned as indiscriminate.
column8: Not always literally random; key idea is lack of appropriate distinction/selectivity.

column5: To distribute or serve something; figuratively, to give out criticism, punishment, abuse, praise, advice, etc., often freely or forcefully.
column6: serve, hand out, dole out, mete out
column7: She dished out soup to everyone. / The coach dished out harsh criticism after the loss.
column8: Literal food-serving origin + figurative distribution. Common phrase 'dish it out but can't take it' = criticize others but cannot handle criticism.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb usage::informal usage::figurative topic::food discovery::figurative_extension discovery::criticism discovery::recommendation discovery::social_approval

column5: To distribute, provide, or issue something in measured/organized fashion; to give advice or justice; in 'dispense with', to do without or get rid of.
column6: distribute, issue, provide; do without (dispense with)
column7: The machine dispenses tickets. / The pharmacist dispensed the medication. / We can dispense with the formalities.
column8: Important separate pattern dispense with. Formal-neutral, common in medicine, machines, law, and institutional contexts.

column5: Not returned, reciprocated, or answered, especially of love or affection.
column7: He wrote poems about unrequited love. / Her affection remained unrequited.
column8: Most strongly associated with love/affection. Can occasionally modify other feelings or efforts, but not broadly interchangeable with 'unanswered'.

column5: Romantic love or deep affection that is not returned by the person loved.
column7: She spent years trying to move on from unrequited love.
column8: Useful phrase card independent from adjective if retrieval value is desired. Compare WID1195 lexical adjective.

column5: To annoy, bother, or pressure someone repeatedly, especially with repeated questions, requests, or interruptions.
column7: Stop pestering me with questions. / The kids pestered him for another story.
column8: Duplicate-family with WID1037, where the lemma has already been normalized/enriched. Recommend later consolidation unless source/retrieval value justifies both.

column5: Agitated, confused, embarrassed, or nervous because of pressure, surprise, or too much happening at once.
column7: She got flustered when the microphone stopped working. / He looked visibly flustered by the rapid questions.
column8: FIX grammar: adjective meaning, not 'to be'. Related fluster verb = make someone agitated/confused.

column5: A servant, subordinate, or follower who is regarded as excessively obedient, servile, or willing to do another person's bidding.
column7: The dictator surrounded himself with obedient lackeys.
column8: Strongly disparaging. Not a neutral synonym for employee/assistant.

column5: A junior worker or assistant whose job involves running errands and doing routine or menial tasks for others.
column7: He started as a gofer, fetching coffee and delivering scripts.
column8: From 'go for' this/go for that. Informal and sometimes belittling. Avoid gendered 'errand boy' as the primary synonym.

column5: Relating to low-status, routine, repetitive, or undemanding work, often involving little autonomy and traditionally regarded as requiring little specialized skill.
column7: He was stuck doing menial tasks like filing papers and cleaning. / I don't mind menial work if it frees everyone else to focus on the difficult part.
column8: Often carries a dismissive/status judgment about the work, not merely 'boring'. Common: menial task/job/work.

column5: A rude, uncouth, or insensitive low-status servant or worker.
column6: rude servant, uncouth underling, ill-mannered subordinate
column7: The character dismisses him as a 'boorish menial,' combining contempt for his manners with contempt for his status.
column8: Not a standard fixed expression. Analyze compositionally: boorish = rude/uncouth; menial as a noun = a servant or low-status worker, now dated/disparaging.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::literary usage::dated usage::disparaging usage::evaluative topic::work

column5: To make a short visit to someone, especially to check how they are doing or whether they need anything.
column6: check on, drop in on, call in on, stop by to see
column7: I'll look in on Grandma after work to see how she's doing. / Could you look in on the cat while I'm away?
column8: Usually implies a brief welfare/checking visit. Compare look into = investigate; look in = make a brief visit, often followed by on + person.

column5: Attractive or expensive clothes and outward appearance can make a person seem more impressive, refined, or important.
column6: clothes make the man, appearances influence impressions
column7: He dressed impeccably for the interview—fine feathers make fine birds, as the saying goes.
column8: Traditional proverb, often used wryly. It comments on the power of appearance; depending on context it can endorse dressing well or criticize superficial judgment.

column5: 1. A small piece of paper/card punched out to make a hole, famously in punched-card or ballot contexts. 2. Internet slang: a stereotypically confident, attractive, socially or sexually successful man.
column6: paper punch-out; stereotypical alpha male, attractive confident guy
column7: The recount focused on hanging chads on punch-card ballots. / In the meme, the 'Chad' character is exaggeratedly confident.
column8: The slang sense is meme/internet culture and can be admiring, mocking, or ironic. 'Hanging chad' became especially associated with the 2000 U.S. election.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::ironic usage::informal topic::internet

column5: Used to introduce a final additional fact—often the last in a series of problems, but sometimes a pleasant finishing touch.
column6: on top of that, to make matters worse, as a finishing touch
column7: It was raining, the bus was late, and to top it off, I forgot my umbrella. / Dinner was excellent, and to top it off, dessert was free.
column8: Not inherently negative. Compare top something off = finish/complete it, fill a container to the top, or add a final element.

column5: To go and begin working, or simply to begin/do work; in informal AmE, go + bare verb is common where other varieties may prefer go and + verb.
column6: get to work, start working, go and work
column7: Stop wasting time and go work on your project. / I'll go work in the library for a couple of hours.
column8: Not a fixed idiom. AmE commonly uses 'go work'; 'go and work' is also natural and is especially common outside AmE.

column5: Existing as a distinct, self-contained thing with its own character, complexity, or rules.
column6: in itself, self-contained, a thing/world unto itself
column7: That subplot is almost a story unto itself. / New York's subway system can feel like a world unto itself.
column8: Common frames: a world unto itself, a category unto itself, an experience unto itself. Slightly elevated/literary.

column5: a mild or lenient punishment for a wrongdoing
column7: He only got a slap on the wrist for cheating on the exam.
column8: Common pattern: get/receive a slap on the wrist. The phrase often implies that the punishment was surprisingly or unfairly lenient.

column5: late or delayed beyond the expected time
column7: Students who are tardy more than three times will receive detention.
column8: Common in school/work attendance contexts. Tardy is slightly more formal/administrative than simply late.

column5: The purchase of a controlling interest or ownership stake in a company or asset; also a payment/package offered to persuade an employee, tenant, contract holder, etc. to leave or surrender rights.
column6: acquisition, takeover; severance buyout, contract buyout
column7: The investors completed a management buyout. / The company offered veteran employees voluntary buyouts.
column8: Broaden beyond corporate takeover. Common compounds: leveraged buyout (LBO), management buyout, contract buyout, employee buyout.
column12: entry::word usage::professional usage::persuasive usage::businesslike topic::business topic::work topic::law discovery::persuasion discovery::professional_context

column5: to descend a vertical surface, such as a cliff, using a rope
column7: They rappelled down the cliff face with expert precision.
column8: Common pattern: rappel down/off a cliff, wall, or building. The core idea is a controlled descent using a rope.

column5: a symbol or offer of peace and reconciliation
column7: She extended an olive branch by inviting him to the family dinner.
column8: Common collocations: extend/offer an olive branch. Usually figurative: an attempt to restore peace or reopen communication after conflict.

column5: To move or shift even slightly; figuratively, to change one's position, opinion, price, or decision.
column7: The drawer wouldn't budge. / He wouldn't budge on the price. / I tried to change her mind, but she wouldn't budge.
column8: Very common in negatives: won't/wouldn't budge. Covers both literal movement and refusal to compromise.
column12: entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::decision-making topic::debate discovery::figurative_extension discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::debate_language

column2: in a vise / in a vice
column5: Caught in severe pressure or squeezed between competing forces, as if held in a vise.
column6: under pressure, squeezed, trapped, caught in a bind
column7: Small businesses were caught in a vise between rising costs and falling demand.
column8: In AmE the clamping tool is normally 'vise'; BrE uses 'vice'. The metaphor is often 'caught in a vise/vice' or 'like a vise'.

column5: Compensation, repayment, or reward for loss, harm, effort, or service; as a verb, to compensate or repay someone.
column7: He received recompense for the damage. / No amount of money could recompense them for the loss.
column8: Formal/literary. Can be positive reward or compensation for harm. Verb pattern: recompense someone for something.

column5: To display or express emotion, especially in a conspicuous, theatrical, or exaggerated way; more neutrally, to convey emotion in performance.
column7: The actor can emote without overplaying the scene. / Critics said he spent the whole speech emoting for the cameras.
column8: Often mildly critical when it suggests excessive theatricality, but in acting/performance discussion it can be more neutral.

column5: An image taken from beneath a person's clothing to view the crotch or underwear, typically without consent; upskirting is the act/practice of making such images.
column7: The law specifically criminalizes certain forms of upskirting.
column8: Use neutral, consent-centered wording. Legal definitions and offenses vary by jurisdiction; do not assume every jurisdiction uses the same statutory term.

column5: small pieces of fecal matter stuck to the hairs around the anus
column6: dingleberry, fecal residue (clinical/paraphrase; slang term has no exact neutral synonym)
column7: He made a crude joke about dingleberries that grossed everyone out.
column8: Crude slang rather than a neutral clinical term. Usually plural in this sense; use carefully because the word is intentionally graphic/comic.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::informal topic::medicine topic::health

column5: to imitate someone's voice, mannerisms, or behavior, often for humor
column7: He can do impressions of nearly every celebrity you can think of.
column8: Common pattern: do an impression of someone; do impressions of celebrities/characters. The focus is imitating voice, mannerisms, or behavior.

column5: Playful, quick exchange of teasing or joking remarks; as a verb, to exchange such remarks.
column7: Their friendly banter made the podcast feel relaxed. / We bantered about whose team was worse.
column8: Banter is ideally mutual/playful; one-sided insults may be defended as 'banter' but can simply be bullying or hostility. BrE uses the word especially often.

column5: Impossible or extremely difficult to satisfy; continually demanding more.
column7: She has an insatiable curiosity about languages. / The market seemed to have an insatiable appetite for the product.
column8: Common collocations: insatiable curiosity/appetite/hunger/desire/thirst. 'Greedy' is not a general synonym because insatiable need not be morally negative.

column2: have a chip on one's shoulder
column5: To carry a lasting sense of grievance, inferiority, or resentment that makes one defensive, combative, or quick to take offense.
column6: be resentful, feel aggrieved, be defensive, have something to prove
column7: He has a chip on his shoulder about being passed over for promotion.
column8: More than simply 'hold a grudge': often describes an attitude or sensitivity rooted in perceived disrespect or disadvantage.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::persuasive discovery::complaint discovery::persuasion

column5: Large groups of ordinary or common people, especially as contrasted with the elite, authorities or ruling class
column6: common people, general public, populace, the public, the crowd, the majority
column7: His films are not intended to appeal to the masses. The elites pull the strings while the masses suffer the consequences of their court's egregious failures. The new app quickly gained popularity among the masses.
column8: Often contrasts ordinary people with elites, authorities, or specialists. Depending on tone, the phrase can sound sociological, political, or slightly dismissive.

column5: To pivot sharply and face the opposite direction, especially in order to leave abruptly, decisively, or angrily.
column7: She turned on her heel and walked out without another word.
column8: Can be literal movement; the abrupt/angry departure implication comes from context rather than being mandatory.

column5: a dismissive or indifferent mindset toward something important
column7: His so-what attitude during the meeting frustrated everyone.
column8: Usually written with hyphens in the attributive compound: a so-what attitude. The phrase signals dismissiveness or indifference rather than simple uncertainty.

column5: Soft, yielding, and easy to squeeze or compress; figuratively, vague, weakly defined, overly sentimental, or lacking firmness, depending on context.
column6: soft, spongy, mushy, yielding; vague, soft-edged
column7: The stress ball is satisfyingly squishy. / The proposal gets squishy when it comes to enforcement.
column8: Current cake example is unnatural for many contexts; moist/soft is normally preferred for cake. Figurative senses are common in informal speech.

column2: rock someone back on their heels / be rocked back on one's heels
column5: To shock, surprise, or unsettle someone so strongly that they are momentarily thrown off balance, literally or figuratively.
column7: The announcement rocked investors back on their heels. / She was rocked back on her heels by the accusation.
column8: Normalize to the more established pattern 'rock someone back on their heels'. Related 'set someone back on their heels'.

column5: Used to signal that something is extremely obvious, or to react to one's own or another person's foolish oversight.
column7: 'You need a password to log in.' 'Duh.' / Oh, duh—I left my keys on the desk.
column8: Can sound mocking, childish, or rude when directed at someone else. Punctuation: 'Duh!' or 'Oh, duh.'

column2: coast by / coast by on something
column5: To get through or succeed with little effort, often by relying on an existing advantage such as talent, charm, reputation, or prior work.
column6: get by, cruise through, skate by, rely on
column7: He coasted by on charm and let the rest of the group do the work. / You can coast by for a while on talent, but eventually preparation matters.
column8: Related coast through = complete easily; coast on = continue benefiting from an advantage. Often mildly critical.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::critical topic::work discovery::social_approval

column2: lash out / lash out at someone
column5: To suddenly attack someone verbally or physically, especially because of anger, fear, pain, or frustration.
column6: snap at, attack, strike out, vent at
column7: She lashed out at her friend and later regretted it. / Hurt people sometimes lash out when they feel cornered.
column8: Normalize lemma from 'lashing out'. Not necessarily 'without control'; it describes sudden aggressive reaction, often emotional.

column5: used to accept a challenge, bet, or agreement
column7: '$20 says I win.' 'You're on!'
column8: Often used to accept a challenge, wager, or proposed contest. Tone is usually confident, playful, or competitive.
column12: entry::idiom entry::response_formula entry::discourse_expression entry::fixed_expression usage::playful discovery::agreement

column5: a soft toy made of plush fabric, often resembling an animal or character
column6: stuffed animal, cuddly toy, soft toy
column7: She gave her niece a dinosaur plushie for her birthday. She collected plushies from every anime convention she attended.
column8: Informal term for a plush/stuffed toy, especially common in fandom and collecting contexts. Plural: plushies.

column5: informal or humorous term for 'president'
column7: The student body prez gave a rousing speech at the assembly.
column8: Informal shortening of president. Meaning depends on context: student-body prez, company/club prez, etc.; usually playful or casual.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::casual usage::slang usage::humorous usage::playful discovery::terminology

column5: To give someone advance, confidential, or inside information, especially a warning about something that is going to happen.
column6: alert, warn, give a heads-up, inform secretly
column7: An anonymous caller tipped police off about the planned robbery. / Who tipped you off that they were coming?
column8: Normalize productive pattern. Distinguish tip-off (noun) = warning/inside information; tip off can also mean begin a basketball game in a separate sense.

column5: To detract from or disparage; in formal/legal use, 'derogate from' means to depart from, diminish, or restrict the force/effect of a right, rule, or obligation.
column6: detract, disparage; depart from, diminish, impair
column7: Nothing in this agreement derogates from existing statutory rights. / His remarks were intended to derogate his opponent.
column8: Formal and relatively rare. Do not confuse with 'denigrate'. Legal/institutional 'derogate from' is especially important.

column5: An informal term for certain Democratic Party convention delegates who are not pledged through primary/caucus results; their voting role is governed by party rules and has changed over time.
column7: Superdelegates became a major topic during several Democratic nomination contests.
column8: FIX temporal precision: rules have changed. Under current Democratic rules, automatic delegates generally do not vote on the first presidential-nomination ballot unless the outcome is already determined; avoid the old blanket definition 'can vote for any candidate regardless of primary results'.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal topic::politics topic::history discovery::terminology discovery::public_discourse

column5: noun: a person chosen or authorized to represent others, especially at a conference, convention, or organization. verb: to entrust a task, authority, or responsibility to another person.
column7: Delegates cast their votes at the convention. / Good managers know how to delegate responsibility.
column8: Broaden to major verb sense. Pronunciation stress differs in many accents: noun /ˈdɛləɡət/, verb /ˈdɛləɡeɪt/.

column5: To prepare and write a formal document, plan, list, agreement, or proposal; also literally, to move something closer or bring oneself upright in some contexts.
column7: The contract was drawn up by the legal team. / We drew up a shortlist of candidates.
column8: Normalize active/passive family. Core formal-document sense is highly productive: draw up a contract/plan/list.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern usage::formal topic::planning discovery::agreement discovery::suggestion

column5: used to indicate that a number is multiplied by itself
column6: squared, raised to the second power
column7: Three to the power of two is nine.
column8: Equivalent to squared / raised to the second power. Written mathematically as x²; e.g. 3² = 9.

column4: pronoun-like noun / slang; adjective; verb; noun
column5: Slang: nothing or very little, especially in 'know squat' or 'get squat'. Other common senses: to crouch with knees bent; a squat exercise; short/low in build; an unlawfully occupied building/place.
column7: He doesn't know squat about cars. / After all that work, we got squat. / She squatted to pick up the box.
column8: The slang sense is informal and often emphatic. Broaden because squat is highly polysemous; 'diddly-squat' is an even more emphatic slang form.

column5: depressing, gloomy, or of very poor quality
column7: The weather was dismal all weekend, so we stayed indoors.
column8: Can describe weather, conditions, results, performance, or mood. The common thread is bleakness, gloom, or very poor quality.

column5: To yield or give in to pressure, temptation, emotion, exhaustion, illness, injury, or another overpowering force; in formal use, 'succumb to' illness/injuries can mean die from them.
column6: yield, give in, surrender; die from (context-specific)
column7: She finally succumbed to exhaustion. / He resisted the dessert for ten minutes before succumbing. / The patient later succumbed to his injuries.
column8: Pattern: succumb to. The death sense is formal/euphemistic and context-dependent; succumb itself does not always mean die.

column5: To try or hope to make an unpleasant fact, problem, feeling, or situation disappear merely by wishing or refusing to confront it.
column6: will away, hope away, ignore, deny
column7: You can't just wish away the problem; it has to be dealt with. / I wish I could wish this headache away.
column8: Often used negatively: 'You can't wish X away.'

column5: to surprise someone who is not paying attention
column6: take by surprise, catch off guard
column7: The opposing team caught them napping and scored in the final seconds.
column8: Usually figurative: catch someone unprepared or inattentive, not necessarily literally asleep. Closely related to catch someone off guard.

column5: Used to temporarily accept an assumption—not necessarily because you believe it—in order to explore its consequences or continue a discussion.
column6: for the sake of argument, hypothetically, assuming for discussion
column7: For argument's sake, let's say you had one more day—what would you change?
column8: Also very common: 'for the sake of argument'. It marks a provisional assumption, not necessarily agreement.

column5: An informal reaction expressing surprise, disbelief, confusion, or a request to repeat what was said.
column7: 'I quit my job yesterday.' 'Say what?'
column8: Usually written with a question mark. Very informal; can sound comic or emphatic rather than a neutral request for repetition.

column5: torn or ragged, especially from wear
column7: He wore a tattered old coat that had seen better days.
column8: Typically describes clothing, paper, flags, books, etc. damaged by wear so that they are torn, ragged, or frayed.

column5: A friendly parting expression meaning take care, be careful, or have a safe journey.
column6: take care, be safe, safe travels
column7: Thanks for coming—mind how you go!
column8: Chiefly British and somewhat traditional. Depending on region/speaker it can sound warm, old-fashioned, or lightly humorous.

column5: A small container, traditionally glass, for holding liquid, especially medicine, chemicals, perfume, or a sample.
column7: The apothecary kept the liquid in a tiny glass phial.
column8: 'Phial' is a less common spelling/form than 'vial' in modern English and can feel literary or old-fashioned.

column5: adjective: recklessly extravagant or wasteful, especially with money/resources. noun: a recklessly wasteful or morally dissolute person (dated/literary).
column7: The company was criticized for profligate spending. / Critics called the project a profligate use of public money.
column8: Formal. Common collocation 'profligate spending'. The noun/morally dissolute sense is much less common today.
column12: entry::collocation entry::word usage::formal usage::literary usage::dated discovery::resource_allocation

column5: Sexual union/intercourse, especially as a biological or zoological term for mating involving genital union.
column7: The documentary described mating and copulation in several animal species.
column8: Formal/clinical and especially common in biology/zoology; not the usual everyday word for human sex.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::scientific topic::biology topic::science discovery::terminology

column5: Slang for romantic/sexual charm or charisma; as a verb, to charm, flirt with, or successfully attract someone, often 'rizz someone up'.
column7: He's got ridiculous rizz. / He tried to rizz her up with a cheesy pickup line.
column8: Internet/Gen Z slang, originally associated with 'charisma'. Usage is fluid: noun 'rizz' is extremely common; verb patterns include rizz up / rizz someone up.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::slang usage::gen_z usage::informal topic::romance

column5: Done in advance to prevent, forestall, or gain an advantage over an anticipated event or action.
column7: They took preemptive action before the storm arrived. / The military described it as a preemptive strike.
column8: AmE usually 'preemptive'; 'pre-emptive' also occurs. 'Preventive' is broader and not always interchangeable; preemptive often implies acting before another expected action.

column5: to sit in a crouched position with one's weight resting on the heels
column7: He sat on his heels to tie the little girl's shoes.
column8: A literal body-position expression: sitting/crouching with weight resting back on the heels. Keep distinct from figurative heel-related idioms.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::debate_language

column5: established or decided in advance
column7: The outcome of the match seemed predetermined from the start.
column8: Common with outcome, result, course, schedule, fate, or answer. It emphasizes that something was decided/fixed before the relevant event.

column5: a stone used for sharpening cutting tools like knives or blades
column7: He ran the blade across the whetstone to restore its sharp edge.
column8: A whetstone is specifically for sharpening an edge by abrasion. Common collocations: sharpen a knife/blade on a whetstone.

column5: To sharpen a blade with a fine abrasive; figuratively, to refine, improve, or perfect a skill, technique, argument, or ability through practice.
column7: He honed the knife on a stone. / She spent years honing her public-speaking skills.
column8: Do not confuse hone with home in: 'home in on' = move/focus toward a target. 'Hone in on' is widespread but historically disputed; for careful usage, use 'home in on'.

column5: To intrude into someone else's activity, conversation, business, or opportunity, often without invitation and sometimes to gain an advantage.
column6: butt in on, intrude on, muscle in on, interfere in
column7: He tried to horn in on our conversation. / Competitors are horning in on their market.
column8: Usually disapproving. Compare 'home in on' = focus/move toward; 'hone' = sharpen/refine.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb usage::informal usage::critical topic::business topic::communication topic::anatomy topic::health

column5: To confuse, bewilder, perplex, or fluster someone.
column7: The instructions completely bumfuzzled me.
column8: Real but uncommon/playful/regional-sounding. Good recognition word; don't treat it as ordinary everyday slang everywhere.

column5: A person who writes from another's dictation, copies manuscripts, or serves as a literary/secretarial assistant.
column7: The author dictated portions of the memoir to his amanuensis.
column8: Rare/formal. Historically broader than a modern secretary; often encountered in literary or historical contexts.

column5: bad-tempered, argumentative, and uncooperative
column7: The cantankerous old man yelled at kids for walking on his lawn.
column8: Usually describes a person, temperament, or behavior: bad-tempered, argumentative, and difficult to deal with.

column5: Irritable, quarrelsome, unruly, or difficult to manage; also used of groups/situations marked by internal conflict.
column7: The fractious toddler refused to settle down. / The leader struggled to unite a fractious coalition.
column8: Broaden beyond individuals. Common with children, animals, political parties, coalitions, meetings.

column5: rude or disrespectful behavior; lack of respect
column7: The teacher was shocked by the student's impertinence.
column8: A relatively formal noun for rude, disrespectful, or presumptuous behavior. Common frame: the impertinence of doing/saying something.

column5: A blockage, closing, or obstruction of a passage; in dentistry, the contact/alignment relationship between upper and lower teeth; in meteorology, an occluded front/process.
column7: The scan showed an arterial occlusion. / The dentist checked her occlusion.
column8: Major technical polysemy. Medical occlusion and dental occlusion are especially common; exact meaning depends strongly on field.
column12: entry::word usage::technical topic::relationships discovery::process_details discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: childishly sulky or bad-tempered
column7: She became petulant when her requests weren't immediately granted.
column8: Often suggests childish sulking or irritability, especially when someone is denied what they want or feels slighted.

column5: To start, resume, or continue doing something without further delay; often used impatiently to tell someone to proceed.
column6: get going, proceed, carry on, get to it
column7: Stop stalling and get on with it. / After the interruption, we got on with the meeting.
column8: BrE especially common, but widely understood. Tone ranges from practical to impatient.

column5: A dialectal or regional way of getting a girl's/woman's attention or addressing her; exact form and meaning depend heavily on region and source.
column7: 'Eh, lass, you dropped your scarf!'
column8: SOURCE/REGIONAL CAUTION: 'lass' is well established in northern England/Scotland and elsewhere, but 'eh lass' should not be presented as one standardized Northern UK formula. If the source actually says 'ey up, lass', that is a different regional greeting.

column5: relating to or characteristic of winter; cold or bleak
