column7: The wintry wind cut through his jacket like a knife.
column8: Used for winter-like weather, landscapes, light, or atmosphere: cold, bleak, frosty, or seasonally harsh.

column5: To interpret, understand, or form an opinion about someone or something, especially when it is puzzling or ambiguous.
column7: I don't know what to make of him. / What do you make of the ending?
column8: Broaden to someone/something. Very common frame: 'What do you make of X?' = What is your interpretation/opinion?
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::courtroom topic::law discovery::ambiguity discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::evaluation

column5: Literal: to bend/tighten a muscle or joint. Slang: to show off or conspicuously display status, possessions, ability, or success; noun slang can mean an act/thing used to show off.
column6: show off, flaunt, brag; bend, tense
column7: He flexed his arm for the photo. / Posting the first-class ticket was a deliberate flex.
column8: Broaden beyond slang. 'Weird flex, but OK' is a well-known internet formula reacting to an odd boast/display.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::informal topic::anatomy topic::health

column5: the act of charming or enchanting someone, often in a deceptive way
column7: Her beguilement of the crowd was effortless and mesmerizing.
column8: Noun related to beguile. The sense can combine charm/enchantment with deception; context determines how negative it is.

column5: verb: to leave someone or something stuck, isolated, or unable to continue; noun: a single thread/fiber, a shore, or a component/thread of a larger whole.
column6: maroon, leave stuck; thread, fiber, shore
column7: The storm stranded hundreds of travelers. / A strand of hair fell across her face. / The course has several thematic strands.
column8: Major polysemy. Current card covers only the verb; noun senses are common and useful.

column5: suggesting the presence of danger or threat
column7: The dog gave a low, menacing growl as they approached the gate.
column8: Common collocations: menacing look, tone, figure, growl, gesture. It suggests an implied or approaching threat.

column5: firmly loyal or determined; not changing or quitting
column7: Her steadfast belief in justice never wavered.
column8: Common with support, loyalty, belief, commitment, ally, or resolve. The key idea is remaining firm and unwavering.

column5: nervous or easily startled
column7: He was so jumpy after the movie that he flinched at every noise.
column8: Often describes a person who is tense, nervous, or easily startled. Common after stress, fear, too much caffeine, or a frightening experience.

column5: A person who is difficult to pin down, catch, understand, trust, or deal with, often because they are evasive or cunning.
column6: evasive person, tricky character, dodgy customer
column7: He's a slippery customer—you'll have trouble getting a straight answer out of him.
column8: 'Customer' here means person/character, not necessarily a buyer. Informal and especially British.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::british_english topic::business discovery::evasive_language discovery::social_trust

column5: A large amount or number of something; 'a whole heap of other options' means many other choices.
column6: a lot of, loads of, tons of, a whole bunch of
column7: We've got a whole heap of other options. / That created a whole heap of problems.
column8: Teach productive frame rather than freezing the source sentence. Very informal.

column5: I'm willing, interested, or ready to participate in a suggested activity, including something challenging or adventurous.
column6: I'm in, count me in, I'm up for it, I'm down
column7: 'Want to try bungee jumping?' 'Sure, I'm game.'
column8: Game as adjective = willing/ready. Related 'game for something' and 'game to do something'.

column5: Not at all; not even close; by no means.
column6: not even close, by no means, absolutely not
column7: Is the job finished? Not by a long shot. / He's not the best player—not by a long shot.
column8: Often used as a standalone emphatic reply. Contrast WID1285 positive 'by a long shot'.

column5: By a large margin or to a considerable degree, usually in comparisons; much less commonly, 'at all' in certain negative constructions.
column6: by far, easily, by a wide margin
column7: She was the best candidate by a long shot.
column8: Most natural in comparisons. The negative idiom 'not by a long shot' is especially common and semantically stronger.

column5: A person who is easily persuaded, dominated, or taken advantage of; also an opponent, task, or challenge that is very easy to defeat or accomplish.
column6: easy mark, soft touch, doormat; easy win, piece of cake
column7: She's kind, but she's no pushover. / Everyone expected the match to be a pushover, but it wasn't.
column8: Broaden beyond person. 'No pushover' is a common positive formulation meaning not easily defeated or manipulated.

column5: From this point onward, especially in formal/legal writing; as a noun with 'the', the life or existence after death.
column7: Hereafter, all requests must be submitted in writing. / Some traditions describe rewards in the hereafter.
column8: Separate grammatical senses: adverb = from now on; noun 'the hereafter' = afterlife. Formal/old-fashioned outside legal/religious contexts.

column5: to do one's fair share of work or duties
column6: contribute, carry your load, do your part
column7: Everyone on the team has to pull their weight to succeed.
column8: Common in teams, workplaces, households, and shared projects. If someone does not pull their weight, others must carry more than their fair share.

column5: To attack, criticize, tackle, or energetically begin dealing with someone or something; 'Have at it!' can mean go ahead and start/try.
column6: go at, attack, tackle; go ahead
column7: The two critics had at each other for an hour. / 'Can I try fixing it?' 'Sure—have at it.'
column8: Current example 'had at the guy' is awkward. High-value expression is 'Have at it!' and reciprocal 'have at each other'.

column5: To prevent, repel, or keep away something harmful or unwanted, such as danger, illness, an attack, hunger, or criticism.
column6: fend off, stave off, repel, keep at bay
column7: She took a walk to ward off drowsiness. / Vaccination can help ward off certain infections.
column8: Normalize without infinitive 'to'. Garlic-and-mosquito example is distracting; use realistic collocations. Compare stave off = delay/prevent temporarily.

column5: 1. The visible external part of the ear (pinna). 2. An ear-like appendage of an atrium of the heart; historically, 'auricle' was also used for an atrium.
column7: The auricle helps collect sound and direct it toward the ear canal.
column8: CORRECT anatomy precision: in modern cardiac anatomy, auricle usually means the ear-shaped appendage of an atrium, not simply 'an upper chamber of the heart'.

column5: A person, shrine, or medium through which divine prophecy/advice is believed to be given; the prophecy itself; figuratively, a person or source treated as highly authoritative.
column7: Ancient Greeks consulted the oracle at Delphi. / Everyone treated him as an oracle on the subject.
column8: Broaden beyond 'person or medium'. Computing/database proper-name uses are separate and should not be conflated with the common noun.

column5: To steal, especially small amounts or relatively low-value items, often repeatedly or opportunistically.
column7: Someone had been pilfering supplies from the storeroom. / Tourists kept pilfering towels from the hotel.
column8: Often suggests petty theft, but the stolen thing need not literally be worthless.

column5: To crush or grind into very fine particles; figuratively, to defeat, destroy, or criticize overwhelmingly.
column7: The machine pulverized the concrete into dust. / Their team pulverized us in the second half.
column8: Literal + emphatic figurative sense. AmE pulverize; BrE also pulverise.
column12: entry::variant_set entry::phrase usage::figurative usage::american_english usage::british_english topic::romance discovery::figurative_extension discovery::criticism

column5: To die; to fail, break down, be defeated, or come to an end.
column6: die, perish; fail, collapse, go under
column7: Another business idea bit the dust. / My old laptop finally bit the dust.
column8: Often humorous/light when used of objects, plans, or companies; can sound flippant if used about a real person's death.

column5: something that is very pleasant or gratifying to hear
column7: Her praise was music to his ears after a long day.
column8: Figurative expression for news, praise, or information that is especially welcome or gratifying to hear—not necessarily literal music.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::figurative topic::news topic::music discovery::impression

column5: To draw attention away from someone else and make them seem less impressive; in theater, literally to move upstage in a way that can force another actor to turn away from the audience.
column7: The supporting actor upstaged the lead. / The surprise announcement upstaged the product launch.
column8: Normalize lemma. Modern figurative sense is much more common outside theater.

column2: talk someone out of something / doing something
column5: To persuade someone not to do something, not to choose something, or to abandon an intended action.
column6: dissuade, persuade against, convince not to
column7: She talked him out of quitting his job. / Can I talk you out of driving in this weather?
column8: Productive patterns: talk someone out of doing something; talk someone out of a decision/purchase. Opposite: talk someone into something.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::persuasive topic::decision-making discovery::persuasion

column5: Worried, unsettled, disturbed, or agitated; in technical/scientific contexts, altered from a normal state by an external influence.
column7: He seemed perturbed by the sudden change of plans. / The object followed a slightly perturbed orbit.
column8: Everyday sense is moderately formal. Technical sense appears in physics/mathematics/astronomy via perturb/perturbation.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::technical usage::scientific topic::science discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A raised table, platform, or structure used in religious worship, sacrifice, offerings, or ritual; also the ceremonial focal point in many weddings.
column6: sacred table, shrine (not exact), ritual structure
column7: The couple stood before the altar to exchange vows. / Offerings were placed on the temple altar.
column8: Do not use 'sanctuary' as a direct synonym: a sanctuary is a sacred place/area, not the altar itself. Common confusable: altar vs alter.

column5: 1. Intense joy, delight, or ecstasy. 2. In some Christian traditions, the Rapture: an eschatological event in which believers are taken up to meet Christ.
column7: She listened in rapture as the orchestra played. / The novel refers to the Rapture as an end-times event.
column8: Capitalize Rapture for the specific Christian doctrine/event. Religious interpretations differ among Christian traditions; do not present it as a universally held doctrine.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::religious topic::religion topic::transportation discovery::emotional_intensity

column2: I could burst / burst with emotion
column5: Used to say that an emotion feels so strong that it is almost physically overwhelming, especially pride, happiness, excitement, or frustration.
column6: I'm overwhelmed, I'm bursting with pride/joy, I could explode
column7: I'm so proud of her I could burst. / He looked as if he might burst with excitement.
column8: Very natural patterns: 'I could burst,' 'burst with pride/joy,' 'fit to burst' (especially BrE). The emotion is normally supplied by context or with + noun.

column5: To talk at length, especially in a rambling or tedious way, often about something unimportant.
column6: go on and on, ramble, chatter, drone on
column7: He kept rabbiting on about his holiday for twenty minutes.
column8: SPELLING FIX: 'rabbiting', not 'rabbitting'. Chiefly British informal. Often mildly annoyed or teasing in tone.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::form_family entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::british_english discovery::triviality

column2: mind one's P's and Q's / Ps and Qs
column5: To be careful about one's manners, behavior, language, or social etiquette.
column6: mind one's manners, behave oneself, be polite, watch oneself
column7: Mind your P's and Q's at dinner with her parents.
column8: The origin is uncertain. Apostrophe/punctuation styles vary: P's and Q's, Ps and Qs. The productive form is usually 'mind your P's and Q's'.

column5: Avoiding a direct answer, commitment, capture, or clear statement; deliberately or habitually tending to evade.
column7: He gave an evasive answer when asked where the money had gone. / The suspect proved evasive and difficult to track.
column8: For answers/people, often implies avoidance rather than simple vagueness. Distinguish elusive = difficult to find/catch/define; evasive = actively avoiding.

column5: A person, product, work, team, or other thing that attracts little attention at first but later proves unexpectedly successful, effective, or important; 'sleeper hit' is especially common for entertainment/products.
column6: dark horse, surprise success, sleeper hit
column7: The film became a sleeper hit through word of mouth. / That inexpensive player was the sleeper of the draft.
column8: 'Sleeper' has many unrelated senses (a person who sleeps, a railroad tie in BrE, sleeping car, etc.). This card targets the 'unexpected success' sense.

column5: 1. A single crystal/flakelike cluster of snow. 2. Slang insult for a person portrayed as overly sensitive, fragile, self-important, or easily offended.
column6: flake of snow; oversensitive person, fragile person (slang)
column7: No two snowflakes are exactly alike. / He dismissed the critics as 'snowflakes.'
column8: The slang sense is pejorative and politically/culturally charged. It is often used to mock sensitivity rather than neutrally describe it.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::slang usage::critical usage::derogatory usage::informal usage::evaluative topic::weather

column5: A period or process of gradually recovering health and strength after illness, injury, or medical treatment.
column7: She spent several weeks in convalescence after surgery.
column8: More formal than recovery/recuperation. 'Rehabilitation' can overlap but often refers specifically to therapy or retraining, so it is not always a direct synonym.

column5: To place someone across one's knee to spank them; figuratively or jokingly, to threaten old-fashioned physical discipline.
column7: The line 'I'll put you over my knee' is an old-fashioned threat of spanking.
column8: Often old-fashioned, comic, or threatening; can sound inappropriate or infantilizing when used toward an adult. Meaning depends strongly on context.

column5: 1. The medieval ideals, customs, and conduct associated with knights. 2. Courteous, protective, or gallant behavior, especially a traditional style of conduct by men toward women.
column7: The story romanticizes medieval chivalry. / He offered his seat out of old-fashioned chivalry.
column8: Modern use can be approving, ironic, or critical, especially when the behavior is strongly gendered or paternalistic.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::dated usage::critical usage::ironic topic::technology

column5: A performer who does magic tricks or illusions; in older, fantasy, or occult contexts, a person said to summon spirits or supernatural forces.
column7: The conjurer amazed the audience with sleight of hand. / In the fantasy novel, the conjurer summons spirits.
column8: 'Conjurer' is the more common modern spelling; 'conjuror' is also used. The stage-magician sense and supernatural/fantasy sense should be separated by context.

column5: To behave wildly, violently, destructively, or completely out of control.
column7: Vandals ran amok through the abandoned building. / The software bug ran amok and corrupted several files.
column8: 'Run amok' is the standard spelling; 'run amuck' is an established variant. Figurative use need not involve literal violence.

column2: be / find oneself at a loose end
column5: To have nothing in particular to do, or to feel uncertain about how to occupy oneself.
column6: be idle, be unoccupied, have time on one's hands
column7: I found myself at a loose end after the meeting was canceled.
column8: Chiefly British. In AmE, 'at loose ends' is more common and can also suggest feeling unsettled or without direction.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::uncertainty

column5: To escape from, avoid, or remain out of the grasp of someone; figuratively, to remain difficult to remember, understand, achieve, or obtain.
column6: evade, escape, dodge; baffle, escape one's memory
column7: The suspect eluded police for weeks. / Her name eludes me. / A clear solution continued to elude the team.
column8: Normalize from 'eluding'. High-value figurative patterns: 'the answer eludes me,' 'success eluded him.' Distinguish evade = actively avoid; elude can describe something that remains out of reach.

column5: A large marine gastropod or its spiral shell; a conch shell can also be used as a horn or ceremonial instrument.
column7: He blew into a conch shell to signal the start of the ceremony.
column8: Pronunciation varies by region and word tradition; /kɑŋk/ is common in AmE. The word may refer to the animal, shell, or shell used as a horn.

column5: A large, heavy, or scholarly book, often one that seems serious or imposing.
column7: He pulled a dusty tome on medieval history from the shelf. / I don't want to read a 900-page tome on tax law.
column8: Often slightly literary or humorous; it emphasizes size/weight/seriousness more than merely 'book'.
column12: entry::word usage::literary usage::academic usage::humorous topic::work discovery::academic_discussion

column5: To become, or be, strongly attracted or addicted to something; used for substances, habits, games, shows, hobbies, etc.
column6: get addicted to, get into, become obsessed with, be captivated by
column7: I got hooked on the series after one episode. / He became hooked on nicotine as a teenager.
column8: Can range from harmless enthusiasm ('hooked on a show') to genuine addiction ('hooked on opioids'); context controls seriousness.

column5: The act or practice of avoiding, escaping, or sidestepping something, especially a duty, question, rule, payment, or responsibility.
column7: His answers were a form of evasion. / Tax evasion is illegal.
column8: Important contrast: tax evasion = illegal nonpayment/concealment; tax avoidance usually refers to legally arranging affairs to reduce tax.

column5: Chemical element S, a yellow nonmetal used in industry and present in many minerals and compounds.
column7: Sulfur burns with a blue flame. / The spring smelled of hydrogen sulfide, not elemental sulfur.
column8: CORRECTION: elemental sulfur itself has little to no characteristic 'rotten egg' smell; that odor is strongly associated with hydrogen sulfide and some other sulfur compounds. 'Sulfur' is U.S./IUPAC spelling; 'sulphur' remains common in BrE.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::literary usage::archaic usage::british_english topic::chemistry topic::science

column5: Crooked, tilted, or out of alignment; figuratively, out of order or not quite right.
column7: His glasses sat askew on his face. / The whole arrangement looked slightly askew.
column8: Often physical/visual. Figurative use exists, but 'go awry' is generally more idiomatic for plans and events that go wrong.

column5: Wrong, off course, or contrary to what was intended or expected; also literally crooked/out of position in some contexts.
column7: Something went awry with the launch. / Our carefully planned schedule went awry by noon.
column8: Especially common in 'go awry'. Less often used before a noun. Compare askew = visually crooked; awry = plans/events turning out wrong.

column5: An old/literary word for sulfur, especially in the religious expression 'fire and brimstone,' evoking divine punishment or hellfire.
column7: The preacher delivered a fire-and-brimstone sermon.
column8: Rare as an everyday chemistry term. Mostly encountered in literary, biblical-style, or dramatic language and in 'fire and brimstone'.
column12: entry::word usage::literary usage::figurative usage::religious usage::scientific topic::religion discovery::religious_origin discovery::literal_vs_figurative

column5: 1. To misbehave. 2. To malfunction or behave unpredictably. 3. Of a body part or medical problem, to start causing trouble or pain.
column6: misbehave, malfunction, play up, give trouble
column7: The kids started acting up in the restaurant. / My laptop is acting up again. / My knee has been acting up lately.
column8: Very productive informal phrase. The subject can be a person, machine, system, or body part.

column5: To arrive at a conclusion by reasoning from known facts, evidence, or premises.
column7: From the footprints, she deduced that someone had entered through the window.
column8: Common pattern: deduce X from Y. In everyday English, infer is often close; technically, deduce may imply reasoning from premises while infer is broader.

column5: To offer a guess despite uncertainty, often politely or cautiously.
column6: hazard a guess, take a guess, speculate
column7: Would you care to venture a guess at how much it cost?
column8: Often used in questions/requests: 'Care to venture a guess?' Slightly more polished than simply 'guess'.

column5: In an ambiguous, noncommittal, or deliberately unclear way, leaving room for more than one interpretation.
column7: She answered equivocally, refusing to say whether she supported the proposal.
column8: Related: equivocal (ambiguous/uncertain). Opposite: unequivocally = clearly and without ambiguity. 'Equivocal' does not always imply deliberate deception.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::professional usage::academic usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::communication topic::debate topic::rhetoric topic::law topic::politics discovery::ambiguity discovery::noncommittal_language discovery::evasive_language discovery::uncertainty discovery::debate_language discovery::public_discourse discovery::professional_context discovery::academic_discussion discovery::hedging

column5: Commentary and opinion offered by pundits, especially in politics, sports, or mass media; sometimes used critically for confident analysis with limited accountability.
column7: Political punditry often focuses more on strategy than policy.
column8: Can be neutral or mildly dismissive. Related: pundit = commentator/expert figure; pundit class/punditocracy are more openly critical terms.
column12: entry::word usage::critical topic::media topic::politics discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::public_discourse

column5: Frankly, openly, and without trying to hide one's true opinion, feelings, or assessment.
column7: She spoke candidly about the project's failures. / Candidly, I don't think the plan will work.
column8: Can modify a verb ('spoke candidly') or introduce a frank statement ('Candidly, ...').

column5: A drink consumed every night; depending on context, often an alcoholic drink taken as part of an evening routine.
column6: evening drink, nightcap (if taken before bed)
column7: He had developed a habit of having a whiskey every night.
column8: Not a fixed idiom. 'Nightcap' is a more lexicalized word for a final drink, often alcoholic, taken before bed. 'Nightly drink' simply means a drink occurring every night.

column5: To criticize, mock, tease, or put someone down, often repeatedly.
column6: mock, roast, rag on, put down, make fun of
column7: They kept bagging on him for being late. / Quit bagging on your brother.
column8: Regional and informal; familiarity varies by dialect. It can be playful among friends or genuinely insulting depending on tone.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::playful discovery::criticism

column5: An award, honor, or expression of praise and recognition for an achievement.
column7: The film received critical accolades. / She accepted the accolade on behalf of the team.
column8: Often plural in modern use: 'receive/win accolades'. Singular 'accolade' can mean a specific honor or strong praise.

column5: Used informally to mean extremely, super-, or an outstanding/extreme example of something.
column7: He's an uber-fan of sci-fi. / The restaurant is uber-trendy right now.
column8: From German über ('over/above'). Usually attached to another word (uber-rich, uber-geek) or used informally as an intensifier. Distinguish the common word-forming use from the company name Uber.

column5: Short for 'just kidding'; used to signal that the preceding statement was a joke or not meant seriously.
column7: I totally failed the test—jk, I got an A.
column8: Very informal digital shorthand. Capitalization varies. In speech, people may literally say 'jay-kay' for comic effect.
column12: entry::abbreviation entry::form_family entry::word entry::response_formula entry::discourse_expression entry::fixed_expression usage::informal usage::humorous topic::internet

column5: 'One bit' means even a small amount or degree; in the very common negative 'not one bit,' it means not at all.
column6: in the slightest, at all, even a little
column7: I don't regret it one bit. / She wasn't one bit surprised.
column8: CORRECTION: 'one bit' itself does not inherently mean 'not at all'; the negative construction creates that meaning. Common frame: not ... one bit.

column5: The vocabulary or stock of words and fixed expressions used in a language, variety, field, text, or by a speaker.
column7: Academic writing often uses more formal lexis. / The course focuses on grammar and lexis.
column8: More technical than vocabulary. Compare lexicon = the vocabulary of a language/person/field, or a dictionary/list; lexis often refers to vocabulary as a linguistic level of analysis.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::academic usage::technical topic::decision-making topic::language_learning topic::linguistics discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::academic_discussion

column5: Excessively willing to obey or serve others; or lower in rank, importance, or function and made subordinate to something else.
column7: He resented being treated as a subservient assistant. / The design should be subservient to function, not the other way around.
column8: Pattern: subservient to. Often negative when describing a person because it suggests servility; the 'secondary/subordinate' sense can be more neutral.

column5: To die.
column7: The old computer finally kicked the bucket. / He joked about traveling the world before he kicked the bucket.
column8: Usually humorous, irreverent, or euphemistic. Can sound insensitive when referring to a recent or serious real-world death.

column2: the cat is out of the bag
column5: The secret has been revealed or is no longer secret.
column6: the secret is out, the truth is revealed
column7: Once she saw the decorations, the cat was out of the bag.
column8: Normalize from the fragment 'cat out of the bag'. Related active idiom: let the cat out of the bag = reveal the secret.

column2: let the cat out of the bag
column3: /lɛt ðə kæt aʊt əv ðə bæɡ/
column5: To reveal a secret, often accidentally or earlier than intended.
column6: spill the beans, reveal, disclose, give away the secret
column7: He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.
column8: Often implies accidental/premature disclosure, though deliberate revelation is also possible. Pairs naturally with 'the cat is out of the bag'.

column5: Wrong or incorrect, especially because of an error in facts, reasoning, assumptions, data, or belief.
column7: The report was based on erroneous assumptions. / The database contained several erroneous entries.
column8: More formal than wrong. Common: erroneous belief/assumption/information/data/conclusion.

column5: 1. To take shelter or settle in securely, especially during danger or bad weather. 2. To settle in and concentrate on work or endure a difficult period.
column6: take shelter, hole up, dig in, buckle down
column7: We hunkered down in the basement during the storm. / I need to hunker down and finish this report tonight.
column8: Broader than simply 'prepare for a long stay'. Can be physical sheltering or figurative concentrated effort/endurance.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::phrasal_verb usage::informal usage::figurative topic::work topic::weather discovery::risk discovery::resolution

column5: Five times as great, numerous, or large; by a factor of five.
column7: Sales increased fivefold, from 100 units to 500. / There was a fivefold increase in demand.
column8: SPELLING/QUANTITATIVE FIX: normally one word, fivefold. 'Increased fivefold' means became five times the original level (a 400% increase), not 'increased by five times' in the loose sense.

column5: To eject or pour out forcefully in large amounts; to vomit; figuratively, to produce or express a stream of words, abuse, smoke, data, etc.
column6: gush, pour out, eject, vomit; spout
column7: The volcano spewed ash into the sky. / The pipe was spewing water. / The account kept spewing hateful nonsense.
column8: Often vivid and negative. Figurative 'spew hate/nonsense' suggests uncontrolled or excessive output.

column5: 1. To spread a substance messily across a surface. 2. To blur or stain by rubbing. 3. To damage someone's reputation with accusations or insinuations; noun: a mark/stain or a reputational attack.
column6: smudge, spread, stain; slander, vilify, defame
column7: She smeared butter on the toast. / The ink smeared. / The campaign launched a smear against its opponent.
column8: Major literal + figurative polysemy. Related-family overlap exists elsewhere in the Master; retain here for now because this card combines noun/verb and reputational sense.

column5: To toss out rough ideas for discussion without committing to them; noun 'spitball' also literally means a small wad of chewed/wet paper thrown through a tube.
column6: brainstorm, toss around ideas, kick ideas around
column7: We're just spitballing ideas for the title. / Let me spitball a few possibilities.
column8: Normalize from participle-only headword. In business/creative talk, 'spitball ideas' = brainstorm casually; literal schoolroom sense is separate.

column5: A small recessed area opening off a room, hallway, wall, garden, or other space.
column7: She turned the window alcove into a reading nook.
column8: Usually a partly enclosed/recessed architectural space. Nook is similar but need not be architecturally recessed.

column5: noun: a disagreement, controversy, or conflict. verb: to challenge the truth, validity, ownership, or correctness of something, or to argue about it.
column7: The neighbors are in a dispute over the boundary. / The company disputes the allegations.
column8: Important verb pattern: dispute a claim/fact/allegation. 'Debate' is not always a synonym because dispute often means challenge/deny.

column5: noun: 1. something bought or offered at a favorable price; 2. an agreement or deal. verb: to negotiate over price or terms.
column6: good deal, deal, agreement; haggle, negotiate
column7: I got the coat for a bargain price. / They struck a bargain. / We bargained with the seller over the price.
column8: High-value collocations: bargain price, strike a bargain, bargain with/for, drive a hard bargain. Also 'more than I bargained for' = more than expected.

column5: Based on or producing illusion; deceptive or unreal in appearance.
column7: The apparent simplicity was illusive; the problem was actually complex.
column8: IMPORTANT CONFUSABLE: illusive is rare. 'Illusory' is usually the natural word for based on an illusion, while 'elusive' means difficult to find/catch/understand. Many apparent uses of illusive are spelling confusions.

column5: While something is happening, with little or no advance preparation; improvised in real time.
column6: on the spot, as you go, in real time, spontaneously
column7: We had to rewrite part of the presentation on the fly. / The app can translate text on the fly.
column8: Can emphasize improvisation or real-time processing; common in everyday speech, computing, and technical contexts.
column12: entry::idiom entry::adverbial_phrase entry::prepositional_phrase usage::technical usage::presentation-friendly discovery::improvement discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::presentation_language

column5: Using something as the foundation, evidence, source, model, or inspiration for something else.
column6: founded on, grounded in, derived from, inspired by
column7: The film is based on a true story. / The decision was based on the available evidence.
column8: Broad high-frequency phrase. 'Based off (of)' is common in informal AmE, but 'based on' remains the safest standard form.
column12: entry::phrase usage::informal usage::american_english discovery::evidence discovery::origin_etymology discovery::encouragement

column5: Based on observation, measurement, experiment, or real-world evidence rather than purely on theory, intuition, or deduction.
column7: There is little empirical evidence to support the claim. / The researchers tested the theory empirically.
column8: Common collocations: empirical evidence/data/research/findings. Empirical does not automatically mean scientifically conclusive; evidence can still be weak or badly collected.

column5: verb: to understand or figure out something difficult or puzzling. noun: a unit of depth equal to six feet (1.8288 m), traditionally used at sea.
column6: grasp, comprehend, make sense of; six-foot depth unit
column7: I can't fathom why he refused the offer. / The water here is twenty fathoms deep.
column8: The verb is especially common in negatives/questions: 'I can't fathom...' The nautical noun sense explains expressions such as 'fathomless'.

column5: To decode something written in cipher; more broadly, to work out the meaning of writing, speech, signals, behavior, or information that is difficult to understand.
column7: I could barely decipher his handwriting. / Analysts are trying to decipher what the announcement really means.
column8: Broader than cryptography. Common with handwriting, codes, signals, motives, and ambiguous messages.

column5: To refer to someone or something indirectly, without naming or discussing it explicitly.
column6: refer indirectly to, hint at, make an indirect reference to
column7: The article alludes to the scandal without naming anyone.
column8: NORMALIZE from 'alludes'. Required pattern: allude to something. Distinguish elude = escape/avoid; allude = refer indirectly.

column5: To get past the most difficult, critical, or discouraging stage of a task, process, week, recovery, etc.
column6: get past the hardest part, turn the corner, break through
column7: The first few chapters were hard, but once I got over the hump, the book became much easier.
column8: The 'hump' is the difficult peak/barrier, not necessarily the whole problem. Also used literally in playful contexts.

column5: To be gloomy, dejected, or listless, often lingering around without doing much because one feels unhappy or sorry for oneself.
column7: Don't just mope around all weekend—come out with us. / He moped after the rejection.
column8: Often implies visible, prolonged gloom and inactivity. Compare sulk = resentful silence/pouting, often because one feels wronged.

column5: To remain sullen, silent, withdrawn, or bad-tempered because one is annoyed, disappointed, or feels slighted; noun: a period/state of sulking.
column7: He sulked for an hour after losing the game. / She went off in a sulk.
column8: Often more resentful/pouty than mope. A person may sulk to show displeasure to others.

column5: Gloomy, sullen, withdrawn, and often noticeably bad-tempered or pessimistic.
column7: He became morose after the project fell apart and barely spoke at dinner.
column8: Stronger and more literary/formal than sad. Often describes a person's mood, manner, expression, or temperament.

column5: 1. A state or period of low spirits, inactivity, stagnation, or poor performance. 2. A traditionally named equatorial ocean region with light/variable winds.
column7: The industry has been in the doldrums for months. / After the holidays I fell into the winter doldrums.
column8: Normally appears with 'the': in the doldrums. The figurative sense comes from the maritime term.

column5: Unable to be divided, separated, or partitioned; in mathematics, not divisible without a remainder in a specified sense.
column7: The founders argued that the union should remain indivisible. / Seven is not evenly divisible by two.
column8: Abstract/political use is common. In mathematics, 'divisible' normally takes 'by'; 'indivisible' may require context about what kind of division is meant.

column5: To leave or withdraw quickly, usually because a situation has become dangerous, awkward, embarrassing, or unfavorable.
column6: retreat quickly, back off, flee, make a quick exit
column7: When the argument turned ugly, we beat a hasty retreat.
column8: Often humorous when the danger is minor or social rather than literal.

column5: noun: 1. a person represented by an elected official, usually someone in that official's electoral area; 2. a component part of a whole. adjective: forming part of a whole.
column7: The senator met with constituents from across the state. / Carbon is a constituent of many compounds.
column8: Not every constituent is necessarily a voter (for example, minors or nonvoters may still be represented). Broaden beyond 'people who live and vote'.

column5: 1. The body of people represented by an elected official. 2. An electoral district, especially in BrE and some political systems. 3. A group of supporters or stakeholders with shared interests.
column6: electorate, voting district, support base, stakeholder group
column7: The MP returned to his constituency for the weekend. / The proposal appeals to an important constituency within the party.
column8: Broader than merely 'group of voters in a specific area'. In British politics, a constituency is also the electoral district itself.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::british_english topic::politics discovery::support discovery::public_discourse

column5: Originally, a full-time Communist Party functionary, especially in the Soviet system; by extension, an unquestioningly loyal bureaucrat or organizational insider.
column6: party functionary, bureaucrat, party loyalist, operative
column7: The reformers clashed with old party apparatchiks. / Critics dismissed him as a corporate apparatchik.
column8: Historical/political origin is important. Modern extended use is disparaging and suggests rigid loyalty to an institution or party line.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::derogatory usage::disparaging usage::professional usage::bureaucratic usage::businesslike usage::evaluative discovery::loyalty discovery::professional_context

column5: The dead body of an animal, especially one slaughtered for meat, left after predation, or in a state of decay; figuratively, the remains/frame of something destroyed.
column7: Vultures gathered around the carcass. / Only the burned-out carcass of the vehicle remained.
column8: CORRECTION: corpse and cadaver primarily refer to human bodies in ordinary/technical use and are not good default synonyms here. 'Carcass' is strongly associated with animals, though figurative object use is common.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical usage::figurative topic::animals discovery::figurative_extension discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Relating to the medical care, treatment, or diseases of animals.
column7: She took her dog to a veterinary clinic. / He is studying veterinary medicine.
column8: CORRECTION: the ordinary noun for a person who treats animals is 'veterinarian' (AmE) or 'vet'; 'veterinary' is primarily an adjective in modern standard English.

column5: To make an idea, subject, or statement clearer by explaining or analyzing it.
column6: clarify, explain, illuminate, shed light on
column7: The professor used a diagram to elucidate the theory.
column8: Formal and often used in academic/technical prose. Pattern: elucidate something; less commonly elucidate on is used, but plain elucidate is usually cleaner.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::academic usage::technical topic::communication discovery::clarification discovery::explanation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::academic_discussion

column5: A difficult period or sequence of time marked by stress, losses, poor performance, illness, or other setbacks.
column6: rough patch, difficult period, hard spell
column7: The team has had a tough stretch of games. / She's been going through a tough stretch lately.
column8: Not a fixed idiom, but a very natural collocation. 'Stretch' = continuous period/span; context supplies what makes it difficult.
column12: entry::idiom entry::collocation entry::noun_phrase usage::informal topic::performance discovery::emphasis

column5: Secretly cooperating with someone, usually in a dishonest, suspicious, or improper scheme.
column6: in collusion, conspiring, secretly working together
column7: The officials were accused of being in cahoots with the contractors.
column8: Usually plural 'cahoots' and commonly followed by with. Strongly suggests secret cooperation; often negative or jokingly suspicious.

column2: ticked off / ticked off with someone
column5: Annoyed or angry; in some contexts, 'tick someone off' also means to scold or reprimand them.
column7: She was really ticked off with her coworker. / I'm ticked off about the delay.
column8: Regional patterns vary: ticked off at/about/with are all heard. Distinguish 'tick something off' = mark/check an item on a list.

column5: To move smoothly with a twisting, sliding motion, especially like a snake; figuratively, to move or behave in a stealthy, sneaky, or ingratiating way.
column7: A snake slithered across the path. / He slithered out of the room before anyone could stop him.
column8: Normalize from participle-only 'slithering'. Figurative use often carries a negative/sly connotation.

column5: A beginner or person new to an activity, skill, field, or religious order; adjective use means relating to beginners.
column7: I'm still a novice at video editing. / The class is designed for novice climbers.
column8: More neutral/formal than rookie. In religious contexts, a novice is someone in a probationary period before full vows/membership.

column5: Openly shown, done, expressed, or observable rather than hidden or secret.
column7: There was no overt hostility, but the tension was obvious. / The policy permits overt political advocacy.
column8: Core contrast: overt vs covert. Overt does not necessarily mean 'obvious to everyone'; it means not concealed.

column5: Hostile, forceful, threatening, or attacking behavior; also forceful action by a state/group, and in psychology/behavior science, behavior intended to harm or dominate.
column7: The dog's sudden aggression worried the owner. / The country condemned the act of aggression.
column8: Not synonymous with violence in every context. 'Aggression' can be verbal, physical, strategic, or institutional; technical definitions vary by field.
column12: entry::word usage::technical topic::science topic::psychology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column2: insofar as / in so far as
column5: To the extent that; to the degree that a statement is true or applicable.
column6: to the extent that, to the degree that
column7: The rule applies insofar as it does not conflict with federal law.
column8: 'Insofar as' is the common closed spelling; 'in so far as' is also accepted. CORRECTION: 'as long as' often means 'provided that' and is not always a good synonym.

column5: An unknown, irrelevant, or unexpected person, especially someone who appears in a group, online space, or situation without an obvious connection.
column7: Some rando joined the lobby and somehow carried the whole team. / I don't give my number to randos online.
column8: Usually humorous or mildly dismissive, not a formal description. Plural 'randos' is very common.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::formal usage::slang usage::humorous usage::informal topic::internet discovery::lack_of_knowledge

column5: 1. To leave secretly or suddenly with a romantic partner, often to elope. 2. To take or steal something and leave with it.
column6: elope with, abscond with, steal, take off with
column7: She ran off with her boyfriend. / Someone ran off with my umbrella.
column8: Two major senses. Related: 'run off' alone can mean leave quickly, print/copy, drain away, or chase away depending on context.

column2: thrust in the sickle / thrust in your sickle and reap
column5: A scriptural-style harvesting expression meaning to begin reaping when the harvest is ripe; figuratively, it can evoke decisive action when the time has come.
column7: The phrase evokes the biblical image of putting in the sickle when the harvest is ripe.
column8: SOURCE-DEPENDENT: treat this primarily as a biblical/literary allusion, not a standard everyday idiom. Exact wording varies by translation and source; avoid inventing a modern productive phrase around it.
column12: entry::idiom usage::literary usage::figurative usage::religious topic::religion topic::agriculture discovery::religious_origin discovery::figurative_extension discovery::literal_vs_figurative

column5: The practice of seeking hidden knowledge or guidance—especially about the future—through supernatural, occult, ritual, or symbolic means.
column7: Ancient societies practiced forms of divination using lots, entrails, stars, or oracles.
column8: Broader than simple fortune-telling: it can seek information about present/hidden matters as well as the future. Methods differ across cultures and traditions.

column5: The floor/base area of a fireplace; by extension, the fireside, home, family life, or domestic center.
column7: They gathered around the hearth on cold evenings. / The poem treats the hearth as a symbol of home and family.
column8: Not simply identical to 'fireplace': the hearth is specifically the floor/base area in front of or within it. Figurative 'hearth and home' is traditional.

column5: Shockingly unfair, immoral, unreasonable, or excessive; in law, sometimes describing terms or conduct so unfair/oppressive that a court may refuse enforcement or grant relief.
column7: Charging desperate patients that much would be unconscionable. / The court considered whether the clause was unconscionable.
column8: Strong moral/legal word. Legal tests and consequences vary by jurisdiction, so avoid treating the everyday and legal senses as perfectly identical.

column5: A strong, often sexual desire; more broadly, an intense craving for power, money, blood, adventure, etc. Verb patterns include lust after and lust for.
column7: The story is driven by lust and jealousy. / He lusted after power and recognition.
column8: Often strong and somewhat negative, especially outside consensual romantic contexts. 'Lust for power/blood' is common figurative usage.

column5: Financial assistance or economic support—often from a government or public body—intended to lower costs, support an industry/activity, or encourage a policy goal.
column7: The government introduced a subsidy for renewable-energy installations.
column8: Can be direct payments, tax advantages, price supports, or other forms of assistance depending on policy context; not every subsidy is a simple cash grant.
column12: entry::word usage::formal topic::finance topic::economics topic::government topic::politics discovery::policy_discussion discovery::encouragement discovery::support discovery::public_discourse

column5: A person who promotes a product, cause, person, or scheme while appearing more independent or enthusiastic than they really are; as a verb, to promote in that way.
column7: The supposedly independent reviewer was accused of being a paid shill. / Influencers were shilling the token online.
column8: Core connotation is deceptive or undisclosed promotion, though people also use it loosely for aggressive promotion. Strongly disparaging.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::disparaging usage::persuasive usage::evaluative discovery::promotion discovery::persuasion

column5: Away from the correct route, direction, behavior, belief, or course.
column7: We wandered astray in the fog. / He was led astray by bad advice. / The investigation went astray.
column8: Common patterns: go astray, lead someone astray. Often figurative; usually appears after a verb rather than before a noun.

column5: A member of the Episcopal Church, especially the Episcopal Church in the United States; relating to Episcopalians or that church tradition.
column6: Episcopal Church member; Anglican-tradition Christian (broader relation)
column7: She was raised Episcopalian. / The family attended an Episcopalian parish.
column8: PRECISION: Episcopalian is related to the Anglican tradition but is not simply synonymous with Anglican in every context. 'Episcopal' is the official adjective in the name 'The Episcopal Church'.

column5: A person, project, place, or thing that initially seems unattractive, awkward, or unpromising but later develops into something admired, successful, or beautiful.
column6: late bloomer, unlikely success, diamond in the rough
column7: The neglected neighborhood became the city's ugly duckling success story after years of redevelopment.
column8: From Hans Christian Andersen's tale. Can refer to appearance, talent, commercial potential, or broader transformation; avoid awkward phrasing like 'he's a total ugly duckling story'.

column5: A young duck.
column7: A line of ducklings followed their mother across the path.
column8: Simple high-frequency sense is sufficient. 'Duckling' also appears figuratively in 'ugly duckling'.

column4: Spanish phrase used in English contexts
column5: Literally 'go with God'; a traditional farewell wishing someone well or safe passage.
column6: farewell, go in peace, goodbye, adiós
column7: He hugged her goodbye and said, 'Vaya con Dios.'
column8: FIX encoding: adiós, not 'adiÃ³s'. Traditional/formal-sounding in Spanish and often used in English-language pop culture, Westerns, songs, or stylized farewells rather than as the default everyday goodbye.

column5: 1. Doubtful, uncertain, or unconvinced. 2. Questionable in truth, quality, legality, or trustworthiness.
column7: I'm dubious about that explanation. / The site makes several dubious health claims.
column8: Two related senses: a person can be dubious = doubtful/skeptical; a claim/deal can be dubious = questionable/suspicious. Not every dubious thing is proven false.

column2: tear into someone / tear into something
column5: To attack or criticize someone fiercely; also to begin eating or attacking something with great energy.
column6: rip into, berate, lambaste; dig into
column7: She tore into him for missing the deadline. / The kids tore into the pizza as soon as it arrived.
column8: NORMALIZE from past-participle 'torn into someone'. Broaden beyond criticism: 'tear into food' is common and positive/neutral in context.

column5: To strongly desire something—especially something possessed by someone else or something one feels envious of.
column7: He coveted his neighbor's classic car. / She had long coveted the position.
column8: Often carries a moral/negative nuance because of envy or wrongful desire, influenced by biblical usage ('Thou shalt not covet').
column12: entry::word usage::religious usage::debate-friendly discovery::strong_desire discovery::longing discovery::debate_language

column5: Believing in, advocating, or characterized by social, political, or economic equality; noun: a person who supports such equality.
column7: They wanted a more egalitarian workplace. / She describes herself as an egalitarian.
column8: CORRECTION: 'democratic' and 'fair' are related ideas but not direct synonyms. Egalitarian specifically concerns equality in status, rights, opportunities, or distribution.
column12: entry::word usage::professional usage::persuasive topic::politics topic::economics discovery::advocacy discovery::public_discourse discovery::professional_context discovery::persuasion

column5: 1. The introduction of material into the body to induce immunity or resistance; historically includes practices distinct from modern vaccination. 2. The introduction of microorganisms/cells into a culture medium. 3. Figuratively, preparation intended to build resistance to an idea or influence.
column6: vaccination (overlapping, not always identical), immunization; seeding (lab context)
column7: Historically, smallpox inoculation predated modern vaccination. / The media-literacy lesson was designed as an inoculation against misinformation.
column8: PRECISION: inoculation and vaccination overlap but are not perfect historical/technical synonyms. 'Inoculation' is also common in microbiology and in figurative 'inoculation theory'.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::technical usage::figurative topic::culture discovery::figurative_extension discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A person who habitually brings a negative, pessimistic, gloomy, or deflating tone to an otherwise positive situation.
column7: Come on, don't be such a Debbie Downer—we're celebrating.
column8: Usually capitalized because the expression comes from the name of a recurring Saturday Night Live character; now widely used as a generic informal label.

column5: To act according to a rule, law, request, order, standard, or requirement.
column7: All employees must comply with the safety rules. / The company failed to comply with the court order.
column8: Common pattern: comply with + rule/request/order/standard. 'Obey' often takes a direct object ('obey the law'), while comply normally requires with.
column12: entry::collocation entry::word topic::law discovery::expressing_need discovery::evaluation discovery::nonconformity

column5: noun: a person regarded as eccentric, irrational, or obsessed with implausible ideas. adjective: bizarre, implausible, or associated with such a person.
column7: He promoted a series of crackpot conspiracy theories. / Critics dismissed the inventor as a crackpot.
column8: Strongly dismissive and sometimes insulting. Safer for ideas/theories than for describing a person's mental health. Common adjective use: crackpot theory/idea.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::disparaging usage::persuasive usage::evaluative discovery::persuasion

column5: 1. In Mexican Spanish/English food contexts, a concha is a round sweet bread (pan dulce) with a shell-patterned sugary topping. 2. Spanish concha more broadly means shell and has other regional meanings.
column6: Mexican sweet bread, pan dulce; shell (Spanish)
column7: I picked up a chocolate concha from the panadería for breakfast.
column8: For the food sense, 'Mexican sweet bread with a shell-patterned topping' is more precise than merely 'roll shaped like a shell'. Spanish concha has additional regional meanings, including slang, so context matters.
column12: entry::term entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::slang usage::informal topic::food

column5: Criteria or standards that change over time, especially repeatedly or unpredictably.
column6: changing criteria, shifting standards, variable requirements
column7: Applicants struggled to keep up with the fluctuating criteria for approval.
column8: Not a fixed idiom. 'Shifting criteria/standards' may sound more natural when criticizing inconsistent requirements. Fluctuating emphasizes repeated movement/change.

column5: Conspicuously or shockingly bad, offensive, or wrong; especially obvious and serious in a violation, abuse, or disregard of rules.
column7: It was a flagrant violation of the rules. / The referee missed a flagrant foul.
column8: Usually negative and commonly collocates with violation, abuse, disregard, breach, foul. Stronger than merely noticeable.

column5: Expressing criticism, disrespect, or a low opinion of someone or something; tending to belittle.
column7: She made several disparaging remarks about his performance.
column8: Common: disparaging remark/comment/reference. Compare derogatory: explicitly insulting/disrespectful; disparaging often emphasizes belittling or speaking negatively of someone.
column12: entry::word usage::derogatory usage::disparaging usage::evaluative discovery::criticism discovery::subjective_judgment

column2: get a grip / get a grip on something
column5: 1. To regain control of one's emotions or behavior. 2. To gain control over, understand, or manage a situation or subject.
column6: pull oneself together, regain composure; get control of, get a handle on
column7: Get a grip—you’re panicking over nothing. / We need to get a grip on our spending.
column8: 'Get a grip!' can sound blunt or unsympathetic. Productive extension: get a grip on something = understand/control/manage it.

column5: Originally an arcade game in which players hit toy moles as they pop up; figuratively, a situation where solving one problem is immediately followed by another similar problem appearing elsewhere.
column6: endless cycle, recurring problem, reactive problem-solving
column7: Fighting spam can become a game of whack-a-mole. / The team was stuck in whack-a-mole mode, fixing bugs one by one.
column8: The commercial game name is Whac-A-Mole; lowercase 'whack-a-mole' is common figuratively. The metaphor stresses reactive, recurring problems rather than simply any never-ending task.
column12: entry::proper_noun usage::figurative usage::businesslike topic::problem-solving discovery::figurative_extension discovery::iteration

column5: Not serious, sensible, or worthwhile; concerned with trivial matters. In legal contexts, lacking a serious legal basis or merit.
column6: trivial, silly, superficial, petty; baseless (legal context)
column7: She regretted spending so much on frivolous purchases. / The judge dismissed the claim as frivolous.
column8: Legal 'frivolous' is a more specific judgment than everyday 'silly/unimportant'; exact standards vary by jurisdiction.

column5: Severe, bare, or bleak in appearance; strikingly clear or sharply contrasting; complete/absolute in expressions such as 'stark reality' or 'stark naked'.
column6: bleak, bare, severe; striking, sharp, glaring
column7: There is a stark contrast between the two approaches. / The room looked stark without any furniture.
column8: High-value collocations: stark contrast/difference, stark reality, stark warning, stark choice, stark naked. Meaning shifts by collocation.

column5: The national committee of the U.S. Republican Party, responsible for party organization, fundraising, electoral support, and national party operations.
column7: The RNC held its national convention that summer.
column8: Political organization details and leadership can change over time. Avoid treating 'GOP leadership' as a direct synonym; the RNC is a specific party committee.

column5: Used to express relief or satisfaction that an unwanted person, thing, or situation is gone or ending.
column6: glad it's gone, glad to be rid of it/them
column7: He's finally moving out? Good riddance. / Good riddance to that broken old printer.
column8: Usually dismissive and often rude when said about a person. Common expanded form: 'good riddance to bad rubbish' (especially BrE).

column5: Disappointed, upset, or feeling low about something.
column7: I was pretty bummed that the concert got canceled. / She was bummed out about missing the trip.
column8: Usually means disappointed/down, not necessarily clinically depressed. Common patterns: bummed about/that; bummed out.

column5: A person or thing believed to be doomed, finished, beyond saving, or certain to fail/die.
column7: When the car started sliding toward the cliff, I thought I was a goner. / That old laptop is a goner.
column8: Can apply to objects as well as people. Often dramatic or humorous; 'dead meat' is more threatening and not a neutral synonym.

column5: A thug or enforcer paid to intimidate, threaten, attack, or perform coercive work for someone.
column7: The villain sent a couple of hired goons to scare him off.
column8: Compositional rather than a special fixed idiom. 'Hired goon' and 'hired muscle' are often more natural. Strongly negative/criminal connotation.
column12: entry::idiom entry::noun_phrase usage::informal topic::work topic::anatomy topic::health

column2: albatross / an albatross around one's neck
column5: 1. A large oceanic seabird. 2. Figuratively, a persistent burden, handicap, or source of guilt that is difficult to escape.
column7: The debt became an albatross around the company's neck.
column8: The figurative expression is associated with Coleridge's 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner', not simply a generic sailor superstition. 'Albatross around one's neck' is the key idiom.

column5: 'Gooney/goony' can mean silly, goofy, or foolish; 'gooney bird' is an informal name for certain albatrosses, especially in Pacific contexts.
column7: The old nickname 'gooney bird' has been used for albatrosses. / He was acting goofy and goony for the camera.
column8: SOURCE/FORM CAUTION: 'gooney' as a standalone person-label is uncommon and spelling varies with 'goony'. Do not present it as ordinary universal slang.

column5: Unattractively, noticeably, or weakly thin; lacking muscle or healthy-looking bulk.
column7: The stray cat looked scrawny after weeks on the street. / I was a scrawny kid before I started training.
column8: Usually negative or teasing. It describes appearance/build and does not prove someone is medically undernourished.

column5: To be selected as a member of a sports team or other competitive group after trying out or being evaluated.
column6: be selected, earn a spot, make the cut
column7: She trained all summer and finally made the varsity team.
column8: Especially common in sports. Related: make the cut = meet the selection threshold; make a team can also mean assemble/create a team in other contexts.

column5: Tending to inhibit, restrain, hinder, or prevent something.
column6: restrictive, limiting, restraining, prohibitive (if cost prevents action)
column7: The high startup cost proved inhibitive to further development.
column8: Real but uncommon. Depending on context, inhibitory is more technical/biological, while prohibitive is especially natural for a cost so high that it prevents action.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::technical discovery::prevention discovery::containment discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A humorous or ironic apology before or after profanity, swearing, or coarse language.
column6: excuse my language, sorry for swearing
column7: Pardon my French, but this is a damn mess.
column8: The 'French' is not literal French. Often joking and somewhat old-fashioned; it can be used before or after the offending language.
column12: entry::idiom usage::informal usage::dated usage::humorous usage::profane usage::ironic

column5: To save time, money, or effort by doing something in an easier/cheaper way, often by ignoring proper procedures or reducing quality or safety.
column7: The contractor cut corners on materials, and the roof began leaking.
column8: NORMALIZE: standard idiom is plural 'cut corners', not usually 'cut the corner' for this figurative meaning. Literal 'cut a corner' has a separate movement/driving sense.

column5: 1. The process of eliminating or destroying all viable microorganisms from an object/material in a defined context. 2. A medical procedure that intentionally makes a person or animal unable to reproduce.
column7: Surgical instruments undergo sterilization before use. / The law regulates voluntary sterilization procedures.
column8: PRECISION: sterilization is stronger than disinfection; disinfection does not necessarily eliminate all microbial life. Also has a distinct reproductive-medical sense.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::noun_phrase topic::health topic::animals discovery::process_details discovery::procedural_language

column5: Humor, lightness, or lack of seriousness, especially when introduced into a serious situation; sometimes inappropriate lightheartedness.
column7: A little levity helped ease the tension. / His levity during the memorial struck some people as inappropriate.
column8: Not inherently inappropriate: levity can be welcome relief. Context determines whether it is refreshing or disrespectful.

column5: Speaking readily, fluently, and at length; talkative and verbally expressive.
column7: Normally quiet, she became surprisingly voluble once the topic turned to movies.
column8: Often describes abundant/easy speech, not necessarily captivating or annoying. More formal/literary than talkative.

column5: Relating to or affecting an entire system, or arising from the structure/interactions of a system rather than from one isolated part.
column7: The audit found systemic problems in the organization. / The infection became systemic.
column8: Key contrast with systematic: systemic = of/throughout a system; systematic = methodical or organized according to a system.

column5: Done according to an organized method, plan, or system; methodical and thorough.
column7: They conducted a systematic review of the evidence.
column8: Key contrast with systemic: systematic describes method/order; systemic describes something affecting or inherent in a whole system.

column5: 1. A substance or food used as one component of a mixture, dish, or product. 2. Figuratively, an element or factor needed for a result.
column7: Mix the dry ingredients first. / Trust is an essential ingredient in a good partnership.
column8: Broaden beyond cooking. Common figurative frame: 'an ingredient for/in success/disaster'.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative topic::food discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To force an idea, opinion, belief, product, or information on someone aggressively or repeatedly, giving them little choice or room to disagree.
column6: force on, shove down someone's throat, impose on
column7: I hate having political opinions rammed down my throat.
column8: NORMALIZE: 'ram down' alone is incomplete for this figurative sense. Common pattern: ram/shove something down someone's throat. Strongly negative.
column12: entry::idiom entry::collocation entry::construction usage::informal usage::figurative topic::decision-making discovery::disagreement discovery::subjective_judgment

column2: get someone bouncing in their chair / have someone bouncing in their seat
column5: To make someone visibly excited, energized, eager, or physically responsive while seated.
column6: get someone excited, energize, have someone bouncing in their seat
column7: That song had me bouncing in my seat. / The announcement had the kids bouncing in their chairs.
column8: CORRECTION: 'get someone bounce in the chair' is ungrammatical in standard English. Natural patterns include 'get someone bouncing...' or 'have someone bouncing...'. This is descriptive, not a fixed idiom.

column5: A limitation, restriction, or condition that limits what can be done; in technical fields, a requirement that a solution must satisfy.
column7: Time constraints forced us to shorten the meeting. / The design has to satisfy several technical constraints.
column8: Common: time/budget/resource constraints; under/within constraints. Technical optimization/engineering sense is highly productive.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical topic::problem-solving discovery::solution_framing discovery::constraints discovery::expressing_need discovery::resolution discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: 1. Likely to cause disagreement, argument, or controversy. 2. Of a person, inclined to argue or quarrel.
column7: School funding remains a contentious issue. / He can become contentious when challenged.
column8: Two senses: a contentious issue causes dispute; a contentious person tends to argue. 'Controversial' fits the first but not necessarily the second.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::debate_language discovery::disagreement discovery::possibility

column5: Occurring or developing in small steps, stages, or additions rather than all at once.
column7: The software improved through incremental updates. / We made incremental progress each week.
column8: Common in business, policy, software, and science: incremental change/improvement/cost. Contrast transformational/radical change.

column5: A playful, childish-sounding way to say 'same', 'me too', or that two things match.
column7: You hate early meetings? Samesies. / We bought the same shoes—samesies!
column8: Better treated as an interjection/expression than a noun. Very informal and intentionally cute/playful; can sound ironic or juvenile.

column5: Physically strong and muscular, often with a large, powerful build.
column7: The brawny mover lifted the sofa by himself.
column8: Usually describes physical build/strength. Can be approving or simply descriptive; contrasts naturally with scrawny.

column5: Informal credit, favor, or approval gained by doing something that pleases or impresses someone.
column7: He earned brownie points with his boss by volunteering for the extra shift.
column8: Usually plural and often humorous: earn/get/score brownie points with someone. Not literal points.

column5: 1. A male goose. 2. Informal: a look or glance, especially in 'take/have a gander at'.
column7: Take a gander at this photo when you get a chance.
column8: The 'look' sense is informal and strongly associated with the fixed pattern 'take a gander at'.

column5: Marked by turmoil, disorder, intense change, excitement, noise, or emotional upheaval.
column7: They had a tumultuous relationship. / The country went through a tumultuous decade.
column8: Often describes periods, relationships, events, crowds, or political conditions. It need not literally be noisy.

column5: According to a claim or report whose truth is not necessarily established; allegedly or supposedly.
column7: The supplement purportedly improves concentration, but the evidence is weak.
column8: Signals distance from the claim. Compare ostensibly = apparently/on the surface, sometimes implying a hidden reality.

column5: A game played as a single standalone event rather than as part of a regular series; more broadly, 'one-off' means occurring or made only once.
column6: single game, standalone event, one-time event
column7: They arranged a one-off charity match. / It was a one-off mistake, not a recurring problem.
column8: Broaden to productive 'one-off'. Hyphenate before a noun. Very common in BrE and widely understood elsewhere; AmE often uses one-time.

column5: Pitifully sad, lonely, abandoned, or hopeless-looking; also unlikely to succeed in 'forlorn hope'.
column7: The abandoned dog gave us a forlorn look. / He made one forlorn attempt to restart the engine.
column8: Often describes appearance/atmosphere as much as an internal feeling. Literary/emotive compared with simply sad.

column5: A sudden involuntary contraction of a muscle or group of muscles; more broadly, a sudden brief burst of activity, emotion, or movement.
column6: muscle contraction, twitch, cramp (not exact); burst
column7: A muscle spasm woke him during the night. / The market went through a brief spasm of panic.
column8: PRECISION: spasm and cramp overlap but are not identical. 'Spasm' is broader; a cramp is typically a painful sustained muscle contraction. Verb use exists but noun is much more common.

column5: Perfectly clean, neat, or spotless; free from flaws or errors; in Christian theology, capitalized in 'Immaculate Conception'.
column7: The kitchen was immaculate. / Her timing was immaculate throughout the performance.
column8: Common literal and figurative uses. Do not confuse 'Immaculate Conception' with the virgin birth; it refers in Catholic doctrine to Mary's conception free from original sin.

column2: it's high time / it is high time
column5: Used to say that something should happen now and is already overdue or should have happened earlier.
column7: It's high time we replaced this old computer. / It's high time you went to bed.
column8: Grammar note: 'It's high time + past tense' is traditional and very common ('It's high time we left'), even though the meaning is present/future. 'High time to do...' also occurs.

column5: Shockingly wicked, cruel, or morally reprehensible; in looser informal use, extremely bad or unpleasant.
column7: The court heard details of the heinous crime. / That's a pretty heinous color combination.
column8: Strong word in serious contexts. Informal exaggeration exists, but core sense concerns extreme moral badness.

column5: verb: to praise, promote, recommend, or publicize something strongly; also to solicit business aggressively. noun: a person who solicits customers or sells tips, with senses varying by region/context.
column7: The company touted the update as a major breakthrough. / Analysts are touting the stock as undervalued.
column8: NORMALIZE from participle-only 'touting'. 'Tout' does not inherently mean overbearing or dishonest; context determines that. BrE has additional noun/verb senses around soliciting and ticket/scalping contexts.
column12: entry::word usage::british_english usage::persuasive topic::business discovery::promotion discovery::recommendation discovery::social_approval discovery::persuasion

column2: be a 10 / be a ten (out of ten)
column5: To be rated 10 out of 10; especially, to be considered extremely attractive, or more broadly exceptionally impressive, desirable, or excellent in the speaker's eyes.
column6: be a ten out of ten, be top-tier, be extremely attractive, be a perfect 10
column7: She's a 10. / He's a solid 10. / To me, she's a 10 out of 10—not just looks-wise, but personality-wise too. / I'd give that movie a 10.
column8: The rating comes from a one-to-ten scale. When the rating is used as a predicative noun, the article is normally present: 'She's a 10,' not simply 'She's 10.' It often rates physical attractiveness, but context can broaden it to personality, style, skill, an item, or an experience. The judgment is subjective; rating people numerically can sound objectifying in some contexts.

column5: verb: to think moodily or resentfully about something for a long time; noun: a group of young birds/animals produced or cared for together, or figuratively a group of children.
column6: dwell on, mope, sulk; offspring, clutch (context-dependent)
column7: Don't brood over one bad review all week. / The hen gathered her brood beneath her wings.
column8: Verb often takes over/on/about. Noun 'brood' is especially associated with birds and a parent's young; 'nest' is not a synonym for the young themselves.

column5: To spend time looking or feeling dejected, listless, or sorry for oneself, often without doing much.
column7: She spent the afternoon moping after the bad news. / Stop moping around and come with us.
column8: Normalize toward base verb while retaining source form. Compare sulk = resentful/pouty; mope = gloomy/listless.

column5: 1. A person used by another as a subordinate, puppet, accomplice, or fall guy. 2. In comedy, a performer whose role is to feed lines or be the butt of jokes for another performer.
column6: puppet, lackey, dupe, underling; straight man (not exact)
column7: Critics called him a stooge for the regime. / The comedian used a stooge from the audience as part of the act.
column8: Often disparaging. A stooge is not simply a fool: the key idea is serving or being used by someone else; comedy has a distinct performance sense.

column5: noun: the buttocks/rear end; the thicker or blunt end of something; a target of jokes ('the butt of the joke'). verb: to strike or push with the head/horns; 'butt in' = interrupt/intrude.
column7: He slipped and landed on his butt. / She was tired of being the butt of the joke. / The goat butted the fence.
column8: Highly polysemous. Add productive 'butt in' and 'butt of the joke'. Register: butt = informal but generally mild in AmE.

column5: Extremely small; tiny.
column7: Could I have just a teensy bit more? / The kitten had teensy little paws.
column8: Playful/cute informal word. Variants include teeny, teensy-weensy, teeny-weeny.

column5: noun: 1. Fluid circulating in a plant. 2. Informal: a foolish or gullible person. verb: to gradually weaken, drain, or undermine strength, energy, confidence, or resources.
column6: plant fluid; fool, sucker; drain, weaken, deplete, undermine
column7: Maple sap is collected in early spring. / The long delays sapped everyone's morale. / Don't be such a sap.
column8: Major missing slang noun sense. Verb commonly appears as sap someone's strength/energy/confidence/morale.

column2: have a knack for sap / have a knack for sappy stuff
column5: To have a natural talent or tendency for sentimental, emotionally sugary, or 'sappy' material.
column6: have a flair for sentimentality, be good at sappy material
column7: She has a knack for writing sappy love scenes.
column8: NOT a standard idiom. The productive construction is 'have a knack for X'; 'sap' here is source-dependent shorthand for sentimental/sappy material and may sound unnatural without context.

column5: A natural or acquired ability to do something skillfully or easily; a characteristic way or trick of doing something.
column7: He has a knack for explaining complicated ideas simply. / I never got the knack of folding it properly.
column8: High-value patterns: have a knack for + noun/gerund; get the knack of something. Often suggests an intuitive practical skill.

column5: 1. Excessively or cloyingly sentimental. 2. Literally full of or resembling plant sap.
column7: The ending was a little sappy, but I still liked it. / Fresh-cut branches can be sticky and sappy.
column8: Usually mildly negative/teasing in the sentimental sense, but speakers may affectionately call something sappy.

column5: An exaggerated expression of disgust, revulsion, or contempt: roughly 'that's disgusting/gross'.
column7: He said matching outfits were romantic. Gag me with a spoon.
column8: Associated especially with 1980s U.S. 'Valley Girl' speech/pop culture and now sounds dated, campy, or deliberately retro. Remove unnecessary word 'saying' from headword.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::dated usage::humorous usage::informal

column5: A person, event, or device introduced suddenly to resolve an apparently insoluble plot problem, especially when the resolution feels insufficiently prepared or artificial.
column6: contrived rescue, sudden plot solution, plot device
