column7: The last-minute rescue felt like a deus ex machina because nothing earlier in the story had set it up.
column8: Not simply any plot twist or lucky event. From Latin 'god from the machine', referring to ancient theatrical machinery used to bring a god onto the stage.
column12: entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::literary topic::problem-solving discovery::solution_framing discovery::hedging discovery::resolution

column5: Extremely impressive, remarkable, large, or excellent.
column7: The restoration team did a stupendous job. / The project required a stupendous amount of work.
column8: Enthusiastic and somewhat grand/old-fashioned compared with amazing. Can emphasize size/degree as well as excellence.

column5: A small hand-propelled cart, typically with one wheel at the front and two handles, used to carry soil, tools, construction materials, etc.
column7: He filled the wheelbarrow with soil and pushed it across the garden.
column8: Simple concrete sense. A handcart is broader and may have two or more wheels, so it is not exact.

column5: Participation in an organized pattern or enterprise involving specified illegal activities; in U.S. federal law, 'racketeering activity' has a defined statutory meaning under RICO.
column6: organized criminal activity, criminal enterprise activity
column7: Prosecutors charged several defendants with racketeering.
column8: LEGAL PRECISION: not simply any organized illegal activity, extortion, or bribery. Exact elements depend on the statute/jurisdiction; U.S. RICO uses specifically defined predicate acts and enterprise/pattern concepts.

column5: A conspiracy charge alleging an agreement to participate in or further racketeering activity or a racketeering enterprise; exact elements depend on the governing law.
column6: RICO conspiracy (U.S. context), criminal conspiracy involving racketeering
column7: The indictment included a racketeering-conspiracy count.
column8: LEGAL PRECISION: avoid defining this generically as merely 'a criminal plot'. In U.S. federal cases, RICO conspiracy is a specific statutory theory; requirements vary by jurisdiction/statute.

column5: Excessive indulgence in sensual pleasures, especially sex, alcohol, partying, or other behavior portrayed as morally dissolute.
column7: The novel depicts a weekend of drunken debauchery.
column8: Strongly judgmental/old-fashioned or literary in many contexts. It describes perceived moral excess; 'indulgence' alone is much milder.

column5: To be familiar with, experienced in, or accustomed to something, often something difficult, notable, or recurring.
column6: be familiar with, be accustomed to, know well
column7: She's no stranger to criticism. / The region is no stranger to severe storms.
column8: NORMALIZE to productive pattern. Often used with hardships or challenges, but can take neutral/positive experiences too.

column5: Too self-satisfied or unconcerned about risks, weaknesses, or the need for improvement, often because things are currently going well.
column7: After three easy wins, the team became complacent and stopped preparing carefully.
column8: Important nuance: complacent is negative; it is not simply content/satisfied. It implies insufficient concern or vigilance.

column2: the least tight thing / least tight
column5: In a context where 'tight' means cool, impressive, or excellent, 'the least tight' means especially uncool, lame, or objectionable.
column7: Showing my poem to everyone without asking? That's the least tight thing you could do.
column8: SOURCE-DEPENDENT/pop-culture phrasing rather than a standard slang expression. Preserve because of source value; teach productive slang 'tight' = cool/excellent separately. Meaning depends on the quoted context.

column5: A name, nickname, alias, or identifying label, especially one by which someone or something is popularly known.
column7: The singer performs under the moniker 'Night Owl.'
column8: Often used for nicknames/stage names/labels, but can simply mean name. Slightly journalistic/playful tone.

column5: The central character of Victor Hugo's novel 'The Hunchback of Notre-Dame', a bell-ringer of Notre-Dame who is socially marginalized and treated cruelly because of his appearance.
column7: Quasimodo is the bell-ringer at the center of Victor Hugo's novel.
column8: CORRECTION/CAUTION: treat primarily as a proper literary name, not a common noun meaning 'outcast/misfit'. Using 'Quasimodo' to mock someone's appearance or disability can be insulting.

column5: Seemingly, partly, or almost, but not fully or genuinely; having some resemblance or functional similarity.
column7: The study used a quasi-experimental design. / The committee has quasi-judicial powers.
column8: Very productive formal combining form: quasi-legal, quasi-scientific, quasi-governmental. 'Pseudo-' often implies falseness more strongly, so it is not always interchangeable.

column5: To respond to an injury, attack, insult, punishment, or adverse action by taking harmful or punitive action in return.
column6: strike back, get back at, take revenge, respond in kind
column7: They threatened to retaliate if the sanctions were imposed. / He was fired after complaining and alleged that the company had retaliated against him.
column8: Patterns: retaliate against someone; retaliate for something; retaliate by doing something. 'Avenge' normally takes an object (avenge a death/wrong) and is not a direct grammatical substitute.

column5: Distant, reserved, aloof, or unfriendly in manner, especially in a way that discourages closeness.
column7: She seemed standoffish at first, but she warmed up once we started talking.
column8: Describes social manner, not necessarily actual dislike. Can reflect shyness/reserve as perceived by others.

column5: A confrontation or deadlock in which neither side is willing or able to give way or make decisive progress.
column7: Police negotiated for hours during the standoff. / The talks ended in a political standoff.
column8: Broader than 'neither side can win': it can be an armed confrontation, negotiation deadlock, or strategic impasse. Spelling 'standoff' is standard AmE; 'stand-off' also occurs.

column5: A self-righteously proper, moralistic, or pedantic person who annoyingly displays their correctness or superiority.
column6: prude (not exact), pedant, goody-goody, self-righteous person
column7: He comes across as a pompous prig whenever he lectures everyone about etiquette.
column8: Dated/literary flavor. 'Puritan' has historical/religious meanings and is not a safe direct synonym.

column5: noun: the old/common name for mercury. adjective/figurative: rapidly changing, lively, mercurial, or difficult to pin down.
column7: Mercury was once commonly called quicksilver. / She has a quicksilver wit that jumps from idea to idea.
column8: Figurative use is literary and derives from mercury's mobile appearance. Avoid vague synonym 'fast-moving' alone; personality/mood/intellect can be quicksilver.

column5: adjective: very tired, especially after prolonged effort, stress, or experience; also tired of something. verb: to make or become tired.
column7: We were weary after the long hike. / I'm weary of having the same argument every week.
column8: High-value pattern: weary of + noun/gerund = tired/fed up with. Often more literary than tired.

column5: To gently or patiently persuade someone to do something; also to obtain or bring something out gradually through careful effort.
column7: She coaxed him into trying one bite. / He coaxed a smile out of the shy child. / We coaxed the old engine back to life.
column8: Normalize to base verb. Productive patterns: coax someone into doing; coax something out of someone; coax something into/out of a state.

column5: noun: a dried plum. verb: to cut back branches/growth; figuratively, to remove unnecessary parts, reduce, or trim a list/system.
column6: dried plum; trim, cut back, pare down
column7: She pruned the rose bushes in spring. / We pruned several outdated items from the list.
column8: Existing card is good; add productive figurative reduction sense. Related-family overlap with earlier WID961 should be retained for later duplicate-family review.

column5: Triumphantly or intensely joyful, especially after a victory, success, or piece of good news.
column7: The exultant crowd erupted when the final whistle blew.
column8: Often conveys outward, triumphant joy rather than quiet happiness. Related verb: exult in/over.

column5: Thrilled, energized, and intensely excited or happy, often after an exciting, risky, fast, or physically stimulating experience.
column7: I felt exhilarated after the roller-coaster ride. / She was exhausted but exhilarated after the race.
column8: Often combines excitement with heightened energy. Compare elated = very happy; exhilarated more strongly suggests stimulation/energy.

column5: noun: a design made by combining or arranging initials/letters as a personal or organizational mark. verb: to decorate or mark with a monogram.
column7: She had her initials monogrammed on the cuff. / The towels bear the hotel's monogram.
column8: A monogram may combine/interlock letters; it is not simply any written initials or a signature.

column5: Highly polysemous: noun: intersecting lines/symbol, Christian cross, hybrid, burden/trial in some expressions. verb: go from one side to another, intersect, oppose, betray, cross out, etc. adjective (especially BrE): angry/annoyed.
column7: We crossed the street. / Cross that name off the list. / Don't cross him—he holds grudges. / Mum was cross with me for being late.
column8: Current card is too compressed for a very high-frequency polysemous word. Important phrases include cross someone's mind, cross paths, cross out/off, cross the line, and BrE 'be cross with'.
column12: entry::word usage::british_english usage::religious topic::religion topic::courtroom topic::law discovery::disagreement discovery::betrayal

column2: knit one's brows / knit one's brow
column5: To draw the eyebrows together, producing a frown that suggests concentration, worry, confusion, or disapproval.
column6: furrow one's brow, frown, crease one's forehead
column7: She knitted her brows as she tried to make sense of the instructions.
column8: NORMALIZE from participle-only 'knitting brows'. Both brow singular and brows plural occur. 'Knit/knitted' are both standard past forms.

column5: 1. To say that a statement is wrong or assert the opposite. 2. Of facts, actions, or evidence, to be inconsistent with or conflict with something.
column6: deny, dispute, gainsay (formal); conflict with, be inconsistent with
column7: The witness contradicted his earlier statement. / The new evidence contradicts the original theory.
column8: Not limited to verbal assertion: evidence/actions can contradict claims. 'Rebut' specifically means answer an argument/claim with counterargument or evidence.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::formal usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly discovery::evidence discovery::assertion discovery::disagreement discovery::debate_language

column5: To trouble, afflict, or cause pain/problems; in 'what ails someone?', to be wrong with or troubling them.
column7: What ails you? / The company has struggled to fix what ails its outdated system.
column8: Usually appears in patterns such as 'what ails X' or 'an ailing company'. The direct sense 'he ails from...' is uncommon in modern everyday English.

column5: A hot savory preparation made from beef or beef extract, historically given especially to sick or convalescent people as nourishment.
column7: The Victorian-era patient was given beef tea during convalescence.
column8: FIX encoding: consommé. Historical/cultural term; not ordinary modern 'tea'. Recipes varied, and beef broth/consommé are related but not exact equivalents.

column5: A person who is chronically ill, frail, or disabled and considered unable to care for themselves or work normally; historically common, now often dated or offensive when used as a label for a person.
column7: The novel refers to her as 'an invalid,' reflecting the language of its period.
column8: Normalize from plural. REGISTER WARNING: person-label 'invalid' is dated and can be demeaning; use specific modern descriptions such as patient, disabled person, chronically ill person, or convalescent when appropriate.

column5: A bed with four tall vertical posts, one at each corner, sometimes supporting a canopy or curtains.
column7: The room contained an antique four-poster bed with heavy curtains.
column8: Hyphenate four-poster. Not every four-poster is a canopy bed, though many support a canopy or hangings.

column5: A spring-flowering plant of the genus Narcissus, typically with a trumpet/cup-shaped corona and yellow, white, or orange flowers.
column6: Narcissus; jonquil (a type/group, not exact synonym)
column7: Daffodils were blooming along the path in early spring.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. 'Narcissus' is the genus/broader botanical grouping; 'jonquil' refers to particular Narcissus types, not every daffodil.

column5: A small flowering plant of the genus Crocus, with cup-shaped flowers; different species bloom in spring or autumn. Saffron comes from Crocus sativus.
column7: Purple crocuses emerged through the late-winter snow. / Saffron is harvested from Crocus sativus.
column8: CORRECTION: 'autumn crocus' commonly refers to Colchicum, which is not a true Crocus, so it should not be a generic synonym. Saffron is a product of one Crocus species, not a synonym for crocus.

column5: To declare something legally or officially invalid, void, or without effect; commonly used of marriages, laws, contracts, decisions, and elections.
column7: The court annulled the marriage. / The decision was later annulled on procedural grounds.
column8: Normalize to base verb while retaining source form. CORRECTION: a marriage is not ordinarily annulled merely because of 'irreconcilable differences'; annulment generally depends on a legal ground showing the marriage was invalid/voidable under applicable law.

column5: Physically together while each person remains separate, private, emotionally distant, or engaged in their own activity; can be negative, neutral, or intimate depending on context.
column7: We spent the evening alone together, each reading our own book. / They sat alone together, emotionally miles apart.
column8: Not a fixed idiom with only the negative meaning 'emotionally distant'. It can also describe comfortable shared solitude or simply two people alone with each other.

column5: Unimpressed, bored, or indifferent because something has become too familiar, common, or overexperienced.
column7: After years of traveling first class, he had become blasé about luxury hotels.
column8: SPELLING: blasé. Core nuance is jaded/unimpressed through familiarity or overexposure, not merely apathetic or unconcerned.

column5: To stay with or spend time with someone so they are not alone, often while they wait, work, travel, recover, etc.
column6: accompany, stay with, sit with, spend time with
column7: I'll keep you company while you wait. / I stayed up to keep her company while she finished packing.
column8: Natural high-frequency expression. 'Company' here means companionship, not a business.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::business topic::work topic::travel

column5: To be filled to the edge or overflowing; figuratively, to be full of an emotion, quality, energy, or ideas.
column6: overflow, be full of, teem with
column7: The cup was brimming with coffee. / She was brimming with confidence and ideas.
column8: Normalize beyond participle-only form. High-value figurative pattern: be brimming with confidence/excitement/ideas. 'Loaded' is not a general synonym.

column5: To hit hard; figuratively, to defeat decisively, damage severely, or impose a heavy cost/impact on someone or something.
column6: hit, wallop, batter; crush, thrash, hammer
column7: He got clobbered in the first round. / Rising costs are clobbering small businesses. / We clobbered them 8–1.
column8: Normalize to base verb. Very productive figurative use for sports, economics, criticism, and severe impact. BrE noun 'clobber' can also mean clothes/equipment, a separate sense.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::figurative usage::british_english topic::romance discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Past/past participle of clobber: hit hard, defeated decisively, or badly affected/damaged.
column7: He got clobbered over the head. / Our team got clobbered 7–0. / The stock was clobbered after the earnings report.
column8: CORRECTION: 'clobbed' is nonstandard/likely an error for 'clobbered' in this context. Keep separate only if source retrieval value matters; otherwise this belongs to the clobber family.

column5: Slang historically derived from 'spastic'. Depending on dialect, it has been used for clumsiness, overexcitement, losing control, or 'freaking out'; it can be an ableist slur and is especially offensive in British usage.
column6: freak out, lose it, flail, overreact (context-dependent)
column7: In older U.S. slang you may hear 'I totally spazzed out,' but it is safer to say 'I freaked out.'
column8: REGISTER/SAFETY: offensiveness varies geographically but the disability-derived history is important. Avoid using it as a label for a person. Spellings include spaz and spazz; recognition is more useful than active production.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrasal_verb entry::word entry::verb_pattern usage::slang usage::offensive usage::informal usage::evaluative discovery::origin_etymology discovery::excessive_emotion

column5: Foamy bubbles/lather formed by soap, detergent, or another liquid; informally, beer in some dialects/slang.
column7: Rinse until all the soap suds are gone. / They went out for a few suds after work.
column8: Usually plural. 'Suds' can mean soapy foam or, informally, beer; context makes the sense clear.

column5: To spread or move outward in different directions from a point or narrow area; also to arrange something in a fan-shaped spread.
column7: The search team fanned out across the field. / She fanned the cards out on the table.
column8: Both intransitive and transitive uses: people fan out; fan cards/papers out. Often used for searches, troops, crowds, roads, fingers, cards.

column2: scratch someone's eyes out / scratch your eyes out
column3: ʃi wɪl skrætʃ jɚ aɪz aʊt
column5: To attack someone viciously, especially by scratching at the face/eyes; often used hyperbolically for intense anger, jealousy, or hostility.
column6: claw at, attack, go for, lash out at
column7: If she catches you flirting with him, she'll scratch your eyes out. / They were joking that the two rivals would scratch each other's eyes out.
column8: Often hyperbolic rather than a literal threat. Traditionally stereotyped in descriptions of fights between women, so avoid presenting the gender stereotype as part of the core definition.

column5: A red-yarn-haired rag doll character created by Johnny Gruelle and featured in American children's books and related dolls.
column7: She still keeps her childhood Raggedy Ann doll on the shelf.
column8: Capitalize as a proper name. More precise than defining it as merely a generic doll; Raggedy Ann is a specific character/design with a long U.S. children's-book/toy history.

column5: Ragged, shabby, tattered, worn-looking, or untidy; sometimes used dismissively of a person's appearance or possessions.
column7: He showed up in the same raggedy old coat. / The fence looked pretty raggedy after the storm.
column8: Informal extension of ragged. Can sound judgmental when applied to a person. Common in AmE speech.

column5: An eccentric, strange, or foolish person, especially someone with unusual ideas or behavior.
column7: Everyone thought he was a kook until one of his predictions turned out to be right.
column8: Can be playful or insulting depending on tone. Related adjective: kooky = eccentric/odd in a quirky way.

column5: Wildly impulsive, reckless, eccentric, or amusingly chaotic; noun historically: a reckless or impulsive person.
column7: They came up with a madcap scheme to drive across the country overnight.
column8: Often literary/journalistic and playful. Common collocations: madcap scheme, adventure, comedy, escapade.

column5: A spout or opening designed to make liquid easier to pour cleanly and with better control.
column6: pour spout, dispensing spout, easy-pour opening
column7: The carton has an easy-pour spout that helps prevent spills.
column8: Not a fixed lexical expression; common descriptive/product wording. Hyphenate easy-pour before a noun.

column5: A pleasant, desirable, or tasty item; plural 'goodies' commonly means treats, snacks, gifts, prizes, or other desirable things.
column6: treat, sweet, gift, prize, desirable item
column7: The kids came home with bags of Halloween goodies. / The deluxe edition includes a few extra goodies.
column8: Broader than food. Singular goodie can mean a desirable item; 'the goodies' can mean treats or attractive extras. Separate 'goody' spellings/usages exist.

column5: In a way that shows anger or offense at something perceived as unjust, insulting, improper, or undeserved.
column7: She indignantly denied cheating on the exam. / 'How dare you?' he replied indignantly.
column8: Core emotion is moral/offended anger, not generic annoyance. Related adjective WID1535 indignant.

column5: Restlessly worried, uneasy, irritable, or difficult to soothe.
column7: The baby grew fretful after missing her nap. / He spent a fretful night worrying about the results.
column8: Often used of babies/children or anxious sleep, but adults can be fretful too. Combines worry with restlessness/irritability.

column5: noun: 1. Something of little importance or value. 2. A layered dessert, especially BrE, traditionally made with sponge/cake, fruit, custard, and cream. verb: to treat something as unimportant or waste time; 'trifle with' = treat lightly/play with.
column6: trivial matter, small thing; dessert; toy with
column7: Don't worry about such a trifle. / We had strawberry trifle for dessert. / Don't trifle with people's feelings.
column8: Major missing common BrE dessert sense and verb. 'Knickknack' is not a general synonym for trifle in the 'minor matter' sense.

column5: Willing to act dishonestly, unfairly, or unethically because one lacks moral scruples.
column7: Unscrupulous sellers sometimes prey on inexperienced buyers.
column8: Strongly negative. Often collocates with dealer, employer, businessman, tactic, practice. Opposite concept: scrupulous = careful about ethics/principles (and also very thorough).

column5: adjective: practicing strict self-denial and abstention from comforts or pleasures, often for spiritual/religious reasons. noun: a person who follows such a disciplined way of life.
column7: He adopted an ascetic lifestyle with few possessions. / The ascetic spent years in prayer and fasting.
column8: Can be religious/philosophical or figurative. Do not equate every ascetic with a monk/hermit; those are context-dependent roles.

column5: Extremely hungry; figuratively, intensely eager or voracious for something.
column7: After hiking all day, we were ravenous. / She has a ravenous appetite for new information.
column8: Very strong hunger word. Figurative use occurs with appetite/desire, but 'ravenous for X' is less universal than 'ravenous appetite'.

column5: 1. Overwhelming joy, delight, or emotional rapture. 2. Ecstasy/MDMA: a common name for the psychoactive drug MDMA, though illicit tablets sold under that name may contain other substances.
column6: rapture, bliss, elation, euphoria; MDMA (drug sense)
column7: The fans were in ecstasy after the winning goal. / The report discussed risks associated with drugs sold as ecstasy.
column8: Important polysemy. Drug sense is common enough for recognition. Do not imply that every illicit 'ecstasy' tablet is chemically pure MDMA.

column5: A flowering plant of the genus Antirrhinum, named for blossoms that can resemble a dragon's mouth when squeezed.
column7: Snapdragons added bright pink and yellow color to the garden.
column8: 'Dragon flower' is not a standard everyday synonym in English. Antirrhinum is the botanical genus; snapdragon is the normal common name.

column5: A mocking or playful exclamation similar to 'duh', used to suggest that something is obvious or that someone has said/done something foolish.
column7: You forgot your keys again? Doy!
column8: Variant/dialectal slang and much less common than 'duh'. Best treated as an interjection, not a noun. Tone can be teasing or insulting.
column12: entry::interjection entry::slang_expression usage::slang usage::dated usage::playful usage::informal discovery::suggestion

column5: A supportive undergarment for the male genitals, traditionally worn in sports; it may be used with a protective cup but does not itself necessarily provide impact protection.
column7: He wore a jockstrap under his uniform. / For contact sports, the supporter can hold a protective cup.
column8: PRECISION: a jockstrap provides support; protection from impact generally comes from an inserted athletic cup. Avoid defining it as inherently protective.

column5: A temporary organ that develops during pregnancy and enables exchange of oxygen, nutrients, and waste between maternal and fetal circulations while also producing important hormones.
column7: The placenta delivers oxygen and nutrients to the fetus through the umbilical cord.
column8: More precise than 'an organ in the uterus that nourishes the fetus'. 'Afterbirth' can include the placenta plus membranes/other tissues, so it is not an exact synonym.

column5: verb: to throw or move something suddenly/forcefully; to move oneself energetically. noun: a brief casual romantic/sexual relationship; a short period of carefree activity or indulgence.
column6: throw, hurl, toss; affair, dalliance; spree
column7: He flung the keys onto the table. / They had a brief summer fling. / She had one last fling before starting the new job.
column8: Highly productive: fling open, fling oneself into/onto, have a fling. Past tense/past participle: flung.

column5: Having zero successes in two attempts; in baseball-style notation, no hits/successes in two tries, extended informally to everyday failures.
column6: oh-for-two, two misses in two attempts
column7: I tried two different fixes and neither worked—I'm 0 for 2 today.
column8: Often written 0-for-2 or 0 for 2 depending style. Productive pattern: 0 for 3, 1 for 4, etc. Everyday extension comes from sports/statistical language.

column5: Spoken form of '0 for 2': zero successes in two attempts; extended informally beyond sports.
column7: I called twice and got voicemail both times, so I'm oh-for-two.
column8: Hyphenated spelling is common when treated as a unit. This is essentially the spoken lexicalization of WID1521, but separate retrieval may be useful because learners hear it before seeing the notation.

column2: roll of quarters / rolls of quarters
column5: A paper or plastic coin wrapper containing quarters; in the U.S., a standard full roll normally contains 40 quarters, totaling $10.
column7: I grabbed a roll of quarters for the laundromat.
column8: CORRECTION: the current definition says merely 'stacks of twenty-five-cent coins' and omits the standard U.S. quantity. A standard U.S. quarter roll is 40 coins = $10.

column5: A cocktail made with Scotch whisky and vermouth, classically sweet vermouth in the standard version, plus bitters; related to a Manhattan but made with Scotch.
column7: He ordered a Rob Roy with dinner.
column8: Capitalize the cocktail name. Classic recipes normally include bitters, which the old definition omitted. Variants such as dry/perfect Rob Roy alter the vermouth.

column5: A joking slang term for the skin around or over the elbow; spelling varies.
column7: He banged his elbow and joked that he'd injured his wenis.
column8: Nonstandard joke word with unstable spelling: wenis, weenis, wenus, etc. It is not an anatomical term. Best for recognition/source context rather than formal use.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::formal usage::slang usage::humorous usage::informal discovery::terminology

column5: To touch or stroke gently and affectionately; noun: a gentle affectionate touch or stroke. Figuratively, something such as wind or light can caress a surface.
column6: stroke, touch gently, fondle (often more sexual)
column7: She caressed the baby's cheek. / A warm breeze caressed his face.
column8: 'Fondle' can carry a stronger sexual connotation and is not always a safe synonym. Caress is affectionate/tender and can be literary.
column12: entry::word usage::literary usage::affectionate usage::warm topic::weather discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Popular with or geared toward tourists; often implying crowdedness, commercialization, clichés, or reduced local authenticity, though not necessarily bad.
column7: We skipped the touristy waterfront and explored a quieter neighborhood.
column8: Can be neutral ('popular with tourists') or mildly negative ('overcommercialized/inauthentic'). Avoid building the negative judgment into every use.

column5: A humorous inversion or variation on 'quick and painless', used to acknowledge that something unpleasant will be brief but not comfortable.
column6: short and brutal, over quickly but painfully
column7: Let's make this meeting quick and painful so we can all go home.
column8: Not a fixed idiom in the same way as 'quick and painless'; often deliberate dark humor or wordplay on that familiar phrase.

column5: noun: an extra benefit or advantage, especially one attached to a job, role, membership, or situation. verb: 'perk up' = become more lively/cheerful; 'perk' also has specialized senses.
column7: Flexible hours are a major perk of the job. / One perk of living downtown is being able to walk everywhere.
column8: Core card should emphasize noun. 'Bonus' may be money whereas a perk can be noncash. Related but separate phrasal verb: perk up.

column5: A powered gardening/maintenance tool that blows a stream of air to move leaves, grass clippings, and other light debris; some models can also vacuum/mulch.
column7: He used a leaf blower to clear leaves from the driveway.
column8: A leaf vacuum/blower is a related combination tool, not a synonym for every leaf blower.

column5: A person, deity, character, or figure described as bearing, wielding, carrying, or bringing lightning; the exact symbolic meaning depends on the source.
column6: wielder of lightning, bearer of lightning
column7: In the story, the warrior is called the lightning bearer because he carries the storm god's weapon.
column8: Not a standard English archetype with a fixed meaning such as 'bringer of enlightenment'. Preserve as source-dependent/poetic wording and interpret from context.

column5: A dentist with specialized training in diagnosing, preventing, and treating malpositioned teeth and jaws, commonly using braces, aligners, and other orthodontic appliances.
column7: The orthodontist adjusted her braces and checked her bite.
column8: 'Braces specialist' is an informal description, not a professional synonym. Orthodontics concerns tooth/jaw alignment and bite, not only braces.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::professional usage::specialist topic::medicine topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::professional_context

column5: The scientific study of ancient life through fossils and other evidence preserved in the geological record.
column7: She studied paleontology and specialized in dinosaur fossils.
column8: AmE paleontology; BrE palaeontology. Broader than dinosaurs and not simply 'prehistoric biology': it covers ancient plants, animals, microorganisms, ecosystems, evolution, etc.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::american_english usage::british_english usage::specialist usage::scientific topic::science discovery::evidence discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To become pregnant or get someone pregnant; informal and potentially crude/disrespectful depending on context.
column7: She joked that she got knocked up right after the wedding.
column8: Register warning: casual/slang and can sound crude, especially about someone else's pregnancy. In older BrE, 'knock someone up' historically also had unrelated senses such as waking someone by knocking.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrasal_verb usage::informal usage::casual usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::british_english

column5: Angry or offended because one believes something is unjust, insulting, improper, or undeserved.
column7: She was indignant at being accused of cheating. / He gave an indignant reply.
column8: More specific than generic angry/annoyed: indignation involves a sense of injustice or affront. Related adverb WID1508 indignantly.

column5: To tell, show, or explain an idea, plan, question, or proposal to someone in order to get their reaction, opinion, or approval.
column6: check with, consult, get someone's take on
column7: Can I run something by you before I send this email?
column8: NORMALIZE productive pattern: run something by someone. Often casual workplace/conversation English.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::casual usage::professional topic::communication discovery::explanation discovery::suggestion discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::social_approval discovery::professional_context

column5: To step heavily or repeatedly on and crush/damage something; to injure people by stepping on them in a crowd; figuratively, to disregard or violate rights, feelings, or principles.
column6: stomp on, tread on, crush; violate, ride roughshod over
column7: The crowd trampled the flowers. / Several people were injured in the crush. / The policy was criticized for trampling on basic rights.
column8: Normalize to base verb while retaining source form. Important figurative pattern: trample on/over rights, feelings, traditions.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative topic::romance discovery::process_details discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To reduce, restrict, limit, or cut short the extent, duration, or amount of something.
column7: We had to curtail our travel plans. / The new rules could curtail access to the service.
column8: Usually transitive: curtail spending/activity/freedom/rights/operations. Slightly formal.

column5: Annoying, frustrating, puzzling, or troublesome, especially in a persistent or difficult-to-resolve way.
column7: It's a vexing problem with no obvious solution.
column8: Can combine annoyance with difficulty/puzzlement. Related verb vex is somewhat formal/literary in modern English.

column5: Best friend forever; a very close friend. Often used playfully even without a literal promise of permanence.
column7: She's been my BFF since middle school. / We became instant BFFs on the trip.
column8: Usually pronounced letter by letter. Can pluralize: BFFs. Often affectionate/playful rather than literally 'forever'.

column5: The branch/basic practice of mathematics involving numerical calculation, especially addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division; adjective: relating to such calculation.
column7: Mental arithmetic gets easier with practice. / Check the arithmetic before submitting the budget.
column8: Pronunciation often differs by POS: noun commonly /əˈrɪθmətɪk/; adjective often /ˌærɪθˈmɛtɪk/ in AmE. Broader 'math' is not an exact synonym.

column5: noun: a number or fractional part written in base-ten notation using a decimal point; adjective: relating to a system based on powers of ten.
column7: Write the answer as a decimal. / Round it to two decimal places.
column8: 'Fractional' is not a direct synonym: decimals can represent whole or fractional values, and fractions can be written non-decimally. High-value terms: decimal point, decimal place, recurring/repeating decimal.

column5: A library classification system that organizes works by subject using numerical classes and decimal subdivisions.
column7: I found the book by looking up its Dewey Decimal number.
column8: CORRECT spelling/capitalization: Dewey, not 'dewy'. Formal name: Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC); 'Dewey Decimal System' is the familiar name.

column2: get some perspective / gain perspective / put something in perspective
column5: To develop a clearer, broader, or more balanced understanding of a situation, often by viewing it in a larger context.
column6: gain perspective, see the bigger picture, get a sense of proportion
column7: Taking a few days away helped me get some perspective. / The comparison puts the cost in perspective.
column8: 'Get perspective' without a determiner is possible in some contexts but 'get some perspective' and 'gain perspective' are often more natural. Also teach productive 'put X in perspective'.

column5: Odd, eccentric, silly, or comically unconventional; sometimes wildly impractical.
column7: It's a wacky idea, but it might actually work. / The show is full of wacky characters.
column8: Usually playful rather than seriously condemning. Can describe ideas, humor, designs, people, situations.

column5: To greatly impress, surprise, excite, or amaze someone.
column7: The finale will knock your socks off. / Her audition knocked the judges' socks off.
column8: CORRECT: standard idiom is plural 'socks'. Common imperative: 'Knock their socks off!' = impress them greatly.

column5: Surprised or shocked, especially suddenly and enough to momentarily unsettle someone.
column7: I was taken aback by how rude he was. / Her blunt question took me aback.
column8: Usually appears in passive/adjectival 'be taken aback', but active 'take someone aback' is also useful. Often followed by by/at.

column5: noun: a young bird that has recently acquired flight feathers or begun flying. Figuratively, an inexperienced person. adjective: new, young, or still developing, especially an organization, industry, or career.
column7: A fledgling had fallen from the nest. / The fledgling company is already attracting investors.
column8: Important literal bird sense was missing. Figurative adjective is very common: fledgling company/industry/democracy/career.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative topic::work topic::travel topic::animals discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Bitter, hostile, and angry, especially in an argument, dispute, separation, or relationship.
column7: The negotiations became increasingly acrimonious. / They went through an acrimonious divorce.
column8: Usually describes exchanges/relationships characterized by bitterness, not simply any angry event. Related noun: acrimony.

column5: To understand an indirect suggestion or signal and respond appropriately, especially by stopping, leaving, or changing behavior.
column6: get the message, catch on, read the signs
column7: He finally took the hint and stopped asking. / I kept yawning, but she didn't take the hint.
column8: Often implies the speaker thinks the hint should have been obvious. Can sound mildly annoyed.

column2: put someone off / put something off
column5: 1. put someone off: cause dislike, discomfort, loss of interest, or reluctance. 2. put something off: postpone or delay it. 3. BrE: distract someone ('Don't put me off').
column7: His rude manner really put me off. / We had to put the meeting off until Friday.
column8: Major polysemy: person-object and thing-object constructions differ. 'Put someone off doing something' = discourage/deter them from doing it.

column5: Traditionally, a woman who gives massages professionally.
column7: The hotel arranged a massage therapist for the appointment.
column8: Modern professional English usually prefers gender-neutral 'massage therapist'. 'Masseuse' can sound dated and in some contexts may carry unwanted sexual-service associations.

column5: Traditionally, a man who gives massages professionally.
column7: He trained and worked professionally as a massage therapist.
column8: Modern professional English usually prefers gender-neutral 'massage therapist'. 'Masseur' remains understandable but is less common in many current professional contexts.

column5: Emotionally hardened and insensitive to other people's feelings, pain, or suffering.
column7: It was callous of him to joke about her loss. / The policy was criticized as callous.
column8: Do not confuse with callus (WID1555), the hardened skin noun. Callous can also historically relate to hardened tissue, but emotional sense dominates everyday adjective use.

column5: noun: a thickened, hardened area of skin caused by repeated friction or pressure. verb: to form a callus or make skin calloused.
column7: Guitar practice gave him calluses on his fingertips.
column8: CORRECTION: blister is not a synonym; a blister is a fluid-filled skin lesion, whereas a callus is thickened hardened skin. Confusable with adjective callous = emotionally insensitive.

column5: A person intensely knowledgeable about or absorbed in the details of a specialized subject, especially public policy, politics, economics, or technical matters.
column7: She's a policy wonk who can explain every line of the bill.
column8: Can be admiring, neutral, or teasing; not necessarily 'excessive'. Productive compounds: policy wonk, data wonk. Related adjective wonky has several separate senses.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::technical usage::specialist topic::politics topic::economics topic::government discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::policy_discussion discovery::specialist_register discovery::expertise discovery::public_discourse

column5: A socially awkward, unfashionable, or nerdy person; often used teasingly rather than as a serious description.
column7: I was a total dweeb in middle school. / Quit being a dweeb and come dance with us.
column8: Informal insult with variable harshness. Not inherently about being studious, and 'loser' can be harsher.

column5: Lively, spirited, assertive, determined, and ready to resist or argue; sometimes combative.
column7: She's small but feisty and never backs down from a challenge.
column8: Often applied to someone perceived as small/young/older/underestimated, but that is not required. Can be approving or mildly critical.
column12: entry::word usage::critical usage::debate-friendly discovery::debate_language discovery::assertion discovery::determination

column5: Cautious and watchful because of possible danger, deception, problems, or unwanted consequences.
column7: I'm wary of deals that sound too good to be true. / She was wary of giving the app access to her contacts.
column8: Common patterns: wary of + noun/gerund; wary about. Confusable with weary = tired.

column5: To perform extremely well, succeed impressively, or exceed expectations.
column6: kill it, nail it, dominate, do amazingly well
column7: You're crushing it at your new job. / Go out there and crush it!
column8: Normalize to productive base phrase while retaining source form. Very common positive informal expression in work, sports, performance, fitness, etc.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::form_family entry::phrase usage::informal usage::slang topic::romance

column5: Relating to sexual intercourse; especially in the older term 'venereal disease' for infections transmitted through sexual contact.
column7: Older medical texts often use the phrase 'venereal disease.'
column8: Modern health communication generally uses sexually transmitted infection (STI) or sexually transmitted disease (STD), not 'venereal disease'. 'Venereal' survives in historical/formal contexts.

column5: Abbreviation for 'venereal disease', an older umbrella term for sexually transmitted diseases/infections.
column7: Older public-health posters warned about VD.
column8: Historical/dated terminology. Modern usage generally prefers STI, or STD depending context. STI and STD are related but not perfectly identical conceptually: infection may be present without symptomatic disease.
column12: entry::abbreviation usage::dated usage::specialist topic::health discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Very rapidly and in large amounts, especially in making, spending, gaining, or losing money.
column6: rapidly, at a great rate, in large amounts
column7: The company was making money hand over fist. / They were losing customers hand over fist.
column8: Commonly financial but can extend to other countable gains/losses. Usually conveys both speed and quantity, not merely 'quickly'.

column5: Containing, covered with, or forming lumps; uneven rather than smooth; figuratively, awkward or uneven in quality in some contexts.
column7: The gravy turned lumpy. / The mattress felt old and lumpy.
column8: Choose synonym by context: clumpy for material with clumps; bumpy for uneven surfaces. Not all lumpy things are 'covered with' lumps.

column5: A narrow crack, split, or opening, especially in rock or another solid surface.
column7: Dust collected in the crevices between the floorboards. / Small plants grew in a rock crevice.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Often suggests a narrow/deep opening. Fissure can be more technical or larger depending context.

column5: noun: a fluid/paste-like material used to fill joints, gaps, or voids, especially between tiles. verb: to fill or seal with grout.
column7: The bathroom grout had started to discolor. / We grouted the new tile floor yesterday.
column8: Not simply used to 'secure tiles in place'—adhesive/thinset typically bonds tile, while grout fills joints; structural grouting has additional construction uses.

column5: noun: a cutting/shaping tool with a sharpened edge used on wood, stone, metal, etc. verb: to cut or shape with a chisel; informal 'chisel someone out of something' = cheat them out of it.
column6: carving tool; carve, cut; cheat, swindle
column7: He used a chisel to shape the wood. / The scammer chiseled investors out of thousands of dollars.
column8: Important figurative/informal verb family: chisel someone out of money. 'Sculpt' is broader and not a direct synonym for the tool action.

column5: To take or steal something and leave/escape with it, often quickly or secretly.
column6: steal, run off with, abscond with
column7: Someone made off with my umbrella while I was inside.
column8:
Productive pattern includes object: make off with something. 'Make off' alone = leave/escape quickly; 'make off with' often implies taking something.

似た表現の比較一覧　表現　主なニュアンス・特徴よくある使われ方

make off with「急いでその場を去る」に焦点。泥棒がサッと盗んで逃げる。泥棒、強盗、計画的な持ち逃げ

run off with「人目を盗んで姿を消す」に焦点。（人に対して使うと「駆け落ちする」）持ち逃げ、横領、駆け落ち

walk off with「平然と、または誤って」持って行く。あるいは「（賞などを）楽々とさらう」。置き引き、勘違い、賞の総なめ、悪びれもせず堂々とのニュアンス

make away withやや古い・堅い表現。意味はmake off withとほぼ同じ。犯罪のニュース、小説など

He run off with all the company's money.（彼は会社の金をすべて持ってドロンした/横領した）人： She ran off with her boss.（彼女は上司と駆け落ちした）

Someone walked off with my umbrella.（誰かが私の傘を（平然と、または間違えて）持って行ってしまった）受賞： The movie walked off with three Oscars.（その映画はオスカーを3部門も楽々とさらっていった）

The thief made away with the secret documents.（その泥棒は秘密文書を持ち去った）

column2: be called to the scene / call someone to the scene
column5: To be summoned or requested to go to the place where an incident, emergency, crime, or other event has occurred.
column6: be summoned, be dispatched, respond to the scene
column7: Police were called to the scene shortly after midnight.
column8: NORMALIZE: most common reporting pattern is passive 'police/officers/emergency crews were called to the scene'. 'Dispatched' is related but not identical.

column5: To listen to everything someone wants to say before judging, interrupting, rejecting, or deciding.
column6: listen fully, give someone a hearing, let someone finish
column7: I know you're angry, but hear me out. / Let's hear her out before we decide.
column8: Very common imperative 'Hear me out.' Usually implies the listener may initially disagree or be reluctant.

column5: To make someone very tired; intransitively, to become tired in some uses.
column7: That hike really tired me out. / The kids tire out quickly in the heat.
column8: Common and neutral. Compare wear someone out = exhaust, often suggesting repeated/prolonged strain.

column5: Historically, a person who prepared and sold medicines and medicinal substances; by extension, an apothecary's shop. The profession's role varied by place and period.
column7: The museum recreated an eighteenth-century apothecary's shop.
column8: Historical role is not identical to a modern pharmacist. In modern branding, 'apothecary' is sometimes used decoratively for shops selling cosmetics/herbs/home goods.

column5: verb: cheat, overcharge, steal from, or copy someone/something. noun: an unfairly expensive deal/scam, or an imitation/copy. adjective: exploitative or derivative.
column6: cheat, overcharge, scam; steal; copy; swindle
column7: They ripped us off on the repair bill. / Forty dollars for that is a rip-off. / The design looks like a rip-off of the original.
column8: Broader than overcharging. Spelling: verb 'rip off'; noun/adjective 'rip-off'. Productive: rip someone off, rip off an idea/design.

column5: Suggested, understood, or contained without being directly stated; also inherent or unquestioning in certain collocations.
column7: His message carried an implicit threat. / There was an implicit assumption that everyone would agree.
column8: Contrast explicit = directly stated. Common: implicit meaning/assumption/bias/threat; implicit trust = complete/unquestioning trust, a distinct collocation.

column5: The characteristic values, beliefs, attitudes, and guiding spirit of a person, group, institution, culture, or era.
column7: The school's ethos emphasizes independence and curiosity.
column8: More than a simple 'culture': ethos specifically emphasizes characteristic values/principles/spirit. In rhetoric, ethos also refers to credibility/character as a mode of persuasion.

column5: Something or someone remarkably good, striking, difficult, intense, or otherwise notable.
column7: That was a humdinger of a storm. / She told us a humdinger of a story.
column8: CORRECTION: standard word is 'humdinger', not 'hamdinger'. It need not be positive; a storm/problem can be a humdinger too.

column5: Quick and not thorough, detailed, or careful.
column7: He gave the report a cursory glance. / A cursory inspection didn't reveal the problem.
column8: Common collocations: cursory glance/look/examination/inspection/review. Usually implies insufficient depth.

column5: Ordinary, unimaginative, or lacking poetic/romantic excitement; in literary discussion, resembling ordinary prose rather than poetry.
column7: The explanation turned out to be disappointingly prosaic. / The film gives a poetic treatment to a prosaic subject.
column8: Not simply 'bad writing'. Core figurative contrast is ordinary/mundane vs imaginative/poetic. Related to prose (WID1581).

column5: Written or spoken language in ordinary grammatical form rather than verse/metre; also a writer's characteristic style of written prose.
column7: Her prose is clear and economical. / The book mixes poetry with short passages of prose.
column8: 'Narrative' is not a synonym: prose can be narrative, expository, argumentative, etc. Contrast prose vs verse/poetry.
column12: entry::word usage::conversational topic::grammar topic::literature topic::lyrics topic::music discovery::lyrics_language

column5: To travel, roam, or go around from place to place for pleasure, amusement, or social activity, often when one is thought to have other responsibilities.
column6: roam, gad about, traipse around, travel around
column7: They spent the summer gallivanting around Europe. / Where have you been gallivanting off to?
column8: Normalize to base verb. Often playful or mildly disapproving; not the same as frolicking, which emphasizes playful movement.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::humorous usage::playful usage::critical topic::travel

column2: spur-of-the-moment / on the spur of the moment
column5: Done or decided suddenly, without advance planning; 'on the spur of the moment' = impulsively at that moment.
column7: It was a spur-of-the-moment decision. / We booked the trip on the spur of the moment.
column8: Hyphenate before a noun: a spur-of-the-moment decision. This card overlaps an earlier family entry but remains useful as a form/collocation card.

column5: A source-specific comic expression suggesting that a man lacks vigor, responsiveness, or sexual potency; exact intended nuance depends on context.
column6: no pep in his step, lacking vigor; sexual-performance euphemism (context-dependent)
column7: He joked about getting older and having 'no snap in his turtle.'
column8: NOT a standard English idiom. Preserve for source recognition only. Do not teach as a generally established euphemism; the sexual reading may be source/context dependent.

column2: take credit for something / take credit for someone's work
column5: To claim or accept recognition for an achievement, idea, result, or action; negatively, to claim recognition that properly belongs to someone else.
column6: claim credit, claim responsibility; steal credit (if undeserved)
column7: She took credit for solving the problem. / He keeps taking credit for his colleague's ideas.
column8: CORRECTION: 'take credit for someone' is not the normal pattern for the intended meaning. Use take credit for something / for doing something / for someone's work. It is not inherently wrongful; context determines whether the credit is deserved.

column5: An American dish of seasoned ground beef formed into patties and typically served with gravy, often mushroom or onion gravy.
column7: The diner served Salisbury steak with mashed potatoes and gravy.
column8: Capitalize Salisbury. It is not literally steak cut from a whole muscle, and 'meatloaf steak' is not a standard synonym.

column5: To make someone very angry; in other contexts, 'burn up' can mean be consumed by fire, use up fuel/energy, or become very hot.
column7: It really burns me up when people take credit for someone else's work.
column8: For anger, common patterns include 'That burns me up' and 'It burns me up that...'. Distinguish from literal/other phrasal-verb senses.

column5: 1. A person's usual temperament or tendency of mood/behavior. 2. The arrangement or positioning of things. 3. The action/result of disposing of, transferring, or resolving something, especially in legal/business contexts.
column7: She has a cheerful disposition. / The report describes the disposition of the assets.
column8: Highly polysemous formal word. Everyday personality sense is common, but legal/business 'disposition of a case/assets' and arrangement senses are important.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::formal topic::business topic::law topic::nature

column5: 1. Used to show surprise or ask whether something is really true: 'Really?' 2. Used to strongly agree with an obvious statement: 'Seriously / tell me about it.' 3. Literally, 'I'm not joking.'
column6: really?, seriously, you're telling me, I'm not joking
column7: 'She quit yesterday.' 'No kidding?' / 'This traffic is awful.' 'No kidding.' / No kidding—I actually won.
column8: Intonation changes function. Can express genuine surprise, emphatic agreement, or insistence on truth.
column12: entry::interjection entry::polysemy_set entry::idiom usage::informal usage::humorous discovery::agreement

column5: A traditional English-language way of approximating seconds by saying 'one Mississippi, two Mississippi...' at a steady pace.
column7: Count 'one Mississippi, two Mississippi' before you start chasing us.
column8: Approximate, not an accurate timing method. Common in children's games and informal timing; other regional counting words exist.

column5: Used to say that something is extremely obvious, often with sarcasm or mild mockery.
column7: 'You need a password to log in.' 'Well, duh.'
column8: 'Well, duh' adds conversational emphasis to duh. Can sound dismissive or rude. Related WID1230/1516 family should be considered in later duplicate-family QA.

column5: Bullwinkle J. Moose, the good-natured but dim-witted cartoon moose from 'The Rocky and Bullwinkle Show' franchise.
column7: The joke compares him to Bullwinkle, the cartoon moose.
column8: CORRECTION: treat as a proper character reference, not a common noun meaning 'goof'. Any implication of clumsiness/goofiness comes from the comparison/context and should not be universalized.

column2: I can't even send back soup
column3: aɪ kænt ˈivən sɛnd bæk suːp
column5: A self-deprecating line suggesting extreme reluctance to complain, assert oneself, or confront someone—even in a low-stakes situation such as returning unsatisfactory food.
column6: I'm too nonconfrontational, I hate complaining, I'm not assertive
column7: Confront my boss? I can't even send back soup when it's cold.
column8: Not a standard idiom with a fixed dictionary meaning. Preserve as source/contextual humor. It evokes nonconfrontational behavior or low assertiveness; do not label it clinically as 'social anxiety' without context.
column12: entry::idiom usage::humorous topic::food discovery::assertion discovery::complaint discovery::suggestion

column5: Bad-tempered, irritable, and prone to complaining or snapping at people.
column7: The crotchety neighbor complained whenever the kids played outside.
column8: Often stereotypically used of older people, but age is not part of the definition. Can be humorous or insulting.

column5: Irritable, petulant, or easily annoyed, often over small matters.
column7: He grew peevish after waiting for an hour. / She answered in a peevish tone.
column8: Somewhat literary/formal. Often suggests petty or childish irritability more than general anger.

column5: Not becoming less severe, intense, demanding, or persistent; not giving way or showing mercy.
column7: The unrelenting heat lasted for weeks. / She faced unrelenting criticism.
column8: Can describe weather, pressure, pain, criticism, pace, effort, etc. 'Uncompromising' overlaps mainly for a person's stance, not all uses.

column5: A source-specific comparison whose intended joke or implication depends on its original context; it should not be treated as an established English idiom.
column7: The speaker joked, 'It's like cocktails in Appalachia,' using the contrast for comic effect.
column8: CORRECTION/CAUTION: not a standard idiom meaning simply 'an unlikely combination'. The line may rely on cultural/class/regional stereotyping of Appalachia, so preserve the source wording but do not generalize or recommend it as a neutral expression.

column5: Loud, energetic, lively, and somewhat rough or rowdy.
column7: A boisterous crowd spilled out of the stadium. / The children became boisterous after dessert.
column8: Not necessarily cheerful: the core is noisy, energetic, exuberant/rowdy behavior. Can be positive, neutral, or mildly disapproving.

column5: 1. Playful, lively, and energetic, especially of an animal. 2. Informally, sexually playful, flirtatious, or aroused.
column7: The puppy was feeling frisky and raced around the yard. / He was getting a little frisky after a couple of drinks.
column8: Important second sense is stronger than merely 'a hint of flirtation'. Context matters; sexual sense is informal and can imply unwanted advances depending on behavior.

column5: Full of lively energy, excitement, enthusiasm, or joy; also very abundant or luxuriant in some formal uses.
column7: The kids were exuberant after hearing the news. / Her exuberant personality filled the room.
column8: Usually strongly positive and outwardly expressive. Related noun: exuberance. Formal extension: exuberant growth/vegetation = abundant/luxuriant.

column5: Noisily energetic, boisterous, and difficult to control, especially of children, animals, or groups.
column7: The rambunctious kids ran around the house all afternoon.
column8: CORRECTION: the headword is already 'rambunctious'; remove the erroneous note calling it a misspelling, and fix the example typo 'rambuncrious'.

column5: To work together by sharing ideas and thinking jointly about a problem or plan.
column7: We put our heads together and came up with a cheaper solution.
column8: Normalize from the past-tense sentence to the productive idiom 'put one's heads together'. Usually implies collaborative thinking/problem-solving.

column5: Pajamas; sleepwear, especially in casual, affectionate, or child-directed speech.
column7: I'm changing into my jammies and calling it a night.
column8: Usually plural. Cute/childlike register, though adults may use it jokingly.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::casual usage::affectionate topic::family topic::public_speaking

column5: A feminine given name or nickname; also commonly used as a pet or fictional-character name. Its specific referent depends on context.
column7: Mitzi jumped onto the couch and curled up beside me.
column8: Proper name, not a vocabulary word with a fixed lexical meaning. Preserve for source/name recognition rather than assigning a generic character type.

column5: Used to say that an action, amount, adjustment, or solution should be sufficient to achieve the intended result.
column6: that should do it, that should work, that ought to be enough
column7: One more turn of the screw—there, that ought to do it.
column8: Common conversational phrase. 'Ought to' here expresses confident expectation, not moral obligation.
column12: entry::phrase usage::conversational topic::work topic::problem-solving discovery::solution_framing discovery::resolution

column5: To close, grip, or tighten something firmly, especially the fists, jaw, teeth, or muscles; clenching is the act/state of doing so.
column7: He clenched his fists in anger. / I catch myself clenching my jaw when I'm stressed.
column8: Normalize to base verb while retaining source form. Common: clench your fists/teeth/jaw; teeth clenching.

column2: well up / well up with tears
column5: Of liquid, tears, or emotion: to rise, gather, or become intense until it is close to overflowing or being expressed.
column7: Tears welled up in her eyes. / I could feel anger welling up inside me.
column8: CORRECTION: not gender-specific. Tears can well up in someone's eyes; emotions can well up inside someone. 'Tear up' is related but grammatically different.

column5: Impossible or extremely difficult to achieve, obtain, reach, or realize.
column6: unachievable, unreachable, out of reach, impossible
column7: Perfection is an unattainable goal. / For most buyers, homes in that neighborhood are financially unattainable.
column8: Often describes goals, ideals, standards, prices, objects of desire. 'Unreachable' is most natural for literal/figurative reach, not every use.

column5: To scatter things loosely over a surface or area; often appears in the past participle 'strewn'.
column7: Petals were strewn across the floor. / The beach was strewn with driftwood.
column8: High-value patterns: be strewn with something; something is strewn across/along something. Past: strewed; past participle commonly strewn, also strewed.

column5: Lacking an organized plan, method, or order; done or arranged in a random, careless, or unsystematic way.
column7: The files were stored in a haphazard way. / We can't keep making changes haphazardly.
column8: Not necessarily chaotic in outcome; the key is absence of method/system. Related adverb: haphazardly.

column5: A smaller room leading into a larger or more important room, especially in a formal, historical, ceremonial, or grand building.
column7: The delegation waited in an antechamber before entering the throne room.
column8: More formal/historical than foyer. It need not be an entrance from outdoors; it specifically precedes another room.

column5: A small entrance hall, lobby, or enclosed space between an outer entrance and the main interior; also a technical term for entrance-like cavities in anatomy.
column7: We left our wet boots in the vestibule. / The word also appears in anatomical terms such as the nasal vestibule.
column8: Broader/technical polysemy. In buildings, foyer/lobby overlap but are not exact; vestibule often emphasizes a small transitional entrance space.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::specialist topic::anatomy topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_register

column5: To severely damage, mutilate, deform, or distort something; figuratively, to badly mispronounce, misquote, edit, or otherwise spoil something.
column7: The machine mangled the metal. / He completely mangled my name. / The article mangled the original argument.
column8: Normalize to base verb. Very useful figuratively: mangle a name, quote, sentence, translation, explanation.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::rhetorical topic::grammar discovery::figurative_extension discovery::debate_language

column5: The dead body of an animal, especially after slaughter, decomposition, or removal of usable parts; figuratively, the stripped or ruined framework/remains of a machine or structure.
column6: animal remains, dead animal; shell, wreck (figurative)
column7: Vultures circled above the carcass. / The burned-out carcass of the car was left by the road.
column8: This overlaps WID1366, already corrected there. Do not use corpse/cadaver as default synonyms: those primarily refer to human bodies.

column5: A small mischievous supernatural creature, traditionally a minor demon or sprite; figuratively, a mischievous or naughty child/person.
column7: You little imp—you hid my keys again!
column8: Often playful when applied to a child. Fantasy/religious folklore sense is older and may be darker than the affectionate figurative use.
column12: entry::word usage::playful usage::figurative usage::affectionate usage::religious topic::family discovery::figurative_extension

column5: A contemptible, dishonest, cowardly, or sneaky person; a creative insult rather than a precisely defined character type.
column7: That crapweasel took the credit and blamed everyone else when it failed.
column8: Strong informal insult. Meaning is flexible/contextual; not a neutral personality descriptor.

column5: 1. A dental appliance used after orthodontic treatment to maintain tooth position. 2. A fee paid to secure ongoing professional services/availability. 3. A person retained in service, especially historically. 4. Something that holds another thing in place.
column6: orthodontic retainer; advance/standing fee; attendant; retaining device
column7: I wear my retainer at night. / The firm keeps the lawyer on retainer.
column8: Major missing common legal/professional-fee sense. A dental retainer is not the same thing as braces.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::professional usage::debate-friendly topic::debate topic::medicine topic::health discovery::professional_context discovery::continuity discovery::debate_language

column5: noun: an object propelled through the air or space by force, whether as a weapon or otherwise. adjective: relating to or capable of being projected.
column7: The blast sent debris flying as dangerous projectiles. / The experiment measured projectile motion.
column8: Not every projectile is a weapon or bullet. Physics sense is important: projectile motion.

column5: Bethel is a biblical place-name meaning 'house of God'; lowercase bethel has also been used by some Christian communities for a chapel, meeting house, or place of worship.
column7: The biblical town of Bethel appears repeatedly in the Hebrew Bible. / Some congregations historically called their chapel a bethel.
column8: PRECISION: not a generic everyday synonym for any holy place. Capitalization and meaning depend on whether it is the biblical proper name or a denominational/historical common-noun use.
column12: entry::proper_noun entry::form_family entry::word usage::religious topic::religion discovery::professional_context discovery::religious_origin

column5: A very small amount, quantity, or degree of something.
column7: Add a smidge more salt. / I'm a smidge nervous about the interview.
column8: Variant smidgen is also common. Can modify concrete quantities or figurative degrees.

column5: To cause all or many members of a group to die/disappear, or to eliminate a character, species, idea, habit, business line, etc.
column6: wipe out, eliminate, eradicate, do away with
column7: The disease killed off much of the local population. / The writers killed off a major character.
column8: 'Off' often suggests elimination from a group/story/system, sometimes one by one or extensively. It does not always mean literally every member.

column5: Swollen, enlarged, or overfilled with blood, fluid, food, or another substance.
column7: The tick was engorged with blood. / Breast tissue can become engorged with milk after childbirth.
column8: Medical/biological contexts are common. More specific than generic bloated; often implies abnormal or marked filling.

column2: spell something out / spell it out
column5: 1. To say or write the letters of a word one by one. 2. Figuratively, to explain something very clearly, explicitly, or in detail.
column6: spell, explain explicitly, make clear, lay out
column7: Could you spell your last name out for me? / Do I really have to spell it out?
column8: Major literal + figurative senses. Normalize from gerund-only form. Figurative 'spell it out' can sound impatient when the point should be obvious.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::figurative topic::communication discovery::clarification discovery::explanation discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To put, drop, set, or seat someone/something down abruptly, heavily, or casually; intransitively, to sit oneself down.
column7: He plunked the groceries down on the counter. / She plunked herself down on the sofa.
column8: Broader than sitting someone down. Objects and oneself are very common. 'Plunk down money' can also mean pay a sum, especially readily.

column5: A story, image, work, or extended representation in which characters/events stand for broader moral, political, religious, or abstract meanings; also the technique itself.
column6: symbolic narrative, extended metaphor (related, not exact), parable (specific type)
column7: The novel can be read as a political allegory. / The cave story functions as an allegory of ignorance and enlightenment.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Allegory is sustained/systematic symbolic representation; not every metaphor, fable, or parable is interchangeable.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative usage::religious topic::work topic::politics topic::religion discovery::public_discourse discovery::religious_origin discovery::literal_vs_figurative

column5: A later-created work whose story is set before an already existing work, showing earlier events in the same fictional continuity.
column7: The new series is a prequel set twenty years before the original film.
column8: A prequel is defined relative to an existing work and is usually produced/released later. An 'origin story' can be a prequel but is not necessarily one.

column5: To come, happen, or exist before something/someone in time, order, rank, or position; to go in front of.
column6: come before, predate, go before, lead
column7: A short speech will precede the ceremony. / The warning signs preceded the crash by several minutes.
column8: Confusable with proceed = continue/go forward. Common passive: be preceded by.

column5: noun: a statement expressing approval, praise, experience, or recommendation, often used in advertising; historically, evidence/tribute of character or service. adjective: relating to a tribute or recommendation.
column7: The site features testimonials from customers. / Celebrity testimonials don't necessarily prove a product works.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. A testimonial is not automatically an independent review; promotional testimonials are selected endorsements.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::persuasive topic::business discovery::evidence discovery::recommendation discovery::social_approval discovery::persuasion

column5: To reveal publicly or to others a private identity, status, affiliation, or secret about someone—especially their sexual orientation or gender identity—without their consent; broader uses also exist.
column7: Are you outing him without his permission?
column8: NORMALIZE from 'are you outing'. In LGBTQ+ contexts, outing someone without consent can cause serious harm. 'Out' also has many unrelated meanings.

column5: The 200th anniversary of an event, institution, place, etc.; adjective: relating to a 200th anniversary or period.
column7: The city celebrated its bicentennial with a week of events.
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling is bicentennial, not 'biccentennial'. Compare centennial = 100th anniversary; semiquincentennial = 250th (rare/formal).

column5: Unpleasant, disgusting, sticky, messy, or emotionally uncomfortable in a way that makes one recoil.
column7: The floor felt icky and sticky. / The conversation left me with an icky feeling.
column8: Childlike/casual but common. Can describe physical texture/smell or a vague moral/emotional discomfort.

column5: A condition, requirement, term, or provision explicitly specified as part of an agreement, arrangement, or decision; in law, also an agreement between parties on a fact/procedure.
column7: I'll agree, with one stipulation: we leave by nine. / The parties entered a stipulation regarding the evidence.
column8: Legal sense can be more specific than generic 'condition'. Productive pattern: with the stipulation that...
column12: entry::word topic::law topic::decision-making discovery::process_details discovery::procedural_language discovery::agreement discovery::expressing_need

column5: Elaborately and often richly decorated, with many details or embellishments.
column7: The room had an ornate carved ceiling. / The invitation used an ornate typeface.
column8: Usually visual/design-focused. Intricate emphasizes complexity, while ornate emphasizes decoration.

column5: Writing that is excessively ornate, elaborate, flowery, or emotionally overwrought in a way that draws attention to style and can impede clarity or story.
column7: The scene slips into purple prose whenever the narrator describes the sunset.
column8: Usually critical, but judgments are subjective and genre-dependent. 'Purple passage' is a related term for an especially ornate section.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::literary usage::critical topic::literature discovery::criticism discovery::excessive_emotion

column5: An intense feeling of disgust, loathing, or repugnance that makes one want to turn away or reject something.
column7: She recoiled in revulsion at the smell. / He felt revulsion at the cruelty described in the report.
column8: Stronger than ordinary dislike. Common: feel revulsion at/toward; recoil in revulsion.

column5: To speak or write at length and in detail about a subject.
column6: elaborate, enlarge, discourse, dwell at length
column7: He expatiated on the history of the building for nearly an hour.
column8: Common pattern: expatiate on/upon something. Formal/literary and uncommon in casual speech.
column12: entry::collocation entry::word usage::formal usage::casual usage::literary usage::informal topic::communication

column5: Growing thickly, richly, or abundantly; also richly elaborate or abundant in appearance, especially hair or vegetation.
column7: The path wound through luxuriant tropical vegetation. / She had luxuriant dark hair.
column8: Do not confuse luxuriant = abundant/lush with luxurious = providing great comfort/expense.

column5: Reluctant or restrained about speaking, revealing thoughts, or sharing information.
column6: reserved, reluctant to speak, guarded, uncommunicative
column7: He was reticent about discussing his childhood.
column8: Traditional precise sense concerns reluctance to speak/disclose. Modern use sometimes broadens to 'reluctant' generally, but 'reticent to do X' is criticized by some usage guides; 'reluctant' is safer there.

column5: adverb: completely, absolutely, or unmistakably, often intensifying something negative or surprising. adjective: plain, direct, or complete in certain uses.
column7: That was downright rude. / The idea is downright dangerous. / She gave me a downright refusal.
column8: Not limited to negative words: 'downright amazing' occurs, though negative intensification is common. 'Blatantly' is not a general synonym.

column5: To be unfaithful to a romantic partner by secretly having another romantic or sexual relationship.
column6: cheat on, be unfaithful to, betray
column7: He discovered that his partner had been two-timing him.
column8: Hyphenate the verb: two-time. Related noun: two-timer. Strongly associated with romantic infidelity.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal topic::relationships topic::romance discovery::betrayal

column5: Grossly insensitive, tactless, vulgar, or lacking refinement, especially in a way that ignores other people's feelings or social standards.
column7: Making jokes about his salary at dinner was pretty crass.
column8: 'Lacking intelligence' is not the core meaning. Crass emphasizes coarse insensitivity/lack of refinement or judgment.

column5: To become strongly upset, anxious, angry, excited, or emotionally agitated about something.
column6: get upset, get agitated, get wound up, stress out
column7: Don't get so worked up over one comment. / Everyone got worked up about the announcement.
column8: Not always negative anxiety: people can get worked up with anger or excitement. Common: get worked up about/over something.

column5: Mentally energized, excited, and prepared for a challenge, performance, competition, or event.
column6: pumped up, fired up, amped up, ready
column7: I put on my favorite song to get psyched up before the interview.
column8: Usually positive preparation/arousal. Distinguish psyched = excited; psyched out = psychologically unnerved.

column2: psych someone out / get psyched out
column5: To intimidate, unnerve, confuse, or undermine someone's confidence psychologically; 'get psyched out' = become unnerved or overthink oneself into poor performance.
column6: unnerve, intimidate, rattle, get inside someone's head
column7: He tried to psych his opponent out before the match. / I psyched myself out before the test.
column8: CORRECTION/NORMALIZE: active form is usually 'psych someone out', not 'psyched out' as a phrasal verb headword. Also common reflexive: psych yourself out.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::informal topic::psychology topic::performance

column5: Very excited, enthusiastic, or eager about something.
column7: I'm psyched for the concert. / She's psyched about starting the new job.
column8: Common patterns: psyched for/about/to do. Distinguish 'psyched up' = mentally prepared/energized and 'psyched out' = unnerved.

column5: An exclamation of discomfort, disgust, exasperation, surprise, or mild alarm; spelling varies by speaker/source.
column7: Eesh, that looks painful. / Yeesh, what a mess.
