column8: SOURCE/FORM CAUTION: 'eeshk' is not a standard established spelling. Preserve it as a source transcription if needed, but teach the broader interjection family eesh/yeesh/sheesh rather than presenting eeshk as a fixed dictionary form.

column5: To use tough, uncompromising, aggressive, or highly competitive tactics to get what one wants, especially in negotiation, politics, business, or disputes.
column6: take a hard line, use tough tactics, be uncompromising
column7: If they refuse to negotiate, we may have to play hardball.
column8: Does not necessarily mean ruthless/illegal; it means abandoning a soft/cooperative approach for tougher tactics. From baseball imagery.
column12: entry::idiom usage::informal topic::business topic::politics discovery::negotiation discovery::public_discourse

column5: A group of parasitic or hemiparasitic plants that grow on trees; in Western Christmas tradition, sprigs are hung as decorations and kissing beneath them is customary.
column7: They hung mistletoe over the doorway. / The couple kissed under the mistletoe.
column8: The kissing custom is cultural, not an inherent botanical property. Mistletoe refers to multiple related plant groups/species.

column5: verb: to take great pleasure or delight in something ('revel in'); also to celebrate noisily or festively. noun: lively celebration or festivity, especially in plural/revels.
column7: She reveled in the attention. / Fans reveled in the streets after the victory.
column8: Major productive pattern is 'revel in something' and need not involve drinking/dancing. Past/participle: reveled/revelled depending spelling convention.

column2: talk someone out of something / talk someone out of doing something
column5: To persuade someone not to do something or not to pursue a plan, purchase, decision, etc.
column6: dissuade, persuade against, convince not to
column7: She talked me out of quitting. / Can you talk him out of buying that car?
column8: Normalize from fixed 'it' to productive construction. Contrast talk someone into something = persuade them to do it.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::persuasive topic::decision-making discovery::persuasion

column5: Expressed or done with force, certainty, clarity, or strong emphasis; leaving little doubt.
column7: She gave an emphatic no. / The team responded with an emphatic 4–0 victory.
column8: Can describe speech/gestures and, in sports/journalism, decisive results. 'Assertive' describes a person's communication style and is not always a synonym.

column5: Useless, ineffective, or serving no practical purpose.
column7: The committee concluded that further debate would be inutile.
column8: Very rare in modern everyday English; often literary, learned, or deliberately unusual. 'Useless' is the normal everyday choice.

column5: 1. Biologically capable of reproducing. 2. Of soil/land, able to support abundant plant growth. 3. Figuratively, productive or rich in ideas, possibilities, imagination, etc.
column7: The valley has fertile soil. / The discussion proved fertile ground for new ideas.
column8: Highly polysemous. Common figurative collocation: fertile ground for. 'Rich' applies well to soil but not every sense.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::collocation entry::word usage::formal usage::figurative discovery::figurative_extension discovery::support discovery::possibility

column5: 1. Not biologically able to reproduce successfully, or having impaired fertility. 2. Of land/soil, unable to support much growth; unproductive.
column7: The soil is too infertile for most crops. / Some medical conditions can make a person infertile.
column8: PRECISION: infertility in people is a medical concept and does not necessarily mean absolute impossibility of conception. 'Sterile' can imply complete inability and is not always interchangeable.

column5: To reach a conclusion by reasoning from known facts, evidence, or premises.
column7: From the wet footprints, she deduced that someone had just come inside.
column8: Normalize to base verb while retaining source form. Pattern: deduce X from Y. This overlaps WID1324 and should be handled as a usage-family duplicate later rather than silently deleted here.

column5: A dentist specializing in periodontology: prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of diseases affecting the gums and other supporting structures of the teeth, and often placement/management of dental implants.
column7: My dentist referred me to a periodontist for advanced gum treatment.
column8: More precise than generic 'dental surgeon'. Periodontists are dental specialists, not simply anyone who treats gums.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::specialist topic::medicine topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A chronic inflammatory disease of the tissues supporting the teeth, associated with microbial dental plaque and progressive loss of periodontal attachment and supporting bone.
column7: Untreated periodontitis can damage the bone supporting the teeth and lead to tooth loss.
column8: PRECISION: more than a generic 'dental infection'. It is a specific inflammatory periodontal disease; gingivitis is a related but distinct, less advanced condition.

column4: phrasal verb (euphemistic; one of several senses)
column5: In one euphemistic sense, to die. 'Pass on' also commonly means transmit/give something to another person or decline an opportunity, so context is essential.
column7: Her grandfather passed on peacefully. / This card targets the death euphemism; elsewhere 'pass on a message' means transmit it.
column8: Do not define the whole phrasal verb only as death. The death sense is gentler/euphemistic and less common than 'pass away' in some varieties.

column5: To die; a common gentle or polite euphemism used when speaking about someone's death.
column7: Her grandmother passed away peacefully last night.
column8: Very common euphemism. 'Deceased' is normally adjective/noun, not a direct verb synonym.

column5: A strongly insulting label for a person regarded as bizarre, irrational, extreme, or dangerously unpredictable.
column7: The character dismisses him as a 'whack job.'
column8: REGISTER WARNING: disparaging and can stigmatize mental illness; better treated as recognition vocabulary than a neutral way to describe a person. Spelling varies.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::variant_set entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::derogatory usage::disparaging usage::informal usage::evaluative topic::work

column5: Slang with several meanings depending on era/dialect: to hit/strike; to have sex with; noun uses can include a blow or other specialized senses.
column7: The old comic scene has one character boff another on the head. / In some slang, 'boff' means have sex with someone.
column8: Register and meaning are highly context-dependent and somewhat dated. Do not assume the sexual sense in every occurrence.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::dated usage::specialist usage::informal discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Cheerfully carefree, unconcerned about consequences, and sometimes recklessly bold.
column7: He had a devil-may-care attitude toward money.
column8: Hyphenate before a noun/adjectivally: devil-may-care attitude. It can sound admiring (bold/free) or critical (reckless).

column5: A large, powerful breed of draft horse originating in Scotland, traditionally used for heavy work and known for feathering on the lower legs.
column7: A team of Clydesdales pulled the wagon through the parade.
column8: Capitalize breed name. 'Horse' and 'draft horse' are categories, not exact synonyms.

column5: As written, 'you swell' is not a standard modern compliment meaning 'you look great'. The source may involve 'swell' as an old-fashioned adjective ('You're swell') or a transcription/context issue.
column6: you're swell, you look great (if intended)
column7: You're swell—you really helped me out. / If the source literally says 'you swell', preserve it as source wording until context confirms the intended meaning.
column8: CORRECTION/CAUTION: do not teach 'You swell in that suit!' as standard English. 'Swell' can be an old-fashioned adjective meaning excellent/fine: 'You're swell.' It is also a verb meaning become enlarged.

column5: To strike, propel, brush, or move someone/something with a quick light movement, especially of a finger, wrist, or small object.
column7: He flicked me on the back of the head. / She flicked a crumb off her sleeve. / He flicked the switch on.
column8: Broader than lightly hitting a person. Common constructions: flick something off/away, flick through pages, flick a switch.

column5: To clean between teeth with dental floss; noun floss = thin thread used for this purpose. 'Flossing' also names a dance move in pop culture, a separate sense.
column6: clean between the teeth; dental floss
column7: I floss every night before bed. / The dentist showed me a better flossing technique.
column8: CORRECTION: brushing is not a synonym for flossing; they clean different tooth surfaces. Normalize to base verb while retaining source form.

column5: The buttocks or rear end.
column7: The toddler fell on his tushie and started laughing.
column8: Cute/child-directed euphemism. Spellings tushie and tushy both occur. Related WID1677 tush.

column2: julienne / cut something into julienne strips
column5: To cut food, especially vegetables, into thin matchstick-like strips; noun/adjective 'julienne' refers to the cut or food prepared that way.
column6: cut into matchsticks, shred finely (not exact)
column7: Julienne the carrots and bell peppers. / Cut the vegetables into thin julienne strips.
column8: CORRECTION: 'do julliene' is misspelled and unnatural. Standard culinary term is julienne (one l after ju-), used as a verb or noun/adjective.

column5: A historical Spanish gold coin, and later related gold coins used in Spain and its colonies; popularly associated with pirates and treasure.
column7: The story's treasure chest was filled with gold doubloons.
column8: CORRECTION: doubloons were gold coins, not generically 'gold or silver coins'. Exact values/types varied historically. Normalize singular/plural.

column5: 1. To drive back, ward off, or resist an attack, force, pest, or unwanted thing. 2. To cause strong dislike or disgust. 3. In physics, to push away through a force such as like electric charges or magnetic poles.
column6: drive back, ward off, resist; disgust, repulse
column7: The defenders repelled the attack. / His arrogance repels me. / Like magnetic poles repel each other.
column8: Major missing emotional and physics senses. 'Defend' is not a direct synonym: one can defend without successfully repelling.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::scientific topic::physics topic::science discovery::prevention

column5: To hit hard; defeat decisively; or badly damage/affect someone or something.
column7: Our team got clobbered 5–0. / Higher costs are clobbering small businesses.
column8: This duplicates the clobber family around WID1496–1497. Preserve for now under the no-auto-delete rule; later duplicate-family QA can decide whether separate retrieval value remains.

column5: verb: to masturbate. noun: an act of masturbation; in some insulting uses, contemptible nonsense/person-related usage appears, but 'wanker' is the standard noun insult for a person.
column7: He called the movie pretentious wank. / The verb 'wank' is vulgar slang for masturbate.
column8: CORRECTION: 'wank' itself is not normally the standard BrE noun meaning 'an idiot'; 'wanker' is the common person-insult. Very vulgar; recognition-focused.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::british_english usage::informal discovery::evaluation

column2: be a wanker / act like a wanker (source: being a wank)
column5: To behave like an obnoxious, contemptible, foolish, or selfish person.
column6: be a jerk, act like an asshole, be obnoxious
column7: Stop acting like a wanker and give me a hand.
column8: CORRECTION: 'being a wank' is nonstandard/likely source-specific for the intended person-insult. Standard BrE insult is 'wanker'; 'wank' has other vulgar noun/verb uses.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::british_english usage::informal

column5: The buttocks; rear end.
column7: He slipped and landed on his tush.
column8: Mild, playful/euphemistic. Related to tushie/tushy WID1669. Do not confuse with Yiddish-derived 'tuchus/tuchis', though they overlap in meaning.

column5: A small quick up-and-down or rhythmic movement of the head; depending on context it can signal acknowledgment/agreement, keep time with music, or simply be involuntary movement.
column7: She gave me a quick head bob of acknowledgment. / He bobbed his head to the beat.
column8: A head bob is not always a nod of agreement; meaning depends on movement and context.

column5: A medical doctor (or osteopathic physician in the U.S.) specializing in eye and vision care, including diagnosis and treatment of eye disease and eye surgery.
column7: The optometrist referred him to an ophthalmologist for possible surgery.
column8: CORRECTION: spelling ophthalmologist, not 'opthamologist'. Do not list optometrist as a synonym: training and scope differ.

column5: Strongly attracted to, infatuated with, or charmed by someone or something; historically also the past participle of smite.
column7: He was completely smitten with her. / I'm smitten with that little café.
column8: Common pattern: smitten with/by. Can apply affectionately to things, places, pets, ideas—not only romantic love.

column2: be an item / be something of an item
column5: To be a romantic couple, especially one that other people know about or speculate about; 'something of an item' can soften or hedge the claim.
column6: be a couple, be together, be seeing each other
column7: Are those two an item now? / The tabloids said they were something of an item.
column8: NORMALIZE from awkward gerund headword. Often gossip/journalistic or slightly old-fashioned/playful.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::dated usage::playful usage::softening usage::journalistic topic::relationships topic::romance discovery::assertion discovery::speculation discovery::hedging

column5: To touch or grope someone's body sexually, especially breasts, buttocks, or genitals; often implies unwanted or inappropriate touching unless consensual context is explicit.
column7: She said a stranger tried to feel her up on the crowded train.
column8: NORMALIZE word order: feel someone up, not 'feel up someone'. Consent matters: the phrase is frequently used in allegations of unwanted touching, though consensual use is possible in context.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::slang usage::informal

column5: A stated reason or excuse used to justify an action while concealing or distracting from the real motive.
column6: excuse, cover, ostensible reason, cover story
column7: He called under the pretext of asking for advice, but he really wanted information.
column8: Unlike a neutral reason, pretext usually implies the stated reason is not the true one. Common: under/on the pretext of; a pretext for.

column5: To deny responsibility for, connection with, knowledge of, or support for something; to publicly reject or renounce it.
column6: deny, repudiate, renounce, disclaim, distance oneself from
column7: The organization disavowed the statement and said it did not reflect its views.
column8: Often formal/public. Patterns: disavow responsibility/knowledge; disavow someone's actions; disavow a belief.

column5: To engage in youthful, reckless, pleasure-seeking, or sexually adventurous behavior before settling into a more conventional life.
column6: have a wild phase, live it up, play the field (sexual context)
column7: He spent his early twenties sowing his wild oats before settling down.
column8: Old-fashioned and historically gendered, often applied to young men. Can carry moral judgment or a double standard; use with awareness.

column5: Literally, wild oat plants; idiomatically best known from 'sow one's wild oats', meaning youthful reckless or sexually adventurous behavior.
column7: The phrase usually appears as 'sow your wild oats,' rather than 'a wild oats phase.'
column8: CORRECTION: 'wild oats' by itself does not normally mean 'the period of life'. The established idiom is 'sow one's wild oats'. Keep this card as the component/family form.

column2: a romp in the sack / have a romp in the sack
column3: hæv ə ˈlɪtl rɑmp ɪn ə sæk
column5: A playful or casual way to refer to having sex.
column6: have sex, sleep together, hook up (not exact)
column7: The comedy treats their brief romp in the sack as an awkward mistake.
column8: Normalize from 'have a little romp in a sack': the idiomatic phrase is 'a romp in the sack'. Informal/euphemistic and somewhat dated/playful; 'make love' can imply more tenderness/romance and is not exact.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::idiom usage::informal usage::casual usage::slang usage::dated usage::playful topic::wellness

column5: Cheerful, lively, self-confident, and stylishly or casually spirited; also describing something set at a lively angle or with a brisk rhythm.
column7: He wore his hat at a jaunty angle. / The song has a jaunty rhythm.
column8: Common collocations: jaunty angle, jaunty tune, jaunty walk. Can describe style/manner, not only mood.

column5: Prestige, status, or special appeal associated with being respected, fashionable, exclusive, or distinctive; historically also a seal/mark.
column7: The neighborhood has acquired considerable cultural cachet.
column8: Pronounced roughly 'cash-AY'; do not confuse with cache /kæʃ/ = hidden store/computer cache. 'Cachet of sophistication' is possible, but often simply 'has cachet'.

column5: Relating to, representing, or resembling a penis or phallus, especially in shape, symbolism, art, psychology, or cultural analysis.
column7: Critics described the tower as phallic imagery.
column8: Can be literal-shape or symbolic/interpretive. 'Penis-shaped' is a plain paraphrase, not a full synonym for symbolic uses.
column12: entry::word usage::technical topic::psychology topic::culture topic::art discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A person who is excessively concerned with displaying or enforcing precise rules, minor details, technical correctness, or book learning, especially in an annoying way.
column7: Don't be a pedant about one misplaced comma when the argument is clear.
column8: 'Scholar' is not a synonym. Pedant is usually negative; related adjective pedantic.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::rhetorical discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::debate_language

column2: be hung up on something/someone / get hung up on
column5: To be preoccupied, fixated, emotionally stuck, or excessively concerned about someone/something; 'hung up on someone' can mean romantically fixated.
column6: fixated on, preoccupied with, obsessed with, stuck on
column7: She's still hung up on her ex. / Don't get hung up on one tiny mistake.
column8: CORRECTION: 'She's still being hung up on...' is unnatural for the state meaning; use 'She's still hung up on...'. Distinguish telephone 'hang up'.

column5: 1. To begin to take effect or operate. 2. To contribute money/resources ('kick in $20'). 3. To break something inward by kicking ('kick in a door').
column6: take effect, start working; contribute; break in
column7: The painkiller should kick in soon. / We each kicked in twenty dollars. / Firefighters kicked the door in.
column8: Major polysemy. For effects, common subjects: medicine, caffeine, adrenaline, instinct, rules, benefits.

column5: To report someone's wrongdoing or misbehavior to a parent, teacher, authority figure, etc., often with a childish or disapproving nuance.
column6: tattle on, report, inform on, rat on (stronger slang)
column7: Don't tell on me—I only took one cookie. / His little sister told on him.
column8: Especially common in children's contexts. 'Snitch/rat out' are stronger slang and can imply betrayal.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::slang usage::critical topic::family topic::education

column5: adjective: designed or treated to slow ignition or the spread of flame. noun: a chemical/substance used to reduce flammability.
column7: The curtains are made from flame-retardant fabric. / Some products contain added flame retardants.
column8: CORRECTION: flame-retardant does not mean fireproof or nonflammable. Hyphenate adjective before noun; noun usually open: flame retardant.

column5: noun: a substance that slows or inhibits a process, especially fire retardant. adjective: slowing or inhibiting a process.
column7: Aircraft dropped fire retardant ahead of the wildfire. / The coating has flame-retardant properties.
column8: Broader than fire, though fire retardant is the most familiar phrase. 'Deterrent' acts by discouraging behavior and is not a general synonym.

column5: 1. One of a pair of long supports used to raise a person above the ground for walking/performing. 2. A post/pile supporting a building above ground or water. Also a name for certain long-legged wading birds.
column7: The house stands on stilts above the floodplain. / The performer walked on stilts.
column8: Normalize singular/plural and add bird sense for recognition. 'Pole' is too broad to be a synonym.

column5: To release an oocyte (egg cell) from an ovary during ovulation.
column7: Many people ovulate roughly once per menstrual cycle, though timing varies.
column8: CORRECTION: reproduce and menstruate are not synonyms. Ovulation is a distinct biological event and does not necessarily coincide with menstruation.
column12: entry::word usage::scientific topic::biology topic::medicine topic::science topic::health discovery::release

column5: 1. In many animals, a reproductive organ that produces oocytes and secretes hormones. 2. In flowering plants, the part of the pistil that contains ovules and develops into fruit after fertilization.
column7: The ovaries produce oocytes and hormones. / In a flower, the ovary can develop into the fruit.
column8: Add important botanical sense. 'Egg producer' is an informal description, not a synonym.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::informal usage::technical topic::anatomy topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: interjection: used to tell someone to be quiet. verb: to tell or cause someone to be quiet, often by saying 'shush'.
column7: Shush! The movie's starting. / She shushed the kids when the announcement began.
column8: Can be gentle/playful or sharp/rude depending tone. Unlike 'silence' as a verb, shush is distinctly informal.

column5: To astonish, overwhelm, or make the mind recoil in disbelief; also, to hesitate or be daunted by something.
column7: The mind boggles at how much data they collected. / I boggled at the price.
column8: CORRECTION: remove the contaminated example 'The project got bogged down...'—bog down is a different verb. Common pattern: the mind boggles at something.

column5: A competitive event in which players play Boggle, the word game where they find words in a grid of lettered dice/letters under time pressure.
column7: He placed second in a Boggle tournament last weekend.
column8: Capitalize Boggle when referring to the branded game. 'Boggle tournament' is compositional rather than a fixed idiom.

column5: A marine crustacean that, as an adult, typically lives attached to rocks, ship hulls, whales, docks, or other surfaces; figuratively, a clingy person/thing in some contexts.
column7: The hull was covered in barnacles. / The comedy portrays him as a barnacle who won't leave his friend alone.
column8: Add figurative cling-on sense for recognition. Not all barnacles are literally 'permanently' fixed throughout every life stage.

column5: A highly contagious viral disease caused by varicella-zoster virus, typically producing an itchy blister-like rash and fever.
column7: She had chickenpox as a child. / Vaccination greatly reduces the risk of severe varicella.
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling is one word, chickenpox. Medical precision: caused by varicella-zoster virus; severity varies.

column5: A severe contagious disease caused by variola virus, historically associated with fever and a characteristic rash; eradicated worldwide through vaccination.
column7: Smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide in 1980.
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling is one word, smallpox. The disease is eradicated in natural transmission; use historical context carefully.

column5: Characterized by excessive anxiety, worry, insecurity, or obsessive concern; historically related to 'neurosis', a broad older psychiatric category.
column7: I'm getting neurotic about checking whether I locked the door.
column8: Modern everyday use is informal and can be judgmental; 'neurosis/neurotic disorder' has a complicated/dated psychiatric history. Avoid treating it as a precise diagnosis.

column5: At a right angle (90°) to a given line, plane, or surface; noun: a perpendicular line or direction.
column7: The two lines are perpendicular. / The pole is perpendicular to the ground.
column8: CORRECTION: 'vertical/upright' are not general synonyms. A line can be perpendicular to another line without being vertical.

column5: Used to introduce or emphasize an observation, concession, or opinion; 'I'll say!' can also independently express strong agreement.
column6: I have to say, I must admit; absolutely (I'll say!)
column7: I will say, the second episode was much better. / 'That was intense.' 'I'll say!'
column8: Distinguish sentence-initial 'I will say...' from standalone emphatic 'I'll say!' meaning strong agreement.
column12: entry::discourse_expression usage::rhetorical topic::rhetoric discovery::debate_language discovery::concession discovery::emphasis discovery::agreement discovery::subjective_judgment

column5: As written, not a standard fixed English expression. It may refer literally to a count associated with a particular night, but the intended meaning requires the original source/context.
column6: nightly count, count for tonight (if intended)
column7: If the intended meaning is a literal tally, 'tonight's count' or 'the count for this night' may be more natural depending on context.
column8: Do not teach as an established phrase. Preserve source wording until context identifies what is being counted.

column5: Taking something into account; given the circumstances. As a participle, also the act of thinking about or contemplating something.
column6: given, taking into account, in view of
column7: Considering the traffic, we made good time. / Considering that he had no experience, he did remarkably well. / I'm considering moving.
column8: Important grammar: preposition 'considering the weather'; conjunction 'considering that...'; verb 'I'm considering doing...'.

column5: To disturb the smooth arrangement of something; to unsettle or annoy someone; noun: a gathered/frilled strip of fabric or a disturbance.
column7: The wind ruffled her hair. / The criticism didn't ruffle him. / The blouse has ruffles at the collar.
column8: Major literal + figurative + clothing noun senses. Common idiom: ruffle someone's feathers = annoy/offend.

column5: Informal abbreviation for the University of Pennsylvania, a private Ivy League university in Philadelphia; the university commonly brands itself as Penn.
column7: She was accepted to Penn. / Online, people also write UPenn.
column8: Precision: 'Penn' is the institution's common self-name; 'UPenn' is widely understood but less central to official branding. Capitalization matters.

column5: To suppress, restrain, or prevent expression, action, development, or breathing; 'stifling' can also mean oppressively hot or restrictive.
column7: He stifled a laugh. / Excessive rules can stifle creativity. / The room felt stifling.
column8: Normalize to base verb. Productive: stifle a laugh/yawn/cry; stifle debate/innovation. Literal suffocation sense exists.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::grammar discovery::prevention discovery::containment discovery::debate_language

column5: To group or classify someone/something together with others, often too broadly or unfairly.
column7: Don't lump me in with the people who cheated. / The report lumps several very different cases together.
column8: Normalize productive pattern: lump X in with Y. Can be neutral categorization but often implies overgeneralization.

column5: Difficult to control, unpredictable, or deviating from what is expected, proper, or intended; also wandering from a course.
column7: The story follows a wayward teenager. / A wayward ball rolled into the street.
column8: Broader than behavior: wayward child, wayward ball, wayward strand of hair. Often implies straying from the expected path.

column5: To cut through completely or separate; figuratively, to end a relationship, connection, tie, or communication.
column6: cut off, detach, separate; break off
column7: The cable was severed in the accident. / The company severed ties with the supplier.
column8: Normalize to base verb. Very common figurative collocation: sever ties/relations/connections.
column12: entry::collocation entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative topic::relationships topic::communication topic::grammar discovery::figurative_extension

column5: The boundary or distance around a circle; by extension, the distance around a roughly circular object.
column7: The circle has a circumference of 20 centimeters. / Measure the tree's circumference at chest height.
column8: In geometry, circumference can mean the circle's boundary or its length. Perimeter is broader; girth is contextual.

column5: A localized area where subcutaneous fat is concentrated or visibly bulges; common descriptive/cosmetic wording rather than a precise fixed anatomical term.
column6: localized fat deposit, area of fat
column7: The article discussed a small fat pocket under the chin.
column8: Compositional/descriptive. Avoid implying a formal anatomical structure. Medical/cosmetic contexts may use more specific terminology depending on location.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::formal usage::specialist topic::communication topic::anatomy topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A purported or source-specific euphemistic slang expression for male masturbation; not a broadly standard modern English euphemism.
column7: The character used 'feed the geese' as a joking euphemism.
column8: CAUTION: highly source-dependent/nonstandard. Preserve for recognition but do not teach as a generally established slang phrase.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::humorous usage::informal discovery::evaluation

column5: The measurement around the middle or circumference of a body or object; also overall thickness/bulk. In equestrian use, a strap around a horse securing the saddle.
column7: Measure the tree's girth. / The horse's girth needed tightening.
column8: Broader than body size and not synonymous with width. Can sound sensitive/objectifying when used about a person's body.

column5: The area where the legs join the torso; the corresponding part of trousers or other clothing; also a forked junction in a tree/structure in some uses.
column7: His jeans tore at the crotch. / The ball hit him in the crotch.
column8: Groin is related but not perfectly identical. Crotch is common everyday wording and can refer to clothing.

column5: The fleshy muscular back part of the lower leg below the knee; plural calves. Also, calf means the young of cattle and certain other large mammals.
column7: My calves were sore after the hike. / The cow stayed close to her calf.
column8: Important polysemy and irregular plural: calf → calves.

column5: To work through correspondence that has accumulated—typically by reading, sorting, answering, and otherwise dealing with letters, emails, or messages one has fallen behind on.
column6: catch up on email, answer correspondence, deal with accumulated messages
column7: I need an hour tonight to catch up on my correspondence. / I spent Sunday morning catching up on emails and other correspondence.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'catch up on + something' means deal with work, reading, messages, sleep, news, etc. that has accumulated or that you have fallen behind on. 'Correspondence' means exchanged written communications such as letters and emails. So 'catch up on one's correspondence' naturally means work through the backlog: read it, organize it, reply where needed, and get up to date. The original 'catch my correspondence' is not natural for this meaning.

column5: The prerecorded greeting callers hear when they reach a person's or organization's voicemail.
column7: I finally changed my outgoing voicemail message. / Her voicemail greeting says she'll return calls tomorrow.
column8: Normalize to common wording. 'Outgoing message' can be abbreviated OGM in telecom contexts; 'voicemail greeting' is very natural everyday English.

column5: To betray someone, one's principles, or a group—often for personal advantage, safety, money, or approval. Also 'sell out' can mean sell all available stock/tickets.
column6: betray, sacrifice, inform on, throw under the bus (context-dependent)
column7: He sold me out to save himself. / Critics accused the band of selling out commercially.
column8: Add broader sell-out family distinction. 'Snitch on' is only one possible betrayal context.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::transportation discovery::persuasion discovery::betrayal discovery::social_approval

column2: fall out of the socket / come out of the socket
column5: To become detached or dislodged from the socket or receptacle in which something normally sits.
column6: come loose, pop out, become dislodged
column7: The bulb fell out of the socket. / His shoulder came out of its socket during the fall.
column8: Normalize to base/productive form. 'Socket' can be electrical/mechanical or anatomical; context determines meaning.

column5: A mildly insulting/playful term for a foolish or inept person; also a placeholder name for an object whose proper name is unknown or forgotten.
column7: You dingus, you left your phone in the car. / Hand me that little dingus next to the screwdriver.
column8: Two useful senses: person-insult and unnamed gadget/object. Usually comic/mild rather than vicious.

column5: To guide someone step by step through a process, procedure, explanation, or sequence of events.
column6: guide, explain step by step, take someone through
column7: Can you walk me through the setup process? / She walked us through what happened.
column8: Normalize full construction: walk someone through something. Very common in work/tech/instructional English.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::presentation-friendly topic::communication discovery::explanation discovery::process_details discovery::procedural_language discovery::presentation_language

column5: Completely naked; wearing no clothes at all.
column6: stark naked, completely naked, butt naked
column7: He came running out of the bathroom buck naked.
column8: Common AmE informal expression. 'Butt naked' is a later/parallel form (WID1789); both are used.

column5: To reach a point where total revenue/gains equal total costs/losses, so there is neither net profit nor net loss; more broadly, to end up neither ahead nor behind.
column7: We need to sell 500 tickets to break even. / After fees, I basically broke even.
column8: Useful noun/adjective: break-even point, break-even analysis. Not simply 'zero out'.

column5: To throw, send, or move something suddenly or forcefully; also to move oneself energetically. 'Flingin'' represents informal pronunciation of 'flinging'.
column7: He was flingin' clothes everywhere while packing. / She flung the door open.
column8: CORRECTION: 'fling' is not an informal variant of 'flinging'; it is the base verb. Flingin' is eye-dialect/informal spelling. Past: flung.

column5: Hyperbolically, to be regarded as hopeless, incurable, irredeemable, or beyond help in some respect; exact slang force depends on community/context.
column6: hopeless, beyond help, a lost cause
column7: He's terminal when it comes to fixing anything—he somehow makes it worse.
column8: CAUTION: terminal primarily has serious medical and other standard meanings ('terminal illness', endpoint, computer terminal). Slang person-label use is contextual and can sound harsh.

column5: A foolish, silly, awkward, or inept person; shortened/variant form related to 'doofus'.
column7: You doof—you locked the keys in the car again.
column8: Usually mild/comic insult. Familiarity varies by speaker/region.

column5: To continue an action or commitment to completion; in sports, to complete the natural motion after striking/throwing. Noun: follow-through.
column7: You promised to call, so follow through. / She followed through on the plan. / His golf follow-through is smooth.
column8: Major sports + commitment senses. Hyphenate noun: follow-through.

column5: Praise, approval, or formal recognition, especially an official award/citation for meritorious conduct or service.
column7: She received a commendation for bravery.
column8: An award can be a commendation, but commendation can also mean the act/expression of praising. Formal register.

column5: To praise or express approval of someone/something; to recommend as worthy; in formal/older use, to entrust something to someone's care.
column7: I commend you for staying calm. / The report commends the program to other schools.
column8: Common patterns: commend someone for something; commend something to someone. 'Endorse' overlaps only some senses.

column5: A stupid or foolish person.
column7: Only a dimwit would send a password in a public post.
column8: Direct insult; stronger and less playful than some words such as dingus/doof.

column5: A person who reacts cheerfully and graciously to losing, teasing, inconvenience, embarrassment, or participation in something awkward.
column7: Thanks for being such a good sport about the prank.
column8: Broader than accepting defeat in a game. Often used after someone tolerates teasing, inconvenience, or being volunteered for something.

column5: Circles that have the same center but different radii; figuratively, layers/groups arranged around a common center.
column7: The target is made of concentric circles. / Information spread through concentric circles of advisers.
column8: Precise geometry term; 'nested circles' is descriptive but does not always guarantee a common center.

column2: the lake where the curse lifted / lift a curse / a curse is lifted
column5: The full phrase is source-specific, but it contains the productive English collocation 'lift a curse' / 'a curse is lifted': to remove or end a curse, spell, persistent run of bad luck, or figuratively a long-standing burden/misfortune.
column6: break a curse, remove a curse, end a curse; break the spell
column7: In the story, they returned to the lake where the curse lifted. / The hero finally lifted the curse. / After decades without a championship, fans joked that the curse had finally been lifted.
column8: IMPORTANT COLLOCATION: 'lift' combines naturally with 'curse' in the sense 'remove/end it.' Active: 'lift a curse'; passive/inchoative-style result: 'the curse was/is/has been lifted.' Literal fantasy/folklore: a magical spell or hex is broken. Figurative everyday use: a long losing streak, persistent bad luck, or a heavy long-standing problem finally ends. The source phrase 'the lake where the curse lifted' should not be generalized into a fixed idiom meaning 'place of healing'; its learning value is the source reference PLUS the productive curse/lift collocation.
column12: entry::idiom entry::collocation usage::figurative topic::nature discovery::figurative_extension discovery::removal

column5: To be unable to get away from, replace, return, or avoid someone/something, often when the situation is unwanted; sometimes neutral/fond in joking contexts.
column6: be saddled with, be left with, have no choice but to keep
column7: I got stuck with the middle seat. / You're stuck with me now.
column8: Broaden beyond people. Also 'stuck with a bill/problem/task'. Distinguish 'stick with someone' = remain loyal/continue.

column5: 1. In cooking, to moisten food repeatedly with fat, juices, or liquid while it cooks. 2. In sewing, to stitch loosely and temporarily to hold fabric in place.
column7: Baste the turkey with its juices. / She basted the seam before sewing it permanently.
column8: Important sewing sense missing. 'Glaze' is not a general synonym for culinary basting.

column5: To gather closely together, especially for a quick private discussion, team planning, warmth, or mutual support.
column7: Huddle up, everyone—we need a plan for the final play.
column8: Common sports/team imperative. 'Huddle' alone is often sufficient; 'up' adds conversational/team flavor.

column5: In American football, to run a deep route downfield for a long pass. Figuratively, it can sometimes suggest taking a longer-term or ambitious approach, depending on context.
column7: Go long—I'll try to hit you near the end zone. / The investment strategy is designed to go long on growth.
column8: CAUTION: the figurative meaning is not simply 'take a big risk'. In finance, 'go long' has a specific meaning: take a position that benefits if an asset rises.
column12: entry::phrase usage::informal usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::sports discovery::figurative_extension discovery::suggestion discovery::debate_language

column2: pull something like this / pull stuff like this
column5: To do, attempt, or perpetrate a particular kind of trick, stunt, troublesome act, or surprising behavior.
column6: do something like this, pull a stunt, try something
column7: Why do you always pull stuff like this at the last minute?
column8: Productive 'pull + stunt/trick/move/something like this'. Usually expresses disapproval or surprise.

column5: Dishonest, secretive, or unfair in method; designed to gain an advantage without being open about it.
column7: That was an underhanded way to win the contract.
column8: AmE spelling underhanded; BrE often underhand. 'Underhand' also has a literal throwing/action sense.

column5: To break suddenly; make a sharp sound/movement; speak sharply; suddenly lose emotional control; take a quick photograph; fasten with a snap; noun/adjective uses are numerous.
column6: break, crack; lose it; retort; photograph (informal)
column7: The branch snapped. / He finally snapped under the pressure. / She snapped at me. / I snapped a photo.
column8: Highly polysemous. Important patterns: snap at someone, snap out of it, snap a picture, snap shut, snap decision.

column2: get mono / come down with mono
column5: To contract infectious mononucleosis ('mono'), commonly caused by Epstein–Barr virus and often involving fatigue, fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes.
column7: He missed school after coming down with mono.
column8: Medical precision: mono is not defined only by saliva transmission; EBV spreads mainly through bodily fluids, especially saliva. 'Get mono' is casual wording.

column5: Enlarged or tender lymph nodes, often noticed in the neck, armpits, or groin during infection or inflammation.
column6: swollen lymph nodes, enlarged lymph nodes
column7: I had a sore throat and swollen glands in my neck.
column8: In everyday speech, 'swollen glands' usually refers to lymph nodes, not glands in the strict anatomical sense.

column5: A clear-to-pale fluid in the lymphatic system containing immune cells and substances collected from tissues; it returns fluid to the bloodstream and participates in immune function.
column7: Lymph flows through lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes.
column8: CORRECTION: avoid simplistic 'removes waste and toxins' wording. The lymphatic system maintains fluid balance, transports certain fats, and supports immune function.

column5: In North American construction, a common dimensional-lumber size whose nominal dimensions are 2 by 4 inches; finished actual dimensions are typically smaller (commonly about 1.5 by 3.5 inches). Figuratively, something blunt/heavy may be compared to a two-by-four.
column6: piece of dimensional lumber, stud (specific use)
column7: We framed the wall with two-by-fours. / It felt like I'd been hit with a two-by-four.
column8: Important precision: 2×4 is a nominal size, not normally an actual finished 2 in × 4 in board.

column5: To get directly to the main point or important part without unnecessary preliminaries or detail.
column6: get to the point, skip the preliminaries, get down to business
column7: Let's cut to the chase: how much will it cost?
column8: Informal but common. Often used to redirect a long explanation.

column5: Cheerful enjoyment, laughter, festivity, and lively good spirits.
column7: The room was filled with music and merriment.
column8: Somewhat literary/formal compared with 'fun'. Often associated with celebrations.

column5: Great amusement and loud laughter; also, sometimes, a situation or reaction characterized by such laughter.
column7: His impression caused general hilarity.
column8: Stronger than ordinary amusement. Often in phrase 'much hilarity ensued'.

column5: Unable or unwilling to believe something because it seems surprising, improbable, or absurd.
column7: She gave me an incredulous look. / 'You paid how much?' he asked, incredulous.
column8: CORRECTION: 'suspicious' is not a core synonym. Incredulous describes disbelief, not distrust of motives.

column5: To inhale suddenly and audibly because of surprise, shock, pain, fear, exertion, or lack of breath; noun: such an intake of breath.
column7: She gasped in surprise. / He came up from the water gasping for air.
column8: 'Gulp' and 'wheeze' are not general synonyms. Useful: gasp at, gasp in surprise, gasp for breath, last gasp.

column5: Initialism for 'Am I the Asshole?', used for posts or discussions asking whether the poster behaved wrongly in an interpersonal conflict; strongly associated with a well-known Reddit community and copied formats elsewhere.
column6: Am I the Asshole?, AITAH (related variant)
column7: She posted an AITA-style story asking whether she was in the wrong.
column8: Internet/community-specific and contains profanity. 'AITA' can refer to the question format as well as the subreddit/community context.
column12: entry::initialism entry::internet_term entry::slang_expression usage::informal usage::internet_slang usage::profane usage::slang topic::internet topic::social_media topic::communication topic::relationships discovery::self-assessment discovery::disagreement discovery::social_approval discovery::evaluation

column5: adjective: relating to an artificial replacement for a missing body part. noun: an artificial body part or device used to replace a missing body part or function.
column7: He uses a prosthetic leg. / The clinic specializes in prosthetics.
column8: Precision: prosthetic is broader than artificial limb. Formal noun for an individual device is also 'prosthesis'; plural 'prostheses'.

column5: An orthotic/orthosis is an externally applied device used to support, align, protect, or improve function of a body part; common examples include foot orthotics, braces, and splints.
column6: orthosis, brace, support, shoe insert (specific type)
column7: The podiatrist prescribed custom foot orthotics. / She wears an ankle-foot orthosis.
column8: Precision: an orthotic is not only a shoe insert. 'Orthosis' is the formal device noun; usage varies.

column5: Very bad, poor, unpleasant, or disappointing; feeling unwell; literally, infested with lice (older/literal sense).
column7: The service was lousy. / I feel lousy today.
column8: Important 'feel lousy' = feel sick/bad. Literal lice sense explains the word historically but is uncommon in everyday use.

column5: To record/register someone for an item, amount, choice, contribution, reservation, or commitment.
column6: sign up, register, mark down, reserve
column7: Put me down for two tickets. / You can put me down for $20 toward the gift.
column8: Normalize from 'put me' to productive pattern. Can involve quantities/contributions, not only events.

column5: To interrupt someone; stop supplying money/service/access; end contact; block a vehicle's path; isolate; or stop serving alcohol, among other senses.
column6: interrupt; disconnect; stop supporting; block; sever contact
column7: Sorry to cut you off, but we're out of time. / They cut off his internet. / That driver cut me off.
column8: Major polysemy. 'Disown' is only one extreme context and not a general synonym.

column5: A name used for laser-light shows synchronized to music by Pink Floyd, especially planetarium-style presentations; the exact producer/program varies by venue and era.
column7: We went to a Laser Floyd show at the planetarium.
column8: Source/cultural reference rather than a generic vocabulary term. Do not assume one single official production called 'Pink Floyd Laser Spectacular'; venue/program names vary.

column5: To release or allow out; emit a sound/breath; make clothing larger; disclose a secret; or, of school/events/venues, finish and release the people inside.
column7: School lets out at three. / The movie let out around 9:30. / She let out a sigh. / The tailor let the waist out.
column8: Major polysemy. For an event/movie, 'let out' is especially AmE and means end/discharge the audience.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb usage::american_english topic::education topic::fashion discovery::impression discovery::release

column2: Laser Floyd was letting out of the planetarium
column3: /ˈleɪzɚ flɔɪd wəz ˈlɛtɪŋ aʊt əv ðə ˌplænəˈtɛriəm/
column5: A contextual sentence meaning that a Laser Floyd show was ending and its audience was coming out of the planetarium.
column6: the show was letting out; the crowd was coming out
column7: Laser Floyd was letting out of the planetarium just as we arrived.
column8: Do not treat as a standalone idiom. It illustrates AmE 'a movie/show lets out' = ends, combined with a specific cultural reference. More natural alternatives may focus on the show or crowd depending context.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::american_english topic::public_speaking topic::construction discovery::audience_engagement

column5: A strong desire to eat snack food; especially, the increased appetite commonly associated with cannabis intoxication, but also used more generally.
column7: I've got the munchies—want some chips? / Cannabis can give some people the munchies.
column8: Usually 'the munchies' or 'have/get the munchies'. Cannabis association is strong but not mandatory.

column2: not have a lead / have no leads
column5: To have no useful clue, information, contact, prospect, or line of inquiry to pursue. In sales, a lead is a potential customer/opportunity; in investigations, a lead is information worth following.
column6: have no clue, have no leads, have no prospect/contact
column7: Police said they had no leads. / I don't have any sales leads yet.
column8: Broaden and normalize. 'I don't have a lead' is grammatical, but plural 'no leads' is especially common in investigative contexts.

column5: An uncommon slang term that can refer to dirt/grime, something unpleasant or worthless, or a contemptible person; exact sense varies by speaker/source.
column7: Get that scrud off the floor. / In the source, he uses 'scrud' as an insult.
column8: CORRECTION/CAUTION: broader and less stable than a fixed insult meaning. Uncommon; source/context should determine sense.

column2: bat for someone / go to bat for someone
column5: To support, defend, advocate for, or intervene on behalf of someone; 'go to bat for' is the especially common fixed expression.
column6: go to bat for, stand up for, advocate for, defend
column7: My manager went to bat for me when the promotion was discussed.
column8: NORMALIZE: 'go to bat for someone' is the standard idiom. 'Bat for someone' can occur but is less self-contained and may be literal/contextual.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::persuasive discovery::advocacy discovery::support discovery::persuasion

column2: loan something to someone / lend someone something
column5: To give someone temporary use of money or property with the expectation that it will be returned or repaid.
column7: I loaned my calculator to Sam. / I lent Sam my calculator.
column8: Usage: 'loan' as a verb is standard, especially AmE; 'lend' is standard across varieties. Loan commonly takes 'loan X to Y'; lend allows 'lend Y X' or 'lend X to Y'.

column5: A U.S. Navy nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, the lead ship of the Nimitz class, commissioned in 1975 and named for Fleet Admiral Chester W. Nimitz.
column7: The USS Nimitz served for decades as a U.S. Navy aircraft carrier.
column8: Proper-name knowledge card. Avoid vague 'known for major global missions' filler; the key lexical recognition is ship name/class and aircraft-carrier context.

column5: To become or make someone more cheerful, lively, alert, interested, or energetic; also for ears/features to rise or become more attentive.
column7: She perked up when dessert arrived. / The dog's ears perked up at the sound.
column8: Can be intransitive or transitive: perk up / perk someone up. Compare noun 'perk' WID1529.

column5: Used to give someone permission or invite them to do something; depending on tone, it can be warmly welcoming or dismissively mean 'go ahead if you insist'.
column6: go ahead, feel free, help yourself
column7: 'Can I use your charger?' 'Be my guest.' / If you want to argue with him, be my guest.
column8: Tone matters: polite permission vs ironic/dismissive challenge.

column5: A woman who sews, especially professionally; depending on work, 'sewer', 'dressmaker', 'tailor', or 'sewist' may be more specific or gender-neutral.
column7: The seamstress altered the dress for the ceremony.
column8: Gendered traditional term. Tailor is not an exact synonym: tailoring often implies skilled construction/alteration of fitted garments and is not gender-specific.

column5: So astonished, shocked, or confused that one is temporarily unable to react or speak.
column7: I was dumbfounded when they offered me the job.
column8: Strong surprise word; can be positive or negative.

column5: To waste time, behave playfully/sillily, or not act seriously; also, depending on context, to engage in romantic/sexual activity, especially casually or outside a committed relationship.
column6: mess around, horse around; hook up (sexual context, not exact)
column7: Stop fooling around and finish your homework. / He admitted he'd been fooling around with someone else.
column8: Major context-dependent sexual sense. 'Fool around with' can also mean experiment/tinker with something, so context matters.

column2: stick one's tongue down someone's throat
column5: A crude or exaggerated description of deep, forceful, or conspicuously passionate kissing.
column7: They weren't just kissing—he practically stuck his tongue down her throat.
column8: CORRECTION: pronouns must refer to two people: one's tongue down someone else's throat, not one's own throat. Often disapproving/humorous and intentionally graphic.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction usage::slang usage::humorous usage::critical usage::vulgar usage::informal

column5: To annoy or anger someone. Separately, 'tick something off' can mean mark an item on a list or reprimand someone in chiefly BrE usage.
column7: That really ticks me off. / Tick each item off as you finish it.
column8: Add distinct checklist sense. This overlaps WID1371 'ticked off' family.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::vulgar usage::british_english

column5: Light-headed or dizzy; or so excited, delighted, nervous, or exhilarated that one feels silly/unsteady.
column7: I felt giddy when I stood up too fast. / She was giddy with excitement.
column8: Two core senses: physical dizziness and excited silliness. Common: giddy with excitement.

column5: To walk/move unsteadily; shock or astonish; arrange events/payments/working times at different intervals; noun: an unsteady movement.
column6: reel, stumble; astonish; space out, phase
column7: He staggered to the door. / The cost staggered me. / We staggered lunch breaks to keep the desk staffed.
column8: Major missing transitive 'astonish' and scheduling sense. Related adjective: staggering = astonishingly large.

column5: A device consisting of a pole with footrests and a spring or other mechanism, used to bounce/jump while standing upright.
column7: The kid bounced down the driveway on a pogo stick.
column8: Straightforward object card. 'Bouncing stick' is descriptive, not a standard synonym.

column5: A branded series of study guides providing summaries, analysis, and explanatory material for literature and other subjects; figuratively, 'the CliffsNotes version' means a very condensed overview.
column7: Give me the CliffsNotes version—I only have five minutes.
column8: Important trademark/brand capitalization. Do not define it merely as summaries; guides also contain analysis and study material. Figurative genericized use is common.
column12: entry::proper_noun usage::figurative topic::literature discovery::summary discovery::figurative_extension discovery::iteration

column5: A shortened version of a book, speech, recording, or other work that omits material while preserving the main content; also the act of shortening, and in formal contexts a reduction/curtailment of a right.
column7: This audiobook is an abridgment of the novel. / The law was challenged as an abridgment of free speech.
column8: Both spellings occur; abridgment is common in AmE, abridgement common in BrE. Add important formal 'abridgment of rights' sense.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::formal usage::american_english usage::british_english topic::work topic::public_speaking discovery::iteration

column5: An 1859 novel by Charles Dickens set mainly in London and Paris before and during the French Revolution, centering on characters including Charles Darnay, Sydney Carton, and Lucie Manette.
column7: We read A Tale of Two Cities in high school.
column8: Keep as literary-reference recognition card. Avoid turning interpretive themes into the lexical definition; themes can be noted separately if source study requires them.

column5: A trusted person with whom one shares private thoughts, feelings, or secrets. 'Confidante' traditionally refers to a woman; 'confidant' is traditionally masculine but is now often used gender-neutrally.
column7: She became my closest confidante. / He was the president's longtime confidant.
column8: Useful gender/form distinction. Pronunciation/spelling can be confused with 'confident' (adjective).

column5: To count aloud in a steady sequence or rhythm, especially to cue the start/tempo of music, exercise, marching, or coordinated action; 'count off' can also assign people numbers.
column6: count in, cue, call the count
column7: The drummer counted the song off: 'One, two, three, four!' / The coach had us count off by twos.
column8: Broaden beyond a countdown: musical count-offs often count upward to establish tempo.

column5: Completely naked; wearing no clothes.
column6: buck naked, stark naked, completely naked
column7: He ran through the sprinklers butt naked.
column8: Common informal variant alongside buck naked (WID1729). 'Butt-naked' is also written with a hyphen in some styles.

column5: To form, compose, or make up a whole; to amount to or be regarded as; formally, to establish/create something.
column6: make up, form, compose; amount to; establish
column7: Women constitute a majority of the staff. / That could constitute a breach of contract. / The committee was formally constituted in May.
column8: CORRECTION: normalize to base verb and replace unnatural progressive example 'are constituting the foundation'. Stative/classificatory uses often prefer simple tense.

column5: Noun: a limit, deadline, threshold, stopping point, or route shortcut; adjective: isolated or truncated. Verb 'cut off' is separate and has many senses.
column7: The application cutoff is Friday. / The cutoff score was 80. / The village was cut off by snow.
column8: Spelling depends on function/style: verb two words 'cut off'; noun/adjective commonly 'cutoff' in AmE, 'cut-off' also common. Also 'cutoffs' = shorts made by cutting trousers.

column5: Delicately small, pretty, graceful, or refined; also small/light in movement or appetite. Can carry stereotypically feminine or faintly critical connotations.
column7: She wore a dainty gold necklace. / He took dainty little bites.
column8: Not simply fragile. Tone can be admiring or patronizing depending context.

column5: Used to express strong agreement, certainty, willingness, or a friendly response to thanks; roughly 'certainly', 'absolutely', or 'you're welcome' depending context.
column6: absolutely, certainly, of course, you're welcome
column7: 'Can you help me?' 'You bet.' / 'Thanks!' 'You bet!'
column8: Important pragmatic range: affirmative answer and response to thanks. Related 'you betcha' is more folksy/regional.

column5: Noun: a broad, usually flat-bottomed vessel used especially for carrying freight, often towed or pushed. Verb: to move or enter abruptly, heavily, or rudely; commonly 'barge in/into'.
column6: cargo vessel; burst in, push in, intrude
column7: Coal was carried by barge. / He barged into the room without knocking.
column8: Productive phrasal uses: barge in, barge into. A barge may be self-propelled or moved by tug depending type.

column5: To leave or run away quickly, especially to avoid trouble or because one is being hurried along.
column6: scram, bolt, flee, make oneself scarce
column7: We'd better skedaddle before the storm hits.
column8: Often humorous/folksy rather than genuinely urgent. Also used as an imperative: 'Skedaddle!'
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::dated usage::humorous usage::playful discovery::prevention

column5: An enthusiastic response meaning that a new suggestion, improvement, amount, or development is much more appealing or satisfactory.
column6: that's more like it, now that's better, yes!
column7: 'How about pizza and beer?' 'Now we're talking!' / A 30% discount? Now we're talking.
column8: Not merely agreement; often signals a noticeable improvement over what was previously proposed.

column5: As a figurative phrase meaning 'stuck, slow, or delayed', this is not a standard general English idiom. Any such meaning depends on the original source/context.
column7: If the source says 'it's on the barge', determine whether a literal shipment/barge or an in-group metaphor is intended.
column8: CORRECTION: do not teach 'on the barge' as an established metaphor for 'in limbo/not progressing'. Preserve source wording pending context.

column2: hair of the dog / have a hair of the dog
column5: An alcoholic drink taken to relieve a hangover, from the longer phrase 'the hair of the dog that bit you'.
column7: He swore by a little hair of the dog the morning after a party.
column8: NORMALIZE: the established expression is 'hair of the dog' / 'a hair of the dog', not usually 'take a hair of the dog' as the headword. It is folk practice, not a medically recommended hangover treatment.

column5: Especially in 'think/be all that': to be or consider oneself especially impressive, attractive, important, or desirable; often used skeptically or sarcastically.
column6: impressive, special, hot stuff; think highly of oneself
column7: He walks around like he's all that. / She thinks she's all that just because she got promoted.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'be all that' and especially 'think you're all that' are the productive patterns. Often followed by dismissive contrast: 'He's not all that.' Do not reduce it to merely 'flashy'.

column3: /maɪ ˈnɪpəlz kʊd kʌt ɡlæs ˈoʊvɚ hɪr/
column5: A crude comic exaggeration meaning one's nipples are very hard/erect, usually because it is extremely cold; context can also be sexual.
column6: I'm freezing, it's freezing in here
column7: Turn up the heat—my nipples could cut glass in here.
column8: The image is hyperbolic: cold can make nipples become erect/hard. 'Over here' is optional source wording, not part of a fixed idiom. Vulgar/body-based humor; recognition-focused.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::idiom usage::slang usage::humorous usage::vulgar usage::informal

column5: A violation or breach of a rule, regulation, law, or code, typically a relatively minor one.
column7: The player received a penalty for a rules infraction. / Repeated traffic infractions can lead to higher insurance costs.
column8: Common collocations: traffic infraction, minor infraction, rules infraction. Often less serious than 'crime' or major 'offense'.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word topic::technology topic::law topic::government topic::politics discovery::policy_discussion discovery::public_discourse

column2: 'Cause mine get me out of tickets. — Phoebe, Friends
column3: /kəz maɪn ɡɛt mi aʊt əv ˈtɪkɪts/
column5: A source-specific joke whose meaning depends on the omitted noun: Phoebe says that hers—contextually her breasts—help her avoid receiving tickets by charming or distracting the person issuing them.
column6: talk one's way out of a ticket, get out of a ticket
column7: 'Cause mine get me out of tickets.' / She joked that flirting had gotten her out of a parking ticket before.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'get someone out of + trouble/a ticket/a fine/an obligation' = enable that person to avoid or escape it. The humor also depends on 'mine' replacing a previously mentioned plural noun. Preserve as a source quote rather than a general idiom.

column5: A strong metal bar, often with a curved or forked end, used as a lever for prying, lifting, or forcing things apart/open.
column7: He used a crowbar to pry the boards apart. / Someone had tried to force the door with a crowbar.
column8: 'Jimmy' is a verb and not a synonym for the tool itself. Productive verbs: use a crowbar to pry/force something open.

column2: jimmy something open / jimmy a lock
column5: To force or manipulate a door, window, lock, etc. open, usually with a small tool or by prying; often associated with unauthorized entry.
column7: Someone had jimmied the window open. / The thief tried to jimmy the lock.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'jimmy + object (+ open)'—jimmy a lock/door/window; jimmy something open. It is a transitive verb, not a phrasal verb. Historically related to 'jemmy', a small crowbar.

column5: Something regarded with intense disgust, hatred, or moral/religious condemnation; also the state/act of being abhorrent in older/formal use.
column7: They called the practice an abomination. / The novel describes the experiments as abominations against nature.
column8: Strong word. Common frames: 'an abomination to/against...' and 'consider/regard X an abomination'. 'Atrocity' specifically suggests extreme cruelty and is not always interchangeable.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal usage::religious topic::religion discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: A person, team, organization, product, etc. that defeats or outperforms a much stronger, larger, or more established rival.
column7: The lower-division club earned a reputation as a giant-killer after beating two top teams.
column8: Sports is a classic context, but business/competition uses occur. A giant-killer is not simply an underdog; it is an underdog/smaller rival that actually defeats 'giants'.

column5: To make noticeable progress, especially on something difficult, slow, or resistant.
column7: We're finally making headway on the project. / Investigators made little headway at first.
column8: KEY COLLOCATION: 'make headway on/with/in something'; common modifiers: make good/some/little/no headway. Normalize from progressive to base construction.

column5: An exclamation used to attract attention or express surprise, protest, approval, or emphasis; now often sounds old-fashioned, theatrical, or stereotypically British.
column7: I say! That's rather impressive. / I say, could you keep the noise down?
column8: Do not confuse with ordinary reporting 'I say that...'. As an interjection, intonation and period style matter; recognition value is higher than modern AmE production.
column12: entry::interjection entry::discourse_expression usage::dated usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::emphasis discovery::social_approval

column5: noun: a committed supporter of a party, cause, or side. adjective: strongly supporting one side, often implying political bias or lack of neutrality.
column7: The proposal drew partisan opposition. / He was a loyal partisan of the movement.
column8: Two POS. 'Partisan' need not mean irrationally biased, but adjective use often contrasts with bipartisan/nonpartisan. Also historical 'partisan' = guerrilla/resistance fighter in some contexts.

column5: Used to say that a son resembles his father in behavior, character, habits, talents, or other traits.
column6: a chip off the old block, takes after his father
column7: He's just as stubborn as his dad—like father, like son.
column8: FORMULA: 'like X, like Y' can be creatively extended ('like mother, like daughter'). Can be affectionate, neutral, or critical depending on the trait.

column2: have had it up to here (with someone/something)
column5: To have reached the limit of one's patience or tolerance; to be extremely fed up.
column6: have had enough, be fed up, be at the end of one's rope
column7: I've had it up to here with these excuses. / She's had it up to here with the constant delays.
column8: KEY FRAME: 'I've had it up to here with + noun/gerund'. Often accompanied by a hand gesture indicating a high level on the body. Normalize from past-only 'had it'.

column5: By doing the action just mentioned; as a result or in the course of doing that.
column6: thereby, in doing so, by doing that
column7: He apologized and, in so doing, repaired some of the damage.
column8: COLLOCATION/FORM: 'in so doing' is formal; everyday English more often uses 'in doing so'. It refers back anaphorically to the preceding action.

column5: A blunt ultimatum meaning that others must accept the speaker's preferred method, decision, or authority or leave/refuse participation.
column6: take it or leave it, no compromise
column7: His management style is basically my way or the highway.
column8: Fixed contrast: 'my way' versus 'the highway' (= leave). Usually critical of authoritarian/inflexible behavior.

column5: A ruler with unchecked or highly concentrated personal power; figuratively, an overbearing person who insists on controlling decisions.
column7: The country was ruled by an autocrat. / At home he behaved like a petty autocrat.
column8: Political meaning is primary. 'Dictator' overlaps but has its own historical/legal uses. Related: autocratic.

column5: An academic distinction meaning 'with great praise/honor', used by some institutions for graduates meeting a high level of achievement.
column7: She graduated magna cum laude.
column8: Institutional criteria vary widely, so do not attach a universal GPA threshold. Related honors: cum laude, summa cum laude.

column5: Except for; if it were not for / if it had not been for. Used to identify a condition without which the result would be different.
column6: if not for, were it not for, except for
column7: But for your help, I would have missed the deadline. / But for the rain, we would have gone out.
column8: KEY FRAME: 'but for + noun phrase, result clause'. Formal/literary. In law, 'but-for causation' asks whether an outcome would have occurred without the alleged cause.

column5: Elementary school or the elementary grades; exact grade span varies by school system and speaker.
column7: I haven't seen him since grade school.
column8: Do not hard-code K–5/6 as universal. In North America the term generally refers to early compulsory schooling before secondary school.

column5: Especially sensitive to sexual stimulation or capable of producing sexual arousal when stimulated.
column7: The neck can be an erogenous area for some people.
column8: Most commonly occurs in the collocation 'erogenous zone'. Individual sensitivity varies; not every person's body responds the same way.

column5: An area of the body whose stimulation may produce sexual arousal or pleasure.
column7: The neck is an erogenous zone for many people, though sensitivity varies.
column8: KEY COLLOCATION: 'erogenous + zone' is the standard phrase. Zones can be primary or secondary depending on framework; avoid presenting any body area as universally responsive.

column5: A state of increased physiological or psychological activation, alertness, or responsiveness; in sexual contexts, sexual excitement and associated bodily responses.
column7: Stress can increase physiological arousal. / Sexual arousal varies greatly between people and situations.
column8: Important broader psychology/physiology sense: arousal is not inherently sexual. Collocations: emotional/physiological/sexual arousal, level of arousal.

column2: know squat about something / not know squat
column5: To know nothing or almost nothing about a subject. 'Squat' here means 'nothing' in informal negative constructions.
column6: know nothing, know zilch, not know a thing
column7: He doesn't know squat about fixing cars. / I know squat about tax law.
column8: NORMALIZE: not 'squat about something' alone. Productive frame: 'don't/doesn't know squat about + topic'. Informal and mildly crude.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::idiom entry::construction usage::informal usage::slang usage::vulgar

column5: A strong urge or felt need to perform an action, sometimes repetitive and difficult to resist; in OCD, compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to obsessions or rigid rules.
column7: She felt a compulsion to check the lock again. / In OCD, compulsions can be behavioral or mental.
column8: PRECISION: compulsion is broader than OCD, and OCD compulsions are not simply 'irrational habits'. Distinguish obsession = intrusive thought/urge/image from compulsion = behavior/mental act.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::ceremonial topic::communication discovery::urge discovery::expressing_need

column2: cough something up / cough it up
column5: To hand over, pay, reveal, or produce something, often reluctantly; literally, to expel something by coughing.
column6: hand over, fork over, pay up; reveal
column7: Come on, cough up the money. / He finally coughed up the name. / She coughed up a piece of food.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'cough up + money/information/name' or 'cough it up'. Figurative sense suggests reluctant production; literal bodily sense remains productive.

column5: Temporarily used or improvised as a substitute because the proper thing is unavailable; noun: a temporary substitute.
column7: They built a makeshift shelter from tarps. / A stack of books served as a makeshift stand.
column8: Common collocations: makeshift bed/shelter/desk/bandage. 'Makeshift' emphasizes improvised substitution, not merely temporary duration.

column2: Where am I giving birth—in a hospital or a big box under the stairs?
column3: /wɛr æm aɪ ˈɡɪvɪŋ bɜrθ ɪn ə ˈhɑspɪtəl ɔr ə bɪɡ bɑks ˈʌndɚ ðə stɛrz/
column5: A source-specific sarcastic comparison contrasting an appropriate place for childbirth with an absurdly inadequate one, used to complain about poor arrangements or treatment.
column6: what kind of conditions are these?, this is ridiculous
column7: Where am I giving birth—in a hospital or a big box under the stairs?
column8: Do not generalize this exact wording into a standard idiom. Learning value comes from the rhetorical pattern 'Where am I doing X—in A or absurd B?' and the comic contrast. Preserve the source quote.
column12: entry::idiom entry::rhetorical_question_pattern usage::rhetorical topic::health topic::rhetoric topic::medicine discovery::insufficient_quality discovery::comparison discovery::complaint discovery::debate_language

column5: Used mainly in emphatic expressions such as 'scare/beat/annoy the bejesus out of someone', where it intensifies the action; also appears as an exclamation.
column7: That noise scared the bejesus out of me. / They beat the bejesus out of the old machine.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION is not standalone 'bejesus' so much as 'the bejesus out of someone'. Historically a euphemistic alteration associated with 'by Jesus'; informal and comic.

column2: the score is X–Y in favor of someone / in someone's favor
column5: Used to state that a team/person is leading by a particular score; more generally, 'in someone's favor' means to that person's advantage.
column7: The score is 3–1 in favor of the home team. / The ruling went in her favor.
column8: Natural sports order is often 'The score is 3–1 to the home team' (BrE) or 'The home team leads 3–1' (AmE). Teach broader collocation 'in someone's favor'.

column2: rile someone up / get riled up
column5: To make someone angry, agitated, excited, or emotionally stirred; 'get/be riled up' describes that state.
column6: agitate, provoke, stir up, get worked up
column7: Don't rile him up before the meeting. / She got riled up about the decision.
column8: KEY FORMS: 'rile someone up'; 'get/be riled up about/over something'. Usually anger/agitation, though excited stirring is possible.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::adjective_phrase entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::informal discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: An informal claim to have or use something before others, usually established by saying 'dibs' or 'I call dibs'.
column7: I call dibs on the front seat. / Dibs on the last slice!
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'call dibs on + thing' or simply 'Dibs on X!' Normally treated as plural-form 'dibs', not singular 'a dib'.

column5: To claim the front passenger seat of a vehicle before others, traditionally by saying 'shotgun!'
column6: call the front seat, claim shotgun
column7: I call shotgun! / She called shotgun before we even reached the car.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'call shotgun' or shout 'Shotgun!' It is a specific cultural seat-claiming convention, closely related to 'call dibs'.

column5: 1. An affectionate/childlike word for a doll. 2. A wheeled platform or cart for moving loads. 3. In film/TV, a wheeled camera platform; related verb 'dolly' for camera movement.
column7: The child lined up her dollies. / We moved the cabinet on a dolly. / The camera dollied toward the actor.
column8: Important polysemy. A hand truck and flat furniture dolly are different types; in cinematography, 'dolly shot' and 'dolly in/out' are productive.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::form_family entry::word usage::affectionate topic::film topic::television topic::entertainment

column5: To develop, turn out, or succeed in a particular way, especially after uncertainty; often used negatively or with 'if'.
column7: Let's see how the plan pans out. / The job offer didn't pan out.
