column8: KEY FRAME: 'pan out well/badly' or simply 'it didn't pan out'. Origin relates to panning for gold, where material either yields something valuable or not.

column5: To hit someone hard, especially in the face/head. In other slang, 'clock' can also mean notice/recognize something or measure a speed/time.
column6: hit, punch, deck; notice (other slang sense)
column7: He threatened to clock the guy. / I clocked the new tattoo immediately.
column8: Add modern recognition sense 'clock = notice/identify', common in some communities. Context separates it from punch and time-measurement senses.

column5: A person regarded as weak, cowardly, timid, or unable to tolerate discomfort; 'wuss out' = withdraw because of fear/reluctance.
column7: Don't be a wuss—just ask. / I almost went, but I wussed out at the last minute.
column8: Productive family: wuss, wussy, wuss out. Insulting and tied to toughness norms; use cautiously.

column5: A nonalcoholic version of a cocktail or mixed drink that normally contains alcohol.
column7: I'll have a virgin mojito, please.
column8: KEY PATTERN: 'virgin + cocktail name' = prepared without alcohol (virgin margarita/mojito). 'Mocktail' is a broader modern term and need not imitate an alcoholic recipe.

column5: Used to express regret or longing that more people do not know or understand the proposition that follows.
column6: I wish more people knew, if people only realized
column7: If only more people knew how useful this feature is.
column8: KEY GRAMMAR: 'if only + past form' commonly expresses a present unreal wish/regret: 'If only I knew'; 'If only more people knew...'. It can stand as an exclamation or introduce the wished-for proposition.

column2: lay someone off / be laid off
column5: To end someone's employment, typically because the employer is reducing staff or work rather than because of individual misconduct; usage can vary by jurisdiction/context.
column7: The company laid off 100 workers. / I was laid off during the restructuring.
column8: KEY FORMS: lay someone off; be/get laid off. Distinguish 'fire' = termination often framed around performance/conduct; 'furlough' = temporary unpaid/part-paid leave, not the same.

column5: Irritable, grouchy, easily annoyed, or in a bad mood.
column7: I'm crabby when I haven't slept enough.
column8: Casual and often mildly teasing rather than severe. 'Crabby about X' and 'feel crabby' are natural.

column5: To complain persistently, especially about something regarded as minor; noun 'bellyache' literally also means a stomachache.
column7: Stop bellyaching about the chores. / He spent the whole trip bellyaching about the weather.
column8: Normalize to base family. Figurative verb is informal; literal noun 'a bellyache' = stomach pain.

column5: noun: a small cut, notch, or chip. verb: make a small cut; chiefly BrE slang steal; BrE informal arrest ('get nicked').
column6: small cut, notch; steal, pinch; arrest (BrE)
column7: I nicked myself shaving. / Someone nicked my bike. / The police nicked him outside the pub.
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling for these senses is 'nick', not 'knick'. 'Knick' survives mainly inside words such as knickknack.

column5: Slightly hungry; ready for a small amount of food.
column7: I'm feeling a bit peckish—shall we get something to eat?
column8: Mild hunger. CORRECTION: 'famished' is the opposite end of intensity and should not be listed as a synonym.

column5: A situation in which underwear is wedged tightly between the buttocks, whether accidentally or because someone pulls it up as a prank.
column7: I've got a wedgie. / The bullies gave him a wedgie.
column8: Useful construction: 'have/get a wedgie'; 'give someone a wedgie'. The prank sense is only one route; it can happen accidentally.

column5: In BrE, especially 'chippy', a fish-and-chip shop. In older U.S. slang, 'chippie/chippy' could disparagingly refer to a young woman/prostitute or mistress.
column7: Let's get dinner from the chippy.
column8: Spelling 'chippy' is very common for the UK shop. The U.S. woman-label is dated and derogatory; recognition only. Meanings are dialect-dependent.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::dated usage::derogatory usage::british_english usage::evaluative

column5: A surgical incision into the larynx. The exact procedure and purpose depend on clinical context; it is distinct from tracheotomy/tracheostomy.
column7: The historical report described an emergency laryngotomy.
column8: PRECISION: do not gloss simply as 'throat surgery' or assume it is the standard emergency airway procedure. Rare technical term; distinguish laryngotomy from cricothyrotomy and tracheotomy.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::specialist topic::health topic::medicine discovery::process_details discovery::procedural_language discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: One of the paired tubes connecting the region near an ovary with the uterus; an oocyte travels through it, and fertilization commonly occurs in the ampulla.
column7: Fertilization most commonly occurs in a fallopian tube before the embryo reaches the uterus.
column8: Precision: the tube does not directly attach to the ovary; fimbriae help capture the ovulated oocyte. 'Uterine tube' is a standard anatomical alternative.

column5: To travel on the London Underground railway system.
column6: take the Tube, use the Underground
column7: We took the Tube to Piccadilly Circus. / Do you usually ride the Tube to work?
column8: Capitalize 'Tube' when referring to London's Underground. 'Take the Tube' is especially natural; 'ride the Tube' is also understandable/common.

column2: give someone a piece of one's mind
column3: /ɡɪv ˈsʌmwʌn ə pis əv maɪ maɪnd/
column5: To tell someone frankly and angrily what one thinks of their behavior, usually as a reprimand.
column6: tell off, scold, chew out, give someone an earful
column7: I was so angry I gave him a piece of my mind.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'give + person + a piece of my/your/her... mind'. Despite 'piece', it means an angry verbal rebuke, not sharing an opinion neutrally.

column5: Very thin, dry, crisp toast, traditionally made by toasting thin slices and often served with spreads, soups, salads, or appetizers.
column7: The pâté was served with Melba toast.
column8: CORRECTION: repair mojibake 'pÃ¢tÃ©' → 'pâté'. Capitalize Melba; named after Australian soprano Nellie Melba.

column2: inflate someone's ego / overinflate someone's ego
column5: To increase someone's self-importance or self-esteem, especially excessively through praise, attention, or success.
column6: feed someone's ego, flatter, puff someone up
column7: Don't inflate his ego any more—he already thinks he's a genius.
column8: KEY COLLOCATION: 'inflate someone's ego' is the more established phrase; 'overinflate' is understandable/intensifying but less necessary. Related: 'have an inflated ego'.

column5: To question someone intensely and persistently, often in an accusatory way.
column7: My parents gave me the third degree when I got home late.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'give + person + the third degree'. Modern everyday use is often humorous exaggeration for lots of probing questions; historical origin is disputed/complex, so avoid asserting one certain origin.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::humorous topic::testing

column2: you want a piece of me?
column5: A hostile challenge roughly meaning 'Do you want to fight me?' or 'Are you challenging me?'
column6: you got a problem?, wanna fight?, come at me
column7: He stepped toward me and said, 'You want a piece of me?'
column8: Fixed confrontational pattern. 'A piece of me' here is not literal and is unrelated to 'give someone a piece of my mind'. Often theatrical/comic outside real conflict.

column2: toe the line / thread the needle
column5: 'Toe the line': conform to a rule, standard, or authority. 'Thread the needle': succeed in navigating a very narrow, difficult path between competing constraints; literally, pass thread through a needle's eye.
column6: conform, comply; navigate a fine line, strike a difficult balance
column7: Employees were expected to toe the line. / The policy tries to thread the needle between safety and convenience.
column8: IMPORTANT: two separate idioms, not one fixed combined expression. 'Toe' is spelled TOE, not 'tow': metaphorically place one's toes at a line. 'Thread the needle' has literal sewing and figurative precision/balance senses.

column5: To begin or start; transitive or intransitive, especially in formal, ceremonial, legal, or official contexts.
column7: The ceremony will commence at noon. / Construction commenced in May.
column8: Common formal collocations: commence proceedings/work/operations; 'commence at/on'. In everyday speech, 'start/begin' is usually more natural.

column2: bum someone out / bum me out
column5: To make someone feel sad, disappointed, discouraged, or emotionally deflated.
column7: That ending really bummed me out. / Rainy weekends bum her out.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'bum + person + out'; passive/state 'be bummed out'. Normalize from first-person-only headword.

column5: Material spread over soil to conserve moisture, suppress weeds, moderate temperature, and/or improve soil; verb: to apply mulch or reduce material into mulch.
column7: We spread mulch around the shrubs. / I mulched the garden beds in spring.
column8: Compost can be used as mulch but is not synonymous with mulch. Mulches may be organic (bark, straw) or inorganic (stone, plastic).

column5: To receive a favorable opportunity, stroke of luck, relief, or respite—especially after repeated problems; often in negative 'can't catch a break'.
column6: get lucky, get a lucky break, get some relief
column7: I've had three things go wrong today—I can't catch a break. / She finally caught a break when a position opened up.
column8: KEY PATTERN: 'can't catch a break' is extremely common and emphasizes repeated bad luck. Positive 'finally catch a break' = receive needed luck/opportunity.

column5: A playful request for affection, especially a kiss; in some contexts it can literally mean give me sugar, so tone/context matter.
column6: give me a kiss, give me some love
column7: Come here and give me some sugar!
column8: KEY IDIOMATIC USE: 'sugar' metaphorically = affection/kisses, especially Southern/U.S. folksy or playful speech. The conditional 'If you give me...' is source wording, not the core expression.

column5: Literally, to lie or relax in pleasant warmth/light; figuratively, to enjoy and take satisfaction in praise, attention, success, glory, etc.
column7: The cat basked in the sun. / She basked in the applause.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: bask in the sun/sunshine/warmth; bask in glory/praise/attention. The literal warmth sense motivates the figurative 'soak up enjoyment' sense.
column12: entry::collocation usage::figurative usage::warm topic::grammar discovery::figurative_extension discovery::social_approval

column2: pack my ass off / verb + one's ass off
column5: In the source, 'pack my ass off' means pack extremely hard/intensively. More broadly, 'verb + one's ass off' intensifies an activity: do it very hard, a lot, or to an extreme degree.
column6: pack like crazy, work extremely hard
column7: I'm gonna pack my ass off tonight. / We danced our asses off. / She worked her ass off for that promotion.
column8: IMPORTANT CONSTRUCTION: 'V + my/your/his/her/our/their ass off' is productive vulgar intensification, not an idiom limited to 'pack'. Common with work, laugh, dance, study, freeze, sweat, etc.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::idiom entry::construction usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::persuasive usage::informal topic::work topic::construction discovery::escalation discovery::persuasion

column2: roll the bones / roll some bones
column5: To roll dice, especially in gambling; by extension, to take a chance or gamble on an uncertain outcome.
column6: roll the dice, gamble, take a chance
column7: Let's roll the bones. / We rolled the bones and invested in the risky project.
column8: 'Bones' is old slang for dice, historically connected with dice made from bone. Figurative risk use is understandable, but 'roll the dice' is much more common in modern general English.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::figurative usage::informal discovery::uncertainty discovery::possibility

column5: To take attention, credit, impact, or praise away from someone, especially by announcing or doing something first.
column6: upstage, overshadow, preempt, take the spotlight
column7: I was about to announce my promotion, but she stole my thunder.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'steal + person's + thunder'. Often involves preempting someone's news/idea/moment, not merely being more impressive.

column5: The tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body; in males it also carries semen during ejaculation.
column7: Urine leaves the bladder through the urethra.
column8: Anatomical precision: urethra ≠ ureter. Ureters carry urine from kidneys to bladder; the urethra carries it from bladder outward.

column5: An animal belonging to Vertebrata, characterized by a vertebral column/backbone or its developmental equivalent; adjective: relating to such animals.
column7: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals are vertebrates.
column8: Normalize singular/plural and add adjective. Contrast invertebrate.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::scientific topic::biology topic::animals topic::science

column5: Working or being paid for work time; also literally while a timer/clock is running, as in sports, tests, or timed tasks.
column7: Don't run personal errands while you're on the clock. / We still have two minutes on the clock.
column8: Broader than employment: 'with ten seconds on the clock'. Contrast 'off the clock' = not working/not officially timed.

column5: To behave playfully, foolishly, or unseriously, often instead of doing what one is supposed to do.
column6: fool around, mess around, horse around
column7: We were goofing around instead of studying.
column8: Usually harmless silliness. 'Goof around with + object' can also mean experiment/play casually with something.

column2: a long shot / be a long shot
column5: A possibility, attempt, candidate, or bet with a low probability of success; something unlikely but still worth trying.
column7: Getting tickets this late is a long shot, but I'll try. / She was a long-shot candidate.
column8: Normalize from one sentence. Productive: 'It's a long shot'; 'a long-shot candidate'; 'by a long shot' is a separate idiom already in the Master.

column5: To go to a place quietly or secretly, often to avoid being noticed. 'Snuck' is a common informal/standard past form especially in AmE; 'sneaked' is also standard.
column6: slip over, creep over, sneak across
column7: He snuck over to her house after everyone went to bed. / We sneaked over there quietly.
column8: KEY FRAME: 'sneak over to + place/person'; 'over there' is deictic source wording, not part of the lexical unit.

column5: To make a person or animal consume food against their will; figuratively, to impose information, propaganda, entertainment, etc. on someone aggressively.
column6: compel to eat; impose, ram down someone's throat (figurative)
column7: The prisoners alleged they were force-fed. / Viewers felt they were being force-fed advertising.
column8: Normalize base + past. Figurative construction: 'force-feed someone + information/propaganda'. Strong word; literal use can involve serious ethical/medical issues.
column12: entry::word entry::form_family usage::figurative topic::food topic::entertainment topic::animals discovery::figurative_extension

column2: get it out / have to get it out
column3: /aɪ dʒəst hæv tə ɡɛt ɪt aʊt/
column5: To express or release something one has been holding inside—such as a thought, confession, emotion, sound, or physical substance—depending on context.
column6: let it out, say it, unload, release
column7: I just have to get it out: I hated the ending. / She cried until she felt she'd gotten it all out.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'get + it/something + out' is highly context-dependent. Emotional speech sense = verbalize/release what has been bottled up; don't define the whole phrasal verb only by that sense.

column5: The sound conventionally attributed to a dog's bark; as an interjection, can express being overwhelmed, discomfort, or a strong reaction. Some dated slang uses refer disparagingly to an unattractive person.
column7: Woof—that was a rough meeting. / The dog gave one loud woof.
column8: Modern reaction 'woof' is context/tone dependent and can mean 'that's rough/intense'. The attractiveness insult is dated/derogatory; recognition only.
column12: entry::interjection entry::slang_expression usage::slang usage::dated usage::derogatory usage::informal usage::evaluative topic::animals discovery::impression

column5: A sleep or nap; to sleep, especially briefly or informally.
column7: I'm going for a quick kip. / We kipped on the floor after the party.
column8: KEY FORMS: 'have/take a kip'; 'kip down' = sleep somewhere temporarily. Not necessarily only a short nap in every use.

column5: To remove, extract, or take something from a container, opening, text, context, etc., often by lifting; figuratively, material can be 'lifted out of context'.
column7: Lift the tray out carefully. / The quote was lifted out of context.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'lift + object + out (of X)' or 'lift out + object'. Add figurative textual sense: lift a passage/quote out of a source/context.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::figurative discovery::figurative_extension discovery::removal

column5: A reproductive cell that fuses with another gamete during sexual reproduction; in humans, sperm and oocytes are gametes.
column7: Fertilization involves the fusion of two gametes.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Avoid oversimplifying all gametes as simply 'sperm and egg' across biology; gamete forms vary among organisms.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::scientific topic::biology topic::anatomy topic::science topic::health

column5: An organ that produces gametes and typically sex hormones; testes and ovaries are the human gonads.
column7: The ovaries and testes are gonads.
column8: 'Sex organ' is too broad as a synonym because many reproductive structures are not gonads. Related adjective: gonadal.
column12: entry::word usage::scientific topic::biology topic::anatomy topic::science topic::health

column5: Available to be won, claimed, taken, chosen, or obtained by whoever acts or succeeds; not yet assigned or decided.
column6: available, unclaimed, anyone's for the taking
column7: The last slice is up for grabs. / With no incumbent running, the seat is up for grabs.
column8: Common with prizes, jobs, political seats, opportunities, objects. Can imply competition, not merely free availability.

column5: A special festive event, often formal and associated with celebration, fundraising, performance, or an institution.
column7: They attended the museum's annual fundraising gala.
column8: A gala need not be a ball or banquet. Common: charity gala, gala dinner, gala performance, opening gala.

column5: A male member of a U.S. college fraternity; often used stereotypically for a young man seen as party-oriented, boisterous, immature, entitled, or conventionally masculine.
column7: The comedy turns him into a stereotypical frat boy.
column8: Distinguish literal membership from stereotype. Not every fraternity member fits the stereotype; 'jock' is not a synonym.

column5: To cause someone to stumble or fall, deliberately or accidentally; 'trip someone up' also figuratively means cause someone to make a mistake or expose an inconsistency.
column7: He stuck out his foot and tripped me. / The interviewer tried to trip her up with a tricky question.
column8: KEY DISTINCTION: 'trip someone' = cause a physical stumble; 'trip someone up' can be physical or figurative.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::figurative topic::travel discovery::figurative_extension

column5: noun: a long narrow rod, column, passage, or vertical opening; verb slang: to treat someone unfairly, cheat them, or leave them with a bad outcome.
column6: rod, spindle; cheat, screw over, rip off
column7: The elevator descended through the shaft. / They really shafted him on the deal.
column8: Highly polysemous noun: drive shaft, arrow shaft, mine/elevator shaft, shaft of light. Slang verb is coarse/informal but not necessarily sexual.

column5: Conjunction: in a way that suggests an imagined, apparent, or unreal situation. Standalone/sarcastic: used to reject an idea as ridiculous or highly unlikely.
column7: He talks as if he owns the place. / 'You'd date him.' 'As if!'
column8: KEY GRAMMAR: 'as if + clause'; unreal comparisons often use past forms ('as if he knew everything'), though tense choices depend on meaning. Standalone 'As if!' is strongly sarcastic.

column5: The act or ability of keeping, retaining, or continuing to hold something; common domains include memory/information, employees/customers/students, fluids, and rights/property.
column7: Employee retention improved after salaries rose. / Sleep can affect memory retention. / The condition can cause fluid retention.
column8: Domain-specific collocations are crucial: employee/customer/student retention, memory retention, fluid/water retention. 'Maintenance' is not a universal synonym.

column5: To abruptly stop being in an unwanted mental/emotional state such as shock, sadness, daydreaming, panic, or fixation and return to normal attention/control.
column6: come to one's senses, shake it off, pull oneself together
column7: I kept replaying the mistake until I told myself to snap out of it.
column8: KEY FRAME: 'snap out of + state/it'. As an imperative to another person, 'Snap out of it!' can sound harsh or dismissive, especially with grief or mental-health distress.

column2: something doesn't add up / something isn't adding up
column5: Used when facts, numbers, explanations, or behavior seem inconsistent, illogical, or suspicious.
column6: something doesn't make sense, something is off, the story doesn't hang together
column7: Something doesn't add up—the timeline keeps changing. / The numbers aren't adding up.
column8: CORRECTION/NORMALIZE: 'something really couldn't add up there' is unnatural for the intended present suspicion. Productive forms are 'something doesn't add up' and 'something isn't adding up'. Literal arithmetic 'the numbers add up' underlies the figurative sense.

column5: Embarrassed, self-conscious, or mildly ashamed, especially after being caught making a mistake or doing something awkward.
column7: He gave me a sheepish grin after admitting he'd forgotten.
column8: Common collocations: sheepish grin/smile/look. Usually mild embarrassment rather than deep shame.

column2: crank something up a notch / crank it up a notch
column5: To increase the intensity, energy, difficulty, pressure, volume, or quality of something by one noticeable degree.
column6: step it up, turn it up, intensify, raise the stakes
column7: Let's crank the difficulty up a notch. / The second act cranks the tension up a notch.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'crank + X + up a notch' or 'crank it up a notch'. 'A notch' metaphorically = one level/step. Original example incorrectly made the subject itself 'crank up' without an agent in a less natural way.

column5: A photograph capturing a person in a natural, unposed moment rather than a deliberately posed portrait; it may be taken with or without the subject noticing.
column7: The photographer captured candid photos of guests laughing.
column8: CORRECTION: candid does not necessarily mean 'without the subject's knowledge'; the defining contrast is unposed/natural. Consent/privacy still matter independently.

column5: To make sure, arrange, or take responsibility for ensuring that something happens or is done.
column6: make sure, ensure, take care that
column7: Please see to it that the door is locked. / I'll see to it that everyone gets a copy.
column8: KEY FRAME: 'see to it that + clause'. Related but different: 'see to + noun/person' = deal with/take care of ('I'll see to the repairs').

column5: noun: mocking treatment or speech intended to make someone/something seem foolish or contemptible. verb: to subject to such mockery.
column6: mockery, derision; mock, make fun of
column7: He faced ridicule for the idea. / Critics ridiculed the proposal.
column8: Formal/stronger than casual teasing. Patterns: expose/subject someone to ridicule; ridicule someone for something.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::casual usage::informal topic::public_speaking topic::medicine topic::health discovery::criticism discovery::impression

column5: To shout or utter mocking, insulting, or contemptuous remarks; noun: such a taunt or mocking cry.
column7: The crowd jeered at the referee. / His speech was met with jeers.
column8: KEY FRAMES: 'jeer at + person/thing'; 'jeer someone' is possible but 'jeer at' is common. Heckle specifically involves disruptive shouted comments, often during a performance/speech.

column5: A person's collection of clothes; a tall cabinet for hanging/storing clothes; in theater/film, the clothing/costume department or costumes used in a production.
column7: I need to update my work wardrobe. / The bedroom has a built-in wardrobe. / She works in wardrobe for film productions.
column8: Major production sense added. In AmE, 'closet' usually means built-in storage space, not exactly the movable furniture sense.

column5: A Roman mythological woodland/rustic deity or spirit, typically represented in later art/literature as partly human and partly goatlike; often compared with Greek satyrs.
column7: Mr. Tumnus is a faun in The Chronicles of Narnia.
column8: PRECISION: fauns and Greek satyrs became heavily conflated in later tradition but are not simply exact equivalents in all historical mythology.

column5: Not pretentious, boastful, conspicuous, or eager to attract attention; modest in manner or appearance.
column7: Despite his success, he remained quiet and unassuming. / The restaurant looks unassuming from outside.
column8: Can describe people, buildings, places, objects—not only personality. 'Reserved' means restrained/socially quiet and is not always synonymous.

column5: Informally, dull, uninteresting, low-energy, vaguely unwell, or emotionally flat; 'blah blah blah' can represent boring/irrelevant talk.
column7: I feel kind of blah today. / The room looked a little blah, so we added some plants.
column8: NORMALIZE beyond 'someone is blah'. Common frames: feel/seem/look blah; 'blah' can describe mood, appearance, food, design, etc.

column2: be a hoot / someone is a hoot
column5: To be very funny, entertaining, amusing, or enjoyably eccentric; 'a hoot' can also mean a very enjoyable time/event.
column6: a riot, hilarious, a character; great fun
column7: Your grandmother is a hoot. / The party was an absolute hoot.
column8: Broaden beyond people: 'The trip was a hoot.' Usually affectionate/positive.
column12: entry::fixed_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::affectionate topic::entertainment

column5: The past, especially an earlier era recalled nostalgically or as having a distinctive old-fashioned character.
column6: days gone by, bygone days, the old days
column7: The town still has the charm of yesteryear.
column8: Usually uncountable/singular and literary/nostalgic. Common phrase: 'the ___ of yesteryear'.

column5: Informally, unreliable, inconsistent, or prone to canceling/forgetting commitments. Literally, consisting of or breaking into thin flakes/layers.
column7: He's flaky about plans and cancels at the last minute. / The pastry was light and flaky.
column8: Important literal + figurative senses. For a person, 'flaky' often suggests unreliability or scattered behavior, not simply eccentricity.

column5: A speech or piece of writing praising and remembering someone, especially one delivered at or around a funeral; more broadly, formal praise.
column7: She delivered a moving eulogy for her grandfather.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: give/deliver/write a eulogy; a eulogy for/to someone. It is usually associated with the dead, but the broader historical sense is praise.

column3: /frɛndz doʊnt lɛt frɛndz juz snoʊ kloʊnz/
column5: A humorous warning/advice template modeled on 'Friends don't let friends drive drunk': 'Friends don't let friends + undesirable action.' The source 'Friends don't let friends use snowclones' is itself a meta-snowclone.
column6: meme template, formulaic slogan, phrasal template
column7: Friends don't let friends use Comic Sans. / 'Friends don't let friends use snowclones' jokingly uses the very template it criticizes.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'Friends don't let friends + bare verb'. A snowclone is a recognizable, adaptable phrase template whose slots can be replaced. Repair mojibake in current synonym.

column5: Having or being represented with human form, traits, emotions, intentions, speech, or behavior despite being nonhuman.
column7: The film features an anthropomorphic fox who talks and wears clothes. / People often use anthropomorphic language about computers that 'want' something.
column8: Related noun/process: anthropomorphism; verb: anthropomorphize. Not limited to physical shape—mental/emotional human traits count too.

column5: A branded U.S. fruit-flavored chewy snack sold as a thin flexible sheet that can be unrolled and eaten.
column7: Do we have any Fruit Roll-Ups?
column8: Brand/cultural-reference card. Keep capitalization and plural product name. Ingredient formulations can change, so avoid defining the product by one specific ingredient list.

column5: 'Frat' is an informal abbreviation for a college fraternity. A fraternity is an organized brotherhood/association; in U.S. campus culture, it often means a Greek-letter social organization, traditionally male, though the broader word has other uses.
column7: He joined a fraternity in college. / There's a party at the frat house tonight.
column8: KEY RELATION: frat ← fraternity. 'Frat house' = house associated with a fraternity. Do not define fraternity only by parties; campus fraternities vary, and 'fraternity' also has broader association/brotherhood senses.

column5: To hit, attack, criticize, or surprise someone from an unexpected direction or without warning; figuratively, to catch someone completely unprepared.
column7: The announcement blindsided the staff. / I was completely blindsided by the breakup.
column8: Normalize to productive verb + passive. KEY FRAME: 'blindside someone with/by...' / 'be blindsided by...'. Figurative surprise sense is extremely common.
column12: entry::phrase usage::figurative topic::grammar discovery::figurative_extension discovery::criticism discovery::warning

column5: To understand and respond appropriately to an indirect suggestion, signal, rejection, or request rather than requiring it to be stated explicitly.
column6: get the message, catch on, read the room
column7: I've stopped replying—why won't he take a hint? / Take the hint and give them some privacy.
column8: KEY COLLOCATION: 'take the/a hint'; often negative or imperative: 'can't/won't take a hint', 'Take a hint.' Can sound impatient.

column2: I wanna say... / I want to say...
column5: Used before a tentative answer or recollection to signal that the speaker thinks something is true but is not fully certain; 'want to say' also has its ordinary literal meaning of wishing to express something.
column6: I think, if I remember right, I believe
column7: I wanna say it was around 2003, but I'm not sure. / I want to say her name was Rachel.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION in recall contexts: 'I want/wanna say + tentative answer'. 'Wanna' represents informal speech and should not be used in formal writing. Distinguish literal 'I want to say something'.

column5: To have unexpectedly good luck or obtain a fortunate outcome.
column6: get lucky, catch a break, strike it lucky (BrE)
column7: We really lucked out with the weather. / I lucked out and found the last available ticket.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FRAME: 'luck out with/on...' and 'luck out and + verb'. In modern AmE it normally means GOOD luck.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::form_family entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::american_english usage::british_english

column5: To be later than the expected, scheduled, or appropriate time; of something desirable or necessary, 'That's overdue' means it should have happened earlier.
column6: late, past due; long overdue, about time
column7: The payment is overdue. / An apology is long overdue. / He finally apologized—about time; that was overdue.
column8: Broaden beyond the source sentence. Common collocations: overdue payment/book/bill; long-overdue reform/apology/change. 'Finally' is not a synonym by itself.

column5: To allow someone to touch/grope another person's body sexually. The core phrasal verb is 'feel someone up'; 'let' adds permission: 'let + person + feel + person + up'.
column7: She couldn't believe he expected her to let him feel her up on the first date.
column8: CORRECTION: current example 'let him feel up' is incomplete/unnatural for the intended transitive sense. KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'feel + person + up'; with let: 'let him feel me/her/you up'. Consent must not be inferred merely from the phrase outside explicit context.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::slang usage::informal topic::construction

column5: To attack and seriously injure by tearing, crushing, biting, or battering; figuratively, to defeat or criticize very severely.
column6: mangle, savage, tear into; crush, thrash
column7: The hikers were mauled by a bear. / Their team got mauled in the second half.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Sports/figurative 'maul' is strong informal imagery. 'Attacked' is broader and does not necessarily imply severe injury.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::figurative topic::romance discovery::figurative_extension discovery::criticism

column5: To deceive or misdirect someone with a feint, false move, or misleading appearance, especially in sports; a 'fake-out' can be the deceptive move itself.
column7: She faked the defender out with a quick step. / The apparent ending was a fake-out.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'fake + person + out'; also 'fake-out' as noun/adjective. Sports feints are prototypical, but narrative/prank uses occur.

column5: To restrain physically; prevent progress/development; suppress emotion/information; or keep someone from advancing to the next level/grade.
column7: Fear was holding her back. / He struggled to hold back tears. / The guards held the crowd back.
column8: Major constructions: hold someone back; hold back tears/laughter/information; hold something back from someone. The object and context determine the sense.

column5: To obtain food, money, housing, favors, etc. from someone repeatedly or opportunistically without contributing fairly; also 'mooch something off someone'.
column6: freeload, sponge off, bum something off
column7: He's been mooching off his parents for months. / Can I mooch a ride off you?
column8: KEY FRAMES: 'mooch off someone' = live/take advantage of their generosity; 'mooch something off someone' = obtain a specific thing/favor. 'Mooch from' occurs, but 'mooch off' is especially idiomatic.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrasal_verb entry::idiom entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::slang usage::informal topic::food

column2: patch things up / patch up a relationship
column5: To repair a damaged relationship, disagreement, or situation and restore friendlier relations; literally, 'patch up' can make a temporary repair.
column6: reconcile, make up, mend fences; repair
column7: They patched things up after the argument. / I hope you two can patch up your friendship.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: literal patching repairs a tear/damage; figuratively 'patch things up with someone' repairs a relationship. Also literal 'patch up a hole/wound'.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::idiom entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative usage::rhetorical topic::relationships discovery::disagreement discovery::debate_language

column5: To ignore, dismiss, avoid, or fail to meet/respond to someone, often casually or disrespectfully; also to disregard an obligation or invitation.
column6: ignore, brush off, ditch, stand up (specific context)
column7: He blew us off and never showed up. / She keeps blowing off my messages.
column8: KEY FRAME: 'blow + person/thing + off'. Can blow off a person, meeting, class, responsibility. 'Stand someone up' specifically means fail to appear for an arranged meeting/date.

column5: To deliberately exclude someone from a group, relationship, discussion, information flow, market, or opportunity, often by cold or uncooperative treatment.
column6: exclude, ostracize, shut out, ice out
column7: They froze him out of the meetings. / Smaller competitors were being frozen out of the market.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'freeze + person/group + out (of something)'. Metaphor of social/economic coldness; broader than merely refusing to speak.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative topic::relationships topic::medicine topic::health discovery::promotion

column5: To make someone feel unable to act, grow, breathe, or express themselves freely; to suppress an emotion, sound, idea, debate, or development.
column7: She felt stifled by the rules. / He stifled a laugh. / Excessive control can stifle creativity.
column8: This overlaps the stifle family already reviewed at WID1713. Preserve for now; teach productive objects: stifle a laugh/yawn/cry, stifle debate/innovation, feel stifled.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::debate_language discovery::impression discovery::containment

column5: The lower, narrow portion of the uterus that opens into the vagina; its canal connects the uterine cavity with the vagina.
column7: The cervix dilates during labor. / Cervical screening examines cells from the cervix.
column8: Useful family: cervical = relating to the cervix (also relating to the neck in other anatomical contexts).

column5: Ready-made in standard sizes rather than custom-made or made-to-measure, especially clothing; after a verb, often written 'off the rack'.
column7: It's an off-the-rack suit. / I bought the suit off the rack.
column8: KEY FORM: attributive adjective often hyphenated 'off-the-rack clothing'; after the verb, 'buy it off the rack'. Contrast bespoke/custom-made/made-to-measure.
column12: entry::adjective_phrase entry::adverbial_phrase entry::variant_set topic::culture topic::fashion discovery::evaluation

column5: To assert authority or a firm boundary and refuse to allow something to continue or be negotiated.
column6: stand firm, draw the line, lay down the law
column7: I finally put my foot down and said no more overnight guests.
column8: KEY FRAME: 'put my/your/his/her foot down' often followed by 'about/on/over' an issue or a clause describing the decision. Stronger than merely 'take a stand': it implies enforcing a limit.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::law discovery::negotiation discovery::assertion discovery::boundary-setting discovery::continuity

column5: When imagining, considering, or anticipating something; commonly introduces the trigger for an emotional or physical reaction.
column6: at the idea of, just thinking about
column7: She shuddered at the thought of going back. / My mouth waters at the thought of fresh bread.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: reaction verb/adjective + 'at the thought of + noun/gerund': shudder, cringe, smile, panic, feel sick, get excited at the thought of...

column5: The area of the body between the lower ribs and hips, especially the lower back/sides; in meat, a cut from this region. Plural 'loins' is also literary/euphemistic for the reproductive/genital region or sexual desire.
column6: lower back, flank; loin cut; groin/genitals (literary plural)
column7: Pork loin comes from the animal's back. / The phrase 'gird your loins' means prepare yourself for action.
column8: CORRECTION/PRECISION: singular 'loin' is not simply 'hips, groin, and lower abdomen'. Important collocation: 'gird one's loins' = prepare for strenuous action/challenge, now often humorous/biblical-sounding.
column12: entry::collocation entry::form_family entry::word usage::literary usage::humorous usage::religious

column5: Primarily a masculine given name/surname. Any slang use meaning an exceptionally talented, prestigious, or admirable person is not broadly standard and requires source/community context.
column7: Chauncey is a personal name. / If a source uses 'a Chauncey' as slang, preserve the surrounding context before assigning a meaning.
column8: CORRECTION: do not teach the current flattering 'urban slang' definition as established general English without source support. Treat as proper name/source-dependent usage.

column5: A person who is not a specialist or professional in a particular field; 'layperson' is gender-neutral, while 'layman' is traditional. In religious contexts, a layperson is not a member of the clergy.
column6: nonexpert, nonspecialist, member of the laity (religious)
column7: The guide explains the science in terms a layperson can understand.
column8: Broaden with religious sense. 'Amateur' can mean an unpaid/nonprofessional participant and is not always equivalent. Prefer 'layperson' when gender is irrelevant.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::professional usage::specialist usage::religious topic::religion discovery::professional_context discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Nestlé's U.S. baking brand associated especially with chocolate morsels/chips and cookie products; also a Friends reference in which Phoebe misremembers 'Nestlé Toll House' as the supposed French family name 'Nestlé Toulouse'.
column6: Toll House chocolate chips, baking brand
column7: Phoebe eventually realizes the 'secret family recipe' came from Nestlé Toll House.
column8: CORRECTION: repair mojibake and spelling ('NestlÃ©', 'NeslÃ©' → Nestlé). Cultural-reference card: the Friends joke depends on the sound similarity between 'Nestlé Toll House' and 'Nestlé Toulouse'.

column5: A sudden brief sensation of light-headedness, dizziness, or altered head sensation, commonly after standing quickly; the phrase can also describe a sudden exhilarating/intense feeling in other contexts.
column7: I got a head rush when I stood up too quickly.
column8: Common physical frame: 'get a head rush from/when...'. Standing-related episodes can reflect a temporary drop in blood pressure, but the slang term itself is not a diagnosis.

column5: To feel uncertain, doubtful, uneasy, mildly unwell, or not quite right; things/situations can also be 'iffy' = questionable or uncertain.
column6: uncertain, dubious, shaky; off, mildly unwell
column7: I feel iffy about the plan. / The weather looks iffy. / My stomach feels a little iffy.
column8: Broaden beyond 'feel'. KEY FRAMES: be/feel/look/seem iffy; iffy about something. Context distinguishes doubtful quality from mild physical discomfort.

column2: have too much time on one's hands
column3: /hæv tuː mʌtʃ taɪm ɑn maɪ hændz/
column5: To have more free time than one knows how to use productively, often said humorously or critically when someone does something elaborate, trivial, or odd.
column6: have time to kill, be idle, have nothing better to do
column7: Whoever made this spreadsheet has way too much time on their hands.
column8: KEY FRAME: 'have too much/a lot of time on my/your/their hands'. Often a teasing inference from someone's unnecessary effort, not simply literal boredom.

column5: To lift, pull, push, or throw with great effort; to rise/fall strongly; to breathe/sigh convulsively; to retch or vomit. Noun: a strong pull/effort or upward movement.
column7: He heaved the suitcase into the trunk. / Her chest heaved as she ran. / He leaned over the sink and heaved.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Important patterns: heave a sigh; chest/stomach heaves; heave something over/into; dry-heave.

column2: visit a town a little south of Throw Up
column3: /ˈvɪzɪt ə taʊn ə ˈlɪtl saʊθ əv θroʊ ʌp/
column5: A source-specific comic metaphor for being extremely nauseated or close to vomiting, imagining 'Throw Up' as a place and one's condition as geographically near it.
column6: be nauseated, be close to throwing up, feel sick
column7: After the ride, I felt like I was visiting a town just south of Throw Up.
column8: Do not teach as a standard idiom. WORDPLAY: 'south of X' literally means below X on a map; here the speaker turns 'Throw Up' into a fictional place to locate their nausea just short of vomiting.

column2: come in fourth / came in fourth
column5: To finish or rank in fourth place in a competition, race, vote, ranking, etc.
column6: finish fourth, place fourth, rank fourth
column7: She came in fourth in the regional spelling bee. / Our team came in fourth overall.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'come in + ordinal/position': come in first/second/last; often 'come in fourth in + competition/category'. Normalize base + past.

column5: A traditional saying based on elephants' reputation for strong long-term memory; figuratively used to say that someone remembers things—sometimes especially favors, injuries, or past events—for a long time.
column6: have a long memory, never forget
column7: You remembered that after ten years? Elephants never forget.
column8: Treat as a cultural saying, not a literal scientific absolute. It can be playful, admiring, or mildly threatening depending context.

column5: A mark left by a tire or other object skidding across a surface; crude slang: a fecal stain/streak in underwear.
column7: Police measured the skid marks on the road. / The comedy makes a crude skid-mark joke about his underwear.
column8: CORRECTION: the underwear sense is secondary slang; restore the primary road/tire sense. Spelling 'skid mark' is standard open form; 'skidmark' also occurs, especially slang.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::variant_set entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::informal

column5: Formally engaged or promised to be married; as a noun, one's person to whom one is engaged.
column7: They were betrothed in the spring. / She introduced him jokingly as her betrothed.
column8: CORRECTION: repair mojibake in current definition. 'Betrothed' sounds formal, historical, literary, or playful in modern everyday English.

column2: kick someone in the crotch / a kick in the crotch
column5: Literally, to kick someone in the groin/crotch. Figuratively, 'like a kick in the crotch' can compare an event to a sudden, severe, humiliating or painful blow.
column6: kick in the groin; low blow (figurative related)
column7: He kicked the attacker in the crotch. / The rejection felt like a kick in the crotch.
column8: Not a fixed idiom in every literal occurrence. KEY distinction: action 'kick someone in the crotch' versus simile/metaphor 'a kick in the crotch'.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::figurative discovery::literal_vs_figurative discovery::comparison discovery::figurative_extension

column5: A person who has previously been convicted of a crime and/or imprisoned; exact implication varies, and the label can be stigmatizing.
column7: The program helps formerly incarcerated people find work.
column8: PRECISION: 'ex-con' derives from ex-convict and does not necessarily mean the person is a parolee. Person-first alternatives may be preferable in neutral/formal contexts.

column5: To be a sign that future events are likely to turn out well or badly for someone/something.
column6: augur well/ill, be a good/bad sign, look promising/ominous
column7: The early results bode well for the project. / That silence doesn't bode well for us.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'X bodes well/ill for Y'. Normalize from first-person sentence. 'Bode' is most common in this collocation and sounds somewhat formal.

column5: The handrail at the side of a staircase; in everyday usage, sometimes the whole railing/balustrade system including its supports.
column7: He slid down the banister as a kid.
column8: Usage varies: technically, balusters are the vertical supports and a balustrade is the complete railing assembly; everyday 'banister' often refers broadly to the stair railing.

column2: get in line / have to get in line
column5: Literally, to join a queue; figuratively, to wait one's turn because many others want the same thing, or to conform/fall into line depending context.
column6: join the queue, wait your turn; fall in line (related)
column7: Grandma has to get in line like everyone else. / You want tickets too? Get in line.
column8: Normalize away from source-specific 'grandma'. KEY USE: 'get in line' often jokingly means 'you're not the only one; wait your turn.' Distinguish 'fall in line' = conform.

column5: 'Wafer-thin' means extremely thin. 'On wafer-thin ice' is a humorous intensification/variation of the idiom 'on thin ice' = in a risky position and close to trouble.
column6: paper-thin, extremely thin; on very thin ice
column7: The phone is wafer-thin. / You're on wafer-thin ice after that comment.
column8: KEY RELATION: wafer + thin is a productive intensifier because a wafer is very thin; 'wafer-thin ice' creatively strengthens 'thin ice'. Hyphenate before a noun: wafer-thin ice.
column12: entry::idiom usage::humorous usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::risk discovery::escalation discovery::debate_language

column5: An informal exaggerating pattern meaning something has a quality to such an extreme degree that it is almost painful, embarrassing, or overwhelming; the source uses 'so outdated it hurts'.
column7: That design is so outdated it hurts. / He's so talented it hurts.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'so + adjective + (that) it hurts'. Often humorous/hyperbolic; 'painfully outdated/obvious/awkward' expresses a similar idea.

column5: Figuratively, conventional, plain, safe, basic, or lacking novelty/adventurousness; in sexual contexts, 'vanilla' specifically means conventional/non-kink sexual preferences.
column7: The design feels a little vanilla. / Their tastes are pretty vanilla.
column8: Broaden beyond 'you are'. Metaphor comes from vanilla as a default/plain flavor. Tone ranges from neutral to dismissive; sexual sense is context-specific.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::adjective_phrase usage::slang usage::figurative usage::informal discovery::figurative_extension

column5: A U.S. chocolate-flavored beverage brand. It is marketed as a chocolate drink rather than simply ordinary chocolate milk.
column7: He grabbed a cold Yoo-hoo from the fridge.
column8: Brand-reference card. Avoid locking the definition to a specific formulation because ingredients/products can change.

column5: A seductive woman, especially the femme-fatale archetype of older film/theater; verb: to use seductive charm, or in music/theater, to repeat/improvise an accompaniment until a cue.
column7: She played a glamorous vamp in the silent film. / The pianist vamped until the singer was ready.
column8: Major missing music/theater verb sense. The woman-label is dated and can be sexist/objectifying; best treated as historical/cultural recognition.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::dated usage::informal topic::business topic::music topic::film topic::entertainment discovery::iteration discovery::improvement

column5: Financial support that one former spouse may be required or agree to pay another after separation/divorce; rules, duration, and terminology vary by jurisdiction.
column7: The divorce agreement required monthly alimony payments.
column8: PRECISION: not universally court-ordered and not available in every divorce. 'Spousal support' is a broader/current term in many jurisdictions.
column12: entry::word usage::specialist topic::law topic::finance discovery::terminology discovery::agreement discovery::support discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: An act that goes beyond or violates a moral, religious, social, or legal boundary/rule.
column7: He apologized for his past transgressions. / The novel treats curiosity as a moral transgression.
column8: Word family: transgress (verb), transgressive (adj). Often moral/religious/literary rather than routine legal language.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal usage::literary usage::legalistic usage::religious topic::law topic::religion discovery::boundary-setting

column5: An attack from the air by military aircraft or other aerial weapons against ground targets; historically especially associated with bombing raids.
column7: Civilians took shelter during the air raid.
column8: 'Bombing raid' overlaps but an air raid is the broader concept. Productive collocations: air-raid siren, air-raid shelter.

column5: To switch between states/options, often repeatedly; noun: a control or switch that alternates between states. Also a pin/fastener or toggle mechanism in other domains.
column7: Toggle dark mode on or off. / Use the toggle to enable notifications.
column8: KEY UI CONSTRUCTION: toggle X on/off; toggle between A and B. Not always exactly two settings in software, though binary toggles are common.

column5: Abruptly incongruous, discordant, shocking, or unpleasant in a way that disrupts one's expectations or senses.
column7: The cheerful music was jarring against the grim scene. / The sudden cut felt jarring.
column8: Useful collocations: jarring contrast/change/noise/transition. The core is a disruptive mismatch or shock, not merely 'surprising'.

column5: To be disloyal to or violate someone's trust; to reveal or disclose something, including unintentionally through signs or behavior.
column6: deceive, sell out; reveal, give away
column7: He betrayed his friend. / Her voice betrayed her nervousness.
column8: KEY POLYSEMY: betray a person/trust/secret = disloyalty or disclosure; 'his expression betrayed his fear' = unintentionally revealed it. Normalize base + source form.

column5: Expressed clearly and in few words, without unnecessary detail.
column6: concise, brief, pithy, to the point
column7: Her explanation was succinct but complete.
column8: Nuance: succinct is usually positive—brevity with clarity/completeness. 'Terse' can imply abruptness; 'laconic' suggests habitually using few words.

column5: A person who experiences synesthesia, in which a stimulus in one sensory or cognitive domain consistently and automatically evokes an additional experience in another or related domain.
column7: Some grapheme-color synesthetes consistently experience particular letters as particular colors.
column8: PRECISION: synesthesia is broader than 'one sense perceived as another'; forms can involve letters/numbers, spatial sequences, sounds, tastes, etc. Normalize singular/plural.

column5: A person who enumerates; especially a census or survey worker who collects/counts information from households or respondents. In computing/mathematics the term can have technical senses.
column6: census worker, survey worker; counter/listing agent
column7: Census enumerators visited households that had not responded.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. 'Surveyor' can mean a land-measurement professional, so it is not a safe general synonym.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical usage::professional usage::scientific topic::work topic::mathematics discovery::professional_context discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To list or name items one by one, usually systematically; in some technical contexts, to count or determine the number of members.
column7: She enumerated three reasons for rejecting the proposal.
column8: KEY FRAME: 'enumerate + items/reasons/steps'; often followed by a list. More formal than 'list'. Word family: enumeration, enumerator.

column5: The quality of performing a learned process rapidly and with little conscious attention or effort after sufficient practice.
column7: Repeated practice can build automaticity in decoding common words.
column8: PRECISION: not the same as instinct or reflex; automaticity is often learned through practice. Common education/skill-learning collocation: develop/build automaticity.
column12: entry::collocation entry::word topic::psychology topic::performance discovery::process_details discovery::evaluation

column5: Relating to qualities, characteristics, meanings, or kinds rather than numerical quantity; in research, involving non-numerical data/interpretive analysis, though qualitative work can still use counts or structured methods.
column7: The researchers conducted qualitative interviews about patient experiences. / There was a qualitative change in the tone of the debate.
column8: Contrast quantitative. Important broader sense: 'a qualitative difference/change' = difference in kind or character, not merely research methodology.

column5: A small increase or step in a series; the amount by which a variable changes. As a verb, especially technical/computing, to increase by a specified amount.
column7: Increase the dose in small increments. / The counter increments by one each time.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: in increments of X; small/regular increments; increment a counter/value. Normalize singular/plural.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical discovery::process_details discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To reduce the strength, intensity, effect, concentration, or amplitude of something; in microbiology, to weaken a pathogen's virulence. 'Attenuated' = weakened/reduced.
column7: Walls attenuate the wireless signal. / Some vaccines use live attenuated organisms.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Technical collocations: attenuate a signal/sound/effect; attenuated virus/vaccine. 'Dilute' is only appropriate in some contexts.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical topic::grammar discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To roll and fall/move off a surface; to come off a production line; in audio/electronics, for response/level to decrease progressively beyond a frequency or point.
column7: The bottle rolled off the table. / High frequencies begin to roll off above 10 kHz. / New cars rolled off the assembly line.
column8: KEY technical sense: frequency response 'rolls off'; noun 'roll-off' = rate/character of attenuation. Add productive 'roll off the assembly line'.

column5: For what it's worth; used to introduce an opinion, fact, or suggestion while modestly acknowledging that it may have limited relevance or value.
column6: for what it's worth, if it helps, just my two cents
column7: FWIW, I think the first version reads more naturally.
column8: Register: common in texts/forums/email, often read as the full phrase rather than spoken letter-by-letter in conversation. It can soften a contribution.
column12: entry::initialism usage::conversational usage::softening topic::internet discovery::suggestion discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::evaluation

column5: To expel feces from the bowels through the anus.
column6: pass stool, have a bowel movement, poop (informal)
column7: The patient had difficulty defecating after surgery.
column8: Register ladder: defecate = clinical/formal; have a bowel movement/pass stool = medical/euphemistic; poop = everyday informal. 'Evacuate' alone is ambiguous.

column5: Magnificent beauty, brilliance, grandeur, or impressive display.
column7: We stood in awe of the mountain's splendor. / The palace was restored to its former splendor.
column8: AmE splendor; BrE splendour. Common collocations: in all its splendor; former splendor; natural/architectural splendor.

column5: A mass of lymphoid tissue in the throat region; in everyday usage 'the tonsils' usually means the paired palatine tonsils visible at the back of the throat.
column7: His tonsils were swollen. / She had her tonsils removed as a child.
column8: PRECISION: there are multiple tonsillar tissues (palatine, pharyngeal/adenoid, lingual, etc.); the common pair are palatine tonsils. Not accurately a generic 'throat gland'.

column5: Difficult, harsh, or unsuitable for living/growth; or unwelcoming/unfriendly toward guests or outsiders.
column7: The desert is inhospitable to many plants. / They received an inhospitable welcome.
column8: KEY FRAMES: inhospitable environment/climate/terrain; inhospitable to life/growth; inhospitable host/reception. Literal environment and social-hosting senses share the idea 'not hospitable'.

column2: inhospitable environment for sperm / inhospitable uterine or reproductive environment
column5: A descriptive, non-diagnostic phrase meaning conditions in the reproductive tract are unfavorable to sperm survival/movement, fertilization, implantation, or pregnancy; the exact mechanism must come from the medical/source context.
column7: The Friends dialogue describes an 'inhospitable environment' as part of an infertility explanation.
column8: CORRECTION: current wording 'inhospitable environment for uterus' is grammatically/medically confused. 'Inhospitable to/for X' means unfavorable to X. Do not invent a specific diagnosis from the phrase alone; cervical, uterine, sperm, implantation, and other factors are distinct.

column5: An inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and tissues, associated with elevated urate levels and often causing sudden severe attacks of pain, swelling, redness, and warmth.
column7: He had a painful gout flare in his big toe.
column8: PRECISION: gout is not simply 'caused by excess uric acid' in a one-step sense; hyperuricemia raises risk, while crystal deposition drives inflammation. Common: gout attack/flare.

column5: In or toward the direction from which the wind is blowing; situated on the windward side.
column7: Stand upwind of the smoke so it blows away from you. / The upwind side of the ridge was cooler.
column8: CORRECTION: 'facing the wind' is not always equivalent. Contrast downwind = in the direction the wind is blowing toward. Useful construction: be/stay upwind of something.

column5: Both are minimal underwear styles. A G-string typically has a very narrow string-like strip at the back and minimal fabric; 'thong' is broader and generally has a narrow back strip, often wider than a G-string. Usage/design categories can overlap by brand/region.
column7: A G-string is generally a more minimal subtype/style than a typical thong.
column8: Treat as a comparison card, not exact universal engineering specifications: garment terminology and cuts vary. In AmE 'thong' also historically can mean a sandal/flip-flop depending context.
column12: entry::term entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::american_english usage::specialist topic::fashion topic::language_learning discovery::comparison discovery::contrast discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To remain emotionally fixated, preoccupied, or unable to move past someone/something; with a person, often lingering romantic attachment.
column6: fixated on, preoccupied with, stuck on, obsessed with
column7: He's still hung up on his ex. / Don't get hung up on one small mistake.
column8: This duplicates/overlaps WID1692, where grammar was corrected. Preserve for now under no-auto-delete. KEY STATE: 'be hung up on'; change-of-state: 'get hung up on'.

column2: best two out of three / best-of-three
column5: A format in which the first competitor to win two of a maximum of three games/rounds wins the series or contest.
column7: Let's make it best two out of three. / They played a best-of-three series.
column8: CORRECTION/NATURALNESS: 'best out of three' occurs, but 'best two out of three' (AmE) and 'best of three' / 'best-of-three' are clearer standard forms. It is not necessarily a tiebreaker.

column2: We're taking that home, mister! — Friends
column5: A source-specific emphatic line meaning 'We are taking/keeping that object and bringing it home,' with 'mister' adding mock-authoritative, playful emphasis.
column6: we're keeping that, that's coming home with us
column7: We're taking that home, mister!
column8: Do not assign a generic 'reward/claiming a prize' idiom. Learning value: 'take + object + home' means bring it to one's home; sentence-final 'mister!' can sound mock-stern/playful depending tone. Preserve as source quote.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::playful topic::construction discovery::emphasis discovery::criticism

column5: To staff, operate, or attend a post, station, desk, vehicle, etc.; historically 'man' referred to supplying personnel, though gender-neutral alternatives such as 'staff' are often preferred.
column7: Two volunteers manned the front desk. / The phones are staffed around the clock.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY COLLOCATIONS: man a desk/post/station/ship. In formal inclusive writing, 'staff' or 'crew' may fit better depending object.

column5: A drug or agent that produces loss of sensation, especially pain, with or without loss of consciousness; adjective: relating to anesthesia.
column7: The dentist used a local anaesthetic. / General anesthetic drugs can produce unconsciousness.
column8: BrE anaesthetic; AmE anesthetic. CORRECTION: painkiller and sedative are not synonyms: analgesics reduce pain; sedatives calm; anesthetics produce loss of sensation and sometimes consciousness.

column5: A person, organization, or mechanism that acts between parties, stages, or systems to facilitate communication, negotiation, exchange, or transfer; adjective: intermediate/mediating.
column7: They used an intermediary to negotiate the deal. / The payment passes through an intermediary bank.
column8: Broaden beyond people. A mediator is a specific neutral dispute-resolution role; an intermediary need not be neutral or resolve a dispute.

column2: heat this up on your loins — Friends
column5: A source-specific Friends joke in which 'loins' is used in its literary/euphemistic sexual-body sense and the speaker jokingly imagines sexual heat warming cold coffee.
column7: Damn, this coffee's cold. Hey Rach, do you mind if I heat this up on your loins?
column8: Do not generalize as an English expression. Learning value is the humorous collision of literal 'heat something up' with literary/euphemistic 'loins' associated with sexuality. Preserve as source quote.

column5: Hanging, sagging, or bending downward; looking tired, limp, or lacking firmness/energy.
column7: My eyelids get droopy when I'm tired. / The plant looked droopy after a hot day.
column8: Common collocations: droopy eyes/eyelids/ears/leaves. 'Flabby' specifically concerns soft flesh/material and is not a general synonym.

column5: Capable of being touched; figuratively, clearly perceptible, concrete, definite, or measurable rather than abstract or vague.
column7: The sculpture is a tangible object. / We finally saw tangible progress. / There was tangible tension in the room.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: tangible evidence/benefit/result/progress/asset. 'Palpable' overlaps especially with strongly perceptible atmosphere/emotion.

column5: Any of numerous mostly small fishes in goby-related groups, many of them bottom-dwelling in marine, brackish, or freshwater habitats.
column7: We spotted several gobies resting on the rocks near the bottom.
column8: CORRECTION: repair garbled Japanese text and avoid claiming goby = Japanese 'haze' universally; Japanese common names map to particular species/groups. Culinary use varies by species/region.

column5: A common name applied to various fishes, including freshwater breams and unrelated marine fishes called sea bream; the exact species/group depends on context.
column7: We ordered grilled sea bream. / Freshwater bream are common in parts of Europe.
column8: CORRECTION: repair garbled Japanese text and avoid equating all 'bream' with Japanese 'tai'. Common fish names do not map one-to-one across biological groups/languages.

column5: A mark made by pressure; an idea/opinion/feeling formed about someone/something; an effect produced on someone; an imitation of a person's voice/manner; a printing/copy instance in specialized uses.
column7: She made a great first impression. / The tire left an impression in the mud. / He does a hilarious impression of his boss.
column8: Major polysemy. KEY COLLOCATIONS: first impression; make/leave an impression on; be under the impression that; do an impression of someone.
column12: entry::word usage::specialist discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::impression discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::specialist_register

column5: Toward, facing, or situated on the side of the sea.
column7: We walked seaward. / The house has a seaward-facing balcony.
column8: Adverb 'move/look seaward'; adjective 'seaward side/slope'. Contrast landward.

column5: 'Self-deflecting' is understandable but not a well-established standard personality adjective. The intended behavior is deflecting attention, praise, blame, or vulnerability away from oneself.
column7: Whenever someone compliments her, she deflects the praise and changes the subject.
column8: CORRECTION: choose established language by context. 'Self-effacing' = modest and avoids attention/praise; 'deflect blame/attention' = redirect it. Do not teach 'self-deflecting' as a standard fixed trait term.
column12: entry::construction topic::psychology discovery::evasive_language discovery::criticism discovery::evaluation discovery::social_approval

column5: To design or reorganize something to make it simpler, more efficient, or less wasteful; literally/aerodynamically, to shape something to reduce resistance. 'Streamlined' describes the result.
column7: We streamlined the approval process. / The train has a streamlined shape.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Literal fluid/aerodynamic sense motivates figurative process sense. 'Optimized' may imply best possible performance and is not always exact.

column5: To set, adjust, or calibrate an instrument/scale/sight so its reference is zero or correctly aligned; more broadly, to reduce a value to zero in technical contexts.
column7: Zero the scale before weighing the sample. / The technician zeroed the instrument.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Keep firearm example optional rather than central. Distinguish 'zero in on' = focus/aim increasingly precisely.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical topic::grammar discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column2: zero in on / zeroed in on
column5: To direct attention, effort, or aim increasingly precisely toward a particular target, issue, detail, or person.
column6: focus on, home in on, target, pinpoint
column7: She quickly zeroed in on the real problem. / The camera zeroed in on his face.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'zero in on + target/topic'. Normalize base + source form. Often figurative focus; compare 'home in on', which is closely related.

column5: Occurring, changing, or recurring in cycles; caused by or related to a cycle, especially in economics, business, biology, or natural processes.
column7: The industry is highly cyclical. / The economy experiences cyclical expansions and contractions.
column8: 'Cyclic' and 'cyclical' overlap strongly; cyclical is especially common for recurring economic/social patterns. Contrast seasonal when recurrence specifically follows seasons.
column12: entry::word usage::scientific topic::business topic::biology topic::economics topic::science discovery::iteration

column5: A critical threshold at which accumulated small changes or pressures produce a larger, often rapid change in a system, trend, behavior, or situation.
column7: The company may be approaching a tipping point where growth becomes self-sustaining.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: something gradually leans until it 'tips'. Not every tipping point is irreversible; remove overstatement. Common: reach/pass a tipping point.

column5: In business, to start/build a venture using founders' own resources and operating revenue rather than substantial outside funding. More broadly/technically, to initiate a process using minimal existing resources; computing 'bootstrap' underlies 'boot'.
column7: They bootstrapped the company for three years before raising outside capital. / The system uses a bootstrap process to load the operating environment.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Business meaning is not simply 'without outside help'—a bootstrapped firm may use customers, loans, small grants, etc.; core idea is limited external equity/funding. Related noun: bootstrapping.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word topic::business topic::grammar discovery::resource_allocation discovery::process_details

column5: A state of self-satisfaction or unworried confidence that reduces awareness of problems, risks, or need for improvement.
column7: After years of success, complacency set in. / We can't let a winning streak breed complacency.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: complacency sets in; breed/lead to complacency; guard against complacency. 'Contentment' can be healthy and is not a good general synonym.

column5: The central, decisive, or most difficult point of an issue, argument, problem, or matter.
column7: The crux of the debate is whether the rule is enforceable. / That's the crux of the problem.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'the crux of + issue/problem/argument/matter'. Usually takes THE. Often followed by 'is that/whether...'.
column12: entry::collocation entry::noun_phrase entry::construction usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly discovery::debate_language

column5: Emergency Medical Technician: a trained emergency medical services provider who gives prehospital assessment and care within the scope defined by their certification/jurisdiction.
column6: emergency medical technician, EMS provider; first responder (broader)
column7: An EMT assessed him before transport to the hospital.
column8: CORRECTION/PRECISION: EMT and paramedic are not synonyms; paramedics generally have a higher/different level of training and scope. Capitalize the initialism EMT.
column12: entry::initialism entry::term usage::technical topic::health topic::assessment discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: noun: an undeveloped growth on a plant that may become a leaf, flower, or shoot; figuratively, something/person at an early stage. verb: to produce buds or begin developing.
column7: The rose bush is covered in buds. / Their friendship was just beginning to bud.
column8: Add productive verb and figurative developmental sense. Common: flower bud, taste bud (separate compound), budding artist/talent.

column5: To keep someone alert, attentive, adaptable, and ready to react, often by creating unpredictability, challenge, or constant demands.
column6: keep alert, keep sharp, keep vigilant, challenge
column7: Her unpredictable questions keep me on my toes. / Working in a busy kitchen keeps everyone on their toes.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: being 'on your toes' suggests physical readiness to move. Productive frames: keep someone on their toes; be/stay on one's toes.

column5: noun: an authoritative power or act of rejecting/preventing a proposal or decision; verb: to reject or block by exercising such authority, and informally to reject an idea.
column7: The president vetoed the bill. / I veto that restaurant—we went there yesterday.
column8: Broaden noun + verb. Formal political vetoes depend on the institution; informal 'I veto X' humorously means 'I reject that option'.

column5: To disapprove of something or regard it as improper, undesirable, or socially unacceptable.
column6: disapprove of, look down on, discourage
column7: Cheating is frowned upon. / That kind of behavior is generally frowned on here.
column8: KEY FORM: usually passive 'be frowned upon/on'. 'Upon' is somewhat more formal; 'on' also occurs. Normalize from past participle headword.

column5: to present or constitute (a problem, danger, or question)
column6: present, create, constitute; posture, model; impersonate
column7: The new rule poses a problem for small businesses. / She posed for a photo beside the poster. / He posed as a delivery driver to get inside.
column8: Important patterns: pose a question/problem/threat/challenge; pose for a photo; pose as someone/something = pretend to be. The abstract 'present/constitute' sense is especially common in formal prose.

column5: To step, walk, or place one's feet; to walk on/crush underfoot. Noun: the way/act of stepping, or the patterned surface of a tire/shoe that contacts the ground.
column7: Tread carefully on the ice. / He trod on my foot. / The tire tread is worn.
column8: CORRECTION: current 'He tread carefully' is nonstandard past in most modern usage. Principal forms: tread–trod–trodden (also trod as participle in some use). Important noun: tire/shoe tread.

column5: To preserve something whole, complete, undamaged, unchanged, or not broken apart.
column7: We moved the sculpture carefully to keep it intact. / The adaptation kept the basic structure intact.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'keep + object + intact'; also 'remain intact'. 'Intact' can mean physically unbroken or figuratively preserved (team, structure, reputation, agreement).

column5: To remove or carry something from a place/person; subtract; deprive someone of something; or, figuratively, learn/retain a main message or impression.
column6: remove, carry off; subtract; deprive; learn/retain
column7: Please take these plates away. / Take five away from twelve. / What did you take away from the lecture?
column8: Major polysemy. KEY FRAMES: take X away; take X away from Y; takeaway (noun) = main lesson/message, especially AmE/business.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::american_english topic::communication discovery::figurative_extension discovery::impression discovery::removal

column5: To reach or be at a maximum allowed limit, capacity, rate, level, or benefit.
column7: My contribution is capped out for the year. / The plan caps out at 100 GB.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'cap out at + limit' and 'be capped out'. Often finance, benefits, games, plans, capacity. 'I've capped out on...' is possible but context-specific.

column5: To taste or enjoy something slowly and attentively; figuratively, to enjoy, appreciate, or dwell pleasurably on an experience, moment, victory, etc.
column7: She savored every bite. / Take a minute to savor the moment.
column8: AmE savor; BrE savour. KEY COLLOCATIONS: savor the flavor/moment/victory/experience. Can imply deliberately prolonging enjoyment.
column12: entry::word entry::variant_set usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::figurative_extension discovery::subjective_judgment

column5: A historically Protestant polemical term for Roman Catholic beliefs, institutions, practices, or papal authority, used disparagingly.
column6: papism (historical/derogatory), Roman Catholicism (neutral referent, not synonym in tone)
column7: Accusations of 'popery' were politically charged in early modern Britain.
