column8: Register is essential: not a neutral modern synonym for Catholicism. Recognition/history card; quotation marks may be appropriate when discussing the label.
column12: entry::word usage::derogatory usage::evaluative topic::communication topic::history discovery::terminology

column5: To support, maintain, defend, or confirm the validity of a principle, standard, law, right, decision, or judgment.
column7: The appeals court upheld the ruling. / We have a duty to uphold these standards.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: uphold a law/ruling/conviction/right/principle/standard. In courts, uphold = leave a lower decision in force; 'affirm' is a close legal term.

column5: Causing or capable of causing a major, fundamental, or far-reaching change.
column7: The trip was transformative for her. / AI could have a transformative effect on the workflow.
column8: Common frames: transformative experience/effect/impact/potential. 'Revolutionary' and 'groundbreaking' are stronger/different: novelty is not required for something to be transformative.

column5: The restoration of something to its rightful owner or condition, or payment/compensation ordered or made for loss, damage, or wrongdoing; legal meaning varies by context.
column7: The court ordered restitution to the victims. / The museum agreed to restitution of the looted artwork.
column8: KEY FRAMES: make/pay restitution; restitution to victims; restitution of property. Not identical to reimbursement, which usually repays expenses.

column5: To fill, permeate, or strongly influence someone/something with a quality, feeling, idea, or value.
column7: Her speech was imbued with hope. / The novel imbues ordinary objects with symbolic meaning.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'imbue X with Y'; passive 'X is imbued with Y'. 'Instill' typically takes a different frame: instill Y in/into X.

column5: noun: a burrowing mammal of the mustelid family/group. verb: to repeatedly pester, pressure, or nag someone, especially with requests or questions.
column7: He kept badgering me to lend him the car. / Badgers live in underground setts.
column8: Normalize singular/base. KEY VERB FRAME: badger someone about/for/into something. Animal species differ by region.

column5: A small, sheltered, secluded, or tucked-away corner/place; often a cozy area suited to a particular activity.
column7: She curled up in a reading nook. / There's a little breakfast nook by the window.
column8: Common compounds/collocations: reading nook, breakfast nook. Closely paired in idiom 'every nook and cranny'.

column5: A small narrow opening, crack, crevice, or hard-to-reach recess.
column7: Dust gets into every nook and cranny.
column8: Most familiar in fixed pairing 'nook and cranny / every nook and cranny' = every part, including hidden places. 'Fissure' can be much larger/technical.

column5: A collection or work that gathers a substantial body of information, examples, or material about a subject, often in a concise or organized form.
column7: The book is a compendium of myths from around the world.
column8: Do not require 'concise but comprehensive' in every use. A compendium can be extensive. KEY FRAME: a compendium of + information/stories/rules/knowledge.

column5: A U.S. brand of packaged meat snacks, especially thin meat sticks.
column7: He grabbed a Slim Jim at the gas station.
column8: CORRECTION: brand styling is 'Slim Jim' (two words), not 'slimjim'. Trademark/product-reference card; avoid calling all similar snacks Slim Jims generically.

column5: To present, propose, state, or offer an idea, argument, theory, effort, or candidate; also literally/biologically, to produce or extend growth.
column7: She put forth a compelling argument. / The committee put forth three candidates. / The plant put forth new shoots.
column8: Broaden productive objects: put forth an argument/proposal/theory/candidate/effort. 'Put forth effort' = exert effort; literal plant sense remains.

column2: put in/offer my two cents / give my two cents
column5: To offer one's opinion modestly, often implying it may not be especially authoritative or requested.
column6: offer my opinion, weigh in, chime in
column7: If I can put in my two cents, I'd keep the original ending. / Let me give you my two cents.
column8: NORMALIZE: 'put forth my two cents' is understandable but not the most idiomatic standard combination. Productive forms: put in my two cents; give/offer my two cents; 'my two cents' itself = my opinion.

column5: Soft, loose, or lacking firmness/tone, especially flesh or muscles; figuratively, weak, loose, or lacking discipline/force.
column6: soft, saggy, out of shape; weak, slack (figurative)
column7: My arms felt flabbier after months without training. / The essay's middle section is a little flabby.
column8: Normalize base + comparative. Figurative use can describe writing, organizations, arguments, etc. Body use can sound judgmental.

column2: tick/check a box / tick/check the boxes
column5: Literally, to mark a checkbox; figuratively, to satisfy a requirement, criterion, preference, or expected feature, sometimes mechanically or superficially.
column6: meet a criterion, satisfy a requirement, check off
column7: The candidate ticks all the boxes. / The feature checks an important box for accessibility.
column8: KEY VARIATION: BrE often 'tick a box'; AmE often 'check a box'. Common figurative plural: tick/check all the boxes. Can imply checklist mentality/token compliance.
column12: entry::idiom entry::collocation usage::figurative usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::figurative_extension discovery::expressing_need

column5: To isolate or keep apart; especially to isolate a jury from outside influence. In law/finance, to seize, set aside, or restrict property/funds depending context.
column6: isolate, segregate, set apart; impound (specific legal sense)
column7: The judge sequestered the jury. / The cabin was sequestered deep in the woods.
column8: Normalize base + source form. 'Secluded' overlaps place sense but not legal jury/property senses. Technical meanings vary by jurisdiction.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical topic::law topic::finance topic::grammar topic::courtroom discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Extremely obvious or conspicuous, especially a fault/discrepancy; or shining/bright in a harsh, dazzling way.
column7: There's a glaring error in the first paragraph. / The glaring headlights made it hard to see.
column8: Two core senses connected by 'hard to ignore'. Common: glaring mistake/error/omission/discrepancy; glaring light.

column5: A cord, strap, or line used to secure, carry, suspend, or attach something, commonly worn around the neck/wrist for an ID, keys, whistle, etc.; also has nautical/technical uses.
column7: Wear your badge on the lanyard. / She clipped her keys to a wrist lanyard.
column8: Broaden beyond neck/wrist: the core is a securing/attachment cord or strap. 'Badge holder' may be attached to a lanyard but is not the same object.

column5: Basic, elementary, or only minimally developed; in anatomy/biology, imperfectly or incompletely developed.
column7: I have only a rudimentary understanding of coding. / The device had a rudimentary control system.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: rudimentary knowledge/skills/understanding/system. Often means 'only the beginnings', not simply 'simple'.
column12: entry::word usage::scientific topic::biology topic::anatomy topic::science topic::health

column5: A thorough cleaning traditionally associated with spring; figuratively, a periodic purge, cleanup, or reorganization of files, habits, systems, finances, etc.
column7: We did some spring cleaning and donated three boxes of clothes. / My inbox needs a little digital spring cleaning.
column8: Productive figurative extension: digital/financial/organizational spring cleaning. Often includes decluttering, not only scrubbing.

column5: To combine separate things into a single stronger, simpler, or more coherent whole; to strengthen or make secure; in finance/accounting, combine accounts/statements.
column7: We consolidated three spreadsheets into one. / The victory consolidated her position as leader.
column8: Important second sense: consolidate power/position/gains = strengthen/secure, not merge. Common: consolidate debt/accounts/operations.

column2: wear something out / wore out my first copy — Friends
column3: /aɪ wɔr aʊt maɪ fɝst ˈkɑpi wɛn aɪ wəz wɪð ju/
column5: To use something so much that it becomes worn, damaged, or unusable; also to exhaust a person. In the Friends line, Rachel's 'I wore out my first copy when I was with you' is a sexual joke implying very heavy use of the book while she and Ross were together.
column7: I wore out my first pair of running shoes. / The kids wore me out. / Rachel: 'I wore out my first copy when I was with you.'
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'wear + object + out'; passive 'be worn out'. For objects = deteriorate through use; for people = exhaust. The source joke depends on the ordinary phrasal verb plus sexual context; preserve that context rather than making the quote itself an idiom.

column5: A person seen as excessively virtuous, well-behaved, rule-following, or eager to display goodness.
column7: Don't be such a goody two-shoes—we're five minutes late, not committing a crime.
column8: Tone is usually teasing or critical. 'Prude' concerns sexual/propriety attitudes and is not a general synonym. Often invariant form: a goody two-shoes.

column5: To remove someone from a position, power, office, or place, often forcefully or through political/organizational action; 'ousting' = the act/event.
column7: Shareholders voted to oust the CEO. / His ousting followed months of internal conflict.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FRAME: oust someone from office/power/a role. 'Depose' is especially rulers/leaders; 'evict' is property/tenancy.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::workplace topic::politics topic::debate discovery::removal discovery::debate_language discovery::public_discourse

column2: my legs are like Jell-O / my legs are like jelly
column3: US: /maɪ lɛɡz ɑr laɪk ˈʤɛloʊ/ | UK: /maɪ lɛɡz ɑː laɪk ˈʤɛli/
column5: My legs feel weak, shaky, wobbly, or unable to support me steadily, often from fear, exertion, shock, excitement, or nerves.
column6: my knees are weak, shaky, wobbly
column7: After the climb, my legs were like Jell-O. / When I stepped offstage, my legs felt like jelly.
column8: US branded metaphor often written Jell-O; BrE/general 'jelly'. The image is wobbling gelatin. Related: 'my knees turned to jelly'.

column2: step on someone / step on people to get ahead
column5: Literally, to place one's foot on someone. Figuratively, to exploit, disregard, or harm others in pursuit of one's own advantage, especially in 'step on people to get ahead'.
column6: walk over, exploit, use, trample on (figurative)
column7: He'll step on anyone to get ahead. / Don't let people walk all over you.
column8: CAUTION: 'step on someone' by itself is often literal; the ruthless-ambition sense is strongly supported by context such as 'to get ahead'. Do not present it as a self-contained phrasal verb with only figurative meaning.
column12: entry::construction usage::figurative topic::construction discovery::literal_vs_figurative discovery::process_details discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Continuously or repeatedly without seeming to stop, often to an annoying or exhausting degree.
column7: The dog barked incessantly all night.
column8: Word family: incessant noise/rain/questions. 'Constantly' may be looser in everyday speech; incessantly emphasizes lack of respite.

column5: To act in accordance with a rule, law, standard, request, order, or demand.
column6: obey, conform to, adhere to, follow
column7: All contractors must comply with the safety rules. / She refused to comply with the request.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'comply with + rule/request/order/requirement'. 'Comply' is intransitive here; not 'comply the rule'. Often formal/legal/administrative.
column12: entry::collocation usage::formal usage::bureaucratic topic::law topic::grammar discovery::evaluation discovery::nonconformity

column5: To become stuck, slowed, or unable to progress; transitively, to cause someone/something to become burdened or delayed, often by details, bureaucracy, complexity, mud, etc.
column6: stall, get stuck, slow down, mire
column7: Negotiations bogged down over costs. / Don't get bogged down in minor details. / Bureaucracy bogged the project down.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: a bog is soft wet ground that traps movement. Productive: get/be bogged down in/by; bog something down. Important contrast with WID1701 'boggle'.

column5: Confused, disoriented, flustered, or thrown out of one's normal mental/physical organization.
column6: bewildered, flustered, rattled, out of sorts
column7: Changing trains three times left me completely discombobulated.
column8: Playful word with comic sound; usually less formal than 'disoriented'. Verb 'discombobulate' exists but adjective is especially common.

column5: Having disproportionately more weight, mass, visual emphasis, or strength in the lower part than the upper part.
column6: weighted toward the bottom, lower-heavy, unbalanced
column7: The sculpture looks bottom-heavy. / The roster is bottom-heavy with junior employees.
column8: Hyphenate adjective: bottom-heavy. Can describe bodies, objects, charts/distributions, organizations/rosters. It does not necessarily mean unstable.

column5: A principle in moral reasoning used to distinguish intended effects from foreseen but unintended harmful side effects, under specified conditions, when evaluating an action that has both good and bad effects.
column7: The doctrine of double effect is often discussed in medical ethics.
column8: PRECISION: not simply 'a good action is permissible if harm is unintended'. Traditional formulations also consider the nature of the act, intention, means/end relation, and proportionality; exact formulations differ. 'Ethical paradox' is not a synonym.

column2: mull something over / mull it over
column5: To think carefully about something for a while before deciding, responding, or forming a conclusion.
column6: consider, ponder, think over, chew over
column7: Let me mull it over tonight. / She's mulling over the offer.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'mull + object + over' / 'mull over + noun'. With pronoun, split it: 'mull it over', not normally 'mull over it'.

column5: A loyal subordinate or follower of a powerful person, especially one who carries out violent, criminal, coercive, or dirty work; common in villain stories and political criticism.
column7: The villain sent two henchmen after the hero.
column8: Plural henchmen. 'Sidekick' can be friendly/heroic and is not a close synonym; henchman usually has negative associations.
column12: entry::noun_phrase topic::work topic::politics topic::crime discovery::criticism discovery::loyalty discovery::public_discourse

column5: As an exclamation, used to present a sudden, easy, or seemingly magical result: 'and presto!' In music, a direction meaning very fast.
column6: voilà, just like that; very fast (music)
column7: Click this button and—presto—the chart appears. / The finale is marked presto.
column8: Two distinct uses. In conversational magic/result sense, 'presto!' often theatrically announces a transformation. Music meaning is technical Italian terminology.
column12: entry::interjection usage::conversational usage::technical usage::specialist topic::music discovery::hedging discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To think about or discuss something carefully and at length before reaching a conclusion.
column6: mull over, think over, consider, discuss
column7: Let's chew the idea over before we decide. / I need some time to chew it over.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'chew + object + over'; pronoun split 'chew it over'. Metaphor: mentally 'chew' an idea as food is chewed. Similar to mull over, with slightly more informal flavor.

column5: Literally, a point where a road divides; figuratively, a point where one must choose between different directions, options, or futures.
column7: After graduation, I felt like I was at a fork in the road.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: one path splits into alternatives. Common frame: 'come to/be at/reach a fork in the road'.
column12: entry::idiom entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative usage::instructional topic::decision-making discovery::instruction discovery::figurative_extension

column5: A second attempt at something, usually because the first attempt went badly or should not count.
column7: That interview was awful—I want a do-over. / Can I get a do-over on that question?
column8: KEY FRAMES: want/get/ask for a do-over. Especially AmE and casual; can refer to games, conversations, dates, decisions, etc.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::casual usage::american_english discovery::possibility discovery::iteration

column5: The loss, surrender, or confiscation of property, money, rights, privileges, or another interest as a penalty, legal consequence, or condition.
column7: The court ordered forfeiture of the proceeds of the crime. / Late cancellation may result in forfeiture of the deposit.
column8: Word family with forfeit. Legal asset forfeiture has specific procedures that vary by jurisdiction. Common: forfeiture of property/deposit/rights.

column5: verb: to lose or surrender something as a penalty or consequence, or give up a game/contest. noun: something lost or a penalty; adjective: subject to loss.
column7: The team had to forfeit the match. / You may forfeit your deposit if you cancel late.
column8: KEY FRAMES: forfeit a game/right/deposit; forfeit by failing to appear. Injury may cause withdrawal rather than technically 'forfeit' depending rules, so avoid making injury definitional.

column5: To decrease in monetary/economic value over time; accounting: allocate the cost of a tangible asset over its useful life. Less commonly, to belittle or disparage.
column6: lose value, decline; write down/expense over time (accounting); belittle
column7: Cars often depreciate quickly. / The company depreciates the equipment over five years. / He constantly depreciated his own achievements.
column8: Important distinction: market depreciation vs accounting depreciation. For belittling, 'deprecate' is often confused with depreciate; both have historical overlap, but modern usage differs.

column5: A playful slang form meaning gone, finished, removed, departed, or sometimes mentally 'out of it'; spelling and exact force vary by speaker/source.
column6: gone, done, out of here, out of it
column7: Once the leftovers hit the table, they were gonezo in five minutes.
column8: CORRECTION: do not derive this confidently from journalistic 'gonzo'; the connection is not necessary/secure. Treat 'gonezo/gone-zo' as playful extension of 'gone', with source-dependent meanings/spelling.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::form_family entry::word usage::slang usage::playful usage::journalistic usage::informal

column5: Not shortened by omission; containing the full text/content of a work rather than an abridged version.
column7: I listened to the unabridged audiobook. / This edition is unabridged.
column8: KEY CONTRAST: abridged vs unabridged. Especially books/audiobooks/dictionaries. 'Full-length' may refer to duration/form and is not always equivalent.

column5: A call, text, invitation, or visit whose main purpose is arranging casual sexual activity, often with little expectation of romance/commitment.
column7: That 1 a.m. text sounded like a booty call.
column8: Not synonymous with 'casual fling' (a relationship/encounter rather than the contact/invitation). Informal and potentially objectifying.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::casual usage::slang discovery::commitment

column5: Consistent with a brand's intended identity/image; figuratively, very characteristic of a person's usual style, behavior, preferences, or persona.
column7: The minimalist packaging is on-brand for the company. / Forgetting his own birthday would be completely on-brand for him.
column8: KEY EXTENSION: commercial branding → playful personal-character sense. Opposite: off-brand can mean generic/non-brand-name or inconsistent with one's image, depending context.

column2: anchor something in/to something / be anchored in
column5: To firmly base, ground, secure, or connect something in a foundation, principle, fact, place, or source; literally, to secure with an anchor.
column6: ground in, root in, base on, secure
column7: The argument is anchored in evidence. / She anchors her routine in a few simple habits. / The boat was anchored to the seabed.
column8: NORMALIZE: productive transitive/passive frames are 'anchor X in Y', 'X is anchored in Y', and literal 'anchor X to Y'. 'Anchor in something' alone is incomplete for many figurative uses.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative usage::rhetorical topic::construction discovery::debate_language

column5: Literally, to cut/remove a shape or portion from something; figuratively, to create, obtain, reserve, or establish something through effort—such as time, space, a niche, role, career, or market.
column6: cut out, create, establish, secure, set aside
column7: She carved out time to study. / He carved out a niche in animation criticism. / The river carved out a deep channel.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: create space by cutting it from a larger whole. Productive collocations: carve out time/space/a niche/a career/a role.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::figurative topic::work discovery::promotion discovery::figurative_extension discovery::removal

column5: A creative extension of 'carve out + space/time/niche', meaning to deliberately create a pocket or sense of warmth/comfort within an otherwise cold, bleak, or difficult setting. It is understandable imagery, not a fixed idiom.
column6: create warmth, cultivate comfort, make space for warmth
column7: The film carves out moments of warmth inside an otherwise bleak story.
column8: KEEP AS CREATIVE COLLOCATION: its value comes from applying productive 'carve out' metaphorically to 'warmth'. Do not label it an established idiom; show the underlying construction and contrast with bleak surroundings.

column5: Cold, bare, exposed, or desolate in appearance; grim, depressing, hopeless, or lacking promising prospects.
column7: The winter landscape looked bleak. / The economic outlook is bleak. / The ending is bleak but powerful.
column8: Important physical + figurative senses. Common: bleak landscape/winter/outlook/prospects/future. 'Cold' alone is not sufficient.

column5: Used to acknowledge that another person has made a clever, effective, or fair point against you, especially in witty verbal exchange; originally a fencing term meaning 'touched/hit'.
column6: fair point, well played, you got me
column7: A: You complain about being late, but you were late yesterday. B: Touché.
column8: CORRECTION: spelling takes accent in standard presentation: touché (though touche appears informally). The fencing origin explains the metaphor of conceding a verbal 'hit'.
column12: entry::interjection entry::response_formula entry::discourse_expression entry::fixed_expression usage::figurative usage::presentation-friendly discovery::presentation_language

column2: bum someone out / be bummed out
column5: To make someone sad, disappointed, discouraged, or emotionally deflated; 'be/get bummed out' = feel that way.
column7: The cancellation really bummed me out. / I was bummed out about missing the show.
column8: This overlaps WID1858 and WID2089 family. Preserve for now. KEY ACTIVE/PASSIVE relationship: X bums me out → I am/get bummed out about X.

column5: A joking alteration of 'take it easy', replacing 'easy' with 'sleazy' for comic effect; used as a deliberately unserious farewell.
column7: All right, I'm heading out. Take it sleazy.
column8: KEY WORDPLAY: easy → sleazy rhyme. It is not a general instruction to behave immorally. Strongly associated with humorous/catchphrase use; source context may matter.

column5: Sordid, disreputable, morally dubious, sexually creepy, dishonest, or cheap/shabby in appearance or atmosphere.
column7: The motel had a sleazy feel. / He came across as a sleazy salesman.
column8: Broader than 'corrupt'. Common: sleazy bar/motel/guy/tactic/tabloid. 'Seedy' overlaps shabby/disreputable atmosphere; 'sleazy' often adds moral/sexual unpleasantness.

column2: pity party / throw oneself a pity party
column5: A period or display of self-pity, especially when seen as indulgent, exaggerated, or unproductive.
column7: I gave myself a ten-minute pity party, then got back to work.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: have/throw oneself a pity party; 'pity party for one' is a humorous phrase. Usually mildly mocking, including self-mockery.

column5: The collarbone: either of the paired curved bones connecting the sternum to the shoulder girdle (scapula).
column7: He fractured his clavicle in the fall.
column8: PRECISION: clavicle connects the sternum medially and scapula laterally; 'connects the breastbone to the shoulder' is acceptable everyday shorthand.

column5: A color effect in which one color/tone gradually shades into another, often light-to-dark or between different hues; common in hair, fabric, nails, design, and food decoration.
column7: She chose an ombré hair color that fades from dark brown to copper.
column8: CORRECTION: standard French-derived styling is often 'ombré' (accent commonly retained); 'ombre' also appears in English. The defining feature is gradual transition, not necessarily light-to-dark.

column5: Large, heavy, awkward, complicated, or inefficient enough to be difficult to carry, use, manage, or deal with.
column7: The old camera rig was cumbersome. / The approval process is unnecessarily cumbersome.
column8: Physical + figurative procedural senses. Common: cumbersome equipment/system/process/rules. 'Clumsy' may describe movement/design but is not always equivalent.

column5: Exciting desire, curiosity, or interest by offering something attractive, promising, or suggestive that is not fully available or revealed.
column7: The trailer offered a tantalizing glimpse of the new season. / The smell of bread was tantalizing.
column8: Word derives from Tantalus: something desired is kept just out of reach. Common: tantalizing glimpse/prospect/clue/aroma.

column5: Literally capable of being touched or felt; figuratively, so noticeable or intense that it seems almost physically perceptible.
column7: The tension was palpable. / There was a palpable sense of relief.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: palpable tension/fear/excitement/relief/sense of X. Figurative sense is extremely common. 'Tangible' overlaps but also strongly covers concrete/measurable results.

column5: To turn something upside down or onto its end; figuratively, to overturn, radically disrupt, or transform an established situation, expectation, system, or life.
column6: overturn, tip over; disrupt, overturn, shake up
column7: The wind upended the canoe. / The discovery upended the accepted theory.
column8: Literal physical image motivates figurative disruption. Common: upend assumptions/industry/plans/life.

column2: have a rockin' bod / rocking body
column5: To have a body the speaker considers very attractive, fit, or impressive. 'Rockin''/'rocking' intensifies approval; 'bod' is informal for body.
column6: have a great body, be in great shape, look amazing
column7: She joked that months at the gym had given her a rockin' bod.
column8: KEY COMPONENTS: bod = informal 'body'; rockin'/rocking = excellent/impressive in this slang use. Subjective and body-objectifying, so register/context matter.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::informal usage::slang discovery::social_approval discovery::escalation

column5: To reverse a situation so that the person/group who was disadvantaged gains the advantage, power, or position previously held by the other side.
column6: reverse the situation, gain the upper hand, flip the script
column7: They turned the tables on the defending champions in the second half.
column8: KEY FRAME: 'turn the tables on + person/group'. The idiom specifically involves reversal of roles/advantage, not any generic change.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::debate_language

column5: To mention famous, powerful, or well-connected people one knows or has encountered, especially to impress others or raise one's status; name-dropping = the practice.
column7: He kept name-dropping celebrities he'd met once.
column8: Normalize verb + noun. Can also mention prestigious brands/institutions in broader usage, but people/connections are prototypical. Usually implies showing off.

column5: Lacking social ease, tact, refinement, or sensitivity; awkwardly inappropriate in manner or behavior.
column7: Asking how much the gift cost would be gauche.
column8: Often describes a social act/comment as tasteless or unsophisticated, not merely physically clumsy. French-derived and somewhat educated/formal in tone.

column5: To exercise; to develop or end successfully; to solve/calculate; to devise/arrange; or to understand a result through reasoning.
column6: exercise; succeed; solve, calculate; figure out, arrange
column7: I work out three times a week. / Everything worked out in the end. / Can you work out the total? / We worked out a compromise.
column8: Major polysemy. KEY constructions: work out at the gym; things work out; work out a problem/solution/deal; work out how/why. Noun 'workout' = exercise session.

column5: As a deliberate gesture of acknowledgment, respect, homage, or reference to someone/something.
column6: as a tribute to, in homage to, in recognition of
column7: The costume is a nod to 1980s sci-fi. / They named the room after her as a nod to her contribution.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: a physical nod acknowledges someone; figuratively, a design/detail/reference 'is a nod to' an influence. Also 'a nod toward'.

column5: The act/process or result of erasing, deleting, removing, effacing, or making something absent/invisible; figuratively used of history, identity, culture, contribution, memory, etc.
column7: The essay discusses the erasure of women's contributions from the historical record.
column8: Broader than identity politics. Word family: erase. In social/cultural discussion, 'erasure of X' often means omission or rendering X invisible, not literal deletion.

column5: Spoken, performed, or composed with little or no advance preparation, often using general knowledge or brief notes rather than a fully prepared script.
column7: She gave an extemporaneous response to the question.
column8: NUANCE: in speech/debate education, 'extemporaneous' can mean prepared in a limited period and delivered from notes, not necessarily completely spontaneous. 'Impromptu' may imply even less preparation.

column5: A compact reference containing key facts, formulas, commands, steps, or reminders; originally/also a concealed aid used dishonestly in an exam.
column6: quick-reference sheet, crib sheet, reference guide
column7: I made a cheat sheet of the keyboard shortcuts. / He was caught using a cheat sheet during the test.
column8: Two senses: legitimate quick reference vs academic cheating aid. Modern tech/work use is often entirely neutral.

column5: A compact set of notes used for quick reference; also, especially traditionally, notes secretly used to cheat in an exam.
column6: cheat sheet, crib notes, quick-reference sheet
column7: I keep a crib sheet of Excel shortcuts by my desk.
column8: Very close to cheat sheet. BrE usage may favor 'crib sheet' for a legitimate quick guide as well. 'Crib' can mean copy/plagiarize in other contexts.

column5: For the purpose just mentioned; used to introduce an action, measure, or step intended to achieve a previously stated goal.
column6: for that purpose, with that aim, accordingly
column7: We want to reduce errors. To that end, we're adding a second review pass.
column8: KEY DISCOURSE FUNCTION: previous sentence states GOAL → 'To that end' introduces MEANS/ACTION toward that goal. More formal than 'so'.

column5: To overwhelm or strongly impress someone with charm, romance, excitement, or emotion, especially causing them to fall in love quickly.
column7: He swept her off her feet on their first trip together.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'sweep + person + off their feet'. Romantic sense dominates; metaphor suggests being carried away so strongly one loses ordinary footing/composure.

column5: A diamond represented as not financing armed conflict under a specified sourcing/certification framework. The label does not by itself guarantee that every labor, environmental, or broader human-rights concern is absent.
column6: non-conflict diamond (less common), responsibly sourced diamond (broader/different)
column7: She asked whether the jeweler could document that the diamond was conflict-free.
column8: CORRECTION/PRECISION: 'conflict-free' primarily concerns conflict financing; do not automatically equate it with fully ethical labor practices. 'Ethically sourced' is broader and not a synonym.

column5: Without advance preparation or planning; spontaneously, especially of remarks, answers, speeches, or decisions.
column7: He made the remark off the cuff. / I can give you an off-the-cuff estimate.
column8: KEY FORM: adverbial 'off the cuff'; attributive adjective often hyphenated 'an off-the-cuff remark'. Preserve existing useful contrast: dated AmE 'on the cuff' = on credit, unrelated in meaning.

column2: psych / psyche someone out / psych oneself up / Psych!
column5: Several related informal forms: 'psych someone out' = intimidate, unsettle, or sometimes trick; 'psych oneself/someone up' = mentally energize/prepare; 'Psych!' = a dated/playful reveal that what was just said was a trick/joke. 'Psych' also abbreviates psychology/psychiatry in compounds/context.
column6: intimidate, fake out; hype up, mentally prepare; just kidding!
column7: Don't let him psych you out. / I need to psych myself up for the interview. / 'I got you a car—psych!'
column8: CORRECTION: current card is garbled and conflates constructions. KEY PARTICLES matter: OUT = unsettle/deceive; UP = prepare/energize. Spelling 'sike!' is a nonstandard slang respelling of the interjection.
column12: entry::interjection entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::slang usage::dated usage::playful topic::family topic::psychology topic::planning

column5: To become or cause something to become stuck, wedged, blocked, crowded, or unable to move/function; 'get jammed' describes entering that state.
column7: The paper got jammed in the printer. / The door jammed shut. / Traffic was jammed for miles.
column8: Normalize base + state. Many senses: jam a mechanism, traffic jam, jam something into a space, get jammed in a crowd. 'Jammed' can also mean packed/full.

column5: Sad, disappointed, discouraged, or emotionally deflated.
column7: I was really bummed out about the cancellation.
column8: KEY RELATION with WID2062/1858: something BUMS someone OUT → that person IS/GETS BUMMED OUT. Keep as state-focused recognition card.

column5: To abandon, withdraw from, cancel, or fail to show up for a person, plan, commitment, responsibility, etc., often unexpectedly or at the last minute.
column6: ditch, flake on, back out of, abandon
column7: Don't bail on me tonight. / He bailed on the meeting at the last minute.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'bail on + person/plan/commitment'. Distinguish 'bail out' = escape/rescue, and legal bail.

column5: Money; cash, usually in a playful, informal, or old-fashioned-sounding way.
column7: I don't have enough moolah for a new laptop right now.
column8: CORRECTION: remove unsupported folk etymology connecting cowhide to 'cash cow' and moolah. 'Moolah' is common spelling; origin is uncertain. It does not inherently imply a large sum.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::dated usage::playful

column5: Penance is an act of repentance, self-discipline, or reparation undertaken or assigned in response to wrongdoing, especially in religious contexts; jokingly, 'This is your penance' assigns an unpleasant task as payback.
column7: As penance, he volunteered for the worst chore. / 'You broke it, so cleaning the whole kitchen is your penance.'
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: do penance; as penance; penance for sins/wrongdoing. In Christian traditions, technical meanings vary. Secular use is often humorous and means a corrective/punishing task, not necessarily personal growth.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::conversational usage::technical usage::humorous usage::religious topic::communication topic::religion discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Worn out, weakened, or badly deteriorated through age, long use, or neglect; can describe buildings, vehicles, systems, and sometimes people.
column7: They lived in a decrepit old apartment building. / The bus was ancient and decrepit.
column8: For people, can sound harsh/ageist. 'Dilapidated' is especially buildings/objects; 'frail' specifically physical weakness.

column5: Extremely embarrassed, ashamed, or humiliated; historically/literally related senses exist but modern everyday use overwhelmingly means intensely embarrassed.
column7: I was mortified when I realized my microphone had been on.
column8: KEY FRAME: mortified to discover/learn; mortified by/at something. Stronger than ordinary embarrassed. Do not confuse with 'horrified' = shocked/appalled.

column5: An infection of the throat/tonsils caused by group A Streptococcus bacteria (group A strep), typically causing sore throat and often fever; diagnosis and symptoms vary.
column7: The rapid test was positive for strep throat.
column8: PRECISION: not every bacterial sore throat is 'strep throat'; the common term specifically refers to group A streptococcal pharyngitis. Symptoms such as swollen lymph nodes may occur but are not definitional.
column12: entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist topic::health topic::medicine discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A canopy/sign structure over an entrance, especially a theater, often displaying names/titles; a large event tent in BrE; figuratively/adjectivally, a prominent star, attraction, event, or matchup.
column6: theater sign/canopy; event tent; headline, star
column7: Her name was on the theater marquee. / It was the marquee matchup of the weekend.
column8: Major regional/polysemous senses. KEY figurative collocations: marquee name/player/event/matchup. 'Headliner' is a person/act, not the physical marquee.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::british_english usage::journalistic topic::news discovery::headline_language discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Attractively old-fashioned, picturesque, or charmingly unusual; sometimes used with faint condescension for something seen as outdated or small-scale.
column7: We stayed in a quaint village. / His idea that nobody needs smartphones now seems almost quaint.
column8: Add ironic/condescending extension: 'quaint notion/idea'. Usually positive for places/objects, but tone matters.

column5: Cheerful, lively, energetic, and upbeat; also physically firm/upright or sticking up in some contexts.
column7: She's surprisingly perky this morning. / The puppy's perky ears stood straight up.
column8: Broaden beyond personality. Body-description uses (e.g., 'perky breasts') exist and can be objectifying; recognition depends on context.

column5: Under sustained pressure, criticism, attack, or difficulty; historically/literally besieged or surrounded by hostile forces.
column7: The beleaguered company is trying to regain customers. / Reinforcements reached the beleaguered city.
column8: Literal siege sense motivates figurative 'beset by problems'. Common: beleaguered government/company/leader/team.

column5: Commanding respect because of age, long service, history, wisdom, achievement, or established reputation.
column7: The venerable institution is more than a century old. / A venerable professor introduced the lecture.
column8: Often combines age/history + respect; not simply 'old'. Can describe people, institutions, traditions, buildings. In some religious contexts 'Venerable' is a formal title/status.

column5: To keep thinking, talking, or writing about something for an extended time, especially something troubling or unproductive.
column6: brood over, linger on, fixate on, harp on (talking repeatedly)
column7: Try not to dwell on the mistake. / The review dwells on the film's weakest scene.
column8: KEY FRAME: dwell on/upon + topic/event. 'Upon' is more formal. Often negative, but can neutrally mean discuss/consider at length.

column5: Certainly; absolutely. Used to strongly confirm a statement, answer yes, or intensify certainty.
column6: absolutely, certainly, definitely, without a doubt
column7: 'Would you go back?' 'Most definitely.' / That was most definitely the right choice.
column8: Can stand alone or modify a statement. More emphatic/conversational than plain 'definitely'.

column2: be wound tight / be wound a little tight
column5: To be tense, highly strung, easily stressed, or tightly self-controlled.
column7: He's wound a little tight before big presentations. / She seems pretty tightly wound today.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: like a spring wound tightly and ready to release. Variants: tightly wound; wound too tight. Do not confuse with 'wound up' (WID2104), which can also mean excited/agitated.

column2: be wound up / get wound up
column5: To be or become tense, agitated, excited, or emotionally worked up; also 'wind someone up' can provoke/tease someone, especially BrE.
column6: worked up, agitated, keyed up, excited
column7: She's wound up about the interview. / Don't get so wound up over one comment.
column8: KEY STATE/CHANGE: be wound up; get wound up about/over X. Related active verb 'wind someone up' has additional teasing/provoking sense.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::british_english topic::weather topic::construction discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: Cold, bare, or desolate; figuratively, grim, depressing, or offering little hope.
column7: The outlook looks bleak. / The winter landscape was bleak and empty.
column8: Normalize away from fixed 'something is bleak'. This overlaps WID2060; preserve as a predicative-pattern card under no-auto-delete.

column5: Lacking energy, brilliance, enthusiasm, distinction, or effectiveness; disappointingly dull or mediocre.
column7: The finale was surprisingly lackluster. / Sales remained lackluster all quarter.
column8: AmE lackluster; BrE lacklustre. Common: lackluster performance/results/sales/reception.

column5: An elaborate confidence scheme carried out over an extended period, often by slowly building the target's trust before the payoff.
column6: long-term scam, confidence trick, elaborate fraud
column7: The whole friendship turned out to be part of a long con.
column8: KEY COMPONENT: con = confidence trick/scam; long = extended setup. Contrast a quick/short con. Also used figuratively for a prolonged deception.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::informal topic::crime discovery::social_trust

column5: To complete something in a satisfying or suitable way; also to make a number less exact by rounding it.
column7: We rounded off the evening with dessert. / Round the total off to the nearest dollar.
column8: IMPORTANT POLYSEMY: event/discourse sense 'round off X with Y'; numerical sense 'round X off/up/down'.

column5: To scatter or spread in different directions; transitively, to cause a group/substance to spread; of light/particles, to separate or distribute.
column7: The crowd dispersed peacefully. / Wind dispersed the smoke.
column8: Can be intransitive or transitive. 'Dissolve' is not a general synonym. Related noun: dispersion.

column5: To survive, recover, or successfully get through a serious illness, crisis, danger, or difficult period.
column7: The doctors think she'll pull through. / The company somehow pulled through the recession.
column8: KEY FRAME: pull through + optionally 'a crisis/illness'; often used without object when survival/recovery is understood.

column5: To be consistent, compatible, or in agreement with something; transitively, to bring things into such agreement or physical alignment.
column6: match, correspond with, be consistent with, harmonize with
column7: Her priorities align with mine. / We need to align the schedule with the new deadline.
column8: KEY FRAMES: X aligns with Y; align X with Y. 'Align well/closely' adds degree.

column5: Considering or taking into account a fact or circumstance. 'Given + noun phrase'; 'given that + clause'.
column6: considering, in view of, taking into account
column7: Given the weather, we stayed home. / Given that it's raining, we should reschedule.
column8: CORRECTION: distinguish grammar explicitly. 'Given that' is conjunction-like; 'given + NP' is prepositional. It introduces a premise/circumstance, not necessarily a causal 'because'.

column5: Used to introduce a contrasting, opposite, or balancing aspect of the same issue.
column6: on the other hand, conversely, alternatively
column7: Working from home saves commuting time. On the flip side, it can feel isolating.
column8: KEY DISCOURSE ROLE: presents the other side/trade-off. Informal. Repair punctuation contamination in current example.

column2: a dash of something / add a dash of something
column5: A small amount of something added to a mixture, style, mood, or presentation; literally common with seasonings/liquids and figuratively with qualities.
column6: a touch of, a hint of, a splash of
column7: Add a dash of salt. / The dialogue adds a dash of humor to an otherwise dark episode.
column8: KEY FRAME: a dash of + substance/quality; add a dash of X to Y. Figurative extension comes from adding a small ingredient.
column12: entry::collocation entry::noun_phrase entry::construction usage::figurative usage::presentation-friendly topic::presentations discovery::presentation_language discovery::figurative_extension

column2: run someone's life / run one's own life
column5: To control or manage a person's life and decisions; 'run my own life' = manage one's own affairs, while 'Don't run my life' rejects another person's control.
column7: Don't try to run my life. / She's perfectly capable of running her own life.
column8: KEY POSSESSION determines meaning: run MY OWN life = manage it; run SOMEONE ELSE'S life = control them. Repair current punctuation.

column5: With conspicuous success or distinction, especially in passing a test, inspection, challenge, or evaluation.
column7: She passed the exam with flying colors. / The system passed every test with flying colors.
column8: Established form normally includes WITH. Historical imagery relates to victorious ships displaying colors/flags.

column2: get the hang of something / get the hang of it
column5: To learn the practical knack or become comfortable with how to do something after some practice.
column6: get used to, figure out, master the basics of, pick up
column7: It took a few tries, but I got the hang of it. / You'll soon get the hang of using the controls.
column8: KEY FRAME: get the hang of + noun/gerund/it. Usually suggests practical familiarity rather than complete mastery.

column5: A concise summary that preserves the essential points or structure of a longer text, speech, or argument.
column7: The assignment was to write a précis of the article.
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling is 'précis' (often 'precis' when accents are omitted). Pronunciation varies by variety. More formal/academic than ordinary 'summary'.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::academic usage::rhetorical topic::public_speaking discovery::summary discovery::academic_discussion discovery::debate_language

column5: Following a familiar formula, template, or conventional pattern, often so predictably that it lacks freshness or originality.
column7: The plot is formulaic, but the characters are charming.
column8: Can be neutral in technical contexts (formulaic language/sequences), but criticism often implies mechanical predictability.

column2: be onto something / you're onto something
column5: To have found or be developing an idea, clue, explanation, or approach that seems promising, important, or correct.
column6: be on the right track, have something, be getting somewhere
column7: I think you're onto something with that theory. / The researchers may be onto something.
column8: NORMALIZE from gerund headword. KEY FRAME: be onto something with + idea/approach. Distinguish 'be onto someone' = suspect/understand what a person is doing.

column5: To include or integrate something as part of a larger whole; also, legally, to form a corporation.
column6: integrate, include, build in; form a corporation
column7: We incorporated more examples into the lesson. / The business was incorporated in Delaware.
column8: KEY FRAME: incorporate X into Y. Add important corporate/legal sense. 'Combine' is broader.

column5: To simplify or redesign a process/system to make it more efficient; literally, to shape something to reduce resistance. 'Streamlining' is the process.
column7: We're streamlining the review workflow. / The streamlined body reduces drag.
column8: Normalize family and connect to WID1992. Figurative efficiency sense comes from aerodynamic streamlining.

column5: A gesture or expression of emphatic approval meaning something is exceptionally good, satisfying, stylish, or perfectly executed.
column7: That final shot was chef's kiss. / The sauce? Chef's kiss.
column8: Originally evokes a chef kissing fingertips in approval; now common online/textual shorthand. Can be sincere or ironic.

column5: To irritate or annoy someone.
column6: annoy, irritate, bother, vex, grate on
column7: It irks me when people cut in line. / His smug tone really irked her.
column8: Productive frame: X irks someone / it irks me that... This is the normalized form previously chosen for nonstandard 'irk out'.

column5: A return phone call; a request to return for a later audition/interview; in comedy/storytelling, a deliberate reference back to an earlier joke/detail; in programming, a function invoked later in response to an event/result.
column6: return call, second audition; recurring reference; callback function
column7: She got a callback after the audition. / The finale contains a clever callback to episode one.
column8: CORRECTION: current definition misses major comedy/storytelling and programming senses. Normalize singular/plural.

column5: Verb: to move or fluctuate in small rapid irregular movements, especially technically. 'The jitters' = nervousness/anxious shakiness. 'Jitter' is also variation in timing/latency in technical systems.
column7: The image jittered on screen. / Too much coffee gives me the jitters. / Network jitter can disrupt real-time audio.
column8: CORRECTION: not 'typically a present participle'. The nervous-person sense is much more idiomatic as 'have/get the jitters' than 'jittered at every sound'.
column12: entry::idiom entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Serious or persistent difficulty, hardship, misfortune, or unfavorable circumstances.
column7: She stayed focused in the face of adversity.
column8: Often uncountable/general: face/overcome adversity; adversity can also refer collectively to adverse circumstances.

column5: A physical position offering a useful view, or figuratively a position/perspective from which something can be understood or judged.
column7: From this vantage point, we can see the whole valley. / From a historian's vantage point, the change looks gradual.
column8: KEY FRAME: from a vantage point / from the vantage point of X. Physical view → figurative perspective.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::figurative_extension discovery::evaluation discovery::debate_language

column5: Verb: to restrain, limit, or control something undesirable. Noun: the raised edge beside a street (AmE; BrE 'kerb'), and figuratively a restraint/check.
column7: The city wants to curb pollution. / He parked beside the curb.
column8: Major noun sense missing. Common verb objects: curb spending/emissions/violence/enthusiasm.

column5: To say something suddenly and impulsively, without sufficient thought or restraint.
column7: I accidentally blurted out the answer. / She blurted the secret out before I could stop her.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: blurt out + content; blurt X out. Often accidental revelation, but not always.

column5: To argue, object, or raise minor distinctions about small or technical points, often avoiding the main issue; noun: a minor objection or criticism.
column6: nitpick, split hairs, haggle over details
column7: We're quibbling over wording instead of solving the problem. / I have one small quibble with the conclusion.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FRAME: quibble over/about X; noun 'a quibble'.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical usage::debate-friendly discovery::debate_language discovery::criticism discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To suffocate by depriving of air; cover thickly/completely; extinguish by cutting off oxygen; or overwhelm someone with excessive affection, attention, or control.
column7: She smothered the fire with a blanket. / The fries were smothered in cheese. / He felt smothered by constant attention.
column8: Major productive senses. KEY: smother X with/in Y; be smothered by affection/control.

column5: To defeat or surpass someone by a small margin; also to gradually displace or exclude someone/something from a position or market.
column6: narrowly beat, pip (BrE); displace, squeeze out
column7: She edged him out by one vote. / Streaming gradually edged DVDs out of the market.
column8: Add displacement sense. KEY FRAME: edge X out (of Y); narrow-victory sense often 'edge out a rival'.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::british_english usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::promotion discovery::debate_language

column5: An activity done regularly for enjoyment or relaxation rather than as one's main work.
column7: Reading is one of my favorite pastimes.
column8: CORRECTION: remove unrelated 'pastoral village' sentence from example. Spelling: pastime, not 'past time'.

column5: A sign or expression of endorsement, acceptance, or authoritative approval, whether formal or figurative.
column7: The proposal finally got the CEO's seal of approval. / Her recommendation gave the restaurant a seal of approval.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: an official seal authenticates/authorizes; figuratively, someone's support functions as that seal. Common: get/give/receive someone's seal of approval.

column5: To deliberately provoke, bait, disrupt, or deceive people online for reaction/amusement; 'troll' can mean the person or the act. Broader online use sometimes labels insincere provocative behavior.
column7: He's trolling the replies for attention. / Don't feed the trolls.
column8: Modern usage is broader than simply posting 'off-topic' messages. KEY phrase: 'Don't feed the trolls' = don't reward provocation with engagement.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::form_family entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::informal topic::internet

column2: play off / playoff / play off against
column5: In sports, teams/players may 'play off' or 'play off against each other' to decide a tie/qualification; noun 'playoff' = deciding postseason/tiebreak competition. 'Play X off against Y' also means manipulate rivals against each other.
column6: play a decider, face off; pit against
column7: The teams will play off for the final spot. / The manager played the two departments off against each other.
column8: CORRECTION: 'play off with each other' is unnatural for the intended sports sense. Distinguish verb 'play off' from noun/adjective 'playoff'.

column2: get off / get off on something
column5: A highly polysemous phrasal verb: leave a vehicle/surface; finish work; escape punishment; remove something; and slang 'get off on X' = derive strong excitement, pleasure, or sexual arousal from X.
column6: leave, disembark; escape; enjoy, be turned on by
column7: We get off the train at the next stop. / He got off with a warning. / She gets off on taking risks.
column8: KEY PARTICLE FRAME for pleasure sense: get off ON + stimulus. Without 'on', context may instead mean orgasm, disembark, finish work, escape punishment, etc.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::slang usage::informal topic::work topic::automotive discovery::removal

column5: Anger or strong displeasure aroused by something perceived as unjust, insulting, improper, or morally wrong.
column7: She reacted with indignation to the accusation.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: righteous indignation; indignation at/over/about X; express indignation. Implies a judgment of wrongness, not generic anger.

column5: Bold or daring willingness to take risks; very often, shameless or presumptuous boldness that shocks or offends.
column7: She had the audacity to blame me for her mistake. / I admired the audacity of the plan.
column8: IMPORTANT polarity: can be admiring ('boldness') or indignant ('the audacity!'). Current definition overfocuses personal safety.

column5: Flexible, pliant, and able to bend/move smoothly; figuratively, adaptable or responsive.
column7: Yoga kept her body supple. / The leather stays supple with proper care.
column8: Can describe body, leather/material, prose/mind metaphorically. 'Lithe' usually describes graceful bodies/movement.

column5: To secure or settle something decisively, especially a victory, title, deal, or argument; to grip/hold tightly. Noun: a close grappling hold, especially in boxing/wrestling.
column7: The goal clinched the championship. / The fighters fell into a clinch.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: clinch a deal/victory/title/nomination. Add combat-sports noun sense.
column12: entry::word usage::rhetorical usage::military discovery::title_language discovery::resolution discovery::debate_language

column5: A thin, flexible layer of tissue or material that covers, lines, separates, or selectively controls passage between structures.
column7: The cell membrane controls movement of substances into and out of the cell. / The eardrum is a thin membrane.
column8: Biological membranes often have functional permeability; engineered membranes can filter/separate. 'Tissue' is not a universal synonym.

column5: To gradually damage or be damaged by chemical/electrochemical reaction; figuratively, to gradually weaken or destroy trust, values, institutions, etc.
column7: Salt water corroded the metal. / Years of secrecy corroded public trust.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Rusting is one type of corrosion, not a synonym for all materials.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word topic::chemistry topic::grammar topic::science discovery::figurative_extension discovery::social_trust

column5: A broad, thick, relatively flat piece of solid material such as concrete, stone, wood, or food; informally, a large thick piece.
column7: They poured a concrete slab. / He cut a thick slab of bread.
column8: Productive: concrete slab, stone slab, slab of meat/bread. 'Plate' is only a technical/contextual overlap.

column5: A spiral/helical boring tool used to drill holes or move material, especially in wood, soil, ice, grain, or plumbing; verb: to bore/drill with an auger.
column7: We used an ice auger to drill a fishing hole. / The crew augered holes for the posts.
column8: Broaden noun + verb. A gimlet is a smaller hand boring tool, not a general synonym.

column5: To soothe or cause someone to become calm, sleepy, or less alert; figuratively, to make someone feel falsely safe. Noun: a temporary quiet period.
column6: soothe, calm; reassure falsely; quiet spell
column7: The waves lulled me to sleep. / Early success lulled them into complacency. / There was a lull in the conversation.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTIONS: lull someone to sleep; lull someone into a false sense of security/complacency. Add noun sense.

column5: A plant/root (Glycyrrhiza species) with a distinctive sweet flavor, and products/candies flavored with licorice or similar flavorings.
column7: Black licorice has a distinctive flavor. / Licorice root is used in some teas and confections.
column8: CORRECTION: not inherently 'a chewy candy'; the word also names the plant/root/flavor. AmE licorice; BrE liquorice.

column5: Of clothing/fabric, loose, soft, draping, and able to move or flow freely rather than fitting tightly or stiffly.
column7: She wore a flowy summer dress. / I like flowy shirts in hot weather.
column8: Common fashion term; informal but established. 'Billowy' suggests more volume; 'breezy' can describe feel/style.

column5: To make or produce a continuous low humming, vibrating, or rhythmic sound; noun: such a sound/vibration. Also historically to strum/pluck.
column7: The engine thrummed beneath us. / The room thrummed with bass and conversation.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Figurative 'thrum with energy/activity' is productive.

column5: The inside part of something; adjective: situated within or relating to the inside. Also the inland part of a country/region.
column7: The car's interior is spacious. / Interior walls were repainted. / They traveled into the country's interior.
column8: Add adjective and geographic sense. Contrast exterior.

column5: To prevent someone from accomplishing a plan or prevent an action/outcome from succeeding.
column7: The alarm thwarted the burglary. / Bad weather thwarted our plans.
column8: KEY OBJECTS: thwart a plan/attempt/attack; thwart someone. 'Foil' is especially close for preventing a plan.

column5: A fresh start in which previous mistakes, obligations, records, or conflicts are treated as cleared or no longer controlling the future.
column7: Moving gave him a chance to start with a clean slate. / Let's wipe the slate clean and begin again.
column8: Related construction: wipe the slate clean = forgive/erase past problems. Metaphor comes from erasing writing from a slate.

column5: To gradually become smaller, fewer, weaker, or less plentiful.
column7: Our savings began to dwindle. / The crowd dwindled to a handful of people.
column8: Usually intransitive. KEY FRAMES: dwindle to + small amount; dwindle away. Suggests gradual reduction.

column5: To enter, begin, or become accustomed to something gradually and gently rather than abruptly.
column6: transition gradually, settle into, gradually start
column7: I'm easing back into exercise. / She eased into her new role over several weeks.
column8: Broaden beyond familiarity. KEY FRAME: ease into + role/routine/activity/conversation; also ease back into.

column5: Historically, a large traveling case/suitcase opening into compartments; in linguistics, a blend word combining form and meaning from two or more words, such as brunch.
column7: 'Brunch' is a portmanteau of breakfast and lunch.
column8: CORRECTION: a portmanteau word is a BLEND, not generally a compound. The linguistic sense comes from Lewis Carroll's metaphor of packing meanings into one word.

column5: At the same time or during overlapping periods; in law, of sentences served at the same time rather than consecutively.
column6: simultaneously, in parallel, at the same time
column7: She worked two jobs concurrently. / The judge ordered the sentences to run concurrently.
column8: Add important legal collocation: concurrent vs consecutive sentences. In computing, concurrent processes need not execute at the exact same instant.

column5: To take a short pause or rest, especially to recover physically or mentally before continuing.
column6: take a break, pause, catch one's breath
column7: Let's take a breather before the next section.
column8: Usually a brief temporary break, not a long vacation. Literal breathing image → figurative pause.

column5: Noun, dated: a regular walk taken for health/exercise, especially 'take one's constitutional'. Adjective: relating to a constitution; inherent in a person's physical/mental makeup.
column7: He took his morning constitutional. / The court considered a constitutional question.
column8: CORRECTION: current card omits overwhelmingly common adjective senses. Preserve quirky noun but teach the family.

column5: A foolish, annoying, obnoxious, or contemptible person; generally childish/comic rather than highly severe.
column7: Don't be a butthead—just apologize.
column8: Repair punctuation. Register: juvenile/informal insult; also culturally recognizable from 'Beavis and Butt-Head'.

column5: A military formation consisting of multiple battalions/regiments depending system; also an organized group for a task (fire brigade). Online, 'brigade' can mean coordinate a group to flood/interfere with another community.
column6: military unit, organized group; coordinate mass participation
column7: The fire brigade arrived quickly. / The post was accused of sending users to brigade another forum.
column8: Major modern internet sense useful alongside military/civic sense. Exact military organization varies by armed force.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::military usage::informal topic::internet topic::military

column5: A large organized meeting; an accepted custom/practice; an agreed rule or standard; a formal international agreement; in storytelling/art, a familiar genre device.
column7: The fan convention drew thousands. / By convention, variables are written this way. / The treaty is an international convention.
column8: Highly polysemous. Common: social convention, naming convention, genre convention, political convention.
column12: entry::word usage::formal topic::culture topic::art discovery::professional_context discovery::agreement discovery::evaluation

column5: The underlying reasoning, basis, or set of reasons explaining why something is done, believed, designed, or decided.
column7: What's the rationale for changing the rule? / She explained the rationale behind the design.
column8: KEY FRAMES: rationale for + action; rationale behind + decision. More than a single 'reason': often the reasoning structure.

column5: The process/state of being raised to a higher-energy or activated state; used technically in physics, chemistry, neuroscience, physiology, and engineering.
column7: Absorption of light can cause electronic excitation. / Neural excitation increases the likelihood that a neuron will fire.
column8: CORRECTION: current atom/electron wording is awkward. Technical meaning depends on field; ordinary emotional 'excitement' is normally preferred outside technical contexts.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::scientific topic::physics topic::chemistry topic::engineering topic::science discovery::process_details discovery::transition discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The act/process of restraining, suppressing, or reducing an action/process; psychology: conscious/social restraint; biology/neuroscience: reduction of activity or response.
column7: Alcohol can reduce social inhibitions. / Neural inhibition helps regulate activity.
column8: Important plural 'inhibitions' = self-conscious restraints. Technical excitation/inhibition are paired concepts in neuroscience.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::scientific topic::communication topic::psychology topic::biology topic::science discovery::constraints discovery::process_details discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A deadlock or situation in which progress cannot continue because the parties or available paths cannot resolve an obstacle.
column7: Negotiations reached an impasse after both sides refused to compromise.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: reach/hit an impasse; break the impasse. Current examples are duplicative; consolidate.

column5: An old-fashioned minced oath expressing surprise, alarm, or emphasis.
column7: Gadzooks! What happened here?
column8: Archaic/comic recognition word. Historically a euphemistic oath, traditionally explained as a shortening of 'God's hooks' (the nails of the Crucifixion), though etymological accounts should be treated cautiously.

column5: A simple brass wind instrument, traditionally without valves, used especially for military signals; verb: to sound a bugle or make a bugle-like call.
column7: The bugle sounded reveille. / An elk bugled in the distance.
column8: CORRECTION/PRECISION: not simply 'similar to a trumpet'; traditional bugle lacks valves and plays notes of the harmonic series. Add animal-call verb sense.

column5: A connected cluster of boils caused by bacterial infection beneath the skin; figuratively, an ugly or intrusive building/object, especially in BrE commentary.
column6: cluster of boils, skin abscess; eyesore (figurative)
column7: The doctor treated a carbuncle on his back. / Critics called the proposed tower an architectural carbuncle.
column8: Medical distinction: a carbuncle is typically a deeper interconnected cluster of furuncles/boils, not just any abscess. Add established figurative eyesore sense.

column5: A playful or rare formation that may be used for cozy sleeping/snuggling/nuzzling, but it is not a broadly standard everyday English verb with one stable meaning.
column7: The caption jokingly described the puppy as 'snoozling' into the blanket.
column8: CORRECTION: do not teach a stable standard definition. Likely blends/echoes snooze, snuggle, nuzzle; preserve only with source context.

column5: Used to say that a person was unaware at the time of an important, surprising, or ironic fact that would become clear later.
column7: Little did I know, that conversation would change everything. / Little did she know that he had already left.
column8: KEY GRAMMAR: negative/fronted 'Little' triggers subject–auxiliary inversion: 'Little did I/she/they know...', not 'Little I knew'. Productive pronoun substitution.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::ironic topic::construction discovery::lack_of_knowledge discovery::perception

column5: Habitually avoiding effort or activity; lazy. In medicine, 'indolent' can mean slow-growing or causing relatively little pain.
column7: He led an indolent life of leisure. / The tumor was described as indolent.
column8: Important medical sense: indolent disease/tumor = slow-progressing, not 'lazy'. Formal/literary for people.

column5: Suffocating/covering; figuratively, excessively protective, affectionate, controlling, or attention-heavy in a way that restricts another person.
column7: Her parents' constant checking felt smothering. / Smoke was smothering the room.
column8: Connect to base verb WID2139. As adjective, 'smothering attention/love/parenting' emphasizes excessive restriction.

column5: Physically unsteady or emotionally overwhelmed by fear, attraction, excitement, shock, admiration, etc.
column7: That roller coaster left me weak at the knees. / His smile makes her weak at the knees.
column8: Not limited to romance. KEY FRAME: make/leave someone weak at the knees; go/feel weak at the knees.

column2: meet in the middle / meet halfway
column5: To compromise by each side moving away from its original position toward a mutually acceptable solution.
column6: compromise, split the difference, meet halfway
column7: I wanted 8 and she wanted 10, so we met in the middle at 9. / Can we meet halfway on the deadline?
column8: KEY METAPHOR: both sides move toward the center. 'Split the difference' specifically averages a numerical gap; broader compromises need not be exactly equal.
column12: entry::idiom usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::problem-solving topic::debate discovery::compromise discovery::solution_framing discovery::trade-off discovery::resolution discovery::debate_language

column5: To secure, stabilize, or ground something physically or figuratively; 'anchoring' is the act/process. In psychology/decision-making, anchoring is bias toward an initial reference value.
column7: Her routine anchors her during stressful weeks. / The first price can create an anchoring effect in negotiation.
column8: Connect to WID2057. Add major cognitive-bias sense: anchor/anchoring effect.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word topic::psychology topic::decision-making discovery::process_details discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Certainly; please do; used to grant permission or strongly encourage an action. In some contexts, also emphatically 'in every possible way'.
column7: 'May I open the window?' 'By all means.'
column8: Most common conversational use grants permission/encouragement. Do not confuse with 'by any means' = using whatever method is necessary.
column12: entry::idiom entry::discourse_expression entry::prepositional_phrase usage::conversational discovery::encouragement discovery::possibility

column5: A new, unfamiliar, unexplored, or unprecedented situation where established guidance or experience is limited.
column6: unknown territory, new ground, unexplored area
column7: We're entering uncharted territory with this technology. / The company is navigating uncharted waters.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: places not yet mapped → situations without a known map/precedent. Common variant 'uncharted waters'.

column5: To have a strong ambition or hope to achieve, become, or attain something, usually elevated or difficult.
column7: She aspires to become a writer. / The project aspires to something more ambitious.
column8: KEY GRAMMAR: aspire TO + noun / TO BE or TO DO. 'Aspire for' is generally nonstandard for this meaning.

column5: To compete eagerly for something, or compete with someone for superiority, attention, position, etc.
column7: Several companies are vying for the contract. / Two candidates vied with each other for the nomination.
column8: KEY FRAMES: vie for + prize/position/attention; vie with + competitor. Usually intransitive; 'battle' can imply stronger conflict.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::debate-friendly topic::debate topic::construction discovery::debate_language

column5: Historically, a crew car attached to the rear of a North American freight train; informally, the rear/end of something and sometimes the buttocks.
column7: The old freight train had a red caboose. / Move your caboose!
column8: PRECISION: cabooses are no longer standard on most modern North American freight trains. Slang body sense is playful/dated.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::slang usage::dated usage::playful usage::north_american_english topic::history topic::transportation topic::automotive

column5: The act/state of severing a connection; especially employment compensation/benefits provided when a job ends ('severance pay/package').
column7: She negotiated a severance package. / The severance of diplomatic ties shocked observers.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: severance pay/package/agreement; severance of ties/relations. It is compensation associated with termination, not the dismissal itself.

column5: A sharp, forceful blow or the sound of one; to strike with such a blow.
column7: The ball hit the fence with a thwack. / She thwacked the cushion with a pillow.
column8: Onomatopoeic/sound-symbolic. Can emphasize either impact or sound.

column5: A foolish, silly, awkward, or inept person, usually a mild/comic insult.
column7: You doofus—you left your keys inside again.
column8: Connect with WID1734 doof and WID1727 dingus. Usually lighter than 'idiot' depending tone. Repair punctuation.

column5: To stare openly, fixedly, or rudely, often from curiosity, amazement, or lack of social restraint.
column7: Tourists stopped to gawk at the enormous sculpture. / Stop gawking and keep moving.
column8: Normalize base + source form. 'Ogle' usually adds sexual/appraising interest; not a general synonym.

column5: A foolish, inept, or clueless person; generally a mild/comic insult.
column7: I locked myself out again—what a numpty.
column8: Chiefly British/Scottish-associated informal usage. Often affectionate/self-deprecating as well as insulting. Repair punctuation.

column5: Suggesting or implying something indirectly; often specifically sexually suggestive, but also capable of suggesting an idea, diagnosis, interpretation, or resemblance.
column7: The dialogue is mildly suggestive. / The symptoms are suggestive of an infection.
column8: IMPORTANT FRAME: suggestive OF + interpretation/condition. Sexual meaning is common but not inherent.

column5: Arousing pleasurable excitement, curiosity, or interest, especially through provocative, sensational, or mildly sexual material.
column7: The headline was titillating but not very informative.
column8: Often carries a slightly disapproving implication of superficial/sensational stimulation. Sexual association is common but not mandatory.

column5: A flirtatious game of touching another person's feet/legs under a table; figuratively, 'play footsie with' can mean flirt, court favor, or maintain cozy dealings with someone/group.
column6: flirt, flirt under the table; cozy up to (figurative)
column7: They were playing footsie under the table. / The politician was accused of playing footsie with extremists.
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling is 'footsie', not 'footsy'. Add important figurative 'play footsie with' sense.
column12: entry::idiom entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::figurative topic::romance discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To try to equal or surpass someone/something admired by imitating their methods, qualities, or achievements; in computing, to reproduce the behavior of another system.
column6: imitate, model oneself on, match; simulate (computing context)
column7: She tried to emulate her mentor's discipline. / The software emulates an older game console.
column8: Important computing sense. Nuance: emulate often implies imitation with aspiration to equal/match, not mere copying.

column5: A trusted person with whom one shares private or confidential thoughts, feelings, or information.
column7: She became his closest confidant during a difficult year.
column8: Do not confuse with 'confident' (adjective). 'Confidant' is now commonly used for any gender; 'confidante' is a traditional feminine form.

column5: Wrongdoing, misconduct, or an unlawful act, especially by a public official or someone in a position of responsibility.
column6: misconduct, wrongdoing, corruption, abuse of office
column7: The investigation found evidence of official malfeasance.
column8: Often occurs as 'malfeasance in office'. In legal usage, exact distinctions among malfeasance, misfeasance, and nonfeasance vary by jurisdiction/context.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::debate-friendly topic::workplace topic::law topic::debate discovery::debate_language

column5: An insulting, old-fashioned term for a woman regarded as brazen, sexually improper, or badly behaved.
