column7: The period drama has a character sneer, 'You little hussy!'
column8: Strongly gendered and dated; recognition-focused. Avoid treating other misogynistic slurs as clean synonyms because tone/severity differ.

column5: To hit a mailbox with enough force that it falls over, accidentally or deliberately.
column7: He lost control of the car and knocked over a mailbox.
column8: CORRECTION: this is not an idiom. KEY CONSTRUCTION: 'knock + object + over' = cause it to fall/topple; mailbox is simply the source object.

column3: /ɪt ɪz ˈnʌθɪŋ tə raɪt hoʊm əˌbaʊt/
column5: Not especially good, impressive, unusual, or noteworthy; merely ordinary or mediocre.
column7: The food was fine, but nothing to write home about.
column8: Common frame: 'X is/was nothing to write home about.' Often mildly negative rather than strongly critical.

column5: To continue through difficulty, resistance, fatigue, discomfort, or an obstacle until reaching the other side or completing something; transitively, also to force a proposal/process through.
column6: persevere, power through, press on; force through
column7: I was tired, but I pushed through and finished the workout. / They pushed the bill through despite opposition.
column8: KEY FORMS: push through; push through it; push X through. CAUTION: pain/illness is not always something one should simply 'push through'; source example with fever was poor general advice.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern usage::journalistic topic::media topic::problem-solving discovery::process_details discovery::suggestion discovery::continuity

column5: To expose one's bare buttocks to someone as a prank, insult, or act of provocation, sometimes from a moving vehicle.
column7: A passenger leaned out and mooned the car behind them.
column8: CORRECTION: 'moon in driving' is not a natural English construction. Productive forms are 'moon someone', 'moon at someone', or describe 'mooning from a car'.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::slang topic::automotive

column5: Being prosecuted or punished again for the same offense after a legally significant prior proceeding; the precise protection and when it attaches vary by legal system.
column6: second prosecution for the same offense (descriptive)
column7: The defense argued that a second trial would violate the rule against double jeopardy.
column8: PRECISION: do not state a universal rule across all legal systems. In U.S. constitutional law, the Double Jeopardy Clause has specific requirements/exceptions; 'repeat trial' is not a true synonym.
column12: entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist topic::law discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column2: wouldn't put it past someone (to do something)
column5: Used to say you believe someone is quite capable of doing something surprising, sneaky, dishonest, extreme, etc.
column6: wouldn't be surprised if, consider someone capable of
column7: I wouldn't put it past him to fake the whole thing. / I wouldn't put that past her.
column8: CORRECTION: core idiom is normally NEGATIVE: 'I wouldn't put it past someone (to...)'. 'Put it past you' alone does not mean the same thing.

column2: loose end / tie up loose ends
column5: An unresolved detail, unfinished task, or remaining problem; 'tie up loose ends' = finish or resolve the remaining details.
column6: unfinished business, unresolved detail, outstanding matter
column7: I have a few loose ends to tie up before I leave. / Let's tie up the loose ends before launch.
column8: Teach the productive idiom, not only the noun. Singular 'a loose end'; plural is especially common in 'tie up loose ends'.

column5: A cereal grass (genus Sorghum) cultivated for grain, animal feed, syrup, biofuel, and other uses; also the grain/product itself.
column7: Sorghum is drought-tolerant and widely grown in hot, dry regions.
column8: CORRECTION: remove mojibake/garbled text. Sorghum is not simply a synonym of millet; they are different cereal crops.

column5: Bold, cheeky, or disrespectful talk/attitude; verb: to speak back to someone in an impudent or cheeky way.
column6: backtalk, cheek, lip; talk back to
column7: Don't give me any sass. / He got in trouble for sassing his teacher.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: give someone sass; sass someone; sassy. Tone can range from playful boldness to disrespect depending context.

column5: To cause extensive damage, disruption, confusion, or disorder.
column7: The storm wreaked havoc on the coastline. / The bug wreaked havoc with the database.
column8: Normalize from past tense. KEY COLLOCATION: WREAK havoc—not 'wreck havoc'. Common prepositions: wreak havoc on/with.

column5: To select and remove members/items from a group, especially animals, plants, data, or material; often to reduce numbers or remove unwanted cases. Noun: the act or selected group removed.
column6: thin out, remove selectively, weed out
column7: Officials culled infected animals from the herd. / We culled duplicate entries from the list.
column8: Broaden beyond 'inferior or surplus': disease/control/data selection may motivate culling. 'Cull' can also mean select/gather choice items in older/formal use.

column2: don't break your arm patting yourself on the back
column3: /doʊnt breɪk jʊɚ ɑrm ˈpætɪŋ jʊɚˈsɛlf ɑn ðə bæk/
column5: A sarcastic warning not to congratulate or praise yourself too enthusiastically.
column6: don't be so self-congratulatory, don't get smug
column7: You fixed one typo—don't break your arm patting yourself on the back.
column8: KEY BASE IDIOM: 'pat yourself on the back' = congratulate yourself. This expression exaggerates it into an injury for sarcasm.

column5: To be determined (and sometimes contextually 'to be decided'): used as a placeholder when a detail has not yet been settled.
column7: The venue is TBD. / Start time: TBD.
column8: Common in schedules, project plans, event listings, tables. Distinguish TBA = to be announced and TBC = to be confirmed/continued depending context.

column5: A box/area of sand for play; in computing/security, an isolated environment in which code, files, or changes can run with restricted effects on the wider system. Verb: to isolate in such an environment.
column7: Run the untrusted code in a sandbox. / The app sandboxes third-party processes.
column8: Broaden beyond merely 'safe testing': isolation/containment is the key computing idea. Also used metaphorically for experimentation.

column5: A person qualified or engaged to estimate the monetary value of property, assets, art, jewelry, etc.
column7: We hired an appraiser to value the house before refinancing.
column8: KEY WORD FAMILY: appraise = estimate value; appraisal = valuation. An 'assessor' may have a specific tax/official role and is not always interchangeable.

column5: Protection from or reduced susceptibility to disease; exemption/protection from a legal duty, prosecution, suit, or consequence; more broadly, freedom from an effect.
column7: Vaccination can produce immunity to a disease. / The witness received immunity from prosecution.
column8: KEY FRAMES: immunity to/from disease/effect; immunity from prosecution/liability. Legal forms include diplomatic, sovereign, qualified immunity, etc., with distinct rules.

column5: Legal responsibility for harm/debt; a financial obligation/debt; or a person/thing that creates disadvantage, risk, or burden.
column6: legal responsibility, obligation, debt; drawback, burden
column7: The company denied liability for the accident. / The loan appears as a liability on the balance sheet. / His temper became a political liability.
column8: Important legal + accounting + figurative senses. Contrast asset vs liability in accounting.

column5: Literally, to give someone less change than they are owed; figuratively, to give someone less than they deserve, expect, or were promised.
column6: cheat, underpay, deprive, give short shrift to (different construction)
column7: The cashier accidentally shortchanged me. / The adaptation shortchanged the supporting characters.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FRAME: shortchange someone (on something). Figurative use is common for inadequate attention, credit, value, etc.

column5: A final demand or set of terms whose rejection will trigger stated or implied consequences.
column7: She gave him an ultimatum: apologize or leave. / The union rejected the company's ultimatum.
column8: Repair punctuation. KEY COLLOCATIONS: issue/give/deliver an ultimatum; ultimatum to someone; deadline may accompany it but is not required.

column5: A social organization for women students/alumnae, especially in U.S. colleges and universities; some are part of Greek-letter systems, while organizations and membership practices vary.
column7: She joined a sorority during her first year of college.
column8: 'Female fraternity' can describe historical naming but is not a clean everyday synonym. Sororities may be social, professional, service-based, etc.

column2: walk on eggshells / be walking on eggshells
column5: To behave extremely carefully around someone or a sensitive situation because a small mistake may cause anger, conflict, or trouble.
column6: tread carefully, tiptoe around, be extremely cautious
column7: Everyone was walking on eggshells around him after the argument.
column8: Normalize to productive base/state. KEY FRAME: walk on eggshells around + person; metaphor = fragile surface that may crack.

column5: To flow over, surround, cover, or overwhelm completely; figuratively, emotions, darkness, chaos, etc. can engulf someone/something.
column7: The building was engulfed in flames. / She was engulfed by panic.
column8: Normalize base + passive. KEY PATTERNS: engulf X; be engulfed in flames/smoke/darkness; engulfed by emotion.

column5: To cross back and forth or form a network/pattern of intersecting lines; a crossing pattern or movement.
column7: Power lines crisscross the neighborhood. / We crisscrossed the city all afternoon.
column8: Broaden grammar. 'Crisscross the country/city' = travel repeatedly across it; not necessarily a literal visible X pattern.

column5: Giving rules or recommendations about how something should be done; in language, prescribing 'correct' usage rather than merely describing actual usage.
column7: The guide is deliberately prescriptive about punctuation. / Prescriptive grammar tells speakers how they ought to use language.
column8: Important contrast: prescriptive vs descriptive, especially linguistics. 'Dictatorial' is too strong as a general synonym.

column5: To perform, speak, decide, or handle something with little or no preparation, relying on improvisation.
column6: improvise, ad-lib, make it up as one goes
column7: I didn't prepare a speech, so I'll just wing it.
column8: Repair punctuation. KEY FRAME is fixed 'wing it'; the object is usually the pronoun 'it'.

column5: To dance or move rhythmically, especially casually to music; to move along briskly/casually; to hit lightly. Noun: a bop can be a dance/movement, and slang 'a bop' can mean a catchy/good song.
column7: We were bopping along to the music. / I'll bop over to the store. / That song is a bop.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Modern slang noun 'a bop' = enjoyable/catchy song is highly useful.

column5: An obstetrician-gynecologist, or the medical specialty/practice of obstetrics and gynecology; can also modify clinic/appointment/care.
column7: I have an OB-GYN appointment next week. / She works in OB-GYN.
column8: CORRECTION: standard styling commonly OB-GYN, ob-gyn, or OB/GYN—not 'obgyn' only. It can refer to the doctor or specialty/context.

column5: The external sac of skin and associated tissues that contains the testes and helps regulate their temperature.
column7: The testes are located within the scrotum.
column8: PRECISION: 'testicle sac' is informal/nontechnical. Temperature regulation involves scrotal muscles and vascular mechanisms; avoid implying the skin alone does all regulation.

column5: Not harmful, dangerous, offensive, or likely to cause trouble; seemingly harmless.
column7: It looked like an innocuous question, but it revealed a major problem.
column8: Often 'seemingly innocuous' when something later proves consequential. 'Benign' overlaps medical/general harmlessness but has technical senses.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::offensive usage::evaluative discovery::possibility discovery::hedging discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Loyalty, commitment, or duty of support to a person, group, country, cause, institution, etc.
column7: The soldiers swore allegiance to the crown. / His political allegiances changed over time.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: pledge/swear allegiance to; allegiance to a country/cause. Can be formal or figurative.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::figurative discovery::support discovery::loyalty discovery::commitment

column5: Loyalty owed or pledged to a lord or superior, especially in a feudal relationship; figuratively, devoted loyalty.
column7: The vassal swore fealty to his lord. / Critics accused the board of fealty to the CEO.
column8: Historical sense is specific to feudal obligation/homage. Figurative modern use is elevated and often critical.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::figurative usage::critical topic::relationships topic::history discovery::figurative_extension discovery::loyalty

column2: bend the knee to someone / bent the knee
column5: Literally, to kneel as an act of submission, homage, or allegiance; figuratively, to submit to someone's authority or dominance.
column6: submit to, bow to, yield to, swear allegiance to
column7: He refused to bend the knee to the new ruler. / Eventually, the rival faction bent the knee.
column8: Normalize base + source past. KEY CONSTRUCTION: bend the knee to + person/power. Strong fantasy/historical resonance in modern usage.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::ceremonial topic::history discovery::figurative_extension discovery::loyalty

column5: To influence or change someone's opinion, decision, feelings, or course of action; literally, to move slowly from side to side.
column7: The evidence swayed several undecided voters. / Her argument didn't sway my opinion. / The trees swayed in the wind.
column8: Normalize from 'to sway someone'. Add literal motion. KEY frames: sway someone; sway someone's opinion/vote; be swayed by.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::rhetorical usage::persuasive topic::decision-making topic::construction discovery::persuasion discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::debate_language

column5: A strong, noticeable, or habitual liking/tendency for something.
column7: He has a penchant for elaborate metaphors.
column8: KEY FRAME: a penchant for + noun/gerund. Slightly formal; 'predilection' is similarly formal.

column5: To break suddenly; make a sharp sound/movement; speak sharply; or suddenly lose emotional self-control under pressure.
column6: break, crack; lash out, lose it
column7: The branch snapped. / She snapped at me. / After weeks of stress, he finally snapped.
column8: CORRECTION: current card captured only one sense. KEY distinctions: snap at someone = speak irritably; snap = lose control; object can physically snap.

column5: Unable to pay debts as they fall due and/or having liabilities exceeding assets under an applicable legal/accounting test; exact definition varies by jurisdiction.
column6: unable to pay debts, financially insolvent
column7: The company became insolvent after months of cash-flow problems.
column8: PRECISION: 'bankrupt' is not a universal synonym; bankruptcy is a legal status/process, while insolvency is a financial condition/test.

column5: Soldiers trained and organized primarily to fight on foot, including modern infantry that may be transported by vehicles or aircraft.
column7: The infantry advanced after the artillery barrage.
column8: PRECISION: 'fight on foot' describes combat role, not necessarily how troops travel. Types include light, mechanized, motorized, airborne infantry.

column5: To understand, mentally grasp, or come to terms with something difficult, complex, surprising, or emotionally hard to accept.
column6: grasp, comprehend, get one's mind around, process
column7: I'm still trying to wrap my head around how the system works. / I can't wrap my head around the ending.
column8: KEY FRAME: wrap my/your/his... head around + noun/clause. Can mean intellectual comprehension or emotional acceptance.

column5: Mentally or emotionally exhausted, stressed, disorganized, or agitated, especially after too many demands.
column6: stressed out, harried, rattled, worn out
column7: I was completely frazzled after answering messages all afternoon.
column8: Not simply physically 'exhausted'. Often combines stress + scattered attention. 'Fraught' is not a synonym for a person in this sense.

column5: To settle into a curled, comfortable position with a book, blanket, drink, pet, person, etc., often for relaxation.
column6: snuggle up with, cozy up with, settle in with
column7: I curled up with a novel and a cup of tea. / The cat curled up with me on the couch.
column8: KEY FRAME: curl up with + companion/object. 'Curl up' itself describes body position; 'with' adds what accompanies the cozy activity.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::resolution discovery::debate_language

column5: Noun: a self-propelled underwater weapon. Verb: to attack with a torpedo; figuratively, to ruin, sabotage, or abruptly destroy a plan, deal, career, chances, etc.
column7: One careless comment torpedoed the deal. / The submarine fired a torpedo.
column8: Add literal noun/verb behind the metaphor. Figurative collocations: torpedo a deal/bill/career/chances.

column5: To spread or distribute information, ideas, knowledge, or material widely among people or places.
column7: The agency disseminated the guidance to local offices.
column8: Usually transitive: disseminate information/findings/results. More formal than 'spread'.

column5: To obtain, arrange, or maneuver something through cleverness, persuasion, manipulation, or sometimes trickery.
column7: She finagled us a better table. / He finagled his way into the sold-out event.
column8: KEY FRAMES: finagle + object; finagle one's way into/out of X. Trickery is possible but not required; can be resourceful persuasion.

column5: To investigate, examine, or question deeply and systematically; physically, to explore with an instrument. Noun: an investigation or an exploratory instrument/device.
column7: Reporters probed the allegations. / The doctor gently probed the wound. / The agency opened a probe into the incident.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Add noun and physical/technical senses.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical topic::finance discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: An unlucky accident, mistake, or minor unfortunate incident, usually not catastrophic.
column7: Aside from a small mishap with the cake, everything went smoothly.
column8: Often mildly euphemistic/light in tone. A serious disaster would usually not be called merely a 'mishap'.

column5: Anger, especially strong anger provoked by something; commonly used in journalism/formal writing.
column7: The decision drew the ire of local residents.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: draw/raise/provoke someone's ire; incur the ire of. 'Indignation' specifically includes perceived injustice/wrongness.

column5: A person shown speaking directly to camera, especially an expert/commentator/interview subject; a 'talking-head segment' is a video/TV section dominated by such on-camera speech rather than action or illustrative footage.
column6: on-camera commentator, interview segment, direct-to-camera segment
column7: The documentary cuts from archival footage to a talking-head interview.
column8: Teach underlying term 'talking head'. It can be mildly dismissive when referring to TV pundits, but is also a neutral production term.
column12: entry::noun_phrase topic::media topic::public_speaking topic::television topic::entertainment discovery::expertise

column5: To cause intense awe, surprise, beauty, excitement, or other strong emotion; literally, something can also momentarily make breathing difficult.
column7: The view took my breath away. / The sudden impact briefly took his breath away.
column8: Normalize possessive: take my/your/her... breath away. Figurative awe is common, but literal physical sense also exists.

column5: Peanut butter and jelly, especially a peanut-butter-and-jelly sandwich.
column7: I packed a PB&J for lunch.
column8: CORRECTION: remove speculative Pam Beesly/Jim material from the definition. In ordinary English, PB&J means peanut butter and jelly. Any The Office wordplay would be source-specific, not the lexical meaning.

column5: A sideways gymnastic movement in which the body rotates with hands and feet contacting the ground in sequence; verb: to perform or move like a cartwheel.
column7: She did a cartwheel across the lawn. / The car cartwheeled down the slope after the crash.
column8: Add figurative/extended verb for objects tumbling end-over-end/sideways. A cartwheel is not simply a 'flip'.

column5: Noun: an unreliable person who often fails to follow through. Verb phrase 'flake on someone' = cancel, fail to show, or abandon a commitment, often at the last minute.
column6: unreliable person; bail on, stand up, cancel on
column7: He's a total flake. / Don't flake on me again tonight.
column8: KEY FAMILY: be a flake; flake out; flake on + person/plan. 'Quitter' is not a clean synonym.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::slang discovery::commitment

column5: To malfunction, become chaotic, behave unpredictably, or go badly out of control.
column6: malfunction, go wrong, go crazy, act up
column7: My phone went haywire after the update. / The schedule went haywire when three flights were canceled.
column8: Normalize from progressive. Used for machines, systems, plans, emotions/body processes figuratively.

column5: Elastic, resilient, or bouncy; tending to spring back after pressure; also light and energetic in movement.
column7: The mattress is firm but springy. / She walked with a springy step.
column8: Broaden beyond material property. Common: springy texture/hair/turf/step.

column5: Jealousy personified, especially possessive or romantic jealousy.
column7: The green-eyed monster appeared when he saw his ex with someone else.
column8: Usually appears with article 'the'. Shakespearean allusion from Othello; modern use can be playful/literary. Jealousy and envy overlap but are not identical.

column5: To direct attention, effort, investigation, or targeting increasingly precisely toward a specific person, issue, location, cause, etc.
column6: focus on, home in on, target, pinpoint
column7: The investigation zeroed in on one account. / Let's zero in on the main problem.
column8: KEY FRAME: zero in on + target. 'Home in on' is a close established alternative; 'hone in on' is common but historically contested.

column5: Deliberately or unreasonably contrary to what is expected, sensible, or desirable; showing obstinate wrongheadedness; also, in some contexts, morally/sexually deviant in an older or judgmental sense.
column7: He took a perverse pleasure in proving everyone wrong. / The rule created a perverse incentive to waste money.
column8: Important collocations: perverse incentive, perverse pleasure, perverse outcome. Sexual/moral labeling can be dated or stigmatizing; context matters.

column5: To display something conspicuously or ostentatiously, often to attract admiration, envy, or attention.
column7: He loves to flaunt his wealth online. / She flaunted the award jokingly.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Commonly confused with 'flout' = openly disregard a rule/law.

column5: Having any real value, quality, usefulness, competence, or importance, especially in negative statements/questions.
column7: None of these batteries are worth a damn. / Is that advice worth a damn?
column8: Especially common under negation: not worth a damn. Related 'give a damn' concerns caring, not value.

column2: scrub / can't scrub out; scrub (gaming slang)
column5: Standard 'scrub' = clean by rubbing hard; 'can't scrub X out/off' = cannot remove a stain/mark by scrubbing. Separately, 'scrub' can be an insulting slang noun for an inexperienced/bad player or incompetent person in some gaming/sports communities.
column7: I can't scrub the stain out. / He called the new player a scrub.
column8: CORRECTION: 'can't scrub' is not itself an established slang phrase meaning an incompetent person, and 'he's a can't scrub' is unnatural. Separate the standard verb construction from slang noun 'a scrub'.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::informal topic::games discovery::incompetence discovery::evaluation discovery::removal

column2: back burner / put something on the back burner
column5: A lower-priority state in which something is postponed while more urgent matters receive attention.
column7: We put the redesign on the back burner until next month.
column8: CORRECTION: standard idiom is normally two words, 'back burner'. KEY FRAME: put X on the back burner; X is on the back burner.

column5: One repetition/cycle of a process; a particular version produced through repeated development; in computing/math, one execution of a repeated procedure.
column7: This is the third iteration of the design. / Each iteration of the loop updates the value.
column8: Clean duplicated definition/example. KEY PRODUCTIVE USE: next/current/earlier iteration of a product/design; iterative = repeated refinement.
column12: entry::word topic::mathematics discovery::implementation discovery::process_details discovery::procedural_language discovery::iteration

column5: An interruption or disturbance that prevents something from continuing normally; also a major change that unsettles an established system/industry.
column7: The outage caused major disruptions. / Streaming created major disruption in the media business.
column8: Normalize singular/plural and add innovation/industry sense. 'Disruption' can be temporary interruption or structural upheaval.

column2: dish it out / dish something out
column5: To give or distribute something; especially to hand out criticism, insults, punishment, advice, etc. freely. In 'can dish it out but can't take it', someone attacks others but cannot tolerate the same treatment.
column6: hand out, dole out; criticize, attack
column7: He can dish it out, but he can't take it. / The coach dished out harsh criticism.
column8: Broaden underlying construction: dish out + food/criticism/punishment. The famous idiom uses pronoun 'it' for harsh treatment.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::idiom entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::informal topic::food topic::medicine topic::health discovery::criticism discovery::recommendation

column5: The act/process of getting rid of something; also availability/control for use in the idiom 'at someone's disposal'.
column7: Safe disposal of batteries is important. / We have several tools at our disposal.
column8: Important second construction: at one's disposal = available for one to use/control. Also garbage disposal = kitchen appliance in AmE.

column2: tank / tank a game; tank it
column5: To perform very badly or fail; transitively, to deliberately lose/underperform, especially in sports for strategic advantage; also of prices/ratings, to fall sharply.
column7: The movie tanked at the box office. / Critics accused the team of tanking for a better draft position.
column8: CORRECTION: 'tank it' is possible but not the core idiom. Distinguish ordinary fail badly from deliberate sports tanking.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::idiom usage::informal usage::slang usage::debate-friendly discovery::debate_language

column2: draw lots / draw lots to decide...
column3: /lɛts drɔ lɑts tə dɪˈsaɪd hu slips wɛɚ/
column5: To choose among people/options randomly, traditionally by drawing marked slips, objects, straws, etc.
column6: choose by lot, decide by chance, randomize
column7: We drew lots to decide who would sleep where. / If nobody volunteers, we'll draw lots.
column8: Normalize from full source sentence. KEY FRAME: draw lots to decide + wh-clause; draw lots for + role/order.

column5: A person's social position, rank, role, or circumstances in society, especially in older class-conscious language.
column7: The novel treats everyone as bound by their station in life.
column8: Often historical/literary and can imply a fixed social hierarchy. Not simply current income.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::formal usage::literary usage::dated usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::debate_language

column5: To be doomed, defeated, ruined, caught, or in serious trouble.
column6: be doomed, be finished, be done for
column7: If she sees the broken screen, I'm toast. / Without that contract, the project is toast.
column8: Normalize productive 'be toast'; subjects can be people, plans, businesses, objects. Often humorous exaggeration.

column5: Traveling from place to place, especially for work or as part of one's way of life; noun: an itinerant worker/preacher/etc.
column7: He worked as an itinerant musician. / Itinerant traders moved between villages.
column8: 'Nomadic' can imply a broader lifestyle/community pattern; itinerant often emphasizes repeated travel for occupation.

column5: A conventional nonsense magic word used theatrically to accompany a trick, transformation, or magical act.
column7: The magician waved the wand and cried, 'Alakazam!'
column8: Recognition/cultural word. 'Presto' can announce a result but also has a separate musical meaning.

column5: Deliberately or affectedly shy, modest, or reluctant to reveal information, often playfully/flirtatiously; can also mean evasively noncommittal.
column7: She gave him a coy smile. / The company was coy about the release date.
column8: Important non-romantic use: be coy about details/plans = deliberately avoid saying much. 'Reserved' may be genuine rather than affected.

column5: In relation to or compared with; facing/opposite; noun historically can mean a person/object situated face-to-face.
column6: regarding, in relation to, compared with, opposite
column7: We need to clarify our position vis-à-vis the new rules.
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling is 'vis-à-vis' (accents/hyphens often retained). Modern common use = 'in relation to/regarding', somewhat formal.

column5: A Spanish conqueror/explorer involved in the conquest and colonization of parts of the Americas, especially in the 16th century.
column7: Spanish conquistadors overthrew major Indigenous states and helped establish colonial rule.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. 'Explorer' alone understates the conquest role; term is historically specific.

column5: A small compartment, recess, or enclosed storage space, often one of a set for personal belongings.
column7: Each child has a cubby for a backpack and coat.
column8: 'Cubicle' is generally a larger partitioned workspace and is not a close synonym. Common in schools/daycare/entryways.

column5: Covered or marked with many small spots, flecks, or patches of contrasting color.
column7: The bird has a speckled breast. / Sunlight speckled the floor through the leaves.
column8: Can describe naturally spotted surfaces or figurative/light patterns. Related verb: speckle.

column2: that's a stretch / be a stretch
column5: Used to say a claim, interpretation, comparison, or expectation goes beyond what seems reasonable, plausible, or supported.
column7: Calling that tiny mistake 'fraud' is a stretch. / Winning from here would be a stretch.
column8: Broaden productive frame: 'That's a stretch'; 'X is a bit of a stretch'; 'It would be a stretch to say...'.

column5: So awkward, embarrassing, tasteless, or uncomfortable that it makes one metaphorically cringe.
column7: The dialogue is painfully cringeworthy in places.
column8: Both closed and hyphenated spellings occur; 'cringeworthy' is common modern styling. Related slang adjective 'cringe' is more informal.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::evaluative usage::slang topic::communication topic::media topic::entertainment discovery::criticism discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::evaluation

column5: A quadrilateral with all four sides equal in length; under standard definitions, a square is a special rhombus.
column7: A square is a rhombus with four right angles.
column8: CORRECTION: 'diamond' is an informal visual label, not a precise geometry synonym; a rhombus need not be oriented like a diamond.

column5: A quadrilateral defined in many U.S. texts as having at least one pair of parallel sides; some curricula use an exclusive definition requiring exactly one pair. BrE terminology differs, often using 'trapezium'.
column7: Under the inclusive definition, every parallelogram is also a trapezoid.
column8: CORRECTION: current definition says 'at least one pair' but example says 'only one pair', an internal contradiction. Flag inclusive vs exclusive conventions.
column12: entry::word usage::american_english usage::british_english usage::specialist topic::mathematics discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A polygon with four sides (and therefore four vertices/angles); adjective: having four sides.
column7: Squares, rectangles, rhombuses, and many trapezoids are quadrilaterals.
column8: Add adjective. 'Tetragon' is technical/rare. Exact trapezoid subclass relation depends on convention noted at WID2286.

column5: For a continuous period of time, often a noticeable but unspecified span.
column6: for a while, for a period, for a spell
column7: I worked nights for a stretch before switching schedules.
column8: KEY COMPONENT: 'a stretch' = an uninterrupted period. Related: 'for long stretches'; distinct from 'That's a stretch' (WID2282).

column5: A mathematically describable figure/form such as a circle, triangle, polygon, polyhedron, etc., in two or more dimensions depending context.
column7: The lesson introduces basic geometric shapes such as circles and triangles.
column8: CORRECTION: 'polygons' are only one subset of geometric shapes; circles are not polygons. Normalize singular/plural.

column5: Altogether; in total, used to state the complete number or amount after counting components.
column7: There were fifteen people in all. / The repairs cost $800 in all.
column8: Often appears after the quantity or at clause end. 'Collectively' is not always interchangeable.

column5: Happening, existing, or operating during the same period; in law, concurrent sentences run at the same time rather than one after another.
column7: The conference has three concurrent sessions. / He received concurrent sentences.
column8: Connect to WID2167 'concurrently'. In computing, concurrency can involve overlapping progress without literal same-instant execution.

column5: Relating to the medical care, health, or diseases of infants, children, and adolescents.
column7: She works in pediatric medicine. / The hospital has a pediatric emergency department.
column8: AmE pediatric; BrE paediatric. Remove awkward pseudo-synonyms such as 'pediatrician's'.

column5: Mutual compromise, exchange, adjustment, or reciprocal concession between people; also the back-and-forth exchange of conversation/interaction.
column7: A good partnership requires give and take. / I enjoyed the give-and-take of the debate.
column8: As noun before another noun often hyphenated: give-and-take relationship. Not necessarily equal concessions.
column12: entry::idiom entry::variant_set entry::discourse_expression usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::communication topic::rhetoric discovery::compromise discovery::debate_language discovery::trade-off discovery::concession

column5: To become stable after rising/falling or to make something even/flat; 'level off' is especially common for a trend that stops rising/falling.
column6: stabilize, flatten out, even out, plateau
column7: Prices rose quickly, then leveled off. / The road levels out after the hill.
column8: Normalize from third-person. Distinguish physical flattening and trend stabilization; 'level off' often more idiomatic for graphs/rates.

column5: Capacity to be shaped, deformed, or changed; in neuroscience/biology, capacity of systems/tissues—especially the nervous system—to adapt structurally or functionally in response to experience or conditions.
column7: Neural plasticity allows the brain to change with learning and experience. / Clay has high plasticity when wet.
column8: Important technical meanings differ by field (materials science, neuroscience, developmental biology). 'Flexibility' is broader.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::scientific topic::communication topic::biology topic::science discovery::flexibility discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Without order, planning, discrimination, or control; haphazardly. Historically it can also mean whether one wants to or not.
column7: Don't add features willy-nilly. / Files were scattered willy-nilly across the folders.
column8: CORRECTION: standard styling commonly hyphenated 'willy-nilly'. Add older 'whether willing or unwilling' origin/sense for recognition.

column5: Something that fails to work, explode, succeed, or meet expectations; a person/thing considered ineffective or disappointing. Attributive adjective: dud check, dud product, etc.
column7: The firework was a dud. / The sequel turned out to be a dud.
column8: Broaden beyond malfunction. 'Dud' originally/commonly covers ammunition/explosives that fail, then figurative failures.

column5: Required by law, rule, authority, or circumstances; mandatory rather than optional.
column7: Attendance is compulsory for all first-year students.
column8: 'Enforced' is not a direct adjective synonym. Common: compulsory education/service/attendance.

column5: A small pouch worn around the waist or hips; AmE commonly 'fanny pack'.
column6: fanny pack (AmE), waist bag, belt bag
column7: I kept my passport in a bum bag while sightseeing.
column8: Styling varies: 'bum bag' is common; 'bumbag' also occurs. Register note: 'fanny' has a vulgar anatomical meaning in BrE, making the AmE term amusing/awkward there.
column12: entry::variant_set entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::vulgar usage::american_english usage::british_english

column5: A vulgar British slang term for the vulva/female genital area; can also occur in insulting sexualized language.
column6: vulva (neutral anatomical referent); pussy, twat (vulgar, not exact in tone/anatomy)
column7: The word 'minge' is vulgar and would be inappropriate in most formal settings.
column8: PRECISION: avoid presenting other slurs as straightforward synonyms. This is recognition-focused British vulgar slang; exact anatomical reference in slang can be loose.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::formal usage::slang usage::offensive usage::vulgar usage::british_english usage::informal usage::evaluative topic::communication topic::anatomy topic::health discovery::terminology

column5: To criticize, insult, or speak disparagingly about someone or something.
column7: She slagged me off in front of the whole team. / They were slagging off the new policy.
column8: Normalize from source pronoun. KEY FRAME: slag someone/something off. Strongly British; informal and often fairly harsh.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::informal usage::slang usage::british_english topic::communication discovery::criticism

column5: Not sufficiently strict, careful, controlled, or attentive to standards or duties.
column7: Security was surprisingly lax. / The company was lax about enforcing the rule.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: lax security/standards/enforcement; be lax about/in doing something. 'Lenient' focuses permissiveness; 'negligent' can be stronger/legal.

column5: Verb: to lead, organize, or initiate an important effort, campaign, project, or movement. Noun: the leading force/person; literally, the pointed head of a spear.
column7: She is spearheading the campaign. / He spearheaded the redesign.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FRAME: spearhead a campaign/initiative/effort. Usually implies active leadership, not merely participation.

column2: boil down to / boil something down
column5: To reduce to the essential point or result; transitively, to condense information or literally reduce liquid by boiling.
column6: come down to, amount to; condense, reduce
column7: It all boils down to trust. / Can you boil the report down to three points?
column8: KEY DISTINCTION: X boils down to Y = Y is the essence; boil X down to Y = reduce X into Y. Literal cooking sense underlies metaphor.

column5: Stern, severe, gloomy, or persistently unsmiling in manner, appearance, or mood.
column7: He wore a dour expression throughout the meeting. / The film has a deliberately dour tone.
column8: Often describes expression/personality/tone. Pronunciation varies: /dʊr/ and /daʊr/ occur.

column5: To break apart into small pieces or components; figuratively, to lose cohesion, structure, or existence.
column6: break apart, crumble, fall apart, collapse
column7: The material began to disintegrate. / Their alliance disintegrated within months.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Can be physical or figurative; not necessarily decay.

column5: To cry or shout very loudly; 'bawl one's eyes out' = cry intensely.
column7: The child was bawling after the fall. / I bawled my eyes out at the ending.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Bawl can mean loud crying OR loud shouting; common construction 'bawl someone out' = scold loudly is distinct.

column5: To weaken, damage, or make less effective gradually or indirectly; literally/historically, to erode or excavate beneath a foundation.
column7: Constant criticism can undermine confidence. / The leak undermined the foundation.
column8: KEY OBJECTS: undermine confidence/authority/credibility/efforts. 'Sabotage' often implies deliberate action; undermine need not.

column5: A person shown speaking on camera, especially an interview subject, expert, commentator, or pundit; sometimes used dismissively for media commentators perceived as repetitive or superficial.
column7: The documentary alternates archival footage with talking-head interviews.
column8: CORRECTION: lack of insight is not inherent in the term. It is also a neutral production term. Overlaps WID2253, retained as a core-term recognition card.

column5: By or because of a thing's inherent nature; in itself, rather than because of external circumstances or relationships.
column7: The task isn't intrinsically difficult; it just takes practice. / Gold is intrinsically valuable in some arguments, though value claims depend on context.
column8: KEY CONTRAST: intrinsically vs extrinsically/instrumentally. Often used with valuable, motivated, interesting, good/bad.

column5: A foolish or inept person (dated/mild); also informal slang for a breast.
column7: I felt like a boob for forgetting the appointment. / The comedy uses juvenile jokes about boobs.
column8: IMPORTANT POLYSEMY: person-insult sense can sound dated; plural 'boobs' commonly means breasts. Register is informal.

column2: put one's foot in one's mouth
column5: To say something tactless, embarrassing, insensitive, or inappropriate, usually accidentally.
column6: say the wrong thing, make a verbal blunder, misspeak
column7: I really put my foot in my mouth when I asked about the party she wasn't invited to.
column8: Normalize possessives. KEY IMAGE: an awkward verbal mistake one wishes one could take back. BrE also 'put one's foot in it'.

column2: my ride bailed me out / bail someone out
column5: In the source phrase, 'my ride' means the person/vehicle providing transportation, and 'bailed me out' means rescued me from an awkward or difficult situation. More broadly, bail someone out = rescue from trouble, including financially or by posting legal bail.
column6: rescue, get someone out of trouble, save
column7: Thankfully, my ride bailed me out of the awkward conversation. / My brother bailed me out when I couldn't cover the bill.
column8: CORRECTION: current headword is ungrammatical ('my ride bail me out'). Teach underlying 'bail someone out' and source-specific 'my ride bailed me out'.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction topic::law topic::transportation topic::automotive

column5: To be unable to tolerate, accept, watch, hear, or endure something because it is disgusting, upsetting, offensive, or otherwise unbearable.
column6: can't stand, can't bear, be unable to tolerate
column7: I can't stomach cruelty to animals. / She couldn't stomach watching the surgery scene.
column8: KEY FRAME: can't/couldn't stomach + noun/gerund. Figurative verb comes from physical stomach/nausea; stronger than simple dislike.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative usage::offensive usage::evaluative

column5: Making someone feel energized, refreshed, stimulated, or more alive; also intellectually/emotionally stimulating.
column7: The cold morning air was invigorating. / We had an invigorating discussion.
column8: Broaden beyond physical health/strength. Related verb invigorate; noun invigoration.

column5: Evidence, proof, or a strong sign of a quality or fact, especially in the construction 'a testament to X'; also a will/testament or a biblical division/title in other contexts.
column7: Her recovery is a testament to her persistence. / The building is a testament to the architect's skill.
column8: KEY FRAME: be a testament to + quality/person/effort. 'Proof' can be stronger than the figurative rhetorical use. Add legal/religious recognition senses.
column12: entry::collocation usage::figurative usage::rhetorical usage::religious topic::religion topic::construction discovery::religious_origin discovery::title_language discovery::evidence discovery::evaluation discovery::debate_language

column5: A vivid, non-fixed metaphor for a person or presence perceived as absorbing or draining a room's energy, charm, or social momentum rather than generating it.
column7: The character is written as a charisma black hole who drains every scene of energy.
column8: SOURCE/CREATIVE: not a standard dictionary idiom. Teach composition: charisma + black hole → metaphorically 'absorbs' social energy. Can be harshly judgmental.
column12: entry::idiom entry::fixed_expression usage::informal usage::figurative discovery::perception discovery::building_on_success

column5: A V-shaped point of the hairline descending toward the center of the forehead.
column7: He has a pronounced widow's peak.
column8: Common appearance term. The name comes from historical associations with widow's hoods and later folklore; it does not imply anything about actual widowhood.

column5: Short for pectoral muscle(s), especially the chest muscles; usually plural 'pecs' in everyday fitness/body talk.
column7: Bench presses work the pecs. / He strained his left pec.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. 'Chest' is broader anatomy, not an exact synonym. Informal but very common in fitness contexts.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal topic::wellness topic::anatomy topic::health

column5: Noun: a curtain or hanging fabric, especially a long/heavy window covering; verb: to hang, arrange, or fall loosely over something.
column7: She chose velvet drapes for the room. / A blanket was draped over the chair.
column8: Add productive verb. In 'does the carpet match the drapes?', drapes metaphorically refers to head hair; see WID2325.

column5: Rough, basic, or not refined; offensively vulgar; or in a natural/unprocessed state, as in crude oil.
column7: They built a crude shelter. / He made a crude joke. / Crude oil prices rose.
column8: Major polysemy: crude design/tool, crude language, crude oil/material. 'Offensive' is only one branch.

column2: does the carpet match the drapes?
column5: A crude sexualized question asking whether someone's pubic-hair color ('carpet') matches their head-hair color ('drapes').
column6: no neutral synonym; sexualized hair-color joke
column7: He made the crude 'carpet and drapes' joke, and everyone looked uncomfortable.
column8: KEY METAPHOR: carpet = pubic hair; drapes = head hair. Often invasive/objectifying; recognition-focused rather than recommended usage. Repair punctuation.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::sentence_pattern usage::slang usage::figurative usage::vulgar usage::informal

column5: A party at which beer is served from one or more kegs, stereotypically associated with U.S. college/fraternity culture but not limited to it.
column7: They hosted a keg party after the game.
column8: Related slang 'kegger'. 'Rager' means a wild party generally, not specifically a keg party.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::american_english topic::education topic::culture

column5: The act/process of marking or establishing a boundary, or the boundary/distinction itself.
column7: There's a clear demarcation between public and private space.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: line of demarcation; clear/sharp demarcation between X and Y. Can be physical, conceptual, organizational.

column2: get the axe / give someone the axe
column5: To be fired, dismissed, canceled, or eliminated; 'give someone/something the axe' = terminate or cut it.
column6: get fired, be cut, be dropped; fire, cancel
column7: Several employees got the axe. / The network gave the show the axe after one season.
column8: Normalize from third-person. Broader than jobs: shows/projects/features can get the axe.

column2: be under someone / report to someone
column5: In an organizational hierarchy, 'be under someone' can mean be lower-ranking or under that person's supervision, though 'report to someone' is often clearer. Literally, 'under' can describe physical position; sexual double entendres depend on context.
column6: report to, work under, be subordinate to
column7: I report to Maya; two analysts work under me. / The phrase can sound suggestive in the wrong context.
column8: CORRECTION: not a stable sexual-dominance expression. Teach hierarchy use plus why physical 'under' can create contextual double entendre.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::debate-friendly topic::work topic::debate discovery::debate_language

column5: To vomit, especially forcefully; a vivid, juvenile/informal expression.
column7: He got carsick and started blowing chunks.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Not inherently alcohol-related. Graphic/comic register; avoid formal contexts.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::idiom entry::form_family usage::formal usage::informal usage::slang

column5: In contemporary slang, 'cap' = a lie, exaggeration, or false claim; 'that's cap' = that's false; 'no cap' = honestly/for real/no lie.
column7: He says he ran a four-minute mile—that's cap. / No cap, that was the best episode yet.
column8: Useful productive frames: that's cap; stop capping; no cap. Slang is strongly informal and generational; usage can shift.

column5: Money sent to a person or organization, especially payment or money sent by migrants/workers to family in another place/country; also the act of remitting payment.
column7: She sends a monthly remittance to her family abroad. / Please include the invoice number with your remittance.
column8: Broaden beyond mail. In economics, migrant remittances are important cross-border household transfers.

column5: The act of becoming involved to change, improve, stop, or influence a situation; also a planned confrontation/support meeting concerning harmful behavior, and a treatment/action in medicine or research.
column7: Early intervention can improve outcomes. / The family staged an intervention about his drinking.
column8: Highly polysemous: medical intervention, military intervention, government intervention, crisis intervention, family 'intervention'. 'Interference' can be negatively loaded.
column12: entry::word usage::military topic::research topic::medicine topic::health discovery::professional_context discovery::support discovery::improvement

column5: To add or attach something to the end of a document, list, file, string, or other sequence.
column7: She appended a note to the report. / The program appends each new record to the file.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FRAME: append X to Y. In computing, append specifically adds at the end.

column5: Touching along a boundary or directly adjoining; forming an unbroken connected area or sequence.
column7: The contiguous United States excludes Alaska and Hawaii. / The files occupy a contiguous block of memory.
column8: Important technical use: contiguous memory/data. 'Neighboring' does not necessarily mean touching; 'continuous' is not always interchangeable.

column5: Repeatedly pressing keys or sending excessive/repetitive keyboard input, often randomly, rapidly, or disruptively.
column7: The chat filled with keyboard spam after everyone started mashing keys.
column8: 'Keyboard spamming' is descriptive rather than a tightly fixed idiom. Distinguish key mashing (rapid/random keystrokes) from message/chat spamming (repeated messages).

column5: Bold, daring, or surprisingly ambitious, sometimes impressively so and sometimes recklessly or shamelessly so.
column7: It was an audacious plan, but it worked. / The audacious claim drew criticism.
column8: Like 'audacity', polarity can be admiring or disapproving. Not automatically 'fearless'.

column5: According to what one has heard or learned, or judging from available evidence; sometimes marks that the speaker is not personally confirming the fact.
column7: Apparently, the meeting has been canceled. / He was apparently unaware of the change.
column8: NUANCE: often means 'I hear/it seems that...', not simply visual appearance. 'Allegedly' has stronger legal/skeptical implications; 'evidently' can sound more inferential.

column5: A person or thing that someone cherishes especially dearly or regards with great affection/pride.
column7: Her youngest grandson is the apple of her eye.
column8: Usually takes 'the'. Can refer to a person or occasionally a prized thing. Strong affectionate tone.

column5: To question, reconsider, or doubt a decision/judgment, often after it has been made; also to try to anticipate another person's actions or reasoning.
column7: Don't second-guess yourself—you made the best call you could. / Analysts tried to second-guess the central bank.
column8: Standard verb often hyphenated 'second-guess'. Add less-common 'anticipate/guess in advance' sense.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::decision-making discovery::uncertainty discovery::speculation discovery::evaluation

column5: In a formal meeting, to formally support another person's motion so it can be considered or debated; noun: an act/person giving such support. More broadly/informally, 'I second that' = I agree/support that.
column7: 'I move that we adjourn.' 'I second the motion.' / 'We need coffee.' 'I second that.'
column8: KEY MEETING CONSTRUCTION: move/make a motion → another member seconds it. Informal 'I second that' is common outside parliamentary procedure.
column12: entry::phrase usage::formal usage::informal usage::professional discovery::professional_context discovery::agreement discovery::support

column5: 'Rolling on the floor laughing'; used in text/online speech to signal that something is extremely funny, often hyperbolically.
column7: That clip had me ROFL.
column8: Usually written as letters/online text; pronunciations vary and many users simply read the letters or treat it visually. Somewhat older internet slang but still recognizable.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::initialism usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::informal topic::internet topic::public_speaking

column5: To settle closely into a warm, comfortable position, often beside or against someone/something.
column7: She snuggled up to him on the couch. / I snuggled up with a blanket and a book.
column8: KEY FRAMES: snuggle up to + person/object; snuggle up with + companion/object. 'Huddle' often emphasizes grouping for warmth/protection.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern usage::warm usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::resolution discovery::debate_language

column2: in spirit / be there in spirit
column5: Emotionally, symbolically, or in intention despite not being physically present; also 'in spirit' can mean in underlying character rather than literal form.
column7: I can't attend, but I'll be there in spirit. / The remake is faithful to the original in spirit.
column8: Broaden beyond absence-at-event. KEY: there in spirit; similar/faithful in spirit.

column5: To grip and not let go; figuratively, to keep, retain, preserve, or remain emotionally attached to someone/something.
column6: cling to, keep hold of, retain
column7: Hold on to me while we cross the ice. / She held on to the old letters for years.
column8: Normalize away from fixed 'hold on to me'. KEY FRAME: hold on to + person/object/hope/memory. Distinguish 'hold on' = wait.

column5: To sweat; to release perspiration through the skin.
column7: He began to perspire during the workout.
column8: More formal/euphemistic than everyday 'sweat'. Common humorous saying contrasts 'horses sweat, men perspire, ladies glow'—dated gendered joke, not usage guidance.

column5: To repeatedly inhale through the nose with short audible sounds, often because of a cold, crying, or allergies; noun: such a sound or a mild cold ('the sniffles').
column7: She sniffled through the sad scene. / I've had the sniffles all week.
column8: 'Whimper' and 'sob' are different vocal crying sounds, not synonyms. Useful noun plural: have the sniffles.

column5: Intended or expressed ironically, playfully, or not entirely seriously, often with a straight-faced appearance.
column7: The article makes a tongue-in-cheek proposal to ban Mondays. / He said it tongue in cheek.
column8: FORM: attributive adjective usually hyphenated 'tongue-in-cheek'; adverbial phrase can appear 'tongue in cheek'. Not necessarily sarcastic.

column5: At every stage throughout a process, journey, development, or difficult experience; often emphasizing continuous involvement or support.
column6: throughout, from start to finish, all along
column7: She supported me every step of the way. / We documented the process every step of the way.
column8: Not inherently 'providing support'; the phrase itself means throughout every stage. Support is a common context.

column2: keep something intact / remain intact; love remained intact
column5: To keep something whole, undamaged, unchanged, or unbroken; 'love remained intact' creatively applies the ordinary adjective to a relationship/feeling that survived difficulty.
column6: preserve, remain whole, stay undamaged; endure
column7: Despite the argument, their friendship remained intact. / Years apart couldn't keep their affection entirely intact.
column8: CORRECTION: 'love intact' alone is not a fixed expression. Teach productive 'keep/remain intact' construction and retain love as a figurative source application. Overlaps WID2007 intentionally.
column12: entry::collocation entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative usage::rhetorical topic::relationships discovery::debate_language

column5: To break or split; make a sharp sound; solve a difficult problem/code; tell a joke; lose composure under pressure; noun: a narrow break, an attempt ('have a crack'), a witty remark, and other context-specific senses.
column7: The glass cracked. / She cracked the code. / He cracked a joke. / He cracked under pressure.
column8: CORRECTION: 'succeed under pressure' was wrong; 'crack under pressure' means FAIL/lose composure. Highly polysemous card; teach collocations rather than one slang gloss.
column12: entry::word usage::slang usage::informal topic::technology discovery::solution_framing discovery::impression

column5: A sudden moment of insight, realization, or understanding when something becomes clear.
column7: I had an aha moment when I saw how the two ideas connected.
column8: Both 'aha moment' and 'a-ha moment' occur. Related interjection 'Aha!' signals discovery/recognition.

column5: Gloomily or resentfully silent, withdrawn, and bad-tempered.
column7: He sat in sullen silence after the argument.
column8: Often combines silence/withdrawal with resentment. Common: sullen mood/look/silence.

column2: give someone the cold shoulder / get the cold shoulder
column5: To deliberately ignore, snub, or treat someone with unfriendly indifference; 'get the cold shoulder' = receive that treatment.
column7: She gave me the cold shoulder after our argument. / I got the cold shoulder all evening.
column8: NORMALIZE: 'cold-shoulder treatment' is understandable but less idiomatic than productive give/get the cold shoulder.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::rhetorical topic::medicine topic::health discovery::debate_language

column5: To charm, delight, or win someone over extremely effectively.
column7: He can charm your socks off when he wants to.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: verb + someone's socks off is an intensifying humorous pattern; compare 'knock/blow someone's socks off' with different meanings.

column5: A social event designed to help people meet and mingle; also a machine/tool for mixing, a person/device that mixes audio, and a nonalcoholic drink combined with spirits.
column6: social gathering; mixing machine; audio mixer; mixed-drink ingredient
column7: They met at a freshman mixer. / Use an electric mixer for the batter. / Tonic water is a common mixer.
column8: Major polysemy missing. Context determines social, kitchen, audio, or beverage sense.

column5: Preserved in a can; prepared/pre-recorded/formulaic rather than spontaneous; informally, fired/dismissed or canceled.
column7: We used canned tomatoes. / The audience heard canned laughter. / He got canned from his job.
column8: Broaden core literal sense. 'Canned response' = standardized/prepared; 'canned laughter' prerecorded. Informal 'get canned' = get fired.

column5: A claim or position asserted in an argument; disagreement/conflict; or the state of competing for something, as in 'in contention'.
column7: Her main contention is that the rule is unfair. / The issue remains a point of contention. / The team is still in contention for the title.
column8: IMPORTANT THREE USES: contention that...; point of contention; in contention for. Repair repetitive examples.
column12: entry::word usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::assertion discovery::disagreement discovery::debate_language

column5: A person who falsely pretends to be another person or to have an identity, role, status, or qualifications they do not possess.
column7: The impostor posed as a doctor. / She worried that colleagues would discover she was an imposter.
column8: Both spellings are standard; 'impostor' is traditional and 'imposter' common. Related 'impostor syndrome' is a psychological experience, not actual deception.

column5: To state, say, or emphasize something again, usually to make it clear or reinforce it.
column7: Let me reiterate the main point. / She reiterated that the deadline had not changed.
column8: Normalize base + source form. 'Reiterate again' is usually redundant because re- already means again.

column5: Action taken in response to an injury, attack, criticism, or perceived wrong, especially to punish or get even; in employment/law, adverse action for protected reporting/activity has specific legal meanings.
column7: He feared retaliation after reporting the misconduct. / The strike prompted military retaliation.
column8: KEY FRAME: retaliation for/against/in response to. Legal 'retaliation' is context-specific; not every negative response meets a legal definition.
column12: entry::word usage::military topic::work topic::communication topic::law discovery::criticism discovery::perception

column5: A pleasantly comforting, affectionate, sentimental feeling; can describe something that produces such feelings. Literal 'warm and fuzzy' can also simply describe temperature/texture.
column7: The reunion gave me a warm and fuzzy feeling. / The ad has a warm-and-fuzzy tone.
column8: FORM: 'warm and fuzzy' predicative/noun phrase; hyphenation may appear attributively. Often playful and sometimes mildly ironic.
column12: entry::idiom entry::adjective_phrase entry::variant_set usage::playful usage::affectionate usage::warm usage::ironic topic::weather

column5: To converse/chat (older/formal sense); in clinical neuropsychology, to produce false or distorted memories without conscious intent to deceive, often filling memory gaps.
column7: The patient confabulated details she genuinely believed were true. / The older sense means to converse informally.
column8: CORRECTION: clinical confabulation is not simply 'fabricating imaginary experiences as compensation' and does not imply deliberate lying. Normalize base and noun.

column2: Have you ever pooped a balloon?
column5: A bizarre humorous question whose meaning depends on source context. Literally it evokes expelling a balloon rectally; in a medical context this can allude to the balloon expulsion test (BET), used in evaluating defecatory disorders. It is not an established figurative English idiom.
column6: balloon expulsion test (medical context); absurd joke
column7: The unexpected question, 'Have you ever pooped a balloon?', may be a comic way of referring to a balloon expulsion test.
column8: CORRECTION: remove unsupported metaphorical senses such as 'release tension' or 'shatter illusions'. Preserve as source-specific humor; medical BET connection only when context supports it.
column12: entry::sentence_pattern usage::humorous usage::figurative topic::health topic::testing discovery::evaluation

column5: A doe is an adult female deer and, for some species, a female rabbit/goat/antelope or similar animal. Separately, DOE is an abbreviation used by multiple organizations, including the U.S. Department of Energy.
column6: female deer; Department of Energy (context-specific abbreviation)
column7: A doe and her fawn crossed the trail. / The U.S. DOE released the report.
column8: CORRECTION: lowercase lexical word and uppercase abbreviation are unrelated homographs. Do not fold DOE into the animal definition without distinction.

column5: Noun: shameless boldness/nerve; bitterness or resentment; bile (historical/anatomical term); a swelling on a plant. Verb: to irritate/chafe or annoy deeply.
column7: She had the gall to complain after arriving an hour late. / The unfairness galled him.
column8: Highly polysemous. Common idiom-like frame 'have the gall to do X'. Do not reduce to resentment.

column5: To rub and cause skin/material irritation; to become irritated by rubbing; figuratively, to feel annoyed or constrained by a rule, restriction, or authority.
column7: The strap chafed my shoulder. / He chafed at the restrictions. / Anti-chafing cream can reduce friction.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FIGURATIVE FRAME: chafe at/under + restriction/control.

column5: Impudent = boldly disrespectful, rude, or shamelessly forward; impudence = that behavior/quality.
column7: The impudent reply shocked the teacher. / He had the impudence to demand an apology.
column8: CORRECTION: current POS says adjective/noun form while headword only adjective. Teach family cleanly. Tone stronger/more formal than playful 'cheeky'.

column2: pop a balloon / popping a balloon
column5: Literally, to burst a balloon. Figuratively, a speaker may creatively compare puncturing optimism, tension, fantasy, or a social setup to popping/deflating a balloon, but there is no single fixed idiomatic meaning. Also appears literally in dating-show formats involving balloons.
column6: burst a balloon; deflate hopes (creative context)
column7: He popped the balloon with a pin. / Her blunt answer felt like popping the bubble of everyone's optimism.
column8: CORRECTION: do not teach a broad list of fixed figurative meanings. Distinguish literal action, creative metaphor, and source-specific dating-show usage.
column12: entry::form_family entry::phrase usage::figurative topic::dating discovery::comparison discovery::figurative_extension

column5: A man known for being charming to, pursuing, or attracting women, often with many romantic interests.
column7: He had a reputation as a ladies' man.
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling is 'ladies' man' (plural possessive), not 'lady's man'. Tone can be admiring, teasing, or critical.

column5: To conflict because of incompatible ideas, styles, interests, or personalities; 'clashing personalities' = people whose characteristic ways of behaving repeatedly conflict.
column7: They have clashing personalities and argue constantly. / Their working styles clash.
column8: Teach underlying productive verb: X clashes with Y; personalities/styles/colors clash. Not merely a static 'situation'.

column5: An economic doctrine favoring minimal government interference in markets; more broadly, a hands-off, noninterventionist attitude or style.
column7: The manager takes a laissez-faire approach to scheduling. / They debated laissez-faire economics.
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling hyphenated 'laissez-faire'. General-use adjective can imply relaxed/noninterfering, sometimes excessively so.

column2: as much as the next person/guy
column5: As much as an ordinary person would; used to claim a normal degree of liking, dislike, ability, etc., often before introducing a qualification or contrast.
column6: like anyone else, as much as anyone
column7: I love shortcuts as much as the next person, but this one creates more work.
column8: Productive pattern: 'I like X as much as the next person/guy, but...'. 'Guy' is informal and can be generic; 'person' is more neutral.

column5: To talk indiscreetly or excessively, especially to reveal information or a secret that should have been kept private.
column7: Don't blab about the surprise party. / Who blabbed the secret to them?
column8: KEY FRAMES: blab about X; blab X to someone. Often implies careless/indiscreet disclosure, not necessarily accidental.

column2: put oneself down / constantly put oneself down
column5: To criticize, belittle, or speak negatively about oneself; when habitual, it can be described as constantly/compulsively putting oneself down.
column7: You keep putting yourself down even when you've done well. / His humor often involves self-deprecation.
column8: NORMALIZE: 'compulsively put oneself down' is not a fixed expression and the current note speculates about causes. Teach productive 'put oneself down' without diagnosing why someone does it.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::communication topic::construction discovery::criticism

column5: Driven by a strong, difficult-to-control urge or habit; also, extremely habitual or persistent. In clinical contexts, 'compulsive' has more specific meanings and should not be used casually as a diagnosis.
column7: He is a compulsive checker of notifications. / The behavior became repetitive and difficult to resist.
column8: NUANCE: compulsive ≠ obsessive. Obsessions are intrusive thoughts/urges; compulsions are repetitive behaviors/mental acts in OCD terminology, though everyday use is looser.
column12: entry::word usage::specialist topic::self-help topic::medicine topic::health discovery::urge discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To mentally or emotionally prepare oneself to face something difficult, unpleasant, frightening, or painful.
column6: brace oneself, prepare oneself, fortify oneself
column7: She steeled herself for the bad news. / I steeled myself to make the call.
column8: KEY FRAMES: steel oneself for + noun; steel oneself to + verb. Metaphor: make oneself hard/strong like steel.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative topic::planning topic::construction

column5: A measure of market concentration calculated by summing the squares of firms' market shares; often called the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index (HHI). Scale depends on whether shares are expressed as fractions or percentages.
column7: Regulators may use the HHI as one indicator of market concentration.
column8: PRECISION: if market shares are percentages, HHI ranges up to 10,000; with fractions, up to 1. Interpretation thresholds depend on authority/time and should not be hard-coded here.

column2: be a tease / you're such a tease
column5: To call someone a 'tease' is to say they deliberately arouse curiosity, anticipation, flirtation, or desire without immediately following through; can be playful or accusatory depending context.
column6: teaser, flirt (context-dependent), someone who keeps you guessing
column7: You won't tell me the ending? You're such a tease. / He called her a tease after the flirtatious exchange.
column8: Broaden beyond sexual/flirtatious use: teasing information/surprises can prompt the phrase too. Sexual use can be loaded or blaming; context/tone matters.

column2: stuff something with something / stuff oneself; 'stuff with me' (source-dependent)
column5: Standard 'stuff X with Y' = fill X tightly/full; 'stuff oneself with food' = eat too much. 'Stuff with me' by itself is not a standard phrasal verb with a stable meaning; any sexual/vulgar reading requires specific source context.
column7: She stuffed the bag with clothes. / We stuffed ourselves with pizza.
column8: CORRECTION: separate productive constructions from the unclear source fragment 'stuff with me'. Do not teach a generic UK sexual meaning without the actual construction/context.

column5: A playful, cheerful, sometimes deliberately goofy way of saying yes.
column7: 'Are you coming?' 'Yeppers!'
column8: Informal/comic. Strongly associated for some speakers with pop-culture character voices, but usable as general playful 'yes'.

column5: To take a short break for roughly the stated number of minutes. 'Take five' is the most established idiom; 'take ten/15' are transparent extensions.
column6: take a break, take a breather, pause
column7: Let's take 15 and meet back here at 2:30. / We've been at this for hours—take five.
column8: Teach productive pattern rather than treating 'take 15' as uniquely fixed. Often an instruction in work/rehearsal contexts.

column2: clean someone out / get cleaned out
column5: To take or cause the loss of all or most of someone's money/valuables, especially through theft, gambling, high costs, or exploitation; also to empty a place/container completely.
column7: The casino cleaned him out. / We got cleaned out by unexpected repairs. / They cleaned out the garage.
column8: KEY ACTIVE/PASSIVE: clean someone out → someone gets/is cleaned out. Separate financial-loss sense from literal emptying.

column5: To deliberately and persistently avoid, reject, or exclude a person, group, practice, or thing.
column6: avoid, ostracize, reject, steer clear of
column7: He was shunned by former friends. / She shuns social media.
column8: Can take people or things/practices. 'Ostracize' specifically emphasizes social exclusion; shun can simply mean deliberately avoid.

column5: To deteriorate or descend into a worse/less organized state ('devolve into'); separately, to transfer power, responsibility, or duties to a lower/local level ('devolve to/on').
column7: The debate devolved into shouting. / Some powers were devolved to regional governments.
column8: CORRECTION: current card misses the major governance/transfer sense. KEY FRAMES: devolve into chaos; devolve power/responsibility to a lower level.

column5: Verb /ˈdɛləˌɡeɪt/: to entrust a task, responsibility, or authority to another person. Noun /ˈdɛləɡət/: a representative sent to a meeting/conference.
column7: A good manager delegates routine tasks. / Each branch sent a delegate to the convention.
column8: IMPORTANT pronunciation/POS distinction: verb stress differs from noun. KEY FRAME: delegate X to Y.

column5: To switch the positions/order of two or more things; in music, to rewrite/perform in a different key; in math, to interchange rows/columns or move terms according to context.
column7: I transposed two digits in the phone number. / Can you transpose the song into C major?
column8: Normalize base + source form. Add major music/math senses; accidental digit/letter swapping is common.

column5: Military: missing in action. Informally, unexpectedly absent, unreachable, or not showing up/communicating for a period.
column6: missing, unaccounted for, absent, off the radar
column7: He went MIA for three days and didn't answer anyone. / The soldier was listed as MIA.
column8: Keep military origin distinct from casual figurative use. Usually pronounced as letters.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::initialism usage::casual usage::slang usage::figurative usage::military usage::informal topic::communication topic::military

column5: A graduating student selected for the valedictory role/honor, often—but not universally—the student with the highest academic rank; selection rules vary by school.
column7: She was named valedictorian and delivered the graduation address.
column8: CORRECTION/PRECISION: not universally defined solely as highest GPA, and the speech role can vary. Contrast salutatorian in systems that use the term.

column2: get some Z's / catch some Z's
column5: To get some sleep, usually a modest amount or a needed rest.
column6: sleep, get some shut-eye, catch some sleep
column7: You look exhausted—go get some Z's. / I'm going to catch a few Z's before the flight.
column8: Repair punctuation. Z represents the conventional written sound of snoring/sleep. Common variants get/catch some Z's.

column5: To devise, arrange, or bring about something through ingenuity or planning; often implies artificiality, manipulation, or implausible construction, but not always deceit.
column7: They contrived a way to fit everyone into one car. / The plot feels contrived.
column8: Important adjective 'contrived' = artificial/forced. Verb can be clever/ingenious without wrongdoing; current tax-evasion example overweights deceit.

column5: To specify or require something explicitly as a condition, term, or provision; in legal procedure, parties may also formally agree to a fact/point.
column6: specify, require, state as a condition; agree formally
column7: The contract stipulates that payment is due within 30 days. / The parties stipulated to the authenticity of the document.
column8: KEY FRAME: stipulate that + clause; stipulate X as a condition. Legal 'stipulate to' = formally agree/admit for purposes of proceeding.
column12: entry::phrase usage::formal topic::law discovery::process_details discovery::procedural_language discovery::agreement

column5: To distort, bias, or shift something away from a balanced/representative result; to turn or lie at an angle. In statistics, skew/skewness describes asymmetry of a distribution.
column7: A few extreme values skewed the average. / The distribution is skewed to the right.
