column8: Broaden to statistical and physical senses. KEY: skew results/data; skew toward X; right/left-skewed distribution.

column2: I won't state our stances so as not to skew the results / withhold one's stance to avoid biasing results
column3: /aɪ woʊnt ˈstɪpjəˌleɪt aʊɚ ˈstænsɪz æz tu nɑt skju rɪˈzʌlts/
column5: A naturalized way to say the speaker will not reveal participants' positions/opinions because doing so might influence the outcome. The original use of 'stipulate our stances' is unnatural for simply 'state/reveal our positions'.
column6: withhold one's position, avoid biasing the results, remain neutral
column7: I won't state our stances beforehand so as not to skew the results. / Let's withhold our opinions until everyone has answered.
column8: CORRECTION: 'stipulate' normally means specify as a condition or formally agree, not merely 'state an opinion'. KEY PURPOSE FRAME: so as not to + verb = in order not to.
column12: entry::construction usage::debate-friendly topic::debate topic::construction discovery::prevention discovery::debate_language

column2: keep one's head held high / hold one's head high
column5: To maintain dignity, confidence, or self-respect despite criticism, failure, embarrassment, or hardship.
column6: hold one's head up, stand tall, keep one's dignity
column7: Even after the loss, she held her head high. / Keep your head held high—you handled it well.
column8: More idiomatic base is 'hold your head high'; 'keep your head held high' is also natural. Physical posture metaphor → dignity/pride.

column5: While confronting hardship, misfortune, opposition, or difficult circumstances; despite such adversity.
column6: despite hardship, amid difficulty, when facing adversity
column7: She remained optimistic in the face of adversity.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: in the face of + danger/opposition/criticism/adversity = when confronted by/despite. Connects to WID2134 adversity.

column5: A person who creates illustrations—images made to explain, decorate, interpret, or accompany text/content, especially for books, magazines, advertising, games, and digital media.
column7: The children's-book illustrator gave each character a distinctive look.
column8: 'Designer' is a different role and 'drawer' is not a natural professional synonym. Related: illustrate, illustration.
column12: entry::word usage::professional topic::communication topic::technology topic::media topic::art discovery::explanation discovery::professional_context

column5: Language that sounds persuasive, grand, principled, or impressive but is regarded as lacking substance, concrete action, evidence, or sincere commitment.
column6: hollow rhetoric, empty words, hollow promises, hot air (informal)
column7: Voters dismissed the promise as empty rhetoric without a concrete plan.
column8: KEY COMBINATION: rhetoric + empty/hollow = persuasive language judged substantively vacant. Often political, corporate, or promotional; evaluative phrase.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::evaluative usage::professional usage::rhetorical usage::persuasive usage::businesslike topic::rhetoric discovery::evidence discovery::commitment discovery::professional_context discovery::persuasion discovery::debate_language

column5: Language and persuasive techniques used in political argument, campaigning, public debate, or messaging; the term itself is neutral, though context may criticize rhetoric as manipulative, inflammatory, or lacking substance.
column6: political discourse, political messaging, campaign language
column7: The candidate's political rhetoric became sharper as the election approached. / Critics said the speech offered rhetoric rather than concrete policy.
column8: CORRECTION: 'rhetoric' does not inherently mean insincere or empty language. Compare WID2400 'empty rhetoric', which explicitly adds that negative judgment.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::politics topic::debate topic::rhetoric discovery::debate_language discovery::public_discourse discovery::criticism

column5: Content or language that adds little substance, information, or value; 'fluff' can refer to padding in writing/media, while 'filler' is material used mainly to fill space/time.
column6: fluff, filler, padding, empty talk, filler language
column7: Cut the fluff and get to the main point. / The article has useful information, but there's a lot of filler.
column8: CORRECTION: 'saying fluff' is not a natural fixed English expression. Teach productive nouns/phrases such as 'fluff', 'filler', 'filler language', or 'empty talk'.

column5: Covered with, made of, or resembling soft fine down—small soft feathers or fine hair/fuzz; by extension, very soft and fluffy.
column7: The chick was covered in downy feathers. / A downy layer of hair covered the fruit.
column8: KEY WORD FAMILY: down (soft feathers) → downy. Do not confuse with Down syndrome; unrelated word/history.

column5: Shared, used, owned, or experienced by members of a group or community rather than privately by one person; relating to community life.
column7: The hostel has a communal kitchen. / Meals were eaten at a communal table.
column8: Common collocations: communal kitchen/bathroom/space/living/dining. 'Public' is not always equivalent: communal may be restricted to members of a particular group.

column4: adjective; noun; verb (informal, verb less common)
column5: Having practical knowledge, good judgment, or shrewd understanding, especially in a particular area; noun: practical know-how. Historically/colloquially, verb 'savvy?' can mean understand.
column7: She's financially savvy. / He has a lot of business savvy. / You need to be more media-savvy.
column8: KEY PATTERNS: tech-/media-/business-savvy; have the savvy to do X. 'Smart' is broader; savvy emphasizes practical understanding.

column5: Directly opposed to or fundamentally incompatible with something in principle, character, or effect.
column6: opposed to, contrary to, incompatible with
column7: That approach is antithetical to the values the organization claims to uphold.
column8: KEY FRAME: X is antithetical to Y. More formal/stronger than simply 'different from'. Related noun: antithesis.

column5: Abrupt, curt, and lacking social warmth or politeness in manner or speech, sometimes unintentionally.
column7: His brusque reply sounded ruder than he intended.
column8: Brusque describes manner, not necessarily hostility. A person can be efficient/direct but come across as brusque.

column5: Literally, 'lean in' = incline one's body toward something. Figuratively, 'lean in' can mean engage more actively or assertively; 'lean into X' commonly means embrace, commit to, exploit, or deliberately intensify a challenge, role, quality, or tendency.
column6: engage, commit, embrace, press into, take initiative
column7: She leaned in to hear him better. / Instead of hiding the weirdness, the show leans into it. / He decided to lean into the challenge.
column8: CORRECTION: simplify garbled note. 'Lean In' was popularized as a leadership/workplace slogan by Sheryl Sandberg, but figurative uses are broader. KEY CONTRAST: lean in (often engagement) vs lean into + object (actively embrace/use X).
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::figurative usage::professional usage::journalistic topic::media discovery::assertion discovery::audience_engagement discovery::figurative_extension discovery::evaluation discovery::commitment discovery::escalation discovery::professional_context

column5: An extremely rapid, striking rise in fame, success, status, popularity, value, etc.
column6: rapid ascent, sudden rise, spectacular rise
column7: The singer's meteoric rise from local clubs to stadium tours took only two years.
column8: KEY COLLOCATION: meteoric rise to fame/prominence/success. Despite the image, meteors visually fall through the sky; the phrase conventionally means spectacularly rapid ascent.

column5: Likely or inclined to experience, suffer from, or do something, especially something undesirable, recurring, or characteristic.
column6: susceptible to, liable to, inclined to, likely to
column7: This road is prone to flooding. / I'm prone to overthinking when I'm tired.
column8: KEY FRAME: prone to + noun/gerund. Not restricted to innate tendencies and not always negative, though negative contexts are especially common.

column5: A silly, goofy, playful, or mildly ridiculous person, often used affectionately rather than as a serious insult.
column7: You're such a goofball—you had the whole room laughing.
column8: Tone is often warm/playful. 'Dork' can overlap but has different social/awkward connotations.

column5: To excite, stimulate, or arouse interest—often in a superficial, sensational, or mildly sexual way.
column7: The tabloid story was designed to titillate readers. / The audience was titillated by the scandalous details.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Often carries a slightly disapproving sense of cheap/sensational stimulation; sexual undertone is possible but not required.

column5: To hold someone's attention completely; fascinate or captivate intensely.
column7: The story enthralled me from the first page. / The children sat enthralled by the performance.
column8: KEY ACTIVE/PASSIVE: X enthralls someone; someone is enthralled by/with X. Stronger than merely 'interest'.

column5: To charm, delight, or fascinate someone, sometimes in a way that distracts or deceives; older/literary uses can mean deceive or trick.
column7: The old town beguiled us with its narrow streets. / He beguiled investors with promises that proved false.
column8: IMPORTANT: deception is possible but not inherent in every modern use. Can be positively charming or negatively deceptive depending context.

column5: To link or join things into a chain or series. 'Concatenate' is the much more common computing/data term for joining strings or sequences end-to-end; 'catenate' is rarer/technical.
column7: The program concatenates the first and last names into one string. / In technical writing, 'catenate' can mean link into a chain.
column8: USAGE: retain catenate for recognition, but for programming/data, 'concatenate' is normally the word learners will encounter and use.

column5: A geminate is a consonant that is phonologically or phonetically long/doubled relative to a singleton consonant; adjective 'geminate' describes it; verb 'geminate' means make/become geminate in linguistic analysis.
column7: Italian contrasts singleton and geminate consonants; for example, consonant length can distinguish words.
column8: CORRECTION: gemination is not simply 'two identical letters' and does not generally refer to vowels in the same way. Spelling may signal gemination in some languages, but the linguistic concept concerns sound/phonological length.

column5: To divide something into two equal or roughly equal parts; or to reduce an amount, number, rate, distance, etc. by half.
column6: cut in half, divide by two, reduce by half
column7: She halved the apple. / The new process halved the time needed to finish the task.
column8: Broaden productive use: halve costs/time/risk/number. Pronounced /hæv/; the 'l' is silent.

column2: take a fall / take the fall
column5: 'Take the fall' = accept or receive blame/punishment, often for others or as a scapegoat. 'Take a fall' can also literally mean fall down and, in some contexts, deliberately lose or suffer a setback.
column6: take the blame, take the hit, be the scapegoat
column7: He took the fall for the accounting scheme. / She took a nasty fall on the stairs.
column8: CORRECTION: for the blame/cover-up sense, the standard idiom is usually 'take THE fall', not 'take A fall'. Preserve 'take a fall' for literal/contextual uses.

column5: A farm implement used to turn or break soil; verb: to turn soil with a plough/plow. Figuratively, to move or work through something forcefully, steadily, or with difficulty.
column6: till, cultivate; push through, forge through
column7: They ploughed the field before planting. / She plowed through three chapters in one evening.
column8: CORRECTION: repair garbled definition. BrE 'plough'; AmE 'plow'. Productive figurative forms: plough/plow through work, traffic, snow, a crowd.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative usage::american_english usage::british_english topic::work topic::agriculture discovery::implementation discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To filter or pass gradually through a porous substance; of liquid, to circulate/filter in coffee-making; figuratively, for ideas, information, feelings, or changes to spread or develop gradually.
column6: filter, seep, trickle; spread gradually, develop
column7: Water percolates through the soil. / The idea took time to percolate through the organization. / Let that thought percolate for a while.
column8: Useful figurative patterns: percolate through + group/system; idea percolates = gradually develops/sinks in.

column5: To joke with or tease someone playfully; 'josh around' = engage in lighthearted joking or teasing.
column7: Relax—I was just joshing you. / We were joshing around after dinner.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FRAMES: josh someone; josh around. Repair punctuation in source example.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::word entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::humorous discovery::audience_engagement

column5: A period of supervised release in the community imposed in criminal justice under specified conditions; more broadly, a trial/evaluation period at work, school, or an organization.
column6: supervised release; trial period, provisional period
column7: He was sentenced to probation. / New employees have a three-month probation period.
column8: IMPORTANT: legal probation is not simply 'testing after a mistake'; it is a formal legal status whose rules vary by jurisdiction. Common frames: on probation; probation period.
column12: entry::word usage::formal topic::work topic::education topic::crime topic::courtroom topic::law discovery::evaluation discovery::release

column2: cop out / cop out of something
column5: To avoid a responsibility, commitment, challenge, or difficult action, often by making an excuse; noun 'cop-out' = an evasive excuse or avoidance.
column7: Don't cop out of the presentation just because you're nervous. / Calling it 'too complicated' felt like a cop-out.
column8: KEY FORMS: cop out; cop out of + noun/gerund; a cop-out (noun, hyphenated).
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::informal usage::presentation-friendly discovery::evasive_language discovery::prevention discovery::commitment discovery::presentation_language

column5: To roam, travel, or go around from place to place for pleasure, amusement, or social activity, often carefree and sometimes with a teasing implication of neglecting responsibilities.
column6: roam, gad about, traipse around, wander
column7: He spent the summer gallivanting around Europe. / Where have you been gallivanting off to?
column8: CORRECTION/NORMALIZE: 'gallivant' is the standard spelling; 'galavant' is a recognized variant. The flirtation/courting association is historical/occasional, not required in modern use.

column5: To touch or stroke someone or something gently and repeatedly; often affectionate, but frequently sexual when referring to a person's body.
column7: She fondled the cat's ears absentmindedly. / In sexual contexts, 'fondle' can describe intimate touching.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Current hair example is possible, but the word often has a sexual connotation with people; 'caress' is usually warmer/less clinical.

column5: A small supernatural being in Irish folklore, typically portrayed as a solitary male fairy associated with shoemaking, trickery, and hidden treasure; modern popular imagery often includes green clothing and pots of gold.
column7: Stories about leprechauns have changed substantially in popular culture. / The children set up a playful 'leprechaun trap' for St. Patrick's Day.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. 'Guarding pots of gold' is popular-culture shorthand, not a complete folklore definition.

column5: To irritate, anger, or agitate someone; 'rile someone up' can intensify this and may also mean excite/stir a group into agitation.
column6: annoy, irritate, anger, agitate, work up
column7: The comment really riled him. / Don't rile the crowd up. / She was still riled about the decision.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FRAMES: rile someone; get/be riled; rile someone up.

column5: Offended, resentful, or upset—often with the speaker implying the reaction is excessive or petty. As a noun, 'butthurt' can mean such resentment.
column7: He was still butthurt about losing the argument.
column8: Register: crude and dismissive; calling someone butthurt judges their reaction rather than neutrally describing emotion. Avoid in formal/respectful contexts.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::formal usage::slang usage::derogatory usage::vulgar usage::rhetorical usage::informal usage::evaluative discovery::evaluation discovery::debate_language

column2: seal something up / seal it up
column5: To close or secure something tightly so air, liquid, people, etc. cannot pass; figuratively/contextually, to finish or secure a result, though 'seal the deal' is more idiomatic for completing an agreement.
column6: close tightly, secure, seal off; finalize (context-dependent)
column7: Seal the bag up before you put it in the freezer. / They sealed up the opening with tape.
column8: CORRECTION: do not overteach 'seal it up' as a generic idiom meaning wrap up a project. Core construction is literal/productive 'seal X up'; compare fixed 'seal the deal'.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::idiom entry::verb_pattern entry::construction discovery::figurative_extension discovery::agreement

column5: To scold or criticize someone angrily and severely, often at length.
column7: The manager berated him for ignoring the safety procedure. / She was berated in front of her coworkers.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FRAME: berate someone for + noun/gerund. Stronger than simply criticize.

column5: A strong adverse reaction by a group or the public against a change, decision, trend, person, or action.
column7: The policy triggered a backlash from local residents. / The company faced backlash over the ad.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: face/provoke/trigger/spark a backlash; backlash against/over X. Usually negative reaction, often collective.

column5: The state or quality of being mediocre—only average in quality, ability, or achievement; can also refer disparagingly to a mediocre person or thing.
column7: He feared settling for mediocrity. / The critic accused the studio of rewarding mediocrity.
column8: Often strongly evaluative: 'average' can be neutral, whereas 'mediocrity' usually implies disappointing lack of excellence.

column5: The science and technology of producing, maintaining, and studying very low temperatures and their effects on materials and systems.
column7: Cryogenics is essential for technologies that use liquefied gases and superconducting systems.
column8: PRECISION: cryogenics is not the same as cryonics, the controversial preservation of human bodies/brains after legal death in hopes of future revival.

column5: Having a bad reputation or not considered respectable, trustworthy, or socially acceptable.
column7: He was associated with several disreputable businesses. / They stayed in a disreputable-looking hotel.
column8: Can describe people, businesses, places, practices. 'Infamous' means famous for something bad and is not always interchangeable.

column2: out of line / be out of line
column5: Beyond acceptable limits of behavior, authority, propriety, or fairness; inappropriate, disrespectful, or presumptuous.
column6: inappropriate, unacceptable, over the line, presumptuous
column7: That comment was completely out of line. / I was out of line to speak to you that way.
column8: Normalize from 'being out of line'. KEY FRAME: be out of line; tell someone they're out of line. Also literal 'out of line' = not aligned/in sequence.

column5: A container, typically with a handle and narrow opening, for holding/pouring liquids. Plural 'jugs' is also vulgar/dated slang for breasts.
column7: She filled a jug with water. / The comedy used a crude joke about 'jugs'.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Slang sense is objectifying and somewhat dated; recognition-focused. A pitcher and jug overlap but regional/object differences exist.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::form_family entry::word usage::slang usage::dated usage::vulgar usage::informal

column5: A person who is killed or suffers severely because of a belief, cause, or identity; figuratively, someone who conspicuously suffers or sacrifices and may seek sympathy. Verb: to kill/persecute as a martyr, or figuratively 'martyr oneself'.
column6: sufferer for a cause; self-sacrificer (figurative), victim (not exact)
column7: She was remembered as a martyr for the movement. / Stop martyring yourself and ask someone else to help.
column8: Do not make attention-seeking part of the core historical/religious definition. Figurative 'play the martyr' often criticizes performative self-sacrifice.

column5: Self-righteously convinced of or displaying one's moral superiority over others.
column7: His holier-than-thou tone made a reasonable point sound unbearable.
column8: Standard fixed form is 'holier-than-thou'. Usually attributive/predicative adjective: a holier-than-thou attitude; don't get holier-than-thou with me.

column5: A person regarded as excessively well-behaved, virtuous, rule-following, or eager to win approval; adjective can describe such behavior.
column6: goody two-shoes, teacher's pet (specific), excessively virtuous
column7: He was teased for being a goody-goody who never broke a rule.
column8: Repair punctuation. 'Prude' specifically concerns sexual/modesty standards and is not a general synonym. Compare WID2034 goody two-shoes.

column2: an undeniable pull between people / feel a pull toward someone
column5: A strong sense of attraction, emotional draw, or compelling interest between/toward people; 'pull' metaphorically conceptualizes attraction as a force drawing someone closer.
column6: mutual attraction, chemistry, magnetic pull, draw
column7: There was an undeniable pull between them. / I felt a strange pull toward her from the start.
column8: Teach productive construction: feel a pull toward X; there is a pull between X and Y. 'Undeniable' intensifies but is not part of a fixed idiom.
column12: entry::idiom entry::collocation entry::construction usage::figurative usage::scientific topic::romance topic::chemistry topic::science

column5: Literally, to inhale air, scent, smoke, etc.; poetically, 'breathe someone/something in' can mean deeply take in and savor a person's presence, scent, atmosphere, or moment.
column7: She stepped outside and breathed in the cold air. / He held her close and breathed her in.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTION: breathe X in. Romantic use is creative/poetic rather than a fixed idiom; literal inhalation is the base meaning.

column5: With deep respect, awe, solemn regard, or religious devotion.
column7: She reverently touched the old manuscript. / The congregation listened reverently.
column8: Word family: revere (verb), reverence (noun), reverent (adj), reverently (adv). Can be religious or secular.

column2: cup someone's face / cup something in one's hands
column5: To hold something gently in curved hands as if forming a cup; 'cup someone's face' means gently hold the sides of their face, often affectionately or reassuringly.
column7: She cupped his face in her hands. / He cupped the tiny bird in his palms.
column8: Teach productive verb 'cup + object', not only romantic phrase. Common: cup one's hands, cup someone's cheek/face.

column5: To sleep, especially briefly or somewhere temporary/informal; 'kip down' = settle down to sleep. Noun: a sleep/nap.
column7: You can kip on the sofa tonight. / We kipped down in the spare room. / I need a quick kip.
column8: Broaden to core BrE 'kip'. 'Kip down' is possible, but simply 'kip' and 'have a kip' are very common.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::word entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::british_english topic::wellness discovery::resolution

column5: To snore, especially loudly; the sound is humorously compared to sawing wood/logs.
column7: He was sawing logs before the movie even ended.
column8: 'Saw logs' is especially common in AmE; 'saw wood' also occurs. 'Wheeze' is not a synonym for snoring.

column2: cop some Z's / get/catch some Z's
column5: To get some sleep or take a nap.
column6: get some sleep, catch some Z's, get some shut-eye, snooze
column7: I'm exhausted—I'm going to cop some Z's. / Try to catch a few Z's on the plane.
column8: 'Cop some Z's' is less common than get/catch some Z's but understandable, especially AmE slang. Z's represent sleep/snoring.

column5: A person or thing regarded as an outstanding model or perfect example of a particular quality.
column7: She remained a paragon of patience even during the delay. / The building was once considered a paragon of modern design.
column8: KEY FRAME: a paragon of + virtue/quality/type. Often elevated or slightly ironic depending context.

column2: catch forty winks / catch some winks; '10,000 winks' (playful hyperbole)
column5: To take a short sleep or nap. 'Forty winks' is an established idiom; 'catch some winks' is also natural. 'Catch 10,000 winks' is a playful exaggeration, not a standard idiom.
column6: take a nap, get some sleep, catch some Z's, get some shut-eye
column7: I'm going to catch forty winks before dinner. / After that week, I feel like I need 10,000 winks.
column8: CORRECTION: normalize the established expressions and preserve '10,000 winks' only as transparent humorous hyperbole. Number formatting standardized.

column5: To retire someone because of age or eligibility for a pension; by extension, to make/consider something obsolete through age. 'Superannuated' can mean retired or antiquated/outdated.
column7: He was superannuated after decades of service. / The office finally replaced its superannuated equipment.
column8: Current machinery example is possible figuratively but uncommon as active verb. Recognition-focused formal word; 'superannuation' is a pension/retirement term in several countries.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal usage::dated usage::british_english topic::grammar

column5: A person who behaves in a ridiculous, foolish, or clownish way, often making themselves an object of amusement or contempt.
column7: He made himself look like a buffoon by interrupting everyone with bad jokes.
column8: Can be comic or insulting. 'Idiot' emphasizes stupidity; buffoon emphasizes ridiculous/clownish behavior.

column2: that won't fly / something won't fly
column5: Used to say that an excuse, idea, behavior, proposal, or arrangement will not be accepted, tolerated, believed, or succeed.
column6: won't be accepted, won't work, won't pass, won't be tolerated
column7: That excuse won't fly with the professor. / Charging extra after we agreed on the price isn't going to fly.
column8: KEY FRAME: X won't fly; X won't fly with + person/group. Meaning depends on context: unacceptable, implausible, or unworkable.

column2: put one's foot in it / put one's foot in one's mouth
column5: To say or do something tactless, embarrassing, or socially awkward, especially accidentally.
column6: say the wrong thing, make a faux pas, blunder
column7: I really put my foot in it when I asked why she wasn't married. / In AmE, 'put my foot in my mouth' is especially common.
column8: Normalize source sentence to productive forms. BrE commonly 'put one's foot in it'; AmE commonly 'put one's foot in one's mouth'.

column5: An exclamation expressing disbelief, scorn, or emphatic rejection of what was just said—roughly 'nonsense!' or 'yeah, right!'
column6: nonsense!, yeah right!, no way!, rubbish!
column7: 'He's an expert.' 'Expert, my foot! He started yesterday.'
column8: CORRECTION: remove invented 'someone stepping on your toes' exasperation sense. This expression is figurative/dismissive, not normally a literal complaint about one's foot.

column2: succumb to something / get someone to give in to something
column5: 'Succumb to X' means yield to a force, temptation, pressure, illness, injury, etc.; if another person causes the yielding, English usually says 'persuade/get someone to give in' rather than treating 'get someone to succumb to' as a fixed phrase.
column6: give in to, yield to, surrender to; persuade, wear down
column7: He finally succumbed to temptation and bought it. / She eventually got him to give in and take a vacation.
column8: CORRECTION: teach the productive lexical frame 'succumb to + noun' separately from causative 'get someone to give in'. 'Succumb' can also mean die from an illness/injury.

column5: To divert or remove part of a liquid, money, resources, people, attention, etc. from a larger supply or intended destination, literally or figuratively; it may be secret/illegal but need not be.
column6: divert, drain off, draw away, skim off (often illicit)
column7: The pipe siphons off excess water. / The scheme siphoned off public funds. / The new service siphoned customers off from its rivals.
column8: CORRECTION: illegality/secrecy is common in financial contexts but not inherent. KEY FRAME: siphon off + resource / siphon X off from Y.

column5: To perform calculations or analyze quantitative data, especially to reach a decision, estimate, forecast, or comparison.
column6: calculate, analyze the figures, run the numbers
column7: Let's crunch the numbers before deciding whether the move is affordable. / The analysts spent the afternoon number-crunching.
column8: Not necessarily 'complex' calculations. Related noun/adjective: number cruncher; number-crunching.

column5: A person who keeps and manages honey bees; a beekeeper.
column7: The apiarist inspected the hives for signs of disease.
column8: 'Beekeeper' is the normal everyday word; 'apiarist' is more formal/technical. Commercial activity is not required.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::technical usage::businesslike discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: An organized revolt or refusal to obey lawful authority by members of a military force or a ship's crew, especially against commanding officers; figuratively, a group rebellion against leadership. Verb: to mutiny.
column7: The sailors staged a mutiny against the captain. / The crew threatened to mutiny over the conditions.
column8: Add verb. Historically/legal definitions can be specific; figurative use is common for humorous workplace/team rebellion.
column12: entry::word usage::humorous usage::figurative usage::professional usage::military topic::military topic::nautical discovery::figurative_extension discovery::nonconformity discovery::professional_context

column5: High-pitched, piercing, and often unpleasantly sharp in sound; figuratively, strident or aggressively insistent in tone. Verb: to make a shrill cry/sound.
column7: A shrill alarm woke us. / The debate became increasingly shrill.
column8: CAUTION: figurative 'shrill' can be a loaded/subjective criticism, especially of a person's voice or advocacy. Describe tone precisely when possible.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::communication discovery::figurative_extension discovery::impression discovery::debate_language

column5: To continue doing something at the same level or in the same way. Often encouraging ('You're doing well—keep it up'), but can also be a warning ('Keep it up and you'll get in trouble').
column7: Your pronunciation is improving—keep it up! / Keep it up and I'm leaving.
column8: IMPORTANT POLARITY: not always praise. Tone/context determines encouragement vs threat/warning.

column5: Rumor, gossip, or informal information circulating among a group, especially workplace, military, or organizational talk.
column7: What's the scuttlebutt about the reorganization?
column8: Origin: nautical 'scuttlebutt' was a cask of drinking water, where sailors gathered and exchanged gossip—roughly analogous to 'water-cooler talk'.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::professional usage::military topic::workplace topic::military discovery::professional_context

column5: A playful formation modeled on 'rumor has it', meaning informal gossip suggests that something is true.
column6: rumor has it, word has it, the scuttlebutt is that
column7: Scuttlebutt has it that the office is moving downtown.
column8: USAGE: understandable and playful, but less established than 'rumor has it'. More ordinary: 'The scuttlebutt is that...' or 'According to the scuttlebutt...'.

column5: Lacking liveliness, interest, intelligence, flavor, or stimulating substance; dull and insipid.
column7: The interview was full of vapid celebrity chatter. / The drink tasted strangely vapid.
column8: Often used for conversation, entertainment, remarks, personalities; literal 'flat/tasteless' sense is older/less common.

column5: An endoscopic examination of the colon, typically using a flexible colonoscope inserted through the rectum; used for screening, diagnosis, surveillance, and sometimes treatment such as polyp removal.
column6: endoscopic examination of the colon, colon screening (when used for screening)
column7: She scheduled a screening colonoscopy after discussing it with her doctor.
column8: PRECISION: not merely 'a flexible camera'; the instrument is a colonoscope. Not every colonoscopy is routine screening; indications vary.

column5: Verb: to make a model, draft, or preliminary representation of something for evaluation, demonstration, design, or testing. Noun 'mock-up': that model/draft.
column7: Can you mock up a new homepage layout? / They showed us a mock-up of the packaging.
column8: FORM: verb 'mock up' two words; noun/adjective commonly 'mock-up' hyphenated. A mock-up may be nonfunctional, unlike some prototypes.

column5: Making an exaggerated, hypocritical, or irritating display of moral superiority, piety, or righteousness.
column7: His sanctimonious lecture about honesty was hard to take seriously after he lied.
column8: Stronger/more negative than simply 'moral'. Compare WID2440 holier-than-thou.

column5: A German harvest-thanksgiving festival or observance ('harvest thanksgiving festival'), generally celebrated in autumn in churches and communities; customs and timing vary by region.
column7: The church decorated the altar with produce for Erntedankfest.
column8: CORRECTION: capitalize German noun. It is comparable to harvest-thanksgiving traditions but is not simply a German version of U.S./Canadian Thanksgiving.

column5: To be in the same situation or predicament as another person/group, often—but not necessarily—a difficult one.
column6: be in the same situation, share the same predicament
column7: Neither of us knows the answer, so we're in the same boat.
column8: Commonly negative/difficult context, but core meaning is shared circumstances. KEY FRAME: be in the same boat as + person.

column5: To share the same understanding, expectations, interpretation, or plan; often used to check alignment before acting.
column6: be aligned, agree, share an understanding, see eye to eye
column7: Before we start, let's make sure we're on the same page about the deadline.
column8: Not necessarily complete agreement on every opinion; often means shared understanding of the current plan/facts.

column5: To decide not to do something because of fear, nervousness, or lack of courage.
column6: back out, lose one's nerve, wimp out, bottle out (BrE)
column7: I was going to try the ride, but I chickened out. / He chickened out of asking her.
column8: KEY FORMS: chicken out; chicken out of + noun/gerund. More specifically fear-based than generic 'back out'.

column5: To feel or display little or no deep regret or guilt about wrongdoing or harm one has caused.
column6: be unremorseful, be unrepentant, show no regret
column7: The court heard testimony that he showed no remorse for the harm he caused.
column8: CORRECTION: 'cold-hearted' is an inference, not a synonym. Distinguish internal 'lack/feel no remorse' from observable 'show no remorse'.

column2: creep someone out / creep me out
column5: To make someone feel uneasy, disturbed, disgusted, or frightened in an eerie or unsettling way.
column6: unsettle, freak out, give the creeps, disturb
column7: That empty hallway creeps me out at night. / The doll really creeped her out.
column8: Normalize productive frame: X creeps someone out. Related: give someone the creeps. Usually eerie discomfort rather than ordinary fear alone.

column2: avail / to no avail / avail oneself of
column5: Noun 'avail' = use, benefit, or advantage, now especially in fixed phrases such as 'to no avail' (= without success). Verb: to help/benefit; reflexive 'avail oneself of X' = make use of X.
column6: use, benefit, advantage; make use of
column7: We tried everything, but to no avail. / She availed herself of the free legal advice.
column8: KEY CONSTRUCTIONS are more useful than bare word: to no avail; of little avail; avail oneself of. Bare transitive verb is formal/less common.

column5: To press/squeeze so something is damaged or deformed; defeat overwhelmingly; emotionally devastate. 'Crushed' can mean physically compressed or deeply disappointed/heartbroken.
column7: The box was crushed in transit. / Our team crushed them 6–0. / I was crushed when the trip was canceled.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Add common competitive sense 'crush someone/team' = defeat decisively.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::journalistic topic::romance topic::media topic::grammar

column5: A productive vulgar intensifier meaning to an extreme degree or with great effort, used after many verbs: laugh/work/dance/run/freeze one's ass off, etc.
column7: I laughed my ass off. / She worked her ass off to finish on time. / We froze our asses off outside.
column8: Teach as construction, not standalone 'ass off'. Meaning varies by verb: intense action/effort or extreme state. Pronoun must agree with subject.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::informal topic::work discovery::escalation

column5: An insulting term for a supposedly unsophisticated, awkward, or naive person from the countryside.
column6: hick, yokel, country bumpkin, rustic (less insulting in some contexts)
column7: They dismissed him as a country bumpkin because of his accent.
column8: Register matters: stereotypes rural people as unsophisticated. 'Country folk' is neutral/plural and not a synonym.

column5: A naive, unsophisticated, or gullible person, traditionally stereotyped as being from the countryside.
column6: gullible person, simpleton, bumpkin, sucker (gullibility focus)
column7: He thought I was some rube he could scam. / She's kind of a rube when it comes to online ads.
column8: Normalize from full source sentence while preserving usable frame. Often emphasizes easy-to-fool naivety more than literal rural origin.

column5: Sincere remorse, guilt, and regret for having done wrong, often accompanied by a desire to make amends.
column7: He expressed genuine contrition for the harm he had caused.
column8: Stronger/more formal than ordinary regret. Common: show/express contrition; genuine/deep contrition.

column2: not hold a candle to someone/something
column5: To be clearly inferior to someone or something in quality, ability, attractiveness, importance, etc.
column6: not compare to, pale in comparison with, be nowhere near as good as
column7: The remake doesn't hold a candle to the original. / He says that singer is good, but she doesn't hold a candle to you.
column8: Normalize productive negative frame. Historically connected to the lowly task of holding a candle for a skilled worker/performer, though exact origin stories vary.

column5: A U.S.-origin frozen-yogurt brand and chain. The initials currently expand to 'The Country's Best Yogurt'; the company originally used a different name before adopting TCBY.
column7: We stopped at TCBY for frozen yogurt.
column8: Brand/reference card. Avoid treating 'dessert place' as a lexical synonym. Corporate branding/history can change, so core learning value is recognizing the chain/initialism.
column12: entry::proper_noun entry::initialism usage::professional usage::businesslike topic::business discovery::origin_etymology discovery::professional_context

column5: Literally, a fire involving tires, which can be difficult and polluting; figuratively, a disastrously chaotic, dysfunctional, or badly managed situation.
column6: disaster, dumpster fire, train wreck, mess
column7: The rollout turned into a complete tire fire. / Firefighters struggled to contain the tire fire.
column8: Add literal source image. Figurative use is vivid/informal; 'dumpster fire' is a close modern metaphor.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::figurative topic::transportation discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To give evidence or make a formal statement as a witness, especially under oath in a legal proceeding; more broadly, to declare/attest to something, including religious usage.
column6: give evidence, bear witness, attest, declare
column7: She testified that she saw the car leave. / Several witnesses testified in court.
column8: KEY FRAMES: testify that + clause; testify about/to X; testify against/for someone. 'Swear' is not a synonym; witnesses may be sworn in before testifying.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::religious topic::law topic::religion discovery::evidence

column5: To witness, observe, or attest to something; also for evidence or facts to demonstrate/confirm something.
column6: witness, attest to, testify to, demonstrate
column7: She bore witness to the destruction firsthand. / These records bear witness to decades of change.
column8: KEY FRAME: bear witness to + event/fact. Can mean personally witness OR serve as evidence. Past tense 'bore witness'.

column5: To stand or move with unsteady, wavering steps as if likely to fall; figuratively, a system/institution can totter on the brink of collapse.
column7: The toddler tottered across the room. / The regime was tottering on the brink of collapse.
column8: Remove duplicate example. KEY: totter toward/across; totter on the brink of X. Often evokes weakness, infancy, age, or instability.

column5: To reproduce, transmit, arrange, or report words/data in a distorted, confused, or unintelligible form; 'garbled' describes the result.
column7: The bad connection garbled his voice. / The message arrived garbled and incomplete.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Can be speech/audio, text, data, or retelling.

column5: The act/process of becoming smaller, shorter, tighter, or reduced; a shortened linguistic form such as 'can't'; a tightening of muscle, including uterine contractions; and in economics, a decline in economic activity.
column7: 'Can't' is a contraction of 'cannot.' / She felt another contraction. / The economy entered a sharp contraction.
column8: Major polysemy missing: grammar, muscles/childbirth, economics, physical reduction. 'Abbreviation' is broader and not the same as grammatical contraction.
column12: entry::word topic::economics topic::linguistics topic::anatomy topic::health discovery::process_details

column5: A naturally occurring compound made from amino-acid precursors and stored largely in skeletal muscle as phosphocreatine, helping rapidly regenerate ATP during high-intensity activity; creatine monohydrate is also a widely used dietary supplement.
column6: creatine monohydrate (common supplement form), phosphagen-system compound (descriptive)
column7: Creatine helps supply rapid energy during short bursts of high-intensity exercise. / He uses creatine monohydrate as a supplement.
column8: CORRECTION/PRECISION: creatine is not itself an amino acid; it is synthesized from amino acids. Supplement effects/appropriate use depend on context; avoid promising muscle growth or recovery as guaranteed outcomes.

column5: Morally low, dishonorable, selfish, or ignoble; 'baser' is the comparative, especially common in phrases such as 'baser instincts' or 'baser motives'.
column7: The speech appealed to the crowd's baser instincts. / He suspected a baser motive behind the generosity.
column8: Normalize base + comparative. This moral sense of 'base' is formal/literary and distinct from base = foundation, military base, chemical base, etc.

column5: Not honorable, noble, or worthy in character, motive, action, or purpose; morally base or shameful.
column7: Jealousy was an ignoble motive, but at least he admitted it.
column8: Common: ignoble motive/action/end. Contrast noble. Slightly elevated/literary.

column5: To provide food, services, facilities, or what a group needs/wants. BrE commonly uses 'cater for' a group/event; 'cater to' is especially common in AmE for serving needs/tastes, and can imply excessive accommodation in some contexts.
column7: The hotel caters for families with young children. / The app caters to beginners. / A local company catered the wedding.
column8: Broaden dialect distinction. Also transitive 'cater an event' = provide food/service. 'Cater to someone's whims' can be mildly critical.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern usage::critical usage::american_english usage::british_english topic::food

column5: A sudden, often passing desire, idea, or change of mind that is not based on a strong reason or plan.
column7: We drove to the beach on a whim. / He changes the rules on a whim.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: on a whim; at someone's whim; whim of fate. 'Caprice' is more formal and often stresses unpredictability.

column5: A minor weakness, eccentricity, or mildly annoying peculiarity in someone's character or behavior.
column7: His habit of labeling everything is one of his harmless foibles.
column8: Usually relatively minor and often spoken of tolerantly. 'Shortcoming' can be more serious.

column5: Playful, fanciful, imaginative, or charmingly odd quality, humor, design, or behavior; sometimes an individual fanciful notion.
column7: The hand-drawn signs add a touch of whimsy to the café.
column8: KEY COLLOCATION: a touch/sense of whimsy. Unlike 'whim', whimsy often describes an aesthetic or playful imaginative quality.

column5: Not capable of bending; figuratively, unwilling or unable to change, adapt, negotiate, or make exceptions.
column7: The material is strong but inflexible. / The policy is too inflexible for unusual cases.
column8: Add literal physical sense. Can describe schedules/rules/systems as well as people; 'stubborn' specifically describes a person/stance and is not always equivalent.

column5: Stiff and not able to bend; figuratively, fixed, strict, or unwilling/unable to adapt.
column7: The frame is rigid. / The schedule is too rigid to accommodate last-minute changes.
column8: Important literal + figurative senses. Compare WID2500 inflexible: rigid often suggests structural stiffness or strict fixedness.

column2: a little bit of apprehension / feel apprehensive
column5: A mild degree of anxiety or uneasiness about something expected or possible; 'apprehensive' is the corresponding adjective.
column7: I felt a little bit of apprehension before the interview. / I'm apprehensive about driving in the storm.
column8: KEY FRAMES: apprehension about/over X; feel/be apprehensive about X. 'Apprehension' can also mean arrest or understanding in other contexts.

column5: To deliberately avoid, reject, or abstain from something, especially as a matter of choice or principle.
column6: avoid, shun, abstain from, steer clear of
column7: She eschews social media. / He eschewed flashy effects in favor of a simple design.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Usually transitive: eschew + noun/gerund. Formal; unlike 'avoid', often suggests deliberate preference/principle.

column5: Untidy, shabby, or somewhat dirty in appearance; can describe people, hair, clothing, animals, or places.
column7: He showed up looking scruffy and unshaven. / The little dog looked scruffy after the rain.
column8: Often mildly negative but can be affectionate. 'Shabby' can focus worn condition; 'disheveled' focuses disorder.

column5: Verb: to emphasize or make the importance of something especially clear. Noun: the '_' character, especially in writing/computing.
column7: The results underscore the need for better testing. / Use an underscore instead of a space in the filename.
column8: Add major noun/computing sense. Figurative verb comes from literally underlining text.

column5: To reduce the severity, harmfulness, seriousness, or impact of something; not necessarily eliminate it.
column7: Trees can help mitigate urban heat. / The apology did little to mitigate the damage.
column8: KEY FRAME: mitigate + risk/damage/impact/effects. Contrast 'prevent': mitigation reduces consequences or likelihood rather than guaranteeing prevention.

column5: To repeat by reading aloud information that has just been written, received, or recorded, especially to verify accuracy.
column7: Could you read the address back to me? / Air-traffic controllers may require a pilot to read back an instruction.
column8: KEY FRAME: read X back (to someone). 'Repeat back' overlaps, but read back specifically implies reading/reciting recorded or received wording.

column5: To cause something/someone to fall or collapse; reduce a level, price, rate, or number; defeat/remove a government or powerful person; or make someone feel sad.
column7: The new supply helped bring prices down. / The scandal brought down the government. / Don't let one bad comment bring you down.
column8: Highly polysemous. KEY PATTERNS: bring X down; bring down X. Add emotional and political senses.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb topic::mental_health topic::government topic::politics discovery::removal discovery::public_discourse

column5: Not candid or fully sincere; presenting oneself, an argument, or a question in a misleadingly innocent, incomplete, or strategic way.
column7: It's disingenuous to pretend you had no idea what the rule meant.
column8: CORRECTION: not limited to 'pretending to know less'. Often describes arguments/questions that conceal relevant knowledge, motives, or implications.

column5: Seeking to influence or control people or situations, especially through indirect, unfair, deceptive, or emotionally exploitative means.
column7: The message felt manipulative because it tried to make customers feel guilty.
column8: Usually negative. 'Persuasive' is neutral; manipulative implies problematic methods or concealed control.

column5: So unpleasant, irritating, arrogant, tedious, or extreme that it is very difficult to tolerate.
column7: His smugness became insufferable. / The heat was insufferable by midday.
column8: Can describe people/behavior or conditions. Often hyperbolic in everyday speech.

column5: A contemptuous way to call someone a bad/despicable informer or tattletale. 'Lousy' intensifies the insult; 'snitch' is the core noun.
column7: He called me a lousy snitch for telling the teacher what happened.
column8: Teach composition: lousy = contemptible/very bad + snitch = person who informs. Informal and hostile; 'informer' is more neutral/formal.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::formal usage::informal usage::slang discovery::escalation

column5: Noisy, boisterous, and difficult to control, often because a group is excited, unruly, or disorderly.
column7: The bar got rowdy after the game. / A rowdy group was shouting in the hallway.
column8: Often group/crowd behavior. 'Boisterous' can be cheerful without being disorderly; rowdy more strongly suggests loss of control.

column2: stake out / stake something out; stakeout
column5: To watch a place secretly over time, especially for police/investigative purposes; also to mark or claim an area/position. Noun 'stakeout' = surveillance operation.
column7: Detectives staked out the warehouse. / We staked out a spot near the stage. / The police conducted a stakeout.
column8: Normalize base + source form and add non-police sense. Verb two words; noun usually one word.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::debate-friendly topic::finance topic::debate topic::policing topic::law discovery::assertion discovery::debate_language

column5: A passage connecting the middle ear with the nasopharynx; it helps ventilate the middle ear and equalize pressure across the eardrum.
column7: Swallowing can help the Eustachian tube open during a flight.
column8: Anatomical term; often capitalized Eustachian, though lowercase also occurs in medical style. Pressure equalization is one important function.

column5: Either of the paired joints connecting the mandible (lower jaw) to the temporal bone of the skull, enabling jaw movement.
column7: Pain around the temporomandibular joint can make chewing uncomfortable.
column8: TMJ names the joint; TMD/temporomandibular disorders refers to disorders affecting the joint/masticatory system. Do not use TMJ as if it inherently means a disorder.

column5: Abnormally reduced tolerance to ordinary sounds, so sounds that are comfortable to most people may feel excessively loud, uncomfortable, or painful.
column7: Someone with hyperacusis may find ordinary dishes clattering painfully loud.
column8: PRECISION: not simply 'good hearing' or generic dislike of noise. Related sound-tolerance conditions/terms are not interchangeable.

column5: To describe the distinctive features or nature of something; in passive construction, 'be characterized by X' = have X as a typical or defining feature.
column7: The author characterizes him as cautious. / The region is characterized by dry summers.
column8: Normalize base + source form. KEY FRAMES: characterize X as Y; X is characterized by Y.

column5: Used when there is no strong reason not to do something or no better alternative; also used with resigned acceptance when circumstances make an option effectively inevitable.
column6: may as well, there's no reason not to, we may as well
column7: We're already here, so we might as well look around. / If nobody else is coming, we might as well leave.
column8: Preserve two key axes: practical 'no reason not to' and resigned 'given the situation, this is what remains'.

column5: The exercise of holding a plank position to train core stability; also a late-2000s/early-2010s internet fad involving lying face-down rigidly in unusual places.
column7: We did three sets of planking. / Old photos show people planking on benches and signs.
column8: Separate fitness and meme senses. In fitness, 'plank' is more commonly the exercise noun: do/hold a plank.
column12: entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::internet topic::wellness topic::debate topic::transportation discovery::debate_language

column5: To interrupt, disturb, or seriously interfere with the normal operation, continuity, activity, or development of something.
column7: The storm disrupted train service. / The protest disrupted the meeting.
column8: Normalize base + source form. 'Disrupt' often implies more substantial interference than a brief interruption.

column5: To keep, continue to have, preserve, or remember something; also to hire/engage a professional's services, especially a lawyer.
column7: The company retained control of the patent. / I retained very little from the lecture. / They retained an attorney.
column8: Add memory and professional-services senses. KEY: retain information; retain ownership/control; retain counsel.

column5: The tendency to change rapidly or unpredictably; in finance, the degree of variation in prices/returns; also emotional/political instability or a substance's tendency to vaporize.
column7: Market volatility increased sharply. / The region's political volatility worried investors.
column8: CORRECTION: change is not necessarily 'for the worse'. Technical meanings vary by domain; finance volatility measures variation, not direction.
column12: entry::word usage::technical topic::finance topic::politics discovery::public_discourse discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Eager or quick to argue, quarrel, or fight; aggressively combative in manner.
column7: His pugnacious style turned every discussion into a fight.
column8: Formal/literary flavor. Can describe rhetoric/attitude as well as people.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::literary usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly discovery::debate_language

column5: A strong desire or impulse to travel, roam, and experience unfamiliar places.
column6: urge to travel, travel bug, desire to roam
column7: After a year at home, her wanderlust came roaring back.
column8: Borrowed from German and fully established in English. Usually positive/romanticized; not the same as general restlessness.

column2: ovulation is cyclical / ovulation occurs in cycles
column5: A statement that ovulation is part of a recurring reproductive cycle. In humans, timing and cycle length vary substantially; ovulation is not guaranteed to occur once every calendar month.
column7: Ovulation occurs as part of the menstrual cycle, but its timing can vary from cycle to cycle.
column8: CORRECTION: remove overgeneralized 'typically monthly/once a month in most women'. Preserve the language-learning point while keeping biological wording accurate.

column2: grow tired of / have grown tired
column5: To gradually become physically tired or, more commonly with 'of', bored, dissatisfied, or fed up over time.
column6: become weary of, tire of, get fed up with
column7: I've grown tired of hearing the same excuse. / By evening, we had grown tired from walking.
column8: KEY FRAME: grow tired of + noun/gerund = gradually lose patience/interest. 'Have grown tired' is present perfect; source form alone is incomplete.

column5: To be deliberately reserved, evasive, or teasing about one's intentions, knowledge, or feelings; sometimes flirtatiously shy.
column6: be evasive, play shy, be teasingly reserved
column7: Don't be coy—just tell me what you think. / She was coy about whether she'd accept the offer.
column8: Repair punctuation. Coy can be flirtatious, but also strategically evasive/noncommittal; not simply genuine shyness.

column5: To say something strikingly bizarre, extreme, implausible, or unconventional; 'outlandish' is the productive adjective.
column7: He said something outlandish just to get a reaction. / The rumor sounded completely outlandish.
column8: Teach the adjective beyond the source phrase: outlandish claim/outfit/idea/behavior.

column5: To dispatch, distribute, transmit, or emit something outward or to multiple recipients; can also send a person somewhere for a purpose.
column7: We'll send out invitations tomorrow. / The antenna sends out a signal. / They sent a technician out to inspect it.
column8: Broaden beyond mail/email. KEY FRAME: send X out; send out X.

column2: nobody knows how to drive in the rain
column3: /ˈnoʊˌbɑdi noʊz haʊ tə draɪv ɪn ðə reɪn/
column5: A common hyperbolic complaint that other drivers seem unusually slow, reckless, or incompetent when it rains.
column6: people drive badly in the rain, rainy-day traffic gripe
column7: Every time traffic slows in a storm, somebody says, 'Nobody knows how to drive in the rain.'
column8: Not a factual universal claim or fixed idiom; preserve as conversational hyperbole. 'Nobody knows how to...' is a productive exaggerated complaint pattern.
column12: entry::idiom usage::colloquial usage::conversational usage::informal topic::weather topic::transportation discovery::incompetence discovery::complaint discovery::impression

column2: roads are slickest when rain first begins / first-rain slickness
column3: /ju noʊ ðə roʊdz ɑr ˈslɪkəst ɪn ðə fɜrst hæf ˈaʊɚ əv reɪn/
column5: Road surfaces can become especially slippery near the beginning of rainfall when water mixes with accumulated oil, dust, and debris; conditions vary by surface, rainfall, traffic, and maintenance.
column7: Be extra careful when rain first starts; residue on the road can make the surface unusually slick.
column8: CORRECTION: avoid presenting 'the first half hour' as a universal fixed rule. Teach 'slick' + driving context and the underlying caution accurately.

column2: the plants are going to love this / plants will love the rain
column3: /ðə plænts ɑr ˈɡənə lʌv ðɪs wɛn ɪt reɪnz/
column5: A casual, personifying way to say that rain will be beneficial for plants.
column6: the rain will be good for the plants, the garden needs this
column7: Finally some rain—the plants are going to love this.
column8: KEY DEVICE: 'X is going to love this' personifies plants and is common casual speech. Source wording 'when it rains' is redundant if spoken during/just before rain.
column12: entry::phrase usage::casual usage::colloquial usage::conversational usage::informal topic::weather

column2: I sleep better when it rains
column3: /aɪ ˈækʧuəli sliːp ˈbɛtɚ wɛn ɪt reɪnz/
column5: A natural personal statement that one's sleep tends to be better during rainy weather; the reason is left to context.
column6: rain helps me sleep, I find rain soothing
column7: I actually sleep better when it rains—the sound relaxes me.
column8: Teach productive comparative frame: sleep better/worse when + condition. This is personal preference, not a general claim about sleep quality.

column2: curl up with a good book / curl up with
column3: /ðɪs ˈwɛðɚ meɪks mi wɑnt tə steɪ æt hoʊm, kɜrld ʌp wɪð ə ɡʊd bʊk/
column5: To settle into a comfortable curled or tucked position with a book, person, blanket, drink, etc., usually for relaxation.
column6: cozy up with, settle in with, snuggle up with
column7: This weather makes me want to stay home and curl up with a good book. / I curled up with a blanket and watched a movie.
column8: Normalize to productive construction. KEY FRAME: curl up with + book/person/object; also curl up on/in + place.
column12: entry::idiom entry::collocation usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::resolution discovery::debate_language

column5: Verb: to deduct money from pay; bring a ship/spacecraft to a dock or connect vehicles/devices; cut short/removal in some contexts. Noun: a structure for boats/loading, or a docking location.
column7: They docked his pay for the missed shift. / The ferry docked at noon. / Put the laptop back on the dock.
column8: Major polysemy: current card only has wage deduction. 'Fine' is not exact because docking specifically subtracts an amount/benefit.

column5: 'Cookie-cutter' describes things made to the same standardized pattern and lacking individuality; 'a cookie-cutter world' is a creative application to a conformist environment.
column7: He hated the cookie-cutter houses in the development. / The film imagines a cookie-cutter world where everyone is expected to fit the same mold.
column8: CORRECTION: standard modifier is 'cookie-cutter', not possessive 'cookie cutter's'. Teach productive adjective; 'world' is source-specific application.

column5: An especially sharp, clever, funny, or devastating insult/comeback; often used jokingly to praise a roast.
column7: 'Even your GPS gives up on you.' 'Ooh, sick burn.'
column8: Internet/youth slang; can be sincere or ironic. 'Burn' is the insult; 'sick' intensifies positively = impressive.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::ironic usage::informal discovery::social_approval

column2: back at you / right back at you
column5: Used to return a greeting, compliment, wish, insult, gesture, or sentiment to the person who just directed it at you.
column6: same to you, likewise, you too, right back at you
column7: 'Have a great weekend!' 'Back at you!' / 'You're amazing.' 'Right back at you.'
column8: CORRECTION: repair garbled example. Can return positive or negative sentiment; 'right back at you' is emphatic.

column5: To rise and fall or vary irregularly in level, amount, value, condition, or intensity over time.
column7: Prices fluctuate throughout the year. / Her energy level fluctuated from day to day.
column8: Usually intransitive: X fluctuates; fluctuate between A and B; fluctuate around a level.

column5: To formally approve, confirm, or give official validity to an agreement, treaty, decision, or action through the required authority/process.
column7: The legislature voted to ratify the agreement.
column8: KEY COLLOCATIONS: ratify a treaty/agreement/amendment. Ratification is formal approval, not merely informal support.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::informal topic::law topic::decision-making topic::politics discovery::process_details discovery::agreement discovery::public_discourse

column5: A word or short expression used as an independent exclamation, reaction, greeting, hesitation, etc., often grammatically separate from the surrounding sentence.
column7: 'Wow!', 'ouch!', and 'hey!' can function as interjections.
column8: CORRECTION: interjections do not have to express 'strong emotion'; they can signal hesitation, response, greeting, attention, and more.

column5: To achieve the intended effect, be accurate, or satisfy the relevant standard/goal.
column6: be accurate, succeed, land well, be on target
column7: Her criticism hit the mark. / The joke didn't quite hit the mark with this audience.
column8: Literal target metaphor → figurative effectiveness/accuracy. Useful negative: miss the mark.

column5: A narrow passage or lane, especially between/behind buildings; in bowling, the long lane down which the ball is rolled; also appears in compounds/idioms such as alleyway and 'right up my alley'.
column7: We cut through the alley behind the theater. / She rolled the ball straight down the bowling alley.
column8: Clarify bowling sense: 'bowling alley' can mean the venue or lane depending context. Related idiom 'up one's alley' = suited to one's interests/skills.

column5: Dismal = gloomy, depressing, bleak, or very poor/unsatisfactory. 'Dismal days' can mean gloomy-weather days or a bleak period.
column7: It was a dismal rainy afternoon. / The team ended a dismal season with another loss.
column8: Teach productive adjective beyond source phrase: dismal weather/performance/results/prospects.

column5: To cut or break something completely; figuratively, to end a connection, relationship, communication channel, or tie.
column7: The cable was severed. / The company severed ties with the supplier.
column8: KEY COLLOCATION: sever ties/relations/connections. Stronger/more complete than merely weaken.

column5: Noun 'share-out' = a distribution/division of money, resources, etc., or sometimes the resulting shares; verb 'share out' = divide and distribute among people.
column7: They agreed on a share-out of the profits. / The money was shared out equally among the partners.
column8: FORM: noun often hyphenated 'share-out'; verb 'share out' two words. Chiefly British.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::variant_set entry::word entry::verb_pattern usage::british_english discovery::resource_allocation

column5: To continue, survive, remain effective, or endure longer than another person or thing.
column6: last longer than, survive, outlive, endure beyond
column7: This battery outlasted the others. / She outlasted every opponent in the tournament.
column8: Transitive comparison is built into the verb: X outlasts Y. Not limited to people.

column5: 'Make someone squat' literally means cause/require someone to lower into a squat. The verb 'squat' also means crouch, occupy property without permission, or reside temporarily in such a place. Unrelated slang 'not do/know squat' means nothing.
column7: The coach made us squat and hold the position. / They squatted in the abandoned building. / He doesn't know squat about cars.
column8: CORRECTION: remove unsupported metaphor 'force into a powerless situation'. Separate causative exercise phrase, property sense, and 'squat = nothing' slang.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::slang usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly usage::informal discovery::debate_language

column5: Pretentiously grand, fancy, sophisticated, or important-sounding, especially in language, ideas, tastes, or behavior.
column7: Skip the highfalutin jargon and explain it plainly.
column8: Often playful rather than severe. Variant spellings include highfalutin and highfalutin'.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::humorous usage::playful usage::critical usage::specialist discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To become sulky or visibly displeased, often with a protruding-lip expression associated with pouting.
column7: He gets pouty when he loses. / She was getting pouty after being told no.
column8: Normalize to productive adjective/construction. 'Pouty' can describe facial appearance or behavior; often mildly teasing.

column5: A place or business where beer is brewed; can range from a small craft brewery to a large industrial operation.
column7: We toured a local craft brewery. / The brewery produces several seasonal beers.
column8: 'Beer factory' is understandable but not the normal synonym. Related: brewer, brew, brewing.

column5: Easily influenced, shaped, or affected by other people, ideas, experiences, media, or surroundings.
column7: Young viewers can be especially impressionable. / He was impressionable and eager to fit in.
column8: Not equivalent to naive: someone can be impressionable without lacking intelligence. Often used for children/young people but not exclusively.

column5: An alternative method used to bypass or cope with a problem, limitation, bug, or unavailable feature without fixing the underlying cause.
column7: We found a workaround for the login bug. / These workarounds keep the system usable until the patch arrives.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. A workaround can be temporary or long-lived; unlike a true fix, it usually leaves the root issue in place.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word topic::security topic::problem-solving discovery::solution_framing discovery::resolution

column5: To officially receive goods, property, a vehicle, securities, etc. 'On taking delivery' = when/upon receiving them. In some markets, taking delivery can mean receiving the underlying asset rather than settling otherwise.
column7: Payment is due on taking delivery of the equipment. / She took delivery of her new car on Friday.
column8: KEY FRAME: take delivery of + item; on/upon taking delivery = at the time of receipt. Formal/logistical/business usage.

column5: Regarding, concerning, or with respect to a topic; also used in constructions expressing uncertainty or questions about a detail.
column7: As to the budget, we need another estimate. / There was some confusion as to who was responsible.
column8: Not specifically 'business' English. Formal/written; productive frames include as to whether/how/why/who.

column5: In the exact capacity, category, or sense just mentioned ('as such'); sometimes used to draw a consequence from that status, but it does not simply mean 'therefore' in all contexts.
column6: in that capacity, in itself, strictly speaking
column7: He's not an employee as such; he's an independent contractor. / She is the team lead and, as such, approves final changes.
column8: CORRECTION: 'therefore/accordingly' is only licensed when it follows from a previously established role/status. Not merely a generic transition.

column2: in the event of / in the event that
column5: Used to introduce a possible future contingency: 'in the event of + noun' or 'in the event that + clause', roughly 'if' or 'if it happens that'.
column7: In the event of a power failure, use the emergency exit. / In the event that the server fails, traffic will be redirected.
column8: Teach grammar explicitly. Formal/legal/business style; 'in case' may imply precaution and is not identical in every sentence.

column5: 'Make up' has many senses: invent, constitute, reconcile, apply cosmetics, complete missed work/time, etc. 'Make up for X' specifically means compensate for a loss, deficiency, mistake, or disadvantage.
column7: We need to make up the missed hours. / Women make up half the team. / She apologized to make up for the delay.
column8: CORRECTION: broaden highly polysemous 'make up'. KEY CONTRAST: make up X (e.g. missed time) vs make up for X (compensate for a problem).

column5: An established system of rules, procedures, conventions, or technical standards governing conduct, communication, operations, or data exchange.
column7: Follow the lab's safety protocol. / HTTPS is a protocol for secure web communication.
column8: Add computing/network sense. Also diplomatic protocol = formal rules of official conduct.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::technical topic::communication discovery::process_details discovery::procedural_language discovery::evaluation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: An organizational environment in which people are expected to own commitments, explain decisions/results, follow through, and address failures rather than routinely deflect responsibility.
column7: Clear roles and follow-through can help build a culture of accountability.
column8: Evaluative management phrase, not a technical guarantee of performance or ethics. 'Accountability' involves answerability/ownership; implementation varies.
column12: entry::collocation usage::technical usage::evaluative topic::communication topic::culture topic::environment discovery::explanation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Providing or associated with a sense of emotional release, relief, or cleansing; also historically/medically related to purging.
column7: Writing the letter was surprisingly cathartic. / The final scene felt cathartic after so much tension.
column8: Everyday use often means emotionally relieving. Do not assume emotional expression is clinically therapeutic merely because it feels cathartic.

column5: A feeling or process of emotional release or relief, especially after intense emotion; in literary theory, famously associated with emotional effect in tragedy.
column7: The confession gave him a sense of catharsis. / The ending provides emotional catharsis for the audience.
column8: Related adjective cathartic. Modern psychology does not make every 'venting' episode beneficial; lexical meaning is broader than a clinical claim.

column5: To be less strict, critical, or demanding toward someone; allow extra tolerance or leeway because of circumstances.
column6: go easy on, give someone a break, show leniency
column7: Cut her some slack—it's her first day.
column8: CORRECTION: standard idiom normally includes 'some': cut someone some slack. Repair punctuation.

column5: So exceptional, distinctive, or extreme that no adequate comparison/equal is available; in some contexts, simply not meaningfully comparable.
column7: The view from the summit was incomparable. / The two datasets are incomparable because they use different definitions.
column8: IMPORTANT POLYSEMY: laudatory 'without equal' vs literal/technical 'cannot fairly be compared'. Context decides.

column5: A topic-focused community on Reddit, conventionally identified by an r/ name such as r/AskHistorians.
column7: She posted the question in a photography subreddit.
column8: Platform-specific term. A subreddit is not merely any discussion group; it is a community within Reddit.

column5: Repetition of the same or similar initial consonant sound in nearby words, especially for stylistic effect.
column7: 'Peter Piper picked...' is a familiar example of alliteration.
column8: CORRECTION: fundamentally about sounds, not necessarily the same written letter. Some definitions extend the term more broadly, but initial consonant-sound repetition is the core teaching sense.

column5: A return to success, popularity, health, competition, or prominence after decline/absence; also a quick reply or retort, especially a witty one.
column6: return, resurgence, recovery; retort, comeback line
column7: The singer made a comeback after years away. / I couldn't think of a good comeback until five minutes later.
column8: CORRECTION: remove '(literal)'—the success-return sense is itself figurative/established, and the retort sense is major.

column5: Literally, to pedal a bicycle backward; figuratively, to retreat from, soften, reverse, or qualify a previous statement, promise, or position.
column6: retreat, reverse course, walk back, retract
column7: He started backpedaling after the comment drew criticism. / The company backpedaled on its earlier promise.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Figurative use often implies reaction to pressure or realizing a position is untenable.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative usage::softening usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::qualification discovery::figurative_extension discovery::debate_language

column2: let someone in / let someone in on something
column5: Literally, allow someone to enter; figuratively, allow emotional access/trust; 'let someone in on X' = share a secret, plan, or information with them.
column6: admit, open up to; confide in, tell
column7: You really let me in when you told me how scared you were. / Can you let me in on the plan?
column8: Normalize source phrase to productive constructions. Distinguish let someone in (access) from let someone in on + information.

column5: A person or entity belonging to a group, organization, body, or set; also a body part/limb in formal or old usage, and euphemistically the penis ('member').
column7: She's the newest member of the committee. / In older or euphemistic writing, 'member' can refer to a body part or penis.
column8: CORRECTION: remove unsupported claim that 'the other member' is established Hong Kong Cantonese slang for a gay man. Preserve attested English group/body-part/euphemistic senses.

column5: Literally, move quietly on one's toes; figuratively, avoid addressing a sensitive issue directly or behave extremely carefully around a person/topic to avoid conflict.
column7: Everyone kept tiptoeing around the real problem. / I feel like I have to tiptoe around him when he's angry.
column8: Add literal base and productive frames. Compare 'walk on eggshells around someone' for stronger ongoing caution.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative topic::construction discovery::figurative_extension discovery::prevention

column5: A unit of phonological timing/weight used in analyses of syllable structure and rhythm; a syllable may contain one or more morae depending on the language.
column6: timing unit, unit of syllable weight
column7: In Japanese, rhythm is often analyzed in morae: 'Nippon' has more morae than syllables.
column8: CORRECTION: 'each kana represents one mora' is a useful rough teaching shortcut but has exceptions/orthographic complications. Plural: morae or moras.

column5: Something that hinders, obstructs, or slows progress, action, movement, or communication; in 'speech impediment', a condition affecting speech production/fluency.
column7: Cost was the biggest impediment to expansion. / The character is described as having a speech impediment.
column8: KEY FRAME: impediment to + noun/gerund. Broader than physical barrier.
