column7: The dog sniffed out the hidden food. / The reporter sniffed out inconsistencies in the story.
column8: Add literal source metaphor. Often suggests skill at detecting something concealed.

column5: To make a deep, rough sound like a frog; speak in a hoarse/raspy voice; slang, to die. Noun: the sound itself.
column7: A frog croaked outside. / 'Water,' he croaked. / The old joke says he'll probably croak at ninety.
column8: Add speech sense. Death sense is informal and can sound insensitive/humorous.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::slang usage::humorous topic::communication discovery::impression

column5: To smile in a self-satisfied, smug, knowing, or sometimes irritating way; noun = such a smile.
column7: He smirked when he realized he'd been right. / Wipe that smirk off your face.
column8: Normalize base + source form. A smirk need not indicate superiority specifically; context may suggest amusement, knowingness, or smugness.

column5: A common respiratory virus that usually causes cold-like illness but can cause serious lower-respiratory disease, particularly in infants, some older adults, and other higher-risk people.
column7: RSV can cause bronchiolitis or pneumonia in vulnerable patients.
column8: CORRECTION: 'lung infection' and 'bronchiolitis virus' are not synonyms. Standard capitalization is usually lowercase common name + uppercase initialism.

column5: Chance or accident; a chance occurrence. Depending on context it may be fortunate, but good luck is not inherent in the word.
column7: By sheer fortuity, we arrived just as the doors reopened.
column8: CORRECTION: distinguish from 'serendipity', which typically involves a fortunate discovery/outcome. Fortuity primarily means chance occurrence.

column5: Adjective: importantly helpful in causing/achieving a result; relating to instruments; music performed without sung lyrics. Noun: an instrumental musical piece/version.
column7: Her advice was instrumental in getting the project approved. / I prefer the instrumental version of this song.
column8: Add noun and broader instrument-related sense. 'Essential' may overstate: instrumental means playing an important causal role.

column5: Existing in imagination rather than as a physical/actual entity; in mathematics, relating to multiples of the imaginary unit i.
column7: He had an imaginary friend. / The equation has imaginary solutions.
column8: CORRECTION: mathematical imaginary numbers are rigorous mathematical objects, not 'unreal' in the everyday sense; separate technical sense.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::scientific topic::mathematics discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To be removed, consumed, or disappear through burning/heat; by extension, sunlight/heat can cause fog/cloud to dissipate. Figurative emotional uses are creative.
column7: The paint burned away in the fire. / The morning fog burned away by ten.
column8: CORRECTION: do not lexicalize broad poetic 'erase/purge emotions' as a standard sense. Keep creative metaphor recognizable.

column5: 'Ear infection' is a broad everyday term for infection in parts of the ear. 'Otitis media' specifically means inflammation of the middle ear and is not synonymous with every ear infection; acute otitis media commonly involves infection.
column7: The child was diagnosed with acute otitis media. / Not every ear infection is a middle-ear infection.
column8: CORRECTION: separate broad everyday term from specific medical term.
column12: entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist topic::media topic::health discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: ENT = ear, nose, and throat; otolaryngology is the medical specialty concerned with these areas and related head/neck conditions; an otolaryngologist is the physician specialist.
column7: My doctor referred me to an ENT. / She specializes in otolaryngology.
column8: CORRECTION: 'ENT' can refer informally to the specialty or doctor; otolaryngologist is a person, not a synonym for the specialty.

column5: To become too large for clothing/space; or, with age/development, stop having a habit, behavior, interest, fear, or condition.
column7: He grew out of those shoes in six months. / She eventually grew out of her fear of dogs.
column8: Add literal clothing/size sense. Also 'grow out one's hair' is a different construction.

column5: To read/open someone's message so it is marked as seen/read but not reply, especially for a noticeable period.
column6: read without replying, ignore the message
column7: I accidentally left him on read all afternoon.
column8: It may be intentional or accidental; does not necessarily mean rejection or ghosting. 'Read' is pronounced /rɛd/ here.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::slang usage::informal topic::communication topic::internet

column5: To leave someone's message unopened/unread, often deliberately; a newer parallel formation modeled on 'leave someone on read'.
column6: leave unopened, not open the message
column7: I left the group chat on unread until I had time to deal with it.
column8: CORRECTION: motive such as avoiding confrontation is contextual, not inherent. Less established than 'leave on read'.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::playful usage::informal topic::communication topic::internet

column2: pull something off / pull it off
column5: To succeed in doing something difficult, unlikely, or ambitious; also literally remove an item by pulling, depending object.
column7: I didn't think we'd finish in time, but we pulled it off.
column8: KEY FRAME: pull X off / pull it off. Success sense often implies difficulty or surprise.

column5: To stay awake throughout the night instead of sleeping, commonly to study, work, travel, socialize, etc.
column7: I pulled an all-nighter to finish the report.
column8: CORRECTION: not limited to study/work. Noun 'all-nighter' can refer to the sleepless night/activity itself.

column2: kick oneself for something / for doing something
column5: To feel strong regret or annoyance with oneself about a mistake, missed chance, or poor decision.
column6: regret, reproach oneself, beat oneself up
column7: I'm kicking myself for not buying the tickets yesterday.
column8: KEY FRAME: kick oneself for + noun/gerund. Often less severe than 'beat oneself up', which can imply sustained self-criticism.

column5: Two people/things or a combination that creates extra difficulty, danger, mischief, or challenge; also used playfully for an especially formidable pair.
column6: twice the trouble, troublesome pair, compounded trouble
column7: Those two puppies together are double trouble.
column8: CORRECTION: remove 'double jeopardy' as synonym; that is a distinct legal concept/common phrase.

column5: To restrain oneself or refrain from doing something, whether from hesitation, caution, self-control, fear, or another reason.
column6: refrain from, stop oneself from, hesitate to
column7: She held back from criticizing him in public.
column8: KEY FRAME: hold back from + gerund. Also 'hold someone/something back' = restrain/prevent progress.

column5: To receive an unintended insult, criticism, joke, or other negative hit while someone/something else was the main target; derives from the image of being hit by a stray shot.
column6: get hit indirectly, catch collateral criticism, get dragged unexpectedly
column7: Why did my favorite show catch a stray in an argument about something else?
column8: Modern internet/slang use often humorous. Underlying violent metaphor; 'stray' = stray bullet/shot in the image.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::humorous usage::figurative usage::rhetorical usage::informal discovery::criticism discovery::debate_language

column5: To criticize someone or something very severely or forcefully.
column7: Critics lambasted the sequel for its weak script.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Stronger than ordinary criticize.

column5: To criticize, reprimand, or rebuke someone for wrongdoing or perceived fault; historically can also mean punish.
column7: She chastised him for ignoring the instructions.
column8: Formal/stronger than everyday 'tell off' in many contexts. Physical-punishment sense is historical/less common.

column5: Quotations attributed to Marcus Aurelius, especially from or associated with his Stoic work Meditations; exact wording and attribution should be checked against a reliable translation/source because popular quote lists often paraphrase or misattribute sayings.
column7: If you want to quote Marcus Aurelius, check the passage and translation rather than relying on a quote graphic.
column8: CORRECTION: do not preserve a bundle of quotations as unquestionably authentic. Some widely circulated lines attributed to Marcus Aurelius are paraphrased, disputed, or from other sources. Card becomes a source-verification/reference reminder.

column5: To officially revoke, cancel, or withdraw a law, order, policy, offer, agreement, decision, or similar action.
column7: The university rescinded the offer. / The rule was later rescinded.
column8: Normalize base + source form. 'Repeal' is especially for laws/statutes and is not universal synonym.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal topic::law topic::decision-making discovery::policy_discussion discovery::agreement

column5: Unoriginal, overly sentimental, old-fashioned, or embarrassingly obvious in an attempt to be funny, romantic, charming, etc.
column7: The joke was corny, but it still made me laugh.
column8: Repair mojibake 'cliché'. Corny can be affectionate: something may be corny and enjoyable.
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::dated usage::affectionate topic::romance topic::security

column5: Something made, done, or occurring once rather than as part of a continuing/repeated series; adjective: occurring once or unique.
column6: one-time event, single instance, unique item
column7: It was a one-off special. / We hope the outage was just a one-off.
column8: In AmE, 'one-time' is often more natural in some contexts. 'One of a kind' emphasizes uniqueness, not necessarily nonrecurrence.

column5: Grammar: the part of a clause that says something about the subject (definitions vary by grammatical framework). Logic: an expression/property predicated of arguments. Verb 'predicate X on/upon Y' = base or found X on Y; 'predicate X of Y' = assert X of Y.
column6: base on, assert of; grammatical predicate
column7: In 'She laughed', 'laughed' functions as the predicate. / The argument is predicated on an assumption that may be false.
column8: CORRECTION: distinguish noun and verb constructions; verb does not simply mean 'affirm or base something upon a proposition'.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::rhetorical topic::grammar discovery::assertion discovery::debate_language

column5: Ease noun = absence of difficulty/discomfort or relaxed manner. Verb = reduce pain/difficulty/tension or move gently. Ease off = lessen in intensity or reduce pressure/effort.
column6: comfort, facility; relieve, lessen; let up
column7: She answered with ease. / The medicine eased the pain. / The rain eased off by evening.
column8: Broaden major noun/verb senses. Common: at ease, with ease, ease into, ease up/off.

column2: pull someone in / pull someone into something
column5: To attract someone's attention/interest; physically draw someone inward; recruit/involve someone; or draw someone into a situation, conversation, conflict, etc.
column7: The opening scene pulled me in immediately. / Don't pull me into your argument. / They pulled another engineer in to help.
column8: CORRECTION: distinguish pull someone in (attract/recruit) from pull someone into + situation. Emotional impact is contextual, not a separate core sense.

column2: the long haul / for the long haul
column5: A long, difficult, or sustained period of effort, activity, recovery, travel, etc.; 'for the long haul' means for a long period or with long-term commitment.
column7: Recovery will be a long haul. / We're in this for the long haul.
column8: Teach the productive article/preposition patterns. Literal 'long-haul flight/trucking' is related but distinct.

column5: To have information, tools, resources, or abilities immediately available and easy to access or use.
column6: have readily available, have easy access to
column7: With the database, we have years of records at our fingertips.
column8: Possessive varies: at my/your/her fingertips. Can also suggest ready command of knowledge/skill.

column2: a short/narrow window for conversation / a short window to talk
column5: A limited period during which a conversation can happen before time, attention, access, or circumstances change.
column6: brief opportunity, narrow window, limited time
column7: We only have a short window to talk before my next meeting.
column8: CORRECTION: 'conversation window is short' is understandable but not a fixed expression. Teach productive 'a short/narrow window to/for X'.

column5: Vlad III, a 15th-century voivode of Wallachia, remembered for impalement as punishment and later associated—indirectly and debatably—with the Dracula literary/cultural tradition.
column7: Vlad the Impaler ruled Wallachia during periods of conflict with the Ottoman Empire.
column8: PRECISION: Bram Stoker's Dracula should not be presented as simply 'based on' Vlad III; the historical-to-literary connection is limited and debated.

column5: Unreasonably or excessively high, especially in price, cost, fee, demand, or amount.
column7: They charged an exorbitant fee for changing the reservation.
column8: Common collocations: exorbitant price/cost/fee/rent/rate. Stronger than merely expensive.

column5: To have the recognized right/attention to speak in a meeting, debate, or conversation, often for an extended time; context may imply dominating the discussion, but that is not inherent.
column6: have the floor, speak at length, command attention
column7: She held the floor for ten minutes before taking questions.
column8: Normalize base form. 'Have the floor' emphasizes recognized turn; 'hold the floor' emphasizes continuing to speak.
column12: entry::idiom usage::debate-friendly topic::communication topic::debate discovery::professional_context discovery::debate_language

column5: To take a personal, social, professional, or other risk by supporting someone, expressing an opinion, making a prediction, or taking action.
column6: take a risk, put oneself on the line, take a stand
column7: I'm sticking my neck out by recommending him for the job.
column8: Normalize base construction. Often: stick one's neck out for someone / to do something.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::professional discovery::professional_context discovery::risk discovery::subjective_judgment

column5: Used to indicate that one understands the implication, request, or situation and needs no further explanation; sometimes signals enthusiastic agreement.
column6: I understand, got it, enough said
column7: 'Can you keep this quiet?' 'Say no more.'
column8: Tone can be serious, playful, conspiratorial, or enthusiastic. Distinct from literal instruction to stop speaking.
column12: entry::idiom usage::conversational usage::playful usage::instructional topic::communication discovery::explanation discovery::agreement

column5: To be appropriate, advisable, or incumbent on someone to do something; chiefly used impersonally: 'it behooves someone to...' (AmE spelling behoove; BrE behove).
column6: be advisable for, be appropriate for, be incumbent on
column7: It behooves us to check the facts before making the claim.
column8: CORRECTION: not necessarily moral/ethical or strictly necessary. Formal and somewhat old-fashioned.

column5: Adjective: currently holding an office/position; or required as a duty, especially in 'it is incumbent on/upon X to...'. Noun: the current holder of an office or position.
column7: The incumbent mayor is running again. / It is incumbent upon us to disclose the conflict.
column8: Separate office-holder sense from duty construction. 'Mandatory' can be too strong outside specific contexts.

column5: An alcoholic drink taken late in the evening, often shortly before bed; also historically/rarely a cap worn at night.
column7: We had one nightcap at the hotel bar before turning in.
column8: Alcohol sense is the common modern one. Does not imply a particular type of drink.

column5: A stakeout is covert or sustained observation of a place/person, especially by police or investigators. 'Stake out' = conduct such surveillance; separately, claim/mark a position or territory.
column7: Detectives kept the building under stakeout. / Reporters staked out the courthouse entrance.
column8: FORM: noun one word; verb two words. Add productive non-police 'stake out a spot/position' sense.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::variant_set entry::word entry::verb_pattern usage::debate-friendly topic::finance topic::debate topic::policing topic::law discovery::assertion discovery::debate_language

column5: To save time, effort, or money by omitting steps or doing something less thoroughly; often implies reduced quality, safety, or compliance.
column7: They cut corners on testing to meet the deadline.
column8: Not every shortcut is 'cutting corners'; the idiom usually carries criticism or risk.

column2: off the top of one's head
column5: From immediate memory or spontaneous thought, without checking, calculating carefully, or researching.
column7: Off the top of my head, I'd say there were about thirty people.
column8: Possessive varies. Often used to hedge estimates/answers.

column2: names and natures do often agree
column5: A proverbial/literary observation that a person's name sometimes seems fitting for their character, occupation, or qualities.
column7: A baker named Baker is the kind of coincidence that makes people joke that names and natures do often agree.
column8: Source-style proverb; not common everyday modern English. 'Nominative determinism' is a related modern concept, not an exact synonym. Remove corrupted Japanese text.

column5: To defeat, outdo, or get the better of someone in a contest, argument, challenge, or comparison.
column7: She bested the defending champion in the final. / He refused to admit he'd been bested.
column8: Normalize base + passive/past form. Verb 'best' is somewhat literary/formal compared with beat/defeat.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::formal usage::literary usage::rhetorical discovery::comparison discovery::debate_language

column5: A casual invitation to give a high five, typically said while raising one's hand.
column7: You nailed it—up top!
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling is normally two words 'up top'. Primarily a high-five prompt, not a general expression of agreement.

column5: A firefighting emergency vehicle carrying firefighters and equipment; terminology and vehicle types vary, and 'fire engine' and 'fire truck' may be used broadly in everyday speech but can have technical distinctions.
column7: A fire engine arrived within minutes and crews connected a hose to the hydrant.
column8: Avoid defining every fire engine as simply a vehicle 'used to extinguish fires'; apparatus roles/equipment differ.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::technical usage::specialist topic::public_speaking topic::automotive discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column2: fire ladder / aerial ladder / ladder truck
column5: A ladder used for firefighting/rescue; depending on context this may be a portable ground ladder or an aerial ladder mounted on specialized apparatus such as a ladder truck.
column6: firefighting ladder, aerial ladder, ground ladder
column7: Firefighters raised an aerial ladder to reach the upper floor.
column8: CORRECTION: 'fire ladder' is broad/nontechnical. Distinguish portable ground ladders from vehicle-mounted aerial ladders.
column12: entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_register

column5: To arrange/thread things on a string or in a series; 'string someone along' = keep someone interested or hopeful without sincere commitment or full information.
column6: thread, link; lead on, keep dangling
column7: She was stringing beads. / He kept stringing her along instead of giving a clear answer.
column8: CORRECTION: deception/false hope belongs specifically to 'string someone along', not bare 'stringing'.

column5: A sentence in which two or more independent clauses are improperly joined without adequate punctuation or conjunction; common types include fused sentences and comma splices.
column7: 'I was tired I went home' is a fused run-on sentence.
column8: PRECISION: a very long sentence is not automatically a run-on. The issue is clause joining, not length.

column5: To walk in a slow, relaxed, unhurried manner; noun: a leisurely walk.
column7: He sauntered into the café as if he had all day.
column8: Normalize base + source past tense; repair mojibake in café.

column5: A group authorized to represent others; or the act/process of assigning authority, responsibility, or tasks to another person.
column7: A delegation met with the minister. / Good delegation frees managers to focus on higher-level work.
column8: Two distinct common senses. In management, delegation may include authority, not merely dumping tasks.

column5: Impudent, irreverent, or boldly playful, often in a way considered amusing or endearing; can also be genuinely disrespectful depending context.
column7: She gave me a cheeky grin. / That's a bit cheeky, asking for another discount.
column8: Strong BrE association. Positive/negative tone depends on relationship and context.

column5: A habitually gloomy, grumpy, sulky, or sour-tempered person.
column7: Don't be such a sourpuss—we're supposed to be celebrating.
column8: CORRECTION: remove unrelated 'dog-in-the-manger/contrarian' framing and corrupted Japanese text. Sourpuss is about sour mood/disposition.

column5: Rude, disrespectful, or improperly bold, especially by showing insufficient respect for authority, status, privacy, or convention.
column7: The interviewer asked an impertinent question about her private life.
column8: Broaden beyond behavior toward a superior. Formal word; can describe questions/remarks as well as people.

column2: Rome wasn't built in a day / Rome was not built in a day
column3: /roʊm wəz nɑt bɪlt ɪn ə deɪ/
column5: Important, complex, or worthwhile achievements take time and should not be expected to happen immediately.
column6: great things take time, be patient
column7: The project is improving—remember, Rome wasn't built in a day.
column8: Contraction is common in conversation. Not specifically about perseverance; core message is time/gradual development.

column5: Gradually and methodically, one small part or step at a time; literally by placing bricks and figuratively by building progress, trust, skills, institutions, etc.
column6: step by step, piece by piece, gradually
column7: They rebuilt trust brick by brick after the dispute.
column8: Teach literal metaphor + broad figurative productivity.

column5: To cause someone to remember something that was partly forgotten or difficult to recall.
column6: remind, prompt someone's memory, trigger recall
column7: Maybe this photo will jog your memory. / Seeing it jogged my memory of the trip.
column8: Normalize productive frame: jog + possessive/person's memory. 'Jogging my memory' is a source inflection.

column5: Serving as a symbol or representative example of a person, group, quality, period, problem, or idea.
column7: The case became emblematic of a wider problem in the industry.
column8: KEY FRAME: emblematic of + noun. Can mean symbolically representative, not only literal emblem.

column5: Shortness in duration or expression; especially concise use of words.
column7: For the sake of brevity, I'll skip the background details. / Brevity is useful when the point is simple.
column8: Common phrase: for the sake of brevity. 'Terseness' can imply abruptness and is not always neutral.

column5: Two people or things that are strikingly alike, especially in personality, behavior, interests, or appearance.
column6: very alike, birds of a feather (related), extremely similar
column7: Those two are like two peas in a pod—they even laugh the same way.
column8: CORRECTION: 'inseparable/close-knit' is not inherent; similarity is the core meaning. Often 'like two peas in a pod'.

column5: A standard, reference point, principle, or exemplary work by which other things are tested, judged, or understood; originally a stone used to test precious-metal alloys.
column7: The novel became a touchstone for later writers in the genre.
column8: Add literal origin as memory hook. Common: a touchstone for/of X.

column5: To stop running (especially an engine) or stop making progress/developing, often after having started.
column6: stall, grind to a halt, lose momentum
column7: The engine stalled out at the light. / Negotiations stalled out after the first round.
column8: Add literal engine sense that motivates figurative progress sense.

column2: stall someone / stall for time; stall out
column5: To deliberately delay someone or delay action by evasion, excuses, or tactics; 'stall for time' = intentionally create delay. Separately, 'stall out' means stop functioning/progressing and is not normally a transitive 'stall me out' idiom.
column6: delay, hold up, stonewall; buy time
column7: I think he's stalling me until the deadline passes. / She stalled for time while the team checked the figures.
column8: CORRECTION: normalize nonstandard 'stall me out'. Remove corrupted unrelated Japanese/otaku comparison. Teach stall + person and stall for time vs intransitive stall out.

column5: A dismissive or exasperated way to say 'don't subject me to that'—often rejecting excuses, details, sentimentality, lectures, or claims.
column6: save it, give me a break, enough
column7: Spare me the excuses—I already know what happened.
column8: Derived from literal 'spare someone something' = refrain from inflicting it. Tone can be sarcastic/rude.

column2: for lack of a better word
column5: Used before or after a word/description to acknowledge that it is imperfect, approximate, or not quite the term one wants.
column6: so to speak (not exact), roughly speaking, for want of a better term
column7: The ending felt, for lack of a better word, hollow.
column8: Not equivalent to 'if you will' in all contexts. It explicitly comments on word choice.

column5: In the wrong position; unsuitable or incongruous in a setting; or socially uncomfortable/not belonging.
column7: That modern lamp looks out of place in the old room. / I felt out of place at the formal dinner.
column8: Three useful patterns: object is out of place; something looks/seems out of place; person feels out of place.

column2: ride the wave / ride a wave of something
column5: To benefit from, continue with, or adapt to a period of momentum, popularity, enthusiasm, change, or other strong trend while it lasts.
column6: capitalize on momentum, go with the trend, surf the wave
column7: The band is riding a wave of renewed popularity. / Let's ride the wave while interest is high.
column8: Normalize productive base. Not always passive 'going with the flow'; can imply strategically exploiting momentum.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::figurative topic::construction discovery::continuity discovery::building_on_success

column5: A feeling, atmosphere, impression, smell, sound, or other effect continues to be present after its source/event has passed.
column6: remain, persist, hang in the air
column7: Tension lingered in the room after the argument. / The good vibe lingered long after the party ended.
column8: CORRECTION: teach productive verb 'linger' rather than lexicalizing 'energy or vibe is lingering' as a fixed modern expression.

column5: To make a process, action, delivery, decision, etc. happen sooner or proceed more quickly.
column7: Could you expedite the shipment? / We changed the workflow to expedite approval.
column8: Common transitive frame: expedite + process/order/shipment/request. Does not mean skip required steps.

column5: To deal with, respond to, or give attention to an issue/question; to speak to a person/audience; to direct remarks to someone; or to write an address on an item.
column6: deal with, tackle; speak to, direct; label
column7: We need to address the underlying problem. / She addressed the audience. / Address the envelope clearly.
column8: Normalize from infinitive 'to address' and add major senses/constructions.

column5: To reduce the amount or supply of a resource substantially; depleted = greatly reduced or drained. Informally, a person can feel depleted of energy.
column7: The drought depleted the reservoir. / After the trip, I felt mentally depleted.
column8: Normalize base + source adjective. Not necessarily completely exhausted/empty.

column5: To become or make larger in size, amount, range, scope, detail, or influence; 'expand on/upon X' = give more detail.
column7: The company expanded into Europe. / Could you expand on that point?
column8: Add important intransitive/transitive and 'expand on' construction.

column5: Having a rough, harsh, breathy, or strained voice, commonly from irritation, illness, overuse, or other causes.
column7: My voice was hoarse after shouting at the game.
column8: Avoid implying sore throat/overuse are the only causes. Common: become/go hoarse.

column2: take it down a notch / take something down a notch
column5: To reduce the intensity, volume, aggressiveness, ambition, emotional heat, or degree of something by a small amount.
column6: tone it down, dial it back, ease off
column7: The music is too loud—take it down a notch. / We may need to take the rhetoric down a notch.
column8: Productive object variant. 'A notch' metaphorically means one step/degree.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::rhetorical topic::communication discovery::debate_language

column5: To deliberately refrain from giving, providing, disclosing, granting, or paying something that could otherwise be given.
column6: hold back, retain, keep back, refuse to disclose
column7: The company withheld part of his pay. / She withheld the information until the investigation ended.
column8: CORRECTION: source example 'withhold judgment' was wrong; standard idiom is 'withhold judgment' = refrain from forming/expressing judgment, not a judge ordering a company to do so.

column5: Boldly rude, disrespectful, or contemptuous behavior or speech, especially toward someone in authority or entitled to respect.
column7: The teacher would not tolerate open insolence in class.
column8: Related adjective: insolent. Often stronger/more openly defiant than ordinary rudeness.

column5: To waste time doing unimportant things, proceed inefficiently, or fuss with something instead of getting on with the task.
column7: Stop faffing around and get your shoes on. / I spent an hour faffing about with the settings.
column8: Normalize base. 'Faff' can also be noun: 'What a faff!' = what a hassle/fuss.

column2: put one's foot in one's mouth / put one's foot in it
column5: To say something tactless, embarrassing, or inappropriate, usually accidentally.
column6: say the wrong thing, make a faux pas, blunder
column7: I put my foot in my mouth when I asked about a job she'd just lost.
column8: Normalize full possessive construction. AmE strongly uses 'put one's foot in one's mouth'; BrE often 'put one's foot in it'.

column2: be slow to reply / take a while to reply
column5: To take longer than expected or desired to respond to a message, email, question, etc.
column6: reply slowly, take a while to respond, be a slow responder
column7: Sorry I'm slow to reply when work gets hectic. / He sometimes takes a while to reply to texts.
column8: Not an idiom; motive is not encoded. Teach natural variants and 'reply to + message/person'.

column5: In slang, bad, unfair, strange, ridiculous, or uncool. Spelling 'wack' is especially common for this adjective, while 'whack' is also seen and is the standard spelling for hit/strike senses.
column7: That rule is wack—it punishes people who did nothing wrong.
column8: PRECISION: slang spelling varies. Keep distinct from 'whack' = hit/strike and 'out of whack' = out of order/alignment.

column5: Extremely angry, shocked, or offended because something is perceived as seriously wrong, unfair, immoral, or insulting.
column7: Residents were outraged by the sudden closure.
column8: Often implies moral offense/indignation, not merely high-intensity anger. Related noun/verb: outrage.

column5: Literally relating to the internal organs (viscera); figuratively, felt deeply and immediately at a bodily/gut level rather than through detached analysis.
column7: I had a visceral reaction to the scene. / The film creates a visceral sense of danger.
column8: Add literal origin/sense. Figurative visceral can describe fear, disgust, excitement, impact, experience—not only emotion.

column5: An opening segment that begins before the title sequence, opening credits, or standard introduction, often to hook the audience or set up the episode.
column7: The episode starts with a cold open before the theme song.
column8: PRECISION: not limited to TV/film and not necessarily comedic. 'Teaser' overlaps but production terminology varies.
column12: entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist topic::media topic::public_speaking topic::television topic::entertainment discovery::title_language discovery::audience_engagement discovery::evaluation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To feel strong romantic or sexual attraction toward someone.
column6: be attracted to, be into, have a crush on
column7: He's had the hots for her for months.
column8: KEY FRAME: have the hots for + person. More overtly physical/sexual than 'have a crush on' in many contexts.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::slang topic::romance

column5: A closet or small storage room used for supplies, commonly in offices, schools, workplaces, or institutions.
column7: Extra paper and toner are in the supply closet.
column8: A utility closet often houses building equipment and is not a clean synonym.

column5: To badly damage/destroy something; defeat someone decisively; or emotionally/physically overwhelm someone.
column7: The storm wrecked the roof. / Their team wrecked us. / That ending absolutely wrecked me.
column8: Broaden from person-only slang to core verb. Online 'that wrecked me' often means emotionally devastated or overwhelmed.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::slang usage::informal topic::romance topic::construction

column5: Latin 'unconquered/unconquerable'; especially the title of William Ernest Henley's poem 'Invictus', widely associated with endurance and self-mastery.
column7: The final lines of 'Invictus' are often invoked as a statement of resilience.
column8: Distinguish Latin word from poem title. Avoid making 'resilient' a literal translation.

column5: To allow events or a situation to develop over time without trying to control every step or force an immediate outcome.
column6: let things develop, wait and see, allow events to play out
column7: We don't have enough information yet, so let's let things unfold.
column8: Built from unfold = develop/reveal gradually. Does not necessarily mean passive acceptance of everything.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern entry::fixed_expression usage::figurative topic::construction discovery::process_details

column5: To spoil, abruptly change, or drain the enjoyable mood/atmosphere of a social situation.
column6: spoil the mood, ruin the atmosphere, bring everyone down
column7: Don't bring up the argument right now—you'll kill the vibe.
column8: Productive: kill the mood is more established/general; vibe is casual contemporary wording.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction usage::informal usage::casual usage::slang usage::rhetorical topic::construction discovery::debate_language

column5: Lose face = suffer humiliation or loss of social standing/dignity; save face = avoid or reduce such humiliation.
column6: be humiliated, lose standing; preserve dignity
column7: He refused to back down because he feared losing face. / The compromise let both sides save face.
column8: Useful pair. 'Face' concerns socially recognized dignity/reputation, often especially salient in interpersonal/cultural contexts.

column5: A change in direction; figuratively, a tactic or response that redirects attention away from a question, criticism, blame, or uncomfortable issue.
column7: Instead of answering the question, he used a joke as deflection.
column8: Add literal/general direction sense. In conversation/politics, 'deflection' often implies avoidance but motive should be inferred from context.

column5: Originally a bet in which the first three finishers are selected in exact order; figuratively, a set or combination of three notable things, often three successes/advantages.
column7: The restaurant hit the trifecta: great food, fair prices, and friendly service.
column8: CORRECTION: figurative trifecta need not be three things happening 'at once', though it is often positive. Add horse-racing origin.

column2: tell people/things apart / tell X from Y
column5: To distinguish similar people or things by recognizing differences.
column7: I can't tell the twins apart. / Can you tell the fake from the real one?
column8: CORRECTION: productive frame is usually plural/object pair: tell X and Y apart, tell them apart, or tell X from Y—not generic singular 'tell something apart'.

column5: To accumulate, incur, score, or achieve a relatively large amount/number of something over time.
column6: accumulate, amass, run up, chalk up
column7: She racked up thousands of miles. / He racked up a huge phone bill. / The team racked up five wins.
column8: Can be positive or negative: points/wins/awards vs debt/charges/penalties.

column2: box someone/something in / be boxed in
column5: To surround or restrict someone/something so movement or options are limited; figuratively, to constrain choices or freedom.
column7: A truck boxed my car in. / The contract left us feeling boxed in.
column8: Normalize active + passive. Literal spatial restriction motivates figurative limited-options sense.

column5: To feel or express wonder, surprise, or admiration at something.
column6: wonder at, be amazed by, admire
column7: We marveled at how quickly the city had changed.
column8: KEY FRAME: marvel at + noun/wh-clause. Wonder can be admiration or astonishment.

column2: lead to a tangent / go off on a tangent
column5: A remark/topic can lead to a tangent, causing discussion to move away from the main subject; a speaker can 'go off on a tangent'.
column7: That question led us off on a tangent about old movies. / I went off on a tangent and forgot my original point.
column8: CORRECTION: normalize the productive idiom 'go off on a tangent' and causative variants; 'lead to some tangents' is merely compositional.

column2: a pantheon of / the pantheon of
column5: Originally, the collective gods of a religion or a temple dedicated to them; figuratively, an elite or highly revered group of people/things in a field.
column6: elite group, canon, hall of fame (informal analogy)
column7: She belongs in the pantheon of great jazz singers.
column8: KEY FRAME: in/join the pantheon of + celebrated group. 'Hall of fame' is only an analogy, not a synonym in all uses.
column12: entry::construction usage::informal usage::religious topic::religion topic::construction discovery::figurative_extension discovery::commitment

column5: A mischievous, cheeky, or troublesome person, often a child; can be affectionate, humorous, mildly scolding, or historically more negative.
column7: You little rascal—you hid my keys again!
column8: Tone matters. 'Rogue' can be affectionate similarly but has broader meanings.

column5: Get behind X = support or endorse X; get behind on X = fall behind schedule/progress with tasks, payments, work, etc.; literal spatial senses also occur.
column6: support, back; fall behind, be overdue
column7: I can get behind that idea. / I got behind on my email after vacation.
column8: CORRECTION: preposition changes the construction: get behind + cause/idea vs get behind on + work/payments.

column2: now you're talking / now you're talking my language
column5: Used to show enthusiastic approval because a suggestion or topic strongly matches one's preferences or interests.
column6: that's more like it, I like the sound of that
column7: Pizza and a movie? Now you're talking my language.
column8: 'Now you're talking!' is the shorter common form; 'my language' adds 'that's exactly my kind of thing'.

column5: To cause something to appear as if by magic; or evoke/create a mental image, memory, feeling, explanation, idea, or resource, sometimes with effort.
column6: summon, evoke, call up, dream up
column7: The smell conjured up memories of childhood. / Somehow she conjured up a solution before the deadline.
column8: Broaden beyond memory/image. 'Conjure' without up is also common.

column5: A language descended from varieties of Vulgar Latin; major examples include Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian, and Romanian, alongside many others.
column7: Romanian is a Romance language even though it is geographically separated from many western Romance languages.
column8: CORRECTION: capitalize Romance. 'Latin family' is imprecise; Romance is a branch of the Indo-European family.

column2: back on the books / get something back on the calendar
column5: To restore something to an official schedule, calendar, roster, or record after cancellation/removal. For appointments, 'back on the calendar/books' is natural; singular 'back on the book' is generally nonstandard for this meaning.
column6: reschedule, put back on the calendar, restore to the schedule
column7: Let's get the session back on the calendar for Friday. / The event is back on the books for next month.
column8: CORRECTION: rebuild nonstandard 'back on the book'. 'On the books' can also mean officially recorded/existing, but bookkeeping uses require context-specific wording.

column5: To move in a twisting/circling way; figuratively, a place, mind, or situation can be full of rapidly moving thoughts, emotions, rumors, questions, activity, etc.
column6: teem with, be full of; churn with
column7: My mind was swirling with questions. / Rumors were swirling around the office.
column8: Teach both 'X is swirling with Y' and 'Y is swirling around/in X'. Not inherently overwhelming.

column5: More complex, significant, interesting, capable, or mysterious than is apparent at first glance.
column6: deeper than it looks, not as simple as it seems
column7: There is more to this case than meets the eye.
column8: CORRECTION: most productive full pattern is 'there's more to X than meets the eye' or 'X is more than meets the eye' in some contexts.

column5: To resonate emotionally or intellectually with someone, especially because something feels familiar, meaningful, relevant, or true.
column6: resonate with, hit home, connect with
column7: Her story struck a chord with viewers who had gone through the same thing.
column8: KEY FRAME: X strikes/struck a chord with + person/group. 'Touch a nerve' can be negative/sensitive and is not a clean synonym.

column5: To continue moving, working, recording, progressing, or proceeding without stopping; exact sense depends on context.
column7: We're making good time, so let's keep rolling. / The camera kept rolling after the mistake.
column8: Add literal/media sense. Informal encouragement; not a fixed idiom with one meaning.

column5: To start dancing or show a dance move; more broadly and less consistently, to take action or make a move.
column6: dance, make a move, get moving
column7: When the music started, he jumped up and busted a move.
column8: Dance sense is the core established slang use. General 'take action' is contextual/extended.

column5: To emit, release, radiate, or produce something perceptible such as heat, light, smell, gas, sound, or an impression/vibe.
column7: The heater gives off a lot of heat. / He gives off a calm, confident vibe.
column8: KEY FRAME: X gives off Y. For impressions, 'give off a ... vibe' is especially productive.

column5: Having a pleasantly sharp, lively, acidic, or piquant taste; sometimes extended to smell.
column7: The sauce is creamy but tangy from the lemon and yogurt.
column8: CORRECTION: tangy is not simply 'slightly sour'; it can involve sharp/pungent flavor more broadly. Usually positive/neutral.

column5: To form theories/guesses without firm evidence; or to take financial risk in hopes of profit, especially by buying/selling assets.
column6: conjecture, theorize, guess; invest speculatively, gamble
column7: We can only speculate about why she left. / He speculated in property during the boom.
column8: KEY FRAMES: speculate about/on + question; speculate that + clause; speculate in + asset/market (financial).

column5: To exert great effort; stretch or injure through excessive force; place pressure on a relationship/resource; filter through a strainer; noun has related physical/injury/pressure/type senses.
column7: I strained to hear her. / The workload is straining the team. / He strained his back lifting the box.
column8: Normalize base + source form and add major senses. 'Straining' as adjective is less central than participle.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word topic::relationships topic::grammar discovery::resource_allocation discovery::emphasis

column2: it happens to the best of us
column3: /ɪt ˈhæpənz tə ðə bɛst əv ʌs/
column5: A consoling phrase meaning that even capable, careful, or experienced people sometimes make mistakes or suffer ordinary mishaps.
column6: everyone makes mistakes, it can happen to anyone
column7: You sent it to the wrong address? It happens to the best of us.
column8: Often minimizes embarrassment kindly; can also be lightly humorous.

column5: A wide, continuous area or extent, especially of land, water, sky, space, or another visible surface.
column7: A vast expanse of desert stretched to the horizon.
column8: CORRECTION: abstract 'expanse of thought/imagination' is possible but uncommon/poetic; concrete spatial uses are central.

column5: A substance that produces mobile ions when dissolved or molten and can conduct electric current; in physiology, electrolytes such as sodium and potassium ions help regulate fluid balance, nerve signaling, muscle function, etc.
column7: Sweat contains water and electrolytes such as sodium and chloride.
column8: CORRECTION: electrolytes are not defined by being 'essential for hydration'; that's a physiological application. 'Ion solution' is not a synonym.
column12: entry::word usage::scientific topic::chemistry topic::anatomy topic::science topic::health

column5: An opaque, microcrystalline variety of silica/chalcedony, often patterned or colored by impurities and used as an ornamental stone/gem material.
column7: The pendant was carved from red jasper.
column8: CORRECTION: normalize headword to jasper. Often described as an opaque variety of chalcedony; avoid oversimplifying it as simply 'quartz'.

column5: To think, talk, or write about past experiences, often with nostalgia or pleasure.
column7: We spent the evening reminiscing about college. / He reminisced with old friends.
column8: KEY FRAME: reminisce about + past topic; reminisce with + person. Fondness is common but not logically required in every use.

column5: To approach people systematically to seek votes, support, opinions, orders, or information; also to examine/discuss a subject thoroughly. 'Canvas' is the fabric; 'canvass' is the verb.
column7: Volunteers canvassed the neighborhood for votes. / The committee canvassed several options.
column8: Normalize base + source form. 'Proselytize' specifically seeks converts to beliefs and is not a general synonym.

column5: To pronounce speech clearly and distinctly; also, more formally, to state or formulate a principle, idea, or doctrine clearly.
column7: Please slow down and enunciate. / The report enunciates three guiding principles.
column8: CORRECTION: 'enunciate words more clearly' is redundant but natural; distinguish pronunciation sense from formal 'state clearly' sense.

column5: Seeming not of this world: supernatural, eerie, extraordinarily strange, or exceptionally intense/beautiful in a way that feels beyond ordinary experience.
column7: An unearthly howl came from the woods. / The singer had an unearthly beauty to her voice.
column8: Can be frightening or positively awe-inspiring. Common with sound, silence, glow, beauty.

column5: In North American informal usage, 'possum' commonly means an opossum (family Didelphidae). In Australia and nearby regions, 'possums' are different marsupials in the suborder Phalangeriformes.
column6: opossum (North American colloquial use); possum (Australasian animals)
column7: A Virginia opossum wandered across the yard. / Australian possums are not the same animals as American opossums.
column8: CORRECTION: original card wrongly grouped American and Australasian animals as one animal known for playing dead. Playing dead is especially associated with opossums.

column2: on the edge of one's seat / keep someone on the edge of their seat
column5: Extremely interested, excited, anxious, or suspensefully engaged while waiting to see what happens.
column7: The finale kept me on the edge of my seat.
column8: CORRECTION: standard possessive construction is 'on the edge of my/your/their seat', not generic 'the seat'.

column5: A dried Turkish chili pepper/flaked seasoning associated with Şanlıurfa, known for dark color and a complex smoky, earthy, raisin-like flavor with moderate heat.
column7: I sprinkled Urfa biber over roasted vegetables for smoky heat.
column8: Food/cultural term. Flavor and heat vary by product; capitalize Urfa. 'Biber' is Turkish for pepper.

column5: Playful, silly, mischievous, attention-getting, or sometimes foolish/outrageous behavior or actions.
column7: The kids' antics kept everyone laughing. / His online antics eventually annoyed his coworkers.
column8: Usually plural. Can be affectionate/amused or critical depending context; not necessarily intended to amuse.

column5: A tendency or recurring trait in someone that makes them more easily deceived or tricked.
column7: He's usually skeptical, but he has a gullible streak when it comes to online deals.
column8: Productive pattern: have a + ADJECTIVE + streak = have a recurring side/tendency (a stubborn streak, a competitive streak). Here gullible modifies streak; it is not a fixed idiom.

column5: Both mark contrast. 'In contrast' commonly stands alone or appears in 'in contrast to/with X'; 'by contrast' is especially natural as a sentence-level connector meaning 'when compared with what was just mentioned'.
column6: conversely, on the other hand, however
column7: In contrast to her brother, she's very quiet. / The first version is cluttered. By contrast, the revised one is easy to scan.
column8: Do not reduce the distinction to sentence position. KEY FRAME: in contrast to/with + noun; By contrast, + clause/sentence. Both can connect discourse, with overlapping use.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::discourse_expression entry::prepositional_phrase usage::debate-friendly topic::language_learning discovery::comparison discovery::contrast discovery::debate_language

column5: A small window in the side of a ship or other vessel, traditionally round; the term can also be used for similar small round windows elsewhere.
column7: I looked through the porthole and saw nothing but ocean.
column8: CORRECTION: standard spelling is one word, 'porthole'. It is especially associated with ships; 'aircraft window' is not a useful defining synonym.

column5: A fire apparatus equipped with an aerial ladder and related equipment for access, rescue, ventilation, and other firefighting operations; exact apparatus terminology varies by department/region.
column6: aerial ladder truck, aerial apparatus, truck company apparatus
column7: The ladder truck arrived quickly to help rescue people trapped on the upper floors.
column8: Avoid treating every ladder truck as simply a fire engine with a ladder. Fire-service classifications and equipment configurations vary.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist topic::business discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To eat food very quickly and hungrily.
column6: devour, gobble down, scarf down, inhale (slang)
column7: He wolfed down his sandwich in less than a minute.
column8: CORRECTION: standard expression is 'wolf down' / 'wolf something down', not normally 'wolf out'. KEY FRAME: wolf + FOOD + down.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::informal usage::slang topic::food

column5: Having irregular, wavy, or curly lines or shapes; often used to describe handwriting, lines, or motion.
column7: Her squiggly signature was hard to read but full of personality. He drew a squiggly line to decorate the edge of the page.
column8: Common collocations: squiggly line, squiggly handwriting, squiggly shape. Informal/descriptive; suggests repeated bends/waves rather than a precise geometric pattern.

column5: extremely peaceful, picturesque, and pleasant, often in an idealized or romanticized way.
column7: They spent the weekend at an idyllic cottage by the lake. They spent their honeymoon in an idyllic village by the sea.
column8: Often describes places/scenes/lifestyles as attractively peaceful and picturesque, sometimes idealized: idyllic village, setting, childhood, life.

column5: Extremely hungry; very hungry in ordinary modern use.
column7: After the long hike, we were absolutely famished.
column8: 'Famished' is commonly hyperbolic and does not literally imply starvation. Stronger than hungry; compare WID1843 peckish = slightly hungry.

column5: Irrelevant or unnecessary; not essential to the matter at hand.
column7: Try to remove any extraneous details from your report to make it more concise.
column8: Common: extraneous detail/information/noise/factor/material. Means unnecessary or irrelevant to the purpose; not necessarily false.

column5: 'Perk up' = become or make more lively, cheerful, alert, or energetic. Bare 'perk' also occurs, especially in related senses, but 'perk up' is the central everyday construction here.
column7: She perked up when she heard they were getting ice cream. / A cup of coffee might perk me up.
column8: KEY FRAME: PERSON perks up; THING perks PERSON up. Keep separate from noun 'perk' = benefit.

column5: A non-wage benefit or extra advantage offered as part of a job, membership, or situation.
column7: One of the perks of working here is unlimited coffee.
column8: Common frame: a perk of + job/situation; job perks. A perk can be formal compensation (insurance, discounts) or an informal advantage ('a perk of living downtown').

column5: As a verb, 'perk' can mean percolate or make coffee in a percolator. Noun uses referring to percolated coffee/percolator are dialectal or uncommon and should not be treated as general standard English.
column7: Let the coffee perk for a few minutes.
column8: CORRECTION: prioritize the established verb use. 'Fresh perk' as a noun is regional/uncommon; do not teach it as a general synonym for brewed coffee.

column5: Not representative of a type, group, or norm; unusual or irregular.
column7: It was an atypical response from someone usually so calm.
column8: KEY FRAME: atypical of + person/group; atypical for + situation/person. Means not typical, not necessarily abnormal or bad.

column5: Apparently or purportedly, but perhaps not actually; used to express something that seems true on the surface.
column7: He was ostensibly on vacation, but people suspected he was still working.
column8: Often carries a gap between stated/apparent purpose and suspected reality: ostensibly to do X; ostensibly about X. It does not itself prove deception.

column5: To overdo, overembellish, or exaggerate something so that the effect becomes excessive; from the expression 'overegg the pudding'.
column7: The final scene overegged the emotion. / Don't overegg the pudding with too many dramatic effects.
column8: Normalize base form. Chiefly British. Can apply to claims, performances, descriptions, decoration, drama, etc.

column5: To begin growing or expanding rapidly; burgeoning = growing/flourishing quickly.
column7: A small scene began to burgeon around the club. / The city's burgeoning tech sector attracted investors.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Often: burgeoning industry/market/population/interest. It emphasizes vigorous growth, not merely existence.

column5: To gradually extract, identify, clarify, or reveal subtle information, distinctions, implications, or threads through careful effort.
column7: The interviewer teased out the differences between the two accounts.
column8: Normalize base. KEY FRAME: tease X out / tease out X. Common in analysis, research, interviews, interpretation.

column5: 1. Stretched or pulled tight, with no slack. 2. (figuratively) Showing tension, discipline, or emotional strain.
column7: She wrapped the rope taut around the pole. / His taut expression revealed the pressure he was under.
column8: Literal: taut rope/wire/skin = tightly stretched. Figurative: taut prose/plot = tightly controlled with little excess; taut nerves/expression = tense. 'Tight' is broader.

column5: 'On tenterhooks' means in a state of anxious suspense or nervous anticipation. Tenterhooks were hooks used to hold cloth stretched on a tenter.
column6: edge of the seat, suspense, nervous tension, high alert
column7: We were on tenterhooks waiting for the results.
column8: KEY FORM is 'on tenterhooks', not simply tenterhooks = suspense. Historical literal origin is a useful memory hook.

column5: A protective glove, historically part of armor; figuratively in established expressions such as 'run the gauntlet' = endure a series of attacks, criticisms, tests, or difficulties. 'Throw down the gauntlet' = issue a challenge.
column7: The knight wore armored gauntlets. / The candidate ran the gauntlet of hostile questions. / She threw down the gauntlet to her rival.
column8: Add two major idioms. Note historical spelling/etymological overlap around 'gantlet/gauntlet'; modern 'run the gauntlet' is standard.

column5: Irritable bowel syndrome: a disorder of gut-brain interaction characterized by recurrent abdominal pain associated with changes in bowel habits, without a single structural lesion explaining the symptoms.
column7: IBS can involve constipation, diarrhea, or both, along with abdominal pain.
column8: Medical precision: symptoms and treatment vary. Avoid treating 'gut sensitivity' as a synonym or implying one universal management plan.

column5: To compel or pressure someone to act through force, threats, intimidation, or other coercive pressure.
column7: They coerced him into signing the agreement. / She said the confession had been coerced.
column8: KEY FRAME: coerce + PERSON + into + gerund/noun. Stronger than persuade or pressure; lack of genuinely free choice is central.

column5: To pacify, calm, or satisfy someone, often by yielding to their demands.
column7: The manager tried to appease the angry customer with a refund.
column8: Common: appease a person/group/critics; appease anger/fears (less central). Can be neutral 'calm/satisfy' or critical when concessions are seen as excessive. Historical/political 'appeasement' carries special associations.

column5: Causing interruption, disorder, or major change to normal activity; in business/technology, 'disruptive' can describe innovations that significantly alter established markets or practices.
column7: His behavior in class was disruptive. / The new app is seen as a disruptive force in the taxi industry.
column8: Do not use 'groundbreaking' as a blanket synonym: disruptive describes effect on an existing system, not simply novelty.

column5: Without help from anyone else; independently.
column7: She single-handedly organized the entire fundraiser event.
column8: Can be literal credit for doing something alone, or hyperbolic emphasis: 'That one scene single-handedly saved the episode.' Hyphenated.

column5: To pass, spread, or filter gradually from one level/group to another, especially from higher levels to lower ones; strongly associated with debates over 'trickle-down' economics but usable more broadly.
column7: The policy changes eventually trickled down to local offices.
column8: Separate neutral phrasal verb from political/economic label 'trickle-down economics', whose effectiveness is a contested empirical/policy question.

column5: A nonclinical popular term for sadness, loss, loneliness, or adjustment difficulties some parents/caregivers may experience after children leave home.
column6: empty-nest adjustment, feelings of loss after children leave home
column7: After her last child went to college, she struggled with empty nest syndrome.
column8: CORRECTION: not a formal psychiatric diagnosis and not equivalent to depression or 'parental separation anxiety'. Experiences vary widely.

column5: To reduce spending, consumption, activity, production, or another amount/extent; 'cut back on X' is the common frame for reducing one's use of something.
column7: We're cutting back on eating out. / The company cut back production.
column8: KEY FRAMES: cut back on + noun/gerund; cut back + production/spending. Contrast 'cut down on' (very similar in consumption contexts).

column5: Something given or done in exchange for something else; a reciprocal arrangement. In legal/political contexts, the phrase may describe an exchange relevant to bribery, contracts, harassment, etc., but is not inherently illegal.
column6: exchange, reciprocal arrangement, something for something
column7: They agreed to a quid pro quo: technical support in exchange for access to the data.
column8: Latin literally 'something for something'. CORRECTION: 'trade-off' is not always equivalent; a trade-off is a compromise between competing benefits/costs.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::technical topic::law topic::politics discovery::public_discourse discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To irritate or anger someone intensely.
column7: Her constant lateness exasperated the team leader.
column8: Transitive: X exasperates PERSON; PERSON is exasperated by/with X. Means intensely irritate/frustrate, often after repeated difficulty rather than explosive rage.

column5: To annoy, frustrate, puzzle, or worry; often literary/formal. Also used in 'vexed question/issue' for a difficult, much-debated problem.
column7: The inconsistency vexed the researchers. / It remains a vexed question.
column8: Broaden beyond small/repeated annoyance. 'Vexed' has an important adjectival use = difficult/controversial.

column5: Verb 'peeve' = annoy or irritate. A 'pet peeve' is a particular thing that especially annoys someone; bare noun 'peeve' exists but is much less common than 'pet peeve'.
column7: It peeves me when people block the doorway. / Loud chewing is one of my pet peeves.
column8: CORRECTION: prioritize common noun construction 'pet peeve'. Verb is transitive: X peeves someone.

column5: To renovate, revise, or give a new and improved form to something.
column7: The company is revamping its website to attract more users.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Verb: revamp a site/system/process. Noun: a revamp. Often modernization/substantial redesign, not a guarantee of improvement.

column5: To show that a claim, myth, theory, or belief is false or unsupported, typically by evidence or argument.
column6: disprove, refute, expose as false, challenge successfully
column7: The scientist debunked the popular but incorrect health myth.
column8: 'Invalidate' is broader/technical; 'debunk' often targets widely believed myths/claims. Avoid claiming a debunk succeeds unless the evidence actually establishes it.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::rhetorical discovery::evidence discovery::assertion discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::debate_language

column5: To anticipate something with strong fear, anxiety, or reluctance; noun 'dread' = strong apprehension/fear.
column6: fearing, anticipating with anxiety, worrying about
column7: I'm dreading the meeting tomorrow. / She felt a sense of dread as the deadline approached.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Dread can include strong reluctance without literal terror.

column5: To investigate, explore, or examine something deeply and thoroughly.
column7: The journalist delved into the company's financial records.
column8: KEY FRAME: delve into + topic/question/records/history. Slightly formal; implies going beneath the surface, though 'deeply and thoroughly' can be contextual rather than guaranteed.

column5: Deprived of the right to vote (core political/legal sense); more broadly, deprived of rights, power, or meaningful participation.
column7: The law disenfranchised many eligible voters. / Some residents felt politically disenfranchised.
column8: CORRECTION: voting-rights sense is central and precise. Broader figurative use exists, but 'marginalized/oppressed/silenced' are not exact synonyms.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative topic::law topic::politics discovery::public_discourse

column5: Using force, threats, pressure, or other means that constrain a person's free choice or compel compliance.
column7: The regime was accused of using coercive tactics to silence opposition.
column8: Related verb coerce. 'Manipulative' may overlap but is not necessarily coercive; coercion specifically involves constrained choice/pressure.

column5: A brief, casual, or not-very-serious involvement, especially a romantic/sexual affair; also a temporary flirtation with an activity, idea, or pursuit.
column6: fling, flirtation, brief affair; brief involvement
column7: His dalliance with acting ended when he realized it wasn't his true calling.
column8: KEY FRAME: a dalliance with + person/activity/idea. 'Dabble' is a verb and not a noun synonym.

column5: To fail to experience, obtain, enjoy, or take advantage of something; with a person, to lose the opportunity for a relationship/experience with them depending context.
column6: lost the chance, passed up, didn't get to experience
column7: I missed out on the concert. / If you never talk to her, you might miss out on getting to know her.
column8: Normalize base. KEY FRAME: miss out on + noun/gerund. Distinguish 'miss someone' = feel their absence.

column5: A signed opinion/commentary article, traditionally associated with the page opposite a newspaper's editorial page; today used broadly for contributed opinion pieces.
column6: opinion piece, guest commentary, opinion essay
column7: She wrote an op-ed criticizing the government's climate policy.
column8: CORRECTION: an op-ed need not be in a magazine/newspaper nor written by someone outside editorial staff in every modern usage. 'Editorial' usually represents an editorial board/institutional position and is not synonymous.

column5: A flashing vehicle turn signal/indicator (especially AmE). Separately, 'blinkers' in BrE can mean horse blinders; figurative limited-perspective uses usually come from 'blinkers/blinkered', not the vehicle light.
column7: Use your blinker before changing lanes. / His blinkered view ignored the alternatives.
column8: CORRECTION: separate vehicle 'blinker' from figurative 'blinkers/blinkered' = restricted outlook.

column5: To grasp or hold tightly, often suddenly or from fear/urgency; noun 'clutch' can mean a tight grasp and has important mechanical/other senses.
column7: The child clutched her teddy bear during the storm. / He clutched the railing as the boat rocked.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Emotional motivation is common but not required.

column5: Noun: a person, group, or country that cooperates with/supports another, especially toward a shared goal. Verb: to join or associate with another party for a purpose.
column7: They became allies during the campaign. / The group allied itself with local organizers.
column8: KEY VERB FRAMES: ally oneself with X; be allied with X. In social-justice contexts, 'ally' can specifically mean a supporter outside a marginalized group, but that is one contextual sense.

column5: To exclude someone from a group, society, or social circle.
column7: He was ostracized by his former friends after the scandal.
column8: KEY FRAME: ostracize + person/group; be ostracized from/by. Social exclusion is central; 'exile/expel' can imply formal/physical removal and are not exact.

column5: A bitter, forceful, often lengthy verbal or written attack on someone or something.
column7: He launched into a diatribe against the new policy.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Common: launch into a diatribe; a diatribe against/about X. Stronger and more sustained than ordinary criticism.

column5: A mischievous trick or practical joke, usually intended to surprise or amuse, though pranks can also be harmful or unwelcome; verb = play such a trick.
column7: They pulled a prank by covering her office in balloons.
column8: Intent to amuse does not guarantee the target finds it funny. Common: play/pull a prank on someone; prank someone.

column5: To move a finger across a touchscreen; steal/take quickly (informal); strike with a sweeping motion; noun 'a swipe' can be such a motion or a critical attack/remark ('take a swipe at').
column6: steal, snatch, jab, dig, roast, tap
column7: Swipe left to delete it. / Someone swiped my umbrella. / The columnist took a swipe at the mayor.
column8: CORRECTION: consolidate major senses rather than label all of 'swipe' as slang. KEY IDIOM: take a swipe at + person/idea.

column5: Adverb/adjective: in a haphazard, random, or uncontrolled way; also, whether willing or unwilling / inevitably, especially in older/formal use.
column7: He tossed clothes into the suitcase willy-nilly.
column8: Two historically related senses remain: haphazardly and willy-nilly = whether one likes it or not. Context usually disambiguates.

column5: Relating to legislation or a legislature—the making of laws or the lawmaking branch/body.
column7: The legislative branch debated the bill for over three weeks.
column8: Common: legislative branch/body/process/power/agenda. 'Statutory' means established/required by statute and is not a general synonym.

column5: To engage in a casual, leisurely conversation.
column6: chat, shoot the breeze, gab, jaw
column7: We stayed up all night chewing the fat about high school memories.
column8: Informal/old-fashioned flavor in some varieties. Means chat at length in a relaxed way; not necessarily gossip. Compare shoot the breeze.
column12: entry::idiom usage::informal usage::casual usage::dated topic::communication discovery::audience_engagement

column5: For a ruminant, to regurgitate partially digested material from the foregut and chew it again as part of rumination.
column7: The cow lay in the field chewing the cud as the sun set.
column8: Literal biological construction. 'Digest again' is not a synonym; chewing cud is one stage in the ruminant digestive process.

column5: Figuratively, to think or talk reflectively at length; this use is less common than literal 'chew the cud'. 'Chew over X' is a more productive modern expression for consider/discuss carefully.
column7: He sat quietly chewing the cud over what had happened. / Let's chew the idea over before deciding.
column8: Register caution: figurative 'chew the cud' can sound old-fashioned or deliberately humorous. Do not overstate it as a common British idiom.
column12: entry::idiom usage::dated usage::humorous usage::figurative usage::british_english discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Partially digested food that a ruminant regurgitates from the foregut to the mouth and chews again.
column7: The cow lay in the field chewing its cud.
column8: CLEANUP: remove corrupted text and overlong anatomy dump. Figurative 'chew the cud' belongs on the separate idiom card.

column5: Noun: a mammal that digests plant material through foregut fermentation and rumination, typically using a multi-compartment stomach; adjective: relating to such animals or, figuratively, deeply contemplative.
column7: Cattle, sheep, goats, and deer are ruminants. / He had a slow, ruminant manner of thinking.
column8: PRECISION: avoid reducing the class to 'herbivore with a four-chambered stomach'; camelids are ruminating foregut fermenters but are not true ruminants. Figurative person-noun use is rare.

column5: To think repeatedly or deeply about something; in psychology, often to engage in repetitive, difficult-to-disengage thinking, frequently about distress. Zoology: to regurgitate and rechew cud.
column7: She kept ruminating on the mistake. / Cattle spend hours ruminating.
column8: Important nuance: everyday/literary ruminate can be reflective; psychological rumination often has repetitive negative content/process. KEY FRAME: ruminate on/about X.

column5: Characterized by sustained, reflective thought; in psychological contexts, involving repetitive rumination, which may be negative or self-focused.
column7: His ruminative gaze lingered on the empty street. / The novel had a quiet, ruminative tone that made it linger in your mind. / She grew more ruminative after the loss of her mentor.
column8: Do not build depression into the lexical definition. Common: ruminative thinking/style/mood/tone.

column5: To bring swallowed material back up to the mouth; in some animals this is a normal feeding/digestive behavior. Figuratively, to repeat information or ideas mechanically without meaningful processing.
column6: bring back up; repeat mechanically, parrot
column7: Birds regurgitate food to feed their young. / He just regurgitated the talking points without understanding them.
column8: CORRECTION: regurgitation is not simply synonymous with vomiting; vomiting is a distinct forceful physiological process. Figurative 'regurgitate facts/talking points' is strongly negative.

column5: A thought, reflection, or period of reflective/speculative thinking; plural 'musings' often means informal reflections on a subject.
column7: The essay is a collection of musings on memory and travel.
column8: CORRECTION: 'musing' as adjective is uncommon compared with 'musing' noun and 'musingly' rare; prioritize noun/plural. Related verb: muse on/about/over.

column5: Dark, gloomy, or dull in tone or mood. Often associated with sadness, melancholy, or seriousness.
column7: The movie had a somber tone throughout. / He wore a somber expression at the funeral.
column8: AmE spelling 'somber'; BrE also 'sombre'. Can describe mood, expression, colors, music, atmosphere, occasion. Means serious/gloomy/subdued, not always explicitly sad.

column5: A famously long, playful invented word popularized by Disney's 1964 film Mary Poppins, used humorously to suggest something extraordinarily wonderful or to revel in the sound of the word.
column7: The concert was simply supercalifragilisticexpialidocious!
column8: Cultural/reference word rather than ordinary productive adjective. Capitalization usually lowercase unless title/context requires. Do not treat it as a precise synonym for 'excellent'.
column12: entry::word usage::playful topic::film topic::entertainment discovery::suggestion discovery::impression

column5: A small contextual information box that appears near a user-interface element, commonly on hover, focus, or other interaction, to explain or label it.
column7: Hover over the icon to display its tooltip.
column8: Normalize singular/plural. Modern touch interfaces may trigger tooltip-like help without mouse hover, so hover is common but not definitional.

column5: In Japanese television/anime scheduling, a roughly three-month broadcast block, commonly around 10–13 weekly episodes; a series may run for one or multiple cours.
column7: This show is getting a second cour starting next summer.
column8: Loanword from French 'cours' via Japanese industry/fandom usage. CORRECTION: a cour is not exactly synonymous with 'season'; English-language fandom may distinguish a multi-cour season from separate seasons.
column12: entry::term entry::fandom_term entry::word usage::technical topic::anime topic::media topic::entertainment topic::fandom topic::television discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To secure oneself/someone with straps or a safety restraint; figuratively, 'strap in' can mean prepare yourself for an intense, surprising, or eventful experience.
column7: Strap in before the ride starts. / Strap in—this story gets wild.
column8: Normalize active + passive. Figurative imperative 'strap in' is related to 'buckle up' and is informal.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::figurative topic::planning discovery::figurative_extension discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: Next to or at the side of someone or something.
column7: She sat beside him during the meeting.
column8: Contrast beside = next to with besides = in addition to/except for (depending construction). Common: beside me, beside the bed; figurative 'beside the point' is a separate idiom.

column5: Noun (formal/literary): painful, arduous labor, hardship, or suffering. Verb (rare/archaic/literary): to toil or suffer laboriously.
column7: After years of travail, the project finally succeeded.
column8: Modern active vocabulary is mainly the noun. The verb is rare; do not encourage routine productive use.

column5: Tentative emphasizes uncertainty, hesitation, or lack of final commitment; provisional emphasizes temporary/conditional status pending a final arrangement or confirmation.
column6: tentative: uncertain, cautious, hesitant; provisional: temporary, interim, conditional
column7: We made tentative plans for Saturday. / The committee gave provisional approval pending inspection.
column8: Useful contrast: a tentative date may be uncertain; a provisional date/status is temporarily adopted. They overlap when something is both uncertain and temporary.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::emphasis discovery::uncertainty discovery::commitment

column5: A traditional story handed down over time, often with a historical basis but not reliably verifiable; also an exceptionally famous/admired person, especially in a field or community; map/chart keys are another major sense.
column6: traditional tale; icon, great; map key
column7: The story became a local legend. / She's a jazz legend. / Check the map legend for the symbols.
column8: CORRECTION: add major cartographic sense. Distinguish legend (person/story/key), legendary (famous or relating to legend), legacy (what is left behind).

column5: To be crazy, irrational, extreme, or astonishing; often humorous/hyperbolic rather than a literal statement about mental illness.
column6: crazy, insane, out of their mind
