column2: take something home / take that paddle home
column5: Ordinarily, 'take something home' means bring it home, keep it, or leave with it; in competition contexts, 'take home + prize/trophy' means win it. In the Friends Barbados ping-pong scene, 'We're taking that paddle home, mister' literally refers to taking the ping-pong paddle home, with a playful trophy/souvenir-like reading available on the surface.
column6: bring something home; take home a prize/trophy; keep as a souvenir
column7: We're taking that paddle home, mister. / She took home the trophy after winning the tournament.
column8: SOURCE CONTEXT: Friends, 'The One in Barbados.' First preserve the literal reading: paddle here is the table-tennis paddle, and Phoebe says they are taking it home. The line can play like keeping the paddle as a trophy/souvenir after the impressive display. There is also a strong sexual subtext: Phoebe is visibly turned on and shortly afterward says, 'It's like watching porn!', so the paddle line can additionally suggest kinky/spanking play at home. Do not treat that innuendo as the only literal meaning, and do not teach 'take that paddle home' as an established idiom. Productive learner pattern: take + THING + home; take home + prize/trophy/award.

column2: Japanese sea bream / madai (red sea bream)
column5: In Japanese food/cultural contexts, 'tai' can refer broadly to sea-bream-like fishes; the especially important celebratory fish is madai, the red sea bream (Pagrus major).
column6: red sea bream, madai, tai (contextual Japanese term)
column7: Grilled madai is served for celebratory occasions in Japan.
column8: CORRECTION: 'Japanese bream' is vague. Do not imply all 'tai' is one species or specifically a New Year dish; sea bream is associated broadly with auspicious celebrations.

column5: A medical examination after death to determine cause/pathology; figuratively, a retrospective analysis after a project/event to learn what happened and why. Also adjective: postmortem examination/analysis.
column7: The coroner ordered a postmortem. / We held a project postmortem to identify what to improve.
column8: Spelling varies by dialect/style. A project postmortem need not focus only on failure; it can examine successes and lessons too.

column5: Sealed so air cannot readily enter or escape; figuratively, extremely strong, complete, or difficult to challenge, especially an argument, case, alibi, or plan.
column7: Store it in an airtight container. / The prosecutor thought the timeline was airtight.
column8: CORRECTION: standard modern spelling is usually one word 'airtight'. Figurative use means hard to challenge, not literally flawless.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative usage::rhetorical discovery::figurative_extension discovery::debate_language

column5: To show very great, often indulgent or adoring affection toward someone/something.
column6: adore, lavish affection on, fuss over
column7: She dotes on her grandchildren. / He absolutely dotes on that dog.
column8: KEY FRAME: dote on/upon + person/animal. 'Fawn over' often implies excessive/flattering attention and is not a clean synonym.

column5: A small quick movement of an animal's tail. Its meaning depends heavily on species, individual, and context and may reflect arousal, attention, irritation, excitement, hunting focus, etc.
column7: The cat's tail began twitching as it watched the bird.
column8: CORRECTION: do not assign a universal emotional meaning to tail twitching across animals. Treat behavioral interpretation as context/species dependent.

column5: Without achieving the desired result; unsuccessfully, despite an attempt or effort.
column7: I restarted the app several times, but to no avail.
column8: Common pattern: try/search/argue/etc., but to no avail. Clean definition punctuation.

column5: Incapable of producing the desired or useful result; ineffective or pointless because it is unlikely to succeed.
column7: It was futile to argue with someone who refused to listen. / Their rescue attempts proved futile.
column8: Common frames: futile attempt/effort/gesture; it is futile to + verb. 'Vain' overlaps in 'in vain' but has other unrelated senses. Remove duplicate synonym.

column5: In stand-up, an additional punchline or short joke following the main punchline, extending the laugh. In TV/story structure, 'tag' can also mean a short closing scene/beat after the main action; terminology varies by medium.
column7: The punchline got a laugh, and the comic added two quick tags. / The episode ends with a short comedic tag.
column8: Keep comedy and narrative senses distinct. 'Stinger' overlaps with post-credit/closing material but is not always identical.
column12: entry::word usage::specialist topic::television topic::entertainment discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A humorous scene, line, or event that concludes a story or performance, often providing a final laugh or twist.
column6: final joke, closing joke, closing gag
column7: The movie ended with a clever ending gag that left the audience laughing. Every episode of the sitcom featured an ending gag during the credits.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: The act or process of undermining, destabilizing, or overturning an established system, authority, convention, or expectation; also the result/strategy of doing so.
column7: The regime accused the group of subversion. / The novel plays with a subversion of the traditional hero narrative.
column8: Capitalize only sentence-initially. In politics the word can imply attempts to undermine authority; in art/storytelling, 'subversion of expectations/tropes' is broader and need not imply rebellion or sabotage.

column5: The punctuation mark —, longer than an en dash, used to mark a strong break, interruption, parenthetical insertion, or emphatic shift in a sentence.
column7: I was going to call—but then I changed my mind. / The answer—surprisingly—was yes.
column8: CORRECTION: show the actual em dash (—), not an apostrophe-like placeholder. Style conventions differ on spacing around it.

column2: fall for an illusion / fall for something
column5: To be deceived or taken in by something false, misleading, or merely apparent. 'Fall for + trick/lie/scam' is the productive idiomatic frame; with a literal magician's illusion, 'fall for' can mean be fooled by it.
column6: be fooled by, be taken in by, believe
column7: I can't believe I fell for that trick. / The investors fell for the illusion of easy money.
column8: Normalize reusable construction: fall for + trick/lie/scam/illusion. Distinguish 'fall for someone' = become romantically attracted.

column5: To increase speed, intensity, or activity, energy, excitement; originally refers to increasing an engine's speed.
column7: The runners revved up their pace during the final lap. The manager's speech revved up the entire sales team. The company is revving up production for the holiday season.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column2: knock it off / knock something off
column3: /nɑk ðæt dɔɡ ɔf hɜr hɛd/ ; /nɑk ɪt ɔf/
column5: 'Knock it off!' is an informal command meaning stop doing something annoying or unacceptable. 'Knock X off Y' literally means cause X to fall/be removed from Y by a blow or force.
column6: stop it, cut it out; knock/remove off
column7: Knock it off—you two are making too much noise. / The ball knocked the hat off her head.
column8: CORRECTION: 'knock that dog off her head' is not itself a standard vulgar idiom. Treat it as a literal/source-specific construction if that wording occurred; teach the reusable 'knock it off' and 'knock X off Y' patterns.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::idiom entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::informal usage::vulgar discovery::removal

column5: Bright, flashy, and showy in a way that is intended to attract attention but may lack depth or substance.
column7: The awards ceremony was full of glitzy outfits and dazzling lights. Despite the glitzy exterior, the restaurant's food was disappointing.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Glamorous or stylish, especially in a dazzling or flashy way.
column7: She looked totally glam in her shimmering dress. The party had a glam theme, with everyone dressed to impress.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Noun: a fraud, scam, trick, or dishonest scheme; also a disadvantage in 'pros and cons'. Verb: to deceive someone, often to obtain money or cooperation.
column7: He conned investors out of thousands of dollars. / One con of the apartment is the long commute.
column8: KEY FRAME: con PERSON out of MONEY/THING; con PERSON into doing X. Add separate 'pro/con' sense.

column5: An elaborate confidence scheme carried out over an extended period, often by building trust before the final deception or payoff.
column7: The plot revolves around a long con that takes months to set up.
column8: Usually noun 'long con'; hyphenation may appear attributively ('a long-con setup'). Related: con, confidence trick.

column5: To fill something to the top or add a final amount; figuratively, to complete an experience or sequence with a final addition.
column6: fill up, finish, complete, cap off
column7: Could you top off my coffee? / We topped off the evening with dessert.
column8: KEY FRAMES: top off + container; top X off; top off an event/meal with + final addition. Compare 'cap off', which more strongly suggests a culminating finish.

column2: become a significant thread / a thread running through something
column5: A 'thread' can metaphorically be a recurring theme, idea, relationship, or line of development connecting parts of a larger work/discussion. Something can 'become a significant thread' as it grows in importance.
column7: Her fear of failure becomes a significant thread in the story. / Memory is a thread running through the whole novel.
column8: Not a fixed idiom. Teach productive THREAD metaphor: a thread in/through X; a thread running through X; pick up/follow a thread.

column5: A small quantity of something, especially added to improve flavor, interest, or variety.
column6: a little bit, a small amount, a touch of
column7: Add a dash of cinnamon to enhance the flavor. The play included a dash of humor to lighten the serious theme.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Not meant to be taken completely seriously; humorously ironic, playful, or mock-serious.
column7: It was a tongue-in-cheek apology. / He said, tongue in cheek, that he deserved a statue.
column8: Hyphenate before a noun ('a tongue-in-cheek remark'); usually unhyphenated in adverbial 'with tongue in cheek'. Not necessarily sarcastic.

column5: For emotions to become so strong that they are expressed freely or seem impossible to contain; 'overflow with + emotion' is a common productive metaphor.
column6: be overwhelmed with emotion, be overcome, well up
column7: She overflowed with joy when she heard the news. / At the reunion, emotions overflowed and several people cried.
column8: Not a fixed idiom. Teach CONTAINER metaphor: overflow with joy/gratitude/love; emotions spill/overflow. 'Emotional flooding' is a more specialized term and not a simple synonym.
column12: entry::idiom usage::figurative usage::specialist discovery::impression discovery::containment discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To annoy or irritate someone.
column7: It irks me when people leave the door open. / His constant interruptions irk everyone.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Transitive frame: THING irks PERSON. Related adjective: irksome.

column5: For a continuous period without interruption ('for hours at a stretch'); or, in a different use, only with difficulty or by stretching what is plausible/possible ('at a stretch').
column6: continuously, in one go; at most, with difficulty (contextual)
column7: She can work for four hours at a stretch. / At a stretch, we could fit six people in the car.
column8: Separate the two constructions. For plausibility, 'that's a stretch' is often more natural than 'believe it at a stretch'.

column5: A dirty or disapproving look given to someone to show anger, distrust, resentment, disapproval, annoyance, or irritation.
column7: She gave him the stink eye after he cut in line. He shot me a stink eye when I brought up the embarrassing story.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::figurative usage::critical usage::informal discovery::social_trust

column5: A slang term for mosquitoes, especially in southern or rural American English.
column7: The camp was swarming with skeeters by sunset. Don't forget the bug spray ' the skeeters are vicious this time of year. The skeeters were out in full force after the rainstorm.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::figurative usage::american_english usage::informal discovery::terminology

column5: In negative contexts, to do nothing or almost nothing; 'squat' here means anything of value/amount and commonly appears after negatives.
column7: He doesn't do squat around the house. / I studied all afternoon and still didn't get squat done.
column8: KEY PATTERN: don't/doesn't/didn't do squat; know squat = know nothing. Informal and mildly crude.

column2: break one's arm patting oneself on the back
column3: /breɪk wʌnz ɑrm ˈpætɪŋ jɔrˈsɛlf ɑn ðə bæk/
column5: A humorous exaggeration used to mock excessive self-congratulation or boasting.
column6: pat oneself on the back, congratulate oneself, brag
column7: Don't break your arm patting yourself on the back—you had plenty of help.
column8: Normalize pronouns consistently: break your arm patting yourself... / break one's arm patting oneself.... Built on 'pat oneself on the back' = congratulate oneself.

column5: To cross back and forth in different directions; a pattern/network of intersecting lines or paths.
column7: Trails crisscross the park. / The fabric has a crisscross pattern.
column8: Standard modern spelling often 'crisscross' in AmE; 'criss-cross' also occurs. Avoid unhyphenated two-word 'criss cross' as the main headword.

column5: To shake or move in small rapid irregular movements; noun 'jitter' can mean such variation/movement, especially technically in electronics/networking. 'The jitters' = nervousness.
column7: The image jittered on the screen. / Too much coffee gives me the jitters.
column8: CORRECTION: 'jittering with nerves' is less natural than 'jittery' or 'have the jitters'. Add technical movement/timing sense; normalize base.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::technical topic::grammar discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: 'Round out X' = make X fuller, more balanced, or complete by adding something. 'Cap off X' = conclude X, often with a final notable event/addition.
column7: A salad rounded out the meal. / Fireworks capped off the festival.
column8: Useful contrast: round out focuses on completeness/balance; cap off focuses on the culminating ending. They overlap but are not interchangeable everywhere.

column5: To bring something to a conclusion, often with a final event, achievement, or addition that serves as a culmination.
column6: conclude, crown, finish off, top off
column7: They capped off the trip with a sunset cruise.
column8: Not necessarily 'satisfying' or positive; a final disaster can cap off a terrible day. KEY FRAME: cap off X with Y.

column5: Not certain or definite, fixed, or confident; done hesitantly or subject to change.
column7: We scheduled a tentative meeting for next week. Her tentative smile suggested she was still unsure. They made a tentative plan to meet next week.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: A catastrophic event resulting in widespread destruction or devastation; also refers to the end of the world or final judgment in religious contexts.
column6: catastrophe, end of the world, disaster, doomsday
column7: The movie depicted a zombie apocalypse wiping out humanity. Some ancient texts describe an apocalypse as a final reckoning between good and evil. The movie depicts an apocalypse brought on by climate change.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: A V-shaped point of the hairline descending toward the center of the forehead.
column7: His widow's peak gives him a distinctive hairline.
column8: CORRECTION: possessive spelling is 'widow's peak'.

column2: carry that weight / carry the weight
column5: To bear an emotional burden, responsibility, consequence, or pressure. 'Carry That Weight' is also the title/lyric phrase of a Beatles song, which can add an allusive layer.
column6: bear the burden, shoulder the responsibility, live with the weight
column7: He carried the weight of that decision for years. / The phrase 'carry that weight' can evoke the Beatles song in the right context.
column8: Teach productive metaphor 'carry/bear the weight of X'. 'That' is source/context-specific rather than required.
column12: entry::phrase usage::figurative topic::music topic::lyrics discovery::title_language discovery::lyrics_language

column2: pop the balloon / burst someone's bubble
column5: 'Pop a/the balloon' literally means burst it. Figuratively it can be used creatively for abruptly ending excitement or momentum, but the established idiom for disappointing someone by destroying an optimistic belief/hope is 'burst someone's bubble'.
column6: burst someone's bubble, deflate, dash hopes
column7: I hated to burst her bubble, but the tickets were already sold out. / His comment popped the balloon of excitement—a creative metaphor.
column8: CORRECTION: do not teach 'popping the balloon' as a standard idiom equivalent to 'burst someone's bubble'. Preserve as creative/source wording.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::figurative discovery::comparison discovery::figurative_extension discovery::building_on_success

column5: To leave secretly or quietly, often to avoid attention.
column6: sneak away/out, slip away, sneak off, leave quietly
column7: They decided to steal away during the wedding reception for a private moment. The child tried to steal away without saying goodbye. He managed to steal away during the commotion without anyone noticing.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: The act of forcing or officially requiring a person/group to leave an institution, organization, place, or country; also the act of forcing a substance/object out.
column7: His expulsion from school shocked everyone. / The test measures expulsion of the balloon.
column8: Avoid 'international expulsion' without a specific organization/context. Add physical expulsion sense, useful with the earlier balloon-expulsion card.

column5: Literally, incline or press one's body into/toward something. Figuratively, embrace, emphasize, or engage fully with a situation, quality, role, or difficulty.
column6: embrace, commit to, play up, engage with
column7: The actor leaned into the character's awkwardness. / She leaned into the challenge.
column8: Overlaps WID3026 comparison card; retain because this card gives focused active-use practice. KEY FRAME: lean into + noun/gerund.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative usage::journalistic topic::media topic::construction discovery::emphasis discovery::audience_engagement discovery::figurative_extension discovery::evaluation discovery::commitment

column5: 'Surefire' means very likely or certain to succeed or produce a result. 'A surefire sale' is a compositional use meaning a sale/deal considered highly likely, not a fixed expression.
column7: A big discount is a surefire way to attract attention. / The agent thought the house would be a surefire sale.
column8: Normalize around productive adjective 'surefire': surefire way/method/hit/success. 'Infallible' is too absolute in many contexts.

column5: Archaic second-person singular object form of 'thou', used as the object of a verb or preposition; survives in older literature, hymns, prayers, and stylized speech.
column7: I give this gift unto thee. / How do I love thee?
column8: PRECISION: 'thee' is specifically objective case; 'thou' is traditionally subject, 'thy/thine' possessive forms. Modern 'you' replaced these distinctions.

column5: To ask or beg someone urgently and earnestly; implore.
column7: I beseech you to reconsider. / They beseeched the king for mercy.
column8: Frames: beseech PERSON to do X; beseech PERSON for X. Formal/literary and often dramatic.

column5: To speak angrily or severely to someone because you think they have done something wrong.
column6: scold, reprimand, rebuke, give someone a dressing-down
column7: She told him off for being rude.
column8: KEY FRAME: tell PERSON off for + noun/gerund. 'Lash out' is broader and need not involve corrective scolding.

column5: An informal way to express strong agreement with what someone has just said.
column7: A: "This traffic is terrible!" B: "You can say that again!" A: "That movie was amazing." B: "You can say that again."
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: 'Dead lie' is not a broadly standard modern idiom for 'blatant lie'. In some source/dialectal wording it may intensify 'lie'; for general active use, 'outright lie', 'blatant lie', 'barefaced/bald-faced lie', or 'flat-out lie' are natural.
column6: outright lie, blatant lie, bald-faced lie, flat-out lie
column7: That was an outright lie, and everyone knew it.
column8: CORRECTION: retain 'dead lie' for recognition/source fidelity only; do not teach it as a normal general-purpose idiom without source/dialect context. Clean corrupted punctuation.

column2: draw a line in the sand / a line in the sand
column5: To establish a firm boundary, limit, or position beyond which one will not compromise or permit something.
column6: set a boundary, draw the line, set a limit
column7: She drew a line in the sand: no more unpaid overtime.
column8: Teach full productive construction 'draw a line in the sand'. The noun phrase alone names the boundary.
column12: entry::idiom usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::compromise discovery::trade-off discovery::boundary-setting discovery::debate_language

column5: A recognizable phrase template with one or more variable slots, reused to create new expressions, often from a familiar quotation or cliché.
column7: 'X is the new Y' is a classic snowclone: 'Orange is the new black,' 'Quiet is the new loud,' etc.
column8: CORRECTION/CLEANUP: repair mojibake and corrupted example. A snowclone is not simply any cliché; its reusable variable template is central.

column5: To admit one's mistake or defeat, especially in a way that is humiliating or humbling.
column6: admit fault, swallow pride, confess defeat
column7: After losing the bet, he had to eat crow and apologize. The CEO ate crow after the product failed miserably.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column2: say that / I would say that / to say that...
column5: Bare 'say that + clause' reports or states a proposition. 'I would say that...' softens/presents an opinion; 'to say that X is Y would be...' is a separate evaluative construction.
column7: I would say that the second version is clearer. / To say that she was surprised would be an understatement.
column8: CORRECTION: 'say that' alone is too broad to have one discourse function. Preserve the useful source patterns explicitly rather than treating them as one idiom.
column12: entry::idiom entry::discourse_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::evaluative usage::debate-friendly topic::construction discovery::debate_language discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::evaluation

column5: Causing a person to become more serious, reflective, or realistic; reducing feelings of excitement or idealism.
column7: The sobering news of the disaster made everyone quiet. Hearing about the risks was a sobering experience.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Used to introduce a contrasting point or qualification to what was just said; similar to 'however' or 'nevertheless.'
column7: The car is very old. That said, it still runs perfectly. The hike was exhausting. That said, the view at the top was worth it.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To use something until it becomes damaged, unusable, or exhausted. To tire someone completely.
column7: After years of hiking, his boots finally wore out. Long meetings wear me out mentally.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column2: that being so / with that said / having said that
column3: /ðæt ˈbiɪŋ soʊ/ , /wɪð ðæt sɛd/ , /ˈhævɪŋ sɛd ðæt/
column5: 'That being so' means given that this is true and often introduces a consequence. 'Having said that' and 'that said' introduce a qualification or contrast. 'With that said' is a common variant, especially AmE, with similar qualifying/transition use.
column6: given that; that said, nevertheless, even so
column7: The road is closed. That being so, we'll take the train. / The plan is expensive. Having said that, it may still be our best option.
column8: CORRECTION: these are not interchangeable transition markers. Separate consequence ('that being so') from qualification/contrast ('having/with that said').

column5: To exist in large numbers or quantities; to be plentiful.
column7: Wildlife abounds in the Amazon rainforest. Opportunities abound for those willing to work hard.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Extremely valuable or important goods, people, or things being transported, protected, or handled with special and great care.
column6: valuable load, important freight, treasured load, valuable freight, cherished person
column7:
The ambulance was transporting precious cargo to the hospital. She guarded her newborn twins like precious cargo. The ship carried precious cargo across the ocean. The bus driver ensured the safety of his precious cargo.
She always treated her baby as her precious cargo.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: By or because of a basic, intrinsic characteristic of something; as part of its nature rather than because of an external circumstance.
column7: Investing is inherently risky. / The tool isn't inherently good or bad; it depends on how it's used.
column8: Avoid defining it as necessarily 'permanent'. An inherent property is intrinsic, but whether it can ever change depends on what is being described.

column5: The act of violating, damaging, or treating with serious disrespect something regarded as sacred, holy, or deeply revered.
column7: Vandalizing the shrine was condemned as desecration.
column8: 'Violent' is not required; disrespectful use, damage, or profanation can constitute desecration.

column5: Unable to make decisions quickly or confidently; characterized by hesitation or uncertainty.
column7: His indecisive nature made team meetings drag on. She was indecisive about which college to attend.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Having or occurring in two distinct phases, components, or stages; exact meaning depends on field (medicine, physiology, chemistry, electronics, etc.).
column7: The drug produced a biphasic response: stimulation at first, followed by sedation.
column8: Technical term; do not assume the second phase is relapse. Common: biphasic response/pattern/waveform.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::specialist usage::scientific topic::chemistry topic::medicine topic::science topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To return to sleep after having awakened.
column6: go back to sleep, drift back to sleep, doze off again
column7: I woke up at six but fell back asleep and missed my alarm.
column8: CORRECTION: three words 'fall back asleep', not 'fallback asleep'. 'Fallback' is a noun/adjective in other contexts.

column2: a second nap / take another nap
column5: A second period of daytime sleep or dozing; ordinary compositional wording rather than a fixed expression.
column6: another nap, an extra nap, nap again
column7: I took a second nap after lunch. / I was still tired, so I took another nap.
column8: Not an idiom. 'Second nap' means literally another nap; after briefly waking during nighttime sleep, 'fall back asleep' is usually more natural.

column5: To obtain some additional sleep, usually because one is tired or has time to sleep longer.
column6: get some more sleep, catch a little more sleep, sleep a little longer
column7: I'm going back to bed to get a bit more sleep.
column8: Does not inherently mean recovery from exhaustion. Natural related phrases: get some sleep; catch a few more hours/winks.

column5: To return to bed and get under the blankets/bedcovers, often to sleep, rest, hide, or seek warmth/comfort.
column6: get back under the covers, crawl back into bed
column7: It was freezing, so I crawled back under the covers.
column8: Normalize from first-person source sentence to reusable construction. Literal action; emotional/comfort implication comes from context.

column5: To manage to fit an activity/person into limited time, or fit something into limited physical space.
column6: fit in, make time for, cram in
column7: I squeezed in a workout before work. / Can we squeeze one more chair in?
column8: KEY FRAMES: squeeze X in; squeeze in X; squeeze PERSON in for an appointment. Covers both time and physical space.

column5: Unreadable, incorrect, or scrambled-looking text characters, often caused by an encoding/decoding mismatch. 'Mojibake' is the specific computing term for garbled text produced by character-encoding problems.
column7: The file opened with garbled characters because it was decoded with the wrong character encoding.
column8: PRECISION: not all garbled characters are caused by encoding, but mojibake specifically is. Useful given earlier café/détente corruption in this Master.
column12: entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::technical usage::specialist discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_register

column5: A person or thing that is a perfect or highly representative example of a quality or type.
column7: She is the epitome of professionalism.
column8: KEY FRAME: the epitome of + quality/type. Pronounced /ɪˈpɪtəmi/ (four syllables), a common pronunciation trap.

column5: A model, pattern, or framework; especially a broad conceptual framework or accepted way of understanding/approaching a field or problem.
column7: The discovery helped create a new paradigm for understanding the disease.
column8: Avoid using 'prototype' as a blanket synonym. Common: paradigm shift; within a paradigm; a paradigm for/of X.

column5: A recurring, prototypical model or pattern of a character, image, situation, or concept; also an original model/type from which similar examples are understood.
column7: The wise mentor is a familiar story archetype.
column8: 'Perfect example' is not always central; in literary/psychological discussion, recurring fundamental pattern/type is important.

column5: A person or thing regarded as an outstanding or near-perfect example of a particular quality.
column7: She was regarded as a paragon of patience.
column8: KEY FRAME: a paragon of + virtue/quality. Often elevated/formal and can be ironic.

column5: An ode is traditionally a lyric poem of praise or elevated reflection. Figuratively, a film, album, design, etc. can be 'an ode to X' when it lovingly celebrates, evokes, or pays tribute to X.
column7: The film is an ode to 1980s action movies.
column8: KEY FRAME: an ode to + person/place/era/style. 'Eulogy' is not a synonym; it specifically praises/commemorates, often after death.
column12: entry::construction entry::fixed_expression usage::figurative topic::music topic::literature topic::lyrics topic::film topic::construction topic::entertainment discovery::lyrics_language discovery::figurative_extension discovery::social_approval

column5: Standardized, reusable text or language used with little change, especially in contracts, policies, press releases, or software/templates; adjective: boilerplate language/code.
column6: standard text, stock language, template text
column7: The contract contains standard boilerplate on liability. / I replaced the boilerplate introduction with something specific.
column8: Can be neutral or mildly critical. In programming, 'boilerplate code' is repetitive setup code, not necessarily copied blindly.
column12: entry::word usage::critical usage::journalistic topic::technology topic::media discovery::evaluation

column5: To add or attach something at the end of a document, list, string, file, or other sequence.
column6: add to the end, attach, concatenate (contextual)
column7: Append your initials to the filename. / The program appends each new record to the log.
column8: KEY FRAME: append X to Y. Contrast prepend = add to beginning.

column5: Forward in space or progress; from a specified time/point and continuing after it.
column7: From 2025 onward, the rule applies to all new accounts. / They pressed onward despite the rain.
column8: AmE commonly 'onward'; BrE also 'onwards' as adverb. Useful frame: from X onward(s).

column5: An easing of strained or hostile relations, especially between countries, through reduced tension and improved diplomacy.
column7: The talks helped produce a period of détente between the two countries.
column8: CORRECTION/CLEANUP: restore 'détente'. A détente is not necessarily a truce, ceasefire, armistice, or peace agreement; those are more specific arrangements.

column5: 'Apron belly' is an informal term for an overhanging fold of abdominal skin and/or fatty tissue. 'Pannus' or 'abdominal pannus' is a clinical/anatomical term used in some contexts. 'Flap belly' is not a standard general term.
column7: After major weight loss, some people are left with an overhanging fold of abdominal skin.
column8: CORRECTION: normalize away from nonstandard 'flap belly'. Avoid implying surgery is required; management depends on symptoms, goals, and clinical context.
column12: entry::term entry::phrase usage::informal usage::technical usage::specialist topic::health topic::medicine topic::anatomy discovery::terminology discovery::evaluation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A small piece, extract, or brief portion of text, speech, code, audio, video, information, etc.
column7: She posted a short snippet of the interview. / I copied a code snippet into the editor.
column8: Common technical collocation: code snippet. Clean stray translation/backtick formatting from Example.
column12: entry::collocation entry::word usage::technical topic::technology topic::media topic::public_speaking discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To use, provide, or spend less of something than is needed or appropriate, often to save money/time/effort.
column6: scrimp, stint, cut back excessively, be sparing
column7: Don't skimp on sleep. / The builder skimped on materials.
column8: Normalize base + source past. KEY FRAME: skimp on + noun. Often implies false economy or inadequate quality.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word topic::finance topic::work topic::decision-making discovery::cost-cutting discovery::insufficient_quality discovery::resource_allocation discovery::trade-off

column5: A slang term associated especially with high-energy partying and Southern hip-hop; can mean extremely excited/hyped, and in some contexts intoxicated. 'Crunk' also names a hip-hop subgenre/style.
column7: The crowd got crunk when the beat dropped.
column8: CORRECTION: the popular 'crazy + drunk' blend explanation is folk etymology/uncertain and should not be stated as fact. Register is dated/era- and culture-marked in some uses.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::term entry::word usage::slang usage::dated usage::informal topic::culture topic::music

column5: An error in reasoning or a deceptive/unsound argument; more broadly, a mistaken belief, especially one based on faulty reasoning.
column7: It's a fallacy to assume that correlation by itself proves causation.
column8: In logic, a fallacy is specifically a flaw in reasoning/argument. 'Falsehood', 'delusion', and 'illusion' are not general synonyms.

column5: A horizontal bar hanging by two ropes, used by acrobats in circus performances.
column7: The trapeze artist swung high above the amazed audience.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Verb: make playful jokes at someone's expense, provoke playfully, tempt without satisfying, or reveal a small preview. Noun: a person who teases, or a preview/teaser-like act in some contexts; 'a tease' can also carry flirtatious/sexual implications.
column6: joke with, rib, taunt (harsher), tempt, preview
column7: I'm just teasing you. / The trailer teased the villain without showing him. / He's such a tease.
column8: Broaden major senses. 'Taunt' is usually more hostile. Sexual/flirtatious noun use can be judgmental depending context.

column5: The punctuation mark ’ or ' used chiefly to mark possession and omitted letters/numbers; also a rhetorical/literary figure in which a speaker directly addresses an absent person, abstract idea, or nonhuman thing.
column7: Use an apostrophe in 'Sarah's book' and 'don't'. / 'O Death, where is thy sting?' is an example of apostrophe in rhetoric.
column8: Add major rhetorical sense. Apostrophe and single quotation mark may look similar but are functionally distinct.

column5: To contact someone without a prior relationship, invitation, or appointment, traditionally by phone, often for sales, recruiting, fundraising, research, or outreach; noun 'a cold call'.
column7: I spent the morning cold-calling potential clients. / The recruiter made a cold call to a candidate.
column8: Broaden beyond sales while keeping it central. Also used metaphorically in classrooms: 'cold-call a student' = call on someone without advance volunteering.

column5: Not invited; arriving, occurring, or becoming involved without an invitation. Depending context, it may imply unwelcome, but the two are not identical.
column7: He showed up uninvited. / An uninvited thought popped into my head.
column8: CORRECTION: 'uninvited' does not inherently mean unwelcome. 'Gatecrashing' is an action, not a direct adjective synonym.

column5: Swollen or uncomfortably full, especially in the abdomen; figuratively, excessively large, complicated, expensive, or filled with unnecessary material.
column7: I felt bloated after dinner. / The software became bloated with unnecessary features.
column8: Common figurative: bloated bureaucracy/budget/software/code. Physical bloating can have many causes; lexical card should not imply one.

column5: A source-specific or translated proverb-like expression suggesting people share the same origin, type, or dubious affiliation. It is not a standard everyday English idiom.
column6: birds of a feather, cut from the same cloth, from the same mold
column7: In natural everyday English, I'd usually say, 'They're birds of a feather' or 'They're cut from the same cloth.'
column8: SOURCE CAUTION: retain for recognition if it appeared in the source, but do not present it as a common English idiom. Exact cultural/source origin should be preserved separately if known.
column12: entry::idiom entry::proverb entry::quotation discovery::origin_etymology discovery::suggestion discovery::evaluation

column5: Very similar in character, attitudes, behavior, or essential nature, as if made from the same material.
column6: alike, similar in nature, birds of a feather
column7: Those two executives are cut from the same cloth.
column8: Often implies shared character rather than merely same background. Can be positive, neutral, or critical.

column2: badger someone / badger someone into doing something
column5: To repeatedly pester, question, urge, or pressure someone, often until they respond or comply.
column7: She badgered him into calling the landlord. / Reporters badgered the spokesperson with questions.
column8: KEY FRAMES: badger PERSON about/for X; badger PERSON into doing X. Usually repeated pressure.

column5: A weapon/device that projects a stream of burning fuel or flame. Figuratively, 'flamethrower' may be used creatively for an extremely aggressive attack, critic, pitch, etc., but this is context-dependent rather than a fixed person-label.
column7: The historical display included a flamethrower. / The columnist went full flamethrower on the proposal.
column8: Standard spelling is usually one word 'flamethrower'. Figurative person sense is creative/contextual; 'roaster' is not a clean synonym.

column5: 'Instrumental' (adjective) means important as a means in bringing about a result: 'X was instrumental in Y.' 'Leverage' (verb) means use a resource, position, relationship, or advantage strategically to achieve a result.
column6: instrumental = crucial/helpful means; leverage = use strategically
column7: Her expertise was instrumental in the launch. / He leveraged his contacts to get an introduction.
column8: They are different grammatical/semantic tools, not direct alternatives. KEY FRAMES: instrumental in + noun/gerund; leverage + asset/resource/relationship.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::debate-friendly topic::relationships topic::debate topic::language_learning discovery::comparison discovery::contrast discovery::resource_allocation discovery::debate_language

column5: Done as a routine duty or formality with little care, enthusiasm, attention, or genuine interest.
column7: He gave a perfunctory apology and changed the subject.
column8: Often implies the action technically fulfills an obligation but lacks genuine engagement. Clean duplicate definition and stray comma.

column5: A tendency to distrust people's motives or sincerity, often assuming self-interest; more broadly, a skeptical, disillusioned attitude toward institutions, ideals, or claims.
column7: Years of broken promises fed her cynicism about politics.
column8: Skepticism is not the same: skepticism questions claims/evidence; cynicism more specifically expects selfishness, insincerity, or bad faith.

column5: A person, event, allegation, issue, or development judged to have little or no substance or significance, especially after receiving attention or hype.
column6: non-event, non-issue, much ado about nothing (contextual)
column7: The supposedly explosive revelation turned out to be a nothingburger.
column8: Informal, dismissive, and often political/media slang. Calling something a nothingburger expresses the speaker's judgment, not an objective fact.

column5: A mocking internet term for imagined 'coping substance'—wishful thinking, rationalization, or denial used to soften disappointment or an unwelcome reality.
column7: Fans insisting the loss was 'actually good for the team' were accused of huffing copium.
column8: Portmanteau of 'cope' + 'opium'. Common playful collocations: inhale/huff copium, pure copium. Often used mockingly toward others, so tone can be antagonistic.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::playful usage::softening usage::informal topic::internet discovery::terminology

column5: To remove duplicate copies or records so that only one instance of each item remains; deduplicated = processed in this way.
column7: We deduplicated the contact list before importing it. / The backup system stores deduplicated data.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Common in data/storage workflows. Deduplication may remove exact duplicates or identify duplicates by defined matching rules; it does not simply mean general cleanup.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::technical topic::grammar discovery::removal discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: In grammar, to change a word's form to express grammatical information such as tense, number, person, case, gender, or degree, depending on the language.
column6: conjugate (verbs, narrower), decline (nouns/adjectives, narrower), modify grammatically
column7: English verbs inflect for forms such as walks/walked. / In Latin, nouns are inflected for case and number.
column8: Normalize base + source form. 'Conjugate' and 'decline' are narrower grammatical processes, not blanket synonyms.

column5: To put forward, assume, or postulate a proposition, explanation, or entity as a basis for argument or reasoning.
column7: The theory posits that the two systems developed independently.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Formal/academic. KEY FRAME: posit that + clause; posit + noun/entity.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal usage::academic usage::rhetorical discovery::explanation discovery::assertion discovery::speculation discovery::academic_discussion discovery::debate_language

column5: Having or showing keen mental discernment and good judgment.
column7: His sagacious advice helped me avoid a costly mistake.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: A person, thing, or element essential to the stability, functioning, or success of a system, plan, group, or argument; literally, a pin that keeps a wheel on an axle.
column6: key element, cornerstone, keystone, backbone, crucial link
column7: Trust is the linchpin of the agreement. / She became the linchpin of the team.
column8: Correct typos and overbroad synonyms. Productive frame: the linchpin of + system/plan/team. Literal origin helps explain the metaphor.

column5: Not working together harmoniously; not aligned in timing or agreement.
column7: Their schedules were completely out of sync.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column3: /tu bi ɑn ðə vɜrdʒ əv ˈsʌmθɪŋ/
column5: To be very close to a state, event, or action happening; the following event can be negative, positive, or neutral.
column6: be about to, be close to, be on the brink of
column7: She was on the verge of tears. / The company is on the verge of a breakthrough. / I was on the verge of giving up.
column8: KEY FRAME: be on the verge of + noun/gerund. CORRECTION: not restricted to dramatic/negative events. 'On the brink of' often sounds more dramatic and is especially common with danger/crisis.

column5: To fall down in an uncontrolled or dramatic way; figuratively, for a structure, plan, belief, reputation, or system to collapse rapidly.
column6: collapse, crumble, fall apart, come crashing down
column7: The wall came tumbling down. / Once the evidence appeared, his whole story came tumbling down.
column8: Normalize around productive patterns. 'Come tumbling down' is especially common and vivid; bare 'tumbling down' is a participial form, not itself a phrasal verb.

column5: The leading or most important position in a field, movement, or situation.
column6: vanguard, front line, cutting edge, spearhead
column7: She has been at the forefront of medical research for decades.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To cause a person or thing to fall or overturn by hitting, pushing, or bumping it; informally, 'knock over' can also mean rob a place.
column7: The wind knocked over the bins. / I knocked my coffee over. / In the crime movie, they planned to knock over a bank.
column8: CORRECTION: the physical action is not necessarily unintentional. Common particle alternation: knock over the vase / knock the vase over.

column5: To move unsteadily from side to side; figuratively, to become uncertain, unstable, or less firm in a decision/position. Noun: an unsteady movement or temporary loss of confidence/stability.
column7: The table wobbles. / Her confidence wobbled after the criticism. / The market had a brief wobble.
column8: Add common figurative sense. Compare WID2985 wobble/flip-flop distinction.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::decision-making topic::debate discovery::figurative_extension discovery::uncertainty discovery::debate_language

column5: Highly polysemous: noun = pointed/end part; useful piece of advice; gratuity; small amount/indication ('tip of the iceberg'). Verb = tilt/cause to tilt; give a gratuity; give private information; empty/pour by tilting.
column6: point, end; advice, hint; gratuity; tilt
column7: The chair tipped backward. / Here's a useful travel tip. / I tipped the server 20 percent. / That's just the tip of the iceberg.
column8: Major polysemy card. Do not compress 'tip' into one core sense. Common frames: tip over, tip X into Y, tip someone, a tip for/on X.

column5: A person who invents, creates, or initiates something.
column7: She was the originator of the community outreach program.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: A sarcastic or frustrated comment made when someone gives important information too late.
column6: too late now, that would've been nice to know earlier
column7: "Oh, the meeting was canceled? Now you tell me!"
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Dingy: dark, dirty, or shabby in appearance. Dinghy: a small boat, often used to travel between a larger ship and the shore.
column6: dirty, gloomy (dingy); small boat, skiff, tender (dinghy)
column7: The hotel room was dingy and smelled musty. We used a dinghy to reach the yacht anchored offshore.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::adjective_phrase usage::figurative topic::travel topic::nautical topic::language_learning discovery::contrast

column5: Literally, to become stuck in boggy ground; figuratively, to become slowed, stuck, or excessively occupied by difficulties, details, bureaucracy, work, etc.
column6: get stuck, become mired, stall, get caught up
column7: The truck bogged down in the mud. / We got bogged down in paperwork. / Don't get bogged down in minor details.
column8: Teach literal source + figurative construction. KEY FRAME: get/be bogged down in + noun.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative usage::bureaucratic topic::work discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Uncomfortably small, restricted, or confined in space.
column7: The cabin was cramped and barely had enough room for two people. The room felt cramped with so many people inside.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To act as if one is not easily available or interested, often to seem more desirable.
column6: be elusive, act aloof, feign disinterest
column7: She decided to play hard to get to see if he would make an effort.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To have doubts, concerns, or misgivings about a plan, idea, person, or course of action.
column6: have doubts about, have misgivings about, be hesitant about
column7: I have reservations about signing the contract without reading it carefully.
column8: KEY FRAME: have reservations about + noun/gerund. Distinguish from 'have a reservation' = a booking.

column5: Nearness or closeness in space, time, or sometimes relationship/context.
column7: The apartment's proximity to the station is convenient. / The two events occurred in close temporal proximity.
column8: KEY FRAME: proximity to + noun; also 'in close proximity to'. 'Close proximity' is common despite being somewhat redundant. 'Presence' is not a synonym.

column5: To be in an unstable or precarious position very close to a major state or event, commonly a negative one such as collapse, bankruptcy, war, or extinction.
column6: be on the brink/verge of, hover near, be close to
column7: The company is teetering on the brink of bankruptcy. / The species teetered on the edge of extinction.
column8: Internal metaphor: teeter = wobble unsteadily; brink/edge = boundary before a fall/change. Correct typo 'verbe'. Stronger instability/danger than neutral 'on the verge of'.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::debate topic::construction discovery::debate_language

column5: Engaged in deep or serious thought, often marked by sadness or melancholy.
column7: He looked pensive as he stared out the window. She stared out the window with a pensive look on her face.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To escape or liberate oneself from physical, mental, or emotional restraints.
column6: escape, liberate, free oneself, get away, get out of
column7: She struggled to break free from the toxic relationship.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: A senior official in a college or university, often responsible for/in charge of a department, faculty or group of students.
column7: The dean of students announced new campus regulations. The dean welcomed all the new students with a speech.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: A formal agreement, contract, or promise, often in religious or legal contexts.
column7: The two companies entered into a covenant to cooperate on research. The tenants signed a covenant to keep the property clean.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::figurative usage::religious topic::law topic::religion discovery::agreement

column5: A word related to another through descent from the same ancestral word; adjective: related by common linguistic origin. More broadly/formally, 'cognate' can mean related or akin.
column6: related word, etymological relative, akin (broader adjective)
column7: English 'mother' and German 'Mutter' are cognates. / English 'father' and Spanish 'padre' are cognate forms.
column8: CORRECTION: cognates are not merely words that look/sound alike, and they need not have identical meanings. Replace incorrect Spanish/French 'comer' example. Distinguish false friends and loanwords.

column5: Having knowledge or awareness of something.
column7: He was fully cognizant of the risks involved. You should be cognizant of your surroundings when walking alone at night.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Literal noun: meat from cattle. Informal noun: a complaint, grievance, feud, or conflict. Verb: complain ('beef about X') or feud/quarrel in slang contexts.
column7: I've got a beef with the way this was handled. / Those two rappers have had beef for years. / He kept beefing about the schedule.
column8: KEY FRAMES: have beef with PERSON; have a beef with/about X; beef about/over X. Remove duplicate synonym.

column5: In slang, 'I'm not tripping' commonly means I'm not upset, worried, overreacting, or making a big issue of it; 'tripping' can also mean behaving irrationally/strangely or experiencing effects of hallucinogens, depending context.
column6: I'm not stressing, I'm not bothered, I'm chill; overreacting (trip)
column7: Don't worry about me—I'm not tripping. / Why are you tripping over something so small?
column8: Register: informal slang, strongly associated with AAE and broader U.S. youth/pop culture. Meaning is context-sensitive; do not assume drug use.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::informal usage::slang topic::travel discovery::excessive_emotion

column5: A mild condition involving repeated sniffing, a runny or stuffy nose, often from a cold or allergies; informally, 'the sniffles' can mean a mild cold-like illness.
column6: runny nose, mild cold symptoms, nasal congestion
column7: I've got the sniffles today, but I otherwise feel fine.
column8: CORRECTION: not necessarily 'a cold' and not caused by playing in rain. Common phrase: have/get the sniffles.

column5: To make a series of short, sharp popping sounds.
column7:
The fire crackled warmly in the fireplace.
I could hear the radio crackling with static.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To think creatively, unconventionally, or from a new perspective.
column6: innovate, brainstorm creatively, break the mold
column7:
To solve this problem, we need to think outside the box.
He encouraged his team to think outside the box during the meeting.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: In a hidden or secret way; not openly shown.
column7:
She covertly passed him a note during the meeting.
They covertly filmed the transaction for evidence.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: In a secretive, concealed manner, often to hide illicit activity.
column7:
The two agents met clandestinely in the alley.
Documents were clandestinely moved across the border.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column2: water with no flow will rot
column5: A proverb-like metaphor meaning that stagnation can lead to decline and that continued movement, renewal, or growth may be necessary. The exact wording is not a standard widely established English proverb.
column6: stagnation leads to decay; keep moving/growing (paraphrases)
column7: The speaker's point was essentially, 'Water with no flow will rot'—if we stop learning, we stagnate.
column8: SOURCE CAUTION: retain the source wording for recognition, but do not teach it as a conventional English proverb unless its specific source/tradition is known. Natural English parallels include 'stagnant water...' imagery and 'use it or lose it,' depending context.
column12: entry::proverb entry::quotation usage::figurative topic::communication discovery::cause_and_effect discovery::evaluation

column5:
1. Awkwardly heavy, bulky, or lacking grace.
2. Inelegant, especially in design or style.
column7: The old laptop felt clunky and heavy. / The app works, but the navigation still feels clunky. / The dialogue is informative but a little clunky.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5:
1. Smoothness and elegance of movement or behavior.
2. A pleasing or attractive quality or feature.
column7:
She danced with effortless grace.
His speech was delivered with grace and sincerity.
Even under pressure, she handled herself with grace.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To strike or pick at something repeatedly with a beak; figuratively/related, 'pecking order' means a social hierarchy of rank or status.
column7: The chickens pecked at the ground. / Everyone quickly learned the office pecking order.
column8: Normalize base + source form. 'Pecking order' comes from observed dominance hierarchies in chickens and is now widely figurative.

column5: A formal agreement between individuals or groups.
column7: The two countries signed a peace pact to end the conflict. They made a pact to stay friends no matter what.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To come or flow out from a source, especially light, sound, smell, heat, influence, or an impression/quality.
column6: radiate, issue, come from, flow from
column7: A strange smell emanated from the basement. / Warmth seemed to emanate from her voice.
column8: KEY FRAME: X emanates from SOURCE. For qualities, 'PERSON emanates confidence' occurs, but 'confidence emanates from PERSON' or 'PERSON exudes confidence' is often more natural.

column5: To make the deep rough call associated with frogs; to speak in a rough/hoarse voice; informal slang 'croak' can also mean die.
column6: rasp, make a frog call; die (slang)
column7: Frogs croaked by the pond. / He croaked out a reply through a sore throat.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Related to earlier WID2774; retain as inflection/recognition card only if useful.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::slang topic::communication topic::grammar

column5: To settle, place, or lie snugly and comfortably in/against something; also for a place/object to sit sheltered or closely surrounded.
column7: She nestled into the couch. / The village nestles in a valley between two mountains.
column8: Add important non-affectionate spatial use. Frames: nestle into/against/between; be nestled in/among.

column5: A mixture made by combining ingredients, often unusual or improvised; figuratively, an invented story, explanation, plan, or fabrication.
column7: He made a strange concoction of fruit and spices. / The alibi sounded like an elaborate concoction.
column8: Literal mixture and figurative invented-story/scheme senses are both useful. Tone can be playful, skeptical, or neutral.
column12: entry::word usage::playful usage::figurative usage::skeptical discovery::explanation discovery::figurative_extension discovery::improvement

column5: Permission that is explicitly stated or communicated, rather than merely implied by circumstances or conduct.
column6: explicit permission, explicit consent, stated authorization
column7: You may not reproduce the material without express permission from the copyright holder.
column8: LEGAL/FORMAL contrast: express permission/consent vs implied permission/consent. 'Express' here means explicitly stated, not fast.

column5: To play, move, or behave in a lively, carefree, playful way; noun 'a frolic' can mean playful activity or, in some formal/legal contexts, a personal deviation from assigned duties.
column7: The dogs were frolicking in the snow. / The children frolicked along the beach.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Everyday sense is playful movement; 'cavort' is close but can sound more literary.

column5: Noun: influence, power, or pull, especially social/political/business influence; also a hard blow. Verb: to hit hard (less common in everyday AmE than noun influence sense).
column7: She has enough political clout to get the proposal heard. / He gave the ball a clout.
column8: Online 'clout' can specifically mean social influence/status/attention; 'clout-chasing' = seeking attention/status.

column5: A sudden and major change that causes disorder or turmoil.
column7: The company faced major upheaval after the CEO resigned. The political upheaval left the country in a state of uncertainty.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column2: bottom line / the bottom line is...
column5: In finance/accounting, the final profit/net-income figure or ultimate financial result; figuratively, the essential point, conclusion, or decisive practical consideration.
column6: net result, profit/result; key point, essence, takeaway
column7: The bottom line is that we can't afford another delay. / Rising costs hurt the company's bottom line.
column8: Teach literal business origin + figurative discourse frame: the bottom line is (that) + clause.

column5: To take a firm position, assert authority, or refuse to allow something to continue.
column6: draw the line, insist, take a firm stand, lay down the law
column7: I finally put my foot down and said no more last-minute changes.
column8: Normalize possessive. Often follows a period of tolerance, but 'finally' is contextual rather than part of the definition.

column2: my circuits must be crossed / one's wires are crossed
column5: 'My circuits must be crossed' is a humorous technology/brain metaphor for being confused or mentally mixed up. The established idiom 'get/have one's wires crossed' means misunderstand one another or mix up information.
column6: my wires are crossed, I'm mixed up, I'm confused
column7: I wrote down Tuesday instead of Thursday—my circuits must be crossed. / We got our wires crossed about the meeting time.
column8: SOURCE/CREATIVE CAUTION: 'circuits must be crossed' is understandable wordplay, but 'get/have one's wires crossed' is the conventional idiom. Clean corrupted apostrophe.

column5: To continue successfully, energetically, or in good condition over time. The most common construction is 'be still going strong'.
column6: keep going, thrive, remain strong, hold up
column7: Their business is still going strong after twenty years. / At midnight, the party was still going strong.
column8: CORRECTION: not normally a noun, and 'went strong throughout the season' is less idiomatic than 'was going strong'. Teach BE + going strong.

column5: Visually appealing, distinctive, or photogenic in a way that makes something suitable for sharing on Instagram or social media.
column7: That café's desserts are extremely Instagrammable.
column8: Clean mojibake. Capitalization varies as the brand-derived adjective becomes lexicalized; formal brand-sensitive writing may prefer 'Instagrammable'.

column2: hair of the dog / hair of the dog that bit you
column5: An alcoholic drink taken to relieve a hangover, based on the older phrase 'the hair of the dog that bit you'. More broadly/historically, the expression reflects the idea of treating an ailment with a little of its cause.
column7: He ordered a Bloody Mary as a bit of hair of the dog.
column8: Usage note: common joking expression, not medical advice; more alcohol does not 'cure' the underlying effects of drinking.

column2: may as well / might as well
column5: Used when an action seems reasonable because there is little reason not to do it, no better alternative, or the circumstances already point that way; can also express resigned acceptance.
column6: might as well, could just, no reason not to
column7: We're already here, so we may as well go inside. / If the train is canceled, we might as well walk.
column8: Compare WID4391 later source if relevant: two useful shades are 'no reason not to' and resigned/practical acceptance. 'Might as well' is generally more common in many varieties; 'may as well' is fully standard.

column5:
1. (noun) An act of breaking a rule, law, or contract.
2. (noun) A gap or break in a barrier or relationship.
3. (verb) To break through or violate something.
column7: The company was fined for a serious data breach.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To clearly and precisely describe, portray, or outline something.
column7: The guidelines delineate the responsibilities of each team member. The report clearly delineates the responsibilities of each department.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: A fortunate occurrence or turn of events caused largely by chance.
column6: lucky break, piece of good fortune, fortunate coincidence
column7: Finding the last available ticket was a real stroke of luck.
column8: Fix grammar. 'Fluke' can imply an unlikely accidental result and is not always positive; not a clean synonym.

column5: Highly polysemous. Noun: a single movement/blow/mark; a swimming movement/style; a clock strike; a medical stroke (acute brain injury from interrupted blood flow or bleeding). Verb: move a hand gently over something; make a stroke; in rowing, set the pace as stroke/stroke seat.
column7: She painted with broad strokes. / He had a stroke and was taken to the hospital. / She stroked the cat's fur. / His golf stroke has improved.
column8: MEDICAL PRECISION: a stroke is not simply 'loss of brain function'; it is an acute neurological event caused by disrupted cerebral blood flow or bleeding. Keep other senses clearly separate.

column5: Holding or being led to hold a false belief despite reality/evidence; often implies a significant mismatch between belief and reality.
column7: He's deluded if he thinks no preparation is necessary. / She had been deluded into believing the offer was genuine.
column8: KEY FRAMES: be deluded about/into believing; delude oneself. Stronger and more judgmental than merely 'mistaken'.

column5: Disappointed after discovering that a person, idea, institution, or situation is less good, true, admirable, or ideal than previously believed.
column7: She became disillusioned with the industry after seeing how decisions were made.
column8: KEY FRAME: disillusioned with/by + noun. Core is loss of illusion/idealism, not simply disappointment.

column5: Broken, crushed, or divided into multiple small fragments; medically, a comminuted fracture is a bone fracture in which the bone is broken into more than two pieces/fragments.
column7: The X-ray showed a comminuted fracture of the femur. / The material is comminuted before further processing.
column8: Technical. Remove speculative metaphorical use unless sourced; common in medicine and particle-size/material processing.

column5: An emphatic way of saying 'you can be sure of it' or 'definitely.'
column7: You can bet your butt I'm not going to miss that concert.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Slightly indecent or suggestive, often in a sexual or provocative way.
column7: The comedian's jokes were a bit too risqué for prime-time TV. Her risqué performance drew both laughs and gasps from the audience.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To seek someone's affection or support, often romantically or politically.
column7: He spent weeks trying to woo her with flowers and poems.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Ordinarily, information heard from another person rather than known directly. In law, 'hearsay' has a specific rule-based definition concerning out-of-court statements offered to prove the truth of what they assert, subject to exclusions/exceptions depending jurisdiction.
column7: That's just hearsay—I didn't hear it from her directly. / The judge considered whether the statement was inadmissible hearsay.
column8: CORRECTION: legal hearsay is not simply 'unsubstantiated information,' and it is not always inadmissible. Keep everyday and legal senses distinct.

column5: Slang for romantic charm or ability to attract/flirt successfully; 'rizz up + person' means charm or flirt with them successfully. 'Unspoken rizz' refers to charisma conveyed without much talking.
column7: He's got rizz. / She rizzed him up in about five minutes. / People joked about his 'unspoken rizz.'
column8: Modern internet/youth slang. Often linked to 'charisma' as a clipping/derivation in popular accounts. Tone can be playful/ironic; not limited to smooth talking.

column5: Short for 'be right back', used to say that the speaker is leaving a chat/activity briefly and expects to return soon.
column7: BRB—I'm grabbing something from the kitchen.
column8: Initialism pronounced letter by letter if spoken, though mainly written. Clean corrupted punctuation.

column2: rub off on someone / be rubbing off on someone
column5: For a quality, habit, attitude, style, or behavior of one person/group to gradually influence another through contact or exposure.
column7: Her optimism is rubbing off on me. / After working together for months, some of his habits rubbed off on her.
column8: Normalize reusable frame: QUALITY/person's habit rubs off on PERSON. Influence can be positive or negative; not necessarily emotional.

1. To accumulate or pile up.
2. To compare favorably or measure up.
3. To appear plausible or make sense.
4. (Aviation) Circling aircraft waiting to land.

column5: To return/store something in its place; eat/drink a surprisingly large amount; imprison; defeat/finish off; euphemistically kill/euthanize in some contexts; save money can appear in 'put money away'.
column7: Put the dishes away. / He can put away a whole pizza. / The criminal was put away for years. / She puts a little money away each month.
column8: Polysemy hub. Meaning is strongly object/context dependent. 'Put an animal down' is much more common than 'put away' for euthanasia.

column5: A structured framework or representation. In cognitive psychology, an organized mental framework for knowledge/expectations; in databases/computing, a formal structure describing how data is organized and related.
column7: A restaurant schema helps us predict what normally happens when dining out. / The database schema defines tables, fields, and relationships.
column8: Plural can be 'schemas' (common) or 'schemata' (technical/traditional). Piaget-related assimilation/accommodation is one theoretical context, not the definition of schema itself.

column5: To be likely or destined to experience something soon. The thing may be unpleasant, surprising, enjoyable, difficult, etc., depending context.
column6: be about to face/experience, have coming
column7: You're in for a surprise. / If the forecast is right, we're in for a beautiful weekend.
column8: CORRECTION: not inherently negative/challenging. Common collocations: in for a shock/surprise/treat/rough night/good time.

column2: out of context / take something out of context
column5: Without enough surrounding information to understand something properly; 'take/quote X out of context' means present it separated from context, sometimes causing a misleading impression.
column7: That sentence sounds terrible out of context. / The clip was taken out of context.
column8: CORRECTION: being out of context does not automatically mean distortion or intentional misrepresentation. Teach productive take/quote X out of context.

column5: Learning and Development: the organizational function/practice concerned with employee learning, skills, capability development, training, and professional growth.
column6: learning and development, employee development, workplace learning, training
column7: She works in L&D and designs leadership-training programs.
column8: Normalize capitalization. L&D may refer to a function/team/field, not merely a single 'initiative'.

column5: Indirectly or not straightforwardly in expression; also at a slanting/diagonal angle in literal or technical contexts.
column7: She referred obliquely to the disagreement without naming anyone. / The line crosses the axis obliquely.
column8: Keep figurative and literal senses. 'Evasively' implies avoidance and is not always appropriate.

column5: 'There goes + noun' is an ordinary productive construction used to observe that something is going, disappearing, being lost, or predictably happening. 'There goes the shirt' can therefore work literally as a playful/resigned meta-comment when a character predictably removes or loses his shirt; in Galaxy Quest, the line jokes about the heroic captain ending up shirtless again.
column6: there goes + noun; there it goes; there goes X again
column7: There goes the shirt—right on cue. / There goes our chance of catching the train. / There goes the neighborhood.
column8: SOURCE/CONSTRUCTION NOTE: Keep this as source-specific humor, not a general fixed idiom meaning 'lose money,' 'lose dignity,' or 'get angry.' The reusable pattern is THERE GOES + NOUN, often used to comment wryly, playfully, or resignedly when an expected event happens or something is lost/gone. In Galaxy Quest, 'And there goes the shirt...' functions as a literal/meta running-gag observation about the heroic captain taking off/losing his shirt, parodying the familiar shirtless sci-fi-hero trope. Do not confuse it with separate idioms 'lose your shirt' = lose a great deal of money and 'keep your shirt on' = calm down / be patient.
