column5: To rise/increase very rapidly; grow taller quickly; attack a place/person with gunfire ('shoot up'); or inject a drug, especially illicitly (informal). 'Shot up' is the past form in all these senses.
column6: soar, spike, surge; grow rapidly; fire on; inject
column7: Prices shot up overnight. / David has really shot up since last year. / The building was shot up. / The character was shown shooting up heroin.
column8: Normalize base + source past. Distinguish intransitive increase/growth from transitive gunfire and drug-use senses. Register/safety context varies.

column5: Increasing, resulting, or calculated through successive additions over time; representing the total accumulated amount/effect up to a point.
column7: The cumulative effect of several small delays was significant. / Her cumulative GPA includes all completed terms.
column8: Remove 'collective' as loose synonym and stray comma. 'Cumulative' does not necessarily mean continuously increasing; it concerns accumulation.

column5: The punctuation mark '...' used to indicate omitted material or, in informal/literary writing, a pause/trailing off; in grammar/rhetoric, omission of words that are understood from context.
column7: 'I'm not sure...' she whispered. / In 'I ordered coffee and she tea,' the omitted 'ordered' is an example of ellipsis.
column8: CORRECTION/CLEANUP: repair corrupted ellipsis character/example. Distinguish punctuation ellipsis from grammatical ellipsis.

column2: not bat an eye / bat an eye
column5: To show a visible reaction, especially surprise, concern, or hesitation; overwhelmingly common in the negative 'not bat an eye' = show no reaction.
column7: She didn't bat an eye when the price doubled.
column8: Normalize around the common negative construction. Literally 'bat' here = blink/move the eyelid, not hit.

column5: For a TV series, franchise, creator, product, etc. to make a conspicuous move seen as gimmicky, implausible, or desperate, often taken as a sign that its creative peak has passed.
column6: go downhill, become gimmicky, show creative desperation
column7: Some fans said the series jumped the shark when it introduced the bizarre twist.
column8: Origin: Happy Days scene in which Fonzie jumps over a shark on water skis. It refers to a perceived turning point/sign of decline, not simply 'the point quality begins declining' in an objective sense.

column2: burn that bridge when we get to it
column3: /bɝn ðæt brɪdʒ wɛn wi ɡɛt tu ɪt/
column5: A humorous blend/alteration of 'cross that bridge when we get to it' and 'burn one's bridges', joking that one will deal with a future problem by making it worse or destroying options.
column7: We haven't even decided whether to move yet—let's burn that bridge when we get to it.
column8: Explain the wordplay: cross that bridge = handle problem later; burn one's bridges = destroy routes/options. The humor comes from combining them.

column5: Identical; referring to the exact same person or thing.
column7: The CEO and the anonymous donor turned out to be one and the same.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column2: by the seat of one's pants / fly by the seat of one's pants
column5: To do something mainly by instinct, feel, experience, or improvisation rather than a detailed plan, data, or formal guidance.
column6: wing it, improvise, go by feel
column7: We didn't have time for a full plan, so we ran the event by the seat of our pants. / The pilot was said to fly by the seat of his pants.
column8: Normalize possessive. Aviation-origin story is commonly associated with flying by bodily feel before/relying less on instruments; avoid overclaiming a single precise origin.

column5: A nonstandard reinterpretation of a word/phrase based on a similar sound that produces a semantically plausible expression, e.g. 'for all intensive purposes' for 'for all intents and purposes'.
column7: 'Old-timers' disease' for 'Alzheimer's disease' is often cited as an eggcorn-like reanalysis.
column8: KEEP. Distinguish from malapropism: an eggcorn is typically a plausible reanalysis of a fixed expression, not merely substitution of a similar-sounding word.

column5: The mistaken use of a word in place of a similar-sounding one, often producing an absurd or humorous result.
column7: 'He's the pineapple of politeness' for 'pinnacle of politeness' is a classic malapropism.
column8: KEEP. Named after Mrs. Malaprop in Sheridan's The Rivals. Contrast eggcorn: malapropism need not create a semantically plausible reinterpretation.

column5: An outward appearance, form, or manner of presentation. In the common construction 'under/in the guise of X', something is presented as X, often while its true nature or purpose is different.
column7: He entered under the guise of a consultant. / The policy was criticized as censorship in the guise of safety.
column8: KEY FRAME: under the guise of + noun/gerund. Deception is common in this construction but 'guise' itself can simply mean outward form/appearance.

column5: Vulgar, sexually explicit, or crude in a way that's intended to be humorous or provocative.
column7: The comedian's raunchy jokes weren't suitable for a family audience.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Messy, untidy, or careless in appearance, habits, or work.

column7: The kids came back from the park looking grubby and exhausted.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: In modern slang, 'slay' means perform exceptionally well, look especially impressive, or succeed brilliantly; 'it slayed' means a performance/look/work was extremely effective or impressive.
column6: kill it, crush it, nail it, be amazing
column7: Her performance absolutely slayed. / That outfit slays. / The finale slayed.
column8: Normalize reusable base + source form. Traditional 'slay' = kill; modern praise use is informal and can be playful/hyperbolic.

column2: beg the question / begging the question
column5: In its traditional logical sense, to assume in the premises what the argument is supposed to prove—circularly presupposing the conclusion. In everyday modern use, 'begs the question' is also widely used to mean 'raises/prompts the question', though this is distinct from the logical sense.
column6: reason circularly, assume the conclusion; raise the question (modern separate use)
column7: Saying 'This policy is best because it's superior to all alternatives' begs the question if 'superior' is never independently established. / The delay raises the question of whether the deadline is realistic.
column8: Important distinction: logical 'beg the question' ≠ simply raise a question. However, the 'raises the question' use is widespread in contemporary English, so recognize it while using 'raises the question' when precision matters.

column5: A particular way or method of doing something, especially one that is characteristic or habitual (typical or well-established)
column7: The thief's modus operandi involved disabling security cameras before breaking in. His modus operandi is to tackle the hardest task first thing in the morning.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Both mean a purpose, aim, or plan. 'Intent' often sounds more formal, focused, or legally significant and commonly appears in 'intent to do X / intent on doing X'. 'Intention' is common in everyday language for plans or purposes and in 'intention to do X / intention of doing X'.
column7: His intent was to deceive the buyer. / I had every intention of calling you back. / She is intent on finishing tonight.
column8: Avoid an overly rigid formal-vs-everyday split: the words overlap substantially. Also distinguish noun 'intent' from adjective 'intent on' = determined/focused.

column5: To end or interrupt something before it was expected to finish.
column7: The meeting was cut short due to a fire alarm.

column5: A 'slip-up' is an unintentional mistake. 'Faux slip-up' is understandable creative wording for an apparently accidental mistake that is actually staged or deliberate, but it is not a standard fixed idiom. It should not be used to mean an ordinary social faux pas.
column7: The supposedly accidental remark looked more like a staged slip-up for publicity.
column8: CORRECTION: 'faux' = false/artificial, so 'faux slip-up' naturally suggests a fake/staged mistake. Do not merge this with 'faux pas', which means a social blunder. For active use, 'staged slip-up' or 'deliberate gaffe' is clearer.

column5: To be planning, hoping, seeking, or intending to do something, often in the near or foreseeable future.
column6: plan to, aim to, intend to, hope to
column7: We're looking to hire two more people this fall. / I'm looking to replace my laptop soon.
column8: KEY FRAME: be looking to + verb. Depending context it can sound less definite than 'plan to' and may express a goal rather than a fixed plan.

column5: To attempt or try something, especially something difficult or new.
column6: give it a shot, try, attempt
column7: I've never fixed a leaky faucet before, but I'll take a crack at it.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To listen attentively in order to detect or notice a particular sound, word, signal, or other audible event.
column6: keep an ear out for, listen out for (esp. BrE), be alert for
column7: Listen for your name to be called. / I lay awake listening for the sound of the door.
column8: CORRECTION: not a phrasal verb in the narrow sense; productive verb + preposition construction. Contrast listen to X = direct attention to X already audible; listen for X = try to detect X.

column5: Noun: a broad, often flat-bottomed boat used especially for transporting goods. Verb: move clumsily or forcefully; 'barge into + place/conversation' = enter or interrupt abruptly and intrusively.
column6: boat; push in, burst in, intrude
column7: A barge carried cargo down the river. / He barged into the room without knocking. / Sorry to barge into your conversation.

column5: Historically, a dealer or trader in a specified commodity; in modern compounds, often a person who promotes, spreads, or traffics in something, frequently something viewed negatively: warmonger, fearmonger, scaremonger, rumormonger.
column7: Critics accused him of fearmongering. / 'Warmonger' and 'fishmonger' show the two major patterns.
column8: Better learned as a productive compound element. Not all -monger words are negative: 'fishmonger' is simply a seller of fish. Hyphenation varies by compound; fearmonger is commonly one word.

column6: uh...; wow; hubba hubba (related comic reaction)
column7: Hummina hummina... I completely forgot what I was going to say.

column5: Verb 'compound' means make a problem, difficulty, or situation worse by adding another factor. 'Compounding issues/problems' are problems that add to or intensify one another; 'compound issues' can also simply mean complex/multi-part issues depending context.
column6: worsen, aggravate, exacerbate; mutually reinforcing problems
column7: A staffing shortage compounded the delays. / The team faced several compounding problems at once.

column5: A condition of pain, suffering, or distress caused by illness or misfortune.
column7: Chronic back pain is a common affliction among office workers.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To state from personal knowledge or confidence that a person or thing is trustworthy, genuine, reliable, good, or true.
column6: attest to, endorse, stand behind, guarantee (contextual)
column7: I can vouch for her reliability. / I haven't tried that restaurant, so I can't vouch for it.
column8: KEY FRAME: vouch for + person/thing. Usually implies personal basis/confidence; it is not always a formal guarantee.

column5: The act/process of recalling past experiences, or a remembered story/recollection from the past, often but not necessarily nostalgic.
column6: recollection, memory, recollection of the past
column7: He published reminiscences of his years abroad. / The photo prompted a reminiscence about their first apartment.
column8: Distinguish 'reminiscence' (a recollection or act of recalling) from 'nostalgia' (a feeling of longing/sentiment for the past).

column5: To serve as a typical or excellent example of something.
column7: His calm response exemplified true leadership under pressure.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To draw or remove a blade or other object from a sheath; figuratively, can be used creatively for bringing out something sharp/aggressive, but literal weapon/tool use is core.
column7: The knight unsheathed his sword. / She unsheathed the knife carefully.
column8: Productive pair: sheath / unsheathe. Do not overstate metaphorical use; 'reveal/expose' is only contextual.

column5: A person, thing, style, or feature resembling or evoking an earlier time or type; also, in biology, a reversion-like resemblance to an ancestral type (less common everyday use).
column6: retro reminder, relic, callback (contextual), atavistic feature (technical/contextual)
column7: Her jacket is a throwback to the 1990s. / The diner feels like a throwback to another era.
column8: KEY FRAME: a throwback to + era/style. 'Nostalgia' is a feeling, not a direct synonym. Social-media 'Throwback Thursday' is a related usage.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::technical usage::scientific topic::biology topic::science discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The reappearance of an ancestral characteristic after it has been absent for generations; more broadly, a reversion to an older or more primitive-seeming trait, practice, or style.
column7: The trait was described as an atavism. / Critics called the policy an atavistic throwback to an earlier era.
column8: Technical biological sense + broader figurative use. Avoid treating 'regression' as an exact biological synonym.

column5: To return to a previous state, condition, practice, version, or subject. In technical workflows, 'revert a change/commit' can also mean undo it, though standard general-English syntax is usually 'revert to X'.
column6: return, go back, roll back (technical/contextual), undo (technical/contextual)
column7: After a week, I reverted to my old routine. / We reverted to the previous version. / The developer reverted the faulty commit.
column8: KEY FRAME: revert to + state/version. Note Indian/South Asian business English 'revert' = reply/respond is regionally common but not the usual meaning in broader international English.
column12: entry::word entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern usage::technical topic::linguistics discovery::evaluation discovery::iteration discovery::commitment discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Having a damp, stale, or moldy smell.
column7: The basement smelled musty after the flood.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Noun: money/security used to secure temporary release from custody pending proceedings. Informal verb 'bail' = leave abruptly; 'bail on + person/plan' = abandon/cancel; 'bail out' = leave an aircraft/boat, rescue financially, or get someone out of difficulty.
column7: I bailed after the second episode. / He bailed on our plans. / The judge set bail at $5,000. / The government bailed the company out.
column8: Polysemy hub. Do not equate bail with 'jail release money' only; legal details vary by jurisdiction. Distinguish bail on vs bail out.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern entry::phrasal_verb entry::word usage::informal topic::security topic::law topic::aviation topic::nautical discovery::release

column5: Without causing or involving guilt; often used to frame a choice as something one need not feel guilty about. Common in marketing and casual lifestyle language.
column6: without guilt, guiltlessly (less common), without feeling bad
column7: I dropped the show guilt-free after four episodes. / The ad promises 'guilt-free' snacking.
column8: CORRECTION: 'innocent' and 'blameless' are not direct synonyms. Marketing uses can imply health/morality claims rather than literally describing nutrition.
column12: entry::word usage::casual usage::informal topic::business topic::decision-making discovery::expressing_need

column5: To do or deliver something with little effort, enthusiasm, or engagement, as though merely going through the motions; 'phoned-in' before a noun is the adjective form.
column6: go through the motions, half-ass (vulgar), give minimal effort
column7: The actor phoned in the performance. / It felt like a phoned-in sequel.
column8: Normalize verb + adjective forms. Origin is associated with doing something remotely/by telephone rather than showing up, later extended to low-effort performance; avoid claiming a single precise origin without source.

column5: To briefly stop at a place, often casually or without a long stay.
column6: drop by, pop in, stop over
column7: I'll swing by your place after work to drop off the book.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Literally, at very close range, especially of a shot. Figuratively/adverbially, directly, bluntly, and without evasion: ask/tell/refuse point blank.
column7: She asked him point blank whether he had lied. / The shot was fired at point-blank range.
column8: Hyphenate attributively: point-blank range/refusal; often unhyphenated adverbially: asked point blank. Literal firearms sense is about very close range, not one exact universal distance.

column5: In everyday speech, excessively or unreasonably suspicious, fearful, or worried that something bad is happening. In clinical contexts, 'paranoid' has more specific mental-health meanings and should not be inferred casually.
column7: I'm probably being paranoid, but did I lock the door? / He became increasingly suspicious of everyone's motives.
column8: For everyday learner use, note that people often say 'I'm being paranoid' hyperbolically. Do not use the casual card to diagnose a person or equate ordinary overthinking with a clinical condition.
column12: entry::adjective_phrase usage::casual usage::colloquial usage::informal topic::health topic::public_speaking topic::medicine

column5: In common contemporary social commentary, 'performative' describes actions presented publicly in a way seen as more concerned with appearance, signaling, or audience reaction than substantive commitment. In linguistics/philosophy, 'performative' also has technical senses unrelated to insincerity.
column7: The company was accused of making a performative gesture without changing its practices.
column8: PRECISION: 'performative' does not objectively prove insincerity; it often expresses a critic's interpretation. 'Virtue signaling' is a more loaded related term, not a neutral synonym. Separate from technical 'performative utterance'.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::technical topic::public_speaking topic::philosophy topic::linguistics discovery::audience_engagement discovery::commitment discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Intensely irritated and frustrated.
column7: She gave an exasperated sigh and walked away.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: A consonant produced with a complete closure followed by a fricative-like release at the same or a nearby place of articulation, functioning as a single consonantal unit; English /tʃ/ in 'chip' and /dʒ/ in 'judge' are common examples.
column7: The /tʃ/ in 'church' is a voiceless affricate, and /dʒ/ in 'judge' is voiced.
column8: Technical precision: an affricate is not merely any stop followed by any fricative; the coordinated release and single-segment analysis matter.
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::religious topic::linguistics topic::courtroom topic::law discovery::evaluation discovery::release discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To move away or create distance; for a vehicle, begin moving away; emotionally, become less close/engaged; in competition, increase one's lead.
column6: move away, withdraw, distance oneself; open up a lead
column7: The train pulled away from the station. / He started to pull away emotionally. / The runner pulled away from the pack.
column8: Add common competition sense. Particle meaning is productive across physical, emotional, and comparative distance.

column5: To leave, cancel, drop, or opt out without feeling guilty. This is understandable casual wording built from slang 'bail' + adverbial 'guilt-free', not a fixed idiom.
column6: bail without feeling guilty, opt out guilt-free
column7: If a show isn't working for me after a few episodes, I'll bail guilt-free.
column8: SOURCE/COMPOSITION NOTE: teach the components rather than treating the whole string as an established idiom. Related cards: bail; guilt-free.

column5: Done in an orderly, systematic, and deliberate way.
column7: Her methodical approach made the project a success.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Something yielded or granted in response to demands/negotiation; an acknowledgment of a point in argument; also a special right/privilege, a reduced-price category ('concession' in some varieties), or a concession stand/business selling refreshments.
column7: They made a concession on the deadline. / His statement was a concession that the original plan had flaws. / We bought popcorn at the concession stand.
column8: Polysemous. A concession is not always 'surrender'. Common frames: make a concession to X; concession on X; concession that + clause.
column12: entry::word entry::discourse_expression usage::rhetorical topic::business topic::communication topic::rhetoric discovery::compromise discovery::negotiation discovery::debate_language discovery::trade-off discovery::concession

column5: Remorse displayed in a way a speaker judges to be more about appearances, reputation, or audience expectations than genuine regret or corrective action.
column6: show of remorse, image-management apology (contextual), insincere regret (if established)
column7: Critics dismissed the statement as performative remorse because it offered no concrete change.
column8: Do not define the person's inner sincerity as fact unless evidence supports it. 'Performative' here marks a critical interpretation; 'virtue signaling' is not a clean synonym.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::critical topic::public_speaking discovery::audience_engagement discovery::evaluation discovery::social_approval

column5: An embarrassing or tactless act or remark in a social situation.
column7: Forgetting her name at the party was a major social blunder.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: To create emotional or physical distance from someone, often due to fear, anger, or discomfort.
column7: She tends to push people away when they get too close.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: A public or artistic expression of respect, admiration, or tribute; especially a work, scene, style, or detail deliberately honoring/invoking an earlier creator or work.
column7: The film pays homage to classic horror. / It contains several homages to silent cinema.
column8: Normalize singular + plural. Common frame: pay homage to. Pronunciations with /h/ and without /h/ occur; usage varies by speaker and region.

column5: To say something incorrectly or unintentionally express oneself wrongly; sometimes used by speakers as a softer way to characterize a verbal error.
column6: say incorrectly, misstate, make a verbal slip
column7: I misspoke earlier—the meeting is Thursday, not Tuesday. / She said she had misspoken during the interview.
column8: KEY FORMS: misspeak–misspoke–misspoken. It does not inherently mean 'misleading'; whether euphemistic depends on context.

column5: Official permission to proceed with a project or plan.
column7: We finally got the go-ahead to launch the campaign.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Modern slang 'slay' = perform exceptionally well, look impressive, or succeed brilliantly. 'Let's slay it' is an understandable motivational use, though 'Let's crush it' / 'Let's kill it' may be more idiomatic for a task depending speaker/context.
column6: crush it, kill it, nail it, do great
column7: Let's crush this presentation. / You absolutely slayed that performance. / Okay—let's slay it.
column8: Keep source phrase but teach productive SLAY. Cultural note: strongly visible in drag/LGBTQ+ and Black/online/pop-culture speech, then spread broadly; avoid presenting it as belonging exclusively to one group.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::presentation-friendly usage::informal topic::romance discovery::encouragement discovery::presentation_language

column5: A nonstandard construction that may suggest physically straining/lifting someone or mentally/physically taxing someone. For the common stress/pressure sense, standard English normally uses 'put a strain on someone/something,' 'put someone under strain,' or 'tax someone.'
column6: tax someone, wear someone down, put pressure on someone; cf. put a strain on someone, put someone under strain
column7: Nonstandard/source wording: The constant criticism was straining everyone in the group. / Standard: The constant criticism was putting a strain on everyone in the group. / The workload put the whole team under considerable strain.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.
column12: entry::construction usage::figurative topic::construction discovery::emphasis discovery::suggestion discovery::evaluation

column5: A style of mocking, cutting, or sarcastic commentary, often witty and dismissive; also the remarks themselves.
column6: sarcasm, mockery, biting wit, snide commentary
column7: The review is full of snark, but it still makes a serious point.
column8: Related adjective 'snarky'. Snark is not identical to sarcasm: it often emphasizes a cutting, smart-alecky tone.

column5: A person regarded as ordinary, mainstream, or outside a particular subculture/community; often dismissive, ironic, or self-aware.
column7: The meme escaped the niche community and reached the normies.
column8: Normalize singular + plural. Pejorative force varies; often used as in-group internet slang rather than a neutral demographic label.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::form_family entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::critical usage::ironic usage::informal topic::internet

column5: Lacking a clear connection or order; incoherent or fragmented.
column7: The report was disjointed and hard to follow.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Not welcoming, attractive, or pleasant.
column7: The cold, gray room felt uninviting.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Unpleasant, objectionable, or difficult to deal with; of a person, inclined to be unpleasant or uncooperative.
column7: The smell was disagreeable. / He became disagreeable when the discussion turned to money.
column8: Remove duplicate synonym. Can describe experiences, conditions, tastes/smells, tasks, or people—not merely grumpiness.

column5: Pleasant or acceptable to the taste; figuratively, acceptable or easier to accept/consider.
column7: The sauce made the vegetables more palatable. / They softened the proposal to make it more palatable to voters.
column8: KEY figurative frame: make X more palatable to PERSON/group. Often means acceptable rather than actively appealing.

column5: Unpleasant, morally questionable, disreputable, or offensive, especially of people, activities, details, or reputations. Historically/literally can mean unpleasant to taste or smell, but figurative moral/social use is especially common.
column7: The investigation uncovered some unsavory business practices. / He was linked to several unsavory characters.
column8: Do not imply food sense is equally common in modern use; 'unappetizing' is usually more natural for food. BrE spelling: unsavoury.
column12: entry::adjective_phrase usage::figurative usage::offensive usage::british_english usage::evaluative discovery::subjective_judgment

column5: Not appealing to the appetite or senses.
column7: The leftovers looked cold and unappetizing.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: A city on the east coast of Scotland, on the Firth of Tay; known for universities, design/culture, publishing, and the video-game industry.
column7: Dundee is one of Scotland's major cities and has a notable game-development history.
column8: Clean corrupted Crocodile Dundee punctuation. Do not conflate Dundee, Scotland with the fictional Australian character Crocodile Dundee; the shared name is incidental.

column5: A close companion or assistant who accompanies a more central or prominent person, especially in fiction, comedy, adventure, or informal descriptions.
column7: The detective and her sidekick solved the case together. / Robin is famously portrayed as Batman's sidekick.
column8: 'Partner-in-crime' can be playful but is not a clean synonym. Sidekick often implies secondary status relative to the main figure.

column5: Noun: a signal or prompt to begin/say/do something; a hint/indication; also a billiards stick. Verb: give a signal or prompt, or prepare/start media/action at the right moment.
column7: That was my cue to leave. / Cue the music. / The stage manager cued the actor. / He chalked his pool cue.
column8: Polysemy card. Distinguish cue from queue (line/list). Productive discourse phrase: 'That's my cue to...'.

column5: Adjective: causing strong dislike/disgust, or tending to repel/resist something. Noun: a substance used to repel insects, water, etc. 'Repellent' is the standard spelling; 'repellant' also occurs, especially for the noun/adjective in some usage.
column7: His behavior was repellent. / Apply insect repellent before hiking. / The jacket has a water-repellent coating.
column8: Separate evaluative and functional senses. 'Deterrent' is related but not identical: a deterrent discourages; a repellent drives/keeps away.

column5: Noun: intense anger/indignation caused by something seen as wrong or offensive; also an act/event regarded as grossly offensive or shocking. Verb: to cause such anger or shock.
column7: The decision sparked public outrage. / The remarks outraged many viewers. / They called the attack an outrage.
column8: Remove 'wrath' as awkward synonym. Useful collocations: spark/provoke outrage; outrage over/at X; be outraged by/at.

column5: On the top of; at or on a higher position.
column7: A flag waved atop the building.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::debate topic::grammar discovery::debate_language

column5: Informal technical shortening of 'deduplicate': remove duplicate records/items according to the chosen matching criteria.
column7: We deduped the email list before importing it.
column8: Normalize base + source past. Related WID3201 'deduplicate'. Keep if separate card helps recognition of common technical shorthand.
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::technical discovery::removal discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The process of moving an employee to a different role, team, or location within an organization.
column7: Her employee reassignment came after the department restructure.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.

column5: Alterations in staffing, including hiring, firing, promotions, or transfers.
column6: staff turnover, workforce shifts, HR changes
column7: The memo outlined upcoming personnel changes across the company.
column8: Core meaning retained. Depth QA: strengthen natural collocations, grammatical frame, register, and reusable literal/figurative patterns where useful.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative usage::persuasive topic::work discovery::promotion discovery::persuasion

column5: In spreadsheets, a formula is an expression entered to calculate a result, usually beginning with '='; a function is a predefined operation such as SUM or IF that can be used inside a formula. A formula may contain functions, operators, references, constants, or combinations of them.
column6: formula = calculation expression; function = predefined operation
column7: Formula example: =A1+A2 uses no function. / Formula example: =SUM(A1:A2) uses the SUM function.
column8: CORRECTION: a formula is not simply 'user-defined' and a function is not the opposite of a formula. This card is spreadsheet-specific; mathematical 'function' and 'formula' have broader meanings.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase topic::language_learning discovery::comparison discovery::contrast discovery::containment

column5: A polynomial function of degree 2, commonly written f(x) = ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Its graph is a parabola.
column7: f(x) = 2x² - 3x + 1 is a quadratic function. / The graph opens upward when a > 0 and downward when a < 0.
column8: CORRECTION/CLEANUP: repair corrupted 'a ≠ 0'. If a = 0, the function is not quadratic.

column5: An additional item or section added to a document, contract, report, book, etc., especially to supply information, corrections, terms, or updates after the main text.
column7: The contract includes an addendum covering remote-work terms.
column8: Plural traditionally 'addenda'; 'addendums' also occurs. An appendix is usually planned supplementary material and is not always interchangeable with addendum.

column5: Integers are ..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... . In common school usage, whole numbers are the nonnegative integers 0, 1, 2, 3, ... . Terminology can vary somewhat by educational source.
column7: Zero is both a whole number and an integer; -3 is an integer but not a whole number under the common school definition.
column8: Technical precision: 'whole number' is less universally standardized than 'integer', so preserve the convention being used.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::technical usage::specialist topic::education topic::language_learning discovery::terminology discovery::comparison discovery::contrast discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A member of the counting-number set; depending convention, natural numbers are {1,2,3,...} or {0,1,2,3,...}.
column7: Seven is a natural number under every common convention. / Check whether a text includes 0 in ℕ.
column8: The inclusion of zero is convention-dependent; good mathematical writing defines the convention when ambiguity matters.

column5: A graphic shape in comics/cartoons containing a character's spoken words, usually with a tail pointing toward the speaker. Thought bubbles/balloons are related but conventionally distinct.
column7: The character's words appear in a speech bubble above her head.
column8: CORRECTION: a speech bubble normally represents speech, not thoughts; thoughts are typically shown with a thought bubble/cloud or other conventions.

column5: A condition resulting from deficiencies, excesses, or imbalances in a person's intake of energy and/or nutrients; it includes undernutrition as well as overweight/obesity and diet-related noncommunicable-disease dimensions in broad public-health usage.
column6: undernutrition (narrower), nutrient deficiency (narrower), poor nutritional status
column7: Malnutrition can result from too little food, an imbalanced diet, impaired absorption, or other factors.
column8: Precision: 'malnutrition' is broader than 'undernourishment'. Avoid making a diagnostic claim from appearance alone.

column5: Tissue composed of closely arranged epithelial cells that covers body surfaces, lines cavities and organs, and forms many glands; functions include protection, absorption, secretion, filtration, and sensation depending on type/location.
column7: The intestinal epithelium is specialized for absorption. / Skin contains a protective stratified squamous epithelium.
column8: CORRECTION: it does not simply 'protect internal organs from infection'. Major classifications include simple/stratified and squamous/cuboidal/columnar; glandular epithelium is a functional category.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist usage::scientific topic::biology topic::anatomy topic::science topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column2: square a number / squaring a number
column5: To multiply a number or quantity by itself; equivalently, raise it to the second power.
column7: Squaring 5 gives 25: 5² = 5 × 5 = 25.
column8: Normalize reusable verb form. For algebraic quantities, square X means X².

column2: raise something to the second power / square something
column5: To use 2 as the exponent of a number/expression: x². For a number x, this equals x × x.
column6: square, raise to the power of two
column7: Raise 4 to the second power: 4² = 16. / Squaring (a+b) gives (a+b)².
column8: KEY FRAME: raise X to the nth power. 'Exponentiate' is broader and more technical, not an exact synonym for specifically squaring.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::technical topic::construction discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Adjective: remaining after the main part/process has ended or been removed. Noun: a remainder; in statistics/regression, an observed value minus its model-predicted value; in entertainment, a residual is a repeat-use/reuse payment under applicable agreements.
column7: The medication had residual effects. / The model's residuals were small. / The actor receives residuals when the show is reused under the contract.
column8: Technical senses differ by field. 'Residual error' is sometimes used, but a statistical residual is specifically observed minus fitted/predicted value and is not identical to an unobservable theoretical error.
column12: entry::word usage::technical topic::entertainment discovery::process_details discovery::iteration discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Insufficiently thought through, developed, prepared, or completed; poorly conceived.
column7: The plan was half-baked and ignored several obvious risks. / The plot twist felt half-baked.
column8: Informal metaphor from something not fully baked. 'Half-assed' is more vulgar and often emphasizes low effort rather than poor development.

column5: To perform or produce something with little effort or enthusiasm; adjective 'phoned-in' describes such work/performance.
column6: go through the motions, perfunctory, half-hearted, low-effort
column7: Season two felt completely phoned-in. / The actor seemed to phone in several scenes.
column8: Related to WID3338; this card can serve adjective-focused recognition. Hyphenate before a noun/adjectivally: a phoned-in performance.

column5: At full intensity; complete, extreme, or unabashedly intense. Can modify nouns or function informally after verbs/with descriptions.
column7: By the finale, it was full-on chaos. / The argument turned full-on hostile.
column8: Usually hyphenated. Meaning depends on collocation: full-on attack, full-on panic, full-on weird, etc. Not always negative.
column12: entry::collocation entry::word usage::informal usage::rhetorical discovery::emotional_intensity discovery::maximum_effort discovery::debate_language

column5: No satisfying result, reward, resolution, or return after effort, setup, investment, or narrative buildup. 'Zero payoff' is emphatic compositional wording, not a fixed idiom.
column6: no reward, no return, no resolution, no satisfying outcome
column7: The mystery got ten episodes of buildup and zero payoff. / All that work had almost no payoff.
column8: Teach productive PAYOFF: payoff for buildup/setup; emotional/narrative payoff; payoff from investment/effort. 'Payoff' also has financial and bribery-related senses.

column5: To do, perform, express, identify, or reproduce something extremely well or exactly right.
column6: ace it, crush it, get it right, hit the mark
column7: That confession scene nails it. / She nailed the pronunciation on her first try.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Productive objects include performance, answer, impression, landing, timing, pronunciation.

column5: To fail to produce the intended effect, response, humor, excitement, or emotional impact.
column6: flop, fail to land, miss the mark, bomb (performance/contextual)
column7: The final joke falls flat. / His attempt at reassurance fell flat.
column8: Normalize base + source form. Often used of jokes, speeches, reveals, campaigns, gestures, or dramatic moments.

column5: A situation, project, event, or process regarded as disastrously bad, chaotic, and difficult to fix.
column7: That rollout turned into a complete dumpster fire.
column8: Informal, vivid, strongly negative. Often hyperbolic; calling something a dumpster fire expresses a judgment rather than an objective category.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::vulgar topic::transportation discovery::process_details discovery::resolution

column5: Mediocre, unimpressive, or merely average, especially relative to hype or expectations.
column7: Honestly, the new series is kind of mid.
column8: Contemporary slang, often dismissive. It can mean 'not very good' rather than a mathematically neutral midpoint; tone/context matter.

column5: A state of severe exhaustion and reduced functioning/engagement associated with prolonged stress or demands; in occupational-health usage, burnout specifically concerns chronic workplace stress, while everyday speech uses the word more broadly for exhaustion from sustained activity/repetition.
column7: I'm getting anime burnout after watching too many similar shows in a row. / She took time off after months of workplace burnout.
column8: PRECISION: everyday 'burnout' is broad, but WHO's occupational concept is work-specific and not classified as a medical condition. Do not equate any tiredness with clinical/occupational burnout.
column12: entry::word usage::professional topic::workplace topic::mental_health topic::health topic::public_speaking discovery::professional_context discovery::emphasis

column5: A gesture—kissing the fingertips and opening the hand outward—or the phrase describing it, used to express that something is excellent, perfect, or especially satisfying.
column6: perfect, exquisite, flawless, just right; perfection
column7: The final shot of the episode was chef's kiss. / That tiny musical cue at the end? Absolute chef's kiss.
column8: Common internet/spoken patterns: 'X is chef's kiss', 'absolute chef's kiss', or simply 'chef's kiss' as a reaction. It is informal and often playful; the expression refers to the stereotyped approving chef gesture.

column5: To stay or continue longer than people want, so that one's presence—or an event, joke, scene, trend, etc.—becomes unwelcome or tiresome.
column6: stay too long, drag on too long, wear out one's welcome, linger too long, become tiresome
column7: I didn't want to overstay my welcome, so I left after dinner. / The beach arc was fun at first, but it overstayed its welcome.
column8: Productive frame: PERSON/THING + overstay + one's/its welcome. Literal with guests; figurative with scenes, jokes, trends, sequels, story arcs, and anything that continues past the point of enjoyment.

column5: An avoidance of a difficult responsibility, decision, or challenge; an easy or unsatisfactory way out. Attributively, 'a cop-out ending/excuse/answer' describes something evasive or disappointingly easy.
column6: easy way out, evasion, dodge, escape, lame excuse (contextual)
column7: Calling it 'just a dream' felt like a cop-out. / That ending was a total cop-out.
column8: Usually negative. Distinguish noun 'a cop-out' from verb 'cop out (of something)' = avoid doing something difficult or responsible.

column5: To manipulate someone over time into doubting their own memory, perception, judgment, or grasp of reality. In looser modern use, it is sometimes used for persistent denial or distortion, but not every lie, disagreement, or misleading narrative is gaslighting.
column6: psychologically manipulate, make someone doubt their perception, distort or deny someone's reality
column7: He kept denying conversations that had happened and tried to gaslight her into doubting her own memory. / Saying a story 'gaslights the audience' is a loose figurative use, not the core interpersonal meaning.
column8: Core frame: gaslight + PERSON; gaslight someone into doubting/believing X. The term is often overextended in casual speech, so use it carefully when precise psychological manipulation is meant.
column12: entry::term entry::word usage::evaluative usage::casual usage::figurative usage::informal topic::psychology topic::relationships topic::communication discovery::perception discovery::social_trust discovery::betrayal discovery::disagreement discovery::uncertainty discovery::evaluation

column5: Apparent narrative protection that lets an important character survive, escape, or succeed despite dangers that would realistically defeat or kill them, because the story needs that character to continue.
column6: narrative immunity, protagonist immunity, story protection
column7: He survives three impossible attacks in a row because the plot armor is doing overtime. / Fans complained that the villain suddenly lost only because the hero's plot armor kicked in.
column8: Usually critical or joking. It is a meta-narrative term: the 'armor' is not literal protection inside the story but perceived protection supplied by the writer/plot.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::humorous usage::critical topic::media discovery::criticism discovery::continuity

column5: To feel, affect, or resonate with someone in a noticeably different—often stronger or more emotional—way than usual or than before.
column6: land differently, feel different, resonate differently, affect someone more strongly
column7: That scene hits different once you know what happens later. / This song hit different after I moved away from home.
column8: Common frame: X hits different (when/after/because...). Highly informal. The expression became widespread through internet and youth speech; 'different' functions adverbially in this slang construction.

column5: To keep someone informed about relevant developments, decisions, or progress so they remain included in the flow of information.
column6: keep informed, keep updated, keep posted, keep apprised
column7: I'll keep you in the loop if the schedule changes. / Please keep me in the loop on anything that affects the launch.
column8: Productive frame: keep + PERSON + in the loop; often followed by 'on/about + topic'. Opposite: leave/keep someone out of the loop.

column5: 1. Relating to the countryside, shepherds, or rural life, often in an idealized, peaceful way. 2. Relating to the care or guidance provided by a pastor or clergy member. As a noun in art/literature/music, a work depicting idealized rural life.
column6: rural, rustic, bucolic, idyllic (sense 1); clerical, ministerial (sense 2)
column7: The film opens with a peaceful pastoral landscape. / The school offers pastoral care to students who need personal support.
column8: Do not reduce it only to 'countryside'. Common combinations: pastoral landscape/scene/poetry; pastoral care/counseling/ministry. 'Bucolic' is close for the rural-literary sense.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::literary usage::specialist topic::work topic::art topic::music topic::literature discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To strengthen one's commitment to a position, strategy, claim, or course of action, especially after it is challenged or becomes risky.
column6: recommit, intensify, dig in, stand firm, press ahead
column7: Instead of apologizing, he doubled down on the claim. / After the first version succeeded, the studio doubled down and ordered two sequels.
column8: Key frame: double down on + NOUN/GERUND. From blackjack, where doubling down increases the wager under specific rules; figuratively it means committing more strongly rather than backing off.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern usage::journalistic usage::debate-friendly topic::media topic::debate discovery::risk discovery::assertion discovery::commitment discovery::escalation discovery::debate_language

column5: 'Hunker down' is the standard idiom meaning take shelter, settle in, or prepare to endure a difficult period. 'Bunker down' is also used, especially when literal shelter or bunker imagery is salient, but it is less established as the general idiom.
column6: take shelter, shelter in place, settle in, dig in, brace oneself
column7: We hunkered down for the night as the storm moved in. / The team bunkered down in the basement during the warning.
column8: NORMALIZATION: teach 'hunker down' as the default reusable idiom. 'Bunker down' is understandable and attested but often sounds like a blend with 'bunker'.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::idiom entry::verb_pattern topic::planning discovery::evaluation discovery::resolution

column2: weigh A against B / weigh A and B
column5: To compare competing options, factors, costs, or benefits carefully before deciding; literally, 'weigh' means determine weight, while figuratively it means evaluate relative importance.
column6: compare, evaluate, balance, weigh up, consider
column7: We need to weigh the risks against the potential benefits. / She weighed both options carefully before deciding.
column8: Most explicit comparison frame: weigh A against B. Also natural: weigh A and B, weigh the pros and cons, weigh one's options. Do not treat literal weighing and figurative evaluation as unrelated words.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative topic::construction discovery::comparison discovery::figurative_extension discovery::evaluation

column5: A job or paid work done in addition to one's main job, usually to earn extra income.
column6: second job, extra job, secondary job, moonlighting (activity)
column7: He has a side job at a café on weekends. / I picked up a side job to cover some extra expenses.
column8: Usually means additional employment. Contrast 'side hustle', which often suggests a self-directed gig, freelance activity, or small business and may carry a more entrepreneurial tone.

column5: Paid work, a gig, freelance activity, or small business pursued alongside one's main job or primary commitments, often for extra income and sometimes with entrepreneurial ambitions.
column6: side gig, freelance gig, extra work, small venture, secondary income stream
column7: Her side hustle selling prints online turned into a full-time business. / I'm looking for a side hustle I can do on weekends.
column8: More informal and entrepreneurial than 'side job'. A side hustle may be self-employed or irregular rather than conventional employment.

column5: Used to introduce something without any delay or further talk.
column6: without delay, let's begin, let's proceed
column7: Without further ado, let's begin the ceremony.
column8: Often used in formal events or scripted introductions.

column5: Exactly right, accurate, appropriate, stylish, or impressively well-executed.
column6: spot-on, excellent, sharp, accurate, just right
column7: Your analysis was on point. / Her outfit was completely on point for the event.
column8: Informal and flexible: can praise accuracy, timing, style, performance, or presentation. Usually predicative ('was on point'), though attributive uses also occur informally.

column5: To belittle, insult, or criticize someone in a way that makes them feel inferior. 'Don't put him down' is the negative imperative form.
column6: belittle, demean, disparage, insult, run down
column7: Don't put him down just because he made a mistake. / She constantly puts herself down even when she does well.
column8: Key frame: put + PERSON/oneself + down. This card targets the 'belittle' sense. 'Put down' also has unrelated senses such as place something on a surface, write something down, suppress, and euthanize an animal.

column5: A term for social, political, and economic arrangements associated especially with medieval Europe in which landholding, lord-vassal relationships, obligations, and localized authority played major roles. Historians debate how broadly and precisely the label should be applied.
column7: Feudalism is often used as a broad label for medieval European systems of landholding and obligation. / Historians disagree about whether 'feudalism' is too broad a term for the varied institutions of the period.
column8: PRECISION: avoid reducing feudalism to 'peasants worked for nobles in exchange for protection'. That describes only part of a much more complex set of relationships, and 'manorialism' specifically concerns the economic organization of estates/manors.
column12: entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::politics topic::debate topic::economics discovery::terminology discovery::debate_language discovery::public_discourse

column5: A fan trip to real-world places associated with an anime, manga, game, or other work—especially locations depicted in or used as models for scenes.
column6: anime location visit, location pilgrimage, seichi junrei (Japanese cultural term)
column7: We made an anime pilgrimage to the town that inspired the series' setting. / Fans travel there to photograph the same viewpoints shown in the anime.
column8: Related Japanese term: 聖地巡礼 (seichi junrei), literally 'pilgrimage to sacred sites', widely used for visiting real-life locations connected with media works. In English, 'anime pilgrimage' is natural fan-community wording; 'holy land of anime' is usually a literal/playful translation rather than a fixed English expression.
column12: entry::fandom_term entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::playful topic::travel topic::anime topic::manga topic::fandom topic::culture topic::work

column5: A tour or trip focused on visiting places where a film, TV series, anime, or other production was filmed, set, or modeled.
column6: filming-location tour, film-location tour, set-location tour, location visit
column7: We joined a filming-location tour that stopped at several places used in the movie. / Fans made their own location tour of the drama's most recognizable spots.
column8: 'Location tour' is understandable but broad; 'filming-location tour' or 'film-location tour' is clearer when the point is visiting screen locations. For anime/model locations, 'anime pilgrimage' may be more culturally specific.
column12: entry::noun_phrase topic::travel topic::anime topic::film topic::television topic::entertainment

column5: 1. The system or rank of hereditary or life peers and their titles, especially in Britain. 2. The body of people who hold such titles. 3. A particular peerage title or dignity.
column6: nobility, titled nobility, aristocracy (overlapping); peerage system
column7: He was elevated to the peerage and took a seat in the House of Lords. / The British peerage includes ranks such as duke, marquess, earl, viscount, and baron.
column8: A 'peer' is a holder of a peerage title. 'Peerage' can mean the institution/body or an individual title. Count is the continental equivalent of British 'earl', not a standard British peerage rank name.

column5: Having just come from, completed, experienced, or achieved something; very recently following a place, event, success, failure, trip, or other experience.
column6: just back from, straight from, newly returned from, immediately after
column7: She was fresh off the plane and already heading to a meeting. / The team came in fresh off a big win. / He's fresh off finishing a six-month project.
column8: Productive frame: fresh off + NOUN/GERUND. Common combinations: fresh off the plane/boat, fresh off a win/loss, fresh off doing something. 'Fresh off the boat' can be neutral literally but has also been used as a stereotype/pejorative about immigrants, so context matters.

column5: A social system or pattern of organization in which men disproportionately hold authority, power, property, or leadership roles, especially in family, political, economic, or institutional life.
column7: The novel critiques the patriarchal rules governing inheritance and marriage. / Scholars debate how patriarchy operates differently across societies and institutions.
column8: More precise than simply 'a government controlled by men'. The term may refer to family structure, institutions, cultural norms, or broader social systems. Adjective: patriarchal.
column12: entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::family topic::politics topic::economics discovery::public_discourse discovery::debate_language

column5: A Japanese humorous label for adolescent behavior in which someone acts as though they possess special powers, secret knowledge, a dark past, or an unusually dramatic identity; often translated as 'eighth-grader syndrome'.
column6: chuunibyou, adolescent delusions of grandeur (rough description)
column7: The character's eyepatch and talk about forbidden powers are classic chūnibyō. / The show lovingly makes fun of 'eighth-grader syndrome'.
column8: NORMALIZATION: repair corrupted Japanese text. Japanese: 中二病 (chūnibyō; also romanized chuunibyou). The English translation is explanatory, not a medical diagnosis.
column12: entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::humorous usage::specialist topic::culture discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A person who deliberately uses shocking, offensive, nihilistic, or provocative statements or imagery to seem edgy, transgressive, or impressively unconcerned with social norms.
column6: provocateur, shock poster, try-hard contrarian (contextual), troll (overlapping)
column7: Posting the most offensive take in every thread just makes him look like an edgelord. / The villain's dialogue sometimes slips into edgelord territory.
column8: Usually mocking or insulting. Not every provocative person is a troll: 'edgelord' specifically targets performative edginess or shock value.
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::derogatory usage::offensive usage::informal usage::evaluative topic::internet discovery::impression

column5: Flexibility or freedom to make decisions or act within limits.
column6: latitude, flexibility, room to maneuver, margin
column7: The boss gave us some leeway with the project deadline. The boss gave me some leeway in how I manage the team.
column8: Common in business, planning, and negotiations.

column5: Showing luminous colors that appear to change as the viewing angle or lighting changes, like soap bubbles, oil films, some feathers, shells, or certain fabrics.
column7: The beetle's shell had an iridescent blue-green sheen. / The fabric looked purple from one angle and green from another because of its iridescent finish.
column8: CORRECTION: the old example treated 'iridescent' as if it meant ambiguous or 'どっちつかず'. That is not its normal meaning. Figurative uses can suggest shifting/multifaceted color or quality, but ambiguity itself is not the definition.

column5: Open to more than one interpretation, uncertain, or deliberately noncommittal; often suggesting that a speaker is avoiding a clear answer or commitment.
column7: His answer was deliberately equivocal, so neither side could claim his support. / The evidence is equivocal and does not clearly favor either explanation.
column8: Two useful patterns: equivocal answer/statement = ambiguous or evasive; equivocal evidence/results = inconclusive or mixed. Opposite: unequivocal = clear and unambiguous.
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::professional usage::academic usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::communication topic::debate topic::rhetoric topic::law topic::politics discovery::ambiguity discovery::noncommittal_language discovery::evasive_language discovery::suggestion discovery::uncertainty discovery::hedging discovery::commitment discovery::debate_language discovery::public_discourse discovery::professional_context discovery::academic_discussion

column5: To remove breast milk from the breast by hand or with a pump, usually for feeding, storage, comfort, or milk-supply management.
column6: pump milk, hand-express milk, remove breast milk
column7: She expressed milk before work and stored it in the refrigerator. / Some parents hand-express a small amount of breast milk for relief.
column8: Key frame: express + milk/breast milk. In this sense 'express' means press or squeeze out a liquid. CORRECTION: remove the typo 'xpress' and avoid implying that 'express air from a container' is a standard everyday extension.

column5: An unexpected gain, advantage, or piece of good fortune, especially a sudden amount of money or profit that was not earned or anticipated in the usual way.
column6: unexpected gain, unexpected profit, bonanza, stroke of luck, lucky break
column7: The company received a tax windfall after the rule changed. / Selling the old property gave them an unexpected windfall.
column8: Originally 'windfall' referred to fruit or wood blown down by the wind and therefore obtained unexpectedly. Common modern combinations: financial windfall, tax windfall, windfall profit/gain.

column5: A person or thing that arrives at exactly the right time and is extremely helpful or welcome, as if sent by providence.
column6: blessing, lifesaver, boon, stroke of luck, timely help
column7: That portable charger was a godsend during the trip. / The extra childcare turned out to be a godsend.
column8: Often strongly appreciative but not necessarily literally religious. Common pattern: X was/is a godsend.

column5: Unexpected money or good fortune that seems to arrive without effort, like a small blessing from above.
column6: windfall, unexpected bonus, lucky break, godsend
column7: The refund felt like pennies from heaven after an expensive month. / To them, the surprise royalty payment was pennies from heaven.
column8: CORRECTION: no article—'pennies from heaven', not 'a pennies from heaven'. The phrase is associated with the 1936 song and later works, giving it a somewhat nostalgic or whimsical flavor.

column5: 1. The dry husks or other light plant material separated from grain during threshing or winnowing. 2. Figuratively, material regarded as worthless, trivial, or less valuable than what matters.
column7: The wind carried the chaff away from the grain. / We had to separate the useful evidence from the chaff.
column8: Important idiom: separate the wheat from the chaff = distinguish what is valuable/good from what is worthless/poor. Do not treat 'chaff' simply as generic waste in every context.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::idiom entry::word usage::figurative discovery::triviality discovery::figurative_extension

column2: edgeways / get a word in edgeways
column5: 'Edgeways' literally means with the edge first or sideways. In 'get a word in edgeways', it means manage to say something when another person is talking continuously.
column6: edgewise (AmE); manage to speak, get a chance to speak (idiom)
column7: She talked for twenty minutes and I couldn't get a word in edgeways. / In American English, 'get a word in edgewise' is more common.
column8: CORRECTION: 'interrupt' is not a synonym for edgeways. The fixed conversational expression is chiefly BrE 'get a word in edgeways'; AmE commonly uses 'edgewise'.
column12: entry::idiom usage::conversational usage::american_english usage::british_english topic::communication discovery::possibility

column5: A person, effort, situation, or objective considered hopeless, beyond saving, or no longer worth pursuing because success is extremely unlikely.
column6: hopeless case, no-win situation, dead end, futile effort
column7: Repairing that water-damaged laptop is probably a lost cause. / After months of arguing, he decided changing their minds was a lost cause.
column8: Common frame: X is a lost cause. It can be harsh when applied to a person, because it implies the person is beyond help or improvement.

column5: To surprise, confuse, shock, or unsettle someone so that they momentarily do not know how to respond.
column6: catch off guard, bewilder, stun, unsettle, take aback
column7: Her sudden resignation threw everyone for a loop. / That plot twist really threw me for a loop.
column8: CORRECTION: standard form is 'throw someone for a loop', not 'throw someone a loop'. Pattern: X threw + PERSON + for a loop.

column5: Punishment from a higher power or deity for wrongdoing.
column7: He believed the storm was divine retribution for their wrongdoing.
column8: Appears in religious or mythological contexts; often implies moral consequence.

column5: Playfully imaginative, fanciful, or charmingly unusual; sometimes also changeable or unpredictable in a way driven by whim.
column6: fanciful, playful, quirky, imaginative, capricious (in the less-charming sense)
column7: The film has a whimsical visual style full of tiny magical details. / She decorated the room with whimsical illustrations and mismatched lamps.
column8: Often positive with art, design, stories, humor, or personality. 'Whimsical' can also shade toward capricious/unpredictable, but the common modern descriptive use is playful and fanciful.

column5: A substance or medicine that promotes bowel movements and is used to relieve constipation; as an adjective, relating to or having this effect.
column6: constipation medicine, bowel stimulant (specific type), stool softener (specific type, not exact synonym)
column7: The doctor recommended a mild laxative for temporary constipation. / Some laxatives work by drawing water into the bowel, while others stimulate intestinal movement.
column8: CORRECTION: 'stool softener' is one type of constipation treatment, not a perfect synonym for all laxatives. Laxatives treat constipation rather than generally 'helping digestion'.
column12: entry::word usage::persuasive topic::medicine topic::health discovery::promotion discovery::persuasion

column5: A religious protector associated with children; in Japanese Buddhism, Jizō (地蔵, Jizō Bosatsu) is especially associated with protecting children, travelers, and the vulnerable.
column7: Small Jizō statues are often dressed with bibs or hats and may be associated with prayers for children.
column8: CORRECTION: repair mojibake 'JizÅ''. Jizō is a Buddhist bodhisattva (Kṣitigarbha), not simply a generic Shinto 'guardian god'. The exact religious meaning depends on cultural context.

column2: head mound / burial mound for severed heads (kubizuka)
column5: A burial or memorial mound associated with severed heads, especially in historical Japanese contexts; Japanese 首塚 (kubizuka) literally means 'head mound'.
column6: head mound, memorial mound, burial mound (contextual)
column7: Local tradition identifies the site as a kubizuka, a mound associated with the burial or memorialization of severed heads.
column8: CORRECTION: repair corrupted Japanese text. This is a descriptive historical/cultural phrase, not a common everyday English lexical item; preserve the Japanese term when source context matters.

column2: when unreasonableness prevails, reason retreats / 無理が通れば道理が引っ込む
column5: A Japanese saying meaning that when unreasonable force or demands are allowed to prevail, sound reason and proper principles are pushed aside.
column6: when force overrides reason; might overrules reason; reason gives way to power
column7: The saying 無理が通れば道理が引っ込む can be translated roughly as 'When unreasonableness prevails, reason retreats.'
column8: SOURCE-SPECIFIC: do not present this English wording as an established native English proverb. It is a translation of 無理が通れば道理が引っ込む. Depending context, natural paraphrases include 'reason gives way to force' or 'when might makes right, reason loses out.'

column5: The cynical idea that those with superior power or force can impose their will and define what is treated as 'right', regardless of moral or legal justice.
column6: power determines right, the strong rule, force over justice
column7: The regime operated on the principle that might makes right. / The phrase is usually used critically, not as an endorsement.
column8: 'Might' here = power/strength, not the modal verb. The expression often condemns the substitution of raw power for justice or moral legitimacy.

column2: where might is master, justice is servant
column3: /weə maɪt ɪz ˈmɑː.stər ˈdʒʌs.tɪs ɪz ˈsɜː.vənt/
column5: An aphoristic way of saying that when raw power dominates a society or system, justice becomes subordinate to those who hold power.
column6: power subordinates justice, might overrules fairness
column7: The line 'where might is master, justice is servant' presents power and justice as master and servant to criticize an unjust system.
column8: SOURCE CAUTION: treat this as an aphoristic sentence or quotation-like wording, not as a standard fixed English proverb unless a specific source establishes one. The reusable idea is closely related to 'might makes right'.

column2: when might is right, then justice there is none
column3: /wɛn maɪt ɪz raɪt ðen ˈdʒʌs.tɪs ðeər ɪz nʌn/
column5: A rhetorical statement arguing that if power alone determines what is considered right, genuine justice disappears.
column6: if power defines right, justice disappears; might over justice
column7: The line 'When might is right, then justice there is none' condemns systems in which force substitutes for justice.
column8: SOURCE CAUTION: retain as a quotation-like or aphoristic expression rather than teaching it as a common English proverb. Compare the established phrase 'might makes right'.

column5: 1. The dome-shaped muscle beneath the lungs that plays a major role in breathing. 2. A thin flexible membrane or partition in various devices. 3. A dome-shaped contraceptive barrier placed over the cervix.
column6: breathing muscle (sense 1); membrane, partition (sense 2); contraceptive diaphragm (sense 3)
column7: The diaphragm contracts and moves downward when you inhale. / A contraceptive diaphragm is used with spermicide and placed over the cervix.
column8: Multiple senses share the idea of a separating membrane or sheet-like structure. In photography/optics, a diaphragm controls the aperture/opening. Replace the old placeholder definition/example.

column5: A change in staffing, personnel allocation, roles, or assignments within an organization; the exact scale can range from a few reassignments to a broader staffing change.
column6: staffing change, personnel change, workforce reallocation, staff reorganization
column7: The department announced a personnel shift that moved several employees to new teams. / The personnel shift was meant to align staff with changing priorities.
column8: CORRECTION: remove encoding garbage. 'Personnel shift' is a broad descriptive phrase, not a highly fixed HR term; use more specific terms such as reassignment, transfer, reshuffle, or reorganization when the type of change is known.

column5: Reorganization of roles within an organization.
column7: There was a staff reshuffle after the new manager took over.
column8: Often triggered by leadership changes or internal restructuring.

column5: The transfer or reallocation of an employee or employees to different duties, roles, teams, departments, or locations within the same organization.
column6: employee reassignment, internal transfer, role reassignment, staff reallocation
column7: The staff reassignment moved two analysts from finance to operations. / Temporary staff reassignments helped the hospital cover the busiest unit.
column8: Usually focuses on where existing staff are moved rather than on hiring or firing. A reassignment may be temporary or permanent and may or may not involve a change in rank or pay.

column5: A temporary authorized absence from work or duty. In employment contexts, especially in the U.S., a furlough often means a temporary period of unpaid leave or reduced work imposed by an employer while the employment relationship continues.
column6: temporary unpaid leave, temporary layoff (overlapping), leave of absence; furlough someone
column7: The company furloughed hundreds of workers during the shutdown. / Federal employees were placed on furlough when funding lapsed.
column8: Distinguish furlough from permanent layoff/termination: a furlough is intended to be temporary, though details vary by employer and jurisdiction. The word also has military/prison-leave senses in some contexts.

column5: To approach someone indirectly or cautiously in order to discover their opinion, feelings, intentions, or willingness before making a direct proposal or commitment.
column6: sound someone out, gauge someone's reaction, probe gently, test the waters
column7: Could you feel her out about joining the project? / I asked a friend to feel Joe out on how he felt about the gift.
column8: Core pattern: feel + PERSON + out, optionally about/on + TOPIC or followed by a clause. Similar to 'sound someone out'. It implies tactful probing rather than bluntly asking.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal topic::testing topic::construction discovery::suggestion discovery::impression discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::commitment

column2: feel out the room / read the room
column5: 'Feel out the room' means cautiously gauge the people or atmosphere before acting; 'read the room' is the more established idiom for noticing the mood, reactions, and social atmosphere and adjusting accordingly.
column6: gauge the room, read the room, test the waters, sense the mood
column7: Let's feel out the room before we pitch the idea. / He should have read the room before making that joke.
column8: 'Feel out' is productive with people/situations ('feel someone out', 'feel out the situation'). 'Read the room' is the idiomatic default when the focus is perceiving the group's mood or social cues.
column12: entry::idiom entry::fixed_expression usage::informal topic::testing topic::performance discovery::comparison

column5: To present an idea, proposal, product, project, or story persuasively in order to win approval, support, funding, or interest.
column6: propose, present, sell, make a pitch, pitch a proposal
column7: We need to pitch the idea to the client tomorrow. / She pitched three concepts to the producers.
column8: Productive frame: pitch + THING + to + PERSON/GROUP. Also: pitch someone an idea. 'Pitch' emphasizes persuasive presentation, not merely mentioning or suggesting an idea.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::presentation-friendly topic::construction discovery::support discovery::suggestion discovery::social_approval discovery::presentation_language

column5: The most important or decisive point of an issue or argument.
column7: The crux of the matter is whether the new policy will benefit small businesses. / He missed the crux of her argument entirely.
column8: よく「the crux of the matter」で使われる。「essence」と似ているが、重要な決定点のニュアンスが強い。

column5: 1. The process by which organic remains become fossils. 2. In second-language acquisition, the stabilization of non-target or incomplete linguistic forms in a learner's interlanguage so that they become resistant to further change.
column7: Fossilization can preserve hard biological material over geological time. / In language learning, repeated non-target forms may become fossilized even in otherwise fluent speakers.
column8: PRECISION: linguistic fossilization is not simply 'incorrect usage becoming a bad habit'; it is a technical concept about persistent interlanguage features that resist further development.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::technical topic::linguistics discovery::process_details discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A state of balance in which opposing forces, influences, reactions, or tendencies are equal or stable; also a figurative state of emotional or systemic stability.
column7: The chemical reaction eventually reached equilibrium. / It took her a few days to regain her emotional equilibrium after the shock.
column8: Common in physics, chemistry, economics, biology, and figurative writing. Equilibrium does not necessarily mean nothing is happening; in dynamic equilibrium, opposing processes continue at equal rates.

column5: 1. A person who holds that the existence or nature of God or the ultimate cannot be known, or who does not claim knowledge on the question. 2. More broadly, not committed to a particular view, system, platform, or solution because the evidence or preference is not decisive.
column6: undecided, noncommittal, uncommitted (extended sense); skeptic (overlapping, not exact)
column7: He describes himself as an agnostic rather than an atheist. / The software is platform-agnostic, so it can run across several operating systems.
column8: CORRECTION: 'nonbeliever' is not an exact synonym; agnostic concerns knowledge/commitment, while atheist concerns belief in gods. Extended compounds such as platform-agnostic or vendor-agnostic mean not tied to one option.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word topic::problem-solving topic::nature discovery::noncommittal_language discovery::solution_framing discovery::evidence discovery::assertion discovery::resolution

column5: To combine two or more distinct things, ideas, issues, or categories into one, often in a way that obscures important differences between them.
