column6: sign, sign panel, placard; billboard (large advertising sign)
column7: The old wooden signboard above the shop had faded lettering. / The sign outside says the café closes at six.
column8: 'Signboard' is standard English but can sound more literal/formal than simply 'sign'. A billboard is specifically a large outdoor advertising display, not a synonym in every context.

column5: One repetition or version in a repeated process of testing, revising, or developing something; also the act/process of repeating.
column6: version, cycle, pass, repetition, revision round
column7: The third iteration of the design finally solved the navigation problem. / We improved the script through several iterations.
column8: Common in software, design, engineering, math, and product development. 'Iterate on X' = repeatedly refine X.

column5: 1. A writing material traditionally made from specially prepared animal skin. 2. A document or surface resembling it. 'Parchment paper' is a separate modern heat-resistant paper used in cooking/baking.
column6: prepared animal skin; vellum (related, not always identical); baking parchment/parchment paper
column7: The medieval text was copied onto parchment. / Line the tray with parchment paper before baking.
column8: FIX: parchment paper is not the same material as historical parchment. 'Vellum' traditionally refers to a finer kind of prepared skin, though terminology varies historically.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::specialist topic::food topic::animals discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A navigation trail showing the user's current location within a site's hierarchy, typically as a sequence such as Home > Category > Page.
column7: Breadcrumbs let users jump back to the parent category without using the Back button.
column8: NORMALIZATION: standard web term is 'breadcrumbs' or 'breadcrumb navigation', not 'breadcrumbs for webpage'. Inspired by the trail motif from Hansel and Gretel. Useful for orientation and hierarchical navigation, but not literally 'essential' on every site.

column5: A written declaration of one's core beliefs, principles, values, goals, or intended way of acting.
column6: statement of principles, personal creed, declaration of intent, values statement
column7: She wrote a personal manifesto describing the principles she wanted to follow in her creative work.
column8: Compositional phrase rather than a fixed genre with one required format. Can be private/self-development oriented or public/activist/creative depending context.

column5: (v.) Appear as a large, often indistinct shape; or seem imminent and potentially threatening/important. (n.) A machine or frame used for weaving cloth.
column6: appear, tower, emerge; approach, threaten; weaving frame/machine
column7: A dark shape loomed through the fog. / The deadline is looming. / She wove the fabric on a hand loom.
column8: High-value figurative use: deadline/problem/crisis looms = it is approaching and feels significant or threatening. Common frame: loom over + PERSON/PLACE.

column2: line break / break a line / start a new line
column5: A 'line break' is the point where text ends on one line and continues on the next. To create one, you can 'insert a line break', 'start a new line', or in some technical contexts 'break the line'. Automatic movement at the margin is 'line wrapping'.
column6: newline, line break; start a new line, insert a newline; wrap
column7:
Insert a line break after the heading. / The editor wraps long lines automatically. / In HTML,
inserts a line break.
column8: FIX: 'break the line' is not the best general headword for 改行する. Distinguish manual line break/newline from automatic line wrapping.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::technical usage::instructional discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To function as something that cushions, separates, protects, mediates, or reduces the impact between two sides, forces, risks, or systems.
column6: serve as a cushion, act as a shield, provide a buffer, mediate, absorb impact
column7: Emergency savings can act as a buffer against unexpected expenses. / A neutral colleague served as a buffer between the two managers. / Extra memory can serve as a buffer during bursts of data.
column8: INTENTIONAL-CONSTRUCTION VALUE: keep separately from WID3614 'buffer' because this card teaches the productive frame serve/act as a buffer + against/between. WID3614 teaches the lexical senses; this card teaches how to deploy the noun naturally in a construction.

column5: The act of identifying or crediting the source, creator, author, or cause of something; also, the process of assigning responsibility or causation.
column6: credit, acknowledgment, source identification; assignment of cause
column7: The article reproduced the image with proper attribution. / Researchers disagreed about the attribution of the effect to one particular cause.
column8: Broader than copyright credit alone. Common areas: source/author attribution; causal attribution in psychology; attribution models in marketing; attribution of a quotation/artwork.

column5: 'To the brim' means completely full up to the edge of a container. Figuratively, 'filled/full to the brim with X' means completely full of X. 'Brim with X' means be full of a feeling, quality, or thing.
column6: completely full, overflowing, packed; be full of
column7: The glass was filled to the brim. / Her eyes were brimming with tears. / The episode is brimming with clever visual jokes.
column8: FIX: not 'the brim with' as a standalone phrase. Useful frames: full/filled to the brim with; brim with; be brimming with.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::construction discovery::figurative_extension discovery::evaluation

column5: A state, concept, or structure involving two contrasting, complementary, or interrelated aspects; plural 'dualities' refers to multiple such pairs or two-sided relationships.
column6: two-sidedness, polarity, opposition, paired contrast; dichotomy (not always exact)
column7: The novel explores the duality of freedom and responsibility. / Its characters embody several moral dualities.
column8: 'Duality' does not always imply a strict either/or split; 'dichotomy' more strongly suggests division into two contrasting categories.

column5: A substitute or representative that takes the place of another person or thing; figuratively, something used to represent a larger group, idea, or category.
column7: The actor used a stand-in while the lights were being set. / The character functions as a stand-in for the audience. / In the essay, one family becomes a stand-in for the masses.
column8: Reusable frame: X is/serves as a stand-in for Y. Literal entertainment-industry sense and figurative representative/proxy sense are both common.

column5: Academic disciplines concerned with human culture, thought, expression, and interpretation, such as literature, philosophy, history, languages, religious studies, and many of the arts.
column6: humanistic disciplines, arts and humanities (contextual), liberal arts (broader category)
column7: She studied philosophy and literature in the humanities. / Funding for the humanities includes support for archives, languages, and historical research.
column8: FIX: social sciences are generally distinguished from the humanities, though boundaries can overlap. 'Liberal arts' is broader and may include humanities, social sciences, natural sciences, and mathematics depending institution. Humanities ≠ simply Japanese 文系.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::academic usage::religious usage::scientific topic::culture topic::religion topic::history topic::philosophy topic::literature discovery::academic_discussion

column5: 'Science' is the systematic investigation of the natural and social world through observation, evidence, theory, and testing, depending on the field. 'STEM' is a broader educational/professional grouping: science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.
column6: natural science, scientific disciplines; STEM fields
column7: She studied physics, one of the natural sciences. / The scholarship supports students across STEM, including engineering and mathematics.
column8: FIX: science and STEM are not synonyms. STEM includes fields beyond science, while 'science' itself can include natural and social sciences depending context. Japanese 理系 is culturally broader/different and should not be treated as an exact translation.
column12: entry::abbreviation usage::professional usage::scientific topic::technology topic::science topic::finance topic::mathematics topic::engineering discovery::professional_context discovery::evidence

column5: Bad-tempered or resentful, typically in a silent and withdrawn way.
column7: He sat in the corner with a sulky expression after losing the game.
column8: Describes a mood of silent resentment or pouting. 日本語では「ふてくされた」「不機嫌な」にあたる。

column5: A plant with long flexible stems that trail along the ground or climb/support themselves on other structures; some vines use tendrils, twining stems, roots, or other mechanisms.
column7: Grapes grow on vines trained along wires. / A vine climbed the fence and covered most of the wall.
column8: Do not assume every vine has tendrils. 'Vine' is also used in compounds such as grapevine. Figurative uses exist but are less central than the botanical sense.

column5: Placed, organized, or contained inside another structure of the same or related kind, often at multiple hierarchical levels.
column7: The folders are nested three levels deep. / The function contains a nested loop. / The HTML elements are incorrectly nested.
column8: Common in computing: nested folders, loops, functions, conditions, elements, data structures. A nested structure is specifically inside another, not merely 'layered'.

column5: Used to add a qualification, contrast, reminder, or important afterthought to what was just said—roughly 'though', 'however', or 'I should add'.
column6: though, however, that said, I should add
column7: The room is tiny. Mind you, the rent is surprisingly low. / He's difficult to work with—mind you, he's brilliant at the technical side.
column8: Often parenthetical and conversational. It does not literally mean 'pay attention to me'; it signals a qualifying comment or counterpoint.
column12: entry::discourse_expression usage::informal usage::conversational usage::technical discovery::contrast discovery::qualification discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A short descriptive or promotional piece of text, especially on a book cover/jacket, webpage, film page, product page, etc.; also, a brief endorsement quote.
column6: promotional copy, short description, endorsement, jacket copy
column7: The back-cover blurb gives away too much of the plot. / The publisher asked several authors to provide blurbs.
column8: 'Blurb' can mean neutral short descriptive copy or explicitly promotional praise depending context. Verb: blurb a book = provide promotional copy/endorsement (less common).
column12: entry::word usage::persuasive topic::film topic::entertainment discovery::promotion discovery::persuasion

column5: Money used in a way that proves worthwhile, useful, enjoyable, or good value.
column6: worthwhile expense, good investment, good value
column7: The tickets were expensive, but it was money well spent.
column8: FIX: usually written without a hyphen after the noun: 'money well spent'. Hyphenation may appear attributively in other constructions, but this fixed phrase is normally open.

column5: Clearly worth paying the stated price because the quality, benefit, experience, or result justifies the cost.
column6: worth the cost, worth every penny, good value
column7: The tour is expensive, but it's well worth the price. / For the build quality alone, the upgrade is well worth the cost.
column8: 'Well worth' intensifies 'worth'. Related frames: well worth the money/time/effort; worth every penny. 'Worth the price' does not necessarily mean cheaper than alternatives—only that the value justifies the cost.

column5: Deeply thoughtful, reflective, or meditative; encouraging or characterized by sustained inward thought.
column7: The film becomes quieter and more contemplative in its final act. / He sat in contemplative silence by the window.
column8: Can describe a person, mood, artwork, practice, or atmosphere. 'Pensive' can carry more sadness/worry; 'contemplative' emphasizes sustained reflection.

column5: A small, thin, light strand, tuft, streak, or trace of something, especially smoke, cloud, hair, grass, or a faint sign of a feeling/quality.
column7: A wisp of smoke rose from the candle. / A few wisps of hair fell across her face. / There was a wisp of a smile.
column8: Common frame: a wisp of + smoke/cloud/hair. Conveys thinness, lightness, and small quantity.

column5: A slender, curling plant organ that coils around a support and helps a climbing plant hold on; figuratively, a thin curling strand or extension resembling one.
column6: clasping shoot, curling stem; curl, strand (figurative)
column7: The pea plant's tendrils wrapped around the wire. / Tendrils of smoke drifted toward the ceiling.
column8: Botanically, a tendril is a specialized climbing structure, not simply any vine shoot. Figurative uses often describe smoke, hair, mist, or branching shapes.
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::specialist topic::anatomy topic::health discovery::figurative_extension discovery::support discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Thin, light, fine, delicate, or sparse in a way that resembles wisps.
column7: Wispy clouds stretched across the sky. / He had a few wispy strands of hair over his forehead.
column8: Common with clouds, smoke, hair, beard, fabric, and thin shapes. Can imply attractive delicacy or insufficient thinness/sparseness depending context.

column5: A shrewd, unprincipled person, especially a politician motivated by personal advantage rather than principle.
column6: opportunist, schemer, unscrupulous politician, political operator
column7: The columnist jokingly dismissed the candidate as an old-fashioned snollygoster.
column8: Rare, colorful 19th-century U.S. slang that is occasionally revived for humorous political commentary. Not a normal modern everyday word; register is intentionally quirky/archaic.
column12: entry::word usage::slang usage::dated usage::archaic usage::humorous usage::informal topic::politics topic::history discovery::encouragement discovery::public_discourse

column5: A noisy fuss, uproar, or excited public reaction, often over something relatively minor or overblown.
column7: The casting announcement caused a huge brouhaha online.
column8: Often humorous or mildly dismissive: calling something a 'brouhaha' can imply people are making a big fuss.

column5: A fuss, commotion, or minor disturbance, often caused by disagreement, confusion, or a small conflict.
column7: There was a brief kerfuffle over who had reserved the room.
column8: Light/humorous tone and especially associated with British/Commonwealth usage, though widely understood elsewhere. Usually less serious-sounding than 'uproar'.

column5: Very excited, enthusiastic, or pleased about something. 'I'm not super jazzed about it' softens a negative reaction to mean 'I'm not especially enthusiastic about it.'
column6: excited about, enthusiastic about, pumped about, thrilled about
column7: I'm pretty jazzed about the trip. / I'm not super jazzed about changing the plan again.
column8: NORMALIZATION: teach reusable 'be jazzed about + NOUN/GERUND'. Informal, especially North American. The sentence-form source expression is a softened negative use of the same construction.

column5: A person, team, or entry that finishes immediately behind the winner; most commonly second place.
column6: second-place finisher, finalist (broader), silver medalist (when applicable)
column7: She was runner-up in the national spelling bee. / Two runners-up received smaller prizes.
column8: INTENTIONAL-DUPLICATE CHECK: WID3611 already teaches runner-up in greater depth. Keep this card for now rather than deleting automatically; normalize spelling to hyphenated 'runner-up' and preserve position. Plural: runners-up.

column5: 1. An aria is an extended solo vocal piece, especially in opera, usually with instrumental accompaniment. 2. ARIA in web development stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications, a WAI specification whose roles/states/properties help expose interface semantics to assistive technologies.
column6: operatic solo; Accessible Rich Internet Applications
column7: The soprano sang a famous aria in the second act. / The button uses an ARIA label so a screen reader can announce its purpose.
column8: FIX: distinguish unrelated terms by capitalization/context. ARIA attributes do not automatically make a site accessible; native semantic HTML is generally preferred when available, with ARIA supplementing semantics where needed.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::abbreviation entry::form_family entry::word topic::internet topic::linguistics

column5: 'Purposely' means intentionally or on purpose. 'Purposefully' can also mean intentionally, but often emphasizes acting with determination, resolve, or a clear purpose.
column6: purposely: intentionally, deliberately; purposefully: deliberately, with purpose, resolutely
column7: He purposely left the door unlocked. / She walked purposefully toward the stage.
column8: The two words overlap, but 'purposely' is the clearest choice for simply 'intentionally'; 'purposefully' often adds manner/resolve.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase topic::performance topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::emphasis discovery::resolution discovery::determination

column5: 1. Care for, look after, or attend to someone/something. 2. Be likely or inclined to behave or develop in a particular way.
column6: care for, look after, attend to; be inclined, be likely
column7: She tends the garden every morning. / I tend to overthink small decisions.
column8: NORMALIZATION: use base form 'tend'. Important frames: tend + OBJECT = care for; tend to + VERB = be inclined/likely to.

column5: To improvise, elaborate, or create variations based on an existing idea, theme, joke, style, or work.
column6: improvise on, build on, play off, vary, elaborate on
column7: The episode riffs on classic detective movies. / The comedian riffed off a comment from the audience.
column8: 'Riff on' is especially common for creative variations on a theme; 'riff off' also occurs, particularly when emphasizing the source one is building from. Originates in music, where a riff is a recurring phrase.

column5: A relationship between learning/practice and performance over time; in everyday speech, the amount or difficulty of learning needed to become competent at something.
column6: learning progression, rate of learning, learning difficulty (informal sense)
column7: There's a steep learning curve when you first start using the software. / After a few weeks, the learning curve flattened as the team became proficient.
column8: FIX/NUANCE: technically, a steep learning curve can mean rapid improvement with experience, but popular usage often uses 'steep learning curve' to mean 'difficult to learn'. Be aware of the mismatch between technical and colloquial interpretations.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::colloquial usage::technical topic::relationships topic::performance topic::public_speaking discovery::competence discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The practice of improving a website or content so it can be discovered and rank appropriately in unpaid/organic search results.
column6: search engine optimization, organic search optimization
column7: We improved the page titles, content structure, internal links, and technical setup as part of the site's SEO work.
column8: Includes on-page/content work (search intent, keywords/topics, titles, content quality), technical/site-structure work (crawlability, performance, indexing, internal linking), and authority/link-related work such as backlinks. Distinguish SEO from paid search advertising/SEM. MERGE NOTE: useful details from WID3769 are folded here, so WID3769 can be removed without losing learning value.
column12: entry::initialism entry::word usage::technical topic::internet topic::automotive discovery::improvement discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: 1. Soft, light material or loose fibers. 2. Superficial or nonessential content added without much substance. 3. A mistake in a performance/line. As a verb, make something fuller/fluffier or make a mistake in delivery.
column6: lint, soft fibers; filler, padding; mistake, flub
column7: The article has useful data but a lot of fluff. / She fluffed the pillows before the guests arrived. / The actor fluffed one line and recovered quickly.
column8: Do not assume all 'fluff' is negative: literal fluff is neutral, while content 'fluff' often means low-substance filler. Related informal verb 'flub' is common for a mistake.

column5: Literally, a vivid or disturbing dream experienced during a fever; figuratively, an experience, work, or memory that feels bizarre, surreal, chaotic, or unreal.
column6: surreal experience, bizarre vision, delirious dream
column7: The movie plays like a fever dream full of abrupt cuts and impossible imagery. / I barely remember the trip—it feels like a fever dream now.
column8: The figurative use is common in reviews and internet speech and does not imply an actual fever.

column5: 1. A comedy built around exaggerated, improbable situations, physical humor, misunderstandings, and rapid complications. 2. Figuratively, an event or process so badly handled, absurd, or insincere that it seems ridiculous.
column6: comedy, slapstick comedy (overlap); travesty, sham, absurdity
column7: The play is a fast-paced bedroom farce. / The hearing turned into a farce when nobody could answer the basic questions.
column8: Figurative 'farce' is strongly negative and implies a supposed serious process has become absurd or meaningless.

column5: (v.) To confuse, puzzle, or make something difficult to understand. (n.) A plate, wall, or device used to control, redirect, or reduce the flow of sound, fluid, light, etc.
column6: bewilder, perplex, puzzle, mystify; barrier/deflector (technical noun)
column7: The sudden error baffled the developers. / Acoustic baffles help reduce echoes in the room.
column8: The technical noun and the 'confuse' verb are separate common senses. Adjective: baffling; past participle: baffled.

column5: 1. Offer goods/services at a lower price than a competitor. 2. Weaken, undermine, or reduce the effectiveness/credibility of something. 3. Cut away from beneath; also refers to an undercut hairstyle.
column7: The discount chain undercut local shops on price. / His later comments undercut the credibility of his earlier argument.
column8: High-value figurative pattern: undercut an argument/claim/position/authority. Haircut sense is separate.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::figurative usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly discovery::social_trust discovery::debate_language

column5: Consisting of various kinds or types, often without clear category.
column7: The box contained miscellaneous items from the attic.
column8: Common in labeling for uncategorized content. 日本語では「種々雑多な」。

column5: 'Disciple' is a devoted follower or student of a teacher, leader, religion, philosophy, or school of thought. 'Apprentice' is a learner who receives practical training in a skilled trade, craft, or profession under an experienced practitioner.
column6: disciple: follower, adherent, pupil; apprentice: trainee, learner, protégé (overlap)
column7: He became a disciple of the philosopher. / She trained as an apprentice carpenter for three years.
column8: Both can translate loosely as 弟子, but the relationship differs: disciple emphasizes following teachings/ideas; apprentice emphasizes hands-on vocational training.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::noun_phrase usage::religious topic::education topic::religion topic::philosophy topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::expertise

column5: By performing the action just mentioned; as part of that action, with the following result or consequence.
column6: by doing that, thereby, in the process
column7: He admitted the mistake and, in doing so, took responsibility for the delay.
column8: Useful cohesion device in formal and everyday writing. 'In doing so' normally refers back to a previously stated action.

column5: As an adjective, restrained, understated, or not intense. As informal adverbial slang, somewhat/quietly, or sometimes privately/without making a big deal of it.
column6: understated, subdued, discreet; kind of, quietly, mildly
column7: We had a low-key dinner at home. / I'm low-key excited about the new season.
column8: 'High-key' exists as slang contrast but is less neutral/common. Do not assume low-key always means 'secretly'; often it simply softens intensity.

column5: The purest, most perfect, or most characteristic embodiment of a quality, style, or type.
column7: The village is the quintessence of rural charm. / To him, that performance was the quintessence of elegance.
column8: Common frame: the quintessence of + ABSTRACT QUALITY/TYPE. More literary/formal than 'perfect example'.
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::construction usage::formal usage::literary topic::construction discovery::evaluation

column5: Consistent with a brand's established image or, figuratively, with a person's recognizable habits, personality, or public persona.
column6: in character, consistent with the image, fitting, characteristic
column7: The minimalist packaging is very on-brand for them. / Forgetting his umbrella again is completely on brand for him.
column8: Marketing origin, now widely used jokingly about people. Hyphenation varies; predicative 'that's on brand' is common.
column12: entry::adjective_phrase entry::variant_set entry::prepositional_phrase usage::informal topic::psychology discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To make a sudden small movement away or tense involuntarily in response to pain, fear, shock, or surprise; figuratively, to hesitate or recoil from something difficult.
column6: wince, recoil, shrink back, jerk back; hesitate
column7: She didn't flinch when the needle went in. / He never flinched from making the unpopular decision.
column8: Useful frames: flinch at/from + THING; not flinch = show no visible fear/hesitation. 'Wince' more specifically involves a facial/body reaction to pain or embarrassment.

column5: 1. Successfully deal with, control, or defeat a problem, obstacle, fear, or opponent. 2. In passive form, be strongly affected or overwhelmed by an emotion, smoke, heat, etc.
column7: She overcame her fear of flying. / He was overcome with emotion after the announcement.
column8: Key contrast: overcome + OBJECT = defeat/manage it; be overcome by/with + FEELING/force = be overwhelmed by it.

column5: A cat with a characteristic coat pattern of stripes, spots, swirls, or bands; also the pattern itself/adjective. 'Tabby' describes coat pattern, not a specific breed.
column7: Their orange tabby sleeps on the windowsill every afternoon.
column8: FIX: foreground the cat-pattern sense. The historical textile sense is rare today. Do not confuse with 'tubby' = short/fat/rounded. A tabby can be many colors and breeds.

column5: To make a high-pitched cry, shriek, or screeching sound; used for people, pigs and some animals, tires/brakes/machinery, etc. Informally, 'squeal on someone' means inform on or betray them.
column6: shriek, screech, yelp; inform on, snitch on
column7: The brakes squealed as the car stopped. / The kids squealed with excitement. / He refused to squeal on his friends.
column8: Cats can sometimes make a sound someone might describe as a squeal, especially in distress, but their typical vocalizations are meow, yowl, hiss, caterwaul, etc.

column5: To have a useful function, role, or reason for existing, even if it is not ideal or generally useful.
column6: have a function, fulfill a role, be useful for something
column7: The old script is ugly, but it still serves a purpose. / Every section should serve a clear purpose.
column8: Common singular/plural: serve a purpose; serve no purpose; serve several purposes. Often implies functional adequacy rather than excellence.

column5: 1. Delay or postpone an action, especially 'hold off on doing X'. 2. Prevent someone/something from approaching, attacking, or succeeding for a time. 3. Wait before starting because conditions are not yet right.
column6: postpone, delay, wait; fend off, keep back
column7: Let's hold off on buying it until the price drops. / The defenders held off the attack until help arrived.
column8: Important frame: hold off on + NOUN/GERUND. Transitive defensive sense: hold off + attacker/threat.

column5: Figuratively, a feature, condition, or factor shared by different people or things; 'common denominator' is the usual expression.
column6: common factor, shared element, shared trait
column7: Curiosity was the common denominator among all the successful applicants.
column8: NORMALIZATION: teach 'common denominator' as the common figurative phrase. 'Denominator' alone can occasionally be figurative but is less natural. Distinguish 'lowest common denominator', which carries a separate negative evaluative sense.

column5: Figuratively, the simplest, broadest, or least demanding level of taste, intelligence, standards, or appeal shared by a large audience, often used critically.
column6: lowest standard, broadest basic appeal, lowest level of common taste
column7: The show relies on jokes aimed at the lowest common denominator.
column8: From mathematics. Figurative use is usually negative and often implies sacrificing quality or sophistication to maximize mass appeal.
column12: entry::idiom entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative usage::scientific topic::public_speaking discovery::audience_engagement discovery::figurative_extension discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::evaluation

column5: 'Squeal' describes a high-pitched cry or sound. It is strongly associated with pigs, children, brakes, and some small animals. A cat may occasionally make a sound described as a squeal, but more typical cat verbs are meow, yowl, hiss, caterwaul, or shriek depending on the sound.
column7: The kitten gave a brief squeal when startled, but an adult cat in distress is more often described as yowling or shrieking.
column8: INTENTIONAL-DUPLICATE VALUE: keep separately from WID3700 because this card answers a specific usage/confusability question about animal-sound verbs.

column5: 1. Containing grit or having a rough, sandy texture. 2. Showing courage and determination. 3. In art/media, realistic in a harsh, raw, or unglamorized way.
column6: grainy, sandy, rough; tough, determined; raw, hard-edged, realistic
column7: The sauce tasted gritty. / It was a gritty comeback after a terrible first half. / The series has a gritty, street-level tone.
column8: FIX: 'gritty' does not mean 'core/essential'; that association belongs to 'nitty-gritty', a separate expression meaning practical/basic details.

column5: Bored, tired, cynical, or no longer impressed because of too much experience, repetition, or exposure.
column7: After reviewing hundreds of nearly identical shows, he became jaded. / The city's constant nightlife eventually left her jaded rather than excited.
column8: Usually emotional/attitudinal fatigue from overexposure, not simply physical tiredness.

column5: To embarrass or humiliate someone, especially by making their mistake, weakness, or inferiority obvious; sometimes by outperforming them conspicuously.
column6: embarrass, humiliate, outshine, make someone look bad
column7: I didn't mean to show him up in front of the whole team. / Her flawless performance showed up the more experienced players.
column8: Different from 'show up' = arrive/appear. Construction: show + PERSON + up.

column5: 1. Arrive and stop, especially a vehicle. 2. Attract or draw people, attention, business, etc. 3. Earn or receive money. 4. Move something inward or closer.
column6: arrive; attract, draw; earn, bring in; move inward
column7: The train pulled in at noon. / The festival pulled in thousands of visitors. / The film pulled in $50 million worldwide.
column8: Highly polysemous; context decides. Compare 'bring in' for revenue and 'draw' for attracting crowds.

column5: (n.) Delicate skill, tact, subtlety, or refined technique in handling a difficult situation. (v.) To handle, maneuver, or achieve something skillfully and subtly, sometimes by finding a clever workaround.
column6: tact, dexterity, subtlety, skill; maneuver, manage deftly
column7: She handled the awkward question with finesse. / We finessed the layout by reducing the spacing slightly.
column8: Can be admiring or slightly skeptical if it implies clever maneuvering around a problem rather than solving it directly.

column5: Able to increase or decrease in size, capacity, workload, or scope effectively; especially, a system/business can grow without requiring disproportionate cost or losing unacceptable performance.
column7: The architecture is scalable enough to handle ten times the current traffic. / They want a business model that is scalable beyond one city.
column8: Not simply 'can be resized'. In computing/business, scalability concerns how well something handles growth in demand, users, data, operations, etc.

column5: Laughing My Ass Off; used online to express strong amusement.
column7: That joke had me lmao.
column8: Informal chat/SNS expression; stronger than 'LOL'. 日本語では「爆笑した」。
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::slang usage::internet_slang topic::internet

column5: Rolling On the Floor Laughing My Ass Off; used online to express extreme amusement.
column7: That video had me roflmao.
column8: Combines ROFL and LMAO; stronger laughter intensity than 'lmao'. 日本語では「床を転げ回るほど爆笑」。
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::informal topic::internet

column5: A person who records, recounts, or documents events, often over time and sometimes in a formal historical chronicle.
column7: She became the unofficial chronicler of the local music scene.
column8: Can be literal/historical or figurative for a writer/journalist/artist who persistently documents a place, era, movement, or community.

column2: walk the walk / talk the talk
column5: To act in a way that proves one's stated beliefs, claims, or promises; 'walk the walk' is often contrasted with 'talk the talk', meaning speak convincingly without necessarily acting.
column6: practice what you preach, back up words with actions, follow through
column7: If the company really cares about sustainability, it needs to walk the walk, not just talk the talk.
column8: NORMALIZATION: base idiom 'walk the walk'; WID3744 is another related card. Retain both for now because one may serve as an inflected/source-form reinforcement rather than deleting automatically.

column5: Concerned with explaining, presenting, or expressing the meaning/significance of something rather than merely stating facts.
column7: The museum uses interpretive panels to explain the site's history. / Her performance is highly interpretive rather than literal.
column8: Common combinations: interpretive display/signage, interpretive dance, interpretive framework, interpretive reading. 'Interpretative' is a variant.

column2: choose/pick a day / choose that day
column5: To select a particular day or date. 'Choose that day' is grammatical when a specific previously mentioned day is being selected, but it is not a fixed scheduling expression.
column6: pick a day, choose a date, settle on a day, set a date
column7: Let's pick a day that works for everyone. / We looked at the calendar and chose that day for the kickoff.
column8: FIX: teach the productive construction rather than treating 'choose that day' as a phrase. For scheduling, 'pick a date', 'settle on a day', and 'set a date' are often more natural.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::dating topic::decision-making topic::grammar topic::construction discovery::resolution

column5: 1. A soothing or healing ointment/preparation. 2. Figuratively, something that comforts, calms, or relieves emotional pain or distress.
column7: Use lip balm before going out in the cold. / Her message was a balm after a terrible week.
column8: Common figurative frames: a balm to/for + pain/soul/nerves; soothing balm. Related adjective 'balmy' has different senses and should not be inferred directly.

column5: To work, walk, or continue through something with sustained effort when it is difficult, tiring, or tedious; as a noun, a long exhausting task/journey.
column6: toil, grind, trudge, plow through; arduous task
column7: We slogged through three hours of paperwork. / The last mile was a real slog.
column8: Focuses on sustained arduous effort. Compare 'plod' = move/proceed slowly and heavily; 'slog' = labor through difficulty.

column5: To walk with slow, heavy steps; figuratively, to continue working or progressing slowly and laboriously.
column6: trudge, lumber, trample along; grind away
column7: We plodded through the mud. / I kept plodding through the report one section at a time.
column8: Emphasizes slow, heavy progress more than overall hardship. Compare slog = work through something arduous.

column5: A house where people engage in sexual activity with sex workers.
column7: The district was once known for its brothels before the reforms.
column8: Historical/legal term; registers vary by region and era (e.g., red‑light district). 日本語では「売春宿」。

column5: A small salamander in the family Salamandridae; many species are semiaquatic or aquatic as adults. In some species, the terrestrial juvenile stage is called an eft.
column6: salamander (broader category), eft (juvenile stage in some species)
column7: We found a newt under a damp log near the pond.
column8: FIX: newts are salamanders, but not all salamanders are newts. Japanese イモリ usually corresponds to newt, while ヤモリ is a gecko (a reptile), so they should not be conflated.

column5: An ordinary, typical, non-specialist person, traditionally framed as an ordinary man.
column6: ordinary person, regular guy, person in the street, everyday person
column7: The article explains the tax change in terms the average Joe can understand.
column8: Casual and gendered/traditional. 'Average Jane' exists as a playful female counterpart; in neutral/formal writing prefer 'ordinary person', 'average person', or 'member of the public'.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::formal usage::informal usage::casual usage::playful usage::specialist discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: 1. Sexually deviant in a way the speaker condemns—strongly judgmental/derogatory. 2. Distorted, corrupted, or diverted from an original proper purpose or meaning.
column6: depraved, sexually deviant (sensitive); distorted, corrupted, warped
column7: The original goal was perverted into a tool for personal gain. / Calling a person 'perverted' is a harsh sexual/moral judgment.
column8: Use with care. In nonsexual abstract contexts, 'perverted' can mean twisted/corrupted, but 'distorted' or 'corrupted' is often clearer and less loaded.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::derogatory usage::evaluative topic::grammar discovery::evaluation

column5: (n.) An amount beyond what is necessary, normal, desirable, or allowed; also excessive behavior/indulgence. (adj.) More than needed or allowed.
column7: Trim the excess from the budget. / He regretted the excesses of the weekend. / Airlines charge for excess baggage.
column8: Insurance: BrE 'excess' often corresponds to AmE 'deductible'. Common plural 'excesses' = immoderate behavior. Pronunciation/stress differs between noun/adjective in some usage.

column5: A very wealthy, powerful, and influential person in a particular industry or field of business.
column7: A media magnate bought the newspaper chain.
column8: Common compounds: media magnate, oil magnate, shipping magnate, tech magnate. Stronger than simply 'rich person' because influence/power is central.

column5: English does not normally use 'someone in excess' to mean a person who habitually overdoes things. More natural choices are 'an excessive person' in limited contexts, 'over-the-top', 'too much', 'extra' (slang), or a specific description such as 'overly dramatic'.
column6: over-the-top, excessive, too much, extra (slang), overly dramatic
column7: He's a bit over-the-top—every small problem becomes a crisis. / She's so extra about birthday parties.
column8: NORMALIZATION: 'someone in excess' is not a standard reusable phrase for this meaning. Choose the adjective that names the excess: overly dramatic, extravagant, excessive, intense, etc.

column5: (n.) A fastening device for a door, gate, lid, etc. (v.) Fasten with a latch. 'Latch onto' means grasp, attach oneself to, become strongly interested in, or seize on an idea/opportunity.
column6: catch, fastener; fasten; seize on, cling to, attach to
column7: She latched the gate. / The press quickly latched onto the rumor. / The child latched onto his mother's arm.
column8: Productive distinction: literal latch; phrasal 'latch onto + idea/person/opportunity'.

column5: Describes someone whose emotional development, expression, coping, or relational skills are perceived as unusually limited or immature.
column6: emotionally immature, emotionally underdeveloped, emotionally restricted
column7: The character is emotionally stunted and avoids vulnerability by turning everything into a joke.
column8: Can sound judgmental or quasi-clinical; it is descriptive, not a formal diagnosis. Prefer specific behavior descriptions when precision or sensitivity matters.

column5: Temporarily shocked, dazed, or unable to react normally because of surprise, emotion, or a physical blow.
column7: She stood there stunned after hearing the result. / He was briefly stunned by the impact.
column8: NORMALIZATION: 'stunned person' is a compositional phrase; teach the reusable adjective. Can be physical or emotional.

column5: So overwhelmed by an emotional event that one is temporarily speechless, dazed, or unable to respond normally.
column7: He was emotionally stunned by the sudden announcement and couldn't answer at first.
column8: INTENTIONAL-NUANCE CHECK: retain separately from general WID3738 because this card isolates the emotional-overwhelm sense rather than merely repeating the adjective.

column5: So intense, extreme, moving, beautiful, terrible, etc. that ordinary language seems inadequate to express it.
column6: indescribable, inexpressible, ineffable, impossible to put into words
column7: I was grateful beyond words. / The destruction was horrific beyond words.
column8: Works with positive or negative emotion. Common patterns: be beyond words; + adjective beyond words ('beautiful beyond words').

column2: translate X from A into/to B
column5: For languages, 'translate X from A into B' is a classic explicit source→target construction; 'translate X from A to B' is also common. Beyond language, 'translate into' often emphasizes transformation into a result/form, while 'translate to' often emphasizes correspondence, effect, or applicability.
column7: She translated the novel from Japanese into English. / That advantage doesn't always translate to higher sales. / The idea translated well into animation.
column8: Do not overstate a rigid rule: both 'into' and 'to' occur in language translation. Productive patterns differ by context: translate into results/action/value; translate to another audience/context/medium.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::language_learning topic::construction discovery::contrast discovery::emphasis

column5: To demonstrate through action that one's stated beliefs, promises, or claims are genuine; to practice what one preaches.
column6: practice what you preach, back up words with actions, follow through
column7: It's easy to promise better service; now the company has to walk the walk.
column8: INTENTIONAL-RELATED CARD CHECK: WID3721 teaches the paired contrast 'walk the walk / talk the talk'; retain this card as the clean headword/retrieval card rather than deleting it.

column5: The process or system of dividing content into pages; in publishing, arranging/numbering pages, and in web/software interfaces, splitting result sets/content into separate navigable pages.
column6: page division, page numbering, paged navigation
column7: The search results use pagination with 20 items per page. / The editor checked the pagination before the book went to print.
column8: Web pagination commonly contrasts with infinite scroll or 'load more'. APIs may also use pagination to return large result sets in chunks.

column5: 1. Position or distribute troops, equipment, people, or resources so they are ready for use. 2. In software, release/install a build or service into a target environment where it can run.
column6: position, station, allocate; release, roll out, put into production
column7: The company deployed extra staff during the launch. / We'll deploy the new version to production tonight.
column8: Computing frame: deploy X to + environment (production/staging/cloud). Broader business use: deploy capital/resources/personnel.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::technology topic::debate topic::environment discovery::resource_allocation discovery::release discovery::debate_language

column5: Made more modest or less self-important by an experience; also commonly used to express gratitude when receiving praise, support, or recognition. In harsher contexts, 'humble' as a verb can mean defeat or lower someone's pride/status.
column6: made modest, grateful, chastened; defeated (contextual verb sense)
column7: I was humbled by how many people offered to help. / The heavily favored team was humbled by the underdogs.
column8: FIX: 'humiliated' is not a normal synonym for the positive 'I feel humbled' sense. Humbled can be appreciative/modest without shame.

column5: Emotionally disturbed, shocked, frightened, or unsettled; also the past participle of physically shake.
column7: He was visibly shaken after the near miss. / She sounded shaken but said she was okay.
column8: Common emotional frame: be shaken by + EVENT. 'Shaken up' often emphasizes temporary emotional disturbance.

column5: To set or mark the boundaries or limits of something. In computing/data, to separate fields or items using a delimiter such as a comma, tab, or pipe.
column6: bound, define, mark off; separate with delimiters
column7: The fields are delimited by commas. / The study area was delimited by the river and two highways.
column8: NORMALIZATION: use base verb 'delimit'. Related terms: delimiter, delimited text, comma-delimited.

column5: A place, system, or container where things are stored or accumulated; in computing, a managed storage location for source code, packages, artifacts, data, etc.
column6: storehouse, archive, storage location; repo (informal tech)
column7: The documents are kept in a digital repository. / Push the change to the Git repository.
column8: A Git repository is a specific version-control repository, not simply any central folder. 'Repo' is common informal tech shorthand.

column5: To arrange things in alternating order or insert layers/items between other layers/items.
column7: The book interleaves historical chapters with present-day scenes. / The pages were interleaved with protective tissue.
column8: Computing uses include memory/data interleaving. NORMAL lexical family: interleave (verb), interleaved (adj./past participle).

column5: Memorizing material primarily through repetition, often with limited emphasis on understanding or application.
column7: Rote memorization can help with forms and vocabulary, but it should be combined with meaningful use.
column8: INTENTIONAL-DUPLICATE CHECK: WID3502 already covers this phrase in depth. Retain rather than delete automatically because this later card may reflect intentional reinforcement; if a future global dedupe pass is desired, compare provenance/order before removal.

column5: 'Rote' is mechanical repetition used for learning; 'by rote' means by repeated memorization, often without deep understanding.
column7: We learned the multiplication table by rote. / He could recite the speech by rote but couldn't explain the argument.
column8: Usually appears in 'by rote', 'rote learning', or 'rote memorization'. Rarely used as a free-standing countable noun.

column5: Slang for a man who pays for sexual services.
column6: sex buyer, client (of a sex worker)
column7: The police arrested several johns during the sting operation.
column8: US/Canada slang; can also mean ‘toilet’ in US slang. 日本語では「買春客」。
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::informal topic::business topic::work discovery::professional_context

column2: go out on a limb / reach out
column5: 'Go out on a limb' means put oneself in a risky or vulnerable position, often to support a belief or person. 'Reach out' means contact, offer support, or extend help. 'Reach out on a limb' is a blend/creative combination, not a standard idiom.
column6: take a risk, stick one's neck out; contact, offer help
column7: I'll go out on a limb and say the sequel will be better. / She reached out to him after hearing the news.
column8: FIX: do not teach 'reach out on a limb' as a conventional phrase. If a source deliberately blends the two images, preserve it as wordplay and explain the standard expressions behind it.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::idiom usage::debate-friendly topic::debate topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::risk discovery::support discovery::evaluation discovery::debate_language

column5: A person who shams—someone who pretends, feigns, or presents something false; a faker or pretender.
column7: The old text dismisses him as a shammer and a fraud.
column8: Rare/dated compared with 'faker', 'fraud', 'impostor', or 'phony'. Useful mainly when encountered in older or unusual sources.

column5: To confront, acknowledge, and deal seriously with a difficult fact, problem, consequence, history, or powerful force.
column6: confront, come to terms with, face up to, grapple with, address
column7: The industry is reckoning with years of poor labor practices. / She had to reckon with the consequences of her decision.
column8: NORMALIZATION: base form 'reckon with'. Common in moral/social contexts: reckon with the past, consequences, legacy. Separate sense 'a force/person to be reckoned with' = formidable.

column5: Noticeably delayed, slow to respond, or affected by lag, especially in games, video calls, interfaces, networks, or devices.
column7: The controls feel laggy whenever the frame rate drops. / The video call got really laggy.
column8: Informal but very common in tech/gaming speech. Depending cause, 'slow', 'high-latency', 'stuttering', or 'low frame rate' may be more precise.

column5: A sharp, witty, surprising, or memorable remark, especially a punchy joke, comeback, or criticism; more broadly, a striking surprise or twist.
column6: quip, barb, one-liner, comeback, punch line; surprise
column7: She ended the speech with a zinger that got the biggest laugh. / The final zinger is that the supposedly cheap option costs more overall.
column8: Tone can be admiring ('great line') or critical if the remark is cutting.

column5: To increase the level, rate, scale, intensity, production, staffing, effort, or activity gradually or deliberately.
column6: increase, scale up, step up, intensify, boost
column7: The factory ramps up production before the holidays. / We need to ramp up testing before launch.
column8: NORMALIZATION: use base form 'ramp up'. Can be transitive or intransitive: ramp up production; production ramps up.

column5: A nagging unresolved thought, curiosity, question, or sense of incompleteness that keeps demanding attention.
column6: nagging thought, unresolved curiosity, cognitive itch
column7: That unexplained detail gave me a mental itch I couldn't stop thinking about.
column8: Creative/productive metaphor rather than a fixed idiom. Often pairs naturally with 'scratch the itch' = satisfy the curiosity or urge.

column5: Focused on the future and on anticipating, planning for, or shaping what comes next rather than only reacting to the present or past.
column7: They adopted a forward-looking policy on energy and infrastructure.
column8: Common in business, policy, strategy, investing, and design. Does not automatically mean 'good'; it describes orientation toward future conditions.

column5: To deprive someone of something valuable, desirable, or important, either literally through robbery or figuratively by causing them to lose an opportunity, quality, experience, time, dignity, etc.
column6: deprive someone of, strip someone of, take away
column7: The injury robbed her of the chance to compete. / Constant worry robbed him of sleep.
column8: Productive frame: rob + PERSON + of + THING. Often figurative and does not require literal theft.
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative topic::construction discovery::figurative_extension discovery::evaluation

column5: A person from the countryside viewed in contrast with more urban, sophisticated people; can be gently humorous or patronizing depending tone.
column6: rural relative, provincial person; country bumpkin (much more insulting)
column7: He joked that he felt like a country cousin at the fashionable city party.
column8: Somewhat dated. 'Country bumpkin' is more openly derogatory and implies ignorance/clumsiness; do not treat the two as equal-strength synonyms.
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::dated usage::humorous usage::derogatory usage::evaluative topic::communication discovery::contrast

column5: A person, event, fact, or comment that ruins or sharply reduces a good mood, excitement, fun, or enthusiasm.
column7: The rain was a buzzkill, but we stayed outside anyway. / Don't be a buzzkill—let them celebrate.
column8: Can refer to a person or thing. 'Killjoy' focuses more on a person; 'downer' can be a depressing event/topic.

column5: 1. A member of the extinct dinosaur groups of reptiles. 2. Figuratively, a person, organization, technology, or practice considered old-fashioned, obsolete, or resistant to change.
column7: That software is a dinosaur by modern standards. / He jokes that he's a dinosaur who still prints every document.
column8: Figurative use can be teasing or insulting. Literal zoological sense is far broader than 'large extinct reptile'; dinosaurs ranged greatly in size.
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::dated usage::figurative topic::technology discovery::figurative_extension

column5: A person viewed as old-fashioned, conventional, fussy, or resistant to new ideas, fashions, or fun.
column6: old fogey, stick-in-the-mud, square (dated), traditionalist (more neutral)
column7: Don't be such a fuddy-duddy—try the new place with us.
column8: Usually teasing/humorous rather than vicious, but still potentially insulting. Often evokes age/conservatism stereotypes.

column5: A 'compilation album' is any album assembled from previously released or otherwise separately sourced tracks rather than conceived as one original album. An 'anthology' is a type of curated collection, often broader or more archival/comprehensive in scope, but the terms can overlap and are not separated by a strict rule.
column7: The label released a compilation of the band's singles. / The box-set anthology includes hits, B-sides, demos, and rare live tracks.
column8: FIX: do not define anthology as necessarily covering an entire career or compilation as necessarily hits/theme-based. In music marketing, usage varies; 'anthology' often signals breadth/retrospective prestige, while 'compilation' is the general category.
column12: entry::term entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::specialist topic::media topic::music topic::language_learning discovery::terminology discovery::contrast discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: With the understanding that the person choosing to proceed accepts the possibility of harm, loss, failure, or other consequences.
column6: at your own peril, taking responsibility for the risk, proceed at your own risk
column7: Use the unofficial patch at your own risk. / Visitors enter the trail at their own risk.
column8: Common warning wording: 'Proceed/use/enter at your own risk.' Legal effect varies by jurisdiction/context; the phrase itself does not automatically eliminate another party's legal responsibility.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::prepositional_phrase discovery::risk discovery::warning discovery::possibility

column5: No longer included on a literal list or, figuratively, removed from consideration, eligibility, selection, or priority.
column6: removed, excluded, no longer under consideration
column7: After the price increase, that hotel is off the list. / His name was taken off the candidate list.
column8: Compositional phrase. Common verbs: be off the list, take/remove X off/from the list, cross X off the list.

column5: A major advance, discovery, or achievement that overcomes an important barrier or creates significant new progress; adjectivally, 'breakthrough' can describe such a development.
column6: major advance, discovery, leap forward, milestone
column7: The treatment was hailed as a medical breakthrough. / Researchers reported breakthrough results.
column8: Stronger than ordinary 'progress'; implies crossing a barrier or achieving something previously difficult/unavailable.

column5: The relationships, loyalties, obligations, experiences, or shared values that connect people or groups and keep them attached to one another.
column6: bonds, connections, shared ties, social bonds
column7: Despite their arguments, family history remained one of the ties that bind them.
column8: Often has a literary/emotional tone and may imply that bonds can both support and constrain.

column5: To cause a strong feeling of recognition, agreement, sympathy, or emotional resonance in someone.
column6: resonate with, hit home, connect with, speak to
column7: That scene struck a chord with me because I'd gone through something similar.
column8: Productive frame: strike a chord with + PERSON/AUDIENCE. Music metaphor. Compare 'hit home' = often makes truth/significance feel personally real.

column5: Several nouns can describe someone who fakes or falsely presents something, but they differ: a faker pretends or produces something false; a fraud is a deceptive person or thing; an impostor pretends to be another person or to hold an identity/status they do not have; a charlatan falsely claims special knowledge or skill; a pretender claims a role, title, or quality without full legitimacy.
column6: faker, fraud, impostor, charlatan, pretender, phony
column7: He's a fraud who lied about his credentials. / The impostor pretended to be a doctor. / The so-called healer was exposed as a charlatan.
column8: NORMALIZATION: replace the question-form headword with a reusable contrast card. Standard spelling is 'impostor' or 'imposter'; both occur. Choose the noun according to what is being faked.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::noun_phrase topic::crime topic::language_learning discovery::title_language discovery::contrast discovery::evaluation

column5: To gradually but firmly establish an idea, feeling, or habit in a person's mind.
column7: Parents try to instill good values in their children.
column8:
Nuance differences:
- instill: gradual, steady introduction of values or attitudes (日本語: 徐々に植え付ける)
- implant: put deeply into (often physical or strong emotional idea) (日本語: 埋め込む)
- impart: communicate or bestow (knowledge/information) (日本語: 伝える)
- inculcate: teach persistently by repetition (日本語: 繰り返し教え込む)
Examples:
• The teacher instilled confidence in her students.
• The coach implanted a sense of discipline in the team.
• The mentor imparted wisdom to the new employees.
• The parent inculcated table manners in their children.

column5: A beveled edge is an edge cut or shaped at an angle rather than at 90 degrees to the main faces. A bevel is the angled surface/cut itself; as a verb, to bevel means create such an angled edge.
column7: The mirror has a beveled edge. / The carpenter beveled the edge of the tabletop.
column8: NORMALIZATION: 'beveled edge' is more natural than 'bevel edge' as the descriptive phrase. A chamfer is a specific flat beveled transition, so the terms overlap but are not always identical.

column2: a cascade of / trigger a cascade of
column5: A 'cascade of X' is a series of events, effects, messages, failures, etc. that follow one another, often because one triggers the next. To cause this, say 'trigger/set off/cause a cascade of X'.
column6: chain reaction, series, succession; trigger a chain of
column7: The announcement triggered a cascade of reactions online. / One server failure caused a cascade of errors.
column8: FIX: 'make a cascade of' is not the usual reusable construction. The waterfall image motivates the figurative sense.

column2: follow your plan to the letter
column5: To follow instructions or a plan exactly as written or intended.
column7: She followed her doctor’s advice to the letter.
column8: Emphasizes strict, literal compliance. 日本語では「一字一句忠実に従う」。

column5: Noun: a large piece of cut wood. Verb: to record information or events.
column7: The sailor logged the ship’s position every hour.
column8: Nautical origins for record-keeping; IT usage for system events. 日本語では「丸太」「記録する」。

column5: Prepared mentally or emotionally for an expected letdown.
column7: I was braced for disappointment after hearing the rumors.
column8: From brace oneself = prepare for impact/difficulty. 日本語では「失望に備える」。

column2: serve someone up / serve up someone
column5: To present, hand over, expose, or make someone available to another person/group, sometimes for criticism, punishment, exploitation, or some unwanted role.
column6: hand over, offer up, deliver, sacrifice, expose
column7: The scandal served up an easy scapegoat for the press. / They practically served him up to the critics.
column8: Context determines the implication. It can suggest treating a person as something to be consumed/used, but it is not a fixed phrasal verb meaning only 'make someone a scapegoat'.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::figurative usage::journalistic discovery::criticism

column2: serve someone up to/for something (source construction)
column5: A contextual extension of 'serve someone up': present or put someone forward so that they become available for a task, role, audience, criticism, punishment, etc. The exact meaning comes from the following complement.
column6: put someone forward, hand someone over, present someone, volunteer someone (contextual)
column7: They served me up to give the closing speech. / The show served the rookie up for ridicule.
column8: FIX: not a standard phrasal verb with the fixed meaning 'arrange for someone to perform a task'. Keep as a construction/source card because the complement to/for + PURPOSE/RECIPIENT supplies the interpretation.

column5: Harsh or jarring because of a lack of harmony; disagreeing or incongruous.
column7: The discordant notes made the song unpleasant to hear.
column8: Can describe sounds, ideas, colors, or relationships. 日本語では「不調和な」「対立する」。

column5: Verb: to weaken or undermine; to sell at a lower price. Noun: a cut made underneath something.
column7: Cheap imports undercut domestic manufacturers.
column8: Figurative and literal meanings; also hairstyle term. 日本語では「切り下げる」「弱体化させる」。

column5: Noun: a break or burst in something. Verb: to break or burst suddenly.
column7: The pipe ruptured due to extreme pressure.
column8: Also used figuratively for relationships (‘rupture in diplomatic relations’). 日本語では「破裂」「決裂」。

column5: Refreshing and invigorating; or causing one to prepare for something challenging.
column7: The bracing sea air revived him.
column8: Can refer to weather, actions, or attitudes that strengthen or prepare. 日本語では「爽快な」「身構えさせる」。

column5: Verb: to shout or cry out loudly. Noun: a loud shout or cry.
column7: He hollered across the street to get her attention.
column8: Southern U.S. dialect also uses 'holler' to mean a small valley. 日本語では「大声を出す」「呼びかける」。

column5: Delve into: to investigate, research, or explore something deeply and methodically. Dive into: to begin something eagerly, energetically, or without hesitation.
column7: She delved into the archives for her research, while he dove into his new project with enthusiasm.
column8: Nuance: 'delve' = methodical depth; 'dive' = energetic entry. Delve emphasizes depth, detail, and thoroughness; often about study, research, or analysis. e.g., “delve into history” (歴史を掘り下げる). Dive emphasizes speed, enthusiasm, and immersion; often about starting an activity. e.g., “dive into work” (仕事に飛び込む). 日本語では「delve into＝掘り下げる」「dive into＝勢いよく取り組む」。
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase topic::research topic::finance topic::language_learning discovery::contrast

column5: A claim that some aspect of how humans conceptualize, divide, measure, or socially organize time is constructed rather than simply given in exactly that form by nature.
column6: time is socially constructed (stronger/specific claim), time is a human construct
column7: When people say 'time is a construct,' they may be talking about calendars and social conventions rather than denying physical change or temporal order.
column8: FIX: add the article 'a'. Avoid defining the phrase as the settled claim that time itself is merely human-created; philosophy and physics distinguish multiple concepts of time, and 'construct' claims vary in strength.

column5: To propose or suggest something for consideration.
column7: They put forward a plan to improve public transport.
column8: Also means to present oneself or one's ideas prominently. 日本語では「提案する」「前面に出す」。

column5: A slant is a slope or angle away from horizontal/vertical; figuratively, it is a particular biased angle or point of view. 'Slanted' can mean physically angled or biased.
column6: angle, slope; bias, spin; tilted, skewed
column7: The roof rises at a steep slant. / The article gives a slanted account of the dispute.
column8: NORMALIZATION: 'slanting manner' is not a useful fixed phrase. For physical posture say 'at an angle/on a slant'; for biased presentation use 'slanted' or 'a slant on X'.

column5: Not straight or symmetrical; biased or distorted.
column7: The statistics were skewed by incomplete data.
column8: Used for physical alignment or abstract data/opinions. 日本語では「歪んだ」「偏った」。

column2: at the same time: simultaneously / concurrently / at once
column3: /æt ðə seɪm taɪm; ˌsaɪməlˈteɪniəsli; kənˈkɝəntli; æt wʌns/
column5: 'Simultaneously' means at exactly or effectively the same time. 'Concurrently' means during overlapping periods or in parallel, not necessarily beginning/ending at the same instant. 'At once' can mean simultaneously, but also immediately.
column7: Both alarms went off simultaneously. / She was working on two projects concurrently. / He tried to answer both questions at once.
column8: NORMALIZATION: replace question-form headword with a reusable contrast card.

column5: Adjective: emotionally or financially committed. Verb: past tense of invest.
column7: She was deeply invested in the success of the project.
column8: Emotional investment refers to personal attachment, not just money. 日本語では「投資した」「感情的に関与している」。

column2: pin something on someone / pin the blame on
column3: /pɪn ˈsʌmθɪŋ ɑn ˈsʌmwʌn; pɪn ðə bleɪm ɑn/
column5: To attribute blame, responsibility, a crime, or a negative outcome to someone, especially when the attribution may be unfair or strategically convenient.
column6: blame, lay/put the blame on, frame (stronger/criminal), saddle someone with blame
column7: They tried to pin the mistake on the intern. / He pinned the blame on inadequate training.
column8: Productive frame: pin + BLAME/CRIME/PROBLEM + on + PERSON/CAUSE. 'Throw someone under the bus' is related when sacrificing another person to protect oneself, but it is not an exact synonym in every case.
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::construction topic::crime discovery::criticism

column5: To attack someone verbally with strong, angry criticism; 'tear into' can also mean attack physically or begin eating/doing something vigorously depending context.
column6: berate, lambaste, lash out at, rip into, come down hard on
column7: The coach laid into the team after the loss. / The reviewer tore into the film for its sloppy ending.
column8: NORMALIZATION: teach the core pair cleanly. 'Pick on', 'put down', 'run down', and 'call out' have different meanings and should not be treated as interchangeable synonyms.

column5: Willing to accept different opinions, beliefs, or behaviors without prejudice.
column7: She is broad-minded about different cultural practices.
column8: Opposite: narrow-minded. 日本語では「心が広い」「寛容な」。

column5: To lift or pick up something quickly, often in one motion.
column7: He scooped up the toys before guests arrived.
column8: Can also mean acquiring quickly (e.g., 'scoop up a bargain'). 日本語では「すくい上げる」「素早く集める」。

column5: Permanently; forever, with no intention or expectation of returning to the previous state.
column6: permanently, forever, once and for all
column7: She left the city for good. / Is the restaurant closed for good?
column8: FIX: 'running for good' is not a general fixed phrase. The reusable expression is 'for good', which attaches to many verbs: leave, quit, close, move away, disappear, etc.

column5: Sarcastic, critical, or mocking in an unkind but often witty way.
column7: He made a snarky comment about her new haircut.
column8: Colloquial. Often playful but can be hurtful. 日本語では「嫌味っぽい」「皮肉屋な」。
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::colloquial usage::slang usage::playful usage::critical usage::informal

column5: Short for 'in real life'; referring to events or situations in the physical world rather than online.
column7: We finally met irl after months of chatting online.
column8: Used in online communication to contrast with virtual interactions. 日本語では「現実世界で」。
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::abbreviation usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::informal topic::internet

column5: Relating to earthquakes; or having a very great effect or impact.
column7: The policy change had seismic consequences for the industry.
column8: From Greek 'seismos' = earthquake. 日本語では「地震の」「重大な影響を与える」。

column5: To be very angry and express it forcefully.
column7: The boss was breathing fire after the mistake.
column8: Imagery from dragons exhaling flames. 日本語では「激怒する」。

column5: To burn slowly without flame; or to have strong, suppressed emotions.
column7: The campfire logs smoldered until morning.
column8: Emotions like anger or passion can 'smolder'. 日本語では「くすぶる」「感情を内に秘める」。

column5: A small, glowing piece of coal or wood in a dying fire.
column7: Only a few embers remained after the fire died down.
column8: Figurative: lingering feelings or remnants. 日本語では「燃え残りの炭火」。

column5: Noun: a temporary period of quiet or inactivity. Verb: to soothe or calm, often by gentle sounds or motions.
column7: There was a lull in the conversation before she spoke again.
column8: Verb often used with babies ('lull a baby to sleep'). 日本語では「一時的な静けさ」「安心させる」。

column5: Verb: to smile in an irritatingly smug, conceited, or silly way. Noun: such a smile.
column7: He smirked when he realized he had won the bet.
column8: Often implies arrogance or self-satisfaction. 日本語では「にやりと笑う（皮肉・優越感）」。

column5: To reveal one's innermost thoughts and feelings.
column7: She bared her soul to her best friend.
column8: Often involves trust and vulnerability. 日本語では「心の内をさらけ出す」。

column5: To speak while someone else is speaking, preventing them from being heard.
column7: He kept talking over me during the meeting.
column8: Considered rude in conversation. 日本語では「話を遮る」「かき消すように話す」。

column2: grill / give someone the third degree / pump someone for information
column3: /ɡrɪl; ɡɪv ˈsʌmwʌn ðə θɝd dɪˈɡri; pʌmp ˈsʌmwʌn fər ˌɪnfərˈmeɪʃən/
column5: 'Grill someone' means question them intensely and persistently. 'Give someone the third degree' means subject them to severe/prolonged questioning. 'Pump someone for information' means question them in order to extract information, often informally.
column6: question closely, interrogate, quiz, cross-examine (legal), press for answers
column7: My parents grilled me about where I'd been. / The detective gave him the third degree. / Reporters pumped the witness for details.
column8: NORMALIZATION: 'phrasal verb for interrogate' is a search-question card, not a reusable headword. Also, 'grill' and 'cross-examine' are not phrasal verbs. 'Sweat someone' can mean pressure/interrogate but is more slangy/contextual.
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::journalistic topic::media topic::law topic::testing topic::language_learning discovery::contrast

column5: Unable to be explained or accounted for
column6: unaccountable, unexplainable, incomprehensible, , mysterious, baffling unfathomable
column7: His sudden disappearance was inexplicable. for some inexplicable reason her mind went completely blank
column8: Often used for puzzling or irrational events. 日本語では「説明できない」「不可解な」。

column5: To take responsibility for something; to rise to the occasion, especially when action is required.
column6: take responsibility, rise to the challenge
column7: When the team needed a leader, she stepped up to the plate.
column8: From baseball: stepping into the batter’s box to face the pitcher. 日本語では「責任を引き受ける」「挑戦に臨む」。

column5: A small quantity of something, especially when added to improve flavor, character, or atmosphere.
column7:
1. Add a dash of salt to the soup.
2. Her speech had a dash of humor that kept everyone engaged.
3. This room needs a dash of color to feel more lively.

column2: small differences, completely different meanings: thing for/about; plans/a plan; an only child/only a child; had fun/was fun
column5: A contrast set showing how a small change in preposition, number, article placement, or grammatical structure can produce a substantially different meaning: 'have a thing for X' expresses a liking or attraction, while 'have a thing about X' signals a particular issue, fixation, sensitivity, or hang-up about X; 'I have plans' commonly means I already have arrangements, while 'I have a plan' means I have a particular plan/strategy; 'I am an only child' means I have no siblings, while 'I am only a child' means I am merely/still a child; 'I had fun' means I enjoyed myself, while 'I was fun' describes me as enjoyable, entertaining, or good company.
column6: have a thing for/about; have plans/have a plan; an only child/only a child; had fun/was fun
column7: I have a thing for dogs, but she has a thing about dogs. / Sorry, I have plans tonight. / I have a plan for how we can fix this. / I am an only child. / I am only a child—how was I supposed to know? / I had fun at the party. / I was fun at the party, apparently; everyone kept laughing at my stories.
column8: Preserve this as a multi-contrast learning card rather than the generic YouTube title. (1) 'Have a thing for someone/something' normally means have a liking, attraction, or special fondness. 'Have a thing about something' does NOT automatically mean 'hate/dislike it'; it means have a particular concern, fixation, sensitivity, hang-up, or strong feeling about it, which can be negative depending on context. Thus 'I have a thing about dogs' could suggest discomfort or an issue with dogs, but context is needed. (2) 'I have plans' is the idiomatic way to say you already have arrangements/commitments, especially when declining an invitation. 'I have a plan' means one particular plan, idea, or strategy. The plural is common for 'arrangements,' but it is not a grammatical rule that one must always use plural whenever one has a scheduled event. (3) 'an only child' is the fixed noun phrase for a person with no siblings; 'only a child' has focusing 'only' modifying 'a child' = merely/still a child. (4) 'I had fun' reports the speaker's experience of enjoyment; 'I was fun' predicates 'fun' of the speaker, meaning the speaker was enjoyable/entertaining to be with. The difference is not literally an -ed/-ing contrast; it is 'have fun' versus 'be fun.'

column5: When viewed in the broader or long-term context, rather than focusing on one small detail or event.

column5: When next June arrives; at or by that future point in time.
column6: when next June comes, by next June
column7:
Come next June, I'll have been here for five years.
Come Monday, we'll know the result.
Come summer, this place gets packed.
Come next year, the new rules will already be in effect.
column8: Productive pattern: come + time expression = when that time arrives. Common examples: come Monday, come summer, come next year, come next June. Slightly more idiomatic/literary than simply saying next Monday/next summer.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0103 | searches: come next june meaning

column5: To eat something steadily or noisily, often in small bites, especially as a snack.
column6: chew on, snack on, nibble on
column7: We munched on popcorn during the movie.
column8: Munch can be transitive ('munch an apple') or used with on ('munch on chips').
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0103 | searches: munching on meanng

column5: To disgust or repel someone.
column7: That video really grossed me out.

column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0101 | searches: gross out meaning

column5: Quiet, restrained, modest, or not drawing much attention; informally as an adverb, somewhat, secretly, or in an understated way.
column7: I'm low-key excited about the trip.

column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0107 | searches: low key meaning in social media

column7: After fertilization, the ovule develops into a seed.

column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0100 | searches: ovule

column5: To rob someone by threatening them, traditionally with a weapon.

column8: Compare stick up for someone = defend/support them; completely different meaning.

column5: Treating a serious subject with deliberately inappropriate humor or flippancy.
column7: I was being facetious—I didn't actually mean it.
column8: Likely correction of raw 'physicious.' Facetious often means joking when seriousness is expected.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0108 | searches: physicious

column5: To fail a test, course, or student; in transitive use, to give someone a failing grade.

column5: To trip or lose balance while moving; or figuratively, to speak, perform, or proceed with difficulty.
