column8: Base verb. Keep distinct from 'stumble upon/across' = discover unexpectedly.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | reviewed improved card

column5: To faint; more commonly in figurative modern use, to react with intense admiration, romantic excitement, or delight.
column7: Fans were swooning over the actor's new look.
column8: The literal fainting sense can sound old-fashioned/dramatic; swoon over someone/something is common for intense attraction or admiration.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0101, voca_0103 | searches: swoon definition

column5: To force an idea, opinion, product, or message on someone aggressively or excessively.

column8: Raw 'rammed down' is commonly part of this idiom. Strongly negative.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0102 | searches: rammed down

column5: To pull a plant out by its roots; figuratively, to force or cause someone to leave a home/community or to remove something deeply established.
column7: The move uprooted the family from the community they had known for years.
column8: Figurative senses include uproot a family/person and uproot a tradition/system/problem.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0099 | searches: uproot meaning

column5: i.e. means 'that is' and restates or specifies the same thing; e.g. means 'for example' and introduces one or more examples.
column7: Bring something waterproof, e.g., a rain jacket. We meet on the final weekday, i.e., Friday.
column8: i.e. comes from Latin id est; e.g. from exempli gratia. A useful shortcut: i.e. = in essence; e.g. = example given.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0108 | searches: i.e. or e.g. meaning

column5: To start touching another person excessively, especially in a sexual, intrusive, or unwelcome way.
column7: He got all handsy after a few drinks, and she told him to stop.
column8: Informal; often negative and implies boundary-crossing.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0108 | searches: get all handsy meaning

column5: To gradually discover, extract, clarify, or separate information, meaning, differences, or details that are difficult to see clearly.
column7: The interviewer teased out the reasons behind her decision.
column8: Often used in analysis/research: tease out implications, differences, patterns, meaning.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0102 | searches: teasing out meaning

column7: We stopped for poutine after the game.
column8: Strongly associated with Quebec and Canadian cuisine.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0104 | searches: poutine

column5: A short soft or electronic-sounding noise; in baseball, a softly hit fly ball that drops between fielders. As a verb, it can mean make such a sound or hit a bloop ball.

column7: The device made a quiet bloop. / The batter blooped a single into shallow right.
column8: FIX: do not teach 'bloop' as a general everyday verb meaning 'botch/ruin'; 'blooper' is the much more established noun for an amusing mistake. Core reusable senses here are sound + baseball.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0108 | searches: blooping meaning

column7: Oh yeah, that's the jam—turn it up.
column8: Keep this exact searched chunk alongside the base word jam. Compare 'That's my jam,' the much more common pattern meaning 'that's a song/thing I really like.' 'That's the jam' is less fixed and more context-dependent, but can enthusiastically identify something as especially good or appealing.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0108 | searches: that's the jam meaning

column5: Three related terms for obtaining consistent results again: repeatability usually emphasizes the same method and conditions; reproducibility and replicability often involve changed teams, data, methods, or settings, but their exact definitions vary by field and standards body.
column7: The paper distinguishes repeatability within one setup from reproducibility across independent setups.
column8: There is no single universal mapping across all disciplines. Interpret the three terms according to the field's stated convention. In addition to this comparison card, create separate supplemental cards for repeatability and replicability; the existing reproducibility card remains the individual reproducibility entry.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0108 | searches: reproducibility vs repeatability vs replicability

column5: To hide or remain ready and watchful until a suitable moment to attack, surprise, catch, or confront someone or something.
column7: The predator lay in wait near the edge of the water.
column8: Past tense: lay in wait; -ing: lying in wait. Can be literal or figurative: a problem may be lying in wait.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0106, voca_0107 | searches: lying in wait meaning

column5: To have something inside; to keep something within limits; to control or prevent something from spreading.
column7:
The box contains old photographs.
Firefighters managed to contain the blaze.
column8: Important senses: contain = include/hold; contain an outbreak/fire/problem = keep it from spreading; contain oneself = control emotion/reaction.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0108 | searches: contain meaning

column5: A creative way to describe an emotion, tension, idea, or problem gradually developing inside someone; adding 'in one's chest' emphasizes the bodily sensation accompanying the buildup.
column6: building up, simmering, welling up, stirring inside
column7: I could feel anger brewing inside me. / A strange mix of anxiety and excitement was brewing in my chest.
column8: NORMALIZATION: 'brewing in your chest' is not a fixed idiom. Teach the productive metaphor SOMETHING IS BREWING = something is developing, plus the optional body-location phrase 'in my chest/inside me.' Common broader uses include trouble is brewing and a storm is brewing.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0101 | searches: brewing in your chest

column5: Partial darkness/coolness from blocked light; a slight degree or color variation; in slang, subtle or indirect criticism or disrespect.
column7: Was that comment meant to throw shade at me?
column8: Internet/pop-culture: throw shade = express contempt or criticism indirectly. Also shades of meaning/color and literal shade.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0109 | searches: shade meaning

column5: Luxuriously self-indulgent, rich, or excessive; historically, morally or culturally declining through excess or luxury.
column7: The dessert was unbelievably rich and decadent.
column8: Modern everyday use is often positive/playful for rich food or luxury; older/formal use can be strongly negative: morally/culturally decayed.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0101 | searches: decadent meaning

column5: Able to be used up, sacrificed, or discarded because it is considered replaceable or not essential.
column7: The soldiers felt they were being treated as expendable.
column8: Can describe people, equipment, resources, or items intended to be consumed.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0106 | searches: expendable meaning

column5: The influence of a speaker's first-language rhythm, stress, intonation, or other prosodic patterns on pronunciation in another language.
column7: Prosodic transfer can make otherwise accurate speech sound noticeably non-native.
column8: Useful in L2 pronunciation: transfer may involve rhythm, pitch movement, stress placement, timing, or phrasing.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0102 | searches: prosodic transfer

column5: Small decorative objects or miscellaneous little items, usually of little monetary value.
column7: The shelves were crowded with souvenirs and knick-knacks.
column8: The raw 'nicks and nacks' is a phonetic/misspelled rendering. Standard spelling is knick-knacks (also knickknacks).
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0108 | searches: nicks and nacks

column5: A person sent on a special mission to represent someone, negotiate, or convey a message.
column7: The king sent an emissary to negotiate peace.
column8: 'Envoy' is especially diplomatic/formal; 'messenger' mainly carries a message; 'emissary' emphasizes being sent as an agent or representative on a mission.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | reviewed improved card

column5: Unusual in an interesting, distinctive, playful, or slightly odd way.
column7: The café has a quirky interior full of vintage signs.
column8: Often positive or affectionate, unlike weird, though context can make it mildly critical.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0109 | searches: quirky meaing

column8: Raw unperishable is understandable but nonperishable is the standard word for food/goods that do not spoil quickly.

column5: Common grammatical patterns for concur when it means agree: concur with a person, statement, finding, or opinion; or concur that + clause.

column7:
The new report concurs with previous findings.
The board concurred that the offer should be accepted.
I completely concur with what you said.
column8: Keep this as a separate pattern card because the preposition/clause structure is the part worth memorizing. Think agree with someone/something and agree that..., but in a more formal register. The bare response “I concur” is also common enough to remember.

column8: Keep the searched collocation alongside the base adjective as a narrative chunk.

column2: A dry air advisory has been issued from Houston to tuna.
column5: A deliberately nonsensical weather-report-like sentence heard by Asa in Journal with Witch when ordinary adult speech stops registering as meaningful language. The words remain audible, but their semantic connections have broken down, creating the sense of hearing sounds without truly hearing the meaning.
column6: deliberate nonsense, semantic disconnection, words without meaning
column7: “A dry air advisory has been issued from Houston to tuna.” The sentence sounds like a weather bulletin, but “Houston to tuna” makes no literal sense.
column8: Preserve this exact line because the nonsense is the point. In the scene, Asa has just lost her parents and is surrounded by relatives discussing, in a practical and emotionally cold way, who will take responsibility for her. Their speech is rendered to her as scrambled, semantically incoherent language: she can hear the sounds, but cannot emotionally process the words as meaningful communication. The weather-report syntax makes the line sound superficially normal while the content is impossible ('from Houston to tuna'), dramatizing psychological distance/dissociation from the adults' conversation. The image of a 'dry air advisory' also resonates with the dry/desert-like emotional imagery associated with Asa's isolation. Raw Japanese search: ヒューストンからマグロに乾燥注意報. User specifically wants this personally memorable anime line retained. More specifically, the keyword 'dry' also functions as important foreshadowing: it leads into the later desert-like inner landscape that visualizes Asa's loneliness. The apparently random 'dry air advisory' therefore does double work—it expresses her present inability to process the adults' words and quietly anticipates the dry, isolated emotional imagery that follows.

column5: 'Have a thing for X' usually means to be attracted to, fond of, or especially interested in X. 'Have a thing about X' means to have a particular fixation, sensitivity, hang-up, concern, or strong feeling about X; it can be negative, but does not automatically mean dislike.

column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0107 | searches: stoked about meaning

column5: To spread over, occupy, or overwhelm a place in large numbers; to exceed a planned limit of time or cost. As a noun, an overrun is an excess beyond a limit.
column7:
The garden was overrun with weeds.
The project had a major cost overrun.
column8: Common patterns: be overrun with; cost/time overrun. The verb can also describe military forces taking control of territory.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0109 | searches: overrun meaning

column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0109 | searches: lead someone down the garden path

column7: The cafeteria seemed divided into different cliques.

column10: voca_0099–0109 | reviewed improved card

column7: She coaxed him into talking about what happened.
column8: Patterns: coax someone into doing something; coax something out of someone; coax a machine into working.
column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0107 | searches: coax meaning

column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0107 | searches: deversification

column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0109 | searches: assembly area meaning

column10: voca_0099–0109 | unmatched | folders: voca_0107 | searches: lapel

column5: To cause liquid or contents to flow out; figuratively, to express feelings, words, or thoughts freely and in large quantity.

column8: Literal ecological sense + strongly negative figurative insult.

column2: 蛙化現象: coined in 2004 → popularized from around 2019
column5: The term 蛙化現象 is traced to a 2004 Japanese psychology conference presentation by Shinsuke Fujisawa; it later spread beyond the original academic sense, with online explanatory articles/videos appearing around 2019 and much broader youth/pop-culture use by the early 2020s.
column7: The term was already used academically in 2004, long before it became a widely recognized youth-culture expression.
column8: The 2004 presentation was titled 『女子が恋愛過程で遭遇する蛙化現象』. The original sense concerned aversion arising when one's romantic interest is reciprocated. Later popular usage broadened toward suddenly losing attraction because of a small behavior or perceived flaw. Thus 'when did people start using it?' has two answers: academic coinage/use in 2004, and wider internet/youth diffusion much later, around 2019 onward, with major mainstream visibility in the early 2020s.

column8: Existing WID6123 has conscientious; this card preserves the raw malformed search as a correction/memory hook. Conscious = awake/aware; conscience = moral sense; conscientious = careful/dutiful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: consciousful

column5: A dismissive metaphor for flashy, rapidly changing, attention-grabbing stimuli used to keep an audience engaged, likened to jingling keys in front of a baby; often paired online with talk of 'constant dopamine hits.'
column6: cheap stimulation, attention bait, sensory bait, constant novelty
column7: The critic complained that the editing felt like jingling keys—cuts, captions, sound effects, and constant novelty every few seconds. / Calling it 'dopamine hits' is a loose popular metaphor, not a precise measurement of dopamine release.
column8: Preserve the combined search context. The criticism is about attention capture/overstimulation. Popular 'dopamine hit' language often oversimplifies neuroscience: dopamine is involved in motivation, learning, salience, reward prediction, and more, not simply a pleasure chemical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: jingling keys / constant dopamine hits

column5: To put someone or something in danger or at serious risk.
column6: endanger, jeopardize, threaten, put at risk
column7: A prolonged strike could imperil the launch schedule. / The character's impulsive decision imperils everyone in the group.
column8: More formal/literary than endanger or put at risk. Jeopardize often focuses on chances, plans, careers, success; imperil vividly suggests exposure to danger.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: imperil meanig

column5: Relating to appeals or to a court that reviews decisions made by a lower court.
column7: The case moved from the trial court to the appellate court. / Appellate judges generally review alleged legal errors rather than retrying the entire case from scratch.
column8: Common collocations: appellate court, appellate jurisdiction, appellate review, appellate judge. Contrast trial court. Exact scope/standard of review depends on the legal system and issue.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: appellate

column5: To criticize, nag, pressure, question, or repeatedly bother someone about something they should do or have done.
column6: nag, hassle, ride, pressure, give someone a hard time
column7: My boss got on my case about the late report. / Don't get on his case—he already apologized.
column8: Especially AmE. 'Be on someone's case' can mean already be nagging/pressuring them; 'get on' emphasizes starting to do so.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119, voca_0120 | search: get on your case meaning
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::american_english discovery::criticism

column5: A narrow horizontal surface or projection, especially one sticking out from a wall, cliff, window, or other vertical surface.
column7: The cat was sitting on the window ledge. / They rested on a narrow rock ledge halfway up the cliff.
column8: Contrast ledger /ˈledʒər/. Window ledge overlaps with windowsill, though sill is specifically the bottom horizontal part of a window opening/frame.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: ledge meaning

column5: To remove or neutralize toxic substances from something; in general/wellness language, to rid the body or environment of supposed toxins.
column7: The liver helps detoxify substances in the bloodstream.
column8: In medical/scientific contexts the object and mechanism matter; commercial 'detox' claims can use the word much more loosely.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: detoxify synonym
column12: entry::word usage::scientific usage::businesslike topic::wellness topic::environment discovery::removal

column5: Extremely or unmistakably grim; here positively functions as an intensifier meaning definitely or downright.
column7: By late afternoon, the weather looked positively grim.
column8: Positively does not mean 'optimistically' here. It intensifies a negative adjective, often with slightly emphatic or literary flavor.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: positively grim meaning

column5: To feel a light prickling, buzzing, stinging, or pins-and-needles sensation; figuratively, to experience a thrill of excitement, fear, anticipation, etc.
column6: prickle, buzz, pins and needles; thrill
column7: My fingers started to tingle after being out in the cold. / I felt a tingle of excitement when the opening music started. / The spicy sauce left my lips tingling.
column8: Physical sensation can have many causes and is not itself a diagnosis. Figurative 'a tingle of excitement/fear' is common. Tingle is lighter/finer than throb or ache.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: tingle

column5: To cause one's own problem, punishment, criticism, misfortune, or other consequence through one's actions or choices.
column6: bring it upon oneself, cause one's own trouble, ask for it (more blaming), have oneself to blame
column7: He brought the criticism on himself by making promises he couldn't keep. / I feel bad for her, but some of this trouble was brought on by her own decisions.
column8: Usually negative and can sound blame-oriented. 'Bring it on yourself' is conversational; 'bring it upon yourself' is slightly more formal/dramatic. Avoid using it to dismiss harm where responsibility is complex.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: bring something on yourself meaning
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::formal usage::conversational topic::construction discovery::criticism discovery::expressing_need

column5: The act/process of getting something back or accessing stored information; in memory, bringing stored information into active use; in computing, finding and returning stored data.
column7: Flashcards strengthen retrieval because you have to produce the answer from memory. / Search indexing speeds information retrieval. / The dog was trained for game retrieval.
column8: Important learning-science sense: retrieval practice = actively recalling information, not merely rereading it. Also computing/information-retrieval and physical recovery senses.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: retrieval

column5: A mocking label for someone accused of claiming to be an incel ('involuntarily celibate') despite supposedly having realistic romantic/sexual opportunities, prior experience, or other traits that disqualify them in the speaker's view.
column7: Forum users called him a fakecel because they believed he could date if he actually tried. / The label reflects community gatekeeping about who counts as 'truly' involuntarily celibate.
column8: Incel-community jargon, not neutral social-science vocabulary. The criteria are unstable and ideological. -cel is highly productive online: fakecel, volcel, femcel, etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: fakecel meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::specialist usage::informal topic::romance topic::internet discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Used to say that an idea or possibility never entered your mind or was never considered.
column6: I never thought of it, it didn't cross my mind
column7: It never occurred to me that she might already know.
column8: Pattern: it occurs to someone that... = the thought comes into that person's mind.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: it never occurred to me meaning

column5: When approach is a noun meaning method or way of dealing with something, use approach to + noun/gerund: 'an approach to learning,' not normally 'an approach to learn.' As a verb, approach can take a direct object.
column6: method of doing, way of dealing with
column7: I like your approach to learning vocabulary. / We need a different approach to solving the problem. / We approached the problem cautiously.
column8: Here 'to' is a preposition, so it takes a noun or -ing form. Compare 'plan to do,' where to is infinitival.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: approach to doing or do

column5: An American brand known for folding knives and knife-design features; the name in a text usually refers to a Spyderco-branded knife rather than a generic knife type.
column7: The character pulled out a Spyderco—here the brand name identifies the knife, not a special generic category called a 'spyderco.'
column8: Proper brand name. Preserve because source context may use it metonymically ('a Spyderco' = a knife made by the brand). No need to learn product specifications for vocabulary purposes.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: spyderco knife

column5: A being characterized as sapient—wise or, especially in speculative fiction, possessing advanced reasoning and intellectual capacities comparable to or beyond humans.
column6: intelligent being, rational being, advanced-thinking being
column7: The treaty recognizes every sapient species as a legal person. / In fantasy and science fiction, 'sapient beings' may include humans, aliens, androids, or magical species.
column8: 'Sapient person' is grammatically possible but uncommon in ordinary speech; 'sapient being/species' is more natural in SF/worldbuilding. Do not use sapient as a simple synonym for sentient.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: sapient person

column5: To force an idea, message, belief, product, or content on someone aggressively or repeatedly, leaving little room to refuse or ignore it.
column6: force on, ram down someone's throat
column7: Viewers complained that the message was being shoved down their throats.
column8: Strongly negative metaphor; often used hyperbolically about media, advertising, ideology, or unwanted advice.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: shove it down their throat meaning

column5: Originating in and having deep historical ties to a particular land or region; especially, describing peoples who inhabited a place before colonization or later dominant settlement and maintain distinct cultural/social identities.
column7: The museum worked with Indigenous communities to revise the exhibit. / This plant is indigenous to the region. / Capitalization is common when referring to Indigenous peoples as a broad identity category.
column8: For plants/animals, indigenous ≈ native to a place. For peoples, terminology is political, historical, and region-specific; prefer the community's own name when known. 'Aboriginal' is appropriate in some official/local contexts but not universally interchangeable.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: indigenous meaning
column12: entry::term entry::word usage::specialist topic::culture topic::history discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column2: a handful of vs a mouthful of
column5: A handful of = a small number/amount, literally enough to fit in a hand; a mouthful of = an amount of food/drink that fills the mouth, and is not normally a general small-number quantifier.
column6: a few, a small number; one bite/sipful
column7: Only a handful of people stayed until the end. / He took a mouthful of water before answering. / Don't use 'a mouthful of people' to mean a few people.
column8: Handful has productive figurative quantity use and also 'someone is a handful' = difficult to manage. Mouthful is about what fits in the mouth or, separately, a long/difficult word/phrase.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: a handful of vs a mouthful of
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::figurative topic::food topic::language_learning discovery::contrast

column5: To admit that a particular argument, observation, or part of another person's case is valid, often while continuing to disagree with the larger conclusion.
column6: grant a point, admit a point, acknowledge a point
column7: I'll concede that point: the first season was paced better. But I still think the sequel has stronger characters. / She conceded the point without abandoning her overall argument.
column8: Excellent debate phrase because concession can be partial. Conceding a point ≠ conceding the whole argument. Common pattern: 'I concede that..., but...'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: concede a point meaning
column12: entry::collocation entry::discourse_expression usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly discovery::disagreement discovery::debate_language

column5: The capacity to have subjective experiences or feelings—especially sensations such as pleasure and pain; definitions vary somewhat across philosophy, ethics, neuroscience, and AI discussion.
column6: capacity for feeling, conscious experience (overlapping), phenomenal experience
column7: Animal-ethics arguments often treat sentience—the capacity to suffer or enjoy—as morally important. / Debates about AI sometimes blur sentience, consciousness, intelligence, and self-awareness even though they are not identical.
column8: Sentience is often narrower than consciousness: roughly capacity for felt experience. Sapience = wisdom/intelligence (especially humanlike higher reasoning); self-awareness = awareness of oneself. Existing sentientism cards assume this concept but do not define it standalone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: sentience meaning

column5: Sounding or feeling like a rant: overly angry, prolonged, complaint-heavy, heated, or uncontrolled in tone.
column7: I want the review to be critical without being ranty. / He gets a little ranty whenever that topic comes up.
column8: 'Not being ranty' means avoiding a rant-like tone, not necessarily avoiding criticism. Informal productive adjective from rant + -y.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: not being ranty

column5: Literally, a blanket that provides warmth; figuratively, something comforting, familiar, safe, reassuring, or emotionally cozy.
column6: comfort, security blanket, cozy familiarity, reassurance
column7: I wrapped myself in a warm blanket and watched an old anime. / Rewatching that series feels like a warm blanket after a stressful week.
column8: The figurative metaphor is common in reviews: a familiar show/book/game can 'feel like a warm blanket.' 'Security blanket' more specifically suggests a source of emotional reassurance/dependence.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: warm blankets meaning
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative usage::warm topic::security discovery::figurative_extension discovery::reassurance

column5: The state of being annoyed, frustrated, worried, or troubled; something that causes such irritation or distress.
column7: To my great vexation, the same error returned after the update. / He sighed in vexation when the train doors closed just before he reached them.
column8: More formal/literary than annoyance. Can convey a blend of irritation and frustrated distress. Related verb vex = annoy, trouble, puzzle.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: vexation meaning

column2: life is like climbing a mountain
column5: A common metaphor framing life as an upward journey involving effort, obstacles, stages, setbacks, perspective, and goals/summits.
column6: life is a journey, uphill climb, climb toward a goal
column7: He described life as climbing a mountain: you struggle upward, stop to catch your breath, and see the landscape differently as you rise.
column8: Not a single fixed proverb; meaning depends on speaker. Preserve as conceptual metaphor rather than inventing a canonical quotation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: someone says life is something like a climbing a mountain

column5: To give a loud, high-pitched, piercing cry, often from fear, excitement, pain, or laughter.
column7: She shrieked when the spider landed on her sleeve. / The kids shrieked with laughter on the ride. / The brakes gave a metallic shriek.
column8: Shriek is high-pitched and piercing. Scream is broader; screech can describe harsh human/animal/mechanical sound; squeal may be excitement or a high-pitched sound.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: shriek meaning

column5: A person who flatters or ingratiates themselves with someone in authority to gain approval or advantage.
column7: Everyone thought he was a suck-up because he praised the boss no matter what. / Don't be such a suck-up.
column8: Hyphenated noun. Strongly negative. Compare suck up to someone (verb). 'Teacher's pet' overlaps in school contexts but is not identical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: suck-up meaning

column5: Genuine, real, authentic, and made or acting in good faith.
column7: She is now a bona fide expert in the field.
column8: Distinct from existing bona fides (plural noun = credentials/evidence of legitimacy). In AmE the adjective is often pronounced BOH-nuh fide.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: bona fide meaning

column5: A highly informal, profanity-heavy expression whose exact meaning depends on source/community; it may function as an exclamation, stylized persona-speech, or a compound around 'fuckshit' (nonsense, bad behavior, chaotic stuff) plus 'brah/bro.'
column7: The phrase reads more like stylized internet speech than a standard idiom. / 'What is this fuckshit, brah?' would roughly convey irritated disbelief at some nonsense or chaos.
column8: Raw search preserved because spelling/segmentation is uncertain. 'Brah' is a bro-like address associated with surf/skater/internet speech. Do not assign a precise fixed definition without the original source context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: fuck shit bra meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::profane topic::internet topic::public_speaking topic::chemistry topic::science discovery::uncertainty

column5: To come together toward the same place, result, conclusion, target, or solution.
column6: meet, come together, home in on, agree on
column7: Several lines of evidence converge on the same explanation. / The roads converge on the town center.
column8: Physical and abstract. Contrast diverge = move/develop apart.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: converge on something meaning
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::problem-solving discovery::solution_framing discovery::agreement discovery::resolution

column5: To create doubt about the truth, validity, reliability, legitimacy, wisdom, or acceptability of something.
column6: cast doubt on, call into question, undermine, raise doubts about
column7: The missing data brings the conclusion into question. / His inconsistent account called his credibility into question.
column8: 'Call X into question' is more established/common; 'bring X into question' also occurs. Different from 'bring up a question' = raise a question for discussion.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: bring into question meaning

column5: To steal goods or valuables by force, especially during war, invasion, piracy, or disorder; as a noun, stolen goods or wealth taken by such force. Figuratively, to exploit or strip resources.
column6: loot, pillage, ransack, despoil, rob; booty
column7: Pirates plundered the merchant ship. / The invading force carried off its plunder. / Critics accused the company of plundering the region's natural resources.
column8: Close to pillage, but plunder works especially well for taking valuables/resources and can be a noun. Pillage often foregrounds violent destructive looting of a place. Loot is broader and more everyday.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define plunder

column5: In animation/anime discussion, flattening can refer to reducing visual depth, dimensionality, tonal variation, character complexity, or production distinctions; the exact technical meaning depends on the source context.
column6: simplification, loss of depth, homogenization, leveling
column7: The compositing gives the scene a flattening effect, making foreground and background feel less separated. / Critics sometimes talk about adaptation flattening when a nuanced character becomes much more one-note.
column8: The raw search says 'flattening in anime industry' but does not preserve the original source sentence. Do not pretend it names one standardized anime-industry process. Keep as contextual recognition vocabulary and check surrounding context when encountered.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: flattening in anime industry meaning
column12: entry::term entry::phrase usage::technical usage::specialist topic::anime discovery::criticism discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Outside the permitted playing area; outside an allowed physical area; figuratively, beyond what is acceptable, appropriate, permissible, or relevant.
column6: off-limits, prohibited, beyond the line, unacceptable
column7: The ball went out of bounds. / That part of the building is out of bounds to visitors. / Asking about her medical history in a job interview felt completely out of bounds.
column8: Sports sense is literal boundary. Figurative use is common for topics/behavior. Contrast 'off-limits' (explicitly prohibited) and 'out of line' (behavior socially unacceptable).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116, voca_0117 | search: define out of bounds

column5: Cleverness, inventiveness, and skill in designing, solving, or creating something.
column7: The repair showed remarkable ingenuity. / It took real ingenuity to build a working prototype from spare parts. / I admire the ingenuity of a simple solution that removes three unnecessary steps.
column8: Ingenuity = clever inventiveness in solving/creating, often under constraints. Important contrast: 'ingenious' = cleverly inventive; 'ingenuous' = innocent/candid; 'disingenuous' = insincere/misleading. Those look similar but are different word families in modern use.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: ingenuity

column5: To treat favors, sacrifices, mistakes, harms, or obligations as if they were credits and debits that should be made even; in relationships, often implies scorekeeping or restoring perceived fairness.
column6: even the score, settle accounts, keep score, restore balance
column7: Healthy reciprocity doesn't require balancing the ledger after every tiny favor. / He apologized partly because he felt he needed to balance the emotional ledger.
column8: Not a single fixed relationship idiom, but a natural accounting metaphor. Can criticize transactional scorekeeping or describe a genuine desire to restore fairness.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: balancing the ledger in relationships
column12: entry::idiom usage::figurative topic::relationships topic::finance topic::assessment discovery::perception discovery::resolution

column5: A context-dependent playful phrase rather than a broadly fixed English idiom. It can literally or jokingly evoke hugs involving a buffalo and may also occur as a community-specific saying, title, nickname, or proper-name expression.
column6: context-dependent; big/tight hug (possible playful reading), hugs from afar (contextual/proper-name use)
column7: They ended the message with 'buffalo hugs,' using it as an affectionate in-group sign-off. / Without the original source, ask what 'buffalo hugs' refers to rather than assuming a fixed slang meaning.
column8: KEEP, but preserve uncertainty. Possible contexts include communities using 'High, Low, and Buffalo' check-ins, playful associations with a large/tight buffalo hug, and proper-name/business uses such as 'Buffalo Hugs & Heart.' These associations do not establish one universal dictionary meaning. The verb 'buffalo' can mean intimidate, bewilder, or bamboozle, but that does not by itself prove a fixed idiom 'buffalo hug.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: buffalo hugs
column12: entry::idiom usage::slang usage::playful usage::affectionate usage::informal discovery::title_language discovery::possibility

column5: A condition in which ordinary consciousness, perception, awareness, thought, emotion, or sense of self is significantly changed, whether through sleep, meditation, substances, illness, trance, etc.
column6: altered state of consciousness, nonordinary state, trance-like state
column7: The documentary discusses meditation as one route to an altered state of consciousness. / The character seems to enter an altered state after the ritual.
column8: Broad descriptive term, not automatically drug-related and not itself a diagnosis. In psychology/neuroscience, definitions and boundaries vary; always use context to identify the cause/type.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: altered state meaning

column2: come across vs come through vs come off
column5: Come across can mean encounter/find or give an impression; come through can mean survive, arrive/be delivered, or succeed when needed; come off can mean detach, succeed, or give a particular impression.
column6: come across: encounter, find; seem/appear | come through: survive, deliver, succeed when needed | come off: detach; succeed; seem/appear
column7: I came across an old photo. / She came through when we needed help. / His joke came off as rude.
column8: Preserve because the original search explicitly compared three confusable phrasal verbs. Existing come off card covers one member, but the contrast itself is useful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: come across vs come through vs come off

column5: Having an excessively high opinion of oneself, one's abilities, appearance, or importance.
column6: vain, arrogant, self-important, egotistical, full of oneself
column7: He comes across as conceited because he constantly talks about how talented he is. / Confidence isn't the same as being conceited.
column8: Usually negative. Conceited emphasizes inflated self-opinion; arrogant additionally emphasizes superiority and often dismissive behavior toward others.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: conceited meaning

column5: To force something out using leverage or effort; figuratively, to extract information, an admission, a secret, or a response from someone with difficulty.
column6: lever out, wrench out; extract, drag out, coax out
column7: I pried the nail out with a tool. / It took twenty minutes to pry the story out of him. / She wouldn't volunteer the answer, so I had to pry it out of her.
column8: Physical pry = use leverage to force apart/open/remove. Figurative pattern often 'pry information/the truth out of someone.' Do not confuse with pry into = intrude curiously into private matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: pry it out meanig

column5: A person who criticizes, disparages, or expresses a negative view of someone or something.
column7: The film has passionate fans and equally vocal detractors. / Even his detractors admitted the presentation was effective.
column8: Unlike adversary, a detractor need not be actively competing against you; the core is criticism/disparagement.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: define detractors

column5: To force, chase, intimidate, or drive someone away from a place; in driving, 'run someone off the road' means force their vehicle off the roadway.
column6: drive away, chase off, scare off, force out
column7: The locals ran the trespassers off the property. / The truck nearly ran us off the road. / He felt as if the hostile atmosphere was designed to run newcomers off.
column8: Often run someone off + place/property/road. Distinct from 'run off' = leave suddenly, print copies, drain liquid, etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: run someone off meaning

column5: To run or move quickly with light, short steps, often playfully, nervously, or like a small animal/child.
column7: The children scampered across the playground. / A mouse scampered behind the cabinet. / The puppy scampered over when it heard the treat bag.
column8: Compare scuttle = hurried short steps, often furtive/crablike; scamper often feels lighter/playful and is common with children/small animals. As a noun: 'a quick scamper.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: scamper

column5: To perform magic or seemingly summon something by magic; figuratively, to bring an image, memory, feeling, or idea vividly to mind; conjuring = the act/practice of doing so.
column6: summon, evoke, call up, invoke; magic
column7: The magician seemed to conjure a coin from nowhere. / That soundtrack conjures images of late-night city streets. / 'The Conjuring' uses the magical/supernatural sense in its title.
column8: Common phrase conjure up. Figurative evoke sense is very useful. Pronunciation often /ˈkʌndʒər/ in BrE and /ˈkɑːndʒər/ in AmE.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: conjuring meaning
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::figurative_extension discovery::hedging

column5: A person who talks a lot, especially continuously, loudly, or about trivial things.
column7: I'm a certified yapper once I get comfortable around people.
column8: From yap = talk noisily/at length. Contemporary internet use is often playful and self-deprecating.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: yapper meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::playful usage::informal discovery::triviality

column5: To treat a sacred, respected, or solemn place or object with violent disrespect or irreverence.
column7: The vandals were accused of desecrating the memorial.
column8: Related noun desecration already existed in prior review/merge history; base verb is independently useful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112, voca_0113 | search: desecrate meaning

column5: A mild, indirect, or less offensive expression used instead of one considered harsh, embarrassing, unpleasant, taboo, or too direct.
column6: softened expression, indirect term, polite substitute
column7: 'Passed away' is a euphemism for 'died.' / Calling layoffs a 'workforce adjustment' can sound like a corporate euphemism designed to soften what happened.
column8: A euphemism changes how something is framed, not necessarily the underlying fact. Compare understatement (deliberately presents something as less extreme), circumlocution (wordy indirectness), and doublespeak (language that obscures/manipulates meaning, usually critical).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: euphemism meaning
column12: entry::word usage::critical usage::offensive usage::softening usage::professional usage::businesslike usage::evaluative discovery::professional_context

column5: An authoritative order; authority/control over people or a situation; mastery of a skill or language. As a verb, to order authoritatively, control, lead, or deserve/attract something such as respect or attention.
column6: order, directive; control, authority; mastery; order, lead, dominate
column7: The officer gave the command to stop. / She has an impressive command of English. / The hill commands a view of the harbor. / His calm competence commands respect without him demanding it.
column8: Key patterns: command someone to do X; be in command; have a good command of X; command respect/attention/a high salary. In 'command respect,' command = naturally inspire or merit it, not literally order people to respect you.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define command

column5: The state of not being intoxicated; especially, sustained abstinence from alcohol or drugs. More formally, it can also mean seriousness, moderation, or clear-headed restraint.
column6: abstinence, being sober, recovery (not identical); seriousness, temperance
column7: He celebrated five years of sobriety. / Early sobriety changed how she organized her social life. / The report was praised for the sobriety of its tone.
column8: In recovery contexts, sobriety can be personally defined and may involve abstinence from particular substances. 'Recovery' is broader than simply not using. Formal 'sobriety of tone/judgment' = seriousness and restraint.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: sobriety meaning

column5: Literally, to make someone fall over; figuratively, to overwhelm, astonish, strongly impress, or suddenly weaken someone.
column6: floor, bowl over, blow away, overwhelm, sweep off one's feet (romantic nuance)
column7: The wave knocked me off my feet. / Her performance completely knocked me off my feet. / That flu knocked him off his feet for nearly a week.
column8: Compare sweep someone off their feet: especially romantic enchantment. Knock someone off their feet can be physical, impressive, shocking, or illness-related.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: knock off one's feet

column5: To find out or determine whether something is true, has happened, or meets a condition, usually through investigation, checking, or evidence.
column6: determine whether, establish whether, find out whether, verify whether
column7: We need to ascertain whether the two files contain the same records. / The doctor tried to ascertain whether the symptoms had changed.
column8: Formal. Whether introduces the yes/no uncertainty being determined. In everyday speech, 'find out whether/if' is usually more natural.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: ascertain whether meaning

column5: Literally, to light a fire again; figuratively, to revive or renew a feeling, relationship, interest, hope, memory, conflict, or enthusiasm that had faded.
column6: revive, reignite, renew, reawaken, resurrect, spark again
column7: The trip rekindled my interest in photography. / They met again years later and rekindled their friendship. / The documentary rekindled an old debate.
column8: Re- + kindle. Often positive with romance/interest/hope, but can also rekindle conflict, resentment, controversy. 'Reignite' is close and preserves the fire metaphor more transparently.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: rekindle meaning
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::relationships discovery::figurative_extension discovery::debate_language

column5: To feel a personal connection, similarity, sympathy, or shared perspective with a person, character, group, or experience.
column6: relate to, connect with, see oneself in, empathize with
column7: I identified with the character's difficulty fitting in. / Many viewers identify with her frustration even if they disagree with her choices.
column8: Different from identify as = state one's identity/category, and identify someone/something = recognize/name.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: identify with definition

column5: A person who writes, edits, researches, or compiles dictionaries.
column6: dictionary writer, dictionary editor, lexicology professional (overlapping)
column7: Lexicographers track how words are actually used before deciding how to describe them in a dictionary. / Modern lexicographers often work with huge searchable corpora.
column8: Lexicography = practice/study of dictionary making. Lexicology = study of words/vocabulary more broadly. A lexicographer does not simply 'invent definitions'; evidence of usage is central.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define lexicographers

column5: Influence or power that comes from an institution's established status, resources, authority, reputation, networks, or position within a system.
column6: institutional influence, organizational power, establishment leverage
column7: The small group had good ideas but lacked the institutional clout to change policy. / A university's name can carry institutional clout beyond the work of any one professor.
column8: Builds on clout = influence. Institutional clout is structural/organizational, not merely personal popularity.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: institutional clout meaning
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::resource_allocation discovery::social_approval discovery::debate_language

column5: Embarrassing, shameful, scandalous, or damaging secrets from someone's past that they want to keep hidden.
column6: dirty secrets, hidden scandals, buried secrets
column7: Every family has a few skeletons in the closet. / The documentary starts digging into the politician's old skeletons in the closet.
column8: BrE commonly says skeletons in the cupboard. The image is of a hidden secret that would be shocking if discovered.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: skeletons in the closet meaning

column2: you can see up my nose
column5: The camera/viewing angle is so low or close that the inside of my nostrils is visible—usually said self-consciously about an unflattering shot.
column6: the camera is looking up my nose, low-angle close-up
column7: Can you move the camera higher? You can see up my nose from that angle. / I hate this webcam position—it looks straight up my nose.
column8: Natural 'see up someone's nose.' Useful for camera/video calls. 'Look up someone's nose' can describe the viewing direction; unrelated to 'look down one's nose at' = act superior.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: you can see up my nose meaning

column5: To think about, worry about, or focus on someone or something persistently and excessively; also to dominate someone's thoughts.
column6: fixate on, dwell on, preoccupy oneself with, be consumed by, get hung up on
column7: I spent way too long obsessing over one awkward sentence in the review. / Fans are still obsessing over that tiny detail in the final scene. / Don't obsess about getting every word perfect when you're speaking.
column8: Common patterns: obsess over/about X; be obsessed with/by X. Obsess often implies disproportionate or hard-to-stop attention, stronger than simply focus on.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113, voca_0116 | search: obsess

column5: To have someone sit, often so you can speak to them seriously, explain something, or deal with an issue directly.
column6: have a talk with, speak seriously to
column7: I sat him down and explained exactly what had happened.
column8: Often implies a deliberate, focused conversation rather than merely causing someone to sit physically.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: sit someone down meaning

column5: Historically, a free man/small landholder or a servant/official of a particular rank; in modern phrases, 'yeoman's work/service' means diligent, valuable, hard work.
column7: The volunteers did yeoman's work sorting thousands of records. / In historical England, yeoman referred to a social rank below the gentry, though its exact status changed over time.
column8: Modern learners most often meet 'yeoman's work/service,' praising dependable hard labor. Also appears in naval ranks/titles and historical institutions such as Yeomen Warders.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: yeoman

column5: To move one's head suddenly and sharply, often to look, signal, recoil, or indicate a direction.
column6: snap one's head, whip one's head, nod sharply, motion with one's head
column7: She jerked her head toward the door, silently telling me to leave. / He jerked his head around when he heard his name.
column8: Jerk emphasizes abrupt sharp motion. 'Jerk one's head toward X' can function as a quick directional gesture; 'snap/whip one's head around' emphasizes sudden turning.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: jerk one's headmeaning

column5: A makeshift or improvised knife or stabbing weapon, especially associated with prisons; as a verb, to stab someone with such a weapon.
column7: The prison drama shows an inmate hiding a homemade shiv. / In crime fiction, 'shiv' immediately evokes a crude concealed stabbing weapon.
column8: Slang with strong prison/crime association. This is descriptive vocabulary, not a technical category: improvised weapons vary widely.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: shiv
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::technical usage::vulgar usage::military usage::informal discovery::improvement discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: What I said, wrote, made, cooked, recorded, printed, etc. did not turn out or get expressed the way I intended; often used after wording accidentally sounds wrong/offensive.
column6: that came out wrong, it didn't turn out right, I didn't express that well
column7: Sorry, that didn't come out right—I meant that I was surprised, not disappointed. / The photo didn't come out right, so I took another one.
column8: Come out can refer to words being expressed, a result/product emerging, photos developing/printing, information becoming public, etc. In conversation 'that came out wrong' is especially common for misphrasing.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: it didn't come out right meaning
column12: entry::phrase usage::conversational usage::offensive usage::evaluative topic::communication topic::food

column2: boggle someone's mind / something boggles someone
column5: To astonish, overwhelm, or confuse someone because something is extremely surprising, complex, or hard to comprehend.
column6: astound, bewilder, blow someone's mind, be mind-boggling
column7: It boggles my mind that they made the same mistake three times. / The sheer number of possible combinations boggles me. / The scale of the project is mind-boggling.
column8: Existing boggle WID? has 'mind began to boggle'; this card preserves the searched argument pattern. Most idiomatic: it boggles the mind / it boggles my mind; 'X boggles me' is grammatical but less formulaic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: something boggles you meaning

column5: To change oneself or something so it becomes suitable for new conditions, purposes, audiences, or environments; to modify a work into another form such as a film adaptation.
column6: adjust, modify, acclimate, tailor, convert, transform
column7: It took me a while to adapt to living in a different country. / We adapted the workflow after the first few batches. / The novel was adapted into an animated series.
column8: Patterns: adapt to X (oneself changes); adapt X for Y / from X / into Y (modify something). Contrast adopt = take/accept/use as one's own. Existing 'adopt vs adapt' card compares them; standalone adapt adds full constructions.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define adapt

column5: Actions taken to limit, contain, repair, or reduce harm after a mistake, scandal, accident, leak, failure, or other damaging event.
column6: containment, crisis management, mitigation, cleanup, reputation management
column7: After the disastrous interview, the PR team went into damage-control mode. / We spent the next hour doing damage control after the bad update went live.
column8: Originally literal emergency control of damage, especially ships; now extremely common figuratively in PR/work/relationships. 'Do damage control'; 'damage-control mode.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: damage control

column5: To add game-like mechanics or incentives—points, levels, streaks, badges, challenges, competition, feedback—to a non-game activity to increase engagement or motivation.
column6: turn into a game, add game mechanics, game-ify
column7: The app gamifies vocabulary review with streaks and levels. / You can gamify chores, but rewards can also distract from the underlying goal.
column8: Noun gamification. Does not necessarily mean creating a full game; usually means applying selected game-design elements.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: gamify meaning

column2: blow someone/something out of the water
column5: To defeat, outperform, disprove, or impressively surpass someone or something by a very large margin.
column7: Their new prototype blew the competition out of the water.
column8: Also used of arguments, expectations, records, or previous versions—not only direct competitors.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: blow out of water

column5: To speak with involuntary pauses, repetitions, or difficulty producing sounds/words; also, in nonclinical description, to speak haltingly because of nervousness or shock.
column6: stutter, falter, stumble over one's words, speak haltingly
column7: He stammered out an apology when everyone turned to look at him. / She began stammering with nerves during the presentation. / A persistent stammer can be a speech disorder, not simply nervousness.
column8: Stammer and stutter overlap heavily; regional/preference differences exist, and clinical terminology may favor stuttering. Avoid using speech disfluency as shorthand for stupidity or dishonesty.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: stammering meaning

column5: A cnidarian of class Cubozoa, named for its roughly box-shaped bell; some species have extremely potent venom.
column7: Box jellyfish live mainly in warm coastal waters. / Some box jellyfish species can cause severe envenomation.
column8: Not one single species. 'Sea wasp' may refer to particular dangerous species and is not a perfect synonym for every box jellyfish.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: Box jellyfish

column5: To enthusiastically indulge in, gush over, or display one's anime/Japanese-pop-culture fandom, often self-deprecatingly or playfully.
column6: geek out over anime/Japan, nerd out, go full weeb
column7: Give me ten minutes to weeb out over this ridiculously good transformation sequence. / We spent the whole train ride weebing out about old anime openings.
column8: Productive slang built from weeb + out, modeled on geek out/nerd out. Usually playful among fans, but weeb can also be insulting depending on speaker/context. Does not literally imply the harsher stereotype every time.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: weeb out meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrasal_verb usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::playful usage::informal topic::internet topic::anime topic::fandom topic::culture

column5: You have full responsibility, control, or choice in the matter; depending on tone, it can mean 'the decision is yours' or 'you will bear the consequences.'
column6: it's up to you, it's your responsibility, the burden is on you
column7: I've explained the options; from here, it's all on you. / If you ignore the backup warning and lose the file, that's all on you. / The final call is all on you.
column8: More responsibility-heavy than neutral 'it's up to you.' Tone can be supportive ('I trust you') or accusatory ('don't blame me'). Context/prosody matter.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: it's all on you meaning

column5: Carefully watchful and alert for possible danger, wrongdoing, problems, or changes.
column6: watchful, alert, attentive, wary, on guard
column7: Security staff remained vigilant throughout the event. / You have to be vigilant about small changes in the data when the sample is this noisy.
column8: Often vigilant about/against/for. Wary emphasizes suspicion/caution; vigilant emphasizes active sustained watchfulness.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: vigilant meaning

column5: A verb that can be used both transitively and intransitively without changing its form, with a systematic relationship between the arguments.
column6: ambitransitive verb, ergative verb (in some English-grammar uses)
column7: The chef boiled the water. → The water boiled. / I moved the chair. → The chair moved.
column8: Labile is broader terminology than the English-teaching use of ergative. Not every transitive/intransitive alternation behaves identically: compare 'I ate the cake / I ate' (object omission) with 'I broke the glass / the glass broke' (affected object becomes intransitive subject).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: labile verbs
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist topic::relationships topic::linguistics topic::grammar discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: In a weak, slight, uncertain, or only loosely connected way.
column6: weakly, loosely, precariously, faintly, only marginally
column7: The theory is only tenuously connected to the evidence. / The sequel is only tenuously connected to the original story. / He was still tenuously holding on to hope.
column8: From tenuous = thin/weak/slight. Common with connected/linked/related, supported, held. Often signals that a claimed relationship or evidential link exists, but only weakly. 'Precariously' fits physical/security senses better than logical connection.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: tenuously

column4: adjective / noun; medical history / offensive slang
column5: Relating to muscle spasticity in medical contexts; historically a noun/adjective for people with cerebral palsy or motor disabilities. In British English especially, slang uses meaning clumsy/stupid are highly offensive ableist insults.
column7: The clinician described increased spastic muscle tone in the patient's leg. / In British conversation, calling someone 'spastic' as an insult is strongly offensive and should be avoided.
column8: Important regional difference: the insult has long been especially severe in the UK because of its disability history. U.S. 'spaz' historically became more casual, but it shares the same ableist origin and can still offend. Existing WID1414 notes this link.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: spastic meaning

column5: A person regarded as dishonest, troublesome, unreliable, or morally bad.
column6: bad apple, troublemaker, shady character, rotten person
column7: His uncle warned him that the new business partner was a bad egg. / The character looks respectable at first, but you gradually realize he's a bad egg.
column8: Old-fashioned but still readily understood, often playful. 'Bad apple' is more common and can imply one corrupting a group; bad egg simply labels the person.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: A bad egg

column5: A person who habitually lives off others or takes their money/help without giving back; as a verb, to obtain things by freeloading or absorb information readily ('sponge it up').
column7: He's a sponge who never pays for anything himself. / Kids can sponge up new expressions surprisingly fast.
column8: Freeloader sense is disparaging. Literal sponge absorbs liquid, motivating 'sponge up information.' Distinct from the animal/material senses.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: sponge in slang
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::slang usage::figurative usage::disparaging usage::evaluative

column5: A brief mental lapse in which you forget something obvious, say the wrong thing, or momentarily fail to think clearly.
column7: I knew her name, but I had a total brain fart when I introduced her.
column8: Very informal and mildly vulgar; usually humorous and self-deprecating.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111 | search: brain fart meaning

column5: Quick/slow to understand, notice, or grasp what is being implied or explained.
column6: quick-witted, catch on quickly; slow to catch on
column7: She was quick on the uptake and understood the joke immediately. / I'm a little slow on the uptake before coffee.
column8: Existing WID6411 covers 'slow on the uptake.' This card preserves the broader productive pattern, especially the positive 'quick on the uptake.' Uptake here = mental reception/understanding.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: on the uptake meaning

column5: Describing a man or boy as having mannerisms, appearance, voice, or qualities culturally stereotyped as feminine.
column7: The actor was mocked as effeminate simply because of his voice and gestures. / What one culture labels 'effeminate' may be completely ordinary masculine behavior in another.
column8: Often judgmental or pejorative because it relies on gender stereotypes; use carefully when describing a person. It does not imply sexual orientation. 'Feminine' is more neutral and not restricted to men.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define effeminate

column5: To reveal information accidentally or carelessly, often something intended to remain secret; also literally allow something to escape one's grasp/control.
column6: blurt out, accidentally reveal, give away, disclose inadvertently
column7: He let slip that they were planning a surprise party. / She accidentally let the name slip during the interview.
column8: Very common pattern: let slip that... / let a detail/name slip. Existing 'slip out' card mentions it, but this construction is independently useful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: let slip meaning

column5: To postpone or delay an action. In this sense, put off is followed by a noun or gerund, not an infinitive.
column7: I kept putting off replying to the email. / Don't put off studying until the night before the test.
column8: Existing put off card covers postpone and repel senses; this card preserves the gerund complementation: put off doing, not *put off to do.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: put off doing something

column5: A person with substantial knowledge, learning, or expertise across many different subjects or fields.
column6: Renaissance person, universal scholar, multidisciplinary thinker
column7: Leonardo da Vinci is often described as a polymath. / He wants to be a polymath, not merely dabble in ten hobbies.
column8: Raw 'polymas' appears to be a misspelling/mishearing. Polymath is the standard word; plural polymaths.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: polymas meaning

column5: To acknowledge the credit, ability, good qualities, or achievement someone deserves, often despite criticism or dislike.
column6: give credit where it's due, give someone credit, acknowledge someone's merits
column7: I disagree with him on almost everything, but I'll give him his due: he knows how to hold an audience. / Give the animators their due—the action scenes look fantastic even when the story drags.
column8: Often concessive: 'I don't like X, but to give X their due...' Similar 'give credit where credit is due' emphasizes fair recognition.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: give someone one's due meaning

column5: Wary = cautious, watchful, or suspicious because danger/problem may exist. Weary = tired, exhausted, or fed up after prolonged effort or experience.
column6: cautious vs tired; guarded vs exhausted
column7: I'm wary of links from unknown senders. / I'm weary after answering emails all day. / She grew weary of the argument but remained wary of trusting him.
column8: Classic spelling/pronunciation confusable. Memory hook: wary = beware; weary = wearied/tired. Existing standalone cards remain useful; contrast card targets the common mix-up.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: wary vs weary

column5: To give someone a small concession, reward, or token benefit, often to placate them while withholding something more important.
column6: give a token concession, toss someone a crumb
column7: The company wouldn't raise salaries, but it threw employees a bone by adding an extra day off.
column8: Raw search included 'a formidable foe'; formidable already exists in Master. The idiomatic learning target is throw someone a bone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: throw a formidable foe a bone meaning

column5: A boundary or point beyond which something cannot or should not go; as a verb, to keep something within such a boundary.
column7: There is a limit to how much information I can absorb at once.
column8: Core image: a boundary marking 'this far, but no farther.' Useful for understanding limited, limitation, off-limits, speed limit, etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: core idea of the word "limit"

column5: To allow the opposing side to score a goal, point, run, etc.; in some sports/competitions, also to admit defeat or surrender a hole/match without completing play.
column6: allow, give up, let in; surrender
column7: They conceded two goals in the final ten minutes. / The defense has conceded only six goals all season. / In match play golf, a player can concede a putt or hole.
column8: Especially common in football/soccer: concede a goal / goals conceded. AmE sports may prefer 'give up/allow' in many contexts. Related but distinct from concede = reluctantly admit a point.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: conceded meaning in sports

column5: To lengthen a scene, episode, story, or runtime with material that adds little essential plot/information, often to meet length requirements or slow pacing.
column6: filler, stretch out, bulk out, pad the runtime
column7: The adaptation pads the scene with repeated reaction shots. / That entire subplot feels like padding added to reach twelve episodes.
column8: Padding is often critical, but extra material can still add atmosphere/character even if not plot-essential. Also pad = cushion/protect or add false expenses/numbers.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: padding the scene

column5: To obtain, collect, or gradually attract something, especially attention, support, praise, votes, information, or awards.
column7: The video garnered millions of views within a week. / Her performance garnered praise even from critics who disliked the film. / The proposal failed to garner enough support.
column8: Common with abstract/countable results rather than ordinary physical possession: garner attention/support/praise/votes/interest. Slightly more formal/journalistic than get.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: garner meaning

column5: Literally, the place where one particular melon belongs or originates; unlike 'home of the melon,' it does not naturally sound like a slogan for a region famous for melons.
column6: place where a melon comes from
column7: If you're describing a farming region, 'home of the melon' or 'home to famous melons' is more natural than 'home of a melon.'
column8: Search-intent contrast. Article choice changes interpretation: a = one nonspecific melon; the = a known/type-symbolic melon. Exact intended source remains uncertain.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: home of a melon meaning

column5: In Disney's Lady and the Tramp, Tramp is the male stray dog's name; the word evokes a roaming, unattached drifter, contrasting with Lady's sheltered, respectable identity.
column7: The title itself sets up the contrast: Lady belongs to a comfortable home, while Tramp lives as a free-roaming stray.
column8: The raw search asks for quotes, but without the original quote there is no supported exact line to preserve. This card keeps the likely vocabulary reason behind the search without inventing copyrighted dialogue.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: lady and the tramp quotes

column5: To react or escalate in an extremely aggressive, drastic, or all-out way; to use the most severe option available. Literal contexts can refer to adopting/using nuclear power or weapons.
column6: go ballistic, go scorched-earth, escalate drastically, use the nuclear option
column7: He went nuclear when he found out the files had been deleted. / The company went nuclear in the lawsuit and demanded every available remedy.
column8: Hyperbolic figurative expression. 'Nuclear option' often means an extreme procedural/strategic measure. Avoid reading literal nuclear meaning unless context supports it.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: go nuclear meaning

column5: Determined to do what one wants despite advice, objections, or consequences; stubbornly self-willed.
column7: He was talented but headstrong and rarely listened to advice.
column8: Can suggest admirable determination or frustrating stubbornness, but usually leans critical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: headstrong definition

column2: I dare you to do something
column5: A direct challenge urging someone to do something risky, difficult, embarrassing, or confrontational, often implying they may be afraid or unwilling.
column6: I challenge you to, go on—do it, bet you won't (slang)
column7: I dare you to watch that scene without laughing. / 'Say that again. I dare you.' can sound genuinely threatening depending on tone. / We dared each other to try the ridiculous dessert.
column8: Dare can be playful or hostile. Patterns: dare someone to do X; I dare you; don't you dare do X (strong prohibition). 'How dare you!' expresses outrage, not a challenge.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: i dare you to do something meaning
