column5: A long, narrow ditch cut into the ground, especially for drainage, utilities, defense, or warfare; as a verb, to dig or form such a trench.
column7: Workers dug a trench for the new cable. / Soldiers sheltered in trenches during the fighting.
column8: Basis of figurative 'in the trenches.' Also ocean trench = very deep elongated depression in the seafloor.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: trench meaning

column5: Excessive concern with minor rules, details, technicalities, or displays of learning, especially when they distract from the real point.
column7: Correcting one typo is helpful; derailing the whole conversation over it can become pedantry. / The review is knowledgeable without slipping into academic pedantry.
column8: Usually negative. Precision is not inherently pedantry: the criticism is that the detail is disproportionate, irrelevant, showy, or rigidly enforced. Pedantic = adjective; pedant = person.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: pedantry

column5: Literally a basic arithmetic truth; rhetorically, it can symbolize an obvious fact, objective reality, or something so self-evident that denying it seems absurd.
column6: an obvious fact, basic truth, self-evident reality
column7: You don't need an expert to prove that two plus two equals four. / In arguments about truth, '2 + 2 = 4' is often used as shorthand for an objective fact.
column8: Meaning depends on discourse. Often contrasted with 'two plus two equals five' as truth versus imposed falsehood.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: two plus two equals four meaning

column5: Feeling uneasy, disturbed, disgusted, or frightened because someone or something seems creepy, uncanny, intrusive, or threatening.
column6: spooked, unnerved, freaked out, disturbed, weirded out
column7: That empty hallway really creeped me out. / I got creeped out when he knew details I'd never told him. / The doll is cute in daylight but kind of creepy at night.
column8: Usually 'be/get creeped out' or 'X creeps me out.' More specifically uneasy/creepy than general freaked out, which can mean panic, anger, or excitement.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: creeped out meaning

column5: The flexible cord connecting a developing fetus to the placenta, containing blood vessels that carry oxygen/nutrients toward the fetus and waste products away through placental circulation.
column7: The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta. / After birth, the cord is clamped and cut, leaving the umbilical stump.
column8: Usually contains two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein. Figuratively, 'cut the umbilical cord' can mean end excessive dependence, though 'cut the cord' is more common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: umbilical cord

column5: The imagined or narrative satisfaction of a desire, especially one that is difficult or impossible to realize in ordinary life.
column7: The story works partly as wish fulfillment for anyone who has dreamed of starting over.
column8: Used in psychology and especially in criticism of fiction/media.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: wish fulfillment meaning

column5: An organized rebellion against authority; as a verb, to rebel. Also, to disgust or repel someone strongly.
column6: rebellion, uprising, insurrection; rebel; disgust, repulse
column7: The soldiers revolted against the regime. / The tax increase sparked a revolt. / The cruelty of the scene revolted her.
column8: Two major verb senses: revolt against authority vs X revolts someone = disgusts them. 'Revolting' commonly means disgusting in BrE/general English, not merely rebellious.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: revolt meaning

column2: talk the talk and walk the walk
column3: /ˌtɔːk ðə ˈtɔːk ən ˌwɔːk ðə ˈwɔːk/
column5: To both say the right things/claim certain values and actually behave consistently with those claims. Often contrasted: it's easy to talk the talk; harder to walk the walk.
column6: practice what you preach, back up words with actions
column7: He talks the talk about work-life balance, but does he walk the walk with his employees? / She doesn't just talk the talk—she walks the walk.
column8: Existing WID3501 covers walk the walk; this full paired construction preserves the rhetorical contrast the search asked for.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: walk the walk talk the talk meaning

column5: To not know something at all; also used emphatically to say someone cannot imagine the extent of something.
column7: I had no idea the meeting had been moved.
column8: Very common conversational expression. 'You have no idea how...' can be emphatic rather than literally about knowledge.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: I had no idea meaning

column5: The organ in the neck between the pharynx and trachea that contains the vocal folds and is involved in breathing, voice production, and protecting the airway.
column7: The vocal folds are located in the larynx. / Inflammation of the larynx can make the voice hoarse.
column8: Commonly called the voice box. Related: laryngeal /ləˈrɪndʒiəl/; laryngitis = inflammation of the larynx.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: larynx meaning

column5: Small, neatly packaged pieces of information, advice, insight, or content designed to be easily consumed, remembered, or shared, sometimes at the cost of context or nuance.
column6: bite-sized insights, digestible takeaways, snippets, sound bites
column7: The course turns complex research into packaged nuggets of advice. / Social media rewards packaged nuggets, but the missing context can matter more than the takeaway.
column8: Not a fixed idiom. Nugget already metaphorically means a small valuable piece of information; packaged emphasizes pre-shaped, consumable presentation and may sound mildly critical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: packaged nuggets metaphor meaning
column12: entry::idiom usage::informal usage::figurative usage::critical usage::presentation-friendly discovery::recommendation discovery::impression discovery::presentation_language

column5: A silly, goofy, awkward, or foolish person, often used affectionately rather than harshly; regionally/historically, also a peanut.
column6: goofball, dork, silly person, doofus; peanut (regional)
column7: You absolute goober—you left your keys in the fridge. / The character is a lovable goober who somehow keeps saving the day. / 'Goober pea' is an old regional term for peanut.
column8: Tone is highly context-dependent but often warm/playful. Less harsh than idiot when affectionate. Peanut sense is associated especially with Southern U.S. usage/history.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define goober

column5: To hit repeatedly with a heavy object; figuratively, to force, overwhelm, or batter someone into accepting something through pressure, repetition, or heavy-handed argument.
column6: club, batter, beat; browbeat, hammer, force
column7: He was bludgeoned with a heavy object. / The film doesn't trust the audience; it bludgeons you with the message in every scene. / They tried to bludgeon the committee into accepting the proposal.
column8: Figurative bludgeon is vivid and strongly negative: bludgeon someone with statistics/a message; bludgeon someone into submission/agreement. Compare hammer home = emphasize repeatedly, which can be neutral/positive; browbeat = intimidate through bullying words.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define bludgeoned

column5: To intrude inquisitively into someone's private affairs, relationships, history, or personal information.
column6: nose into, snoop into, meddle in, probe into
column7: I don't want to pry into your personal life, so you don't have to answer. / The tabloids kept prying into her family life.
column8: Pry into = investigate intrusively/curiously. Distinct from pry information out of someone = extract it with persistent effort.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: pry into someone's life meaning

column5: Very tough, hard, intimidating, or impressive; well functions as an intensifier. 'Wellard' can represent a fused/nonstandard spelling or a name depending on context.
column7: He was acting well hard in front of his mates.
column8: The raw search 'wellard' is ambiguous: in British speech/writing, well hard can sound/fuse like wellard; Wellard is also known as a proper name. Preserve the likely slang target without erasing ambiguity.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: wellard meaning

column5: To identify, recognize, or articulate exactly what something is—especially a subtle problem, feeling, difference, cause, or quality that is hard to describe.
column7: Something about his delivery feels off, but I can't quite put my finger on it. / You just put your finger on the real problem.
column8: Often negative 'can't quite put my finger on it.' Related 'put your finger on X' = identify precisely.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: put my finger on it meaning

column5: The state of being important, noticeable, salient, or standing out; in speech/prosody, the perceptual highlighting of a syllable, word, or phrase through stress, pitch, duration, etc.
column7: The issue rose to national prominence. / In speech, contrastive focus can give a word extra prominence.
column8: Broad general noun plus important linguistics/prosody sense given surrounding searches. Related prominent.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: prominence

column5: The quality of treating sides or people fairly without favoritism, bias, or improper preference.
column7: Judges are expected to maintain impartiality. / Complete impartiality is difficult when you are personally involved.
column8: Impartial does not necessarily mean having no values/opinions; it means not improperly favoring one side in the relevant judgment/process.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: Impartiality

column5: The place, route, stage, or conceptual starting point through which someone or something enters a system, location, subject, market, body, etc.
column6: entry point, access point, gateway, starting point
column7: Investigators found the burglar's point of entry at a rear window. / That short film is a good point of entry into the director's work. / The skin can be a point of entry for infection.
column8: Very flexible literal/figurative phrase. 'Entry point' is often more idiomatic in computing/markets; 'point of entry' is common in security, medicine, travel, and formal prose.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: at the point of entry meaning

column5: Literally, to roll or lie about in mud, water, etc., especially animals. Figuratively, to indulge deeply and often excessively in an emotion/state, especially self-pity, misery, nostalgia, or luxury.
column7: The pigs wallowed in the mud. / I gave myself one evening to wallow in self-pity, then moved on. / She wallowed in nostalgia while rewatching old shows.
column8: Common patterns: wallow in self-pity/misery/guilt/luxury. Figurative use often implies excessive or self-indulgent immersion. Related personal phrase 'wallow on one's own' can emphasize doing it alone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: define wallowing

column5: In an attractive, charming, appealing, or becoming way.
column7: She smiled fetchingly at him across the table. / The hat was tilted fetchingly to one side.
column8: From fetching = attractive/charming. 'Smile fetchingly' has an old-fashioned romantic/narrative flavor and may sound deliberately quaint today.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: smiles so fetchingly meaning

column5: A word, phrase, sound, or speech habit that a person repeats frequently, often automatically or without noticing.
column6: speech habit, filler habit, repeated mannerism
column7: Saying 'you know' every few seconds had become a verbal tic.
column8: Can refer to habitual fillers/catchphrases; not necessarily a clinical tic disorder.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111 | search: verbal tic

column5: To endure and push through pain, fatigue, difficulty, or adversity through determination rather than quitting.
column6: tough it out, grind it out, push through, soldier on
column7: My legs were dead for the last mile, but I gutted it out. / We were exhausted, but we gutted out the final hour of work.
column8: Raw 'gutting out' points to gut it out / gut out something. Especially sports/endurance AmE. 'Grit it out' is a related expression.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120, voca_0121 | search: gutting out meaning

column5: High water is the state/level of a tide or body of water near its maximum. A high-water mark is the highest level reached, figuratively the peak or greatest achievement.
column6: high tide, peak level; apex, zenith, peak
column7: The trail disappears at high water. / That album remains the high-water mark of the band's career.
column8: Also appears in 'come hell or high water' = regardless of difficulties (existing related card). 'High-water mark' is common figuratively; 'high water' alone is usually literal unless context supplies an idiom.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: high water meaning

column5: To move quickly with short hurried steps; to deliberately sink a ship by making holes/openings in it; figuratively, to deliberately ruin, abandon, or prevent a plan. As a noun, a hurried run or a container such as a coal scuttle.
column6: scurry, scamper; sink; sabotage, scrap, derail
column7: A crab scuttled under the rock. / The crew scuttled the ship to prevent its capture. / The deal was scuttled at the last minute by a funding dispute.
column8: Three memorable senses: hurried movement, sink one's own ship, kill a plan. Do not confuse with scuttlebutt = rumor/gossip, though historically scuttlebutt has nautical roots.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: scuttle

column5: To attach oneself closely to someone physically, socially, or emotionally; often to begin following, depending on, befriending, or clinging to them, sometimes more persistently than they want.
column6: cling to, attach oneself to, stick with, glom onto (informal), become dependent on
column7: The shy kid latched on to me during the first week of camp. / Once he found someone who shared his obsession, he latched onto him immediately.
column8: Can be neutral/affectionate or mildly negative depending on unwanted dependency. Existing base latch card notes latch onto ideas; this search specifically motivates the person/social sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: latching on to you meaning

column5: Not alike; noticeably different.
column7: The two games look similar at first but are actually quite dissimilar.
column8: Often followed by to or from depending on dialect/style: dissimilar to/from.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: dissimilar meaning

column5: An organized athletics competition consisting of running races and usually jumping/throwing events on or around a track.
column7: Our school hosted a track meet on Saturday. / She ran the 800 meters and the relay at the same track meet.
column8: AmE track meet; BrE often athletics meeting/meet. Track and field includes track races plus field events such as long jump, high jump, shot put, etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: track meet meaning

column4: noun; regional Australian slang / hunting slang
column5: 1. Australian slang, especially associated with Canberra: a disparaging or humorous label for a working-class, uncultivated, or 'bogan'-type person. 2. In North American hunting slang, a trophy animal large enough to qualify for, or evoke, Boone and Crockett record-book standards.
column6: bogan, yobbo (Australian sense; approximate); trophy animal, record-book animal (hunting sense)
column7: The term 'booner' has been used in Canberra slang for a stereotypically rough or uncultivated person. / The hunter called the enormous buck a booner.
column8: KEEP + FIX. This is not merely an undefined internet coinage. Meanings are regional/domain-specific, so context matters. The Australian social label can be disparaging; the hunting sense derives from Boone and Crockett trophy/record-book standards.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: booner meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::slang usage::humorous usage::disparaging usage::north_american_english usage::informal usage::evaluative topic::animals discovery::qualification

column5: To have absolutely no idea or knowledge about something.
column6: have no clue, not have the faintest idea, not have the slightest idea, be clueless
column7: I haven't the foggiest where he put the keys. / I don't have the foggiest idea what that acronym stands for. / 'How does this setting work?' 'Haven't the foggiest.'
column8: Informal idiom, especially associated with BrE: 'I haven't the foggiest' can omit 'idea' because it is understood. Equivalent to 'not have the faintest/slightest idea.' In AmE, 'I don't have the foggiest' also occurs.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: i haven't the foggiest meaning

column5: A basic principle, element, or early undeveloped form of something; usually plural rudiments for the fundamental skills or facts of a subject.
column6: basic, fundamental, element, foundation, first principle
column7: She taught me the rudiments of music theory before we moved on to composition. / He understands the rudiments of editing but not the more technical workflow yet.
column8: Common: the rudiments of X. Rudimentary (existing WID1925) = basic/undeveloped. Singular rudiment is less common in everyday speech and can also mean a vestigial/undeveloped structure in biology.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: rudiment

column5: To get or ask for something from someone for free, especially a small item such as a cigarette, ride, food, or money.
column6: mooch, cadge (BrE), sponge, scrounge, borrow/get for free
column7: Can I bum a cigarette off you? / He was always bumming rides off his friends. / I bummed a charger off someone at the café for ten minutes.
column8: Informal, especially AmE. Pattern 'bum X off someone' or simply 'bum X.' It can imply casual freeloading but is often lighthearted for small favors/items.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: bum off you meaning
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::casual usage::american_english usage::british_english topic::food discovery::expressing_need

column5: The natural coloring of skin, hair, eyes, tissue, or another material caused by pigments.
column7: The condition can affect skin pigmentation.
column8: General biological/descriptive term; pigment is the coloring substance, pigmentation the coloring or pattern/process.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: pigmentation meaning

column5: To gather together in a group or crowd.
column7: Fans began to congregate outside the theater before the doors opened.
column8: Often used of people gathering in a particular place.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: congregate meaning

column5: A playful or mocking coinage modeled on 'weeaboo,' referring to a non-American person seen as excessively idealizing, imitating, or obsessing over U.S. culture.
column6: America-obsessed person, U.S.-culture fan (neutral paraphrase), reverse-weeb (joking)
column7: His friends jokingly called him an Americaboo because he romanticized diners, pickup trucks, college football, and every American cliché. / The term is usually internet wordplay, not a stable identity label.
column8: Productive -boo formation modeled on weeaboo; meanings and tone vary. Usually humorous/pejorative and often critiques idealization of a country through media stereotypes.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: americaboo meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::humorous usage::playful usage::critical usage::informal topic::internet topic::culture

column2: get / be brought up to speed
column5: To become fully informed about the current situation, recent developments, procedures, or knowledge needed to participate effectively.
column6: get caught up, get updated, get briefed, become current
column7: Give me ten minutes to get up to speed on what happened yesterday. / Can you bring Maya up to speed before the meeting? / It took me a week to get up to speed with the new workflow.
column8: Raw 'caught up to speed' blends 'caught up' and 'up to speed.' Standard: get/be up to speed; bring someone up to speed. 'Catch someone up' is also natural.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: caught up to speed

column2: no wonder / it's no wonder that
column5: It is not surprising; the preceding facts make the result easy to understand.
column7: He slept three hours—no wonder he's exhausted. / It's no wonder that people were confused by the instructions.
column8: Raw 'there's no wonder that' is generally less idiomatic for this meaning. Prefer 'it's no wonder that...' or simply 'no wonder...'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: there's no wonder that meaning

column5: A defiant or dismissive retort meaning roughly 'leave me alone,' 'screw you,' or 'I don't care what you think.'
column6: screw you, get lost, kiss my ass, go to hell
column7: You don't like my haircut? Bite me. / 'You can't do that.' 'Bite me.' / Among close friends it can be mock-defiant, but to a stranger it will usually sound hostile.
column8: Confrontational and rude, though sometimes playful among friends. It rejects criticism, authority, or unwanted advice rather than literally inviting biting. Tone is crucial; it is much stronger than 'whatever.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: bite me meaning

column5: To cause someone to form a particular belief, perception, or feeling, intentionally or unintentionally.
column6: make it seem that, create the impression that, suggest, convey the impression that
column7: The trailer gives the impression that she's the main character, but she disappears after episode two. / I didn't mean to give the impression that I was angry; I was just tired.
column8: Useful when separating appearance from fact. 'Give the impression of being X' is another pattern. Can be intentional or accidental; 'pretend' specifically implies intention.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: give the impression that meaning

column2: let up vs chill out vs stop
column5: Let up means become less intense or stop pressing/harassing; chill out means relax or calm down; stop is the broad neutral verb for ceasing an action.
column7: The rain finally let up. / Chill out—it's not a big deal. / Stop shouting.
column8: Raw search said 'chill up'; normalized to the idiomatic chill out. Preserve as a contrast because the three are not interchangeable.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: let up vs chill up vs stop

column5: Thoroughly tough, rebellious, dangerous, or impressively 'bad' all the way through; sometimes admiring rather than condemning.
column7: The character walks in like he's bad to the bone.
column8: Popularized strongly in modern culture by the George Thorogood song/title; bad may carry a swaggering, admiring sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: bad to the bone meaning

column5: To leave someone waiting, uncertain, unsupported, or without the response/completion they expect; also to fail to return an offered high-five.
column6: keep someone waiting, leave someone in suspense, abandon someone, leave someone high and dry (stronger/contextual)
column7: You can't say 'I have huge news' and then leave me hanging. / She never replied, so I was left hanging for three days. / Don't leave me hanging—high five!
column8: Meaning depends on situation: unanswered message/question, unresolved information, lack of support, or literal social gesture. Leave high and dry usually implies more serious abandonment.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: leave someone hanging meaning
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal topic::communication discovery::uncertainty

column2: pull a fast one on someone
column5: To trick, deceive, or cheat someone, especially through a clever maneuver or by exploiting their inattention.
column6: trick, fool, deceive, con, put one over on
column7: Don't try to pull a fast one on me—I checked the numbers already. / They pulled a fast one by changing the terms at the last minute.
column8: Usually implies crafty deception rather than a huge elaborate fraud. Common: 'Are you trying to pull a fast one on me?'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: pulling a fast one on me meaning

column5: Still possible, available, or under consideration; not ruled out.
column7: A later launch is not off the table if testing takes longer.
column8: Off the table = removed from consideration; not off reverses that.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: it's not off the table meaning

column5: Punishment that deliberately inflicts physical pain on a person's body, traditionally including practices such as spanking or caning.
column7: Corporal punishment is banned in schools in many places. / The debate was not about ordinary discipline but specifically about whether physical punishment should ever be permitted.
column8: Corporal here means bodily/physical, not the military rank corporal. Distinguish capital punishment = execution/death penalty.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: corporal punishment

column5: To have as much of something as one wants or can tolerate; depending on context, to be satisfied by abundance or to be thoroughly tired/fed up with it.
column6: get enough of, have enough of, be satiated with; be fed up with
column7: At the buffet, you can have your fill of both dishes. / I've had my fill of pointless online arguments for one day. / 'I can have my fill of both of you' could be positive, sensual, playful, or hostile depending on source context.
column8: Literal origin is eating/drinking until satisfied, then figurative abundance. Tone is highly context-dependent with people; preserve ambiguity rather than forcing one reading.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: I can have my fill of both of you meaning

column5: Resistance, opposition, criticism, or negative reaction against a proposal, change, claim, policy, request, or pressure.
column6: resistance, opposition, backlash, objections, resistance to change
column7: The new policy faced immediate pushback from employees. / I expected some pushback when I suggested changing the workflow. / The claim received pushback from other researchers.
column8: Pushback is often direct resistance to a specific move; backlash can suggest a broader/stronger public reaction after something happens. Very common in work, politics, media, and discussion.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define pushback

column5: Excessively submissive, deferential, or slave-like obedience to authority, implying loss of independence, dignity, or critical judgment.
column6: slavish obedience, abject submission, unquestioning obedience, subservience
column7: The essay criticizes servile obedience to authority rather than ordinary cooperation. / He expected servile obedience from everyone beneath him.
column8: Servile is strongly negative and historically relates to servitude/slavery. Stronger than obedient; suggests degrading subordination or fawning compliance.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: servile obedience

column5: A broad claim about a whole group that ignores important differences and can reinforce prejudice, stigma, or harmful assumptions.
column6: overgeneralization, blanket statement, harmful stereotype, broad-brush claim
column7: Saying that an entire generation is lazy is a sweeping harmful generalization, not a useful description of millions of individuals. / The criticism identifies both problems: the claim is sweeping, and the stereotype can cause harm.
column8: Not a fixed dictionary idiom, but the searched phrase captures a useful distinction: 'sweeping' describes overbreadth; 'harmful' describes consequences/content. A broad generalization is not automatically false, but needs evidence and qualification.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: sweeping harmful generalization meaing

column5: A small, interesting piece of information or a small tasty piece of food.
column7: She shared a few interesting tidbits about how the film was made.
column8: Also spelled titbit in British English.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: tidbits meaning

column2: sit in the corner and think about what you did
column3: /ˌsɪt ɪn ðə ˈkɔːrnər ən ˌθɪŋk əˌbaʊt wʌt ju ˈdɪd/
column5: A humorous or exaggerated command treating someone like a misbehaving child who should go away, reflect on their behavior, and feel ashamed.
column6: go to the corner, think about what you've done, go sit in time-out
column7: That pun was terrible. Go sit in the corner and think about what you did. / After recommending that awful movie to me, you can sit in the corner and think about what you've done.
column8: Evokes old-fashioned child discipline/time-out. Often playful online or among friends, not a fixed formal idiom.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: sit in the corner and think about what you did meaning
column12: entry::idiom usage::formal usage::dated usage::humorous usage::playful topic::family discovery::criticism

column2: as in vs as to vs as for
column5: As in introduces an example or intended sense; as to means regarding/about or introduces an indirect question; as for shifts the topic to a particular person or thing.
column6: as in: for example, in the sense of | as to: regarding, concerning | as for: regarding, turning to
column7: 'Cold' as in unfriendly. / There is doubt as to whether it will work. / As for the price, we can discuss it later.
column8: Preserve as a contrast card because the original search explicitly compared three similar-looking structures.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: as in vs as to vs as for

column5: Repeatedly or persistently troubled, harmed, or beset by something unpleasant, as though by a plague.
column6: beset by, afflicted by, dogged by, troubled by, riddled with
column7: The production was plagued by delays and budget problems. / He was plagued with doubts before the interview. / The game launched with servers plagued by crashes.
column8: Stronger sense of persistent/recurrent trouble than simple 'affected by.' Plagued by is broadly common; plagued with often emphasizes being full of/repeatedly experiencing a problem. Existing examples use plagued but no standalone productive card.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: plagued

column5: A large box/chest; the enclosed luggage compartment of a car (AmE; BrE boot); the main stem of a tree; an elephant's long flexible nose; the main body/torso; also various main channels/lines.
column6: car boot (BrE), chest, tree stem, elephant proboscis, torso
column7: Put the suitcase in the trunk. / The elephant lifted its trunk. / The tree trunk was too wide to wrap my arms around. / The nerves branch from the main trunk.
column8: Highly polysemous. For cars: AmE trunk vs BrE boot. 'Swimming trunks' = men's swim shorts, usually plural.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: trunk

column5: A metal fastener; a sliding door lock; a flash of lightning; a projectile for a crossbow. As a verb, to fasten, suddenly run away, move abruptly, or swallow food very quickly.
column6: fastener, latch; dash, flee, make a run for it; gulp
column7: The horse bolted when it heard the explosion. / He bolted the door before going upstairs. / A bolt of lightning struck nearby. / Don't bolt your food—you'll make yourself sick.
column8: Highly polysemous. 'Bolt from the blue' is a separate idiom already in the Master. Motion sense implies sudden rapid escape. Food sense = swallow/eat too quickly.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: bolt meanig

column5: Time that was unavailable, wasted, missed, or taken away from normal activity/work; also time one later tries to recover or compensate for.
column6: wasted time, missed time, downtime (contextual), time lost
column7: We worked late to make up for lost time. / The injury resulted in several weeks of lost time at work.
column8: Common fixed collocation in 'make up for lost time.' In employment/safety contexts, lost time can have technical meanings such as absence caused by injury.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: lost time meaning
column12: entry::collocation entry::noun_phrase usage::technical topic::work discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: In Superman stories, a fictional substance that weakens Superman; figuratively, a person's particular weakness, temptation, vulnerability, or thing they find unusually hard to resist or handle.
column6: Achilles' heel, weakness, downfall, weak spot
column7: Chocolate is my kryptonite—I can ignore most desserts, but not that. / Public speaking is basically his kryptonite even though he's confident one-on-one.
column8: The figurative use is extremely common and often playful. Unlike Achilles' heel, kryptonite can be a temptation ('cheesecake is my kryptonite') as well as a vulnerability.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: kryptonite

column5: To walk with short steps while swaying from side to side, like a duck or penguin; can be humorous or insulting when used of a person.
column7: The penguins waddled toward the water. / After putting on three layers of winter clothes, I could barely do anything except waddle.
column8: Often cute/humorous for animals/children, but describing an adult's body or gait as waddling can sound mocking. Motion combines short steps + side-to-side sway.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: waddle meaning

column5: Relating to or affected by anorexia, especially anorexia nervosa; historically also meaning causing or characterized by loss of appetite.
column6: having anorexia, affected by anorexia nervosa
column7: The article describes the difficulties faced by anorexic patients during recovery. / Calling a merely thin person 'anorexic' is inaccurate and can be hurtful.
column8: In ordinary speech, anorexic is sometimes misused as a casual synonym for extremely thin; medically, anorexia nervosa is an eating disorder and cannot be inferred from appearance alone. 'Person with anorexia' is often preferable when discussing an individual.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define anorexic

column5: To make an attempt at doing, solving, answering, or guessing something, especially without certainty of success.
column6: have a go at, try, take a shot at
column7: I'll take a stab at explaining why the code fails.
column8: Can also be 'take a stab in the dark' for a guess made with little information.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: take a stab meaning

column5: In The Good Place, the deliberately absurd name for the afterlife's nonlinear conception of time: its timeline loops and curves in a shape resembling the written words 'Jeremy Bearimy.'
column6: nonlinear afterlife time, Jeremy Bearimy timeline
column7: Michael explains that time in the afterlife doesn't move in a straight line; it moves in a 'Jeremy Bearimy.' / The joke lets the show hand-wave impossible chronology while making the explanation itself part of the comedy.
column8: Search provenance: 'good place michael's explanation jeremy.' This is a show-specific cultural reference rather than ordinary English vocabulary. The dot over the i is itself part of the joke and represents especially inexplicable temporal states.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: good place michael's explanation jeremy

column5: Of a bird, to clean and arrange its feathers with its beak; of a person, to groom oneself carefully or behave with visible self-satisfaction/pride.
column6: groom, primp; congratulate oneself, strut, bask
column7: The parrot spent several minutes preening its feathers. / He preened in front of the mirror before the interview. / The politician was preening over the favorable headlines.
column8: Human figurative sense often carries mild criticism: visibly pleased with oneself. 'Preen oneself on X' = take self-satisfied pride in X. Bird sense is literal grooming.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define preening

column5: A small child, especially an energetic or mischievous one; historically, it has also had other regional or insulting senses.
column7: The little tyke had already figured out how to open the gate.
column8: Common affectionate/informal child sense. Historical senses include dog and a rude/uncouth person; Yorkshire 'Tyke' can also be a regional nickname.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: define tyke

column5: A two-beat gait faster than a walk and slower than a canter/gallop, especially of horses; by extension, to move at a brisk, short-stepped pace.
column7: The horse broke into a trot. / The dog trotted over to greet us. / She trotted down the stairs to answer the door.
column8: Also figurative phrasal 'trot something out' = repeatedly present an argument/excuse; existing card covers that separately.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: trot meaning

column5: In charge of or directing an organization, project, government, team, or other undertaking.
column6: in charge, in control, leading, at the controls, running the show
column7: The company changed dramatically with a new CEO at the helm. / Who was at the helm when the project began?
column8: Helm is literally the steering position/control of a ship. Figurative leadership metaphor. Related recent card 'in the driver's seat' emphasizes control; at the helm often emphasizes leadership/management.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: at the helm meaning
column12: entry::idiom usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly topic::government topic::politics discovery::public_discourse discovery::debate_language

column5: Literally, to drive something in by striking it; figuratively, to make an idea, lesson, rule, or fact stick through forceful emphasis or repetition. 'Hammer home' is especially idiomatic for emphasizing a point.
column6: drill in, drive home, pound in, impress upon, reinforce
column7: The teacher hammered the rule into us until nobody forgot it. / The final scene hammers home the cost of his decision. / He hammered the nail in with three blows.
column8: For ideas, 'hammer home a point/message' and 'hammer something into someone' are very natural. 'Hammer in' alone is more literal/compositional.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: hammer in

column5: Gameplay in which human players compete directly against other human players, as opposed to fighting only computer-controlled enemies.
column7: I mostly play PvE, but my friend lives for PvP. / The patch completely changed the PvP meta. / Some games let you toggle PvP on or off.
column8: Contrast PvE = player versus environment. PvP can describe a mode, combat, server, build, meta, etc. Exact rules vary by game.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116, voca_0119 | search: pvp meaning
column12: entry::initialism entry::word usage::military topic::technology topic::games discovery::contrast

column5: People regarded as disreputable, undesirable, low-class, or socially inferior.
column6: rabble, undesirables, lowlifes, scum (stronger), hoi polloi (different nuance)
column7: The snobbish character complained that the neighborhood was filling up with riffraff. / The bouncer was told to keep the 'riffraff' out—a deliberately contemptuous way to describe people.
column8: Disparaging and often reveals the speaker's class prejudice/snobbery. Usually collective and uncountable: 'the riffraff,' not normally 'a riffraff.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: riffraff

column5: An Anglican parish priest; more broadly in some usage, a clergy member serving a parish or acting as a representative/deputy in ecclesiastical contexts.
column7: The village vicar conducted the wedding. / In an old British comedy, the local vicar is often a recognizable social character.
column8: Do not treat priest, vicar, rector, pastor, and minister as exact synonyms; titles depend on denomination and church structure. Vicar is strongly associated with the Church of England/Anglican context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113, voca_0114 | search: vicar
column12: entry::word usage::british_english usage::religious topic::performance topic::government topic::politics discovery::public_discourse

column5: In an overly self-confident, smug, or brash manner, especially when confidence seems unjustified or irritating.
column7: He cockily predicted a sweep before the first game had even started. / She leaned back and said, a little too cockily, 'I've got this.'
column8: Cocky is informal and usually negative, though playful admiration is possible. Confident is neutral/positive; cocky adds excessive self-assurance and often showiness.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: in a cocky way meaning

column5: A city in the West Midlands of England; also appears in the idiom 'send someone to Coventry,' meaning deliberately ignore or socially ostracize someone.
column7: The factory was based in Coventry. / After the argument, they practically sent him to Coventry.
column8: Preserve both place recognition and the culturally specific idiom likely to arise in British contexts.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: Coventry

column5: Continuing for a long time or longer than usual or expected.
column7: The region suffered a prolonged period of drought. / Prolonged eye contact can start to feel awkward. / After a prolonged silence, he finally answered.
column8: Often suggests that the duration is notable, burdensome, or longer than desirable. Common collocations: prolonged period, exposure, illness, absence, silence, conflict, use. 'Protracted' is more formal and often stresses troublesome length; 'extended' is more neutral.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: prolonged

column5: To treat or worship someone/something as a god; figuratively, to idolize or elevate a person to an unrealistically exalted status.
column7: Some rulers were deified after death. / Fans sometimes deify creators and then react harshly when they turn out to be ordinary people.
column8: Strong word. Figurative deify goes beyond admire: it suggests near-worship or placing someone above normal criticism.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: deified meaning

column5: Justified, reasonable, or supported by the circumstances or evidence.
column7: Given the evidence, further investigation is warranted.
column8: Opposite of existing unwarranted. Common formal pattern: concern/action is warranted.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: define warranted

column5: The state of being famous for something extremely bad, shameful, or notorious; an infamous reputation.
column7: The attack became a date that would live in infamy. / The disastrous finale achieved a kind of internet infamy.
column8: Infamy is stronger and darker than ordinary notoriety. Famous = widely known; notorious/infamous = widely known for something bad.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: define infamy

column5: A derogatory internet label for a man portrayed as weak, unmasculine, overly sensitive, submissive, or politically/culturally progressive, based on a pseudoscientific stereotype linking soy consumption with feminization.
column6: weak man, unmanly man (insult), beta male (related insult)
column7: The comment section dismissed anyone who disagreed as a 'soyboy' instead of answering the argument. / The insult relies on a culture-war stereotype, not a serious nutritional diagnosis.
column8: Pejorative manosphere/culture-war slang. The soy→feminization premise grossly misrepresents the effects of dietary phytoestrogens. Useful for understanding rhetoric, not as a neutral description.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: soyboy
column12: entry::variant_set entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::critical usage::derogatory usage::rhetorical usage::informal usage::evaluative topic::internet topic::politics discovery::public_discourse discovery::debate_language

column5: Ask someone to repeat or explain what they just said, often because it was unclear, surprising, complicated, or hard to believe.
column6: say that again, go over that again, repeat that, walk me through that again
column7: Sorry, run that by me again—are you saying the meeting moved to tomorrow? / Run that last part by me again; I think I missed the distinction.
column8: Productive construction: run something by someone = tell/show them an idea or plan to get their reaction: 'Can I run something by you?' With again, it often means repeat/explain.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: run that by me again meaning
column12: entry::phrase usage::informal usage::presentation-friendly topic::communication discovery::explanation discovery::uncertainty discovery::iteration discovery::presentation_language

column5: The geologic period from about 145 to 66 million years ago, the final period of the Mesozoic Era, ending with the mass extinction that eliminated non-avian dinosaurs.
column7: Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops lived near the end of the Cretaceous. / Flowering plants diversified dramatically during the Cretaceous.
column8: Comes after Jurassic and before Paleogene. 'Late Cretaceous' is especially common in dinosaur contexts. Existing cards mention Cretaceous incidentally; standalone period is useful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: cretaceous meaning

column5: A disappointment: someone or something that fails to meet expectations, hopes, or promises; the feeling/result of being disappointed.
column6: disappointment, anticlimax, disappointment after hype, bust
column7: After all that hype, the finale was a bit of a letdown. / The hotel looked amazing online, so the tiny room was a real letdown.
column8: Usually countable: a letdown. 'Anticlimax' specifically emphasizes a weak/disappointing culmination after buildup. 'Let someone down' is the related verb phrase.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: letdown meaning

column5: A very close, affectionate, emotionally significant friendship between men, framed playfully with the language of romance but usually understood as nonsexual/nonromantic.
column6: close male friendship, male bonding, buddy relationship
column7: Their off-screen bromance became almost as popular with fans as the show itself. / The movie is basically a road-trip bromance disguised as an action comedy.
column8: Blend of bro + romance. Can normalize male affection, but sometimes carries an assumption that intimacy between men needs a joking heterosexual frame. Context/tone varies.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: bromance meaning
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::humorous usage::affectionate topic::friends topic::relationships

column5: To apply or bring to bear force, effort, influence, authority, pressure, or another power; reflexively, to make a strong effort.
column6: apply, exercise, use, bring to bear; strain oneself, make an effort
column7: You don't need to exert much force to close the latch. / The studio exerted enormous pressure on the director to shorten the film. / He rarely exerts himself unless the deadline is immediate.
column8: Common collocations: exert force/pressure/influence/control/authority/effort; exert oneself. Exercise influence/authority is close; exert often emphasizes active force or pressure.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: exert meaning

column5: A person or business that sells fish and seafood, especially at a shop or market.
column6: fish seller, seafood seller, fish dealer
column7: The fishmonger recommended a whole sea bass for dinner. / We bought fresh scallops from the local fishmonger.
column8: Traditional occupational compound. -monger historically means dealer/trader; in modern figurative compounds such as fearmonger it can be disparaging.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: fishmonger meaning
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::disparaging usage::evaluative topic::business discovery::promotion

column5: The act or process of rising to a higher position, level, rank, or spiritual realm.
column7: Her rapid ascension to the top job surprised the industry.
column8: Often more elevated/formal than rise. Capitalized Ascension has specific Christian religious meanings.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: define ascension
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::religious usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::process_details discovery::debate_language

column5: Extremely worried, upset, distressed, or emotionally agitated.
column6: distressed, devastated, frantic, beside oneself, deeply upset
column7: She was distraught after realizing her dog was missing. / He sounded distraught on the phone and could barely explain what happened. / The parents were understandably distraught while they waited for news.
column8: Strong emotional word: more intense than 'upset' and often suggests someone is overwhelmed by worry, grief, fear, or shock. Common collocations: distraught mother/parent/family, visibly distraught, become distraught.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: define distraught

column5: A rapidly rotating column of air; figuratively, a fast, intense burst of activity, events, or emotion.
column7: The week after the announcement was a whirlwind of interviews and meetings.
column8: Common figurative patterns: a whirlwind of activity/emotions; a whirlwind romance; a whirlwind tour.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: whirlwind meaning

column5: A clicking sound made with the tongue to express disapproval, annoyance, impatience, or mild reproach; to make that sound.
column7: She tutted when she saw the muddy footprints on the floor. / 'Tut, tut,' he said, pretending to be scandalized.
column8: Especially associated with British English; U.S. speakers more often write 'tsk.' Can be genuinely disapproving or theatrically/playfully judgmental.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: tut meaning

column5: To remove or send something away with a quick, light, sharp movement, usually of a finger or hand.
column6: brush away, swat away, flip away, knock away
column7: She flicked the bug away from her sleeve. / He flicked away the notification without reading it. / The character casually flicks the blade away as if it weighs nothing.
column8: Can be literal or figurative/digital. Flick away emphasizes a small quick dismissive motion; brush away is often gentler; swat away suggests a broader/stronger strike.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: flick away  meaning

column5: A person who tends to prefer lower-stimulation environments, solitude, or smaller-scale social interaction and who may restore energy through time alone; not simply a shy, antisocial, or socially unskilled person.
column6: introverted person, inward-oriented person (rough); opposite: extrovert
column7: I'm an introvert, but I still enjoy long conversations with people I know well. / Being introverted doesn't automatically mean being shy—you can be socially confident and still need a lot of alone time afterward.
column8: Everyday personality label, not a diagnosis. Introversion concerns temperament/energy/stimulation preferences more than fear of social judgment. Ambivert is commonly used for people showing a mix of introverted/extroverted tendencies.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: introvert

column5: For a quality, habit, attitude, or influence to be transferred from one person to another through close contact or association.
column7: Her optimism started to rub off on the rest of the team.
column8: Raw search was 'rub it off on someone'; the idiomatic form for transferred influence is rub off on someone. Do not confuse with literally rubbing something off a surface.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: rub it off on someone
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::self-help discovery::evaluation

column5: To pursue a similar career, role, lifestyle, achievement, or course of action as someone who came before you.
column6: follow someone's example, emulate, take the same path
column7: She followed in her mother's footsteps and became a doctor. / The sequel tries to follow in the original's footsteps without simply copying it.
column8: Usually about a life/career path or precedent, not literal walking. Can be admiring or neutral. 'Follow someone's lead' is more immediate/situational.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: follow in someone's footsteps

column5: Used to say that something will never happen or is extremely unlikely.
column6: never, not in a million years, when hell freezes over, fat chance (related)
column7: He'll apologize when pigs fly. / 'Do you think he'll voluntarily wake up at 6 a.m.?' 'Yeah, when pigs fly.' / She joked that she'd give up coffee when pigs fly.
column8: Built on an obviously impossible image and normally means 'never' or 'extremely unlikely.' Often sarcastic/playful rather than a neutral probability statement. 'When hell freezes over' is stronger/rougher; 'fat chance' expresses skepticism rather than a time clause.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: when pigs fly meaning

column5: Irritable, bad-tempered, or easily annoyed; also sometimes not working smoothly, especially of a machine or system.
column7: I'm always cranky when I haven't slept enough.
column8: Common conversational American English. Machine/system sense is less central but useful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: cranky

column5: To carry social status, esteem, cachet, or perceived distinction because people associate it with an institution, role, label, product, tradition, etc.
column6: carry prestige, have status, confer cachet, be prestigious
column7: The degree had a lot of prestige attached to it in that industry. / Certain job titles have prestige attached to them even when the work is similar.
column8: Natural construction: X has prestige/status/stigma/value attached to it. 'Attached' emphasizes socially associated rather than inherent quality.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: had prestige attached to it

column5: To punish someone conspicuously or severely so that others will be deterred from doing the same thing.
column6: punish as a warning, set an example through punishment
column7: The school made an example of the students who organized the prank.
column8: Usually negative/coercive; distinct from 'set a good example.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: make an example of someone

column5: The process of carefully checking a person's background, qualifications, reliability, security risk, claims, or suitability before approval, hiring, publication, selection, etc.
column6: screening, background checking, due diligence, verification, review
column7: Every candidate goes through a fairly extensive vetting process. / The article was published without enough vetting of its sources. / I do a little vetting before recommending a channel I barely know.
column8: Vet = examine/check carefully. Background check is one kind of vetting; due diligence is broader and common in business/legal contexts. 'Vetting' often implies filtering before trust/access/selection is granted.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: vetting
column12: entry::word topic::security discovery::risk discovery::process_details discovery::qualification discovery::social_approval

column5: By repeating a process in successive cycles, using each result or round to refine, improve, or advance the next one.
column6: repeatedly in cycles, incrementally, through iteration
column7: We improved the flashcard pipeline iteratively: test a batch, inspect the problems, then adjust the next batch. / The model is refined iteratively rather than designed perfectly in one pass.
column8: Important distinction: iterative = repeated cycles; incremental = built in small additions. A process can be both, but they are not identical. Common in software, design, optimization, and research.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: Iteratively

column5: Knowledge or recognition gained from experience or repeated exposure; also an easy, informal manner arising from closeness.
column7: Her familiarity with the software made the task much faster.
column8: Common patterns: familiarity with; breed familiarity; undue familiarity. Related adjective familiar.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: familiarity

column5: To make someone's appearance look especially attractive or favorable, especially when said of clothing, colors, lighting, or a style.
column7: That shade of blue is really flattering on you.
column8: Also simply 'That dress is flattering.' Compare flatter as a verb meaning praise someone, often excessively.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: something is flattering on me meaning

column2: I don't have time vs I don't have the time
column5: I don't have time = I lack enough available time. I don't have the time can mean the same with more emphasis, or 'I don't know what time it is' in certain contexts; 'the time' may also refer to a specific required amount/opportunity.
column6: I have no time; I don't have enough time
column7: I don't have time to watch a two-hour video tonight. / I don't have the time to argue about this right now. / 'Do you have the time?' can mean 'Do you know what time it is?'
column8: Article changes nuance rather than creating a simple correctness rule. For ordinary lack of availability, no article is extremely common. 'Don't have the time for X' can sound emphatic/dismissive: I won't devote my time/energy to it.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: I don't have time vs I don't have the time
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::debate-friendly topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::emphasis discovery::lack_of_knowledge discovery::debate_language

column5: In a way relating to hearing or the sense of sound; by means of auditory perception.
column7: The two consonants are hard for me to distinguish auditorily, even though I can see the difference on a spectrogram. / The scene is easy to follow visually but confusing auditorily.
column8: Raw 'auditorially' is a plausible formation but auditorily is the more standard dictionary adverb from auditory. 'Aurally' is shorter and often more natural. Do not confuse auditory (hearing) with auditor (person who examines accounts).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: auditorially

column5: Poorly regulated or unable to maintain normal control/stability; used of emotions, physiology, behavior, biological systems, markets/processes, etc.
column6: poorly regulated, unstable, out of balance
column7: After the argument he felt emotionally dysregulated and had trouble calming down. / Dysregulated immune signaling can contribute to disease.
column8: Broad technical/clinical adjective. Emotional dysregulation has specific psychological uses, but casual internet use can be looser. Avoid treating it as a diagnosis by itself.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: dysregulated
column12: entry::word usage::casual usage::technical usage::rhetorical usage::informal topic::biology topic::science discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::debate_language

column5: A fan-made scanned and translated version of a comic, especially manga/manhwa/manhua, typically produced and distributed without the official publisher's authorization.
column6: fan translation, scanlated manga, fan-translated comic
column7: I first read the series through an old scanlation before an official English edition existed. / Scanlation quality can vary widely between groups.
column8: Blend of scan + translation. Scanlation groups may handle scanning, cleaning, typesetting, translation, proofreading, etc. Legal/copyright status differs from licensed translation; the term itself describes the fan-production practice.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: scanlation
column12: entry::fandom_term entry::term entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::technical usage::slang topic::manga topic::fandom topic::internet topic::media discovery::iteration discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To enter a place secretly, quietly, or without permission or notice.
column7: They sneaked into the theater through a side door.
column8: Both sneaked and snuck are common past-tense forms, with regional/style variation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: sneaked into meaning

column5: Designed to attach to a surface by means of adhesive; as a noun, something attached this way.
column7: She used stick-on labels to organize the storage boxes.
column8: Usually before a noun: stick-on label, patch, decoration, hook. Hyphenated as an attributive adjective.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: stick-on meaning

column5: Adopting or promoting an extremely pessimistic, fatalistic worldview in which a problem is seen as largely hopeless or beyond meaningful change.
column7: Hours of doom-focused content left him blackpilled about the future.
column8: Internet metaphor derived from red-pill language. Meaning varies by community and can occur in misogynistic/incel spaces as well as broader political/cultural pessimism.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: blackpilling
