column5: Tamper normally takes a thing, evidence, system, witness process, etc. With a person, the intended meaning may be improper influence/manipulation—especially 'tamper with a witness'—but ordinary English usually chooses manipulate, interfere with, mess with, or pressure depending on context.
column6: manipulate, interfere with, pressure; tamper with a witness
column7: The defendant was accused of tampering with a witness. / For ordinary interpersonal manipulation, 'he tampered with her' sounds unusual without special context.
column8: Do not generalize object-style tamper to people. Legal phrase witness tampering / tamper with a witness is established; other person objects require context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: tamper with someone meaning

column2: leave at the last possible moment
column5: To delay departure until the latest time one believes will still allow arrival or completion, leaving little or no buffer for delays.
column6: leave at the last minute, cut it fine, leave no margin for error
column7: I always leave at the last possible moment, so one delayed train can ruin everything. / He cuts it fine every morning and reaches the gate just before boarding closes.
column8: 'At the last minute' is broader; 'last possible moment' emphasizes deliberately using nearly all available buffer. BrE 'cut it fine' is a useful near-equivalent.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: always leave at the last possible moment meaning

column5: To argue repeatedly about small, petty, or relatively unimportant things, often in an irritated back-and-forth way.
column6: squabble, quarrel, wrangle, snipe at each other
column7: The siblings bickered over who got the front seat. / I like their chemistry—the constant bickering feels more affectionate than genuinely hostile.
column8: Not specifically slang. Bickering often sounds smaller/pettier than arguing or fighting. Squabble is close; banter is playful and need not involve genuine irritation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: bickering meaning slang

column5: Messy, flattened, or tousled hair caused by sleeping.
column6: messy morning hair, sleep-mussed hair, tousled hair
column7: I woke up with terrible bedhead and had no time to fix it. / His bedhead was sticking up in every direction. / I joined the video call with full-on bedhead.
column8: Also styled 'bed head.' Usually humorous/informal and refers to the messy hairstyle caused by sleeping, not the person. 'Tousled' can be deliberately stylish; bedhead specifically evokes having just gotten out of bed.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: bedhead meaning

column5: So dead—or figuratively so exhausted, numb, detached, or beyond concern—that caring is impossible.
column6: beyond caring, too exhausted to care
column7: After the all-nighter, I joked that I was too dead to care.
column8: Not a fixed idiom. Preserve the searched phrase because its hyperbolic/dark-humor force is the point.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: too dead to care meaning

column5: To move or drift away from a place, group, path, subject, rule, or expected course. 'Stray from' is usually more idiomatic for departing from a path, topic, plan, or norm.
column6: wander away, drift away, deviate from, depart from
column7: Try not to stray from the marked trail. / The adaptation strays pretty far from the original novel. / One sheep strayed away from the rest of the flock.
column8: For abstract departures, prefer stray from: stray from the topic/plan/path/tradition. 'Stray away' is possible, especially physical movement, but often sounds less idiomatic than wander away or stray from.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: stray away meaning

column5: A person or animal that lives in or occupies a particular place.
column7: The island has fewer than a thousand permanent inhabitants. / The documentary looks at the forest and its animal inhabitants. / In the fantasy novel, the cave's inhabitants rarely come to the surface.
column8: Used for people, animals, fictional beings, or populations occupying a place. 'Resident' is the most neutral for people; 'dweller' often appears in compounds (city-dweller); 'denizen' can sound literary and often means a characteristic inhabitant.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: define inhabitants

column5: To go back along the same route; figuratively, to reverse or modify a previous statement, decision, or position.
column7: The company backtracked after customers objected to the change.
column8: Often used for retreating from a public claim or policy.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0118 | search: backtrack meaning

column5: To feel physically unwell, emotionally bad, guilty, low, or generally lousy.
column6: feel lousy, feel awful, feel rough, feel under the weather (physical), feel bad
column7: I slept badly and feel pretty crummy today. / I felt crummy about canceling at the last minute, even though I had a good reason.
column8: Crummy is informal and mild-to-moderate. Physical 'feel crummy' is broader than under the weather; emotional use can mean guilty/down. Crummy can also describe poor-quality things: a crummy hotel.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: feel crummy meaning

column5: In a way relating to knowledge, justification, evidence, belief, or what one is rationally entitled to know/believe.
column6: with respect to knowledge/evidence, evidentially (contextual), epistemologically (not exact)
column7: The two claims may be morally similar but epistemically very different: one is supported by direct evidence and the other is speculation. / We should stay epistemically humble when the available evidence is weak.
column8: Epistemic = relating to knowledge/justified belief. Epistemically justified = justified as a belief. Epistemological often describes the theory/study of knowledge itself, so the adverbs are not always interchangeable. Common phrase: epistemically irresponsible/humble/justified.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: what does epistemically means

column5: An unexpected complication, variation, subtlety, or new feature that makes a situation or idea less straightforward.
column7: The new rule adds an interesting wrinkle to the debate.
column8: Distinct from a skin/fabric wrinkle. Common review/analysis phrase: an interesting/new wrinkle.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: interesting wrinkles meaning

column5: Causing a strong loss of energy, patience, emotion, money, or other resources; literally, removing liquid from something.
column7: That conversation was emotionally draining. / Long meetings are surprisingly draining when you're concentrating in a second language. / The plumber is draining the tank before replacing the valve.
column8: As adjective, emotionally/mentally/physically draining are very common. Compare exhausting (often stronger physical/general fatigue) and taxing (demanding effort/concentration).

column7: I know I sound like a broken record, but please back up your files.
column8: From a damaged vinyl record repeatedly playing the same groove.

column5: Existing in name only or very small in amount; also relating to a name, noun, stated face value, or unadjusted monetary amount depending on field.
column7: He is the nominal head of the organization, but someone else makes the decisions.
column8: Common senses: nominal leader, nominal fee, nominal value/GDP. Meaning varies substantially by domain.

column5: A natural way to say that one's English still needs substantial improvement. 'Could use some/a lot of work' means would benefit from improvement, repair, practice, or attention.
column6: My English still needs a lot of work; I still have a lot to improve in my English
column7: My English could still use a lot of work, especially when I have to explain something spontaneously. / The pronunciation is pretty good, but the rhythm could use some work.

column5: To turn something over; or to reverse, invalidate, or abolish a decision, law, judgment, or established situation.
column7: The appeals court overturned the earlier ruling.
column8: Useful synonyms depend on sense: reverse/strike down a ruling; topple a government; tip over a vehicle.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: overturn synonym

column5: To decline an offer, opportunity, activity, or question; to choose not to participate.
column6: pass, decline, sit this one out
column7: I'm taking a pass here—I don't know enough to comment responsibly.
column8: Often softer/more casual than refuse. 'I'll pass' is even more common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: I’m taking a pass here

column5: To politely lead, guide, or direct someone into a room, especially as a host, receptionist, servant, or staff member.
column6: usher in, escort in, lead in, see someone in
column7: The receptionist showed me into a small meeting room. / Please show our guests into the lounge while I finish setting the table.
column8: Here show = guide/escort, not display. Related: show someone out = escort them to the exit; show someone around = give a tour; show someone to their seat/room.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: show someone into a room meaning

column5: A loosely used term for migraine-related visual symptoms. It may refer to migraine with visual aura, while 'retinal migraine' is a rarer condition involving temporary visual disturbance in one eye.
column6: visual migraine, migraine with visual aura (often intended), retinal migraine (not always equivalent)
column7: She described flashing zigzags before the headache and called it an ocular migraine. / Because 'ocular migraine' is used inconsistently, a clinician may ask whether the visual symptoms affected one eye or both.
column8: Terminology is imprecise in everyday use. Migraine aura often produces visual phenomena perceived in both eyes/visual fields; retinal migraine is rare and monocular. New or sudden vision loss needs medical assessment rather than assuming migraine.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: ocular migraine
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::specialist topic::health discovery::terminology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Larva is an immature stage of an animal such as an insect; lava is molten rock that reaches Earth's surface.
column6: larva: immature form, grub (for some insects) | lava: molten rock
column7: A caterpillar is a larva; molten lava flowed from the volcano.
column8: Useful near-sound contrast. Plural of larva is larvae /ˈlɑːrviː/ (also larvas in some nontechnical use).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: larva vs lava

column5: To collapse violently inward; figuratively, for an organization, relationship, plan, career, argument, etc. to collapse or destroy itself from internal pressure/problems.
column6: collapse inward, cave in; collapse, unravel, self-destruct
column7: The damaged container imploded under external pressure. / The team imploded after weeks of internal conflict. / His argument imploded once the contradictory evidence appeared.
column8: Opposite image of explode, though real physical usage is more specific than simply 'collapse.' Figurative implode strongly suggests internal failure rather than destruction imposed entirely from outside.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: implode
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::rhetorical topic::work topic::relationships discovery::figurative_extension discovery::debate_language

column5: A flowering plant genus native to southern Africa, known for tall stems topped with rounded clusters of blue, purple, or white trumpet-shaped flowers; commonly called lily of the Nile or African lily.
column6: lily of the Nile, African lily
column7: Agapanthus lined the walkway with large blue flower clusters. / Despite the common name 'lily of the Nile,' agapanthus is not a true lily and is native to southern Africa.
column8: Botanical genus Agapanthus. Common names can mislead geographically/taxonomically. The name derives from Greek elements meaning love + flower.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define agapanthus

column5: I'm extremely angry or furious, often with the image of anger so intense that one is metaphorically giving off smoke or fumes.
column6: I'm furious, I'm livid, I'm seething, I'm pissed off
column7: I'm absolutely fuming—they cancelled it after we'd already traveled two hours. / He looked calm in the meeting, but afterward he told me, 'I'm fuming.'
column8: Very common especially in BrE, but understood broadly. Fuming usually means intense anger, stronger than annoyed. 'Seething' often suggests anger being contained rather than openly expressed.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: i'm fuming meaning

column5: Emotionally or socially distant, reserved, detached, or unwilling to become friendly/involved; sometimes seeming cold or superior.
column7: He seemed aloof at first, but he was actually just shy. / Her aloof manner made the group think she disliked them.
column8: Aloof describes outward social distance; it does not tell you the cause. Can be intentional, shy, self-protective, or arrogant.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: define aloof

column5: To begin an activity with a particular goal or intention.
column6: aim to, intend to, embark on, undertake, begin with the goal of
column7: We set out to build a simpler system, not a larger one. / She set out to prove the theory wrong but ended up supporting it. / The documentary sets out to explain how the industry changed.
column8: Focuses on the intention at the beginning; it does not guarantee the goal is achieved. Very useful narrative pattern: 'set out to X, but ended up Y.' Distinguish 'set out for + place' = begin a journey toward a destination.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: set out to do meaning

column5: A small, insignificant, weak, young, or unimpressive person, especially one regarded as having more confidence or attitude than their status warrants.
column6: small fry, runt, nobody, twerp, squirt
column7: Who does that little pipsqueak think he is, ordering everyone around? / The villain dismisses the young hero as a pipsqueak.
column8: Comic/old-fashioned insult. Often attacks size, age, status, or perceived insignificance rather than intelligence.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: pipsqueak

column2: go off on a tangent / get sidetracked / digress
column5: To leave the main subject, route, or task and move into a side topic or distraction—Japanese 脇道にそれる depending on context.
column6: digress, get sidetracked, go off track, veer off, wander off-topic
column7: Sorry, I went off on a tangent about pronunciation. / We got sidetracked and never returned to the original question.
column8: Recent cards already cover several members individually; this search-intent card maps the Japanese concept to natural English choices. Digress is more formal; tangent emphasizes a side topic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: 脇道にそれる 英語

column5: The scientific study of birds.
column7: Her interest in migration eventually led her to study ornithology. / Ornithology covers bird behavior, ecology, evolution, physiology, and classification. / A field guide can be useful to both birders and students of ornithology.
column8: A person who studies birds scientifically is an ornithologist. Distinguish ornithology (scientific discipline) from birding/birdwatching (recreational observation), though the interests can overlap.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: define ornithology

column5: Made worse or more severe; annoyed or irritated (especially informal AmE). In legal compounds, aggravated marks a more serious form of an offense because of specified circumstances.
column6: worsened, exacerbated; irritated, annoyed; more serious (legal)
column7: His knee pain was aggravated by running downhill. / I was getting aggravated by the constant interruptions. / 'Aggravated assault' is a legal category whose exact definition depends on jurisdiction.
column8: Important polysemy: aggravate originally/standardly = make worse; 'annoy' is now common, especially AmE. Legal aggravated is technical and should not be inferred from ordinary 'angry.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: aggravated
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::technical usage::american_english topic::law topic::grammar discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To move smoothly with a twisting, sliding motion, especially like a snake; figuratively, to move stealthily, unpleasantly, or insinuatingly.
column7: A snake slithered across the warm pavement. / He somehow slithered through the crowd without anyone noticing. / The villain slithers his way into positions of influence.
column8: Literal snake-like motion is core. Figurative use can make a person's movement/behavior sound sneaky, slimy, or morally repellent. Existing slithering card covers participle; standalone verb is useful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: slither meaning
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::warm topic::presentations discovery::presentation_language discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To suddenly reject or abandon a romantic partner, especially after having seemed committed to the relationship.
column7: He was devastated after being jilted just weeks before the wedding.
column8: Often appears as jilted: a jilted lover, bride, or fiancé(e).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: jilt meaning

column5: Prestige is primarily a noun meaning status/esteem; prestigious is an adjective meaning having or conferring prestige.
column7: The award carries prestige. / It's a prestigious award. / A prestige brand is possible, but 'prestigious brand' is the ordinary adjective construction.
column8: Prestige can function attributively before nouns ('prestige television/brand'), but do not generally replace prestigious after linking verbs: 'the school is prestigious,' not *'is prestige.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: prestige vs prestigious

column2: for hours on end / for several hours on end
column5: Continuously for many hours, with little or no interruption; 'on end' emphasizes an extended uninterrupted stretch.
column6: for hours straight, continuously, for hours at a time
column7: He can talk about old anime for hours on end. / It rained for several hours on end.
column8: Also days/weeks on end. 'On end' can separately mean upright ('hair stood on end'), but this duration idiom means continuously.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: for several hours on end

column5: The area where the lower abdomen meets the upper inner thigh, on either side of the body; in everyday speech it may loosely refer to the genital/pubic region.
column6: inguinal region, crotch (less anatomical), pelvic/genital area (loose context)
column7: He pulled a muscle in his groin during the match. / The ball hit him in the groin. / A groin strain often involves muscles of the inner thigh.
column8: Anatomically groin is not simply a synonym for genitals, though everyday usage can blur them. 'Crotch' refers more to the fork of the body/clothing.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: groin meanig

column5: A compact mass of indigestible material that accumulates in the digestive tract, especially the stomach; historically, bezoars were also believed to have magical or antidotal powers.
column7: The doctors discovered a bezoar in the patient's stomach. / In fantasy stories, a bezoar may appear as an antidote because of the old belief that it could counteract poison.
column8: Medical types include phytobezoars (plant material) and trichobezoars (hair). The historical antidote belief is important in literature/fantasy but is not modern medical treatment.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define bezoar meaning

column5: A sudden episode of violent, involuntary muscular contractions or body movements; figuratively, a violent social/political disturbance or upheaval.
column6: violent spasm, fit, seizure-related movement; upheaval
column7: His body went into convulsions during the medical emergency. / The revolution sent the country into political convulsions.
column8: Medical nuance: convulsion describes the motor phenomenon; it is not identical to seizure, because seizures can occur without convulsions and convulsions can have different causes. Figurative plural 'convulsions' = violent upheavals.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define convulsion
column12: entry::word usage::figurative topic::politics topic::television topic::entertainment discovery::figurative_extension discovery::public_discourse

column5: Restricted, defined, or constrained by oversimplified expectations about what a person/group/character should be like.
column6: boxed in by stereotypes, constrained by clichés, typecast
column7: The character feels less like a person and more like someone bound by stereotypes about masculinity. / Good writing lets characters exist without being bound by stereotypes.
column8: Natural compositional extension of 'bound by.' Often useful in media/social analysis; stereotype can constrain portrayal, expectations, or self-conception.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: bound by stereotypes meaning

column2: pull the rug out from under someone
column3: /ˌpʊl ðə ˈrʌɡ aʊt frəm ˌʌndər ˌsʌmwʌn/
column5: To suddenly remove support, security, assumptions, resources, or plans that someone was relying on, leaving them destabilized.
column6: undermine, destabilize, yank away support, blindside
column7: They approved the project and then pulled the rug out from under us by cutting the budget. / The final reveal pulls the rug out from under the audience's entire interpretation of the story.
column8: Raw search 'put the rug from under' normalized. Often used for abrupt policy/funding changes; in storytelling, a reveal can overturn what the audience thought was true.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113, voca_0114 | search: put the rug from under
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::security discovery::resource_allocation discovery::support discovery::removal

column4: adjective / noun / verb, chiefly BrE slang; polysemous
column5: Slang with several unrelated senses: bad, useless, or defective ('a duff battery'); the buttocks ('get off your duff,' chiefly AmE informal); a type of pudding/dough in older usage; and other niche slang senses depending on context.
column7: The remote stopped working because the battery was duff. / Get off your duff and help me move this table. / 'Duff' is highly context-dependent, so don't assume every slang occurrence means the same thing.
column8: Chiefly BrE 'duff' = no good/faulty is common. 'Up the duff' = pregnant is BrE slang and is treated separately through the pregnancy search cluster. Also appears in names/brands, so source context matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define duff
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::slang usage::american_english usage::british_english

column5: When necessary in a difficult, urgent, or less-than-ideal situation; as an emergency substitute or fallback.
column6: if necessary, in an emergency, when push comes to shove, as a fallback
column7: In a pinch, I can use my phone as a hotspot. / This sauce isn't ideal, but it'll work in a pinch.
column8: Common AmE. Implies not the preferred solution, but adequate when options/time/resources are limited.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: in a pinch meaning

column5: A representative or messenger sent on a diplomatic or special mission, especially by a government or leader.
column7: The president sent a special envoy to negotiate a ceasefire. / She served as the UN envoy to the region.
column8: Especially diplomatic/formal. Emissary overlaps strongly; ambassador is normally a formally accredited diplomatic representative, while an envoy may be appointed for a specific mission.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: envoy definition

column5: To hold something or someone tightly with the hand(s) or arms; to fasten/join with a clasp. As a noun, a fastening device such as on a necklace or bag.
column6: grip, grasp, clutch, embrace; fastener, catch
column7: She clasped both hands around the mug. / They clasped hands before stepping onto the stage. / The clasp on my necklace broke.
column8: Clasp often suggests hands closing firmly around something or two hands joining. Clutch can imply anxiety/desperation; grasp is more neutral. Noun clasp = small fastening mechanism.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: clasp meaning

column5: To eat food very quickly and greedily or hungrily.
column6: gobble up, devour, scarf down, inhale (slang), bolt
column7: I wolfed down a sandwich before the meeting. / He was so hungry after the hike that he wolfed down dinner in five minutes.
column8: Image of a wolf eating voraciously. Scarf down is informal AmE; gobble/devour are broad; bolt food can imply swallowing dangerously fast.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: wolf down meaning

column5: To reverse one's position, policy, attitude, or course completely.
column6: reverse course, make a U-turn, change tack completely
column7: After months of opposition, the mayor did an about-face and supported the proposal. / The company made an about-face on pricing.
column8: Both do an about-face and make an about-face occur; 'make' is especially transparent/common. Preserves raw 'doing an about-face.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: doing an about-face meaning

column5: A person who takes part in a mutiny—organized rebellion or refusal to obey lawful authority, especially by sailors or soldiers against their officers.
column7: The captain ordered the mutineers confined below deck. / Pirate stories often blur the line between a crew overthrowing its captain and a formal naval mutiny.
column8: Especially nautical/military. A mutineer rebels from within an existing crew/unit against its authority; a pirate/privateer describes different legal/occupational relationships.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: mutineer meaning

column5: Literally, to fracture the neck; figuratively in 'break one's neck to do something,' to make an extreme or urgent effort, often more effort than is sensible or appreciated.
column6: go to great lengths, bend over backward, bust one's ass (vulgar), rush
column7: I'm not going to break my neck trying to finish this tonight when nobody needs it until Friday. / She broke her neck to help them, and they barely thanked her. / He could break his neck if he falls from there.
column8: Figurative pattern usually break one's neck to do X. It can imply excessive effort or haste, often with resentment. 'At breakneck speed' is related imagery but means dangerously/very fast.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: break one's neck meaning
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative usage::vulgar discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To bend something over itself; to close/collapse by folding; figuratively, to give in, withdraw, fail under pressure, or stop operating. In poker, to surrender one's hand.
column6: bend, crease, collapse; give in, cave, capitulate; withdraw a hand
column7: Fold the paper in half. / He talked tough online but folded the moment his boss challenged him. / The company folded after losing its main investor. / She folded before the river card.
column8: A recent existing card already develops the pressure/poker sense; this card broadens the raw 'folded' search to the literal base verb and business 'company folded.' 'Fold' and 'crease' are related but not identical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define folded

column5: A bad, immoral, or unhealthy habit or character trait; also criminal activity involving prostitution, illegal gambling, drugs, etc. In titles, vice can mean deputy/subordinate rank (vice president). A vise is a clamping tool in AmE spelling.
column6: bad habit, moral failing, wickedness; illicit activity
column7: Coffee is probably my mildest vice. / The detective worked in the vice squad. / Greed is traditionally described as a vice. / She was promoted to vice president.
column8: Several unrelated-looking uses. Moral vice contrasts with virtue. Vice squad targets certain illicit activities. Prefix-like vice- = deputy/in place of. Tool spelling: AmE vise, BrE vice.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116, voca_0117 | search: vice meaning
column12: entry::word usage::american_english usage::british_english usage::persuasive topic::self-help topic::crime discovery::persuasion

column5: Tangible = physically touchable or concretely perceptible/definite; intangible = not physical/touchable, often abstract, hard to quantify, or nonmaterial.
column6: concrete vs abstract, physical vs nonphysical
column7: The laptop is a tangible asset; brand reputation is an intangible asset. / The trip gave me tangible results but also intangible benefits like confidence.
column8: Tangible can be figurative: tangible progress/evidence = clear and real. Intangible does not mean unreal; trust, goodwill, rights, knowledge, and atmosphere can be real but nonphysical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: tangible vs intangible

column5: In a persistent, continuous, or intensely determined way that does not let up or give respite.
column7: She relentlessly practiced the same passage until it sounded effortless. / The villain relentlessly pursues them across the entire film. / The app relentlessly pushes notifications until you disable them.
column8: Can praise determination or criticize oppressive persistence. Tirelessly often sounds positive; incessantly often sounds annoying; relentlessly emphasizes not easing or stopping. Existing relentless adjective card remains distinct.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: relentlessly doing something meaning

column5: Severe, unpleasant, or unsuitable weather, especially rain, snow, storms, cold, or other conditions that disrupt normal activity.
column7: The event will be moved indoors in case of inclement weather.
column8: Very common formal collocation in closures, travel notices, policies, and event announcements.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: what is inclement weather

column5: Lasting for a very short time; fleeting or short-lived.
column7: Internet fame can be incredibly ephemeral. / The beauty of cherry blossoms is often associated with their ephemeral nature.
column8: More literary/formal than short-lived. Can describe art, trends, emotions, organisms, experiences. Ephemera = items originally meant to be short-lived, such as tickets/posters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: ephemeral

column5: To acquire or be given an unfairly negative reputation or criticism.
column6: get a bad reputation, get unfairly blamed, be unfairly maligned
column7: Frozen vegetables get a bad rap, but they can be just as nutritious as fresh ones. / Dubs get a bad rap from some anime fans even when the performances are excellent.
column8: Usually written bad rap, not bad rep, although speakers may associate it with reputation. Bad rep is a separate shortening of bad reputation. Related bum rap = false accusation/unfair blame.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: get a bad rap meaning

column5: To separate and move in different directions; to become different in opinion, development, pattern, or result.
column7: The two paths diverge after the bridge. / Their interpretations begin to diverge at this point.
column8: Natural contrast with converge. Diverge from = depart from a path/norm; diverge on/over = differ about an issue.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118, voca_0120 | search: diverge

column5: No; a negative vote. Also used rhetorically to correct and intensify what was just said: 'or rather—even more strongly...'
column7: The motion passed with ten ayes and two nays. / It was difficult—nay, almost impossible—to finish in time.
column8: Modern everyday 'no' is far more common. In voting: aye vs nay. Literary/rhetorical 'nay' revises upward: 'good, nay, brilliant.' Strong old-fashioned/pirate/fantasy flavor as a standalone response.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: Nay
column12: entry::interjection usage::formal usage::literary usage::dated usage::archaic usage::rhetorical topic::rhetoric discovery::escalation discovery::debate_language

column5: A loose popular phrase for repeated small bursts of rewarding, novel, or attention-grabbing stimulation—notifications, short videos, game rewards, rapid content changes, etc.
column6: constant stimulation, repeated rewards, novelty hits, quick gratification
column7: Short-form feeds are often criticized as providing constant 'dopamine hits.' / The phrase is useful for understanding internet discourse, but it shouldn't be treated as a literal clinical description of what the brain is doing each second.
column8: Common pop-neuroscience shorthand. Dopamine is not simply 'the pleasure chemical,' and everyday claims about exact dopamine spikes are often much more confident than the evidence warrants. Learn the discourse meaning separately from the neuroscience.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: constant dopamine hits

column2: the gears are turning (in my head)
column5: I'm actively thinking, processing, connecting ideas, or starting to work something out; mental machinery is figuratively beginning to move.
column6: the wheels are turning, I'm thinking it through, my brain is working
column7: I can see the gears turning in your head—you've just thought of something. / Once he mentioned the timeline, the gears started turning.
column8: 'The wheels are turning' is more conventional, but gears turning is transparent and common enough as a mental-mechanism metaphor. Often used visually of someone's expression.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: the gears are turning in my head meaning

column2: make a point of doing something
column5: To deliberately and consistently make sure that one does something because one considers it important or wants it noticed.
column6: make sure to, deliberately do, take care to, go out of one's way to
column7: I make a point of writing down new expressions when I hear them in the wild. / She made a point of thanking everyone individually before she left.
column8: Implies conscious intention, often habitual or emphatic. 'Make a point' can also mean state an argument; 'make a point of X' is the deliberate-action construction.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: make a point of doing meaning

column5: A wasting away or reduction in size, strength, function, or vitality from disuse, disease, poor nourishment, or other causes; figuratively, a skill, institution, relationship, etc. can weaken through neglect.
column6: waste away, shrink, deteriorate, wither, weaken
column7: Muscles can atrophy after long periods of immobilization. / If I stop speaking English for years, some active vocabulary will atrophy. / The institution's capacity slowly atrophied.
column8: More technical than 'wither.' Medical atrophy has specific causes/types; figurative use is common for skills, abilities, institutions, and relationships.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: atrophy meaning
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::figurative topic::relationships topic::health discovery::figurative_extension discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To have the opportunity, privilege, or chance to do something, often something desirable.
column6: have the chance to, be able to
column7: I got to meet the director after the screening.
column8: Different from have to do: get to do often frames the action as an opportunity rather than an obligation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: get to do meaning

column5: Most commonly in computing/AI, natural language processing: computational methods for analyzing, understanding, or generating human language. Also used for neuro-linguistic programming, a distinct self-help/communication approach.
column7: Modern language models are part of the broader NLP landscape. / In a self-help seminar, NLP may instead mean neuro-linguistic programming.
column8: Always resolve by context. In AI/computational linguistics, NLP overwhelmingly means natural language processing. Neuro-linguistic programming is unrelated to that technical field.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: NLP
column12: entry::abbreviation usage::technical topic::communication topic::technology topic::self-help topic::linguistics discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Poorly made, weak, shaky, and likely to collapse or break.
column7: We climbed a rickety wooden staircase to the attic. / The old table was so rickety that my coffee kept wobbling. / A rickety bus carried us up the mountain road.
column8: Suggests physical instability plus age, poor construction, or disrepair. Common with chairs, stairs, bridges, buildings, carts, vehicles. 'Ramshackle' stresses dilapidated construction/appearance; 'flimsy' stresses lack of strength; rickety strongly evokes wobbling/shakiness.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111 | search: what is rickety

column5: To mock, defeat, criticize, or show someone up decisively, especially in public or online.
column7: People kept dunking on the ad for its awkward slogan.
column8: From basketball dunk imagery; online discourse often uses dunk on for performative public ridicule.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: dunk meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern entry::discourse_expression usage::slang usage::informal topic::internet discovery::criticism

column5: To add or include something, often as an extra; to contribute a comment/idea; or to give something as a bonus.
column7: They threw in free delivery with the purchase.
column8: Distinct from throw in the towel = give up. Also literal sports senses exist, e.g. a soccer throw-in.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: throw in meaning

column5: Sensitive to being tickled; figuratively, delicate, awkward, or difficult to handle without causing trouble.
column7: Money can be a ticklish subject in some families.
column8: The figurative sense is useful: a ticklish issue/question/situation needs careful handling.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: ticklish meaning

column2: live off vs live up to
column5: Live off X = survive/support oneself using X as a source of money, food, resources, or support. Live up to X = meet an expectation, standard, reputation, promise, or ideal.
column7: He lives off freelance income. / Some animals live off insects. / The sequel didn't live up to the hype. / She tries to live up to her own standards.
column8: Completely different phrasal verbs despite similar form. Also live off someone can imply financial dependence/freeloading; live on can overlap for food/income.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: live off vs live up to
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase topic::food topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::resource_allocation discovery::support discovery::evaluation discovery::social_approval

column5: To attract, interest, please, or seem desirable to someone; in other contexts, to make an earnest request to someone.
column7: The simpler design appeals to younger customers.
column8: Raw 'appeal A to B' is not the usual pattern for attractiveness: A appeals to B. Another pattern is appeal to someone for something.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: apeal a to b meaning

column5: To have no legitimate reason, right, qualification, or justification to do something; also used hyperbolically when something is unexpectedly good, strong, difficult, etc.
column6: have no right to, shouldn't be, be in no position to; be absurdly/unexpectedly X (hyperbolic)
column7: He has no business telling you how to spend your money. / That cheap little speaker has no business sounding this good. / I had no business trying that trail in ordinary sneakers.
column8: Very productive modern hyperbole: 'X has no business being this good/funny/beautiful.' It literally sounds like prohibition/unsuitability but often means 'surprisingly, almost unfairly X.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: has no business meaning

column5: Most important or fundamental; also a senior Roman Catholic cleric, a red North American bird, or a term used in sets such as cardinal directions and cardinal numbers.
column7: One cardinal rule of the job is to protect confidential information.
column8: Polysemous word. Core adjective sense is 'fundamental/primary.' Context distinguishes the cleric, bird, number, and direction uses.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: define cardinal

column5: A dismissive label for someone seen as a temporary, superficial, inexperienced, or inauthentic participant in a scene, hobby, subculture, profession, or risky environment.
column7: Veterans of the scene dismissed the newcomers as tourists.
column8: Extends literal tourist = temporary visitor. Slang force depends on community and can be gatekeeping or contemptuous.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: tourist meaning slang
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::informal topic::travel topic::environment discovery::risk

column5: To produce remarkably good results or a strong beneficial effect.
column6: do wonders for, greatly improve, be highly effective
column7: A few days off worked wonders for her mood. / That small UI change worked wonders for readability.
column8: Can also be 'work wonders on X.' Hyperbolic but common; doesn't literally imply a miracle.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: it works wonders for meaning

column5: To work or act very quickly because there is little time before a deadline or bad outcome.
column6: race against time, be under severe time pressure
column7: Doctors raced against the clock to identify the cause. / We were racing against the clock to finish before the upload deadline.
column8: Clock emphasizes a visible/fixed time limit. 'Race against time' is near-equivalent.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: racing against the clock

column5: The trajectory of a character's internal development or change across a story—beliefs, values, goals, identity, relationships, behavior, etc.; some arcs are positive, negative, flat, or deliberately incomplete.
column7: His character arc moves from isolation to trusting other people. / A flat arc can still be compelling if the character changes the world rather than changing fundamentally.
column8: Not every sequence of events involving a character is an arc; arc emphasizes development/trajectory. Common review/analysis term.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: character arc

column5: Small, precise, or trivial details, especially details that can absorb attention despite not being central to the main issue.
column6: fine details, tiny details, particulars, trivialities
column7: We spent an hour arguing over the minutiae of the formatting instead of finishing the project. / Fans love analyzing the minutiae of background animation.
column8: Plural of Latin-derived minutia, though singular minutia is rare in ordinary English. Do not confuse pronunciation with minute /ˈmɪnɪt/ (60 seconds). Often 'the minutiae of X.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define minutiae

column5: A set of criteria or instructions used to evaluate or categorize work; especially an assessment scoring guide showing dimensions and performance levels. Historically, also a heading/instruction in a text or liturgy.
column6: scoring guide, assessment criteria, evaluation framework
column7: The teacher shared the grading rubric before the presentation. / Our review rubric scores accuracy, depth, and naturalness separately.
column8: In education, rubric usually means structured assessment criteria, not simply a vague rule. Useful for systematic QA/review workflows.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: rubric meaning
column12: entry::word usage::instructional usage::presentation-friendly topic::work topic::assessment topic::performance discovery::instruction discovery::evaluation discovery::presentation_language

column5: Because of, or driven by, a feeling of frustration.
column7: He slammed the drawer shut out of frustration.
column8: Out of + emotion/motive expresses the feeling or motive that caused an action: out of fear, curiosity, kindness, frustration.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: out of frustration meaning

column5: The French city and, by association, the Palace of Versailles; in historical contexts, 'Versailles' may also refer metonymically to the royal court or the Treaty of Versailles context.
column7: The Palace of Versailles became a symbol of French royal power. / The Treaty of Versailles was signed after World War I.
column8: English pronunciation commonly /vərˈsaɪ/, unlike the French pronunciation. Context determines city, palace, court, or treaty reference.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: VERSAILLES Definition & Meaning | Dictionary.com

column5: A small, involuntary contraction of a bundle of muscle fibers, often visible under the skin as a localized muscle twitch.
column7: A brief fasciculation appeared in the calf after exercise. / Persistent fasciculations can have many possible causes, so the word describes the movement rather than diagnosing why it happens.
column8: More technical than twitch. Fasciculations may occur in healthy people as well as in medical conditions; context, persistence, weakness, and other signs matter clinically. Card is lexical, not diagnostic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define fasciculation

column5: Verb: strengthen, support, reinforce, or improve something such as confidence, an argument, a reputation, demand, or a structure. Noun: a long firm pillow/cushion used for support.
column6: strengthen, reinforce, support, shore up, boost
column7: The new evidence bolstered her argument. / Positive feedback helped bolster his confidence. / The bed had a cylindrical bolster.
column8: Productive figurative verb. 'Bolster an argument/claim/confidence/support.' Noun sense is physical support/cushion and explains the metaphor.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: bolster definition
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::rhetorical discovery::support discovery::social_approval discovery::improvement discovery::debate_language

column5: Latin for 'girl' or 'young woman.' In English-language contexts it most often appears in Latin study, titles, names, or references such as Puella Magi Madoka Magica.
column7: In elementary Latin, puella is a standard first-declension noun meaning 'girl.' / Anime fans may recognize puella from the Latin-styled English title Puella Magi Madoka Magica.
column8: Latin first declension: puella, puellae, etc. It is not an ordinary English synonym for girl; using it in English sounds learned, title-like, or deliberately Latin.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: puella meaning

column5: A small cut or notch; a light clicking/snapping sound; in cricket, a glancing hit off the edge of the bat. As a verb, to nick/cut slightly, click, or edge the ball.
column7: The lock closed with a quiet snick. / The batter snicked the ball to the wicketkeeper. / He made a tiny snick in the edge of the material.
column8: Rare/context-heavy outside cricket and sound-description. Dictionary sources support cut/notch, click, and cricket senses. citeturn0search0turn0search1
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define snick

column5: To adjust one's behavior, appearance, expression, or choices so they fit the expectations and conventions of a social group or society.
column6: fit in, follow social conventions, adhere to norms
column7: People sometimes conform to social norms even when they privately disagree with them. / She felt less pressure to conform to the group's expectations after college.
column8: Conform emphasizes matching group patterns/expectations, which may be informal and unwritten. Distinct from comply with, which more strongly suggests a request/rule/requirement.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: conform to social norms meaning

column5: A fixation on a scenario in which a white person imagines themself rescuing, enlightening, protecting, or elevating nonwhite people, often centering the rescuer's virtue and flattening the agency of those supposedly being helped.
column7: The film was criticized for turning local characters into props for a white-savior fantasy. / In dating or travel discourse, a rescue narrative can become fetishized when one partner is imagined as 'saving' the other from their culture.
column8: Not a clinical diagnosis or fixed technical term. 'White savior complex' is the more established phrase; adding fetish highlights repetitive fascination/desire. Critique concerns paternalism, stereotyping, and displaced agency.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: white savor fetish

column5: At a high level of success or importance; informally, to a very great degree.
column7: After years of small gigs, the band finally hit the big time. / I messed up big time.
column8: Existing 'screw up big time' shows the intensifier in one phrase; this standalone card captures the broader construction and noun sense hit/make the big time.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: big time meaning

column5: A mocking or hostile nickname for the United Kingdom formed with the suffix -stan, typically used to imply that Britain has become culturally or politically alien, especially through immigration or Islamization.
column7: The commenter used 'United Kingdomistan' as a polemical nickname for Britain.
column8: Nonstandard, ideologically loaded coinage rather than neutral vocabulary. Preserve as recognition/context vocabulary; it can carry anti-immigrant or anti-Muslim insinuation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: United Kingdomistan

column5: A source-specific phrase involving circumstantial, likely describing a series shaped by circumstances or a sequence of circumstantial events/evidence; not a standard fixed term by itself.
column7: The phrase 'circumstantial series' needs its original sentence to determine whether series means a TV series, sequence of events, or evidentiary chain.
column8: Preserve because the exact search may encode source context, but do not invent a specialized meaning. See the separate circumstantial card for the adjective's stable core meaning.

column5: A vivid red to reddish-orange color; historically, a bright red pigment traditionally made from mercury sulfide (cinnabar).
column6: scarlet, vivid red, red-orange, cinnabar red
column7: The shrine gates were painted a brilliant vermilion. / The sunset turned the clouds vermilion. / Traditional vermilion pigment has a long history in art and ritual.
column8: Often associated visually with Japanese torii/shrine architecture, Chinese art, and historical pigments. Color boundaries vary. Historical mercury-based vermilion is chemically/toxically distinct from modern safer substitutes.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: vermillion meaning

column5: A romantic and/or sexual relationship that has some features of dating or partnership but lacks clear definition, commitment, labels, or mutually established expectations.
column6: undefined relationship, unlabeled relationship, casual relationship (overlapping), more-than-friends situation
column7: We were seeing each other every weekend, but neither of us knew whether it was a relationship or just a situationship. / Situationships can feel comfortable until the two people realize they have very different expectations.
column8: Not simply 'friends with benefits': a situationship may involve emotional intimacy and dating-like behavior, and sex is not required. Core idea = ambiguity/undefined status.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: situationship meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::casual usage::slang topic::relationships topic::dating topic::romance discovery::commitment

column5: A U.S.-based LGBTQ media advocacy organization that works for fair, accurate, and inclusive representation in media.
column7: GLAAD criticized the coverage and called for more accurate LGBTQ representation.
column8: Formerly expanded as Gay & Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation; since 2013, GLAAD has been used as the organization's primary name rather than as a current acronym.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: glaad meaning

column5: To begin a journey; to arrange or present something clearly; or to state ideas, rules, or plans in an organized way.
column7: We set out before sunrise, and the report later set out exactly what we had found.
column8: Polysemous. Keep separate from set out to do something because the journey/presentation senses are independently common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: set outmeaning

column5: Used to say that something is difficult, intense, disturbing, demanding, spicy, frightening, exhausting, or otherwise requires toughness/tolerance.
column6: not for the faint of heart, not for the squeamish, not easy
column7: That horror movie is not for the weak. / Ten hours of spreadsheet cleanup in one sitting is not for the weak. / This hot sauce is definitely not for the weak.
column8: Internet/casual intensifier. Often humorous exaggeration. 'Not for the faint of heart' is the more established idiom; choose 'not for the squeamish' for gore/disgust.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: this is not for the weak meanig

column5: Clothing, especially considered as a particular style or appropriate dress for an occasion.
column7: The invitation says formal attire. / His everyday attire is much more casual than his stage outfits.
column8: Usually uncountable in modern use: attire, not *an attire. Common collocations: formal/business/wedding/traditional attire.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: define attire

column2: don't judge a gun by its holster
column3: /ˌdoʊnt ˌdʒʌdʒ ə ˈɡʌn baɪ ɪts ˈhoʊlstər/
column5: A nonstandard metaphorical variation on 'don't judge a book by its cover': don't judge the quality, nature, or capability of something by its outward container/appearance.
column6: don't judge a book by its cover, appearances can be deceiving
column7: The line 'don't judge a gun by its holster' uses the familiar proverb structure to say appearances don't tell you everything.
column8: Not a standard established proverb. Preserve as source-specific wordplay. Raw search had 'it's'; possessive is 'its': by its holster.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: don't judge a gun from it's holster meaning

column2: throw a spanner in the works
column5: To cause a problem or unexpected complication that disrupts, delays, or prevents a plan or process from working smoothly.
column6: throw a wrench in the works, disrupt, derail, complicate, create a snag
column7: The sudden visa change threw a spanner in the works of our travel plans. / Everything was ready until the supplier pulled out and threw a spanner in the works.
column8: Classic BrE expression; AmE equivalent is 'throw a wrench in the works.' 'The works' means the mechanism/system as a whole. Usually an unforeseen disruptive factor.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: throw a spanner in the works meaning

column5: Busy or occupied and therefore unavailable; also literally bound, or committed/locked into something such as money or resources.
column7: I'm tied up until three, but I can call you after that.
column8: Several senses share the image of being bound so you cannot move or use something freely.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111 | search: tied up meaning

column5: Suffering from or seriously affected by an illness, problem, hardship, or harmful condition.
column6: suffering from, stricken with/by, troubled by, affected by, beset by
column7: The region was afflicted by years of drought. / He plays a detective afflicted with chronic insomnia. / The afflicted communities received emergency aid.
column8: Often formal/literary and usually negative: afflicted with/by X. 'Affected' is neutral/broader; afflicted implies suffering. As noun phrase 'the afflicted' = people who suffer from a condition.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: define afflicted

column5: A joking response to an odd, unnecessary, or questionable boast or display of pride.
column7: You memorized every fast-food menu in town? Weird flex, but OK.
column8: Often appears as 'weird flex but OK/okay.' Flex = boast/show off. Usually teasing or dismissive.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: weird flex meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::humorous usage::informal topic::communication topic::internet

column5: To ignore someone or not give them attention, consideration, or concern.
column6: ignore, disregard, pay no attention to, take no notice of
column7: Pay the hecklers no mind and finish what you were saying. / She paid him no mind and kept walking.
column8: Also 'pay no mind to someone/something.' Informal and somewhat folksy/regional in feel. Raw 'pay her no mind' is a normal instance.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: pay her no mind meaninmg

column5: Inhuman = not human, lacking normal human qualities, or shockingly cruel/monstrous. Inhumane = cruel and causing unnecessary suffering; not compassionate or humane.
column6: inhuman: nonhuman, monstrous; inhumane: cruel, merciless, brutal
column7: The creature had inhuman strength. / The prisoners were kept in inhumane conditions. / Calling the workload 'inhuman' can mean impossibly harsh; 'inhumane treatment' specifically emphasizes cruelty/lack of compassion.
column8: They overlap in cruelty contexts but are not interchangeable everywhere. An alien can be inhuman without being inhumane. Humane ↔ inhumane concerns compassion; human ↔ inhuman concerns humanity/human qualities.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: inhuman vs inhumane

column5: To explain or demonstrate a process, event, argument, or set of steps to someone in sequence.
column7: Can you take me through what happened after the meeting?
column8: Very common in interviews and explanations: 'Take me through that' asks for a step-by-step account.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111 | search: take me through that meaning
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::rhetorical usage::presentation-friendly topic::communication discovery::explanation discovery::process_details discovery::debate_language discovery::presentation_language

column5: A state of having a bad reputation or losing public respect.
column6: disgrace, dishonor, ill repute, bad name, infamy
column7: The scandal brought the organization into disrepute. / Years of low-quality sequels brought the franchise into disrepute with longtime fans.
column8: Very common fixed pattern: bring X into disrepute / fall into disrepute. Compared with infamy, disrepute focuses on loss/lack of respect rather than spectacular evil or notoriety.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: define disrepute

column5: Small, intermittent signals of attention or interest that keep someone engaged without offering consistent effort, clarity, or commitment; breadcrumbing is the behavior of sending such signals.
column6: mixed signals, intermittent attention, stringing someone along (overlap)
column7: He kept sending flirty messages every few weeks—just enough breadcrumbs to keep her interested. / She realized she was being breadcrumbed and stopped responding.
column8: Existing WID6120 covers breadcrumbing; this card preserves the plural 'breadcrumbs' as the individual signals in relationship context. Different from web-navigation breadcrumbs.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: breadcrumbs meaning relationship

column5: Showing that one is sorry for having caused trouble, offense, inconvenience, or harm; expressing regret.
column7: She sounded genuinely apologetic about missing the meeting. / He gave me an apologetic smile after stepping on my foot.
column8: Contrite/remorseful are stronger and more morally weighted. 'Apologetic tone/look/smile' can communicate regret without an explicit apology.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: apologetic meaning

column5: The attribution of human traits, emotions, intentions, behavior, or form to nonhuman animals, objects, gods, natural forces, machines, etc.
column7: Giving the robot a jealous personality is anthropomorphism. / We should be careful about anthropomorphism when interpreting animal behavior.
column8: Personification is a literary device giving human qualities to nonhuman things; anthropomorphism can be broader and more literal/systematic, including treating animals or AI as humanlike agents.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: anthropomorphism

column5: Describing a person who typically experiences sexual attraction only after forming a strong emotional bond with someone.
column7: She describes herself as demisexual and says emotional closeness is important before attraction develops.
column8: A sexual-orientation label on the asexual spectrum. The exact experience varies by person; it does not simply mean choosing to wait before having sex.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: demisexsual

column5: A work, event, product, or performance that fails badly, especially commercially or with audiences; to fail in that way.
column7: The film flopped at the box office despite strong reviews. / It was a notorious flop when it opened, then became a cult favorite years later. / A financial flop isn't necessarily an artistic failure.
column8: Entertainment use often means commercial failure, but speakers may mean critical/audience failure too. 'Bomb' is close; 'tank' often emphasizes performance/results dropping badly.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: film flops meaning
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::critical usage::businesslike topic::work topic::performance topic::entertainment topic::film

column5: Pleased and honored because someone has praised you, shown interest in you, or treated you as special; sometimes politely used when declining an offer.
column7: I'm flattered that you asked me. / She looked genuinely flattered by the compliment. / 'I'm flattered, but I'm not interested' softens a rejection.
column8: Usually positive, but 'flattered' can coexist with embarrassment or refusal. Related verb flatter can also mean praise insincerely/excessively.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: flattered meaning

column5: A professional who represents authors and their work, often pitching manuscripts to publishers, negotiating contracts/rights, and advising on publishing strategy.
column7: She signed with a literary agent who submitted the novel to editors. / Many traditional publishers accept fiction submissions mainly through agents.
column8: Roles vary; agents typically earn commission rather than charging ordinary reading fees. 'Literary' here covers commercial genres too, not only literary fiction.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: literary agent meaning
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::literary usage::professional usage::businesslike topic::work discovery::negotiation discovery::professional_context

column5: Fresh, juicy, interesting, or scandalous gossip.
column6: juicy gossip, tea, dirt, scoop, dish
column7: Okay, what's the hot goss? You said something happened at the party. / I don't even watch the show, but somehow I know all the hot goss about the cast.
column8: Goss = clipped playful form of gossip. Hot goss often sounds knowingly silly/campy rather than serious. Compare tea = gossip/information, especially juicy inside information; dirt emphasizes damaging information.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: hot goss meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::playful topic::food

column5: A person traveling on foot; figuratively, ordinary, dull, or lacking imagination.
column7: The design is functional but a little pedestrian.
column8: The figurative adjective is often mildly critical: pedestrian prose, ideas, design.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: pedestrian meaning

column5: The ability to make quick, accurate judgments and understand a particular area well, especially business, politics, finance, or practical affairs.
column7: Her business acumen helped turn a tiny shop into a profitable company. / Technical skill alone doesn't guarantee good managerial acumen.
column8: Often appears as business/financial/political acumen. Implies sharp practical judgment, not just accumulated knowledge.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: acumen meaning
column12: entry::word usage::technical topic::business topic::finance topic::politics discovery::evaluation discovery::public_discourse discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To do absolutely nothing, or virtually nothing useful/effective.
column6: do nothing, do jack shit, do bugger all, accomplish nothing
column7: I've been staring at this file for an hour and done fuck all. / They promised to fix the problem, then did fuck all about it.
column8: Fuck all can also mean 'nothing/almost nothing': I know fuck all about cars. Very blunt/vulgar; BrE and other varieties use it readily in frustrated speech. Compare do bugger all (BrE, somewhat milder) and do jack shit (AmE, vulgar).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: done fuck all meaning

column5: To activate something; to suddenly attack or betray someone; to excite or interest someone, including sexually; or to depend on a particular factor.
column6: switch on; attack; excite; depend on
column7: Turn on the lights. / The crowd suddenly turned on him.
column8: Existing turn on someone covers the attack/betray sense; keep the broader base phrasal verb because activation and attraction senses are independently common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: turn on meaning

column5: To choose someone for an official position by voting, with the position used as an object complement.
column6: choose, vote in, appoint by election
column7: The members elected Maya chair of the committee.
column8: Pattern: elect + person + position: elect someone president/chair/treasurer. No 'as' is required in this construction.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: elect someone something meaning
