column5: Past of boot: kicked; forced/removed from a place, group, game, server, job, etc.; started a computer/system ('booted up'); also wearing boots.
column6: kicked out, ejected, removed, expelled; started up
column7: He got booted from the server for cheating. / The laptop booted normally after the update. / She was booted and ready for the snow.
column8: Context decides. 'Get booted' commonly = be kicked out/removed. Computing boot is unrelated in modern meaning to footwear.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: booted meaning

column5: To be extremely energetic, excited, restless, or hyperactive.
column6: be hyper, be bursting with energy, be wired, be bouncing around
column7: The kids were bouncing off the walls after all that candy. / I had so much nervous energy before the trip that I was practically bouncing off the walls. / The puppy had been indoors all day and was bouncing off the walls.
column8: Usually figurative, evoking frantic movement around a room. Can describe excitement, restlessness, excess energy, or hyperactivity. 'Wired' often suggests stimulation/caffeine/nervous arousal; 'bouncing off the walls' is more vivid and playful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: bounced off the walls

column2: take someone up on that / take someone up on an offer
column5: To accept someone's offer, invitation, challenge, or suggestion. Raw 'take it up on that' is usually a malformed version; say 'take you/him/her/them up on that.'
column6: accept the offer, accept the invitation, take up the offer
column7: You offered to help me move—I might take you up on that. / She took him up on his offer of a ride.
column8: Important object pattern: take PERSON up on OFFER/that. Alternatively, 'take up an offer.' Do not normally say *take it up on that for this meaning.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: take it up on that meaning

column5: To pivot or move to one side in an arc, or cause something to do so, clearing the way.
column6: swing away, pivot aside, move aside, swing open
column7: The gate swung aside to reveal the courtyard. / He swung the lamp aside so I could reach the shelf.
column8: Usually compositional rather than a fixed idiom. Aside emphasizes movement out of the way; 'swing open' emphasizes opening. Can be transitive or intransitive depending on structure.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: swing aside meaning

column5: Showing creativity, originality, or a strong ability to form new ideas, images, stories, solutions, or possibilities.
column7: The film has an imaginative visual style even when the plot is simple. / That was an imaginative solution to a boring technical problem.
column8: Imaginative = possessing/using imagination; imaginary = not real/existing only in imagination. Important contrast.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: imaginative meaning

column5: A rapid abbreviated writing system; more broadly, a concise word, label, symbol, or expression used to stand for a larger, more complex idea.
column7: In the article, 'the West' is used as shorthand for a much more complicated set of institutions and societies. / She learned shorthand for taking notes quickly.
column8: Figurative 'X is shorthand for Y' is extremely common. Shorthand can be useful compression but may hide distinctions or nuance.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: shorthand

column5: Lively, energetic, cheerful, enthusiastic, and full of pep.
column7: I'm not very peppy in the morning. / The host has a relentlessly peppy delivery. / She chose a peppy song to wake everyone up.
column8: Often describes personality, voice, music, or mood. Can be affectionate or mildly annoying if the energy feels excessive. 'Pep' = energy/enthusiasm.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: I'm not peppy meaning

column5: Traditionally, a villain or bad person ('the baddie' in a story). In modern social-media slang, especially 'baddie,' an attractive, confident, stylish person—often a woman—with a polished, glamorous image.
column6: villain, bad guy; attractive confident woman, hottie, it girl (overlapping)
column7: The cartoon baddie reveals his plan in the final episode. / Her makeup and outfit are pure Instagram-baddie aesthetic. / Context completely changes whether 'baddie' means villain or attractive person.
column8: Modern beauty/fashion sense usually spelled baddie. Traditional BrE-style baddie = villain. Social-media sense often implies confidence, makeup/fashion polish, and curated aesthetic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: baddy meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::british_english topic::media

column5: Emotions that remain after the event or relationship that caused them has ended or should seemingly be over.
column6: residual feelings, remaining feelings, unresolved feelings, emotional residue
column7: She still had lingering feelings for him years after they broke up. / The ending left me with lingering feelings of sadness and unease for the rest of the night.
column8: Often romantic, but not necessarily: lingering feelings of guilt, resentment, affection, unease, etc. 'Unresolved feelings' implies they have not been psychologically settled; lingering simply means they persist.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: lingering feelings

column5: To discover or expose that someone is lying, often because their story contradicts evidence or something they said earlier.
column6: catch someone lying, expose a lie, catch someone out, bust someone (informal)
column7: She said she'd never met him, but the photo caught her in a lie. / I wasn't trying to interrogate him; I just happened to catch him in a lie when the dates didn't match.
column8: Catch someone in a lie focuses on discovering a specific falsehood. Catch someone out (especially BrE) can mean expose a mistake/deception more broadly.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: catch someone in a lie meaning

column5: A homicide offense based on causing another person's death through legally culpable negligence rather than an intent to kill. Exact offense names, definitions, and required mental states vary by jurisdiction.
column6: criminally negligent homicide, negligent killing; manslaughter (not equivalent in every jurisdiction)
column7: New York law uses the offense name 'criminally negligent homicide'; other jurisdictions may use different labels. / 'Negligent murder' is not a safe universal synonym for negligent homicide.
column8: Raw search 'negligent murder' should not be normalized into a universal offense name. In New York, homicide categories include criminally negligent homicide separately from murder. Legal terminology is jurisdiction-specific.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: negligent murder meaning
column12: entry::term entry::phrase usage::specialist topic::law discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column2: say the quiet part out loud
column5: To openly state an underlying motive, belief, or implication that is normally left unstated because saying it explicitly would be embarrassing or revealing.
column6: state the implicit motive, reveal the subtext
column7: He said the quiet part out loud when he admitted the rule was meant to discourage newcomers.
column8: Raw search 'said the quiet part loud' normalized to the standard phrase with out loud.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: said the quiet part loud meaning

column5: To make, order, or force someone to walk somewhere in a purposeful, controlled, or brisk way, often suggesting authority or lack of choice.
column6: escort, lead, frog-march (stronger), make someone walk
column7: The teacher marched him to the principal's office. / Security marched the protesters out of the building. / She marched the kids upstairs to bed.
column8: Transitive march can imply control: march someone out/in/over to X. 'Frog-march' is stronger and can imply physical force/restraint.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: marching someone meaning

column5: Exactly correct, accurate, or precisely aligned/aimed; in some dialectal contexts, also excellent/fine.
column6: exactly right, spot-on, accurate, bang on
column7: Your guess was dead on. / The timing has to be dead on or the joke won't land.
column8: Common AmE 'dead-on accurate'; 'dead on' = exactly. In Northern Irish usage, 'dead on' can also mean okay/good/nice, so context matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: dead on meanng

column2: cause issues to bubble to the surface
column5: To cause previously hidden, suppressed, unnoticed, or underlying problems to become visible and demand attention.
column6: bring issues to the surface, expose underlying problems, make problems emerge
column7: The sudden workload increase caused old communication problems to bubble to the surface. / The controversy didn't create every tension; it caused several existing issues to bubble to the surface.
column8: Raw 'caused issues to bubbles to surface' needs grammar repair: cause + object + to + base verb → caused issues to bubble to the surface. Strong metaphor of submerged material rising into view.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: caused issues to bubbles to surface meaning

column5: Historically, one of the hunters and later sea raiders active around the Caribbean in the 17th century, especially against Spanish shipping; more broadly, a pirate/adventurer. Figuratively, a bold or unscrupulous operator.
column7: The story turns a historical Caribbean buccaneer into a romantic pirate hero. / The company was run by a group of financial buccaneers who loved risky deals.
column8: Historically more specific than generic pirate. The word is linked to French boucan/boucanier: hunters smoked meat on wooden frames called boucans before some became raiders.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: buccaneer meaning

column5: To speak to someone in a one-sided way without genuinely engaging, listening, or allowing a real exchange.
column6: lecture, monologue at, talk over (overlapping), preach at
column7: He didn't really talk with me; he talked at me for twenty minutes about what I was doing wrong. / Some video essays feel conversational, while others feel like the host is talking at the audience.
column8: Contrast talk to/with: neutral interaction; talk at is critical and emphasizes one-way delivery. Talk over someone = keep speaking while they are trying to speak or drown them out.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: talk at someone
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::conversational usage::critical topic::communication topic::lectures discovery::lecture_language

column5: The act or process of deliberately destroying a building or structure; figuratively, a crushing defeat or thorough dismantling of an argument/performance.
column7: The old stadium is scheduled for demolition next year. / Her rebuttal was a complete demolition of his argument. / The champion delivered a one-sided demolition in the final.
column8: Literal construction sense is core. Figurative sports/debate use is vivid and emphatic. Demolish = verb. Raw 'demolistion' corrected.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: demolistion meaning
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::performance discovery::process_details discovery::figurative_extension discovery::debate_language

column5: A deliberately extreme way to describe reasoning, beliefs, or an intellectual position as wildly irrational, distorted, or detached from sense.
column6: intellectually unhinged, wildly irrational, intellectually incoherent, outlandish
column7: The essay starts with a fair criticism and somehow ends up somewhere intellectually deranged. / I don't merely disagree with that reading; the chain of reasoning feels intellectually unhinged.
column8: Not a fixed idiom or clinical description. Deranged literally has mental-illness associations and is strong/stigmatizing when applied to a person; applied to an argument/worldview it works as hyperbolic rhetorical criticism.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: intellectually deranged
column12: entry::idiom usage::evaluative usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::evaluation discovery::debate_language

column5: Literally, to die or cause someone to be unable to breathe because air is cut off; figuratively, to make someone feel trapped, oppressed, overwhelmed, or deprived of freedom/space.
column6: choke, asphyxiate, smother; stifle, overwhelm, constrain
column7: Smoke can suffocate someone before the flames reach them. / The room was hot and suffocating. / His parents meant well, but the constant monitoring felt suffocating. / Too many rules can suffocate creativity.
column8: Compare smother: can literally block breathing/cover completely and figuratively overwhelm with attention. Stifle often means suppress expression, growth, creativity, laughter, etc. Suffocating emphasizes lack of breathing room, literally or emotionally.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: suffocating meaning

column5: Extremely high or rapidly increased, especially prices, costs, levels, emotions, ratings, or measurements.
column6: sky-high, extremely high, off the charts, soaring
column7: Hotel prices were through the roof that weekend. / My stress level went through the roof when the file disappeared. / After the trailer, expectations were through the roof.
column8: Be through the roof = already extremely high; go/shoot through the roof = rise dramatically. Existing example uses fury level, but standalone idiom has broad high-frequency use.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: something is through the roof meaning

column5: In contemporary dating/looks slang, 'pull women' means attract or successfully get dates/sexual or romantic attention from women; 'chopped' means unattractive/ugly. Thus: how to attract women if you're considered unattractive.
column6: get women, attract women, have dating success; ugly/unattractive (chopped)
column7: The video title 'how to pull women if you're chopped' basically means 'how to attract women if you're ugly.'
column8: Preserve the full search phrase because the slang combination is the learning target. Existing WID4985 covers chopped; 'pull' in this sense is especially common in BrE/internet dating slang and can sound objectifying depending on context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: how to pull women if you're chopped meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::british_english usage::informal topic::dating topic::romance topic::internet

column5: Used to express a strong hope that something bad will not happen; also used sarcastically to criticize the idea that an ordinary or desirable thing would somehow be unacceptable.
column7: God forbid anything happens to the kids. / God forbid we take one day off. / 'Maybe he could admit he was wrong—God forbid.'
column8: Can be sincere (strong hope that a feared event does not occur) or sarcastic (mocking the idea that some ordinary/reasonable thing would be terrible). Tone and context completely change the effect. 'Heaven forbid' is a milder/euphemistic alternative.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: god forbid meaning

column5: A mindset centered on relentless work, hustle, self-discipline, productivity, and pursuing success—often used sincerely or mockingly/critically.
column6: hustle mentality, hustle culture, work-hard mindset
column7: His whole feed is sigma-grindset content about waking up at 4 a.m. and never taking days off. / 'Grindset' often parodies extreme productivity culture.
column8: Blend of grind + mindset. Strongly associated with hustle-culture and sigma-male memes; tone is frequently ironic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: grindset meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::ironic usage::informal topic::work topic::internet topic::self-help topic::culture

column5: The main claim or argument remains valid or relevant despite a correction, objection, exception, or flaw in some supporting detail.
column6: the argument still holds, that doesn't invalidate the point, the core point remains
column7: I got the year wrong, but the point still stands: the policy changed before the second season. / You can criticize his example, but his broader point still stands.
column8: Useful in debate, but don't use it as a magic escape from a rebuttal: whether the point really stands depends on whether the challenged detail was essential to the argument.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: the point still stands meaning
column12: entry::phrase usage::conversational usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly discovery::assertion discovery::debate_language

column5: A mocking or unsympathetic response meaning that someone's situation is unfortunate and they are the one who has to deal with it.
column6: too bad for you, tough luck
column7: You have to work all weekend? Sucks to be you.
column8: Usually sarcastic and insensitive rather than genuinely sympathetic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: sucks to be you meaning

column5: To admit that something is true or valid, often reluctantly; to accept defeat or yield a point; to give/grant something; in sports, to allow the opponent to score.
column6: admit, acknowledge, yield, surrender, grant; allow (a goal/point)
column7: I'll concede that his first point was fair. / She conceded the election after the final count. / The team conceded two goals in the second half. / He refused to concede defeat.
column8: Highly productive: concede a point, concede that..., concede defeat, concede an election, concede a goal. 'Admit' lacks the competitive/yielding flavor; concession often comes after resistance.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: conceded meaning

column5: Besides the ordinary verb, 'Look,' can introduce a blunt explanation or redirect attention ('Look, here's the problem'). 'A look' can mean a distinctive style/outfit or facial expression; slang meanings vary by community.
column6: listen, here's the thing (discourse); style, outfit, expression
column7: Look, I get what you're saying, but I still disagree. / That jacket is a whole look. / She gave me a look that said, 'Don't even try it.'
column8: Raw 'look meaning slang' is too broad for one secret slang definition. Preserve the productive modern uses: discourse-marker Look; 'a look' = style/aesthetic; 'give someone a look' = meaningful facial expression.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: look meaning slang

column5: To squash, press, mash, or push things together, often messily or affectionately; smooshed = flattened, compressed, or crowded together.
column6: squish, squash, mash, smush, press together
column7: The sandwich got smooshed at the bottom of my bag. / The puppies were all smooshed together on the couch. / She smooshed the clay into a rough ball.
column8: Informal and expressive. Smush is a common variant. Often conveys soft compression rather than violent crushing.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: smooshed meaning

column5: To carefully consider the advantages and disadvantages of the available choices before deciding.
column7: I'm still weighing my options before accepting either offer.
column8: Raw search misspelled weighing. Weigh metaphorically = assess relative value or consequences.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: weighning your options meaning

column5: A facial expression in which someone looks fixedly without showing an obvious emotion, reaction, recognition, or understanding.
column6: vacant stare, blank look, expressionless gaze, thousand-yard stare (not identical)
column7: I explained the joke and got nothing but a blank stare. / She answered the shocking news with a blank stare that made it impossible to tell what she was thinking.
column8: Can suggest confusion, shock, dissociation, boredom, nonrecognition, or deliberate lack of reaction; the expression alone does not tell you which. 'Vacant' more strongly suggests absence/disconnection.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: blank stare meaning

column5: To be very knowledgeable, experienced, or skilled in a subject, field, system, or body of knowledge.
column6: be knowledgeable about, be proficient in, be conversant with, know well
column7: She's well-versed in Japanese animation history. / You don't need to be well-versed in linguistics to notice the pattern.
column8: Usually well-versed in + subject/field. Hyphenated before/after noun commonly. 'Versed in' alone is more formal.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: be well-versed in something
column12: entry::idiom entry::adjective_phrase entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::formal discovery::expertise

column5: A highly powerful, extraordinary, or larger-than-life villain, especially in superhero fiction; figuratively, someone portrayed as extravagantly evil or malicious.
column7: The movie spends more time developing the supervillain than the hero. / The internet turned him into a cartoonish supervillain who was supposedly responsible for everything.
column8: Usually one word 'supervillain' in modern usage. Figurative use often mocks exaggerated moral framing: 'treated like a supervillain.' Not every main antagonist is necessarily a supervillain.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: super villain meaning
column12: entry::variant_set entry::noun_phrase usage::informal usage::figurative topic::entertainment discovery::figurative_extension

column5: A small boat propelled with oars by a person rowing.
column7: They crossed the lake in a little wooden rowboat. / He tied the rowboat to the dock before the storm arrived.
column8: AmE rowboat; BrE often rowing boat. Not every small boat is a rowboat: the defining feature is propulsion by rowing with oars.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: rowboat meaning

column5: As a verb, to arrange/manipulate something dishonestly for a desired result, or to equip/set up something with gear. As a noun, equipment/apparatus, a vehicle setup, or an oil-drilling structure, among other senses.
column6: fix, manipulate, tamper with; equip, set up; setup, apparatus
column7: They were accused of rigging the election. / We rigged a temporary light above the desk with a clamp. / His gaming rig takes up half the room.
column8: Very polysemous. Rig an election/game = dishonestly predetermine/manipulate. Rig up = improvise/set up equipment. Gaming rig = computer setup; oil rig = drilling structure. 'Rigged' online often means unfairly fixed.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: rig meaning

column5: Literally, a place presented as especially associated with melons—their origin, production, fame, or local identity. Without source context, it is not a standard English idiom.
column6: melon-producing region, place famous for melons
column7: The town markets itself as the 'home of the melon.'
column8: Preserve exact search. 'Home of X' is a productive slogan meaning a place strongly associated with X. The definite article can suggest a specific/local emblematic melon.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: home of the melon meaning

column5: Clear enough to read or decipher, especially handwriting, print, text, labels, or visual information.
column7: His handwriting is messy but still legible. / The subtitles need to remain legible on a small phone screen.
column8: Legible focuses on whether symbols/text can be read. Readable can also mean pleasant/easy to understand stylistically; intelligible focuses on comprehensibility.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: legible meaning

column5: Feeling and showing sincere remorse, guilt, or regret for wrongdoing.
column7: He looked genuinely contrite after realizing how much his comment had hurt her. / Her apology sounded contrite rather than defensive.
column8: Stronger and more morally weighted than apologetic. Often implies genuine recognition of fault.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: contrite

column5: Making a false emergency report intended to send armed police or other emergency responders to an innocent person's location, often as harassment or intimidation.
column6: false emergency-report attack, malicious police hoax
column7: The streamer was targeted by swatting after someone falsely reported a violent emergency at his home.
column8: Dangerous criminal harassment that can cause injury or death. Named from SWAT, though actual responding agencies vary. Recognition/safety term; not ordinary 'swat' = hit an insect.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: swatting meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::informal topic::internet topic::crime topic::policing topic::law

column5: To warn, advise, or mildly-to-seriously rebuke someone about behavior, often with an implication of correction or guidance.
column6: warn, caution, rebuke, reprimand, reprove, counsel
column7: The teacher admonished them to be more careful with the equipment. / She admonished him for speaking so rudely. / The guide admonished visitors not to touch the paintings.
column8: Patterns: admonish someone for X; admonish someone to do/not do X. Compared with rebuke/reprimand, admonish more readily includes warning or corrective advice, not just condemnation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117, voca_0120 | search: define admonish

column5: To make someone feel happier, more hopeful, or more confident; also to improve someone's social or economic condition.
column7: A good mentor should lift people up along the way, not just advance alone.
column8: Raw search included 'along the way'; the independently useful idiom is lift someone up.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: lift someone up along the way meaning

column5: To lean, be distributed, or be biased disproportionately toward one side, group, result, or characteristic.
column6: tilt toward, lean toward, bias toward
column7: The survey sample skews toward younger respondents.
column8: Existing skew covers distortion; this searched construction highlights the common intransitive/distribution pattern skew toward.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: skew to meaning

column5: A published or written false statement that damages someone's reputation; as a verb, to defame someone in this way.
column7: The newspaper denied that the article was libelous or that it had libeled him.
column8: Traditionally contrasted with slander (spoken defamation). Exact legal rules vary by jurisdiction.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0117, voca_0121 | search: define libel

column5: Extremely small, slight, or precise in degree or detail.
column7: There was only a minute difference between the two versions. / She notices minute changes in pronunciation that I would completely miss.
column8: This adjective is pronounced my-NOOT /maɪˈnuːt/, unlike minute '60 seconds' /ˈmɪnɪt/. Common: minute detail/difference/amount/trace. 'Minutely' can mean in very fine detail.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: minute definition

column5: Let's go proposes or urges that speaker and others leave/start/do something together; go! directly commands or urges another person/people to move, act, or continue. 'Let's go!' also functions as an excited cheer meaning roughly 'yes!/come on!'
column6: come on, let's move; go!, move!; yes! (cheer)
column7: We're going to miss the train—let's go. / The light's green—go! / He hit the winning shot and everyone yelled, 'Let's go!'
column8: Raw 'let's go vs go let's go' points to pragmatic difference. 'Go, let's go!' can occur as stacked urging, but not as a separate fixed grammar. Intonation/context determines whether let's go means departure, encouragement, impatience, or celebration.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: let's go vs go let's go

column5: To undergo or cause chemical breakdown by microorganisms, often producing alcohol, acids, or gases; figuratively, to develop or stir over time, especially ideas, unrest, or social change.
column7: Let the dough ferment overnight for more flavor. / Political discontent had been fermenting for years before the protests began. / The city was a place where new artistic ideas could ferment.
column8: Do not confuse ferment with foment. Foment is specifically to stir up/encourage trouble or unrest; ferment can describe the broader process of active development. Noun ferment = agitation/excitement, pronounced with first-syllable stress.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: ferment meaning

column5: To get beyond a literal barrier or, figuratively, overcome a point of resistance, blockage, exhaustion, or limitation.
column6: break through, get beyond, overcome the barrier
column7: Once I got past the wall of self-doubt, the writing became much easier.
column8: Not a single fixed idiom with one universal meaning; 'the wall' is supplied by context. In endurance sports, the wall can be the sudden point of extreme fatigue.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: get past the wall meaning

column5: An act of violating, conflicting with, or failing to comply with a law, rule, agreement, or requirement.
column7: The construction was carried out in contravention of local regulations. / Sharing the data would be in contravention of the agreement.
column8: Typical formal pattern: in contravention of X. Related verb: contravene. More legalistic than violation and uncommon in casual conversation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define contravention
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::casual usage::legalistic usage::informal topic::law discovery::agreement discovery::expressing_need

column6: trope: motif, convention, device | troupe: company, ensemble, group of performers
column7: The reluctant hero is a familiar trope, while the theater troupe performs it onstage.
column8: Both words already exist separately in Master, but the original search explicitly contrasts the confusable spellings, so retain the contrast card.

column5: To be unable to distinguish one thing from another, implying extreme ignorance or incompetence in that area.
column6: not know the difference between, be clueless about
column7: He doesn't know talent from toilet tissue, but he still judges every performance.
column8: The searched line 'doesn't know talent from toilet tissue' is a playful nonce variation on the template. A famous vulgar version is 'not know shit from Shinola.' Preserve the user's exact contrast in the example.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: doesn't know talent from toilet tissue meaning

column5: To deliberately put someone in a bad position, trick or frame them, especially so they take blame or suffer consequences; literally, to close a wound with stitches.
column6: frame, set up, trick, shaft; suture
column7: He swears the evidence was planted and that somebody stitched him up. / You stitched me up by volunteering me for the presentation without asking. / The doctor stitched him up after the accident.
column8: Strong BrE colloquialism. Figurative sense ranges from serious 'frame for a crime' to joking 'put me in an awkward situation.' Compare set someone up, which can also be positive (arrange a date/opportunity).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: stitch someone up meaning

column5: Implicit processing occurs relatively automatically or without conscious awareness of the rule/process; explicit processing involves conscious attention, deliberate reasoning, or accessible knowledge about what is being processed.
column7: A learner may implicitly pick up a word-order pattern from repeated exposure, while explicitly processing a grammar explanation requires conscious attention. / Native speakers often judge a sentence before they can state the rule explicitly.
column8: The boundary is theory/task-dependent; implicit does not simply mean 'unimportant' and explicit does not guarantee verbalizable perfect knowledge. Useful in language learning and cognitive psychology.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: implicit processing vs explicit processing

column5: To acknowledge that someone's action, choice, or reaction is understandable or not reasonably blameworthy.
column7: I can't fault them for choosing the safer option.
column8: Often conveys reluctant or fair-minded acceptance even if the speaker dislikes the outcome.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: I can't fault them for that meaning

column5: A style of mixed drink traditionally served over crushed ice, often with wine or spirits, sugar, and fruit garnish.
column7: She ordered a sherry cobbler packed with crushed ice and fruit.
column8: Distinct from cobbler = a person who repairs shoes and cobbler = a baked fruit dessert.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: cobbler drink meaning

column5: For an event, plan, launch, trip, ceremony, etc. to happen successfully and smoothly without problems, delays, or complications.
column6: go smoothly, go perfectly, run without problems, go according to plan
column7: The import went off without a hitch. / Somehow the wedding went off without a hitch despite the storm. / We tested everything twice so the launch would go off without a hitch.
column8: Existing hitch card mentions 'without a hitch,' but this preserves the very common full construction 'go off without a hitch.' Here go off = happen/proceed, not explode or become spoiled.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: go off without a hitch meaning

column5: A sport in which players throw flying discs toward elevated metal basket targets, aiming to complete each hole in as few throws as possible.
column7: We played nine holes of disc golf at the park. / Disc golf uses golf-like ideas such as tees, holes, par, drives, and putting, but you throw a disc instead of hitting a ball.
column8: 'Frisbee golf' is commonly understood, but Frisbee is a trademark; disc golf is the standard sport name.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: disc golf

column5: A scarcity or serious lack of something; an insufficient supply.
column7: There's no dearth of opinions online, but there is a dearth of careful evidence. / The town faced a dearth of affordable housing.
column8: Usually 'a dearth of X.' Formal/literary. Opposite idea: abundance, glut (depending context).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: dearth definition

column5: A response to criticism that deflects by accusing the critic of the same or similar wrongdoing instead of addressing whether the original criticism is true.
column6: appeal to hypocrisy, whataboutism (overlapping), 'you too' fallacy
column7: 'You shouldn't pirate games.' 'But you streamed that movie illegally last year.' That's a tu quoque response if it is offered instead of answering the criticism.
column8: Latin 'you too.' Often classified as an ad hominem fallacy. However, pointing out hypocrisy can be relevant to credibility, consistency, enforcement, or fairness; it becomes fallacious when hypocrisy is treated as disproving the underlying claim.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: tu quoque meaning

column5: Prepared as a kipper by splitting, salting, and smoking a herring; figuratively in some British uses, thoroughly defeated, ruined, exhausted, or caught out.
column7: After the overnight shift, he joked that he was completely kippered.
column8: Slang force is context-dependent and less universal than the literal fish sense. Do not assume it always means drunk/exhausted without context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: kippered meaning  uk slang

column5: A taste that remains in the mouth after food or drink is swallowed; figuratively, a lingering emotional impression left by an experience, story, conversation, etc.
column6: lingering taste, finish; lingering impression, residue, aftereffect
column7: The coffee has a slightly bitter aftertaste. / The finale is hopeful, but it leaves a strangely melancholy aftertaste. / His apology fixed the immediate problem, yet the argument left a sour aftertaste.
column8: Literal food/drink sense is core. Figurative use is especially useful in reviews: bitter/sour/unpleasant/strange aftertaste = lingering negative or mixed feeling. 'Afterglow' is usually positive; aftertaste can be positive, negative, or mixed.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: aftertaste

column5: Tamper-proof = intended to be impossible or extremely difficult to tamper with; tamper-resistant = designed to resist interference; tamper-evident = designed so interference leaves visible evidence.
column7: The bottle has a tamper-evident seal. / No system is perfectly tamper-proof, so 'tamper-resistant' may be more precise.
column8: Important distinction: tamper-evident does not prevent opening; it reveals it. 'Tamper-proof' is often marketing language and may overstate absolute protection.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: tamper-proof meaning

column5: A provocative game or joke in which two same-sex participants perform escalating romantic or sexual behavior and the first to pull away is treated as the loser.
column7: The scene plays like a game of gay chicken, with neither character willing to back down.
column8: Informal and culturally loaded; can reinforce stereotypes or trivialize sexuality. Meaning comes from chicken as a contest of who backs down first.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: gay chicken meainng

column5: To introduce or bring up a topic—especially a difficult, sensitive, or potentially awkward one—for discussion.
column7: I wasn't sure how to broach the subject of money. / She waited until dinner was over before broaching the topic.
column8: Broach commonly collocates with subject/topic/issue. Do not confuse brooch /broʊtʃ/ = decorative pin; same pronunciation in many accents.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: broach a subject

column5: Inflammation or irritation of a tendon, often causing pain and tenderness near a joint.
column7: The repetitive motion aggravated the tendinitis in his wrist. / Shoulder pain can have many causes, so 'tendonitis' is not a label to infer from soreness alone.
column8: Tendinitis is the more etymologically regular spelling; tendonitis is extremely common. Tendinopathy is a broader term for tendon disorders and may be preferred when degeneration rather than acute inflammation is involved.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: tendonitis

column5: Extremely based—strongly approved of as bold, unapologetic, authentic, or correct.
column7: Refusing to apologize for that harmless opinion was based AF, according to the comments.
column8: AF = as fuck, a strong vulgar intensifier. Meaning of based remains context-dependent.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112, voca_0113 | search: based AF meaning

column5: To show excessive or smug satisfaction about one's own success or another person's failure.
column7: He couldn't resist gloating over the victory.
column8: Common pattern: gloat over/about something. More specifically smug than ordinary boast.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: gloat meaning

column5: An exclamation expressing relief, surprise, exhaustion, amazement, or being impressed/overwhelmed.
column7: Whew, I thought I'd deleted the whole file. / Whew—that was a long day. / Whew, that price is higher than I expected.
column8: Very conversational and sound-symbolic. Phew overlaps strongly with relief/exhaustion; whew can also express impressed surprise.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: whew meaning

column2: I couldn't bounce ideas off anyone about that
column3: /aɪ ˌkʊdənt ˌbaʊns aɪˈdɪəz ɔːf ˈeniwʌn əˌbaʊt ðæt/
column5: A natural way to say you had nobody with whom you could discuss an issue and test your ideas. Raw 'I couldn't bounce off about that' is incomplete because the idiom normally requires an idea/topic object and a person.
column6: I had no one to run it by, I had no one to discuss it with
column7: Back then I couldn't bounce ideas off anyone about that, so I had to work through it on my own.
column8: Grammar: bounce something off someone. You can also say 'I didn't have anyone to bounce that idea off.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: I couldn't bounce off about that meaning

column5: The process of expressing a mathematical quantity, expression, or object as a product of factors.
column7: Prime factorization expresses 60 as 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
column8: Common in arithmetic and algebra; related verb factor/factorize.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: factorization

column5: To turn someone over physically, cause them to rotate, or—in certain slang contexts—change/recruit someone's allegiance or cooperation. It does NOT by itself normally mean 'give someone the middle finger'; that is flip someone off.
column6: turn over, roll over; convert/recruit, turn (informant)
column7: The instructor flipped him onto his back during the demonstration. / Investigators tried to flip one member of the group into cooperating. / If someone gives you the middle finger, they 'flip you off,' not normally 'flip you.'
column8: Raw search likely tests the missing particle. Important contrast: flip someone off = insult with middle finger; flip someone = turn them over or, contextually, persuade/recruit them to the other side.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: someone flips you meaning

column5: In the direction of; closer to a time or goal; or in relation to one's attitude, behavior, or contribution concerning someone or something.
column7: She walked toward the station. / His attitude toward the proposal changed.
column8: Towards is a common variant, especially in British English. Toward is common in American English.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: toward meaning

column5: An exhaustive, often critical dissection of a cultural work, trend, event, community, or phenomenon to explain what happened, what it reveals, and why it succeeded, failed, or decayed.
column6: deep-dive postmortem, cultural postmortem, exhaustive dissection, forensic analysis
column7: What started as a review turned into a full-blown cultural autopsy of the franchise and the fandom around it. / The video isn't just mocking one bad ad; it's practically a cultural autopsy of the era that produced it.
column8: Autopsy is literal examination of a body after death to determine cause; figuratively it suggests forensic, retrospective dissection. Full-blown intensifies it: fully developed, not merely a passing analysis. Particularly natural for long-form video essays/criticism.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: a full-blown cultural autopsy

column2: rip (slang: do extremely well / tear through)
column5: In some informal contexts, to perform with great energy or effectiveness, move very fast, or tear through a task/opponent; exact meaning depends heavily on construction.
column6: crush it, tear it up, go hard, shred, blaze through
column7: He absolutely ripped on guitar during the last song. / She ripped through the exam and finished early. / 'Go rip!' can work as encouragement, roughly 'go crush it,' but rip by itself does not universally mean 'do my best.'
column8: Raw query asks whether rip means beat/do my best: there is no single slang meaning. 'Rip through X' = move/do quickly; 'rip on guitar' = play intensely/well; 'let it rip' = go ahead at full force; 'rip into someone' = attack verbally. Preserve construction.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: rip means beat or do my best?

column5: Stylish confidence, coolness, or fashionable presentation; promotional/free merchandise; historically, stolen goods or a bundle/garland. As a verb, to hang/droop in a curve (older/specialized).
column6: style, swagger, drip (modern slang); merch, freebies
column7: He walked in with ridiculous confidence and somehow made the outfit look like pure swag. / The conference gave everyone a bag of branded swag. / In current fashion slang, 'drip' often sounds newer than 'swag.'
column8: Very polysemous and era-sensitive. 2010s slang swag ≈ style/cool confidence, related to swagger but not identical. Corporate/event swag = branded freebies. Older meanings survive in specialized/historical contexts.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: swag meaning

column5: To continue working, moving, or progressing steadily and persistently, often slowly and without drama; literally, an engine/machine may make repetitive chugging sounds while operating.
column6: keep going, plug away, chug along, work steadily
column7: The old train chugged away into the distance. / I wasn't making spectacular progress, but I kept chugging away at the vocabulary project.
column8: 'Chug along' is more common for steady progress; 'chug away' emphasizes continued action/sound. Separate from chug a drink = swallow quickly in large gulps.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: chugged away meaning

column5: A strong feeling that someone or something is beneath respect, worthless, despicable, or deserving of scorn; also, deliberate disregard for an authority, especially in legal 'contempt of court.'
column7: She looked at the scammer with open contempt. / He spoke with contempt about anyone he considered weak. / The judge held him in contempt of court for refusing to comply.
column8: Stronger than dislike: contempt combines negative judgment with a sense of superiority or lack of respect. Existing cards use contempt in definitions/synonyms, but this standalone card develops the core concept and legal collocation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define contempt

column5: To be unable to think of an answer, explanation, or solution; completely puzzled by a question or problem.
column6: be baffled, be puzzled, be at a loss
column7: I'm stumped—I can't figure out why the program keeps crashing.
column8: Stumped comes from stump as a verb meaning to puzzle or defeat intellectually.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: I'm stumped meaning

column2: how you show up day to day
column3: /haʊ ju ˌʃoʊ ˈʌp ˌdeɪ tə ˈdeɪ/
column5: How you consistently behave, participate, relate to others, perform your role, and embody your values in everyday life—not merely whether you physically arrive.
column6: how you conduct yourself, how you engage, everyday behavior
column7: Character isn't just what you say you value; it's how you show up day to day. / A manager's culture is shaped by how they show up for the team every day.
column8: Modern coaching/workplace/therapy-style use of 'show up.' 'Show up for someone' specifically emphasizes being present/supportive; 'show up as X' emphasizes the manner/identity you bring.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119, voca_0120 | search: how you show up day to day

column5: To give someone a particular impression; to seem a certain way to someone.
column6: seem to, come across as, appear to
column7: His explanation struck me as unusually careful.
column8: Pattern: X strikes A as B. The thing/person causing the impression is the subject; A is the person receiving it; B is the impression.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: strike A as B meaning

column5: To make a series of small explosive, spitting, or irregular sounds; to speak in a halting, shocked, angry way; or for an engine/process to run unevenly and falter.
column7: The old engine sputtered and died. / He sputtered in disbelief when he saw the bill. / Oil sputtered in the hot pan.
column8: AmE sputter and BrE splutter overlap. Speech sense suggests words coming out brokenly because of emotion. Engine/flame sense = irregular bursts, often before stopping.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: sputtered

column5: To say an activity, attitude, aesthetic, habit, or identity is not just occasional but a characteristic, ongoing way of living—often emphatic or joking.
column6: a way of life, part of how one lives, not just a hobby
column7: For him, cycling isn't a hobby; it's a lifestyle. / 'Being late is a lifestyle for her' is humorous exaggeration meaning it's habitual.
column8: 'Lifestyle' can be neutral marketing/sociology vocabulary or casual hyperbole. Don't assume deep identity in every joke use.

column6: in accordance with, under, according to, following
column7: The records were released pursuant to a court order. / Pursuant to our agreement, payment is due within thirty days.
column8: Strongly formal/legal/administrative. Usually 'pursuant to X,' not bare pursuant in ordinary conversation. In plain English, 'under' or 'in accordance with' is often more natural.

column6: poseur, pretentious thinker, faux intellectual, intellectual show-off
column7: The character throws around philosophers' names to sound deep, but the argument is deliberately written as pseudo-intellectual nonsense. / Calling someone a pseudo-intellectual is itself a strong dismissive judgment.
column8: Disparaging and subjective. Better analysis identifies what is shallow—misused terminology, unsupported claims, name-dropping, fake profundity—rather than using the label alone as an argument.

column5: To formally ask, appeal to, or rely on someone to provide help, action, expertise, support, or another needed thing.
column6: ask, appeal to, request, turn to, rely on
column7: We may need to call upon outside experts for advice. / In a crisis, the town can call upon volunteers for additional support. / The chair called upon each member for a brief response.
column8: Call upon/on someone to do X = formally request that they act. Call upon someone for X = seek X from them. Also 'call on someone' can mean visit them or choose them to speak, so construction/context matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: call upon A for B meaning

column5: Literally, to clean or disinfect; figuratively, to remove offensive, disturbing, controversial, sensitive, or identifying material so something appears cleaner, safer, or more acceptable.
column6: clean up, scrub, bowdlerize, censor, whitewash, redact (contextual)
column7: The adaptation sanitized the darker parts of the original story. / The report was sanitized before publication to remove identifying details. / You can sanitize user input before storing or displaying it.
column8: Nuance: sanitize a story/history can imply making it artificially clean or harmless; whitewash implies concealing wrongdoing; bowdlerize removes supposedly offensive material; redact obscures specific information; in computing/security sanitize can mean clean/validate data or securely remove data.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: sanitize something meaning slang

column5: Medical imaging of the breasts using low-dose X-rays, especially for screening or diagnostic evaluation.
column7: Mammography is used for breast-cancer screening in many health systems. / A mammogram is an image/exam produced through mammography.
column8: Lexical distinction: mammography = imaging technique/process; mammogram = resulting image or commonly the examination itself.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: mammography

column5: A fast-paced form of association football (soccer) played mainly indoors on a hard court, typically with five players per side and a smaller, lower-bounce ball.
column6: indoor five-a-side football, five-a-side soccer (not exact)
column7: We played futsal at the gym because the outdoor field was closed. / Futsal rewards close control, quick passing, and movement in tight spaces.
column8: From Portuguese/Spanish fútbol/futebol + sala/salón ('hall/indoor'). It is a distinct codified sport, not simply any indoor soccer game. Commonly five-a-side including the goalkeeper.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: futsal meaning

column5: Impossible to overcome, solve, or surmount.
column6: insurmountable, unconquerable, unbeatable, impossible to overcome
column7: The funding problem proved insuperable. / At first the language barrier seemed insuperable, but it gradually became manageable. / They faced what looked like an insuperable obstacle.
column8: Formal and much less common than 'insurmountable.' Typically modifies obstacle, difficulty, barrier, problem. It means impossible to overcome, not merely very difficult; in ordinary conversation 'insurmountable' is usually more natural.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: insuperable

column5: It is likely or probable that something is true or will happen.
column6: probably, most likely, odds are, there's a good chance
column7: Chances are, I've already looked that word up once. / If the restaurant is packed every night, chances are the food is pretty good.
column8: Usually followed by a clause: chances are (that).... Informal and natural. 'Odds are' is close.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: chances are meaning

column5: The geologic era from about 252 to 66 million years ago, comprising the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous periods and popularly known as the age of dinosaurs.
column7: Dinosaurs first appeared during the Triassic and diversified throughout the Mesozoic. / The Cretaceous is the final period of the Mesozoic Era.
column8: Order: Triassic → Jurassic → Cretaceous. The era ends at the K–Pg mass extinction about 66 million years ago. 'Age of dinosaurs' is convenient but many other organisms flourished too.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define mesozoic

column5: To cause a sudden shivery physical/emotional sensation because of fear, awe, excitement, disgust, beauty, or another intense reaction.
column6: give someone chills, make one's skin crawl (negative), send a shiver down one's spine
column7: That final line still sends chills down my spine. / The sound of footsteps in the empty hallway sent a chill down her spine. / Her performance gave me chills in the best possible way.
column8: Raw 'chills down me' is incomplete/nonstandard. Standard patterns: send chills/a chill down someone's spine; give someone chills. The reaction can be positive or negative.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: chills down me meaning

column5: Using software to automatically extract data or content from websites, documents, interfaces, or other sources rather than collecting it manually.
column6: web scraping, automated data extraction, crawling (overlaps, not identical)
column7: The research pipeline used automated scraping to collect publicly displayed product prices. / A site may rate-limit or block automated scraping.
column8: Scraping = extracting content/data; crawling = systematically discovering/fetching pages, often as part of scraping/indexing. Legality, terms of service, privacy, copyright, and technical permissions depend on context; the vocabulary term itself is neutral.

column7: I sent the second draft to three beta readers before revising it again.
column8: Common in fiction and fanfiction communities. A beta reader is not necessarily a professional editor or proofreader.

column5: The metaphor that ideas should compete openly in public discussion, with people able to compare, challenge, accept, or reject them rather than having truth determined solely by authority.
column6: free exchange of ideas, open debate, intellectual marketplace
column7: Supporters framed the forum as a marketplace of ideas where bad arguments could be challenged openly. / Critics argue that a marketplace of ideas does not automatically reward truth when attention and power are unequal.
column8: Important concept in free-speech discourse, especially U.S. legal/political rhetoric. It is a metaphor, not a guarantee that true ideas inevitably win. Often associated historically with arguments for open discussion and later U.S. jurisprudence.

column7: The villain mocks the heroes as a bunch of meddling do-gooders. / 'Do-gooder' can turn objectively helpful behavior into something the speaker frames as sanctimonious or naive.
column8: Often pejorative despite literally sounding positive. Tone reveals more about the speaker's attitude than about whether the person's actions are actually good.

column7: The lyric uses 'Mary Jane' as a euphemistic nickname for marijuana. / 'Occasional Mary Jane' would normally mean occasional cannabis use if the context is drugs.
column8: Context matters: Mary Jane is also an ordinary female name and a style of shoe. Cannabis sense can sound retro or euphemistic rather than current neutral terminology.

column2: accept the weight of someone's feelings
column5: To recognize the seriousness, emotional force, responsibility, or burden carried by another person's feelings rather than dismissing or trivializing them.
column6: take someone's feelings seriously, acknowledge their emotional weight, honor someone's feelings, hold space for someone (contextual)
column7: She wasn't ready to return his feelings, but she accepted the weight of what he had confessed. / The scene works because he doesn't try to fix her grief; he simply accepts the weight of it.
column8: Not a fixed idiom, but a natural metaphor: weight = seriousness/burden. 'Accept someone's feelings' may mean acknowledge them; 'reciprocate' means feel the same way and is NOT implied. 'Hold space' is more therapeutic/wellness-register.

column7: Commenters called the celebrity a 'longback,' turning an ordinary body proportion into an insult. / 'Long torso' is the neutral description; 'longback' is mocking internet slang.
column8: Pejorative/body-shaming, not an anatomical term. Definitions vary across online communities and often target women. Useful mainly for understanding social-media insults, not for describing people neutrally.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: longback meaning

column5: A person appointed to a position of authority or supervision; especially, in some British/Commonwealth schools, a senior pupil given limited disciplinary or organizational responsibilities. Historically, also an administrative official.
column7: She was made a school prefect in her final year. / In Harry Potter, prefects are students with extra responsibilities and privileges. / Roman administration also used titles translated as prefect.
column8: School sense is especially familiar from British fiction. A prefect is not simply 'class president'; powers and selection vary by school/system. Latin root relates to someone placed in charge.

column6: viewer retention, watch retention, retention rate

column8: Common YouTube/video/podcast analytics term. Distinguish audience retention (how long they stay) from reach/views (how many arrived) and returning audience (whether they come back).

column6: that's not quite how it works, that's not really the case, reality is more complicated

column6: muddle, mess, mixture, scramble, mix up
column7: My notes were a jumble of half-finished ideas. / The app jumbled the cards into the wrong order. / All the dates got jumbled in my head.
column8: Jumbled = mixed/disordered. 'Jumble sale' is BrE for a sale of donated secondhand goods. Compare scramble, muddle, garble.

column7: The anime episode turns the Pocky game into an awkward romantic challenge. / They stopped halfway because neither of them wanted the joke to become an actual kiss.
column8: Associated with Japanese youth/pop culture and anime/manga portrayals. Similar visual setup to a spaghetti kiss, but deliberately played as a game/challenge using a snack stick.

column5: To marry someone; to become joined to them in marriage.
column6: marry someone, get married to someone, tie the knot with someone
column7: She got hitched to her college sweetheart. / He joked that he never expected to get hitched to anyone.
column8: Natural but 'get married to someone' is more neutral. 'Hitched to' can also literally mean physically attached, so context matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: got hitched to someone meaning

column2: look someone in the eye / look someone in the eyes
column5: To make direct eye contact with someone, especially while speaking seriously, honestly, confidently, or confrontationally.
column6: make eye contact with, meet someone's gaze
column7: Look me in the eye and tell me you didn't know. / She couldn't look him in the eye after lying to him. / 'Look me in the eyes' is also natural, especially when emphasizing both eyes/direct gaze.
column8: Singular 'look someone in the eye' is the conventional idiom; plural 'in the eyes' is also grammatical/natural but often feels more literal or emphatic. Compare 'look someone in the face.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: look someone in the eye or eyes

column5: For a hidden feeling, problem, memory, conflict, fact, or tension to gradually emerge and become noticeable or openly expressed.
column6: surface, emerge, come to light, rise to the surface, resurface
column7: Old resentments began bubbling to the surface during the reunion. / As the story progresses, details about his childhood slowly bubble to the surface.
column8: Often suggests something was already present underneath rather than newly created. 'Come to light' emphasizes discovery; bubble to the surface often feels gradual, organic, and emotionally charged.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: bubbling to the surface meaning

column5: An argument whose reasoning, premises, objections, or justifications reproduce a similar pattern at another level, or whose justification calls for the same kind of justification again.
column6: nested reasoning, recursive justification, regress-like structure
column7: The debate became recursive: every demand for evidence generated another demand to justify the standard of evidence itself. / His reply embedded the same objection inside a new version of the argument.
column8: Not a single standardized logic term. Preserve as conceptual search. Depending on structure, related ideas include regress, circularity, self-reference, or nested argumentation—but these are not identical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: recursive structures in an argument

column5: Dull, old-fashioned, overly conventional, heavy, or lacking imagination; of food, heavy and filling.
column7: The institution has a stodgy image that it is trying to modernize. / The meal was warm but a bit stodgy.
column8: Can criticize people, writing, organizations, design, traditions, or heavy food. BrE especially common for food/institutional dullness.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: stodgy meaning
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::dated usage::warm usage::british_english topic::food

column5: The ability or capacity to reproduce; also the capacity of land/soil to support abundant growth.
column7: Age can affect fertility, but it is only one factor. / Farmers monitor soil fertility before deciding what to plant.
column8: Fecundity can mean biological reproductive capacity/potential and is more technical; fertility often concerns actual reproductive capacity/outcomes. Common: fertility rate, fertility treatment, fertility window, soil fertility.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define fertility

column5: To make a quick, light, sharp movement or strike, often with a finger, wrist, or small object; to move or switch something quickly. As a noun, a quick movement/strike; informally, a movie ('a flick').
column6: snap, flip, twitch, swat lightly; movie (informal)
column7: She flicked the crumb off the table with one finger. / He flicked his eyes toward the door. / I flicked through the channels for a few minutes. / We watched an old horror flick.
column8: Very productive: flick something away/off; flick through pages/channels; flick a switch; flick one's hair/eyes; flick someone lightly. Existing 'flick someone' is only one construction, so standalone card is broader.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: flick meaning

column5: Used to clarify what you mean by giving an example, restatement, spelling cue, or more specific sense of a word.
column7: I mean 'light' as in 'not heavy,' not 'bright.'
column8: Very common clarification pattern: X as in Y. It points to the intended example or sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: as in meaning

column4: proper noun / historical dinosaur genus name
column5: A historical genus name once used for certain hadrosaur fossils, especially material now generally classified within Edmontosaurus; the name is largely obsolete in modern dinosaur taxonomy.
column7: Older dinosaur books may label a duck-billed dinosaur 'Anatosaurus,' while newer references usually place the relevant fossils in Edmontosaurus. / The name survives in older pop-culture and educational material.
column8: Useful as historical vocabulary rather than a current standard genus. Dinosaur taxonomy changes as fossils are re-evaluated; older names can persist long after scientific classification shifts.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: anatosaurus meaning

column5: The shape, progression, or changing pattern of emotion across a story, scene, performance, conversation, or experience.
column7: The scene keeps the same plot beats but changes the emotional contour completely.
column8: Analytical/metaphorical phrase: contour treats emotional rises, falls, transitions, and intensity as a shape.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: emotional contour meaning

column5: To hang, bend, or sink downward limply; to lose firmness, energy, or spirit. As a noun, a downward sag or hanging shape.
column6: sag, hang down, wilt, slump, sink
column7: The flowers drooped in the heat. / His shoulders drooped when he heard the result. / The ears droop naturally on that breed. / By midnight my eyelids were starting to droop.
column8: Useful literal-to-emotional mapping: plants/body parts hang downward; posture can droop with tiredness/disappointment. Existing droopy adjective is related but not a duplicate of the productive verb.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: droops

column5: Sexual intercourse, especially penile-vaginal intercourse in formal, medical, biological, or deliberately clinical language.
column7: The medical questionnaire uses the formal term coitus rather than everyday sexual vocabulary. / In ordinary conversation, 'sex' or 'sexual intercourse' is much more natural than coitus.
column8: Formal/clinical and somewhat old-fashioned outside technical contexts. It can sound comically clinical in casual speech. Do not assume it covers every kind of sexual activity; traditionally it refers specifically to intercourse.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define coitus

column5: To raise a person so their feet leave the ground, physically by force, embrace, impact, etc. Figuratively, 'sweep someone off their feet' is the established romantic idiom.
column6: pick up, hoist, raise; sweep off one's feet (figurative)
column7: He hugged her so hard he lifted her off her feet. / The blast lifted him off his feet.
column8: Raw 'lifted off one's feet' is most naturally literal. Do not automatically substitute 'swept off one's feet,' which means suddenly charm/romance someone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120, voca_0121 | search: lifted off one's feet

column5: Originally shorthand for psychological operation: organized activity intended to influence attitudes, emotions, beliefs, or behavior. Online, jokingly or conspiratorially, 'psyop' labels something suspected of manipulating public perception or taste.
column6: psychological operation, influence operation; manipulation campaign (broader)
column7: The military sense refers to planned psychological operations aimed at influencing an audience. / Online, people jokingly call an aggressively promoted trend a psyop. / 'This movie is a psyop' may be pure hyperbole, not a factual allegation.
column8: Internet use has broadened dramatically and is often unserious. Calling something a psyop does not establish coordinated manipulation. Distinguish actual documented influence operations from meme/conspiracy usage.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: psyop meaning

column5: Dressing or presenting oneself in an exaggerated emo aesthetic as a costume, imitation, or temporary persona; can be neutral description or a dismissive accusation that someone's emo identity/style is performative.
column7: The outfit looked less like everyday emo fashion and more like emo cosplay. / Calling someone's style 'emo cosplay' can imply you think they're only performing the identity.
column8: Not a fixed technical term. Cosplay literally means costume play, but figurative 'X cosplay' often criticizes someone for imitating an identity/role without authenticity.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: emo cosplay meaning

column5: An ability to notice fine differences, quality, flaws, authenticity, or significance and make good judgments about what one sees.
column6: good eye, critical eye, trained eye, perceptive judgment
column7: A discerning eye can spot when an expensive-looking set is actually cheaply dressed. / She has a discerning eye for typography and tiny spacing problems.
column8: Extends existing discerning adjective into a common collocation. 'Critical eye' can emphasize scrutiny; 'trained eye' emphasizes expertise; discerning eye emphasizes selective good judgment.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: discerning eye meaning

column2: be more on alert about something
column5: To be more watchful or ready to notice a possible problem. Raw 'more on alarm about' is unnatural; use 'more alert to,' 'more vigilant about,' 'more on guard against,' or 'on higher alert for.'
column6: be more alert to, be more vigilant about, be on guard against
column7: After that scam, I'm more alert to messages that create artificial urgency. / We're on higher alert for duplicate entries now.
column8: 'On alert' is natural, but 'on alarm' is not the usual expression. Choose preposition by phrase: alert to, vigilant about, on guard against, on alert for.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: being more on alarm about something

column5: To create or convey a particular intuitive impression, atmosphere, personality, or emotional feeling.
column6: give the impression, come across as, exude, radiate, have an X vibe
column7: He gives off a friendly, slightly awkward vibe. / The empty hotel gives off a creepy 1980s-horror vibe even in daylight.
column8: Existing give off WID2740 covers the general phrasal verb; this collocation is independently useful because 'vibe' is an impression rather than literal emission. 'Come across as X' focuses more directly on how a person seems.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: give off the vibe that meaning

column5: The tiring sameness that comes from little or no change, variety, or interest.
column7: Working from the same room every day can become monotonous, so I sometimes go to a café just to break the monotony. / The show's visual style is beautiful, but the pacing eventually settles into monotony.
column8: Common: break/relieve the monotony; the monotony of daily life/work. Monotony emphasizes repetitive sameness; boredom is the feeling that may result from it; tedium emphasizes how tiresome something feels.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: monotony meaning

column5: Grammatically possible, but often less natural than 'conform to social norms' because comply usually suggests explicit rules, demands, requests, or requirements; use it when norms are treated as obligations.
column6: obey, adhere to, conform to (more idiomatic for norms)
column7: Employees must comply with the dress code. / People tend to conform to social norms. / 'Comply with social norms' works when the norms are framed as rules one is expected to obey.
column8: Search-intent contrast: comply with rules/laws/requests; conform to norms/standards/patterns. Overlap exists, but collocational preference matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: comply with social norms meaning

column5: A jump-rope activity using two long ropes turned in opposite directions while one or more people jump between them; historically/informal BrE, 'double Dutch' can also mean incomprehensible language or gibberish.
column7: The kids practiced Double Dutch in the playground. / The instructions sounded like double Dutch to me—an older expression meaning they were incomprehensible.
column8: Capitalize when treating the sport/activity name. The 'gibberish' sense belongs to a family of old English expressions using Dutch stereotypically and may sound dated; the jump-rope sense is culturally important in U.S. urban communities.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: double dutch meaning

column5: To know something extremely thoroughly, including its details and how it works.
column6: know thoroughly, know backwards and forwards
column7: She knows the software inside out after using it for ten years.
column8: Inside out literally means with the inner surface turned outward; figuratively it suggests complete knowledge from every angle.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111 | search: know something inside out meanign

column5: High status, respect, admiration, or social esteem associated with a person, institution, occupation, product, cultural form, etc.
column7: The university's prestige attracts applicants from around the world. / The job pays less but carries considerable prestige.
column8: Usually uncountable. Prestige can be institutional/social and need not reflect intrinsic quality. Attributive use: prestige brand, prestige project.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: define prestige

column5: A process or situation in which one step is said to lead to a chain of increasingly serious, difficult, or undesirable consequences; also the argument that allowing A will eventually lead to Z.
column6: thin end of the wedge (BrE, related), dangerous progression, chain of escalation
column7: Skipping one workout isn't a slippery slope by itself. / Critics called the policy a slippery slope toward broader surveillance.
column8: A slippery-slope argument is not automatically fallacious: the key question is whether the proposed causal/institutional chain is supported. Often used loosely for habits that may escalate.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: a slippery slope

column7: We discussed how best to explain the change to customers.
column8: Natural compact alternative to 'what is the best way to...'.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: how best to do meaning

column5: A fan who supports a team, person, franchise, or cause mainly when things are going well, but loses interest or loyalty during failure or difficulty.
column6: bandwagon fan (overlapping), fickle fan, glory supporter (BrE sports)
column7: He only started wearing the jersey after they made the finals, so everyone called him a fair-weather fan. / A fair-weather fan disappears as soon as the team starts losing.
column8: From fair-weather friend: someone dependable only in good times. Bandwagon fan emphasizes joining because something becomes successful/popular; fair-weather emphasizes abandoning support in bad times.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: fair weather fan

column5: A picture-like written symbol, especially one in ancient Egyptian hieroglyphic writing; more loosely, an unreadable or mysterious-looking symbol or mark.
column7: The wall was covered in Egyptian hieroglyphs. / His tiny handwritten notes looked like hieroglyphs to me.
column8: Egyptian hieroglyphs are a full writing system using signs that can represent sounds, words, or semantic categories—not simply 'pictures that mean objects.' Informal plural can mean indecipherable marks.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: hieroglyphs

column5: To pause briefly before continuing, often to think, calm down, or let a moment land.
column7: Let's take a beat before we respond to that email.
column8: From beat as a brief unit/pause, especially in performance and conversation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: take a beat meaning

column5: An animal's recorded ancestry/lineage; by extension, a person's, institution's, product's, or idea's distinguished background, origins, qualifications, or track record.
column6: lineage, ancestry, bloodline; credentials, provenance, background
column7: The dog has an impressive pedigree. / The director has a strong comedy pedigree. / The theory has an intellectual pedigree stretching back centuries.
column8: Figurative pedigree often evaluates credibility/status from origins or past associations. Can sound elitist when applied to people/social background.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: pedigree meaning

column4: noun, internet sexual slang; also proper fandom term
column5: In current internet sexual slang, a person who engages heavily in 'gooning'—prolonged, highly absorbed pornography/masturbation sessions. Separately, Gooner is a longstanding nickname for an Arsenal F.C. supporter.
column7: Online, 'gooner' may be thrown around jokingly as an insult for someone perceived as porn-brained. / In football context, 'a Gooner' can simply mean an Arsenal supporter.
column8: Two unrelated senses can collide. Sexual-slang sense is explicit and often insulting/memetic. Arsenal sense comes from the club's 'Gunners' nickname and should not be confused with it.

column6: fit in with, merge with, camouflage oneself among, disappear into
column7: Wear something neutral if you want to blend in with the crowd. / The new character blends in with the group so naturally that you forget she joined halfway through the season.
column8: Blend in emphasizes not standing out visually/socially; fit in emphasizes social acceptance/compatibility. A color/object can blend in with surroundings without any social meaning.

column5: At the amount it cost the seller to obtain or produce something, with no profit added.
column6: at cost price, without markup, at the seller's cost
column7: Employees can buy the equipment at cost. / He sold me the spare part at cost and didn't make a cent on it. / The nonprofit provides the books at cost.
column8: Means for the seller's purchase/production cost, with no profit markup. Crucial contrast: 'at a cost' = with a sacrifice, disadvantage, or expense ('Success came at a cost'). 'Cost price' is common in BrE.
