column5: A scheme for obtaining money, attention, or advantage through deception, manipulation, or opportunistic exploitation; to engage in such a scheme.
column7: Critics accused the influencer of turning the controversy into a grift.
column8: Modern online use can broaden beyond literal fraud to cynical monetization or opportunism.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: grift meaning

column2: make a fool out of someone
column5: To make someone look stupid, ridiculous, gullible, or embarrassed, especially in front of others; 'make a fool out of me' can imply humiliation or deception.
column6: humiliate, embarrass, make someone look stupid, play someone for a fool
column7: Are you trying to make a fool out of me? / He felt the prank had made a fool out of him in front of everyone.
column8: Also 'make a fool of someone'—often more concise and idiomatic. 'Make a fool of yourself' = behave in a way that makes yourself look ridiculous.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: making a fool out of me meaning

column5: To move without much power or effort, especially using momentum; figuratively, to progress or succeed with little effort, often because the hard work is already done or one's advantage is large.
column6: glide, roll, cruise; sail through, breeze through
column7: Take your foot off the pedal and let the bike coast downhill. / The team built a huge lead and coasted to victory. / He coasted through the class on natural ability and barely studied.
column8: Figurative coast can be neutral ('win easily') or critical ('stop trying and rely on past success/talent'). 'Coast along' often suggests easy progress; 'coast through' = complete with little effort.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: coasted

column5: Not called, summoned, requested, or selected; much less common in everyday speech than the idiom 'uncalled for.'
column7: Several numbers remained uncalled in the lottery. / For 'inappropriate or unnecessary,' say 'uncalled for,' not simply 'uncalled.'
column8: Search likely tests distinction. 'Uncalled-for' may also be hyphenated before a noun: an uncalled-for remark.

column5: Weak, indecisive, vague, lacking firm conviction, or insufficiently definite/forceful.
column7: His answer was so wishy-washy that I still don't know what he actually supports. / The ending felt wishy-washy instead of committing to either interpretation.
column8: Usually critical. Can describe opinions, people, language, policy, storytelling, colors/flavors that feel weak or diluted.

column5: Instruction, training, guidance, or protection provided by a teacher, mentor, or guardian; especially in 'under someone's tutelage.'
column7: She studied under the tutelage of a master animator. / Under his coach's tutelage, her technique improved rapidly.
column8: More formal than teaching. Fixed collocation 'under the tutelage of.' Historically also guardianship/protection.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: tutelage

column5: The forces, patterns, interactions, and relationships that shape how a group, relationship, system, or situation behaves and changes.
column6: interactions, interplay, relationships, power structure, forces at work
column7: The show becomes much more interesting once the group dynamics start to shift. / Their friendship has a strange power dynamic because one of them is also the other's boss. / Adding a third character completely changes the dynamics of the scene.
column8: Often plural: family/group/team/relationship/power dynamics. 'Dynamic' can be a single pattern/relationship; dynamics emphasizes the interacting forces as a whole. Not the same as 'dynamic' = energetic/changing.

column5: To appear, arise, grow, or develop suddenly or quickly.
column6: pop up, crop up, emerge, arise, mushroom
column7: New cafés have sprung up all over the neighborhood. / Fan theories sprang up almost immediately after the trailer dropped. / Wildflowers spring up here after the first warm rains.
column8: Can describe buildings/businesses, problems, movements, plants, rumors, ideas. Past: sprang up; past participle: sprung up.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: spring up meaning

column5: Very small, meager, inadequate, or contemptibly insignificant in amount, quality, or value.
column7: They offered a paltry $20 for a full day's work. / The update added a paltry two features after a year of development.
column8: Often conveys contempt: not merely small, but embarrassingly insufficient. Raw companion search 'paultry' was a misspelling.

column5: To avoid conviction or punishment for a criminal charge, especially despite having been accused.
column7: The defendant beat the rap when the key evidence was excluded.
column8: Rap here = criminal charge/accusation in older slang. Often implies escaping legal consequences.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: beat the rap meaning

column6: routine, gag, sketch (bit) vs company, ensemble, group (troupe)
column7: The comedian did a bit about airport security. / The improv troupe performed three shows that weekend. / Their fake argument became a recurring bit on the podcast.
column8: Likely raw question 'a bit is like a troupe?' Answer: no. Bit = piece of material/performance; troupe = people performing. Sketch is usually a more developed scripted comic scene; bit can be much smaller or improvised.

column5: Calm, graceful self-control and confidence, especially under pressure; physical balance/elegance. As a verb, to hold or position something ready for action.
column7: She answered the hostile question with remarkable poise. / The dancer moved with poise and precision. / He stood poised to leave as soon as the meeting ended.
column8: Poise often combines composure + graceful confidence. 'Poised to do X' = ready/in position to do it, often because conditions are favorable.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: poise meaning

column5: The prime, freshest, or most beautiful period of one's youth.
column6: prime of youth, bloom of youth
column7: He remembered those summers as the flower of his youth.
column8: Literary/old-fashioned metaphor: flower = the finest or most flourishing stage of something.

column5: To decipher a code; figuratively, to discover the key principle, pattern, method, or solution needed to understand or succeed at something difficult.
column6: decipher, solve, figure out, unlock the secret, get the hang of
column7: After months of listening practice, I finally felt like I was cracking the code of fast casual speech. / Researchers tried to crack the enemy code.
column8: Figurative use can be playful/hyperbolic: crack the code of dating, marketing, pronunciation. It implies a hidden underlying pattern.

column6: molten rock at the surface, volcanic melt
column7: Lava flowed slowly down the side of the volcano. / The lava cooled into dark volcanic rock. / Thick, viscous lava can move very differently from more fluid lava.
column8: Magma is molten or partially molten rock beneath Earth's surface; once erupted at the surface it is called lava. 'Lava' can refer to the molten material and, in geology, the rock formed from a lava flow after cooling. Do not confuse lava /ˈlɑːvə/ with larva /ˈlɑːrvə/.

column7: The forum uses 'cuck' as a generic insult for any man it considers weak. / In the traditional sense, cuckold refers specifically to a man whose partner is unfaithful.
column8: Highly derogatory and often associated with manosphere/political trolling. Internet insult sense has drifted far from the literal relationship meaning. Do not assume consensual fetish context unless context supports it.

column5: A deep, persistent resentment associated especially with perceived powerlessness, in which hostility may be redirected into moral judgments or value systems that condemn what one cannot attain or confront directly.
column7: Nietzsche's discussion of ressentiment is not simply about feeling annoyed; it concerns resentment becoming psychologically and morally productive. / The critic interpreted the movement through the lens of ressentiment.
column8: French loanword used especially in Nietzschean/philosophical discourse. Do not flatten it to ordinary resentment: the theoretical sense involves reactive value-formation and powerlessness.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: ressentiment
column12: entry::word entry::discourse_expression topic::philosophy discovery::criticism discovery::complaint discovery::perception discovery::evaluation

column5: A self-reinforcing sequence in which one positive development causes another, which feeds back and produces further improvement—the positive counterpart of a vicious cycle.
column6: positive feedback loop, reinforcing loop, upward spiral
column7: More listening improves comprehension, which makes listening more enjoyable, which leads to more listening—a virtuous cycle. / Better service increased trust and repeat business, creating a virtuous cycle.
column8: Common economics/business/policy term. 'Virtuous' here means beneficial, not morally pure. Opposite: vicious cycle.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: virtuous cycle

column5: A strongly stated, provocative, surprising, or quickly formed opinion, often designed to attract attention or spark argument.
column7: Hot take: the sequel is better than the original.
column8: Existing take (noun) mentions hot take, but the compound has its own internet/media connotations and is useful independently.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: hot take meaning

column5: Mental or emotional exhaustion, frustration, boredom, or cynicism caused by prolonged use of dating apps and repeated swiping, messaging, matching, rejection, or shallow interactions.
column6: dating burnout, swipe fatigue, app burnout
column7: After months of repetitive small talk and ghosting, I developed serious dating-app fatigue. / She deleted the apps for a while because swipe fatigue was making dating feel like a second job.
column8: A contemporary descriptive term rather than a clinical diagnosis. Burnout is stronger and broader; fatigue can describe simple weariness/disillusionment. Related phenomena include choice overload and dating-app burnout.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: dating app fatigue

column5: Competition marked by spiteful, snide, gossipy, or cutting interpersonal behavior.
column7: The show turns the friendly contest into catty competition between the leads.
column8: Existing catty card gives the adjective; preserve this searched collocation because it captures how the adjective colors a rivalry/competition.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: catty competition meaning

column5: Experiencing a continuing series of successes or doing something very well repeatedly.
column6: on a winning streak, in the zone
column7: She has won five matches in a row—she's really on a roll.
column8: Usually positive momentum: one success seems to lead naturally into the next.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: on a roll meaning

column5: Lack of candor or sincerity; the quality of being disingenuous or pretending not to know, understand, or intend something.
column7: The apology's careful wording gave it an air of disingenuity.
column8: Less common than disingenuousness, but established. Do not confuse with ingenuity.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: disingenuity

column5: To remain in a place, situation, or relationship instead of leaving; with someone, to continue staying near or associated with them.
column7: I decided to stick around for another hour and see what happened.
column8: The core idiom is stick around. 'Stick around with someone' is possible when the context is staying with that person, but the particle normally belongs to stick around, not *stick around with* as one fixed phrasal verb.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111 | search: stick around with someone
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::relationships discovery::continuity

column5: Said when an annoying, familiar, or predictable situation is starting to happen again.
column6: not this again, same old story
column7: Here we go again—another argument about whose turn it is to clean up.
column8: Usually expresses weary recognition, irritation, or amusement at repetition.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: here we go again meaning

column5: To keep moving along a route; figuratively, to keep pursuing the same course of action, development, behavior, or decision trajectory.
column6: stay on the course, keep going in that direction, proceed
column7: If we continue down this path, the app will become harder to maintain. / The story continues down a darker path in season two.
column8: Common conceptual metaphor: decisions/development as travel along a path. Often used as warning: 'If we continue down this path...'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: continue down the path meaning
column12: entry::fixed_expression usage::figurative topic::decision-making discovery::literal_vs_figurative discovery::figurative_extension discovery::continuity

column5: A small ornament, piece of jewelry, souvenir, or decorative object, usually of little monetary value.
column7: The market stalls sold cheap trinkets and souvenirs. / She kept a few childhood trinkets in a box.
column8: Can be affectionate or dismissive. Unlike keepsake, trinket often suggests small/decorative and not especially valuable.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: trinkets meaning

column5: A heavy, unpleasant, or oppressive atmosphere, vapor, smell, or influence; historically, a supposed disease-causing 'bad air.' Figuratively, a pervasive cloud of corruption, fear, gloom, confusion, etc.
column7: A miasma of smoke hung over the valley. / The story is soaked in a miasma of dread and decay. / Nineteenth-century miasma theory wrongly attributed many diseases to poisonous bad air.
column8: Excellent gothic/literary word. Figurative 'a miasma of X' suggests something diffuse and pervasive. Historical miasma theory is obsolete but culturally important.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: miasma meaning
column12: entry::word usage::literary usage::dated usage::figurative topic::health discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Unauthorized, improper, or secret interference with something in order to alter, damage, manipulate, influence, or compromise it.
column7: The seal is designed to reveal evidence of tampering. / Witness tampering is a serious legal offense. / The results were investigated for possible data tampering.
column8: Common compounds: evidence tampering, witness tampering, product tampering, data tampering. Base pattern: tamper with X. Usually implies improper/unauthorized interference, stronger than ordinary adjustment.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define tampering

column5: In the familiar/current form in which we understand or experience something; used when imagining major change or destruction of that form.
column6: in its present form, as it currently exists
column7: The internet changed publishing as we knew it. / That discovery could transform medicine as we know it. / 'The end of the world as we know it' means the end of the familiar world/order, not necessarily literal planetary destruction.
column8: Tense often follows viewpoint: as we know it now; as we knew it then. Common dramatic phrase: X as we know it.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: as we know it meaning

column2: put all one's eggs in one basket
column3: /ˌpʊt ɔːl wʌnz ˈeɡz ɪn wʌn ˈbæskɪt/
column5: To risk all one's resources, hopes, money, time, or plans on a single option so that one failure could cause a major loss.
column6: bet everything on one thing, concentrate all risk, go all-in (overlapping)
column7: Don't put all your eggs in one basket—apply to more than one program. / I wouldn't put all my savings into one stock.
column8: Usually appears as advice not to concentrate risk. 'Go all-in' can be deliberate/positive; eggs-in-one-basket framing emphasizes vulnerability from lack of diversification.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: Putting all your eggs in one basket
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::decision-making discovery::resource_allocation discovery::risk

column5: Used to say that the same statement, pattern, problem, rule, or observation also applies to another thing.
column6: the same goes for, likewise with, similarly for
column7: The app is slow on my phone, and it's the same with the desktop version. / People overuse that phrase in reviews; same with 'masterpiece.'
column8: Very productive pattern. 'The same goes for X' is often smoother when extending a claim. Compare 'same as' for direct equivalence/comparison.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: same with something meaning

column5: Difficulty or inability to achieve pregnancy/reproduction; medically, definitions use specified periods of regular unprotected intercourse and vary with age/context.
column7: The couple sought medical advice after struggling with infertility. / Some conditions affect fertility without making pregnancy impossible.
column8: Infertility does not necessarily mean absolute sterility. Fertility = capacity/likelihood of reproduction; subfertility = reduced fertility; sterility can imply inability to reproduce. Existing cards mention fertility issues, but the standalone term is useful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define infertility

column5: A stylized slang form of dog used as a friendly way to address a person, similar to dude, bro, or friend.
column7: What's up, dawg? I haven't seen you in forever.
column8: Strongly associated with informal American speech and hip-hop/pop culture. Tone and appropriateness depend on speaker/context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: dawg meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::slang topic::friends topic::animals

column5: A sudden sharp physical pain or brief intense feeling, especially guilt, regret, sadness, jealousy, hunger, or longing.
column6: twinge, stab, ache, pang of emotion
column7: She felt a pang of guilt after reading the message. / A sudden pang of hunger reminded me I'd skipped lunch.
column8: Usually 'a pang of X'; plural pangs common for recurring/intense feelings: pangs of conscience, hunger pangs.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: pangs meaning

column5: In a coma and unable to be awakened; informally/hyperbolically, extremely sleepy, inactive, or unresponsive.
column6: unconscious, in a coma; inert, dead to the world (figurative)
column7: He remained comatose after the accident. / After the overnight flight I was practically comatose on the couch.
column8: Medical sense is serious and specific. Casual hyperbole is common but should not be confused with actual coma. 'Comatose market/room' can figuratively mean lifeless/inactive.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define comatose

column5: A statement that makes something seem greater, stronger, more important, or more extreme than it really is.
column7: Calling the minor delay a disaster was an overstatement.
column8: Natural opposite of understatement; can be deliberate or simply excessive wording.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: overstatement meaning

column5: A large amount or number of something; much/many, especially in casual speech.
column6: lots of, tons of, heaps of, plenty of, a load of
column7: I've got loads of bookmarks left to process. / There were loads of people at the festival. / We still have loads of time.
column8: Very common informal BrE and widely understood elsewhere. Works with count and uncount nouns. 'A load of' can also mean a large amount, but 'a load of rubbish' has its own dismissive flavor.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: loads of synonym

column5: Both boring/uninteresting and slyly contemptuous or mean in tone.
column6: boring and sneering, tedious and cutting
column7: The dialogue felt dull and snide rather than witty.
column8: Not a fixed idiom. Preserve the searched pairing: dull describes lack of interest/liveliness; snide describes contemptuous indirect meanness.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: dull and snide

column5: A complete failure, null result, or situation in which gains and losses cancel out; exact nuance depends on context. More standard related forms are 'a wash' (= no net advantage / roughly even) and 'a washout' (= complete failure).
column6: a wash, a washout, a total loss, a bust (contextual)
column7: If the extra revenue is exactly canceled by the extra cost, it's basically a wash. / If the speaker said 'a total wash' to mean complete failure, 'a total washout' would often be more idiomatic.
column8: Raw phrase is understandable but not a strongly fixed standard idiom. Preserve search provenance while distinguishing 'a wash' from 'a washout' instead of pretending they are identical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: total wash meaning

column5: Wise or possessing wisdom; in science fiction/philosophy, capable of higher reasoning, reflective intelligence, or human-like intellectual understanding, often contrasted with merely sentient.
column6: wise, intelligent, rational, self-aware (overlapping, not identical)
column7: Humans are named Homo sapiens from a Latin root associated with wisdom. / The novel distinguishes sentient animals that can feel from sapient species capable of complex reasoning and civilization.
column8: Everyday English rarely uses sapient outside literary/SF/philosophical contexts. Sentient = capable of sensation/experience; sapient = wise or higher-order reasoning. Real scientific/philosophical boundaries are not perfectly captured by the SF shorthand.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: sapient meaning
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::literary usage::scientific topic::science topic::entertainment topic::philosophy

column5: Covered with soft fibers; blurred or indistinct; or unclear, imprecise, and difficult to define or remember.
column7: My memory of that conversation is a little fuzzy.
column8: Common figurative senses: fuzzy memory, fuzzy logic/boundaries, warm and fuzzy. Existing warm and fuzzy is a specific idiom.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: define fuzzy

column5: Illegally hunting, catching, or taking wildlife; by extension, improperly recruiting someone else's employees/clients or taking resources/opportunities regarded as belonging to another party.
column6: illegal hunting, wildlife trafficking; talent poaching, client poaching
column7: The reserve increased patrols to stop elephant poaching. / The rival company was accused of poaching engineers from the team. / Restaurants sometimes complain about competitors poaching staff.
column8: Core wildlife sense involves illegal taking. Business/sports sense is figurative and may be legal but viewed as aggressive/unethical. Also poach = cook gently in liquid, an unrelated common verb sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define poaching
column12: entry::word usage::figurative topic::business topic::work discovery::professional_context discovery::resource_allocation

column2: when it comes down to it
column5: When the situation reaches the essential point, final decision, or moment when action really matters; ultimately, in practical terms.
column6: ultimately, when all is said and done, at the end of the day, when it really matters
column7: When it comes down to it, I'd rather have a smaller deck I actually use. / He talks confidently, but when it comes down to it, will he actually do it?
column8: Related but different from 'X comes down to Y' = X is essentially determined/reduced to Y. This phrase is a clause-level discourse marker.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: when it comes down to it is this

column5: A being, deity, spirit, or figure believed to guide the souls of the dead to the afterlife.
column7: Hermes is sometimes described as a psychopomp who escorts souls to the underworld.
column8: From Greek roots meaning roughly 'soul guide.' Appears in mythology, religion, fantasy, and literary criticism.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: psychopompとは

column5: Consistent or in agreement with a rule, expectation, policy, trend, value, or standard.
column6: consistent with, in accordance with, aligned with
column7: The change is in line with our long-term strategy.
column8: Often used in formal/business contexts to express conformity or alignment.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: in line with meaning

column5: Simple and straightforward, with neither hassle/ceremony ('fuss') nor unnecessary extras/luxuries ('frills').
column6: simple and straightforward, hassle-free and basic, no-nonsense
column7: The place is no fuss, no frills: good food, quick service, nothing fancy.
column8: Not a rigid fixed idiom, but a natural rhythmic pairing. 'No fuss' emphasizes ease/lack of bother; 'no frills' emphasizes lack of extras.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: no fuss no-frills meaning

column5: To incorporate an expected event, risk, or piece of information into the current price or valuation of an asset, product, or market.
column7: Markets had already priced in the expected rate cut.
column8: Very common in finance: X is priced in / investors price in X.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: price in meaning

column5: To appear or arrive, often unexpectedly; to be found after being missing; also to increase the level of something such as volume or heat.
column7: My missing keys finally turned up under the sofa.
column8: Highly polysemous. Core useful senses: appear/arrive, be found, and increase a setting.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: turn up meaning

column5: To remember and continue considering a fact because it may affect what you think or do next.
column6: bear that in mind, remember that
column7: The road gets icy after dark, so keep that in mind when you leave.
column8: That can refer back to an entire previous statement or warning.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: keep that in mind meaning

column5: Thick and sticky in consistency, resisting flow; in physics, having relatively high viscosity.
column7: Honey is more viscous than water. / The sauce becomes more viscous as it cools. / Lava can range from relatively fluid to extremely viscous depending on composition and temperature.
column8: Physics/materials sense: a viscous fluid strongly resists flow; viscosity is the property. Everyday 'thick' is close but less precise. Do not confuse viscous /ˈvɪskəs/ with vicious /ˈvɪʃəs/.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111, voca_0121 | search: define viscous

column5: Involved in or helping to enable wrongdoing, especially knowingly or through cooperation, support, or acquiescence.
column6: involved, implicated, collusive, accessory to, enabling
column7: The report alleged that several managers were complicit in hiding the problem. / He worried that staying silent would make him complicit.
column8: Common pattern: complicit in X / complicit with someone. Related noun complicity. Stronger than simply 'involved' because wrongdoing is implied.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: complicit meaning

column5: To cause someone to experience something painful, harmful, unpleasant, or damaging; commonly used with injury, pain, suffering, damage, punishment, or a defeat.
column7: The attack inflicted serious damage on the building. / She didn't want to inflict that kind of pain on him. / The team inflicted its first defeat of the season on the defending champions.
column8: Typical pattern: inflict X on/upon someone/something. Usually the object is negative. Compare 'afflict': a disease/problem afflicts a person; a person/action inflicts harm on someone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: inflict

column5: In an overly self-important, grand, formal, or dignified manner that seems affected or ridiculous.
column7: He pompously announced that only he truly understood the film. / The waiter character speaks pompously about an extremely ordinary sandwich.
column8: Usually critical. Pompous describes inflated dignity/self-importance; pretentious more broadly means trying to appear more cultured/important than one really is.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116, voca_0117 | search: pompously

column5: A weighing instrument that compares an unknown mass with known masses by balancing two sides/pans around a central pivot; also a common symbol of justice/fairness.
column7: The old laboratory used a balance scale with weights. / The scales of justice are conventionally shown as a balance.
column8: Often simply 'balance' or 'scales.' Distinct from a modern bathroom/kitchen scale that directly displays weight/mass.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: balance scale

column5: Fully developed, complete, or at the most serious/intense stage.
column6: fully developed, complete, outright, full-scale, fully fledged (contextual)
column7: A small disagreement turned into a full-blown argument. / What started as a hobby became a full-blown business. / By evening, the mild headache had turned into a full-blown migraine.
column8: Means something has developed to a complete, unmistakable, or intense stage. Common with crisis, war, panic, addiction, illness, investigation, obsession. Often marks escalation: 'turn into/become a full-blown X.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: full-blown

column5: The standard, conventional, officially defined, or normalized ordering of items in a system, representation, sequence, language, or dataset.
column6: standard order, normalized order, conventional order
column7: The serializer puts the fields into canonical order before comparison. / The language has a canonical word order, though other orders are possible.
column8: Technical meaning varies by field. Canonical = chosen/recognized standard representation; it need not mean the only possible order.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: canonical order meaning

column5: Details; the important or interesting information about something.
column7: Send me the deets when you know the time and place. / Okay, I saw the post—now give me the deets.
column8: Very informal/playful shortening of details. Existing 'hear the deets on something' card contains it, but the raw definition search justifies a clean standalone base card. Common: get/give/send the deets.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: deets meaning

column5: To become especially prominent, important, visible, or central in attention/discussion.
column6: come to prominence, move to center stage, become salient
column7: Privacy concerns came to the forefront after the data leak. / A minor character comes to the forefront in the final episodes.
column8: Existing forefront card covers 'at the forefront'; this preserves the change-of-state construction come to the forefront.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: come to the forefront meaning

column5: To enter a place, field, subject, or activity that is unfamiliar, uncertain, or potentially risky.
column7: The company ventured into the streaming market.
column8: Can be literal or figurative: venture into the woods / venture into politics.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: venture into meaning

column5: A structure in which a preposition is followed by an -ing form functioning as a gerund, or a participial phrase is used to modify or frame a clause; the two structures should not be conflated.
column7: After finishing the report, she went home. / He left without saying goodbye.
column8: Important distinction: after/without + -ing can be preposition + gerund; 'After finishing...' can also be analyzed as a supplement/participial clause depending on grammar framework. Preserve as a grammar-comparison card rather than force one label.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: preposition + ing  participle phrases

column5: To reduce or stop pressure, criticism, demands, punishment, harassment, or intensity directed at someone.
column6: ease up on, go easier on, stop pressuring, give a break
column7: The coach finally let up on him after he improved. / Can you let up on her a little? She already knows she made a mistake.
column8: Person-target construction makes the pressure sense especially clear. Compare weather/pain 'let up' = become less intense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: let up on someone meaning

column5: A person who habitually obtains things—especially money, food, or help—from others rather than providing for themselves; someone who scrounges.
column7: He's always scrounging cigarettes off people; everyone thinks he's a bit of a scrounger. / The tabloid portrayed benefit claimants as scroungers.
column8: Often derogatory and socially loaded, especially in phrases like 'benefit scrounger.' Scrounge can also neutrally mean search around to obtain something cheaply or from scraps.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: scrounger
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::derogatory usage::british_english usage::evaluative topic::food

column5: To injure, damage, upset, agitate, or otherwise affect someone badly; in other contexts, to raise something or sharply increase a price.
column7: That fall really jacked me up for a few days.
column8: Very context-dependent. 'Jacked me up' can be physical injury, emotional disturbance, or strong stimulation; jack up prices = raise sharply.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: jacked me up meaning

column5: The absence or insufficiency of the thing just mentioned.
column6: absence of it, want of it, deficiency of it
column7: Success depends on preparation—or the lack thereof. / The problem wasn't bad data so much as a complete lack thereof. / Experience, or the lack thereof, can change how the scene is interpreted.
column8: Formal/compact phrase that refers back to the previously mentioned noun and avoids repetition. 'Thereof' = of that/of it. Common construction: 'X—or the lack thereof.' It can sound slightly legalistic or wry in casual prose.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: lack thereof meaning

column5: Variation in neurological/cognitive functioning that diverges from what is treated as typical; often used as an umbrella concept in neurodiversity discourse for conditions or traits such as autism and ADHD.
column7: The discussion focused on neurodivergence and how different people process sensory input. / Neurodivergence is broader than any one diagnosis.
column8: Usage and scope vary by community/context; it is not itself a specific medical diagnosis. Related: neurodivergent (adj/person descriptor), neurodiversity (variation across a population).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: neurodivergence meaning

column5: To perform, pronounce, translate, edit, adapt, explain, or otherwise handle something very badly, damaging or mangling it.
column7: I'm probably going to butcher his last name, so correct me if I say it wrong. / The adaptation butchered the ending. / The subtitles completely butchered the joke.
column8: Very common figurative hyperbole. Literal butcher = slaughter/cut up meat. Figurative use is especially common with names/pronunciation, songs, translations, stories, and performances.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: butcher something meaning
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::figurative topic::communication discovery::explanation

column5: A dismissive label for formulaic, low-effort, derivative, or mass-produced-feeling isekai media; 'flop' instead means a work that fails commercially/critically or is simply mocked as unsuccessful.
column6: generic isekai, formulaic isekai, low-effort content
column7: He called the show 'isekai slop' because it recycled the same overpowered-protagonist setup. / A show can be slop without being a flop if it is formulaic but commercially successful.
column8: Raw search asks slop or flop: use slop for perceived low-quality/formulaic content; flop for failure/poor performance. Both are subjective/informal judgments.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: isekai slop or flop?
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::disparaging usage::evaluative topic::work topic::media topic::fandom

column5: Extra features, enhancements, decorative touches, or impressive add-ons beyond the basic function of something.
column7: The app has lots of bells and whistles, but I mainly care whether the core study mode works. / We chose the basic model without all the bells and whistles.
column8: Often contrasts with no-frills/bare-bones. Can be positive (useful extras) or mildly dismissive (flashy but unnecessary).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: bells and whistles meaning

column5: A company, organization, or sometimes individual with substantial influence, market presence, resources, reputation, or strategic importance within an industry.
column6: major player, industry leader, key competitor, heavyweight
column7: The company grew from a niche startup into a major industry player. / Being famous does not automatically make a firm a major player if its market share is tiny.
column8: Player is figurative: an actor/participant with influence in a field. 'Major player in the industry' is also very common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: to be a major industry player meaning
column12: entry::phrase usage::figurative topic::business discovery::promotion discovery::resource_allocation discovery::social_approval

column5: To have a valid, reasonable, or persuasive argument or observation, even if it is not the whole story.
column6: be right about something, make a valid point, have a case
column7: I don't agree with his conclusion, but he has a point about the pacing. / You may have a point—doing it now would save us another trip tomorrow.
column8: Often useful for partial agreement: 'You have a point, but...' Stronger 'have a case' often implies evidence/argument supporting a position; 'point taken' acknowledges the other person's point.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: have a point meaning

column5: Someone portrayed as dangerously or seriously harmful to the public; jokingly, a chaotic person whose behavior is comically antisocial or troublesome.
column6: public menace, danger to society; absolute menace (joking)
column7: The prosecutor called him a menace to society. / You put pineapple on all three pizzas? You're a menace to society.
column8: The dramatic phrase is often hyperbolically reused online for trivial behavior. This joking register is worth recognizing separately from genuinely serious legal/social condemnation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: menace of society meaning

column5: A long bench with a back, traditionally arranged in rows for people to sit on in a church or other place of worship.
column7: They sat in the back pew during the service. / Sunlight from the stained-glass windows fell across the empty wooden pews.
column8: Not related to internet/comic 'pew pew' gun-sound imitation. In many churches pews are fixed wooden benches, though seating arrangements vary.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: pew meaning

column5: To shake or tremble suddenly, especially from fear, disgust, cold, or a strong emotional reaction; figuratively, a machine/building can shake violently.
column7: I shudder every time I remember that scene. / She shuddered at the thought of doing it again. / The old train shuddered to a stop.
column8: Common patterns: shudder at the thought; shudder with fear/disgust; make someone shudder. Shiver is strongly associated with cold; shudder often conveys a brief involuntary reaction to something disturbing.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: shuddered

column5: An emotional inhibition, insecurity, persistent worry, prejudice, fixation, or psychological difficulty that interferes with relaxed behavior; also, a problem/obstacle.
column7: He has a hang-up about his height. / I used to have a lot of hangups about speaking English in front of people. / Don't let one technical hang-up derail the whole project.
column8: Often 'have a hang-up about/over X.' Plural hangups common. Distinct from 'hang up' verb (end a phone call) and 'a hang-up' can also mean a delay/problem.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: hangups meaning
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::informal usage::technical topic::psychology topic::problem-solving discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A person's or animal's manner or pattern of walking/moving on foot; in animals, also a particular mode such as walk, trot, canter, gallop.
column6: walk, stride, manner of walking, locomotion pattern
column7: I recognized him from his distinctive gait before I saw his face. / The horse changed gait from a walk to a trot.
column8: Medical/biomechanical uses: gait analysis, abnormal gait. Do not confuse gate /ɡeɪt/; they are homophones.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: define gait

column5: Literally, for a ruminant animal to chew cud; figuratively, to think repeatedly and deeply about something. In psychology, rumination often means repetitive, difficult-to-stop focus on distressing thoughts or feelings.
column6: ponder, mull over, reflect on, dwell on, brood over
column7: I've been ruminating on what he said about language learning. / She kept ruminating over the mistake long after everyone else had moved on. / Cows ruminate by regurgitating and rechewing partially digested food.
column8: Neutral/literary ruminate on/about = contemplate deeply. Psychological rumination is often negative and repetitive, closer to dwell/brood than productive reflection. The figurative sense comes from 'chewing over' thoughts like cud.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: what does ruminating means
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::literary usage::figurative topic::psychology topic::animals discovery::figurative_extension

column5: To handle or perform something clumsily or incompetently, causing mistakes or failure; also an instance of such mishandling.
column7: They bungled the rollout by sending customers the wrong instructions.
column8: Existing cards mention bungle as a synonym, but this base verb is independently useful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: bungle meaning

column5: To assess the audience's mood, knowledge, interest, expectations, reactions, or likely response so you can adjust what you say or do.
column6: read the room, assess the audience, take the audience's measure
column7: A good speaker gauges the audience before deciding how technical to get. / I told one joke first to gauge the audience's reaction.
column8: Gauge = estimate/measure. 'Read the room' is more idiomatic for immediate social mood; gauge the audience can be broader and more deliberate.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: gauge the audience
column12: entry::idiom usage::technical topic::communication topic::public_speaking discovery::audience_engagement discovery::possibility discovery::evaluation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To estimate or infer something beyond known data, observations, or experience by extending an existing pattern or trend.
column7: It's risky to extrapolate national trends from such a small sample.
column8: Contrast interpolate, which estimates within the range of known data.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111, voca_0112 | search: extrapolate meaning

column2: light as a feather, stiff as a board
column3: /ˌlaɪt æz ə ˈfeðər ˌstɪf æz ə ˈbɔːrd/
column5: A traditional children's party/sleepover levitation game and chant in which participants try to lift a person while repeating the phrase.
column7: At sleepovers they used to play 'light as a feather, stiff as a board.'
column8: Cultural phrase, not a normal comparison idiom as a whole. The two halves individually use similes: light as a feather; stiff as a board.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: light as a feather stiff as a board

column5: Teacher-facing materials/interfaces are intended for instructors; student-facing ones are intended to be directly viewed or used by learners.
column7: The answer key is teacher-facing, while the quiz itself is student-facing. / We need separate teacher-facing controls and a simpler student-facing screen.
column8: Useful design/education distinction. 'Facing' identifies the primary user/audience, not physical direction.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: teacher facing vs student facing

column5: An abbreviation with many possible expansions; the intended meaning depends entirely on context. Common examples include road traffic accident (especially BrE/medical), real-time attack in gaming, and regional transit/transport authorities.
column6: road traffic accident; real-time attack; regional transit authority (contextual)
column7: The chart listed 'RTA' as the cause of injury, meaning road traffic accident. / In gaming discussion, RTA may refer to a real-time attack or a real-time speedrun category depending on the community.
column8: Do not memorize RTA as one universal meaning. Preserve the source context whenever possible. This card is intentionally context-sensitive because the raw search supplied only the abbreviation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: rta meaning
column12: entry::initialism usage::british_english topic::games topic::health topic::transportation discovery::possibility

column5: To end up behaving like someone who repeatedly raises false alarms. The phrase is grammatical, but whether it fits depends on whether the repeated behavior actually involves exaggerated/false warnings.
column7: If you exaggerate every minor problem as a catastrophe, you'll end up crying wolf. / Merely 'doing that repeatedly' is not enough unless 'that' is false/exaggerated alarming.
column8: Raw sentence 'If you keep doing that, you'll end up crying wolf' needs antecedent context. Preserve the semantic condition: crying wolf is specifically false/exaggerated alarm, not generic repetition.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: If you keep doing that, you’ll end up crying wolf.

column5: To be immediately noticeable, striking, surprising, or attention-grabbing to someone.
column6: stand out, catch one's eye, leap out, be conspicuous
column7: The typo jumped out at me as soon as I opened the page. / Nothing in the first paragraph really jumps out at me.
column8: Figurative visual/mental salience. Also literal 'someone jumped out at me' = suddenly emerged/attacked/startled, so context matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: jump out at me meaning

column5: A person from Liverpool, England; sometimes also someone who speaks with the Liverpool/Scouse accent.
column7: He's a Scouser born and raised near the city centre. / The comedian's unmistakably Scouse accent immediately gave away where he was from. / Not every person from Merseyside necessarily identifies with the label in exactly the same way.
column8: Informal demonym for a person from Liverpool; 'Scouse' also names the Liverpool accent/dialect and historically a type of stew. Usually neutral/in-group but, like many regional labels, tone can make it affectionate, stereotypical, or derogatory. 'Liverpudlian' is the more formal demonym.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: scouser meaning slang
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::informal usage::slang usage::derogatory usage::affectionate usage::evaluative

column5: To advance to a higher position or better situation through persistent, difficult, often fiercely competitive effort.
column6: fight one's way up, struggle upward
column7: She clawed her way up from an entry-level job to senior management.
column8: Vivid image of climbing by gripping with claws; can suggest ruthless competitiveness depending on context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111 | search: claw one's way up meaning

column2: settle for friendship / settle for being friends
column5: To accept a friendship when one wanted a romantic relationship or something more, often implying compromise or disappointment.
column6: accept being friends, remain just friends, settle for less (contextual)
column7: He wanted to date her, but eventually decided he'd rather settle for friendship than lose her completely. / 'Settle for being friends' can sound as though friendship is a consolation prize, so the framing matters.
column8: Natural forms: settle for friendship / settle for being friends. Settle for X generally means accept something less than what one ideally wanted. Compare 'decide to stay friends,' which is more neutral and does not imply second-best.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: settle for friends meanng
column12: entry::phrase topic::friends topic::relationships topic::romance discovery::compromise discovery::trade-off discovery::resolution

column5: To suddenly start discussing or pursuing a topic that is only loosely related—or unrelated—to the main subject.
column6: digress, go off-topic, wander from the point, branch off
column7: I asked about the ending and somehow went off on a tangent about 1990s anime dubbing. / He tends to go off on tangents, but half the time they're the most interesting part.
column8: Especially common for speech/writing/thought. Tangent is a side direction from the main line. Can be mildly critical or affectionate; not necessarily a problem.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: go off on a tangent

column5: Extremely offensive, morally repugnant, hateful, or disgusting.
column7: She described the abuse as morally abhorrent. / I find that kind of cruelty abhorrent.
column8: Strong moral condemnation, more formal than disgusting/awful. Common pattern 'abhorrent to someone' or simply 'morally abhorrent.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: abhorrent meaning

column5: Flirting charm or ability to attract someone romantically; 'rizzing skills' means one's skill at flirting, talking, presenting oneself, or creating attraction.
column7: His rizz is mostly confidence and good timing rather than pickup lines. / She joked that his rizzing skills disappeared the second he actually liked someone.
column8: Existing rizz cards cover the word/action; this contextual card preserves the searched idea of rizz as a learnable 'skill set.' Rizz is playful Gen-Z/internet slang and can already sound self-conscious/ironic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: rizzing skills meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::playful usage::ironic usage::informal

column5: To produce large quantities of something continuously or rapidly, often routinely and sometimes with an implication of formulaic or mediocre quality.
column6: mass-produce, crank out, pump out, turn out
column7: The studio churns out several low-budget sequels a year. / He can churn out competent articles quickly, but they sometimes feel formulaic.
column8: Can be neutral about high output, but often mildly critical: quantity/regularity over care or originality. Common with content, products, graduates, reports.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: churn out definition

column5: A rough, breathy, weak, strained, or raspy quality of the voice, often caused by irritation or problems affecting the vocal folds/larynx.
column6: raspiness, rough voice, huskiness (partial), dysphonia (clinical broader term)
column7: After shouting all night, he woke up with noticeable hoarseness. / Persistent hoarseness can make speaking tiring.
column8: Everyday symptom word. Hoarse = adjective. Dysphonia is a broader clinical term for impaired voice quality/function.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: hoarseness

column5: The property of remaining unchanged under specified changes, transformations, conditions, or variation.
column7: Researchers look for perceptual invariance across different speakers. / In mathematics and physics, an invariant property remains unchanged under a defined transformation.
column8: Technical meaning always depends on 'invariant with respect to what?' In speech perception, the problem of invariance concerns stable linguistic categories despite variable acoustic signals.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: invariance

column5: An open area of uncultivated upland, especially in Britain; as a verb, to secure a boat or vessel in place with ropes, anchors, or similar means.
column7: They walked across the windswept moor. / We moored the boat near the pier.
column8: Two major unrelated senses. Related existing unmoored is figurative 'not anchored/stable.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: moor meaning

column5: That fact, detail, reaction, or omission reveals something significant or revealing about the underlying situation or person.
column7: He praised everyone except his own manager. That's telling.
column8: Telling as an adjective = revealing or significant, as in a telling detail/sign.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: That’s so telling

column5: A feeling of distress, disappointment, alarm, or discouragement caused by something unexpected or unwelcome; as a verb, to cause that feeling.
column7: To my dismay, the file was corrupted. / Fans reacted with dismay when the cancellation was announced. / She was dismayed to discover that the train had already left.
column8: Common pattern 'to someone's dismay.' Stronger/more formal than disappointment and often includes alarm or discouragement. Dismayed = distressed/disappointed by an unwelcome development.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: dismay

column5: In the past and left behind, especially a problem, period, event, or experience one has moved beyond.
column6: behind us, in the past, over and done with
column7: That stressful launch is finally in the rearview mirror. / By then, college was already disappearing in the rearview mirror.
column8: Based on seeing what is behind a car in its rearview mirror. Often 'put/leave X in the rearview mirror.' Can also literally refer to the mirror.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118, voca_0119 | search: rearview mirror phrase

column5: To touch, adjust, experiment with, or make small changes to something, often repeatedly or without a clear plan.
column7: I fiddled with the settings until the picture looked right.
column8: Can imply minor, fussy, or potentially unhelpful adjustments.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: fiddle with meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal topic::research discovery::trial_and_error discovery::minor_adjustment

column5: Not normally a standalone English idiom for irritation or burden. Natural expressions include 'up to my neck in X' = deeply involved/overwhelmed, 'a pain in the neck' = annoying, and 'get on my nerves' = irritate me.
column6: up to my neck in, pain in the neck, get on my nerves
column7: I'm up to my neck in work this week. / That constant buzzing gets on my nerves. / *It's up my neck* is not the normal idiom for 'it's annoying me.'
column8: Preserves a previously discussed confusion. 'Up my neck' can occur literally or inside larger phrases, but do not substitute it for 'on my nerves/under my skin.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: up my neck

column5: To prove stronger or more successful; to be widespread or dominant; or, with upon/on, to persuade someone.
column7: After a long debate, common sense prevailed.
column8: Common patterns: prevail over/against; conditions that prevail; prevail upon someone to do something.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: prevail meaning

column5: To produce, pull out, or bring out something suddenly and quickly, often dramatically or unexpectedly.
column6: pull out, produce, bring out, brandish (weapon-specific/stronger)
column7: He whipped out his phone and showed me the screenshot. / The character suddenly whipped out a gun, changing the whole tone of the scene. / She whipped out a notebook and started taking notes.
column8: Not inherently weapon-related; object can be phone, card, cash, tool, etc. With a weapon, 'brandish' adds threatening display, while whip out focuses on sudden production.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: whip out a gun meaning

column5: A book, file, or record in which financial transactions, credits, debits, or accounts are systematically recorded; figuratively, an imagined record of favors, harms, obligations, or moral credits/debts.
column7: The accountant entered the payment in the ledger. / Relationships become exhausting if every favor goes into a mental ledger.
column8: Key contrast with ledge /ledʒ/: ledger has /-ər/ and is an accounting record. Digital accounting systems still use ledger terminology.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: ledger meaning
column12: entry::word usage::specialist topic::finance discovery::figurative_extension discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A formal copyright-enforcement action against online content or an account, often following a rights-holder complaint and potentially carrying platform penalties.
column7: The channel received a copyright strike after uploading the full clip.
column8: Platform-specific rules differ. A strike is not necessarily the same as an automated claim or simple takedown notice.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: copyright strike

column5: Very strict, conventional, morally proper, or easily shocked by behavior outside accepted rules.
column7: His strait-laced parents hated the show's crude humor. / She looks strait-laced at work but is completely different with close friends.
column8: Historically also straight-laced spelling occurs, but strait-laced is the traditional form; strait = narrow/restricting. Often mildly critical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: Strait-laced

column5: To make an already tense, angry, controversial, or dangerous situation worse by encouraging, intensifying, or adding fuel to it.
column6: inflame, exacerbate, stir up, fuel, aggravate
column7: Posting the rumor only fanned the flames of the controversy. / Instead of calming everyone down, his sarcastic reply fanned the flames.
column8: Literal image: fanning a fire supplies oxygen and makes it burn harder. Common objects: flames of anger, hatred, conflict, controversy. Opposite idea: defuse/de-escalate.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: fanning the flames meaing

column5: Usually the Commonwealth of Nations: a voluntary association of independent countries, many but not all with historical links to the British Empire.
column7: Canada, India, Australia, and many other countries are members of the Commonwealth. / The Commonwealth is not a single country or government.
column8: Internationally, capitalized 'the Commonwealth' commonly refers to the Commonwealth of Nations. Commonwealth can also be part of official state names or describe a political community; U.S. states such as Massachusetts, Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Kentucky use 'Commonwealth' in their formal names without a different constitutional status from other states.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: commonwealth meaning internationaly
column12: entry::proper_noun entry::term entry::word usage::formal topic::politics topic::history discovery::public_discourse

column5: Not open to debate, negotiation, or reconsideration.
column6: nonnegotiable, not open for debate, settled, not up for negotiation
column7: The safety requirement is not up for discussion. / Whether we back up the Master first is not up for discussion. / He made it clear that the deadline was not up for discussion.
column8: Firm, often authoritative wording that closes debate rather than merely expressing a preference. Compare 'not up for debate' (very close) and 'not up for negotiation' (especially terms/deals). Can sound controlling if used in interpersonal contexts.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: not up for discussion meaning

column5: Fond of joking or characterized by joking, playful humor, especially in manner or tone.
column7: He made the comment in a jocular tone, so nobody took it as a serious insult. / Her usually formal emails became surprisingly jocular.
column8: More formal than funny/jokey. Describes manner/tone/person; can coexist with teasing or mild derision.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: Jocular

column5: A scheme or sudden betrayal in which people attract trust, money, or participation and then abruptly withdraw support, liquidity, funds, or the promised project, leaving others with losses; from 'pull the rug out from under someone.'
column6: exit scam, sudden withdrawal, betrayal, pull the rug out
column7: Investors accused the token creators of a rug pull after the liquidity vanished. / Fans joked that cancelling the project after months of hype felt like a rug pull.
column8: Especially common in cryptocurrency/NFT contexts, where it can describe creators draining liquidity or abandoning a project. Broader internet use is metaphorical and does not necessarily allege a literal financial crime.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: rug pull meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::figurative usage::informal topic::internet topic::finance discovery::support discovery::betrayal discovery::social_trust

column5: To make a gesture inviting someone to come closer or follow; figuratively, to attract or seem to invite someone toward an opportunity or destination.
column7: She beckoned me over with one finger. / A new career beckoned.
column8: Common patterns: beckon someone over/in; opportunity/adventure beckons.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: define beckons

column5: Willing to obey or cooperate; also meeting specified rules, standards, or requirements.
column7: The device is fully compliant with the new safety standard.
column8: Two important shades: a compliant person readily yields/cooperates; a compliant product/system conforms to requirements.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: compliant meaning

column5: Able to be inferred or concluded from evidence or reasoning even if not stated directly.
column7: Her disappointment was inferable from the abrupt change in tone.
column8: Also spelled inferrable, with double r, though inferable is common. Related verb infer.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: inferable

column5: To create or add to an index; to organize information so it can be searched/retrieved; to adjust/link a value to an external measure; or to indicate/serve as an indicator of something.
column6: catalog, list, organize, register; link, track
column7: The search engine indexes new pages automatically. / Benefits are indexed to inflation. / The measure is intended to index changes in consumer confidence.
column8: Computing/search sense is very common. Financial/economic 'index X to inflation.' Do not reduce it to the noun stock-market index.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: define indexing as verb

column5: A conventional way of listing the feminine third-person singular pronouns someone uses: she (subject), her (object/determiner), hers (independent possessive).
column7: She said she uses she/her pronouns. / 'I spoke to her about her book; the copy on the desk is hers' shows the three grammatical forms.
column8: Profiles often abbreviate the set as she/her rather than she/her/hers. Listing pronouns communicates how someone wishes to be referred to; it does not by itself tell you every detail of that person's gender identity.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: she/her/hers meaning

column5: To outwardly communicate an impression of self-assurance and willingness to state or defend one's needs, boundaries, or position.
column6: exude confidence, convey self-assurance, appear assertive, carry oneself confidently
column7: Speak clearly and make eye contact if you want to project confidence without sounding aggressive. / The character projects confidence and assertiveness even when she's privately uncertain.
column8: Project here = cause others to perceive a quality. Assertive ≠ aggressive: assertiveness is direct/self-assured expression while respecting others; aggression pushes or attacks.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: project confidence and assertiveness meaning
column12: entry::phrase usage::debate-friendly topic::communication topic::debate discovery::assertion discovery::boundary-setting discovery::impression discovery::debate_language

column5: Polaris is the star currently located close to the north celestial pole, commonly called the North Star or Pole Star; figuratively, a 'North Star' or 'guiding star' is a principle or goal that provides direction.
column6: North Star, Pole Star; guiding principle, lodestar
column7: Polaris appears nearly fixed in the northern sky and has long aided navigation. / Simplicity became the team's North Star when redesigning the app.
column8: Polaris is not the brightest star in the night sky. Figurative North Star is very common in strategy/product language. Lodestar is a literary/formal related metaphor.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: polaris north star guiding star

column5: Doing difficult, practical, frontline work directly rather than observing or managing from a distance; immersed in the demanding day-to-day reality of a field.
column6: on the front lines, doing the hands-on work, in the thick of it
column7: People in the trenches know which parts of the workflow actually waste time. / After years in the trenches as a teacher, she moved into policy.
column8: From military trench warfare. Common business/work metaphor; can sound dramatic when applied to trivial work, sometimes intentionally.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: in the trenches meaning

column5: To naturally inspire, earn, or compel respect because of one's ability, character, authority, presence, or achievements.
column6: earn respect, inspire respect, merit respect, carry authority
column7: She rarely raises her voice, but she commands respect the moment she enters the room. / Years of careful work made him a critic who commands respect even from people who disagree with him.
column8: Not 'order someone to respect you.' Command here means possess qualities that strongly elicit respect. 'Demand respect' can sound more assertive/explicit; 'earn respect' emphasizes gaining it over time.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: command respect meaning

column5: Extremely difficult, frustrating, or laborious because someone is reluctant to cooperate, speak, provide information, or do what is needed.
column6: an uphill struggle, painfully difficult, hard work, like getting blood from a stone (BrE/contextual)
column7: Getting him to tell me what happened was like pulling teeth. / Trying to get everyone to agree on a date was like pulling teeth.
column8: Especially common for extracting answers/cooperation from reluctant people. 'Getting blood from a stone' similarly emphasizes impossibility/reluctance, while uphill battle is broader sustained difficulty.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: pulling teeth synonym

column5: Lacking courage, determination, or strength of character.
column7: He was criticized as spineless for refusing to defend his own decision.
column8: Figurative insult based on the image of having no backbone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0116 | search: spineless

column5: Relating to grammatical inflection: changes in word form that express features such as tense, number, person, case, or comparison without creating a fundamentally new lexeme.
column7: The -ed in walked is an inflectional ending marking past tense.
column8: Contrast derivational morphology, which forms a new word/lexeme or changes word class more readily.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: define inflectional

column5: Ordinary civilian life, especially as contrasted with military service or another uniformed/service life.
column7: After twenty years in the army, adjusting to civvy street took some time.
column8: Chiefly British and informal. Often used in the pattern return/go back to civvy street.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: civvy street meaning

column5: To damage, distort, or ruin something badly; figuratively, to perform, pronounce, quote, or explain something very poorly.
column7: I completely mangled his name when I tried to pronounce it.
column8: Existing Master has mangled; keep the productive base verb because the figurative 'butcher/garble' use is independently useful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111 | search: mangle meaning

column5: To move outward or open while flapping, or to make something extend outward with a flapping motion; in some contexts a loose/nonstandard phrase whose exact sense comes from the physical action.
column6: spread/flap outward, flutter out, open out
column7: The loose fabric flapped out behind him in the wind. / She flapped the blanket out before laying it on the grass.
column8: Not a major fixed phrasal verb in everyday English. Interpret compositionally from flap + out unless the source gives a special slang meaning. Do not confuse with 'flip out' = lose emotional control.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: flap out meaning

column5: To remove the rough, extreme, distinctive, abrasive, or challenging qualities of something, making it smoother, safer, more conventional, or broadly palatable.
column6: smooth out, soften, tone down, round off, domesticate, sanitize
column7: The remake sands off the edges that made the original so strange and memorable. / Corporate messaging tends to sand off the rough edges of what people actually said.
column8: Literal image: sanding sharp/rough edges smooth. In criticism it can be negative: increased accessibility at the cost of personality, bite, specificity, or risk.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: sand off the edges meaning

column5: Near-equivalents include bar crawl, bar-hopping, pub-hopping, and pub tour, but nuance differs: crawl suggests an organized/multi-stop route; hopping emphasizes moving between venues; tour can sound more organized/touristic.
column6: bar crawl, bar-hopping, pub-hopping, pub tour
column7: We went bar-hopping downtown. / The hostel runs an organized pub crawl every Friday.
column8: Search-intent card. 'Bar crawl' is the closest AmE counterpart. 'Bar-hopping' is usually uncountable/activity wording rather than a named organized event.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: pub crawl synonym

column5: Literally, to attack with a nuclear weapon; figuratively, to destroy, delete, reset, or overwhelm something completely or drastically.
column7: I accidentally nuked the whole folder instead of deleting one file.
column8: Informal figurative use is common in tech/gaming: nuke a server, nuke an account, nuke a build.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: nuke meaning
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::figurative usage::military discovery::figurative_extension discovery::removal

column5: A vulgar internet initialism referring to a sexual act involving manual stimulation through or around clothing/pocket area; exact expansions and usage can vary across slang communities.
column7: The acronym appeared in an Urban Dictionary-style slang discussion, not in ordinary formal English. / If you encounter OTPHJ in a sexual context, treat it as explicit internet slang rather than a standard abbreviation.
column8: Highly niche, explicit slang with unstable crowd-sourced definitions. Preserve provenance/context rather than treating it as a standard lexical item; not appropriate for neutral/formal conversation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: Urban Dictionary: OTPHJ
