column5: Of that or of it; referring back to something already mentioned.
column6: of it, of that, from that (in some compounds)
column7: The agreement and any amendment thereof must be kept on file. / The report describes the policy and the consequences thereof. / Preparation—or the lack thereof—made the difference.
column8: Formal/legal/literary anaphoric word meaning 'of that/of it.' Rare in ordinary conversation except set phrases such as 'lack thereof.' Related legalistic forms include therein, thereto, hereby, whereof; avoid them when plain English is clearer.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: define thereof

column5: To break up or cause an organized group to cease operating or existing.
column7: The committee disbanded after completing its work.
column8: Common for bands, military units, committees, organizations, and groups.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: disband meaning

column5: To take possession or control of something for official/military use, often by authority; more loosely, to seize or appropriate something for one's own use without permission.
column7: The soldiers commandeered a truck to evacuate the area. / My friends commandeered the living room for their all-night movie marathon.
column8: Official/military sense can involve lawful requisition under authority. Informal humorous use exaggerates ordinary taking over: commandeer the couch, TV, meeting room, etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define commandeer

column5: Used to introduce a situation the speaker sees as strikingly ironic, contradictory, or unexpectedly fitting.
column6: talk about irony, here's the irony, ironic, isn't it?
column7: How's this for irony? The fire station had to be evacuated because of a fire. / I spent all week fixing my backup system, and then the backup drive died—how's that for irony?
column8: Productive pattern: How's this/that for X? = 'this/that is a remarkable example of X.' Existing irony card explains that irony is not merely any unfortunate coincidence.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: how's this for irony meaning

column5: Having or appealing to an excessive interest in sexual matters, especially in a lurid, scandalous, or gossip-oriented way.
column6: lurid, prurient, racy, lewd, titillating, scandalous
column7: The article focused on the most salacious details of the celebrity's private life. / The series sells itself as serious history, but the marketing leans heavily on salacious gossip.
column8: Salacious often describes stories/details/reporting, not simply anything sexual. Prurient emphasizes an unhealthy/voyeuristic sexual interest; lewd is more directly obscene/crude; racy is milder and can be playful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: SALACIOUS Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster

column5: A foolish, contemptible, or insignificant person; in action/gaming/media discussion, a generic low-level henchman or disposable enemy serving a more important villain.
column6: goon, henchman, minion, lackey, disposable enemy; idiot (contextual)
column7: The hero plows through a hallway full of mooks before reaching the boss. / Games often use weak mooks to teach you a new combat mechanic. / Calling a real person a mook is insulting and somewhat old-fashioned/slangy.
column8: Especially useful in TV Tropes/gaming/action-media vocabulary: unnamed rank-and-file enemies. Broader insult sense predates that specialized fandom use.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define mooks
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::dated usage::specialist usage::military usage::informal topic::media topic::games discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Both can refer to small representations of people/characters, but figurine strongly means a small statue/ornament, while figure is broader and is the standard hobby term in phrases such as action figure, scale figure, anime figure.
column7: I'd call a porcelain angel a figurine, but an articulated Spider-Man toy an action figure. / Anime collectors usually say 'figure' rather than 'figurine.'
column8: Figure has many unrelated senses (number, shape, person, body). Figurine is narrower. In collector communities, product-category conventions matter more than size alone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: figurine vs figure meaning
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase topic::anime topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::evaluation

column5: To deliberately lose a game or intentionally play badly so that one's team does not win, often for strategic, corrupt, gambling, or other reasons.
column6: deliberately lose, tank (overlapping), fix a match (related), take a dive (individual/contextual)
column7: The player was accused of taking money to throw the game. / Fans suspected the team had thrown the match, though there was no proof.
column8: Throw a game implies intentional loss. Tank can mean intentionally lose for strategic incentives (e.g. draft position) but also simply perform terribly. Match-fixing is broader manipulation of a contest/result.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: throw the game meaning in sports

column5: With the edge facing forward/sideways rather than the broad surface; chiefly encountered in the idiom 'get a word in edgewise/edgeways.'
column7: Turn the table edgewise and it might fit through the doorway. / In everyday speech, most people encounter edgewise in 'I couldn't get a word in edgewise.'
column8: Edgewise is common in AmE idiom; edgeways is common in BrE. Literal adverb exists but is much less frequent than the idiom.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define edgewise

column5: A literal prepositional phrase meaning 'by means of grunts' or 'by low-ranking workers/soldiers,' depending on context.
column6: through grunting sounds; by rank-and-file workers
column7: They communicated mostly by grunts and gestures.
column8: Not a fixed idiom. Keep because the search isolates how by combines with the plural noun grunts; existing grunt card supplies the noun senses.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: by grunts

column5: Literally, an illegal or unfair strike below the waist in combat sports; figuratively, an unfair, cruel, or unnecessarily personal attack, especially exploiting a vulnerability.
column6: cheap shot, unfair attack, below-the-belt remark, dirty hit
column7: Punching below the belt is a low blow. / Bringing up his divorce just to win the argument was a low blow. / I expected criticism, but attacking her family felt like a cheap shot.
column8: Figurative low blow and hit below the belt are close. Cheap shot can be any unfair/opportunistic attack. Low blow often emphasizes crossing a moral/personal line.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: low blow
column12: entry::idiom usage::figurative usage::rhetorical usage::military topic::military discovery::figurative_extension discovery::debate_language

column5: A playful way to say that something contains only useful, substantive content and no filler, padding, or unnecessary extras.
column6: no filler, straight to the point, all substance
column7: The guide promises no fluff, just stuff you can actually use.
column8: Fluff = nonessential filler; stuff provides the rhyme and means the actual material/content. Not a fixed universal idiom, but readily understandable wordplay.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: no fluff just stuff meaning

column5: Humility is modesty and freedom from excessive pride; humiliation is the painful experience/state of being made to feel ashamed, degraded, or foolish.
column7: Humility helped him admit he was wrong; public humiliation would have been something entirely different. / Choosing humility is not the same as accepting humiliation.
column8: Crucial lexical distinction despite shared humil- root. Humility can be voluntary/positive; humiliation is typically imposed or experienced as degrading.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: humility vs humiliation

column5: To turn out differently from what people expected, often in a surprising or impressive way.
column7: The sequel defied expectations and became the strongest film in the series.
column8: Can be positive or negative; it simply means the expected pattern/prediction did not hold.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: defy your expectations meaning

column5: Possessing supreme or independent authority; as a noun, a monarch or other supreme ruler.
column7: The country is a sovereign state with authority over its own laws.
column8: Related existing sovereignty = the state/right of having sovereign authority.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: define sovereign

column5: A drawn-out set of polite formulas, social niceties, formalities, or conversational steps that feel obligatory before getting to the real point.
column6: social formalities, polite dance, ritual niceties, ceremony
column7: After the usual polite rigmarole about the weather and the journey, they finally started discussing the contract. / Sometimes I'd rather skip the polite rigmarole and just ask what someone actually means.
column8: Not a fixed idiom, but a natural creative combination. Rigmarole adds mild impatience: the politeness is experienced as elaborate procedure rather than meaningful content.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: polite rigmarole meaning

column5: As a verb, to recoil or feel embarrassed/discomforted. In modern slang, adjective/noun uses describe something painfully embarrassing, awkward, try-hard, or socially embarrassing.
column6: wince, recoil; cringeworthy, embarrassing, awkward, try-hard
column7: I cringed when I heard my old recording. / That dialogue is kind of cringe, but I still love the show. / People sometimes call any open enthusiasm 'cringe' just because it isn't detached or ironic.
column8: Traditional verb predates slang. 'Cringe' as adjective ('that's cringe') is common internet/youth usage. Existing cringe-worthy card overlaps, but standalone cringe has broader modern grammar and cultural use.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: being cringe meaning

column5: Literally in the drainage channel along a street/roof; figuratively, in a degraded, disreputable, vulgar, or very low condition. 'Mind in the gutter' specifically means interpreting things sexually.
column6: down-and-out, degraded; dirty-minded (mind in the gutter)
column7: The ball rolled into the gutter. / His reputation was already in the gutter after the scandal. / Get your mind out of the gutter—I wasn't talking about sex.
column8: Multiple idioms: reputation/economy 'in the gutter' = very low; 'mind in the gutter' = sexual/vulgar interpretation; bowling gutter is another literal sense. Context matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: in the gutter

column5: To be interpreted or mistaken as a sign of weakness, lack of resolve, or inability to resist.
column6: be mistaken for weakness, be seen as weakness, be read as weakness
column7: His patience shouldn't be taken for weakness. / She worried that apologizing too quickly would be taken for weakness rather than maturity.
column8: Common pattern: 'Don't mistake my kindness/silence/patience for weakness.' Passive 'be taken for weakness' is natural but somewhat formal. Take X for Y = mistake/interpret X as Y.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: be taken for weakness meaning

column5: Lubber: a clumsy, awkward, or inexperienced person, especially at sea. Landlubber: someone unfamiliar with ships/seafaring, stereotypically a landsman among sailors.
column6: landlubber, clumsy sailor, novice, awkward person
column7: The pirate captain sneered at the new deckhand as a useless landlubber. / 'Lubber' by itself sounds archaic or deliberately nautical today.
column8: Strong pirate/nautical flavor in modern media. Historically lubber was a broader insult for a big clumsy/lazy fellow. 'Landlubber' remains recognizable largely through pirate fiction and jokes.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: lubbers

column5: A crude insult for a person perceived as fat; sometimes used adjectivally or jokingly/intensifying in compounds.
column6: fatso, lard-ass (insulting), overweight person (neutral description, not synonym in tone)
column7: The character calls him a 'lazy fat-ass' during the argument. / Among close friends it may be used jokingly, but from a stranger it can be openly hostile.
column8: Strongly insulting/body-shaming in many contexts. Spelling varies fat-ass/fatass. Do not use it as a neutral term for someone's body size.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: fatasses
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::vulgar usage::rhetorical topic::communication discovery::perception discovery::escalation discovery::debate_language

column5: An official or serious expression of disapproval for misconduct, especially from someone in authority; to give such a warning/censure.
column7: The employee received a formal reprimand for violating the policy. / The coach reprimanded the players for ignoring the safety rule.
column8: Often institutional/workplace/military/school context and can be formally recorded. More official than scold; rebuke can be sharp without being an administrative sanction.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define reprimand
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::professional usage::bureaucratic usage::military discovery::warning discovery::professional_context

column5: To have a very beneficial, impressive, or restorative effect on someone or something.
column6: work wonders for, greatly improve, be excellent for
column7: A short walk can do wonders for my concentration. / Better lighting did wonders for the room.
column8: Very natural with health, mood, appearance, performance, confidence, etc. 'Do wonders' and 'work wonders' are near-equivalents.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: doing wonders for meaning

column5: A suffix forming nouns that express a state, condition, quality, or extent, as in attitude, aptitude, latitude, magnitude, solitude.
column7: Latitude and magnitude both end in -tude, but modern speakers usually learn the whole words rather than actively deriving them from *-tude.
column8: From Latin -tūdō via French/Latin formations. Not normally a free English word 'titude.' 'Attitude' is not synchronically 'at + titude.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: titude meaning

column5: Preparing or influencing a system/person so that a later response is easier or more likely; meanings occur in psychology, learning, pumps/engines, painting, and other fields.
column7: Seeing one word can sometimes prime recognition of a related word. / The opening scene primes the audience to expect a tragedy. / The wall needs priming before painting.
column8: Psychology: prior exposure can influence later processing. Popular claims about behavioral priming can be broader/stronger than evidence supports; context matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118, voca_0120 | search: priming meaning

column5: Ready to accept something without protest or resistance, often reluctantly or passively.
column7: His acquiescent response suggested that he disagreed but would not fight the decision.
column8: From acquiesce. Often implies passive acceptance rather than enthusiastic agreement.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: define acquiescent

column5: A shortage, lack, or inadequacy of something needed; also a weakness or defect.
column7: Iron deficiency can cause fatigue.
column8: Common in medicine/nutrition, systems, skills, and formal evaluation: nutrient deficiency, deficiency in knowledge, design deficiency.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: define deficiency

column5: A cruel, violent, stupid, or physically forceful person or animal; as an adjective, based on raw physical force rather than skill, subtlety, or reasoning.
column6: thug, beast, bully, savage (often problematic), brute-force
column7: The villain is portrayed as a huge brute who solves every problem with violence. / We used brute force rather than a clever algorithm. / 'Brute strength' means raw physical power.
column8: As a noun, insulting/dehumanizing. Productive compounds: brute force, brute strength, brute fact. Existing 'brute force' card covers the computing phrase; this card supplies the underlying broader word.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define brute

column5: Departing from accepted norms or standards; as a noun, a person characterized as behaving outside such norms.
column7: The study examined behavior the community considered deviant.
column8: Can be neutral/technical in sociology or strongly judgmental/insulting when labeling a person.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: deviant meaning

column5: The same thing is true of me / I am in the same situation or have the same reaction, preference, problem, etc.
column6: same here, me too, likewise for me
column7: 'I can't concentrate when I'm hungry.' 'Same with me.' / 'I loved the first season but dropped the second.' 'Same with me.'
column8: Grammatical and understandable, but 'same here' or 'me too' is often more idiomatic in short replies. 'Same with me' is useful when explicitly mapping a previously stated fact onto oneself.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: same with me meaning

column5: To chat and socialize, especially in a friendly, flattering, or strategic way to build connections, network, or gain advantage.
column6: network, mingle, chat up, hobnob, butter up (stronger)
column7: He spent the reception schmoozing with producers and journalists. / I hate events where you're expected to schmooze for two hours.
column8: From Yiddish. Can be neutral ('socialize/network') or mildly cynical, implying calculated charm. 'Schmooze with someone'; 'schmooze one's way into...'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: schmooze meaning

column5: A quick, light kiss on someone's cheek, usually affectionate, friendly, familial, or mildly romantic depending on culture and relationship.
column6: quick kiss, light kiss, kiss on the cheek
column7: She gave him a quick peck on the cheek before leaving. / In some cultures, cheek kisses are routine greetings and carry little romantic meaning.
column8: Peck emphasizes brevity/light contact. A cheek kiss can be romantic, familial, friendly, or conventional greeting behavior; context matters. 'Peck' also literally means a bird striking with its beak.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: peck on the cheek meaning

column5: To wave or swing the arms, legs, or an object wildly and uncontrollably; figuratively, to struggle ineffectively or chaotically. As a noun, a traditional threshing tool/weapon-like implement with a swinging part.
column7: He slipped on the ice and flailed his arms trying to stay upright. / The company spent months flailing without a clear strategy. / The monster's tentacles flailed in every direction.
column8: Physical flailing is uncontrolled swinging. Figurative flail = struggle without effective direction, close to flounder. Distinct from fail despite similar spelling.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: flail verb meaning

column5: A dismissive way to tell someone to go away or leave you alone.
column6: get lost, beat it, go away, scram, buzz off
column7: If you're only here to complain, take a hike. / He told the salesman to take a hike after the third pushy call. / We literally took a hike through the hills the next morning.
column8: Dismissive idiom = 'go away / leave me alone,' often rude but milder/playful in some contexts. The same words also have the fully literal meaning 'go hiking,' so context and tone matter.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: take a hike

column2: one's opinion counts for about the weight of a feather
column3: /wʌnz əˈpɪnjən kaʊnts fər əˌbaʊt ðə ˌweɪt əv ə ˈfeðər/
column5: A humorous/nonstandard way to say someone's opinion has almost no influence or importance in a discussion.
column6: count for very little, carry little weight, matter hardly at all
column7: In this argument, his opinion counts for about the weight of a feather.
column8: Understandable wordplay, but English normally says an opinion 'carries weight,' not literally 'counts for the weight of.' Preserve as a creative source/search sentence and contrast with the idiomatic version.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: In this argument, his opinion counts for about the weight of a feather.
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::humorous usage::figurative usage::rhetorical discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::debate_language

column5: A state of severe disorder or disturbance; historically/colloquially, mental disturbance or irrationality.
column7: The essay describes the character's growing emotional derangement.
column8: Can sound clinical or stigmatizing when applied to mental health; often appears rhetorically in phrases like 'X derangement syndrome.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: derangement

column5: Bona fide before a noun means genuine, real, or unquestionably qualifying as that thing; with an insult such as 'bona fide asshole,' it emphatically means a genuine/undeniable one.
column7: He wasn't just being rude; he was acting like a bona fide asshole. / What started as a hobby turned into a bona fide business. / She's a bona fide expert, not just someone with a big following.
column8: Existing bona fide WID5770 covers the dictionary meaning; preserve this contextual card because the search tests how it behaves before a strongly evaluative noun. It can intensify positive, neutral, or negative labels.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: bona fide asshole meaning

column5: Very common, easy to find, and therefore not especially valuable, special, or impressive.
column6: commonplace, ubiquitous, ten a penny (BrE), nothing special
column7: Generic isekai premises are a dime a dozen; execution is what makes one memorable. / Cafés like that are a dime a dozen downtown.
column8: Literally 'twelve for ten cents' → cheap because abundant. Often mildly dismissive. BrE counterpart 'ten a penny.' Contrast one-of-a-kind = unique.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: Dime a dozen:

column5: A person who repeatedly engages in crime over a long period and treats criminal activity as an ongoing way of life rather than an isolated offense.
column6: habitual offender, repeat offender, professional criminal
column7: Police described him as a career criminal with a long record of burglaries. / The phrase implies a sustained pattern of offending, not merely someone who committed one serious crime.
column8: Repeat offender is more legal/neutral and simply means repeated offending; professional criminal can imply skill/occupation; career criminal is strongly evaluative and may appear in policing/media rhetoric.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: career criminal meanig
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::evaluative usage::professional usage::rhetorical topic::work topic::crime discovery::professional_context discovery::iteration discovery::continuity discovery::debate_language

column5: To combine disapproving tutting with prolonged chatter or complaining; a context-built phrase rather than a fixed idiom.
column6: tsk and complain, grumble and chatter, tut and ramble
column7: They sat in the corner tutting and yapping about how everything used to be better. / The phrase paints a comic picture: little noises of disapproval plus nonstop talk.
column8: Not a standard lexicalized expression. Tut = click of disapproval; yap = talk noisily/at length, often dismissively. Existing yapping/yapper cards cover modern yap slang.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: tut and yap meaning

column5: Adjective: very loyal, committed, firm, or strong in support/opposition. Verb: to stop or check the flow of blood or another liquid.
column6: steadfast, loyal, committed, unwavering; stem, stop
column7: She's a staunch defender of free expression. / They tried to staunch the bleeding with pressure.
column8: Adjective is common: staunch supporter/ally/opponent. Verb may also be spelled stanch, especially AmE; both forms occur. Existing 'staunchly' is the adverb.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: staunch definition

column5: A response meaning 'what you just said is very true, important, or says a great deal,' often agreeing emphatically with a concise observation.
column6: exactly, you can say that again, that's for sure, well said
column7: 'Working from home saves commuting time, but it can blur every boundary.' 'You said a mouthful.'
column8: Idiomatic mouthful here = a statement containing a lot of truth/meaning, not literally many words. Somewhat old-fashioned but still recognizable. Different from 'give someone a mouthful.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: you said a mouthful meaning

column5: Filled with a powerful feeling of awe, wonder, admiration, or reverence.
column7: We stood awestruck beneath the enormous night sky.
column8: Awe can combine admiration with fear or overwhelming grandeur; awestruck is stronger than merely impressed.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: awestruck meaning

column5: A proposed term for a period in which human activity has become a dominant influence on Earth's climate, ecosystems, geology, and environment.
column7: Plastic pollution and fossil-fuel emissions are often discussed as signatures of the Anthropocene. / The novel imagines what ruins our civilization might leave behind for observers deep in the future.
column8: Widely used in science/humanities, but as of the mid-2020s it was not formally ratified as an official geological epoch by the relevant stratigraphic bodies. Capitalization is common. The proposed start date has been debated.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: anthropocene meaning
column12: entry::proper_noun entry::term usage::informal topic::culture topic::environment discovery::terminology

column5: Not giving way under pressure; firm, rigid, stubborn, relentless, or physically resistant to bending/movement.
column7: She remained unyielding in her refusal to apologize. / The material felt hard and unyielding. / They faced unyielding pressure for months.
column8: Can be positive (steadfast) or negative (inflexible). Literal physical resistance and figurative attitude/conditions.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: unyielding meaning

column5: Stop being so self-important, self-absorbed, dramatic, offended, or preoccupied with your own feelings/image; gain perspective.
column6: stop taking yourself so seriously, lose the ego, get a grip (overlapping)
column7: You made one small mistake—get over yourself and move on. / He acts like everyone is watching him; someone needs to tell him to get over himself.
column8: Usually dismissive and potentially rude. Not the same as 'get over something' = recover from an event/illness/relationship.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: get over yourself meaning

column5: To make a final choice or decision after considering different possibilities.
column7: After comparing several designs, we settled on the simplest one.
column8: Search was 'settled on meaning'; normalize to the base form settle on.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: settled on meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::decision-making discovery::possibility discovery::resolution

column5: Reluctantly and with resentment or unwillingness, even though one does or admits something.
column7: He begrudgingly admitted that her idea had worked.
column8: Often implies giving credit, agreement, help, or compliance while not being happy about it.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: begrudgingly

column5: To do something in a new, unconventional, or distinctive way rather than following an established pattern.
column7: The director broke the mold with a quiet, character-driven superhero film.
column8: Also BrE spelling break the mould. Existing synonym mention does not replace the idiom card.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: break the mold meaning

column5: The state or quality of being unlike or different.
column7: The dissimilarity between the two versions becomes obvious when you compare the endings.
column8: Opposite of similarity; more formal and less common than difference.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: define dissimilarity

column7: The movie starts like a thriller and then becomes increasingly arthouse-y and abstract. / I like slow arthouse films, but this one felt self-consciously obscure.
column8: Also art-house. 'Arthouse-y' can be neutral, admiring, or mildly dismissive ('trying hard to seem artistic'). Not synonymous with simply low-budget or foreign-language.

column8: Existing nifty card covers the adjective; preserve the searched collocation because it captures the common evaluative use in reviews.

column5: To understand or realize something, often gradually; also, for an idea, fashion, product, or practice to become popular.
column6: get it, figure it out, cotton on (BrE); become popular, take off, gain traction
column7: It took me a few episodes to catch on to what the show was doing. / Don't explain the joke—he'll catch on. / The trend caught on surprisingly quickly.
column8: Two core senses: person catches on = understands; thing catches on = becomes popular. 'Catch on to X' = realize/understand X. Related but different catch someone on = physically catch, etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114, voca_0115 | search: catch on

column5: Characterized by playful teasing, joking back-and-forth, or banter.
column7: Their conversation was light and bantery rather than serious.
column8: Informal derivative of banter; less standard/common than 'full of banter' or 'bantering.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: bantery meaning

column5: The place, point, system, factor, or conceptual center where a problem is located or concentrated—the part regarded as its main site/source.
column6: center of the problem, site, focal point, source
column7: The UI isn't the real locus of the problem; the underlying data model is. / Researchers debated whether the locus of the difficulty was perception or memory.
column8: Locus is formal/technical Latin-derived noun meaning place/site. Plural loci /ˈloʊsaɪ/ or /ˈloʊkiː/ depending convention.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: locus of the problem meaning

column5: Clearly different or separate from something else; clearly recognizable or noticeable; definite/unmistakable.
column6: different, separate, discrete, distinctive, unmistakable, clear
column7: These are two distinct meanings of the same word. / I heard a distinct click from the other room. / The character has a distinct speaking style.
column8: Distinct = separate/clearly different; distinctive = characteristic in a way that makes something stand out. 'A distinct possibility' = real/definite possibility.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: distinct

column5: As a noun, a building where horses or other livestock are kept; also a group of horses or, figuratively, a group of people under one management. As an adjective, steady and unlikely to change/fail. As a verb, to house a horse.
column7: The horses were brought back to the stable before dark. / Prices have remained relatively stable. / The agency has a stable of well-known actors and directors.
column8: This card broadens beyond existing emotional-stability uses. Figurative noun 'a stable of writers/talent' = group managed/associated together. Do not confuse stable adjective with static: stable can still change gradually.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: stable

column5: A genus of large herbivorous ceratopsian dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of North America, famous for three facial horns and a large bony frill.
column7: Triceratops lived alongside Tyrannosaurus near the end of the Cretaceous. / The skull's three horns make Triceratops one of the easiest dinosaurs to recognize.
column8: Name means roughly 'three-horned face.' Technically a genus, but everyday English often treats Triceratops as the animal name. It was not from the Jurassic despite common dinosaur mashups.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: triceratops meaning

column5: Trying to maximize one's physical attractiveness through grooming, fitness, fashion, skincare, cosmetic procedures, or other appearance-focused practices.
column7: He started looksmaxxing by changing his haircut, clothes, and workout routine.
column8: Internet slang associated especially with male appearance-rating communities. Spelling varies: looksmaxing / looksmaxxing. Can range from ordinary grooming advice to obsessive or toxic appearance discourse.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: looks maxxxing meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word entry::discourse_expression usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::informal topic::internet topic::wellness topic::fashion

column5: Completely firm and unwilling to change one's decision, opinion, or demand; strongly insistent.
column7: She was adamant that she would pay her own share. / He remained adamant about keeping the original ending even after everyone objected. / I'm not sure why, but she was absolutely adamant.
column8: Common patterns: be adamant that + clause; be adamant about X. Stronger than 'sure' or 'firm': it highlights refusal to be persuaded. Historically adamant was also a legendary extremely hard substance.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: adamant
column12: entry::word usage::persuasive topic::decision-making discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::determination discovery::persuasion

column5: Psych! is a teasing reveal meaning 'just kidding / fooled you.' To psych someone out means to intimidate, unsettle, or manipulate them mentally so they lose confidence or composure.
column6: just kidding, gotcha; intimidate, rattle, mess with someone's head
column7: I told him the tickets were sold out—psych! I already bought them. / Don't let the other team psych you out before the match even starts.
column8: Interjection is commonly spelled psych! (sometimes psyche! informally, though psych reflects the slang). 'Psych oneself up' is different: mentally prepare/excite oneself. 'Psych out' = unsettle/deceive psychologically.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: psych meaning slang
column12: entry::interjection entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::slang usage::informal

column5: Normal operations or behavior continuing despite disruption, controversy, change, or unusual circumstances; sometimes used critically to imply nothing meaningful has changed.
column6: normal operations, same old routine, back to normal, status quo
column7: The storm passed, and by Monday it was business as usual. / After a brief apology, the company went straight back to business as usual.
column8: Can be reassuring ('operations continue normally') or critical ('nothing changed despite the problem'). Often used without article: It's business as usual.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: just business as usual meaning

column5: Holding, containing, or carrying a particular emotional force, mood, attitude, or potential. Understandable metaphorically, though 'harbor' more naturally collocates with feelings/thoughts such as resentment, suspicion, or hope.
column6: carrying the energy, holding that energy, harboring a feeling
column7: The scene feels like it's harboring this nervous energy beneath the surface. / More idiomatically: she was carrying a lot of anxious energy.
column8: Preserve search, but flag collocation. 'Harbor resentment/suspicion/feelings' is conventional; 'harbor energy' is creative/metaphorical rather than a fixed collocation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: harboring the energy meaning

column5: To put all of one's effort, energy, or determination into an attempt.
column6: do one's best, give 100 percent, go all out
column7: We didn't win, but everyone gave it their all.
column8: Raw search 'give it all' normalized to the usual idiom give it one's all / give it your all.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: give it all meaning

column5: Lacking diversity or variety; composed of people, things, or perspectives that are relatively homogeneous.
column7: The panel was criticized for being unusually undiverse. / The recommendations felt undiverse—almost everything came from the same genre and era.
column8: Understandable and used, but 'not very diverse,' 'lacking diversity,' or 'homogeneous' may sound more natural depending on context. For people/groups, diverse refers to representation/variety, not an inherent moral quality of individuals.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: undiverse

column5: Beyond literal animal flesh/food, 'meat' can slangily refer to a person's body or flesh, genitals (especially penis), a muscular person/body, or the substantial/core part of something ('the meat of the argument').
column6: body/flesh; penis (vulgar); substance, core, main part
column7: The discussion used 'meat' as crude sexual slang, not as food vocabulary. / Let's get to the meat of the argument. / Gaming and internet communities also create highly local 'meat' jokes, so the surrounding sentence matters.
column8: Urban Dictionary-style searches are especially context-sensitive. Do not assume the sexual sense whenever 'meat' appears. Common standard figurative sense: the meat of X = the most substantial/important part.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: Urban Dictionary: meat
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::figurative usage::vulgar usage::rhetorical usage::informal topic::food topic::animals discovery::debate_language

column5: A stiff fabric or structured underskirt/hooped framework used to hold a skirt out from the body, especially associated with 19th-century fashion.
column7: The costume department built a crinoline to give the Victorian dress its enormous bell shape. / Walking through a narrow doorway in a full crinoline would have required some care.
column8: Historically crinoline first referred to stiff fabric, then especially the cage crinoline/hooped underskirt. Useful in period fashion, costume design, historical fiction, and visual analysis.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: crinoline

column5: A style of handwriting in which letters are often joined in flowing strokes; Japanese 筆記体 is commonly translated as cursive or cursive handwriting.
column7: I learned cursive in elementary school but rarely use it now. / Can you read her cursive handwriting?
column8: Cursive is broader than one specific school alphabet style. 'Script' can also mean handwriting/typeface and is more ambiguous.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: 筆記体 英語で

column5: To have more important, urgent, or worthwhile matters to deal with than the one currently being discussed.
column6: have more important things to do, have higher priorities, have bigger problems
column7: I'm not going to argue about one typo—we've got bigger fish to fry. / The detective ignored the petty dispute because she had much bigger fish to fry.
column8: Often dismisses a smaller issue in favor of priorities. Can sound slightly brusque. Also 'other fish to fry' = other matters to attend to, without necessarily ranking them as bigger.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: bigger fish to fry meaning

column5: Agree with a person/opinion = share or accept that person's view; agree on something = two or more parties reach/share the same decision, plan, terms, or point.
column6: share someone's view vs reach agreement about
column7: I agree with you about the ending. / We agreed on a date for the meeting. / They agree on most issues but disagree on how to solve this one.
column8: Also agree to a proposal/request/terms; agree that + clause; agree to do something. 'I agree on you' is generally wrong when meaning 'I share your opinion.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: agree with vs on

column5: Humble is primarily an adjective describing a person, attitude, origin, or thing as modest/not self-important; humility is the noun for the quality or state of being humble.
column7: She remained humble despite her success. / Her humility made it easy for her to admit mistakes.
column8: Also humble as verb = make someone less proud / lower in status. 'Humbleness' exists but humility is the standard abstract noun in most contexts.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: humility vs humble
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::origin_etymology discovery::evaluation

column5: Apologetic = showing regret, remorse, or awareness that one has caused inconvenience/offense. Agreeable = pleasant, willing to agree/cooperate, or acceptable/pleasing. They can coexist but describe different things.
column7: He sounded apologetic about being late. / She was agreeable and happy to change the meeting time. / Someone can be apologetic but not agreeable: 'I'm sorry, but I still won't do it.'
column8: Apologetic concerns regret; agreeable concerns pleasantness or willingness. 'Accommodating' is closer to cooperative; 'contrite' is stronger remorse. Do not infer apology merely from a soft/agreeable tone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: apologetic vs agreeable

column5: A grammatical structure in which a constituent can contain another constituent of the same type or a rule can apply repeatedly, enabling potentially unbounded embedding.
column7: The phrase 'the book [on the table [in the room]]' illustrates repeated embedding. / Clauses can be embedded inside clauses: 'I think [she said [he left]].'
column8: Recursion is a major concept in syntax, though theoretical claims about its universality and role in human language are debated. Distinguish recursion from simple iteration.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: recursive structure linguistics

column5: To tell someone private, secret, or previously unknown information or allow them to participate in a plan.
column6: confide in, reveal to, clue in, include, bring into the loop
column7: I'll let you in on a little secret. / They finally let me in on the plan after the details were settled. / Can you let me in on what everyone is laughing about?
column8: Two related ideas: reveal information/secret to someone, or allow someone to participate/share insider knowledge. Pattern: let + person + in on + noun/pronoun. 'Clue someone in' is close and informal.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: let you in on it meaning

column5: Statistical characteristics of a population or audience, such as age, sex/gender categories, income, education, location, occupation, etc.; also population groups defined by such characteristics.
column6: population characteristics, audience segments, population profile
column7: The app is popular across several age demographics. / We need speakers from different demographic backgrounds, not just different accents.
column8: Often plural 'demographics' for data/profile; singular demographic can mean a population segment ('a younger demographic'). Avoid treating personality or speaking style themselves as demographics.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: demographics

column5: To push the lips forward, often to show displeasure, disappointment, or playful sulking; more broadly, to sulk visibly. As a noun, the protruding-lips expression.
column6: sulk, mope, make a face; pursed/protruding lips
column7: She pouted when they said dessert was finished. / He was clearly disappointed, but instead of arguing he just sat there pouting. / She did an exaggerated pout for the photo.
column8: Can be genuinely childish/sullen or deliberately cute/playful, especially in photos. Sulk emphasizes withdrawn bad mood; pout highlights visible facial/lip expression.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: pout

column5: A long, complicated, tedious, or unnecessary procedure; also a lengthy, rambling story or explanation.
column6: fuss, palaver, hassle, song and dance, bureaucratic runaround
column7: I just wanted to change my address, but it turned into a whole rigmarole. / We had to go through the usual airport-security rigmarole.
column8: Often 'go through the whole/usual rigmarole.' BrE also pronounces it roughly /ˈrɪɡmərəʊl/. Usually conveys annoyance at unnecessary steps.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: rigmarole

column5: I'm extremely surprised, stunned, impressed, shocked, or emotionally overwhelmed.
column6: I'm stunned, blown away, gobsmacked, amazed
column7: I'm totally floored by how good the finale was. / When she told me the actual price, I was floored.
column8: Floor as a verb can mean knock someone down physically; figuratively, information/events 'floor' you by overwhelming your expectations or composure.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118, voca_0120 | search: i'm totally floored meaning

column5: To exploit an opportunity, trend, reputation, event, or situation in order to make money or gain some other advantage.
column6: capitalize on, profit from, exploit, monetize, take advantage of
column7: Studios rushed to cash in on the sudden popularity of the genre. / The brand cashed in on nostalgia with a deliberately retro campaign. / He tried to cash in on his brief viral fame.
column8: Often mildly critical because it suggests opportunism, though it can be neutral business language. Distinguish cash in X = exchange chips/coupons/investment for money; cash in on X = profit from an opportunity.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: cash in on

column5: To make something unclear, confusing, difficult to understand, or harder to discover, whether deliberately or as an effect; in computing, to transform code/data to make it harder for humans to interpret.
column7: The jargon obfuscates a fairly simple idea. / The company was accused of obfuscating the true cost. / Developers may obfuscate code to make reverse engineering harder.
column8: Often implies deliberate concealment but not always. Noun: obfuscation. Stronger/more formal than confuse.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: obfuscate meaning

column5: Near-death experience: a vivid subjective experience reported by some people who are close to death or believe they are, sometimes involving sensations such as leaving the body, moving through a tunnel, intense light, peace, or life review.
column7: The memoir describes an NDE after a medical emergency. / Researchers study near-death experiences without assuming that every reported feature occurs in every case.
column8: Raw 'nde' is highly ambiguous, but near-death experience is a common expansion in general discourse. Reports vary widely; interpretations can be neurological, psychological, spiritual, religious, or mixed. The term itself describes the reported experience, not its cause.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: nde meaning
column12: entry::initialism entry::word entry::discourse_expression usage::religious discovery::subjective_judgment discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: Weapons collectively, especially the range, stock, or systems of weapons used by a military, group, character, vehicle, etc.
column7: The documentary examines medieval weaponry. / The mech's weaponry is visually impressive but wildly impractical.
column8: Usually uncountable collective noun: 'advanced weaponry,' not normally 'a weaponry.' Broader/formal compared with weapons.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: weaponry

column5: On the condition that; if and only if the stated requirement is met.
column6: provided that, as long as, assuming that
column7: You can borrow the car, provided you bring it back by ten.
column8: Distinct from provided as the past participle of provide. As a conjunction, provided (that) introduces a condition.

column5: A state of profound unease, dissatisfaction, or distress. In 'gender dysphoria,' distress related to incongruence between experienced gender and assigned sex/sex characteristics, as defined clinically.
column6: distress, unease, dissatisfaction; gender dysphoria (specific term)
column7: The medication can sometimes cause anxiety or dysphoria. / Gender dysphoria refers to distress, not simply to being transgender; not every transgender person experiences it.
column8: Opposite-root concept euphoria = intense well-being. Dysphoria can occur in multiple clinical contexts. Do not use 'dysphoric' as a casual synonym for merely sad without context.

column5: In court, to question a witness called by the opposing side; figuratively, to question someone intensely and skeptically as if testing their story.
column6: question, interrogate, grill; challenge a witness
column7: The defense attorney cross-examined the witness about the timeline. / I only asked where he'd been—there was no need to cross-examine him for twenty minutes.
column8: Legal sense is specific: cross-examination follows/directly challenges testimony, usually by the opposing party. Figurative use can sound humorous: aggressive detailed questioning. Grill is less legally specific.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: cross-examine meaning

column5: Because there is a small or unlikely possibility that something may happen or be true; just in case, despite low odds.
column6: just in case, on the slight chance, in case
column7: I brought an umbrella on the off chance it rained. / I messaged him on the off chance he was still awake.
column8: Often followed by that-clause or used before an action taken as a precaution. 'Off chance' = remote possibility.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: on the off chance meaning

column5: To have extremely little importance, authority, persuasive force, or influence; a playful extension of 'carry weight.'
column6: carry little/no weight, count for little, have little influence
column7: In this argument, his opinion carries about as much weight as a feather. / Without evidence, that claim carries very little weight.
column8: 'Carry weight' is established: have influence/credibility. Adding 'as a feather' is creative humor, exploiting literal vs figurative weight.

column5: A wooden framework/grill used in the Caribbean for smoking or drying meat; by extension associated with the hunters called boucaniers, from whom English 'buccaneer' developed.
column7: Hunters smoked meat over a boucan before the term boucanier became associated with the Caribbean raiders later called buccaneers. / The word gives a useful etymological bridge from smoked meat to 'buccaneer.'
column8: Historical French/Caribbean term with Indigenous Caribbean roots often traced through French. Valuable mainly for understanding buccaneer etymology rather than modern everyday use.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: boucans

column5: To be enough or adequate for a particular purpose or need.
column7: A short explanation will suffice for now. / One example should suffice to show the difference. / If all you need is a quick backup, the free version may suffice.
column8: Often somewhat formal. Patterns: X will suffice; suffice for X; suffice to do X. Existing card 'suffice it to say / suffice to say' is a fixed discourse construction derived from this verb.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: suffice meaning

column5: To throw something casually or forcefully; to discard/get rid of something; in BrE/AusE, also to quit/leave or sometimes vomit in slang. As a noun, a chuck is also a clamping device on a drill.
column6: toss, throw, fling; ditch, dump, throw away
column7: Just chuck the keys over here. / I finally chucked all the cables I hadn't used in ten years. / He chucked the job and went traveling.
column8: Very informal and especially common in BrE for throw/discard. 'Chuck it!' can mean stop it/give it up. Do not confuse with chuckle. Mechanical drill chuck is a separate noun sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: chuck meaning

column5: Done as a final desperate attempt after other options have failed or are nearly exhausted.
column7: They made a last-ditch effort to save the project. / The medication was a last-ditch option after other treatments failed.
column8: Raw 'with last ditched' repaired. Usually before noun: last-ditch effort/attempt/measure. Related 'last resort.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: with last ditched meaning

column5: Columbina (also Columbine) is a witty female servant/maid stock character in commedia dell'arte, often clever, lively, and involved in romantic intrigue. 'Columbine-y' is a playful nonce adjective meaning reminiscent of that character/style.
column7: Her costume has a very Columbina-like, commedia feel. / Calling the performance 'Columbine-y' would be an improvised way to say it evokes the playful maid character.
column8: Raw 'columbiney' is not a standard dictionary adjective. Preserve the search intent by anchoring it to Columbina/Columbine. Do not confuse with Columbine High School or the columbine flower when context is theatre.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: columbiney meaning

column5: A sudden or brief entry into another territory or area, especially a hostile military entry; figuratively, an unwanted intrusion into a domain or activity.
column7: The army reported a cross-border incursion overnight. / The company viewed the startup's move into its market as an unwelcome incursion.
column8: Usually smaller/shorter than a full invasion and often military/political. 'Foray' can be exploratory and non-hostile; incursion normally implies intrusion or violation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define incursion

column5: A characteristic gimmick, routine, comic persona, recurring bit, style, or behavior associated with a performer/person; sometimes an annoying habitual act.
column7: His whole shtick is pretending to be painfully cringe on purpose. / The fake arrogance is part of her online schtick, not necessarily how she acts off camera.
column8: Raw 'being shtik for cringe' appears malformed; likely the key word is shtick/schtick. From Yiddish. 'That's his shtick' = that's his characteristic routine/gimmick.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: what does being shtik for cringe mean

column5: Historically, a New Yorker descended from early Dutch settlers; more broadly an old New York cultural label. 'Knickerbockers/knickers' also refers to loose knee-length trousers. The New York Knicks name derives from Knickerbockers.
column6: old New Yorker; knee breeches / knickerbockers
column7: The word Knickerbocker became strongly associated with old New York and its Dutch heritage. / Vintage illustrations often show boys wearing knickerbockers fastened below the knee.
column8: Multiple cultural senses. Washington Irving's fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker helped popularize the New York association. British 'knickers' now usually means women's underwear, so do not equate the modern words blindly.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: define knickerbocker

column5: Exercise designed to improve cardiovascular fitness through sustained rhythmic movement that raises heart rate and breathing, especially group routines performed to music.
column7: My mother used to do aerobics videos in the living room in the 1980s. / The gym offers dance aerobics as well as strength classes.
column8: Grammatically usually treated as singular as a field/activity: aerobics is good exercise. 'Aerobic' means involving oxygen or cardiovascular endurance; not all cardio is the stereotypical choreographed aerobics class.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: aerobics meaningg

column5: In many English-learning grammars, a verb that can be transitive with an affected object and intransitive with that same participant as subject, without an overt passive marker.
column7: I broke the glass. → The glass broke. / She opened the door. → The door opened. / Heat melted the ice. → The ice melted.
column8: The intransitive sentence is not passive: 'The door opened' has no was/be + past participle. Linguistic terminology varies; many linguists call these labile verbs or discuss the causative–inchoative alternation rather than labeling the English verb itself ergative.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: ergative verbs

column5: To solve, understand, calculate, plan, or reach a satisfactory arrangement concerning something.
column7: We need to work out why the upload keeps failing.
column8: Existing work out card focuses on exercise and 'turn out successfully'; transitive work something out is common enough to preserve separately.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: work stuff out meaning

column5: Harshly irritating or unpleasant, especially a voice, sound, manner, or personality; also the act/result of shredding with a grater or a grid-like structure.
column7: His forced laugh became grating after a while. / The metallic noise was incredibly grating.
column8: Figurative adjective is common. From grate: scrape harshly / irritate.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: grating meaning

column5: Relating to the circumstances surrounding an event rather than direct observation; also dependent on or shaped by particular circumstances.
column7: The case was based largely on circumstantial evidence. / Their success was partly circumstantial—it depended on unusually favorable timing.
column8: Most familiar legal collocation: circumstantial evidence = indirect evidence from which a fact is inferred. Not synonymous with weak evidence; circumstantial evidence can be strong.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: circumstantial meaning

column5: A crude slang expression meaning to masturbate, typically referring to a male masturbating.
column7: The phrase 'beat your meat' is vulgar joking slang for masturbating. / It's the kind of expression you may hear in crude internet humor rather than polite conversation.
column8: Vulgar and often juvenile/comedic. Use neutral 'masturbate' in medical/formal contexts. Preserve because raw search explicitly asked for the slang meaning.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: beat meat meaning slang
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction usage::formal usage::slang usage::humorous usage::vulgar usage::informal

column5: Having broad, deep knowledge or ability across multiple different fields; characteristic of a polymath.
column7: Her polymathic mind jumps easily from linguistics to art history to programming. / A 'polymathic brain' is an informal way to praise unusually broad intellectual interests.
column8: Less common than polymath (noun). Broad curiosity alone does not necessarily make someone a polymath; the word usually implies substantial competence/knowledge across fields.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119, voca_0120 | search: polymathic brain meaning

column5: If or when someone asks for it; available or done when requested.
column7: Additional documentation is available upon request.
column8: Formal/common in notices, policies, and business writing.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: upon request meaning

column5: An abnormal bulging or ballooning of a weakened area in the wall of a blood vessel, most often an artery; rupture can cause life-threatening internal bleeding.
column7: The scan revealed a small cerebral aneurysm. / A ruptured aneurysm is a medical emergency.
column8: Aneurysms can occur in different vessels, including the aorta and cerebral arteries, and many unruptured aneurysms cause no symptoms. Sudden severe symptoms require emergency medical care; the word is also hyperbolically misused online ('this gives me an aneurysm').
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: aneurysm 意味は

column5: While presenting something as if it were a particular legitimate, harmless, or different thing, often concealing the real purpose or identity.
column6: under the pretense of, pretending to be, masquerading as, in the name of (sometimes)
column7: He collected personal information under the guise of conducting a survey. / The villain enters the town under the guise of a traveling doctor.
column8: Usually implies deception/concealment, unlike neutral 'in the form of.' Existing example in Master already uses this construction; standalone phrase retained because it is highly productive.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: under the guise of

column5: In a way that is completely clear, definite, and leaving no room for doubt or ambiguity.
column6: unambiguously, categorically, definitively, unmistakably, without reservation
column7: She unequivocally denied the accusation. / The test results do not unequivocally prove the claim. / He said unequivocally that he would not support the proposal.
column8: Related adjective: unequivocal. Strong formal word meaning there is no ambiguity or room for competing interpretation. Common with state, condemn, reject, support, demonstrate/prove. Stronger and more formal than simply 'clearly.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: unequivocally meaning

column2: the pot calling the kettle black
column5: A criticism of hypocrisy: someone faults another person for a flaw that the critic also has.
column6: that's hypocritical, look who's talking, pot-kettle
column7: He called me disorganized? That's the pot calling the kettle black—his desk is worse than mine.
column8: Raw search omitted 'pot.' Standard form is 'the pot calling the kettle black.' Often shortened jokingly to 'pot, meet kettle.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: calling the kettle black meaning

column5: Small involuntary contractions around the eyelid, commonly called an eyelid twitch; often temporary and associated with factors such as fatigue, stress, caffeine, or eye strain.
column6: eyelid twitch, eye twitch, eyelid myokymia (common benign form)
column7: My eyelid starts twitching when I've been staring at a screen too long. / The twitch disappeared after a few days of better sleep.
column8: Common everyday phrase worth retaining as a concrete body-context card. 'Myokymia' is a more specific medical term often used for benign eyelid twitching; not every twitch should be self-diagnosed from vocabulary alone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: eyelid twitching

column5: The name of the large impact crater buried beneath the Yucatán Peninsula, associated with the asteroid impact about 66 million years ago linked to the end-Cretaceous mass extinction.
column7: The Chicxulub impact released an enormous amount of energy and had global environmental effects. / The crater itself is mostly buried, so you don't see a giant open hole when visiting the region.
column8: Name comes from Chicxulub in Yucatán; English pronunciations vary. The impact is strongly linked to the K–Pg extinction event that eliminated non-avian dinosaurs and many other organisms.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: Chicxulub meaning

column2: game a test / game the test
column5: To exploit the rules, scoring system, predictable patterns, loopholes, or test-taking strategies in order to maximize a score without necessarily improving the underlying ability the test is meant to measure.
column6: game the system, exploit the test, teach to the test (related), optimize for the metric
column7: Students can sometimes game a standardized test by learning its predictable tricks. / If an AI benchmark becomes too predictable, developers may optimize for it in ways that game the test rather than improve general ability.
column8: Game as a verb = manipulate/exploit a system's rules for advantage. 'Game the test' is more natural than 'game a test' when referring to a specific assessment. Good example of Goodhart-style metric optimization.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: to game a test meaning
column12: entry::phrase topic::testing topic::assessment discovery::improvement discovery::exploiting_rules discovery::gaming_the_system discovery::metric_optimization

column2: How many stops in are you?
column5: How far into a multi-stage route/activity are you, measured by completed/current stops? Natural for a pub crawl when context is already clear.
column6: How far in are you?, how many stops have you done?
column7: 'How many stops in are you?' 'We're at the fourth pub.' / How many episodes in are you? uses the same X-in construction with a different unit.
column8: Raw 'How many stops are you in crawling pub?' is unnatural. For pub crawl: 'How many stops in are you?' or 'How many pubs have you hit so far?'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: how many stops are you in crawling pub meaning

column5: Too eager to tell people what is morally right or what they should believe/do, especially in a self-righteous, didactic, or heavy-handed way.
column7: The movie has a clear message, but it rarely feels preachy. / His advice became preachy once he stopped listening and started lecturing.
column8: Common media criticism. A work can be political/moral without being preachy; preachy criticizes delivery/tone, especially overt lecturing.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: preachy meaning

column5: Careful, responsible, diligent, and guided by a desire to do one's work or duties properly and ethically.
column6: diligent, responsible, scrupulous, thorough, careful, dutiful
column7: She's a conscientious editor who checks every citation before publication. / He was conscientious about replying even when he couldn't solve the problem immediately.
column8: Conscientious ≠ conscious. Conscientious = responsible/careful; conscious = awake/aware. Scrupulous can emphasize moral correctness or meticulous care. Often 'conscientious about/in doing X.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: conscientious

column5: To enjoy, approve of, understand, or enthusiastically participate in something; older slang can also mean dance energetically.
column6: be into, be cool with, enjoy
column7: I can get down with that idea.
column8: Do not confuse with get down to = begin serious work. 'Get down with it' often means join in/enjoy it.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: get down with it meaning

column2: move on to the next target
column5: To stop focusing on the current person, task, objective, or object of attention and proceed to the next one.
column6: proceed to the next objective, switch targets, move to the next item
column7: Once this batch is finished, we'll move on to the next target. / The predator abandoned the chase and moved on to the next target.
column8: Compositional rather than a fixed idiom. Target can be literal, strategic, sales/work-related, or figurative; tone changes with context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: move on to the next target meaning

column2: keep your hand over the top of your glass
column3: /ˌkiːp jər ˈhænd ˌoʊvər ðə ˌtɑːp əv jər ˈɡlæs/
column5: To physically cover the opening of a drink glass with your hand as a precaution against spills or someone adding something to the drink.
column6: cover your drink, keep your drink covered
column7: In a crowded club, she kept her hand over the top of her glass while moving through the room. / If you leave a drink unattended, getting a fresh one is safer than assuming it is fine.
column8: This is literal safety advice, not a fixed idiom. 'Cover your drink' is much more compact/natural. The exact phrase may arise in discussions of drink-spiking precautions.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: keep your hand over the top of the glass meaning

column5: The process of treating a person, culture, or group as fascinatingly 'exotic' or fundamentally other, often reducing them to stereotypes, fantasy, novelty, or aesthetic difference rather than seeing them as full individuals.
column7: The essay criticizes the exotification of Japanese women in Western dating fantasies. / Travel media can celebrate cultural difference without turning people into exotic scenery.
column8: Often critical. Exotification can sound positive on the surface ('mysterious,' 'special,' 'exotic') while still objectifying. Fetishization adds stronger obsessive/sexual or reductive fixation; othering is broader.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: exotification

column5: A fiction genre—'literary role-playing game'—in which RPG/game mechanics such as levels, stats, skills, quests, classes, experience points, or system messages are explicit parts of the story/world.
column6: game-system fiction, progression fantasy (overlapping), RPG fiction
column7: The novel is LitRPG: the protagonist can literally see stats, gain levels, and unlock skills. / Not every isekai is LitRPG; explicit game mechanics are the key clue.
column8: Often overlaps with progression fantasy and isekai but is not identical. Progression fantasy focuses on measurable growth even without game UI; isekai focuses on transport/reincarnation to another world.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: lit rpg

column5: Intended or likely to provoke a strong reaction, thought, controversy, anger, or sexual interest.
column6: thought-provoking, challenging, inflammatory, controversial, suggestive, sexually suggestive
column7: The documentary asks a provocative question without pretending there is an easy answer. / His deliberately provocative post was obviously designed to start an argument. / The ad was considered provocative because of its sexual imagery.
column8: Provocative is not automatically sexual. Thought-provoking is usually positive/intellectual; inflammatory emphasizes anger/conflict; suggestive often implies sexual innuendo; provocative can cover all of these depending on what reaction is being provoked.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: provocative

column5: Short for uncle; in contemporary slang, a joking label for an older man or someone perceived as old, out of touch, or 'uncle-aged.'
column7: They started calling him unc because he complained about the music being too loud.
column8: Can be affectionate, teasing, or insulting depending on context. Often used beyond literal family relationships.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111, voca_0116 | search: unc meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::humorous usage::affectionate usage::informal discovery::perception

column5: Certainly; definitely; used to emphasize strong confidence, determination, or contradiction.
column7: I'm sure as hell not paying for something I didn't order.
column8: Informal and mildly vulgar. Often appears as be sure as hell or sure as hell + clause.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: sure as hell meaning
column12: entry::phrase usage::informal usage::vulgar discovery::emphasis discovery::determination discovery::escalation

column5: Women who are neurodivergent; the phrase often appears in discussion of how autism, ADHD, and related traits may be recognized, masked, stereotyped, or diagnosed differently in women because research and diagnostic expectations historically centered other populations.
column6: neurodivergent females (less preferred in ordinary reference), autistic/ADHD women (when specific)
column7: The article focuses on neurodivergent women who learned to mask social difficulties for years. / Discussions of late diagnosis often mention women whose traits did not match older stereotypes.
column8: Not a separate diagnosis. Avoid assuming all neurodivergent women share one presentation. 'Masking' and diagnostic disparities are common discussion themes, but individual conditions and experiences vary widely.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: neurodivergent women meaning
column12: entry::phrase usage::presentation-friendly topic::research topic::medicine topic::health discovery::presentation_language

column5: To have a person available to complain, grumble, or vent to.
column6: have someone to complain to, vent to, gripe to, moan to
column7: Sometimes you don't need advice; you just want someone to bellyache to for five minutes. / He called his brother because he needed somebody to gripe to.
column8: Bellyache as verb = complain persistently, often about relatively minor things; humorous/negative compared with neutral 'vent.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: have someone to bellyache to meaing

column5: To move away from a place, person, group, path, or subject without a clear plan or often without noticing; figuratively, for attention/thought/speech to drift away.
column6: stray, drift away, roam off, walk away, get distracted (figurative)
column7: Don't wander off—we're leaving in ten minutes. / The child wandered off while everyone was looking at the parade. / My mind wandered off halfway through the explanation.
column8: Off highlights departure from a reference point/group/path. Can be literal movement or figurative attention/topic. Stronger safety implication than simply wander around.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: wander off meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb usage::figurative usage::presentation-friendly topic::public_speaking discovery::figurative_extension discovery::presentation_language

column5: To gather or summon people, strength, courage, energy, enthusiasm, or other resources; as a noun, an assembly or formal gathering, especially of troops.
column6: summon, gather, marshal, scrape together, rally
column7: I finally mustered the courage to ask the question. / She couldn't muster much enthusiasm for another sequel. / The commander mustered the troops before dawn.
column8: Very common figurative collocations: muster courage/strength/energy/enthusiasm/support. 'Pass muster' = meet an acceptable standard (different idiom). As noun, military muster = assembly/roll call.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: mustering
column12: entry::idiom entry::word usage::formal usage::figurative usage::military discovery::resource_allocation

column5: In American English, fanny is a mild/childish word for the buttocks. In British English and some other varieties, it is vulgar slang for the female genitals/vulva, so the same word can sound dramatically different across dialects.
column7: An American parent might tell a child to sit on their fanny. / In Britain, that sentence can sound startling because fanny has a much more vulgar anatomical meaning there.
column8: Classic transatlantic false-friend. This dialect difference explains why AmE 'fanny pack' sounds funny or rude to many British speakers, who normally say bum bag.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: fanny meaning america
