column5: A very large, thick-skinned herbivorous mammal with one or two horns on its snout, native to Africa and Asia.
column7: We saw a white rhinoceros resting near the water. / Despite their heavy build, rhinos can move surprisingly fast.
column8: Plural rhinoceroses or rhinoceros; rhinos is far more common conversationally. Five living species remain. The 'white' in white rhinoceros is not a color contrast in ordinary appearance.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: rhinoceros meaning

column5: To hit or beat someone repeatedly/heavily; in vulgar sexual slang, to have vigorous penetrative sex with someone. Context determines the intended sense.
column6: beat, pummel, hammer; have sex with (vulgar slang)
column7: The boxer pounded his opponent with body shots. / In crude sexual dialogue, 'pound you' can be a blunt reference to vigorous sex.
column8: Highly context-sensitive. The ordinary violence sense is common; the sexual sense is vulgar/objectifying. Also pound = strike repeatedly, pound on a door, heart pounds, British currency unit, etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: pound you meaning

column5: In a manner relating to or suggestive of something beyond Earth; a rare adverb formed from extraterrestrial.
column7: The landscape was lit so strangely that it looked almost extraterrestrially beautiful.
column8: Rare and awkward in ordinary prose. It can suggest 'alien / from beyond Earth,' but otherworldly is usually the more natural adjective for an eerie or unearthly quality.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: extraterrestrially can mean other worldly?

column2: go on to do vs go on doing
column5: Go on to do = proceed to a new/subsequent action after finishing or discussing something else. Go on doing = continue the same activity.
column6: proceed to do vs continue doing
column7: After explaining the theory, she went on to give three examples. / She went on talking for another twenty minutes.
column8: Classic gerund/infinitive meaning contrast. 'Go on with + noun' also means continue: go on with the story/work.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: go on to do or doing
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase topic::grammar topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::continuity

column2: in limbo / a state of limbo
column5: In an uncertain, unresolved, or suspended state where progress or a final decision cannot be made.
column7: The project remained in limbo while funding was reviewed.
column8: Natural expressions are in limbo and in a state of limbo; 'limbo state' is understandable but less idiomatic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: limbo state meaning

column5: A critical or mocking label for a racialized sexual/romantic fixation on East Asian people, especially women, based on stereotypes rather than individual attraction. Separately, yellow fever is the name of a viral disease.
column6: Asian fetish, racial fetishization, fetishization of Asian women/men
column7: She disliked being approached by men whose comments suggested an Asian fetish rather than interest in her as a person. / In discussions of dating, 'yellow fever' can refer critically to racial fetishization; in medicine it means an unrelated viral disease.
column8: The phrase uses 'yellow' as a racial label and can itself be offensive. Distinguish ordinary attraction to an individual from stereotyped preference/objectification. Medical yellow fever is a completely separate literal sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: yellow fever fetish
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::term entry::discourse_expression usage::slang usage::critical usage::offensive usage::informal usage::evaluative usage::specialist topic::romance topic::social_media topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: An unusually strong, persistent focus, attachment, or preoccupation with someone or something; also the act of fixing something in position.
column7: His fixation on minor details slowed the entire project.
column8: Psychological/everyday sense often implies excessive focus: fixation on/with something.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: fixation meaning

column5: Used to introduce the surprising, decisive, ironic, especially important, or most striking part of a story or situation.
column6: here's the catch, here's the twist, and the crazy part is, most importantly
column7: The hotel looked cheap—and here's the kicker: breakfast alone cost fifty dollars. / He apologized for being late. Here's the kicker: he'd been sitting in the wrong café for an hour.
column8: Kicker = the detail that changes how you see the whole story. 'Here's the catch' specifically emphasizes a hidden drawback/condition; kicker can be good, bad, ironic, or simply surprising.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: here is a kicker meaning

column5: Something that depicts, stands for, expresses, or models something else; the act of representing; also advocacy on someone's behalf. In cognition/linguistics, a mental or internal encoding/structure used to represent information.
column6: depiction, portrayal, model, symbol, encoding; advocacy
column7: A map is a representation of physical space. / The study asks how words are represented in memory. / The lawyer provided legal representation.
column8: Highly polysemous. In cognitive science, 'representation' is theory-laden: researchers may disagree about what is represented and in what format.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: representation

column5: Wastefully extravagant with money or resources; as a noun, a person who leaves and later returns, especially in the phrase the prodigal son.
column7: After years abroad, the prodigal son finally returned home.
column8: Do not confuse with prodigious. The returnee sense comes from the biblical parable of the Prodigal Son, whose defining trait was wasteful spending.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: prodigal meaning

column5: A situation that looks luxurious, privileged, or desirable from the outside but restricts freedom, autonomy, or happiness.
column6: golden cage, luxurious prison, comfortable captivity
column7: The palace became a gilded cage: she had every luxury except the freedom to leave. / A high-paying job can feel like a gilded cage if the money makes you afraid to quit.
column8: Raw search misspelled 'guilded.' Gilded = covered with a thin layer of gold / made outwardly splendid. The metaphor contrasts attractive exterior with confinement.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: guilded cage meaning

column5: A person learning English as a foreign language, typically in a setting where English is not the main language of everyday life.
column7: The textbook is designed for intermediate EFL learners.
column8: EFL = English as a Foreign Language. Traditionally contrasted with ESL, though EL/ELL and other terms are also used depending on context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: efl learners

column5: To keep moving restlessly in bed, especially because you cannot sleep.
column6: sleep restlessly, lie awake, fidget in bed
column7: I tossed and turned all night before the interview. / The room was too hot, so I kept tossing and turning.
column8: Usually describes sleepless restlessness rather than ordinary repositioning.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: toss and turn definition

column5: To change direction away from the intended physical route, plan, subject, or course, often gradually or unexpectedly.
column6: go off course, drift off track, deviate, stray, swerve away
column7: The conversation veered off track once everyone started arguing about terminology. / The project began well but veered off track after the requirements changed.
column8: Veer emphasizes a change of direction; off track emphasizes departure from intended course. Existing veer is broad; this collocation is useful figuratively for discussions/projects.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115, voca_0119 | search: veer off track meaning

column5: The fish has gone bad or is no longer fresh enough to eat; more broadly, off can mean spoiled or stale of food.
column6: spoiled, gone bad, not fresh, turned
column7: Don't eat that—the fish smells off. / I think the fish is off; it's got a strange sour smell.
column8: For food, be off / smell off / taste off commonly means spoiled or suspiciously unfresh. Separate idiom 'something is off' = something seems wrong, strange, or not quite right.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: the fish is off meaning

column5: To; toward; or in relation to, especially in biblical, archaic, or deliberately elevated language.
column7: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.
column8: Existing unto itself is a specific phrase; bare unto is useful for recognizing older/biblical constructions.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: define unto
column12: entry::word usage::literary usage::archaic usage::religious topic::religion topic::grammar discovery::religious_origin

column2: make something easy / make it easy for someone to do something
column5: To reduce the difficulty, effort, friction, or complexity of an action or situation; commonly framed as make X easy or make it easy for someone to do X.
column6: simplify, facilitate, streamline, make easier, lower the barrier
column7: The app makes it easy to review ten cards at a time. / Clear examples make difficult vocabulary easier to remember. / He didn't exactly make things easy for himself by arriving unprepared.
column8: Raw search 'something made easy' may appear in titles such as 'grammar made easy,' meaning explained/simplified so it becomes easy to learn or do. 'Facilitate' is more formal.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: something made easy meaning

column5: Unsung means deserving praise or recognition but receiving little of it. 'Unsung hero' is the established phrase; 'unsung king' is a creative extension meaning an underrecognized person who is exceptionally good or dominant in some area.
column7: He's the unsung king of background reaction shots—half the comedy comes from his face. / The editor was an unsung hero of the production.
column8: Preserve 'unsung king' because the search may come from a specific praise context, but note that unsung hero is the fixed/common collocation. Unsung literally evokes someone whose praises are not sung.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: unsung king meaning

column5: To predict what background, clarification, context, definitions, or connections a listener will need in order to follow you, and supply them before the listener has to ask.
column6: preempt confusion, provide context proactively, audience-design one's explanation
column7: Good speakers anticipate the listener's information needs before they've expressed them. / If I mention a niche anime term, I should anticipate what context the listener needs to understand the point.
column8: Preserves exact conceptual search with typos repaired. Closely related to audience design and common ground: tailoring an utterance to what the listener likely knows/needs.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: You're anticipating the listner's information needs before thery've expressed them.
column12: entry::phrase topic::communication topic::public_speaking discovery::clarification discovery::explanation discovery::audience_engagement discovery::expressing_need

column5: With effect applied backward to an earlier date, event, period, or already-completed action; by reinterpreting or changing something after the fact.
column6: with retrospective effect, after the fact, retrospectively
column7: The pay increase was applied retroactively to January. / The platform changed the rule but said it would not punish users retroactively. / Later episodes retroactively changed how I understood the first scene.
column8: Legal/admin sense = effect reaches backward in time. Narrative/everyday sense can mean later information changes one's interpretation of earlier material. Retroactive ≠ merely retrospective: retrospective looks back; retroactive changes/applies to the past.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: retroactively

column5: Very serious, severe, sharp, or intense; also, in medicine, beginning suddenly and often lasting a relatively short time.
column7: The hospital is dealing with an acute shortage of nurses.
column8: Common senses include acute pain, acute awareness, acute shortage, acute angle, and acute illness. Contrast medical acute with chronic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: acute definition

column5: To stop extremely quickly and within a very short distance; figuratively, to halt or change immediately.
column6: stop dead, stop instantly, halt abruptly, turn on a dime (related)
column7: The dog can sprint across the yard and stop on a dime. / The actor's expression can go from manic to blank on a dime. / The project couldn't simply stop on a dime once contracts were signed.
column8: A dime is tiny, creating the image of stopping within a tiny space. Compare 'turn on a dime' = change direction very quickly. Often used for vehicles, athletes, animals, behavior, or processes.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: stop on a dime

column5: A word carrying strong emotional, ideological, evaluative, historical, or cultural associations beyond its basic descriptive meaning, so its use can frame a discussion.
column6: emotionally charged term, value-laden word, loaded term
column7: Calling the policy 'radical' can be a loaded word choice depending on the context. / 'Natural' is often a loaded word in debates about behavior.
column8: Loaded does not mean false or forbidden; it means the term brings connotations/framing that should be noticed.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: loaded word meaning

column5: To leave a remote, rural, sparsely populated area and go somewhere more urban or connected.
column6: leave the countryside, get out of the boonies, move to town/the city
column7: He couldn't wait to get out of the sticks and move to New York. / We finally got out of the sticks and found a café with decent Wi-Fi.
column8: Existing 'in the sticks' = in a remote rural area. This card preserves the searched motion construction 'get out of the sticks.' Informal; can sound dismissive toward rural places.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: to get out of the sticks meaning

column5: To leave or go away quickly, especially when ordered to; 'Scram!' means 'Get out of here!'
column6: get lost, beat it, clear out, run along, leave
column7: Scram before the guard sees you. / 'You kids, scram!' the old man shouted. / We heard sirens and decided to scram.
column8: Strongly informal, often comic/old-fashioned in modern dialogue. As an imperative it can sound rude. Not related to scramble despite superficial resemblance.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: scram mean ing

column5: Characterized by voyeurism—taking intrusive or sexualized interest/pleasure in observing others' private, intimate, vulnerable, or sensational experiences; more broadly, uncomfortably prying as a viewer.
column7: The camera lingers in a way that feels voyeuristic rather than empathetic. / Critics called the coverage voyeuristic because it turned private grief into spectacle.
column8: Can be literally sexual or broader media criticism. Broader use still implies an ethically uncomfortable spectator relationship, not simply 'watching closely.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: voyeuristic meaning

column5: Inflammation or irritation of the synovial sheath surrounding a tendon, causing pain and sometimes swelling or impaired movement.
column7: De Quervain tenosynovitis can cause pain near the thumb side of the wrist. / Trigger finger is a form of stenosing tenosynovitis affecting a finger's flexor tendon sheath.
column8: Tendinitis concerns the tendon itself; tenosynovitis concerns its sheath, though they can coexist. Spelling raw search 'tendosinovitis' corrected to tenosynovitis.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: tendosinovitis

column2: what made you feel that way?
column5: What caused or led you to have that feeling, impression, reaction, or belief?
column6: what gave you that impression?, why did you feel that way?
column7: You said the conversation felt awkward—what made you feel that way? / What made you feel that the ending was rushed?
column8: Often gentler/more exploratory than blunt 'Why?' because it asks about the cause/evidence behind the feeling. Can refer to emotion or impression/judgment.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: what made you feel that way meaning

column5: Dox means reveal someone's private identifying information online; dunk on means publicly mock, criticize, defeat, or show someone up. They are not interchangeable.
column6: dox: expose personal information, deanonymize | dunk on: mock, ridicule, roast, show up
column7: Doxing someone exposes private information; dunking on someone is public ridicule or one-upmanship.
column8: Preserve because the original search explicitly asks whether two internet-slang verbs are interchangeable. Existing individual cards cover each term.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: dox and dunk are interchangeable in slang?
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::slang usage::informal topic::internet topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::criticism

column5: A small ornamental or collectible statue representing a person, animal, character, deity, etc.
column7: She has a shelf of ceramic cat figurines. / The limited-edition anime figurine sold out immediately.
column8: Usually emphasizes a small statue/decorative object. In hobby/anime contexts, 'figure' is often more natural for character collectibles; figurine can sound decorative or traditional.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: figurine meaning

column5: To become annoyed, bitter, resentful, defensive, or upset, especially over a loss, criticism, teasing, or perceived slight.
column6: get bitter, get annoyed, get mad, get butthurt (vulgar-ish slang), get sore
column7: Don't get salty just because you lost one match. / He got salty when people pointed out the contradiction in his review.
column8: Internet/gaming slang broadened into general informal speech. 'Salty' often implies visible bitterness or sore-loser energy, not just ordinary anger.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: get salty meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::vulgar discovery::criticism discovery::perception

column5: Continuous or nearly continuous movement, with little or no pause.
column7: The toddlers seemed to be in constant motion all afternoon.
column8: Transparent phrase, but useful as a common descriptive chunk: be in constant motion.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: constant motion meaning

column5: A violent, intimidating, or criminal person, especially one used to threaten or attack others; also used loosely as an insult for someone perceived as brutish or lawless.
column6: brute, hoodlum, goon, heavy, enforcer, gangster (not exact)
column7: The gang sent two thugs to intimidate the shop owner. / The film's villain surrounds himself with anonymous thugs. / Calling protesters 'thugs' can carry strong political and racialized implications depending on context.
column8: Historically from Hindi ṭhag via British colonial usage. Modern English often means violent criminal/enforcer. In U.S. public discourse, applying 'thug' selectively to Black people has been criticized as racially coded; context and speaker matter.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: define thug

column5: To publish a defamatory statement about someone in a form treated as libel; more loosely, to defame someone in writing/publication.
column6: defame, smear, malign, publish defamatory claims about
column7: He threatened to sue, claiming the newspaper had libeled him. / Be careful: calling something 'libel' is a legal claim, not merely saying it was insulting.
column8: Traditional libel/slander distinction is written/published vs spoken, but exact defamation law and categories vary by jurisdiction. Existing noun libel card remains useful.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: libel someone meaning

column5: Labile means liable to change, unstable, reactive, or easily altered; stable means resistant to change and remaining relatively constant.
column6: unstable, changeable, reactive vs steady, fixed, resistant
column7: The compound is chemically labile at room temperature, whereas the comparison compound is stable. / His mood was emotionally labile rather than stable.
column8: Labile is used in chemistry, biology, medicine/psychology, and linguistics. In medicine 'emotionally labile' means emotions shift rapidly/easily. In linguistics a labile verb alternates transitive/intransitive. Stable is the broad everyday opposite only in the 'changeable' sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: labile vs stable

column5: Already achieved, completed, learned, or gained as experience; sometimes, already eaten/drunk.
column6: to one's credit, completed, accumulated, in one's experience
column7: With a few presentations under my belt, I stopped getting quite so nervous. / Once you have a couple of long trips under your belt, packing gets much easier. / He had a good breakfast under his belt before the hike.
column8: Common: have/get X under one's belt. Experience/achievements sense is highly productive. Food sense is more literal-humorous and less central.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: under one's belt

column5: Easily annoyed, irritable, and somewhat touchy.
column7: The interview became tetchy when the subject of money came up. / Everyone was getting a bit tetchy after hours of delays. / His tetchy reply made it obvious I'd hit a nerve.
column8: Especially common in British English. Close to 'testy': easily irritated and showing it in speech/behavior. 'Touchy' can also mean sensitive about a particular subject; 'tetchy' more directly describes an irritable mood/manner.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: tetchy

column5: To cut, chop, or remove a part, especially a branch, limb, end, or unnecessary section, often in a quick/rough way; figuratively, remove a chunk from a price, runtime, budget, etc.
column6: chop off, cut off, trim off, remove
column7: They lopped off several dead branches. / The editor lopped ten minutes off the runtime. / A sale lopped $50 off the price.
column8: Often implies a substantial piece rather than delicate trimming. 'Lop' historically associated with pruning branches; productive figurative extension.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: lopping off meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::form_family entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative topic::finance discovery::resource_allocation discovery::figurative_extension discovery::removal

column5: To regard or handle a person as a risk, burden, disadvantage, or source of potential trouble rather than as an asset.
column6: see as a burden, regard as a risk, treat as dead weight
column7: After the scandal, the party began treating him as a liability. / She hated being treated as a liability just because she needed extra training.
column8: Builds on figurative liability = person/thing likely to cause loss or problems. Often organizational/political, but also interpersonal.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: treat someone as a liability

column5: The use of force, threats, pressure, intimidation, or other means to make someone do something they would not freely choose to do.
column7: Consent obtained through coercion is not freely given. / The confession was challenged on the grounds that it had been obtained by coercion. / Economic pressure can become coercive depending on the circumstances.
column8: Stronger than persuasion or ordinary social pressure: coercion undermines meaningful freedom of choice. Legal definitions vary by context. Related: coerce, coercive.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: coercion

column5: To make a mistake, fail to do one's responsibility, or mishandle something through inattention, poor follow-through, or negligence.
column6: mess up, fail, let something slip, fumble
column7: I dropped the ball and forgot to send the file. / The company really dropped the ball on customer support.
column8: From sports image of failing to hold/control the ball. Often implies responsibility: 'I dropped the ball on X.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: drop the ball meaning

column5: As an adjective, stylishly attractive, confident, energetic, and adventurous in a somewhat old-fashioned or romantic way; as a participle, moving/running quickly.
column6: debonair, gallant, handsome, stylish; rushing, darting
column7: He plays a dashing young pilot in the old adventure film. / She looked dashing in the tailored suit. / He came dashing down the stairs when he heard the crash.
column8: Attractive-person sense has a classic/romantic flavor and historically skews masculine, though it can describe anyone. 'Dashing' motion comes from dash = move quickly. Debonair is polished/charming; dashing adds energy/adventure.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: dashing

column5: Adjective: extraordinarily beautiful, impressive, elevated, or awe-inspiring, often beyond ordinary beauty. Verb: in chemistry, to change directly between solid and gas without passing through the liquid state.
column7: The final movement is sublime—quiet, overwhelming, and almost impossible to put into words. / Dry ice sublimes directly from solid carbon dioxide into gas.
column8: Important contrast with WID6110 sublimate. Sublime adjective is aesthetic/philosophical; sublime can also be the chemistry verb. 'Sublimation' additionally has the psychological redirection sense. Do not confuse sublime with subliminal.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: sublime meaning

column5: A line, fold, ridge, or wrinkle made by folding, pressing, or bending material or skin; as a verb, to make or develop such a line. In sports, 'crease' can name a marked area near a goal/wicket.
column7: The shirt had a deep crease down the sleeve. / Try not to crease the poster. / He smiled and the skin around his eyes creased. / Hockey goalies defend the crease in front of the net.
column8: Useful physical distinctions: wrinkle is often irregular/natural; crease often comes from folding/pressure and can be sharper. Sports senses vary by sport.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define crease

column5: Literally, for a bird/animal to produce an egg; figuratively, especially in AmE, to fail badly or give a poor performance.
column7: The comedian laid an egg with a set that got almost no laughs. / The sequel laid an egg at the box office despite a huge marketing campaign.
column8: Figurative use is informal and somewhat old-fashioned/colorful. Related 'goose egg' = zero. Do not confuse with 'lay the groundwork' etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: To lay an egg
column12: entry::idiom usage::informal usage::dated usage::figurative usage::american_english topic::performance topic::animals discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Requiring great physical or mental effort, energy, or exertion; also vigorous or forceful.
column7: The hike is beautiful but fairly strenuous, especially in the last mile. / She made strenuous efforts to keep the project alive.
column8: Common: strenuous exercise/activity/work/effort. Arduous emphasizes difficulty and sustained labor; vigorous emphasizes energetic intensity and can be positive; strenuous emphasizes exertion.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: strenuous

column5: An incident in which protected, confidential, or sensitive data is accessed, exposed, stolen, or disclosed without authorization.
column7: The company notified customers after a data breach exposed account information.
column8: Existing examples mention data breaches, but no standalone card covered the term.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: data breach meaning

column2: is that offer still on the table?
column3: /ɪz ðæt ˌɔːfər stɪl ɑːn ðə ˈteɪbəl/
column5: Is the previously discussed offer, option, proposal, or possibility still available for consideration or acceptance?
column6: is the offer still open?, does the offer still stand?
column7: Is that job offer still on the table? / You mentioned I could stay at your place— is that offer still on the table?
column8: 'On the table' = available for discussion/consideration. Contrast 'off the table' = no longer being considered/available.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: is that offer still on the table? meaning

column5: Noun: a projecting tube/lip through which liquid pours; a jet/stream of liquid. Verb: to send liquid or other material out forcefully; figuratively, to talk at length, especially glibly or dogmatically ('spout nonsense').
column6: nozzle, outlet; jet; gush, spew; ramble, pontificate
column7: Steam spouted from the pipe. / The kettle has a narrow spout. / He spent twenty minutes spouting conspiracy theories he had just read online.
column8: Existing easy-pour-spout card is narrow. Figurative spout + ideas/nonsense/opinions is often critical, implying effortless/unreflective talk. Compare spew, which is more forceful/disgusting.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: spout meaning

column5: Both can suggest instability, but labile emphasizes ease of change/reaction; volatile can mean rapidly changeable/unpredictable and, in chemistry, readily evaporating.
column7: The molecule is labile and reacts readily with water. / Oil prices have been extremely volatile this month. / Ethanol is more volatile than water because it evaporates more readily.
column8: Do not use volatile as a general chemistry synonym for labile: volatility specifically concerns vaporization tendency. For mood, emotionally labile = rapidly shifting affect; volatile person = liable to sudden, potentially explosive anger/change, often stronger and more dangerous-sounding.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: labile vs volatile
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::scientific topic::chemistry topic::language_learning topic::science discovery::contrast discovery::emphasis discovery::suggestion

column5: The people who watch, listen to, read, or otherwise receive a performance, speech, broadcast, publication, work, or message; also a formal meeting granted by an important person.
column6: viewers, listeners, readers, spectators, public, readership
column7: The video found an audience outside its original fandom. / Know your audience before choosing the level of explanation. / The ambassador was granted an audience with the king.
column8: Audience can be collective singular/plural depending dialect. Modern media: target audience, audience retention, audience demographics. Formal 'an audience with X' = official meeting.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: audience meaning
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::professional topic::work topic::communication topic::media topic::performance topic::public_speaking discovery::professional_context discovery::concession discovery::audience_engagement

column5: Decease means death or to die in formal/legal language; deceased means dead and is commonly used formally for a person who has died.
column7: The property passed to his heirs upon his decease. / The deceased was identified the next morning.
column8: As a verb/noun decease sounds legal/archaic. In normal conversation say die/death. 'The deceased' is a formal noun phrase.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: decease
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal usage::archaic usage::legalistic topic::law

column4: noun / verb / adjective, chiefly BrE slang
column5: Slang with several senses: excrement or defecation; rubbish/nonsense or something poor-quality; in expressions such as 'cack-handed,' awkward or clumsy. Exact sense depends strongly on context.
column7: That printer is absolute cack—it jams every ten minutes. / The word can also refer crudely to excrement, so context matters. / 'Cack-handed' means clumsy or awkward.
column8: Chiefly British/Irish informal slang and vulgar in its bodily sense. Do not confuse with 'cackle.' Because raw search lacks context, retain the polysemy rather than forcing one definition.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define cack
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::british_english discovery::evaluation

column5: To cut, tear, or remove the limbs or major body parts from a person or animal; figuratively, to break a country, organization, or system into separate pieces.
column6: cut apart, sever limbs, mutilate; break up, partition (figurative)
column7: The horror film shows a dismembered body. / The empire was gradually dismembered by war and political settlements.
column8: Graphic literal meaning. Existing 'dismembering' is a gerund/context card; this preserves the base verb and figurative historical/political use. Dismantle is much less bodily/violent.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: dismembered meaning
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::figurative topic::grammar topic::animals discovery::figurative_extension discovery::removal

column5: To customize, decorate, or upgrade something in an extravagant, flashy, or attention-grabbing way.
column6: trick out, deck out, customize, bling out
column7: He pimped out the old car with huge wheels, custom lights, and a ridiculous sound system. / They pimped out the gaming room with LEDs and wall-to-wall displays.
column8: Popularized strongly by makeover/car culture such as 'Pimp My Ride.' The underlying word pimp has sexual-exploitation meanings, so this slang can sound dated or insensitive; 'trick out/deck out' are safer alternatives.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: pimp out meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrasal_verb usage::slang usage::dated usage::informal discovery::improvement

column5: Named in the title of a work or holding the title of a position; sometimes having a title without the full power normally associated with it.
column7: Hamlet is the titular character of Shakespeare's play.
column8: Titular character = character named in the title. Do not automatically equate titular with main/protagonist; a title character need not be the central protagonist.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: titular meaning
column12: entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::work topic::debate discovery::title_language discovery::debate_language

column5: Relating to a theme, central idea, recurring subject, or organizing motif.
column7: The two episodes are very different in plot but thematically connected. / The final image gives the story a neat thematic payoff. / I like the character arc, but I'm not sure it fits the film's thematic focus.
column8: Common criticism vocabulary: thematic depth, thematic resonance, thematic throughline, thematically consistent. Theme is the underlying idea; motif is a recurring element that may express a theme.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: thematic meaing

column5: Of the heart, to seem to miss or interrupt a beat; figuratively, to feel a sudden jolt of fear, surprise, excitement, or attraction.
column6: miss a beat; heart leap, startle
column7: My heart skipped a beat when I saw the message. / For a second, her heart seemed to skip a beat when he walked into the room.
column8: Often figurative/hyperbolic in romance or suspense. Compare 'without missing a beat' = without pausing or losing composure, a different idiom.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: skip a beat me4aning

column5: To cause something to become a particular state; to provide or give; to represent artistically; or in computing, to generate a visual/audio output from data.
column7: The damage rendered the machine useless. / The software renders the scene in real time.
column8: Highly polysemous. Common pattern render + object + adjective: render something useless/impossible. Also render assistance, render a verdict, render an image.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: render meaninng

column5: Polite, respectful, considerate behavior; a polite act or favor. 'Courtesy of' can mean provided by, thanks to, or—sometimes ironically—caused by.
column7: He had the courtesy to call and say he'd be late. / As a courtesy, the hotel waived the fee. / The photos are courtesy of the museum. / We spent two hours in traffic, courtesy of a crash downtown.
column8: Common patterns: common courtesy; have the courtesy to do; as a courtesy; courtesy of. 'Courtesy of' can be neutral attribution or ironic blame. Raw 'cautesy' corrected.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: cautesy meaning

column5: A rare or highly local/nonstandard slang form used by some speakers for someone or something silly, goofy, or foolish.
column7: You're being so gilly today.
column8: Not standard contemporary English. The search 'gilly means silly?' is supported mainly by user-generated slang; older dictionaries also record gilly as 'a fool' and standard dictionaries give unrelated senses such as a variant of gillie. Preserve because the search itself was memorable.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: gilly means silly?

column5: A particular point in time, process, or sequence—especially one at which an important decision or change occurs; also literally a joining point.
column6: point, stage, crossroads, critical moment, junction
column7: At this juncture, changing the entire plan would cost more than finishing it. / The story reaches a crucial juncture when she finally learns who betrayed her.
column8: Very common formal phrase: at this juncture. Compared with crossroads, juncture need not imply a choice, though 'critical juncture' often does. Literal joining sense is less common in everyday speech.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: juncture

column5: Subtle qualities, meanings, feelings, or attitudes present beneath the obvious surface; literally, quieter/lower tones. Often used for emotional, political, sexual, racial, ominous, or comic implications.
column6: subtext, hints, overtones, undercurrents, subtle notes
column7: The scene has ominous undertones even before anything bad happens. / His supposedly neutral comment carried political undertones. / The perfume has warm woody undertones.
column8: Raw 'undertories' appears to be a typo/search slip. Undertone is subtler/background quality; overtone is also commonly figurative and can overlap. 'Undercurrent' often suggests a hidden force/feeling running through a situation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: undertories

column5: A response meaning 'I and/or many others have the same problem, experience, feeling, or situation as you.' Often sympathetic, teasing, or dryly sarcastic.
column6: join the club, you're not alone, same here
column7: 'I can't keep up with all these new slang words.' 'Welcome to the club.' / 'I'm exhausted.' 'Welcome to the club—we all stayed up too late.'
column8: Not necessarily about a real club. 'Join the club' is a near-equivalent, often more dismissive/sarcastic: your problem is common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117, voca_0120 | search: welcome to the club meaning

column5: To feel extremely excited, delighted, or light-headedly enthusiastic about something.
column6: be thrilled about, be excited about, be over the moon about
column7: She was giddy about finally seeing the band live. / I was embarrassingly giddy about a tiny feature working correctly.
column8: Existing base giddy covers excited/dizzy; this preserves the natural 'giddy about' collocation and positive anticipation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: being giddy about meaning

column5: The feeling or process of becoming disappointed after discovering that a person, belief, institution, dream, or situation is less good, true, admirable, or ideal than one had believed.
column6: disenchantment, disappointment, loss of faith, disenchantment
column7: His early idealism gradually turned into political disillusionment. / Dating-app fatigue can include disillusionment with the idea that endless choice makes dating easier.
column8: More specific than disappointment: an illusion/idealized belief is stripped away. Related: disillusion (verb), disillusioned (adj).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define disillusionment

column5: A compact narrative way to say that they departed, set out, or immediately began moving/doing something.
column6: away they went, they set off, they went off
column7: The doors opened, the kids grabbed their bags, and off they went. / I gave them the address and off they went to find the restaurant.
column8: Inversion/fronting with directional particle: off + subject + verb. Similar: off we go!, off he ran, away they went. Often lively/storytelling in tone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: off they went meaning

column2: expose oneself to a wide range of speakers
column5: To deliberately get experience hearing/interacting with speakers from varied ages, backgrounds, accents, personalities, and speaking styles, so comprehension does not overfit to a narrow set of voices.
column6: get exposure to diverse speakers, listen to a wide range of speakers
column7: I want to expose myself to people from different demographics—different ages and backgrounds, with various accents, personalities, and speaking styles.
column8: Important pragmatic caution: 'expose myself to people' can momentarily evoke the sexual sense of expose oneself. In language-learning contexts, 'get exposure to a wide range of speakers' or 'expose myself to a wide range of voices/speakers' is safer/natural.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: I want to expose myself to people from different demographics — people of different ages, backgrounds, with various accents, personalities, and speaking styles.

column5: Having had part cut shorter with a saw; especially used in the fixed weapon term 'sawed-off shotgun' (AmE) / 'sawn-off shotgun' (BrE). More broadly, shortened or truncated.
column7: The prop looked like a sawed-off piece of pipe. / AmE commonly says sawed-off; BrE commonly says sawn-off.
column8: The adjective itself is broader than weapons. Weapon collocations are culturally common but legally regulated; card focuses on language/variant forms rather than operational details.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: sawed-off meaning

column5: Literally, to take someone or something to the area behind a building; context can make it a dark euphemism for taking something away to destroy, kill, discard, or deal with privately.
column6: take out back, deal with privately, put down (contextual)
column7: The broken chair was taken around back to be thrown out. / Joking about taking an old computer out back can imply it's so hopeless it deserves to be 'put out of its misery.'
column8: Raw search 'took it around back' lacks source context. The culturally familiar darker pattern is take X out back, sometimes evoking taking an animal away to be shot/put down. Around back can also be completely literal: 'The delivery driver took it around back.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: took it around back

column5: A condition in which a finger catches, locks, or snaps during bending/straightening because the flexor tendon and its sheath are irritated or narrowed; also literally the finger used to pull a firearm trigger.
column7: My ring finger started clicking and locking, and the doctor said it was trigger finger. / In the literal phrase, keep your trigger finger away from the trigger until appropriate.
column8: Medical name: stenosing tenosynovitis. Symptoms can include pain, stiffness, clicking, catching, or locking. Distinct from carpal tunnel syndrome, which involves compression of the median nerve at the wrist.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: tirgger finger

column5: To sing with maximum enthusiasm, emotion, volume, or wholehearted effort, without holding back.
column6: sing passionately, belt it out, give it everything
column7: We drove home singing our hearts out to old anime openings. / She may not have hit every note, but she sang her heart out.
column8: Pattern X one's heart out also occurs with cry/laugh/dance/play, meaning intensely/to one's fullest. 'Belt out' specifically suggests loud, powerful singing.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: sing your heart out meaning

column5: To depend exploitatively on another person or resource, taking money, support, labor, status, or benefits while giving little back.
column6: mooch off, sponge off, freeload on, exploit, parasitize
column7: He spent years leeching off his parents without contributing anything. / Scam accounts leech off the popularity of real creators by reposting their work.
column8: From leech, a bloodsucking animal, so the metaphor is strongly negative. 'Mooch off' and 'sponge off' are more everyday; leech off suggests parasitic exploitation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: leech off of meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::verb_pattern entry::construction usage::informal usage::figurative usage::critical discovery::resource_allocation discovery::support

column5: Noisy, rough, disorderly, or shaky; sometimes suggesting a loud rattling quality.
column7: The old train made a rackety clatter as it pulled into the station.
column8: Less common than rickety. Rackety emphasizes noise/disorder; rickety emphasizes weak, shaky construction.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: rackety

column5: Content, messaging, or marketing deliberately designed to provoke anger or outrage because strong negative reactions drive attention, sharing, engagement, or sales.
column6: outrage bait, anger bait, controversy marketing, outrage marketing, engagement bait
column7: The ad felt less like a sincere campaign than ragebait designed to dominate the conversation. / Some creators build an audience by posting increasingly obvious outrage bait.
column8: Useful translation for 炎上商法 depends on context: ragebait/outrage bait for content engineered to anger; outrage marketing/controversy marketing for a deliberate promotional strategy; publicity stunt if controversy itself is the stunt. Related: outrage economy WID5829.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: 炎上商法　英語で

column5: Literally, secretly move cash beneath a table; figuratively/idiomatically, make a concealed, unofficial, often illegal payment such as a bribe or undeclared payment.
column6: pay secretly, bribe, make an under-the-table payment, pay off
column7: He slid an envelope of cash under the table. / The contractor was accused of making under-the-table payments to officials.
column8: 'Under the table' commonly means secretly/illegally, especially payment or employment. A literal physical action can evoke that idiom but is not automatically a bribe.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: sliding money under the table meaning

column5: To provide evidence or facts that prove or support a claim, allegation, or statement.
column7: The journalist could not substantiate the allegation.
column8: Formal. Usually substantiate a claim/allegation/account with evidence.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: define substantiate
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::journalistic discovery::evidence discovery::assertion discovery::support

column5: Not justified, necessary, appropriate, or deserved; especially rude, excessive, or unfair behavior/comment.
column6: unnecessary, unwarranted, inappropriate, out of line, gratuitous
column7: That personal insult was completely uncalled for. / The extra sarcasm felt uncalled for.
column8: Often moral/social judgment: 'That was uncalled for.' Different from 'uncalled' alone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: uncalled for

column5: A traditional Scottish savory dish made from sheep's offal (classically heart, liver, and lungs) minced with oats, onion, suet/fat, seasoning, and traditionally cooked in a sheep's stomach or casing.
column7: We tried haggis with neeps and tatties in Edinburgh. / Modern haggis is often sold in an artificial casing rather than an actual sheep's stomach.
column8: Strongly associated with Scotland and Burns Night. 'Neeps and tatties' = turnips/swede and potatoes. Recipes vary, including vegetarian versions; the traditional description is not every modern product.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define haggis

column5: A person, thing, or situation that threatens harm or causes serious trouble; informally, an annoyingly troublesome or chaotic person. As a verb, to threaten.
column6: threat, danger, nuisance, pest; threaten, intimidate
column7: Drunk driving is a menace to public safety. / That kid is an absolute menace—he hid every remote in the house. / The villain menaced the town for years.
column8: Tone ranges from serious threat to affectionate/joking 'you little menace.' Common pattern: a menace to society/public safety.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: menace meaning

column5: A second attempt at recording, filming, performing, or doing something after the first attempt failed or was unsatisfactory.
column6: second take, second attempt, try again, round two
column7: I stumbled over the first line—take two. / The first version of the app was messy, so this redesign is basically take two.
column8: From film/recording terminology: a take is one recorded attempt. Informally 'take two' can announce any redo. 'Take two pills' is unrelated ordinary verb + number.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: take 2 meaning

column5: A former American shoe-polish brand remembered especially through the expression 'not know shit from Shinola,' meaning to be extremely ignorant or unable to distinguish the obvious.
column7: He acts like an expert, but he doesn't know shit from Shinola.
column8: The expression relies on the visual contrast between dark shoe polish and excrement and is vulgar. Modern Shinola is also the name of a Detroit-based lifestyle brand; context distinguishes it.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: define shinola

column2: qi / chi vs psyche vs ki
column5: Chinese qì/chi and Japanese ki are historically related East Asian terms: Japanese ki is the Sino-Japanese reading of 気/氣, associated with breath, vital energy, spirit, mood, etc. English psyche comes from Greek psykhē ('soul, breath, life, mind') and is not etymologically related, despite some conceptual overlap.
column6: qi/chi, ki; psyche, mind, soul (conceptual only)
column7: Japanese 'ki' appears in words such as genki and can refer broadly to spirit/energy/mood. / English 'psyche' refers to the mind or soul. / Similar 'breath/life/spirit' metaphors across cultures do not by themselves prove a shared word origin.
column8: Important distinction: qi/chi ↔ Japanese ki have a real historical linguistic relationship through Chinese characters/borrowings; psyche is Greek and unrelated etymologically. The resemblance is conceptual, not evidence of common origin.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: che in chinese and psyche in english and ki in japanese have some relations?

column5: To hit someone or something repeatedly and forcefully, especially with fists; figuratively, to overwhelm or batter with criticism, attacks, bad news, weather, etc.
column7: The boxer pummeled the heavy bag for three rounds. / The coast was pummeled by wind and rain. / The film got pummeled by critics on opening weekend.
column8: Usually repeated blows/pressure, not one strike. Figurative passive 'be pummeled by criticism/questions/storms' is common. Stronger and more sustained than hit.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: pummeled meaning
column12: entry::word usage::figurative topic::news topic::weather discovery::figurative_extension discovery::criticism

column5: A furnace used to extract or process metals at very high temperatures. A blast furnace specifically produces molten iron from iron ore using a hot air blast; smelting furnace is the broader category.
column7: Iron ore, coke, and limestone are fed into a blast furnace to produce molten iron. / The fantasy city is built around enormous smelting furnaces glowing beneath the foundry.
column8: Japanese 溶鉱炉 is commonly blast furnace when referring to the ironmaking structure; 溶解炉 can be melting furnace. 'Smelter' can mean the industrial plant or furnace operation, not always the individual furnace.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: 溶鉱炉 英語で

column5: To be intensely tormented, distressed, or consumed by worry.
column6: be consumed with worry, be tormented by anxiety, be beside oneself with worry
column7: She was racked with worry while waiting for the test results. / He spent the whole night racked with worry about whether he'd made the right decision.
column8: Rack here evokes torture/strain: racked with guilt, pain, grief, anxiety, doubt. Also spelled wracked in some modern usage, but racked is traditional/common in this sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: be racked with worry meaning

column5: A polite formula used before disagreement, criticism, or contradiction to signal respect—or, depending on tone, to soften or ironically sharpen what follows.
column6: respectfully, with respect, no disrespect, I mean no disrespect
column7: With all due respect, I think that interpretation ignores the last two episodes. / With all due respect, that's simply not what the data says.
column8: Often heard as a warning that disagreement is coming. Sincere in formal settings, but can sound passive-aggressive or sarcastic if followed by a harsh attack. 'No offense' is more casual and similarly may fail to soften what follows.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: With all due respect…
column12: entry::discourse_expression entry::prepositional_phrase usage::formal usage::casual usage::softening usage::ironic usage::informal topic::communication discovery::disagreement discovery::criticism

column5: To avoid something because of fear, discomfort, reluctance, or lack of confidence.
column6: avoid, steer clear of, recoil from
column7: She doesn't shy away from difficult conversations.
column8: Common with challenges, controversy, responsibility, attention, or difficult topics.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: shy away from meaning

column5: To weaken, damage, or erode something gradually or indirectly—confidence, authority, an argument, trust, stability, health, etc.; literally, historically, weaken from beneath.
column7: Constant interruptions undermined her confidence. / That exception risks undermining the whole rule. / His joke was funny without undermining the seriousness of the scene.
column8: Often indirect/gradual rather than openly attack. Distinguish undercut, which overlaps strongly and can also mean sell more cheaply.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: undermining
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::rhetorical topic::health discovery::compromise discovery::trade-off discovery::social_trust discovery::debate_language

column5: The hard or protective pupal stage/casing of a butterfly or moth during metamorphosis; figuratively, a protected transitional state in which something is changing into a new form.
column7: The caterpillar formed a chrysalis and later emerged as a butterfly. / The character spends the middle of the story in a kind of emotional chrysalis before re-entering the world.
column8: Strictly, chrysalis is the pupa of a butterfly/moth; cocoon is a silk casing spun around the pupa by some insects, especially many moths. They are often casually confused. Plural chrysalises or chrysalides.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: chrisalis

column5: To be extremely annoying, troublesome, inconvenient, or disruptive to other people.
column6: be a pain, be a pest, be a bother, be a real nuisance
column7: The construction noise has been a complete nuisance all week. / Sorry to be a complete nuisance, but could you send that file one more time?
column8: Complete is an intensifier here. 'Nuisance' is milder/less insulting than menace and often applies to situations as well as people. 'Sorry to be a nuisance' is a common polite BrE-style request softener.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: being a complete nuisance meaning

column5: Openly revealing attitudes, motives, prejudice, or hostility that were previously concealed or presented more politely.
column7: The reply was a surprisingly mask-off admission of what he really believed.
column8: From 'the mask comes off.' Often used critically in online political/cultural discourse.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: mask-off meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word entry::discourse_expression usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::informal topic::internet

column5: Differences in speech patterns across speakers—or sometimes within the same speaker—such as pronunciation, pitch, timing, accent, voice quality, lexical choices, or realization of linguistic contrasts.
column6: inter-speaker variation, talker variability, speaker variation
column7: Listeners learn to cope with speaker variability: the same vowel can sound quite different across people. / A robust model should handle accent and speaker variability.
column8: In speech research, talker variability is also common. Inter-speaker = between speakers; intra-speaker = within one speaker across situations/time.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: speaker variability
column12: entry::term entry::phrase topic::language_learning topic::public_speaking topic::linguistics discovery::perception discovery::evaluation

column5: Consisting of parts or members that are all the same or very similar in kind, composition, character, or distribution; uniform throughout.
column7: The mixture should be homogeneous before you pour it into the mold. / The school was far more culturally homogeneous than the city around it. / A homogeneous group is not necessarily identical in every respect.
column8: Opposite: heterogeneous. In science, a homogeneous mixture has uniform composition. In social description, homogeneous means relatively similar along the dimension being discussed, not literally identical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: homogeneous

column5: Connected directly to and for the private use of a bedroom, especially a bathroom; as a noun, an en-suite bathroom.
column7: The room has an en-suite bathroom with a shower. / We booked a double room with an en suite rather than a shared bathroom.
column8: From French 'in sequence,' but English hotel/property usage is specialized. Often written en suite or ensuite. In AmE, 'private/attached bathroom' is more ordinary.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define en suite
column12: entry::adjective_phrase usage::american_english usage::british_english usage::specialist discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A highly flexible word whose central image often involves separation, movement away from contact or a normal position, removal, disconnection, or being outside an active/allowed state.
column7: The lid came off, the lights are off, and that room is off-limits.
column8: Not one single meaning. The recurring image is being separated from a surface/path/state or moved away from it. This helps connect take off, cut off, turn off, off-limits, day off, etc. The off in top off/cap off is lexicalized and should be learned with the whole phrasal verb.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: core idea of the preposition "off"
column12: entry::word usage::debate-friendly topic::debate topic::grammar discovery::flexibility discovery::debate_language

column5: Impel = drive/urge someone toward action, often through motivation, feeling, or circumstances. Compel = force or strongly oblige, often leaving little real choice; it can also mean powerfully attract/convince in 'compelling.'
column7: Curiosity impelled her to investigate; the court order compelled her to testify. / Fear may impel action without literally compelling it.
column8: Overlap exists. Impel foregrounds impetus/motivation; compel foregrounds necessity/coercion. Both commonly take object + to-infinitive.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: impel vs compel
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::persuasive topic::decision-making topic::language_learning discovery::persuasion discovery::urge discovery::contrast discovery::encouragement

column5: Very proper, neat, formal, restrained, or easily shocked by behavior considered improper; sometimes disapprovingly prudish or stiff.
column6: proper, prudish, strait-laced, demure, stiff, prissy
column7: She sat with a prim expression and corrected everyone's table manners. / The costume makes the character look deliberately prim and old-fashioned.
column8: Often suggests excessive propriety/restraint. As a verb, 'prim one's lips/mouth' = draw them into a tight disapproving expression.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: define prim

column5: Literally, body tissue that supports, binds, or connects other tissues and organs; figuratively, material or relationships that link separate parts into a coherent whole.
column6: binding tissue; glue, linking material, connective thread
column7: Ligaments are a type of connective tissue. / The quiet character scenes are the connective tissue holding the bigger action sequences together. / Those recurring jokes become connective tissue between otherwise separate episodes.
column8: The figurative use is especially useful in criticism, storytelling, organizations, and systems: not necessarily the flashy 'main content,' but what makes the pieces connect and function together.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: connective tissue meaning

column5: To suddenly attack someone physically or, much more commonly, speak/act toward them angrily and aggressively, often as an emotional reaction.
column6: snap at, attack, strike out, vent at, go off on
column7: He lashed out at everyone who tried to help him. / She later apologized for lashing out when she was overwhelmed. / The cornered animal lashed out with its claws.
column8: Usually lash out at someone/something. Emotional sense often suggests reactive anger rather than planned aggression. 'Vent' can be less targeted/hostile; 'snap at' is usually verbal and briefer.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: lash out meaning

column5: To look foolish or embarrassed because something one said, predicted, or attempted turned out to be wrong or failed.
column6: look foolish, be embarrassed, be humiliated, lose face
column7: He confidently predicted a landslide victory and ended up with egg on his face. / If the rumor turns out to be false, a lot of commentators will have egg on their faces.
column8: Usually result-oriented embarrassment after being publicly wrong. 'Lose face' is broader and culturally loaded; egg on one's face is colloquial and often mildly comic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: To have egg on your face

column5: Not deserving honor or respect because it is shameful, unethical, disloyal, or lacking integrity.
column7: He considered betraying his friend for money dishonorable. / The officer received a dishonorable discharge.
column8: US military 'dishonorable discharge' is a specific severe punitive discharge; ordinary adjective use is broader.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118, voca_0120 | search: dishonorable meaning

column5: A person with exceptional technical skill and artistry, especially in music; more broadly, someone highly accomplished in a particular craft. As adjective, displaying such mastery.
column6: master, expert, prodigy (not exact), highly skilled performer
column7: She's a virtuoso violinist. / The sequence is a virtuoso display of animation and timing.
column8: Traditionally strongly associated with musical performance, but figurative extensions are common: virtuoso performance, a virtuoso of negotiation. Plural virtuosos/virtuosi.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: virtuoso meaning
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::figurative topic::music topic::performance discovery::expertise discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column2: take your like and get out
column5: A joking way to say that something was annoyingly funny, clever, or effective: the speaker gives the post a 'like' while mock-telling its creator to leave.
column6: take my upvote and get out
column7: That pun was awful. Take your like and get out.
column8: Internet-comment phrasing. Often playful rather than genuinely hostile; variants use upvote, award, etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: take your like and get out meaning

column5: To interfere with, alter, damage, manipulate, or meddle with something without authorization, especially in a way that may compromise its proper state, evidence, safety, or function.
column6: interfere with, meddle with, manipulate, alter improperly
column7: Someone tampered with the lock. / The investigation found no evidence that the data had been tampered with.
column8: Tamper is normally used with 'with.' Common: tamper with evidence, equipment, packaging, data. Often implies improper/unauthorized interference.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: tamper meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern discovery::compromise discovery::trade-off discovery::evidence

column5: To smile, curl the lip, speak, or look in a way that shows contempt, scorn, or mocking superiority.
column6: smirk contemptuously, scoff, jeer, mock, curl one's lip
column7: He sneered at the cheap costume, which immediately made him less likable. / 'You call that an apology?' she sneered.
column8: Sneer is contemptuous; smirk is a self-satisfied smile and need not show contempt; scoff is verbal disbelief/mockery. Existing sneering card is adjectival; standalone verb/noun is productive.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: sneer

column5: A person who obtains money, influence, or support through deception, scams, opportunistic persuasion, or cynical exploitation; online, often someone accused of monetizing an audience or cause insincerely.
column6: con artist, scammer, hustler, fraud, charlatan
column7: Critics dismissed him as a political grifter who changes positions whenever there is money in it. / Online, 'grifter' is often thrown around more broadly than 'con artist.'
column8: From grift = swindle/petty fraud. Modern political/media use often implies cynical monetization or bad-faith opportunism, but it remains an accusation, not proof of fraud.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: grifter meaning
column12: entry::word usage::informal topic::internet topic::art topic::public_speaking topic::crime discovery::audience_engagement discovery::support

column5: Some nouns commonly take 'to' as a preposition followed by a noun or gerund, e.g. approach to doing, key to doing, solution to doing, obstacle to doing, objection to doing, commitment to doing.
column6: approach to, key to, solution to, objection to, commitment to
column7: Consistency is the key to building active vocabulary. / They found a practical solution to reducing waste. / She has no objection to working late.
column8: The crucial point is whether 'to' belongs to a prepositional construction rather than an infinitive. Not every noun + to uses a gerund: 'ability to do,' 'decision to do,' 'attempt to do' take infinitives.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: noun word like approach that requires gerund phrase like approach to doing something
column12: entry::construction topic::problem-solving topic::grammar discovery::solution_framing discovery::resolution discovery::commitment

column5: Trying to improve one's identity, image, lifestyle, or perceived status by intensely adopting or performing a chosen persona, aesthetic, role, or subculture.
column7: He jokingly called his new medieval wardrobe LARPmaxxing.
column8: Nonstandard internet formation: LARP + maxxing. Often humorous or mocking, implying that self-improvement has become performative role-play rather than something fully authentic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: larpmaxxing meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::humorous usage::informal topic::internet discovery::perception discovery::improvement

column5: Would benefit from, need, or welcome something; often used to express a mild need or to say that something needs improvement.
column6: could do with, would benefit from, need, could really use
column7: I could use a coffee. / This paragraph could use another example. / You look like you could use some sleep. / The app could use a little polish.
column8: Very common conversational softener. 'I could use X' ≈ I would welcome/need X. 'X could use some work' = X needs improvement. Often gentler than direct 'need.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: could use something meaning
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::conversational topic::construction discovery::expressing_need discovery::improvement

column5: A childbirth emergency in which the umbilical cord descends through the cervix/vagina ahead of or alongside the presenting part of the baby, creating a risk that the cord can be compressed and reduce blood/oxygen flow.
column7: The obstetrics lesson described umbilical cord prolapse as an emergency because cord compression can compromise fetal oxygenation.
column8: Medical vocabulary card. It describes a specific obstetric emergency; management is time-sensitive and belongs to trained medical care, not self-treatment.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: umbilical cord prolapse

column5: To use an earlier success, idea, foundation, result, or development as the basis for further progress; to develop or extend it rather than starting over.
column6: develop, expand on, capitalize on, extend
column7: The pilot had a strong start, but the series never really built on it. / Let's build on what worked in the first version instead of redesigning everything.
column8: In 'it never really built on that strong start,' the subject failed to turn the promising beginning into sustained development. Distinct from literally building on land/a foundation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: it never really built on that strong start. in this sentence, what "built on" means?

column5: Extremely neat, correct, respectable, restrained, and concerned with proper manners or behavior.
column6: very proper, decorous, strait-laced, prudish, buttoned-up
column7: She acts prim and proper around her grandparents. / The prim-and-proper school uniform contrasts with the character's chaotic personality.
column8: Can be admiring, teasing, or critical. Often implies stiffness or excessive concern with appearances/manners.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: prim and proper meaning

column5: To spin or rotate quickly and lightly, or to make something do so; as a noun, a spinning movement.
column7: She twirled the pen between her fingers.
column8: Raw search 'TWIRLE' is most plausibly a spelling variant/typo for modern twirl. Historical spelling twirle exists, but the normal modern headword is twirl.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: TWIRLE MEANIG

column5: A risky or uncertain undertaking, especially a business project; as a verb, to dare to go, say, or do something despite risk or uncertainty.
column7: The new venture could be profitable. / Few hikers ventured beyond the marked trail.
column8: Existing venture a guess is one specific construction; this card captures the broader noun and verb.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: venture meaning

column5: For something to be noticed, recognized, understood, or produce a mental reaction; if something 'doesn't register,' the person fails to notice, process, or treat it as significant.
column6: sink in, be noticed, be processed, click, land
column7: I heard the words, but they didn't register until a few seconds later. / If 'native English doesn't register' was the source wording, it likely means native/natural English isn't being recognized or mentally registering as such, though the exact intended subject needs source context.
column8: This is the cognitive sense of register, not sign up/record. Existing cards mention 'sink in/register'; this search is useful because 'X doesn't register' is highly productive. Raw sentence is semantically incomplete/odd, so preserve uncertainty.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: what does the word "register" mean in the following sentence, "native english doesn't register."

column5: Inflammation or disease of one or more joints, causing symptoms such as pain, stiffness, swelling, or reduced movement; an umbrella term covering many different conditions.
column7: Her knee stiffness is caused by osteoarthritis. / Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease and is very different from ordinary wear-and-tear osteoarthritis.
column8: Arthritis is not one single disease. Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, psoriatic arthritis, etc. differ substantially in cause and treatment. Existing gout card is one specific form.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: arthritis

column5: A position or period of increasing or dominant power, influence, or control.
column7: The party's rapid ascendance changed the political landscape.
column8: Ascendance is valid, though ascendancy is also very common for a state of dominant influence. Do not confuse with ascent = the act of rising/climbing.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: ascendance meaning in english

column5: A person, team, animal, product, or other competitor that enters a contest, race, examination, market, or field.
column7: The race attracted more than 500 entrants. / The new company is a strong entrant in the streaming market.
column8: Entrant emphasizes entering/being entered. In business, 'new entrant' = a firm newly entering a market. Not every participant is necessarily an entrant in all contexts.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: define entrants

column5: Verb: remove an animal's reproductive capacity; figuratively, deprive something of power, force, effectiveness, or distinctive character. Adjective/noun: a grammatical gender/category neither masculine nor feminine in languages that use it.
column6: spay/castrate (context-specific); weaken, emasculate, defang, render ineffective
column7: The cat was neutered at the clinic. / The compromise neutered the proposal by removing its strongest provision. / German has neuter nouns.
column8: Raw 'neutere' repaired. In animal care, neuter can be generic, though castrate/spay are sex-specific. Figurative use can be forceful/negative.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: neutere meaning
column12: entry::word usage::figurative topic::grammar topic::animals discovery::figurative_extension discovery::removal

column5: A meme phrase used to praise a moment as extraordinarily dramatic, beautiful, satisfying, ridiculous, or 'cinematic'; often sincere and ironic at the same time.
column6: peak cinema, cinema, masterpiece (hyperbolic), kino (internet slang)
column7: The villain entered exactly as the music dropped—absolute cinema. / The cat knocked over the cup, stared into the camera, and walked away. Absolute cinema.
column8: Associated online with a reaction image of filmmaker Martin Scorsese raising his hands. Often applied humorously to things that are not films at all. Hyperbolic internet praise rather than literal film criticism.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: absolute cinema meaning
