column2: pry it out of my cold, dead hands
column3: /ˌpraɪ ɪt aʊt əv maɪ ˌkoʊld ded ˈhændz/
column5: A dramatic way to say one will never willingly give something up: the only way to take it is after the speaker is dead.
column6: you'll never get it from me, over my dead body, I'm never giving it up
column7: You can pry this old controller out of my cold, dead hands. / I know the app is outdated, but you'll have to pry it from my cold, dead hands.
column8: Often humorous when applied to trivial possessions/preferences. Related to the famous 'from my cold, dead hands' formulation in U.S. gun-rights rhetoric, but now widely repurposed as hyperbole.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: pry it out of my cold dead hands meaing

column2: the opposite of a double whammy
column5: There is no single fixed opposite of 'double whammy.' Depending on context, say a double win, two wins at once, a one-two boost, a double benefit, a win-win, or 'two birds with one stone.'
column6: double win, double benefit, win-win, two birds with one stone
column7: The new schedule saves money and gives us more free time—a double win. / It's the opposite of a double whammy: we got two benefits at once.
column8: Double whammy = two bad blows/problems together. 'Win-win' emphasizes benefits for multiple sides, while 'two birds with one stone' emphasizes achieving two goals with one action; neither is an exact lexical antonym.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: double whammy opposite

column2: have trouble / difficulty / a problem / struggle / a hard time with something
column5: All express difficulty, but nuance differs: have trouble doing X is very natural/general; have difficulty is more formal; have a problem with X may mean difficulty OR objection/disapproval; struggle with emphasizes ongoing effort; have a hard time is conversational and can include emotional difficulty.
column6: have difficulty, struggle with, find difficult
column7: I have trouble remembering names. / She had difficulty understanding the legal wording. / I have a problem with that policy (= I object to it). / He struggles with pronunciation. / I had a hard time adjusting after the move.
column8: Grammar: trouble/difficulty/a hard time + -ing; struggle with + noun/-ing; have a problem with + noun/-ing. 'I have a problem doing X' exists but 'with' is often clearer.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: have trouble vs difficulty vs problem vs struggle vs a hard time with something
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::formal usage::conversational topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::emphasis discovery::continuity

column5: The crucial, difficult, or especially interesting question whose answer would resolve the main uncertainty.
column6: the big question, key question, crucial question
column7: Why did the system fail in the first place? That's the million-dollar question. / The million-dollar question is whether users will actually pay for it.
column8: Hyperbolic; not literally worth a million dollars. Variants use other large amounts ('$64,000 question') historically.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: million dollar question meaning

column5: Broken or not working; caught doing something wrong or illegal; in some contexts, exposed or found out.
column7: The printer is busted, and I got busted trying to fix it without permission.
column8: Very informal. Multiple common senses derive from bust: broken/damaged and caught/arrested/exposed.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: busted meanig

column5: Used to give someone information you think they should be aware of, often as a warning, clarification, or heads-up.
column7: Just so you know, the last train leaves at eleven.
column8: Tone ranges from helpful to mildly pointed or defensive depending on delivery.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111, voca_0117 | search: just so you know meaning

column5: To manipulate or exploit a system, rules, metrics, or process to gain an advantage; also to gamble/play games in other contexts.
column6: exploit, manipulate, work, rig (stronger), optimize around
column7: Companies learned how to game the ranking algorithm. / If a test rewards memorizing one pattern, students will naturally learn to game it.
column8: Very common construction game the system. Unlike cheat, gaming a system can exploit loopholes while technically following rules. 'Game' can also mean play video games ('I game on PC'), a separate verb sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: game verb meaing

column5: To ultimately be determined by, reduced to, or depend on one essential factor or choice.
column6: boil down to, depend on, hinge on, amount to, ultimately be about
column7: In the end, the decision comes down to cost. / Whether I keep the card comes down to one question: will I actually use it? / A lot of the disagreement comes down to different assumptions.
column8: Often used after stripping away complexity: 'It all comes down to...' The complement is usually a noun, noun phrase, or wh-clause. 'Boil down to' emphasizes reduction to essentials; 'come down to' can also emphasize the decisive factor/choice.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: come down to meaning

column5: The act of insulting, attacking, or belittling someone by applying offensive, mocking, or derogatory labels instead of addressing the substance of an issue.
column7: The debate collapsed into name-calling within ten minutes. / Calling everyone who disagrees an idiot is name-calling, not an argument.
column8: Can range from childish insults to politically loaded labels. In argument analysis, name-calling is often treated as ad hominem-style rhetoric, though not every negative descriptive label is automatically fallacious.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: name-calling meaing
column12: entry::word usage::derogatory usage::offensive usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly usage::evaluative discovery::debate_language

column5: To change from supporting, liking, or favoring someone or something to opposing or rejecting them.
column6: oppose, become hostile to, abandon support for
column7: Public opinion turned against the proposal.
column8: Unlike turn on someone, this often emphasizes a change in allegiance or attitude rather than a sudden attack.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: turn against meaning

column5: To be an extremely enthusiastic or devoted fan of someone or something; as a noun, such a fan.
column7: I've stanned that singer since her first album.
column8: Originated from Eminem's song 'Stan' and broadened in internet/fandom language. Can be playful/self-aware or imply excessive devotion.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: stan someone meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::slang usage::playful usage::informal

column5: A casual way to acknowledge that another person's point, reaction, preference, limitation, or criticism is reasonable or understandable, even if you do not fully agree.
column6: fair enough, that's reasonable, I can see that, valid
column7: 'I stopped after three episodes because the pacing was too slow.' 'Yeah, that's fair.' / 'I don't want to spend $30 on an app.' 'That's fair.'
column8: Often functions as low-key concession/validation rather than literal judgment of fairness. 'Fair enough' is very close and sometimes sounds slightly more final.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: that's fair meanig
column12: entry::discourse_expression usage::casual usage::conversational usage::rhetorical usage::informal discovery::agreement discovery::criticism discovery::debate_language

column5: Designed to be seen, used, or managed by teachers rather than directly by students.
column7: The platform has a teacher-facing dashboard for assignments and analytics.
column8: Product/education jargon built on X-facing = oriented toward/intended for X.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: teacher facing meaning

column5: A 180-degree turn, literally in drill/marching; figuratively, a complete reversal of opinion, policy, plan, or behavior.
column7: The company made an abrupt about-face on remote work. / About-face! the drill instructor ordered.
column8: Hyphenated noun. Figurative 'do/make an about-face.' Compare 'U-turn,' especially BrE/politics.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: about-face meaning
column12: entry::interjection usage::figurative usage::british_english discovery::policy_discussion discovery::figurative_extension discovery::subjective_judgment

column5: The siphonophore genus that includes the Portuguese man o' war (Physalia physalis) and related bluebottle forms.
column6: Physalia genus, Portuguese man o' war genus
column7: Physalia physalis is the scientific name commonly used for the Portuguese man o' war. / Physalia floats at the ocean surface and trails long tentacles below.
column8: Useful taxonomy hook for カツオノエボシ. Physalia is a hydrozoan siphonophore genus; the organism is colonial, with specialized zooids rather than one ordinary jellyfish body.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: Physalia
column12: entry::proper_noun usage::specialist usage::scientific topic::biology topic::science discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A person's face or facial appearance, especially when described dramatically, artistically, or in older/literary language.
column7: A grim visage appeared in the doorway. / The statue's serene visage contrasts with the violence of the scene.
column8: Much more literary than face. Often used for striking expressions/appearances or personified objects. Compare countenance, also formal/literary.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: visage meaning

column5: To work through details, disagreements, or difficulties through sustained discussion/effort until an agreement, plan, wording, or solution is produced.
column6: work out, thrash out, hash out, negotiate, iron out
column7: We spent an hour hammering out the final wording. / The two sides are trying to hammer out a deal.
column8: Metaphor of shaping metal by repeated blows. Common: hammer out an agreement/deal/compromise/details. Suggests effort and back-and-forth.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: hammer things out meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative topic::work topic::communication topic::problem-solving discovery::negotiation discovery::solution_framing discovery::agreement discovery::resolution

column5: To be wearing one's complete outfit, costume, uniform, or distinctive set of clothes/accessories.
column6: be fully dressed up, have the whole outfit on, be in full costume
column7: He showed up with his full cowboy get-up on—boots, hat, belt buckle, everything. / Once I had my full get-up on, the costume suddenly looked much better than it did piece by piece.
column8: Get-up = outfit, often conspicuous, themed, old-fashioned, humorous, or costume-like. 'Full get-up' emphasizes the whole ensemble, not merely being dressed.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: have my full get up on meaning
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::dated usage::humorous topic::fashion

column5: To flatter, please, or act excessively deferential toward someone—especially a superior—in order to gain favor or advantage.
column6: brown-nose, butter up, curry favor with, ingratiate oneself with
column7: He's always sucking up to the manager before promotion season. / She refused to suck up to people just because they had status.
column8: Object usually person/authority. Butter up can be a one-off attempt; suck up to often suggests habitual servility/opportunism.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: suck-up to someone meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::disparaging usage::persuasive usage::evaluative discovery::persuasion

column5: Descendants or offspring; in supernatural fiction, can refer to beings created, sired, or descended from another being.
column7: The vampire's progeny were expected to show loyalty to their maker.
column8: Existing progeny card gives the general sense; preserve this contextual card because the original Anne Rice search asks how the kinship/lineage term functions in a fictional social system.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: do progenies pledge allegiance in Anne Rice's books?

column5: Distorted, bizarre, ugly, unnatural, or disturbingly exaggerated; in art, a fantastic ornamental form combining strange human, animal, or plant elements.
column7: The creature has a grotesque smile that is almost human but not quite. / The contrast between the cheerful music and the grotesque violence makes the scene deeply unsettling. / Medieval buildings sometimes feature carved grotesques.
column8: Grotesque can describe appearance, behavior, inequality/excess ('a grotesque waste of money'), or an artistic mode mixing comic and horrifying. A grotesque is not necessarily a gargoyle: gargoyles specifically function as waterspouts.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: grotesque

column5: A weight suspended so it can swing freely back and forth; figuratively, something that shifts repeatedly between opposing positions or extremes.
column7: Public opinion often seems to swing like a pendulum between the two extremes.
column8: Common metaphor: the pendulum swings back/toward X.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: pendulum meaning

column5: To fail badly, decline sharply, or deliberately perform poorly; also to cause something to fail or plunge.
column7: The stock tanked after the announcement.
column8: Existing 'tank it' focuses on intentionally losing; standalone tank also commonly means fall/fail dramatically without intentionality.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: tank verb meaing

column5: The most powerful, successful, dominant, or important person or group in a situation.
column7: After the merger, everyone wondered who would emerge as top dog.
column8: Existing cards use top dog as a synonym, but no standalone card covers the expression.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: top dog meaning

column5: Expressing approval of someone or something seen as confidently authentic, unapologetic, bold, or correct despite social pressure.
column7: She said exactly what she thought and the comments called her based.
column8: Highly context-dependent internet slang. It can be sincere, ironic, political, or simply mean 'I approve.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112, voca_0113 | search: based meaning slang
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::ironic usage::informal topic::internet discovery::social_approval

column5: A playful or context-built expression, likely wordplay around flapjack rather than a widely established idiom; its exact intended meaning depends on the source scene.
column7: 'Flap your jacks' sounds like deliberately silly wordplay rather than ordinary English. / If a character says it as a command, the humor may come from splitting 'flapjack' into flap + jacks.
column8: Not a standard dictionary idiom. Preserve rather than invent a fixed meaning. Nearby searches for 'flap out' and 'flapjack' strongly suggest the original context involved wordplay or misunderstanding.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: flap your jacks meaning

column5: Organized into relatively independent components that can be combined, replaced, rearranged, reused, or developed separately; figuratively used for ideas, workflows, software, courses, writing structures, etc.
column7: A modular workflow lets us improve the enrichment stage without rebuilding the whole pipeline. / The course is modular, so students can take units independently.
column8: Existing modular-vs-single-unit card covers structural contrast. Figurative use preserves the same core metaphor: separable/recombinable components.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: modular meaning figuratively

column5: Forming, resembling, or relating to a network or netlike structure.
column7: The tissue has a reticular pattern. / The reticular formation is a network of neurons in the brainstem.
column8: Technical anatomy/biology adjective from Latin reticulum 'small net.' Common in reticular formation, reticular fibers, reticular pattern.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: reticular

column5: To try to enjoy the advantages of two incompatible alternatives or positions while avoiding their disadvantages; often used critically.
column6: have the best of both worlds (not always critical), want both sides, eat one's cake and have it too
column7: You can't demand total creative freedom and then blame everyone else for every decision—you can't have it both ways. / He wants privacy but also constant public attention; he can't have it both ways.
column8: Usually critical because the two desired positions conflict. 'Best of both worlds' can describe a genuinely compatible combination and is more positive.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: have it both ways

column5: An outward appearance of magnificence, importance, wealth, dignity, or greatness that hides a less impressive, insecure, ordinary, or flawed reality.
column6: pretense of grandeur, grand exterior, veneer of magnificence
column7: The hotel maintained a façade of grandeur even as the rooms behind the lobby fell apart. / His pompous language created a façade of grandeur around a fairly simple idea.
column8: Not a fixed idiom, but a natural metaphor. Façade = front/appearance concealing reality; grandeur = magnificence/greatness. Related 'delusions of grandeur' concerns an exaggerated belief about one's own importance, not merely appearance.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: facade of grandeur meaning

column5: Trying to control other people in an overbearing, bossy, or authoritarian way.
column7: Her manager was so domineering that nobody felt comfortable making decisions without permission. / The character can be protective without becoming domineering.
column8: Strongly negative and specifically interpersonal. Dominant can be neutral/descriptive; domineering implies excessive control over others.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: define domineering

column5: A person who deliberately provokes strong reactions, controversy, anger, or conflict; agent provocateur can specifically mean someone who incites others into illegal acts, sometimes as an infiltrator.
column7: He's less a serious commentator than a professional provocateur who knows exactly what will make people angry. / The character acts as a provocateur, constantly pushing the others into confrontation.
column8: Existing cards use provocateur as a synonym, but the word itself has useful nuance: provoking reaction may be the person's role/strategy, not merely incidental offensiveness.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: provocateurs

column5: Constrained, obligated, shaped, or strongly limited by inherited customs, conventions, or traditional expectations.
column6: constrained by tradition, tied to custom, tradition-bound
column7: The family felt bound by tradition to continue the ceremony. / The genre isn't bound by tradition; creators can reinvent the format.
column8: Bound by = restricted/obligated by. Can be neutral (connected through shared tradition) but often implies reduced freedom.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: bound by tradition meaning

column2: spaghetti kiss / Lady and the Tramp kiss
column5: A romantic-comedy image in which two people eat opposite ends of the same strand of spaghetti/noodle and unexpectedly meet in a kiss, strongly associated with Disney's Lady and the Tramp.
column7: The scene parodies the classic Lady and the Tramp spaghetti kiss. / They tried the spaghetti-kiss bit as a joke and immediately started laughing.
column8: Not a formal idiom; it is a recognizable visual trope/cultural reference. Useful for describing recreations/parodies without quoting copyrighted dialogue.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: lady and the tramp style spaghetti kiss

column5: Slow to understand, notice, or grasp what someone means, especially a joke, hint, or situation.
column6: slow to catch on, not quick on the draw, dense (harsher), a bit slow
column7: It took me a minute to realize she was joking—I'm a little slow on the uptake today. / He's not stupid; he's just sometimes slow on the uptake with sarcasm.
column8: Can be mildly self-deprecating/playful, but calling someone else slow on the uptake may sound insulting. Uptake here = understanding/mental reception.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: slow on the uptake meaning

column5: A media and attention environment in which anger, controversy, and moral outrage are repeatedly produced or amplified because they drive clicks, engagement, influence, or revenue.
column6: attention economy driven by outrage, ragebait ecosystem
column7: The creator argued that the outrage economy rewards the most inflammatory interpretation.
column8: Analytical phrase rather than a single fixed technical term; closely related to ragebait and engagement incentives.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: outrage economy
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::technical usage::specialist topic::business topic::media topic::environment discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To behave, look, or develop according to a rule, standard, pattern, convention, or group expectation; also to match/be consistent with something.
column7: He felt pressure to conform at school. / The design must conform to accessibility standards. / The results conform to the predicted pattern.
column8: Patterns: conform to a standard/norm; conform with can mean be consistent with, but 'conform to' is very common. Conformity can be voluntary or pressured.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: conform meaning

column5: Honestly or directly, without exaggeration or disguise; also used as an intensifier meaning genuinely or simply.
column7: Straight up, I didn't expect the movie to be that good.
column8: Informal. Other literal senses exist ('vertically upward', drinks served without ice depending on context), so context matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111 | search: straight up meaning

column5: Existing only in, belonging specifically to, or characteristic of one particular person, thing, group, place, system, etc.
column6: specific to, peculiar to, exclusive to, distinctive of
column7: That pronunciation pattern isn't unique to you; lots of learners do it. / The feature is unique to the paid version.
column8: Natural pattern unique to X. Strictly, unique means one-of-a-kind, but modern usage also commonly means distinctive/specific to a limited entity/group.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: unique to you meaning

column5: To reduce in quality, condition, status, dignity, or performance; to humiliate or treat someone as less worthy; scientifically, to break down or deteriorate chemically/physically.
column6: deteriorate, decline, erode, break down; demean, humiliate, debase
column7: Image quality degrades each time the file is recompressed. / The plastic slowly degrades in sunlight. / He felt degraded by the way they spoke to him in front of everyone.
column8: Can be intransitive ('the signal degraded') or transitive ('compression degraded the image'). Human/dignity sense = demean. Scientific degradation is neutral process language, unlike moral/social degrading.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: degrade meaning

column5: The process of creating/searching an index or organizing data for retrieval; in finance/economics, linking values to an index or following an index-based investment strategy.
column7: Database indexing can make queries much faster. / Wage indexing links pay adjustments to a price index. / Passive index investing aims to track a market index.
column8: Meaning varies strongly by domain: databases/search, publishing, economics, investing, cognition. Related verb index.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: define indexing

column5: To accept an unexpected situation and adapt to it rather than resisting or becoming upset.
column6: go with the flow, adapt, take it in stride
column7: The schedule changed again, so we just rolled with it.
column8: Often suggests flexibility in the face of uncertainty or inconvenience.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: roll with it meaning

column5: In North American English, a pancake. In British English, a baked oat bar made with oats, butter, and syrup/sugar.
column7: The diner served a stack of flapjacks with maple syrup. / In Britain, a flapjack is usually a chewy baked oat square rather than a pancake.
column8: A classic AmE/BrE lexical difference. Context can radically change the food image. Also useful for understanding playful compounds/wordplay such as the nearby raw search 'flap your jacks.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: flapjack

column5: To use a supply, resource, experience, knowledge, or ability; also, for time to pass/approach, or literally to pull clothing on.
column6: draw upon, tap into, rely on, make use of
column7: She drew on years of teaching experience to explain the concept simply. / The film draws heavily on 1970s horror. / As evening drew on, the streets became quieter.
column8: Highly polysemous. Resource sense often takes experience/knowledge/reserves/tradition. 'Draw on/upon' can mean use as a source. Time sense: night/evening/winter draws on. Do not confuse draw on paper = make a picture on a surface.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: draw on meaning

column5: To act as though an embarrassing, awkward, suspicious, or important event is insignificant, intentional, or not worth noticing.
column6: brush off, laugh off, pretend it was nothing
column7: I tripped onstage but tried to play it off like it was part of the joke.
column8: Often means conceal embarrassment or significance through casual behavior.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: play it off | WordReference Forums

column5: Very strongly or keenly conscious of something, especially a problem, risk, difference, or uncomfortable fact.
column7: He was acutely aware that everyone in the room was watching him.
column8: Stronger than simply aware; often used when the awareness is impossible to ignore.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: acutely aware meaning

column5: To keep evil, harmful forces, bad luck, or danger away through protection, ritual, magic, belief, or metaphorical preventive action.
column6: repel, avert, keep at bay, protect against, drive away
column7: The villagers hung charms above the doors to ward off evil. / In the story, the repeated line functions like an incantation meant to ward off evil spirits.
column8: Ward off is broader: ward off illness, attack, criticism, danger. Incantation WID153 = spoken magical formula; apotropaic describes something whose purpose is to avert evil/harm.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: it's an incantation to ward off evil
column12: entry::phrase usage::conversational usage::figurative usage::ceremonial discovery::risk discovery::prevention

column5: To be distracted or diverted from the main subject, task, route, or goal by something secondary.
column6: get distracted, get diverted, go off track, lose the thread
column7: I opened the article to check one word and got sidetracked for forty minutes. / We got sidetracked talking about the soundtrack and never answered the original question.
column8: Often unintentional. Sidetrack someone = divert them; get sidetracked = become diverted. Compared with go off on a tangent, sidetracked can involve activity/tasks as well as conversation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115, voca_0121 | search: get sidetracked

column5: A loose network of online communities and ideologies focused on men, masculinity, dating, gender relations, or men's grievances, including groups such as men's-rights activists, pickup artists, incels, and red-pill communities.
column6: male-oriented online ecosystem, men's-rights sphere (partial), red-pill ecosystem (partial)
column7: The documentary traces how several influencers moved from dating advice into the broader manosphere. / 'Manosphere' is an umbrella label, so two communities placed under it may disagree sharply with each other.
column8: The term is broad and often critical; it does not mean every online space for men. Some parts focus on men's issues, while others are associated with misogyny, anti-feminism, or extremist rhetoric. Use specific subgroup labels when precision matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: manosphere
column12: entry::term entry::word usage::critical usage::rhetorical topic::dating topic::internet topic::culture topic::environment discovery::debate_language

column5: The clear expression/formulation of ideas; the production of speech sounds by positioning/moving speech organs; a joint or connection permitting movement; in figures/models, movable joints and their range.
column7: Her articulation of the problem was clearer than mine. / Good articulation makes consonants easier to understand. / This action figure has excellent articulation in the shoulders and hips.
column8: Important polysemy for the surrounding figurine/figure search context: collectors use articulation for movable joints. Existing 'articulation disorder' is only the speech-clinical compound.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: articulation meaning

column5: To interpret or frame a behavior, trait, emotion, identity, or social phenomenon primarily as a disease, disorder, or psychological abnormality, sometimes excessively or inappropriately.
column6: medicalize (overlapping), diagnose, treat as pathological, problematize (not exact)
column7: Not every awkward social habit needs to be pathologized as a disorder. / Critics argue that the framework pathologizes normal grief. / Medicine can identify genuine pathology without pathologizing every variation in human behavior.
column8: Often critical in psychology/social discourse. Medicalize = bring something under medical framing/treatment; pathologize more specifically casts it as abnormal/diseased. It does NOT mean merely 'study pathology.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: pathologize
column12: entry::word entry::discourse_expression usage::critical usage::debate-friendly topic::psychology topic::health topic::medicine discovery::debate_language

column5: A dramatic statement of moral or cultural disappointment meaning that people or society seem to have declined to an embarrassingly, shockingly, or morally degraded level.
column6: how far we've fallen, society has sunk so low, what has humanity come to?
column7: I opened the comments, saw people cheering for the scam, and thought, 'Humanity has fallen so low.' / It's often used half-seriously or hyperbolically about something absurdly disappointing.
column8: 'Fall/sink so low' is the productive idiom; 'humanity has fallen so low' applies it to society as a whole. Tone can range from genuine moral despair to melodramatic internet humor.

column5: Legally responsible for something; or likely to do, experience, or suffer something, often undesirable.

column6: adjust vs take up vs skilled
column7: We adapted the workflow to the new format. / The team adopted a new policy. / She's adept at spotting subtle wording differences.
column8: Pronunciation matters: adapt /ə-DAPT/, adopt /ə-DOPT/ (AmE), adept /ə-DEPT/. Patterns: adapt to/for/from; adopt a policy/method/child; adept at + noun/gerund.

column5: Short for 'voluntary celibate': a person who is not having sex or pursuing sexual relationships by choice, often contrasted with incel ('involuntary celibate').
column7: He described himself as a volcel because dating was simply not a priority for him. / In forum slang, volcel is often contrasted with incel, though people argue about where the boundary lies.
column8: Internet coinage from voluntary + cel(ibate). May be sincere, ironic, or used accusatorily ('you're a volcel, not an incel'). Do not assume religious celibacy; motivation varies.

column5: Feeling deep wonder, admiration, reverence, or amazement toward someone or something.

column8: Raw search 'since the slice of bread' likely points to this fixed expression. Usually playful or ironic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: since the slice of bread meaning

column5: A feeling of relief after a worry, burden, responsibility, or uncertainty is removed.
column6: a load off one's mind, relief, burden lifted
column7: Finishing the project was a huge weight off my shoulders. / Hearing that the test was negative took a weight off her shoulders.
column8: Common forms: be a weight off my shoulders; take a weight off someone's shoulders. Metaphorical burden.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: weight off my shoulders

column5: A point at which lines, routes, branches, or connections meet; a distinct point or unit in a network, structure, anatomy, or data system.
column6: junction, connection point, vertex, hub, network point
column7: Each computer on the network acts as a node. / In a graph, an edge connects one node to another. / The city's central station is a major transportation node.
column8: Meaning varies by field: network node, graph/tree node, lymph node, plant node, transportation node. Core image is a distinct point in a larger connected structure. In graph theory 'vertex' is the precise counterpart; in networks 'hub' usually means a particularly connected/important node.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: define nodes

column5: At an early stage or early in a period of time; sometimes simply early.
column6: early on, at an early stage
column7: It's early doors, but the new manager already looks promising.
column8: Distinctive British expression, especially common in sports commentary and informal speech.

column5: Good at noticing, understanding, or interpreting subtle details, feelings, or situations.
column7: That was a perceptive observation about why the scene feels unsettling.
column8: Usually complimentary: it suggests noticing more than is immediately obvious and understanding its significance.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: perceptive

column5: Browsing possible partners, jobs, homes, options, or opportunities without serious commitment or immediate intention to choose/buy; a metaphorical extension of literal window-shopping.

column7: He was on the dating app mostly window-shopping rather than trying to meet anyone. / Employees sometimes start window-shopping for other jobs before they actually decide to leave.
column8: Not one fixed slang definition: the metaphor transfers 'look but don't buy/commit' into other domains. In dating it can sound objectifying, so tone/context matter.

column7: People in the comments said the model mogged everyone else in the photo.

column6: consider a dreamer; require a dreamer

column6: bite/sipful; tongue-twisting phrase; earful; well said (contextual)
column7: That's a mouthful of a title. / He took a mouthful of soup. / She gave him a mouthful for being late. / 'You said a mouthful' means strong agreement, not criticism.
column8: Existing WID2477 covers the core noun senses. This card exists because the search explicitly asked for 'mouthful expressions' and links the idiom family without collapsing their distinct meanings.

column2: hold oneself out to be/as something
column5: To represent or present oneself to others as having a particular identity, status, qualification, or authority.
column6: represent oneself as, present oneself as
column7: He held himself out as an expert despite having no formal training.
column8: Common in legal/formal contexts, especially when discussing how a person represented their qualifications or status.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: hold oneself out to be meaning

column5: To practice fighting with controlled blows, especially in boxing/martial arts; figuratively, to exchange arguments, teasing, or verbal attacks in a lively competitive way.
column6: practice fight, box; trade barbs, joust, banter, clash
column7: The two fighters sparred for three rounds without going full force. / The hosts spent half the podcast sparring over which sequel was worse.
column8: Figurative spar often suggests back-and-forth rather than one-sided hostility. Spar with someone over/about an issue. A spar is also a pole/beam in nautical/structural contexts—a separate sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: spar meaning

column5: A difficult struggle in which success requires sustained effort because circumstances are unfavorable.
column6: hard struggle, difficult fight, steep challenge, fight an uphill battle
column7: Convincing people to switch after years of habit is an uphill battle. / The anime had almost no marketing, so finding a large audience was always going to be an uphill battle.
column8: Metaphor of fighting while moving uphill. Often 'face/fight an uphill battle.' Does not mean impossible—just significantly disadvantaged/difficult.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114, voca_0115 | search: uphill battle meaning

column5: To discover, determine, or establish something with reasonable certainty, especially by investigation, checking, or evidence.
column6: determine, establish, find out, verify, learn
column7: Investigators could not ascertain the cause of the failure. / I checked the workbook to ascertain which WordID was actually correct.
column8: More formal than find out. Common objects: facts, identity, cause, extent, whether/what/how. Does not mean merely guess or assume.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: ascertain meaning

column5: Adopt = take something up, accept it, begin using it, or legally become a parent. Adapt = change something—or oneself—so it fits new conditions, purposes, or media.
column7: The team adopted a new workflow, then adapted it to fit the smaller project. / The film adapts the novel rather than adopting it unchanged.
column8: Memory hook: adopt = take it as yours/use it; adapt = alter to fit. A company adopts a policy; it adapts the policy to local law. An organism adapts to its environment.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: adopt vs adapt

column2: the boulder of Sisyphus / Sisyphus's boulder
column5: The huge stone Sisyphus must repeatedly push uphill in Greek myth; figuratively, a burden or task that must be struggled with again and again without permanent resolution.
column6: Sisyphean burden, endless burden, recurring task
column7: Every morning the backlog returned like Sisyphus's boulder. / For him, maintaining the old system became a boulder he pushed uphill only to watch it roll back down.
column8: Not a fixed idiom as such; 'Sisyphus's boulder' is a recognizable allusion. The key image is not merely heaviness but repetition: apparent progress is repeatedly undone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: boulder of sisyphus meaning

column5: Disparaging something you cannot have or failed to obtain, often as a way to protect your pride by pretending it was undesirable anyway.
column6: rationalization, dismissing what one can't have, resentment disguised as contempt
column7: He didn't get the promotion and suddenly started saying the job was terrible anyway—classic sour grapes.
column8: From Aesop's fable 'The Fox and the Grapes': the fox cannot reach the grapes and concludes they must be sour. Japanese 酸っぱい葡萄 maps directly to this concept.

column5: A magic spell or curse intended to cause harm or bad luck; as a verb, to cast such a spell on someone or something. In computing/mathematics, hex can also abbreviate hexadecimal.
column6: curse, spell, jinx, bewitch; hexadecimal (technical abbreviation)
column7: The witch put a hex on the prince. / He joked that the team must be hexed after losing five finals in a row. / In programming, FF is a common hex representation of 255.
column8: Magic sense is common in fantasy. Hex vs curse: hex often suggests a deliberately cast magical spell; curse is broader. Technical hex = base-16/hexadecimal is unrelated in meaning.

column7: The article says the DSA requires certain online platforms to follow EU rules—there DSA means Digital Services Act. / In a cryptography textbook, DSA may mean Digital Signature Algorithm.
column8: There is no single context-free definition. Preserve the acronym card because the raw search lacks context. NIST uses DSA for Digital Signature Algorithm; other fields use the same letters differently.

column6: individual speech variety, personal dialect, individual language use
column7: Everyone has an idiolect shaped by where they've lived, what they watch, and whom they talk to. / Her idiolect includes expressions she picked up from several regions.
column8: Raw 'ideolect' repaired to idiolect. Contrast dialect/sociolect, which characterize groups; idiolect focuses on an individual.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: ideolect meaning

column5: To say something that has been worrying, burdening, irritating, or emotionally weighing on you, so that you feel relieved afterward.
column6: unburden oneself, vent, confess, air something, get it out
column7: Can I tell you something? I just need to get it off my chest. / She finally got years of resentment off her chest. / Writing the message helped me get the whole thing off my chest, even though I never sent it.
column8: Raw 'get the load off your chest' blends this idiom with 'take a load off.' Standard is get something/it off your chest. Vent = express frustration; confess = admit something hidden/wrong; this idiom covers many emotional burdens.

column5: To feel hesitant, embarrassed, or reluctant about doing or discussing something because of shyness or self-consciousness.
column6: feel hesitant about, be embarrassed about
column7: Don't feel shy about asking for clarification.
column8: Natural pattern: be/feel shy about + noun or -ing form.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: feel shy about meaning

column5: Originally an evil spirit or devil; also a cruel/wicked person. Informally, someone intensely devoted or addicted to something, especially in compounds such as coffee fiend.
column6: demon, devil; monster; addict, fanatic, junkie (contextual)
column7: The legend describes a fiend that haunts the forest. / She's a coffee fiend—she knows every café in the neighborhood. / The villain is portrayed as a sadistic fiend.
column8: Existing fiending WID4515 derives from fiend. Modern playful compounds X fiend often mean someone who craves/loves X intensely; 'drug fiend' is harsher and historically stigmatizing.

column5: To firmly decide, promise, or agree to devote oneself, one's time/resources, or future action to a person, plan, responsibility, relationship, or goal.
column6: commit, pledge, promise, dedicate oneself, undertake
column7: Before buying the annual plan, I wanted to be sure I could make the commitment. / They weren't ready to make a long-term commitment to the relationship. / She made a commitment to practice every day.
column8: Common patterns: make a commitment to someone/something; make a commitment to do something. Commitment can be practical, moral, financial, or romantic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: make a commitment

column5: Extremely tiring, demanding, and difficult, especially over a sustained period.
column7: The last section of the hike was grueling. / Editing a two-hour video on a tight deadline turned into a grueling week of late nights.
column8: Grueling emphasizes exhausting ordeal. Strenuous emphasizes effort/exertion; arduous emphasizes difficulty and sustained labor; punishing suggests exceptionally harsh demands.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define grueling

column5: To gradually disperse, fade, or disappear; to cause something such as heat, energy, smoke, tension, fear, or clouds to spread out and vanish. Also, to waste money/energy through careless living.
column6: disperse, scatter, fade, evaporate, dissolve; squander
column7: The morning fog dissipated by noon. / The heat is dissipated through the metal fins. / Her anxiety began to dissipate once she understood what had happened. / He dissipated much of his fortune.
column8: Can be intransitive or transitive. Scientific use: dissipate energy/heat. Emotional/atmospheric use: tension, fear, doubts dissipate. 'Dissipated' can also mean dissolute/self-indulgent, a less common literary sense.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define dissipates

column5: Both mean move away while wandering. Wander off more strongly frames leaving a specific place/person/group or going where one should not; wander away emphasizes increasing distance or gradual movement away.
column6: stray off/away, drift away, roam away
column7: The toddler wandered off in the store, so we had to look for him. / We watched the deer wander away into the trees. / My attention wandered off is possible, but 'my mind wandered' is usually more natural.
column8: Often interchangeable physically, but off commonly carries a 'left the group/place' event boundary; away highlights direction/distance. For abstract deviation from rules/topics, stray from or drift away from may be more natural.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: wander off vs wander away

column5: A very small opening in skin, plant/animal tissue, rock, or another material through which substances may pass; especially openings associated with hair follicles and sweat/sebum on skin.
column7: Sweat reaches the skin surface through pores. / The material's tiny pores absorb moisture.
column8: Plural pores common in skincare. Do not confuse pore over = study/read closely, or pour = cause liquid to flow; all can sound similar depending accent.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: pores meaning

column5: A time so far in the past that human memory cannot reach it; since an unimaginably ancient time.
column6: time immemorial, beyond living memory, since ancient times
column7: The custom has existed from time out of mind. / In fantasy narration, the phrase can give a place the feeling of having been ancient beyond memory.
column8: Literary/archaic flavor. Closely related to 'time immemorial,' which is much more common as 'since/from time immemorial.' Bob Dylan also used Time Out of Mind as an album title, but the phrase predates it by centuries.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: time out of mind

column5: To remain watchful, alert, and attentive to possible danger, problems, deception, or changes.
column6: stay alert, remain watchful, keep one's guard up, stay on the lookout
column7: Travelers were advised to stay vigilant in crowded stations. / Even after the obvious scam message is deleted, stay vigilant for follow-up attempts.
column8: Vigilant implies sustained attention to possible threat/problem. 'Stay alert' is broader and more everyday; 'keep your guard up' suggests defensive caution.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: stay vigilant meaning

column5: Publicly expressing values or moral positions in a way perceived as intended mainly to display one's own virtue, social alignment, or moral standing.
column7: Critics dismissed the company's statement as virtue signaling.

column7: The documentary was accused of whitewashing the regime's abuses. / Fans criticized the adaptation for whitewashing the character. / The team whitewashed its opponent in the series.

column7: Soldiers watched the valley from the old stone ramparts.

column7: A driver flipped me off even though he was the one blocking the intersection. / I got flipped off for honking when the light turned green.
column8: Common in North America. Strongly rude/hostile but not necessarily accompanied by words. 'Flip out' is unrelated = become extremely upset/excited.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: get flipped off meaning

column5: The internal or external framework of bones/supporting structures of a person or animal; by extension, the bare framework, outline, or minimal supporting structure of something.
column6: bony framework, framework, structure, outline, bare bones
column7: The museum displays a complete dinosaur skeleton. / I wrote the skeleton of the argument first, then filled in the details. / The building's steel skeleton was visible during construction.
column8: Literal anatomical sense is core. Figurative uses emphasize a stripped-down supporting framework: skeleton crew = minimum staff; skeleton key = key designed to open multiple locks; skeleton of a plan/argument = basic structure. Distinct from 'skeletons in the closet' = hidden embarrassing secrets.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: skeleton meaning

column5: To predict a counterargument, concern, or challenge that someone is likely to raise and consider/address it in advance.
column6: foresee a counterargument, preempt an objection, address a likely objection
column7: A strong essay anticipates the objection that correlation does not prove causation. / She anticipated his objection and explained the cost before he asked.
column8: Useful rhetoric/argumentation skill. Anticipating ≠ automatically refuting; you can anticipate an objection and then concede, qualify, or answer it.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: anticipating an objection meaning
column12: entry::phrase usage::rhetorical usage::debate-friendly topic::debate discovery::debate_language discovery::possibility

column5: A king in Greek mythology condemned in the underworld to push a huge stone uphill forever; each time he nears the top, it rolls back down, making his punishment an image of endless futile labor.
column6: mythological figure; symbol of endless labor
column7: The essay compares modern bureaucracy to Sisyphus pushing his stone uphill. / Once you know the myth of Sisyphus, the adjective Sisyphean becomes instantly memorable.
column8: The myth has many ancient variants. In modern philosophy/literature, especially Camus, Sisyphus can also symbolize confronting absurd, repetitive existence rather than merely 'failure.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: sisyphus meaning

column5: Literally/historically, to castrate or remove male reproductive power; much more commonly figurative, to make a man feel less masculine, powerful, confident, or effective, or to weaken something's force/power.
column6: make feel less masculine, humiliate, disempower, weaken, neuter (figurative)
column7: He felt emasculated by the constant jokes about his masculinity. / Critics argued that the revised law had been emasculated by so many exceptions that it could no longer work effectively.
column8: Figurative use reflects cultural ideas about masculinity and power, so it can reinforce gender stereotypes depending on framing. Non-person figurative sense = deprive of strength/effectiveness.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: emasculate

column5: To be in a state of heightened watchfulness and readiness because a threat, risk, or important event may occur.
column6: be highly vigilant, be on guard, be on heightened alert
column7: The airport was on high alert after the security warning. / After the first suspicious email, I was on high alert for follow-up scams.
column8: Stronger than simply 'be alert.' Often institutional/security language, but everyday figurative use is common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: being on high alert

column5: To look at goods in store windows or browse shops without intending to buy anything immediately.
column6: browse, look around, shop without buying
column7: We spent an hour window-shopping in SoHo without buying anything. / I like window-shopping for watches even when I know I won't get one.
column8: Usually literal shopping/browsing. Can extend metaphorically to dating, jobs, houses, etc., but that figurative use depends on context and can sound cynical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: window-shop meaning

column5: In automotive customization, to lower a vehicle body over its frame by modifying the floor/body so the body sits lower relative to the chassis.
column6: body drop, lower the body over the frame
column7: The custom shop channeled the body several inches over the frame.
column8: This is a specialized hot-rodding/custom-car sense, distinct from the existing general/spiritual 'channeling' card.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: channeled meaning in a automotive industry
column12: entry::phrase usage::technical usage::specialist topic::automotive discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To postpone something; to make someone dislike, distrust, or lose interest; or to distract/discourage someone.
column7: We put off the meeting until Friday. / His rude tone really put me off.
column8: Important contrast: put something off = postpone; put someone off = repel/discourage/distract.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: put off

column5: Capable of being inherited genetically; in quantitative genetics, describing variation in a trait that is statistically attributable to genetic differences within a particular population/environment.
column7: Some disorders have a strong heritable component. / Height is highly heritable, but that does not mean an individual's height is fixed entirely by genes.
column8: Important nuance: heritable ≠ inevitable/genetically determined. Heritability is population- and environment-specific. In everyday nontechnical use, inheritable is often used for property/rights as well as traits; heritable strongly suggests biological genetics.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define heritable

column5: To stop moving, operating, progressing, or continuing, often completely or after slowing/disruption.
column6: stop, grind to a halt, come to a stop, cease
column7: Traffic came to a halt after the accident. / The conversation came to a sudden halt when his name was mentioned. / Without funding, the project gradually came to a halt.
column8: 'Grind to a halt' emphasizes slow/difficult stopping; 'come to a screeching halt' emphasizes abruptness. Can describe physical motion or processes/activities.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: came to a halt

column5: To turn a person, event, place, or story into a myth or legend; figuratively, to portray it in an idealized, simplified, heroic, or larger-than-life way.
column6: romanticize, idealize, lionize, turn into legend, mythicize
column7: Biopics often mythologize their subjects by smoothing away contradictions. / Fans have mythologized that production disaster so much that the real story is almost beside the point.
column8: Can be neutral in scholarship (create/treat as myth) or critical when it means distort through heroic/romantic storytelling. Unlike simply fictionalize, mythologize stresses symbolic/legendary status.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: mythologize

column5: Very discouraged, dejected, or without hope, especially after disappointment or failure.
column7: He looked despondent after hearing the project had been canceled. / The ending leaves her exhausted but not completely despondent.
column8: Stronger/more literary than sad. Usually a temporary emotional state; does not by itself imply a clinical diagnosis.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120, voca_0121 | search: define despondent

column5: A story, image, or work in which characters and events systematically represent broader moral, political, religious, or abstract ideas.
column7: The novel can be read as an allegory of political revolution.
column8: Unlike a single symbol, an allegory typically sustains a larger pattern of correspondences across a work.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0115 | search: allegory
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::religious topic::work topic::politics topic::religion discovery::public_discourse discovery::religious_origin discovery::literal_vs_figurative

column5: A context-dependent phrase likely expressing that nothing important is at risk or that an event has little/no consequence. Standard English would normally say 'there are no stakes,' 'the stakes are nonexistent,' or 'nothing is at stake.'
column6: no stakes, nothing at stake, no consequences, low stakes
column7: If nobody can lose anything, there are basically no stakes. / 'Stakes of none' sounds stylized or nonstandard; I'd normally say 'nothing is at stake.'
column8: Preserve raw search provenance but do not teach 'stakes of none' as a standard fixed phrase. Stakes = what can be gained/lost; high-stakes/low-stakes are standard compounds.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: stakes of none

column5: A short, confused, relatively small physical fight or struggle involving pushing, grabbing, or blows; as a verb, to engage in such a struggle.
column7: A scuffle broke out near the entrance, but security separated them quickly. / The two players scuffled after the whistle.
column8: Usually smaller/less organized than a fight or battle. Also historically can mean move with shuffling feet. Do not confuse scuffle (minor fight) with scuff (surface scrape/mark).
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: scuffle

column5: An activity labeled 'EVT'; the abbreviation is too context-dependent to assign one reliable expansion without the original source.
column7: The schedule lists an 'EVT activity,' but the surrounding program is needed to know what EVT stands for.
column8: Preserve ambiguity rather than invent an expansion. EVT can stand for many unrelated terms across education, engineering, medicine, events, etc. Source context should control.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: evt activity meaning

column5: A humorous euphemism for a man's testicles/genitals; literally, valuable jewelry or heirlooms belonging to a family.
column7: The ball hit him right in the family jewels. / The museum displayed the royal family's jewels—literal family jewels, not the euphemism.
column8: Usually humorous and old-fashioned/euphemistic in the anatomical sense. Context disambiguates literal heirlooms from the genital joke.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: family jewels meaning
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::fixed_expression usage::informal usage::dated usage::humorous usage::vulgar topic::family topic::anatomy topic::health

column5: To live at another person's expense or repeatedly get money, food, housing, etc. from them without contributing fairly.
column6: mooch off, freeload on, leech off, scrounge from
column7: He spent months sponging off his parents instead of looking for work. / I don't mind helping once; I just don't want anyone sponging off me.
column8: Negative and stronger than casually 'bum X off someone' for a small item. Often suggests an ongoing dependent/freeloading pattern.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: sponge off meaning

column5: To go through life without a usual aid, buffer, distraction, medication, entertainment, or preparation—deliberately extending raw-dog from its sexual slang sense to mean 'without protection/help.'
column6: do it with no buffer, go without, white-knuckle it (contextual), go in unassisted
column7: My headphones died, so I had to raw-dog the entire flight with no music or podcast. / He's raw-dogging life without social media, caffeine, or a calendar.
column8: Originally vulgar sexual slang for sex without a condom; modern internet usage productively means doing something with no usual comfort/protection/distraction. Still crude, so register matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: raw dog life meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::form_family entry::phrase usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::informal topic::internet topic::entertainment topic::animals

column5: The style of continuous written language used in scholarly articles, books, essays, theses, and similar academic work, as distinct from verse, dialogue, notes, or informal speech.
column6: scholarly writing, academic writing, formal expository prose
column7: The argument is interesting, but the academic prose is so dense that I keep rereading each paragraph. / Clear academic prose can still be precise without stuffing every sentence with jargon.
column8: Prose simply means ordinary written/spoken language not organized as verse; academic prose is a register/style, not necessarily 'good' or 'bad' writing. It can range from lucid to highly technical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: academic prose

column5: A structure that contains or refers to another instance of the same kind of structure, allowing patterns to be nested or repeatedly applied.
column7: A folder can contain another folder, creating a recursive structure. / The definition points to a rule that can apply again inside its own output.
column8: General concept across computing, mathematics, linguistics, logic, and organization. Recursion is repeated self-embedding/application, not merely repetition.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: recursive structure

column5: To feel relaxed, comfortable, calm, and free from anxiety or awkwardness; in military drill, 'at ease' is also a command/posture allowing limited relaxation.
column6: feel comfortable, be relaxed, feel at home, be unworried
column7: I felt more at ease once the conversation became informal. / Her warm tone put everyone at ease. / The soldiers stood at ease.
column8: Patterns: be/feel at ease; put someone at ease. Opposite: ill at ease. Military sense is distinct but related to relaxation from strict attention.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: be at ease
column12: entry::idiom usage::informal usage::warm usage::military topic::mental_health topic::military

column5: The idea that accepting the possibility of looking embarrassing, uncool, or overly earnest frees you to enjoy things and express yourself without excessive self-consciousness.
column6: embrace the cringe, be unapologetically yourself, kill the part that cringes (related meme)
column7: I almost didn't post it because it felt cheesy, but being cringe is being free. / The phrase pushes back against ironic detachment: sometimes sincerely loving something is worth looking uncool.
column8: Not a traditional proverb; contemporary internet culture. Often used sincerely-but-playfully to defend enthusiasm, fandom, hobbies, fashion, dancing, etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: being cringe is being free
