column2: learn about other cultures vs learn other cultures
column5: Learn about other cultures = gain knowledge/information about them, the normal phrasing. Learn a culture can mean acquire/internalize its practices and norms through experience, but 'learn other cultures' is usually less natural for general study.
column6: study other cultures, learn about cultures; become familiar with a culture
column7: Travel can help you learn about other cultures. / Living with a host family helped her learn the local culture from the inside.
column8: Use learn about for knowledge as topic. Learn X directly is normal for languages/skills and can work for a culture when emphasizing acquisition/enculturation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: learning about other cultures vs learning other cultures

column5: Having multiple related meanings or senses.
column7: 'Head' is highly polysemous: it can refer to a body part, a leader, the top/front of something, and more. / 'Off' is so polysemous that memorizing one Japanese translation won't get you very far.
column8: Polysemy = multiple related senses of one word. Homonymy = same form associated with historically/semantically distinct words/meanings. The boundary can be debatable, which is why dictionaries may analyze senses differently.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: polysemous

column5: Able to seal itself automatically; figuratively, structured so that apparent counterevidence is reinterpreted as support, making a belief or argument resistant to disconfirmation.
column7: The tire uses a self-sealing layer around small punctures. / A self-sealing belief can treat every objection as further proof of the conspiracy.
column8: Literal technical uses exist in tires, containers, materials, etc. Figurative epistemic use is especially useful with 'self-sealing argument/belief.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: self-sealing
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::figurative usage::rhetorical discovery::figurative_extension discovery::support discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::debate_language

column5: Literally, loam (fertile soil with a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay) that is free/no-cost or unrestricted; 'free loam' is not a standard fixed English expression.
column7: The listing advertised free loam for anyone willing to haul it away.
column8: Preserve because it was explicitly searched, but no special idiomatic meaning should be invented without source context. Possible typo/mishearing is also possible. Loam itself is a common soil term.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: free loam meaning

column5: Without suffering injury, damage, harm, or serious negative consequences; unharmed despite danger, attack, criticism, or difficulty.
column7: Everyone escaped the crash unscathed. / The character somehow came through the scandal relatively unscathed. / Very few businesses emerged from the crisis completely unscathed.
column8: Often 'escape/come through/emerge unscathed.' Can be physical or figurative. Scathe is rare as a modern verb, but scathing and unscathed remain common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: unscathed meaning

column5: Revealing or indicating something that is otherwise hidden or not immediately obvious; as a noun, historically a person who tells on others, and in technical contexts an indicator/device.
column7: There was a telltale pause before he answered. / The telltale smell of smoke made us check the kitchen.
column8: Common collocations: telltale sign, telltale signs, telltale mark/smell. As adjective it means 'giving the game away.' Do not confuse with 'tell a tale.' Existing cards mention telltale as synonym but not standalone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: telltale meaning

column5: A structural suspension component that supports and locates part of a vehicle's wheel assembly and often incorporates a shock absorber.
column7: The mechanic found a leaking front strut.
column8: Automotive struts are load-bearing suspension members; they are not simply another name for every shock absorber.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: what is car struts

column5: An activity occurring around noon; especially, a sexual encounter during the middle of the day. In some contexts it can also mean a midday event, drink, meal, or broadcast.
column6: midday quickie (sexual sense), lunchtime encounter; midday event
column7: The sitcom joke was about sneaking home for a nooner. / Outside sexual slang, local contexts sometimes use nooner for a lunchtime event or gathering.
column8: The sexual sense is the best-known informal meaning. Formation: noon + -er. Context is necessary because organizations/events sometimes independently use 'Nooner' as a name for midday programming.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: nooner meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::slang topic::media topic::food

column5: That makes sense or fits with the known facts, pattern, or person's usual behavior.
column6: that makes sense, that checks out, figures
column7: He forgot the deadline again? Yeah, that tracks.
column8: Contemporary conversational use of track = align/correspond with evidence or expectations.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: that tracks.

column5: To stop intervening closely and allow a person, process, team, or system to operate with greater independence.
column6: step back, back off, stop micromanaging, take a hands-off approach
column7: Once the team understood the workflow, I went mostly hands-off. / The game goes hands-off during some story sequences and just lets the scene play out.
column8: Hands-off can describe management, parenting, policy, technology, etc. Contrast laissez-faire: often specifically an ideology/policy of minimal intervention; hands-off is broader everyday English.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: go hands-off meaing

column5: Calling someone/something 'the shit' means excellent, impressive, or the best; calling someone/something 'shit' usually means terrible, worthless, or contemptible.
column6: awesome/excellent vs terrible/worthless; the bomb (positive, dated-ish) vs crap
column7: That band is the shit. / That band is shit. / This ramen is the shit means high praise; this ramen is shit means the exact opposite.
column8: The definite article completely reverses the slang evaluation: 'the shit' = excellent/top-tier; bare 'shit' as a predicate adjective-like noun = terrible. Highly informal/vulgar. Compare 'my shit' which can mean my stuff/music/work depending context and is different again.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: you are the shit vs you are shit
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::dated usage::vulgar topic::language_learning discovery::contrast

column5: To openly disclose a previously hidden sexual orientation or gender identity; by extension/jokingly, to reveal another identity, preference, or affiliation one had kept secret.
column6: come out, disclose one's identity, reveal
column7: He came out of the closet to his family in college. / The phrase is sometimes extended jokingly to tastes or fandoms, but that can trivialize the LGBTQ+ meaning depending on context.
column8: The central modern meaning is LGBTQ+ coming out. 'Come out' is usually the more natural shorter form when context is clear. Distinguish from skeletons in the closet: that phrase concerns shameful/hidden secrets generally.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: come out of the closet

column5: To temporarily distance oneself from a situation or activity in order to reconsider it more calmly/broadly; also literally move backward.
column6: pause and reassess, gain perspective, pull back, reconsider
column7: I took a step back and looked at the whole workflow instead of fixing one cell at a time. / We need to take a step back and ask what problem we're actually solving.
column8: Very common figurative management/conversation phrase. Can also mean reduce involvement/responsibility.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: take a step back meaning

column5: To increase speed; to cause a process, rate, growth, change, or development to happen faster.
column6: speed up, quicken, hasten, expedite, intensify (contextual)
column7: The car accelerated as it entered the highway. / Remote work accelerated changes that were already happening in the industry. / The final episodes accelerate the pace almost too much.
column8: Can be transitive or intransitive: the car accelerates; X accelerates change. Expedite means actively make a process faster; intensify means become stronger, not necessarily faster. Raw 'accerlerate' corrected.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: accerlerate meaning

column5: The quality of being sticky; figuratively, the ability of a product, idea, website, habit, or experience to keep people engaged or be remembered.
column7: The app's daily streak feature increases user stickiness.
column8: Figurative business/product use concerns retention or staying power; context determines the specific metric.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: stickiness meaning
column12: entry::word usage::figurative topic::internet topic::self-help discovery::figurative_extension discovery::evaluation

column5: For many people to attack, criticize, mock, or pressure one person at the same time, especially online.
column7: Hundreds of accounts dogpiled on her after the clip went viral.
column8: From literal dogpile = a heap of bodies. Online sense often concerns mass criticism/harassment.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: dog piled meaning

column5: Relating to a grammatical alignment in which the subject of a transitive verb is marked differently from the subject of an intransitive verb; in English grammar discussions, 'ergative verb' is also used for certain verbs that alternate between transitive and intransitive uses with the affected participant as object/subject.
column7: Basque is often described as having ergative-absolutive alignment. / In 'I opened the door' and 'The door opened,' open shows the alternation often called ergative in English teaching materials.
column8: Two related but distinct uses of ergative appear in linguistics. Typological ergative-absolutive alignment is not the same thing as the English 'ergative verb' alternation, also called causative/inchoative or labile alternation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define ergative

column5: To become deliberately friendly or ingratiating toward someone, often to gain favor, influence, or advantage.
column6: curry favor with, ingratiate oneself with
column7: The lobbyist spent months cozying up to influential officials.
column8: Can imply insincerity or strategic friendliness. Also literal cozy up = get physically comfortable/close.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: cozy up to meaning

column5: Benign = harmless, gentle, mild, or not dangerous; medically, noncancerous/not malignant. Raw 'been benigning' is not standard English; likely intended 'being benign' or 'has been benign.'
column7: The tumor turned out to be benign. / What looked threatening was actually fairly benign. / If the intended sentence was 'it's been benign,' use benign as an adjective—not *benigning as a normal verb.
column8: Benign is normally an adjective, not a productive verb. Medical benign ≠ guaranteed irrelevant: a benign condition can still cause problems depending on location/size. Contrast malignant.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: been benigning

column5: To take, buy, obtain, or seize something quickly, especially before someone else can.
column7: Fans snatched up the remaining tickets within minutes.
column8: Often implies speed and limited availability; snap up is especially common for purchases/opportunities.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: snatch up meaning

column5: Relating to the voice or singing; also, openly and forcefully expressing opinions or feelings. As a noun, especially in music, a sung part or recorded singing track.
column7: She's been very vocal about wanting the adaptation to stay faithful. / The song's lead vocal is almost completely dry. / Vocal cords are more precisely called vocal folds.
column8: 'Vocal about X' = outspoken about it. Musical plural 'vocals' is very common. Do not confuse vocal = voice-related/outspoken with verbal = relating to words/language.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: vocal meaning

column5: A characteristic clue that clearly reveals the presence, cause, identity, or true nature of something.
column6: dead giveaway, revealing sign, giveaway, clear indication, red flag (often warning-specific)
column7: The tiny bubbles are a telltale sign that the water is beginning to boil. / Avoiding every specific question can be a telltale sign that someone is hiding something.
column8: Telltale sign is often diagnostic/revealing, not necessarily negative. Red flag specifically warns of danger/problem; giveaway emphasizes revealing a secret/answer.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: telltale sign meaning

column5: To feel unfamiliar, unnatural, strange, or outside one's usual experience.
column6: feel unfamiliar, feel alien, feel strange
column7: Speaking in such a formal style still feels foreign to me.
column8: Foreign extends metaphorically from 'from another country' to something that feels unfamiliar or alien to one's habits or experience.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: something feels foreign meaing

column5: Literally, to stop being able to see something; figuratively, to forget, neglect, or stop focusing on an important goal, fact, principle, or bigger picture.
column6: forget, overlook, lose track of, neglect
column7: We lost sight of the boat in the fog. / Don't lose sight of why you started learning English in the first place.
column8: Figurative use is extremely common: lose sight of the goal/point/bigger picture. Opposite: keep sight of / keep X in sight.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: lose sight of somehting meaning

column5: A joking gaming metaphor meaning that a new trait, problem, ability, obsession, chapter, or piece of life experience has suddenly appeared, as though downloadable game content had been unlocked.
column6: new feature unlocked, new lore unlocked, achievement unlocked (related meme)
column7: I started getting back pain at thirty—new DLC unlocked. / After learning that detail about the character, it felt like new lore DLC had unlocked.
column8: DLC = downloadable content added to a game. In meme use, life/personality is treated like a game receiving expansion content. Usually playful, absurd, or self-deprecating.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: new DLC unlocked
column12: entry::phrase usage::humorous usage::playful usage::figurative topic::internet topic::games

column5: To have strong control or influence over someone, often by manipulating their emotions, attention, hope, or dependence so they remain responsive to you.
column6: have someone wrapped around one's finger, string someone along, control, manipulate
column7: She knows he'll cancel any plan the moment she calls—she has him on a string. / The villain keeps both rivals on a string by feeding each of them different information.
column8: Image of a puppet controlled by strings. 'String someone along' specifically means keep them waiting/hopeful without committing; 'have someone on a string' emphasizes control.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: have someone on a string

column5: To make a decision or take action despite uncertainty and without having enough evidence or guarantees, because you trust, hope, or believe it will work.
column6: take a chance, make the jump, trust and go for it, take a risk
column7: Moving abroad without knowing exactly how it would work was a leap of faith. / At some point you have to take a leap of faith and submit the application. / The relationship requires a leap of faith from both of them.
column8: Often positive/hopeful but inherently acknowledges uncertainty. Not necessarily religious. 'Blind faith' can sound uncritical; leap of faith emphasizes the decision to cross an evidential/psychological gap.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: take a leap of faith
column12: entry::idiom usage::religious topic::work topic::decision-making topic::religion discovery::risk discovery::evidence discovery::possibility discovery::social_trust

column2: How many stops into the pub crawl are you?
column3: /haʊ ˌmeni ˌstɑːps ˌɪntuː ðə ˈpʌb krɔːl ɑːr ju/
column5: A natural way to ask how far someone has progressed through a pub crawl, measured by venues/stops visited.
column6: How far into the pub crawl are you?, how many pubs have you hit?
column7: How many stops into the pub crawl are you? / We're three pubs in and taking a food break.
column8: Also very natural: 'How far into the pub crawl are you?' and 'How many pubs have you been to so far?'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: how many stops are you in pub crawl

column5: To move, divert, or redirect someone or something to another place, track, route, or function; medically, a shunt is a passage/device that diverts fluid or blood.
column7: The train was shunted onto a side track. / The company shunted the complaint from one department to another. / A surgical shunt can redirect fluid to relieve pressure.
column8: Often implies being pushed aside or redirected rather than simply moved. BrE railway use is especially common. Figurative 'shunt someone aside' can suggest marginalization.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: shunt

column5: Clumsy or awkward, especially in physical movement or handling things.
column7: I'm so klutzy that I knocked over my glass twice.
column8: Related noun: klutz, from Yiddish.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0112 | search: klutzy meaning

column5: Appraise = assess or estimate the value, quality, condition, or significance of something. Apprise = inform someone about something.
column7: We hired someone to appraise the painting. / Please apprise me of any changes to the schedule. / I appraised the situation first, then apprised the team of the risk.
column8: Classic confusable pair. Appraise usually takes an object being evaluated; apprise commonly appears as 'apprise someone of something.' Appraiser is a person who values property.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: appraise vs apprise

column5: A slang term for temporary aching or discomfort in the testicles associated with prolonged sexual arousal without orgasm; also used figuratively for frustrated anticipation.
column6: epididymal hypertension (technical label sometimes used), sexual frustration; frustrated anticipation
column7: He complained of 'blue balls' after making out for a long time. / People jokingly described the cliffhanger as cinematic blue balls because the promised reveal never came.
column8: Vulgar/informal. The discomfort does not create an obligation for another person to provide sexual activity; it typically resolves on its own. Figurative use = prolonged buildup without payoff.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: get blue balls meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::informal usage::slang usage::technical usage::figurative usage::vulgar discovery::terminology discovery::figurative_extension discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Freed from responsibility, blame, obligation, punishment, or a difficult situation; no longer required to answer for or do something.
column6: in the clear, excused, released, absolved, no longer responsible
column7: Since Maya volunteered to present, I'm off the hook. / The new evidence doesn't necessarily let him off the hook. / Don't think one apology gets you off the hook for fixing the problem.
column8: Common patterns: be off the hook; let/get someone off the hook. Originally associated with a fish escaping a hook; modern figurative use is extremely common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: off the hook meaning
column12: entry::idiom usage::informal usage::conversational usage::figurative topic::communication topic::workplace topic::law discovery::release discovery::resolution discovery::criticism

column5: To quickly assess someone's character, abilities, intentions, threat level, or suitability, often by observing them.
column6: assess, evaluate, appraise, take someone's measure, scope someone out
column7: I could tell he was sizing me up the moment I walked into the room. / The interviewer spent the first few minutes sizing up how confident each candidate was.
column8: Can sound strategic, wary, competitive, or judgmental. 'Check someone out' may mean look at/evaluate but can also imply attraction; size up emphasizes assessment.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: size up peopl meaning

column5: Accessible only after paying, subscribing, or passing through a site's paywall.
column7: I found the article, but it's paywalled. / Half the sources I wanted to read were stuck behind a paywall.
column8: Very common internet/media adjective. Paywall = access barrier requiring payment/subscription. Hard paywall allows no free access; metered/soft paywall allows some free content.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: something is paywalled meaning

column5: The habit of compulsively scrolling through a stream of distressing, alarming, or negative online news and content.
column6: compulsive negative-news scrolling, compulsive bad-news consumption
column7: I lost an hour to doomscrolling before bed. / I opened the app to check one headline and ended up doomscrolling until 2 a.m. / Doomscrolling can make a bad news cycle feel inescapable.
column8: Also 'doomscroll' as a verb. Refers to compulsively consuming distressing/negative online content, especially news and social feeds, even when it worsens one's mood. Related 'doomsurfing' exists but is less common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: doomscrolling meaning
column12: entry::internet_term entry::word usage::informal usage::journalistic topic::internet topic::social_media topic::news topic::mental_health topic::wellness topic::self-help

column5: To speak to someone in a condescending, patronizing way, as if they are less intelligent, mature, knowledgeable, or important than you.
column6: patronize, condescend to, speak condescendingly to
column7: I hate it when customer-service scripts talk down to people. / Explain it simply, but don't talk down to me.
column8: Distinct from 'talk someone down' = persuade someone to calm down, lower a price, or come down from a dangerous place. Word order changes meaning.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: talk down to someone meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::persuasive topic::communication discovery::persuasion

column5: Having a mouth cut or split unusually wide; Japanese 口裂け is context-dependent and may be translated descriptively as slit-mouthed, a slit mouth, or a mouth slit/cut open.
column7: Kuchisake-onna is commonly rendered 'the Slit-Mouthed Woman.' / The creature was drawn with a mouth slit unnaturally wide.
column8: For 口裂け女, established English rendering is Slit-Mouthed Woman. For a generic injury/design, choose descriptive wording rather than assuming the folklore reference.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: 口裂け 英語で

column5: To make someone feel a fluttery nervous excitement in the stomach, often from attraction, anticipation, or anxiety.
column6: make someone's heart flutter, make someone nervous/excited, give someone butterflies in their stomach
column7: He still gives me butterflies even after all this time. / I always get butterflies right before I have to speak in front of a group.
column8: Commonly romantic, but not exclusively. Get/have butterflies (in one's stomach) = experience the feeling; give someone butterflies = cause it. Can be pleasant excitement or nervous anxiety.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: give someone butterflies meaning

column5: To a state of complete destruction, disappearance, unconsciousness, forgetfulness, or extreme excess; used after verbs such as bomb, blast, drink, beat, grind, or consign depending on context.
column6: into nothingness, completely, into unconsciousness, beyond recognition (contextual)
column7: The base was bombed into oblivion. / He played the game until three in the morning and ground the same mission to oblivion. / The old scandal was eventually consigned to oblivion.
column8: Oblivion literally/abstractly means being forgotten or unknown, or unconsciousness. 'Verb + into/to oblivion' is hyperbolic and productive; the exact result comes from the verb.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: to oblivion meaning

column2: I can only do so much
column5: There is a limit to how much I can accomplish, help, control, or compensate for given my time, ability, resources, or role.
column6: there's only so much I can do, I have limits
column7: I can help you practice, but I can only do so much—you still have to use the language yourself. / With two hours left, I can only do so much.
column8: Often sets a boundary or explains limitations without saying 'I won't.' Tone can be resigned, defensive, realistic, or empathetic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: i can only do so much meaning

column5: Clear and easy to understand; mentally clear and rational; in 'lucid dream,' aware that one is dreaming while the dream continues.
column7: She gave a lucid explanation of a complicated idea. / He was tired but still lucid. / I realized I was dreaming and briefly became lucid.
column8: Major senses: clear expression; clear mental state. 'Lucid interval' has medical/legal uses. Lucid ≠ vivid, though lucid dreams can be vivid.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: define lucid

column2: whether to do something or not
column5: Used when considering a choice between doing something and not doing it, or between alternative courses of action.
column6: whether or not to, decide if
column7: I haven't decided whether to go or not.
column8: Whether can introduce alternatives; 'or not' may be omitted when the yes/no contrast is already clear.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: English Phrase: whether to (do something) or not | PhraseMix.com

column5: The state of being widespread or common; in statistics/epidemiology, the proportion of a population having a condition at a given time or over a period.
column7: The study measured the prevalence of the condition among adults.
column8: Often used formally: prevalence of X; high/low prevalence. Distinct from incidence, which concerns new cases/events.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: prevalence define

column5: To angrily tell someone off, criticize them, or say a lot of harsh words to them.
column6: give someone an earful, tell someone off, bawl someone out, give someone a piece of one's mind
column7: When he finally arrived two hours late, she gave him a mouthful. / The driver leaned out the window and gave the cyclist a mouthful.
column8: Chiefly British/Irish/Australian-style usage; 'give someone an earful' is more familiar in AmE. Distinct from literal a mouthful of food/drink and 'a mouthful' = long hard-to-say phrase.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: Give someone a mouthful
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::criticism

column5: To circulate among people/places; to visit a series of people or locations; for news, rumors, images, jokes, etc. to spread widely.
column6: circulate, go around, spread; visit in turn
column7: The clip started making the rounds on social media. / The doctor made the rounds before breakfast. / I made the rounds at the party and talked to everyone for a few minutes.
column8: Major senses: information circulates; a person visits a sequence of places/people. Medical 'rounds' is especially common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: make the rounds meaning

column5: Safe and unharmed after danger or a difficult journey; also physically whole, not broken into separate pieces.
column6: safe and sound, intact, unharmed, whole
column7: Text me when you get home in one piece. / Somehow the fragile figure arrived in one piece despite the terrible packaging.
column8: Raw 'in piece' normally needs one: in one piece. Compare 'piece by piece' and 'in pieces' = broken apart or, figuratively, emotionally devastated.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: in piece meaning

column5: To be unwilling to make the effort to do something because it feels too troublesome, uninteresting, or not worth one's energy.
column6: can't be arsed (vulgar BrE), don't feel like it, can't be fussed, won't make the effort
column7: I know I should cook, but I can't be bothered tonight. / He couldn't be bothered to read the instructions before complaining.
column8: Usually 'can't/couldn't be bothered to do X.' It often means lack of motivation rather than literal inability. Very natural BrE; widely understood elsewhere.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: i can't be bothered eanig

column5: To examine a large amount of material, information, evidence, files, etc. carefully in order to find what is useful or important; literally, pass material through a sieve.
column6: sort through, comb through, go through, screen
column7: We sifted through hundreds of bookmark searches to find useful candidates. / Detectives sifted through the evidence.
column8: Literal sifting separates fine/coarse material; figurative sense implies patient filtering of a mass of information/items.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: sift through meaning

column5: Search + place/person/system means examine it in order to find something; search for + target means try to find that target. Search can also be intransitive or take a database/web object.
column7: Police searched the house for evidence. / We searched for the missing file all morning. / I searched the website for the old review. / 'Search the answer' is usually unnatural if you mean 'look for the answer.'
column8: Core frame: search [AREA] for [TARGET]. Compare look for X = seek X; look through X = examine X. In web usage, 'search Google/the database' is normal; 'search for X' names the query target.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: search vs search for

column5: Something that is thoroughly tedious, exhausting, slow, or laborious to get through.
column6: a grind, an ordeal, hard going, a chore
column7: The middle ten episodes were a total slog for me. / Cleaning thousands of messy rows by hand would be a total slog.
column8: Built from existing noun slog = long difficult tiring effort. 'Total' intensifies it conversationally; useful especially in reviews of games/books/shows/work.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: total slog meaning

column5: The particular choice, arrangement, or style of words and phrases used by a person, group, text, or field.
column6: wording, phrasing, diction, formulation, turns of phrase
column7: The meaning is fine, but the phraseology sounds oddly formal for casual conversation. / Legal phraseology can make a simple idea feel much harder than it is.
column8: Useful distinction: wording = exact words; phrasing = how something is expressed; diction = choice/style of words, often literary; phraseology can refer broadly to characteristic expressions of a language/person/field.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: phraseology
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::casual usage::literary usage::informal topic::communication topic::decision-making

column5: Nose contour makeup with lines, shading, or contrast that looks too strong, sharp, obvious, or insufficiently blended rather than creating a subtle sculpted effect.
column6: heavy nose contour, severe contour, unblended contour, strong contour
column7: The lighting made her nose contour look much harsher on camera than it did in person. / If the contour lines are too dark and close together, the result can look harsh rather than sculpted.
column8: Harsh describes visual effect, not a formal makeup technique. Existing contour card notes cosmetics generally; this preserves a useful beauty-review collocation and evaluative nuance.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: harsh nose contour

column5: A learned or culturally shared expectation about how people are supposed to behave, speak, or sequence actions in a familiar social situation.
column6: social norm, behavioral script, expected routine, cultural script
column7: A first date comes with a social script about who asks questions, when to flirt, and what counts as progress. / Moving between cultures can make invisible social scripts suddenly obvious.
column8: Useful for dating/culture discussions: scripts are not literal written rules and individuals can reject or improvise them. 'Norm' is broader; script emphasizes expected sequence/roles in a situation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: social script meaning
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::discourse_expression topic::communication topic::psychology topic::culture topic::sociology

column5: Literally removing weapons or the ability to attack; figuratively, reducing suspicion, hostility, or defensiveness through charm, openness, humor, vulnerability, etc.
column6: charming, winning, reassuring, endearing; neutralizing, disarming
column7: She has a disarming smile that makes even skeptical people relax. / His willingness to admit he was nervous was unexpectedly disarming. / Officers began disarming the militia.
column8: Figurative disarming does not merely mean charming; it suggests lowering another person's guard. 'Disarmingly honest' = so candid that resistance/suspicion drops.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: disarming meaning
column12: entry::word usage::figurative usage::skeptical topic::grammar discovery::figurative_extension discovery::reassurance

column2: can you go one day without ...?
column5: A frustrated or teasing way to ask whether someone can refrain from a repeated behavior even for a single day; usually implies the speaker thinks they do it constantly.
column6: do you have to keep...?, can you stop... for once?
column7: Can you go one day without complaining? / Can you go one day without turning every conversation into an argument?
column8: Usually rhetorical, not a literal request for information. Tone ranges from playful teasing to sharp criticism.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: can you go one day without complaining meaning
column12: entry::phrase usage::playful usage::rhetorical topic::rhetoric discovery::complaint discovery::debate_language

column5: Very serious, gloomy, harsh, unpleasant, or depressing; also stern or forbidding in appearance.
column6: bleak, gloomy, dire, harsh, forbidding, stern
column7: The latest economic forecast looks grim. / The movie paints a grim picture of life after the collapse. / She gave me a grim smile and went back to work.
column8: Broad adjective: grim news/prospects/conditions = very bad; grim expression = stern/gloomy; grim determination = serious and resolute. 'Dire' focuses on severity/urgency; 'bleak' often adds hopelessness. The malformed search 'in a grim' normally requires a following noun.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: define grim

column5: Initialism for 'not gonna lie,' used to introduce a candid opinion, admission, reaction, or sometimes simply to add conversational emphasis.
column6: not gonna lie, honestly, to be fair (sometimes), I have to admit
column7: NGL, that ending hit me much harder than I expected. / I was skeptical, but ngl, the food was great. / NGL can function almost like a discourse marker rather than a literal claim that one normally lies.
column8: Very informal, common in texting/social media. Usually written ngl/NGL. Can signal frankness, soften an admission, or just add casual emphasis. Avoid in formal writing.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: ngl
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::formal usage::informal usage::casual usage::conversational usage::slang usage::skeptical usage::softening topic::internet discovery::emphasis discovery::subjective_judgment

column5: A performer or performance that appears before the main/headlining act; figuratively, an earlier event that serves as a prelude to something bigger.
column6: support act, opener, warm-up act; prelude
column7: The opening act played for thirty minutes before the headliner. / The scandal was only the opening act of a much larger political crisis.
column8: Raw 'openinng' repaired. In concerts/comedy, 'opener' is common. Figurative use frames the first event as setup for the main event.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: openinng act meaning
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative usage::warm topic::performance discovery::figurative_extension discovery::support discovery::prelude

column5: Easily startled, nervous, wary, or unpredictable; originally/common with animals, especially horses, and figuratively with people, markets, investors, etc.
column7: The horse became skittish around the traffic. / Investors are skittish after weeks of bad news.
column8: Suggests readiness to react or bolt, not just generalized anxiety. Figurative 'skittish market/investors' is common.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: skittish

column5: A very small but noticeable sign or amount of hope in an otherwise discouraging situation.
column6: ray of hope, faint hope, spark of hope
column7: The final test result gave them a glimmer of hope. / Even one positive reply was a glimmer of hope after weeks of silence.
column8: Glimmer = faint light, hence a small sign of something positive. Common 'glimmer of hope/recognition/understanding.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: glimmer of hope meaning

column5: Humor that is somewhat dry: understated, restrained, deadpan, or delivered without obvious signals that a joke is being made.
column6: somewhat dry humor, understated humor, deadpan-ish humor
column7: His humor is dry-ish rather than fully deadpan—you can usually hear a little smile in his voice.
column8: -ish deliberately softens categorization: 'kind of dry.' Dry humor often relies on understated delivery and incongruity rather than big emotional cues.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: dry-ish humor meaning

column5: A sudden, repetitive, involuntary movement or sound; figuratively, a habitual mannerism or recurring verbal/behavioral quirk.
column7: Saying 'you know' every few seconds had become a verbal tic.
column8: Keep broad lexical sense. Existing 'verbal tic' from Batch 01 is a specific phrase; this base noun also covers physical/vocal tics.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: define tics

column5: To continue moving, working, or progressing steadily, usually without dramatic speed; similar to 'chug along' or 'keep plugging away.'
column6: chug along, keep going, plug along, carry on
column7: The project is trucking along nicely now. / I wasn't moving fast, but I kept trucking along.
column8: Informal, especially AmE. Often 'keep on truckin'' in older/pop-cultural usage. Raw 'trucking along' is not necessarily about literal trucks.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: trucking along meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::form_family entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::american_english discovery::continuity

column5: A mocking label for a man who aggressively promotes hustle culture—constant work, entrepreneurship, optimization, wealth-building, discipline, and productivity as identity or moral virtue.
column6: grindset bro, hustle-culture guru, entrepreneur bro (overlapping)
column7: My feed suddenly filled up with hustle bros telling me that sleeping eight hours is a character flaw. / The video starts as business advice and gradually turns into full hustle-bro grindset rhetoric.
column8: Usually pejorative/mocking. 'Bro' marks a stereotype, not literally a brother. Related to grindset, entrepreneur-influencer, manosphere/self-improvement ecosystems, but not identical to them.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: hustle-bro
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::critical usage::rhetorical usage::persuasive usage::informal topic::work topic::internet topic::culture discovery::promotion discovery::persuasion discovery::debate_language

column5: Willing or eager to please others; obliging, sometimes excessively so.
column7: He was so complaisant that he rarely challenged anyone's requests.
column8: Do not confuse with complacent = self-satisfied and insufficiently concerned. The words are pronounced differently.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0117 | search: define complaisant

column5: Get Ready With Me: a social-media video/post in which someone talks to the audience while getting dressed, doing makeup/hair, or preparing for an event/day.
column7: I put on a GRWM while I was making breakfast and ended up listening to the whole story. / Her GRWM is less about makeup than about chatting through what happened on her date.
column8: Common on TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, etc. Often functions as a conversational/storytime format rather than purely a beauty tutorial.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: grwm
column12: entry::initialism usage::conversational usage::instructional topic::media topic::public_speaking discovery::audience_engagement

column3: /ˌtuːt wʌnz ˌoʊn ˈhɔːrn/; /ˌbloʊ wʌnz ˌoʊn ˈhɔːrn/
column5: To praise, advertise, or boast about one's own achievements, abilities, or qualities.
column6: brag, boast, sing one's own praises, self-promote
column7: I don't mean to toot my own horn, but I finished the whole project in one day. / She's talented but uncomfortable blowing her own horn in interviews.
column8: 'Not to toot my own horn, but...' is a common humorous preface before self-praise. Toot is especially AmE; blow one's own trumpet is common BrE equivalent.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: toot my own horn meaning
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::humorous usage::american_english usage::british_english usage::persuasive discovery::promotion discovery::social_approval discovery::persuasion

column5: Spreading, occurring, or existing unchecked and very widely, especially something undesirable such as corruption, disease, rumors, abuse, or speculation.
column6: widespread, unchecked, rife, pervasive, out of control
column7: Rumors were rampant after the announcement. / Corruption had become rampant throughout the organization. / Speculation is rampant whenever a show ends on a cliffhanger.
column8: Usually negative and stronger than widespread: suggests lack of control. Common patterns: rampant corruption/speculation/inflation; X is rampant. Heraldry has a separate technical sense of an animal standing upright on hind legs.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: rampant
column12: entry::word usage::technical topic::health discovery::speculation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: General practitioner: a doctor who provides primary/general medical care and is usually the first point of contact for non-emergency health problems.
column6: general practitioner, family doctor, primary-care doctor/physician
column7: I couldn't get a GP appointment until Friday. / If the pain doesn't improve, you should probably speak to your GP.
column8: In UK English GP is extremely common. U.S. speakers more often say primary-care doctor/physician or family doctor, though general practitioner is understood. GP can mean other things in specialist contexts, so context matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: GP
column12: entry::word usage::british_english usage::specialist topic::family topic::health discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Return on investment: a measure of how much benefit, profit, or value an investment produces relative to its cost; figuratively, the payoff obtained for time or effort spent.
column6: return, payoff, cost-effectiveness, value for money/time
column7: The campaign had a strong ROI because sales increased far more than the ad spend. / Spending two hours polishing that tiny detail has terrible ROI for me.
column8: In finance, ROI is commonly calculated as net gain relative to investment cost, though exact definitions vary. Casual figurative use is common for time/effort: 'low-ROI task.' Do not assume every organization calculates it identically.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: roi meaning
column12: entry::initialism entry::word usage::casual usage::figurative usage::informal topic::finance discovery::figurative_extension

column5: A task requiring endless or repeatedly renewed effort while producing little lasting progress, like Sisyphus eternally pushing a boulder uphill only for it to roll back down.
column6: endless task, futile labor, never-ending struggle, uphill battle
column7: Trying to keep every inbox permanently at zero can feel like a Sisyphean task. / Fixing one bug only to create two more turned the cleanup into Sisyphean labor.
column8: From the Greek myth of Sisyphus. 'Sisyphean' emphasizes repetitive, seemingly futile effort; an 'uphill battle' is difficult but can still clearly end in success.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: sisyphean task

column5: A female attendant at a Shinto shrine who assists with rituals, sacred dance, purification, charms, shrine duties, etc.; commonly called miko in English, with 'shrine maiden' as an accessible translation.
column7: The anime character is a miko who works at her family's Shinto shrine. / Visitors watched a miko perform a ceremonial dance.
column8: Japanese 巫女. 'Shrine maiden' is conventional but can evoke fantasy/maiden imagery; miko is often preferable in Japan-specific contexts. Role/history vary by period and shrine.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: 巫女 英語で

column5: To perform many difficult, annoying, arbitrary, or bureaucratic requirements in order to achieve something or satisfy someone.
column6: go through hoops, navigate red tape, bend over backwards (related), meet endless requirements
column7: I had to jump through five different hoops just to reset the account. / International paperwork can make you feel like you're constantly jumping through hoops.
column8: From trained animals/circus performers jumping through hoops on command. Usually implies the requirements feel excessive or unreasonable, not merely that there are several normal steps.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: jump through hoops

column5: To publicly accuse or expose someone in connection with sexual harassment, assault, or misconduct in the cultural context of the #MeToo movement; sometimes used loosely or polemically.
column6: accuse publicly of sexual misconduct, expose, call out (broader)
column7: The commentator claimed the producer had been 'MeTooed' after multiple allegations became public. / Using 'MeToo' as a verb can compress very different allegations and processes into one loaded label.
column8: Informal and politically/socially loaded. #MeToo is primarily a movement/hashtag; verbal uses such as 'get MeTooed' can sound dismissive, sensational, or imprecise. Prefer precise description of allegations when factual accuracy matters.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: metoo verb meaning

column5: Slang, dated: a marijuana cigarette/joint, or marijuana. Nautical: a refrigerated ship/container/truck used to transport perishable goods.
column7: The old movie uses 'reefer' as slang for marijuana. / The fruit was shipped overseas in refrigerated reefers.
column8: Very context-dependent. Drug sense is strongly associated with older 20th-century slang ('Reefer Madness'). Logistics sense remains current industry vocabulary.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: reefer meaing
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::slang usage::dated usage::informal topic::transportation topic::nautical

column5: A confrontation in which two sides keep escalating or refusing to yield, each hoping the other will back down first; if neither yields, both may suffer serious consequences.
column7: The two companies are playing a game of chicken over licensing fees. / In the classic driving image, two drivers head toward each other and the first to swerve is labeled 'chicken.'
column8: Used in politics, negotiations, relationships, and game theory. Key structure: mutual danger + incentive to make the other side yield first.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: the game of chicken

column5: The act of reducing complexity, depth, variation, hierarchy, or nuance so that different things are treated as simpler or more uniform than they really are.
column7: The adaptation's biggest problem is the flattening of morally complicated characters into heroes and villains. / Compressing the data caused some flattening of the differences between groups.
column8: Literal flattening = making physically flat. Figurative criticism often means loss of nuance, dimensionality, contrast, or hierarchy.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: flattening meaning

column5: To stop being trapped in one's own thoughts, overthinking, or self-conscious internal focus; in other contexts, to stop thinking about someone or something.
column6: stop overthinking, get out of one's own thoughts
column7: I needed to get out of my head and just enjoy the conversation.
column8: Context matters: 'I can't get it out of my head' instead means one cannot stop thinking about it.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: getting out of my head

column5: A style or aesthetic associated with the elegance, dress, ornament, or visual codes of a royal/aristocratic court; not a single standardized fashion category.
column6: courtly style, regal aesthetic, aristocratic chic
column7: The costumes mix modern tailoring with a kind of court chic—ornate fabrics, jewelry, and rigid silhouettes.
column8: Preserve exact search. 'Court' likely means royal court, but without source context the phrase is descriptive rather than a fixed technical term. Chic = stylish/elegant.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: court chic
column12: entry::phrase usage::technical usage::specialist topic::fashion discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To display, show, lead, or move someone/something publicly and conspicuously, often to impress, celebrate, shame, or make a point; sometimes critically, to show off.
column6: display, show off, flaunt, march, exhibit
column7: The company paraded its new executives in front of the press. / He kept parading his credentials as if they settled the argument. / Prisoners were paraded before the cameras.
column8: Tone depends on object/context. 'Parade someone around' can imply treating a person as a trophy or spectacle. Literal parade = move ceremonially in procession.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: parade someone meaning
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::journalistic usage::rhetorical usage::ceremonial discovery::debate_language

column5: To work extremely hard or make an intense effort; in other contexts, to fall hard and hurt oneself, or 'bust someone's ass' can mean punish/catch/defeat them.
column6: work one's ass off, grind, work extremely hard, go all out
column7: I busted my ass getting this finished before the deadline. / She busted her ass for years to build the business. / Be careful on the ice or you'll bust your ass.
column8: Vulgar but common. Work-one's-ass-off sense is usually positive/self-emphatic. Object changes meaning: bust someone's ass may mean discipline, arrest, beat, or harass depending on context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: bust my ass meaningi
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction usage::vulgar topic::work discovery::emotional_intensity discovery::maximum_effort

column5: To acknowledge that one has lost or can no longer succeed in a contest, struggle, argument, campaign, or effort.
column6: admit defeat, surrender, give up, accept loss
column7: After three failed attempts to repair it, I finally conceded defeat and called a technician. / The candidate conceded defeat after the results became clear.
column8: More formal than 'give up' and emphasizes acknowledgment of loss. One can concede defeat without literally surrendering to an enemy; useful figuratively for stubborn tasks/problems.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: concede defeat meanign
column12: entry::collocation usage::formal usage::rhetorical topic::politics discovery::public_discourse discovery::debate_language

column5: Noun: a person's face or facial expression, especially literary/formal. Verb: to accept, tolerate, approve of, or permit something, often in negatives.
column6: face, visage, expression; tolerate, sanction, permit
column7: His countenance remained calm. / The school will not countenance bullying of any kind.
column8: Important polysemy: the verb is pronounced the same and often appears as 'will not countenance X.' More formal/literary than face.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: define countenance

column5: To transfer pollen to the reproductive part of a flower, enabling fertilization; figuratively, ideas can cross-pollinate between groups or fields.
column7: Bees pollinate many flowering plants. / Conferences can help ideas cross-pollinate between different disciplines.
column8: Pollination precedes fertilization; they are related but not identical biological processes. Nouns: pollination, pollinator.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: pollinate meaning

column5: An adjustment made to bring a journey, project, strategy, behavior, model, or process back toward its intended direction or goal after drift or new information.
column6: adjustment, recalibration, corrective change, change of course
column7: The team made a small course correction after the first round of user feedback. / AI systems may need course corrections when evaluation reveals a recurring failure mode.
column8: Originally/navigation metaphor: correct the course of a vessel/aircraft. Figuratively usually implies adjustment rather than total abandonment. 'Pivot' often suggests a larger strategic change.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: course correction AI

column5: Rep can mean reputation ('a bad rep'), representative ('sales rep'), or one repetition of an exercise. Reps is commonly the plural exercise repetitions and can also mean representatives. Context determines the sense.
column7: He has a good rep in the industry. / Ask your sales rep. / I did three sets of ten reps. / You need more reps speaking spontaneously if you want the phrasing to become automatic.
column8: Very polysemous abbreviation. In gym/skill-training talk, 'get your reps in' = accumulate repeated practice attempts. Don't confuse 'bad rep' (reputation) with 'bad rap' (unfair criticism/blame), though speakers sometimes blur them.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117, voca_0120 | search: rep vs reps
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase topic::business topic::wellness topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::social_approval

column5: The origin, source, history, and chain of custody or derivation of an object, work, data item, claim, artifact, etc.
column6: origin, source history, lineage, pedigree, chain of custody
column7: The museum documented the painting's provenance. / We preserve each card's search provenance so we can remember why it entered the vocabulary list.
column8: Especially art/archives/data/research. Data provenance records where information came from and how it was transformed. Distinct from provenience in some archaeological usage.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: provenance

column5: To complain repeatedly or make unkind, critical remarks about someone or something.
column7: They spent the whole lunch break bitching about their boss.
column8: Raw search 'bitching someone' is not the usual standard pattern for this sense; normally bitch about someone/something. Distinguish bitch someone out = scold someone harshly.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: bitching someone meaning
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::critical usage::vulgar discovery::complaint

column5: An area in a game world where player-versus-player combat is enabled, encouraged, or governed by special rules.
column6: combat zone, contested zone, PvP area
column7: Once you cross the bridge, you're in a PvP zone and other players can attack you. / I accidentally wandered into the PvP zone with a gathering build.
column8: Game-specific mechanics vary: PvP may be automatic, opt-in, faction-based, full-loot, etc. Zone emphasizes geographic/area-based activation rather than a whole-game mode.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: pvp zone meaning

column5: Simple, basic, and inexpensive or practical, without extra features, decoration, luxury, or unnecessary services.
column7: We stayed at a no-frills hotel near the station. / I want a no-frills flashcard app that loads quickly.
column8: Usually positive/neutral when simplicity/value is desired, but can imply austere/basic. Frills literally = decorative extras.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: no-frills meaning

column5: A temporary bruise-like mark on the skin caused by sucking or kissing strongly, usually on the neck; also has a few unrelated regional/technical slang senses.
column7: She wore a scarf to hide a hickey on her neck. / A hickey is basically a superficial bruise caused by broken tiny blood vessels under the skin.
column8: Common informal AmE; BrE 'love bite.' Usually associated with romantic/sexual activity. Do not confuse with hiccup.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: hickey meaning
column12: entry::word usage::informal usage::slang usage::technical usage::american_english usage::british_english discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A contest in which two teams pull opposite ends of a rope; figuratively, a prolonged struggle between opposing people, forces, desires, or interests.
column7: We played tug-of-war at the school festival. / She felt a constant emotional tug-of-war between staying and leaving. / The negotiations became a tug-of-war over control.
column8: Usually hyphenated as the noun. Figurative use often describes competing motives or power. 'Tug' itself = pull with force.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117, voca_0118 | search: tug of war

column5: Caused by one's own actions, choices, or behavior, especially harm, injury, difficulty, or suffering.
column6: self-caused, brought on oneself, of one's own making
column7: The injury was self-inflicted. / Missing the deadline was largely a self-inflicted problem—we kept changing the scope. / The phrase can describe literal injury or figurative trouble.
column8: Common collocations: self-inflicted wound/injury/damage/problem/crisis. Literal self-injury contexts can be serious; figurative use is extremely common in commentary and analysis.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: self-inflicted

column5: A machine that converts energy into motion; relating to bodily movement; as a verb, to travel by motor vehicle or move along quickly.
column6: engine (overlapping), electric motor; movement-related; drive, travel
column7: The fan uses a small electric motor. / The injury affected fine motor control in his hand. / We motored down the coast before sunset.
column8: Motor vs engine: an engine often converts fuel/heat into mechanical power; an electric motor converts electrical energy into motion, though everyday usage overlaps. Existing motor skills card covers one adjective use.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: motor meaning

column2: try doing something vs try to do something
column5: Try doing something means experiment with an action to see what happens; try to do something means make an effort or attempt to achieve it.
column7: Try restarting the app. / I tried to restart it, but the button wouldn't respond.
column8: Applied to the raw search: 'try messing up something' would mean experiment with messing it up, while 'try to mess up something' means attempt to mess it up.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: try messing up something or to mess up something?

column5: Having a brain or cognitive style that differs from what is considered neurologically typical; commonly used for autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and other forms of neurological/cognitive difference, with boundaries varying by community and framework.
column7: The group was designed by and for neurodivergent students. / She describes herself as neurodivergent and says noisy open offices drain her quickly.
column8: Originates in the neurodiversity framework and is not itself a medical diagnosis. Usage boundaries vary: some use it broadly for any meaningful neurological divergence; others use narrower community conventions. Neurotypical is the common contrast.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: neurodivergent meaning

column5: To give praise that also contains, implies, or smuggles in an insult, criticism, stereotype, or demeaning assumption.
column6: damn with faint praise, give a left-handed compliment, compliment-insult
column7: 'You're surprisingly articulate' can be a backhanded compliment because the praise implies low expectations. / Telling someone 'you look great for your age' may land as a backhanded compliment.
column8: Existing backhanded card mentions the phrase; this preserves the productive construction with a recipient. Whether something feels backhanded depends on implication and context.

column5: I'm in serious trouble, stuck, ruined, or unlikely to succeed because the situation has gone badly.
column6: I'm screwed, I'm toast, I'm done for, I'm in trouble
column7: If that backup is corrupted too, I'm hosed. / I missed the last train and my phone's at one percent—I'm completely hosed.
column8: North American informal slang. Usually less vulgar than 'I'm fucked/screwed' but still casual. Hose can also mean cheat/overcharge or spray with a hose; context distinguishes them.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: I'm hosed meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::informal usage::casual usage::slang usage::vulgar usage::north_american_english discovery::possibility

column5: A major administrative region in some countries; figuratively/formally, a person's proper area of knowledge, responsibility, or activity.
column6: region, administrative division; domain, sphere, remit
column7: Ontario is a province of Canada. / Budget decisions are outside my province; I only handle the technical side.
column8: Political meaning varies by country. Figurative 'the province of X' is formal: 'That question is the province of philosophy.' Do not assume province equals U.S. state in powers/status.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: province meaning

column5: Relating to the Caribbean Sea, its islands and surrounding coasts, or the peoples/cultures of that region; the Caribbean = the region itself.
column7: Piracy and privateering are strongly associated in popular imagination with the Caribbean. / Caribbean cultures are highly diverse in language, history, ethnicity, and colonial experience.
column8: Both common English pronunciations are standard, with regional/speaker variation. The Caribbean is not culturally homogeneous; avoid treating it as one single island culture.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define caribbean

column5: Unique; unlike anything or anyone else; having distinctive qualities that make it the only one of its type.
column6: unique, singular, unparalleled, distinctive, sui generis (formal)
column7: The handmade jacket is genuinely one-of-a-kind. / She has a one-of-a-kind voice that I can recognize immediately.
column8: Hyphenate before a noun: a one-of-a-kind design. After be, hyphens are still common: the design is one-of-a-kind. Natural conceptual opposite of 'a dime a dozen.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: one-of-a-kind

column5: Historical records arranged by year; more broadly, the recorded history of a field, place, institution, or human activity.
column7: The upset went down in the annals of sports history. / It may be one of the strangest production decisions in the annals of anime.
column8: Usually plural. Common grand/formal phrase: in the annals of history / go down in the annals of X. Do not confuse annals /ˈænəlz/ with anals.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define annals

column5: Unwanted or inappropriate interference in other people's affairs or in matters that are not one's responsibility.
column7: She resented his constant meddling in her relationships. / The villain complains about 'meddling kids.'
column8: Usually negative and interpersonal/social. Meddle in/with. Compared with tamper, meddle often concerns affairs/decisions; tamper more often objects, systems, evidence, packaging, etc.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: define meddling

column5: A protective guard worn on the forearm, especially by archers to keep the bowstring from striking the arm; historically, also a stimulating drink or something that braces/strengthens.
column6: arm guard, vambrace (not identical), archer's guard
column7: The archer tightened the leather bracer on his forearm before shooting. / Fantasy costumes often use decorative bracers even when the design is not historically functional.
column8: In archery, a bracer protects the inside forearm. A vambrace is armor for the forearm and is not exactly the same thing. Older 'a bracer' can mean a strengthening/stiff drink, but that sense is uncommon today.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: bracer meaning

column5: A comprehensible but unusual phrase suggesting exposure that does not let up, relent, or give the learner relief—continuous, relentless exposure. More idiomatic choices are relentless, sustained, constant, or intensive exposure.
column6: relentless exposure, sustained exposure, constant exposure, intensive exposure
column7: Months of relentless exposure to fast conversational English changed what sounded 'too fast' to me. / 'Unyielding exposure' is understandable, but 'relentless exposure' is more idiomatic.
column8: Preserve exact search while correcting naturalness. Unyielding usually modifies people, positions, pressure, surfaces, resistance—not exposure itself.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: unyielding exposure meaning

column5: Raw 'same with yesterday' is context-dependent and often less natural than 'same as yesterday' when asking whether today's situation/order/schedule is identical to yesterday's. 'Same with yesterday' works only when extending a prior statement to yesterday as another case.
column6: same as yesterday; the same goes for yesterday (contextual)
column7: 'Same order as yesterday?' is natural. / 'It rained Monday, and the same with yesterday' is possible but 'the same was true yesterday' sounds smoother.
column8: Key contrast: same as X = comparison/equivalence; same with X = the same statement applies to X. Preserve the raw search because this is exactly the sort of preposition choice that causes uncertainty.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: same with yesterday meaning

column5: To undergo menstruation: to discharge blood and tissue from the uterus as part of the menstrual cycle.
column7: Some people menstruate regularly while others have irregular cycles. / The medical article distinguishes ovulation from menstruation—they are related parts of the cycle but not the same event.
column8: Neutral medical/biological verb. In everyday conversation, 'have/get one's period' is more common. Not everyone who menstruates identifies as a woman, and not every woman menstruates.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: menstruate meaning

column5: A departure or difference from an expected, normal, planned, or standard course, value, or behavior.
column7: Any significant deviation from the plan must be reported.
column8: Also technical/statistical: standard deviation.

column5: Physically present in person rather than seen in a photo, video, recording, imagination, or description.
column7: I'd only seen the painting online, so it was amazing to see it in the flesh. / After years of video calls, they finally met in the flesh.
column8: Can refer to people or impressive objects/art seen physically. Slightly vivid/dramatic compared with ordinary 'in person.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: in the flesh meaning

column5: To change gradually or smoothly in form, appearance, character, or function; in digital media, transform one image/shape into another through a continuous transition.
column7: The conversation slowly morphed into an argument. / The animation shows one face morphing into another.
column8: Informal/productive figurative verb. Often morph into X. Digital-image sense helped popularize modern usage.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: morphing meainig

column5: A comic or exaggerated imitation of a serious style; also a stage-entertainment tradition combining comedy, theatricality, and often striptease.
column7: The show was a playful burlesque of old Hollywood melodramas.
column8: Two important senses: literary/theatrical parody, and the entertainment tradition now strongly associated with glamorous striptease.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: burlesque

column5: To admit that one did something wrong, embarrassing, or previously hidden, and accept that it is true.
column6: admit, confess to, acknowledge, come clean about, fess up to
column7: Who broke the mug? Just own up to it. / He finally owned up to lying about where he'd been. / She owned up to the error before anyone else noticed it.
column8: Pattern: own up to + noun/gerund. 'Confess' can sound more serious/legal/religious; own up is conversational and strongly suggests taking responsibility.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: owning up to meaning

column2: skirt around / skirt over an issue
column5: To avoid dealing directly with a difficult, sensitive, or inconvenient subject; 'skirt around the issue' is standard. 'Skirt over' is less idiomatic and may blend skirt around with gloss over.
column6: avoid, evade, sidestep, dance around, gloss over
column7: He kept skirting around the real issue instead of answering the question. / If you mean 'treat it too briefly,' gloss over the issue is more natural than *skirt over it.
column8: Useful correction card from raw 'skirt over.' Skirt = move along the edge of something, hence figuratively avoid the center/core. Standard collocations: skirt the issue, skirt around the issue.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: skirt over meaning

column5: The highest point, peak, tip, or culmination of something; literally the topmost point of a shape/object and figuratively the highest level of achievement, power, development, etc.
column7: At the apex of his career, he was directing two major films at once. / The apex of the triangle points upward.
column8: Often 'at the apex of.' In anatomy, apex can mean the pointed/end part of an organ, e.g. apex of the heart/lung. Figurative apex emphasizes highest point.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: apex meaning

column5: To start talking too much, boasting, gossiping, insulting, revealing things, or speaking recklessly—especially when the speaker thinks you should have kept quiet.
column6: shoot your mouth off, talk shit, blab, mouth off
column7: Don't go running your mouth about something you don't understand. / He went running his mouth to everyone about the argument.
column8: Confrontational and often threatening/accusatory in tone. 'Run your mouth' = talk recklessly/excessively; 'go running your mouth' adds a sense of setting off and doing it.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: go runnning your mouth meaning

column5: A genus of large flying pterosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of North America, notable for a long cranial crest and lack of teeth.
column7: Pteranodon was a pterosaur, not a dinosaur. / Reconstructions often emphasize the animal's long backward-pointing head crest.
column8: Important distinction: pterosaurs are flying reptiles closely related to dinosaurs, but are not dinosaurs themselves. Pteranodon means roughly 'wing without tooth' and was toothless.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: PTERANODON Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster

column5: A nonstandard slang combination likely meaning haters who are doomed, defeated, exposed, exhausted, or otherwise 'cooked'; exact nuance depends on source context.
column7: After the comeback, fans joked that the haters were cooked. / 'Cooked haters' is understandable meme language, but not a stable dictionary phrase.
column8: Cooked is highly context-sensitive internet slang: doomed, finished, exhausted, mentally fried, exposed, etc. Preserve uncertainty rather than invent one exact source meaning.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: cooked haters meaning

column5: Used to jump quickly to a surprising or rapid next development: before you realize it, suddenly the situation has changed.
column6: before you know it, suddenly, and then, one thing led to another
column7: We stopped for one drink, and next thing you know it was two in the morning. / I watched one episode, and next thing I knew I'd finished the whole season.
column8: Tense often shifts: 'next thing I knew' when narrating past events; 'next thing you know' for vivid/general storytelling. Suggests rapid progression or omitted intermediate steps.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: next thing you know meaning

column5: Amusingly strange, wildly unconventional, absurd, or clownishly energetic; historically, a comic fool or clown.
column6: wacky, goofy, madcap, eccentric, absurd, offbeat
column7: The show has a zany sense of humor without becoming completely random. / He plays a zany inventor who solves every problem in the worst possible way.
column8: Usually playful rather than harsh. 'Wacky' and 'goofy' are close; madcap suggests hectic comic energy. Historical noun sense connects to comic theatre.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define zany

column5: To express, designate, or issue an amount/value in a particular unit or currency; 'denominated in dollars' means stated/payable in dollars.
column6: express in, state in, price in, designate
column7: The bond is denominated in U.S. dollars. / Prices were denominated in euros. / The notes are issued in several denominations.
column8: Especially finance/economics. Don't confuse denomination = religious subgroup, although both share naming/category sense historically.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: denominated meaning

column5: A form of Italian popular theatre that flourished from roughly the 16th to 18th centuries, featuring professional performers, improvised scenarios, masks, physical comedy, and recurring stock character types.
column6: Italian improvised comedy, masked comedy, commedia
column7: Harlequin, Pantalone, and Columbina are stock figures associated with commedia dell'arte. / The production borrows commedia-style masks, exaggerated movement, and comic archetypes.
column8: Literally Italian 'comedy of the profession/art.' Performances were structured around scenarios and stock roles rather than being completely improvised from nothing. Influential on European comedy, pantomime, clowning, and character archetypes.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: Commedia dell'arte

column2: allow doing vs allow someone to do
column5: Allow + object + to-infinitive is standard when naming who performs the action: 'allow users to edit.' Allow + gerund can describe a permitted activity generally: 'The rules don't allow smoking.'
column6: permit doing; permit someone to do
column7: The app allows users to switch modes. / The building doesn't allow smoking. / This setting allows editing without an account.
column8: Do not say *allow someone doing* for the ordinary permission meaning. Passive: users are allowed to edit; smoking is allowed.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: allow doing something vs allow someone to do something
