column2: call the shots / be calling the shots
column5: To be the person who makes the important decisions and controls what happens.
column6: be in charge, run the show, call the tune, be in the driver's seat
column7: She owns the company, but her investors are really calling the shots. / Once you're the director, you get to call the shots.
column8: Informal control/authority idiom. Can imply actual power differs from official title.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: calling the shots meaning

column5: Rough, noisy, energetic play or fooling around that can become unsafe or disruptive.
column6: roughhousing, fooling around, messing around, rowdy play
column7: The teacher told them to stop the horseplay before someone got hurt. / What started as harmless horseplay ended with a broken lamp.
column8: Usually uncountable. Roughhousing is very close and often physical; horseplay commonly appears in safety rules/workplace warnings: 'No horseplay.' Not related to horses literally.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: define horseplay

column5: A privately owned armed ship—or its commander/crew—authorized by a government through a commission such as a letter of marque to attack and capture enemy shipping during wartime.
column6: licensed raider, corsair (overlapping), state-authorized sea raider
column7: A privateer could legally attack enemy merchant ships under authorization from its government. / To the enemy, the distinction between privateer and pirate could feel rather academic.
column8: Key distinction: pirate operates without state authorization; privateer is privately operated but officially commissioned against designated enemies. Legal status depended on period, jurisdiction, and commission.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define privateer
column12: entry::word usage::academic topic::fandom topic::history topic::nautical topic::government topic::politics discovery::public_discourse discovery::academic_discussion

column5: Cutting away unwanted branches/parts to improve growth or shape; figuratively, removing unnecessary elements; in computing/AI, eliminating branches, parameters, connections, or possibilities to simplify or speed a system.
column7: After pruning, the tree produced healthier growth. / We pruned redundant cards from the candidate list. / Model pruning can reduce computational cost by removing less useful parameters or connections.
column8: Useful literal→technical metaphor. Exact technical method depends on field: decision trees, neural networks, search algorithms, gardening.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: what is pruning
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::figurative discovery::figurative_extension discovery::possibility discovery::improvement discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Easily irritated, impatient, or quick to become annoyed.
column7: He got testy when the same question was asked for the third time.
column8: Often describes a temporary mood or interaction rather than a permanent personality.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: testy definition

column5: A ceremony, event, ordeal, or experience marking a transition from one social status or life stage to another; figuratively, a common formative experience people in a group are expected to go through.
column6: initiation, milestone, coming-of-age ritual, formative experience
column7: The ceremony functions as a rite of passage into adulthood. / Getting hopelessly lost on your first solo trip can feel like a travel rite of passage.
column8: Anthropological term associated with transitions such as birth, adulthood, marriage, death, initiation. Figurative everyday use is broader and often humorous. Rite = ritual; right/write are unrelated.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: rite of passage definition
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::discourse_expression usage::humorous usage::figurative usage::ceremonial discovery::transition discovery::figurative_extension

column5: One of the four primary compass directions: north, south, east, and west.
column7: The map marks each cardinal direction with a large letter. / North is a cardinal direction; northeast is an intercardinal direction. / The trail signs show all four cardinal directions.
column8: The four cardinal directions are north, east, south, and west. Intercardinal (ordinal) directions lie between them: northeast, southeast, southwest, northwest. 'Cardinal' here means principal/fundamental, not the bird or church rank.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: cardinal direction meaning

column5: Very broad, extensive, comprehensive, or far-reaching, often affecting many people/things or making a claim with little qualification; also the participle of sweep.
column7: The law introduced sweeping changes to the tax system. / That's a sweeping claim to make from three anecdotes. / The review makes several sweeping judgments about an entire generation.
column8: Common collocations: sweeping changes/reforms/powers/victory/generalization/statement. With claims/generalizations it often implies overbreadth; with reforms it can simply mean extensive.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define sweeping

column5: To be extremely nervous, anxious, frightened, or under intense pressure, often visibly sweating.
column6: be extremely nervous, panic, be on edge
column7: I was sweating bullets waiting for the interview result. / He started sweating bullets when the teacher asked to see his homework.
column8: Hyperbolic, not literal. Common progressive: 'I was sweating bullets.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0118 | search: sweating bullets meaning

column5: Very poor and lacking the money or resources needed for basic necessities; as a noun, an indigent person.
column7: The program provides legal representation for indigent defendants. / The hospital historically served indigent patients who could not afford private care.
column8: Formal and common in legal/administrative contexts, especially 'indigent defendant.' Stronger/more institutional than simply low-income. Do not confuse with Indigenous.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define indigent

column5: The act of going by, transferring, or dying; temporary/brief as an adjective; in identity contexts, being perceived as belonging to a social category, sometimes one different from an assigned or known identity.
column6: brief, fleeting; death/decease; being perceived as (identity context)
column7: I only made a passing comment about the ending. / We were saddened by his passing. / In some identity discussions, 'passing' means being perceived by others as a member of a particular group.
column8: Highly polysemous. Common: passing interest/remark = brief; someone's passing = death (euphemistic); passing grade = sufficient to pass; passing in race/sports; identity 'passing' has specific social histories and can be sensitive. Context is essential.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: define passing

column5: To an intense, severe, or highly perceptive degree.
column7: She was acutely conscious of the awkward silence. / I became acutely aware of how different the two accents were. / He was acutely ill and needed immediate treatment.
column8: Two useful clusters: (1) intensely/keenly aware or sensitive—acutely aware/conscious/embarrassed; (2) medically/severely—acutely ill, acute pain. It often signals high intensity rather than merely 'very.' Contrast chronically in medical duration.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: acutely definition

column5: Clever at gaining an advantage through tricks, strategy, deception, or resourcefulness; crafty and hard to outmaneuver.
column7: The wily negotiator never revealed his real limit. / A wily fox is a classic storybook image.
column8: Often admiring and suspicious at once: intelligence plus craftiness. More literary/playful than simply clever.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: wily meaning

column5: To support, reinforce, strengthen, or prevent something from weakening, collapsing, or failing—literally with supports or figuratively with resources/actions.
column6: reinforce, strengthen, bolster, prop up, support
column7: The company raised cash to shore up its balance sheet. / The rewrite shores up the weak middle of the story. / Workers shored up the damaged wall.
column8: From shore = prop/support with a brace. Figurative collocations: shore up finances, support, defenses, confidence, a position.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: shore up meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb usage::figurative usage::debate-friendly discovery::resource_allocation discovery::figurative_extension discovery::support discovery::prevention discovery::debate_language

column5: Criminal, violent, dishonest, or suspicious wrongdoing, especially when investigating an unexplained death/disappearance; in sports, unfair or illegal play.
column6: wrongdoing, crime, misconduct; cheating, dirty play
column7: Police said there was no evidence of foul play in the disappearance. / Investigators began to suspect foul play after finding the door forced open. / The referee penalized the team for foul play.
column8: Common investigative collocation: 'no foul play suspected.' It does not name a specific crime; it signals possible malicious/criminal involvement. Sports sense is more literal rule-breaking/unfair conduct.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define foul play

column5: Physical exercises using body weight and little or no equipment, often to develop strength, flexibility, and coordination.
column7: Push-ups, squats, and pull-ups are staples of calisthenics.
column8: Usually treated as an uncountable/plural-form noun: do calisthenics.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: calisthenics meaning

column5: An online publishing platform associated especially with subscription newsletters, essays, podcasts, and independent writers; by metonymy, 'a Substack' can mean someone's publication/newsletter hosted there.
column7: She publishes a weekly essay on Substack. / I subscribed to his Substack after reading one free post.
column8: Brand/proper noun. 'A Substack' is common conversational shorthand for a publication hosted on the platform, though the generic item is a newsletter/publication.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: substack meaning

column5: A usually mocking label for a non-Japanese person perceived as obsessively idealizing Japanese culture, especially anime/manga, in an exaggerated, shallow, or identity-consuming way; 'weeb' is the common shortened form and can be self-deprecating.
column7: He jokingly calls himself a weeb because half his shelves are manga. / 'Weeaboo' is harsher when it implies fetishizing Japan rather than simply enjoying Japanese media.
column8: Existing Master references the term but lacks a standalone card. Historically emerged from internet replacement/filter culture around an earlier slur. Modern 'weeb' ranges from affectionate self-label to insult; Japanophile is much more neutral.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: weeaboo
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::critical usage::affectionate usage::informal topic::internet topic::anime topic::manga topic::culture discovery::perception

column2: up to one's ears in something
column5: Extremely busy, deeply involved, or overwhelmed by a large amount of work, trouble, debt, paperwork, etc.
column6: swamped, buried in, snowed under, overwhelmed, knee-deep in
column7: I'm up to my ears in vocabulary cards this week. / By Friday she was up to her ears in paperwork. / They were up to their ears in debt.
column8: Image: submerged so deeply that only the head/ears remain above the pile. Commonly negative/overwhelmed, though playful exaggeration is frequent. Usually 'up to my/your/his ears in X.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: up to my ears

column5: A sudden attack, entry, or search carried out to seize, damage, arrest, steal, or obtain something; as a verb, to conduct such an action against a place/group or to take resources from it.
column6: attack, storm, search, bust, plunder, loot
column7: Police raided the warehouse before dawn. / The village was repeatedly raided for supplies. / In games, our guild raids the same boss every Friday.
column8: Wide range: police raid, military raid, robbery raid, game raid, pantry/fridge raid. 'Be raided' focuses on the target. Gaming raid is a coordinated group encounter and may be semantically specialized.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: define raided
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist usage::military topic::weather discovery::resource_allocation discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The visible plume above a whale when it exhales forcefully through its blowhole; it consists mainly of warm moist breath condensing in cooler air, often mixed with seawater/mucus droplets.
column6: whale blow, blowhole plume, exhalation plume
column7: We spotted the whale first by its tall spout on the horizon. / Different whale species can have characteristically shaped blows, though distance and weather affect what you see.
column8: Whales do not simply shoot stored seawater from their lungs. The visible 'spout' is primarily exhaled warm moist air condensing, plus droplets around the blowhole.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: whale spout meaning

column5: To be especially noticeable, distinctive, memorable, or significant to a particular observer.
column6: stick out to someone, catch someone's attention, strike someone, be noticeable
column7: One line in the review really stood out to me. / What stands out to you most about the animation? / Her pronunciation immediately stood out to me as unusually natural.
column8: Existing WID4376 notes this as the standard alternative to raw 'stock out to someone'; retained because this exact productive pattern is highly useful. 'Stand right out to me' simply intensifies it.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: stand right out to me meaning

column5: Very loud, rough, disorderly, and energetic, especially of voices, laughter, crowds, parties, or entertainment.
column7: A raucous crowd spilled out of the bar after the game. / The episode ends with a raucous party scene full of shouting and laughter.
column8: Often combines loudness with rowdy energy. Can be positive ('raucous fun') or negative ('raucous disturbance'). Existing appearances as a synonym do not replace a standalone card.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: raucous

column5: The indefinitely remote past, beyond human memory or record; used especially in 'since/from time immemorial.'
column6: time out of mind, since ancient times, beyond living memory
column7: People have told stories around fires since time immemorial. / The village claimed the right had existed from time immemorial.
column8: Immemorial literally means extending beyond memory. The fixed phrase 'time immemorial' is much more common than using immemorial alone. Often rhetorical rather than a literal historical claim.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define immemorial

column5: A planned piece of work or undertaking; as a verb, to estimate or predict, to display outward, to cast an image, or to attribute one's own feelings to someone else.
column7: The team projected higher sales for the new project.
column8: Stress changes in common AmE pronunciation: noun PRO-ject, verb pro-JECT. The verb is highly polysemous, including psychological projection.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: project

column2: slide in the direction of something
column5: To move gradually toward a physical direction, state, tendency, position, or outcome.
column7: The discussion slowly slid in the direction of politics.
column8: Not a fixed idiom; slide adds a sense of smooth or gradual movement/change.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: slide in the direction meaning

column5: To land a movement, note, accent, edit, or action exactly on the musical beat or rhythmic accent.
column6: land on the beat, match the beat, strike on the beat
column7: The dancer hits the beat perfectly with each shoulder movement. / The cut hits the beat right as the chorus starts.
column8: Compositional but common in dance/music/editing talk. Contrast 'miss the beat' and 'keep the beat.' 'Beat' also has police/reporting/story senses.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: hit the beat meaning

column5: Unpleasantly bright, showy, colorful, or ornate in a way that feels excessive or lacking in taste.
column7: The hotel lobby was decorated in garish gold and purple. / I like colorful animation, but that scene's neon palette was so garish that it distracted me from the characters.
column8: Garish is usually negative. Gaudy emphasizes tasteless showiness; lurid can suggest shockingly vivid color or sensational content; flashy can be neutral/positive depending on context.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: garish meaning

column2: have an inflated sense of self
column5: To have an exaggerated view of one's own importance, ability, status, attractiveness, virtue, or uniqueness.
column6: have an inflated ego, be self-important, have an exaggerated self-image, think too highly of oneself
column7: Social media can encourage some people to develop an inflated sense of self. / He has an inflated sense of his own importance and assumes every disagreement is about him.
column8: Not a clinical diagnosis. 'Sense of self' can be neutral; inflated marks excessive self-evaluation. Related: grandiose self-image, ego inflation.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: people have an inflated sense of self meaning

column5: Completely different or contrary in a relevant respect; also a person or thing on the other side or at the other extreme.
column7: Her reaction was the exact opposite of what I expected.
column8: Broad core word useful across opposite direction, opposite effect, the opposite of, and sit opposite someone.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: opposite meaning

column5: A tall layered ice-cream sundae, traditionally served in a long glass with fruit, sauces/syrups, cream, and other toppings.
column7: I ordered a Knickerbocker glory mostly because I'd heard the name in British TV. / The dessert arrived in a tall glass layered with ice cream, fruit, sauce, and whipped cream.
column8: Classic British dessert; recipes vary. The name is culturally distinctive and sounds old-fashioned/retro. Not simply any sundae, though sundae is the closest broad category.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0115 | search: knickerbocker glory meaning

column5: To state or say that one did/experienced something, using report + gerund when the subject of report is also the understood subject of the -ing action.
column6: say one did, state having done, report that one did
column7: Several users reported seeing the same error. / She reported feeling dizzy after the ride.
column8: Common pattern: report doing/having done something; also report that + clause. Not normally 'report to do' for this meaning.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: report doing meaning

column2: depth with a few voices, breadth with different ones
column3: /depθ wɪð ə ˌfjuː ˈvɔɪsɪz bredθ wɪð ˌdɪfrənt wʌnz/
column5: A listening-learning strategy: repeatedly listen to a small number of familiar speakers for deep adaptation and detailed comprehension, while also rotating through many different speakers for robust generalization across voices/accents/styles.
column6: deep repeated exposure + broad speaker variability
column7: For listening practice, I want depth with a few voices and breadth with different ones: learn a handful of speakers deeply, but keep testing myself on unfamiliar voices too.
column8: Preserve Jin's/search-source formulation as a useful conceptual contrast. 'Depth' supports adaptation to individual idiolects; 'breadth' counters overfitting and builds tolerance for speaker variability.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: Depth with a few voices, and breadth with different ones

column5: A period of intense optimism, euphoria, confidence, or relief sometimes experienced early in recovery from addiction, when life may feel unusually hopeful and problems seem easier than they are.
column7: He felt amazing during the first weeks of sobriety, but his counselor warned him about the 'pink cloud.' / Pink-clouding can make someone underestimate the work of long-term recovery.
column8: Recovery-community term, not a formal diagnosis and not experienced by everyone. Often discussed as temporary; avoid treating later difficulty as inevitable.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: pink cloud meaing
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::formal usage::slang usage::informal discovery::impression discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: Extra time added at the end of a half to compensate for time lost to substitutions, injuries, delays, goal celebrations, video reviews, and other stoppages.
column7: They scored the winner in the fifth minute of stoppage time. / The board showed seven minutes of added time.
column8: Football/soccer term. Not the same as extra time, which is an additional period played in some knockout matches after regulation ends tied.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: stoppage time meaning

column5: To make a loud, harsh cry like a bird; figuratively, to complain loudly or noisily. As a noun, the cry or a loud complaint.
column6: screech, cry, shriek; complain, gripe, protest
column7: The parrot squawked every time someone entered the room. / Customers started squawking about the new fee. / One angry squawk from the bird woke everyone up.
column8: Bird sense is primary. Human complaint sense is informal and can sound dismissive. In aviation, 'squawk' also means transmit/set a transponder code: 'squawk 7700' for an emergency.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116, voca_0118 | search: squawk

column5: An uneasy feeling of doubt, guilt, or concern about whether something is right or wise.
column7: She had no qualms about rejecting the offer. / I have a few qualms about giving the app that much access. / He accepted the deal without a qualm.
column8: Most common in plural: 'have qualms about + noun/gerund,' 'no qualms about doing.' A qualm is a moral/practical uneasiness, not simply uncertainty. 'Scruple' leans moral; 'reservation' is broader and often milder.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: define qualms

column5: Behaving in a way associated with the 'sigma' meme archetype: independent, self-contained, cool, dominant, unfazed, or performatively unconcerned with social approval—often used ironically.
column6: acting like a sigma, sigma behavior, lone-wolf meme behavior
column7: He ignored the drama and walked away; the comments called it 'being sigma.' / 'Being sigma' is often more of a joke than a serious personality category.
column8: Existing sigma card defines the label. This preserves the productive phrase 'being sigma.' Meaning is meme-driven and unstable; frequently ironic/parodic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0120 | search: being sigma meaning
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::phrase usage::slang usage::internet_slang usage::ironic usage::informal topic::internet topic::performance discovery::social_approval

column5: You are difficult to manage, control, supervise, or keep up with—often because you are energetic, mischievous, demanding, unpredictable, or emotionally intense.
column6: hard to handle, a lot to deal with, demanding, mischievous
column7: That puppy is adorable, but he's such a handful. / 'You're such a handful,' she said, half annoyed and half amused.
column8: Can be affectionate/playful or genuinely critical depending on tone. Distinct from 'a handful of people' = a small number, covered in Batch21.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: you're such a handful meaning
column12: entry::idiom usage::conversational usage::playful usage::critical usage::affectionate discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: Learn by heart = memorize something so thoroughly that you can reproduce it from memory, often word for word. Rote memorization = memorizing through repetition, often with little emphasis on understanding.
column6: memorize, commit to memory; learn by rote, drill
column7: We had to learn the poem by heart for class. / Flashcards can become rote memorization if you repeat definitions without learning how the words actually behave in context. / I know the dialogue by heart.
column8: They overlap but focus differently: by heart describes the result (known from memory); by rote describes the method (mechanical repetition). Rote can be critical when contrasted with understanding, but repetition itself is not inherently useless.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: learning by heart by rote memorazation
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::critical topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::emphasis discovery::commitment

column5: To pray for someone or something, or formally present prayers as an act of worship, remembrance, gratitude, or supplication.
column6: pray, say prayers, send prayers, pray for
column7: People gathered to offer prayers for the victims. / At the shrine, visitors offered prayers for good health and success.
column8: Offer prayers sounds more formal/ceremonial than simply pray. In religious contexts 'offer' conceptualizes the prayer as something presented to God/deity. 'Thoughts and prayers' is a separate modern phrase and can be sincere or criticized as formulaic.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: offer prayers meaning

column5: A doctor who specializes in diagnosing and treating cancer.
column7: Her GP referred her to an oncologist for further tests. / The oncologist explained the treatment options and what to expect from each one.
column8: Oncology = study/treatment of cancer. Medical oncologists, surgical oncologists, and radiation oncologists have different roles.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0113 | search: oncologist
column12: entry::word usage::specialist topic::health topic::medicine discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A problem, reversal, delay, or difficulty that interrupts progress or makes success harder, usually without necessarily ending the effort.
column7: Losing a week of work was a setback, but the project recovered. / She treated the rejection as a temporary setback.
column8: Usually implies progress can resume. Stronger 'defeat' may imply losing; setback is often temporary/partial.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: define setbacks

column5: Used to express an intuition, impression, or expectation that something is true or will happen, without claiming certainty.
column6: I suspect, I have a hunch
column7: I have a feeling that you're going to love it.
column8: A feeling here means intuition, not necessarily emotion.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0111 | search: I have a feeling that you love it meaning

column5: Too obvious, direct, literal, or unsubtle, especially in writing, symbolism, dialogue, or interpretation; in other contexts, exactly correct.
column7: The symbolism works, but the dialogue is a little too on the nose.
column8: Raw phrase 'be a little more on the nose with it' means make the intended point more explicit/obvious. Context distinguishes 'too obvious' from 'exactly right.'
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0112 | search: be a little more on the nose with it

column5: Giving or expressing a warning, caution, reproof, or moral advice; intended to admonish.
column7: She gave him an admonitory look when he reached for his phone during the ceremony. / The story ends on an admonitory note about pride and greed.
column8: Formal/literary and much less common than cautionary or warning. Can combine warning + mild reproof rather than pure anger.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define admonitory
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::literary usage::ceremonial discovery::warning discovery::recommendation

column5: Showing or involving empathy—the ability/willingness to understand and share or imaginatively enter another person's feelings or perspective.
column7: She was empathetic without pretending she knew exactly how he felt. / An empathetic response can acknowledge someone's frustration before offering advice.
column8: Empathic is a common variant, especially technical/professional. Empathetic ≠ sympathetic exactly: sympathy is concern/pity; empathy emphasizes understanding another perspective/feeling.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0119 | search: define empathetic
column12: entry::word usage::technical usage::professional discovery::professional_context discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To strongly desire or yearn to be in a particular state, role, place, relationship, etc.
column6: yearn to be, ache to be, deeply wish to be
column7: As a teenager, he longed to be taken seriously. / She longed to be somewhere quiet.
column8: Long as verb is literary/emotional compared with want. Pattern: long to do; long for + noun/person; long for someone to do.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0121 | search: long to be meaning

column5: To gradually become weaker, smaller, thinner, less vigorous, or less significant until nearly disappearing; literally of plants/bodies and figuratively of institutions, hopes, skills, etc.
column6: waste away, shrivel, fade away, dwindle, atrophy
column7: Without water, the plant slowly withered away. / The old organization withered away after its funding disappeared. / Skills can wither away if you never use them.
column8: Wither alone often means dry/shrivel or lose vitality; away emphasizes gradual disappearance/decline. 'Waste away' is especially associated with bodily emaciation; atrophy can be literal or figurative and more technical.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0116 | search: wither away meaning
column12: entry::phrasal_verb usage::technical usage::figurative discovery::figurative_extension discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To perform the official duties at a ceremony, especially a wedding or religious service; or to act as an official/referee in a sporting event.
column7: Her uncle officiated at the wedding. / A licensed celebrant officiated the ceremony. / She has officiated college basketball games for ten years.
column8: Common patterns: officiate at a wedding/service; officiate a wedding (also common); officiate a game. Officiant = person conducting a ceremony.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0117 | search: define officiated

column5: The systematic way a word changes form to express grammatical information such as tense, number, person, case, gender, or comparison.
column6: inflectional paradigm, conjugation pattern, declension pattern, morphological pattern
column7: Sing–sang–sung follows a different inflection pattern from regular verbs like walk–walked–walked. / Learning common inflection patterns makes unfamiliar forms easier to recognize.
column8: Existing inflection WID374 is primarily illustrated with voice/pitch. Here the target is grammatical morphology. Conjugation is usually for verbs; declension for nouns/adjectives/pronouns in languages with case; inflection is the umbrella term.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0114 | search: inflection patterns

column5: To take control of driving; figuratively, to assume control, leadership, or responsibility for a situation.
column7: I was exhausted, so she took the wheel for the last hour of the drive.
column8: Literal driving sense readily extends metaphorically to taking control.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110 | search: take the wheel meaning

column5: Decorative flags or strips of material hung for celebrations; also the name of several small seed-eating birds.
column7: Red, white, and blue bunting hung across the porch.

column8: Often figurative: arbiter of taste/style/truth. Related arbitrate, arbitration, but an arbiter need not always be a formal arbitrator.

column5: Used after many forceful verbs to mean doing the action to an extreme or very intense degree.
column6: the hell out of, the heck out of

column8: Pattern: verb + the crap out of + object, e.g. beat/scare/kick/clean the crap out of something. Raw search 'crap out of it' likely came from this intensifier construction.
column10: voca_0110–0121 | folders: voca_0110, voca_0111, voca_0112 | search: crap out of it meaning

column5: The part of an utterance or discourse that is highlighted as especially informative, contrastive, new, or currently central to the communicative point.
column7: In 'JOHN bought the book,' stress on John can mark discourse focus when contrasting who bought it. / Prosody helps listeners identify discourse focus.
column8: Exact definitions differ across information-structure theories. Focus interacts with givenness, topic, contrast, syntax, and prosody; not merely 'what the conversation is about.'

column5: An element best known from topsy-turvy, sometimes echoed in playful formations to suggest inversion, disorder, or reversal; not normally a productive standalone suffix in standard English.
column7: Topsy-turvy is the established word; a writer might coin a playful X-turvy formation for comic effect, but readers would hear it as an echo of topsy-turvy.
column8: Existing topsy-turvy WID5144 covers the standard adjective. Raw search 'something-turvy' suggests curiosity about the reusable-looking second half. Treat novel -turvy formations as wordplay, not a normal suffix you can freely attach to anything.

column5: A person who participates in LARP (live-action role-playing), physically portraying a character in an improvised or structured fictional setting; online, sometimes used derisively for someone seen as performatively pretending to be a type of person.
column7: The park was full of LARPers in fantasy costumes. / Online critics called him a 'revolutionary LARPer,' implying the persona was performative.
column8: Capitals vary: LARPer/larper. Internet extension can be insulting and often means 'someone acting out an identity/ideology without genuine stakes.'

column2: circumvent vs qualify vs hedge vs carefully frame
column5: To circumvent is to avoid or get around a rule, obstacle, or issue; to qualify a statement is to limit or modify its force; to hedge is to make a claim less direct or certain; to carefully frame something is to deliberately choose how it is presented.
column6: circumvent = get around; qualify = limit/modify; hedge = soften uncertainty; frame = present strategically
column7: He tried to circumvent the restriction by using another account. / I'd qualify that claim: it applies mainly to beginners. / She hedged by saying 'in some cases' and 'I think.' / He carefully framed the criticism as a suggestion.
column8: These are not interchangeable. Qualifying changes the scope or strength of a claim; hedging signals uncertainty/caution; framing concerns presentation and perspective; circumventing means bypassing something rather than wording it cautiously.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrase usage::academic usage::softening usage::presentation-friendly topic::decision-making topic::language_learning topic::problem-solving discovery::contrast discovery::assertion discovery::qualification discovery::hedging discovery::prevention discovery::academic_discussion discovery::presentation_language

column5: A communication-security design in which data is encrypted so that only the communicating endpoints possess the means to read the message content, rather than intermediate service providers being able to read it in transit.
column7: The messaging app uses end-to-end encryption, so the service is not supposed to be able to read the message content in transit.
column8: Usually abbreviated E2EE. It protects message content between endpoints, but it does not automatically hide all metadata, protect a compromised device, or guarantee the identity of the person at the other endpoint.
column10: voca_0122

column5: To officially exclude a person from participation in the sacraments or membership privileges of a church; figuratively, to cast someone out of a community or group.
column7: He was excommunicated from the church after openly rejecting its doctrine. / Jokingly, they said he'd be excommunicated from the fandom for admitting he hated the finale.
column8: The literal sense is specifically religious and formal. Figurative uses are often humorous or exaggerated. Do not confuse with communicate.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::formal usage::humorous usage::figurative usage::religious topic::religion discovery::figurative_extension discovery::religious_origin discovery::literal_vs_figurative

column5: To stop dealing in generalities and begin discussing or working on the most important practical details of something.
column6: get down to business, get into the details, get to the heart of the matter
column7: We've talked about the overall plan; now let's get down to the nitty-gritty. / Once we got down to the nitty-gritty of the contract, several problems appeared.
column8: Usually takes of + noun: get down to the nitty-gritty of the budget/deal/problem. More specific than simply get down to it: nitty-gritty emphasizes the concrete, often messy details.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::idiom usage::informal usage::conversational usage::professional usage::presentation-friendly topic::business topic::communication topic::work topic::presentations topic::planning topic::problem-solving discovery::practical_details discovery::presentation_language discovery::professional_context discovery::nuts_and_bolts discovery::process_details discovery::implementation

column5: To work for a large company, institution, government, or other conventional authority, especially as viewed from an anti-establishment or independent-minded perspective.
column6: work for a corporation, work for the establishment, have a conventional job
column7: After years of freelancing, he joked that he was finally going to work for the man. / She left her corporate job because she was tired of working for the man.
column8: the Man can mean institutional authority or the establishment. The phrase often carries joking, countercultural, or mildly rebellious overtones; it does not simply mean 'work for a male boss.'
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::idiom usage::informal usage::humorous usage::professional usage::businesslike topic::business topic::work topic::culture topic::government topic::politics discovery::public_discourse discovery::professional_context

column5: The criteria or level of evidence and justification a person or field requires before accepting a belief or claim as warranted.
column6: standards of justification, standards of evidence, belief criteria
column7: Scientific and everyday decisions may operate with different epistemic standards. / We should apply roughly comparable epistemic standards to competing claims.
column8: Broader than evidentiary standards: epistemic standards can include evidence quality, source reliability, coherence, inference rules, and acceptable uncertainty. Useful when discussing double standards in belief formation.
column10: voca_0122

column5: To isolate or separate someone or something from others; in law, to take possession of property by authority; in trials, to isolate a jury from outside information.
column7: The jury was sequestered during the high-profile trial. / The researchers sequestered the samples from potential contaminants. / The policy aims to sequester carbon underground.
column8: Broad verb with domain-specific uses. Carbon sequestration = capturing/storing carbon. Existing adjective/past participle sequestered describes something kept apart; this card centers the active verb.
column10: voca_0122

column5: A trap, especially one made with a loop or wire for catching animals; as a verb, to catch or trap, literally or figuratively.
column7: The ranger found an illegal snare in the woods. / The scam was designed to snare inexperienced buyers. / His foot was snared by a loop of rope.
column8: A snare is a kind of trap; it may use a tightening loop, but snare is broader than noose. Snared = caught/trapped. Also snare drum is a completely separate common compound.
column10: voca_0122

column5: Bringing many old, unrelated, or already resolved grievances into a current argument so that the original issue gets buried under a pile of complaints.
column6: gunnysacking (related), piling on grievances, bringing up everything at once
column7: We started arguing about the dishes, but within five minutes we were kitchen-sinking and fighting about things from three years ago.
column8: Named after 'everything but the kitchen sink.' Often discussed in relationship/conflict communication. Gunnysacking is related but emphasizes storing grievances up and unloading them later; kitchen-sinking emphasizes throwing many grievances into the present fight.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::variant_set entry::noun_phrase usage::rhetorical topic::relationships topic::communication discovery::complaint discovery::debate_language

column5: To prevent something threatening, unpleasant, or unwanted from approaching, worsening, or having its full effect.
column6: hold off, fend off, keep away, stave off
column7: Regular exercise helps keep stress at bay. / The medication kept the symptoms at bay for several months. / They lit a fire to keep the insects at bay.
column8: Often used with illness, fear, hunger, danger, attackers, insects, or problems. It usually means control or delay rather than permanently eliminate.
column10: voca_0122

column5: Agreeable can mean pleasant, acceptable, or willing to agree; disagreeable means unpleasant, objectionable, or difficult to deal with—not simply 'a person who disagrees.'
column6: agreeable: pleasant, amenable; disagreeable: unpleasant, objectionable
column7: The weather was surprisingly agreeable. / She was agreeable to the proposed change. / He became increasingly disagreeable as the meeting dragged on.
column8: Agreeable to a plan = willing to accept it. Disagreeable often describes unpleasantness in temperament, sensation, or conditions; it does not normally mean 'holding a different opinion.' For that, use disagreeing, opposed, or in disagreement.
column10: voca_0122

column5: To get rid of, escape from, or shake off someone who is following, accompanying, or bothering you.
column6: ditch, shake off, lose, get rid of
column7: We took a side street and finally gave the guy the shake. / She was trying to give her unwanted companion the shake.
column8: A relatively uncommon/dated idiom. It is different from give someone a fair shake = give someone a fair chance. Modern speakers are more likely to say shake someone off, lose someone, or ditch someone.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::dated discovery::removal

column5: The transfer of pollen between different plants; figuratively, the exchange and mixing of ideas, methods, styles, or influences between different people, fields, or cultures.
column7: Bees help with cross-pollination between plants. / The project benefited from cross-pollination between linguistics and computer science. / Anime has long involved cross-pollination with games, music, and online fan culture.
column8: The figurative sense is common in discussions of culture, research, business, and creativity. It suggests productive transfer across boundaries, not just random mixing.
column10: voca_0122

column5: A lack of the respect or solemnity normally considered appropriate toward a person, institution, belief, or serious subject.
column7: The show's irreverence toward authority is part of its appeal. / His jokes mix affection with a deliberate irreverence toward tradition.
column8: Can be negative ('disrespect') or approving when it suggests refreshing refusal to treat something too solemnly. Adjective: irreverent. Contrast reverence = deep respect.
column10: voca_0122

column2: not as much as I should
column5: Less often, less intensely, or to a smaller degree than the speaker believes would be appropriate or desirable.
column6: less than I ought to, not enough, less often than I should
column7: I read in English, but not as much as I should. / I call my parents, just not as much as I should.
column8: The omitted action/degree is recovered from context. Very natural self-evaluative phrasing. Compare not as much as I used to = a comparison with the past, not with an obligation or ideal.
column10: voca_0122

column5: A loop in a rope or cord formed with a sliding knot that tightens when pulled, historically used for hanging or for catching things.
column7: The rope had been tied into a noose. / The image of a tightening noose is also used metaphorically for mounting pressure or danger.
column8: A noose describes the tightening loop itself, whereas a snare is a trap and may or may not involve a noose. Because of its strong association with execution and lynching, the word can carry heavy historical and emotional weight.
column10: voca_0122

column5: To add a limitation, condition, exception, or clarification that makes a statement less absolute or more precisely accurate.
column6: limit, modify, nuance, add a caveat to
column7: I'd qualify that statement by saying the effect is strongest in younger learners. / She qualified her criticism with 'at least in the cases I've seen.'
column8: This is the academic/discourse sense of qualify, not 'be eligible.' A qualifier narrows or modifies a claim. Qualifying can overlap with hedging, but a qualification may be precise and confident rather than uncertain.
column10: voca_0122

column5: To support, encourage, defend, or stand by someone, especially when they face difficulty or opposition.
column6: support, back, stand by, have someone's back, root for
column7: Even when the project was going badly, I knew she was in my corner. / It's easier to take risks when you have someone in your corner.
column8: From boxing, where a fighter's corner team advises and supports them between rounds. 'Someone is always in your corner' means they consistently support you; it does not require physical presence.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative usage::conversational usage::warm topic::relationships topic::friends topic::communication discovery::support discovery::encouragement discovery::solidarity discovery::loyalty

column5: The name of an Irish musical group, later used as the title of Key's visual novel/anime CLANNAD; in the game context it is strongly associated with the theme of family.
column7: I finally looked up why CLANNAD is called Clannad. / The title fits the story's focus on family, even though the linguistic history is more complicated than 'Clannad means family.'
column8: The Irish band says its name was formed from Clann as Dobhar ('family from Dore'), shortened into Clannad. The visual novel's creators treated CLANNAD as meaning 'family' in Gaelic, but Irish 'clann' is the actual ordinary word related to family/children; CLANNAD itself is a proper name, not simply the Irish common noun for 'family.'
column10: voca_0122

column5: To be a sign or warning that something, usually important or unpleasant, is likely to happen in the future.
column7: The sudden drop in sales may portend a difficult year ahead. / Dark clouds portended the storm.
column8: Portend describes a real-world sign indicating what may come. Foreshadow is especially common in storytelling, where an earlier detail anticipates a later event. 'Bode well/ill' is closely related. Portend often sounds formal or ominous.
column10: voca_0122

column5: Showing disrespect toward something sacred or religious; by extension, outrageously disrespectful toward something people treat as almost sacred.
column7: Defacing the shrine would be considered sacrilegious. / Anime fans might jokingly call skipping the opening theme sacrilegious.
column8: Correct spelling: sacrilegious, not *sacrelegious*. Despite its connection to sacrilege, the word is pronounced with /-lɪdʒ-/. Figurative use is often playful hyperbole.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::word usage::playful usage::figurative usage::profane usage::religious topic::religion discovery::religious_origin discovery::literal_vs_figurative

column5: Extending across an entire process, system, route, or workflow from the initial starting point all the way to the final endpoint.
column6: complete, full-process, from start to finish, comprehensive
column7: We tested the workflow end to end. / The company offers an end-to-end service from design through delivery.
column8: Hyphenate before a noun: an end-to-end test/solution. Often unhyphenated after the verb: test the system end to end. It does not mean 'done entirely by one person'; the focus is coverage from one endpoint of a process to the other.
column10: voca_0122

column3: /fər ɔːl aɪ noʊ/; /fər ɔːl wiː noʊ/
column5: Used to emphasize that the true situation is unknown and that a possibility, sometimes an extreme one, cannot be ruled out.
column6: as far as I/we know, possibly, maybe for all anyone knows
column7: For all I know, he could already be on the train. / For all we know, this may have been planned months ago.
column8: For all I know foregrounds the speaker's own lack of knowledge; for all we know frames the uncertainty as shared by a group. Often followed by could/may/might. It can sound skeptical, speculative, or slightly dismissive depending on tone.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::idiom entry::prepositional_phrase usage::skeptical usage::speculative discovery::emphasis discovery::possibility discovery::lack_of_knowledge

column5: To give someone a fair opportunity, fair treatment, or an unbiased chance to prove themselves.
column6: give a fair chance, treat fairly, give a fair hearing
column7: I didn't love the first episode, but I want to give the series a fair shake. / New employees deserve a fair shake before they're judged.
column8: Usually positive: give someone/something a fair shake. Also 'not get a fair shake' = be treated unfairly. Distinct from give someone the shake = get rid of/escape someone.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::idiom entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal topic::medicine topic::health discovery::possibility

column5: A long, deep cut or wound; also a deep cut or split in a surface. As a verb, to cut deeply.
column7: He had a nasty gash on his leg after the fall. / The collision gashed the side of the boat.
column8: Stronger than cut: gash typically suggests a relatively long, open, or deep wound. In some varieties of British slang, gash also has crude/offensive senses; context matters.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::word usage::slang usage::offensive usage::vulgar usage::informal usage::evaluative

column5: Rules or thresholds governing what counts as acceptable evidence and how strong evidence must be to justify a conclusion, claim, or legal finding.
column6: standards of evidence, proof requirements, evidential criteria
column7: Different courts apply different evidentiary standards. / A scientific claim should be judged by evidentiary standards appropriate to the field.
column8: Legal contexts may distinguish admissibility rules from burdens/standards of proof such as preponderance of the evidence or beyond a reasonable doubt. In broader academic use, the phrase concerns what evidence is considered sufficient and reliable.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::academic usage::scientific topic::law discovery::evidence discovery::assertion discovery::academic_discussion

column5: In a secretive, stealthy, or sly way intended to avoid being noticed.
column7: He sneakily checked his phone under the table. / The cat sneakily crept into the room while the door was open.
column8: Sneakily is the standard adverb from sneaky. *Sneakishly* is rare/nonstandard-sounding and is usually not the form a native speaker would choose.
column10: voca_0122

column5: A powerful whirlpool; figuratively, a chaotic, violent, or overwhelming situation involving many forces, events, or emotions.
column7: The small boat was pulled toward the maelstrom. / The scandal dragged the company into a maelstrom of lawsuits, media attention, and internal conflict.
column8: The figurative pattern maelstrom of + plural/uncountable noun is common: a maelstrom of emotions/events/controversy. Stronger and more dramatic than simple confusion or busyness.
column10: voca_0122

column5: To catch in a trap or snare; figuratively, to trap or entangle someone in a difficult situation, scheme, obligation, or relationship.
column7: The animal became ensnared in wire. / He found himself ensnared in a web of debt and legal problems.
column8: Often figurative and somewhat literary: be ensnared by/in something. Compared with trap, ensnare paints a stronger image of becoming caught in something difficult to escape.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::form_family entry::word usage::literary usage::figurative topic::relationships discovery::literal_vs_figurative discovery::figurative_extension

column5: A word or expression invented for a single occasion or narrow context rather than established as a conventional part of the language.
column6: nonce word, ad hoc coinage, occasionalism
column7: The reviewer called it a 'plotquake,' probably a one-off coinage rather than established slang.
column8: In linguistics, nonce word/nonce formation is the more technical term for an item coined for a particular occasion. A one-off coinage may be transparent and memorable without ever becoming conventional.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::technical usage::specialist usage::informal topic::linguistics discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A continuous range in which adjacent points differ only gradually and there are no clear-cut breaks between categories.
column7: Political views do not always fit into two boxes; they can lie on a continuum. / Language proficiency is better thought of as a continuum than a simple beginner/advanced split.
column8: Plural: continua /kənˈtɪnjuə/ or continuums. Often used in academic discussion when categories shade gradually into one another. Similar to spectrum, though continuum emphasizes continuity.
column10: voca_0122

column5: A statement in set theory proposing that there is no size of infinity strictly between the cardinality of the integers and that of the real numbers.
column7: The continuum hypothesis asks whether there is a cardinality between that of the natural numbers and the real numbers.
column8: A famous result in mathematical logic: within the standard ZFC axioms of set theory, the continuum hypothesis can neither be proved nor disproved if ZFC is consistent. This is a specialized mathematical term, not the ordinary continuum sense.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist usage::scientific topic::research topic::mathematics discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Attrition is gradual reduction through repeated losses, departures, wear, or pressure; depletion is the reduction or exhaustion of a stock, supply, or resource through use or loss.
column6: attrition: gradual loss, erosion; depletion: exhaustion, reduction, drain
column7: The team lost staff through attrition as people resigned over several months. / Heavy pumping caused depletion of the groundwater supply.
column8: Attrition often emphasizes a process of wearing down or losing members over time—employee attrition, war of attrition. Depletion emphasizes that a finite resource is being used up—battery depletion, resource depletion. They can overlap, but the conceptual focus differs.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::noun_phrase usage::academic topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::resource_allocation discovery::academic_discussion

column5: A broad, stable recreational boat supported by two or more hollow pontoons rather than by a conventional single hull.
column7: They rented a pontoon boat for a lazy afternoon on the lake. / Pontoon boats are popular for cruising, fishing, and group outings.
column8: Pontoons are buoyant tubes or floats underneath the deck. Pontoon boats prioritize stability and deck space over high-speed performance.
column10: voca_0122

column5: To cause or bring about a result; to persuade or lead someone to do something; in medicine, to deliberately initiate a physiological process such as labor.
column6: cause, bring about, provoke; persuade, prompt
column7: The drug can induce drowsiness. / Nothing could induce him to change his mind. / Doctors decided to induce labor the following morning.
column8: Common patterns: induce something; induce someone to do something. More formal than cause in many contexts. Medical induce is often understood as induce labor when context is clear.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::academic usage::persuasive topic::medicine topic::health discovery::persuasion discovery::process_details discovery::academic_discussion

column5: A faint design or identifying mark embedded in paper or superimposed on an image, video, or document; as a verb, to mark content in this way.
column6: embedded mark, identifying mark, logo overlay
column7: Hold the bill up to the light and you can see the watermark. / The preview images were watermarked with the photographer's logo.
column8: Traditional paper watermarks are formed in the paper itself and become visible in transmitted light. Digital watermarks may be visible overlays or hidden signals used for attribution, tracking, or authenticity.
column10: voca_0122

column5: A metaphor for a state in which someone seems to have exhausted their emotional resources, empathy, resilience, or capacity to keep investing in a relationship or situation.
column6: emotional exhaustion, depletion, burnout, emotional insolvency (metaphorical)
column7: After months of conflict, he described himself as being on the edge of emotional bankruptcy. / The phrase suggests there is simply nothing left in the emotional account.
column8: Not a precise clinical diagnosis or standardized psychological term; it is a financial metaphor. Depending on context it may mean burnout, inability to give more emotionally, or a perceived lack of empathy/inner resources.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::noun_phrase usage::figurative topic::relationships topic::psychology topic::mental_health topic::finance discovery::resource_allocation

column5: A treatise is a systematic, often book-length work on a subject; a thesis is either a central proposition or an academic research work, especially a master's/undergraduate thesis in AmE; a dissertation is a substantial degree research work, especially a doctoral dissertation in AmE, though usage varies by country.
column6: treatise = systematic scholarly work; thesis/dissertation = degree research works
column7: Darwin's book is a scientific treatise, not a student dissertation. / She wrote a master's thesis on bilingual education. / He defended his doctoral dissertation last spring.
column8: Terminology varies internationally. In U.S. usage, master's thesis and doctoral dissertation are common; British universities often use dissertation for substantial undergraduate or master's projects as well. Japanese 卒論 often maps naturally to undergraduate/senior thesis depending on institution, not automatically dissertation.
column10: voca_0122

column5: Consistency in the standards, assumptions, or reasoning one uses when deciding what to believe or regard as justified knowledge.
column6: consistency of reasoning, consistent epistemic standards
column7: If you demand strong evidence for claims you dislike but accept weak evidence for claims you favor, your epistemic consistency is questionable.
column8: A philosophical/critical-thinking phrase rather than a fixed technical test. Epistemic = relating to knowledge, belief, justification, or evidence. Often invoked when comparing how a person evaluates different claims.
column10: voca_0122

column5: Contrary to what instinct, common sense, or an initial guess would lead you to expect.
column7: It sounds counterintuitive, but slowing down can make you finish the task faster. / The result was counterintuitive: the smaller group remembered more.
column8: Does not mean merely complicated or wrong. A counterintuitive result specifically conflicts with an intuitive expectation. Opposite: intuitive.
column10: voca_0122

column5: Crisis is the singular form meaning a time of intense difficulty, danger, or decisive change; crises is its irregular plural.
column7: The company is facing a financial crisis. / The report compares several economic crises from the last century.
column8: Spelling and pronunciation change: crisis /ˈkraɪsɪs/ → crises /ˈkraɪsiːz/. Compare analysis → analyses, basis → bases. Do not pronounce crises like 'crisis-es.'
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::noun_phrase usage::academic usage::critical topic::grammar topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::risk discovery::emotional_intensity discovery::academic_discussion

column5: Extremely dry from heat or lack of water; very thirsty; dried out or withered because of insufficient moisture.
column7: After the hike I was absolutely parched. / Weeks without rain left the soil parched and the trees visibly stressed. / Her lips felt parched in the dry air.
column8: Can describe a person/throat/mouth ('very thirsty/dry') or land, plants, and surfaces. Do not confuse with perched /pɝːtʃt/ = sitting or positioned on a raised/narrow place.
column10: voca_0122
column12: entry::word topic::grammar topic::anatomy topic::health discovery::insufficient_quality discovery::contrast

column5: Ideas or opinions formed in advance, before enough evidence or direct experience is available.
column7: Try to set aside your preconceived notions and judge the proposal on its merits. / I went into the class with preconceived notions about what the students would be like.
column8: Usually plural. A preconceived notion is not merely any prior belief; it often suggests an assumption that may distort how later evidence is interpreted.
column10: voca_0123

column2: wash over someone vs. overcome by vs. overwhelmed by
column5: Three ways to describe strong feelings: a feeling can wash over someone as it spreads through them; someone can be overcome by a feeling when it takes control; someone can be overwhelmed by a feeling when its intensity is too much to handle.
column6: sweep over; be overcome by; be overwhelmed by
column7: Relief washed over me when I heard the news. / She was overcome by grief. / He felt overwhelmed by the number of decisions he had to make.
column8: Pattern: FEELING washes over PERSON, but PERSON is overcome/overwhelmed by FEELING. 'Wash over' is often narrative and can be pleasant or unpleasant; 'overcome by' suggests being taken over; 'overwhelmed by' stresses excessive intensity or burden. Preposition nuance: be overcome by + FEELING is the normal pattern. Be overwhelmed by + CAUSE/FEELING focuses on what overwhelms you; be overwhelmed with + FEELING can emphasize being filled/flooded with that emotion. 日本語の感覚では wash over = 感情がさーっと押し寄せて包む、overcome by = 感情にのみ込まれる、overwhelmed by/with = 強すぎて圧倒される／感情でいっぱいになる。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::construction usage::figurative topic::communication topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::emotional_intensity discovery::literal_vs_figurative

column5: A thin flexible tube inserted into the body to drain fluid, deliver medication, or provide access to a vessel or organ.
column7: The nurse inserted a catheter to drain the patient's bladder. / A catheter was used to deliver the medication directly into the blood vessel.
column8: Common types include urinary catheters and intravenous/cardiac catheters. The word refers to the tube itself, not the procedure.
column10: voca_0123
