column5: Names for a small dot placed at midline height, such as ·. Interpunct is the typographic term; middle dot and centered dot are descriptive names.
column7: The Japanese title uses a middle dot between the two names. / In typography, the symbol · can be called an interpunct.
column8: Do not automatically call every · a multiplication dot: the same glyph can serve different functions in typography, mathematics, phonetics, or word separation. Search-intent anchor: 'center dot' is understandable, but 'middle dot' is the standard Unicode-style name and 'interpunct' is the typographic name when it separates words/elements. The same visible dot can have different names by function.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::term usage::technical topic::language_learning topic::technology discovery::terminology discovery::contrast discovery::specialist_knowledge

column5: A blend or formulation whose composition, proportions, method, or branding is controlled by a company and is not presented as a generic standard formula.
column7: The serum contains a proprietary complex of peptides and lipids. / The label lists the total amount of the proprietary complex but not the exact proportion of every ingredient.
column8: Common in supplements, cosmetics, and product marketing. 'Proprietary' means privately owned/controlled; 'complex' here means a formulated combination, not necessarily a formally defined scientific category. 日本語でざっくり言うと「メーカー独自配合／独自ブレンド」。A proprietary complex is a company-controlled or branded formulation, not a universal scientific category. It may bundle several ingredients under one branded name, and the exact proportions or formula may not be fully disclosed.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::term usage::technical usage::businesslike topic::business topic::science discovery::terminology discovery::professional_context

column2: used to do vs. would do
column5: Both can describe repeated past habits, but used to can also describe past states; would normally needs an established past-time context and is generally not used for states in the same way.
column7: When I was a kid, I used to walk to school every day. / When I was a kid, I would walk to school every day. / I used to live in Boston, not normally I would live in Boston.
column8: Use 'used to + base verb' for past habits or states that no longer hold. Use 'would + base verb' for repeated actions after a past frame has been established. Do not write *use to* in affirmative statements. Spelling/grammar hook: affirmative is 'used to + base verb' (I used to live there). After did/didn't, 'use to' is standard because did carries the past tense: Did you use to...? / I didn't use to.... 日本語感覚では used to =「昔は〜した／〜だった（今は違う）」、would = 過去の場面を置いたうえで「よく〜したものだった」。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::verb_pattern entry::construction topic::grammar topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::clarification

column5: An interruption or halt in an activity, process, work, or movement.
column7: A power failure caused a brief stoppage in production. / The match resumed after a short stoppage.
column8: Compare 'stoppage time' in soccer/football, which is a specific sports term. General stoppage can describe work stoppages, traffic, machines, production, or play.
column10: voca_0123

column5: A person who regularly uses marijuana, especially one stereotypically associated with a laid-back or intoxicated lifestyle.
column7: The comedy plays with the stereotype of a harmless stoner roommate.
column8: Informal and potentially judgmental. It describes a person, not simply anyone who has used marijuana once.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::slang usage::north_american_english topic::culture discovery::social_approval

column5: Short for 'if you know, you know,' used when a reference, experience, or joke is expected to make sense mainly to people already familiar with it.
column7: That tiny ramen shop after midnight—IYKYK. / The post had no explanation, just 'IYKYK.'
column8: Often signals insider knowledge or a shared experience. Usually written in capitals, but lowercase iykyk is common online.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::initialism entry::internet_term usage::internet_slang usage::informal topic::internet topic::social_media discovery::social_trust

column5: A conventionally attractive man portrayed as kind, lovable, and not especially intelligent or sophisticated.
column7: The character is a classic himbo: gorgeous, sweet, and completely clueless.
column8: Often affectionate rather than purely insulting, depending on context. Formed from 'him' + 'bimbo.'
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::internet_term entry::word usage::slang usage::informal usage::playful topic::internet topic::culture discovery::social_approval discovery::subjective_judgment

column5: An association of companies, organizations, institutions, or people formed to cooperate on a shared project or objective.
column7: A consortium of universities is funding the research. / The contract was awarded to an international construction consortium.
column8: Plural: consortiums or consortia. Usually implies organized cooperation while the members remain separate entities.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::professional topic::business topic::work discovery::professional_context

column5: A contagious skin infestation caused by tiny mites that burrow into the skin, typically causing intense itching and a rash.
column7: The clinic treated several family members for scabies after the rash spread through the household.
column8: The noun is grammatically singular in modern medical usage despite ending in -s. It is a condition, not the name of the mite itself. 日本語では「疥癬（かいせん）」。ぶっちゃけ、ヒゼンダニが皮膚に入り込んで強いかゆみを起こす皮膚感染・寄生症。The Japanese anchor is useful for recognition, but the English card should still keep the medical distinction from the mite itself.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word entry::term usage::scientific usage::specialist topic::health topic::medicine discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A fixed or limited amount of something allocated to a person or group; as a verb, to limit or distribute something according to such allowances.
column7: Each hiker received a daily ration of water. / During the shortage, the city had to ration fuel.
column8: Common patterns: a ration of food/water; ration something to someone; ration out supplies. Do not confuse with rationale = underlying reason.
column10: voca_0123

column5: A group of infectious diseases caused by Rickettsia-related bacteria and spread by vectors such as lice, fleas, or mites, typically involving fever and rash.
column7: The historical outbreak was identified as epidemic typhus. / Flea-borne typhus still occurs in some regions.
column8: Do not confuse typhus with typhoid fever; they are different diseases with different causes and transmission. 日本語では「発疹チフス」などのリケッチア性疾患群を指す。Typhus と typhoid fever（腸チフス）は名前が似ているが別物。検索時に「意味は」と確認した語なので、まず「発疹チフス系」と一発で結びつける。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word entry::term usage::scientific usage::specialist topic::health topic::medicine discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: To die or be destroyed, especially violently, suddenly, or because of harsh conditions.
column7: Several sailors perished in the storm. / The documents perished in the fire.
column8: For spoiled food, modern English normally says 'went bad,' 'spoiled,' or 'was moldy'; 'perished food' is not the normal equivalent of Japanese 消費期限切れ. Related adjective: perishable = liable to spoil.
column10: voca_0123

column5: The act or crime of making a false copy, signature, document, artwork, or other item in order to deceive; also the fake item itself.
column7: The signature turned out to be a forgery. / He was charged with forgery after altering the checks.
column8: Forge can mean make a fraudulent copy/signature, but it also has unrelated senses such as shape metal or create a relationship.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::legalistic topic::law topic::crime topic::art discovery::evidence discovery::risk

column2: in high school vs. at high school
column5: In American English, in high school normally means enrolled in and attending high school; at high school can refer more literally to being at the school location and is also more natural in some other varieties of English.
column7: I learned Spanish when I was in high school. / She's at the high school now for a parent-teacher meeting.
column8: For life stage/status in AmE, 'in high school' is the natural default. 'When I was in high school' often means 'during my high-school years.'
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::construction usage::american_english usage::british_english topic::grammar topic::education discovery::contrast discovery::terminology

column2: hear someone do / doing vs. hear that someone did
column5: Hear + object + bare infinitive presents an event as a whole; hear + object + -ing focuses on the event in progress; hear that + clause reports information rather than direct perception.
column7: I heard her sing the whole song. / I heard her singing in the next room. / I heard that she sang at the concert last night.
column8: With perception verbs such as hear/see/watch, bare infinitive and -ing normally imply direct perception. 'Hear that...' means receive information or a report and does not imply you personally heard the event.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::verb_pattern entry::construction topic::grammar topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::perception

column2: be in a hurry to do / be in a hurry + -ing
column5: To need or want to do something quickly. The normal pattern is be in a hurry to + verb; an -ing clause can follow when it describes the rushed activity, but forms such as *I'm hurry* are incorrect.
column6: be rushed, be pressed for time
column7: I'm in a hurry to get to the station. / I was in a hurry getting ready this morning. / I'm in a hurry—not *I'm hurry*.
column8: Use the noun phrase 'in a hurry.' For a destination/action, 'I'm in a hurry to get to the station' is usually clearer than 'I'm in a hurry going to the station.' Original-query correction: 'I'm hurry ...' is wrong; use 'I'm in a hurry.' 'I'm in a hurry going to the station' is possible only in special contexts and sounds awkward for the intended meaning; normally say 'I'm in a hurry to get to the station.' 日本語なら「急いでいる／急いで〜しなきゃ」。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::verb_pattern entry::construction topic::grammar topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::clarification

column5: The symbol < is a less-than sign in mathematics and comparison expressions; the same shape can be called an opening/left angle bracket when it functions as a delimiter in markup, notation, or typography.
column7: In 3 < 5, the symbol is a less-than sign. / In HTML, < begins a tag and is often informally called a left angle bracket.
column8: Name the symbol by function. In programming discussions, people may say 'less-than' or 'angle bracket' for the same glyph, but the intended role differs. Technical precision: the character < is U+003C LESS-THAN SIGN. In code/markup people often call the same glyph a left/open angle bracket by function, but true mathematical angle-bracket characters such as ⟨ ⟩ are distinct Unicode characters. 見た目が似ても「何として使っているか」で名前が変わる。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::term usage::technical topic::mathematics topic::technology discovery::terminology discovery::contrast

column5: A badge, emblem, mark, or distinctive symbol that indicates rank, membership, office, organization, or identity.
column7: The uniform bears the unit's insignia on the shoulder. / The car displayed the company's insignia on the hood.
column8: Singular and plural are both often insignia; insignias is also used. More formal than logo when the symbol marks rank, affiliation, or official identity.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::military topic::military topic::culture discovery::specialist_register

column5: Mechanistic explains something as if it operates through fixed causal mechanisms, often reducing a complex process to machine-like parts; mechanical more directly means relating to machines or done automatically without thought.
column7: The theory offers a mechanistic account of memory. / The repair was a mechanical problem. / His response sounded mechanical, as if he had rehearsed it.
column8: 'Mechanistic' is common in science and criticism of overly reductionist explanations. 'Mechanical' can be literal (machinery) or figurative (routine, automatic). 日本語anchor: mechanistic =「機械論的・メカニズムに還元して説明する感じ」; mechanical =「機械の／機械的な／型どおりで自動的な感じ」。A mechanistic explanation explains a system through fixed causal mechanisms; a mechanical response can sound automatic, routine, or emotionless.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::word usage::academic usage::technical topic::science topic::philosophy discovery::contrast discovery::terminology

column5: Juicy, tender, or rich in moisture; as a noun, a plant with thick fleshy leaves or stems that store water.
column7: The roast was tender and succulent. / Aloe and many cacti-like plants are succulents.
column8: The food sense is strongly positive. As a plant term, succulent is broader than cactus: many succulents are not cacti.
column10: voca_0123

column5: To move or rush out suddenly and quickly, often in an unexpected direction.
column6: dash out, shoot out, bolt out
column7: A cat darted out into the road. / She darted out of the room before anyone could stop her.
column8: Dart emphasizes sudden, quick movement. Common pattern: dart out of/from somewhere; something can also dart across/into a place.
column10: voca_0123

column5: To apply a vehicle's brakes suddenly and forcefully.
column7: I had to slam on the brakes when a dog ran into the street. / The driver slammed on the brakes just before the intersection.
column8: Normally plural 'brakes.' 'Slam on' adds sudden force; 'hit the brakes' is a close informal alternative.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::collocation entry::verb_pattern usage::informal topic::automotive topic::transportation discovery::emphasis discovery::warning

column5: To turn a vehicle around in roughly the shape of the letter U so that it travels in the opposite direction.
column7: We missed the entrance, so I made a U-turn at the next light.
column8: The noun is U-turn. Common collocations: make/do a U-turn, illegal U-turn, U-turn lane. Figuratively, make a U-turn can mean reverse a policy or opinion completely.
column10: voca_0123

column2: concord / in concord vs. in harmony
column5: Concord means agreement, harmony, or peaceful relations. In concord (with) is formal and relatively uncommon; in harmony with is more natural in everyday English for things that agree or fit well together.
column7: The two groups lived in concord for years. / The design is in harmony with the surrounding landscape.
column8: 'Concord' is formal and also appears in specialized senses such as grammatical agreement. If you simply mean compatible or harmonious, 'in harmony with' or 'in agreement with' is usually more idiomatic than 'in concord with.' 日本語では concord =「一致・調和・協調」だがかなりformal。'in harmony with' はもっと普通に「〜と調和して／うまく噛み合って」。Search typo 'harmory' should be normalized to harmony.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::word usage::formal topic::communication discovery::agreement discovery::contrast

column5: A home and the land around it, especially a farm or property established and occupied by a family; historically, land settled under homesteading laws.
column7: They restored an old homestead at the edge of town. / The family homesteaded in the region in the nineteenth century.
column8: In modern use, 'homestead' can also evoke self-sufficient rural living. The legal/historical meaning varies by country and period.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::formal topic::history topic::agriculture discovery::specialist_knowledge

column5: In disagreement or conflict with someone or something; inconsistent with something.
column6: in conflict with, contrary to, incompatible with
column7: His explanation is at odds with the evidence. / She found herself at odds with the rest of the committee.
column8: Pattern: be at odds with PERSON/THING. 'Odds' is plural in this idiom. It can describe people disagreeing or facts/principles being incompatible.
column10: voca_0123

column5: Impressively large or ambitious in a way that is often excessive, unrealistic, self-important, or showy.
column7: He announced a grandiose plan to transform the entire city in six months. / The speech was full of grandiose claims about his own importance.
column8: Can describe plans, language, architecture, or self-image. Often carries criticism: impressive-sounding but inflated beyond what is reasonable.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word usage::critical usage::evaluative topic::psychology discovery::criticism discovery::subjective_judgment

column2: snitch on someone vs. tip someone off
column5: To snitch on someone is to report their wrongdoing to an authority or other person; to tip someone off is to secretly give them advance information or a warning.
column7: Someone snitched on him to the teacher. / A friend tipped him off that the police were asking questions.
column8: The direction of information is different: snitch ON offender → authority; tip offender/person OFF → give them information. 'Tip-off' is also a noun: an advance warning or piece of secret information. 日本語でぶっちゃけると snitch on X =「Xの悪事をチクる／密告する」; tip Y off =「Yにこっそり情報・警告を流す」。構造も重要: snitch on [wrongdoer] → authority, but tip [recipient] off about/to [information]. The recipient of a tip-off can be a suspect, police, a friend, etc.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrasal_verb usage::informal topic::communication topic::crime discovery::contrast discovery::betrayal discovery::warning

column5: Augean describes an extremely dirty, corrupt, or difficult-to-clean situation; the Augean Stables are the mythic filthy stables cleaned by Hercules and figuratively a deeply entrenched mess requiring enormous cleanup.
column7: Reforming the department felt like cleaning the Augean Stables. / The audit exposed an Augean mess of neglected records and conflicts.
column8: The bookmark's 'Augean staples' is a typo for 'Augean Stables.' The figurative expression comes from the labor of Hercules; use it for a mess whose cleanup seems Herculean. 日本語感覚では「手のつけようがないほど汚れた／腐敗したものを大掃除する」。'Clean the Augean Stables' evokes a gigantic, long-neglected mess or entrenched corruption that needs a Herculean cleanup.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::form_family entry::idiom usage::literary usage::figurative topic::literature topic::history discovery::origin_etymology discovery::figurative_extension discovery::excessive_emotion

column5: To officially cancel a legal prohibition on an activity or thing.
column6: revoke a ban, rescind a prohibition, lift a ban
column7: The council voted to repeal the ban on backyard sheds. / Lawmakers proposed repealing the ban on Sunday sales.
column8: Structure: repeal + the ban + on + NOUN/-ing. 'Lift a ban on X' is often more idiomatic in general news; 'repeal' emphasizes formally canceling the law or rule that created the ban. Usage contrast: laws/statutes are commonly repealed; bans/restrictions/sanctions are very often lifted. 日本語で repeal =「法律そのものを正式に廃止」、lift =「禁止・制限措置を解除」。So 'lift the ban on X' is often the most idiomatic general-news phrasing.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::collocation entry::verb_pattern usage::formal usage::legalistic topic::law topic::government topic::politics discovery::policy_discussion discovery::removal

column5: An organization in a residential community that manages shared property and enforces community rules, usually funded by homeowner fees.
column7: The HOA requires approval before residents can change the exterior color of their homes. / Our monthly HOA fee covers landscaping and pool maintenance.
column8: Common in U.S. planned communities, condominiums, and subdivisions. Rules and legal powers vary by jurisdiction and governing documents.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::abbreviation entry::term usage::north_american_english usage::professional topic::law topic::government discovery::terminology discovery::professional_context

column2: bump a version / build / dependency / cache token
column5: To increment or change a version-like value so software, dependencies, builds, or caches treat something as a newer revision.
column7: We bumped the app version from 1.8.6.377 to .378. / Bump the dependency version before release. / I changed the query string to bump the cache.
column8: Technical jargon. 'Bump' means move a number/token forward, often by a small amount. A 'cache bump' usually changes a version/query/hash so clients fetch a fresh asset; the exact mechanism depends on the system. 日本語感覚では「番号・バージョンをちょっと上げる／値を進める」。A cache bump does not necessarily mean +1; it can mean changing a query token, hash, filename, or version so clients fetch a fresh asset.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::collocation entry::verb_pattern usage::technical usage::informal topic::technology discovery::minor_adjustment discovery::iteration discovery::implementation

column5: A softened or altered expression used in place of a stronger swear word, often by changing its sounds while preserving the emotional function.
column7: Words such as 'darn' and 'gosh' are classic minced oaths. / The character uses comic minced oaths instead of profanity.
column8: Examples vary by dialect and era. A minced oath is not simply any mild exclamation; it historically or functionally substitutes for a taboo expression.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::term usage::informal topic::linguistics topic::culture discovery::terminology discovery::emotional_intensity discovery::origin_etymology

column5: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion, attitude, or course of action, especially despite persuasion or moral pressure.
column7: The committee remained obdurate despite months of criticism. / He was obdurate in his refusal to apologize.
column8: Formal and strongly negative. More severe than merely stubborn: it suggests hardened resistance to reason, pressure, or compassion.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word usage::formal usage::literary topic::psychology discovery::nonconformity discovery::determination

column5: Requiring a great deal of effort, endurance, or sustained difficulty.
column7: The rescue team faced an arduous climb through deep snow. / Rebuilding the database by hand would be an arduous task.
column8: Usually describes tasks, journeys, processes, or work—not something merely unpleasant. Emphasizes sustained effort.
column10: voca_0123

column5: To cry or make a long, loud, mournful sound; wailing is the act or sound of doing so, and can also describe a sustained high-pitched sound such as a siren.
column6: cry out, lament, howl; sobbing, wailing
column7: The child wailed for several minutes. / We could hear the child wailing from the hallway. / Sirens were wailing in the distance.
column8: 日本語で一発なら「泣きわめく／泣き叫ぶ」「長く悲しげに鳴り響く」。Memory hook: a wailing child goes「わーっ」と長く泣き続け、a wailing siren goes「ウーッ」と長く鳴り続ける。人にも、sirens/guitars/windのような持続する大きな音にも使う。
column10: voca_0123

column5: To provoke, mock, or insult someone deliberately, often by making cruel or challenging remarks; also such a remark or action.
column7: The crowd taunted the opposing player. / He ignored their taunts and kept walking.
column8: Unlike ordinary teasing, taunting is typically hostile or provocative and is meant to upset or challenge the target.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::critical topic::communication discovery::criticism discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: To do, read, watch, learn, or complete something that you have fallen behind on or not had time for.
column6: get up to date on, make up, clear a backlog of
column7: I need the weekend to catch up on email. / She spent the flight catching up on sleep. / Let's meet so I can catch up on what happened.
column8: Pattern: catch up on + TASK/NEWS/READING/SLEEP. Different from catch someone up on something = bring someone up to date by telling them, and catch up with/to someone = reach the same position. 日本語では「溜まって遅れているものを片付けて追いつく」。catch up on email/work/reading/news/sleep/correspondence. 'catch my correspondence' だけでは通常この意味にならず、'catch up on my correspondence' が自然。
column10: voca_0123

column5: As an adjective, dependent on a condition or uncertain event; as a noun, a group of people representing or belonging to a larger body.
column7: The offer is contingent on financing. / A large contingent of supporters traveled with the team.
column8: Common pattern: contingent on/upon. The noun sense explains names such as the Bromley Contingent, a labeled group of followers associated with the early UK punk scene.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::formal topic::planning topic::work discovery::possibility discovery::constraints

column5: Under no circumstances; absolutely not.
column7: On no account should you share that password. / You must on no account open the door while the machine is running.
column8: When fronted at the start of a clause, this negative expression normally triggers subject-auxiliary inversion: 'On no account should you...' not *On no account you should...*
column10: voca_0123

column5: To do something concrete in response to an issue, report, request, or information.
column7: The agency promised to take action on the complaints. / We need to take action on the findings before the next release.
column8: Structure: take action on + issue/information/request. Compare act on something, which is more compact and can also mean follow advice or information.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::collocation entry::verb_pattern usage::professional topic::work topic::planning discovery::call_to_action discovery::implementation

column5: Having enough money to live comfortably; financially prosperous.
column7: She grew up in a well-off family. / The neighborhood is relatively well-off.
column8: Usually attributive or predicative. Do not confuse with better off = in a more favorable situation, which is not necessarily about money.
column10: voca_0123

column5: To lower one's body or head in respect or submission; figuratively, to submit to someone's authority or superiority.
column7: The crowd bowed down before the statue. / He refused to bow down to political pressure.
column8: Common figurative pattern: bow down to + PERSON/POWER/PRESSURE. The physical sense can express worship, respect, or submission depending on context.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::phrasal_verb usage::figurative topic::culture topic::religion discovery::literal_vs_figurative discovery::social_approval

column5: A type of work or occupation, especially one felt to be a strong calling or particularly suited to a person's abilities and values.
column7: Teaching was more than a job for her; it was a vocation. / He eventually found his vocation in public service.
column8: Often implies a sense of calling or purpose more strongly than job or occupation. Related: vocational = connected with practical career training.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word usage::formal topic::work topic::education discovery::professional_context discovery::strong_desire

column5: To suddenly become very popular, widely noticed, or rapidly successful, especially online or in entertainment.
column6: go viral, take off, explode in popularity
column7: Her video blew up overnight and reached millions of views. / The band really blew up after that single.
column8: One of several meanings of blow up: it can also explode, enlarge an image, lose one's temper, or destroy something. Context identifies the popularity sense. 日本語anchor: このsenseは「一気にバズる／急に有名になる／急に売れる」。'Her video blew up overnight.' =「動画が一晩でバズった」。Explode / enlarge / lose one's temper など別senseも多いので、popularity contextで見分ける。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::phrasal_verb entry::slang_expression usage::informal usage::figurative topic::internet topic::entertainment discovery::figurative_extension discovery::promotion

column5: A small bean-shaped structure in the lymphatic system that filters lymph and helps coordinate immune responses.
column7: The doctor checked the lymph nodes in her neck for swelling. / Enlarged lymph nodes can occur during an infection.
column8: Lymph nodes are not glands in the strict anatomical sense, although 'lymph glands' is a common older term. They are part of the immune and lymphatic systems.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::term usage::scientific usage::specialist topic::anatomy topic::medicine discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A gland in the skin that produces sweat, helping with temperature regulation and other skin functions.
column7: Sweat glands become more active when body temperature rises.
column8: Two major types are eccrine and apocrine glands. The everyday term is sweat gland.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::term usage::scientific usage::specialist topic::anatomy topic::biology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A gland that produces saliva and releases it into the mouth.
column7: The major salivary glands include the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands.
column8: Use plural 'salivary glands' when referring to the group. Saliva lubricates the mouth and contributes to digestion.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::term usage::scientific usage::specialist topic::anatomy topic::biology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A butterfly-shaped endocrine gland in the neck that produces hormones involved in metabolism, growth, and energy regulation.
column7: The thyroid gland sits at the front of the neck. / Blood tests can help evaluate thyroid hormone levels.
column8: In everyday medical language, 'thyroid' alone often refers to the gland. Do not confuse it with the parathyroid glands.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::term usage::scientific usage::specialist topic::anatomy topic::medicine discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: Relating to a college or colleges, especially college-level education, institutions, or sports.
column7: She competed in collegiate athletics. / The organization oversees several collegiate programs.
column8: The bookmark spelling 'colligeate' is a misspelling. Do not confuse collegiate with collegial, which means cooperative and friendly among colleagues.
column10: voca_0123

column5: The combining or relational capacity of an element; in linguistics, the number and type of arguments a word—especially a verb—can take; in chemistry, the combining capacity of an atom.
column7: The verb 'give' has a valency pattern that can include a giver, a thing given, and a recipient. / In chemistry, valency describes an element's combining capacity.
column8: Valency and valence are related terms. In linguistics, think of the 'slots' a predicate naturally opens for participants.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word entry::term usage::technical usage::academic topic::linguistics topic::chemistry discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::terminology

column5: As a noun, a liquid or other substance that dissolves another substance; as an adjective, financially able to pay debts.
column7: Water is the solvent in this solution. / The company remained solvent despite the downturn.
column8: The chemical and financial senses are distinct but both common. Opposite financial adjective: insolvent. 日本語anchor: noun (chemistry) =「溶媒／溶剤」; adjective (finance) =「支払い能力がある、債務を払える」。同じ綴りでもsenseがかなり違う。The bookmark likely targeted the chemistry sense, so that should be the first mental hook.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::technical usage::formal topic::chemistry topic::finance discovery::contrast discovery::specialist_knowledge

column5: A shelter, enclosure, or facility for keeping dogs; as a verb, to place or keep a dog in such a facility.
column7: The dog sleeps in a kennel in the yard. / We kenneled our dogs while we were away.
column8: Plural kennels can refer to a boarding/breeding facility as a whole. Doghouse is more specifically a small individual shelter.
column10: voca_0123

column5: An unrealistically optimistic way of seeing a person, situation, or the past, emphasizing positives and overlooking problems.
column7: He's looking back at college through rose-colored glasses. / Take off the rose-colored glasses and look at the costs too.
column8: Also rose-tinted glasses, especially in British English. Common pattern: see/look at something through rose-colored glasses.
column10: voca_0123

column5: A person's outward behavior, manner, or appearance, especially the impression created by how they act.
column7: Her calm demeanor helped reassure the nervous patients. / His friendly demeanor changed as soon as the interview began.
column8: American spelling demeanor; British spelling demeanour. It describes outward manner, not necessarily a person's true inner feelings. 日本語で一言なら「物腰・態度・立ち居振る舞い」。内面そのものではなく、外から見える振る舞い・表情・話し方から受ける印象。'a calm demeanor' =「落ち着いた物腰」、'a friendly demeanor' =「親しみやすい態度」。Personalityより“表に出ている様子”に焦点がある。
column10: voca_0123

column2: moldy / have mold on / be covered in mold
column5: Moldy means affected by or covered with mold; have mold on it states the presence of mold more neutrally; be covered in mold emphasizes a large visible amount.
column7: The bread was moldy. / Every bun had mold on it. / The forgotten fruit was covered in mold.
column8: 'Moldy' is the natural compact adjective. For visible extent, 'has mold on it' or 'is covered in mold' is often more precise. Molded normally means shaped in a mold, not 'covered with mold.' 日本語anchor: moldy =「カビてる」; have mold on it =「カビが付いてる／生えてる」; be covered in mold =「カビだらけ／カビに覆われてる」。'have mold on itself' is usually unnatural for an ordinary object; say 'have mold on it.' 'Molded' normally means「型で成形された」.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::adjective_phrase topic::health topic::everyday_life discovery::contrast discovery::clarification

column5: Expressing a contrast in which one fact is acknowledged but does not prevent the main statement from being true.
column7: Although it was raining, we went out anyway. / 'Although' introduces a concessive clause in that sentence.
column8: Common concessive markers include although, though, even though, while, and despite/in spite of in different grammatical structures.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word entry::term usage::academic usage::formal topic::grammar topic::linguistics discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::terminology

column5: A particular way of interpreting, representing, or mentally framing something.
column7: That construal of the sentence makes the pronoun refer to the teacher. / The two theories offer different construals of the same event.
column8: Formal/technical, especially in linguistics, psychology, philosophy, and law. Related verb: construe = interpret.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word entry::term usage::formal usage::technical usage::academic topic::linguistics topic::psychology topic::philosophy discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::subjective_judgment

column5: To fill a vehicle or machine with gasoline or other fuel.
column7: Let's gas up before we get on the highway. / I stopped to gas up the rental car.
column8: Common in North American English. 'Fuel up' is broader because it is not limited to gasoline. 'Gas up the car' and 'gas the car up' are both possible.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::phrasal_verb usage::north_american_english usage::informal topic::automotive topic::transportation discovery::procedural_language

column5: A tube that carries an egg from an ovary toward the uterus or another reproductive structure; in humans, a fallopian tube.
column7: Fertilization usually occurs in the oviduct before the embryo reaches the uterus.
column8: Oviduct is the broader biological term across animals. In human anatomy, fallopian tube or uterine tube is more common.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word entry::term usage::scientific usage::specialist topic::anatomy topic::biology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: A task, project, or piece of work that is accepted and carried out, often one that is substantial or demanding.
column7: Moving the entire archive to a new system was a major undertaking. / Restoring the old theater became a five-year undertaking.
column8: Related verb undertake = begin/accept responsibility for a task. Undertaking can also mean a formal promise in legal contexts, and in older usage the funeral business.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::formal usage::professional topic::work topic::law discovery::professional_context discovery::commitment

column5: The part of a scene nearest the viewer; as a verb, to make something especially prominent, visible, or important.
column7: A tree fills the foreground of the photograph. / The report foregrounds the risks rather than the benefits.
column8: The verb is common in academic, design, media, and technical writing: foreground X = deliberately bring X to attention. Opposite: background or de-emphasize.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::academic usage::technical usage::figurative topic::media topic::technology topic::communication discovery::literal_vs_figurative discovery::emphasis

column5: To begin to have a strong effect, become established, or gain control; literally, to obtain a firm grip.
column7: The new habit took hold after a few weeks. / Panic began to take hold of the crowd. / She reached for the rail and took hold.
column8: Common patterns: IDEA/TREND takes hold; FEELING takes hold of someone; take hold of an object. The abstract sense suggests increasing influence or establishment.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::verb_pattern entry::fixed_expression usage::figurative topic::communication discovery::figurative_extension discovery::continuity

column5: As soon as the earliest indication of something appears.
column6: at the earliest indication of, as soon as
column7: Stop the machine at the first sign of smoke. / He leaves at the first sign of conflict.
column8: Pattern: at the first sign of + NOUN. It emphasizes acting immediately when an early warning or indication appears. 日本語で「〜の兆候が少しでも最初に見えた時点で／気配がしたらすぐ」。'At the first sign of trouble, call me.' =「少しでもヤバそうならすぐ連絡して」。Here sign = 兆候・気配, not a signboard.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::prepositional_phrase entry::fixed_expression topic::planning discovery::warning discovery::prevention discovery::early_stage

column2: shout-out / give a shout-out to someone
column5: A public expression of thanks, praise, recognition, or greeting; to give such recognition to someone.
column7: A quick shout-out to everyone who helped with the launch. / She gave a shout-out to her teacher during the interview.
column8: Noun is usually hyphenated: shout-out. The verb 'shout out' can also simply mean yell loudly, so context matters. 日本語で一言なら、文脈に応じて「〇〇にも拍手！」「〇〇に感謝！」「名前を出して称える／感謝を送る」。'Big shout-out to John for helping us.' =「手伝ってくれたJohnにも大感謝／拍手」。単なる praise より、公に名前を出してrecognitionを送る感じ。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::form_family entry::noun_phrase entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::conversational topic::social_media topic::communication discovery::social_approval discovery::audience_engagement

column5: Pottery made from clay fired at relatively low temperatures, usually remaining more porous than stoneware or porcelain unless glazed.
column7: The museum displayed painted earthenware bowls. / The village is known for traditional earthenware pottery.
column8: Write earthenware as one word. Earthenware, stoneware, and porcelain are all ceramics but differ in clay body, firing temperature, density, and vitrification.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::form_family entry::term usage::technical topic::art topic::culture discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::terminology

column5: A small prehistoric Japanese clay figurine, especially one made during the Jōmon period; in general English it can be described as a clay or earthenware figurine.
column7: The exhibition includes several Jōmon dogū clay figurines. / The small earthenware figurine dates to prehistoric Japan.
column8: Dogū is the established Japanese archaeological term and is commonly retained in English-language writing rather than translated away completely. 「土偶」を英語で言いたいとき、考古学・縄文の文脈なら dogū をそのまま使える。一般向けに説明するなら a clay figurine / an earthenware figurine. 'earthenware pottery' だけだと「土器・陶器類」寄りで、figurineという人形・像の形が落ちる。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::term entry::noun_phrase usage::specialist topic::history topic::art topic::culture discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::terminology

column5: A comparison showing differences between two versions of text, files, or data; as a verb, to compare versions and display those changes.
column7: Check the diff before you merge the patch. / I diffed the two config files to see what changed.
column8: Common in software development and version control. A diff may show added, removed, and modified lines; it is not merely any 'difference.'
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word entry::term usage::technical usage::informal topic::technology discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::process_details

column5: A person who writes or creates a work; as a verb, to write, create, or formally produce a document, book, specification, policy, or other work.
column7: She is the author of three novels. / The engineering team authored the migration plan.
column8: The verb is common in formal and technical contexts. For ordinary messages, 'write' is usually more natural than 'author.'
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::formal usage::professional topic::literature topic::work discovery::professional_context

column5: To lose one's job because the position is no longer needed, often because of restructuring, closure, or reduced staffing rather than personal misconduct.
column6: be laid off, lose one's position
column7: Several employees were made redundant when the two offices merged.
column8: British English. The closest common American expression is 'be laid off,' although legal and employment details vary. It does not normally imply the employee was fired for poor performance. 日本語でかなり近いのは「リストラされる／人員整理で職を失う」。特にBrE。発想は「その人が無能だからクビ」ではなく、「その役職・人員が組織上不要になった」。AmEでは 'be laid off' が日常的。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::verb_pattern entry::fixed_expression usage::british_english usage::professional topic::work topic::workplace discovery::professional_context discovery::terminology

column5: Immediately; without delay.
column7: Call me straightaway if anything changes. / She knew straightaway that something was wrong.
column8: Especially common in British English; 'right away' is very common in American English. Also written straight away as two words.
column10: voca_0123

column2: despite + noun / despite the fact that + clause
column5: Despite is a preposition: it normally takes a noun phrase or -ing form, not a finite clause directly. To introduce a full clause, use despite the fact that.
column7: Despite the products displayed at the trade show, this model attracted the most attention. / Despite being expensive, it sold well. / Despite the fact that it was expensive, it sold well.
column8: Do not write *despite it was expensive*. Compare although/even though + clause. 'Despite the products that were displayed...' is grammatical if 'the products...' is the object of despite, though context may make 'among all the products...' more natural. Search-sentence nuance: 'Despite the products that were displayed at the trade show, this model attracted the most attention.' is grammatical because 'the products...' is a noun phrase, but it can sound semantically odd if the intended meaning is simply「展示商品の中でこれが最も注目された」。Then 'Among all the products displayed at the trade show, this model attracted the most attention.' is more natural. If the contrast is「多くの他商品と並んでいたのに」, say 'Despite being displayed alongside many other products, ...'. Grammar and intended meaning are separate questions.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::construction entry::verb_pattern topic::grammar topic::language_learning discovery::contrast discovery::clarification

column2: pass something over to someone / hand something over to someone
column5: To transfer an object, information, topic, task, or responsibility to another person; hand over is especially common for responsibility or control, while pass over can describe physically or conversationally passing something along.
column7: I'll pass the next point over to Maya. / Let me hand this issue over to the support team. / Could you pass the paper over to Sam?
column8: 'Pass this point over to someone' is possible in meeting handoffs, but 'hand this over to...' or 'pass the next point/question to...' is often more natural. Do not confuse pass over someone = skip/not choose that person. Meeting-handoff nuance: 日本語の「このpointを相手に渡す」を直訳して 'pass this point over to John' にすると不自然になりやすい。Depending on context, say 'I'll hand this over to John,' 'I'll turn it over to John,' 'I'll let John take this point,' or 'I'll pass this question on to John.' 'Pass over someone' can also mean skip/not choose them, so construction matters.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::phrasal_verb topic::communication topic::work discovery::contrast discovery::professional_context

column5: Medieval means relating to the Middle Ages, the historical period in Europe conventionally placed between antiquity and the early modern era.
column7: The castle was built in the late medieval period. / The Middle Ages are often dated roughly from the 5th to the late 15th century in European history.
column8: Exact boundaries vary by historian, region, and topic; dates such as c. 500–1500 are a convenient approximation, not a universal hard cutoff.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::contrast_set entry::form_family usage::academic topic::history discovery::terminology discovery::contrast

column5: A country on the Caribbean coast of Central America, bordered by Mexico and Guatemala, with Belmopan as its capital.
column7: Belize is the only Central American country whose official language is English. / They traveled from Guatemala into Belize.
column8: Belize was formerly known as British Honduras. It is geographically in Central America and culturally connected to the Caribbean as well.
column10: voca_0123

column5: A combining form appearing in words about systems of rules, arrangement, management, classification, or fields of organized knowledge.
column7: Taxonomy concerns systems of classification. / Astronomy historically contains the same Greek-derived -nomy element.
column8: From Greek nomos, 'law, custom, arrangement.' The meaning shifts by word, so -nomy should not be translated mechanically as one fixed English noun. 日本語で一語に固定しないのがコツ。「体系・ルール・整理の仕方に関わる感じ」。Greek nomos = law/custom/arrangement. Taxonomy = 分類体系、astronomy = 天体を体系的に扱う学問、economy も同根だが意味は歴史的に変化している。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::term entry::construction usage::technical usage::academic topic::linguistics topic::language_learning discovery::origin_etymology discovery::terminology

column5: The portion of a home's value that the owner effectively owns: the property's current market value minus outstanding debt secured by it.
column7: If the house is worth $500,000 and the mortgage balance is $300,000, the homeowner has about $200,000 in home equity.
column8: Home equity can rise through mortgage repayment or higher property values and fall through borrowing or lower values. Distinct from equality; this is the ownership/value sense of equity. 日本語で直感的には「今その家を売って住宅ローン等を差し引いたあと、自分の持ち分として残る価値」。$500k home − $300k mortgage ≈ $200k home equity. 文脈により「住宅の純資産価値／自己持分」。社会政策の equity = 公平 とは別sense。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::noun_phrase entry::term usage::professional topic::finance topic::economics discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register

column5: The condition in which one word or expression has multiple related meanings.
column7: The word 'head' shows polysemy: a body part, a leader, and the top or front of something are historically and conceptually related senses.
column8: Compare homonymy, where identical forms represent meanings treated as unrelated. Adjective: polysemous. 日本語なら「多義性」。一つの単語が“関連のある複数の意味”を持つこと。head = 頭 → 組織の長 → 物の先端、のようにsense同士につながりがある。Compare homonymy: same form but meanings are treated as unrelated.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word entry::term usage::technical usage::academic topic::linguistics discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::terminology

column5: To react with an angry, dramatic outburst or tantrum.
column6: throw a fit, have a tantrum, blow up
column7: Don't pitch a fit just because the plan changed. / He pitched a fit when the restaurant lost his reservation.
column8: Informal and often dismissive of the person's reaction. 'Throw a fit' is a very common equivalent. 日本語感覚では「癇癪を起こす／キレて大騒ぎする／そんなことで騒ぐなよ」。子どものtantrumだけでなく、大人が些細なことで怒って大げさに反応する場合にも使う。'Don't pitch a fit.' は相手の反応を大げさだと見る、ややdismissiveな響き。'Throw a fit' is very common.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::idiom entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::critical topic::communication discovery::emotional_intensity discovery::criticism

column5: To destroy something explosively or violently into extremely small pieces.
column7: The blast blew the shed to smithereens. / In the game, the ship gets blown to smithereens.
column8: Smithereens is normally plural and occurs mainly in fixed expressions such as 'blow to smithereens' or 'smash to smithereens.'
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::idiom entry::verb_pattern usage::figurative usage::informal topic::military discovery::emotional_intensity discovery::figurative_extension

column2: with no trace left / leave no trace
column5: With nothing remaining that can be seen, found, or used as evidence; to disappear or remove something completely.
column6: without a trace, leave nothing behind
column7: The cabin burned down with no trace left of the original interior. / By morning, the snow had melted without a trace.
column8: 'Without a trace' is the most idiomatic fixed phrase for disappearance. 'With no trace left' is grammatical and emphasizes the remaining result.
column10: voca_0123

column2: be born yesterday / I wasn't born yesterday
column5: To be extremely naive or inexperienced; the common negative form 'I wasn't born yesterday' means 'I'm not so naive that I will believe that.'
column7: Do you really expect me to believe that? I wasn't born yesterday. / He talks to me as if I were born yesterday.
column8: The idiom is normally negative or hypothetical. It does not refer literally to age. Exact frame from the search: 'You treat me as if I was/were born yesterday.' =「俺を昨日生まれた世間知らずみたいに扱うなよ」。'I wasn't born yesterday.' =「そんな見え透いた話に騙されるほどウブじゃない／世間知らずじゃない」。Literal ageではなく naive/inexperienced のmetaphor.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::idiom entry::sentence_pattern usage::informal usage::rhetorical usage::skeptical topic::communication discovery::figurative_extension discovery::lack_of_knowledge

column2: don't bother doing / then don't bother asking
column5: Used to tell someone not to make the effort to do something because it is pointless, unwelcome, unnecessary, or too late.
column6: don't trouble yourself, don't waste the effort
column7: If you aren't going to listen, don't bother asking. / If the file is already deleted, don't bother looking for it.
column8: Pattern: bother + -ing, not normally *bother to asking*. Tone can be dismissive or irritated, especially in 'then don't bother...'.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::critical topic::communication discovery::boundary-setting discovery::criticism

column5: Serious trouble or a difficult situation.
column7: If the audit finds those missing records, we're in deep doo-doo. / That mistake could put him in deep doo-doo.
column8: Humorous/euphemistic slang based on doo-doo = feces. Less vulgar than 'deep shit' but still very informal. 日本語で「かなりヤバいことになる／深刻なトラブルに入る」。doo-doo は子どもっぽい「うんち」の婉曲語なので、'in deep shit' をsoft/humorousにした感じ。Meaning can be serious even though the wording is playful.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::slang_expression entry::noun_phrase usage::slang usage::informal usage::humorous topic::communication discovery::risk discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: Dirt, grime, residue, or unpleasant material; informally, worthless or poor-quality stuff, nonsense, or a mild exclamation.
column7: There was sticky crud around the edge of the keyboard. / I don't want to install a bunch of useless crud on the laptop. / Crud, I forgot my keys.
column8: Broad informal word. The physical sense means accumulated dirty material; figurative uses depend heavily on context. Sense map: ① physical =「こびりついた汚れ・カス・ベタベタしたゴミ」 ② slang =「くだらないもの／粗悪なもの／いらないもの」 ③ interjection 'Crud!' =「ちぇっ／しまった」。一語の固定訳よりcontextで切り替える。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::slang_expression entry::word usage::informal usage::slang topic::everyday_life discovery::literal_vs_figurative discovery::evaluation

column5: To pressure someone strongly in order to obtain money, information, a concession, or some other thing from them.
column7: The reporter tried to squeeze him for details about the deal. / They squeezed the contractor for a lower price.
column8: This is figurative squeeze = apply pressure. Compare squeeze something in = find room/time for it, which is a different construction. 日本語で「相手に圧をかけて、金・情報・値引き・譲歩などを絞り出す／締め上げて出させる」。'squeeze him for information' =「圧をかけて情報を引き出す」。Physical squeezeの「絞る」イメージがfigurativeになっている。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::verb_pattern entry::fixed_expression usage::informal usage::figurative topic::communication topic::business discovery::negotiation discovery::resource_allocation discovery::figurative_extension

column5: Running lengthwise; or, in research, following the same subjects or phenomenon over an extended period of time.
column7: The fibers run in a longitudinal direction. / The researchers conducted a longitudinal study that followed the children for ten years.
column8: Contrast cross-sectional study, which examines a population at one point or short period rather than tracking change over time.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word entry::term usage::academic usage::technical topic::research topic::science discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::contrast

column5: The ability of different systems, devices, programs, or organizations to work together and exchange or use information effectively.
column7: The new standard improves interoperability between the two platforms. / Data portability is useful only if the receiving system has enough interoperability to use the data.
column8: Stronger than simple coexistence: interoperable systems can communicate or function together in a meaningful way. 専門訳は「相互運用性」。でも腹落ちする言い方なら「別々のsystem同士がちゃんと通じて、一緒に使える力」。Compatibility = 互換性がある、より一歩進んで、interoperabilityは実際に情報をやり取りして連携・機能できるところまで含む。
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word entry::term usage::technical usage::professional topic::technology topic::engineering discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::implementation

column5: Extremely cold; figuratively, emotionally cold or unwelcoming.
column7: A frigid wind swept across the platform. / The meeting opened with a frigid exchange between the two executives.
column8: The older use meaning sexually unresponsive is dated, judgmental, and potentially offensive; avoid it in neutral modern descriptions of a person.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::polysemy_set entry::word usage::figurative usage::dated topic::weather topic::psychology discovery::literal_vs_figurative discovery::impression

column5: To drink alcohol and celebrate noisily or exuberantly, especially for an extended time.
column7: They spent the night carousing after the championship win.
column8: Literary or somewhat old-fashioned compared with 'party.' Often implies alcohol and rowdy enjoyment.
column10: voca_0123

column5: A Filipino double-edged sword related to the Southeast Asian kris or keris, often with a partly or fully wavy blade.
column7: The museum displayed a Mindanao kalis with a broad double-edged blade.
column8: A Philippine cultural and martial-arts term. The kalis is generally sword-sized, unlike many dagger-sized keris forms.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::word entry::term usage::specialist topic::culture topic::military discovery::specialist_knowledge discovery::specialist_register discovery::terminology

column5: An overnight flight that departs late at night and arrives the following morning, often leaving passengers with little normal sleep.
column7: I'm taking a red-eye flight to New York tonight. / We caught the red-eye and landed just after sunrise.
column8: 'Black-eye flight' is not the standard expression. Red-eye refers to the tired, bloodshot eyes associated with traveling overnight. 具体像: たとえば夜10時〜深夜に出て、翌朝6〜8時ごろ着くようなovernight flight（時間帯は固定定義ではない）。到着時に寝不足で目が充血して red-eyed になりやすい → red-eye. 時間を有効利用できたり便によっては安かったりする一方、到着後がしんどい。'Black-eye flight' can occur as a misremembered or mistaken form, but the standard expression is 'red-eye flight'.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::form_family entry::noun_phrase entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::north_american_english topic::travel topic::aviation discovery::terminology discovery::practical_details

column5: A name or term that is inaccurate, misleading, or inappropriate for the thing it describes.
column7: Calling the device 'wireless' is a bit of a misnomer because it still needs a power cable.
column8: A misnomer is specifically a naming problem, not simply any factual error.
column10: voca_0123

column2: to a T / down to a T
column5: Exactly, perfectly, or in every detail; 'have something down to a T' means to have mastered or organized it very precisely.
column7: The description fits him to a T. / She has the morning routine down to a T.
column8: Also written 'to a tee.' Common patterns: fit/suit/follow something to a T; have/get something down to a T. 日本語なら「寸分違わず／ぴったりその通り／完璧に」、くだけて「ドンピシャ」。'It fits her personality to a T.' =「彼女の性格にドンピシャ」。'You described him to a T.' =「まさにその通りに言い当てた」。Core idiom is 'to a T'; 'down to a T' also occurs and can feel influenced by 'down to the last detail'.
column10: voca_0123

column5: To talk too much, especially boastfully, disrespectfully, recklessly, or about things one should keep quiet.
column7: He keeps running his mouth about things he doesn't understand. / Stop running your mouth and listen for a minute.
column8: Informal and often confrontational. Depending on context, it can imply boasting, insulting, gossiping, or revealing too much. 日本語はcontextで「ベラベラしゃべる」「余計なことをペラペラ言う」「でかい口をたたく」「ごちゃごちゃ言う」あたり。単なる talk a lot ではなく、話しすぎ・生意気・不用意・自慢・悪口など“話す内容に問題がある”感じ。'Stop running your mouth.' can be quite confrontational:「ごちゃごちゃ言ってんじゃねえ／黙れ」.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::idiom entry::verb_pattern usage::informal usage::critical topic::communication discovery::criticism discovery::emotional_intensity

column5: The act, route, or means of going out or leaving a place; in computing, data or traffic leaving a system or network.
column7: Emergency egress routes must remain clear. / The provider charges separately for network egress.
column8: Opposite: ingress. Common in building codes, networking, cloud computing, and formal technical writing.

column5: A complete, undivided whole or self-contained entity; an older/formal sense related to the Latin idea of something whole, intact, or untouched.
column6: whole, intact whole, complete entity, undivided unit
column7: The parts were treated as one integer—an undivided whole—rather than as separate fragments.
column8: This sense is rare in modern everyday English; the mathematical meaning「整数」is overwhelmingly more common. Etymological/figurative hook: Latin integer = whole, intact, untouched. That idea helps explain related 'integrity': wholeness, soundness, and—figuratively—moral character that is not corrupted or divided. Applied metaphorically, integer can evoke ① completeness/self-sufficiency: a person or thing whole on its own, needing no external pieces to be complete; ② an unbroken entity: a group/state/system that remains unified rather than fractured; ③ by etymological association, incorruptible wholeness or strong moral integrity. Treat these as rare/literary or explanatory senses, not as an everyday synonym for 'honest person.'

column5: A system in which a price, rate, benefit, requirement, or other amount changes according to another variable such as income, usage, or need.
column7: The clinic charges on a sliding scale based on income. / The penalty increases on a sliding scale as the violation becomes more serious.
column8: Common pattern: on a sliding scale. The value is not fixed; it moves according to defined criteria. 日本語で要するに「条件に応じて額や基準が変わる仕組み」。料金なら「所得などに応じた可変料金制／段階料金制」。Core image: the value is not fixed; it slides according to another variable.
column10: voca_0123

column5: A structured inventory or record describing what is included in a data or system migration, often including identities, versions, counts, hashes, status, or other metadata needed to verify the move.
column7: The migration manifest lists every dataset, its version, and its checksum. / We compared the imported records against the manifest before declaring the cutover complete.
column8: 'Manifest' broadly means an inventory or list of contents, especially in transport and computing. 'Migration manifest' is a practical technical term rather than one universal standardized schema. 日本語でざっくり「移行対象一覧／移行台帳」。何を移すか・何が移ったかをIDs, versions, counts, hashes, statusなどで記録し、移行内容を照合・検証するためのinventory。WLPのCanonical作業でもまさにこのsense。No single universal schema is implied by the phrase.
column10: voca_0123

column5: To extinguish something such as a flame; figuratively, to end, suppress, or destroy something, and in violent slang to kill someone.
column7: She snuffed out the candle. / The policy could snuff out small competitors. / In crime fiction, 'snuff someone out' can mean kill them.
column8: The violent-person sense is slang and should be interpreted from context. For ordinary lights/flames, snuff out simply means extinguish.
column10: voca_0123

column5: Not limited to a fixed set of answers, a definite end point, or a predetermined duration or outcome.
column7: The interview began with an open-ended question. / They signed an open-ended agreement with no fixed completion date.
column8: Hyphenate before a noun. Common contrasts: open-ended question vs closed question; open-ended commitment vs fixed-term commitment.

column5: To read, examine, or look through something, traditionally with careful attention; in modern use it can also mean browse or look over.
column7: She perused the contract before signing it. / I spent a few minutes perusing the menu.
column8: The older/core sense is 'examine carefully,' but casual modern use often means 'browse.' Context determines how thorough the reading is.
column10: voca_0123

column5: To return to a situation, idea, position, or condition similar to the starting point after a series of changes or developments.
column6: return to the starting point, complete the cycle
column7: After years abroad, her career came full circle when she returned to teach at her old school. / The debate has gone full circle.
column8: Usually figurative. 'Come full circle' often carries a sense of completion or irony, not merely physically moving in a circle.

column5: A time-travel paradox in which information or an object exists in a causal loop with no clear point of origin because it is passed from the future to the past and back again.
column7: In the story, the scientist learns the formula from his future self and later gives it to his younger self, creating a bootstrap paradox.
column8: Named by analogy with 'pulling oneself up by one's bootstraps.' Distinct from bootstrap in computing, where a small initial process starts a larger system.

column5: Clumsy, awkward, heavy-handed, or lacking skill and sensitivity.
column7: The company's ham-fisted response made the controversy worse. / He made a ham-fisted attempt to repair the delicate mechanism.
column8: Can describe physical clumsiness or an insensitive, poorly handled approach. Also ham-handed.

column5: A major transformation in form, character, condition, or appearance; in biology, a developmental change such as a caterpillar becoming a butterfly.
column7: The novel traces her metamorphosis from outsider to leader. / A butterfly undergoes metamorphosis.
column8: Plural: metamorphoses /ˌmetəˈmɔːrfəsiːz/. Related verb: metamorphose; broader everyday verb: transform.

column5: A possible future event or condition, especially one that may cause problems; a contingency plan is a prepared alternative course of action for such a possibility.
column7: We set aside extra funds for unexpected contingencies. / The team has a contingency plan in case the primary server fails.
column8: Compare contingent on = dependent on a condition. 'Contingency' names the possible event or provision; 'contingency plan' is the plan for dealing with it.

column5: A remark quoted ironically after events prove it overconfident, premature, or badly wrong.
column6: so much for that prediction, ill-fated prediction
column7: "This will only take five minutes." Famous last words—we were still working three hours later.
column8: Often said immediately after someone makes an overly confident prediction, even before it is disproved, to joke that trouble is likely. 日本語の会話感覚では、皮肉に「はいはい、そう言ってたらどうなることやら」「それフラグじゃん」「そう言ったそばから…」。'This will only take five minutes.' — 'Famous last words.' =「そう言って長引くやつだろ」。まだ失敗していなくても、あとで外れそうな自信満々の発言に先回りして言える。
column10: voca_0123

column5: An operation that intentionally does nothing or has no observable effect, often used as a placeholder, safe fallback, or way to preserve an interface.
column7: When the condition is false, the handler becomes a no-op. / The migration step is idempotent and effectively a noop when everything is already current.
column8: From 'no operation.' Spellings include no-op, NOP, and noop depending on language/project. A no-op may still execute code internally but leaves relevant state unchanged.

column2: account for X percent of Y
column5: To constitute, represent, or make up a stated proportion of a total.
column7: Online sales account for 42 percent of total revenue. / The top three categories account for nearly half of all responses.
column8: Pattern: X accounts for NUMBER percent of Y. Do not confuse with account for = explain or justify, as in 'That doesn't account for the discrepancy.' 日本語で「XがYの○%を占める」。This is the item-level percentage expression. Compare 'show the breakdown of Y' =「Yの内訳を示す」for the whole composition.
column10: voca_0123
column12: entry::construction entry::verb_pattern usage::academic usage::presentation-friendly topic::research topic::presentations discovery::presentation_language discovery::process_details

column5: To display how a total is divided into categories, components, or shares.
column6: show the composition of, show the distribution of
column7: The pie chart shows the breakdown of household spending by category. / The table shows a breakdown of users by age group.
column8: Use 'the breakdown of X by Y' when Y is the grouping dimension. A pie chart is appropriate only when the categories form parts of a meaningful whole. 日本語で「〜の内訳を示す」。'breakdown by age/region/category' =「年齢別／地域別／カテゴリー別の内訳」。Compare 'X accounts for 35% of Y' = 個々の割合を述べる; 'the breakdown of Y' = 全体がどう分かれているかを見る。
column10: voca_0123

column2: catch up to / catch up with someone
column5: To reach the same position, level, or progress as someone or something that was ahead; catch up with can also mean meet and exchange news.
column6: draw level with, reach, close the gap
column7: I walked faster to catch up to them. / Smaller companies are catching up with the market leader. / Let's catch up over coffee next week.
column8: 'Catch up to' strongly emphasizes reaching a target. 'Catch up with' works for reaching someone and also has the social sense of reconnecting. Past form: caught up. 日本語: catch up to someone = 前を行く人に「追いつく」。catch up with someone も追いつく意味で使えるほか、「久しぶりに会って近況を話す」senseもある。Compare catch up on work/email = 遅れているものを片付けて追いつく。up to / with / on で関係が変わる。
column10: voca_0123

column5: The planned transition from an old system, process, environment, or method to a new one, especially the point or period when the new one becomes authoritative.
column7: The database cutover is scheduled for Saturday night. / We completed the cutover and froze the new canonical baseline.
column8: Common in IT, telecom, infrastructure, and operations. A cutover is the actual transition, not the entire migration project. 日本語なら「本番切替／移行切替」。Migration = 移行プロセス全体; cutover = 準備・テストのあと、実際のtraffic/read/writeやauthorityを旧側から新側へ切り替える局面。WLP Canonical cutoverでproduction defaultを新経路へ切り替えたのがまさにこのsense.
column10: voca_0123

column5: Used to say that a behavior or situation is typical or characteristic of a person, group, thing, or system, often with irony, resignation, or mild criticism.
column6: that's typical of X, that's how X is
column7: "The form needs three signatures for a one-line change." "That's bureaucracy for you." / He apologized and then did it again—that's Tom for you.
column8: X is the person/category being characterized: 'That's politics for you,' 'That's kids for you.' Tone often carries shared exasperation or irony. 日本語感覚は「まあXってそういうもんだよ」「これがXってやつだ」「さすがXというか…」。'That's bureaucracy for you.' =「まあ官僚組織ってそういうもんだよ」。'That's Tom for you.' =「まあトムらしいよ」。Xの典型的な性質を、共感・諦め・皮肉・軽い批判などのtoneで指すproductive pattern。The original search was vague, so keep the pattern broad rather than pretending one literal 'something' was intended.
column10: voca_0123

column5: A crude label for someone alleged to hide sexually perverted or inappropriate interests behind an outwardly ordinary appearance.
column7: The character jokingly calls him a closet perv, but the phrase is insulting and highly informal.
column8: 'Perv' is short for pervert and is derogatory; 'closet' means hidden or secret in this construction. Use with caution and do not treat it as a neutral description. 日本語なら「隠れスケベ／隠れ変態」くらい。ただし 'perv' is derogatory/teasing, not neutral. Productive pattern: 'closet X' = 人に見せず隠しているX／公には認めていないX. Keep the register warning.
column10: voca_0123

column5: A construction in which only emphasizes how recently or late someone provided information, often implying that the speaker had little time to act.
column6: told me only yesterday, gave me very little notice
column7: You only told me to do this yesterday—how was I supposed to finish it by this morning? / She only told us about the deadline yesterday.
column8: Placement of only can be flexible in speech. Here the intended scope is temporal: 'not until yesterday / no earlier than yesterday,' not 'you did nothing except tell me.' Context and stress clarify the focus. 日本語で「昨日になって初めて言ったじゃん／昨日言われたばっかりなのに」。Here 'only' highlights recency/lateness, often implying 'you gave me almost no time.' Stress + context determine scope; it does not mean 'the only thing you did was tell me.'
column10: voca_0123

column5: A check or preparation performed before a flight; by extension, a validation step carried out before a deployment, operation, export, or other important action.
column7: The pilot completed the preflight inspection. / Run the preflight checks before deploying the release.
column8: In technical work, 'preflight' often means verify prerequisites, configuration, permissions, or integrity before making changes. It does not itself imply the main operation has begun.
